title: [RFC] [QeRL]: Online Quantization and Model Reloading
author: kylesayrs
body: >! Note: This design has changed slightly since it was originally posted. LayerwiseLoader is no longer necessary # Motivation ## What is Quantized Model Reloading and Why is it Useful? vLLM serves not only as a inference runtime for serving requests from end users, but also as a means of serving requests for large language model post-training. One particularly important use case is using vLLM to serve rollouts (required by RL pipelines) using a quantized model to serve the requests. For more information, see [QeRL: Beyond Efficiency – Quantization-enhanced Reinforcement Learning for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.11696v1). These quantized models must be reloaded every couple of seconds in order to make sure that the rollouts match the distribution that would have been generated by the base model weights. ## Existing Features in vLLM vLLM already has some pathways for enabling these kinds of workflows. However, the current implementations have caveats which can make usage difficult. ### Weight Reloading After a model has been loaded once, the weights are stored in kernel format (see nomenclature). However, kernel format does not always match checkpoint format. There is an existing implementation which restores the original model format in order to allow reloading (implemented [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/online_quantization.py), but “restore” step is done eagerly and effectively doubles the amount of required memory, which is unideal. The current implementation has also only been enabled for torchao configs. ### Online Quantization There are two styles of online quantization implemented in vLLM. Originally, there was on the “offline” style of [FP8](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/fp8.py#L222C14-L222C42), where all unquantized weights are loaded synchronously, and then all weights are quantized synchronously after loading via `process_weights_after_loading`. This style works, but requires as much memory as the unquantized model, despite the final model being quantized, which is unideal (see Memory Requirements section). Recently, @vkuzo implemented a means of online quantization by [adding a hook to the `weight_loader`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/29196/files) which calls `process_weights_after_loading` to quantize the weights as they are loading. This reduces the amount of memory that is required to online quantize models, but has only been implemented for CT_FP8_CHANNELWISE and doesn't support currently post processing operations which require multiple parameters, such as marlin repacking. ## Design Considerations ### Nomenclature - “Checkpoint format” refers to the format in which weights are loaded from disk or provided by a user. - “Model format” refers to the state of the model after `init` but before weights are processed with `process_weights_after_loading` . The mapping between “checkpoint format” and “model format” is implemented by `model.load_weights`. - “Kernel format” refers to the state of the model after `process_weights_after_loading` - In the case that checkpoint format is unquantized, but the kernel format is quantized, we call this “online quantization”, where unquantized weights are quantized by vLLM during/after loading. ### Model Cuda Graph After models are loaded for the first time, a cuda graph is captured of the model which is used to accelerate inference. This cuda graph shares the same tensor data pointers as the model used to load weights. As of now, the data pointers used by the cuda graph cannot be updated after capture. This means that any time reloading happens, the new data must be copied into the cuda graph tensors. Regenerating the model cuda graph is far too slow for the required cadence of model reloading (on the order of a few seconds). ### Memory Requirements An ideal solution would use as little memory as is required to load model weights. Some implementations, such as the current implementation of online quantization, require eagerly duplicating all model weights prior to loading, which effectively doubles the amount of memory required to load a model. This is a blocker for enabling reloading of large (600Gb+) models. Additionally, an ideal solution would only use as much memory as is required to store the quantized model, not the unquantized model. In cases such as NVFP4, this would cut the memory requirements of using vLLM reloading by one fourth. ### Existing Quantized Reloading Scripts Although online quantization and quantized weight reloading support is limited in vLLM as of now, there already exist users who are using vLLM to do online quantized reloading. Below are a list of examples. 1. [MoonshotAI](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/checkpoint-engine/blob/44d5670b0e6aed5b9cd6c16e970c09f3dc888ad0/checkpoint_engine/worker.py#L167) 2. [Verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl/blob/f332fc814718b9ea7968f6d264211460d4e90fff/verl/utils/vllm/vllm_fp8_utils.py#L209) 3. Periodic Labs, which calls `model.load_weights` with subsets of weights, rather than a weight iterator containing all weights An ideal solution would not require changing the code in these scripts, although that may not possible or a reasonable expectation given that online quantized reloading has never been officially supported by vLLM. ### Weight Repacking and Recreation After Loading Some kernels such as the marlin kernel recreate and rename parameters in `process_weights_after_loading`. These recreation operations can make techniques which eagerly restore original weights (such as the current weight reloading implementation) more memory intensive, as both the original loading tensor and the recreated packed tensor must be alive at the same time, effectively doubling memory requirements. ### Proposed Change I'd like to propose a design which achieves the following: 1. Supports online quantization via `process_after_weight_loading` (most online quantization is implemented this way) 2. Minimizes the peak memory required to load an online quantized model 3. Minimizes the peak memory required to reload a quantized model (online or otherwise) 4. Supports reloading chunks of weights 5. Supports loading weights which are already in kernel format ## Layerwise Wrappers ## The core idea is to wrap existing weight loaders. These wrappers will allow us to know exactly when all of a layer's weights are loaded, and thus the earliest moment when `process_after_weight_loading` can be safely called. ## Online Quantization ## Online quantization requires that tensors are materialized and processed on a layer-wise basis. This can be achieved using a `layerwise_process` function. ```python3 class OnlineFP8Scheme: def create_weights(..., layer, weight_loader): layer.weight = Parameter(..., device="meta") layer.weight.weight_loader = weight_loader layerwise_process(layer) def process_weights_after_loading(self, layer): if layer.weight.dtype == "fp8": return self.weight, self.scale = fp8_quantize(layer.weight) def layerwise_process(layer): # get parameters for later copying original_parameters = get_module_tensors(layer) # move layer onto meta device for name, param in get_module_tensors(layer).items(): setattr(layer, name, param.to("meta")) # track loading progress to determine when to process load_numel_remaining = get_layer_size(layer) for name, param in get_module_tensors(layer).items(): original_weight_loader = getattr(param, "weight_loader", default_weight_loader) @wraps(original_weight_loader) def process_loader(param, loaded_weight): nonlocal load_numel_remaining # materialize meta tensor if necessary if param.device == torch.device("meta"): param = materialize_meta_tensor(param) setattr(layer, name, param) # load weight into target original_weight_loader(param, loaded_weight) # process and copy when weights are loaded load_numel_remaining -= loaded_weight.numel() if load_numel_remaining <= 0: process_weights_after_loading(layer) param.weight_loader = restore_and_process_loader ``` ## Model Reloading ## In the case that we are *reloading* weights, the layer starts in kernel format. We must restore the layer to model format before weights can be loaded again. After all weights are loaded, we again call `process_weights_after_loading`. However, because these are now new tensors, the data from the new tensors must be copied into the original tensor data in order for the changes to be reflected in the cudagraph. The core of this design is the `layerwise_restore_and_process` function. This function wraps parameter weight loaders with a function which initializes processes parameters **as they are being loaded**. Layer-wise initialization and processing avoids eagerly allocating too much memory, or duplicating memory after processing. ### Restoring Layers ### When `reload_weights` is first called, the model weights have already been processed into **kernel format**. However, in order to support reloading with weights which are in **checkpoint format**, the model must be $${\color{green}restored}$$ to **model format**. This is achieved by recording the metadata of parameters shapes, dtypes, and weight loaders of the model when it is in checkpoint format, then using this metadata to reconstruct the model into checkpoint format. ```python3 def record_metadata_for_reloading(model): for module in model.modules(): module.restore_metadata = {} for name, param in get_module_tensors(module).items(): meta = param.to(device=torch.device("meta")) for attr_name in RESTORE_ATTRS: if hasattr(param, attr_name): setattr(meta, attr_name, getattr(param, attr_name)) module.restore_metadata[name] = meta def initialize_model(...): model = model_class(**kwargs) record_metadata_for_reloading(model) return model ``` ## Reload Weights Entrypoint ## In order to apply the reloading wrappers, we encourage reloading users to use the existing `reload_weights` entrypoint. This entrypoint would accept reloading weights both in "checkpoint format" or "kernel format". This would require users to begin using `reload_weights` in order to get the benefits of support for loading in original checkpoint format, online quantization, and reduced memory usage. ```python3 def reload_weights(self, weights_iterator = None, kernel_format: bool = False) -> None: if weights_iterator is None: # load from disk model_loader = get_model_loader(self.load_config) weights_iterator = model_loader.get_all_weights(self.model_config, model) if not kernel_format: model.apply(layerwise_restore_and_process) model.load_weights(weights_iterator) model.apply(unwrap_layerwise_restore_and_process) else: model.load_weights(weights_iterator) ``` ## Summary ## Current implementations of both model reloading and online quantization use much more memory than is required (almost double) and are only implemented for limited use cases. The proposed design uses minimal memory to perform loading and reloading and is fully compatible with existing model definitions and online quantization implementations. The PR associated with these changes can be found here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32133 Related: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/31848 ### Feedback Period. ~2-3 weeks ### CC List. @jerryzh168 @mgoin @vkuzo @dsikka @luccafong @robertgshaw2-redhat ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Consolidate FP8 min/max values into somewhere reasonable (Python only)
author: rasmith
body:
### Motivation.

On platforms such as MI300 that have `torch.float8_e4m3fnuz` as their fp8 dtype, it is necessary to use `-224.0/224.0 ` for fp8 min/max values for better accuracy when making fp8 computations.

There are two problems that exist:
1) There is code that uses the default min/max values that torch provides and not the recommended ones:
     * currently, this doesn't cause errors because the tests and implementations agree on these values
2) There are mismatches between the default and recommended values (+-224 vs +=240)
    * this causes test failures due to mismatches between test and implementation:
       * there are PRs to fix the mismatches that occur
          * https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/30292
          * https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/30291

Of course there can be future reoccurrences of the mentioned problems.


### Proposed Change.

I'm proposing to:
1.  Consolidate the recommended fp8 min/max values into fp8_utils, 
2.  Update usage of fp8 min/max values to use the newly consolidated values,

title: [RFC]: Multi-Process Benchmark Architecture for Scaling Beyond Single-Core Limits
author: GaoHuaZhang
body: ### Motivation. The current `vllm benchmark` tool relies on a **single-core, single-process** load generator. Under moderate or high request rates or high concurrency levels, the benchmark becomes limited by the CPU capacity of that single core. The overhead of coroutine scheduling prevents the client from: 1. **Sending requests at the configured request rate**, and 2. **Consuming server-side streaming chunks in real time**. As a result, the observed metrics deviate significantly from the actual behavior of the target service. This reduces benchmark reliability and makes it difficult to evaluate scenarios where models or serving systems are optimized for **high-concurrency** or **dense request** workloads. In these cases, the benchmark fails to reflect the true performance characteristics of the service. For example, I created a synthetic service using gunicorn with a fixed **TTFT = 100 ms** and **TPOT = 10 ms**. When running: ``` vllm bench serve --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1 ``` (without specifying a `--request-rate`, i.e., effectively `inf`), both TTFT and TPOT became **significantly distorted**. When specifying `--request-rate 100`, the metrics returned to normal: ``` vllm bench serve --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1 --request-rate 100 ``` However, increasing the request rate to 200 again caused severe metric distortion: ``` vllm bench serve --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1 --request-rate 200 ``` In addition, even with a modest request rate, **concurrency ceiling effects** still degrade measurement accuracy. When increasing the maximum output length (thus increasing per-request service time and instantaneous concurrency), results again became inaccurate.Moreover, many requests failed without any indication.: ``` vllm bench serve --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1 --request-rate 100 \ --random_output_len 2048 --num-prompts 2000 ``` The version of vLLM used in this experiment is as follows: The corresponding hardware environment is: **12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-12700** This demonstrates that the current single-core coroutine-based load generator is insufficient for high-concurrency, high-throughput benchmarking scenarios. There are tools in the industry that address this problem—such as [aiperf](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aiperf)—which use multi-process architectures to overcome single-core limitations. However, the goal of this RFC is to **integrate scalable, high-concurrency load-generation capabilities directly into vLLM**, eliminating the need to deploy and operate a separate benchmarking tool. ### Proposed Change. This proposal requires substantial modifications to `benchmarks/serve.py`. Specifically, the existing `run_benchmark` function will be refactored into a dedicated `BenchmarkWorker` class. The `get_request` logic will be replaced by a centralized flow-control mechanism powered by a `TokenProducer`, which issues permission tokens using a Linux kernel–backed semaphore (`multiprocessing.BoundedSemaphore`) to ensure accurate global rate and concurrency control across all worker processes. To avoid redundant memory loading and improve throughput, the `BenchmarkDataset` output will be preloaded into shared memory. Only lightweight metadata (e.g., starting offset and length) will be passed to each worker. When generating a request, a worker retrieves the metadata and reconstructs the corresponding prompt locally without copying large buffers across processes. The high-level architecture is illustrated as follows: **Coordinator (controller process)** — manages worker processes, global configuration, TokenProducer, metrics aggregation and ProcessBar UI. **BenchmarkWorker (sub-process)** — each is an OS process; inside each worker run an async event loop (e.g., asyncio) that spawns many coroutines to send requests, parse responses, and push parsed outputs to a local queue. **OutputHandler (per worker)** — consumes parsed results from worker coroutines and handles aggregation/forwarding to coordinator (non-blocking, avoids delaying coroutines). **RPSController (flow controller)** — central component that issues “tokens”(the permit subprocess need to acquire before send request) granting permission to issue requests; implements RPS, concurrency cap, ramp-up schedule, burst windows, jitter, and per-scenario rate policies. **ProcessBar (progress & summary)** — receives per-worker progress events, aggregates, and displays a consolidated progress view with throughput, per-worker statuses, latency percentiles, and error counts. #### Component Responsibilities **Coordinator** Spawn/monitor worker processes and restart policy. Instantiate TokenProducer and broadcast tokens or token leases to workers. Aggregate metrics, compute percentiles, and produce final reports. Expose run modes: single-node, distributed coordinator (leader) + remote workers. **RPSController ** API: acquire_token(worker_id) -> token_id and release_token(token_id) (or push model). Support multiple token allocation strategies (global, per-worker quotas). **BenchmarkWorker** Configurable concurrency (number of coroutines), batch sizes, request payloads. Async request lifecycle: prepare → request → await → parse → enqueue result for consumer thread. Periodically report local metrics to coordinator. **OutputHandler** Consume parsed results without blocking the event loop. Optionally write per-request logs to disk or stream to coordinator. **ProcessBar** Accept progress events over IPC (e.g., pipes or a lightweight socket). Display per-worker progress and overall aggregated stats in the console and optionally a machine-readable logfile. ### Feedback Period. two week ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Consolidate Intel Quantization Toolkit Integration in vLLM
author: yiliu30
body: **Authors**: Intel Neural Compressor Team, Intel vLLM Team **Related**: [RFC: vLLM Quantization Cleanup](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30136) ### Motivation. In alignment with vLLM's quantization consolidation effort, we propose to streamline Intel's quantization support, currently fragmented across three implementations: | File | Scope | Capabilities | | --------------- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------- | | `inc.py` | Intel Gaudi (HPU) | Online W8A8_FP8 quantization | | `auto_round.py` | Intel CPU/GPU | WnA16 (AutoRound models) | | `ipex_quant.py` | Intel CPU/GPU | W4A16,W4A8, W8A16_FP8 via IPEX backend | This fragmentation creates maintenance overhead and inconsistent user experience. Consolidation will: - Reduce code duplication and maintenance burden - Provide a unified entry point for Intel quantization - Enable future formats (`MXFP4`/`MXFP8`/`NVFP4`, and advanced mixed-precision recipes ### Proposed Change. The overall status and proposal are below: #### 1. Consolidate Intel CPU/GPU Quantization → `inc.py` - Merge `auto_round.py` into `inc.py` as unified Intel quantization backend - Extend `inc.py` to support: - `WnA16` inference (from AutoRound) - Future formats (`MXFP4`/`MXFP8`/`NVFP4`, advanced mixed-precision) #### 2. Migrate CPU/GPU Support → `compressed_tensors` - Move `ipex_quant.py` kernel (use vllm-xpu-kernel instead of IPEX) support to `compressed_tensors` backend - Ensure Intel CPU/GPU compatibility with standard compressed tensor formats - Deprecate `ipex_quant.py` after successful migration #### 3. Finalize Gaudi Migration → vLLM-Gaudi Plugin - Verify `W8A8_FP8` capabilities fully available in vLLM-Gaudi plugin - Update documentation to reference plugin ### Backward Compatibility This consolidation ensures seamless migration for existing users: - **Compressed Tensors**: Standard compressed tensor models will be deployable on Intel CPU/GPU through the enhanced backend, providing broad compatibility with the vLLM ecosystem. - **AutoRound Models**: Existing AutoRound quantized [models on HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/models?search=AutoRound) will remain backward compatible via the consolidated `inc.py`. Both compressed tensor format and INC support are essential to serve different user needs: compressed tensors for standardization and interoperability and INC for Intel-optimized quantization recipes. ### Estimated Timeline - Phase 1 (Target: Jan 2026) : merge `auto_round.py` into `inc.py` - Phase 2 (Target: Q1 2026) : migrate `ipex_quant.py` to `compressed_tensors` ### Feedback Period. Please comment on the proposal or suggest alternatives. If there are no strong objections, we will proceed with the timeline above and submit implementation PRs. Thanks! ### CC List. cc @hshen14 @thuang6 @wenhuach21 @jikunshang @kzawora-intel @xuechendi ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Per-instance EPLB metrics
author: markmc
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

(co-authored with @sallyom and Claude)

In replicated vLLM deployments behind a load balancer, the load balancer has no visibility into EPLB (Expert-Parallel Load Balancing) state when making routing decisions. EPLB dynamically replicates heavily-used experts across EP ranks to balance load, and instances experiencing high expert load imbalance or active rebalancing operations have degraded capacity. Without metrics exposing this state, load balancers cannot avoid routing traffic to struggling instances, leading to suboptimal performance and increased tail latencies.

EPLB already tracks and logs this information to stdout when `--eplb-log-balancedness` is enabled:

```
EPLB step: 2500: avg_tokens=1024, max_tokens=2048, balancedness=0.5000
```

But these are obviously not queryable by load balancers. This proposal exports the same data that's currently logged as Prometheus metrics, enabling intelligent load balancing decisions based on instance health.

Note - these stats are EP-group-wide, and should not be reported per-engine (i.e. with the `engine_idx` label), instead they should probably only be recorded on DP rank 0.

## Proposed Metrics

| Metric Name | Type | Description
|-------------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank` | Gauge | Average tokens per EP rank in current interval |
| `vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank` | Gauge | Maximum tokens across EP ranks in current interval |
| `vllm:eplb_rebalancing` | Gauge | Whether EPLB is currently rebalancing (0 or 1) |
| `vllm:eplb_rebalance_events_total` | Counter | Total number of EPLB rebalancing operations |

## Sample PromQL

```promql
# Imbalance ratio - 0.5 means 50% balanced
(vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank)

# Relative imbalance: avoid instances where one rank is 2x overloaded
(vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 2.0

# Absolute imbalance: avoid instances with severe token gap
(vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank - vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 5000

# Hybrid: high load AND poor balance (most dangerous)
vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank > 15000
AND (vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 1.5

# Alert on thrashing
rate(vllm:eplb_rebalance_events_total[5m]) > 2

# Reduce traffic to instance currently rebalancing
vllm:eplb_rebalancing == 1
```

title: [RFC]: Token Padding Strategy for FP8 GEMM Performance Optimization
author: 0xjunhao
body:
### Motivation.

This RFC proposes implementing a token padding mechanism in the vLLM execution loop to ensure the number of tokens (batch size M) is a multiple of 4 when running FP8 models. This alignment significantly improves performance on NVIDIA B200/H200 GPUs.

FP8 GEMM kernels (both DeepGEMM and CUTLASS-based implementations) exhibit distinct performance characteristics based on input dimensions. Benchmarks on B200 hardware demonstrate substantial throughput degradation when the number of tokens (M) is not aligned to specific boundaries.

### Benchmark Data
- End-to-End serving

`vllm serve` and `vllm bench serve --backend vllm --dataset-name sharegpt --dataset-path ./ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json  --base-url http://localhost:8000  --endpoint /v1/completions --model
[model] --tokenizer [model] --num-prompts 2000 --max-concurrency 100`

| GPU | model | Total Token throughput (tok/s) Before | Total Token throughput (tok/s) After | Speedup |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| B200 | Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 | 15455.37 | 17350.65 | 10.9% |
| B200 | Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 | 6350.89 | 8016.02 | 26.2% |
| H200 | Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 | 15810.43 | 16136.04 | 2.0% |
| H200 | Qwen/Qwen3-32B-FP8 | 6049.23 | 6161.02 | 1.8% |

- GEMM only (B200)
`python3 benchmarks/kernels/deepgemm/benchmark_fp8_block_dense_gemm.py` with shape modifications

| m    | n     | k     | Time DeepGEMM (μs) | TFLOPS DeepGEMM | GB/s DeepGEMM | Time vLLM CUTLASS (μs) | TFLOPS vLLM CUTLASS | GB/s vLLM CUTLASS |
|------|-------|-------|--------------------|------------------|---------------|----------------|-------------|-----------|
| 63   | 24576 | 1536  | 103.1              | 46.1             | 397.2         | 20.5           | 232.3       | 1999.9    |
| 64   | 24576 | 1536  | 63.8               | 75.7             | 642.2         | 19.1           | 253.0       | 2146.2    |
| 127  | 24576 | 1536  | 103.4              | 92.7             | 427.3         | 31.6           | 303.5       | 1398.8    |
| 128  | 24576 | 1536  | 63.8               | 151.4            | 693.2         | 18.5           | 521.6       | 2387.7    |
| 4095 | 24576 | 1536  | 168.5              | 1835.3           | 1456.3        | 778.0          | 397.4       | 315.3     |
| 4096 | 24576 | 1536  | 161.0              | 1921.3           | 1524.4        | 204.3          | 1513.9      | 1201.2    |

H200 GEMM benchmark requires m to be a multiple of 4 and thus not run.

### The Problem

Currently, gpu_model_runner.py passes the raw number of tokens to the execution backend. While CUDA Graph capture handles padding for small batches (typically up to 512), it does not guarantee M%4==0 for all graph slots, and it does not handle batches larger than the graph capture limit.

Analysis of production-like traffic (ShareGPT, 3000 prompts, concurrency 100) reveals that for batches > 512 tokens (which bypass CUDA graphs), they constitute a significant part of the engine steps and the remainder modulo 4 is evenly distributed:

```
[Distribution of the unpadded number of tokens]
Counts: 0-63: 1183 | 64-127: 4309 | 128-255: 542 | 256-511: 545 | 512-1023: 554 | 1024-2047: 86 | 2048-4095: 1
Residual Counts (tokens % 4 for tokens > 512): 0: 166 | 1: 163 | 2: 154 | 3: 156
```

Roughly 74% of large batches currently run on unoptimized kernel paths.

### Proposed Change.

We propose introducing a padding logic within `_determine_batch_execution_and_padding` in `gpu_model_runner.py`.

Instead of a blanket if `quantization == "fp8"`, the padding logic should be:

- Selective: Trigger only when the backend kernel benefits from alignment, including DeepGEMM/FP8 and CUTLASS/FP8 on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper.

- Alignment: Pad num_tokens to the nearest multiple of 4.

- Safety: Ensure padded "dummy" tokens are masked out or handled such that they do not affect model accuracy or trigger Out-Of-Bounds (OOB) memory access.

### Alternatives Considered

#### Option A: Pad at the Kernel Level

Modify every GEMM kernel invocation to handle padding internally.

- Pros: Keeps Model Runner logic clean.

- Cons: Requires padding input tensors at every layer. For a deep LLM, this results in hundreds of unnecessary copy operations per forward pass, reducing performance gains.

- Verdict: Rejected due to high runtime overhead.

#### Option B: Rely on CUDA Graphs

Expand the CUDA Graph capture range or modify capture steps to enforce alignment.

- Pros: Uses existing infrastructure.

- Cons: CUDA graph capture sizes typically increase in steps of 8 or 16 and by default cap at 512 tokens. Throughput-heavy scenarios often exceed this (large batches). Benchmarks show significant regression for M > 512 when unaligned. Expanding the capture sizes to larger M significantly increases VRAM usage. In addition, steps of 8 or 16 introduce even more computational overhead than enforcing the mod-4 padding.

- Verdict: Rejected, as it requires significantly more VRAM and incurs greater computational overhead than mod-4 padding.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@LucasWilkinson @mgoin @robertgshaw2-redhat

title: [RFC] DBO fallout tracking metrics
author: markmc
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

(co-authored with @sallyom and Claude)

## Motivation

Production WideEP deployments exhibit unpredictable throughput variance (10-50% degradation) with no clear diagnostic signal. Dual Batch Overlap (DBO) is a technique that splits batches into two micro-batches (ubatches) to overlap computation and communication, significantly improving throughput in Data-Parallel deployments. However, DBO is fragile and falls out silently when conditions aren't met—such as when the second ubatch would be empty (common at 256-token boundaries) or when DP ranks disagree on ubatching decisions.

Currently, there is no instrumentation to confirm whether DBO is engaged or why it disengages. Operators cannot distinguish between DBO working as expected, falling out due to batch size alignment issues, or failing due to coordination problems across DP ranks. This makes root-causing throughput degradation nearly impossible.

See [this slack thread in llm-d #sig-deepseek](https://llm-d.slack.com/archives/C08TFSU2PFY/p1765216364703649?thread_ts=1765213004.840599&cid=C08TFSU2PFY) for context

## Proposed Change

Add metrics to track DBO engagement and fallout reasons.

| Metric Name | Type | Description | Cardinality |
|-------------|------|-------------|-------------|
| `vllm:dbo_active` | Gauge | Whether DBO is currently engaged (1=active, 0=inactive) | 2 per instance (phase=prefill/decode) | 
| `vllm:dbo_fallout_total` | Counter | Count of DBO fallout events by reason | 3 per instance (reason label) | 
| `vllm:ubatch_token_count` | Histogram | Distribution of ubatch sizes in tokens | 2 per instance (ubatch_index label) | 

**Fallout reasons tracked**:
- `empty_second_ubatch` - Second ubatch would be empty after padding
- `below_threshold` - At least one DP rank had token count below DBO threshold
- `other` - Other reasons

**Label schema**: All metrics include `{model_name, engine}` labels. `dbo_active` adds `{phase}` (prefill/decode). `dbo_fallout_total` adds `{reason}`. `ubatch_token_count` adds `{ubatch_index}` (first/second).


### Alternatives

title: [RFC]: FlashMask Attention Backend for PrefixLM Models
author: lucianommartins
body:
### Motivation.

PrefixLM models like Gemma3 multimodal require mixed attention patterns: bidirectional attention for image tokens (prefix) combined with causal attention for text tokens. Currently, vLLM handles this pattern using TritonAttention (or FlexAttention as fallback), which is slower than FlashAttention-2.

The core issue is that FlashAttention-2 only supports pure causal or pure non-causal attention—it cannot represent the hybrid mask pattern:

```
Image Tokens [0, N):      Bidirectional (attend to all image tokens)
Text Tokens [N, seq_len): Causal + attend to prefix
```

This forces PrefixLM models to use slower backends, creating a significant performance penalty for multimodal inference.

From benchmarks on A100-80GB:

| Backend | gemma3-4b seq=512 | gemma3-27b seq=512 | Notes |
|---------|-------------------|---------------------|-------|
| **FlashAttention-2** | 0.072 ms | 0.082 ms | Text-only baseline |
| **TritonAttention** | 0.18 ms | 0.16 ms | Current PrefixLM path |
| **FlexAttention** | 0.29 ms | 0.33 ms | Fallback |
| **Ratio** | 2.5x slower | 2x slower | Overhead vs FlashAttn |

The 2-4x overhead applies to every attention layer, accumulating to significant end-to-end latency.

Models with `is_mm_prefix_lm=True` that would benefit:
- Gemma3 (4B/12B/27B) - Multimodal with bidirectional image prefix
- Future multimodal models - Any model requiring partial bidirectional attention
- PrefixLM architectures - T5-style prefix attention patterns

Strategic value:

1. Significant performance improvement for multimodal: Closing the gap with FlashAttention
2. O(N) memory for attention masks vs O(N²): critical for long context
3. Unified backend: Single backend for text and multimodal (simpler codebase)
4. Future-proof: Extensible to other complex mask patterns

### Proposed Change.

FlashMask (ICLR 2025 Accepted, Wang et al.) extends FlashAttention-2 with column-wise sparse mask representation, enabling arbitrary attention patterns with O(N) memory complexity.

Paper: "FlashMask: Efficient and Rich Mask Extension of FlashAttention"
Status: ICLR 2025 Poster
Authors: Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Xiyuan Xiao, Siming Wu, Jiabin Yang, et al.

Column-Wise Sparse Mask Representation

Instead of storing a dense O(N²) mask, FlashMask represents attention patterns as column indices per row:

```
# For each query row i, store the start/end columns that can be attended to
mask_representation = {
    "col_left": [left_bound_0, left_bound_1, ...],   # [seq_len]
    "col_right": [right_bound_0, right_bound_1, ...]  # [seq_len]
}

# Attention allowed: col_left[i] <= j <= col_right[i]
```

For Gemma3 PrefixLM pattern with 256 image tokens:

```
# Image tokens (rows 0-255): attend to all image tokens
col_left[0:256] = 0
col_right[0:256] = 255

# Text tokens (rows 256+): causal + attend to all prefix
col_left[256:] = 0      # Can attend back to token 0 (prefix)
col_right[i] = i         # Causal: attend up to current position
```

This representation is O(seq_len) instead of O(seq_len²).

The FlashMask kernel extends FlashAttention-2's tiling algorithm:

```cpp
// FlashAttention-2 base (simplified)
for (int k_block = 0; k_block < num_k_blocks; k_block++) {
    // Load Q, K, V tiles
    // Compute attention scores
    for (int j = 0; j < BLOCK_N; j++) {
        // Causal mask: if (col > row) mask = -inf
        bool valid = (k_block * BLOCK_N + j) <= query_row;
        scores[j] = valid ? qk_dot[j] : -INFINITY;
    }
    // Online softmax, accumulate output
}

// FlashMask extension
for (int k_block = 0; k_block < num_k_blocks; k_block++) {
    int col_start = k_block * BLOCK_N;
    
    // Load column bounds for current query rows
    int left = col_left[query_row];
    int right = col_right[query_row];
    
    // Column-wise sparse mask
    for (int j = 0; j < BLOCK_N; j++) {
        int col = col_start + j;
        // Check against column bounds (replaces causal check)
        bool valid = (col >= left) && (col <= right);
        scores[j] = valid ? qk_dot[j] : -INFINITY;
    }
    // Rest unchanged: online softmax, accumulate output
}
```

The mask check remains O(1) per element—only the comparison changes.

Proposed implementation plan

Phase 1: FlashMask Kernel Integration

Implement FlashMask CUDA kernels based on the paper algorithm:

```
Target: vllm/attention/ops/flashmask/

Files to create:
├── flashmask_fwd.cu          # Forward pass kernel
├── flashmask_bwd.cu          # Backward pass (if needed for training)
└── flashmask_utils.cuh       # Shared utilities
```

Modifications required:
- Adapt to vLLM's tensor layouts and dtypes
- Add paged attention block table support
- Integrate with vLLM's CUDA graph capture

Python wrapper:

```
# vllm/attention/ops/flashmask.py

def flashmask_attention(
    query: torch.Tensor,      # [batch, seq_q, num_heads, head_dim]
    key: torch.Tensor,        # [batch, seq_k, num_kv_heads, head_dim]  
    value: torch.Tensor,      # [batch, seq_k, num_kv_heads, head_dim]
    col_left: torch.Tensor,   # [batch, seq_q] - left column bounds
    col_right: torch.Tensor,  # [batch, seq_q] - right column bounds
    scale: Optional[float] = None,
    window_size: Optional[int] = None,  # For sliding window layers
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """FlashMask attention with column-wise sparse masking."""
    ...
```

Phase 2: vLLM Backend Integration

2.1 Backend registration

```
# vllm/attention/backends/flashmask.py

class FlashMaskBackend(AttentionBackend):
    """FlashMask attention backend for PrefixLM models."""
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_name() -> str:
        return "FLASHMASK"
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_impl_cls() -> type["FlashMaskImpl"]:
        return FlashMaskImpl
    
    @classmethod
    def supports_mm_prefix(cls) -> bool:
        return True  # Critical: enables selection for PrefixLM
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_supported_head_sizes() -> list[int]:
        return [64, 96, 128, 192, 256]  # Include Gemma3 variants
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_min_capability() -> int:
        return 80  # Ampere minimum (same as FlashAttention-2)
```

2.2 Metadata extension

```
# Extend attention metadata for FlashMask

@dataclass
class FlashMaskMetadata(AttentionMetadata):
    # Column bounds for FlashMask sparse representation
    col_left: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None   # [total_tokens]
    col_right: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None  # [total_tokens]
    
    # Per-layer sliding window (for Gemma3's 5:1 pattern)
    layer_sliding_window: Optional[int] = None
```

2.3 Mask construction

```
# vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py

def _build_flashmask_metadata(
    self,
    seq_lens: List[int],
    mm_prefix_ranges: List[Optional[Tuple[int, int]]],
    sliding_window: Optional[int],
) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    """Build FlashMask column bounds from mm_prefix_range.
    
    For each sequence with prefix range [start, end):
    - Rows in [start, end): col_left=start, col_right=end-1 (bidirectional)
    - Rows >= end: col_left=0, col_right=current_row (causal + prefix)
    """
    col_left_list = []
    col_right_list = []
    
    for seq_len, mm_range in zip(seq_lens, mm_prefix_ranges):
        if mm_range is None:
            # Pure causal (no prefix)
            col_left_list.append(torch.zeros(seq_len, dtype=torch.int32))
            col_right_list.append(torch.arange(seq_len, dtype=torch.int32))
        else:
            prefix_start, prefix_end = mm_range
            col_left = torch.zeros(seq_len, dtype=torch.int32)
            col_right = torch.arange(seq_len, dtype=torch.int32)
            
            # Bidirectional within prefix region
            col_right[:prefix_end] = prefix_end - 1
            
            col_left_list.append(col_left)
            col_right_list.append(col_right)
    
    return torch.cat(col_left_list), torch.cat(col_right_list)
```

2.4 Backend selection update

```
# vllm/attention/selector.py

def get_attention_backend(model_config, ...):
    if model_config.is_mm_prefix_lm:
        # Priority order for PrefixLM models
        if FlashMaskBackend.is_available():
            return FlashMaskBackend  # NEW: Preferred
        elif TritonAttentionBackend.is_available():
            return TritonAttentionBackend  # Fallback
        else:
            return FlexAttentionBackend  # Last resort
    # ... rest unchanged
```

Phase 3: Testing & Validation

3.1 Correctness tests

```
# tests/attention/test_flashmask.py

def test_flashmask_causal_matches_flashattn():
    """Pure causal should match FlashAttention exactly."""
    
def test_flashmask_prefixlm_matches_tritonattn():
    """PrefixLM pattern should match TritonAttention output."""
    
def test_flashmask_gemma3_multimodal():
    """End-to-end Gemma3 multimodal produces correct output."""
    
def test_flashmask_sliding_window():
    """Sliding window + PrefixLM works correctly."""
    
def test_flashmask_paged_attention():
    """Works with PagedAttention block tables."""
```

3.2 Performance benchmarks

```
# benchmarks/attention/benchmark_flashmask.py

configs = [
    ("gemma3-4b", "text-only", [128, 512, 2048, 8192]),
    ("gemma3-4b", "multimodal-256", [128, 512, 2048]),
    ("gemma3-27b", "text-only", [128, 512, 2048, 8192]),
    ("gemma3-27b", "multimodal-256", [128, 512, 2048]),
]

# Targets:
# - Text-only: Close to FlashAttention-2
# - Multimodal: Significant improvement over TritonAttention
```

Hardware support

| GPU | SM Version | FlashMask Support | Fallback |
|-----|------------|-------------------|----------|
| H100 | SM 9.0 | Full | N/A |
| A100 | SM 8.0 | Full | N/A |
| RTX 4090 | SM 8.9 | Full | N/A |
| RTX 3090 | SM 8.6 | Full | N/A |
| V100 | SM 7.0 | No | TritonAttention |

FlashMask requires SM 8.0+ (same as FlashAttention-2).

File changes summary

| Path | Change | Description |
|------|--------|-------------|
| `vllm/attention/backends/flashmask.py` | NEW | Backend registration |
| `vllm/attention/backends/flashmask_impl.py` | NEW | Implementation |
| `vllm/attention/ops/flashmask.py` | NEW | Python wrapper |
| `csrc/flashmask/` | NEW | CUDA kernels |
| `vllm/attention/selector.py` | MODIFY | Add FlashMask selection |
| `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` | MODIFY | Build FlashMask metadata |
| `tests/attention/test_flashmask.py` | NEW | Correctness tests |
| `benchmarks/attention/benchmark_flashmask.py` | NEW | Performance benchmarks |

Alternatives considered

1. Continue using TritonAttention

Status: Current solution
Pros: Already implemented, correct behavior
Cons: 2-4x slower than FlashAttention, not optimal for production

2. FlexAttention

Status: Available as fallback
Pros: Supports arbitrary masks
Cons: slower than FlashAttention, high compile overhead

3. Fused QKNormRoPE optimization

Status: Investigated, not viable for Gemma3
Reason: GemmaRMSNorm uses `x*(1+w)` formula, incompatible with existing fused kernel
Impact: Would only provide small performance gains even if implemented

4. Hybrid backend runtime switching

Status: Not possible in current vLLM architecture
Reason: vLLM selects attention backend once at model initialization
Would require: major architectural changes to support per-request backend selection

### Feedback Period.

2 weeks (14 days) from submission date.

### CC List.

- @WoosukKwon (vLLM maintainer, attention backends)
- @ywang96 (vLLM maintainer, attention backends)
- @zhuohan123 (vLLM maintainer, PagedAttention author)
- @youkaichao (vLLM committer, model integration)
- @DarkLight1337 (vLLM committer, multimodal models)
- @Isotr0py (vLLM committer, attention backends)
- @mgoin (vLLM committer, performance optimization)

### Any Other Things.

Implementation Commitment

I am prepared to contribute the implementation with maintainer guidance.

Risk Mitigation

1. Correctness: Extensive numerical testing against TritonAttention reference
2. CUDA Graph compatibility: Test with PIECEWISE mode early
3. Fallback: Keep TritonAttention as fallback for unsupported GPUs

Related Work

- PR #30386: Already added TritonAttention PrefixLM support
- FlexAttention: torch.compile-based solution
- This RFC: Natural evolution toward improved multimodal performance

Success Criteria

Correctness (Required):
1. FlashMask output matches TritonAttention output within numerical tolerance
2. All existing tests pass: `tests/models/decoder_only/vision_language/test_gemma3.py`
3. GGUF multimodal tests pass: `tests/models/decoder_only/vision_language/test_gguf_multimodal.py`

Performance (Required):
4. Text-only latency ≤ FlashAttention-2 latency (no regression)
5. Multimodal latency < TritonAttention latency (improvement amount TBD during implementation)
6. Memory usage for masks: O(N) verified via `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()`

Integration (Required):
7. Compatible with PagedAttention block tables
8. Compatible with CUDA graph capture (PIECEWISE mode)
9. Fallback to TritonAttention on unsupported GPUs (SM < 8.0)

Tests to Add:
- `tests/attention/test_flashmask_correctness.py`
- `benchmarks/attention/benchmark_flashmask.py`

title: [RFC]: Enabling Zero-Copy Video with PyNvVideoCodec and IPC
author: brandonpelfrey
body:
### Motivation. This RFC proposes a set of changes for enabling HW-accelerated video decoding and zero-copy transfer to CoreEngine for improving VLM latency/throughput and reducing CPU pressure for (eventual) multi-GPU scaling. These changes are aimed at improving the basic DP=1 case first with future improvements to support more complex DP>1 or TP cases. # Benchmark Data A comparison of throughput for video captioning tasks consistently showed a 2-3% improvement in overall throughput. This testing was performed on a single H100 GPU. All testing performed on ``` CPU Model: AMD EPYC 7413 24-Core Processor System Memory: 256 GB GPU: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 ``` Benchmarking serving was single vLLM instance with 3 API Server Processes. ``` VLLM_VIDEO_LOADER_BACKEND=pynvvideocodec \ VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \ vllm serve nvidia/cosmos-reason1-7b \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"video": 1}' \ --allowed-local-media-path / \ --mm-processor-cache-gb \ --trust-remote-code \ --max-model-len 65536 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 \ --no-enforce-eager \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --api-server-count 3 \ --media-io-kwargs '{"video":{"num_frames":10}}' \ --mm-processor-kwargs '{"max_pixels": 151200}' \ --maximum-concurrent-videos 140 ``` ## Default CPU Encoding + CPU->GPU Transfer Data Path ``` vllm bench serve \ --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --backend openai-chat \ --model nvidia/cosmos-reason1-7b \ --dataset-name sharegpt --dataset-path /workspace/data/sharegpt/llava_v1_5_mix665k_with_video_chatgpt72k_share4video28k.json \ --disable-shuffle \ --num-warmups 20 \ --num-prompts 1000 \ --max-concurrency 200 \ --sharegpt-output-len 128 ============ Serving Benchmark Result ============ Successful requests: 1000 Failed requests: 0 Maximum request concurrency: 200 Benchmark duration (s): 309.01 Total input tokens: 16003 Total generated tokens: 111204 Request throughput (req/s): 3.24 Output token throughput (tok/s): 359.88 Peak output token throughput (tok/s): 2332.00 Peak concurrent requests: 208.00 Total token throughput (tok/s): 411.67 ---------------Time to First Token---------------- Mean TTFT (ms): 40142.06 Median TTFT (ms): 42035.58 P99 TTFT (ms): 59058.94 -----Time per Output Token (excl. 1st token)------ Mean TPOT (ms): 169.17 Median TPOT (ms): 173.85 P99 TPOT (ms): 269.43 ---------------Inter-token Latency---------------- Mean ITL (ms): 172.21 Median ITL (ms): 271.29 P99 ITL (ms): 395.90 ================================================== ``` CPU utilization during this test was consistently hovering around 30% on all 24 cores during this test based on video decoder usage. ## PyNvVideoCodec + GPU IPC (zero-copy) Data Path Note: All testing with CUDA MPS enabled to avoid the cost of GPU context switching between CoreEngine processes and multiple PyNvVideoCodec work happening in API Server processes. ``` vllm bench serve \ --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --backend openai-chat \ --model nvidia/cosmos-reason1-7b \ --dataset-name sharegpt --dataset-path /workspace/data/sharegpt/llava_v1_5_mix665k_with_video_chatgpt72k_share4video28k.json \ --disable-shuffle \ --num-warmups 20 \ --num-prompts 1000 \ --max-concurrency 200 \ --sharegpt-output-len 128 ============ Serving Benchmark Result ============ Successful requests: 1000 Failed requests: 0 Maximum request concurrency: 200 Benchmark duration (s): 301.32 Total input tokens: 16003 Total generated tokens: 111878 Request throughput (req/s): 3.32 Output token throughput (tok/s): 371.30 Peak output token throughput (tok/s): 2821.00 Peak concurrent requests: 206.00 Total token throughput (tok/s): 424.41 ---------------Time to First Token---------------- Mean TTFT (ms): 38948.64 Median TTFT (ms): 26945.85 P99 TTFT (ms): 74324.50 -----Time per Output Token (excl. 1st token)------ Mean TPOT (ms): 164.79 Median TPOT (ms): 169.49 P99 TPOT (ms): 219.31 ---------------Inter-token Latency---------------- Mean ITL (ms): 163.15 Median ITL (ms): 283.04 P99 ITL (ms): 295.42 ================================================== ``` CPU utilization while using the zero-copy path was consistently *much* lower at <5% on nearly every core. # The Problem Inference workloads involving many videos, for instance video captioning, currently incur the cost of copying pre-processed frame data within the API Server process into a shared ring buffer, and then from the shared ring buffer to GPU in the CoreEngine Process. There is also significant CPU overhead involved from the current CPU video decoding method. ### Proposed Change. This RFC proposes three mechanisms which improve throughput and lower CPU utilization. ## Hardware Video Decoding Provide PyNvVideoCodec as a VideoLoader backend for HW-accelerated video decoding directly to VRAM. This also reduces CPU pressure from video decoding. PyNvVideoCodec is available under an MIT license and is officially supported by NVIDIA. PyNvVideoCodec may be installed for users utilizing NVIDIA GPUs. ## GPU Shared Memory IPC A new queue-based transport for "sending" GPU-resident tensors from API Server loading processes to CoreEngine processes via GPU shared memory IPC. This pairs with HW-accelerated video decoding to avoid any CPU-GPU or GPU-GPU transfers. Each CoreEngine process will have a single queue and that queue is shared to all API Server processes. When an API Server will send a request to a CoreEngine, any GPU tensors within multimodal content are replaced with a generated handle, and that handle is sent over the existing ZMQ channel. The original tensor is sent using `torch.multiprocessing.Queue` for the relvant CoreEngine at that time. Because there can be multiple API Servers producing into a single queue for a CoreEngine and ZMQ queue messages referring to a tensor may arrive in any order, when a CoreEngine process is retrieving a Tensor over the Queue, it drains all available Tensors into a table until the desired one is found. Future queries to get a Tensor from the queue first check the table of received-but-not-yet-consumed Tensors. The approach of using Queues with PyTorch Tensors is advantageous is already functionality to ensure that ref-counting semantics are already obeyed and GPU shared memory is transparently used over Queues to enable zero-copy transfer in the above approach. The cost of releasing shared memory tensors appears to have no tangible impact on performance. ### GPU IPC Data Flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant API as API Server
(Video Loader) participant GPU as GPU VRAM
(Shared Memory) participant Q as torch.mp.Queue
(Data Plane) participant ZMQ as ZMQ Socket
(Control Plane) participant Core as CoreEngine
(Model Executor) Note over API, GPU: 1. Hardware Decode API->>GPU: Decode directly to VRAM (PyNvVideoCodec) activate GPU GPU-->>API: Return GPU Tensor Reference deactivate GPU Note over API, Core: 2. Split Transport API->>API: Generate Handle (UUID) replacing Tensor in Request par Async Transfer API->>Q: torch.multiprocessing.Queue Put(GPU Tensor) Note right of Q: PyTorch ref-counting ensures
VRAM allocation remains alive API->>ZMQ: ZMQ Send(Request Metadata + Handle) end Note over Core, GPU: 3. Reconstruction & Inference ZMQ->>Core: Recv(Request Metadata + Handle) Core->>Q: Get() -> Returns GPU Tensor Core->>Core: Reconstruct Request
(Match Handle to Tensor) Core->>GPU: Execute Model Inference Note right of GPU: Zero-Copy: Data stayed in VRAM
the entire time ``` ## Limiting Video Decode VRAM Utilization PyNvVideoCodec allocates VRAM on its own during the decode process. Because this is not accounted for in the KV Cache memory utilization budgeting, another mechanism will ideally prevent users from reaching an OOM state for VRAM. We propose that a new parameter (e.g. "max-concurrent-videos") is provided by the user which tracks the maximum number of "live"/in-flight videos across all requests. That value is divided amongst the API Servers, and each API Server during VideoLoader will use a process-wide counting semaphore so that if the number of outstanding requests is already at the max, a new decode process will block until a previous request on that API Server completes and releases one resource from the semaphore. Note that the failure mode this attempts to protect against is not a new issue: A large influx of video decoding work on a vLLM instance using CPU-based video decoders will also OOM. The difference is that GPU VRAM is commonly in contention with activations, KV Cache, etc. so we believe something like this is required to enable production use cases. # Alternatives Considered With respect to HW-accelerated Video Decoding... We did not see another solution which provided official support, pypi-installable, permissive licensing, and interacted with PyTorch to support zero-copy. With respect to IPC... We have additionally considered a two-way ref-counting approach where API Server processes retain all tensors and send a descriptor based on pytorch-internal functions. The descriptor is used to re-construct the tensor on the CoreEngine side. When the CoreEngine drops references to a tensor, a "release" message is sent back to the appropriate API Server to "down-ref" (and deallocate) that storage. It was found that the cost of closing an IPC mapping in the Core Engine process is negligible (commonly ~100 microseconds from traces), additional complexity, and requirement of ensuring the release message is sent back properly disqualified this approach. With respect to guarding against VRAM OOM... Client tooling can often limit workload pressure which can avoid this issue. In cases of many distinct clients which are not cooperating, or in the case of a malicious client attempting to (D)DOS the system, we did not see another approach. Additionally, semaphore based on bytes instead of video count would adapt to varying resolutions, but the VRAM requirements of a video would require first querying the length/resolution of a video to determine the probable storage requirements. The idea with tracking video count assumes that all videos are a "maximum number of total pixels (resolution * frames)" ### Feedback Period. Concurrent with PR coming in a few days. ### CC List. @benchislett ### Any Other Things. For supporting DP>1 cases immediately following this change, we recommend running one vLLM instance in a container, each container with one GPU, and using an external load balancer across containers. In this way, each vLLM instance maintains a simplified view of resources. Draft PR: Coming in a couple of days. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Draft] [RFC]: vLLM + UCC Backend
author: lengrongfu
body:
### Motivation.

Integrating UCC (Unified Collective Communication) https://github.com/openucx/ucc into vLLM as an optional communication backend. 
### Strengthening vLLM’s Backend Abstraction
- UCC supports a wide range of hardware backends,
- It decouples vLLM’s distributed engine from any single communication API.
- It allows developers to register new communication backends through UCC’s standardized API.
- This modularity supports future frameworks, accelerators, or transport technologies with minimal changes to vLLM internals.
- Through UCC vLLM can advantage of many UCC’s key design philosophies, such as:
   -  Enabling framework to use optimized collective implementations provided by the underlying transport (eg. ROCm/UCX for AMD, Level-Zero for Intel, and CUDA for NVIDIA).
- By providing a unified interface through UCC vLLM takes advantage of many of its benefits.
- Enable performance-optimized collectives on diverse hardware platforms through existing vendor or community-supported UCC transports.
- Abstract away vendor-specific libraries behind a common API, reducing direct dependencies in vLLM’s communication layer.
- Provide cross-platform support across CPU, GPU, and multi-node environments through UCX and UCC’s pluggable backends.

### Enabling Broader Hardware Ecosystem Participation
By integrating UCC as an optional backend, vLLM gains several architectural advantages:
- Backend-agnostic communication layer
- Extensible design
- Improved interoperability
- Simplified maintenance and evolution

### Community and Ecosystem Benefits
- Lower contribution barrier – backend introduction or algorithm optimizations through UCC’s plugin model without modifying vLLM directly.
- Shared maintenance effort – allows vLLM to benefit from upstream advancements with minimal internal changes.
- Cross-project collaboration – UCC is used by various HPC and AI frameworks. Adoption in vLLM enables shared expertise and potential interoperability with existing distributed infrastructure.
- Broader hardware inclusion – Support for new accelerator architectures can be achieved upstream in UCC, automatically extending vLLM’s compatibility scope.
- HPC/AI Community alignment – The integration positions vLLM within the shared ecosystem of HPC and AI communication frameworks, fostering collaboration between performance engineers, AI researchers, and hardware vendors.

### Potential Performance Improvements
- Native collective algorithms – UCC provides built-in implementations of established parallel algorithms (e.g., pairwise exchange, Bruck, recursive doubling).
- Small-message and irregular traffic patterns – UCC’s adaptive scheduling can help mitigate overheads in workloads that involve many small or uneven communication patterns, such as KV-cache migration or chunked prefill stages in multi-node inference.
- Topology-aware execution – UCC can leverage system topology information (intra-node vs inter-node) to choose transport layers dynamically.
- Multi-protocol interoperability – UCC supports combining transports in a single collective operation, which can be beneficial in heterogeneous or partially connected environments.
- Performance experimentation framework – With UCC integrated, developers can benchmark and explore new algorithmic strategies for collective operations within vLLM without modifying its core communication layer.

### Proposed Change.

## all_reduce or reduce_scatter etc.

1. we only need use  `torch.distributed` and set backend is `ucc`.
```python
self.ucc_group = torch.distributed.new_group(self.ranks, backend="ucc")
```

2. then we can use this group to exec all_reduce or other torch support method.

```python
dist.all_reduce(tensor, op=op, group=self.ucc_group)
```

everything is natively supported by PyTorch.

PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/24426

## all_to_all

- Path one
 
   Implement a similar interface and functionality as DeepEP using UCC.

   TODO..

- Path two

   Implement a vllm alltoall backend using PyTorch Symmetric Memory, and then integrate it into the PyTorch Symmetric Memory backend via UCC. Currently, only three backends are supported: "NVSHMEM", "CUDA", and "NCCL".

   TODO...

title: [RFC]: DRY Dependencies for Better Hardware-Specific vLLM Dependency Management
author: wjhrdy
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM currently maintains **16 separate `requirements/*.txt` files** (cuda.txt, rocm.txt, tpu.txt, xpu.txt, cpu.txt, plus build/test variants) with **no centralized dependency specification for common dependencies**. This creates three critical issues:

#### 1. No Single Source of Truth Creates CI Fragility

- Each hardware target has **divergent torch versions**:
  - CUDA: `torch==2.9.0`
  - XPU: `torch==2.9.0+xpu` with custom index URLs
  - TPU: Completely different dependency set
- **Non-CUDA builds discover breakages only after CUDA CI passes** → CI flakes and delayed feedback

#### 2. Development vs CI Install Paths Have Diverged

- Developers: `pip install -e .` → relies on `pyproject.toml` dynamic dependency resolution
- CI: Explicitly installs from hardware-specific requirements files
- **Result**: Changes that work locally fail in CI (or vice versa)
- **Evidence**: pyproject.toml contains `# Should be mirrored in requirements/build.txt` admitting synchronization debt
- **No guardrails** to detect drift until builds break

#### 3. Lack of Automated Validation

- When PyTorch or common dependencies are updated, manual effort required to validate across 16 files
- High likelihood of missing one hardware variant → CI flakes
- Each dockerfile manually specifies dependencies → duplication

#### Current System Costs

- Setup.py runs **3 times during build**, causing precompiled wheels to download 3x (inefficient)
- Manual synchronization burden on maintainers
- Setup.py deprecation is **blocking other improvements**

### Proposed Change.

Implement a setuptools custom build backend that **uses `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE` as the single source of truth**:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools"]
build-backend = "backend"
backend-path = ["_custom_build"]
```

Custom `_custom_build/backend.py` implements:

- `get_requires_for_build_wheel(config_settings)`
- `get_requires_for_build_sdist(config_settings)`
- `get_requires_for_build_editable(config_settings)`

These functions return hardware-specific torch requirements based on `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE` environment variable.

#### Benefits

- DRY dependency definition per hardware target  
- Seamless install E.g.: `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu uv pip install git+https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm@v0.12.0`
- Works with uv, pip, and standard package managers  
- Eliminates 3x wheel downloads (improves build speed)  
- Dev/CI paths converge on same logic  
- Automated validation via CI (all hardware paths tested)

#### Implementation Scope

1. **Custom build backend**: Migrate from setup.py to custom setuptools backend
2. **Dependency definitions**: Consolidate hardware-specific torch versions
3. **Dockerfile updates**: Use `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE` variable
4. **Documentation**: Update installation guides for each hardware target
5. **Testing**: Validate backend behavior across hardware targets
6. **Deprecation**: Remove setup.py (currently causes 3x build overhead)

#### Success Criteria

- [ ] DRY dependency definitions
- [ ] Dev install (`pip install -e .`) and CI install use identical dependency resolution
- [ ] Installation docs work for all hardware targets with `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE` env var
- [ ] CI flakes from dependency mismatches eliminated or significantly reduced

#### Considerations

**Complexity**: Build system migration requires coordinated updates across:
- `pyproject.toml` configuration
- All Dockerfiles (CUDA, ROCm, TPU, XPU, CPU) need to be updated
- CI pipeline configuration
- Installation documentation
- Developer guides

**Backward compatibility**: Must support installation workflows:
- `pip install vllm`
- `pip install -e .` (from source, dev mode)
- `git+` URLs with `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=<target>`
- `uv pip install` workflows


### Feedback Period.

3 weeks (until January 14th, 2025)


### CC List.

@dtrifiro @khluu @Harry-Chen 

### Any Other Things.

#### Related Work

- [**PR #13480**](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/13480) by @dtrifiro: Previous implementation (outdated, needs rebase) — implements exact approach described above
- [**Draft PR #30901**](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/30901) by @dtrifiro: Working skeleton being updated in coming weeks

#### References

- [Slack discussion consolidating dependency management approaches](https://vllm-dev.slack.com/archives/C07R5PAL2L9/p1765923836906189) (Dec 2025)
- PEP 517/518: Custom build backends
- [uv package manager index pinning docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/indexes/#pinning-a-package-to-an-index)

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: AMD-Quark Online Quantization
author: hangy-amd
body: # Motivation. Online quantization has many advantages. For example, it simplifies the model deployment by eliminating the need to use third party quantization tools for quantization. As a major quantization backend of vLLM, Quark is planning to implement online quantization in vLLM. Users can take unquantized models or even offline quantized models as input and simply set the attribute `quantization` during LLM initialization. Then, they'll get the expected online quantized models. # Proposed Change. There's an existing pipeline of running offline quantized models. We'll reuse the existing pipeline as much as possible for online quantization. ## Run offline quantized model The current pipeline of running offline quantized model is as follows: - model init - init model layers - init `quant_method` for each layer according to `quant_config` - call `create_weights` method of `quant_method` to init weight and weight_scale as torch.nn.Parameters - attach `weight_loader` to weight and weight_scale - load weights - the weight_loader attached to weight and weight_scale will be called - process_weights_after_loading - model inference: - the method `apply_weights` of `quant_method` will be called ## Online quantization pipeline Online quantization pipeline is almost the same as that of running offline quantized model except for inserting some quantization operations and some other minor differences: - model init - init model layers - init `quant_method` for each layer according to `quant_config` - call `create_weights` method of `quant_method` to init weight and weight_scale as torch.nn.Parameters (the dtype of weight could be float dtype compared to quantized dtype in running offline quantized model) - attach `weight_loader` to weight and weight_scale - load weights - the `weight_loader` attached to weight and weight_scale will be called (weight_loader attached to weight_scale may or may not be called depending on the format of input model) - process_weights_after_loading - take weight as input and do quantization and get quantized weight and weight_scale - model inference: - the method `apply_weights` of `quant_method` will be called ## API design We want to design the API as simple as possible. The simplest way of enabling online quantization would be setting `quantization` attribute to specific values, for example `quark_online_fp8_ptpc`, like the pseudo code shows: ```python llm = LLM( model_name=model_name, quantization="quark_online_fp8_ptpc", ... ) output = llm.generate_greedy(["some prompt"]) ``` Under the hood, the quant_config parsing process is like this: - Read quant_config from huggingface config, this would be none for unquantized float models - If the `quantization` attribute is set to "quark_online_xxxx" (we'll follow the current naming pattern, which is quant backend + quant scheme), Quark will provide a default quant_config with an API like `quark.config.get_default_config` - Quark online quantization will reuse offline quant_method with an attribute `is_online_quant` set to `True` to distinguish online and offline quantization. We'll also provide a way of customizing the default quant_config for users. Users can get the default quant_config at the outer most layer, make some modification and insert the config with hf_override. ```python import quark quant_config = quark.config.get_default_config(scheme="fp8_ptpc") # modifying quant_config hf_overrides = { "quantization_config": quant_config } llm = LLM( model_name=model_name, hf_overrides=hf_overrides, ... ) output = llm.generate_greedy(["some prompt"]) ``` ## Online quantizing offline quantized models The pipeline of online quantizing offline quantized models is almost the same as that of online quantizing float models except for inserting addtinal dequantization before quantization in method `process_weights_after_loading` ### Feedback Period. 1 ~ 2 weeks ### CC List. @vkuzo ### Any Other Things. # Discussion One example use case of online quantizing offline quantized weight models I can think of would be changing the quant scheme of the offline quantized model. For example, The offical Deepseek R1 is per-block fp8 quantized. With online quantization, we can change the quantization scheme from per-block fp8 to mxfp4 of mxfp6 during model loading. Is a valuable use case? If so, is it appropriate to do it with online quantization? ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Optional Hidden States Transfer in `KVConnectorBase_V1` to Eliminate Decoder Prefix-Prefill in P/D Disaggregation
author: xinyu-intel
body: ### Motivation. vLLM supports **Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregation**, where prefill and decode are executed in separate vLLM instances and communicate via connector abstractions such as `KVConnectorBase_V1`. A key motivation of this design is to prevent prefill work from interrupting decode execution and to improve tail inter-token latency (ITL) under high concurrency. In the current vLLM v1 design, P/D disaggregation typically transfers **KV cache only** from the prefill worker to the decode worker. As a result, the decode worker must still recompute the **last-token hidden states** in order to sample the first output token. This recomputation is implemented by scheduling a **decoder-side prefix prefill**, leveraging existing prefix caching infrastructure. While functionally correct, this design introduces performance issues in certain deployment configurations. ### Deployment context This RFC is motivated by deploying **DeepSeek-R1 (MLA attention)** on Intel accelerators (Gaudi and Intel XPU) with the following configuration: - **Prefill**: Tensor Parallel (TP) - **Decode**: Data Parallel (DP) - **Connector**: NIXL connector with GDR enabled ### Observed issues Take the following line chart as an example, which was captured on one of the DP decode rank(DP16) during 8k/1.5k serving task. 1. **Decode pipeline interruption** Decoder-side prefix prefill injects prefill-style computation into the decode execution timeline. Hardware event traces show that: - steady-state decode steps execute in a stable regime (tens of milliseconds), - prefix-prefill injections introduce large step-time spikes (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds), - these spikes directly inflate TPOT and tail ITL, - the effect worsens with higher concurrency and longer context lengths. 2. **Inefficiency under DP decode for MLA** For MLA models, DP decode is often preferred. However: - prefix prefill is also scheduled in DP mode, - only one DP rank is required to produce hidden states for sampling, - other ranks perform redundant or dummy work, - this causes unnecessary token dispatch overhead and scheduler pressure. These issues contradict the original goal of disaggregated prefilling: **keeping decode execution in a stable steady state**. The decode worker already has all required information to proceed **if last-token hidden states are available**, making the decoder-side prefix prefill fundamentally avoidable. ### Proposed Change. This RFC proposes an **optional, backward-compatible enhancement** to `KVConnectorBase_V1` (v1-only) to transfer **last-token hidden states** alongside KV cache under P/D disaggregation. ### High-level design When enabled, the prefill worker transfers: - KV cache blocks (existing behavior), and - **last-token hidden states** corresponding to tokens that are ready for decoding. The decode worker can then: 1. Receive KV cache and hidden states 2. Perform **sampling only** for the first token 3. Immediately enter steady-state decoding without scheduling a decoder-side prefix prefill This preserves the existing async scheduling model while eliminating decode pipeline interruptions caused by prefix prefill. ### Hidden states definition - Tensor: `hidden_states_last` - Shape: `(num_tokens, hidden_dim)` - Semantics: final-layer hidden states corresponding to the *last prefill token* for each token ready for decoding - Dtype: model activation dtype (e.g., bf16 / fp16), consistent with the input to `lm_head` > `num_tokens` is used instead of `batch_size` to reflect vLLM’s token-centric scheduling model. It may differ from request count due to chunked prefill, prefix caching, or scheduler packing. ### Tensor Parallel prefill considerations For TP prefill: - hidden states may be sharded across TP ranks, - the prefill worker should materialize full `(num_tokens, hidden_dim)` hidden states on a designated producer rank (e.g., TP rank 0), - only the materialized tensor is transferred to the decode worker. This avoids requiring TP collectives on the decode side. ### Decode behavior (DP decode) When hidden states transfer is enabled: - A single DP rank (e.g., local rank 0) computes logits and performs first-token sampling. - Sampled token IDs are broadcast to other DP ranks using existing mechanisms. - The scheduler proceeds with normal decode steps. No changes are required to async scheduling semantics. ### Configuration and compatibility - The feature is **opt-in** (disabled by default). - Applies to **vLLM v1 only** (`KVConnectorBase_V1`). - Existing behavior is preserved when the feature is disabled or unavailable. - If hidden states transfer fails at runtime, the system falls back to the existing decoder-side prefix prefill path to preserve correctness. ### Lifecycle considerations Hidden states are **ephemeral model outputs** and are not managed by an existing cache allocator. Implementations are expected to: - manage hidden states with a request/token-scoped lifecycle, - ensure deterministic reclamation after sampling, - avoid introducing long-lived cache semantics. One possible implementation approach is to use pre-registered, connector-managed ephemeral buffers (similar in spirit to encoder cache registration in NIXL-based designs), but the exact mechanism is left to implementation. --- This change aligns with broader vLLM efforts toward richer intermediate tensor transfer (e.g., fully disaggregated pipelines and encoder–prefill disaggregation) while keeping the scope narrowly focused on eliminating unnecessary decoder-side prefix prefill for improved decode latency and efficiency. ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. @xuechendi @jikunshang @NickLucche @hlin99 ### Any Other Things. ### Reference: [[RFC]: Elastic DP Rank Recovery: Graceful Handling of GPU Hardware Failures Without Full Cluster Restart · Issue #30112 · vllm-project/vllm](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30112) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30112 [[RFC]: OmniConnector for Multimodal Full Disaggregation (Encode/Prefill/Decode/Generator) · Issue #62 · vllm-project/vllm-omni](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/62) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/62 ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Supporting Multi MTP layers in Speculative Decoding (EagleProposer)
author: DingYiBin
body:
### Motivation.

The EagleProposer for speculative decoding is only able to utilize the first MTP layer.
However, the model [XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2-Flash](https://huggingface.co/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2-Flash) has 3 MTP layers.
Is there any plan or ongoing PR to extend support for multi MTP layers in speculative decoding?
btw, [hugo-wind-ding/qwq-32b-mtp](https://huggingface.co/hugo-wind-ding/qwq-32b-mtp) has 7 mtp layers for QwQ-32B

### Proposed Change.

EagleProposer needs a new member function to pass spec_step_idx to mtp models, when num_nextn_predict_layers > 1 and num_speculative_tokens > 1.
