title: [RFC]: Sampling Optimization: move gather of logits after argmax.
author: whx-sjtu
body: ### Motivation. As shown in the left part of the following picture, in the original sampling procedure we perform `llm_head` and `gather` first, then perform `argmax` to full `logits`. However, we can in fact move `gather` after `argmax` to reduce both the communication volume of `gather` and the computation load of `argmax`. The test results during the puncturing phase show that this feature can optimize the `logits_processor + sampler` time consumption by more than 200 us in certain scenarios. In speculative decoding scenarios, where multiple rounds of post-processing are required for each step, the benefits of this feature can become even more pronounced. So I think this is an important optimization especially when eagle3 become more and more popular. Later I will propose a PR to implement this. ### Proposed Change. Implementing PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32021 1. Remove the `gather/all_gather` operation from logits processor. 2. Add two `gather/all_gather` operations to sampler to gather both max value and max index of `argmax`. Then perform `max` to obtain the global max value and related max index. ### Results. Original argmax: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8aa31aa6-0a1f-41df-8029-248c683c40bd) Optimized: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4cb0c786-673b-407a-9356-dae57e1ff395) _No response_ ### CC List. @youkaichao @zhuohan123 @WoosukKwon ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Early-Fail Tokenization Guard for Completions or Chat Completions
author: scratch-ml
body: ## Motivation. ### Problem Extremely long chat inputs (e.g., hundreds of millions of tokens) are fully tokenized before length checks, causing CPU OOM (e.g., ~300GB per vllm instance) and hanging the single-threaded async tokenizer, blocking all other requests. More concretely, in RL scenarios, many request inputs come from agent–environment interactions and can sometimes become huge. This should ideally be mitigated by client-side validation before sending the request, but in practice callers often aren’t aware of it. We also need safeguards in vLLM itself, because diagnosing a service hang after it occurs can be time-consuming and difficult. ### Root Cause `_normalize_prompt_text_to_input` (chat path) always tokenizes the entire prompt, then checks `max_model_len` afterward. `Tokenizer `runs in a single-thread `AsyncMicrobatchTokenizer` executor; huge prompts monopolize it and allocate large intermediate buffers. `truncate_prompt_tokens` is optional and usually unset, so no protective truncation/early stop is applied. ## Proposed Change. ### Recommended Fixes #### 1) Protective truncation during tokenization (default path) In `_normalize_prompt_text_to_input` and `InputPreprocessor._tokenize_prompt`, pass `truncation=True` with `max_length = max_model_len (+1)` when no user override is set. If returned input_ids reaches max_model_len, immediately raise a length error instead of continuing. #### 2) Pre-tokenization raw-size guard Add a character-count (or byte) hard cap derived from max_model_len (configurable, e.g., 32–64×). If the rendered prompt exceeds this cap, reject before calling the tokenizer. #### 3) Optional async tokenizer guard Allow a `max_length_guard/max_raw_chars_guard` kwarg in AsyncMicrobatchTokenizer’s encode loop to fast-fail obviously excessive work, preventing the single executor thread from being tied up. ### Effects Long requests fail fast with clear errors; tokenizer never builds gigantic BatchEncodings or stalls the executor thread. Normal requests are unchanged; near-limit requests still get the same validation error but much earlier and with bounded memory. ## Feedback Period. _No response_ ## CC List. _No response_ ## Any Other Things. _No response_

title: [RFC]: Improve environment variable declaration and handling
author: ProExpertProg
body:
### Motivation. Currently, all environment variables are declared twice: the type definition and the custom getter lambda function (shown below). Due to the sheer amount of env vars, it is difficult to keep these in sync, often leading to incorrect type declarations and defaults. Documentation is usually in the form of comments near the getter instead of a docstring on the type declaration, making it unavailable to the IDE. Finally, apart from strings, most variables are ints, bools, or paths, reimplementing custom parser logic. While #25700 argues for limiting the use of envvars (which I agree with), we should still handle the env vars we do have in a robust way.
Current structure of envs.py ``` if TYPE_CHECKING: VLLM_HOST_IP: str = "" VLLM_PORT: Optional[int] = None VLLM_CACHE_ROOT: str = os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/vllm") ... environment_variables: dict[str, Callable[[], Any]] = { # Root directory for vLLM cache files # Defaults to `~/.cache/vllm` unless `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is set "VLLM_CACHE_ROOT": lambda: os.path.expanduser( os.getenv( "VLLM_CACHE_ROOT", os.path.join(get_default_cache_root(), "vllm"), )), # used in distributed environment to determine the ip address # of the current node, when the node has multiple network interfaces. # If you are using multi-node inference, you should set this differently # on each node. 'VLLM_HOST_IP': lambda: os.getenv('VLLM_HOST_IP', ""), # used in distributed environment to manually set the communication port # Note: if VLLM_PORT is set, and some code asks for multiple ports, the # VLLM_PORT will be used as the first port, and the rest will be generated # by incrementing the VLLM_PORT value. 'VLLM_PORT': get_vllm_port, ... } ```
### Proposed Change. Instead of duplicating the type annotations and getter dictionary, I propose the following: - Use the type-hinted declaration as the single source of truth, including defaults and custom parsing, and move them into `envs/_variables.py` - Import those directly `if TYPE_CHECKING` , otherwise use them as a default store - Allow lazy defaults - Standardize argument parsing for `str`/`int`/`float`/`bool`/`Path`/`list[str]` "trivial" types - Add a pre-commit check to validate _variables.py (check lazy default type consistency) and that they are never imported directly I worked on a prototype of this a while ago in #23601 (warning: I couldn't get GH Copilot to clean up the code as intended so it's not nearly finished). Example declarations: ``` VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL: str = env_factory("INFO", lambda x: x.upper()) """Logging level for vLLM. Default is "INFO".""" VLLM_HOST_IP: str = "" """ Used in distributed environment to determine the ip address of the current node, when the node has multiple network interfaces. If you are using multi-node inference, you should set this differently on each node. """ def get_vllm_port(env_port: str) -> int: ... VLLM_PORT: Optional[int] = env_factory(None, get_vllm_port) """ Used in distributed environment to manually set the communication port. Note: if VLLM_PORT is set, and some code asks for multiple ports, the VLLM_PORT will be used as the first port, and the rest will be generated by incrementing the VLLM_PORT value. """ VLLM_CACHE_ROOT: Path = env_default_factory(lambda: parse_path( os.getenv("XDG_CACHE_HOME", "~/.cache")) / "vllm") """Root directory for vLLM cache files. Defaults to `~/.cache/vllm` unless `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is set.""" ... ```
Skeleton for vllm/envs/__init__.py: ``` from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, get_type_hints import envs._variables from envs._variables import _defaults as _env_defaults from envs.utils import EnvFactory, parse_list, parse_path, unwrap_optional, is_type_with_args if TYPE_CHECKING: # This way IDEs & type checkers get the declarations directly from envs._variables import * _type_hints = get_type_hints(_variables) def __getattr__(name): if name not in _env_defaults: raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__} has no attribute {name}") default = _env_defaults[name] if (value := os.getenv(name)) is None: # Not found, return default value if isinstance(default, EnvFactory): default = default.default_value # Call if lazy-initialized return default() if callable(default) else default if isinstance(default, EnvFactory): # If factory provided, use it to parse string return default.parse(value) # Automatic parsing of "trivial" data types var_type = get_type_hints(_variables)[name] # type(default_value) var_type = unwrap_optional(var_type) if var_type is str: return value if var_type in (int, float): return var_type(value) if var_type is bool: return value.strip().lower() in ("1", "true") if var_type is Path: return parse_path(value) if is_type_with_args(var_type, list,[str,]): return parse_list(value) raise ValueError(f"Unsupported type {var_type} for " f"environment variable {name}") ```
Alternatively, we could create a class `Envs` with variables as properties and use function decorators, but the above proposal seems the most scalable (we have a lot of env vars so the simpler the declaration for each the better). ### Feedback Period. 12/23 - 1/5 ### CC List. @hmellor @aarnphm @simon-mo @zhuohan123 @ywang96 @DarkLight1337 ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: a efficient adaptive rejection sampling for accelerating speculative decoding.
author: sunchendd
body:
### Motivation.

Description:
This proposal introduces an enhancement to the rejection sampling mechanism at the core of speculative decoding. The current method relies on a fixed, context-independent random threshold, which leads to a significant "random rejection" problem. In high-uncertainty generation scenarios, plausible candidate tokens proposed by the draft model are frequently rejected merely because their acceptance ratio falls slightly below this fixed threshold due to random chance. This wastes the computational effort spent on verifying subsequent draft tokens and severely limits the acceleration potential of speculative decoding for creative or open-ended tasks.

Motivation:
We observe a dramatic drop in draft acceptance rates as generation uncertainty increases—from over 80% at temperature=0 to only around 30% at temperature=1. This efficiency loss stems from the fixed threshold's inability to account for the intrinsic uncertainty of the target model's predictions at different generation steps. There is a clear need for an adaptive threshold mechanism that is aware of the model's confidence. Such a mechanism could intelligently relax acceptance criteria in high-uncertainty scenarios, reducing wasteful rejections and substantially improving inference throughput without significantly compromising output quality.



### Proposed Change.

Proposed Solution:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13194 propose the Efficient Adaptive Rejection Sampling (EARS) method. Its core innovation is to dynamically adjust the acceptance threshold based on the target model's predictive confidence:
1、Define Uncertainty: Measure the model's uncertainty at the current step as Uncertainty = 1 - max(P_target).
2、Compute Dynamic Tolerance: Introduce a tolerance term proportional to this uncertainty: Tolerance = β * (1 - max(P_target)), where β is a tunable hyperparameter.
3、Modify Acceptance Condition: Change the traditional rule P_target / P_draft ≥ U (where U is a uniform random number) to:
P_target / P_draft ≥ U - Tolerance.

When the model is highly uncertain (low max(P_target), high Tolerance), the effective acceptance threshold is lowered, "pardoning" plausible candidates that would have been randomly rejected. When the model is confident (high max(P_target), low Tolerance), the criterion remains strict, preserving generation quality.

Key Benefits:
1、Significant Efficiency Gains: Achieves up to ~18.12% higher token throughput in open-ended generation tasks.
2、Minimal Impact on Quality: Incurs only a negligible accuractony drop (e.g., <=0.84% on GSM8K) in tasks requiring precision.
3、Easy Integration: Requires no modifications to model architectures. It can be seamlessly integrated into existing speculative decoding frameworks with minimal engineering overhead via optimizations like pre-computation.

title: [RFC]: Decouple page_size_bytes calculation in AttentionSpec for TPU/RPA Compatibility
author: Lumosis
body:
### Motivation.

In the current vLLM V1 implementation, `AttentionSpec` (in `kv_cache_interface.py`) calculates the `page_size_bytes` as a fixed product of `num_kv_heads`, `head_size`, `dtype`, and `block_size`.

The issue: Ragged Paged Attention (RPA) on TPUs often requires the KV cache to be padded to specific byte boundaries (e.g., for XLA memory alignment or specific TPU tiling).

* Because page_size_bytes is a @property, it cannot be overridden during initialization.

* Backends are currently forced to use "hacky" workarounds like `num_gpu_blocks_override` to trick the system into allocating the correct amount of memory, which leads to technical debt and fragile integration in uLLM.

* Multi-host executor (RayExecutor) cannot use `num_gpu_blocks_override` to override num_gpu_blocks. When creating workers across a cluster, `vllm_config` is passed by value (serialized via Ray). The updates made in the `tpu_worker` do not propagate back to the `EngineCore`.

### Proposed Change.

Convert page_size_bytes from a @property to a field that is assigned during __post_init__. This allows a backend to either:

* Accept the default calculation (platform-agnostic).

* Provide a pre-calculated, padded value during initialization.

```
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AttentionSpec(KVCacheSpec):
    num_kv_heads: int
    head_size: int
    dtype: torch.dtype
    use_mla: bool
    page_size_bytes: Optional[int] = None 

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.page_size_bytes is None:
            # Platform-agnostic default logic
            coef = 1 if self.use_mla else 2
            calc_size = (coef * self.block_size * self.num_kv_heads * self.head_size * get_dtype_size(self.dtype))
            object.__setattr__(self, "page_size_bytes", calc_size)
```

title: [RFC]: Integrate omni-ai-npu/omni-infer's Topology-Aware Placement and Execution Optimizations into vLLM EPLB
author: taostronger
body:
### Motivation.

As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, the efficiency of Expert Parallelism Load Balancing (EPLB) becomes a bottleneck. Based on our analysis of the current vLLM architecture and our experience with OmniInfer (https://github.com/omni-ai-npu/omni-infer), we have identified three key areas for optimization within the existing EPLB modules:

Placement Algorithm: The current default policy (deepseek-eplb) does not fully exploit hardware topology awareness (e.g., NVLink vs. PCIe bandwidth differences).
Initialization Flexibility: Currently, EplbState defaults to Round-Robin initialization. Users lack the interface to inject a pre-calculated or specific initial expert layout (e.g., from a file).
Execution Efficiency: The instruction scheduling for expert movement (rebalance_execute.py) can be optimized to reduce bus contention. Furthermore, calculating the schedule in Python during the inference step introduces overhead.

### Proposed Change.

The EPLB module in Omniinfer is called omni_placement. We propose a modular integration plan from omni_placement that respects the current vLLM architecture (Policy -> State -> Execution).

2.1. Policy Module: Register OmniPlacementPolicy

Current State: New algorithms are added by inheriting the abstract base class.
Proposal: We will implement and register OmniPlacementPolicy as a new EPLB algorithm.
Detail: This policy integrates OmniInfer's topology-aware algorithm. It constructs a weighted graph of the physical hardware (identifying high-bandwidth islands) to generate placement plans that minimize cross-node communication latency.

2.2. EPLB-State Module: Custom Initialization Support

Current State: The EplbState initializes expert placement using a default Round-Robin logic.
Proposal: Extend the initialization logic to support user-defined layouts.
Detail: We will add functionality to load the initial expert mapping from external files (e.g., .npy or JSON). This allows users to start inference with a known optimal static layout or restore a specific state, bypassing the warm-up phase for the load balancer.

2.3. Execution Layer: Instruction Reordering & C++ Solver

Current State: rebalance_execute.py calculates rank pairs for weight transfer, and async_worker.py handles the background transfer.
Proposal A (Instruction Reordering): We will integrate OmniInfer's instruction scheduling primitives into rebalance_execute.py. By implementing a "Reorder Mechanism" for the dynamic expert movement instructions, we can optimize the sequence of P2P (isend/irecv) operations to minimize network congestion and maximize bandwidth utilization.
Proposal B (High-Performance Solver Backend): OmniInfer utilizes a C++ based host-side scheduler for efficient activation data collection and algorithm calculation.
We propose porting this logic as an optional high-performance backend.
This module will handle the heavy lifting of schedule calculation on the host side (C++) and dispatch instructions via H2D communication. This significantly reduces the CPU overhead compared to the pure Python implementation, especially under high-frequency rebalancing scenarios.

### Implementation Plan
Phase 1 (Policy & Init): Implement OmniPlacementPolicy and add .npy loading support to EplbState.
Phase 2 (Execution Optimization): Port the instruction reordering logic into rebalance_execute.py.
Phase 3 (C++ Integration): Introduce the C++ scheduler as an optional extension, exposing it via Pybind to the Python control loop.

title: [RFC]: Video Frame Sparsification via Pixel-Level Similarity for Efficient Multimodal Long-Video Inference
author: rayleeku
body:
### Motivation.

The exponential growth of video content and rising demand for "long-video intelligence" (e.g., video summarization, multimodal QA, video generation) have made long-video inference a standard requirement for multimodal large models. However, current models suffer from critical efficiency bottlenecks, necessitating a lightweight, adaptive, and scalable sparsification solution. Key challenges include:
1.1 High Redundancy
Videos exhibit inherent temporal redundancy (e.g., near-identical consecutive frames in static scenes) and spatial redundancy (e.g., repeated encoding of similar content across frames), causing models to waste computation on duplicated information.

1.2 Input Sequence Overflow
Video encoding generates excessive visual tokens that frequently exceed the context window limits of language models.


### Proposed Change.

This solution implements adaptive sparsification through three stages:
1. Downsampling Preprocessing: Apply spatial downsampling (e.g., 4× reduction) to raw frames to lower computational load.
2. Similarity Assessment: Compute SSIM + L1 loss between adjacent frames to generate inter-frame similarity sequences.
3. Adaptive Keyframe Extraction:
- Calculate retained frame count: K = int(total_frames × sparsity_ratio) based on user-defined sparsity ratio
- Apply constraint: K = max(2, min(total_frames, 2 × (K // 2))) → ensures K is even and ≥2
- Select Top-(K-1) lowest-similarity frames as segmentation points to divide the video into K segments
- Extract the temporal midpoint frame from each segment as the keyframe; discard others.

<!-- Failed to upload "image.png" -->

Design Notes:
- Retained frame count is auto-derived from sparsity ratio, eliminating manual specification
- Minimum 2-frame constraint prevents single-frame segments and preserves semantic integrity

2.2 Implementation
Integrate sparsification module in vllm/input/preprocess.py:
- Insert VideoSparsifier processing logic before feeding frames to ViT
- Enable/disable functionality via environment variables
- Consolidate new feature code under vllm/multimodal/ directory

title: [RFC]: Native Weight Syncing APIs
author: hao-aaron
body: ### Implementation Progress - [x] PR 1: New APIs, NCCL, new examples, quantized reloading integration https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31943 - [x] PR 2: IPC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/34171 - [x] new IPC weight engine - [x] new examples (offline and http) - [ ] PR 3: Follow ups - [ ] caching metadata for NCCLWeightTransferUpdateInfo - [x] Confirm this works okay with quantized models - [x] investigate memory usage with layerwise reloading - [x] qwen 30b example: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37334 - [x] enable multigpu IPC examples/ optimizations https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL/discussions/1189 - [ ] Alternative method for enabling endpoints (currently using `DEV_MODE`) - [ ] figuring out how to make this work without `VLLM_ALLOW_INSECURE_SERIALIZATION` - [x] ~Make trainer side functions for each engine into separate library~ - [x] ~APIs for dynamically adding/destroying NCCL groups~ - [ ] ensure create process groups works with all parallelisms - [ ] tracking weight versions https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31943#issuecomment-3834098959 - [x] remove old weight_sync examples: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36188 - [x] update docs/ more detailed docs. - [x] Stateful Trainer send: [design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HgHmEvohLRrRqaWT66y7dJqWPql1Zr0sYL1Hpqf8TV4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.2ec7ge3026mw). - [x] New trainer send abstractions - [x] update nccl to use stateful trainer - [x] update ipc to use stateful trainer - [ ] RDT weight transfer engine - [ ] **WPI zero-copy weight transfer**: [#40828](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40828) — Kubernetes-native shared memory, ~20 GB/s measured - [x] **NCCL M2N sharding-aware transfer**: [#46439](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/46439) — trainer TP ≠ inference TP ### Correctness Tracked in separate RFC: [#48312](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48312) — 5 open weight reload bugs + 5 KV cache invalidation bugs. ### Motivation. Authors: @hao-aaron @SumanthRH vLLM serves not only as an inference runtime for serving requests from end users, but also as a means of serving requests for large language model post-training. The vLLM model weights must be synced periodically in order to make sure that the rollouts match the distribution that would have been generated by the base model weights during post-training. Currently, the official methodology for performing weight sync is to inject additional functionality to each worker class to support the creation of process groups and broadcasting functionality, see: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/examples/offline_inference/rlhf.py. However, there are no standardized methods for performing online weight syncing. Open source projects like [SkyRL](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL/blob/01b4ee09f9983e8452258a8fa88a6fc025da6cfb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/vllm/vllm_engine.py#L69), [VeRL](https://github.com/volcengine/verl/blob/252d76908b903ad8fb6969eb3a5e5f873c95ea2b/verl/experimental/one_step_off_policy/fsdp_workers.py#L52), and [TRL](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/blob/42cce51cf016e3c9502274a0ed05da53d488506c/trl/scripts/vllm_serve.py#L83) need to include their own implementations of the weight syncing infrastructure, leading to added complexity for developers seeking to adopt vLLM as their inference server for post-training workloads. The lack of consistent weight syncing APIs leads to duplicated efforts on the side of users attempting to adopt vLLM. It requires users to version lock to specific implementations of the weight syncing infrastructure, as well as locking into specific torch.distributed backends. Other relevant RFCs [Online quantization with model_loader](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30359): This RFC proposes a way to improve the online quantization which matches the proposal here about having a step for finalizing the weight syncing operation ### Background Weight syncing with NCCL (with disaggregated training and inference) is typically done in many RL frameworks (SkyRL, SLIME, OpenRLHF etc) by having rank 0 of the trainer form a process group with all ranks of the inference engine. There are two methods that are typically implemented per worker: `init_weight_update_group(master_address, master_port, rank_offset, world_size)` - Initializes the process group. Should run on all the worker ranks. - master_address and master_port are the IP and a free port for the machine with rank 0 of the trainer - rank_offset is the rank offset in the process group for this particular worker. For example, if you have 2 vLLM replicas with TP 2, then the TP rank 0 for the 2nd replica has rank_offset of 3 (1 for rank 0 of trainer + 2) - world_size is the global world size `update_weight(name, src_dtype, shape)` Initiates a weight update with NCCL. Should run on all the worker ranks. Each worker will allocate a fixed buffer based on src_dtype and shape and then update the weights. The data is received by a NCCL broadcast operation from rank 0. We then simply call model_runner.model.load_weights after receiving weights. Most of the logic can stay the same → just issue torch.distributed.broadcast in a loop, and call load_weights once. Trainers can still just call this one by one if needed by just formatting a single input as a list. ### Proposed Change. We propose native support for weight syncing, both through offline inference via LLM and AsyncLLM, as well as through HTTP calls via the OpenAI-compatible API. A first draft implementation can be found here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...ahao-anyscale:vllm:weight_transfer_prototype ### New API Endpoints The main features of this new API include exposing the following new endpoints: #### `POST /init_weight_transfer` Initializes the weight transfer mechanism by creating a process group between the trainer and all vLLM workers. **Parameters (NCCL backend):** | Parameter | Type | Description | |-----------|------|-------------| | `master_address` | string | IP address of the trainer (rank 0) | | `master_port` | int | Free port on the trainer machine for NCCL rendezvous | | `rank_offset` | int | Starting rank for vLLM workers in the process group. Typically 1 (trainer is rank 0) | | `world_size` | int | Total number of processes (1 trainer + N vLLM workers across all DP/TP ranks) | **Worker Behavior:** 1. Each worker computes its unique global rank: `rank = (dp_rank * world_size_per_dp + tp_rank) + rank_offset` 2. Creates a `StatelessProcessGroup` connected to the trainer's master address/port 3. Initializes a `PyNcclCommunicator` on the current CUDA device for subsequent broadcasts While this is being called, a process on the trainer side must also simultaneously join the process group. #### `POST /update_weights` Receives weight tensors from the trainer and loads them into the model. Weights are transferred and loaded incrementally to avoid OOM. **Parameters (NCCL backend):** | Parameter | Type | Description | |-----------|------|-------------| | `names` | list[str] | List of parameter names matching the model's state dict keys | | `dtype_names` | list[str] | List of torch dtype names (e.g., "bfloat16", "float32") | | `shapes` | list[list[int]] | List of tensor shapes for each parameter | **Worker Behavior:** 1. For each weight in the batch: - Allocates an empty CUDA tensor with the specified dtype and shape - Receives the tensor data via `nccl.broadcast(src=0)` from the trainer - Immediately calls `model.load_weights([(name, tensor)])` to load into the model - Frees the temporary tensor to avoid memory accumulation The trainer must issue corresponding `broadcast` calls for each weight in the same order. #### `POST /finalize_weight_update` Finalizes the weight update by running post-processing required for quantized or custom kernel formats. **Request Body:** None **Worker Behavior:** 1. Calls `process_weights_after_loading(model, model_config, device)` 2. This handles any necessary weight transformations such as: - Quantization to target precision (e.g., FP8, INT8) - Packing weights for optimized CUDA kernels - Re-computing any cached values derived from weights NOTE: this may change depending on the results of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30359 **EDIT: this endpoint is made redundant by https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30359, and will not be included in final version** ### Architecture The implementation introduces a pluggable `WeightTransferEngine` abstraction that separates weight transfer transport logic from the worker implementation, allowing different backends to be plugged in. **Supported Backends:** - **NCCL**: Uses NCCL broadcast operations for distributed weight transfer - **IPC**: Uses CUDA IPC for same-node weight transfer via shared memory handles ### Configuration Weight transfer is configured via WeightTransferConfig: from vllm.config import WeightTransferConfig ``` # For programmatic usage llm = LLM( model="...", weight_transfer_config=WeightTransferConfig(backend="nccl"), ) ``` ### Usage Example A full RL example with the LLM interface can be found [here](https://github.com/ahao-anyscale/vllm/blob/weight_transfer_prototype/examples/offline_inference/new_weight_syncing/rlhf.py). An http example is [here](https://github.com/ahao-anyscale/vllm/blob/weight_transfer_prototype/examples/offline_inference/new_weight_syncing/rlhf_http.py). The main structure of the two are the same. We begin by initializing process groups. The following code is from a process on the trainer side. We launch an LLM instance as a Ray actor, and save the handle so the trainer can make calls. ``` # Set up the communication channel between the training process and the # inference engine. master_address = get_ip() master_port = get_open_port() handle = llm.init_weight_transfer.remote( WeightTransferInitRequest( init_info=asdict( NCCLInitInfo( master_address=master_address, master_port=master_port, rank_offset=1, world_size=3, ) ) ) ) model_update_group = stateless_init_process_group( master_address, master_port, 0, 3, torch.device("cuda:0") ) ray.get(handle) ``` We then sync the weights by asynchronously calling the vllm endpoint while also broadcasting the trainer side weights ``` # Synchronize the updated weights to the inference engine using batched API. # Collect all weight metadata names = [] dtype_names = [] shapes = [] for name, p in train_model.named_parameters(): names.append(name) dtype_names.append(str(p.dtype).split(".")[-1]) shapes.append(p.shape) # Issue update_weights call with NCCL-specific update info handle = llm.update_weights.remote( WeightUpdateRequest( update_info=asdict( NCCLUpdateInfo( names=names, dtype_names=dtype_names, shapes=shapes, ) ) ) ) # Broadcast all weights from trainer for name, p in train_model.named_parameters(): model_update_group.broadcast(p, src=0, stream=torch.cuda.current_stream()) ray.get(handle) # Finalize the weight update (processes weights for quantization/kernel format) ray.get(llm.finalize_weight_update.remote()) ``` ### Open Questions - How should we handle online quantization? Should we merge /finalize_weights together with the /update_weights API? There could be situations where update weights API is called multiple times before calling finalize weights which would motivate disaggregating the apis. Our pattern of calling update_weight before finalizing seems to align with https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30359 One answer is that the API keeps the flexibility of keeping the operations separate, regardless of how the engine handles the weight syncing under the hood, i.e. whether it is fusing load_weights and process_weights or keeping them separate. - The existing pause and resume endpoints can be combined with the above API to implement fully async RL training workflows, see [here](https://skyrl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/fully_async.html) for various async RL strategies. Are the current pause and resume APIs sufficient for current and future RL use cases? ### Feedback Period. 1-2 weeks ### CC List. @SumanthRH @kouroshHakha @robertgshaw2-redhat @simon-mo @kylesayrs @rizar ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: EPLB Implementation Refactoring
author: ilmarkov
body:
### Motivation.

### Current Pain Points

The existing EPLB implementation, while functionally correct, suffers from several issues that impact development velocity and system reliability:

1. **Coordination Complexity**: The async EPLB uses multiple variables (`rebalanced`, `ep_buffer_ready`, `pending_global_ready_check`, `layer_to_transfer`) to coordinate between threads, making it difficult to reason about system state and leading to debugging challenges.

2. **Testing Challenges**: Race conditions are hard to test due to implicit state machines and unclear thread ownership boundaries.

3. **Code Duplication**: Sync and async rearrangement paths share code but have different control flow, resulting in complex conditional logic scattered throughout `rearrange()`.

4. **No Recovery Mechanism**: If synchronization fails mid-layer (e.g., due to network issues or hanging ranks), there is no recovery path, requiring full process restart.

5. **Unclear Thread Semantics**: The async worker daemon pattern with complex lifecycle management makes it unclear when threads own which variables.

6. **Mysterious Synchronization**: The `torch.cuda.synchronize()` call in sync EPLB (`rebalance_execute.py`) is required but unexplained, suggesting potential hidden race conditions.

7. **Complex Transfer Logic**: The `move_to_buffer()` function (~200 lines) mixes planning, local copies, and remote transfers, making it hard to understand and test.

8. **Terminology Confusion**: "Physical experts" is ambiguous - they are actually slots that can hold different logical expert weights over time.


### Proposed Change.

### 1. Replace Async Worker Daemon with Fork-Join Pattern

**Current State**: A long-lived daemon thread waits on events and maintains complex state across multiple rebalancing operations.

**Proposed**: Use a fork-join pattern where a worker thread is spawned for each rebalancing operation and joined when complete.

#### Rationale

- **Simpler Lifecycle**: Each rebalancing operation has a clear start and end
- **Easier Resource Management**: No persistent thread to manage
- **Better Error Isolation**: If a transfer fails, the thread dies and we can detect it

---

### 2. Separate Sync and Async Rearrangement Paths

**Current State**: A single `rearrange()` method with `if self.is_async:` branches throughout.

#### Design

```python
class EplbState:
    def rearrange(self, ...):
        if self.is_async:
            return self._rearrange_async(...)
        else:
            return self._rearrange_sync(...)
    
    def _rearrange_sync(self, ...):
        # Simple sequential logic:
        # 1. Compute new mappings
        # 2. For each layer: transfer weights (blocking)
        # 3. Update mappings
        # 4. Done
        
    def _rearrange_async(self, ...):
        # Fork-join logic:
        # 1. Validate no transfer in progress
        # 2. Prepare transfer context
        # 3. Fork worker thread
        # 4. Return immediately
```

#### Rationale

- Each path is easier to understand in isolation
- No complex conditional logic

---

### 3. Rename Physical Experts to Slots

**Current State**: The term "physical expert" is used for what are actually weight storage locations that can be reassigned to different logical experts.

**Proposed**: Rename throughout the codebase:
- `num_physical_experts` → `num_expert_slots`
- `physical_to_logical_map` → `slot_to_logical_map`
- `num_local_physical_experts` → `num_local_slots`

#### Rationale

- **Clearer Semantics**: A "slot" can hold different expert weights over time
- **Avoids Confusion**: "Physical" suggests hardware or location, but these are logical storage slots
- **Better Mental Model**: Slots are reassigned during rebalancing, experts are logical entities

---

### 4. Simplify Async Handshake Protocol with State Machine

**Current State**: Multiple variables track coordination state:
- `rebalanced: bool`
- `ep_buffer_ready: int` (0 or 1)
- `pending_global_ready_check: bool`
- `layer_to_transfer: int`

**Proposed**: Single atomic state variable with explicit state machine.

#### State Machine Design

```python
class AsyncTransferState(Enum):
    """State machine for async EPLB transfers."""
    IDLE = 0
    RANKS_READY = 1         # All ranks ready, can transfer/consume
    PLAN_STAGED = 2         # New mappings computed, ready to transfer
    LAYER_TRANSFERRING = 3  # Worker filling buffer for current layer
    LAYER_CONSUMING = 4     # Main thread consuming buffer
    ERROR = 99              # Transfer failed, needs recovery

```

#### Rationale

- **Single Source of Truth**: One variable tells you system state
- **Explicit Transitions**: Can validate and log transitions
- **Clear Ownership**: Each state defines who can act
- **Testable**: Can mock states and test transitions
- **Debuggable**: Log shows clear state progression

---


### 5. Add Recovery Mechanism for Synchronization Failures

**Current State**: No recovery if transfer hangs or fails mid-layer.

**Proposed**: Timeout detection and recovery state.

#### Rationale

- Prevents indefinite hangs
- Graceful degradation (continue without rebalancing)
- Synchronized recovery across ranks
- Logged error information for debugging

---

### 6. Resolve torch.cuda.synchronize() Mystery

### 7. Simplify move_to_buffer()

**Current State**: 200-line function mixing planning, execution, and communication.

**Proposed**: Split into components.

---

### 8. Improve new_mapping Lifecycle Handling

**Current State**: `new_*_map` fields are set/read/cleared in multiple places with implicit lifecycle.

**Proposed**: Explicit lifecycle functions with validation.

title: [RFC]: Online Quantization Roadmap
author: vkuzo
body:
### Motivation.

Online quantization (weights passed to vLLM in high precision, quantization of weights done inside of vLLM) is emerging as an important use case for quick experimentation and RL.  Today vLLM supports online quantization with a single recipe (float8 per-tensor scaling).  I wanted to align on the high level future direction of the specifics of how online quantization is implemented in vLLM as we extend this to more recipes / more hardware types / more use cases.

### Proposed Change.

### Guiding principles

* prefer inlining online quantization logic in vLLM directly over calling third party libraries, for simplicity of the common case.
* separate online quantization code from offline quantization code as appropriate, sharing underlying utilities as needed. 
* the basic dtype of the weight (fp8, int8, etc) should be the high level organization axis for online quant UI and code.  For example, the high level entrypoint for online quant for fp8 (currently `fp8.py` and `--quantization=fp8` in the CLI) should be the entry point for all fp8 weight recipes (tensorwise, rowwise, deepseek-style blockwise, etc) across all hardware types (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, etc).

### Planned improvements

#### fp8 (fp8.py, --quantization="fp8")

  * improve code organization wrt offline quant (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32189)   
  * optimize memory usage (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31914)
  * add support for online quantization for rowwise and blockwise fp8 (currently only tensorwise scaling is supported). This would involve some UI design of how the user can choose the scaling from the command line (not yet done), how to ignore layers, whether there should be a way to mix-and-match different recipes per layer, etc.  See https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32412 .
  * improve support for other hardware platforms (as needed)

#### other dtypes

* `mxfp8.py` / `--quantization=mxfp8` could be added for online quant with other mxp8, similar with int8, nvfp4, etc (as needed)

### Open questions

* how should we implement numerics matching between training and inference code? For example if the training code calls a specific `quantize_to_fp8_rowwise` kernel, what is the recommended mechanism to guarantee the same kernel being used in vLLM?  Is it an env var, an out-of-tree kernel registration mechanism, something else?

### Feedback Period.

one to two weeks

title: [RFC]: Expose Sharding Metadata from vLLM Model Layers
author: chunzhao
body:
### Motivation.


Currently, downstream systems that need to understand how vLLM model weights are sharded must infer sharding patterns from tensor names using heuristics:

```python
# Current approach: Pattern matching on tensor names
def infer_sharding(tensor_name: str) -> ShardingType:
    if "gate_proj" in tensor_name or "up_proj" in tensor_name:
        return COLUMN_PARALLEL  # [tp_size, 1]
    elif "down_proj" in tensor_name:
        return ROW_PARALLEL  # [1, tp_size]
    elif "embed_tokens" in tensor_name:
        return VOCAB_PARALLEL
    # ... many more patterns
```

This approach has several problems:

1. **Fragile**: Different model architectures use different naming conventions (e.g., Llama uses `gate_proj`, other frameworks use `w13`, some use `fc1_weight`)

2. **Incomplete**: New layer types or model architectures require updating all downstream pattern matchers

3. **Error-prone**: Subtle naming differences can lead to incorrect sharding inference, causing silent data corruption during distributed operations

4. **Duplicated logic**: Every system that needs sharding info must implement and maintain its own pattern matching

5. **No support for complex sharding**: Advanced patterns like Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with head-aware reshaping, or MoE with Expert Parallel (EP) + Expert Tensor Parallel (ETP), are difficult to express through naming conventions alone

**Use cases affected:**
- RL training systems that transfer weights between vLLM inference and training workers
- Checkpointing with different parallelization strategies
- Model parallelism conversion (TP/PP/DP resharding)
- Distributed debugging and visualization


### Proposed Change.

### Overview

Each vLLM layer that performs weight sharding should attach sharding metadata to its parameters at construction time. This metadata describes the global shape, sharding dimensions, and sharding type.

### Sharding Metadata

Define `vllm/model_executor/layers/sharding.py`:

```python
class ShardingType(enum.Enum):
    REPLICATED = "replicated"
    COLUMN_WISE = "column_wise"
    ROW_WISE = "row_wise"
    VOCAB_PARALLEL = "vocab_parallel"
    EXPERT_PARALLEL = "expert_parallel"
    QKV_PARALLEL = "qkv_parallel"

@dataclasses.dataclass
class Sharding:
    shape: Sequence[int]           # Global (unsharded) shape
    nd_num_shards: Sequence[int]   # Number of shards per dimension
    sharding_type: ShardingType    # Semantic type
```

### Layer Integration

Each parallel layer attaches sharding to its weight parameter:

```python
class ColumnParallelLinear(LinearBase):
    def __init__(self, input_size, output_size, ...):
        super().__init__(...)
        self._setup_sharding_metadata()

    def _setup_sharding_metadata(self) -> None:
        self.sharding = Sharding(
            shape=[self.output_size, self.input_size],
            nd_num_shards=[self.tp_size, 1],
            sharding_type=ShardingType.COLUMN_WISE,
        )
        self.weight.sharding = self.sharding
```

### Layers to Update

| Layer | nd_num_shards | Notes |
|-------|---------------|-------|
| `ColumnParallelLinear` | `[tp, 1]` | Output dim sharded |
| `RowParallelLinear` | `[1, tp]` | Input dim sharded |
| `QKVParallelLinear` | `[1, tp, 1, 1]` | 4D head-aware reshaping for GQA |
| `MergedColumnParallelLinear` | `[tp, 1]` | Gate+Up fused |
| `VocabParallelEmbedding` | `[tp, 1]` | Vocab dim sharded |
| `ParallelLMHead` | `[tp, 1]` | Output vocab sharded |
| `FusedMoE` | `[ep, etp, 1]` | Expert + tensor parallel |
| `ReplicatedLinear` | `[1, 1]` | No sharding |

### QKV with Grouped Query Attention

For GQA where `num_q_heads > num_kv_heads`, QKV weights are reshaped to 4D for correct all-gather:

```python
class QKVParallelLinear(ColumnParallelLinear):
    def _setup_qkv_sharding(self) -> None:
        qk_ratio = self.total_num_heads // self.total_num_kv_heads
        # Shape: (qk_ratio + 2, kv_heads, head_dim, hidden_size)
        self.sharding = Sharding(
            shape=[qk_ratio + 2, self.total_num_kv_heads, self.head_size, self.hidden_size],
            nd_num_shards=[1, self.tp_size, 1, 1],
            sharding_type=ShardingType.QKV_PARALLEL,
        )
```

### Access Pattern

Downstream code queries sharding directly from parameters:

```python
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    sharding = getattr(param, "sharding", None)
    if sharding is not None:
        print(f"{name}: shape={sharding.shape}, shards={sharding.nd_num_shards}")
```

### Backward Compatibility

- Existing code continues to work (sharding metadata is additive)
- Parameters without sharding metadata are treated as replicated
- Pattern matching can coexist during migration period

### Example: Llama-style Dense Model (TP=4)

| Layer | Local Shape | Global Shape | nd_num_shards |
|-------|-------------|--------------|---------------|
| `embed_tokens` | `[8000, 4096]` | `[32000, 4096]` | `[4, 1]` |
| `q_proj` | `[1024, 4096]` | `[4096, 4096]` | `[4, 1]` |
| `o_proj` | `[4096, 1024]` | `[4096, 4096]` | `[1, 4]` |
| `gate_proj` | `[2752, 4096]` | `[11008, 4096]` | `[4, 1]` |
| `down_proj` | `[4096, 2752]` | `[4096, 11008]` | `[1, 4]` |

### Example: MoE Model (EP=2, ETP=2)

| Layer | Local Shape | Global Shape | nd_num_shards |
|-------|-------------|--------------|---------------|
| `router` | `[8, 4096]` | `[8, 4096]` | `[1, 1]` |
| `expert.w13` | `[4, 7168, 4096]` | `[8, 14336, 4096]` | `[2, 2, 1]` |
| `expert.w2` | `[4, 4096, 7168]` | `[8, 4096, 14336]` | `[2, 1, 2]` |

title: [RFC]: Extending vLLM Pause/Resume API to support in-flight requests and DPEP scenarios
author: kouroshHakha
body:
## Overview

This document specifies the design for vLLM's pause/resume API to support online RL weight updates. It covers both single-engine and DPEP (Data-Parallel Expert-Parallel) deployments.

**Goals**:
1. Enable zero-downtime weight updates for online RL training
2. Support three pause modes: `abort`, `finish`, `keep`
3. Decouple cache management from pause/resume operations
4. Work seamlessly in both single-engine and multi-engine DPEP setups

**Key Innovation**: The `keep` mode pauses the scheduler loop while preserving request state, enabling fast weight updates with minimal disruption.

---

## Mental Model: System Architecture

### Three Layers

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CLIENT                                         │
│  Concerns: finish reasons, partial outputs      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FRONTEND (AsyncLLM)                            │
│  - Request admission control                    │
│  - abort/finish modes operate here              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCHEDULER (EngineCore)                         │
│  - Busy loop: schedule() → execute() → update() │
│  - keep mode pauses this loop                   │
│  - running/waiting queues, KV cache             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Request Lifecycle States

```
Waiting → Running → Completed
   ↑         ↓
   └─────────┘ (preemption)
```

---

## Core Concept: Three Pause Modes

### Mode: `abort`

**What happens**:
- Frontend blocks new requests
- Abort in-flight requests immediately
- Return partial outputs with `finish_reason="abort"`

**Client impact**: Client-aware (must handle retry)

**Use case**: Fast pause, client can retry

**Current API equivalent**:
```python
POST /pause?wait_for_inflight_requests=false&clear_cache=false
```
(Note: `clear_cache` is decoupled in new design - use `/reset_prefix_cache` explicitly)

---

### Mode: `finish`

**What happens**:
- Frontend blocks new requests
- Wait for in-flight requests to complete normally
- Return with normal finish reasons (`stop`, `length`)

**Client impact**: Client-transparent

**Use case**: Weight-consistent trajectories, no client changes

**Current API equivalent**:
```python
POST /pause?wait_for_inflight_requests=true&clear_cache=false
```
(Note: `clear_cache` is decoupled in new design - use `/reset_prefix_cache` explicitly)

---

### Mode: `keep` (NEW)

**What happens**:
- Frontend blocks new requests
- **Pause EngineCore busy loop** (no scheduling, no execution)
- Requests frozen in `scheduler.running` queue
- KV cache preserved

**Client impact**: Client-transparent (stream appears slow, then continues)

**Use case**: Async RL with minimal latency

**Current API equivalent**: **Not available** (this is the new feature)

**Key distinction**: Unlike abort/finish (which drain requests), `keep` pauses the engine itself.

---

## Single-Engine Design (Non-DPEP)

### API Endpoints

```
POST /pause
Body: {"mode": "abort" | "finish" | "keep"}

POST /resume
Body: {}

POST /reset_prefix_cache
Query: ?reset_running_requests=true&reset_external=false
```

### Pseudo-code: Pause Flow

```python
class AsyncLLM:
    async def pause_generation(mode: PauseMode):
        # 1. Pause frontend (all modes)
        async with self._pause_cond:
            self._paused = True
            self._pause_mode = mode

        # 2. Mode-specific behavior
        if mode == ABORT:
            # Abort all requests
            await self.abort(all_request_ids, internal=True)
            await self.output_processor.wait_for_requests_to_drain()

        elif mode == FINISH:
            # Wait for natural completion
            await self.output_processor.wait_for_requests_to_drain()

        elif mode == KEEP:
            # Pause the engine busy loop
            await self.engine_core.pause_scheduler_async()
            # Returns only when scheduler acknowledges pause
```

### Pseudo-code: Scheduler Pause

```python
class EngineCore:
    def step() -> list[EngineCoreOutput]:
        # Check if pause requested
        if self._scheduler_pause_requested:
            self._scheduler_paused = True
            self._pause_ack_event.set()  # Acknowledge
            return []

        # Check if paused
        if self._scheduler_paused:
            return []  # No work while paused

        # Normal operation
        scheduler_output = self.scheduler.schedule()
        model_output = self.model_executor.execute_model(scheduler_output)
        engine_outputs = self.scheduler.update_from_output(...)
        return engine_outputs

    def pause_scheduler(ack_event: asyncio.Event):
        self._scheduler_pause_requested = True
        self._pause_ack_event = ack_event
        # Pause takes effect after current step

    def resume_scheduler():
        self._scheduler_paused = False
```

**Critical detail**: Acknowledgment ensures scheduler is truly paused before weight update.

---

## Cache Management (Orthogonal)

Cache management is **decoupled** from pause/resume. Use existing `/reset_prefix_cache` API.

### Two Scenarios with `keep` Mode

#### Scenario 1: Stale KV (fast)

```bash
POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}
POST /update_weights {...}
POST /resume
```

**Result**: Requests continue with stale KV cache (old embeddings + new predictions). RL-safe.

---

#### Scenario 2: Clean Prefill (clean boundaries)

```bash
POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}
POST /reset_prefix_cache?reset_running_requests=true
POST /update_weights {...}
POST /resume
```

**What happens**:
1. `reset_prefix_cache` moves requests: `running → waiting`
2. Clears KV cache
3. On resume: scheduler auto-schedules from waiting queue with prefill

**Implementation**: Uses existing vLLM preemption mechanism (`Scheduler._preempt_request()`). No new code needed.

---


## DPEP Design (Multi-Engine)

### Key Challenges

1. Multiple DP engines must coordinate pause/resume
2. DeepEP collectives (MoE all-to-all) require all engines participating
3. Engines are at different step counts at any moment
4. Need to avoid deadlocks during pause

### Key Insights

1. **Step-count synchronization**: Engines naturally stay within ~2-5 steps of each other and synchronize at every 32-step boundary via AllReduce. Use `max(steps)` as dynamic sync target.

2. **Dedicated ZMQ messages**: New message types (`PAUSE_DP`, `RUN_UNTIL_STEP`, `RESUME_DP`) for explicit pause coordination. Event-driven acknowledgment via `pause_ack` and `step_reached` responses.

3. **PAUSE_DP wakes idle engines**: When between waves, engines are blocked in `input_queue.get()`. The `PAUSE_DP` message itself wakes them - no dummy request injection needed.

4. **Between-wave is fastest**: All engines at step 0 (counter resets at wave boundary) → already synchronized → no `RUN_UNTIL_STEP` needed.

5. **Any-rank entry**: Any DP rank can receive `/pause` HTTP request, forwards to `DPCoordinatorProc`.

6. **Broadcast + response pattern**: Coordinator broadcasts to all engines, collects responses via existing output socket.

---

### DPEP Architecture

```
                External Controller
                       |
         /pause to ANY DP rank (e.g., Rank 2)
                       |
    ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
    |                                     |
Rank 0 (has DPCoordinatorProc)       Rank 2
    |                                     |
    |←────── Forward PAUSE_REQUEST ───────┘
    |
    └──► Broadcast PAUSE_DP to all engines
              (via ZMQ publish socket)
```

### New ZMQ Messages

| Direction | Message | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| Coord → Engines | `PAUSE_DP` | Pause immediately, respond with step count |
| Coord → Engines | `RUN_UNTIL_STEP(target)` | Resume until target step, then auto-pause |
| Coord → Engines | `RESUME_DP` | Resume normal operation |
| Engines → Coord | `pause_ack(step)` | Current step when paused |
| Engines → Coord | `step_reached(step)` | Step when target reached |

---

### DPEP Communication Flow

#### Pause Flow: Two Paths

**Path 1: Between-Wave (Fast - engines_running=False)**

```
1. Controller → Rank 2: POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}
2. Rank 2 → DPCoordinator: PAUSE_REQUEST
3. DPCoordinator broadcasts: PAUSE_DP
4. Each engine (blocked in input_queue.get()):
   - Wakes up, receives PAUSE_DP
   - Sets engine_pause=True
   - Sends pause_ack(step=0) to coordinator
   - moves on from the loop that gets it blocked on `input_queue.get()` and pauses. 
5. DPCoordinator receives all pause_acks
   - All at step 0 → already synchronized!
   - No RUN_UNTIL_STEP needed
6. Rank 2 → Controller: HTTP 200 OK
```

**Path 2: Mid-Wave (Step Sync - engines_running=True)**

```
1. Controller → Rank 2: POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}
2. Rank 2 → DPCoordinator: PAUSE_REQUEST
3. DPCoordinator broadcasts: PAUSE_DP
4. Each engine:
   - Sets engine_pause=True
   - Sends pause_ack(step=N) to coordinator
   - The engine moves on to the paused condition
5. DPCoordinator receives all pause_acks: [13, 15, 14, 13]
   - Calculates target = max(steps) = 15
   - Broadcasts: RUN_UNTIL_STEP(15)
6. Each engine:
   - Clears engine_pause, sets target_step=15
   - Runs until step >= 15
   - Sends step_reached(15) to coordinator
7. DPCoordinator receives all step_reached
8. Rank 2 → Controller: HTTP 200 OK
```


---

#### Resume Flow

```
1. Controller → Rank 1: POST /resume
2. Rank 1 → DPCoordinator: RESUME_REQUEST
3. DPCoordinator broadcasts: RESUME_DP
4. If engines_running==False (between waves):
   DPCoordinator broadcasts: START_DP_WAVE
5. Each engine:
   - Clears engine_pause
   - If between waves: receives START_DP_WAVE, resumes stepping
6. Rank 1 → Controller: HTTP 200 OK
```

---

### DPEP Pseudo-code

```python
class DPEngineCoreProc:
    def _handle_client_request(request_type, request):
        if request_type == PAUSE_DP:
            self.engine_pause = True
            self.output_queue.put(EngineCoreOutputs(
                engine_index=self.engine_index,
                pause_ack=self.step_counter,
            ))

        elif request_type == RUN_UNTIL_STEP:
            target_step = request
            self.target_step = target_step
            self.engine_pause = False
            if self.step_counter >= target_step:
                self._send_step_reached()

        elif request_type == RESUME_DP:
            self.engine_pause = False
            self.target_step = None

    def _process_input_queue(self):
        # Critical: exit loop when paused (enables between-wave pause)
        while (
            not self.engines_running
            and not self.scheduler.has_requests()
            and not self.engine_pause  # NEW
        ):
            req = self.input_queue.get()
            self._handle_client_request(*req)

    def is_engine_paused(self) -> bool:
        if self.engine_pause:
            return True
        if self.target_step and self.step_counter >= self.target_step:
            self._send_step_reached()
            return True
        return False

class DPCoordinatorProc:
    def handle_pause_request(self):
        # Broadcast PAUSE_DP
        self._broadcast_pause_dp()
        self._pending_acks = set(range(self.engine_count))

    def handle_pause_ack(self, engine_index, step):
        self._collected_steps[engine_index] = step
        self._pending_acks.discard(engine_index)

        if not self._pending_acks:
            target = max(self._collected_steps.values())
            if all(s >= target for s in self._collected_steps.values()):
                # Already synchronized (between-wave case)
                self._paused = True
            else:
                # Need to sync to target (mid-wave case)
                self._broadcast_run_until_step(target)
```

---


## Usage Patterns

### Pattern 1: Fast Async RL (Single-Engine)

```bash
POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}
POST /update_weights {...}
POST /resume
```

**Pause cost**: Complete current engine step, then pause
**Behavior**: Stale KV, client-transparent

---

### Pattern 2: Clean Async RL (Single-Engine)

```bash
POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}
POST /reset_prefix_cache?reset_running_requests=true
POST /update_weights {...}
POST /resume
```

**Pause cost**: Complete current engine step + prefill overhead on resume
**Behavior**: Clean prefill, client-transparent

---

### Pattern 3: Fast Async RL (DPEP)

```bash
# Controller sends to ANY rank
POST /pause {"mode": "keep"}  # Any rank accepts
POST /update_weights {...}    # Update all ranks
POST /resume                  # Any rank accepts
```

**Pause cost**:
- Between waves: Message round-trip only
- Mid-wave: Up to 31 engine steps
**Behavior**: Stale KV, client-transparent, coordinated across all DP ranks

---

### Pattern 4: Weight-Consistent (Single or DPEP)

```bash
POST /pause {"mode": "finish"}
POST /reset_prefix_cache
POST /update_weights {...}
POST /resume
```

**Pause cost**: Wait for all in-flight requests to complete naturally (unbounded)
**Behavior**: Each request uses single weight version

---

## Comparison Tables

### Mode Comparison

| Mode | Frontend Pause | Engine Busy Loop | Requests | Client Notified | Use Case |
|------|----------------|------------------|----------|-----------------|----------|
| `abort` | ✅ Yes | ❌ Keeps running | Aborted | ✅ Yes (abort) | Fast, client retries |
| `finish` | ✅ Yes | ❌ Keeps running | Complete normally | ✅ Yes (normal) | Weight-consistent |
| `keep` | ✅ Yes | ✅ **PAUSED** | Frozen in memory | ❌ No | Async RL, minimal latency |

---

## Key Design Principles

1. **Separation of concerns**: Pause/resume is orthogonal to cache management

2. **Client transparency for RL**: `keep` mode enables zero-downtime updates without client changes

3. **Acknowledgment for safety**: Pause waits for engine acknowledgment before returning (prevents race conditions)

4. **Reuse existing primitives**:
   - DPEP uses 32-step sync points (already exists)
   - Cache management uses preemption (`_preempt_request()`)
   - No new coordination mechanisms

5. **Idempotency**: Multiple pause/resume calls are safe

6. **Any-rank entry in DPEP**: No single point of failure

7. **Simplified synchronization in DPEP**: Only one all-reduce (on `engines_running`), not on pause_mode


### Feedback Period.

1-2 weeks

title: [RFC]: Support function calling using `structural_tag`.
author: chaunceyjiang
body:
### Motivation.


1. When using vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API, if `tool_choice="required"` is set to force the model to call a tool, the model’s output behavior does not match expectations.
   **Specific concern:** When `tool_choice="required"` is enabled, vLLM converts the tool schema into a JSON Schema and constrains the model output via `structured_outputs`. Since the schema is defined as `{"type": "array", ...}`, does this mean the model’s first token is forcibly constrained to be `"["`? , this would skip the model’s native `tool_calls_start_token` (e.g. `<|tool_calls_section_begin|>`), completely bypassing the model’s native tool-calling format and its thinking output.

2. **Tool parsing logic:** The current function-calling parsing logic looks quite hacky and fragmented. Most of the logic relies on regular expressions to extract the tool-calling portion, and then uses JSON parsing to extract the tool name and arguments. In practice, the tool-calling output produced by the model does not always strictly conform to the expected JSON format, which can lead to parsing failures or incorrect results. Therefore, introducing a `structural_tag` mechanism would allow more reliable marking of the start and end of tool calls, making the parsing process more robust and accurate.


### Proposed Change.

xgrammar has recently introduced a series of new structural tags.  
We can use a trigger mechanism: detect the start tag of a tool call; once detected, immediately initiate guided generation until the closing tag is encountered.  
This approach also supports multiple types of tool_call formats.

-----

Llama JSON-based tool calling, Gemma:
```
{"name": "function_name", "parameters": params}
```
Corresponding structural tag:
```
{
    "type": "structural_tag",
    "format": {
        "type": "triggered_tags",
        "triggers": ["{\"name\":"],
        "tags": [
            {
                "begin": "{\"name\": \"func1\", \"parameters\": ",
                "content": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": ...},
                "end": "}"
            },
            {
                "begin": "{\"name\": \"func2\", \"parameters\": ",
                "content": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": ...},
                "end": "}"
            },
        ],
    },
}
```
Qwen 2.5/3, Hermes:
```
<tool_call>
{"name": "get_current_temperature", "arguments": {"location": "San Francisco, CA, USA"}}
</tool_call>
```
Corresponding structural tag:

```
{
    "type": "structural_tag",
    "format": {
        "type": "triggered_tags",
        "triggers": ["<tool_call>"],
        "tags": [
            {
                "begin": "<tool_call>\n{\"name\": \"func1\", \"arguments\": ",
                "content": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": ...},
                "end": "}\n</tool_call>",
            },
            {
                "begin": "<tool_call>\n{\"name\": \"func2\", \"arguments\": ",
                "content": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": ...},
                "end": "}\n</tool_call>",
            },
        ],
    },
}
```
DeepSeek:

There is a special tag `<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜> ... <｜tool▁calls▁end｜> `quotes the whole tool calling part.
```
<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜><｜tool▁call▁begin｜>function<｜tool▁sep｜>function_name_1
```jsonc
{params}
```<｜tool▁call▁end｜>

```jsonc
{params}
```<｜tool▁call▁end｜><｜tool▁calls▁end｜>
```


Corresponding structural tag:
```
{
    "type": "structural_tag",
    "format": {
        "type": "triggered_tags",
        "triggers": ["<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜>"],
        "tags": [
            {
                "begin": "<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜>",
                "end": "<｜tool▁calls▁end｜>",
                "content": {
                    "type": "tags_with_separator",
                    "separator": "\n",
                    "tags": [
                        {
                            "begin": "<｜tool▁call▁begin｜>function<｜tool▁sep｜>function_name_1\n```jsonc\n",
                            "content": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": ...},
                            "end": "\n```<｜tool▁call▁end｜>",
                        },
                        {
                            "begin": "<｜tool▁call▁begin｜>function<｜tool▁sep｜>function_name_2\n```jsonc\n",
                            "content": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": ...},
                            "end": "\n```<｜tool▁call▁end｜>",
                        }
                    ]
                }
            }
        ],
        "stop_after_first": true,

    },
}

```
https://xgrammar.mlc.ai/docs/tutorials/structural_tag.html#examples




**Known issue:**
Currently, only **xgrammar** supports `structural_tag`. **outlines_core**, **lmformatenforcer**, and **llguidance** do not support it.

title: [RFC]: Change `kv_load_failure_policy` Default from "recompute" to "fail"
author: NickLucche
body:
### Motivation.

In disaggregated prefill setups, the `kv_load_failure_policy` controls how the system handles failures when the decode instance loads KV cache blocks from the prefill instance.

Currently, the default is `"recompute"`, which recomputes failed blocks on the decode instance. This may lead to a drop in performance:

1. **Wrong instance, wrong configuration**: Decode instances use low-latency optimizations (e.g., DeepGemm low-latency mode). Recomputing prefill work on decode instances with decode-optimized settings is inefficient and surfaces and amplifies some of the co-location limitations (see next point).

2. **Interference**: Prefill recomputation on decode instances increases tail latency for ongoing decode requests (https://hao-ai-lab.github.io/blogs/distserve-retro/). This will result in higher variance/jitter in tracked metrics such as ITL.

Changing the default to `"fail"` will:
- Prevent performance jitter by avoiding recomputation on decode instances. 
- Surface infrastructure issues immediately via request failures.
- Improve observability leading to a more stable "observation dashboard", making it easier to spot changes in traffic (arguably main drive).


### Proposed Change.

Change the default value of `kv_load_failure_policy` in `vllm/config/kv_transfer.py:67` from:

```python
kv_load_failure_policy: Literal["recompute", "fail"] = "recompute"->"fail"
```


### Behavior Changes

**Current behavior (default="recompute"):**
- When the decode instance fails to load KV cache blocks from the prefill instance, affected requests are rescheduled
- Failed blocks are recomputed on the decode instance

**Proposed behavior (default="fail"):**
- When the decode instance fails to load KV cache blocks, affected requests immediately fail with `FINISHED_ERROR` status
- The error is propagated to the client through the API response with finish_reason indicating the failure


### Migration Path

Users who want to preserve the current behavior can explicitly set the policy:

```bash
# For Python API
engine = LLMEngine(
    kv_transfer_config={"kv_load_failure_policy": "recompute"}
)

# For CLI (decode instance)
--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector": "P2pNcclConnector", "kv_role": "kv_consumer", "kv_load_failure_policy": "recompute", ...}'
```

title: [RFC]: Consolidate Multimodal Related Info
author: charlotte12l
body:
### Background + Motivation
We are introducing `model_arch_config`  https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/28454, which defines explicitly what kind of information vLLM engine need from hugggingface config/ user-defined config, so we could avoid `hf_config`/`getattr(hf_config, xxx)` got passing around in engine.  


### Previous Discussion
For whether `model_arch_config` should contains multimodal related info,  https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/24384#issuecomment-3489703720 suggested that we should put `supports_multimodal` into `model_arch_config` as it's something purely from model architecture, which we hope to get from standardized hugggingface config or user-defined config.
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/28454#issuecomment-3638695628 also suggested to bring more folks related to MM for discussion.


The original plan would be:
- delete `supports_multimodal` in model_info
- in `model_arch_config_convertor`, call registry to check if a model is multimodal. See discussion in  https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/28454#issuecomment-3638695628 
- call `model_arch_config.is_multimodal_model` to know if a model is multimodal 

###  Current Questions
One tricky case is that `ModelConfig` also has `supports_multimodal_raw_input_only`, but this looks to be something not purely from model architecture/config? Not sure if we should move it as well, or we still keep all multimodal related info in `_model_info`.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/0a7dd23754ed5e01303e0eb4e64ace5e70251f46/vllm/config/model.py#L1407

Create this RFC for discussion. 

### Proposed Change.
Original idea:
- delete `supports_multimodal`, `supports_multimodal_raw_input_only` in model_info
- in `model_arch_config_convertor`, call registry to check if a model is multimodal, and if `supports_multimodal_raw_input_only` 
- vLLM only uses `model_arch_config.is_multimodal_model`, `model_arch_config.supports_multimodal_raw_input_only`

 https://github.com/charlotte12l/vllm/pull/7 is a initial draft
