- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Tensor descriptor (TD) adoption strategy for vLLM Triton kernels
author: afierka-intel
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM's Triton kernels load data and store results via raw pointer arithmetic (`tl.load(ptr + offset, mask=…)`). Triton's newer structured memory-access API — `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` (TD) — is the replacement API upstream Triton is steering toward (`tl.make_block_ptr` is officially deprecated) and the path to architecture-accelerated memory on modern hardware: TMA on NVIDIA Hopper, 2D block loads on Intel Xe. Adopting TD in vLLM kernels unlocks significant E2E speedups where backend lowering is mature (Intel Battlemage: +38–83%), creates headroom where lowering is still catching up (NVIDIA Blackwell today), and positions the code base ahead of the deprecation rather than behind it.

This RFC proposes a **strategy for adopting TD across vLLM's Triton kernels**: opt-in TD paths behind a single env var (`VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD`) with per-kernel constexpr gating, a platform-aware default, and graduation criteria that gate every future conversion and every default-on flip. The strategy has been applied to `triton_unified_attention.py` (the unified attention kernels used by the `TRITON_ATTN` backend) in PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327) as the pilot that validates the approach; follow-up PRs extend TD to the remaining XPU-invocable Triton kernels under the same framework, each justified by per-kernel benchmarks meeting the graduation criteria below.

#### Triton surface area in vLLM

vLLM has **245 `@triton.jit` functions** in mainline today. The subset that is **invocable on Intel XPU** — either as default path or via documented opt-in env vars / backend selectors — is our primary scope:

| Category | Count | Invocation path (XPU) |
|---|---|---|
| **Unified attention (pilot)** | 3 | `--attention-backend=TRITON_ATTN` — PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327) |
| **Other attention ops on the TRITON_ATTN path** | ~20 | `TRITON_ATTN` backend: `triton_decode_attention`, `triton_prefill_attention`, `chunked_prefill_paged_decode`, `triton_reshape_and_cache_flash`, `prefix_prefill`, `common.py` token merge, `turboquant_*`, `dcp_alltoall` |
| **MLA Triton kernels** | ~9 | `--attention-backend=TRITON_MLA` (auto-selected for MLA models), plus `xpu_mla_sparse` |
| **LoRA Triton path** | ~16 | `XPU_USE_TRITON_KERNEL=1` env var — routes `PunicaWrapperXPU` through Triton kernels instead of SYCL |
| *(Helpers / pure-compute in same files)* | ~15 | N/A — no memory I/O to wrap with TD |
| **XPU-invocable subtotal** | **~50** | This is the RFC's XPU scope |
| Not currently XPU-invocable (CUDA/ROCm-only today) | ~160 | fused_moe, quantization, sample/spec_decode, mamba, FLA, rotary, deepseek_v4_ops — XPU delegates to SYCL (`vllm-xpu-kernels`) or has no Triton path. Covered by this strategy *if* the ecosystem later adds XPU paths. |
| *(Helpers / pure-compute, other)* | ~20 | Excluded from scope |
| **Total** | **245** | |

This RFC's strategy applies to all 245 kernels in principle, but the empirical evidence and near-term work focus on the ~50 XPU-invocable kernels where Intel has both the data and the motivation to drive conversion. NVIDIA / ROCm conversions of the remaining ~160 kernels are free to follow under the same framework and the same graduation criteria.

#### Why this matters now

1. **XPU enablement gap.** Current raw-pointer Triton attention kernels are functional on Intel XPU (Battlemage) but perform below hardware potential. Measured impact of TD on Battlemage: **+38% to +83% throughput** on Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across prefill-heavy and decode-heavy workloads.

2. **NVIDIA Hopper TMA path underutilized.** On Hopper (H100/H200), TD lowers to Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) instructions, unlocking hardware memory throughput otherwise inaccessible to raw-pointer kernels. We do not include Hopper benchmarks in this RFC; community runs are welcome.

3. **NVIDIA Blackwell: opt-in bridges the gap.** On B200, the TD path currently underperforms raw pointers (–33% to –60% E2E). We attribute this to implementation-level factors — per-tile descriptor reconstruction overhead, autotune configs not yet tuned for TMA — rather than a structural property of the API. `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` carries strictly more information than raw pointers (explicit shape, strides, and block layout), so in principle the backend can always lower it to at least parity. The opt-in design lets Blackwell users take the fast path today and adopt TD later as these optimizations land, without a second kernel migration.

   The asymmetry between the Battlemage speedup and the B200 regression is consistent with the fraction of forward-pass FLOPs each model spends in the attention block. Computed at a representative decoding shape (`seq_q=1, seq_kv=4096`) from public HF configs, the attention block (QKV + QK + AV + O) accounts for ~25% of forward FLOPs on Qwen3-4B, ~22% on Llama-3.1-8B, and ~14% on Qwen2-7B. On Battlemage, Xe 2D block loads make the TD path substantially faster in the attention kernel itself, and the E2E gain tracks this share (+83% / +55% / TD-neutral respectively). On B200, the current Triton→TMA lowering has not closed the gap to the highly tuned raw-pointer path, so the same attention-share multiplier works against the TD kernel rather than for it.

4. **Alignment with Triton's direction.** `tl.make_block_ptr` is officially deprecated in Triton: as of 2026-03-06, it emits a runtime deprecation warning explicitly directing users to `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` (or the `TensorDescriptor` class) as its replacement ([triton-lang/triton#9667](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/9667)). TD is the API Triton upstream is steering toward for lowering to accelerated memory paths — TMA on Hopper, 2D block loads on Xe. Adopting TD in attention kernels aligns with this direction and gives every backend a single API to optimize against, rather than requiring per-platform rewrites as block pointers phase out.

5. **Zero regression by design.** TD is off by default on all NVIDIA platforms. When disabled, the kernel compiles to the exact same code path — same autotuning, same performance, bit-exact output. Enabling TD is a single env-var flip (`VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD=1`) that users can benchmark on their own hardware before committing. This change adds capability; it removes nothing. The engineering cost of converting attention to TD is paid once — every backend benefits as its lowering improves, without a second kernel migration.

6. **Adjacency to [RFC #40458](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40458).** A parallel RFC (#40458) proposes converting simple element-wise kernels (SwiGLU, MRoPE, etc.) to **block pointers**, and asks maintainers: *"`tl.make_block_ptr` vs `tl.make_tensor_descriptor`?"* Given the deprecation of `tl.make_block_ptr` (see point 4) and the fact that on tiled-memory and TMA-capable architectures (Intel XPU, NVIDIA Hopper) TD is the API steering toward the accelerated memory paths while block pointers are not, this RFC complements #40458 by empirically answering that question for attention kernels: **block_ptr and TD are both useful for different kernel classes; for heavy kernels on tiled-memory and TMA-capable HW, TD is the path forward**.

### Proposed Change.

#### Pilot kernel (PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327))

The pilot that validates the strategy is `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_unified_attention.py`. PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327) refactored the file so that the previously separate 2D and 3D attention kernels are now a single unified kernel with two opt-in TD gates; the refactor also added four TD-path `@triton.jit` helpers:

| `@triton.jit` function | Role | TD path status |
|---|---|---|
| `kernel_unified_attention` | Main kernel — prefill / decode / segmented decode in one entry | **Opt-in TD available** (`USE_TD` for K/V cache tile loads, `USE_TD_QO` for Q load + output store). |
| `reduce_segments` | Post-processing kernel (online softmax reduction of per-segment outputs) | Not yet wrapped; access is already contiguous, trivial candidate for follow-up. |
| `_cast_kv_tile` | Helper — cast/dequant K/V tile data | N/A (operates on in-register tile data post-load). |
| `_load_q_td`, `_load_kv_tile_td`, `_store_output_td` | TD-path loaders/storer helpers | **Part of the TD path**; active only when `USE_TD` / `USE_TD_QO` are set. Dead-code-eliminated at compile time otherwise. |

Plus Python helpers (`_is_gemma3_attention`, `_get_tile_size`, entry point `unified_attention`) that are not `@triton.jit` and are not impacted by this RFC.

#### Mechanism

Two independent opt-in constexpr flags at the kernel level:

- **`USE_TD`** (bool, default `False`): TD path for K/V cache tile loads inside the per-tile loop.
- **`USE_TD_QO`** (bool, default `False`): TD path for Q load at kernel entry and output store at kernel exit.

A Python-side env var controls the TD path with **tri-state semantics**:
- unset (default): **auto** — TD on for Intel XPU (where Battlemage evidence shows consistent net-positive impact), off elsewhere;
- `1`: force TD on regardless of platform (used by NVIDIA users who want to evaluate TD on their own HW — Hopper users are the most likely candidates);
- `0`: force TD off regardless of platform (useful for A/B testing and for platforms where TD may be selected by default in the future but the user wants to stay on raw pointers).

The tri-state makes platform-aware defaults the norm without removing user control.

PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327) shipped this as `VLLM_TRITON_ATTN_USE_TD` — specific to the attention pilot. As the strategy extends to other Triton kernels under the same opt-in pattern, we propose **renaming the env var to `VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD`** in a follow-up PR so that a single flag gates the TD path across all kernels (consistent with the single-flag, no-subsystem-subflags design below). The tri-state semantics stay unchanged.

No subsystem subflags. A single flag is enough for the strategy's scope and keeps the interface simple. If finer granularity is ever needed, it can be introduced as a follow-up without breaking this interface.

#### TD path for K/V cache — how paged KV is handled

vLLM's paged KV cache introduces a 2-level indirection: `seq_offset // BLOCK_SIZE → block_table[…] → physical_block_idx → cache_offset`. `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` requires its base pointer (and strides) to be known at descriptor construction time, which conflicts with per-tile dynamic lookups.

The proposed approach is a **hybrid**:

1. Perform block-table lookup with raw pointer (unchanged).
2. Extract scalar `physical_block_scalar = tl.min(physical_block_idx, axis=0)`; this is valid because **all tiles within one block share the same physical block index** when `BLOCK_SIZE % TILE_SIZE == 0`.
3. Construct TD per tile iteration with base `= cache_ptr + physical_block_scalar * stride_cache_0 + kv_head_idx * stride_cache_2`, then load via `desc.load([offset_in_block, 0])`.

#### Required preconditions

The TD path requires:
- `BLOCK_SIZE % TILE_SIZE == 0` (enforced via `tl.static_assert` in the kernel);
- Triton ≥ 3.4.0 (first release shipping the non-experimental `tl.make_tensor_descriptor`; the experimental predecessor in 3.3.x is not sufficient). For XPU, `triton-xpu` ≥ 3.6.0 includes this API.
- Tile caller must clamp `TILE_SIZE` to `BLOCK_SIZE` when `USE_TD=True`.

When these do not hold, the non-TD path (raw pointer + mask) is selected — **no functional regression**.

#### Code layout

TD path is structured as three `@triton.jit` helpers called from `kernel_unified_attention` when the corresponding constexpr flag is set:
- `_load_q_td` — Q load at kernel entry (used when `USE_TD_QO=True`),
- `_load_kv_tile_td` — K/V cache tile load inside the per-tile loop (used when `USE_TD=True`),
- `_store_output_td` — output store at kernel exit (used when `USE_TD_QO=True`).

The raw-pointer path remains inline in `kernel_unified_attention` under the `else` branches of the same constexpr ifs.

Both paths co-exist in the source, but only one is compiled per kernel specialization. `USE_TD` is a `tl.constexpr` parameter, so Triton specializes the kernel per unique value. When `USE_TD=False`, the TD branch is never visited during AST-to-TTIR translation (see [`python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py`](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/main/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py), `visit_If`: after `_unwrap_if_constexpr`, only the active branch is emitted) — the inactive code path is absent from the generated Triton IR and therefore from all downstream artifacts (LLVM IR, PTX, SPIR-V). The compiled binary contains no runtime branch and no instructions for the disabled path. This is a property of Triton's specialization mechanism, applied uniformly across all backends. Long-term, as TD becomes the default across platforms, the raw-pointer path can be removed, simplifying the kernel back to a single code path.

#### Planned kernel conversions beyond the pilot

The strategy proposed here applies uniformly to further kernels; each conversion lands as its own PR, using the same `VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD` env var, the same constexpr-gating pattern, and the graduation criteria below. Near-term targets (all XPU-invocable under the paths in the table above):

1. **Rest of the `TRITON_ATTN` path** in `v1/attention/ops/` — `triton_decode_attention` (4), `triton_prefill_attention` (1), `chunked_prefill_paged_decode` (2), `triton_reshape_and_cache_flash` (3), `prefix_prefill` (2), `common.py` token-merge (~3), `turboquant_*` (5), `dcp_alltoall` (2). ~22 memory-I/O kernels total.
2. **MLA Triton kernels** (`triton_mla.py`, `xpu_mla_sparse.py`) — ~9 kernels, invocable on XPU via `--attention-backend=TRITON_MLA` or the XPU-specific MLA sparse backend.
3. **LoRA Triton kernels** in `lora/ops/triton_ops/` — ~16 kernels, invocable on XPU via `XPU_USE_TRITON_KERNEL=1`.

Non-XPU-invocable kernels (MoE, sampling, spec_decode, mamba, FLA, standard quantization, rotary, DeepSeek V4 ops — ~160 total) are covered by this strategy in principle but are currently routed away from Triton on XPU (delegated to `vllm-xpu-kernels` SYCL ops or simply not supported). Their conversion is open to CUDA / ROCm maintainers under the same framework if and when it makes sense for their platforms.

*Explicit non-goal:* blanket, unconditional conversion of all Triton kernels. The evidence (B200 regression) does not support in-place replacement. Every PR that lands a TD path must be backed by per-kernel, per-backend benchmarks meeting the graduation criteria, and every default-on flip (per platform) requires the same evidence.

#### Validation approach

1. **Numerical equivalence.** Per-kernel tests (`tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_unified_attention.py`) comparing TD and non-TD paths across shapes, dtypes (fp16, bf16), and GQA ratios. Implemented in PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327).
2. **End-to-end throughput.** `vllm bench throughput` on a representative model set spanning standard attention (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B) and non-power-of-2 GQA (Qwen2-7B) × three workloads (ShareGPT, random-prefill, random-decode). Standard `vllm bench throughput` CLI, no custom harness.

#### Evidence: cross-platform impact

TD is not a single-platform feature — its value depends on how each backend lowers it today and where it is headed. We organize results by impact category.

##### 1. Hardware where TD helps today

**Intel Battlemage**, `TRITON_ATTN` backend, `VLLM_TRITON_ATTN_USE_TD=1`.

Throughput median (req/s, 3 runs) vs `TRITON_ATTN` baseline (TD=0):

| Model | Architecture | GQA | random-decode | random-prefill | sharegpt |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 | standard attn | 4:1 | 3.51 → **6.41** (+83%) | 3.50 → **6.41** (+83%) | 5.02 → **8.52** (+70% R1; +38–39% R2/R3 medians) |
| Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | standard attn | 4:1 | 2.83 → **4.38** (+55%) | 2.83 → **4.37** (+55%) | 5.42 → **7.48** (+38%) |

Measured by the Intel XPU team across Battlemage SKUs (B60 and B70). Numbers are expressed as relative deltas; the trend across SKUs is consistent.

Default (flash-attn) backend varies ±1.6% across same runs — TD effect is isolated to the Triton backend.

##### 2. Hardware where TD is safe and neutral

**Qwen2-7B (GQA 7:1) on Intel Battlemage** — TD=0 and TD=1 produce identical throughput (2.28 req/s on random-decode, 4.29 → 5.32 on sharegpt within noise). Confirms TD introduces no regression on non-power-of-2 GQA configurations. The `TRITON_ATTN` vs. default gap on this model is shared by both paths — an autotuning limitation of `TRITON_ATTN` for the 7:1 shape, not a TD issue.

##### 3. Hardware with headroom for future gains

**B200 (NVIDIA Blackwell)** — TD currently underperforms raw pointers (–33% to –60% across Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2-7B). This reflects implementation-level factors — per-tile descriptor reconstruction, autotune configs not yet tuned for TMA — rather than a structural property of the API. TD is off by default on NVIDIA; Blackwell users pay no cost. As these optimizations land in the Triton backend or kernel-side tuning, Blackwell users can opt in without a kernel migration.

**NVIDIA Hopper (H100/H200).** We expect TD to lower to TMA on Hopper, which is the accelerated memory path there. We do not include Hopper benchmarks in this RFC — community runs are welcome and would help map the strategy to Hopper, but they are not required for the decision proposed here: the opt-in design means Hopper users pay no cost until they choose to enable the TD path and validate on their own setup.

#### Graduation criteria for default-on adoption

TD remains opt-in per platform until all three criteria are met on that platform's representative hardware:

1. **Numerical equivalence.** Per-kernel tests pass on TD vs raw-pointer paths across shapes, dtypes, and GQA ratios.
2. **Performance parity or better.** E2E throughput at parity or above the raw-pointer path on ≥3 models spanning different attention configurations (e.g., standard attention, GQA, non-power-of-2 GQA).
3. **Compilation cost.** No autotune-time regression exceeding 2× the raw-pointer baseline.

When a platform meets these criteria for the pilot kernel, a follow-up PR flips its default in `VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD`. Intel Battlemage meets all three today. The same framework applies to every subsequent kernel conversion and every subsequent default-on flip — this is the single bar under which TD spreads across vLLM Triton kernels. Intel holds itself to the same bar, and NVIDIA graduation is expected as Triton-backend optimizations land — a *when*, not an *if*.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@ProExpertProg, @LucasWilkinson, @tdoublep, @bringlein, @jikunshang and @xuechendi

### Any Other Things.

#### Open questions for maintainers

1. **Acceptance of per-backend opt-in strategy.** Is a constexpr-gated dual-path (TD + raw) acceptable as the long-term design, or should vLLM prefer a single-path-with-runtime-switch approach?
2. **Env var design.** We propose a single `VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD` switch with tri-state semantics (unset = auto; `1` = force on; `0` = force off), platform-aware auto-default (on for Intel XPU, off elsewhere), and no subsystem subflags. The pilot landed in PR [#40327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40327) as the more specific `VLLM_TRITON_ATTN_USE_TD`; we would rename it to the general form in a follow-up PR once the strategy is accepted. Does this design and rename plan work for maintainers?
3. **Benchmark gate for future kernel conversions.** What should be the minimum evidence bar for each additional TD conversion? (proposed: numerical equivalence + per-kernel microbench + E2E throughput on ≥1 NVIDIA + ≥1 non-NVIDIA backend.)
4. **Triton version floor.** Are we comfortable depending on Triton ≥ 3.4.0 (first stable `tl.make_tensor_descriptor`) / `triton-xpu` ≥ 3.6.0 for the TD code path? Users on older Triton continue to use the raw-pointer default and see no change.
5. **Relation to [#40458](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40458) scope.** Should #40458 (block_ptr for simple kernels) and this RFC proceed in parallel, or should one be gated on the other's merge?

title: [RFC]: Per-Layer Parallelism Policy
author: sungsooha
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## 1. Motivation

PR #36287 introduced TPA (tensor-parallel-size-attention) to vLLM, and review feedback from Lucas Wilkinson — *"the design shouldn't be attention-specific"* — pointed to a more general need: a per-layer parallelism policy that lets layers declare what they are and have the framework resolve their plan.

## 2. The idea

A single function, owned by the framework, that turns a layer's identity into its parallelism plan:

```
                                ┌─────────────────────────────┐
   (layer instance, prefix) ──▶ │  framework-owned resolver   │──▶  plan
                                │  (consults config + layer)  │
                                └─────────────────────────────┘
```

Layers consult the resolver in `__init__` instead of reading global TP accessors. A *plan* is whatever the layer needs to make local decisions — its TP width, its rank within that group, its communication backend, etc. The plan schema is open-ended; the call shape stays the same as new fields are added.

The plan being a function of the layer is what makes the design non-attention-specific. The resolver doesn't know it's an attention layer — it knows it's *this* layer at *this* prefix and consults config to decide. New strategies (Q-replication, hybrid attention, MTP, future ideas) become resolver-and-config changes, not N-model changes.

## 3. How the policy expresses different models

The mechanism in §2 is one resolver and one plan dataclass. The breadth comes from what the policy declares for which layers. To make the schema concrete, here are illustrative configurations for different model architectures. The exact field names are not part of this RFC's ask — the question is whether the *shape* (named axes, rules with matchers, per-layer-kind plans) covers the architectural patterns we want to support.

### 3.1 Llama family — uniform GQA

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  axes:
    tp: 16
    attn_tp: 4      # TPA: attention layers narrower than full TP
    dcp: 4          # required by TPA invariant: dcp = tp / attn_tp
  rules:
    - match: { kind: attention }
      plan: { tp_size: attn_tp, dcp_size: dcp }
    - match: { kind: mlp }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }
```

One attention rule, one MLP rule. Every block matches the same two rules. Every derivative (Mistral, Phi3, NemotronNAS, TeleChat2, GLM) reuses this verbatim.

### 3.2 Nemotron-H, Jamba — hybrid attention + SSM

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  axes:
    tp: 16
    attn_tp: 4
    dcp: 4
  rules:
    - match: { kind: attention }
      plan: { tp_size: attn_tp, dcp_size: dcp }
    - match: { kind: mamba }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }     # SSM has no attention heads to TPA-shard
    - match: { kind: mlp }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }
```

The resolver dispatches by layer kind, which HF config already declares via `hybrid_override_pattern`. No new metadata source needed — the heterogeneity signal already exists in the model config.

### 3.3 DSV4 — MLA + MoE + sparse indexer

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  axes:
    tp: 16
    attn_tp: 1      # MLA has 1 effective KV head → TPA collapses to DCP-only
    dcp: 16
    ep: 8           # expert parallel for MoE layers
  rules:
    - match: { kind: attention, attention_flavor: mla }
      plan: { tp_size: tp, dcp_size: dcp }
    - match: { kind: indexer }
      plan: { tp_size: 1 }                  # replicate across TP
    - match: { kind: moe }
      plan: { tp_size: tp, ep_size: ep }
    - match: { kind: mlp }
      plan: { tp_size: tp }
```

Three distinct layer-kind rules within one model. MLA attention, sparse indexer, and MoE experts each get a different plan; all expressed through the same schema.

### 3.4 MTP heads — speculative decoding

```yaml
parallelism_rules:
  rules:
    - match: { prefix_pattern: "mtp_*" }
      plan: { tp_size: 1 }      # replicate each MTP head
```

The matcher can target by `prefix` when the architecture attaches sub-modules. The rule applies regardless of the main model's parallelism choices, because the resolver dispatches on `(layer, prefix)` independently for each layer.

## 4. Backward compatibility

Three properties of the design enforce backward compatibility by construction:

- **Sentinel-fallback at every consult site.** The resolver returns a "no policy active" plan by default. Layers fall back to today's global TP accessors and behave bit-identically. Adding the resolver call to a parallel layer is safe in isolation.
- **Whitelist gate per architecture.** A model opts into per-layer policy only when its migration is verified. Non-whitelisted models keep their current global-TP wiring; per-layer CLI flags are rejected at config-validation time with a clear error.
- **Per-strategy delivery.** Each new strategy lands resolver-native for the model families it targets, independently. Existing global parallelism (TP, PP, EP, DCP) stays where it is; existing globals become the resolver's fallbacks for those fields if and when a per-layer override is genuinely needed.

A user who upgrades vLLM and changes no CLI flags sees no behavior change. A user who opts into a per-layer flag on a whitelisted model gets the new behavior. There is no third state.

## 5. Roadmap

What we commit to deliver, with TPA-GQA as the concrete reference:

- **TPA + FlashAttention + Llama family** *(rebased [PR #36287])*. Resolver scaffold, `QKVParallelLinear` consult site, `--tensor-parallel-size-attention` flag, Llama-family migration, FA backend integration, whitelist gate. Enables TPA-GQA on Llama family and its derivatives (Mistral, Phi3, NemotronNAS, TeleChat2, GLM). GSM8K parity vs pure-TP baseline validates both the per-rank semantics and the backward-compat property.
- **TPA + FlashInfer + Llama family**. Backend-specific DCP-wrapper audit. The FA path already validates the policy mechanism; this enables the FlashInfer backend for already-whitelisted models.
- **DSV4 with Q-rep (MLA family)**. Q-rep ships as the second concrete policy feature; MLA models (DSV3, DSV4 and inheritors like GLM4-MoE-Lite, MistralLarge3) join the whitelist. Demonstrates the resolver carrying a non-TPA plan field.
- **Nemotron Super (hybrid attention + SSM)**. Per-layer-kind policy via HF `hybrid_override_pattern`. Demonstrates the resolver dispatching on layer kind (attention vs SSM), the central case from the §3.2 example.

Additional model families are not in our immediate priority but we're happy to extend coverage later, including through community contributions, since adding a new architecture is a small declaration in the schema rather than a deep change.

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Derender Endpoints to Provide Detokenization for Disaggregated Serving
author: hickeyma
body:
### Motivation.

The `/render` endpoints (`POST /v1/chat/completions/render` and `POST /v1/completions/render`) landed in PR #36166 as the preprocessing leg of disaggregated serving. They accept a standard OpenAI request and return a`GenerateRequest` that the GPU inference tier can consume directly without a tokenizer.
unif
After generation, the inference server (`/inference/v1/generate`) returns a `GenerateResponse` containing raw output token IDs, along with logprob entries encoded as `"token_id:N"` placeholder strings because the generate server has no tokenizer. To turn that into a client-facing OpenAI response, we need to:

1. Detokenize the output token IDs back into text
2. Resolve `"token_id:N"` logprob placeholders into real token strings
3. Populate the `bytes` field in logprob entries (required by the OpenAI spec, cannot be filled by the tokenizer-free generate server)
4. Format the result as a `ChatCompletionResponse` or `CompletionResponse`

Currently this postprocessing is coupled to `OpenAIServingChat` /`OpenAIServingCompletion` inside the GPU server. Operators running llm-d, Dynamo or any other disaggregated setup are forced to either run the full vLLM stack on the CPU tier or implement postprocessing themselves.

This RFC proposes exposing the detokenization as `/derender` endpoints on the existing render server which is the direct inverse of `/render`. 

Detokenization is defined as a post processing step of `GPU-less deployment of frontend` in RFC #34407:

> "Allow preprocessing (tokenization, MM input processing) and **postprocessing (detokenization, tool call parsing, reasoning parsing)** to
> run without GPU."

This RFC in addition adopts that full definition as its goal: `/derender` is the inverse of `/render`. A true inverse must emit `reasoning_content` and `tool_calls`, not just `content` (ref: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-4592871058 and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-4621521435). Reasoning and tool call parsing are therefore **in-scope goals of this RFC** built on ~the unified `Parser` from RFC #32713 (its `extract_response_outputs(model_output, model_output_token_ids, request, ...)`~ (`Parser.parse()` for batch and `Parser.parse_delta()` for streaming, the same calls `/v1/chat/completion`s makes, so derender and chat serving parse the same way) is the single source of truth for decode side parsing). This functionality is for disaggregated / RL consumers who need `derender(tokens) -> content` today.

The work is phased as follows:
- **Detokenization** endpoint lands first. The protocol is made parsing ready now so the follow up requires no breaking API change. (#43606)
- **Reasoning/tool call parsing** (non-streaming), built on the unified `Parser`. ~#45045~ Superseded by and landed in **#45919**.
- **Streaming derender + streaming parsing** is specified in the companion RFC #47161. Detokenization landed in #47301 and reasoning/tool parsing in #50550.

Partial #34407 and #22817.

### Proposed Change.

Implementation in:

- #43606 (detokenization)
- ~#45045~ Superseded by #45919 (reasoning/tool parsing)
- #48617 (round trip parity test + docs)
- #49396 (CPU work on the renderer executor)
- Streaming: #47301, #50550 (see #47161)
- #59324, #61852, #62719 (parity fixes)
- #60082 (generate \`output_mode="derender"\`, see #56851)
- #63148 (shared non-streaming chat message assembly, closing #57593)

#### New Endpoints

| Method | Path | Input | Output |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| `POST` | `/v1/chat/completions/derender` | `DerenderChatRequest` | `ChatCompletionResponse` |
| `POST` | `/v1/completions/derender` | `DerenderCompletionRequest` | `CompletionResponse` |

Both endpoints:
- Run on the existing render server (`vllm launch render` PR #36166). No new process or server binary is needed
- Are GPU-free, only the `Renderer` (tokenizer) is required
- Are synchronous, stateless and idempotent. The caller already holds the complete `GenerateResponse` and therefore nothing to stream

#### Protocol Additions

Two new request types in `vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/protocol.py`:

```python
class DerenderChatRequest(BaseModel):
  stream: Literal[False] = False
  model: str | None = None
  generate_response: GenerateResponse  # output_mode="tokens" only (#58588)
  prompt_tokens: int | None = None
  prompt_token_ids: list[int] | None = None
  # GenerateRequest.token_ids from /render (a suffix is enough). Seeds
  # decoding so the first output token keeps its leading space (#59046).
  chat_request: ChatCompletionRequest | None = None
  # The request the client sent to /render, before adjust_request ran.
  # Carries the fields the chat parsers read (tools, tool_choice,
  # include_reasoning, chat_template_kwargs and model-specific fields).
  # Required when a reasoning or tool parser is configured (400 otherwise).
```

```python
class DerenderCompletionRequest(BaseModel):
    stream: Literal[False] = False
    model: str | None = None
    generate_responses: list[GenerateResponse]
    prompt_tokens: list[int] | None = None
    prompt_token_ids: list[list[int] | None] | None = None
     # GenerateRequest.token_ids from /render (a suffix is enough). Seeds
    # decoding so the first output token keeps its leading space (#59046).
    completion_request: CompletionRequest | None = None
    # Original request context. Used for skip_special_tokens. Completions
    # don't run reasoning/tool parsing.
```

`prompt_tokens` is caller-supplied because `GenerateResponse` does not carry the prompt token count (only output tokens per choice are stored). The caller already holds `GenerateRequest.token_ids` from the render step, so passing `len(token_ids)` costs nothing. This avoids a protocol change to `GenerateResponse`.

For completions, `generate_responses` is a list parallel to the `list[GenerateRequest]` returned by `/v1/completions/render`. If `prompt_tokens` is provided its length must equal `len(generate_responses)`. A mismatch will return `400 Bad Request`.

`chat_request` / `completion_request` are optional on the wire and the caller already holds them from the `/render` step, so passing them is free and requires no change to `GenerateResponse`. On a server with a reasoning or tool parser configured, chat derender returns `400` without `chat_request` rather than falling back to plain detokenization which would leak parser markup into `content` (#50550). `model` is optional (#51463). `chat_request` is the request as sent to `/render`. `/render` only returns the `GenerateRequest`, so derender never sees what `adjust_request` changed (see the `adjust_request` row below).

##### Example Requests

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions/derender \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
      "model": "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
      "generate_response": {
        "request_id": "chatcmpl-abc123",
        "choices": [
          {
            "index": 0,
            "token_ids": [9906, 29892, 1128, 508, 306, 1371, 366, 9826],
            "finish_reason": "stop"
          }
        ]
      },
      "prompt_tokens": 8
    }'
```

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/completions/derender \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
      "model": "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
      "generate_responses": [
        {
          "request_id": "cmpl-abc123",
          "choices": [
            {
              "index": 0,
              "token_ids": [9906, 29892, 1128, 508, 306, 1371, 366, 9826],
              "finish_reason": "stop"
            }
          ]
        }
      ],
      "prompt_tokens": [8]
    }'
```

#### Implementation Details

##### Chat: `ServingDerender.derender_chat_response` → `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat`

1. Validate model via `_check_model` and resource bounds (#47260)
2. If a reasoning or tool parser is configured and `chat_request` is missing, return `400`
3. For each choice: reject empty `token_ids` and resolve logprob placeholders
4. Decode incrementally, seeded from the prompt tail (`prompt_token_ids`), the same way the engine primes its detokenizer (#59046)
5. With a parser: decode with `skip_special_tokens=False`, build the parser with `chat_request.tools`, the resolved `chat_template_kwargs` and `model_config`, then run `Parser.parse()` over the text and `token_ids` to get `reasoning`, `content` and `tool_calls`. Without a parser: honour `chat_request.skip_special_tokens` and `spaces_between_special_tokens`
6. Build `ChatCompletionResponse` with `usage` from `prompt_tokens` and the output token counts. Pass `prompt_logprobs` and `kv_transfer_params` through unchanged

CPU work (detokenization, logprob resolution, parsing) runs on the renderer's executor (`renderer_num_workers`), off the event loop (#49396).

> [!NOTE]
> In a disaggregated setup the render tier must be launched with the same `--reasoning-parser` / `--tool-call-parser` / `--enable-auto-tool-choice` and chat template config as the would be chat tier or parity breaks regardless of protocol. This is a deployment/docs requirement and not a code one.

##### Completions: `ServingDerender.derender_completion_response` → `OnlineDerenderer.derender_completion`

Same pattern, iterating over `(generate_response, prompt_token_count)` pairs and emitting `CompletionResponseChoice` objects with an increasing `index` across all responses. Plain detokenization only.

#### Layout

```
vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/
  derender/api_router.py   ← POST /v1/chat/completions/derender
                              and POST /v1/completions/derender
  derender/serving.py      ← ServingDerender: validation, bounds, responses
  token_in_token_out/
    protocol.py            ← Derender*Request / Derender*StreamRequest types

vllm/renderers/
  online_derenderer.py     ← OnlineDerenderer: detokenization, logprob
                              resolution, parsing

tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/
  test_derender.py         ← batch
  test_derender_stream.py  ← streaming
  test_derender_parity.py  ← round trip parity

docs/serving/online_serving/derenderer.md
```

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@DarkLight1337 @noooop @hyeongyun0916 @vMaroon @sagearc @robertgshaw2-redhat @njhill

### Any Other Things.

#### Parsing: status and remaining work

The batch path is complete: detokenization (#43606), reasoning/tool parsing (#45919), parity CI and docs (#48617, #61852). Streaming is tracked in #47161 (#47301, #50550, #62706). All items are done.

| Item | Status |
|------|--------|
| **Streaming derender + streaming parsers** | Done in #47161 (#47301, #50550). Streaming parity CI and docs in #57922, logprobs in #55029. |
| **Thread `chat_template_kwargs` to parsers** | Done in #45919. Docs note ntoken_id:Needed: render tier template config must match the chat tier. |
| **Round trip parity CI** | Done. Batch in #48617. Since #61852 it feeds the engine's `finish_reason` and compares tool call ID format. Generate `output_mode="derender"` parity in #60082. |
| **Build on the unified `Parser`** | Done. `Parser.parse()` (batch) and `Parser.parse_delta()` (streaming) in `vllm/parser`. #32713 was closed as not planned. |
| **Mutated request state (`adjust_request`)** | Limitation recorded. `/derender` gets the request from before `adjust_request`, so decode flags and hy_v4's structural tag can differ ([audit](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-5996086149)). `derenderer.md` (#60082) points to generate `output_mode: "derender"`, which parses the engine's own text. The `reasoning_ended` gap (#60059) was fixed in #60062. |
| **Completion path parsing** | Decided: completions don't parse. `completion_request` is used for `skip_special_tokens` only. |
| **Unify (not mirror) the assembly path** | Done in #63148, closing #57593. `finish_reason` (#59324), tool call IDs (#61852), the parallel tool call filter (#60082) and the tool choice drop branches (Harmony `tool_choice="none"`, `tool_choice: null`) now share one helper. |
| **Stop strings** | Done in #62719 (stop strings and stop tokens), closing #57052. Bug B fixed in #57058. #59510 closed. |
| **Model default parsers on the render server** | Done in #54835. |

#### Out of scope for the Initial Implementation

| Feature | Notes |
|---------|-------|
| gRPC / msgpack transport | Orthogonal, following JSON/pydantic first per consensus in #22817. |
| Engine-parser U+FFFD leak fix | Streaming chat completion U+FFFD leak at the reasoning to content/tool transition (split/`DelegatingParser` mode) is a different code path from the derender-logprob FFFD fix. Root cause identified by @bbrowning and fixed in #46159. |
| Torch free / in-process parser library | RL trainers calling parsing in-process (GPU less, torch light) per #38925. Orthogonal to the endpoint. Tracked as related. |
| `token_id:N` logprob shape redesign | Integer `token_id`s in `GenerateResponse` (e.g. `GenerateLogProbs`) vs. the OpenAI string shape, raised by @sagearc. Done in #58181, closing #57574. |
| Streaming derender | Covered by the companion RFC #47161 (#47301, #50550). |

#### Resolved

- ~`chat_template_kwargs` threading~: done in #45919.
- ~Round trip parity CI~: done in #48617.
- ~Completions parsing~: completions don't parse.
- ~Unify vs. mirror~: unify. Done in #63148 (#57593)
- ~Mutated request state (\`adjust_request\`)~: recorded as a limitation in \`derenderer.md\` (#60082). Use generate \`output_mode: "derender"\` when it matters.
- ~Stop strings~: fixed in #62719.

#### Related

- #22817
- #34407
- #34551
- #35213
- #35684
- #36166
- #47161 (streaming derender)
- #50550
- #56851 (request level `output_mode` on generate)
- #56993 (scale-out components)
- #59324, #61852, #54835, #62719 (parity fixes, merged)
- #53418 (Rust derender parsing)
-  #60059 (reasoning_endedon generate, found in theadjust_request audit, fixed in #60062)
- #59046 (seed derender decode from the prompt)
- #57593 (shared assembly, closed by #63148)

title: [RFC]: Changes in vLLM Model Development
author: WoosukKwon
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM has long pursued the goal of building a unified, fast inference engine across diverse models and hardware. We remain committed to this goal, but we have come to believe that vLLM's current model implementation principles need to be revisited in order to improve both performance and development velocity. Two lessons stand out:

* We were overly reluctant to modify model code directly for op fusion and kernel dispatching. Instead, we accumulated abstractions and compiler passes that ultimately made the code opaque and hard to optimize.  
* We pursued the unrealistic ideal of a single model definition that works well on every hardware. In practice, each hardware backend benefits from its own model implementation, since different hardware favors different fusion strategies.  
* AI coding agents have made manual op fusion and kernel writing much easier, and the agents work best with raw model code.

To address these issues, we are making three fundamental changes to how vLLM implements and optimizes models:

1. Removing full-graph `torch.compile` requirement  
2. Separation of model code across hardware backends  
3. A clear model interface

## **1\. Removing full-graph `torch.compile` requirement**

vLLM enables full-graph `torch.compile` by default and has relied on it for model-specific optimizations. Two problems have emerged:

* **Performance.** Achieving speed-of-light performance on target models on the latest hardware within a tight timeline requires manual optimization. Compiler-driven optimization alone has not been sufficient, and timely performance gains are critical to vLLM's adoption.  
* **Developer experience.** `torch.compile` increases the vLLM startup time and imposes the opacity and constraints inherent to any compiler, both of which slow iteration on model code.

We are therefore **removing vLLM's reliance on full-graph `torch.compile`** and restructuring model definitions accordingly. The migration must **preserve the current user-facing UX and introduce no performance regressions**.

NOTE: we will keep using `torch.compile` to fuse adjacent ops locally, whenever we find it to be beneficial. The removal is only about full-graph compilation.

### **1-1. Compiler fusion → manual fusion**

Historically, vLLM kept model code minimal (pure PyTorch ops) and relied on compiler passes to fuse them. We are reversing this convention: fusion should be expressed directly in model code. Concretely, model code should look like:

```py
class Attention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ...):
        ...
        self.o_proj = RowParallelLinear(..., reduce_results=False)

    def forward(self, ...):
        ...
        hidden_states = self.o_proj(attn_out)  # pre-allreduce
        return hidden_states


class Layer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ...):
        self.attn = Attention(...)
        self.rms_norm = RMSNorm(...)
        self.mlp = MLP(...)

    def forward(self, hidden_states):
        ...
        hidden_states = self.attn(hidden_states)  # pre-allreduce
        # Call the fused kernel here.
        residual, quantized_inputs = add_rms_norm_quant(
            hidden_states,
            residual,
            self.rms_norm.weights,
            self.rms_norm.eps,
            # act_quant_kwargs depends on the quantization scheme
            self.mlp.act_quant_kwargs,
            do_allreduce=self.tp_size > 1,
        )
        hidden_states = self.mlp(quantized_inputs)  # pre-allreduce
        return hidden_states
```

Here, `add_rms_norm_quant` is the call site for the fused kernel. We will introduce such "big fused ops" directly in model code wherever manual fusion is beneficial. This way, we can replace all fusions in vLLM’s compiler passes and even further improve the performance in complex cases such as DeepSeek V3.2 that the current compiler optimizations do not handle well.

### **1-2. CustomOp / vLLM IR**

With manual fusion in place — and the hardware-backend code separation discussed below — there is little reason to further develop the `CustomOp` and vLLM IR abstractions. ~~We will deprecate both and only keep the minimal part of it~~ We will keep them for legacy models, but more recent and complex models will instead have fused ops with a custom dispatching logic (for example, when different kernels must be launched on Hopper vs. Blackwell) possibly with some shared utility methods. For example, the code may look like:

```py
def add_rms_norm_quant(
	hidden_states: torch.Tensor,
	residual: torch.Tensor,
	rms_weights: torch.Tensor,
	rms_eps: float,
	mlp_act_quant_kwargs: dict[str, Any],
	do_allreduce: bool,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, Any]:
	if not do_allreduce:
		# No comm. Launch a simple fused kernel.
		return ...

	device_info = get_device_info()
	if device_info.name in ("GB200", "GB300"):
		# Launch FlashInfer kernel
		...
	elif device_info.name in ("H100", "H200"):
		# Launch some other kernels
 		...
```

### **1-3. Piecewise CUDA graph**

To preserve the piecewise CUDA graph feature without relying on `torch.compile`, we can adopt the "breakable CUDA graph" approach from SGL. @ZJY0516 already implemented a prototype in #42304 We expect this to match the performance of the current compiler-based approach without imposing many constraints on model code.

### **1-4. Hacks for compiler compatibility**

vLLM has accumulated several hacks to keep model code compatible with `torch.compile`. One example is `forward_context`, a global variable used to bypass the compiler's argument checking. These workarounds have hurt readability and introduced rough edges — model inputs are scattered across multiple places, and some global objects are not freed when the vLLM engine is deleted. Removing these hacks will improve the project's maintainability.

## **2\. Hardware separation and model isolation**

vLLM currently uses a single model definition for all in-tree hardware backends and relies on `CustomOp` and `torch.compile` to apply different fusions and dispatch kernels. This has made the code unnecessarily complex and fragile: a change made for one backend can easily break or regress another.

Going forward, **we will separate model code by hardware vendor**. Each model definition can then evolve independently for its target hardware without risk of breaking the others. Just as importantly, each vendor can design fusions around the kernels available to them, rather than conforming to a shared abstraction that fits no one perfectly.

Concretely, we expect the model code to be organized as follows:

```
models/
    deepseek_v4/
        nvidia/
            model.py
            kernels/
                fused_q_kv_norm.py
            tests/
                test_model.py
                test_fused_q_kv_norm.py
        amd/
            model.py
    deepseek_v3_2/
        nvidia/
            model.py
            kernels/
                fused_q.py
            tests/
                test_model.py
                test_fused_q.py
        amd/
            ...
```

Here, `kernels` contains model-specific JIT kernels (and maybe AoT kernels depending on our build structure); commonly used kernels remain in their existing locations. Each model directory also includes unit tests, so we can easily verify basic correctness of the model and its kernels. The code organization will help aggressively leverage AI to optimize models, as well as cleanly deprecate old models from the vLLM codebase.

## **3\. Model interface**

vLLM relies on many implicit assumptions about models and does not cleanly separate model-agnostic logic from model-dependent logic. This has produced a poor developer experience for users bringing custom in-house models. To address this, we are introducing explicit interfaces for both model definition and configuration.

First, we will define vLLM's own `ModelConfig` to hold all the information vLLM needs about a model. It is essentially a union of the typical HF config and vLLM's model protocol. The idea is similar to #24384.

```py
@dataclass
class ModelConfig(ABC):
    num_layers: int
    max_model_len: int
    vocab_size: int
    hidden_states_dtype: torch.dtype
    num_kv_heads: int
    num_query_heads: int
    is_moe: bool
    num_shared_experts: int | None
    num_routed_experts: int | None
    experts_per_tok: int | None
    supports_mm: bool
    supports_pp: bool
    supports_lora: bool
    ...
    model_kwargs: dict[str, Any]  # e.g., "rms_norm_eps": 1e-05
```

This brings three benefits:

1. A single source of truth for all model information.  
2. We currently spawn a subprocess to read certain fields from the model definition; this config eliminates that overhead, which is often dominated by import time.  
3. Model developers no longer need to port their models into HF format to use vLLM. In an extreme case, they can simply hardcode the config with values they already know.

Second, we will introduce vLLM's own model interface to make all contracts explicit. It should look like:

```py
class Model(ABC):
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: ModelConfig,
        parallel_state: ParallelState,
        **kwargs,
    ) -> None:
        # Allows the model to manage its own state.
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def load_weights(self, use_dummy: bool) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def init_kv_cache(self) -> None:
        # KV cache-related API (Needs more thought).
        ...

    def optimize_and_warmup(self) -> None:
        return None

    def add_requests(self, req_indices: list[int], request_data: list[Any]) -> None:
        # For initializing model-specific state (if any) when a request first arrives.
        return None

    @abstractmethod
    def prepare_inputs(self, input_batch: InputBatch) -> dict[str, Any]:
        # Prepare model inputs for a step. May include building attention metadata.
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def forward(self, **kwargs) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Run the model and return the hidden states.
        ...

    def compute_logits(self, hidden_states: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        raise NotImplementedError

    # More optional APIs for LoRA, spec decoding, and multimodal inputs.
    ...
```

The key idea is to let the model manage its own state when needed. For example, Qwen-VL models can manage their pre-computed M-RoPE values within this framework without any changes to the upper-level model runner. Similarly, `prepare_inputs` lets each model define its own inputs. With this design, the model runner handles only model-agnostic work — bookkeeping for continuous batching, sampling, CUDA graphs, and parts of model parallelism — while all model-dependent work lives in the model layer. Part of this idea was already implemented as `ModelState` in [model runner V2](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/interface.py).

Any model definition that implements both the `Model` and `ModelConfig` interfaces should be fully supported by vLLM, with no additional requirements.

### Proposed Change.

# In-Progress
* @ZJY0516 implements PW CUDA graph without relying on `torch.compile` #42304 
* @WoosukKwon implements the initial hardware separation for DeepSeek V4 & @tjtanaa will handle the AMD implementation
* @mgoin tracks and ports the fusions currently implemented through the compiler-based approach #43224

# TODOs
1. When PW CUDA graph & manual fusions are ready, remove `@supports_torch_compile` for DeepSeek V4
2. Port more models (e.g., Kimi, GLM, Qwen, Minimax, Nemotron, etc.) to manual fusion
3. When all models are ported with manual fusion, start deprecate vLLM's `torch.compile` integration
4. (Orthogonally to the above) Define model interface & apply it to all models

Detailed timeline will be updated soon.

title: [RFC]: Add support for Cohere's /v2/chat HTTP API entry point
author: andrewbcohere
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM does not currently support the [Cohere Chat v2 api](https://docs.cohere.com/reference/chat). While similar to chat completions, this api has a number of different fields, including notably, citations present within the assistant messages which should then be rendered into the prompt. This functionality is important to many of our users and so it would be needed for them to be able to use cohere models with vLLM directly.

### Proposed Change.

The proposed change is to add a cohere/v2/chat entry point that renders the request using the Melody library's prompt rendering functions. The flow would be very similar to the create_chat_completion function, but with render_chat calling the melody library to produce the rendered chat template prompt. Common logic could also be potentially refactored into a shared class. Output parsing logic is already in place and would not need to change.

title: [RFC]: Porting compiler fusions to manual fusion
author: mgoin
body:
## Motivation.

#42770 lays out the move from full-graph `torch.compile` to manual fusion expressed directly in model code. This issue tracks the concrete porting work for **section 1-1** of that RFC: enumerating the fusions currently performed by `vllm/compilation/passes/` and mapping each one to a work item to port to a manual call site in model code. To be clear this workstream is meant to touch all existing portable model definitions where compiler fusion pass would apply previously.

The goal is **no performance regression** as we delete each compiler pass. Each fusion below is either:
- ported to a "big fused op" callable from model code,
- collapsed into another fused op,
- or explicitly dropped (with rationale).

## Proposed Change.

### Changes to QuantMethod

This is clearly needed for fusions where we are fusing the input quant op from a downstream Linear layer. When a linear layer ops in, by registering a `self.input_quant_key = QuantKey.XX`, the fused operation will return a new `QuantizedActivation` instead of a `torch.Tensor`. When the linear's kernel sees that the input is not a simple unquantized tensor, it will pass it through directly to the matmul without requantizing.

For an illustrative example for `RMSNorm + Quant` see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42469

### Changes to Attention

TBD

### Changes to model definitions

We will initially implement these fusions for the simplest models that we can start with, and produce several subsequent PRs where we migrate groups of models to use these manual fusions, carefully testing performance and accuracy for at least one model within an architecture.

### Inventory of fusion passes

In rough priority order. Sub-issues will be filed per fused op to track ownership, kernel coverage, and the model PRs that switch over to it.

#### CUDA

- [ ] `allreduce + rms_norm[+quant]` (`AllReduceFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43499
  -  [ ] No quant
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor/per-token
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `rms_norm[+add] + quant` (`RMSNormQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43500
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor/per-token
  -  [ ] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
- [ ] `silu_mul + quant` (`ActivationQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43501
  -  [x] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [x] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
  -  [x] NVFP4
- [ ] `attn + output_quant` (`AttnQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43502
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `mla_attn + output_quant` (`MLAAttnQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43498
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [ ] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `q_norm + k_norm + rope` (`QKNormRoPEFusionPass`) - GLM4/Qwen3 / Gemma path. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43497
- [ ] `rope + kv_cache_write` (`RopeKVCacheFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43503
- [ ] `mla_rope + kv_cache_concat` (`MLARoPEKVCacheCatFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43504
- [ ] `minimax_qk_allreduce + norm` (`MiniMaxQKNormPass`)   https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43410

#### ROCm / aiter

- [ ] `allreduce + rms_norm[+add]` (`RocmAiterAllReduceFusionPass`)
- [ ] `rms_norm[+add] + (group/dynamic) fp8 quant` (`RocmAiterRMSNormQuantFusionPass`)
- [ ] `silu_mul + group fp8 quant` (`RocmAiterSiluMulFp8GroupQuantFusionPass`)
- [ ] `add + rms_norm + router_pad` (`RocmAiterTritonAddRMSNormPadFusionPass`)
- [ ] `mla_dual_rms_norm` (`MLADualRMSNormFusionPass`)

#### Compiler housekeeping (to drop, not port)

These exist only to clean up the IR and keep the compiler-fusion world consistent. With manual fusion they have no role:
- `NoOpEliminationPass`
- `VllmIRLoweringPass`
- `UnsafeCloneEliminationPass`
- `ScatterSplitReplacementPass` + `SplitCoalescingPass`
- `FixFunctionalizationPass`
- `PostCleanupPass`

These will be removed alongside the `torch.compile` integration removal (roughly the end-of-June milestone in #42770).

### Open questions.

1. **Sequence parallelism** SP today is opt-in (`pass_config.enable_sp`) and matters most for long-context + high TP. Basically it is a special case of all-reduce + rms_norm, where it turns `AR + RMSNorm[+Quant]` into `ReduceScatter + RMSNorm[+Quant] + AllGather`. We should decide whether to keep an SP path at all in the manual-fusion world.
2. **Async-TP** Not sure if this is possible to port to manual fusion.

### In-Progress.

- @mgoin tracks per-pass porting and files sub-issues from this list.
- @WoosukKwon's DSv4 NVIDIA implementation will be the reference port for P0 CUDA ops.
- @tjtanaa will handle the P0 ROCm ops.

title: [RFC] NSA is architecturally incompatible with NVIDIA consumer/workstation GPUs — MLA is the only viable sparse attention path
author: piweb-labs
body:
### Motivation.

After extensive production testing on SM120 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 8×96GB, PCIe Gen5), NSA (Native Sparse Attention) cannot be made to work reliably for production serving on NVIDIA consumer/workstation GPUs. This is not a bug — it is an architectural incompatibility.

The fundamental problems:

1. **NSA requires dynamic sparse index computation at every decode step.** This means per-layer, per-token topk selection over the full KV cache. On SM100 (datacenter Blackwell), dedicated FP8 block-scaled GEMM units handle this efficiently. On SM120, these units do not exist — the sparse indexer falls back to software paths that are both slow and correctness-problematic.

2. **PCIe topology makes NSA+MTP catastrophically unreliable.** The b12x PCIe oneshot allreduce has a buffer reuse race under CUDA graph/no-copy mode. The only known fix (a completion barrier in `pcie_oneshot.cu`) costs ~1 tok/s and still does not guarantee correctness under concurrent serving. MTP + TP>1 + concurrent>1 produces deadlocks (see #41402, #41404 — both closed without resolution).

3. **SM120 is not SM100.** FP8 block-scaled GEMM kernels written for SM100 crash or produce garbage on SM120 (#26211, #35566). FP8 KV Cache is slower than BF16 on SM120 because there are no native FP8 block-scaled compute units. NVFP4 KV Cache PRs (#21601 in SGLang) remain unmerged with critical bugs.

4. **NSA's correctness is unacceptably fragile.** The voipmonitor/GLM-5.1 reference image achieves only 93.3% accuracy (28/30), and requires a custom b12x overlay with three patched source files plus a custom vLLM tree. This is not production-grade — it is a fragile experiment.

5. **Every community Docker image for NSA+MTP is broken.** The rtx6kpro wiki images hang or produce incoherent output. Later versions are worse than earlier ones because upstream changes in both vLLM and b12x break the fragile integration points.

MLA avoids all of these problems:
- MLA compresses KV cache structurally (low-rank projection), no per-step sparse indexing needed
- MLA decode is a standard attention path — no custom indexer, no topk, no CUTE DSL kernel instability
- MLA works with existing FP8/BF16 KV Cache backends without SM120-specific kernel requirements
- MLA + MTP integration is straightforward because MLA does not introduce sparse index metadata into the speculative decode path
- MLA gives comparable or better KV cache compression for most workloads without the correctness fragility of NSA

The empirical evidence is clear: after 7+ days of testing every available NSA+MTP Docker image on 8×RTX PRO 6000, none are production-viable. NSA on SM120 is a dead end. Community effort should pivot to MLA as the only sparse attention path that can reach production reliability on consumer/workstation NVIDIA GPUs.

### Proposed Change.

1. Stop investing engineering effort in NSA kernel development for SM120 GPUs. The architectural gap between SM100 and SM120 makes NSA fundamentally unviable on consumer/workstation hardware.

2. Prioritize MLA attention backend as the primary sparse/efficient attention path for vLLM, with first-class SM120 support:
   - Native FP8 KV Cache for MLA decode on SM120
   - MLA + MTP speculative decode integration
   - MLA prefix caching and chunked prefill

3. Document that NSA support on SM120 is experimental/best-effort only, not production-targeted. This saves other teams from repeating the same 7-day dead-end exploration.

4. Re-evaluate whether the b12x NSA indexer integration should remain in vLLM at all, or whether it should be moved to a separate experimental package to avoid destabilizing the main branch.

### Feedback Period.

2 weeks

_No response_

title: [Feature]: [RFC] Bottleneck-aware expansion for PD disaggregation
author: zsn6493
body:
This is an RFC-style feature request for discussion.

I have been reading through the recent PD, KV transfer, and offloading work, and it feels like the next missing step is not replacing PD, but making PD deployments more adaptive when one side becomes the dominant bottleneck.

## Summary

This proposal does **not** replace PD disaggregation.

Instead, it builds on the current PD model and asks whether vLLM should identify the dominant bottleneck at runtime and expand the most effective side first.

Concretely, the idea is:

- keep the current PD architecture
- detect whether runtime pressure is mainly on `prefill`, `decode`, or `decode-side KV capacity`
- expand the easiest and most effective side first
- reduce user-facing contention before relying on stronger competition inside a fixed topology

## Motivation

PD already gives an important separation between prefill and decode pools, and KV transfer / request migration / offloading are all moving in the right direction.

But even with PD, deployments still seem mostly statically provisioned. That means it is still easy to end up in situations like:

- `prefill` is saturated while `decode` is relatively idle
- `decode` is saturated while `prefill` is underutilized
- `decode-side KV capacity` becomes the dominant bottleneck even when compute is still available
- remote KV transfer backlog creates hidden stalls between the two pools

So from my perspective, PD solves mixed-pool interference, but not yet dynamic imbalance between the pools.

## Proposal

Introduce a bottleneck-aware expansion layer for PD disaggregation.

A simple first version could classify runtime pressure into three categories:

1. `Prefill-bound`
   Prefill-side compute or memory pressure dominates.

2. `Decode-bound`
   Decode-side token throughput or scheduling pressure dominates.

3. `Decode-KV-bound`
   Decode-side KV holding capacity dominates, even if decode compute is not yet saturated.

Then the runtime (or a future policy layer built on top of it) could choose the most effective expansion action:

- `Prefill-bound -> add prefill capacity`
- `Decode-bound -> add decode capacity`
- `Decode-KV-bound -> add decode-side KV capacity / tier`

The key point is that this would make PD more adaptive without changing the core PD architecture.

## Suggested First Scope

A practical first step might be:

- expose structured runtime pressure signals
- classify bottlenecks into `Prefill-bound`, `Decode-bound`, or `Decode-KV-bound`
- support one minimal expansion hook or policy target

Even just that would already make PD more adaptive, without requiring full runtime elasticity.

## Non-Goals

This is **not** proposing:

- replacing PD disaggregation
- generic runtime GPU hot-plug
- runtime TP/NCCL topology mutation within an active worker group
- full cluster autoscaling inside vLLM

## Related Work

This seems closely related to, but different from, the following threads:

- PD disaggregation roadmap: #33702
- KV transfer push-model discussion: #36923
- KV cache offloading RFC: #19854
- Multi-tier offloading RFC: #38260
- NIXL handshake / autoscaling decode discussion: #19777

My understanding is that those efforts already provide the right building blocks. What seems missing is a policy/runtime layer that decides which side should be expanded first when pressure emerges inside an already disaggregated deployment.

## Questions

I would really appreciate feedback on a few points:

- does this direction fit the current PD roadmap?
- which bottleneck class would be the best first target?
- should a first step focus only on signaling, or include one minimal expansion hook?
- how should this interact with ongoing KV transfer / request migration work?

title: [RFC]: Add Gumiho speculative decoding to vLLM
author: userljz
body:
### Motivation.

<!--
Open at: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/new?template=750-RFC.yml
Title:   [RFC]: Add Gumiho speculative decoding to vLLM
Labels:  RFC (added automatically by the template)

Paste each section below into the matching field of the RFC template.
-->

## Motivation.

[Gumiho](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10135) (ICML 2025) is a hybrid speculative
decoding drafter:

1. The first two speculative tokens are produced autoregressively by an
   EAGLE-style transformer head.
2. Every additional speculative token is produced **in parallel** by per-step
   MLP heads conditioned on the embeddings and hidden states of the first two
   draft tokens.

The motivation is that **early speculative tokens matter more than late
ones**. Each accepted prefix token unlocks all later tokens in the same draft,
so allocating more compute to the first two positions (a small but
high-quality transformer head) and amortising the rest with cheap parallel
MLP heads yields a better acceptance-rate / drafter-latency trade-off than
either a pure EAGLE drafter (all transformer, sequential) or a pure
MLPSpeculator drafter (all MLP, parallel but lower quality).

Concretely, this means a lower per-step drafter latency than EAGLE/EAGLE3
when `num_speculative_tokens > 2`, with similar end-to-end accepted-token
gains.

We have a working ROCm prototype on top of vLLM v0.16.0 and have already
ported it to current `main` with all CI hygiene applied; the changes are
small and contained.

## Proposed Change.

Add `"method": "gumiho"` as a new V1 speculative decoding method.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43544

### Surface

```python
LLM(
    model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
    speculative_config={
        "method": "gumiho",
        "model": "amd/Gumiho-llama3-8b",
        "num_speculative_tokens": 3,
        "draft_tensor_parallel_size": 1,
    },
)
```

### Implementation

* **New drafter model** `vllm/model_executor/models/gumiho.py`
  (`GumihoLlamaForCausalLM` + inner `GumihoLlamaModel` + `GumihoResBlock`,
  `GumihoNoResBlock`, weight loader). The transformer head reuses
  `LlamaDecoderLayer` from `llama_eagle.py` exactly like EAGLE does.
* **New proposer** `vllm/v1/spec_decode/gumiho.py`
  (`GumihoProposer(EagleProposer)`). Only overrides two new hooks defined on
  `SpecDecodeBaseProposer`:

  | Hook | Default | Gumiho |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `_init_draft_hidden_states_list` | returns `None` | returns `[sample_hidden_states]` so the sequential loop also collects hidden states |
  | `_maybe_get_mlp_draft_token_ids` | returns `None` | after the 2nd draft step, calls `GumihoLlamaForCausalLM.generate_mlp_draft_token_ids(...)` and short-circuits the rest of the loop |

  Both hooks are no-ops in the base class, so existing proposers
  (EAGLE / EAGLE3 / MTP / DFlash / draft_model / ...) are not affected.

* **New HF config wrapper** `vllm/transformers_utils/configs/gumiho.py`
  (`GumihoConfig`), mirroring how `EAGLEConfig` wraps the underlying Llama
  backbone.

* **Wiring**
  * `SpeculativeConfig`: add `gumiho` to `SpeculativeMethod`, `use_eagle()`,
    the draft-TP=1 forced set, the model-type auto-detect path, and add a
    config-wrap branch parallel to the EAGLE one (reusing the existing
    `update_arch_()` helper).
  * `gpu_model_runner.GPUModelRunner.__init__`: add a `method == "gumiho"`
    branch matched **before** `use_eagle()` so we don't fall back to a plain
    `EagleProposer`.
  * `v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/__init__.py`: raise an explicit
    `NotImplementedError` on the V2 GPU runner.
  * Model + HF-config registry entries.

* **Docs + example** under
  `docs/features/speculative_decoding/gumiho.md` and a new
  `--method gumiho` branch in
  `examples/features/speculative_decoding/spec_decode_offline.py`.

* **Unit tests** under `tests/v1/spec_decode/test_gumiho.py` (CPU-only,
