title: [RFC]:Sequence Parallelism (SP) for Vision Transformers (ViT) in VLM Inference
author: BossH2
body:
# RFC: Sequence Parallelism (SP) for Vision Transformers (ViT) in VLM Inference

## Motivation

As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) evolve to process higher-resolution images, video frames, and ultra-long multi-modal contexts, the computational and memory footprint of the visual processing stage—predominantly governed by Vision Transformers (ViTs)—has become a critical bottleneck in distributed inference. 

While modern inference frameworks have successfully laid the groundwork for managing long textual sequences in the Large Language Model (LLM) backbone via sequence-level distribution, the multi-modal visual ingestion pipeline remains highly unoptimized in tensor-parallel (TP) environments. Currently, when handling large visual inputs, the implementation inherits severe performance degradation due to the following structural limitations:

1. **Serial Execution Bottleneck in Multi-GPU Environments:** Although the textual component can leverage distributed prefill parallelization, the long sequence of visual tokens generated by the ViT is often processed without natively aligning to the Sequence Parallelism (SP) boundaries of the downstream LLM. This leads to severe pipeline stalls and fails to fully exploit the concurrent compute budget available across a multi-GPU cluster.
2. **Redundant Visual Weight and Activation Replication:** Under standard Tensor Parallelism (TP) configurations, heavy communication overhead is incurred when slicing the attention weights of large Vision layers across hosts. Furthermore, redundant intermediate states or duplicated visual tokens are often replicated across the TP domain, which severely restricts the system's maximum batch size and prevents the model from scaling to ultra-long multimodal sequences.

To radically resolve these multi-modal scaling efficiency issues, we propose extending the **Sequence Parallelism (SP)** infrastructure specifically to the ViT and visual-projection layers of VLMs. Natively integrating Sequence Parallelism into the vision components yields three game-changing advantages for long-context multi-modal inference:

* **Compute Parallelization & Latency Reduction:** By natively slicing the visual sequences along the sequence dimension across the SP ranks, the intense computational workload of large-scale ViT layers is evenly distributed across multiple GPUs. This directly drives down the Prefill-stage latency, bypassing the structural bottlenecks where the vision encoder acts as a serial gatekeeper before the parallelized LLM backbone.
* **Communication Message Size Reduction:** In distributed, multi-host clusters, standard Tensor Parallelism (TP) incurs prohibitive communication overhead during the intra-layer activation slicing of large Vision layers. Moving to a sequence-parallel paradigm drastically alters the communication boundaries. By maintaining a communication volume that scales with the sequence partitioning rather than the tensor dimensions, it avoids the inter-node network bottlenecks typically seen in large-scale multi-modal deployments.
* **Distributed Memory Footprint:** The memory footprint of visual tokens and their corresponding intermediate activations scales linearly with the image resolution and token sequence length. Introducing natively aligned SP allows the system to split the visual sequence into manageable chunks according to the `SP_SIZE`. Each SP rank independently processes and stores only its designated slice of the visual input, effectively unlocking the ability to support significantly larger batch sizes and ultra-long contexts by simply scaling the SP rank count.

### Proposed Change.

# Proposed Change: Sequence Parallelism for Vision Transformer (ViT) in Multimodal Models

> **RFC Status:** Implemented | **Date:** 2026-05-26 | **Updated:** 2026-06-22
> **Scope:** `qwen2_5_vl.py`, `qwen3_vl.py` (eager-mode ViT sequence parallelism)
> **Approach:** AllGather + ReduceScatter via TP group, attention-only wrapping

---

## 1. High-Level Architecture

### 1.1 Motivation

Current ViT parallelism modes both replicate the visual token sequence across ranks — TP (`mm_encoder_tp_mode="model"`) partitions attention heads but every rank holds the full `[Total_Patches, hidden_size]` activation; DP (`"data"`) shards across images but not within a single image. For high-resolution inputs (e.g., 1024×1024 → 4096+ patches), this `O(Total_Patches)` per-rank activation memory bottlenecks QKV projections and attention score tensors.

**Core invariant:** Under SP, every rank holds exactly `1 / tp_size` of the total visual sequence at the start and end of each VisionBlock. Attention runs on the full (AllGathered) sequence; Norm and MLP operate on the sharded sequence.

### 1.2 SP Pattern: Attention-Only Wrapping

The key insight is that SP reuses the existing **TP communication group** (`get_tp_group()`) and standard collective primitives:

```
Per VisionBlock:
  norm1(sharded) → AllGather(dim=0) → attn(full, reduce_results=False) → ReduceScatter(dim=0) → norm2(sharded) → mlp(sharded)
```

| | LLM SP (graph-mode) | ViT SP (eager-mode, this RFC) |
|---|---|---|
| Communication group | TP group | TP group (reused) |
| Attention type | Causal (unidirectional) | Bidirectional (per-image) |
| SP wraps | LayerNorm (after ReduceScatter) | Attention (after AllGather) |
| Pattern | RS→Norm→AG | AG→(attn→proj)→RS |
| Norm | Full sequence | Sharded (per-token, safe) |
| MLP | Full sequence | Sharded (per-token TP, safe) |
| Comm per block | 1×RS + 1×AG = 2 ops | 1×AG + 1×RS = 2 ops |

**Why AllGather before attention?** ViT uses bidirectional (full) attention — every token must attend to every other token of the same image. Without AllGather, each rank's tokens can only see their own chunk.

**Why ReduceScatter after attention?** The attention output projection (`RowParallelLinear`) uses `reduce_results=False` when SP is enabled, producing partial feature contributions per rank. ReduceScatter both sums these partials (completing the AllReduce) AND scatters the result along the sequence dimension back to sharded form — two actions in one collective.

**Why Norm and MLP on sharded data?** Both are per-token operations. LayerNorm/RMSNorm computes mean/variance per token independently. ColumnParallelLinear and RowParallelLinear split weights along hidden_dim, not sequence dim, so their TP behavior is orthogonal to sequence sharding.

### 1.3 Tensor Shape Lifecycle

The full dataflow through the SP-ViT pipeline (`S = total_patches`, `D = hidden_size`, `P = tp_size`):

```
[1] Patch Embedding (full seq, replicated — no communication)
    pixel_values [S, C_in]  →  hidden_states [S, D]
    e.g., 504×504 image → [1296, 1152]

[2] Pre-processing (model-specific, replicated)
    Qwen2.5-VL: window_index reorder + unsqueeze → [S, 1, D]
    Qwen3-VL:   pos_embed + unsqueeze → [S, 1, D]

[3] SP ENTER — Manual Slice (no communication, data is replicated)
    hidden_states [S, 1, D] → [S/P, 1, D]  via [tp_rank*chunk : (tp_rank+1)*chunk]
    Constraint: S % P == 0

[4] For EACH ViT Block (×24 for Qwen3-VL-30B):
    ┌─ norm1 (local): [S/P, 1, D] → [S/P, 1, D]  (per-token, no communication)
    │
    │  ★ AllGather #1: [S/P, 1, D] → [S, 1, D]
    │    dim=0, TP group. Each rank gets full sequence. ~S×D/P bytes per rank.
    │
    ├─ Attention (full seq, reduce_results=False):
    │  - QKV proj (ColumnParallelLinear): [S, 1, D] → [S, 1, 3×D/tp] per rank
    │  - Reshape to [batch, S, 3, heads/tp, head_dim]
    │  - RoPE (per-token, elementwise)
    │  - Bidirectional attention: each token attends all S tokens
    │    → [batch, S, heads/tp, head_dim]
    │  - Output proj (RowParallelLinear, reduce_results=False):
    │    → [S, 1, D] PARTIAL per rank (no AllReduce inside proj)
    │
    │  ★ ReduceScatter #2: [S, 1, D] → [S/P, 1, D]
    │    dim=0, TP group. SUMs partial features + SCATTERs back to sharded.
    │    ~S×D bytes per rank.
    │
    └─ norm2 + residual + MLP (local):
       x = x_original + x_attn                    → [S/P, 1, D]
       x = x + mlp(norm2(x))                      → [S/P, 1, D]

[5] Transformer Exit — AllGather
    hidden_states [S/P, 1, D] → [S, 1, D]  (restore full sequence for merger)
    Per deepstack layer (Qwen3-VL only): same AllGather before merger.

[6] Patch Merger (full seq, standard TP)
    [S, 1, D] → view(-1) → ColumnParallelLinear → GELU → RowParallelLinear
    → [S/spatial_merge_unit, out_hidden_size]

[7] Downstream LLM Handoff
    ViT output: [num_vision_tokens, out_hidden_size] (full sequence, replicated)
    LLM decoder receives the full visual embedding sequence as usual.
```

**Communication per block:** 1× AllGather + 1× ReduceScatter = 2 ops. Total per block: `3 × S × D / P` bytes (AG sends S/P×D, receives S×D → S/P×D upload, S×D download → 3×S×D/P.

---

## 2. Detailed Component Changes

### 2.1 VisionTransformer Init: SP State Acquisition

Both `Qwen2_5_VisionTransformer.__init__` and `Qwen3_VisionTransformer.__init__` acquire SP state from the existing TP infrastructure:

```python
# In both Qwen2_5_VisionTransformer and Qwen3_VisionTransformer:
use_data_parallel = is_vit_use_data_parallel()
self.tp_size = (
    1 if use_data_parallel
    else parallel_state.get_tensor_model_parallel_world_size()
)
self.tp_group = get_tp_group()
self.tp_rank = parallel_state.get_tensor_model_parallel_rank()
self.sp_min_token_num = 1000  # same threshold as graph-mode LLM SP
```

No new config fields. No new process groups. SP state is derived entirely from TP state.

### 2.2 VisionTransformer Forward: SP Injection + Exit

SP is injected at the transformer entry point, after model-specific preprocessing:

**Qwen2.5-VL** (`qwen2_5_vl.py`, after window_index reorder + unsqueeze):
```python
seq_len = hidden_states.shape[0]
sp_enabled = (
    self.tp_size > 1
    and seq_len >= self.sp_min_token_num        # 1000
    and seq_len % self.tp_size == 0
)
if sp_enabled:
    seq_chunk = hidden_states.shape[0] // self.tp_size
    hidden_states = hidden_states[self.tp_rank * seq_chunk : (self.tp_rank + 1) * seq_chunk]
```

**Qwen3-VL** (`qwen3_vl.py`, after pos_embed + unsqueeze): identical logic.

**Exit (both models):**
```python
if sp_enabled:
    hidden_states = self.tp_group.all_gather(hidden_states, dim=0)
hidden_states = self.merger(hidden_states)  # merger requires full sequence
```

**Why manual slice at entry, not ReduceScatter?** At the entry point, data is replicated (patch_embed + pos_embed produce identical output on all ranks). Manual indexing `[tp_rank * chunk : ...]` is zero-cost — no communication needed. ReduceScatter would unnecessarily SUM replicated data.

### 2.3 VisionBlock Forward: Attention-Only SP Wrapping

Both models insert SP around the attention sub-block only:

**Qwen2_5_VisionBlock.forward** (`qwen2_5_vl.py:511-539`):
```python
def forward(self, x, cu_seqlens, ..., sp_enabled=False, tp_group=None):
    x_normed = self.norm1(x)                           # [chunk, 1, D]
    if sp_enabled:
        x_normed = tp_group.all_gather(x_normed, dim=0)  # → [S, 1, D]
    x_attn = self.attn(x_normed, ..., sp_enabled=sp_enabled)
    if sp_enabled:
        x_attn = tp_group.reduce_scatter(x_attn, dim=0)  # → [chunk, 1, D]
    x_fused_norm, residual = self.norm2(x, residual=x_attn)
    x = residual + self.mlp(x_fused_norm)
    return x
```

**Qwen3_VisionBlock.forward** (`qwen3_vl.py:446-473`):
```python
def forward(self, x, cu_seqlens, ..., sp_enabled=False, tp_group=None):
    x_normed = self.norm1(x)
    if sp_enabled:
        x_normed = tp_group.all_gather(x_normed, dim=0)
    x_attn = self.attn(x_normed, ..., sp_enabled=sp_enabled)
    if sp_enabled:
        x_attn = tp_group.reduce_scatter(x_attn, dim=0)
    x = x + x_attn                                     # x preserved as original input
    x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
    return x
```

**Critical detail — `x_normed` vs `x`:** `x` is NEVER overwritten with norm1 output. This preserves the original block input for the residual connection (`x = x + x_attn`), which is required by the Pre-LN Transformer architecture.

### 2.4 VisionAttention Forward: reduce_results Toggle

**Qwen2_5_VisionAttention.forward** (`qwen2_5_vl.py:404-465`):

```python
def forward(self, x, ..., sp_enabled=False):
    self.proj.reduce_results = False if sp_enabled else True
    # ... QKV projection, RoPE, attention, output projection ...
```

When `sp_enabled=True`, the output `RowParallelLinear` (`self.proj`) skips its internal AllReduce. This leaves each rank with **partial feature contributions** (only the columns of the weight matrix owned by that rank). The subsequent `ReduceScatter` in VisionBlock.forward both SUMS these partials across ranks AND SCATTERs along dim=0 — achieving what a separate AllReduce + manual slice would do in one operation.

**Why no save/restore?** SP state is uniform across all blocks within one forward pass — either every block has `sp_enabled=True` or every block has `sp_enabled=False`. No toggle mid-forward.

**Qwen3-VL note:** `Qwen3_VisionBlock.attn` is an instance of `Qwen2_5_VisionAttention` (line 430 of qwen3_vl.py), so the `reduce_results` toggle is inherited without duplication.

### 2.5 Deepstack Handling (Qwen3-VL only)

Qwen3-VL's `deepstack_visual_indexes` specify intermediate layers whose outputs are fed through separate merger modules:

```python
if layer_num in self.deepstack_visual_indexes:
    ds_input = (
        self.tp_group.all_gather(hidden_states, dim=0)
        if sp_enabled
        else hidden_states
    )
    deepstack_feature = self.deepstack_merger_list[idx](ds_input)
```

**Why AllGather before deepstack merger?** The merger internally does `view(-1, hidden_size)` to group `spatial_merge_unit` consecutive tokens before ColumnParallelLinear. Sharded data would split those consecutive groups across ranks. AllGather restores the full sequence so the view reshape sees contiguous tokens.

**Communication:** 1× AllGather per deepstack layer.

### 2.6 Merger (Both Models)

The main merger (`Qwen3_VisionPatchMerger` / `Qwen2_5_VisionPatchMerger`) runs on the full sequence after the exit AllGather. Its ColumnParallelLinear and RowParallelLinear use standard TP with default `reduce_results=True` — consistent with pre-SP behavior. No merger code was changed.

### 2.7 Window Attention (Qwen2.5-VL)

Qwen2.5-VL alternates full and window attention via `fullatt_block_indexes`. Under SP:

- **window_index reorder happens BEFORE SP injection** — tokens are reordered while data is still replicated. SP's manual slice occurs after reordering, so window pattern correctness is preserved.
- **Attention always runs on AllGathered full sequence** — both full-attn and window-attn blocks see the complete `[S, 1, D]` after AG. The `cu_seqlens` / `cu_window_seqlens` metadata is computed on the full sequence and used with the full sequence.
- **No halo exchange needed** — because attention operates on the full AllGathered sequence, window boundaries naturally align. No special window-attention SP logic required.

---

## 3. Implementation Blueprint

### 3.1 Architecture: Inline Modification (No Wrapper Class)

The implementation follows an **inline modification** pattern rather than a wrapper/decorator pattern. This was chosen because:

1. SP reuses the existing TP group — no new communication groups to manage.
2. The SP code path is a thin veneer of 2 collective ops per block — a wrapper would add indirection without reducing complexity.
3. Each model (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL) has model-specific preprocessing (window_index vs deepstack) that is cleaner to handle in situ.

**Modified files and their roles:**

| File | Class/Method | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `qwen2_5_vl.py` | `Qwen2_5_VisionAttention.forward` | +`sp_enabled` param, toggles `reduce_results` |
| `qwen2_5_vl.py` | `Qwen2_5_VisionBlock.forward` | +2 params (sp_enabled, tp_group), AG→attn→RS wrapping |
| `qwen2_5_vl.py` | `Qwen2_5_VisionTransformer.__init__` | +4 attrs (tp_size, tp_group, tp_rank, sp_min_token_num) |
| `qwen2_5_vl.py` | `Qwen2_5_VisionTransformer.forward` | SP enablement check, manual slice entry, AG exit |
| `qwen3_vl.py` | `Qwen3_VisionBlock.forward` | +2 params, same AG→attn→RS wrapping |
| `qwen3_vl.py` | `Qwen3_VisionTransformer.__init__` | +3 attrs (tp_group, tp_rank, sp_min_token_num; tp_size existed) |
| `qwen3_vl.py` | `Qwen3_VisionTransformer.forward` | SP check, manual slice, deepstack AG, exit AG |

**Unmodified by design:**

| File/Class | Reason |
|---|---|
| `qwen3.py` (LLM decoder) | Phase 2 — decoder SP is separate work |
| `mm_encoder_attention.py` | Attention operates on full AG'd sequence, no SP awareness needed |
| `layernorm.py` | Norms are per-token, SP-transparent |
| VisionMLP classes | Standard TP on sharded data, per-token operations |
| `parallel_state.py` | No new groups; SP reuses `_TP` |

### 3.2 Communication Primitives

No new communication primitives. SP uses standard `GroupCoordinator` methods:

| Primitive | GroupCoordinator method | parallel_state.py |
|---|---|---|
| AllGather | `tp_group.all_gather(x, dim=0)` | Line 543 |
| ReduceScatter | `tp_group.reduce_scatter(x, dim=0)` | Line 574 |

Both internally short-circuit when `world_size == 1`, providing zero-overhead fallback for single-GPU or DP-ViT mode.

### 3.3 Configuration

No new CLI flags or config fields. SP is **auto-enabled** when all three conditions hold:

```python
sp_enabled = (
    self.tp_size > 1                # multi-GPU TP
    and seq_len >= self.sp_min_token_num  # 1000 (same as graph-mode SP)
    and seq_len % self.tp_size == 0       # alignment requirement
)
```

The existing `--tensor-parallel-size` flag implicitly controls SP. DP ViT mode (`is_vit_use_data_parallel()=True`) automatically forces `tp_size=1`, disabling SP.

### 3.4 Constraints & Compatibility

| Constraint | Enforcement | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `seq_len >= 1000` | Runtime check in forward | Short sequences: communication overhead > memory savings |
| `seq_len % tp_size == 0` | Runtime check in forward | Manual slice `[tp_rank*chunk : ...]` requires exact division |
| `tp_size > 1` | Runtime check in forward | Single-GPU has no peer to scatter to / gather from |
| DP ViT mode → tp_size=1 | Init-time override | DP ViT shards across images, not within an image |
| Backward compat: all conditions false | No-op path | SP code branches are invisible when `sp_enabled=False` |
| `reduce_results` toggle | Per-forward assignment | SP state uniform across all blocks; no save/restore needed |

### 3.5 Prefill/Decode Separation (PD Separation)

The ViT runs **exclusively during prefill** — it encodes visual inputs into embeddings before the LLM decoder generates tokens. There is no ViT processing during decode. Therefore:

- **No PD-specific communication patterns** are needed within the ViT.
- The SP communication (AllGather + ReduceScatter) occurs only during the prefill-phase ViT forward pass.
- **PCP compatibility:** The ViT SP operates within the TP group on full visual sequences. PCP subdivides visual tokens for KV cache distribution in the LLM decoder, which is independent of ViT SP. The two mechanisms are orthogonal.

### 3.6 Performance Model

For a ViT with hidden size `D`, full sequence length `S`, `P = tp_size`, `B = num_blocks`:

| Metric | TP-only (no SP) | TP + SP |
|---|---|---|
| Per-rank activation (attention) | `O(S × D)` | `O(S × D)` (full seq after AG) |
| Per-rank activation (norm, mlp) | `O(S × D)` | `O(S × D / P)` |
| Per-block communication | 0 | 1×AG + 1×RS |
| Per-block compute | `O(S × D² / P)` | `O(S × D² / P)` (unchanged) |
| ViT→LLM boundary | 0 | 1×AG at exit |

The `O(P)` memory reduction for Norm and MLP activations is the primary benefit. The attention activations remain `O(S × D)` (by design — attention requires full sequence), but the peak memory is still lower because norm/mlp intermediate buffers are sharded.

title: [RFC]: Streaming API for Real-Time Server State and Metrics
author: liu-cong
body:
### Motivation.

Distributed inference routers (e.g., `llm-d-router`) require real-time visibility into engine capacity to balance load effectively. Current scraping/polling methods (like Prometheus `/metrics` pulling) introduce dual inefficiencies:
1. **Latency & Staleness:** A single large request can instantly saturate a server. Routing layers remain blind to this during the polling window, sending subsequent traffic that causes cascading queuing delays or OOMs.
2. **Resource Waste:** Continuous HTTP requests occur even when the server state is completely static.

While routers try to mitigate this by estimating in-flight load locally, this state is fragile across router restarts and lacks accurate engine-level visibility into metrics like dynamic KV-cache occupancy.

### Proposed Change.

Expose an optional **streaming API endpoint** (e.g.,  `grpc` streaming) from the engine allowing routers to establish a persistent connection. The model server will asynchronously push structured metrics the moment internal scheduling states change, reducing telemetry lag down to network transport latency.

The detailed design will be updated later.

title: [RFC]: Non-blocking core model loop
author: njhill
body:
# Motivation

The vLLM core engine process today **blocks** whenever it has no active requests. The non-DP loop ends up parked in `multiprocessing.Queue.get(block=True)`. In the DP case the wake-up is staged through a dedicated `DPCoordinator` process that broadcasts messages to bring all ranks out of their idle state together.

```python
# vllm/v1/engine/core.py - current non-DP busy loop
def run_busy_loop(self):
    while self._handle_shutdown():
        # 1) Poll the input queue until there is work to do.
        self._process_input_queue()        # blocks on input_queue.get(block=True)
        # 2) Step the engine core and return the outputs.
        self._process_engine_step()
```

The blocking model has worked well, but it has accumulated meaningful cost:

## Limitations of the current design

### 1. Multiplexing more than one wake-up source is awkward

The engine needs to react to more than just new requests: `DPCoordinator` wave messages, KV-connector completion / failure events, FSM/grammar compilation futures, and future signals like async weight updates and elastic-EP changes. Today these are multiplexed via a background ZMQ-poller thread that feeds an in-process `Queue` the main thread blocks on. It works, but every new signal source means another producer thread or another path into that queue.

### 2. Separate DP Coordinator process required

The `DPCoordinator` process is responsible for:

1. **Waking all DP ranks together when a new wave starts.** When a request lands at one idle rank, the coordinator broadcasts `START_DP_WAVE` so the ranks begin a new wave in lockstep. This is the dominant reason the coordinator exists.
2. **Maintaining wave numbering** across engines, including stale-wave handling for requests that arrive between coordinator broadcasts.
3. **Aggregating per-engine queue stats** and publishing them to the front-end(s) for the "internal DP LB" mode.
4. Handling elastic-EP add/remove events.

(1) and (2) only exist because the engine is allowed to fall asleep.

### 3. State machine complexity

Several distributed bits of state - `engines_running`, `current_wave`, `pending_pause`, plus the coordinator's mirror of them - all need to agree across processes. Most exist only to make "wake up together" work. In a non-blocking design "running" is no longer a state at all, just a per-step decision about whether to forward.

# Proposed Change

**Make the engine core loop non-blocking, and shrink the DP coordinator to its remaining intrinsic role.**

### 1. Core engine loop becomes a spin loop

The `EngineCoreProc.run_busy_loop` and `DPEngineCoreProc.run_busy_loop` paths converge on a single non-blocking shape:

```python
def run_busy_loop(self):
    while self._handle_shutdown():
        # Drain any pending client requests / control messages. Non-blocking.
        self._process_input_queue_nowait()

        # Drain any pending async signals (KV connector, grammar futures, etc.).
        self._process_async_signals_nowait()

        # Step the engine. In DP+EP mode this is a dummy batch when no local work
        # is ready but the per-iteration all-reduce says some peer rank has work.
        self._process_engine_step()
```

The background ZMQ-poller thread that feeds `input_queue` is kept; the main thread just stops sleeping on it.

The DP case no longer has a distinct "running" vs "stopped" state - every engine is always looping. What remains is a per-iteration **decision**: should this step run a model forward? In DP+EP that decision must agree across ranks. The dummy-batch / lockstep-forward contract itself is unchanged.

### Idle-throttling policy

A literal busy-spin would burn one CPU core per engine and per worker process even on a completely idle cluster (see Costs). The default policy:

* If there's work, iterate with no sleep. This is identical to today's "busy" DP+EP behaviour.
* If idle, `time.sleep(0)` or similar to yield the GIL, or a configurable short sleep (e.g. `VLLM_ENGINE_IDLE_SLEEP_MS`, default `0`).

The same lever applies to workers: when `dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp` (V2) or `coordinate_batch_across_dp` (V1, if adapted) returns the all-zero descriptor, the model runner sleeps for the configured interval before returning to the dequeue.

### 2. Subsuming the per-iteration all-reduce into the V2 model runner

The V2 model runner already does a per-step CPU-group all-reduce (`dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp`) that exchanges `(num_tokens, cg_mode, uniform_token_count)` across DP ranks and short-circuits when every rank reports zero tokens. This already answers "does any rank have work?" in the same collective that handles per-step DP padding.

In the V2 path we therefore drop the per-iteration outer all-reduce on `has_unfinished_requests` entirely. The loop becomes "always enter the runner; the runner's existing per-step sync handles both jobs." No `engines_running`, no `_has_global_unfinished_reqs`, no 32-step throttle.

The V1 model runner has a structurally identical per-step primitive (`coordinate_batch_across_dp`) but lacks the explicit all-zero short-circuit. Two options, deferrable:

* **Adapt V1 similarly** - add the short-circuit so V1 and V2 share the simpler loop.
* **Keep the outer all-reduce on the V1 path** until the V1 runner is removed, then delete the V1 branch whole. As a side benefit, V1 workers stay blocked on the SHM dequeue at idle rather than spinning.

### 3. Eliminate the DP wake-up machinery

With no engine ever blocking, the entire wave-broadcast path becomes dead code:

* The `START_DP_WAVE` request type and all engine-side wave bookkeeping.
* The `start_wave` engine->coordinator notification and corresponding broadcast.
* The XPUB/XSUB pub-sub leg between coordinator and engines.
* The `current_wave` field on `EngineCoreRequest`.

(Per section 2: under V2 the per-iteration cross-rank all-reduce also goes; under V1 it stays until the V1 runner is removed.)

### 4. Shrink (and eventually retire) the DP coordinator

After section 3 the only remaining responsibilities of `DPCoordinator` are stats aggregation for the "internal DP LB" mode (Python multi-api-server deployment need a near-real-time view of each engine's queue depth) and infrequent elastic-EP scaling events. It's function as a stats broadcaster is also redundant when using the new single-process rust front-end.

* **Short term:** keep `DPCoordinator` for internal-LB Python deployments, trimmed to just the stats-broadcast + control-plane role.

### 5. Simpler async-signal handling

With a spin loop, KV-connector events and grammar-compilation completions are just polled state each iteration. Grammar `Future.done()` becomes a normal step of the loop; future host-side KV signals (out-of-band cache hits, etc.) can be polled inline instead of plumbed through a wake-up queue.

## Benefits

* **Simpler engine state.** No `current_wave`, no `START_DP_WAVE`, no wake-up races, no stale-wave handling.
* **Simpler IPC topology.** The XPUB/XSUB coordinator<->engine fabric goes away.
* **Lower cold-request latency in DP deployments.** One fewer process and IPC hop on the request path.
* **Uniform code path for non-DP and DP.** The two `run_busy_loop` implementations converge.
* **Extension-friendly.** New async signal sources plug in as ordinary polled checks rather than as new wake-up producers.
* **Clear deprecation path** for the DP coordinator.

## Costs

* **CPU usage at idle.** Under V2 (and V1 + adapt option), every engine core *and* every GPU worker process spins at idle - roughly N + NxTxP cores for DP=N, TP=T, PP=P (e.g. ~12 cores for DP=4 TP=2, ~72 cores per node for DP=8 TP=8). Production deployments are rarely idle for long - GPU time is the binding cost - and `VLLM_ENGINE_IDLE_SLEEP_MS` applies to both engine cores and workers as the opt-in escape hatch for dev/test. (Under V1 + Option B in section 2, workers stay blocked on the SHM dequeue at idle as today; only the engine cores spin.)
* **Internal-LB Python deployments** continue to need the coordinator (but not if rust front-end is used.)

## Out of scope

* No change to KV-connector contracts, structured-output backends, or the scheduler itself.

### What other serving engines do

* **SGLang** - scheduler loop busy-spins by default; opt-in `--sleep-on-idle` switches to `zmq.Poller.poll(1000)`. No cross-rank wake signal, so `--sleep-on-idle` is effectively incompatible with DP+EP (idle ranks can stall peers in the per-step collective for up to 1 s).
* **TokenSpeed** - unconditional spin; no blocking path. DP coordination is a per-step CPU-group `all_gather` of rank state, with idle ranks running a dummy forward.
* **TensorRT-LLM** - block-waits at idle, but only on global rank 0. Request intake is centralized on rank 0; every step runs a global broadcast rooted at rank 0, and non-zero ranks sleep inside that collective. No coordinator process; the per-step broadcast is the wake-up.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Claude was used to help draft this RFC, with significant human editing/rework.

title: [RFC]: Debug observation for prefix-cache lookup boundary before request-level stats
author: gustavgauge
body:
### Motivation.

I’m trying to calibrate a narrow vLLM observability boundary, not propose a new serving API, scheduling policy, eviction policy, admission mechanism, offload mechanism, or external framework.

Current read: vLLM exposes useful request/prefill-level prefix-cache signals, including cached-token counts. However, I do not see a native debug record that identifies a specific prefix-cache lookup with:

- lookup boundary,
- event order,
- cache/hash identity,
- local hit length,
- and bounded matched-prefix evidence or an opaque correlation handle.

Is that read wrong? Is there already a native vLLM event, trace field, invariant, or debug artifact that lets a user distinguish:

> “this specific expected prefix span was observed at lookup under this cache/hash identity”

from:

> “this request had some cached tokens”?

The motivating debugging cases are ordinary prefix-cache cases:

- a nonzero cached-token count that may be shorter than the expected prefix;
- a hit from a different cache/hash domain or configuration than the one being debugged;
- repeated lookup paths caused by chunking, batching, retries, or scheduling behavior;
- a user or external debugger needing to know which lookup produced the cached-token count without requiring vLLM to own external semantics.

The goal is not to replace existing cached-token counters. The goal is to understand whether the lookup-level evidence behind those counters is already available, and if not, whether a small disabled-by-default debug observation would be useful.

### Proposed Change.

One concrete boundary I am considering is in the V1 KV cache manager path, immediately after:

```python
coordinator.find_longest_cache_hit(request.block_hashes, max_cache_hit_length)
```

inside:

```text
vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_manager.KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks
```

and before prefix-cache stats recording or later scheduling/allocation effects reinterpret the result.

A possible boundary label would be:

```text
after_find_longest_cache_hit_before_stats
```

I am not attached to this owner or label. A useful answer would be that the observation belongs closer to the prefix-cache coordinator, metrics, tracing, KV events, or another existing debug surface.

The payload I have in mind is disabled by default and debug/trace-only. It might include:

- request id;
- lookup boundary;
- event order;
- local cached-token count from this lookup;
- block size / cache-hash-domain identity where safe;
- bounded matched-prefix summary or opaque handle;
- truncation state.

I would prefer an opaque handle if exposing any matched block-hash summary is unsafe or too unstable.

Non-goals:

- not a serving API;
- not a scheduler API;
- not a cache policy;
- not an eviction policy;
- not an admission mechanism;
- not an offload mechanism;
- not a performance claim;
- not a request for vLLM to own external semantic predicates.

The native event should not need to emit external predicate ids, materialization outcomes, or tool-specific adapter state. External tools can join a generic lookup observation to their own expected prefix span or threshold outside vLLM.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is the evidence gap above real, or is there already a native vLLM surface I missed?
2. If the gap is real, is `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` after `find_longest_cache_hit(...)` a reasonable observation boundary?
3. Would maintainers prefer this as structured logging, tracing, KV events, metrics, or not in vLLM at all?

Useful feedback would be: “existing field X already solves this,” “wrong boundary,” “payload unsafe,” “use a different trace surface,” or “not useful for vLLM.”

### Feedback Period.

At least one week. I am mainly looking for boundary/falsification feedback before attempting any implementation.

Useful outcomes include:

- existing native evidence I missed;
- a better observation boundary;
- a safer payload shape;
- a preferred trace/log/metrics/KV-event surface;
- or a clear signal that this is not useful for vLLM.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

This RFC is intentionally narrow. It is not asking vLLM to adopt an external framework or own external materialization predicates.

I also checked the docs chatbot; it did not identify an existing public debug event/API for lookup boundary, cache/hash identity, or matched-prefix evidence behind `num_cached_tokens`.

I am happy to reduce this to a documentation/debugging question if maintainers think the existing surface already provides the relevant evidence.

title: [RFC]: Deprecate `kv_both` for NIXLConnector and Enforce Explicit P/D Roles
author: NickLucche
body:
### Motivation.

Today, NIXL P/D instances are all configured with kv_role: "kv_both". The actual prefill-vs-decode behavior is determined by incoming request at runtime, via kv_transfer_params (do_remote_prefill / do_remote_decode). This means there is no reliable way for an instance to know whether it is a P or D before the handshake.

In practice, to the best of my knowledge, kv_both does not provide real value:

Instances are never re-purposed at runtime. P and D are already started with distinct configurations: low-latency/high-throughput, different tensor-parallel degrees, or even different GPU types. 
The proxy maintains separate P and D endpoint lists. 
I have observed no real-world scenario where a running P instance gets repurposed as D or vice versa.
If such a need exist please comment on this RFC! :) 

Role ambiguity blocks config-time optimizations. Any optimization that depends on knowing producer vs consumer semantics -- memory allocation strategies, model loading decisions, scheduler behavior -- must either be deferred to request time (adding per-request overhead) or resort to brittle heuristics like `num_computed_tokens == 0` to infer role.

Other connectors already enforce roles. MooncakeConnector, LMCacheConnector, and others already expect explicit kv_producer / kv_consumer roles. NIXL is the outlier.

### Proposed Change.

### Phase 1: Deprecation warning (non-breaking)
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43874

NIXLConnector validates kv_role at init:

- kv_producer or kv_consumer: recorded and used going forward.
- kv_both: logs a deprecation warning pointing to the migration guide, then continues with today's behavior. No functional change for existing deployments

The kv_both literal remains valid in the KVRole type system -- offloading, LMCache, FlexKV, and other connectors that genuinely need dual-role semantics are unaffected. The deprecation is NIXL-specific.

**Migration cost for operators (llm-d/dynamo)**: one config field change per instance. Since the proxy already separates P and D endpoint lists, operators already know which instances serve which role.

### Phase 2: Role-aware optimizations
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45280
- [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45283

With the role known at config time, a number of optimizations become possible:

**Code clarity**: not an optimization per-se, but a lot of the confusion in reading/maintaining NIXL code stems from unclear distinction in code between P/D/Shared behavior.
**Speculative decoding asymmetry:** P can auto-adjust its speculator config (e.g. set num_speculative_tokens = 1) and skip sampling since it never uses draft tokens. This would enable PR such as #39266 to skip proposing using a clear "is_producer" interface.
This eliminates the block-count mismatch that currently requires a scheduler-level workaround (#22317) and avoids regressions for other spec-decode methods (#43733) .
Future optimizations. Any P-vs-D asymmetric behavior (chunked transfer strategies, priority scheduling, health-check semantics) can be cleanly gated on role.

### Phase 3: Hard deprecation (breaking)
After a deprecation period (2/3 minor releases), NIXL rejects kv_both with a clear error message pointing to the migration guide.

### Feedback Period.

1 week

### CC List.

@youkaichao @robertgshaw2-redhat @markmc @benchislett @snadampal @ZhanqiuHu @TheEpicDolphin

_No response_

title: [RFC]:  Move trainer-side weight transfer logic out of `vllm`
author: SumanthRH
body:
### Motivation.

The new vLLM weight transfer APIs were introduced in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31943 (`vllm/distributed/weight_transfer/`). They give RL frameworks a standard way to sync updated weights from a trainer process into running vLLM workers, with pluggable backends (NCCL, CUDA IPC, etc.).

Today, a backend is implemented by subclassing `WeightTransferEngine` and providing the below methods:

```python
class MyWeightTransferEngine(WeightTransferEngine):
    init_info_cls = MyInitInfo
    update_info_cls = MyUpdateInfo

    # vLLM-side (receive)
    def init_transfer_engine(self, init_info: MyInitInfo): ...

    def receive_weights(
        self,
        update_info: MyUpdateInfo,
        load_weights: Callable[[list[tuple[str, Tensor]]], None],
    ): ...

    # Trainer-side (send) — called from the RL framework
    @staticmethod
    def trainer_send_weights(
        iterator: Iterator[tuple[str, Tensor]],
        trainer_args: dict[str, Any] | Any,
    ): ...
```

`init_transfer_engine` and `receive_weights` are vLLM-side logic for setting up transport and receiving weights into the worker. `trainer_send_weights` (and on `NCCLWeightTransferEngine` also `trainer_init`) is a helper meant to be called from the trainer process to send weights to all inference workers.

There are two issues with bundling the trainer-side helper inside vLLM's engine class:

1. **The abstraction conflates send and receive.** `WeightTransferEngine` should be a vLLM-side abstraction concerned only with receive logic. Putting send logic on the same class makes the API harder to reason about, and individual subclasses have already grown extra static methods that exist only for the trainer side (e.g. `NCCLWeightTransferEngine.trainer_init`).

2. **`trainer_send_weights` is too prescriptive.** Its signature is tied to a `(name, tensor)` iterator for example. RL frameworks have diverse needs around how a state dict is materialized and chunked. A single static method on a vLLM class is the wrong place to standardize this functionality.

More broadly: even though `trainer_send_weights` is not required (frameworks can implement their own send path today), adding it as part of the public engine API can imply that this *is* the way to send weights. This is not what we want.

### Proposed Change.


Move the trainer-side helpers fully out of the `vllm` package.

Concretely:

- Remove `WeightTransferEngine.trainer_send_weights` from the base class and from all subclasses (`NCCLWeightTransferEngine`, `IPCWeightTransferEngine`).
- Remove `NCCLWeightTransferEngine.trainer_init` (and any similar trainer-only helpers on other backends).
- Keep on `WeightTransferEngine` only the receive-side contract: `__init__`, `parse_init_info`, `parse_update_info`, `init_transfer_engine`, `receive_weights`, `shutdown`.
- Keep the backend-specific request/info dataclasses (`*InitInfo`, `*UpdateInfo`) where they are. They define the wire format between trainer and vLLM and remain part of the vLLM public API.
- Provide **one reference implementation per backend** under `examples/rl/` (or a sibling `examples/rl/weight_transfer/`) that shows the trainer-side counterpart. The existing example scripts (`rlhf_nccl.py`, `rlhf_ipc.py`, `rlhf_http_nccl.py`, `rlhf_http_ipc.py`, etc.) already call the helpers and will be updated to use the new in-example abstractions.

We still want this reference implementation in the vLLM repo and well tested. For example, `NCCLWeightTransferEngine` uses `packed_nccl_broadcast_consumer` helper function and it's better for trainer rank-0 sender to use the corresponding `packed_nccl_broadcast_producer` method to be consistent.

### Migration

This is a breaking change for users who import `trainer_send_weights` / `trainer_init` directly.

Given the APIs are new (introduced in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31943 and not yet broadly adopted), I think they can be removed outright rather than going through a proper deprecation.

## Example for NCCL

The reference trainer-side class for NCCL becomes:

```python
# examples/rl/weight_transfer/nccl_sender.py
class NCCLBroadcastSender:
    def __init__(
        self,
        master_address: str,
        master_port: int,
        world_size: int,
        packed: bool = False,
        packed_buffer_size_bytes: int = DEFAULT_PACKED_BUFFER_SIZE_BYTES,
        packed_num_buffers: int = DEFAULT_PACKED_NUM_BUFFERS,
    ):
        # Trainer is rank 0 in the stateless process group shared with vLLM workers.
        device = torch.accelerator.current_device_index()
        pg = StatelessProcessGroup.create(
            host=master_address, port=master_port, rank=0, world_size=world_size,
        )
        self.group = PyNcclCommunicator(pg, device=device)
        self.packed = packed
        self.packed_buffer_size_bytes = packed_buffer_size_bytes
        self.packed_num_buffers = packed_num_buffers

    def send_weights(
        self,
        iterator: Iterator[tuple[str, torch.Tensor]],
    ):
        if self.packed:
            packed_nccl_broadcast_producer(
                iterator=iterator, group=self.group, src=0,
                post_iter_func=lambda item: item[1],
                buffer_size_bytes=self.packed_buffer_size_bytes,
                num_buffers=self.packed_num_buffers,
            )
        else:
            for _, tensor in iterator:
                self.group.broadcast(tensor, src=0, stream=torch.cuda.current_stream())
```

The example imports `StatelessProcessGroup`, `PyNcclCommunicator`, and the packed broadcast producer from `vllm`. 

### Feedback Period.

1 week

### CC List.

@hao-aaron  @aoshen02 @robertgshaw2-redhat @kouroshHakha 

### Any Other Things.

## Alternative Designs

The other alternative design is to create a separate `WeightTransferSender` abstraction in vLLM that will only encapsulate the send logic from the trainer - that way we decouple send and receive. However, this will still be trying to standardize trainer side logic as a vLLM API and will be counter-productive.

title: [RFC] External post-generation classifier hook API
author: geodesia-ai
body:
## Motivation

Many production deployments need to attach a post-generation classifier to vLLM so that every completion is scored for safety, hallucination, audit, or A/B routing before the response is returned to the client. Today the only ways to do this are:

1. Monkey-patch `build_app()` in `vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server` to inject a Starlette middleware that wraps the response. Fragile across vLLM minor releases and breaks `streaming=True` because the response body is already partially flushed by the time the middleware sees it.
2. Run vLLM behind a reverse proxy that re-parses the OpenAI JSON, calls the classifier, and re-serializes. Doubles the request latency and loses access to per-engine signals (prompt logprobs, KV state, etc).
3. Subclass `OpenAIServingChat` / `OpenAIServingCompletion` and override `create_chat_completion`. Survives one or two releases at most because vLLM iterates fast on those classes.

None of these survive a vLLM upgrade comfortably. The current state pushes safety vendors into vLLM-version pinning and that hurts the ecosystem.

What is missing is a small, public, opt-in hook surface where an external classifier registers a callable that receives the request, the generated text, and the engine's metadata for that request, and either returns scores (non-blocking) or returns a decision (blocking, with an optional replacement body).

## Proposed API

```python
from typing import Protocol, Optional, Any

class ScoringContext:
    request_id: str
    prompt: str
    generated_text: str
    extra_fields: dict[str, Any]   # from OpenAIBaseModel.get_extra_fields()
    finish_reason: str
    prompt_token_ids: list[int]
    output_token_ids: list[int]
    request_metadata: dict[str, Any]   # opaque per-request state

class ExternalClassifierHook(Protocol):
    name: str
    blocking: bool                  # True = decision; False = annotation only
    timeout_ms: int                 # per-call timeout

    async def score(self, ctx: ScoringContext) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Return a dict of scores. If `blocking` is True and the dict
        contains the key 'block' with a truthy value, the response is
        replaced with `dict['replacement']` or with a default refusal."""
        ...

# Registration on LLMEngine / AsyncLLMEngine:
engine.register_external_classifier_hook(hook)

# Propagation: every classifier's output appears under
# RequestOutput.metadata["external_scores"][hook.name].
```

## Lifecycle

1. Generation completes (or finishes a token boundary, for streaming).
2. The engine builds a `ScoringContext`.
3. All registered hooks are invoked concurrently with `asyncio.gather`, each bounded by its declared timeout.
4. Hook return values are merged into `RequestOutput.metadata["external_scores"]`.
5. If any blocking hook returned a "block" decision, the response is replaced before serialization.
6. The OpenAI serving layer serializes the modified response.

For streaming responses, blocking hooks are invoked at end-of-stream and can replace the final chunk only. Hooks that want to inspect mid-stream tokens go through the (future) forward-hook API, not this one.

## Non-goals

* Mid-stream token mutation. That belongs in a separate RFC about the forward-hook API.
* Synchronous hooks. Everything is async to allow concurrent classifiers without head-of-line blocking.
* Registering hooks via env var or CLI. Registration is programmatic (`engine.register_external_classifier_hook(hook)`) and is meant to be invoked by a `vllm.general_plugins` entry-point.
* New auth/quota surface. Hooks run with the same trust level as the engine; vendors are expected to harden their own hook code.

## Alternatives considered

* Middleware-only. Cannot see prompt_token_ids, prompt logprobs, or the per-request metadata the engine keeps. Also bypassed for `/v1/completions` raw text path.
* gRPC sidecar. Adds a hop, complicates deployment, and makes the per-token APIs (logprobs) unavailable.
* RequestOutput post-processor decorator. Closer in spirit but does not address streaming or the blocking case, and forces every consumer to register at app build time.

## Open questions

1. Should `score()` be allowed to set sampling parameters for a retry? Useful for "if the first generation was flagged, regenerate at temperature=0" but it complicates the contract considerably.
2. Should hook outputs be serialized into the OpenAI response automatically (under a `metadata` field) or kept on the Python side only? My current preference is the latter so that we do not pollute the OpenAI schema.
3. Where exactly to mount the registration: on `LLMEngine`, on `AsyncLLMEngine`, on the `OpenAIServing*` classes, or all of the above? My current preference is `AsyncLLMEngine` because that is what every entrypoint constructs and it shares the lifetime of the engine.
4. Should the hook be allowed to access the KV cache? Probably no for v1, yes for a future RFC.

## Prior art

* Anthropic's "guardrails" approach, conceptually similar but server-internal.
* NeMo Guardrails, runs in front of the model; this RFC would let it run inside.
* Llama Guard, currently has to be wired manually by every vLLM user.

Happy to iterate on the shape. The minimum viable API for me is "an async callable that runs after generation and whose output ends up on `RequestOutput.metadata`". Everything else (timeouts, blocking semantics, replacement body) is negotiable.

title: [RFC]: Offloading Metrics Redesign
author: Srinivasoo7
body:
### Motivation.

The offloading connector currently treats metrics as a transfer-specific concern. That worked while the only exposed metrics were load/store bytes, time, and size, but it does not scale well as offloading managers start exposing their own state.

The immediate example is `vllm:kv_offload_stores_skipped`, which is emitted by the CPU offloading manager when a store is skipped because the reuse threshold is not reached. A near-term follow-up is a CPU KV offload cache usage gauge. These metrics are not transfer operations, so adding them through the existing hard-coded transfer metrics path would keep expanding special cases in the connector.

We need a general offloading metrics path where connector metrics and manager metrics are declared as metadata, registered up front, and observed through the same counter/gauge/histogram machinery. This also makes aggregation semantics explicit: counters are summed, gauges keep the latest value, and histograms accumulate observations.

At the same time, offloading metrics are part of vLLM's public Prometheus surface. Existing metrics such as `vllm:kv_offload_total_bytes`, `vllm:kv_offload_total_time`, and `vllm:kv_offload_size` may already be used by dashboards, alerts, or autoscaling rules. The redesign should therefore improve the internal model and introduce clearer flat metrics without silently removing or renaming existing public metrics. 

### Proposed Change.

## Summary

This RFC proposes a metadata-driven metrics design for the KV offloading connector and offloading managers. The goal is to make offloading metrics general enough for counters, gauges, and histograms while preserving the public Prometheus metrics contract that users may already rely on.

The immediate motivation is the `stores_skipped` metric for CPU offloading. The next expected metric is a CPU KV offload cache usage gauge. The current connector metrics path is hard-coded around transfer statistics, so adding more manager-specific metrics would keep increasing special-case code unless we redesign the path first.

PR: #35669 #43877 

## Background

The current offloading connector exposes transfer metrics as labelled Prometheus metrics:

- `vllm:kv_offload_total_bytes{transfer_type=...}`
- `vllm:kv_offload_total_time{transfer_type=...}`
- `vllm:kv_offload_size{transfer_type=...}`

Internally, the recent flat-metrics work moved toward representing transfer stats and manager stats as metric-name keyed payloads. Review discussion then raised three design requirements:
- Offloading managers should be able to declare their own metrics, not just counters.
- Metrics should be registered up front from metadata, rather than lazily created or discovered during `observe()`.
- Existing public metrics should not be removed casually. If they are ever replaced, the vLLM metrics deprecation process should be followed.

## Goals

- Provide one offloading metrics path for counters, gauges, and histograms.
- Let each `OffloadingManager` define the metrics it emits.
- Let the offloading connector define transfer metrics through the same metadata model.
- Use a flat stats payload, with metric names as keys.
- Make aggregation semantics explicit by metric type.
- Register Prometheus metrics and per-engine labelled children during initialization.
- Preserve existing labelled transfer metrics while introducing any new metric names.
- Support tiered offloading managers that may need the full `OffloadingSpec` when deciding which metrics to expose.

## Non-Goals

- This RFC does not redesign all vLLM metrics.
- This RFC does not remove existing offloading transfer metrics.
- This RFC does not finalize the exact public name for the CPU KV offload cache usage gauge.
- This RFC does not change unrelated metrics such as prefix-cache metrics, request latency metrics, speculative decoding metrics, or KV block sampling metrics.

## Scope

In scope:

- Offloading connector transfer metrics.
- Offloading manager metrics emitted through the offloading connector.
- Internal `OffloadingConnectorStats` aggregation and reduction semantics.
- Prometheus registration for offloading connector metrics.
- Compatibility behavior for legacy offloading transfer metrics.

Out of scope:

- General server/request metrics.
- HTTP metrics.
- NIXL-specific metrics.
- Prefix-cache metrics.
- The legacy swapped-preemption metrics, except where CPU cache usage naming overlaps with historical metrics.

## Existing Public Metrics

The following public metrics already exist and should continue to be emitted
during the redesign:

| Metric | Type | Labels | Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `vllm:kv_offload_total_bytes` | Counter | `transfer_type` | Total bytes transferred by the offloading connector |
| `vllm:kv_offload_total_time` | Counter | `transfer_type` | Total transfer time measured by offloading operations |
| `vllm:kv_offload_size` | Histogram | `transfer_type` | Distribution of KV offload transfer sizes |

The current `transfer_type` values are:

- `CPU_to_GPU`
- `GPU_to_CPU`

These names are not ideal because each metric mixes load and store semantics behind a label, but they are public metrics. Mark's feedback was that removing or replacing them based on an assumption that nobody depends on them is not acceptable. This RFC therefore treats compatibility as a design requirement.

## Proposed Public Metrics

The redesigned connector can expose clearer flat transfer metrics:

| Metric | Type | Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes` | Counter | Total bytes loaded from offload storage to GPU |
| `vllm:kv_offload_load_time` | Counter | Total load time from offload storage to GPU, in seconds |
| `vllm:kv_offload_load_size` | Histogram | Per-operation load size distribution |
| `vllm:kv_offload_store_bytes` | Counter | Total bytes stored from GPU to offload storage |
| `vllm:kv_offload_store_time` | Counter | Total store time from GPU to offload storage, in seconds |
| `vllm:kv_offload_store_size` | Histogram | Per-operation store size distribution |

Manager-defined metrics are also represented in the same registry. Known
examples:

| Metric | Type | Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vllm:kv_offload_stores_skipped` | Counter | Number of KV offload stores skipped because the reuse threshold was not reached |
| TBD CPU KV cache usage metric | Gauge | Current CPU KV offload cache usage |

The CPU KV cache usage metric needs a final naming decision. It should either use a new `vllm:kv_offload_*` name, or explicitly follow the deprecation policy if it is intended to replace or supersede an older CPU cache metric such as `vllm:cpu_cache_usage_perc`.

## Metric Metadata

Offloading metrics should be described with subclasses instead of a generic `metric_type` discriminator:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OffloadingMetricMetadata:
    documentation: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OffloadingCounterMetadata(OffloadingMetricMetadata):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OffloadingGaugeMetadata(OffloadingMetricMetadata):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OffloadingHistogramMetadata(OffloadingMetricMetadata):
    buckets: tuple[float, ...] | None = None
```

Metric names are the dictionary keys:

```python
{
    "vllm:kv_offload_store_bytes": OffloadingCounterMetadata(...),
    "vllm:kv_offload_store_size": OffloadingHistogramMetadata(...),
}
```

This keeps histogram-specific fields on the histogram subclass and avoids duplicating the metric name inside the metadata object.

## OffloadingSpec and OffloadingManager API

`OffloadingSpec` should own the resolved manager metric definitions:

```python
class OffloadingSpec(ABC):
    metric_definitions: dict[str, OffloadingMetricMetadata]

    @classmethod
    @abstractmethod
    def get_manager_cls(cls) -> type[OffloadingManager]:
        ...
```

During spec initialization:

```python
self.metric_definitions = self.get_manager_cls().get_metric_definitions(self)
```

Managers should receive their resolved metric definitions at construction time:

```python
class OffloadingManager(ABC):
    def __init__(
        self,
        metric_definitions: dict[str, OffloadingMetricMetadata] | None = None,
    ):
        self.metric_definitions = metric_definitions or {}

    @classmethod
    def get_metric_definitions(
        cls,
        spec: OffloadingSpec,
    ) -> dict[str, OffloadingMetricMetadata]:
        return {}

    def get_stats(self) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
        return None
```

The thought is to align that metric definitions should be available from the spec/manager relationship and that `OffloadingSpec` should be passed instead of only `VllmConfig`. The spec contains `vllm_config` but can also carry
resolved offloading-specific configuration such as block sizing, tiering configuration, and future manager-specific state.

`None` is the default no-stats return value for managers. Managers should avoid returning `{}` in the common case where they have no metrics to emit.

## Flat Stats Payload

`OffloadingConnectorStats.data` should use metric names directly as flat keys:

```python
{
    "vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes": 1234,
    "vllm:kv_offload_load_size": [1024, 2048],
    "vllm:kv_offload_stores_skipped": 3,
}
```

The stats payload should not use type prefixes such as `counter:` or `histogram:`. Type information comes from the metadata registry. Prefixes would duplicate metadata, require string parsing on the observation path, and make
unknown-key validation less direct. Flat metric-name keys keep the payload close to the Prometheus surface while still allowing strict type checks through the registry.

## Aggregation and Reduction Semantics

Aggregation must be metadata-driven:

| Metric type | `aggregate()` behavior | `reduce()` behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Counter | Sum increments | Return summed value |
| Gauge | Keep latest observed value | Return latest value |
| Histogram | Concatenate samples | Return count and sum for logging; observe each sample in Prometheus |

This avoids branching based on Python value shape. Lists are valid for histograms, scalars are valid for counters/gauges, and unknown metric keys should fail fast.

## Stats Emission Semantics

Worker-side and scheduler-side offloading stats are both valid sources:

- Worker-side stats report transfer metrics collected around asynchronous load and store operations.
- Scheduler-side stats report connector/manager metrics that are only known after scheduler state has been updated.

The scheduler stats path should support three cases:

- worker-side stats only
- scheduler-side stats only
- both worker-side and scheduler-side stats

When both exist, they should be aggregated with the same metadata-driven semantics described above. This refers to transfer stats forwarded from the worker and manager stats collected on the scheduler side within the same connector, not two simultaneously active connector instances. Collection order matters: scheduler-side connector stats should be collected after `update_connector_output()` has run, so manager state reflects the current worker output before stats are emitted.

Long term, `get_kv_connector_stats()` should return `None` when there are no stats to emit. During compatibility work, an empty stats object may be used as a temporary bridge only where the current scheduler aggregation path requires a worker-side stats object before scheduler-side stats can be included. The dedicated scheduler fix should remove the need for that workaround by allowing scheduler-side-only stats directly.

## Prometheus Registration

`OffloadPromMetrics.__init__` should build a complete registry from:

- connector metric definitions
- selected spec's manager metric definitions

It should create all Prometheus metric objects and per-engine labelled children up front. `observe()` should then do only:

1. Look up the metric metadata by key.
2. Validate the observed value type.
3. Dispatch to `inc`, `set`, or `observe`.
4. Update compatibility metrics when applicable.

This removes lazy metric creation, prefix parsing, and string slicing from the hot path.

## Compatibility Metrics

The implementation should update the old labelled metrics from the same flat stats payload:

| New flat metric | Existing compatibility metric |
| --- | --- |
| `vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes` | `vllm:kv_offload_total_bytes{transfer_type="CPU_to_GPU"}` |
| `vllm:kv_offload_load_time` | `vllm:kv_offload_total_time{transfer_type="CPU_to_GPU"}` |
| `vllm:kv_offload_load_size` | `vllm:kv_offload_size{transfer_type="CPU_to_GPU"}` |
| `vllm:kv_offload_store_bytes` | `vllm:kv_offload_total_bytes{transfer_type="GPU_to_CPU"}` |
| `vllm:kv_offload_store_time` | `vllm:kv_offload_total_time{transfer_type="GPU_to_CPU"}` |
| `vllm:kv_offload_store_size` | `vllm:kv_offload_size{transfer_type="GPU_to_CPU"}` |

Compatibility metrics should be emitted for CPU offloading while the existing public metrics are supported. If other offloading managers start using the same connector transfer metrics, we should decide whether the legacy CPU/GPU `transfer_type` labels are semantically correct for them before emitting the old metrics there too.

## Deprecation Plan

The vLLM metrics documentation says metric deprecation should be handled carefully because users may only notice after a release breaks dashboards or autoscaling. The policy calls for clear `/metrics` help text, documentation, release notes, and an escape hatch for hidden metrics.

This RFC proposes the following phased approach:

1. Add the metadata registry and flat metrics.
2. Continue emitting the existing labelled metrics.
3. Add manager-defined metrics through the registry, including `vllm:kv_offload_stores_skipped`.
4. Add the CPU KV offload cache usage gauge as a follow-up using the same registry.
5. If the community agrees to deprecate the existing labelled metrics, update metric help strings, docs, and release notes with the target removal version.
6. Hide deprecated metrics only after the documented grace period, with the project-standard escape hatch.
7. Remove deprecated metrics only after the policy-compliant period has elapsed.


## Implementation Plan

1. Define metric metadata subclasses in `vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py`.
2. Add `OffloadingSpec.get_manager_cls()`.
3. Add `OffloadingSpec.metric_definitions`, populated from `get_manager_cls().get_metric_definitions(spec)`.
4. Add `OffloadingManager.__init__(metric_definitions=...)`.
5. Pass `spec.metric_definitions` into concrete manager constructors.
6. Define connector transfer metric definitions in one place.
7. Convert `OffloadingConnectorStats` to flat metric-name keys.
8. Implement metadata-driven aggregation and reduction.
9. Build Prometheus metric objects and observer mappings during `OffloadPromMetrics.__init__`.
10. Emit both flat transfer metrics and compatibility labelled metrics.
11. Add `stores_skipped` as the first manager-defined counter.
12. Add the CPU KV offload cache usage gauge in a follow-up.
13. Once scheduler-side-only stats aggregation is supported, update `get_kv_connector_stats()` and manager stats plumbing so no-stats paths return `None` instead of an empty stats object.

## Test Plan

Add or update tests for:

- Counter aggregation.
- Gauge aggregation using latest value.
- Histogram aggregation using concatenated samples.
- Unknown metric key failure.
- Prometheus registration for counters, gauges, and histograms.
- Existing labelled transfer metrics still being observed.
- Manager metric definitions being discovered through `OffloadingSpec`.
- Manager stats emitted through the connector scheduler path.
- Scheduler-side and worker-side connector stats being aggregated correctly.
- CPU KV cache usage gauge once implemented.

Suggested placement:

- Offloading stats and Prometheus registry tests should live under the offloading connector unit tests.
- Scheduler aggregation/order tests should live in `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py` and cover scheduler-side only, worker-side only, and both in one focused test.

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Hard-Coded Transfer Metrics

This has the lowest immediate churn, but it leaves every new offloading manager metric as a special case.

### Remove the Existing Labelled Metrics Immediately

This gives the cleanest final public surface, but it violates the spirit of the metrics deprecation policy and risks breaking existing dashboards.

### Prefix Internal Stat Keys by Type

Prefixes such as `counter:` and `histogram:` make dispatch easy, but duplicate information already present in metadata and make the payload less natural.

## Open Questions

- What exact name should the CPU KV offload cache usage gauge use?
- Should CPU cache usage be a percentage, bytes, block count, or more than one metric?
- Should compatibility labelled metrics be emitted only for CPU offloading, or
  for all offloading managers that use load/store transfer metrics?
- What release should begin deprecation, if we decide to deprecate the labelled transfer metrics?
- Should we add a feature flag before hiding/removing any compatibility metric,
  or rely on the project-wide hidden metrics escape hatch?


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@orozery 
@markmc 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: vLLM NaN Reporting
author: elvircrn
body:
# RFC: KV Cache NaN Detection

## Motivation

We discovered that R1 NVFP4 had issues with NaNs in the forward pass. While debugging, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43318 was created to aid debugging, which helped us find and fix the following NaN-inducing bugs:

* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39444: dummy run writing NaN to KV cache null block
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/38148: FP8 scale buffers allocated with torch.empty instead of torch.zeros
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42984: SiLU-Mul quant kernel spreading NaN across row boundaries
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40047: broader sweep of kernels spreading NaN across rows (silu_and_mul_scaled_nvfp4_experts_quantize, scaled_fp4_grouped_quantize)
* https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/issues/621: DeepEP low-latency combine race condition producing incorrect results at batch size 512+
* https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/632: proposed fix for the above
* https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/2861: FlashInfer mm_fp4 NaN sensitivity with 8x4 SF layout
* https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3103: grouped_gemm_nt_masked spreading NaN across row boundaries
* https://github.com/tlrmchlsmth/vllm/pull/33: CUDA graph NaN padding tests for attention/MoE/per-token ops

Also related: https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/issues/1974, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/35219

The main challenge when debugging NaNs in logits is **causality**. When a NaN gets into the KV cache by any of the above mechanisms, it produces NaNs at the next generation step. By the time the NaN shows up in logits, the originating layer, phase, and step are lost. Therefore, causality is the most important design goal for this RFC.

`VLLM_COMPUTE_NANS_IN_LOGITS=1` added logits NaN reporting in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/30187. We wanted to expand on this capability, so we created https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43318 which covers broad kernel-side NaN/Inf detection and was used to debug the above issues. It won't get merged since it was hacked up together and is too intrusive. However, the following Grafana dashboard was created using metrics generated by that PR:

![KV Cache NaN Debug Dashboard](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/aca0e4c8-e59c-4a6b-9944-dd00be9554a2)

Ideally the dashboard should tell us which kernel, in which layer, on which rank, in which phase (prefill/decode) introduced the first NaN into the system. Reporting should distinguish between NaNs in padded vs non-padded regions so that operators can tell whether a NaN originated from CUDA graph padding or from real data.

### Proposed Change.

## Proposed Change

To address causality, we intercept NaN writes at the KV cache rather than observing them after the fact in logits. All phases must work with full CUDA graph capture/replay and have low enough overhead to debug issues that only reproduce under high concurrency or performance-sensitive conditions. We propose splitting the work into mergeable phases:

**Phase 1: MLA KV cache NaN write detection**: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43880 (ready for review)

Detect NaN source values being written to KV cache in `concat_and_cache_mla`, gated by `VLLM_DEBUG_MLA_CACHE=1`. Zero overhead when disabled. Full CUDA graph support. Prometheus counter `vllm:kv_cache_nans` with `layer` and `phase` labels. Tracks which layer/phase introduced the first NaN.

**Phase 2: Broader KV cache write detection**

Extend detection to `reshape_and_cache_flash` and other cache write kernels, covering non-MLA attention backends.

**Phase 3: Op-level NaN debugging utilities**

Decorators/utilities for wrapping arbitrary ops with NaN input/output checks. The prototype in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43318 proved this is valuable during bringup but requires manual insertion in the model forward pass. This makes extending models more difficult and the NaN reporting becomes a nuisance to work around when it is only needed for debugging.

**Phase 4: CUDA graph augmentation**

Detect NaN injection from CUDA graph padding at runtime.

Phases 3 and 4 are not clear on how best to be approached. Feedback and ideas are welcome.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

_No response_

title: [RFC]: hardware agnostic model definitions in vLLM
author: zou3519
body:
### Motivation.

This is a direct follow up to https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42770, which proposes removing full model torch.compile from vLLM and proposes separating model definitions by hardware type in vLLM.

While the [vLLM models proposal](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42770) addresses a lot of the concerns related to achieving maximum performance for the most popular models on the most popular hardware (specifically measured as how many GW of power is expected to be used for inference overall for the next of couple months) it makes supporting a wide set of models and hardwares more challenging.

In this follow up, we argue that this proposal doesn’t completely serve the whole userbase. In particular:

- There is significant interest in the community for alternative hardwares. We think giving users more choice is good for the community in the long-term.
- Supporting many hardwares across many models is a challenging task; we think sharing parts of the stack between hardware is the simplest and most reliable way to do this. 

We propose to embrace this view of the world while setting appropriate boundaries to ensure this will not get in the way of the top GW users’ optimization.



### Proposed Change.

There should be a hardware-agnostic model definition for all models that is maintained by the community in the core vLLM repository. Hardware backends can choose to use this model definition or they can choose to create their own model definition (as per [the vLLM models proposal](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42770))

For tail models: this is keeping the existing vLLM hardware-agnostic model definitions and the CustomOp mechanism in vLLM.
For head models: this is accepting a hardware-agnostic model definition and PRs to CustomOp-ify it.

There are some options for how we can do this. The first is a hardware agnostic model definition that lives alongside the other models:

```
models/
    deepseek_v4/
        nvidia/
            model.py
        amd/
            model.py
        hw_agnostic/
            model.py
    ...
```


Another option could be just to separate it out the existing code into its own folder and spin off a new folder for the new hardware-specific code:

```
vllm/
    model_executor_hw_specific/
      # new path for best perf on specified HW - nv, amd, xpu
      layers/
      kernels/
      models/
      ...
    model_executor_hw_agnostic/
      # could rename/refactor current model_executor to model_executor_hw_agnostic
      # this folder maintained by the community
      layers/
      models/
      custom_op.py
      ...
```

## Maintenance

We're hoping that some combination of the folks who will benefit from these hardware agnostic model definitions (e.g. hardware vendors, model providers, pytorch team) will coordinate to maintain them.

## Requirements

- The model definition **should be hardware agnostic** and be testable in core vLLM. The definition of hardware agnostic is:
    - The model uses native torch ops
    - The model uses custom ops (see next point) that can be abstracted and designed for dispatch to different hardware platforms.
- **We should keep the CustomOp mechanism** and allow people to add more CustomOps. CustomOp has generally been a good way to identify “operator” boundaries that when backends provide implementations for said operators, it can result in decent performance.
    - This might evolve into vLLM IR style of CustomOp management, because vLLM IR is supposed to be an upgrade to the CustomOp system.
- The model definition should **support fullgraph capture** (with torch.compile), because many alternative backends (TPU, Intel Gaudi, IBM Spyre, CPU) benefit heavily from a fullgraph capture.
- **Isolation**: these hardware agnostic model definitions should not affect the hardware-specific (e.g. nvidia cuda) model definitions.

##  Alternatives

- Use HF Transformers backend. It is not clear if this will suffice. For example:
    - many popular models don’t work out of the box (gpt-oss-120b, qwen3.5, etc)
    - it does not have a CustomOp abstraction
    - it does not guarantee implementations are fullgraph capturable
    - we do see a perf gap from using HF transformers backend vs stock vLLM
- Maintain an out-of-tree set of model definitions. We could do this, but it seems like significantly more work (and maintenance cost) because vLLM already provides a long tail of hardware-agnostic model definitions in core.




### Feedback Period.

not sure

### CC List.

@WoosukKwon @tlrmchlsmth @mgoin @LucasWilkinson @ProExpertProg @ZJY0516 @albanD, @tdoublep, @raghukiran1224, @xuechendi, @claudio1212 

### Any Other Things.

Thanks to @albanD, @tdoublep, @raghukiran1224, @xuechendi, @claudio1212 and others (sorry I don't have all of your GitHub handles) for helping author and review an earlier draft of this RFC.
