@ivanium @stmatengss @Pz1116

title: [RFC]:  Profiler support for CUDA graph capture tracing and roofline trace annotations
author: devalshahamd
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM's PyTorch profiler integration today gives a good view of actual model execution under a real workload, but it has two gaps that make trace-driven performance analysis (especially attention roofline analysis) harder than it needs to be.

### 1. The CUDA graph capture phase is invisible to the profiler

When vLLM runs with CUDA graphs (`cudagraph_mode=FULL`, `PIECEWISE`, or `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`), the profiler trace of the actual workload records graph *replay*: the GPU kernels execute from a pre-recorded graph, so the replay trace has GPU kernels but **no CPU-side call stack and no input shapes** for the ops inside the graph. The CPU operators, python call stack, and tensor shapes only exist during the **graph capture phase** at server startup, which the profiler never sees today.

This means that for any deployment using full/piecewise CUDA graphs (the common production configuration), a profiler trace cannot attribute GPU time to module / op / shape without additional, manual instrumentation. The information needed to enrich the replay trace already exists at capture time; we simply do not record it.

### 2. The default execution-step annotation lacks the statistics needed for roofline analysis — even though vLLM already computes them

Each execution step is annotated via `torch.record_function`, but the default annotation only encodes request and token counts:

```
execute_context_1(839)_generation_63(63)
```

For variable-length batched inference, the per-step attention compute and memory traffic depend on more than token counts. As derived in the attention roofline model, the only per-request quantities that appear in the FLOPs / bytes formulas are `N_Q(i)`, `N_KV(i)`, and their products, and these can be reduced to a handful of **per-phase aggregates** (computed separately for context and generation requests):


| Aggregate        | Used in                                              |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `R_C`, `R_G`     | Request counts                                       |
| `Σ N_Q`          | Elements moved (Q read, output write)                |
| `Σ N_KV`         | Elements moved (K read, V read from paged KV cache)  |
| `Σ (N_Q · N_KV)` | FLOPs (full QKᵀ / score·V rectangle term)            |
| `Σ (N_Q²)`       | FLOPs (causal self-attention correction for prefill) |


Because the default annotation does not carry `Σ N_KV`, `Σ (N_Q·N_KV)`, or `Σ (N_Q²)`, an analyst cannot reconstruct the attention roofline (arithmetic intensity, achieved vs. peak FLOPs/bandwidth) for a step **directly from the trace**. They must re-run with detailed logging or correlate against scheduler state that is not present in the trace file.

The detailed annotation emits that same reduction into each step's `record_function` event. The consequence is that **all statistics needed for the roofline live in the single profiler trace file** — kernel timings, shapes, and per-step compute/memory aggregates co-located. This is also complementary to the capture trace, which supplies the graph-mode shapes/call-stacks for those same kernels.



### Proposed Change.

Add two **opt-in, default-off** `ProfilerConfig` flags (prototyped in PR #37524). Both are no-ops unless the torch profiler is enabled, so default behavior is unchanged.

### Flag 1: `capture_torch_profiler_dir` (str, default `""`)

Absolute path to a directory in which to write a PyTorch profiler trace of the **CUDA graph capture phase** (rank 0 only). Requires `--profiler-config.profiler torch`. When set, the capture workflow in `gpu_model_runner.py` wraps graph capture in a `torch.profiler` context (and `nullcontext()` otherwise), producing one trace per captured graph (batch size × compilation mode):

```
torch_trace/
|-- capture_traces
|   |-- graph_capture_rank_0.<...>.pt.trace.json.gz   # per captured graph
|   `-- ...
|-- <workload replay trace>.pt.trace.json.gz
`-- profiler_out_0.txt
```

These capture traces retain the CPU-side call stack and input shapes for every op that ends up inside a replayed CUDA graph. A downstream tool can match a replay step (by batch size / compilation mode) to its capture trace and back-fill shapes and call stacks onto the replay tree.

### Flag 2: `detailed_trace_annotation` (bool, default `False`)

When `True`, the `torch.record_function` annotation for each execution step is extended with per-phase roofline aggregates for context (prefill) and generation (decode) requests. The annotation **format/labels are unchanged from the current prototype** (this RFC does not propose changing the emitted string); variable names in the implementation were made more descriptive following review feedback.

Detailed format:

```
execute_886_context_1(sq824sk824sqsq678976sqsk678976)_generation_62(sq62sk93055sqsq62sqsk93055)
```

where, aggregated per phase:

- `sq`   = `Σ N_Q`        (scheduled/new tokens; Q read + output write traffic)
- `sk`   = `Σ N_KV`       (total KV length; K/V read traffic)
- `sqsq` = `Σ (N_Q · N_Q)` (causal self-attention correction term, dominant in pure prefill)
- `sqsk` = `Σ (N_Q · N_KV)` (QKᵀ / score·V compute term, dominant in decode / chunked prefill)
- leading `bs` = `Σ N_Q` across all requests (effective batch size)

Default (`False`) annotation is unchanged: `execute_context_1(839)_generation_63(63)`.

These are written as `user_annotation` events, so roofline analysis is possible directly from the trace with no extra runtime logging.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@rasmith
@njhill 
@WoosukKwon 

### Any Other Things.

### How these features are used (offline analysis)

Both flags are additive metadata on the existing profiler trace — extra `user_annotation` events and an extra set of capture trace files — so they slot into any existing trace-based analysis flow without changing how the trace is collected or read. Any tool that already walks a PyTorch profiler trace can pick up the per-step roofline aggregates and the capture-phase shapes/call-stacks with no new instrumentation.

As a concrete example, **[TraceLens](https://github.com/AMD-AGI/TraceLens/)** is an open-source PyTorch trace analysis toolkit. It builds a unified CPU/GPU call tree from a profiler trace, attaches per-op input shapes, and attributes GPU kernel time to analytic compute/memory **performance ("perf") models** per op category (GEMM, MoE, attention, norm, etc.) to place each op on a roofline. On top of that core it offers inference-specific workflows: trace splitting into per-step / per-phase (prefilldecode-mix, decode-only) windows, and a capture-merge step that augments graph-replay traces with the call-stacks and shapes recovered from graph-capture traces. The two vLLM flags map directly onto two TraceLens capabilities:



**1. Attention roofline for variable-length inference.** TraceLens parses the detailed annotation directly from the trace's `user_annotation` events and feeds the per-phase aggregates into its attention perf model:



- [`TraceLens/PerfModel/extensions/attention_perf_model_extensions.py`](https://github.com/AMD-AGI/TraceLens/blob/main/TraceLens/PerfModel/extensions/attention_perf_model_extensions.py) consumes those fields in `flops_func()` and `bytes_func()`. The FLOPs implementation is the **same equation** as vLLM's `perf.py` (and the roofline derivation):
  ```python
  # attention_perf_model_extensions.py (flops_func)
  ctx_flops_qk = H_Q * (2 * c_sqsk * d_h_qk) - H_Q * (1 * c_sqsq * d_h_qk)
  ctx_flops_pv = H_Q * (2 * c_sqsk * d_h_v)  - H_Q * (1 * c_sqsq * d_h_v)
  gen_flops_qk = H_Q * (2 * g_sqsk * d_h_qk)
  gen_flops_pv = H_Q * (2 * g_sqsk * d_h_v)
  ```
  i.e. `Σ N_Q·N_KV` drives the QKᵀ/score·V rectangle and `Σ N_Q²` is the causal prefill correction — exactly the `sqsk` / `sqsq` annotation terms. This yields per-step arithmetic intensity and achieved-vs-peak roofline placement, separating prefill-bound (compute) from decode-bound (memory) behavior, all from the single trace.

**2. Analysis of the graph-captured region.** Capture traces supply the shapes and call-stacks that graph-replay traces lack, so graph-mode kernels can be categorized and attributed to modules and shapes. At a high level, each captured graph is labeled with its batch size and compilation mode, and a runtime execution step is mapped to the matching captured graph using two signals already present in the runtime trace: the step's **batch size** and its **number of graph-launch events** (one `*GraphLaunch` for a `FULL` graph, several for a `PIECEWISE` graph). For example, a runtime decode step with batch size 32 and a single graph launch maps to the captured graph labeled `{batch_size: 32, mode: FULL}`; the analysis tool then back-fills that capture's call-stacks and shapes onto the step's replayed kernels.

**Example TraceLens output.** Running `generate_perf_report_pytorch_inference` with `--capture_folder` on the `graph_full` test trace produces a `unified_perf_summary` where each op carries its input shapes/dtypes (recovered from the capture trace), a modeled GFLOPs / data-moved / arithmetic-intensity, the underlying kernel(s), and its share of step time. Top rows (abbreviated) for a batch-size-32 FULL-graph decode step:


| op                                    | Input shape                                            | Input data type | GFLOPs | Data Moved (MB) | FLOPS/Byte | kernel_details                              | %    |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------- | ------ | --------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| `vllm::unified_attention_with_output` | `((32,64,64),(32,8,64),(32,8,64),(32,64,64))`          | bf16            | 0.90   | 108.1           | 7.96       | `kernel_unified_attention_2d`               | 6.8  |
| `vllm::rocm_unquantized_gemm`         | `((32,2880),(5120,2880),(5120,))`                      | bf16            | 0.94   | 28.6            | 31.4       | `Cijk_Alik_Bljk_..._MT32x32x256_MI16x16x1`  | 3.6  |


The `InferenceAttention` row's perf params are populated directly from the detailed annotation for that step (taken verbatim from the test's `unified_perf_summary.csv`):

```
{ 'B': 1, 'N_Q': 32, 'H_Q': 64, 'H_KV': 8, 'd_h_qk': 64, 'd_h_v': 64,
  'causal': False,
  'c_sq': 0, 'c_sk': 0, 'c_sqsq': 0, 'c_sqsk': 0,
  'g_sq': 32, 'g_sk': 55086, 'g_sqsq': 32, 'g_sqsk': 55086 }
```

This is a pure decode step (`c_* = 0`): 32 generation requests contribute `g_sq = 32` query tokens against `g_sk = 55086` cached KV tokens, and `g_sqsk = 55086` drives the modeled attention FLOPs — values that exist in the trace **only** because `detailed_trace_annotation` emitted them. Without the flag, the same row would have no `sk`/`sqsk` and the attention roofline could not be computed for that step.

title: [RFC]: Image Token Pruning for Multimodal Models
author: garrygale
body:
### Motivation.

### Summary

Add image token pruning feature to vLLM. When `--image-pruning-rate` is set, image tokens are pruned before LLM fusion using a configurable pruning method. Pruning is off unless explicitly enabled, similar to EVS.

We choose to intentionally **NOT** describe any specific pruning method in this RFC, but it is assumed that the pruning methods only use the embedding matrix output from the vision encoder, similar to EVS. We include the interface, necessary cli arguments, model integrations, and dispatch mechanism in this RFC.

### Motivation
- Existing Efficient Video Sampling (EVS) integration only applies to video token pruning.
- We should also have entrypoints for image pruning methods.
- There are quite some recent works on vision token pruning. We should allow different existing vision pruning method to be added and called, in addition to EVS, without modifying core vLLM.
- Since not all token pruning method applies to both images and videos (like EVS does not apply to images), image and video pruning should be separate cli args.

### Proposed Change.

### New CLI Arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--image-pruning-rate` | `None` | Float (0.0–1.0). Fraction of image tokens to prune. `None` disables pruning. Can be set to 0 to disable image pruning when video pruning is active |
| `--image-pruning-config` | `None` | Flat JSON dict. Must contain a `"method"` key selecting the pruning strategy, plus method-specific parameters. |
| `--video-pruning-config` | `None` | Flat JSON dict. Optional. Defaults to `{"method": "evs"}` to preserve backward compatibility. |

`--video-pruning-rate` is already introduced with EVS.

### Modified Files

| File | Changes |
|---|---|
| `vllm/multimodal/evs.py` | Add `prune_image_embeds()` and `prune_video_embeds()` dispatch functions. Existing EVS functionality unchanged, but `compute_retained_tokens_count` and `recompute_mrope_positions` might need some change to accomodate image token pruning. |
| `vllm/config/multimodal.py` | Add `image_pruning_rate`, `image_pruning_config`, `video_pruning_config` fields. Add `is_image_pruning_enabled()`. Update `is_multimodal_pruning_enabled()` to check both image and video. |
| `vllm/config/model.py` | Plumb new multimodal config fields into `ModelConfig`. |
| `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py` | Add `--image-pruning-rate`, `--image-pruning-config`, `--video-pruning-config` CLI args. |

plus individual model files (per model, opt-in).

### Interface & dispatch

All pruning methods share a common function signature, and assumed to operate on the final vision embedding matrix, to avoid too much coupling with upstream ViT or downstream LLM, following the discussions in PR #38888, though other inputs can still be sent in via **kwargs.

In `vllm/multimodal/evs.py` we can define lightweight dispatch functions:

```python

IMAGE_PRUNING_METHODS: dict[str, Callable] = {}
VIDEO_PRUNING_METHODS: dict[str, Callable] = {"evs": compute_retention_mask}

# Image pruning method signature
def prune_image(
    image_embeds: torch.Tensor,
    image_size_thw: torch.LongTensor | tuple[int, int, int] | tuple[int, int],
    spatial_merge_size: int,
    q: float,
    **kwargs,                   # additional method-specific params from config dict, and other parameters
) -> Tensor:                    
    method_name = kwargs.pop("method")
    return IMAGE_PRUNING_METHODS[method_name](
        image_embeds, image_size_thw, spatial_merge_size, q, **kwargs
    )

# Video pruning method signature (same pattern as EVS today)
def prune_video(
    video_embeds: torch.Tensor,
    video_size_thw: torch.LongTensor | tuple[int, int, int],
    spatial_merge_size: int,
    q: float,
    **kwargs,               # additional method-specific params from config dict, and other parameters
) -> Tensor:
    method_name = kwargs.pop("method", "evs")
    return VIDEO_PRUNING_METHODS[method_name](
        video_embeds, video_size_thw, spatial_merge_size, q, **kwargs
    )
```

Existing EVS functionality should be kept for backward compatibility, though some modifications to those functions (`compute_retained_tokens_count` and `recompute_mrope_positions`) is likely needed to make them work for both images and videos.

### Model Integration

Using Qwen3-vl as an example, the pruning logic should be added inside the existing `_postprocess_image_embeds_evs` method:

```python
def _postprocess_image_embeds_evs(self, image_embeds, mm_input):

    if self.is_multimodal_pruning_enabled:
        merge_size = self.visual.spatial_merge_size
        grid_thw = image_input["image_grid_thw"]
        grid_thw_list = grid_thw.tolist()
        image_embeds_out = []
        for emb, size in zip(image_embeds_split, grid_thw_list):
+           retention_mask = prune_image_embeds(
+               emb,
+               size,
+               self.visual.spatial_merge_size,
+               self.image_pruning_rate,
+               method = 'a_certain_method',
+           )
            positions = compute_mrope_for_media(size, merge_size).to(emb.device)
            positions = torch.cat(
                [
                    positions,
                    torch.zeros_like(
                        positions[:, 0:1]
                    ),  # Dummy extra fifth channel
                ],
                dim=1,
            )
            emb = torch.cat([emb, positions], dim=1)
+           emb = emb[retention_mask]
            image_embeds_out.append(emb)
            image_embeds_split = tuple(image_embeds_out)
        return image_embeds_split
```
and `get_image_replacement_qwen3vl` method within `_get_prompt_updates`:
```python
def get_image_replacement_qwen3vl(item_idx: int):
    out_item = out_mm_kwargs["image"][item_idx]
    grid_thw = out_item["image_grid_thw"].data
    assert isinstance(grid_thw, torch.Tensor)

    num_tokens = int(grid_thw.prod()) // merge_length

+   image_pruning_rate = self.info.ctx.get_mm_config().image_pruning_rate
+   if image_pruning_rate is not None and image_pruning_rate > 0.0:
+       num_tokens = compute_retained_tokens_count(
+       tokens_per_frame=num_tokens,
+       num_frames=1,
+       q = image_pruning_rate,
+   )
+
    return [hf_processor.image_token_id] * num_tokens
```
mimicking the existing logic with video token pruning.

Some minor changes in `__init__` and `get_mrope_input_positions` are likely also needed.

### Backward Compatibility

- All existing EVS logics are preserved.
- `--video-pruning-rate` alone continues to trigger EVS with default behavior.
- Models that directly call EVS functions continue to work unchanged.
- `is_multimodal_pruning_enabled()` returns `True` when either image or video pruning is enabled to preserve backward compatibility. If this value is true and either the video_pruning_rate or the image_pruning_rate is not set, then they are automatically set as 0.

title: [RFC]: Triton Kernel Dispatcher for Multi-Platform Support
author: wangxiyuan
body:
### Motivation.


### Background

vLLM uses Triton kernels in many places, including sampling, attention, normalization, mamba/copy, and speculative decoding. These kernels are designed and optimized specifically for GPU. Some other hardwares can not run these kernels directly. Here I take Ascend NPU as an example to explain the compatibility problem.

#### Functional limitations

1. **Grid mapping limitations**: GPU uses logical grid dimensions decoupled from physical cores, while NPU uses physical core-bound mapping. Grid size must not exceed AI Core count, and 2D grids must match the hardware topology. Large or multi-dimensional grids commonly used in vLLM kernels cause functional errors on NPU.

2. **Data type limitations**: NPU vector units do not support certain data types (e.g., int64 for Vector ADD, int64/int32 for Vector CMP). Kernels using these types produce incorrect results or fall back to scalar operations.

3. **Memory access alignment**: NPU requires 32-byte alignment for vector operations and 512-byte alignment for cube-vector fused operations. GPU kernels often use different alignment assumptions.

4. **TL.dot constraints**: NPU has specific requirements for M/N/K tile sizes, accumulation dtype, and output dtype in tl.dot operations that differ from GPU Tensor Core constraints.

5. **Missing GPU-specific APIs**: CUDA thread, stream, event, and kernel synchronization APIs are unavailable on NPU.

#### Performance problem

Even when kernels can functionally run on NPU, they suffer severe performance degradation:

1. **Excessive grid parallelism**: GPU kernels often launch grids with far more logical programs than NPU physical cores, causing multi-round dispatch overhead and excessive launch latency.

2. **Lack of NPU-optimized tiling**: GPU kernels lack the inner-loop tiling (XBLOCK/XBLOCK_SUB) pattern that NPU needs for efficient on-chip memory utilization (192KB UB capacity on Atlas 800T/I A2). Without proper tiling, kernels either overflow UB or fail to enable multi-buffer instruction parallelism.

3. **Missing NPU-specific compiler optimizations**: triton-ascend supports AscendNPU IR optimizations like multibuffer, unit_flag, tile_mix_vector_loop, etc. that are not configurable in GPU-oriented kernels.

4. **Synchronization overhead**: tl.load with partial mask filling (default other=0 behavior) causes unnecessary Vector-MTE synchronization on NPU, reducing instruction parallelism.

### Proposed Change.


### Current Status

vllm-ascend now has rewritten over **55 Triton kernels** with NPU-specific implementations. However, the current approach uses **monkey-patching** to replace upstream vLLM kernels at runtime:

```
# vllm_ascend/patch/worker/patch_triton.py
import vllm.model_executor.layers.mamba.ops.causal_conv1d
vllm.model_executor.layers.mamba.ops.causal_conv1d.causal_conv1d_update = causal_conv1d_update_npu
vllm.model_executor.layers.mamba.ops.causal_conv1d.causal_conv1d_fn = causal_conv1d_fn

# vllm_ascend/patch/worker/patch_mamba_utils.py
mamba_utils.batch_memcpy_kernel = batch_memcpy_kernel
mamba_utils.batch_memcpy = batch_memcpy
```
There is no need to explain the problem of monkey-patching again here. In short, it makes the codebase more complex and harder to maintain. Even worse, it can lead to subtle bugs and performance issues.

### Target

I propose adding a **Triton Kernel Dispatcher** module (vllm/model_executor/triton_dispatcher.py) that provides two decorators:

- @pluggable_kernel: Applied to the default (CUDA) Triton kernel in vLLM core code, making it replaceable.
- @register_kernel(name): Applied to a platform-specific override in a hardware plugin, registering it under a unique name.

The dispatcher preserves the standard Triton invocation syntax kernel[grid](...), so existing call sites require zero changes.

1. Marking a kernel as pluggable (in vLLM core):
```
from vllm.model_executor.triton_dispatcher import pluggable_kernel
from vllm.triton_utils import tl, triton

@pluggable_kernel
@triton.jit
def expand_kernel(output_ptr, replace_from, replace_to, ...):
    ...
```

2. Registering a platform-specific override (in a hardware plugin):
```
from vllm.model_executor.triton_dispatcher import register_kernel

@register_kernel("vllm.v1.sample.rejection_sampler.expand_kernel")
def npu_expand_kernel(*args, grid=None, **kwargs):
    # NPU-specific implementation
    ...
```

Or equivalently as a function call:
```
register_kernel("vllm.v1.sample.rejection_sampler.expand_kernel")(npu_expand_kernel)
```

3. Dispatch behavior:

When `kernel[grid](args)` is called:
- If a registered override exists: the dispatcher calls override(args, grid=grid, **kwargs)
- If no override exists: the dispatcher falls back to the default Triton kernel with native kernel[grid](args) syntax

This means:
- On CUDA: no override registered, so default kernel runs with zero overhead
- On NPU: the Ascend plugin registers overrides at startup, and NPU implementations are dispatched
- On Other Platforms: just registers its implementations similarly


4. KernelDispatcher class

The KernelDispatcher wraps a default Triton kernel and provides:

- __call__(*args, **kwargs): Dispatches to override (if registered) or default
- __getitem__(grid): Returns a _KernelLauncher for overrides (passing grid as keyword arg), or delegates to default_kernel[grid] for native Triton behavior



### Feedback Period.

_No response_

@WoosukKwon @ProExpertProg @wxsIcey 

### Any Other Things.

A reference implementation is available at: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43048

title: [Rust Frontend][RFC]: Elastic Expert Parallel support
author: coder3101
body:
### Motivation.

Elastic EP allows an operator to change the data-parallel size (and therefore the EP topology) of a running server without a restart. Today this is not supported due to various assumption such as static set of engines during startup etc. This RFC proposes how to bring the Python frontend-facing half of Elastic EP to the Rust frontend, and because the orchestration does **not** live in the frontend process, how the Rust frontend should co-design with the existing Python control plane.

#### Core Problem

In the python version, the orchestration lives inside the API server process `AsyncLLM` owns the `DPLBAsyncMPClient` which owns ray `CoreEngineActorManager` . In rust however that component is replaced, the python supervisor still runs the `launch_core_engines(…)`, but it then launches the rust binary via `RustFrontendProcessManager` in `frontend` mode, passing only some engine connection details. The rust binary then connects to engine cores over ZMQ with a **fixed** set of engines which were passed, additionally it has no Ray actor to add / remove engines at runtime. So `scale_elastic_ep` is not expressible as the existing per-engine utility call fan-out that powers other operations such as `/sleep` , `/pause` etc. Scaling is a control-plane operation over engine core lifecycle and topology, which in the rust deployment is owned by the Python supervisor/coordination, not the frontend.



### Proposed Change.

Split the feature into a frontend half which is clearly in scope for the Rust frontend such as APIs, middleware etc and an orchestration half that should be delegated to Python control plane. We can work in phases outlined here

#### Phase 1 - Frontend-local primitives

These can be implemented purely in `rust/` and mirror the Python observable behaviour:

1. Scaling-state flag + Rejection : Add a shared scaling `AtomicBool`  flag field in the `AppState`. Add a request middleware after authentication middleware but before load tracking that short circuits with 503 and similar error message. Should we selectively only reject inference request or request for all routes? I think its better to only reject the inference request because then observability/liveliness probes can survive this scale up. (Note: Python rejects **all** HTTP routes during scaling, so inference-only rejection is a deliberate divergence from parity.)
2. `POST /is_scaling_elastic_ep` : checks that atomic flag and returns the status. 
3. `POST /scale_elastic_ep` handler skeleton and validation : A handler that validates the request similar to python and same return code, in phase 1 this just sets/clears the scaling atomic flag in the app state and doesn’t actually performs any orchestration for scaling. Validation must also reject requests when `data_parallel_backend != "ray"`, since only `CoreEngineActorManager` supports scaling. 

#### Phase 2 - Draining request

Implement `wait_for_requests_to_drain(drain_timeout)` in the Rust frontend, gated on the `VLLM_ELASTIC_EP_DRAIN_REQUESTS` semantics. Python only polls `engine_core.dp_engines_running()` until idle or timeout; it never inspects the in-flight request count. The Rust frontend has both signals available:

1. in-flight count via `AppState.server_load` (using it would be an enhancement over Python, not parity)
2. DP idleness via the coordinator: the rust frontend already subscribes to the coordinator’s `(counts, wave, engines_running)` publishes; the global `engines_running` flag is exactly what Python’s `dp_engines_running()` returns.

Which of the two drain inputs should be used or may be both? For strict parity, `engines_running` alone is sufficient.

#### Phase 3 - Orchestration co-design

Because the Rust frontend cannot create/remove engine cores or run the Ray `ReconfigureDistributedRequest` flow, the scale operation must be driven by the component that owns the engine lifecycle. In python these live in one process `DPLBAsyncMPClient` so scaling is a single in-process method. With rust frontend, neither alone can perform a scale and there is **no message path between them** today. Supervisor only passes CLI args to the Rust process at launch and then monitors liveliness. Therefore we propose to introduce a narrow control channel and keep all engine facing choreography in the frontend. We call this channel `control-channel`

##### Control Channel

A dedicated ZMQ request/reply socket, setup exactly like existing supervisor → frontend address handoff:

1. Supervisor binds a control `ROUTER` socket before spawning the frontend, allocating its address with the same helpers used for the other engine addresses.
2. Supervisor passes the address as a new `--control-address` flag to rust frontend
3. Frontend connects a `DEALER` socket at startup, configured via a new optional field in `EngineCoreClient::connect` next to the coordinator connection.
4. Supervisor services it from a small control loop on a background thread, started just before `wait_for_completion_or_failure` . The thread holds `engine_manager` and `vllm_config` 

##### Message contract of Control channel

1. `ScaleUp { new_size }` → Supervisor creates the rendezvous, replies `Ack { rendezvous }` immediately, then runs `engine_manager.scale_up_elastic_ep(vllm_config, new_size)` on a background thread and sends `ScaleUpResult { ok | error }` when it returns.
2. `ScaleDown { new_size }` → Supervisor sets up the rendezvous, drops run refs via `remove_run_refs_for_scale_down`, replies `Ack { rendezvous }`
3. `ScaleDownComplete { new_size }` → Sent by the frontend once every removed rank reports `SHUTDOWN_COMPLETE`. Supervisor calls `engine_manager.scale_down_elastic_ep(old_size, new_size)` to free the removed engines' placement groups, mirroring Python's `SHUTDOWN_COMPLETE` handler.
4. Any request may be answered with `Err { message }` so the frontend can surface 500

The reconfigure "rendezvous" (TCP store + DP master ports created today by `_setup_elastic_ep_reconfig_bootstrap`) must be shared between the workers the supervisor spawns and the `reinitialize_distributed` message the frontend sends to existing engines. Because the supervisor owns the `vllm_config` used to launch workers, **the supervisor creates the rendezvous and returns its ports in the** `Ack`; the frontend relays those ports inside the reconfigure message. This keeps worker spawning and rendezvous creation co-located and leaves the frontend as a pure relay of the port info.

##### EEP notification relay

The reconfigure utility calls returning is **not** the end of a scale operation. Engines emit EEP notifications on the output socket (handled by `eep_process_engine_core_notification` in the Python client), and the Python client runs a small state machine around them that the Rust frontend must replicate:

1. `RECONFIGURE_FINISHED` (sent by engine 0): all engines have switched to the new setup. The frontend must keep the 503 gate on until it arrives.
2. Aggregated notifications such as `NEW_CORE_ENGINES_WEIGHTS_INIT_READY`: once received from all new (or removed) ranks, the frontend relays them to the existing engines as `eep_handle_engine_core_notification` utility calls.
3. `SHUTDOWN_COMPLETE` (scale-down only): once received from all removed ranks, the frontend sends `ScaleDownComplete` on the control channel so the supervisor can release the removed engines' placement groups.

Implementation note: the rust `engine-core-client` today rejects input-socket registrations from engine ids outside the startup set and stores engines in an immutable `Vec<ConnectedEngine>`; accepting post-startup registrations (and additions/removals to the routing set) is a prerequisite change for both sequences below.

##### Coordinator touchpoints

The `DPCoordinator` is a passive bookkeeper during scaling. It participates only in these two ways:

- On scale-up, newly spawned  engines subscribe to its back socket during their normal boot and receive `READY`; the coordinator already accepts mid-run subscriber. No new code needed.
- At the end of either scale up or down, the frontend sends a `(“SCALE_ELASTIC_EP”, new_size)` note on the coordinator front socket, which resizes the coordinator’s engine list so its `(counts, wave, engines_running)` broadcast matches the new headcount. Rust frontend already holds this socket and sends wakeup notes on it; we extend it to send this one additional note.

##### Scale-up Sequence (4 → 8)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
autonumber
participant Op as Operator
participant FE as Rust Frontend
participant SV as Supervisor
participant EX as Existing engines (0-3)
participant NE as New engines (4-7)
participant CO as Coordinator

Op->>FE: POST /scale_elastic_ep {new_size: 8}
FE->>FE: set scaling=true (503 gate on)
FE->>FE: drain in-flight (engines_running)

FE->>SV: ScaleUp{8}  [control pipe]
SV->>SV: create rendezvous (TCP store + ports)
SV-->>FE: Ack{rendezvous ports}  (immediately, BEFORE spawning)
SV->>NE: spawn Ray actors (scale_up_elastic_ep, background thread)

FE->>EX: reinitialize_distributed{size=8, ports}  [input pipe]
NE->>EX: __init__: rendezvous barriers + weight transfer (TCP store)
NE->>CO: subscribe
CO-->>NE: READY
NE->>FE: register [rank, ready_response]  [input pipe]
NE->>FE: notify NEW_CORE_ENGINES_WEIGHTS_INIT_READY  [output pipe]
FE->>EX: relay eep_handle_engine_core_notification  [input pipe]
SV-->>FE: ScaleUpResult{ok}  (scale_up_elastic_ep returned)

FE->>FE: add engines 4-7 to engine list + routing
EX->>FE: notify RECONFIGURE_FINISHED (engine 0)  [output pipe]
FE->>CO: ("SCALE_ELASTIC_EP", 8)
CO->>CO: resize engine list -> 8
FE->>FE: set scaling=false (503 gate off)
FE-->>Op: 200 OK
```

Note: there is no HELLO/INIT/READY handshake between new engines and the supervisor; in Ray mode all addresses are passed at actor creation and `_perform_handshakes` is a no-op.

##### Scale down (8 → 4)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
autonumber
participant Op as Operator
participant FE as Rust Frontend
participant SV as Supervisor
participant KE as Engines kept (0-3)
participant DE as Engines removed (4-7)
participant CO as Coordinator

Op->>FE: POST /scale_elastic_ep {new_size: 4}
FE->>FE: set scaling=true (503 gate on)
FE->>FE: drain in-flight

FE->>SV: ScaleDown{4}  [control pipe]
SV->>SV: create rendezvous (TCP store + ports)
SV->>SV: drop run refs (remove_run_refs_for_scale_down)
SV-->>FE: Ack{rendezvous ports}

FE->>KE: reinitialize_distributed{size=4, ports}  [input pipe]
FE->>DE: reinitialize_distributed{SHUTDOWN_CURRENT_RANK, ports}  [input pipe]
FE->>FE: drop ranks 4-7 from engine list + routing (stop routing now)
DE->>DE: reconfigure remaining group, then exit

FE->>CO: ("SCALE_ELASTIC_EP", 4)
CO->>CO: resize engine list -> 4
KE->>FE: notify RECONFIGURE_FINISHED (engine 0)  [output pipe]
FE->>FE: set scaling=false (503 gate off)
FE-->>Op: 200 OK

DE->>FE: notify SHUTDOWN_COMPLETE (each removed rank)  [output pipe]
FE->>SV: ScaleDownComplete{4}  [control pipe]
SV->>SV: scale_down_elastic_ep -> remove placement groups (async cleanup)
```


### Feedback Period.

Two weeks

### CC List.

cc @BugenZhao 

### Any Other Things.

- Relates to #44280 
- AI assistance was used to analyze the python codebase to understanding existing scale EP implementation but this RFC was written without AI assistance and as author I have understood and taken the accountability for it

title: [RFC]: Extend hidden-state extraction to export verifier KV caches
author: Beichen-Ma
body:
### Motivation.

Reference `speculators` primary [RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/issues/586) for more context.

vLLM already provides an offline hidden-state extraction path used to generate
training data for speculative-decoding draft models. This is sufficient for draft architectures that are self-contained (e.g. eagle3, and Qwen-style MTP).

Gemma4 MTP is not self-contained. Its draft attention is query-only and at
inference borrows the verifier's KV cache (specifically the last sliding-window layer
and the last full-attention layer) via cross-model KV sharing. To support Gemma 4 drafter finetune, the verifier's KV tensors must themselves be extracted and supplied as training inputs, exactly as hidden states are today.

The current extraction system exports hidden states only. There is no supported way
to export a verifier attention layer's KV cache. We propose extending the extraction
system to do so.



### Proposed Change.

High-level: allow the extraction pipeline to export selected verifier attention
layers' KV caches alongside hidden states, into the same per-request `.safetensors`.

The existing `KVConnector` interface already carries most of what's needed. Today the example connector points that mechanism only at the single cache-only layer that stores hidden states. The proposed change makes the verifier's real attention layers eligible save targets and serializes their K/V.

- Phase 1 out-of-tree prototype. Implement as a custom `KVConnector` (selected via
  `--kv-transfer-config`) with no changes to vLLM core, to validate feasibility, tensor
  layout, and position-alignment. This is the experimentation path and needs nothing
  from vLLM maintainers up front.
- Phase 2 upstream. Promote the capability into the extraction system / connector
  interface as a first-class, tested, maintained feature.

The consuming training pipeline lives in `vllm-project/speculators` and is covered by
the primary RFC.




### Feedback Period.

At least one week (longer welcome given the cross-repo nature).

title: [RFC]: AuxOutput Connector — block-keyed outputs and storage roadmap
author: huangyibo
body:
## Summary

AuxOutput Connector (formerly Artifact Connector) manages auxiliary model outputs for post-training workloads. Its first output is routed experts (R3): the expert IDs selected for each executed token of an MoE model.

The foundation is merged in #45635. The next steps are **faster value delivery** (#61086), **distributed storage and key-based delivery** (#57968), and **an extensible response schema** (#61291). This RFC tracks their shared architecture and follow-ups; implementation and validation belong to the linked PRs.

Status below was checked on October 15, 2026. Open proposals are not merged capabilities.

## Requirements and architecture

Two consumption patterns should remain available:

- **Return values:** simple integration for existing RL clients, without a separate remote reader.
- **Return references:** large deployments fetch data from shared storage, avoiding forwarding large payloads through API servers and a central RL controller.

Most initial outputs are token-aligned, so KV-compatible prefix hashes and block boundaries provide a useful basis for reuse. However, KV and auxiliary data need not have the same lifetime: a trainer may still need R3 after inference finishes or a GPU KV cache is reset.

A capture hook produces only the current forward's tensor. The connector handles accepted versus rejected rows, cached prefixes, block assembly, partial tails, and request completion. Storage owns bytes and retention; training coordination stays outside the connector.

```text
GPU Worker process
  model forward -> capture -> async GPU-to-CPU copy
                              |
                     AuxOutputWorkerConnector
                     accepted rows / complete blocks
                       |                    |
                 local SHM             Mooncake Store
                       |                    ^
                       v                    |
EngineCore process: progress, hashes, accepted boundaries/tails
                       |                    |
                       v                    v
API Server process:  R3 values         output references
                       |                    |
                       v                    v
                   RL client        trainer -> Store.get(keys)
```

Mooncake #57968 also has an EngineCore publisher for boundaries/tails finalized after stop and length handling. #61086 batches arrays at existing IPC boundaries on the value path. These are complementary workstreams; their combined runtime behavior still needs validation.

## Main workstreams

### 1. Batch incremental R3 transport — #61086, open

Pack many small per-request arrays into a compact batch array with request spans/row counts. Unpack at the receiver and accumulate into request-owned storage. This reduces Python object and serialization overhead while retaining incremental delivery and partial results on abort.

The original Nemotron/GB200 comparison reported approximately **19% higher output-token throughput** (3 baseline runs, 2 batching runs); this is workload-specific. Packing still copies data and is not a zero-copy or lower-memory claim. Mooncake worker-tail batching requires separate integration and measurements. [Reproduction and results](https://gist.github.com/aoshen02/377db5658721d30b934e9a227a3c19fa).

### 2. Mooncake backend — #57968, open

Store complete blocks and accepted partial tails remotely; return ordered keys so external consumers can fetch the values. Reuse the existing background writer and native Mooncake I/O. SHM remains the default.

The PR records cross-host RDMA retrieval, prefix reuse, preemption, speculative rejection and Mooncake PD handoff experiments. P/D sharing requires matching generation, model/R3 profile, hash configuration and block size. Removing a configuration restriction does not establish support for every KV connector/backend combination.

Retention remains deployment-managed: request completion does not delete remote objects, but the backend does not yet implement trainer-held references or guarantee protection until a delayed trainer reads them.

### 3. Structured HTTP output — RFC #61291 and [fork draft #132](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/132)

Walter's current proposal builds on #57968 and replaces the R3-specific key-list contract with a named `aux_outputs` object:

```text
aux_outputs
  routed_experts
    token_start, num_rows
    metadata: dtype, num_layers, experts_per_token
    chunks: [{key, num_rows}, ...]
  <future output field>
    its own range, metadata and chunks
```

This describes how to decode and place each payload, allowing additional fields without requiring R3-only readers to understand them. Large top-k token logprobs for RL score centering motivate the extension; the schema draft itself does not implement their capture and storage.

The earlier stored-manifest experiment, [fork #131](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/131), has been superseded in the RFC by this simpler HTTP structure. An additional remote manifest object is not required by the current proposal. Review still needs to settle migration from `aux_output_keys`, SHM/value-path compatibility, and preservation of stop/abort/empty-terminal behavior.

## Related implementation roadmap

| Area | Work | Current scope/status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Additional outputs | #60789 | Draft: generated and prompt logprobs through AuxOutput. Selected-token/fixed top-k, raw-logprob mode; full-vocabulary output and online weight updates are excluded. Align its field/range contract with #61291. |
| Avoid repeated prefix delivery | #57966; RFC #56402 | Open: opt-in prefix omission with caller-owned route history and session identity. Does not itself add KV offloading. |
| Custom eviction policy | #58328 | Open: local-store `ExpertCachePolicy` hooks and selection from eligible unreferenced blocks. Worker configuration and Mooncake retention are outside this PR. |
| Pipeline parallelism | #61333 | Open: combine routing rows from all PP stages through existing stage transfers. |
| TP-sharded capture | #61388 | Open: restore the full local token axis when model-level SP shards rows at DP=1. |
| DBO ordering/offsets | #57184 | Related open prototype; does not establish general DBO+R3 correctness. |
| Multimodal token coordinates | #61097 | Open: account for model-expanded prompt ranges and P/D prompt cuts. |

Recent merged foundations/fixes:

- #61000: own SHM out-of-band buffers before releasing reusable queue slots; received arrays must remain valid after subsequent messages.
- #61643: retain all required routing rows during DeepSeek V4.1 decoder replay, using the existing keep-row mechanism. R3 can therefore require work that logits-only inference skips.
- #58150 / #58205: narrow KV-connector restrictions and scope the MRV2 requirement to applicable GPU platforms. These configuration changes do not certify every runtime combination.
- #59060: remove redundant Aux reset guards for the completed-pause workflow. It does not implement arbitrary reset during active inference or preservation across every GPU-only reset.

## Contracts still to define

1. **Output coordinates and identity.** R3 describes executed tokens; logprobs describe predictions and need an explicit target-token convention. Specify dtype/shape, raw versus processed probabilities, model/weight version and reuse compatibility. DSA/index data remains a follow-up; non-token-aligned data needs a concrete use case before adding machinery.
2. **Shared retention across inference and training.** Store one logical R3 object and let multiple training batches reference it. Track acquire/release separately from inference-cache retention; registration must precede exposing a key to a consumer. Reclaim only after all required uses finish. A generation change isolates identity but is not a deletion signal for old training data. This protocol is proposed, not implemented by #57968 or #58328.
3. **Eviction policy versus protection.** The storage/lifecycle layer decides which objects are eligible; a plugin chooses which eligible objects to evict. It must not override live-consumer protection. KV hits also require matching auxiliary data: define coordinated retention or invalidation/recomputation when R3 is unavailable. Sharing a hash does not ensure joint availability.
4. **Bounded capacity and failures.** Define backpressure or tiering when protected data fills the store, cleanup of abandoned consumer holds, and observability for retained bytes and consumer lag. TTL alone cannot guarantee delivery to arbitrarily slow consumers. Remote-store failures also need an explicit request/engine failure policy.
5. **Compatibility validation.** Preserve partial outputs, async ownership and SHM behavior as storage/schema/packing changes compose. Test actual row provenance and slot reuse, plus prefix hits, chunked prefill, speculative rejection, preemption, reset, PD and parallel layouts. Support and performance claims remain tied to the configurations exercised in each PR.

AI assistance was used to research and update this RFC. Linked experiments are reported by their implementation PRs; this roadmap update did not rerun them.

title: [RFC]: FULL cudagraph support for spec-decode drafter chain steps (currently PIECEWISE-only; measured ~15-18% of decode step time)
author: rmarnold
body:
## Summary

Spec-decode drafters are hardcoded to PIECEWISE cudagraphs. The comment in `gpu_model_runner.py` says it plainly:

```python
# Eagle currently only supports PIECEWISE cudagraphs.
# Therefore only use cudagraphs if the main model uses PIECEWISE
# NOTE(lucas): this is a hack, need to clean up.
```

and `SpecDecodeBaseProposer.initialize_cudagraph_keys` pins `eagle_cudagraph_mode = CUDAGraphMode.PIECEWISE` unconditionally. The consequence: **every drafter chain step runs its attention ops eagerly between graph pieces**, paying Python dispatch + per-layer metadata per speculative token. For constant-draft-position drafters (Gemma4 MTP and similar), the chain steps are uniform decode (1 token/req) with **loop-invariant metadata** — the ideal shape for FULL graphs.

## Measured cost (CUDA-event instrumentation; GB10/sm_121, Gemma-4 26B-A4B NVFP4, MTP gamma=3, vLLM 0.22.1.dev)

Per decode step, phases bracketed with CUDA events (means over ~100 steady-state steps):

| | conc=1 | conc=16 |
|---|---|---|
| step wall | 27.7 ms | 100.6 ms |
| target verify forward (FULL graph replay) | 20.8 ms | 79.5 ms |
| **drafter chain (propose)** | **4.9 ms (18%)** | **15.6 ms (15.5%)** |
| → of which sampling | 2.1 ms | 3.2 ms |
| → of which forward+glue residual | 2.7 ms (~1.4 ms/forward) | **15.2 ms (~7.6 ms/forward)** |

The per-forward cost of a 419M W4A4 drafter is ~7.6 ms at 16 concurrent sequences — ~10x its weight-read floor — and it scales with batch, which is the signature of the eager attention + per-call dispatch between the piecewise pieces (confirmed: dispatcher returns PIECEWISE for every drafter shape; zero FULL).

**Estimated prize for FULL chain steps: ~+11% aggregate at conc16, +6–7% single-stream** for this model class; larger for higher gamma.

## Findings from an out-of-tree attempt (11 iterations) — offered to whoever implements this in-tree

We prototyped FULL-graph drafter chain steps via runner/proposer patches and got capture + replay working; the findings below are the practical landmine map:

1. **Keys + wrapper:** `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` keys with `uniform_decode_query_len=1` (chain steps) + a `CUDAGraphWrapper(runtime_mode=FULL)` around the drafter model works. The verify-shaped first pass should stay PIECEWISE.
2. **Pre-capture eager warmup is mandatory:** backend lazy inits (in our case an attention backend's first-use buffer setup) allocate on first forward — illegal mid-capture. One eager pass with the capture metadata before capturing fixes it.
3. **`set_forward_context` silently default-constructs `BatchDescriptor(num_tokens=...)` when the caller passes none** — and the proposer paths never pass one. Capture, replay, and any entry-table lookups then key inconsistently (the dispatcher's descriptors carry `uniform=True/num_reqs`; the default has `uniform=False/num_reqs=None`). The descriptor must be threaded from `dispatch()` through `set_forward_context` exactly as the runner's execute path does.
4. **Phase-aware dummy capture:** once FULL keys exist, naive dummy runs dispatch FULL during the PIECEWISE capture phase too, so the drafter's piecewise graphs never get captured for those sizes — and the runtime first-pass then triggers a (banned) runtime capture. Dummy runs need to know which phase they're capturing for.
5. **KV-store hazard:** drafter attention layers run the standard attention path including the KV store; capture-time `slot_mapping` must be isolated (scratch page) or the store suppressed. Our prototype's zeroed slot_mapping caused replays to write drafter garbage into page 0 of the **target's** KV cache → `<pad>` corruption under concurrent sampling. This is the dangerous failure mode to design against.
6. **Replay-only runtime guard:** dispatching FULL only for descriptors with an actually-captured graph (falling back to PIECEWISE otherwise) converts coverage gaps into graceful degradation instead of `RuntimeError: CUDA graph capturing detected at an inappropriate time`.

Even with all of the above, our out-of-tree version saw most runtime chain dispatches still fall back — aligning the warmup capture grid with runtime chain batch sizes needs the in-tree machinery (the runner controls both grids). That's why we're filing this as an RFC rather than continuing out-of-tree.

## Ask

First-class FULL-cudagraph support for drafter chain steps where metadata is loop-invariant (constant draft positions), with the descriptor threading and KV-store isolation handled in-tree. Happy to share raw measurement data, re-run benchmarks on Blackwell (GB10/sm_121), or test patches.

title: [RFC]: Forward ReqContext from CPUOffloadingManager to CachePolicy for session-aware KV eviction
author: jacklin78911-collab
body:
### Motivation.

This is a follow-up to the KV Offloading Roadmap (#33689), which already lists "Add request ID to RequestContext" (done in #42507) and "Create an offloading policy abstraction" among its items. Since #42507, `ReqContext` carries `req_id` and is available to `OffloadingManager` API calls; vLLM also has request-level offloading semantics via `OffloadPolicy.REQUEST_LEVEL` ([source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/1ae1051b4bf6e7e98d61b15527040f63eda73a0b/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py#L60-L63)). However, for the native CPU backend this context currently stops at `CPUOffloadingManager`: `touch(keys, req_context)` calls `CachePolicy.touch(keys)`, and `prepare_store(keys, req_context)` performs policy get/evict/insert operations without exposing `req_context` or store-batch boundaries to the policy ([source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/1ae1051b4bf6e7e98d61b15527040f63eda73a0b/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/manager.py#L141-L203)). The missing boundary is specifically manager → policy.

This matters for multi-turn serving. The value of offloaded prefix KV is *chain-shaped*: a lookup recovers only a contiguous leading run of a request's blocks, so isolated blocks are worthless without their predecessors. Block-centric policies cannot see this structure. In controlled multi-turn experiments on a capacity-constrained CPU tier (details below), we observed:

- **LRU and ARC deliver zero recoveries.** Across 3 runs each on a cyclic-revisit workload (6 sessions, ~2K-token prefixes, tier sized to ~2 complete prefixes), neither policy served a single load; their store/load traces were bit-identical to each other. Every revisit paid full prefix recomputation.
- **A chain-aware prototype recovers complete prefixes on the same workload.** Grouping blocks by request and evicting/protecting at chain granularity yields 3 complete prefix recoveries per run (verified via the engine's offloaded-tokens accounting: 2,016–2,256 tokens recovered, zero GPU-cache contribution; second-turn TTFT drops from ~0.85 s to 0.07–0.14 s), while issuing ~25% fewer store operations.
- **The prototype's hardest problem was reconstructing request identity.** Without context, chains must be inferred from key-arrival adjacency, which breaks under interleaved store batches; several of our prototype's failure modes were caused or amplified by this reconstruction, rather than by the eviction heuristic alone.

| Policy | load transfer ops ×3 runs | store transfer ops ×3 runs | complete prefix recoveries ×3 runs¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| LRU | 0 / 0 / 0 | 70 / 70 / 70 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| ARC | 0 / 0 / 0 | 70 / 70 / 70 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| chain-aware prototype | 3 / 3 / 4 | 52 / 52 / 52 | 3 / 3 / 3 |

¹ "Complete" = ≥2,000 offloaded tokens recovered for a ~2K-token prefix, per the engine's own per-request accounting (`hit N offloaded tokens` debug log); the recovered token counts (2,256/2,048/2,016) reproduce identically across runs. Counts are transfer operations, not blocks or bytes.

(Experiments on v0.21.0, Qwen2.5-3B-AWQ, RTX 4060; we are preparing a technical report with full methodology and will link it here.)

We also verified end-to-end that application hints injected via `SamplingParams.extra_args["kv_transfer_params"]` reach the manager layer — so with the boundary crossed, hint-aware policies (e.g., "this session will continue") become possible with zero new plumbing elsewhere.

### Proposed Change.

Minimal and backward-compatible: forward the already-present `ReqContext` across the manager→policy boundary, as optional methods with default fallbacks on `CachePolicy`:

```python
class CachePolicy(ABC):
    # existing five methods unchanged

    def touch_with_context(
        self,
        keys: Iterable[OffloadKey],
        req_context: ReqContext,
    ) -> None:
        self.touch(keys)  # default: ignore context

    def on_store_batch(
        self, keys: Collection[OffloadKey], req_context: ReqContext
    ) -> None:
        """Called once at the beginning of prepare_store()."""
        pass  # default: no-op
```

`CPUOffloadingManager.touch()` becomes `self._policy.touch_with_context(keys, req_context)`; `prepare_store()` calls `on_store_batch(keys, req_context)` before its policy operations. Passing the batch's `keys` matters: the batch is the natural chain-segment boundary, and without it a policy must reassemble the batch from individual `insert` calls.

Existing policies (LRU/ARC) are unaffected. This gives opt-in policies (a) request identity per touched key set, (b) store-batch delimitation (one batch = one request's blocks, eliminating identity reconstruction), and (c) access to `kv_transfer_params` hints.

We have working patches and a prototype policy against v0.21.0 and are happy to submit a PR rebased on main if the direction is acceptable. We deliberately do not propose any specific new policy here — only the information plumbing that makes session/chain-aware policies implementable in-tree or out-of-tree.

### Feedback Period.

One week, or as maintainers prefer

### CC List.

@orozery @ronensc

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] RL CI Matrix for vLLM: Behavioral + Physical + Protocol Coverage
author: aoshen02
body:
## Background

vLLM is the dominant rollout engine for post-training frameworks (verl, slime, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, AReaL, prime-rl, NeMo-RL, ROLL, miles, trl, open-instruct). The RL lifecycle exercises a unique code surface: **cumem-based GPU memory management** (`sleep/wake_up`), **scheduler gating** (`pause/resume`), and a **weight-transfer HTTP protocol** (`/start_weight_update` → `/update_weights` → `/finish_weight_update`).

This surface has seen a burst of production bugs in recent months — six currently open as PRs (#45326, #45552, #45363, #45518, #44972, #44483) — yet has **zero dedicated CI coverage** today.

This RFC proposes a structured, 5-tier RL CI matrix covering the production HTTP endpoint surface, grounded in a comprehensive survey of how 12 downstream frameworks already test this surface.

---

## Problem: Current State

### vLLM
- `tests/basic_correctness/test_cumem.py` covers the **internal Python allocator API** only — not the HTTP endpoints that RL frameworks call.
- `tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/test_sleep.py` asserts **flag values** (`is_sleeping`, Prometheus metrics) but never asserts **behavioral consequences**: it never checks whether the scheduler actually blocks requests or whether FlashAttention runs on unmapped KV cache.
- **No test exists** for `/pause`, `/resume`, `/is_paused`, `/start_weight_update`, `/update_weights`, `/finish_weight_update`, `/get_world_size`, PauseMode semantics (`abort`/`wait`/`keep`), or the compound RL training-step sequence.

### Active bugs this CI would catch
| PR / Issue | Bug | Status (updated) |
|---|---|---|
| **#45552** open | `sleep()` / `wake_up()` missing `torch.cuda.synchronize()` → "200 lie": HTTP 200 returned while engine is already dead. | 🟡 OPEN; covered by sleep/wake cycle tests |
| **#45326** open | Request arriving during `sleep()` bypasses scheduler pause → hangs forever. | 🟡 OPEN; CI test: `test_sleep_abort_mode_blocks_new_requests` |
| **#45518** open | `sleep()` on already-sleeping engine returns no idempotency signal in response body. | 🟡 OPEN; CI test: `test_double_sleep_idempotent` |
| **#44972** open | Pages remapped by `wake_up()` may contain stale data → Mamba/GDN models produce NaN logprobs. | 🟡 OPEN; ❌ needs Tier 2 model-specific test |
| **[#46438](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46438)** open | `discard(tag) → sleep() → wake_up()` double `unmap_and_release` → `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`. Found by @AlanFokCo in multi-model hot-swap. | ✅ `test_cumem_physical.py` |
---

## Directory Layout

Tests are organized by roadmap section. Each file covers both single-GPU and multi-GPU (TP≥2) cases via parametrize.

```
tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/rlhf/
├── conftest.py                              ← Shared fixtures (server harness, HTTP helpers, GPU memory query)
│
├── state_transitions/                       ← Section 2: State Transitions
│   ├── test_sleep_wake.py                   ← 2.3 Scheduler: sleep/wake/pause/resume lifecycle
│   ├── test_state_machine.py                ← 2.3 Scheduler: CPU state-machine invariants
│   ├── test_state_machine_enforcement.py    ← 2.3 Scheduler: transition enforcement
│   ├── test_cumem_physical.py               ← 2.3 Scheduler: CuMemAllocator VMM edge cases (@AlanFokCo)
│   ├── test_weight_update.py                ← 2.1 Weight Update: transfer protocol + model matrix (dense/MoE/FP8/VLM)
│   ├── test_weight_checker.py               ← 2.1 Weight Update: SHA-256 checksum verification
│   └── test_weight_update_metrics.py        ← 2.1 Weight Update: Prometheus metrics
│
├── info_retrieval/                          ← Section 3: RL Information Retrieval
│   ├── test_weight_info.py                  ← 3.1 Versioning: /weight_info, /update_weight_label
│   └── test_response_schema.py              ← 3.2 APIs: structured JSON responses for /sleep, /wake_up
│
└── consistency/                             ← Section 4: Consistency
    ├── test_routed_experts.py               ← 4.2 R3: routed_experts capture + replay correctness
    # 4.1 Logprobs: tests live in tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py (upstream)
    #              → see tests/v1/sample/test_prompt_logprobs_mode.py (#47680)
    #              → RL-specific: logprob stability across sleep/wake added in test_sleep_wake.py
```

### Section → file mapping

| Roadmap Section | Test File(s) | Upstream tests (not in this dir) |
|----------------|-------------|----------------------------------|
| 2.1 Weight Update | `state_transitions/test_weight_update.py`, `test_weight_checker.py`, `test_weight_update_metrics.py` (includes KV prefix cache flush after weight update) | — |
| 2.2 Scheduler | `state_transitions/test_sleep_wake.py`, `test_state_machine.py`, `test_state_machine_enforcement.py`, `test_cumem_physical.py` (includes KV invalidation after wake, FP8 KV scale restoration, KV CPU backup) | — |
| 3.1 Versioning | `info_retrieval/test_weight_info.py` | — |
| 3.2 APIs | `info_retrieval/test_response_schema.py` | — |
| 4.1 Logprobs | RL-specific cases in `state_transitions/test_sleep_wake.py` (logprob stability across lifecycle) | `tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py`, `test_prompt_logprobs_mode.py` (#47680) |
| 4.2 R3 | `consistency/test_routed_experts.py` | — |
| 4.3 DSA Index | (not yet implemented) | — |

### Cleanup: scattered RL tests to consolidate

RL-related tests currently scattered across the repo. These should be moved into `tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/rlhf/` when splitting PR #45586.

| Current location | Content | Move to |
|-----------------|---------|---------|
| `tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/test_sleep.py` | Sleep flag + Prometheus metrics (flag-only, no behavioral assertions) | `state_transitions/` — superseded by `test_sleep_wake.py` |
| `tests/v1/worker/test_sleep_mode_backend.py` | Sleep mode backend unit test | `state_transitions/` |
| `tests/basic_correctness/test_mem.py` | CuMemAllocator internal Python API | `state_transitions/` — colocate with `test_cumem_physical.py` |
| `tests/entrypoints/weight_transfer/test_weight_transfer_llm.py` | Weight transfer LLM E2E | `state_transitions/` — same scope as `test_weight_update.py` |

Open PRs — should land directly into `rlhf/` instead of ad-hoc locations:

| PR | Proposed file | Move to |
|----|--------------|---------|
| [#44972](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44972) | `tests/models/language/generation/test_gdn_sleep_wake.py` | `state_transitions/test_sleep_wake.py` as Mamba/GDN parametrize case |

Upstream tests to keep in place (reference via soft link in directory tree):

| Location | Reason to keep |
|----------|---------------|
| `tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py` | General logprobs, not RL-specific |
| `tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py` | General determinism infrastructure |

### `conftest.py` — shared infrastructure

| Component | Reference Pattern |
|---|---|
| `ServerContext` (subprocess launch/teardown) | miles `with_mock_server()` context manager |
| `wait_for_health(url, timeout)` | sglang `wait_for_server` |
| `get_gpu_free_bytes()` | sglang `_platform_mem_usage` |
| `get_prometheus_metrics(url)` | sglang weight_checker |
| `generate_completion(url, prompt, ...)` | common across all |

---

## Test Matrix with Downstream Mapping

### `state_transitions/test_state_machine.py` (CPU, no GPU)

> **Industry-wide gap**: No framework — including PR #45586 — tests sleep/wake state-machine invariants at the CPU level.

title: [RFC]: Partial Cache Hits for Hybrid Models
author: ZJY0516
body:
## Motivation

In attention-only models, full attention can use a small KV cache block size, for example 16 or 32 tokens. This gives prefix caching a fine matching granularity.

For hybrid full-attention + Mamba models, the full-attention block size needs to be aligned with the Mamba state block size. This makes block size super large compared to before. Since vLLM prefix-cache matching is block-size granular, this coarse block size leads to suboptimal cache hit rates.

As a result, full attention loses its natural fine-grained cache-hit behavior. For example:

- full-attention natural block size: 16 or 32 tokens
- Mamba state block size: 1024 tokens
- effective hybrid prefix-cache granularity: 1024 tokens

This hurts prompts whose reusable boundaries are not multiples of the Mamba state block size, such as chat turns, tool-call boundaries, and agentic traces.

This RFC proposes separating prefix-cache matching granularity from block size granularity. We introduce `hash_block_size` to allow to hit a partial cache block.

When a request ends at a hash boundary that is not a block boundary, vLLM can cache and later hit that partial prefix. A later request that diverges after that partial prefix uses copy-on-write before appending new tokens for mamba state.


## Partial Cache Example

```text
hash_block_size   = 2
block size        = 6
request A prompt  = a b c d e f g h
request B prompt  = a b c d e f g h x y
```

Request A registers cache entries at the boundaries that matter:

```text
H2  = hash([a b])                    # prefix key for tokens [0, 2)
H4  = hash(parent=H2, [c d])         # prefix key for tokens [0, 4)
H6  = hash(parent=H4, [e f])         # full-block key for tokens [0, 6)
H8  = hash(parent=H6, [g h])         # partial key for prefix [0, 8)
```

Request B can reuse request A's partial tail and then append two new tokens. Because the hit ends inside a cache block, request B uses copy-on-write instead of modifying request A's block in place:

```text
H8 -> block_A                        # block_A has [g h]
request B copies [g h] to block_B
request B writes x y into block_B
H10 = hash(parent=H8, [x y])         # partial key for prefix [0, 10)
```

This is a partial-to-partial extension. The old partial key `H8` remains valid for request A's block, while request B registers a new partial key `H10` for its copied block:

```text
H8  -> block_A                       # reusable through token 8
H10 -> block_B                       # reusable through token 10
```

There is no separate partial-tail hash formula. The hash at every `hash_block_size` boundary is already prefix-chained over all previous tokens. A partial cache key is simply the fine-grained boundary hash at the reusable prefix length.

If request B's second cache block later becomes full, for example with tokens `z w`, vLLM already has the next fine-grained boundary hash:

```text
H12 = hash(parent=H10, [z w])        # full-block key for tokens [0, 12)
```

When `block_B` is promoted from partial to full, the full-block view for `block_size=6` uses `H12`. The old partial alias `H10 -> block_B` is removed and `H12 -> block_B` becomes the primary full-block key.

After request B, the cache layout is:

```text
block 0: tokens [0, 6) = a b c d e f
block_A: tokens [6, 12), only [6, 8) = g h written
block_B: tokens [6, 12), only [6, 10) = g h x y written
```

Without partial hits, request B can only reuse block 0 and must recompute from token 6. With partial hits, `block_A` is registered under `H8`, so request B can reuse eight tokens and recompute only `x y`.

Both full attention and Mamba use copy-on-write when a later request extends from a partial cache hit. The difference is what needs to be copied.

For full attention, the copied payload is the reusable KV slice inside the cache block. In this example, request B receives a fresh destination block and copies the first two tokens of `block_A` before writing `x y`.

For Mamba, the copied payload is the recurrent state at token 8.

## Proposed Design

### 1. Decouple hash granularity from cache blocks

The cache block is still the unit of memory allocation and ownership. `hash_block_size` only changes the granularity used for prefix-cache lookup.

Request hashes are computed at `hash_block_size` boundaries in one prefix chain. Each hash already includes the previous boundary hash, so the hash at token `N` fingerprints the whole prefix `[0, N)`.

Larger group block keys are derived by taking the last fine-grained hash inside the larger block. For example, with `hash_block_size=2` and `block_size=6`, the first full-block key is `H6`, not a concatenation of `H2`, `H4`, and `H6`, and not a separately recomputed `hash([a b c d e f])`.

In code, `BlockHashListWithBlockSize(fine_hashes, hash_block_size, block_size)` is a lazy larger-block view over the fine hashes. For target block index `i`, it returns `fine_hashes[(i + 1) * (block_size / hash_block_size) - 1]`.

Partial cache aliases use the same boundary hashes. In the example above, `H6` is the full-block key for `[a b c d e f]`, while `H8` is the partial alias key for the boundary after `[g h]`.

The lookup first matches full blocks using the larger-block view (`H6`, `H12`, and so on). When full-block matching stops, vLLM probes the final fine-grained boundary inside the next block. For example, if `H12` is not cached but `H8` is cached, the request can still reuse tokens through token 8.

Partial cache entries are only created for the tail of a request. vLLM still computes fine-grained hashes for each `hash_block_size` boundary, but it does not register every boundary in the block pool. At most one partial cache entry is created for the final under-filled cache block of each request. This keeps the number of partial aliases bounded.

A partial hit also means that the number of returned blocks is no longer enough to describe the reusable prefix length. If lookup returns `block 0` and `block 1` for the boundary at token 8, `len(blocks) * block_size` would incorrectly imply 12 reusable tokens. The hit result therefore carries `hit_length=8` explicitly.

### 2. Allow cache aliases per cache block

The block pool lookup table maps hash keys to cache blocks. Before this change, each cached block was effectively looked up through one full-block hash key. Partial hits need the same cache block to be temporarily reachable through an additional fine-grained boundary hash key.

In the example above, `block_A` owns the memory range `[6, 12)`, but only tokens `[6, 8)` are reusable. The block pool registers `block_A` under `H8` so request B can find the state at token 8.

When `block_B` later becomes full, the cache should replace its partial lookup key `H10` with the full-block key `H12`.

This requires two lookup directions:

```text
cached_block_hash_to_block[hash]         # hash -> block, used by prefix lookup
block.block_hash                         # block -> primary hash
cached_block_hashes_by_block[block_id]   # block -> additional alias hashes
```

The first map is the normal prefix-cache lookup path. The reverse metadata is needed for cleanup. When a block is evicted, reset, or reused, vLLM must remove every hash key that points to it from `cached_block_hash_to_block`; otherwise a later request could hit a stale partial alias and read a block whose contents now belong to another request.

For example, if `H10 -> block_B` was registered for request B's partial tail and `block_B` later becomes full under `H12`, promotion should remove the old `H10` entry before registering `H12`. Likewise, eviction of `block_B` must remove both its primary hash and any alias hashes. KV-cache events for a partial alias use that alias's tail token IDs and the tail length as `block_size`, because the stored chunk associated with the alias is the written tail slice rather than a full cache block.

### 3. Full attention partial hits use copy-on-write

When full attention hits a partial hash boundary inside a cache block, the hit source block cannot be appended to directly by the new request. The manager allocates a fresh block and emits a pending copy:

```text
(kv_cache_group_id, src_block_id, dst_block_id, num_tokens)
```

The worker applies these copies after zeroing new blocks and before forward. For standard full attention, only the reused token range is copied. MLA may need full-block copying depending on compressed layout constraints.

### 4. Mamba final-tail checkpointing

Mamba align mode stores recurrent state, not per-token KV. Intermediate prefill chunks already end at physical Mamba block boundaries, so the running state at those boundaries can be cached naturally.

For the final reusable prompt tail, the hash boundary may fall inside a scheduled chunk. How to cache this boundary is still an open design question. There are two possible approaches:

- **Metadata checkpoint.** Keep the scheduled chunk intact. GDN/KDA metadata carries the checkpoint offset and destination state block, and GDN/KDA materializes the recurrent state at that offset. This avoids adding another scheduler split, but the backend logic is more complex.
- **Scheduler split.** Split the final chunk at the hash boundary. The Mamba running state at the end of the first chunk can then be cached naturally. This is easier to reason about, but it adds another scheduling boundary and may affect batching or performance.

### 5. CLI

Add:

```text
--hash-block-size <int>
```

Example:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --mamba-cache-mode align \
  --hash-block-size 16
```

## Open Design Question: Final-Tail Checkpointing

If the final prompt hash boundary lies inside a scheduled chunk, the cache manager needs a Mamba state at that boundary before it can safely register the partial hash entry. For example, suppose the chunked prefill budget is 20 tokens, `hash_block_size` is 4, and the prompt length is 25. The first forward processes tokens `[0, 20)`. The final reusable hash boundary is token 24, with one prompt token left after it.

There are two candidate ways to get the state at token 24:

Option A is a scheduler split. The scheduler cuts the chunk at the final prompt hash boundary, so the existing Mamba state update at the end of the first forward naturally produces the checkpoint state.

```text
forward pattern: 20 + 4 + 1
scheduled work:  [20, 24), then [24, 25)
checkpoint:      state@24

forward 1:       [20, 24), write state@24
forward 2:       [24, 25), continue from state@24
```

Option B is backend checkpoint materialization. The scheduler keeps the work in one model forward, allocates a snapshot block, and passes checkpoint metadata to the attention backend.

```text
forward pattern: 20 + (4 + 1)
scheduled work:  [20, 25)
checkpoint:      state@24

mamba_checkpoint_offsets_cpu[req_idx]       = checkpoint_pos - chunk_start
mamba_checkpoint_state_indices_cpu[req_idx] = snapshot_block_id
```

The GDN backend then splits only the affected prefill rows internally:

```text
scheduler forward: tokens [20, 25)
checkpoint:        token 24

backend phase 1:   [20, 24), write state@24 to snapshot block
backend phase 2:   [24, 25), continue from state@24
```

Option B keeps the model forward count at `20 + 5` instead of `20 + 4 + 1`, but it adds backend-specific metadata and extra kernel launches inside the attention implementation. The current prototype experiments with Option B for Kimi GDN, but the RFC should keep this as an explicit design decision rather than a settled requirement.

The tradeoff is:

- scheduler splitting is simpler and reuses the existing end-of-forward Mamba state update, but it increases the number of model forwards;
- backend checkpoint materialization can reduce model forward count, but it adds backend-specific metadata, segment construction, and extra backend work.

If backend checkpoint materialization is chosen, GDN internal splitting should only happen when a scheduled chunk actually crosses the final fine-grained prompt boundary.

## Open Design Question: Same-Step Reuse

Finer-grained prefix caching should increase the number of cacheable boundaries and improve hit rate. However, vLLM does not currently support reusing a Mamba state that is produced by another request in the same scheduler step. Forcing that reuse can split two otherwise batchable requests into different chunks or different forward steps, which may hurt end-to-end performance.

One possible policy is to ignore cache entries produced in the same scheduler step and recompute that state for the second request. This may do a small amount of extra work and temporarily use more memory, but it avoids introducing an intra-step dependency that breaks batching. Whether to implement same-step reuse or same-step recomputation is an open question.
