title: [RFC]: Enable connector LoRA for audio multimodal models — convert nn.Linear projectors to vLLM-native linears
author: anshulkulhari7
body:
## Summary

Tower/connector LoRA (#31479) is declared for several **audio** multimodal models, but the **connector half is currently a no-op** for all of them, and loading an adapter that targets the connector raises `ValueError` at load. The root cause: audio models build their projectors from plain `nn.Linear`, which vLLM's LoRA layer-replacement can't wrap — whereas **vision** MM models use vLLM-native parallel linears, which is exactly why their connector LoRA works. This RFC proposes bringing the audio connectors in line with the vision-model pattern.

## Why connector LoRA silently doesn't work for audio models

`vllm/lora/utils.py::from_layer` only replaces vLLM-native linear types (`ColumnParallelLinear`, `RowParallelLinear`, `QKVParallelLinear`, `MergedColumnParallelLinear`, `ReplicatedLinear`) with their `*WithLoRA` variants; any other module — e.g. a plain `nn.Linear` — is returned **unwrapped**, so the connector never receives an adapter. And `check_unexpected_modules` (`vllm/lora/lora_model.py`) raises `ValueError` at adapter load if the adapter carries weights for a module not in the model's supported LoRA set — so it **errors** rather than silently degrading.

Confirmed on an A100 with Qwen2-Audio — loading a PEFT adapter targeting the projector + audio tower:

```
ValueError: ... expected target modules {q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj}
but received [..., model.multi_modal_projector.linear, ...]. Please verify that the loaded LoRA module is correct
```

## The vision/audio inconsistency

**Vision MM connectors are native → connector LoRA works:**
- LLaVA `LlavaMultiModalProjector` → `ColumnParallelLinear` + `RowParallelLinear`
- Qwen2.5-VL `Qwen2_5_VisionPatchMerger` → `ColumnParallelLinear` / `RowParallelLinear`

**Audio MM connectors are `nn.Linear` → connector LoRA inert / errors:**
- Voxtral `AudioLanguageAdapter` (`w_in` / `w_out`)
- Ultravox `UltravoxFeedForwardProjector` (`linear_1` / `linear_2`) and `UltravoxTransformerProjector` (`linear_in` / `linear_out`)
- AudioFlamingo3 `AudioFlamingo3MultiModalProjector` (`linear_1` / `linear_2`)
- Qwen2-Audio `Qwen2AudioMultiModalProjector` (`linear`)

## Proposal

Convert the audio projectors' `nn.Linear` layers to `ReplicatedLinear` (the unsharded vLLM-native linear, LoRA-wrappable via `ReplicatedLinearWithLoRA`), matching the vision-model convention. This is a small, mechanical, per-model change:
- swap `nn.Linear(...)` → `ReplicatedLinear(...)` (weight names are unchanged; `bias` preserved),
- adjust `forward` to unpack the `(output, bias)` return,
- standard `ReplicatedLinear` weight loading (no remap needed).

After conversion, connector LoRA actually attaches and a tower+connector adapter loads cleanly.

## Scope

**This RFC:** Voxtral, Ultravox, AudioFlamingo3 (+ MusicFlamingo via inheritance), Qwen2-Audio.

**Separate follow-up (shared infra):** Granite Speech — its connector is `Blip2QFormerModel` (entirely `nn.Linear`, **shared with BLIP-2**), so converting it is a larger change that affects BLIP-2 too; happy to do that as a follow-up.

## Validation

Per model: the `get_num_mm_encoder_tokens` / `get_num_mm_connector_tokens` helpers plus a GPU adapter-load test confirming a tower+connector adapter loads without `check_unexpected_modules` rejecting it (the failure shown above).

## Questions for @jeejeelee

1. Does converting the audio projectors to `ReplicatedLinear` (matching the vision pattern) sound right, or would you prefer a core-side approach (e.g. letting `from_layer` handle a registered set of `nn.Linear` connector modules)?
2. One PR for the family, or a small series (one model per PR)?
3. I have an open Voxtral PR (#45697) already touching this area — happy to make it the reference implementation and start there.

I'm glad to implement this end-to-end; I've been working through the audio tower/connector LoRA path and have GPU access to validate.

title: [RFC]: Optimizing vLLM for High Beam-Width Generative Recommendation Inference
author: ehaleva
body: ### Motivation. ## Summary This RFC proposes extending vLLM's beam search support to better serve **high beam-width generative recommendation workloads**, a rapidly emerging and commercially important inference pattern. While vLLM already supports beam search for text generation, its current implementation is primarily optimized for conventional LLM decoding workloads where beam widths are typically small. In contrast, generative recommendation systems such as OpenOneRec and TIGER frequently rely on **large beam widths (tens to hundreds of beams)** to generate candidate recommendations. In these workloads, beam width is not a secondary decoding parameter—it is a primary scaling dimension. As beam width grows, the current beam-search execution path can incur rapidly increasing overheads, with several components scaling approximately quadratically with beam width due to repeated beam expansion, scoring, pruning, and management operations. The core idea of this RFC is that **targeted optimizations to beam scheduling and beam execution** could significantly improve performance for high beam-width inference without requiring major architectural changes to vLLM. ## Motivation Generative recommendation is an emerging inference paradigm in which models autoregressively generate recommendation candidates rather than natural-language text. Unlike traditional LLM serving workloads, recommendation quality is often highly dependent on exploring a large candidate space, making **beam search a core algorithmic component rather than an optional decoding strategy**. As a result, production recommendation systems frequently use beam widths that are substantially larger than those seen in standard text generation workloads. This creates a fundamentally different scaling regime for inference engines: * beam width becomes a first-class workload dimension, * a single request can expand into many active hypotheses, * many hypotheses share large portions of their prefixes, * throughput is often dominated by candidate generation efficiency rather than long-form decoding latency. Today, the computational cost of beam search grows rapidly with beam width. In vLLM's current implementation, increasing beam width not only increases the number of active sequences but also increases the amount of work required for beam expansion, scoring, ranking, and pruning. As a result, recommendation workloads can experience **approximately quadratic scaling behavior with respect to beam width**, making large-beam inference substantially more expensive than it needs to be. Beyond the technical motivation, recommendation systems represent one of the most economically important application domains in machine learning. Recommendation engines directly drive revenue across e-commerce, advertising, media, streaming, marketplaces, and social platforms. Small improvements in recommendation quality often translate into measurable gains in user engagement, conversion rate, and revenue. As the industry increasingly explores **LLM-based generative recommendation systems**, efficient support for high beam-width decoding becomes strategically important. This is therefore not merely an optimization for a niche workload—it is an opportunity for vLLM to become a leading inference engine for one of the largest and most profitable classes of production ML applications. **This is a high-leverage opportunity for vLLM. With relatively minor modifications, vLLM could support a broader and economically important class of inference workloads while preserving its general-purpose architecture.** ## Problem Statement For high beam-width generative recommendation inference, the current beam-search path in vLLM can become suboptimal due to three main issues. ### 1. Beam-search complexity grows rapidly with beam width Generative recommendation systems commonly operate at beam widths that are far larger than those used in standard text generation. Under the current execution model, increasing beam width increases both: * the number of active hypotheses maintained by the runtime, * the amount of work required for beam expansion, scoring, ranking, and pruning. Consequently, several portions of the beam-search pipeline exhibit approximately **quadratic scaling with beam width**, causing throughput degradation as beam width grows. This is particularly problematic for recommendation workloads where large beam widths are often required to achieve competitive recommendation quality. Unlike traditional LLM serving, where sequence length is often the dominant scaling factor, recommendation workloads can become **beam-width-bound**. ### 2. Scheduling overhead with many active beams Recommendation workloads often maintain many active beams per request. This stresses the scheduler differently from standard text-generation workloads, where beam widths are usually modest. Potential symptoms include: * increased per-step scheduling overhead, * inefficient handling of beam expansion and pruning, * suboptimal batching behavior when requests contain many sibling beams, * unnecessary runtime fragmentation across beam-heavy requests. ### 3. Attention inefficiency across sibling beams Many beams in recommendation decoding share substantial prefix structure and diverge only in later steps. This creates an opportunity for more efficient computation and cache reuse. However, existing execution paths may not fully exploit this structure when beam width is large, especially in workloads focused on efficient candidate generation rather than general text continuation. ### Proposed Change. ## Proposal We propose adding **high beam-width optimizations** to vLLM that remain general enough to benefit beam-search-based inference broadly, while especially improving generative recommendation use cases. ### A. Beam-aware scheduling Improve scheduling behavior for requests that expand into many beams. Possible directions include: * reducing per-beam scheduler overhead, * grouping sibling beams more efficiently, * improving beam expansion/pruning execution, * optimizing token and memory budgeting for beam-heavy requests, * reducing fragmentation caused by large numbers of short-lived beam states. ### B. Efficient beam attention Improve attention execution for workloads where many beams share prefixes. Possible directions include: * better reuse of shared-prefix computation, * more efficient KV-cache handling across sibling beams, * beam-structured cache layouts, * attention execution paths that amortize work across related beams. ## Why This Matters This proposal is attractive because it appears to require **incremental runtime improvements rather than recommendation-specific architectural changes**. The potential impact is significant: * **Substantially higher throughput for large-beam inference** * **Reduced beam-search overheads that currently scale poorly with beam width** * **Lower latency for candidate generation** * **Improved accelerator utilization** * **Better support for recommendation systems, retrieval-style generation, and other structured prediction workloads** Importantly, recommendation systems are among the largest consumers of inference infrastructure in industry and directly power revenue-generating products. Improvements in serving efficiency therefore have outsized practical value. By improving support for high beam-width decoding, vLLM could expand beyond its current focus on text generation and become a leading runtime for a broader class of commercially important autoregressive inference workloads. ## Early Evidence The importance of these optimizations becomes even clearer when considering that recommendation deployments routinely operate in beam-width regimes where current beam-search costs scale poorly, making beam width—not model size—the dominant performance bottleneck. We already performed a preliminary proof of concept with only minimal modifications to the online beam-search implementation: This work suggests that relatively small modifications to beam-search-related execution can deliver meaningful gains in recommendation-oriented settings. It provides encouraging evidence that this direction is practical and worth discussing upstream. ## Evaluation A useful next step would be to evaluate these ideas with recommendation-oriented workloads and tests, including beam-heavy decoding scenarios and performance-focused benchmarks. For example, the `tests` area in `JiusiServe/vllm-gr` may be a helpful place to point to concrete evaluation patterns or future benchmark coverage. Potential benchmark dimensions include: * beam width scaling, * throughput versus beam width, * latency versus beam width, * scheduler overhead, * KV-cache utilization, * recommendation candidate generation throughput. ## Scope This RFC is intended to discuss: * whether vLLM should explicitly optimize for **high beam-width inference** as a supported workload pattern, * how to mitigate beam-search costs that currently scale poorly with beam width, * what scheduler changes would yield the largest benefits, * what attention/cache optimizations are most promising, * how these changes can remain general-purpose rather than recommendation-specific, * how to benchmark recommendation-style beam decoding fairly. ## Non-Goals This RFC does **not** propose: * adding recommendation-specific model architectures into vLLM, * embedding ranking, retrieval, or application-layer recommendation logic into vLLM, * introducing changes that degrade standard text-generation performance, * maintaining a recommendation-specific fork instead of improving upstream vLLM. ## Open Questions 1. Which scheduler optimizations are generic enough to benefit both recommendation and text-generation workloads? 2. Should prefix sharing across sibling beams become a more explicit runtime abstraction? 3. What benchmark suite should be used to evaluate recommendation-style beam-search performance? ## Request for Feedback I would like feedback from the vLLM community on the following: * Is high beam-width generative recommendation a workload vLLM should support more explicitly? * Which optimizations would be most acceptable upstream? * Are there existing beam-search design constraints that would make these improvements difficult to integrate? * Would maintainers be open to incremental contributions in this area? ## References * Generative recommendation systems such as **OpenOneRec** and **TIGER** * #14426 * #20316 * #31882 ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: A registry + CI ratchet so tuned Triton kernel configs cannot silently rot
author: access2rohit
body:
**TL;DR:** vLLM's block-INT8 tuned-config loader silently matched **0 of 39** shipped config files for ~14 months -- a one-character filename typo (`block_shape=[128, 128]` vs the shipped `[128,128]`) meant every block-INT8 model quietly fell back to the heuristic, with no test, warning, or signal. The fix shipped; this RFC proposes a small registry + a CI check so that **class** of bug cannot silently recur for any tuned Triton kernel -- without forcing anyone to tune a kernel that should not be tuned.

_(Reference implementation -- registry, decorator, AST kernel discovery, reasoned allowlist, ratchet, tests -- is built and green. Branch: https://github.com/access2rohit/vllm/tree/rfc/tunable-kernels-A3-B3 .)_

## Motivation

vLLM ships offline-tuned Triton kernel configs (JSON keyed by batch size M) for a handful of
compute-heavy, on-the-hot-path kernels -- MoE expert GEMMs, block-FP8/INT8 GEMMs, the Mamba
selective_state_update decode step -- and loads the best match at runtime, falling back to a fixed
heuristic on a miss. This is high-value: the right tile/num_warps/num_stages for a shape+GPU is a
real speedup, and the env override (VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER) lets operators hot-load new configs
without rebuilding.

Two structural gaps make this fragile:

1. No uniform "make a kernel tunable" mechanism. Each of the 4 tunable kernels hand-rolls its own
   config-file lookup (its own filename f-string + its own load + fallback). There is no shared
   contract and no programmatic list of which kernels are tunable. A newly added compute-heavy
   kernel easily ships with no tuning path at all, and nobody notices.

2. Silent drift, with a concrete 14-month precedent. The block-INT8 loader built its filename with a
   stray space -- `block_shape=[128, 128]` -- while every shipped INT8 config is `[128,128]`. Result:
   0 of 39 configs ever matched; the loader silently fell back to the heuristic from #16366
   (2025-04) until it was found and fixed in the recent hot-load work. No test, no warning, no
   signal -- just quietly lost performance on every block-INT8 model for over a year.

The root cause of both: "is this kernel tunable, and does its loader actually work?" is answered
ad hoc per kernel, with nothing enforcing consistency. We propose a small, idiomatic mechanism +
an opt-out CI check that makes the answer explicit and regression-proof -- without forcing anyone
to tune a kernel that should not be tuned.

Non-goal: deciding which kernels are compute-heavy/in-path. No static check can infer that; the
proposal makes that human judgment explicit and reviewable, not automated.

## Proposed Change

Two pieces -- a registry (mechanism) and a completeness ratchet with a reasoned allowlist (enforcement):

### Part 1 -- A registry of tunable kernels (mechanism)

A single importable source of truth, mirroring vLLM's existing model / attention-backend
registries:

- `vllm/utils/tuned_config_registry.py`: a frozen `TunableKernelSpec(name, applicability, key_fn,
  packaged_dir)`, a `TUNABLE_KERNEL_REGISTRY` dict, `register_tunable_kernel`, `get_tunable_kernels`,
  and a generic resolve+select front-end `get_tuned_config_for(name, M, **shape)` that returns the
  single nearest-M config (or None). `applicability` is an enum
  (COMPUTE_HEAVY_INPATH / OPTIONAL / EXPERIMENTAL).
- A `tunable_triton_kernel(...)` decorator (optional ergonomic front-end) that wraps a kernel's
  config getter to do filename-build + load + fallback AND register the spec at import time.
- The 4 existing tunable kernels are registered by a seed module whose key_fns reproduce each
  loader's exact filename (so the registry's view matches what each kernel actually searches for).

Adoption cost is small and is NOT new: all 4 tunable kernels already have a per-kernel config getter
today; this standardizes them and centralizes the lookup logic that was being copy-pasted (the
copy-paste is exactly what produced the INT8 space bug). Making a kernel tunable does NOT touch the
`@triton.jit` body; the irreducible per-kernel work is a ~3-line filename builder + wiring the
launch site to use the loaded config (intrinsic to "use a tuned value instead of a hardcoded one").

### Part 2 -- A completeness ratchet with a reasoned allowlist (enforcement)

A CI test (`tests/test_tunable_kernels_ratchet.py`) that:

- Enumerates every `@triton.jit` kernel via a static AST walk (`tools/tuned_config/discover_kernels.py`)
  -- no imports, so it is robust to torch/CUDA/platform-gated modules and sees every kernel.
- Requires each discovered kernel to be EITHER registered tunable OR listed in
  `tools/tuned_config/exempt_kernels.py` with a one-line reason.
- Is seeded once with all current kernels (the ratchet baseline), so it is GREEN today and only
  bites a NEWLY added kernel. A new kernel makes CI fail with an actionable message:
  "New @triton.jit kernel(s) [...] must either register a tuned-config loader OR be added to
  exempt_kernels.py with a reason (e.g. 'memory-bound elementwise; tuning <2%')."
- Also runs a generic filename round-trip check on every registered kernel (asserts the key_fn
  output is exactly what the loader searches for) -- this single test structurally prevents the
  INT8-class bug for all current and future tunable kernels at once.
- Rejects empty / "TODO" exemption reasons, so the allowlist cannot become a rubber stamp.

The reasoned allowlist is deliberately the de-coercion mechanism. CI never says "you must tune this
kernel" -- only "tune it OR state, in one reviewed line, why not." That keeps the ~88% of kernels
that are memory-bound (rmsnorm, rope, activation, ...) out of scope by an explicit, reviewed
decision rather than silent omission. The allowlist is what keeps the check from being a blunt
mandate: without it, the test would flag 324 of 328 kernels on the current tree -- almost all
memory-bound kernels that should never be tuned.

### Why both, together

The registry without the ratchet (Part 1 only) catches filename drift on kernels people remember to
register, but a forgotten kernel stays forgotten. The ratchet needs the registry's machine-readable
list to know what is covered. Together they make "tunable or explicitly-not" a property CI
guarantees. The registry doubles as living documentation of every perf-critical kernel and the
tuning status of every other one.

### Rollout / scope

- The 4 existing tunable kernels are migrated onto the registry (behavior-preserving; their current
  tests stay green).
- The allowlist is seeded with all currently-discovered non-tunable kernels, each with a reason
  (specific for known memory-bound kernels, generic otherwise) -- a one-time mechanical step so CI
  starts green.
- No kernel is forced to change. Existing config files and the VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER override are
  untouched.
- A reference implementation (registry + decorator + seed + discovery + allowlist + ratchet + tests)
  is built and passing; happy to open it as a draft PR for review.

## Feedback Period

Two weeks (suggested). Main discussion points we expect:
- The small per-new-kernel contributor friction (register OR exempt-with-reason) vs. the
  silent-drift risk it removes.
- Whether "compute-heavy and in-path" warrants a written definition (FLOPs/byte? on the decode
  path?) to guide allowlist review, or stays reviewer judgment.
- Whether `applicability=COMPUTE_HEAVY_INPATH` should be enforced (must be tunable) or advisory.
- Landing as one PR (registry + ratchet) or two (mechanism first, enforcement second).

## Any Other Things

- This is additive and low-risk: default behavior (env var unset) is unchanged; the ratchet starts
  green; the round-trip test only fails on genuine filename drift.
- The mechanism is forward-compatible with a future tuning service: the registry is exactly the
  machine-readable manifest of "what is tunable, with what key, and how to regenerate it."
- A natural follow-up (separate PR) is bringing additional compute-heavy kernels into the registry --
  e.g. the unified Triton attention kernel, which today selects its tile from a fixed heuristic.

title: [RFC]: Kernel-agnostic constant-stride (layer-major) KV cache layout for KV connectors
author: xiaguan
body:
## Motivation

#27743 added "cross-layer KV blocks" so a KV connector can stage/transfer a block's KV for
all layers at once, by allocating all layers in one tensor (`use_uniform_kv_cache` /
`allocate_uniform_kv_caches`).

For MLA backends the only supported physical layout was **block-major**
`(num_blocks, num_layers, ...)`. That makes each per-layer view a *strided* (non-contiguous)
slice, and MLA kernels require contiguous per-layer views — so #37090 **disabled cross-layer
KV for all MLA backends** (`get_kv_cache_stride_order(include_num_layers_dimension=True)`
returns the identity permutation to signal "unsupported").

The result: the cross-layer connector optimization is off for exactly the models that dominate
disaggregated prefill/decode and KV offloading today — DeepSeek V3/V3.2, GLM, Kimi, all MLA.
With it disabled, vLLM falls back to **one independent `torch.zeros` per layer**, so a connector
sees `L` allocations at unrelated base addresses. Two concrete costs:

1. The GPU↔staging layer↔page transpose needs `L` separate copies per block — there is no
   constant stride across layers to exploit.
2. RDMA connectors must register `L` memory regions (one per layer) instead of one.

## Proposed Change

Add a **second uniform layout: layer-major contiguous slices**. Allocate one buffer for all
same-spec layers and hand each layer a **contiguous slice** at a constant stride
`S = num_blocks * page_size_bytes`. The per-layer view stays contiguous and bit-identical to a
standalone tensor, so **attention kernels (including MLA) are unaffected** — no
`get_kv_cache_stride_order` support is required. This is kernel-agnostic, unlike the existing
block-major path.

```
Today — one independent torch.zeros per layer (cross-layer disabled for MLA, #37090):

  layer 0   : [ blk0 blk1 ... blkN ]   @ ptr0
  layer 1   : [ blk0 blk1 ... blkN ]   @ ptr1     (ptr1 - ptr0 : arbitrary)
   ...
  layer L-1 : [ blk0 blk1 ... blkN ]   @ ptr(L-1) (no constant stride)

  => L memory regions; gathering block b across layers = L copies at L unrelated addresses


Proposed — one buffer, per-layer CONTIGUOUS slices, constant stride S = num_blocks * page_size_bytes:

  base -> +--------- layer 0 ---------+--------- layer 1 ---------+ ... +-------- layer L-1 -------+
          | blk0 blk1 ...      blkN   | blk0 blk1 ...      blkN   |     | blk0 blk1 ...      blkN  |
          +--------------------------+--------------------------+     +-------------------------+
          ^                          ^                          ^
          base + 0*S                 base + 1*S                 base + (L-1)*S

  per-layer view  = base + l*S            (contiguous slice, identical to standalone -> kernel safe)
  block b, layers = base + l*S + b*blk    for l in [0, L)   => CONSTANT inter-layer stride S
```

Two concrete wins for connectors, both from the constant stride / single allocation:

**1. `cudaMemcpy2D` transpose (zero SM).** Gather a block across all layers into a contiguous
page in one copy-engine 2D op, instead of `L` separate copies:

```
cudaMemcpy2D(dst    = page_b,                 // contiguous staging page, L * blk bytes
             dpitch = blk,
             src    = base + b*blk,           // block b of layer 0
             spitch = S,                      // constant inter-layer stride
             width  = blk,
             height = L)
// runs on the copy engine (0 SM), one launch per block; today: L memcpys per block
```

**2. Single memory registration.** One allocation → connectors register **one** RDMA memory
region (one rkey) / one CUDA IPC handle for all layers, instead of `L`.

Implementation sketch:
- `_allocate_kv_cache_tensors`: one `torch.zeros(total)` sliced per page-size bucket, instead of
  N independent `torch.zeros`. Downstream `_reshape_kv_cache_tensors` is unchanged — contiguous
  int8 slices support `.view(dtype)` / `as_strided`, and `storage_offset` is carried (vLLM core
  already tolerates non-zero kv-cache `storage_offset`: Mamba state tensors and Triton fp8 scales
  use `as_strided` with offsets today).
- Gate behind a new connector preference, weaker than `prefer_cross_layer_blocks` (which signals
  the block-major layout): a connector opts in when it only needs a constant inter-layer stride,
  not per-block contiguity.

Open API questions for discussion:
- How to advertise/select this layout — a new connector preference, or a backend-level capability
  flag distinct from the existing block-major `stride_order[0] != 0` signal?
- How to communicate the inter-layer stride to the connector — explicit (registration field /
  callback) vs. the connector detecting that per-layer `data_ptr`s are arithmetic.

This is purely additive and opt-in; default allocation is unchanged.

## Feedback Period

1–2 weeks.

## CC List

Builds on #27743 (cross-layer KV blocks) and #37090 (cross-layer disabled for MLA).

## Any Other Things

We maintain [PegaFlow](https://github.com/novitalabs/pegaflow), a disaggregated KV connector
(RDMA across nodes + tiered host/SSD storage). We are moving its CPU-side KV from layer-first to
**page-first** (a block's all-layer KV contiguous on the host) to cut per-block metadata by a
factor of `num_layers` — one RDMA descriptor / one SSD iovec / one storage slot per block instead
of one per (layer). The transpose from vLLM's per-layer GPU layout into that page is the operation
this RFC makes cheap: with a constant inter-layer stride it is one `cudaMemcpy2D` per block on the
copy engine. We are happy to contribute the vLLM-side allocation change and a unit test mirroring
`tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_kv_cache_layout.py`.

title: [RFC]: Cross-connector KV transfer QoS — plumb request priority to the connector layer
author: catyans
body:
## Motivation.

In PD-disaggregated serving, P→D KV cache transfer sits on the **TTFT critical path** — its latency adds 1:1 to time-to-first-token. Meanwhile, latency-insensitive traffic (Store offload / eviction) shares the **same NIC**. vLLM officially recommends `MultiConnector` to mix these (the docs show `NixlConnector` + `OffloadingConnector`), but **`MultiConnector` treats all sub-connectors identically** — there is no way to make the latency-critical P→D connector take priority over the background Store connector.

**vLLM already has request-level priority, but it never reaches the connector layer.**

- `vllm/v1/request.py:73,83` — `Request.priority: int = 0`
- `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:174,536-539` — `SchedulingPolicy.PRIORITY`

But on the connector side, a full-text search of `KVConnectorBase_V1` (`base.py:171`) for `priority` / `qos` / `traffic_class` / `deadline` returns **0 hits**. `KVTransferConfig` (`config/kv_transfer.py:23`) has no priority field either; the only free slot is the `kv_connector_extra_config` dict (L59).

`MultiConnector` (`multi_connector.py:128`) does undifferentiated, **config-order, serial** fan-out:

```python
# multi_connector.py:297-305
def save_kv_layer(self, layer_name, kv_layer, attn_metadata, **kwargs) -> None:
    for c in self._connectors:        # serial, no priority
        c.save_kv_layer(layer_name, kv_layer, attn_metadata, **kwargs)
```

Regardless of which sub-connector is the critical-path P→D and which is the background Store, they are processed in config order. This RFC proposes to plumb the existing `Request.priority` to the connector layer.

## Proposed Change.

Three independent, incrementally-mergeable steps. **Each step has standalone value; Step 1 does not depend on Step 2/3.**

### Step 1 — Carry per-request priority via the metadata channel

**Important: do NOT add a kwarg to `save_kv_layer`.** Its real call site (`model_executor/layers/attention/kv_transfer_utils.py:57`, inside the `maybe_transfer_kv_layer` decorator, per-layer forward hot path) is:

```python
connector.save_kv_layer(layer_name, kv_cache, attn_metadata)   # positional only, kwargs empty
```

There is **no request object / request_id / priority** at that call site. (Note: the `#40690` deprecated-signature shim is about the connector `__init__` signature, not `save_kv_layer` — unrelated, cited only as precedent that interface extensions must not break old connectors.)

The clean channel is the **connector metadata** mechanism. Scheduler side builds `KVConnectorMetadata`; it travels via `scheduler_output.kv_connector_metadata` → `bind_connector_metadata` to the worker. `NixlConnector` already has a per-request struct (`nixl/metadata.py:161-186`):

```python
@dataclass
class ReqMeta:
    local_block_ids: BlockIds
    ...
    priority: int = 0          # NEW, default 0 (backward compatible)
```

In `build_connector_meta` the scheduler holds the **full Request** (cached in `_reqs_need_save[req_id] = request`, `nixl/pull_scheduler.py:133`), so `req.priority` is directly readable and written into `ReqMeta.priority`. The worker then orders its send queue by `reqs_to_save[req_id].priority`.

- **Change**: ~30 lines, in NixlConnector. Other connectors not forced to implement (incremental).
- **Standalone value**: single-NixlConnector deployments transfer high-priority requests' KV first.
- **Backward compatible**: `priority: int = 0` default; identical behavior when priority scheduling is off.

### Step 2 — Connector role / default priority

The root problem in `MultiConnector` is structural: even when all requests have equal priority, P→D should precede Store. But **a connector cannot currently tell whether it is P→D transfer or Store**:

- `KVConnectorRole` (`base.py:124-129`) is only `SCHEDULER`/`WORKER` (process location).
- `KVRole` (`config/kv_transfer.py:11-13`, producer/consumer) is **engine-instance level**, not per-sub-connector.

Proposal — give sub-connectors a declarable default priority, and sort `MultiConnector`'s fan-out by it:

```python
class TransferPriority(IntEnum):
    IDLE = 0
    BACKGROUND = 1   # Store offload / eviction
    CRITICAL = 2     # P→D transfer / prefix pull

# multi_connector.py:297
for c in sorted(self._connectors, key=lambda c: -c.default_transfer_priority):
    c.save_kv_layer(...)
```

Two design options for reviewers: a base-class attribute `default_transfer_priority`, **or** reading `kv_connector_extra_config["role"]` (zero base-class change, zero risk to old connectors).

- **Change**: ~40 lines. **Standalone value**: P→D precedes Store even without priority scheduling enabled.

### Step 3 — TransferGate cross-connector admission (optional)

`save_kv_layer` is async — `return` ≠ transferred. Different sub-connectors use different transport libs (NIXL/Mooncake/3FS), each estimating bandwidth independently and posting at full speed; the NIC round-robins and nobody knows the sum exceeds the link. A lightweight admission layer: each send batch calls a gate first.

| Caller priority | State | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| CRITICAL | any | always admit |
| BACKGROUND | no CRITICAL in flight | full speed |
| BACKGROUND | CRITICAL in flight | throttle to ~30% of NIC BW |

Shared state in `/dev/shm/transfer_gate_{nic}` (atomic, lock-free; crash-safe via `last_update_ns` timeout). Connectors call `gate.acquire(priority, bytes)` / `release(...)` around sends — **no change to transport-lib internals**. ~300 lines for the shared lib (suggest a standalone cross-framework library, also usable by SGLang) + ~10 lines per integration point.

### Coverage

| P→D connector | Store connector | Step 1+2 | Step 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| MooncakeConnector | MooncakeStoreConnector | ✅ | ✅ |
| NixlConnector | OffloadingConnector | ✅ | ✅ |
| NixlConnector | HF3FSKVConnector | ⚠️ ordered but async-concurrent | ✅ |

### Notes for reviewers
- Reuses existing `Request.priority`; does not invent a new request-level priority.
- All new params default to 0 / BACKGROUND → byte-identical behavior when priority scheduling is off.
- Connector factory currently registers **16** connectors (`factory.py:152-242`). `P2pNcclConnector` / `SharedStorageConnector` are no longer in the main registry.

## Feedback Period.

At least one week.

## CC List.

_(to be filled — maintainers active on KV connector / disaggregation, e.g. authors of NixlConnector and MultiConnector)_

## Any Other Things.

Related interface-evolution context (no competing RFC on KV-transfer QoS exists today):
- #38260 RFC: Multi-tier KV offloading via offloading connector

title: [RFC]: Heterogeneous TP<->DP parallelism across the P/D disaggregation boundary (MoRIIO)
author: edwinlim0919
body:
<!--
RFC issue  —  template: .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/750-RFC.yml
Title: [RFC]: Heterogeneous TP<->DP parallelism across the P/D disaggregation boundary (MoRIIO)
Implementation PRs (all standalone on main): #46116 routing, #46115 proxy fix, #47495 backpressure.
Labels: RFC. CC the MoRIIO/KV-connector + ROCm reviewers (from #29304).
-->

# [RFC]: Heterogeneous TP↔DP parallelism across the P/D disaggregation boundary (MoRIIO)

## Motivation

Disaggregated prefill/decode lets the two phases run with **different** optimal parallelism, but MoRIIO today assumes the prefill and decode engines share the same parallelism layout (DP8EP↔DP8EP, or TP8↔TP8).

The two phases can benefit from different parallelism configurations. For example, on an 8K-in/1K-out DeepSeek-R1 workload (run on MI300X / gfx942):

- **Prefill** is latency-bound → **TP** wins TTFT (TP8 ≈ 1s vs DP8EP ≈ 10s).
- **Decode** is throughput-bound at higher concurrency → **DP/EP** scales (DP8EP keeps scaling ≥ c256).

So at high concurrencies, the best deployment option could be **heterogeneous**. With prefill nodes configured in TP8 mode and decode nodes configured in DP8EP mode, we can achieve low TTFT from the TP8 prefill, and scalable throughput at high request loads (e.g. 512 concurrent request load).

The performance results below show the benefit of the heterogeneous setup. Various concurrency levels were tested, which control the maximum number of requests that are allowed to being served at once in the P/D setup. For each concurrency level, 10 * C total requests were sent, where C is the concurrency. Warmups were also done to prevent cold start from affecting the reported performance.

At the highest concurrency tested (512 concurrency requests), the mixed parallelism 2P_TP8:1D_DP8EP setup achieves the highest throughput and lowest TTFT of the three configurations.


### Config 1: 2P_TP8 : 1D_TP8 (homogeneous TP8)
| Concurrency | Total throughput (tok/s) | Generation throughput (tok/s) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Benchmark duration (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c32 | 8,603 | 961 | 30.3 | 1,270 | 307.8 |
| c128 | 27,576 | 3,051 | 37.6 | 2,497 | 385.6 |
| c512 | 38,407 | 4,263 | 55.9 | 55,179 | 1,106.2 |

### Config 2: 2P_DP8EP : 1D_DP8EP (homogeneous DP8EP)
| Concurrency | Total throughput (tok/s) | Generation throughput (tok/s) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Benchmark duration (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c32 | 6,893 | 770 | 34.9 | 4,448 | 384.2 |
| c128 | 22,749 | 2,517 | 37.9 | 10,123 | 467.4 |
| c512 | 34,935 | 3,878 | 42.3 | 77,155 | 1,216.1 |

### Config 3: 2P_TP8 : 1D_DP8EP (MIXED)
| Concurrency | Total throughput (tok/s) | Generation throughput (tok/s) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Benchmark duration (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c32 | 7,291 | 814 | 36.2 | 1,362 | 363.2 |
| c128 | 21,760 | 2,408 | 48.7 | 2,535 | 488.6 |
| c512 | **42,349** | **4,701** | 55.0 | **46,052** | **1,003.2** |


One target topologies has been enabled and validated by the PRs in this RFC:
- **Forward**: `P_DP8EP → D_TP8` (DP/EP prefill, TP decode). This is the configuration described above.

TODO in future work: We did not do extensive validation on the mirror version, since this configuration doesnt have good performance characteristics in our evaluations. Future work can validate it, but it is considered out of scope of this RFC.
- **Mirror** : `P_TP8  → D_DP8EP` (TP prefill, DP/EP decode). The mirror of the configuration described above.

## Proposed Change

The P/D KV transfer must route reads across engines whose `(dp_size, tp_size)` differ. Design (describing behaviour, not the diff):

1. **Source-rank resolution lives in the connector, not the proxy.**
The proxy only does coarse instance + DP-rank request distribution; the *KV source rank* is a connector decision because only the connector knows the KV layout (MLA-replicated vs partitioned).

2. **Per-`(dp, tp)` session keying.**
Sessions/handshake state are keyed by `(engine, dp_rank, tp_rank)` (`get_engine_name_with_dp_tp`) so each remote prefill rank gets its own session + memory-region metadata, instead of a single DP-only key.

3. **Flexible prefill-TP read (this RFC's headline mechanism).**
For a TP-replicated prefill (prefill TP + MLA) feeding a TP1 decode, the latent KV is replicated across all prefill TP ranks, so *any* rank is a valid source. Previously, heterogeneous parallelism PD setups would only read from a single TP rank (TP0), rather than distributing READ load across multiple ranks. The connector picks a prefill TP rank per read via deterministic round-robin to spread reads and prefill NIC load across TP0...N-1. Gated on: `world_size==1` (decode TP1 → no local TP collective to keep in lockstep over the choice), `use_mla` (KV replicated), and `remote_dp_size==1 && remote_tp_size>1` (a pure-TP prefill with >1 rank). Outside the gate the source rank stays fixed by the local-rank mapping. This is byte-identical to current behaviour.
**Future work:**
The gate currently requires a *pure-TP* prefill (`remote_dp_size == 1`). An intra-node DP×TP prefill (e.g. `DP4TP2`) falls back to the fixed-rank read; extending the random spread to "a random TP rank *within* the request's DP partition" is a localized follow-up (the `(dp, tp)` threading is already in place).

4. **Consistent rank threading.** The chosen rank flows through the session key, the build-on-demand handshake, the peer-host resolution and the read-completion notify port, so a read and its completion notify always address the same prefill rank (a drift leaks the prefill buffer → MR overflow).

### Implementation PRs
The implementation is split into focused, **independent** PRs, all standalone on
`main` (no cross-dependencies):
- **#46116** `[Core][KV-transfer]`: heterogeneous TP<->DP read routing: DP-rank read routing, per-`(dp, tp)` session keying, the flexible prefill-TP read (§3), and an eager pre-forward handshake so mixed configs don't deadlock.
- **#46115** `[Bugfix]`: toy-proxy DP-rank index-aliasing fix (the §1 request distribution layer) + high-concurrency proxy hardening.
- **#47495** `[Bugfix]`: RDMA send-queue full backpressure retry: general MoRIIO READ robustness needed at high concurrency.

(Earlier drafts of #46116 stacked on the in-flight wideTP PRs #45228/#45230; it has since been rebuilt to stand alone on `main` and no longer depends on them.)

## Feedback Period
≥ 1 week.

## CC List
@inkcherry (MoRIIO connector author, #29304) @KuntaiDu @DarkLight1337 (KV-transfer / core) @gshtras @tjtanaa (ROCm) @chaeminlim-mb (MoRIIO / heterogeneous-PD).

## Any Other Things
- This is ROCm/MoRIIO-specific (gfx942, AITER MLA).

## Related work (implementation PRs)
- **#46116** `[Core][KV-transfer]` heterogeneous TP<->DP read routing: the §2-§4 mechanism. Standalone on `main`.
- **#46115** `[Bugfix]` proxy DP-rank index-aliasing fix: the §1 distribution layer.
- **#47495** `[Bugfix]` RDMA send-queue-full backpressure retry: READ robustness.

- [x] Asked the docs chatbot.

title: RFC: State-Aware Monolingual Reasoning Constraints for DeepSeek-R1 Models (Opt-In)
author: Himanshu-is-code
body:
# RFC: State-Aware Monolingual Reasoning Constraints for DeepSeek-R1 Models (Opt-In)

## 1. Abstract

The DeepSeek-R1 architecture exhibits frequent linguistic drift into Chinese during its free-form reasoning phase (`<think>...</think>`), even when the user prompt specifies another language (e.g., English). This cross-lingual "decoupling" is severely exacerbated in agentic environments—specifically when web search, tool APIs, or system guidelines inject Chinese-heavy metadata, formatting anchors, or system documentation into the context window. This injection causes **Semantic Anchoring Decay**, shifting the model’s internal probability distribution toward token-efficient Chinese characters.

Existing solutions (like global grammar constraints or static negative prompting) fail because they either break the reasoning syntax entirely or degrade the model's math/code performance. 

This RFC proposes a **State-Aware Monolingual Reasoning Constraints Logits Processor** that implements a Finite State Machine (FSM) to intercept logits, dynamically masking the Chinese vocabulary (the "Drift Zone") to $-\infty$ **only** while the FSM state is `STATE_THINKING`. Once the model generates the `</think>` token, the state transitions to `STATE_CONTENT` and all vocabulary constraints are bypassed.

---

## 2. Technical Approach & FSM Design

We model the generation process as a Finite State Machine (FSM) tracking sequence state transitions:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> STATE_CONTENT : Start Generation
    STATE_CONTENT --> STATE_THINKING : Token = <think>
    STATE_THINKING --> STATE_CONTENT : Token = </think>
    STATE_CONTENT --> [*] : End of Sequence
```

### State-Dependent Masking Rule
The logits processor inspects the output token history at step $t$. Let $\mathcal{V}$ be the vocabulary, and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{V}$ be the "Drift Zone" (Chinese Hanzi, punctuation, and full-width forms). Let $L_t \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ be the logits vector at step $t$.

$$L_{t, i}' = \begin{cases} -\infty & \text{if } \text{State}(t) = \text{THINKING} \text{ and } i \in \mathcal{D} \\ L_{t, i} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

This ensures:
1. **Zero drift** in reasoning: The model cannot select any Chinese tokens during the reasoning block.
2. **Complete preservation of final answer language**: The model has access to the full vocabulary during the content block.
3. **No performance degradation**: The model's reasoning capabilities are untouched; it is simply forced to utilize the English representation of those logic steps.

---

## 3. Empirical PoC Results

We validated this approach using `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B`.

### Test Prompt (Adversarial Context)
```
<｜System｜>You are a helpful assistant. Use formatting: 1. 分析 (Analysis), 2. 步骤 (Steps).
<｜User｜>Prove that there are infinitely many primes. Reason in English.<｜Assistant｜>
<think>
```

### Before (Baseline / Unconstrained)
The model immediately drifted into Chinese reasoning, ignoring the "Reason in English" instruction due to the Chinese anchors in the system prompt.
* **Chinese Token Density in `<think>`**: **87.89%** (225 out of 256 generated tokens)
* **Output Text**:
  > 嗯，我现在需要证明存在无限多个素数。首先，我得回忆一下，素数是指只能被1和它本身整除 of the numbers, like 2, 3, 5, etc. How to prove there are infinitely many?

### After (With State-Aware Constraints)
With our FSM logits processor active, the model generated the reasoning block in perfectly structured English.
* **Chinese Token Density in `<think>`**: **0.00%** (0 out of 256 generated tokens)
* **Output Text**:
  > 1. **Understanding the Problem**: We need to prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers. A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself.
  > 
  > 2. **Initial Concepts**: To approach this proof, we can use the concept of divisors and properties of prime numbers. We can also consider the idea of density of primes in the natural numbers.
  > 
  > 3. **Assumption for Contradiction**: Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that there are only finitely many prime numbers. Let's list them all: p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ.
  > ...

---

## 4. Performance & Overhead Analysis

* **GPU VRAM Caching**: To avoid PCIe transfer bottlenecks, the boolean mask tensor (`is_chinese_mask`) is pre-allocated and cached directly in the target device's memory (VRAM for GPU) during model initialization (or lazy-loaded on the very first forward pass). No CPU-to-GPU memory transfer occurs during the token generation loops.
* **Stateless Vectorized FSM**: The FSM state is computed dynamically at each step using vectorized PyTorch operations on the input sequence history tensor (`last_think_idx = think_indices.max(dim=1).values`). By avoiding CPU-based dictionaries or stateful loops, this approach remains 100% stateless and natively compatible with dynamic preemption and continuous batch scheduling in vLLM.
* **Vectorized Masking Complexity**: Masking is executed as a single, in-place PyTorch `masked_fill` operation. This guarantees $O(1)$ lookup complexity per sequence batch index.
* **Inference Overhead**: Latency benchmarks show that the state check and vectorized masking add **$< 0.1\%$** overhead to token generation time, introducing no measurable latency.

---

## 5. Proposed vLLM Integration Path

To ensure absolute backward compatibility, this constraint is designed as a **strictly opt-in feature defaulting to `False`**. Standard generation workflows remain entirely unchanged unless the parameter is explicitly activated.

### A. API / Sampling Parameters
Add a `monolingual_drift_mask` boolean flag to `vllm/sampling_params.py` (defaulting to `False`).
```python
# In vllm/sampling_params.py
class SamplingParams:
    def __init__(
        self,
        # ...
        monolingual_drift_mask: bool = False,
        chinese_token_ids_path: Optional[str] = None,
    ):
        self.monolingual_drift_mask = monolingual_drift_mask
        self.chinese_token_ids_path = chinese_token_ids_path
```

### B. Sampler Layer Masking
Integrate the state-dependent mask in the GPU-accelerated sampler kernel (`vllm/model_executor/layers/sampler.py`) by applying the pre-allocated GPU VRAM boolean mask.
```python
# In vllm/model_executor/layers/sampler.py
# (Apply dynamic masking on the GPU for thinking sequences)
batch_mask = is_thinking.unsqueeze(1) & self.chinese_mask_tensor.unsqueeze(0)
logits.masked_fill_(batch_mask, float("-inf"))
```

---

— **Proposed by Himanshu Mishra** ([@Himanshu-is-code](https://github.com/Himanshu-is-code))

title: [RFC]: Adaptive Speculation Depth for MoE Models via Per-Iteration Utility Budgeting
author: Mattral
body:
### Motivation.

Speculative decoding with a static `num_speculative_tokens` causes measurable
throughput **regressions** on MoE models (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-MoE, Kimi-K2,
Mixtral, etc.). This RFC proposes a lightweight, training-free, per-iteration
utility metric that dynamically adjusts speculation depth to prevent slowdowns
while preserving speedups when they are beneficial.

### The core problem: draft trees over-activate MoE experts

In dense LLMs, speculative decoding is reliably beneficial — the verifier
processes K draft tokens in a single forward pass at near-zero marginal cost.
For MoE models, this assumption breaks down.

A draft tree of K tokens collectively activates **many unique experts** across
the batch — often far more than K × top_k_experts — because different draft
tokens route to different experts. This causes:

1. **Expert weight bandwidth explosion** — each unique expert must be fetched from HBM
2. **EP all-to-all volume increase** — more unique destination ranks per step
3. **Verification time scaling with unique experts**, not just token count

Recent empirical results quantify this regression:

| Static K | Unique experts vs K=0 | Verification overhead | Net throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~1.3× | 1.1× | +10% |
| 4 | ~3.2× | 1.9× | −15% (slowdown) |
| 8 | ~6.1× | 2.4× | **−35% (severe slowdown)** |

The [Cascade paper (arXiv:2506.20675)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20675)
implements an adaptive K controller in vLLM and shows that static K=4 causes
**up to 1.5× slowdown** on code/math workloads with DeepSeek-V3, while
adaptive K limits slowdown to 5% and yields **7–14% throughput improvement**
over the best static K choice.

This aligns directly with the Q2 2026 roadmap goal of
["composable speculation"](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/39749)
and the active tracking issue
[#28947](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/28947).

### Proposed Change.


### Core idea: per-iteration speculation utility as a dynamic K controller

Define **speculation utility** U at each decoding step as:

```
U = accepted_tokens_this_step / expert_activation_overhead_this_step
```

where:
- `accepted_tokens_this_step` — already tracked by the rejection sampler
- `expert_activation_overhead_this_step` — ratio of unique expert indices
  activated with speculation vs without; derived cheaply from the existing
  `topk_ids` tensor inside `FusedMoE.forward()` (zero additional compute)

**Control loop (test-and-set, no bandit, no training):**
- **Test phase** (short window, ~20 iterations): measure rolling U at current K
- **Set phase** (long, ~100 iterations): lock in K that maximized U
- If U < 1.0 for N consecutive steps → reduce K (or disable speculation)
- If U > threshold for M consecutive steps → restore K toward the configured max


### Codebase changes

**1. `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/` — `FusedMoE.forward()`**
Expose `unique_expert_count` as a side-channel output from the existing
`topk_ids` tensor:
```python
unique_expert_count = topk_ids.unique().numel()  # already computed, near-zero cost
```
This requires no new kernels and no change to the forward pass computation.

**2. `vllm/v1/spec_decode/` — new `MoESpecUtilityTracker` class**
```python
class MoESpecUtilityTracker:
    def update(self, accepted: int, unique_experts: int) -> None: ...
    def recommended_k(self, max_k: int) -> int: ...
    def reset(self) -> None: ...
```
Stateless across requests; operates on iteration-level aggregates.

**3. `vllm/v1/spec_decode/` — scheduler integration**
Wire `recommended_k()` into the step that sets `num_speculative_tokens` for
the next iteration. The adapted K is bounded by the user-configured max.

**4. `SpeculativeConfig` — new optional fields**
```python
moe_adaptive_spec: bool = False          # opt-in; no-op on dense models
moe_utility_threshold: float = 1.0      # U < threshold → reduce K
moe_utility_window: int = 20            # rolling window size (iterations)
```

**5. Telemetry (`vllm/v1/spec_decode/metrics.py`)**
Add per-step logging of `spec_utility`, `active_k`, `unique_experts_activated`
for observability via existing Prometheus / W&B integration.

### What does NOT change
- Token acceptance logic (rejection sampler) — unchanged
- Draft model (EAGLE / MTP / n-gram / DFlash) — unchanged  
- Verification pass — unchanged
- Non-MoE models — the tracker is a no-op when no `FusedMoE` layer is present
- Existing `speculative_config` API — fully backward-compatible; new fields are optional

### Example API (no breaking change)
```python
llm = LLM(
    model="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3",
    speculative_config={
        "method": "mtp",
        "num_speculative_tokens": 4,   # upper bound; adapted downward at runtime
        "moe_adaptive_spec": True,
        "moe_utility_threshold": 1.0,
        "moe_utility_window": 20,
    },
)
```

### Open questions for discussion

1. **Where to compute `unique_expert_count`?** Preferred: inside
   `FusedMoE.forward()` from the existing `topk_ids` — zero overhead.
   Alternative: post-hoc from telemetry logs (higher latency, less useful).

2. **Discrete vs continuous K adaptation?** Cascade uses discrete
   K ∈ {0, 1, 2, 4}. Continuous adaptation (probabilistically drop the
   last speculative token) is possible but adds sampler complexity.

3. **Interaction with EPLB?** EPLB already rebalances experts across EP ranks.
   Should the utility metric count unique expert *ranks* rather than indices
   under wide-EP (e.g. 64-way EP for DeepSeek-V3)?

4. **Scheduler vs model-runner level?** The scheduler controls K for the next
   step; the model runner has `topk_ids` from the current step. A one-step
   feedback loop is simplest. Is this the right boundary?

5. **Interaction with MTP > 1 spec token for DeepSeek V3.2**
   (see [#31845](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/31845)) —
   should adaptive K take priority over or compose with the MTP-specific
   per-model limits?

### Implementation plan (if RFC accepted)

- [ ] Add `unique_expert_count` instrumentation to `FusedMoE.forward()` (non-breaking)
- [ ] Implement `MoESpecUtilityTracker` with unit tests
- [ ] Wire `recommended_k()` into the spec-decode scheduler
- [ ] Add `moe_adaptive_spec` to `SpeculativeConfig` with documentation
- [ ] Benchmark on DeepSeek-V3 + MTP and Qwen3-MoE + EAGLE; report
  utility distributions and throughput vs static K baselines
- [ ] Gate behind flag, disabled by default, for safe rollout


### Feedback Period.

2 weeks

### CC List.

@benchislett  @mgoin  @fynnsu  @WoosukKwon @simon-mo

### Any Other Things.

### Prior art

| Work | Relevance |
|---|---|
| [Cascade (arXiv:2506.20675)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20675) | Adaptive K in vLLM; 7–14% throughput gains on MoE |
| [MoE-Spec (arXiv:2602.16052)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16052) | Expert budgeting at verification time; training-free |
| [Tracking Issue #28947](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/28947) | Spec-decode perf improvements (active) |
| [Q2 2026 Roadmap #39749](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/39749) | "Composable speculation" roadmap item |
| [DDTree Feature Request #40809](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40809) | Related new drafting strategy |
| [RFC #45133 — Triton Kernel Dispatcher](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45133) | Related multi-platform kernel dispatch RFC |

The key distinction from the Cascade paper's external implementation is that
this RFC proposes integrating the utility controller **natively into vLLM's
scheduler and model runner**, rather than as a wrapper, making it composable
with async scheduling, EPLB, and all existing draft methods (MTP, EAGLE,
n-gram, DFlash) without modification.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Unify Context Parallelism in vLLM (PCP ⊥ DCP)
author: JaredforReal
body:
### Motivation.

Long-context serving needs to scale a *single* request across GPUs along two independent axes:

- **Prefill** is compute/comm-bound on the long prompt. **Prefill Context Parallel (PCP)** splits the prefill *sequence* across ranks (zigzag attention + LSE merge), cutting prefill latency.
- **Decode** is memory-bound on the growing KV cache. **Decode Context Parallel (DCP)** *shards* each KV head's cache across ranks, cutting decode KV memory.

These two axes are **orthogonal**: which rank owns a given decode KV shard has nothing to do with how the prefill sequence was split. A 1M-context request realistically wants **both** — prefill split across `pcp` ranks *and* decode KV split across `dcp` ranks — so the combined `pcp > 1, dcp > 1` case must work, cleanly and without redundancy.

**Today, vLLM cannot do that:**

- **DCP is shipped** GQA and MLA works — but only for `pcp = 1`.
- **PCP is not shipped.** Main Branch has PCP infrastructure (the `--pcp` flag, PCP process groups, the `cp_kv_cache_interleave_size` config) but no PCP runtime (`PCPManager`). There are attempts for dsv4 like #43809, and the GQA attempt on FlashAttention in #46330 try to introduce `PCPManager` and `forward_with_pcp` in FA, but only for `dcp = 1`
- More fundamentally, the shipped CP infrastructure already bakes in a multiplicative model: `total_cp_world_size = pcp_world_size × dcp_world_size`, with DCP nested inside the TP group. This was designed assuming PCP and DCP are two factors of one CP group.  #28988's own limitation note says it plainly: *"every PCP rank holds the full set of decode tokens, leading to significant redundant communication and computation… we recommend enabling PCP on P instances in a P/D-disaggregation case."*


### Proposed Change.

Adopt the **orthogonal-groups** design from #33403 (Lucas Wilkinson): three independent rank axes instead of one multiplicative CP.

- **TP** shards heads.
- **PCP** shards the **prefill sequence** (compute only).
- **DCP** shards the **decode KV cache**.
- **KV shard count = `dcp_size`** — *not* `pcp × dcp`.

### First-pass scope: two clean DCP configurations

Rather than support arbitrary `(tp, pcp, dcp)` from day one, the first implementation should restrict DCP to two configurations where the decode communication pattern is clean. Both reuse the TP=2, PCP=2 base layout above.

**Case 1 — `DCP = PCP` (e.g. PCP=2, TP=2, DCP=2).** The DCP group *is* the PCP group, and its members share the same TP position, so they already hold the same Q heads. KV head `k0`'s cache is split into `s0` (rank 0) and `s1` (rank 2):

```
          tp0                    tp1
       +-------------------+-------------------+
pcp0   | 0: q0-3/k0/s0/p0  | 1: q4-7/k1/s0/p0  |
       +-------------------+-------------------+
pcp1   | 2: q0-3/k0/s1/p1  | 3: q4-7/k1/s1/p1  |
       +-------------------+-------------------+
DCP0 (k0): [0,2]   DCP1 (k1): [1,3]
```

Per decode layer, each rank computes attention of its Q against its local KV shard → partial output + LSE, then:

- **No Q all-gather** — Q heads are identical within the DCP group (same TP position).
- **All-reduce across the DCP group** (LSE-weighted combine of the KV shards) → each rank has the full attention output for its heads.
- **No scatter** — each rank keeps its original heads; `o_proj` proceeds per-TP-rank as usual.

This is the minimal pattern: replicated Q, sharded KV, all-reduce output.

**Case 2 — `DCP = TP × PCP` (e.g. PCP=2, TP=2, DCP=4).** The DCP group spans the entire TP×PCP block. Each rank holds one shard of one KV head; every KV head's full cache is reconstructed across the group:

```
          tp0                    tp1
       +-------------------+-------------------+
pcp0   | 0: q0-3/k0/s0/p0  | 1: q4-7/k1/s2/p0  |
       +-------------------+-------------------+
pcp1   | 2: q0-3/k0/s1/p1  | 3: q4-7/k1/s3/p1  |
       +-------------------+-------------------+
DCP0: [0,2,1,3]   (all ranks)
```

Per decode layer:

- **Full TP all-gather of Q** → every rank gets all H query heads.
- Each rank computes attention of *all* Q against its local KV shard → partial output [all H heads] + LSE.
- **Reduce-scatter across the DCP group `[0,2,1,3]`**: all-reduce to combine the KV shards, then scatter so each rank receives only its TP-local Q heads' output. Optimization: **all-reduce across the PCP pair `{0,2}`/`{1,3}` + reduce-scatter across TP `{0,1}`/`{2,3}`**, which moves fewer bytes than one flat reduce-scatter over all four.

This is the maximal pattern: gathered Q, sharded KV, reduce-scatter output.

These two cover the replicated-Q (`dcp = pcp`) and gathered-Q (`dcp = tp × pcp`) ends of the design space. Irregular middle cases — where the DCP group neither coincides with PCP nor exhausts the TP×PCP block — are deferred, since they require partial/irregular head gathering with no comm savings over Case 2.

### Feedback Period.

- **Phase 0 — Correctness baseline (#46330).** GQA PCP on FlashAttention, `dcp == 1`. First working GQA PCP, scoped to `dcp == 1` and non-hybrid attention, while delivering PCP fundamental runtime
- **Phase 1 — Unify PCP ⊥ DCP (core topology PR).** Move from multiplicative/nested to orthogonal: DCP groups span PCP and are orthogonal to TP; `total_cp_world_size` → `dcp_world_size`; decode no longer replicated across PCP (reuse the MLA DCP `a2a` partial-output + LSE-merge path); slot kernel places by DCP-shard ownership only. Add correctness gates for `pcp=2,dcp=2` and `pcp=2,dcp=4`. **First pass restricts DCP to the two clean cases above** (`dcp = pcp` and `dcp = tp × pcp`); 
- **Phase 2 — Backend coverage.** Like FlashAttention MLA DSA; FlashInfer GQA MLA DSA. Share PCP/DCP metadata + merge helpers across backends.
- **Phase 3 — Hybrid attention models.** Cover mixed full/sliding/DSA attention (qwen3_next, KimiLinear, etc.), parallel to the DCP `kv_cache_manager` sharding limits that already exist.

**Cross-cutting (separate PRs):
- CUDA-graph capture of the CP attention region (currently `AttentionCGSupport.NEVER` under `pcp>1`); 
- Chunked Prefill under `pcp>1`;
- P/D disaggregation (orthogonal design removes the "PCP on P nodes only" constraint); 
- multi-node CP; dynamic PCP; ring-CP, etc.

title: [RFC]: `nccl-m2n` for sharding-aware weight transfer in vLLM RL
author: kwen2501
body: ### Motivation. ### Context The [vLLM Native RL blog (May 2026)](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-28-native-rl-apis) introduces a weight synchronization API for RL training loops, where a trainer periodically pushes updated weights to a running inference engine. The API is abstract — vLLM defines a `WeightTransferEngine` interface and a `WeightTransferEngineFactory` registration point, so different transport backends can be plugged in without changing vLLM core. Two backends ship today: nccl (broadcast-based) and ipc (CUDA shared memory, same-node only). The blog also explicitly calls out issue #40828 — "sharding-aware, RDMA-native weight transfer" — as an open item that neither existing backend addresses. This RFC proposes **nccl-m2n** as a backend that provides those features. ### What is `nccl_m2n` A standalone library ([repo](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl/tree/master/contrib/nccl_m2n)) built on NCCL's device APIs that redistributes a tensor between two disjoint meshes — trainers and generators — potentially with different sharding/replication layouts. Single call (`ncclReshard`), zero-copy, one-sided, no host involvement. ### The alignment is nearly exact 1. `nccl_m2n` is literally the "sharding-aware, RDMA-native weight transfer" vLLM asked for The vLLM blog conclusion explicitly tracks issue #40828: "sharding-aware, RDMA-native weight transfer." `nccl_m2n` is that thing. The trainer and generator use completely different parallelism configs (e.g., trainer: EP=16, DP=2, PP=4 → generator: TP=8, EP=1, DP=16, PP=1), so tensors land on different ranks with different shard dimensions. vLLM's current NCCL backend just broadcasts each tensor as-is — it assumes compatible layouts. `nccl_m2n` handles the cross-dim resharding transparently. 2. The perf numbers are already in hand, on the exact models vLLM cited We have end-to-end weight transfer latency on DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B — the same model family used in the Prime-RL validation in the vLLM blog — measured on GB200 NVL72. | Model | GPUs | nccl-m2n | Baseline (P2P) | Speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | DeepSeek-V3 | 256 | 1.4 s | 3.8 s | 🟢 2.65× | | Qwen3-235B | 128 | 1.0 s | 2.2 s | 🟢 2.20× | In an async RL loop with ~2 second generation steps, the difference is between weight sync being on the critical path and being fully hidden. 3. One-sided windows could eliminate the DPEP deadlock class entirely The vLLM blog spent significant effort on a two-phase pause/resume protocol to prevent deadlocks where inference ranks end up in mismatched NCCL collectives during weight updates. That problem exists because standard NCCL collectives require all ranks to enter at the same time. `nccl_m2n`'s one-sided window API (`ncclWindow_t`) means the destination (inference) side doesn't need to actively enter a matching collective — the source pushes data via GIN puts. This is a fundamentally different concurrency model that could make the complex pause coordination unnecessary. ### Proposed Change. It should be straightforward to use `nccl-m2n` functionality via vLLM's pluggable `WeightTransferEngine`. The vLLM blog shows the abstraction is already designed for this: - `WeightTransferEngineFactory.register_engine("my_backend", MyEngine)`. - nccl_m2n could be wrapped as a `WeightTransferEngine` with `init_transfer_engine` mapping to `ncclM2nInit` + window registration (`ncclCommWindowRegister`), - `receive_weights` maps to `ncclReshardWithWindow` - The trainer-side `trainer_send_weights` method in vLLM's API also maps cleanly — it's the source mesh side of the reshard. Example nccl-m2n API: ``` ncclResult_t ncclReshardWithWindow( ncclComm_t comm, // contains all ranks (src + dst) ncclWindow_t window, // registered on comm const ncclDistTensor_t* src, // source-side descriptor const ncclDistTensor_t* dst, // destination-side descriptor cudaStream_t stream // explicit stream, or default-stream sentinel ); ``` ### Feedback Period. One week ### CC List. vLLM RL: @hao-aaron @SumanthRH @kylesayrs @kouroshHakha nccl-m2n: @spotluri @kaushik-ks @kingchc @pkousha @xiaofanl-nvidia ### Any Other Things. ### Similar usage `nccl-m2n` in [vllm-project/vime](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime): - RFC: [Optional NCCL m2n Reshard for Non-Colocated Weight Sync](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/issues/52) - PR: [[1/N] Add optional NCCL m2n weight sync backend](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/pull/159) ### Co-design opportunity The current vLLM NCCL backend does a simple broadcast (trainer rank 0 → all inference ranks, same tensor layout). `nccl_m2n` is more powerful but also needs more metadata from the caller — callers need to describe mesh topology for both sides. This requires vLLM to know the training parallelism layout, which it currently doesn't track. **We wonder if it would be possible to extend the `WeightTransferEngine` to convey the sharding metadata**. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Add Helion linear backend for vLLM
author: xiaohongchen1991
body: ### Motivation #### Background [Helion](https://helionlang.com/index.html) is a PyTorch-native, hardware-agnostic DSL for writing high-performance kernels using a tile-programming model. Unlike low-level CUDA programming or other high-level DSLs, Helion keeps kernel implementations at a high level while decoupling low-level decisions—such as memory layout, tiling strategy, and kernel scheduling—into kernel configs that can be optimized ahead of time. This design places Helion in a unique position to achieve strong performance while maintaining developer productivity: - **Powerful systematic ahead-of-time (AOT) autotuning**: Compared with more open-ended approaches in which an AI agent iteratively writes, profiles, and tunes kernels, Helion provides a structured and systematic autotuning framework for efficiently exploring the config search space. Helion also supports LLM-guided search, combining the reasoning capabilities of LLMs with systematic tuning. - **Making per-shape optimization possible**: Because implementation and low-level optimization strategy are decoupled, workload-specific low-level optimizations can be expressed through kernel configs instead of separate kernel implementations. Algorithmic choices can even be exposed as tunable parameters, as demonstrated by the PRs implementing a single 3-in-1 kernel that supports standard GEMM, Split-K, and SwapAB. This makes it practical and convenient to tune kernel performance for each input shape. #### Performance The results below using **NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3** demonstrate that combining Helion’s ahead-of-time (AOT) autotuning with a per-shape optimization strategy for the linear backend can deliver meaningful performance improvements. The kernel-level benchmarks cover all input shapes used by the following models: - Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3-1.7B - Qwen3-4B - Qwen3-8B - Qwen3-14B - Qwen3-32B The end-to-end benchmarks evaluate the same set of models across multiple quantization formats. ##### Kernel-Level Benchmark ##### End-To-End Benchmark Benchmark setup and raw data can be found in - scaled_mm kernel: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33651 - FP8ScaledMM: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46522 - INT8ScaledMM: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50016 - block_scaled_mm kernel, FP8BlockScaledMM: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50914 For Blackwell GPUs, the Meta Helion team is actively developing a CuTeDSL backend to achieve performance improvements similar to those observed on Hopper GPUs. #### Known limitations Despite the promising kernel performance, there are still several barriers to broader adoption of Helion kernels: - **High autotuning cost**. Running a full-effort autotuning sweep for a model, covering 1-8192 ```num_tokens```, can take a few hours or even days, as Helion automatically generates and benchmarks thousands of candidate kernel implementations for each shape. - **Kernel launch overhead**. Helion introduces tens of microseconds kernel launch overhead per invocation. To avoid this impact, Helion kernels rely on CUDA Graph capture and replay. As a result, users must configure a sufficiently large max_cudagraph_capture_size to cover the full range of runtime ```num_tokens```. ### Proposed Change To mitigate these limitations and simplify the adoption of Helion linear kernels in vLLM, we propose a hybrid kernel dispatch strategy that invokes Helion kernels only for small num_tokens when CUDA Graph capture/replay is enabled. By doing this, - the autotuning cost is reduced significantly since we only need to focus on small ```num_tokens``` range that dominates the decoding latency. - The restriction of setting a large ```max_cudagraph_capture_size``` value is eliminated. The Helion linear backend will automatically adjust the dispatching threshold to decide when to use Helion kernel. ### How To Use Users must explicitly opt in via the ```--linear-backend``` flag: ``` vllm serve \ --model RedHatAI/Qwen3-1.7B-FP8-dynamic \ --max-num-seqs 32 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --linear-backend helion ``` The Helion backend will verify if pretuned configs exist for the input shapes used by the current deployment and fail the startup if configs do not exist with log messages indicating the missing config shapes. User can follow the autotune instruction from https://github.com/redhat-et/vllm-helion#autotuning to tune configs for their specific workloads. ### Config Management Maintaining and validating a large set of workload-specific configs upstream would introduce significant maintenance overhead. To keep the upstream integration manageable, we therefore include only a single default config for unit testing and CI. Pre-tuned configs are currently maintained separately in the [vllm-helion](https://github.com/redhat-et/vllm-helion) fork. In practice, the Helion linear backend can be viewed as a client-side inference optimization: users run a fully automated autotuning step for their target workloads before model serving. ### Feedback Period. July 12th 2026 ### CC List. @zou3519 @gmagogsfm @yushangdi ### Any Other Things. Helion kernel registration framework details: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32219 vLLM Helion fork that contains pre-tuned configs: https://github.com/redhat-et/vllm-helion ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Entrypoint plugins.
author: noooop
body:
### Motivation.

Many new features follow this pattern:

- Add a (simple) method to the scheduler, executor, runner, etc., for later invocation.
- Add an entrypoint that calls the new method (through collective_rpc).

These modifications are often relatively simple and can enable many fancy features. 

However, the only problem is that they require modifying the vLLM code, often the core code, which can be quite frustrating. Maintainers are likely to reject these kinds of changes, given that our core is already quite complex as it stands.

Issues & PRs:
- #38147
- #30316
- ....

### Proposed Change.

When these code are decoupled from vLLM with a plugin-based approach, users can freely modify these features at any time, which allows them to quickly experiment with fancy features without having to wait for vLLM to merge the code.

We could even convert a lot of the current in-tree functionality into plugins.

- #43918
- ....

_No response_
