title: [RFC]: Design a shared warmup infrastructure for JITs
author: LopezCastroRoberto
body:
### Motivation.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47451 contains an initial implementation of the proposal described in this RFC.

## Summary

This RFC proposes a standard, extensible warmup infrastructure for JIT kernels in vLLM.

The goal is to let kernels from different JIT backends, including Triton, CuTeDSL, TileLang, and potential future DSLs, expose the set of specializations that should be compiled during engine startup.

This is not intended to be a one-off warmup path for a specific kernel. Instead, it defines a kernel-owned contract where each warmable kernel describes its own compile keys, dispatch logic, warmup search space, and compile-only entry point.

## Motivation

vLLM increasingly relies on JIT-generated kernels from multiple DSLs. Today, warming these kernels is difficult to standardize because each backend exposes different runtime and compilation APIs. This RFC proposes a common infrastructure with several goals:

- Create shared JIT warmup infrastructure for JIT backends in vLLM.
- Keep warmup definitions close to the kernels that own the specialization logic, making the system easier to review and maintain.
- Warm up actual compile keys instead of running representative non-key inputs, such as token sizes, and hoping they map to all required specializations. That mapping is not always obvious or guaranteed, so warmup should target the compile-key space directly.
- Use Python AST dispatch tracing to derive compile-key search spaces from normal Python `dispatch(...)` methods, avoiding duplicated hand-written warmup logic.
- Support compile-only warmup APIs, avoiding dummy runtime launches and dummy tensor allocation. Dummy runs can be expensive and may have side effects; each DSL should expose fake tensor/spec descriptors suitable for compilation only.
- Define a standard interface for new contributors and potentially third-party libraries to expose warmup metadata: compile keys, representative warmup keys, and a compile-only API.

## Proposed Change: Warmup Contract

Each warmable kernel should expose a small wrapper object near the kernel's normal runtime entry point.

The wrapper owns:

- A frozen `CompileKey` dataclass with the fields that identify one compiled specialization.
- A `dispatch(...)` method that maps normal dispatch arguments to `CompileKey`.
- A `get_warmup_keys(...)` method that returns representative keys to compile.
- A `compile(compile_key)` method that compiles one key.

Proposed shape:

```python
class MyKernel(VllmJitKernel["MyKernel.CompileKey"]):

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class CompileKey:
        BLOCK_SIZE: int

    @staticmethod
    def kernel(...):
        ...

    def dispatch(self, *, num_tokens: int) -> CompileKey:
        return self.CompileKey(BLOCK_SIZE= ...)

    def get_warmup_keys(self, vllm_config: VllmConfig) -> list[CompileKey]:
        ...

    def compile(self, compile_key: CompileKey) -> None:
        ...
  
    def __call__(self, ...):
        compile_key = self.dispatch(...)
        ...

MY_KERNEL = MyKernel()
```

CompileKey must be hashable. `get_warmup_keys(...)` should deduplicate keys before returning them if multiple representative inputs map to the same compiled specialization.

## Scope

This RFC covers the warmup contract and the minimal shared infrastructure needed to make JIT warmup kernel-owned and backend-extensible.

The initial scope is limited to:

- A generic wrapper interface for warmable kernels.
- AST-assisted expansion of representative dispatch inputs into compile keys.
- Backend-specific compile-only adapters where needed.
- Initial Triton and CuTeDSL examples that exercise the contract.

It does not attempt to migrate every existing warmup path or define a complete backend-neutral fake tensor API for all DSLs in this first step.

## Current And Prior Work

To my knowledge, PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47451 is the first implementation of this proposal. It adds the shared wrapper contract and demonstrates it with one Triton path and one CuTeDSL path.

Before this proposal, warmup logic was mostly backend-specific and ad hoc. In some cases it used representative runtime-like inputs rather than directly expressing the compile-key space.

#### Unified Runtime monitor
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46167
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46621
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46718

## Risks

- Some specialization fields (compile-keys) may be hidden in backend internals and hard to model.
- Over-warming can increase startup time.
- Third-party libraries may need small API additions to expose compile-only entry points, and potentially methods to get warmup compile keys.

title: [RFC]: ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs instead of state for faster standard and speculative decode (Mamba2 + GDN)
author: Johnny-Liou
body:
### Motivation.

## Summary

[ReplaySSM](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/) is a memory-bandwidth optimization for the decode kernels of state space model (SSM) and linear attention layers. It is a collaboration between Dao AI Lab and NVIDIA; a concurrent cross-framework implementation is in the [TensorRT-LLM PR](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/14203).

SSM decode is memory-bound: today each step reads and writes back the full recurrent state. ReplaySSM instead caches recent inputs, reconstructing the state only when needed and otherwise computing the output directly from the cache. This keeps most steps read-only and writes the full state back only once every L steps. 

ReplaySSM provides three benefits:

1. Memory-traffic reduction in a bandwidth-bound kernel: the per-step state write is replaced by a small input append.
2. Cheap rollback for speculative decoding: caching recent SSM inputs makes rollback a buffer pointer move, avoiding the separate per-draft-token state the current implementation keeps.
3. Parallel verification for speculative decoding: on non-flush steps the output is read directly without materializing the state, so a draft window is verified in one shot instead of by a serial recurrence.

Implementation: we have opened a draft PR (#47576) implementing ReplaySSM in vLLM, based on the [ReplaySSM reference repository](https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM). 

We are aware of the existing feature request #46187, which tracks ReplaySSM in vLLM and is assigned to us as the ReplaySSM authors. This RFC and the accompanying draft PR are the upstream contribution we committed to.

## Motivation

Two problems motivate ReplaySSM.

1. In hybrid models, the SSM (linear-attention) layers are the decode bottleneck at short-to-medium output lengths (Fig 2 in the blog post). SSM decode is memory-bound and its per-step state read/write dominates HBM traffic.
2. Speculative decoding must roll back rejected draft tokens, but the SSM state update is irreversible: once history is summarized into the recurrent state, a token cannot be subtracted back out. To support rollback, the current implementation keeps a separate recurrent state per draft token, which costs extra memory traffic and extra HBM footprint (about (1 + num_spec)× the state), hurting both latency and maximum concurrency.

ReplaySSM addresses both by caching inputs instead of state. It keeps a single checkpoint state S0 and caches the recent SSM inputs in a ring buffer; on a flush step (once every L steps) it folds the cached inputs into the checkpoint, and on every other step it computes the output directly from the checkpoint plus the cached inputs without materializing the full state.

For standard decode, writing the state back only once every L steps (instead of every step) roughly halves the dominant memory traffic. For speculative decode, caching recent inputs makes rollback a ring-buffer pointer move, cutting the per-step rollback cost from O(T) to O(1) (`T = num_spec_tokens + 1`) and removing the per-draft-token state storage, which improves both latency and maximum concurrency.

ReplaySSM speeds up the SSM kernel most at large serving batch sizes, where the kernel is fully memory-bound (small batch is not a relevant operating point: there the kernel is overhead-bound rather than memory-bound, and e2e latency is dominated by the MLP layers). For hybrid models it gives the largest end-to-end speedup at short-to-medium output lengths, where the SSM layers dominate latency.

### Proposed Change.

## Proposed Change

We propose adding ReplaySSM to vLLM as an opt-in decode path for hybrid SSM models, covering both SSM families and both decode modes, with the baseline path unchanged when the feature is off.

### Scope
- Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) SSM layers.
- Standard and speculative decode.
- New Triton kernels plus the vLLM integration (mixer dispatch, attention-metadata cursors, state-shape sizing). The conv path reuses vLLM's existing `causal_conv1d_update` unchanged.

### Integration and backward compatibility
The feature is opt-in through config flags that all default to off; when off, the decode path is byte-for-byte the baseline. The ReplaySSM caches are added as extra tensors on the existing paged mamba state, so they reuse vLLM's paged-block allocation and block-table indexing (continuous batching, per-request allocation and eviction).

### Config flags (all default off)
- `--use-replayssm`: Mamba2/GDN standard cached decode.
- `--use-replayssm-spec`: speculative cached decode (requires speculative decoding and `--mamba-cache-mode none`).
- `--replayssm-buffer-len`: history buffer length (default 16).
- `--replayssm-route` (Mamba2 standard only): `output_only` (default) or `state_and_output`; a temporary knob for the precision study, planned for removal (see Open questions).

### Key integration points
- Paged cache: the input caches and the checkpoint state live in the paged KV block, indexed per request by physical block id; only small per-block cursors live in the metadata builder.
- CUDA graphs and continuous batching: speculative decode uses two device-routed launches (verify and flush) with the flush decision and rollback computed on-device, so the launch sequence is fixed and one captured graph per batch size covers the path.
- What we cache: only the state-building inputs; the output read vector (Mamba2 C, GDN q) is taken from the current activations and never cached.
- Flush decision (spec): we flush when `history + T > B`, where `B` is the history buffer length, and size the ring buffer to `B + T`. This is a slight change from the formulation in the blog post.

### Validation
Correctness is checked at three levels (per-kernel vs an exact reference, prefill-vs-decode equivalence over full sequences, and engine-level parity via `check_logprobs_close`), plus a speculative-decode acceptance-length match on GSM8K. Performance covers standard decode (kernel and end-to-end) and speculative decode (throughput and maximum concurrency). Full numbers are in the draft PR.

## Performance
Please check the detailed experiment results in the draft PR (#47576). Here are brief results.

### Standard decode
Whole-model per-step speedup (baseline / ReplaySSM), fp32 state, buffer length 16:

| Model (SSM, HW) | bs 1 | bs 32 | bs 128 | bs 512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Nano-4B (Mamba2, H100) | 0.99 | 1.17 | 1.40 | 1.55 |
| Qwen3.5-4B (GDN, H100) | 0.99 | 1.08 | 1.21 | 1.31 |
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2, B300) | 0.98 | 1.10 | 1.27 | 1.67 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN, B300) | 0.98 | 1.07 | 1.14 | 1.20 |

### Speculative decode
End-to-end throughput at (B, T) = (16, 4), on B300 with an MTP drafter. `c/std` = ReplaySSM-spec / baseline-spec throughput; `c/AR` = ReplaySSM-spec / no-spec autoregressive throughput.

ReplaySSM-spec vs native-spec (`c/std`):

| Model | bs 1 | bs 32 | bs 256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2) | 1.09 | 1.07 | 1.88 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN) | 0.99 | 1.19 | 1.80 |

ReplaySSM-spec vs no-spec AR (`c/AR`):

| Model | bs 1 | bs 32 | bs 256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2) | 2.12 | 1.90 | 2.21 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN) | 1.90 | 1.93 | 1.85 |

### Feedback Period.

## Feedback Period
One week from posting; we will keep it open longer if discussion is active.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

## Work in progress
1. Tensor parallelism test files (e.g., TP1==TP2) and evaluation.
2. Evaluation on lower-precision (fp16/fp8) state. Current evaluation focus on FP32 state (default in most hybrid models)
3. Numerical-precision benefit: because reconstruction is FP32 and the state is written back only on flushes, a low-precision checkpoint (e.g. FP16) is re-quantized ~`L`× less often than the per-step baseline. Reference: [NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Ultra Technical Report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-Technical-Report.pdf), Section 4.5.

## Open questions
1. Timeline: We plan to split the integration into three stages: Mamba2 standard decode -> GDN standard decode -> Mamba2/GDN speculative decode. 
2. Paged-cache layout: is appending ReplaySSM tensors onto the mamba state the pattern you prefer, or should the caches be a separate allocation?

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Opt-in incremental prompt encoding for multi-turn chat
author: bird
body:
## Motivation

vLLM's frontend re-tokenizes the **entire** prompt on every request. In multi-turn chat this is almost pure waste: each request re-sends the whole conversation, so the rendered prompt of turn `N` is (in the overwhelmingly common case) a strict string prefix of the prompt of turn `N+1`. Tokenization cost is linear in conversation length, so per-turn TTFT degrades linearly with history size even when the KV cache has a 100% prefix hit:

- For a ~200K-token history, a single full encode costs ~0.5 s on a typical host CPU — often *more* than the prefill itself once prefix caching kicks in.
- The cost is paid on the API-server CPU, so under concurrent load it also competes with detokenization, chat-template rendering, and multimodal preprocessing for renderer threads (#39590 tracks frontend tokenization overhead more broadly).

We ship this optimization in production on a DeepSeek-V4-Flash 2×DGX-Spark deployment (agentic coding workload, long conversations): **median multi-turn TTFT dropped from 0.92 s to 0.47 s**, with encode itself ~35× faster at the median, and token-exact output verified on every request (30/30 sampled turns exact; the always-on overlap verifier never had to fall back incorrectly).

### Relationship to existing work

- **PR #45514 (segment-parallel tokenization / segment cache)** is adjacent but different: it splits a single large prompt into segments to tokenize them in parallel and/or cache segment encodings keyed by content. That accelerates *cold* large prompts. This proposal is **exact prefix-incremental** encoding across *requests*: it exploits the multi-turn growth pattern where the previous request's full encoding is already known, and reuses it wholesale up to a verified boundary. The two compose naturally (segment-parallel for the cold miss path, incremental splicing for the warm multi-turn path), and we position this RFC as complementary to #45514, not competing.
- **SGLang** ships an L1 prefix tokenization cache in its SMG frontend as ecosystem precedent that per-conversation prefix reuse at the tokenizer level is worth having in a production serving stack.
- vLLM already reuses *KV* by prefix (Automatic Prefix Caching). This is the same idea one layer up, applied to the CPU-side encode.

## Proposed change

An **opt-in** (`--enable-incremental-encoding`, default off; env fallback `VLLM_INCREMENTAL_ENCODING=1`) renderer-level cache, `vllm/tokenizers/incremental_encode.py` (~450 LOC including docs), wired into `BaseRenderer._tokenize_prompt`:

1. Keep a bounded LRU (default 16 entries) of recently encoded `(text, token_ids)` pairs, optionally partitioned by the request's `cache_salt` (the OpenAI frontend is stateless, so matching is purely longest-string-prefix).
2. On a new prompt, find the longest cached entry whose text is a prefix of the new text.
3. Do **not** trust token alignment at the append point. Back up a `BACKUP=1024`-char window from the end of the cached prefix and ask the HF fast backend pre-tokenizer (`pre_tokenizer.pre_tokenize_str`) for pre-token boundaries at least `MARGIN=96` chars from either window edge. **BPE merges never cross pre-token boundaries**, so tokens strictly before such a boundary are independent of the appended text.
4. Accept the first boundary that (a) has no special-token markers (`<|`) within ±`MARGIN` of the seam, and (b) coincides with an exact token boundary in the *cached* encoding's character offsets (this rules out seams inside added/special tokens).
5. Re-encode only from the boundary, then **verify** that the overlap tokens (ids *and* offsets) match the cached encoding exactly, excluding tokens within `MARGIN` of the cached text's end (which may legitimately merge with appended text). Splice `cached_prefix_ids + tail_ids`.
6. Anything unprovable falls back to a full encode (which also refreshes the cache): no pre-token boundary in the window, seam near special markers, a normalizer that rewrites the window, verification mismatch, incompatible encode kwargs (`add_special_tokens` semantics are probe-validated as a content-independent prefix/suffix template; results that would exceed a `truncation`/`max_length` limit go back to the regular path), prompts under a 16K-char gate.

**Scope**: HF fast tokenizers only (`is_fast` with a `backend_tokenizer.pre_tokenizer`). Mistral, deepseek_v32 and harmony renderers are untouched; on unsupported tokenizers the flag is silently inert. The cache lives *above* the renderer's deep-copied tokenizer pool and is thread-safe — the lock covers only lookup/insert, never tokenizer calls.

**Non-goals**: no cross-process sharing (per API-server-process cache), no persistence, no change to any default behavior.

## Measured results

Unit benchmark (`benchmarks/benchmark_incremental_encoding.py`, transformers-only, Qwen2.5 tokenizer, per-turn encode latency):

| history (tokens) | full encode p50 | incremental p50 | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5K | 3.97 ms | 0.69 ms | 5.8× |
| 32K | 25.67 ms | 1.17 ms | 22.0× |
| 128K | 151.82 ms | 2.77 ms | 54.9× |
| 512K | 782.94 ms | 10.95 ms | 71.5× |

Production (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 2×DGX-Spark, agentic coding traffic): median multi-turn TTFT 0.92 s → 0.47 s.

## Alternatives considered

- **Do nothing / rely on faster tokenizers**: tokenizer throughput has improved, but the cost remains O(history) per turn; at 512K-token contexts (now routine for agents) it's hundreds of ms per turn on every mainstream tokenizer.
- **Cache `apply_chat_template` output / message-level caching**: requires assumptions about template stability and message identity; the string-prefix formulation is agnostic to how the prompt was produced (chat template, raw completion, custom renderers) and is verified against ground truth token ids.
- **Trust token alignment at the cut point (no backup window)**: incorrect — the last tokens of the cached encoding can merge with appended text (and specials/whitespace runs cross naive cut points). The pre-token-boundary + overlap-verify design is what makes this exact rather than heuristic.
- **Segment/content-addressed caching (PR #45514)**: complementary; see above. Segment caching helps cold large prompts and is keyed by content chunks; prefix-incremental exploits the request sequence and reuses one contiguous encoding with a single splice.
- **Do it in the Rust frontend**: attractive long-term (no GIL, closer to the tokenizer), but the Python renderer path remains the default and only universal path today (`VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND` is experimental and does not cover all renderers/modalities). The algorithm is self-contained (prefix match, `pre_tokenize_str` boundary, overlap verify, splice) and ports directly to the Rust frontend when its tokenization path matures; landing the Python version establishes semantics, flags, and tests that a Rust port must match.
- **Unbounded / per-connection caches**: the OpenAI API is stateless and gives no client identity; a small global LRU with longest-prefix matching (plus optional `cache_salt` partitioning) captures the workload without memory growth. Entries store ids as int32 arrays and only trailing offsets, so worst-case memory is a few MB per cached 512K-token conversation.

## Feedback period

Open — feedback welcome, particularly from folks working on #45514 and the Rust frontend.

## CC

@DarkLight1337 @njhill (frontend/tokenizers CODEOWNERS), and folks working on #45514

title: [RFC]: FlashInfer NVFP4 KV serving on pre-SM100 GPUs
author: lesj0610
body:
### Motivation.

This RFC tracks the work needed to make `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` usable with FlashInfer on pre-SM100 GPUs, mainly Ampere/Hopper systems.

The practical target is serving large-context Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4 models with FlashInfer-backed NVFP4 KV cache without relying on the Blackwell-only path. This started from trying to serve those models on SM8x hardware, but I have tried to split the work into generic vLLM/FlashInfer pieces instead of model-specific patches.

vLLM already has Triton-based quantized KV cache paths such as TurboQuant 4bit and int4 per-head. The goal here is different: enable the FlashInfer CUDA path to use NVFP4 KV cache on pre-SM100 systems, so users can combine FlashInfer attention/dequantization support with the roughly 3x KV cache capacity benefit of NVFP4.

### Proposed Change.

The work is split across several PRs:

| PR | Scope | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #46963 | Core pre-SM100 NVFP4 KV cache update path through FlashInfer slot-mapping append | Ready for review |
| #46883 | Consume FlashInfer workspace sizing in vLLM | Ready for review |
| #47547 | Allow Gemma4 to choose FlashInfer when FA4 is unavailable | Ready for review |
| #46558 | FlashInfer MM-prefix attention support | Draft / included for dependency context |
| #47637 | Qwen3-VL shape-specialized pos-embed JIT fix | Draft / separate follow-up |

Some PRs are still draft because I am trying not to add more ready-for-review PRs before the core pieces are triaged. They are included here for context and dependency tracking, not as a request to review everything at once.

The FlashInfer side has been split separately:

- flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3740 — NVFP4 paged KV append with slot mapping
- flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3748 — paged NVFP4 KV dequantization helper
- flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3822 — SM8x-gated h512 NVFP4 FA2 prefill optimization

My current understanding of the review order is:

1. #46883, because it wires FlashInfer workspace sizing into vLLM.
2. #46963, because it is the core pre-SM100 NVFP4 KV cache update path and depends mainly on the FlashInfer slot-mapping append API.
3. #47547, so Gemma4 can actually select FlashInfer when FA4 is unavailable.
4. #46558 and #47637 as follow-up/context PRs, not blockers for the core path.

I would like feedback on whether this split and review order makes sense, and whether any scope or test coverage should be adjusted before deeper review.

### Feedback Period.

At least one week, or until the relevant maintainers have had a chance to comment on the preferred review order and ownership.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

The main local validation target is RTX 3090 / SM86. I have been testing the path with Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4 style workloads using `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`. The detailed capacity, MRCR, and serving benchmark tables are in #46963.

I do not have H100/Hopper hardware locally, so the Hopper side is not hardware-verified by me yet. The intent is still generic pre-SM100 support, not an SM86-only path.

This is also not meant to replace the existing Triton-based quantized KV cache options. The changes are intended to keep the generic vLLM behavior intact while allowing FlashInfer-backed NVFP4 KV cache updates on pre-SM100 systems.

If the design, scope, or tests should be changed before review, I can update the PRs.

title: [Rust Frontend][RFC] Anthropic Messages API: /v1/messages and /v1/messages/count_tokens
author: blasrodri
body:
### Motivation

The Anthropic Messages API is an unclaimed 🧭 item on the roadmap (#44280). The Python frontend serves it today (`vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/`), registered unconditionally alongside the OpenAI routes, and it has become the drop-in surface for Claude Code and Anthropic-SDK clients. The Rust frontend has no `/v1/messages`, so switching on `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1` breaks those clients. All the machinery the endpoint needs — chat template rendering, tool/reasoning parsers, streaming, multimodal, LoRA — already exists in the Rust stack; what's missing is a protocol adapter at the route layer. No engine or `vllm-chat` changes.

_**Refs**: roadmap #44280. Python implementation: `vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/{protocol,serving,api_router}.py`._

### Proposed design

Python implements this as a double adapter: Anthropic request → OpenAI `ChatCompletionRequest` → `create_chat_completion`, then re-parses the OpenAI **SSE strings** back into Anthropic events (`serving.py`). The Rust frontend doesn't need the OpenAI middleman. `vllm-chat` already emits a block-structured event stream (`ChatEvent` in `chat/src/event.rs`: `BlockStart`/`BlockDelta`/`BlockEnd` carrying an `AssistantBlockKind` of `Text`/`Reasoning`/`ToolCall`, plus `ToolCallStart`/`ToolCallArgumentsDelta`/`ToolCallEnd`, terminal `Done`) that maps onto Anthropic's `content_block_*` events with a small state machine (the index remap in the streaming section is the one wrinkle). So the proposal is one new route module that adapts directly against the internal chat layer, at the same layer the `routes/openai/chat_completions/` module sits for OpenAI:

```
Anthropic request ──(convert)──▶ vllm_chat::ChatRequest ──▶ state.chat.chat()
ChatEventStream ──(translate)──▶ Anthropic SSE events / AnthropicMessagesResponse
```

New code lives in `rust/src/server/src/routes/anthropic/` (`messages.rs`, `count_tokens.rs`, plus `types.rs` / `convert.rs` / `validate.rs` mirroring the `routes/openai/chat_completions/` module layout), registered in `routes.rs` as `/v1/messages` and `/v1/messages/count_tokens`. Everything below the route — renderer, tool parsers, reasoning parsers, multimodal finalization, LoRA resolution, sampling validation, mock-engine test infra — is reused unchanged. What the direct approach does *not* reuse is the OpenAI route's own response-assembly layer (`collect_chat_completion` / the chunk-stream builder): the Anthropic route re-implements the `saw_tool_calls`-driven stop reason, tool-call index bookkeeping, and usage assembly against `ChatEvent` directly. So this moves that finish-reason/tool-call machinery to a second consumer rather than deleting it — the trade is a cleaner event source (no SSE re-parse) and two fidelity wins Python can't get, against duplicating logic the OpenAI route already has.

The two fidelity wins:

- **Assistant block ordering.** Python flattens assistant history into OpenAI's `content` + `reasoning` + `tool_calls` fields, losing thinking/text/tool_use interleaving (`serving.py:319-343, 642-666`). `ChatMessage::Assistant { content: Vec<AssistantContentBlock> }` preserves block order end to end.
- **`stop_sequence` stop reason.** Python's converter only sees the OpenAI finish reason (`stop`/`length`/`tool_calls`), so it cannot report `stop_reason: "stop_sequence"` or the matched sequence (open gap, see #45807). Rust's `FinishReason::Stop(Option<StopReason>)` carries the matched stop string natively.

#### Request mapping

| Anthropic | Rust internal |
|---|---|
| `system` (string or text blocks) | leading `ChatMessage::System` |
| `messages[].role: system` (#44283) | `ChatMessage::System` (see open question on merging) |
| user `text` / `image` blocks | `ChatMessage::User` with `ChatContent::Parts`; base64 sources become `data:` URIs on the `ImageUrl` part (same string the OpenAI route forwards; decoding is handled downstream in `llm-multimodal`) |
| assistant `thinking` block | `AssistantContentBlock::Reasoning` |
| assistant `text` block | `AssistantContentBlock::Text` |
| assistant `tool_use` block | `AssistantContentBlock::ToolCall` (`input` serialized to JSON string) |
| `redacted_thinking` | accepted and dropped (opaque), matching Python |
| user `tool_result` block | `ChatMessage::ToolResponse { content, tool_call_id }`; images inside results become a follow-up user message, matching Python |
| `tools[]` (`name`/`description`/`input_schema`) | `ChatTool` |
| `tool_choice` `auto` / `any` / `tool` / `none` | `ChatToolChoice::{Auto, Required, Function, None}` |
| `max_tokens` (required, ≥ 1) | `sampling_params.max_tokens` |
| `stop_sequences` | `decode_options.stop_strings` |
| `temperature` / `top_p` / `top_k` | `SamplingParams` |
| `output_config.format` (`json_schema`) | structured outputs (same lowering as `response_format`) |
| `output_config.effort` | `chat_options.reasoning_effort` |
| `stream` | `intermediate` |
| `metadata` | accepted, unused (matching Python) |
| vLLM extensions: `chat_template_kwargs`, `kv_transfer_params` | `chat_options.template_kwargs` and the `SamplingParams` `vllm_xargs` path (via the existing `merge_kv_transfer_params` helper), matching Python's protocol extensions |

Request types follow the existing route conventions: route-owned serde structs, `validator::Validate` via `ValidatedJson`, unknown fields ignored (Claude Code's `cache_control` deserializes harmlessly, as it does through pydantic).

#### Streaming translation

The translator is a state machine over `ChatEvent`. `vllm-chat`'s output processor already emits blocks in clean open/close order (`structured.rs` synthesizes `BlockStart`/`BlockEnd` and closes on kind change), so no text buffering is needed — the piece Python's converter has to do because OpenAI chunks interleave text into an open tool block. The one real subtlety: `ChatEvent`'s `index` is **two disjoint numbering spaces** — text/reasoning blocks are indexed by `message.content.len()`, tool calls by a separate counter that also starts at 0, so a text block and a tool call can both carry `index: 0` in one response. Anthropic's `content_block_start.index` must be a single monotonic index across text/thinking/tool_use, so the translator maintains its own remap and synthesizes `content_block_stop` when a tool call interrupts an open text block. It's still a small, allocation-light state machine, but it is a remap, not a passthrough. SSE frames use axum's named-event support (`event: <type>\ndata: <json>`); no `[DONE]` sentinel.

| `ChatEvent` | Anthropic event(s) |
|---|---|
| `Start { prompt_token_ids }` | `message_start` (`usage.input_tokens` = prompt length) |
| `BlockStart` (`Text` / `Reasoning`) | `content_block_start` (`text` / `thinking`) at remapped index |
| `BlockDelta` (`Text` / `Reasoning`) | `content_block_delta` (`text_delta` / `thinking_delta`) |
| `BlockEnd` | [`signature_delta` for thinking — see open question] + `content_block_stop` |
| `ToolCallStart { id, name }` | `content_block_start` (`tool_use`, `input: {}`) at remapped index |
| `ToolCallArgumentsDelta` | `content_block_delta` (`input_json_delta`) |
| `ToolCallEnd` | `content_block_stop` |
| `Done { usage, finish_reason }` | close open block, `message_delta` (stop reason + final usage), `message_stop` |
| `LogprobsDelta` | dropped (no Anthropic analog) |
| stream error | `error` event (Anthropic error envelope), stream ends |

#### Stop reason mapping

| `FinishReason` | `stop_reason` |
|---|---|
| `Stop(_)` with tool calls seen | `tool_use` |
| `Stop(None)` | `end_turn` |
| `Stop(Some(Text(s)))` | `stop_sequence`, `stop_sequence: s` |
| `Stop(Some(TokenId(_)))` | `end_turn` (`stop_token_ids` is a vLLM extension with no Anthropic analog) |
| `Length` | `max_tokens` |
| `Error` | error response / `error` event |
| `Abort` | open question below |
| `Repetition(_)` | open question below (carries an optional `StopReason` like `Stop`) |

Usage maps as in Python's `_build_anthropic_usage`: `input_tokens = prompt − cached`, `cache_read_input_tokens = cached`, `cache_creation_input_tokens = 0`, with cache fields omitted unless `--enable-prompt-tokens-details`. `TokenUsage.cached_token_count` already carries the needed number. Non-streaming empty completions emit one empty text block rather than `[]`, matching Python (strict clients index `content[0]`).

#### `count_tokens`

`tokenize_chat` (added for `/tokenize`) already does render → finalize → encode without engine submission, accepting the full `ChatRequest` (system, tools, tool_choice) and returning the prompt token IDs. `count_tokens` converts the request through the same `convert.rs` path (no sampling params), calls `tokenize_chat`, and returns `input_tokens` from the resulting length, plus Python's `context_management: {original_input_tokens}` envelope for response-shape parity. This means the entire request-conversion layer is exercised and testable before any generation code exists.

#### Errors

Anthropic's envelope is `{"type": "error", "error": {"type", "message"}}` with the type/message carried over from the internal error, as in Python's `translate_error_response`. A small `IntoResponse` adapter over the existing `ApiError` covers it; mid-stream failures become `error` SSE events with the sanitized message (in Python the real message is currently masked by a pydantic validation error, #46162 — we should forward it from day one).

### Non-goals / deferred

Mirroring the Python endpoint's scope:

- No server-side tool execution, MCP, or web search; `tools` are client tools only.
- No Message Batches API.
- `cache_control` accepted and ignored (prefix caching is engine-level); no `cache_creation` reporting beyond the constant `0`.
- No `thinking` request parameter (the real API's `{type: enabled, budget_tokens}`); Python doesn't accept it either. Deferred, though Rust already has `thinking_token_budget` so the mapping is cheap later.
- `search_result` content blocks (pending in Python, #45653) and `/v1/messages/render` (#45803): follow Python once merged.
- Image support limited to the currently registered image-model specs, same as the OpenAI route.

### Plan

Three PRs, each independently reviewable and tested against mock-engine fixtures, with the Python implementation as the behavioral oracle:

1. **Request surface + `count_tokens`.** Anthropic request/response/error types, `convert.rs` (Anthropic → `ChatRequest`), validation, route registration, and `/v1/messages/count_tokens` via `tokenize_chat`. Tests: port the conversion cases from `tests/entrypoints/anthropic/test_anthropic_messages_conversion.py` (tool_result shapes, image sources, thinking round-trips, system merging) as expect-test snapshots, plus a mock-engine route test for token counts.

2. **Non-streaming `/v1/messages`.** Sampling/tool-choice/structured-output lowering, `collect_message` → `AnthropicMessagesResponse` (ordered thinking/text/tool_use blocks, stop-reason mapping, usage with cache fields). Mock-engine tests covering text, reasoning, parallel tool calls, forced named tool choice (Python gets this stop reason wrong today, #47598), stop-sequence, `max_tokens`, and the empty-content case.

3. **Streaming.** The `ChatEvent` → Anthropic SSE translator with named events, mid-stream `error` events, and full-sequence snapshot tests (text-only, thinking + text, tool calls, each stop reason). A manual differential check of event sequences against the Python frontend on the same prompts goes in the PR description.

### Open questions

- **Inline system message merging.** Python probes the chat template at startup with a fake `[system, user, system, user]` render and, if it raises, hoists inline system messages into the leading system block (`_detect_merge_inline_system`); #47681 proposes merging by default. Options for Rust: mirror the probe, always merge, or pass system messages through and let the template reject them. Preference from maintainers? (Always-merge avoids a startup Jinja probe and matches where #47681 is heading, but changes default behavior.)
- **Claude Code compat: billing-header stripping.** Python silently drops system text blocks starting with `x-anthropic-billing-header` because the per-request hash defeats prefix caching. It's a client-specific hack, but Claude Code is the flagship consumer of this endpoint. Mirror it, or leave it out of the initial port?
- **Fabricated thinking signatures.** Python emits a random UUID as the `signature` on thinking blocks (and a `signature_delta` before `content_block_stop`) because some strict SDK clients require one when replaying thinking with tools. vLLM can't produce a real signature. Mirror the fabricated signature, or omit and accept signature-less thinking blocks on input only?
- **`Abort` / `Repetition` finish reasons.** Anthropic has no analog. Python maps unknown finish reasons to a null `stop_reason`. Mirror the null, or map to an explicit `end_turn` (which some strict clients handle more gracefully)? `Repetition` also carries an optional `StopReason`, so it needs the same call.
- **Tool-use IDs without model-provided IDs.** Rust's `generate_tool_call_id()` already uses a `call_{uuid}` form, so the collision Python hits with `call_{int(time.time())}` when a response has multiple tool_use blocks (#35667) doesn't arise here — flagging only to confirm we keep the UUID form rather than mirror Python for parity.

### Feedback Period

_No response_

### CC List

cc @BugenZhao @njhill

title: [RFC]: vLLM gRPC server API for downstream integrations
author: connorcarpenter15

title: [RFC]: Separate Flashinfer GQA into TRTLLM and flashinfer backends.
author: pavanimajety
body:
### Motivation.

vllm/v1/attention/backends/flashinfer.py has grown and supports too many kernels at this point. Each has diverse set of features, [standard attention support matrix](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/attention_backends.md#standard-attention-mha-mqa-gqa-backends) captures the support. 

However, we still have variety of backends within each of these wrappers, that make it too complex to add any new features. 

Broadly, these are the supported features from native flashinfer `BatchPrefill*Wrapper` & `*BatchDecode*Wrapper` api. Note that this api also exposes the trtllm_batch* api when `trtllm-gen` backend is supported. 

  | FlashInfer Prefill API / backend | Arch | FP8 compute | FP8 KV | SWA | NVFP4 KV | LSE return |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`, `auto` (routes to fa2 or fa3) | SM80, SM90, SM100 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
  | `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`, `fa3` | SM90 | Yes | Yes, only if Q is FP8 | Yes | No | Yes |
  | `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`, `trtllm-gen` | SM100, SM103 | Yes | Yes | Causal: Yes; Non-causal + SWA: No | Yes | Yes |
  | `BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper`, `auto` | SM80, SM90, SM100 | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
  | `BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper`, `fa2` | SM80, SM90, SM100 | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
  | `BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper`, `cutlass` |  SM100, SM110 | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |

And for decode - 
 
  | FlashInfer API / backend | Arch | FP8 compute | FP8 KV | SWA | NVFP4 KV | LSE return |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`, `auto/fa2` tensor-core | SM80, SM90, SM100 | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
  | `BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`, `fa3` | SM90 | Yes | Yes, only if Q is FP8 | Yes, if FA3 checks pass | No | Yes |
  | `BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`, `trtllm-gen` | SM100, SM103 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

For the standard FlashInfer prefill/decode wrapper paths, backend="auto" resolves to FA3 when FA3 eligibility checks pass, otherwise FA2. It does not auto-select cuDNN, cutlass, cute-dsl, or trtllm-gen. Also note that NVFP4 KV Cache support for attention kernels is available for backend=`fa2` or backend=`trtllm-gen`. In the current code, we only wire through `trtllm-gen`.  When fa2 backend is selected for nvfp4 kv cache, kv is dequantized to `bfloat16` or `float16` for attention compute. This is in place for NVFP4 compatibility with pre-blackwell from flashinfer 0.6.13 and currently not supported through vLLM.


For the trtllm-gen api, the support matrix looks similar to the selected `trtllm-gen` backend.

 | TRTLLM API / backend | Arch | FP8 compute | FP8 KV | SWA | NVFP4 KV | LSE return |
 | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
 | `trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache`| SM100, SM103 | Yes | Yes | Causal yes; non-causal + SWA rejected | Yes | Yes |
  | `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache`, `xqa` | SM90, SM120, SM121 | No FP8 Q | Yes | Yes | No | No |
  | `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache`, `trtllm-gen`| SM100, SM103 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes` | Yes |



### Proposed Change.

Phases -

- [ ] 1. Split the backends in place to enable clean separation and phase 1 testing. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47786
- [ ] 2. Add support for flashinfer_gqa api + DCP + spec decode
- [ ] 3. Split to two files flashinfer_gqa.py and trtllm_attention_gqa.py

I will be testing with existing tests that cover flashinfer & trtllm api backends and running gsm8k on three models - 
1. Llama 3.3 70B
2. GPT OSS
3. nvidia/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4

To ensure compatibility, I will test Spec-decode, DCP, FP8 KV Cache, NVFP4 KV Cache features on SM90 and SM103 with both

Based on my local testing, I combine (1) and (3) into a single PR.

title: [RFC]: Precise group-aware recovery for KV load failures on hybrid models
author: ClockOfDestiny
body:
### Motivation.

`kv_load_failure_policy="recompute"` lets a KV connector recover from a
remote load failure by reporting the affected block IDs back to the
scheduler, which rewinds `num_computed_tokens` and recomputes the affected
tokens. On hybrid-KV models this mechanism has two gaps today.
 
**Gap 1 — scheduler assumes a single KV cache group.**
`Scheduler._update_requests_with_invalid_blocks` does a strong single-element
unpack:
 
```python
# vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py
# TODO (davidb): add support for hybrid memory allocator
(req_block_ids,) = self.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids(req_id)
```
 
`get_block_ids()` returns `tuple[list[int], ...]` — one list per KV cache
group. For a hybrid model the unpack raises `ValueError: too many values to
unpack (expected 1)`, which propagates through `update_from_output` and kills
`EngineCore`. 
 
**Gap 2 — no peer-block linkage, so peer KV stays stale on partial failures.**
 
Even if Gap 1 is fixed, the failure path only marks the single block whose
backend `get` reported an error. In a hybrid layout, the KV for one token
span is spread across multiple groups; when group A's block for span S fails
to load, the peer blocks for S in groups B, C, ... are also unusable, since
the attention compute for S can't produce a correct output with one group's
KV missing. If those peer blocks were loaded successfully they stay in the
cache unmarked, and subsequent decode steps read them as if they were valid —
silent accuracy degradation. 

### Proposed Change.

When `kv_load_failure_policy="recompute"` is set on a hybrid-KV model, a
backend load failure in any group must (a) mark the failed block **and its
peer blocks across all groups** as invalid, and (b) rewind
`num_computed_tokens` to the earliest failed token **across all groups**, so
that all stale KV is identified and recomputed. The change is scoped to the
failure path — the happy path and the single-group path are unchanged.
 
**Mooncake worker — peer-block linkage on load failure.**
 
In `MooncakeStoreWorker`'s receive thread, the per-request `block_id_list`
currently flattens all groups' block IDs into `list[int]`, losing the
group↔block relationship. We change the element type of `block_id_list` to `list[set[int]]`,
where each `set` contains the block IDs of all peer blocks (across every
group) that cover the same token span as the appended block. On each
append, peer block IDs across the other groups are collected using
`token_start // peer_group_block_size` to index into the request's per-group
block-id lists. Mamba align-mode null blocks (`block_id <= 0`) are skipped.

For example, assume that group 0 has a block size of 256, group 1 has a block size of 128, and the current request has 256 tokens. The block id for group 0 is [10], and for group 1 it is [20,21]. The result returned by `batch_get_into_multi_buffers` is [256,128,-5], indicating that block 21 failed to be fetched. The original `block_id_list` would be [10,20,21], with the corresponding failed block list as [21]. After modifying it to [(10,20), (20,10), (21,10)], we can obtain the correct failed block list, which is [10,21].
 
With that, a backend `get` failure fans out to peers naturally:
 
- Per-key partial failure (`batch_get_into_multi_buffers` returns `value < 0`
  for some keys): the failed key's `set[int]` is unioned into
  `invalid_block_ids`, so all peer blocks are included without further
  bookkeeping.
- Oversized-key (whole request skipped) and sub-batch exception: the entire
  request's blocks across all groups already live in `block_id_list`, so the
  existing whole-request failure marking is preserved; only the
  flattening call site is updated to handle `set` elements.
 
`batch_get_into_multi_buffers` only takes keys/addrs/sizes — `block_id_list`
is never passed to the mooncake API, only used for internal error tracking —
so changing its element type does not affect the API call. Rotation and the
disk-offload sub-batch slicing need no special handling, since slicing a
`list[set]` is the same as slicing a `list[int]`.
 
**Scheduler — group-aware rewind.**
 
`_update_requests_with_invalid_blocks` is made hybrid-aware:
 
- Replace the strong unpack with a per-group iteration over
  `get_block_ids(req_id)`.
- For each group, use *that group's* `block_size` (read from
  `self.kv_cache_config.kv_cache_groups[g_idx].kv_cache_spec.block_size`) to
  locate the first failed block and its token position.
- Maintain `rewind_num_computed_tokens = min(failed_token_pos across all
  groups)`. The earliest failure across all groups is the safe rewind point,
  since any token after the earliest failure has at least one group's KV
  missing.
 
The single-group happy path is preserved by construction: when
`len(req_block_ids_by_group) == 1`, the outer group loop runs once,
`group_block_size == self.block_size`, and `rewind_num_computed_tokens ==
idx * self.block_size` — identical to today's behavior.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks from submission.

### CC List.

@LCAIZJ  @Pz1116  

### Any Other Things.

A draft implementation PR can follow within one week of RFC acceptance, based on a working local prototype on vLLM v0.23.0.

title: [RFC]: Packed Variable Length Speculative Decoding
author: benchislett
body:
### Motivation.

In speculative decoding, we can save verification cost by selectively verifying a different number of draft tokens per request in each step. There are various techniques of selecting and tuning which / how many tokens to submit for verification, but all share a common benefit: reducing verification overhead with per-request variable-length query lengths in a batch.



### Proposed Change.

We will support verification input batches with heterogeneous query lengths for each decode request. We will separate the concerns of total verification token budget and allocation of that budget among the draft tokens. The scheduler chooses a host-visible total token budget, and the worker distributes that budget across requests entirely on-device, avoiding serialization of the query lengths to/from the host. This allows us to maintain asynchronous scheduling and CUDA graph compatibility.

This will involve changes to the scheduler, model runner input preparation, cuda graph management, and speculator-scheduler implementations (for the actual logic to decide which tokens to propose).

I propose to build off of the [batch-level Dynamic Speculative Decoding](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45953) support (which already has full-graph compatibility) in ModelRunnerV2.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@TheEpicDolphin @WoosukKwon @LucasWilkinson @mgoin @ekagra-ranjan @simon-mo @zyongye 

### Any Other Things.

## Challenges

### Varlen kernel support

Attention kernels take as input the number of *requests* in addition to the query offset pointers.
For decoding, many attention kernels omit the latter and simply assume either 1 (autoregressive) or N (uniform speculative) query lengths per request.

Many, but not all, attention kernels already support variable length queries per request:
- FlashAttention Decode (Hopper/Blackwell GQA): supports varlen queries via `flash_attn_varlen_func` arguments `max_seqlen_q` and `cu_seqlens_q`. (Definitely FA3, not sure about varlen full-graph for FA4)
- FlashInfer TRTLLM-Gen Decode (Blackwell GQA): supports varlen queries via `max_q_len` and `cum_seq_lens_q`, but not plugged into vLLM yet
- FlashInfer TRTLLM-Gen MLA Decode (Blackwell MLA): no support
- FlashAttention MLA: Currently uniform-query CG compatibility, but supports varlen Q, might be compatible
- DeepSeek V4 Indexed attention: Underlying Sparse MLA kernel supports varlen, but seems to need some plumbing to fully support varlen
- MiniMax M3 Sparse attention: no support
- FlashMLA (Hopper MLA): no support
- GDN: seems possible with some extra work on the metadata builder
- Mamba/Mamba2: seems possible with a bit of plumbing

Thus we will have to gate support to only the attention backends which have varlen support implemented, and it'll take quite a bit of follow-up work to enable this for most backends.

### CUDA Graph Compatibility

We currently have support for FULL CUDA Graphs with different query lengths for different batch sizes.
This is done by keying the graphs by `num_reqs` _and_ `num_tokens` _and_ `uniform_token_count`.

We can extend this: for each `num_reqs` (binned to powers of 2 / multiples of 8 / etc.) from `1` up to `max_num_seqs`, 
we record a separate set of graphs for each `num_query_tokens_per_request` from `1` (no spec tokens) up to (1 + max_num_speculative_tokens).

To unlock true dynamism, we break the connection between `num_query_tokens_per_request` and `max_q_len`: we always permit up to `max_num_speculative_tokens` for a single request, a pass `max_q_len=max_num_speculative_tokens` in every attention kernel invocation,
and thus allow some requests to have fewer than `num_query_tokens_per_request` and some to have more. This means that the scheduler
effectively is only deciding `mean_num_query_tokens_per_request` (and will likely use heuristics from the workers to make that decision, see below).

Then all we need to do is leverage `cu_seqlens_q` to have variable query start locations within the block, mark the remaining tokens in the suffix with `is_padding`, and pad `num_reqs` to `num_reqs_padded` by appending to `cu_seqlens_q` with 0-query-length requests which are ignored by the kernel.

Thus, the attention kernel is, for a given `num_reqs_padded` and `num_tokens = int(mean_num_query_tokens_per_request * num_reqs_unpadded)`, always invoked with inputs of consistent shape and address.

Note, that we can support non-integer `mean_num_query_tokens_per_request` as long as we record more graphs for `num_tokens` values in between `num_reqs * i` and `num_reqs * (i + 1)`, though they will not be perfectly uniform; we will have to support some extra padding or handle this specifically when doing capture.

### Supporting mixed batches

Supporting mixed batches with FULL CUDA Graphs is appealing as host-overhead in short prefills is a real concern, but this is out-of-scope for this RFC.
For PIECEWISE graphs, this is simpler. The main remaining consideration is compatibility with the `is_padding` optimization, which allows some kernels (e.g. MoE kernels) to skip work on graph-padding tokens. With variable query lengths in the decode, we may end up with some decode padding (to match the number of actual query tokens with the number of expected query tokens) in addition to graph padding. This should be avoided, either by packing the decodes tightly in the batch or reordering prefills and extends to the front of the batch, to share the query padding with the graph's total-token-count padding. It's unclear to me if it will be easy to implement the former, as the total number of used query tokens need not be known on the host, but either solution seems feasible here.

The easiest short-term solution seems to be to **enforce no padding in the query block**. Since we always have more draft tokens than we will need to admit in our budget, we can just fill all allocated slots with draft tokens even if our performance model might indicate it's favorable to skip them. Even though they might be skippable via `is_padding`, there are still some attention and constant overheads to be paid, so the price shouldn't be too extreme here.

### Supporting Data Parallelism

Some coordination across workers will be necessary to synchronize which graph is being executed, i.e. which (`num_reqs_padded` x `num_tokens_padded`) pair is active. Seems like this should fit naturally with our existing DP sync, but I'm not an expert in this area.

### Scheduler-Speculator awareness

In vLLM, our scheduler lives in a separate process; yet I propose to let it decide `mean_num_query_tokens_per_request` when scheduling.
In order to have the scheduler make decisions about how many total query tokens to permit, it will need some information from the model runner.
I propose to extend the Speculator interface to allow the scheduler to "query" for "hints" such as how many query tokens should be issued on average per request.

It is important to maintain asynchronous scheduling support here; in the DSpark report, they suggest using information delayed by 2 engine iterations in order to schedule the next step. This seems very reasonable, as acceptance rates over batches generally have significant temporal locality over multiple steps (reasoning v.s. final response, conversation domain, blocks of code/math/formatted output, etc).

This would probably be easier to implement if the scheduler was replicated into each worker, so we don't need to cross an IPC boundary, but this is what we have today.

I'm not certain that the scheduler needs to know about this at all. Conceptually I feel like it's the role of the scheduler
to be choosing how many tokens to put in the batch, but besides allocating KV slots and selecting which requests to run
(both of which are pretty agnostic to the variable-length decode tokens, the scheduler can just allocate the slots optimistically), I'm not sure why the current scheduler would need to be involved.

title: [RFC]   guard-gated sparse MLA topology index policy
author: teerthsharma
body:
## Summary

This RFC is intended to supersede the broad topology-aware KV cache compression framing in #38725 with a narrower, falsifiable vLLM integration target: a disabled-by-default topology policy for sparse MLA logical-token index selection.

The goal is not to introduce a new KV cache compression stack. The goal is to test whether topology-aware replacement of a bounded tail of an existing learned sparse-MLA `topk_indices_buffer` can improve sparse attention quality under the same budget, while preserving vLLM's current sparse MLA coordinate contracts and fail-closed behavior.

## Why this is materially different from #38725

#38725 proposes a broad topology-aware KV cache compression framework with lifecycle compression, directional pruning, NPU-oriented matrix operations, and expected memory/FLOPs gains.

This RFC narrows the surface to sparse MLA index policy only:

- topology object: sparse MLA logical request-local token indices, shape `[num_tokens, topk]`
- invariant: learned-token retention plus segment/witness coverage, optional barrier and diversity terms
- implementation rule: preserve a learned prefix and replace only a bounded tail with topology witnesses
- baseline: existing sparse MLA learned/top-k indices unchanged
- null models: same-budget random, locality, and learned-tail selectors
- fallback: disabled or unsupported paths return the original learned indices unchanged
- hot path: no Python loops or CPU sync in CUDA runtime paths without a separate benchmark gate

## Proposed contract

A topology index policy should satisfy these constraints before runtime wiring:

- disabled by default
- exact `torch.int32` 2D coordinate contract
- logical request-local token offsets, not physical cache slots
- `-1` sentinel padding preserved
- no duplicate selected logical tokens in the produced candidate set
- bounded structural replacement, never unbounded learned-token eviction
- dense or unmodified fallback on dtype, shape, device, budget, coordinate, or guard mismatch
- schedule construction time benchmarked separately from sparse attention execution
- quality guard based on relative L2, cosine similarity, KL, top-1 agreement, and next-token agreement

## Local screening evidence

These are screening-only local results, not a vLLM runtime speedup claim.

CPU `distilgpt2`, seq48, budget8:

| policy | selected ratio | rel L2 | cosine | mean L2 | KL | top1 | last token | total ms | speedup vs dense | guard |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| random | 0.8000 | 0.4593 | 0.9332 | 3689.6 | 1.7548 | 0.2857 | false | 36.19 | 3.810x | fallback |
| locality | 0.8000 | 0.4573 | 0.9050 | 3719.2 | 4.1488 | 0.2143 | false | 38.42 | 3.588x | fallback |
| learned-tail | 0.8000 | 0.4319 | 0.9527 | 3322.3 | 1.9067 | 0.2857 | true | 35.68 | 3.864x | fallback |
| topology index | 0.8000 | 0.4263 | 0.9490 | 3219.1 | 1.9461 | 0.2857 | true | 43.89 | 3.142x | fallback |

CPU `distilgpt2`, seq64, budget16:

| policy | selected ratio | rel L2 | cosine | mean L2 | KL | top1 | last token | schedule ms | total ms | speedup vs dense | guard |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| random | 0.8079 | 0.2480 | 0.9688 | 2984.4 | 2.6708 | 0.2857 | false | 3.631 | 49.31 | 2.746x | fallback |
| locality | 0.8079 | 0.3439 | 0.9398 | 4042.6 | 4.0561 | 0.2143 | false | 0.972 | 45.41 | 2.982x | fallback |
| learned-tail | 0.8079 | 0.2632 | 0.9661 | 2927.0 | 2.0080 | 0.3214 | false | 2.791 | 48.64 | 2.784x | fallback |
| topology index | 0.8079 | 0.2510 | 0.9697 | 2792.6 | 1.9447 | 0.2857 | false | 104.609 | 145.37 | 0.931x | fallback |

The seq64 run selected nonzero topology barrier/diversity and improved mean L2/KL versus the null models, but the prototype schedule cost erased speedup. The guard correctly rejected all sparse policies on relative L2/cosine, and for the topology policy also on speed/schedule overhead.

## Falsification gates before PR-ready runtime wiring

1. Unit tests for disabled passthrough, dtype/shape/device fallback, bounded replacement, learned retention, duplicate removal, padding layout, and coordinate bounds.
2. A CPU reference policy that produces the same 2D logical-token coordinate contract as sparse MLA.
3. A vectorized or kernel-side schedule path before any CUDA hot-path use.
4. `vllm bench` or sparse MLA backend benchmark comparing current sparse MLA, same-budget random, locality, learned-tail, and topology-index policy.
5. Quality gates: relative L2, cosine, KL, top1 agreement, next-token agreement, and task-level eval where applicable.
6. Observable counters: learned tokens retained, structural tokens inserted, fallback reason, and schedule-build time.

## Suggested first PR scope

A first PR should not wire this into runtime serving. It should add only:

- an isolated sparse MLA topology-index helper
- disabled-by-default config object
- explicit result/fallback object
- unit tests for the coordinate and fallback contract
- benchmark notes showing that current evidence is screening-only

That gives maintainers a small reviewable base before any kernel/runtime integration is proposed.

title: [RFC][Frontend/CLI]: Offline prefix-cache workload analyzer
author: raravind007
body:
## Motivation

vLLM's automatic prefix caching reuses KV-cache blocks only when the computed block-hash chain matches at full-block granularity. The hash includes the parent block hash, the current block tokens, and optional extra keys such as LoRA IDs, multimodal input hashes, and cache salts. As a result, small prompt-formatting differences, per-request metadata, different chat templates, LoRA/multimodal metadata, or cache-salt differences can prevent reuse even when prompts look similar to a human.

Today, users can inspect prefix-cache behavior through runtime logs, Prometheus metrics, and benchmark scripts, but there is no user-facing, no-GPU way to analyze a request dataset before deployment and answer whether its prompt structure is cache-friendly. This makes it difficult to reason about RAG, agent, tool-calling, and multi-turn workloads before spending GPU time on a serving run.

Related user pain: #29944, #12077, #24394, and the forum thread "How log kvcache usage and prefix hit rate in offline infer?".

## Proposal

Add an offline prefix-cache analyzer CLI, tentatively:

```
vllm analyze-prefix-cache \
  --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
  --input requests.jsonl \
  --format openai-chat \
  --block-size 16 \
  --output-format text
```

Given a JSONL of requests and a model/tokenizer, the analyzer would:

- Parse OpenAI batch-style requests and/or plain prompt JSONL.
- Apply the selected chat template and tokenize each request.
- Compute the same full-block hash-chain structure used by vLLM prefix caching, reusing existing request/block hashing utilities rather than reimplementing hashing logic.
- Group requests by shared hash-chain prefixes.
- Report offline cacheability estimates, including:
  - total prompt tokens
  - total full-block tokens
  - estimated reusable full-block tokens
  - estimated cacheability ratio
  - top shared prefix groups
  - request groups that diverge after a common prefix
- Support both human-readable text output and machine-readable JSON output.

This is static analysis over tokenized requests and existing hashing utilities. It should not instantiate the engine, execute model weights, or require GPU access.

## Design question: internal API usage

The hashing logic this proposal depends on (`hash_block_tokens`, `generate_block_hash_extra_keys`, `get_request_block_hasher`) currently lives in `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py` — internal to the engine core. A CLI/frontend module importing directly from `v1/core` crosses a layering boundary that may not be acceptable as-is. Before implementation, we'd like maintainer input on whether this warrants a small, stable public helper for offline hash-chain construction, versus importing the internal utilities directly for a first version.

## Scope for v1

- CLI command for offline workload analysis.
- Text output by default.
- JSON output for automation and CI/capacity-planning workflows.
- Support for plain prompt JSONL and OpenAI-compatible chat/batch request JSONL.
- Block-size parameter support, with optional comparison across multiple block sizes.
- Mechanical divergence reporting: show where hash chains stop matching and which request groups share common full-block prefixes.
- Documentation with RAG, agent, tool-calling, and multi-turn examples.

## Explicit non-goals for v1

- Exact runtime prefix-cache hit-rate prediction.
- Modeling scheduler behavior, eviction, memory pressure, request arrival order, preemption, KV offload, or disaggregated serving.
- Natural-language cause classification such as "this miss was caused by timestamps" or "this miss was caused by per-user IDs."
- Full multimodal/LoRA/cache-salt inference unless the relevant metadata is present in the input format and can be passed through the same hashing path.
- Engine behavior changes.

The analyzer should present results as an offline upper-bound or cacheability estimate, not as a guarantee of production hit rate.

## Alternatives considered

**Existing runtime metrics** — Runtime metrics and logs can show prefix-cache behavior after a server or offline inference run, but they do not provide a pre-flight analysis tool for a request corpus.

**`benchmarks/benchmark_prefix_caching.py`** — Benchmarks prefix-caching performance by running an actual model with fixed prompts or ShareGPT-style prompts. This proposal is different: it does not run inference, does not require GPU, and analyzes a user's request dataset structurally before deployment.

**Hash microbenchmarks** — Existing hash benchmarks are useful for comparing hashing throughput and algorithm choices, but they do not estimate cacheability of a real prompt workload.

## Open questions

- Should this be a top-level command such as `vllm analyze-prefix-cache`, or should it live under an existing CLI family such as `vllm bench prefix-cache-analyze`?
- What input formats should v1 support beyond plain prompts and OpenAI-compatible request JSONL?
- Should JSON output be considered stable in v1, or marked experimental?
- How much LoRA, multimodal, and cache-salt metadata should v1 support?
- Should block-size comparison be built into v1, or added later?

Happy to implement this if the design direction is acceptable.

title: [RFC]: Composite Attention Backends
author: MatthewBonanni
body:
### Motivation.

In certain scenarios, it would be beneficial to use different attention backends for prefill and decode requests. For example:

- **Performance:** some kernels perform better at either prefill or decode, so mixing backends will improve overall performance.
- **Feature compatibility:** in the case of `mm_prefix`, the backend must support bidirectional attention for the image prefix, which restricts the set of compatible backends. This is only necessary for prefills, though, so we could use a different (and potentially faster) backend for decodes.

There are two scenarios in which we already do this:

1. **MLA:** MLA has entirely different pipelines for prefill and decode, and uses different backends for each. MLAPrefillBackend is already a formalized object since https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32623
2. **FlashInfer:** The standard FlashInfer GQA backend routes prefills and decodes to different kernels, and there's an intra-FlashInfer selector mechanism distinct from the vLLM-level backend selector.

### Proposed Change.

Establish composite attention backends, which use different backends for prefill and decode. These will be able to be specified by `--attention-config.prefill_backend/--attention-prefill-backend` and `--attention-config.decode_backend/--attention-decode-backend` (mutually exclusive with `--attention-config.backend/--attention-backend`).

The automatic backend selector will now select prefill and decode selectors independently.

**Draft PRs / plan:**

- 1/N: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48024
- 2/N: Unify FlashInfer under this structure
- 3/N: Enable `mm_prefix` for prefill with causal decode on different backends

title: [RFC]: PyTorch vLLM correctness audit
author: morrison-turnansky
body:
### Motivation

#### Fix coincidentally correct tests flagged by numeric stability audit

Our goal is to smoothen the handoff between PyTorch and vLLM during release. Some tests in vllm may either expect a guarantee in correctness from PyTorch that is not valid causing misleading test failures that aren't true failures or they do not verify the property they intend to. This can lead to hard to debug failing tests against new releases costing significant development time and CI costs.

The audit identifies tests that are **coincidentally correct** (CC) — tests that pass today but rely on unstated numeric assumptions that a PyTorch update could silently break. These patterns are identified as a contract of correctness between PyTorch and vLLM, which is documented at [correctness-contract](https://github.com/morrison-turnansky/vllm-test-audit/blob/main/skills/audit-contract/SKILL.md).

While we believe that these tests can be identified automatically via agents, we first want to introduce the idea to the community. All issues and PRs involved with this audit will be reviewed and verified during this initial phase. If the community finds value in this, we can consider adding this agentic linting to the CI or run at regular intervals (nightly, monthly, etc.). We will present evaluation metrics of our agents performance before anything is exposed to upstream CI.

### Proposed Change.

This issue tracks incremental PRs that fix individual CC-flagged tests. Each PR will reference this issue, cite the specific audit clause, and make the test compliant. If a test is made compliant and is now failing that is useful signal, but we should separate source code fixes from test code fixes during out initial pass.
