- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Multimodal Asynchronous Collaborative Architecture Sidecar
author: xiaonaiping114
body: ### Motivation. Motivation In multimodal inference on hardware accelerators, the vLLM API Server process is conventionally responsible for both: 1. **Serving inference requests** (HTTP I/O, scheduling, tokenization, streaming) 2. **Image preprocessing** (network download, PIL decode, HF `processor()`, grid_thw extraction, pixel_values tensor construction) These two responsibilities are architecturally in conflict: - Image preprocessing is **CPU-bound, synchronous, and variable-latency** — network download alone is unbounded, and HF transforms scale with image resolution. - The API Server is **event-loop-driven, async, latency-sensitive** — it must serve many concurrent HTTP requests with sub-millisecond scheduling overhead. - When preprocessing runs inside the API Server process, it competes for the **same event loop, the same GIL, and the same CPU cores** as the inference serving path. The symptom is a **super-linear TTFT inflation under concurrency**: a single-image request pays the full preprocess cost, while N concurrent requests pay it N times serialized through the event loop, plus the gather-callback queueing overhead that emerges when many coroutines compete for the same loop. At high concurrency, the wait for `grid_thw` (the shape tensor needed before accelerator prefill can start) becomes the dominant tail-latency contributor. The root cause is **architectural coupling**: preprocess and serve live in the same process, so no amount of intra-process async or threading can give preprocess its own GIL, its own CPU cores, or its own failure domain. **Why a Separate Process (Not Just Async/Threading)?** | Approach | Problem | |----------|---------| | Inline in API Server | Blocks the event loop; super-linear TTFT inflation under concurrency | | asyncio.gather in API Server | Event-loop gather-callback queueing — wall time far exceeds the sum of sync work in the coroutines; GIL still serializes CPU work | | ThreadPoolExecutor in API Server | GIL serializes PIL/HF preprocess across threads; OpenMP thread oversubscription when torch is loaded (320 cores × N workers) | | **Out-of-process sidecar** | Independent GIL, independent CPU cores, independent memory; horizontal worker scaling; API Server stays purely async | The key insight is that **GIL isolation cannot be achieved intra-process**. CPU-bound preprocessing needs its own Python interpreter, its own event loop (or no event loop at all), and its own CPU cores. Only a separate process provides this. --- ### Proposed Change. Proposed Change ## Summary This RFC proposes a **Multimodal Asynchronous Collaborative Architecture Sidecar** for `vllm` that decouples image preprocessing (download → PIL decode → HF preprocess → grid_thw extraction → pixel_values serialization) from the vLLM API Server process. The sidecar runs as an independent multi-process service that communicates with vLLM via ZMQ PUSH/PULL sockets and shared disk files, enabling horizontal scaling of CPU-side preprocessing without touching the API Server event loop. The architecture introduces a **three-process collaboration model**: 1. **vLLM API Server process** — stays purely async; offloads every image to the sidecar at the earliest possible moment (URL only, ~200 B payload) and waits only for `grid_thw` (a tiny tensor needed to shape the ViT input). 2. **Sidecar service process** — a standalone process running ZMQ PULL/PUSH sockets, a `task_queue` for bounded backpressure, a `pusher` thread for result forwarding, and a `_grid_thw_callback` dispatcher that fires the moment stage ④ of the pipeline completes. 3. **Sidecar worker processes** — N fork-based workers, each running a 7-stage preprocess pipeline with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` and CPU pinning to a dedicated NUMA node, achieving true GIL isolation and L3-cache locality. Two cross-process data channels complete the design: a **fast path** (TP Worker `np.load()` on `.pv.npy` written atomically to shared tmpfs) for pixel_values, and a **fallback path** (`.pv.meta.json` polling) for `grid_thw` when ZMQ delivery is observed to be late. The dual-channel design makes the system correct under all timing regimes and fast under steady state. ## High-Level Architecture The architecture is a **three-process collaboration** with two cross-process data channels. Each process owns a distinct responsibility, a distinct GIL, and a distinct CPU budget. They communicate via ZMQ PUSH/PULL sockets (for tiny control-plane messages) and shared tmpfs files (for large pixel-values tensors). **Process boundaries and responsibilities:** | Process | Responsibility | Concurrency model | CPU budget | |---------|----------------|--------------------|------------| | **vLLM API Server** | HTTP I/O, request scheduling, tokenization, sidecar client | asyncio event loop (single-threaded) | Co-resident with vLLM | | **Sidecar Service** | ZMQ PULL/PUSH sockets, task_queue, pusher thread, _grid_thw_callback dispatcher | 1 main process + 1 pusher thread | Lightweight control plane | | **Sidecar Worker × N** | 7-stage preprocess pipeline per image | N fork processes, OMP=1, NUMA-pinned | Dedicated NUMA node | **Two cross-process data channels:** - **Control plane (ZMQ)**: API Server PUSHes a tiny URL payload (~200 B) to the sidecar; the sidecar PUSHes back `grid_thw` (a small shape tensor, <1 KB) the moment it is extracted. This is the **latency-critical** channel — `grid_thw` return time gates the start of accelerator prefill. - **Data plane (shared tmpfs files)**: The sidecar writes `.pv.npy` (pixel_values, 1–10 MB) and `.pv.meta.json` (grid_thw + metadata) atomically to a shared tmpfs path. TP Workers `np.load()` the `.pv.npy` directly, bypassing the API Server entirely. This is the **throughput-critical** channel — large tensors never traverse ZMQ. The dual-channel split is deliberate: ZMQ is optimized for small frequent messages, while tmpfs file reads are effectively memcpy. Forcing pixel_values through ZMQ would either hit the 1 MB message-size limit or require tuning that hurts steady-state throughput. ## Architecture Diagram ## Core Components | Component | Role | Lives In | |-----------|------|----------| | **Sidecar Service** (`service.py`) | Main process; owns PULL/PUSH sockets, bounded `task_queue` (mp.Queue), a dedicated `pusher` thread that drains `result_queue` into the PUSH socket, and the `_grid_thw_callback` dispatcher | Sidecar process | | **Sidecar Worker** (`worker.py`) | N fork workers; each runs the 7-stage preprocess pipeline and writes `.pv.npy` / `.pv.meta.json` atomically | Sidecar process | | **Sidecar Client** (`client.py`) | API Server-side ZMQ client; `submit()` enqueues URLs, `receiver_loop()` consumes grid_thw messages, `_grid_thw_store` is the in-process map from request_id → grid_thw | vLLM API Server process | | **`_grid_thw_callback`** | The critical handover function: called by a worker the instant stage ④ completes, before stage ⑤ even starts; pushes grid_thw into `result_queue` so the pusher thread can ZMQ-PUSH it back to the API Server | Sidecar process | | **Disk files** (`.pv.npy`, `.pv.meta.json`) | Cross-process data plane; `.pv.npy` carries pixel_values (1–10 MB) for the fast path, `.pv.meta.json` carries grid_thw as a JSON fallback when ZMQ delivery is late | Shared tmpfs | ## Data Flow The four labeled data paths in the diagram: 1. **① ZMQ PUSH URL** — API Server → Sidecar Service PULL socket. The API Server submits only the image URL and a `request_id` (payload ~200 B). The URL is pushed the moment `lite_preprocess` produces a placeholder PIL image — **no image bytes are downloaded by the API Server**. 2. **② grid_thw** — Sidecar Service PUSH socket → API Server `receiver_loop()`. Fired by `_grid_thw_callback` immediately after stage ④ (grid_thw extraction) completes, **before** stage ⑤ (JPEG/meta encode) or stage ⑦ (np.save). This is the latency-critical return: accelerator prefill cannot start without grid_thw. 3. **③ TP Worker `np.load()`** — Sidecar Worker (after stage ⑦) → TP Worker, via shared tmpfs `.pv.npy`. The TP Worker reads pixel_values directly from disk, **bypassing the API Server entirely**. This is the fast path: large tensors never traverse the ZMQ control plane. 4. **④ Fallback polling** — Sidecar Worker (after stage ⑥) → API Server, via shared tmpfs `.pv.meta.json`. If the API Server's `wait_for_grid_thw()` does not receive the ZMQ message within a timeout window, it polls `os.path.isfile(.pv.meta.json)` as a correctness safety net. This guarantees grid_thw is always available before accelerator prefill, regardless of ZMQ timing. The ordering is intentional: stage ④ (grid_thw extract) is the **earliest** point at which accelerator prefill can begin, so the callback fires there. Stages ⑤–⑦ run in parallel with accelerator prefill, hiding their cost completely. ## Key Design Decisions ### 1. Multi-Process over Multi-Thread **Why not threads?** - GIL serializes PIL/HF preprocess across images — CPU-bound work cannot be parallelized by Python threads. - OpenMP thread oversubscription: torch's internal OpenMP pool spawns 320 threads per process on a 320-core host; with N workers this becomes `320 × N` threads competing for the same cores. - Fork workers get independent GILs, independent memory spaces, and independent CPU cores. The only shared state is the inherited `task_queue` (a `multiprocessing.Queue`), which uses kernel-level synchronization. **Why fork (not spawn)?** - HF `processor()` initialization for large vision models loads a 122 B+ config from a network filesystem; cold-start takes 4+ minutes. Fork inherits the parent's already-initialized processor state, so workers reach steady-state immediately after fork. - Lower startup overhead — no re-import, no re-initialization of HF/torch. - `multiprocessing.Queue` is inherited across fork, so the task_queue and result_queue are shared without explicit setup. ### 2. ZMQ PUSH/PULL over Shared Memory **Why not shared memory directly for everything?** - Cross-process synchronization complexity (locks, condition variables) makes the code fragile and hard to reason about. - ZMQ PUSH/PULL provides natural backpressure via the bounded `task_queue` — when workers are saturated, the PULL socket blocks the producer, which is exactly the desired behavior. - Decouples producer (API Server) from consumer (Workers) — the API Server's `submit()` is a non-blocking ZMQ send and returns immediately. **Why a single pusher thread + result_queue (not direct_send from each worker)?** - A single PUSH socket is a single source of truth for ordering and backpressure. - `direct_send=1` (each worker holds its own ZMQ context and PUSH socket) adds per-worker context overhead and makes ordering nondeterministic. - The pusher thread is empirically NOT the bottleneck — `result_queue` is a fast in-process `mp.Queue` and the pusher only forwards tiny grid_thw payloads (<1 KB each). ### 3. File-Based Pixel Values (Fast Path) **Why `.pv.npy` on disk (not ZMQ tensor transfer)?** - `pixel_values` tensors are 1–10 MB per image; ZMQ's default 1 MB message-size limit is inadequate, and raising the limit hurts steady-state throughput. - A disk file allows the TP Worker to `np.load()` directly, **bypassing the API Server entirely**. This is the key architectural win: the data-plane path is `sidecar worker → tmpfs → TP worker`, with no Python hop in the API Server. - On shared tmpfs, `np.load()` is effectively a memcpy from the page cache, not disk I/O. **Why atomic write (`_atomic_np_save`)?** - A TP Worker may `np.load()` the file the instant it appears on disk. A non-atomic write (open + write + close) can expose a half-written file under concurrent access. - `_atomic_np_save` writes to a temporary path then `os.replace()`s into place, giving the reader either the complete file or no file at all. **Fallback (`.pv.meta.json`)**: - If the API Server's `wait_for_grid_thw()` does not receive the ZMQ message within its timeout window, it polls `os.path.isfile(.pv.meta.json)` as a correctness safety net. - This guarantees grid_thw is always available before accelerator prefill, regardless of ZMQ timing or message loss. - The fallback path is rarely hit in steady state but is essential for correctness under burst load. ### 4. Immediate grid_thw Callback (Not Deferred) **Why callback after stage ④ (not after stage ⑦)?** - `grid_thw` is the shape tensor needed to construct the ViT input — accelerator prefill cannot start without it. - Stages ⑤ (JPEG + meta encode) and ⑦ (np.save) take 200–500 ms combined. Deferring the callback until after they complete would gate accelerator prefill on preprocess finishing, eliminating the parallelism benefit. - The `_grid_thw_callback()` fires the instant stage ④ (grid_thw extraction) completes, then stages ⑤–⑦ run **in parallel** with accelerator prefill. This is what hides the entire preprocess cost behind the accelerator-bound prefill time. ### 5. CPU Pinning + OMP=1 **Why pin workers to a specific NUMA node?** - Prevents cross-NUMA memory access on multi-socket hosts. Empirical A/B testing on a 320-core / 8-NUMA-node host showed that single-node pinning (CPUs 160–191, NUMA node 4) outperforms cross-NUMA scheduling. - Isolates sidecar CPU usage from the API Server and TP Worker processes, preventing scheduler-induced interference. - `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` is critical: without it, torch's OpenMP pool spawns 320 threads per forked worker, and `N workers × 320 threads` oversubscribes the host instantly. Setting OMP=1 makes each worker single-threaded, which is the correct concurrency model for CPU-bound preprocess. ### 6. Control Plane / Data Plane Separation **Why split ZMQ (control) and tmpfs files (data)?** - ZMQ is optimized for small, frequent, low-latency messages. The control plane (URL in, grid_thw out) carries payloads under 1 KB and benefits from ZMQ's socket-level backpressure. - Tmpfs files are optimized for bulk transfer. The data plane (pixel_values) carries 1–10 MB per image and would saturate ZMQ's message-size limit. - Splitting the planes lets each channel use the right tool: ZMQ for latency-critical control, tmpfs for throughput-critical data. - This separation also enables independent failure modes: a ZMQ socket failure does not corrupt the data plane, and a tmpfs write failure does not block the control plane. ## Compatibility & Impact ### Scope - **Only affects the target accelerator backend** - Gated by `VLLM_MM_SIDECAR_ENABLED=1` (default: disabled) - No changes to vLLM core code (all patches in `patch_mm_opt/` subtree) ### Other Backends - NVIDIA / AMD / TPU / XPU: zero impact (env var defaults to 0) ### Backward Compatibility - Existing deployments without sidecar env var: unchanged behavior - Existing deployments with sidecar: new fast path, same output ## Proposed PR Plan To keep each PR reviewable, the sidecar architecture is split into 4 PRs: | PR | Title | Scope | LOC (approx) | Dependency | |----|-------|-------|--------------|------------| | 1 | `[Feature] Sidecar service + worker foundation` | service.py (PULL/PUSH/task_queue/pusher), worker.py (7-stage pipeline + fork entry) | ~600 | None | | 2 | `[Feature] Sidecar client + grid_thw return chain` | client.py (submit/receiver_loop/_grid_thw_store), _grid_thw_callback, .pv.meta.json fallback | ~400 | PR1 | | 3 | `[Feature] fast path: .pv.npy atomic save + TP Worker np.load` | _atomic_np_save, .pv.npy write/read, orchestration in phase1.py | ~350 | PR1+PR2 | | 4 | `[Perf] P6 multi-process tuning: fork + CPU pinning + OMP=1` | P6 config, fork mode, NUMA pinning, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 | ~250 | PR1+PR2+PR3 | Each PR includes: - pytest unit tests for pure functions (`_grid_thw_from_pv_result`, `_atomic_np_save`, `_grid_thw_callback`) - Performance benchmark in `benchmarks/` directory - Accuracy validation data (MME 90.27%/90.78%) > Note: Total ~1600 LOC exceeds the 500 LOC threshold, hence this RFC is submitted first. The split ensures no single PR exceeds 600 LOC. ### Feedback Period. We are seeking community feedback on the following open questions: 1. **Should the sidecar architecture be generalized to other hardware backends?** - Currently hardware-specific due to accelerator prefill bottleneck profile - NVIDIA A100/H100 may also benefit from CPU-side preprocess offload at high concurrency 2. **Worker count tuning** - Current: 32 workers on NUMA node4 (CPU 160-191) - Optimal count depends on image resolution, batch size, NUMA topology - Should we expose `VLLM_MM_SIDECAR_NUM_WORKERS` as a first-class config? 3. **Disk I/O vs network filesystem** - `/tmp/vllm_http_temp/` is local tmpfs on our deployment - Network FS (NFS/CephFS) may negate the fast path benefit - Should we detect FS type and fallback to ZMQ tensor transfer on network FS? 4. **Lifecycle management** - Sidecar process is started by `start_sidecar.sh` before vLLM serve - Should vLLM manage sidecar lifecycle (start/stop/restart) natively? - Or keep it as an external service for deployment flexibility? 5. **Integration approach** - Should the sidecar be a separate pip package (`vllm-mm-sidecar`)? - Or keep it as an optional component within vllm core? **Feedback deadline**: [TBD - typically 2-4 weeks] Please share your thoughts, concerns, or suggestions in the comments below. ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] [Feature] [Experimental] Support GigaToken Accelerated Tokenizer Mode
author: Prasannajaga
body: ## Motivation. With recent advancements in high-throughput LLM tokenization, researchers from the Stanford team released [GigaToken](https://github.com/marcelroed/gigatoken) (PyPI: [gigatoken](https://pypi.org/project/gigatoken/)), a next-generation accelerated tokenizer engine designed to eliminate CPU tokenization bottlenecks during large-scale inference and long-context prompt processing. In high-concurrency LLM serving workloads (such as `/tokenize` endpoints or pre-fill prompt tokenization), standard tokenizers can become a latency bottleneck. Currently, vLLM supports a static set of tokenizer modes (`auto`, `hf`, `slow`, `mistral`, `deepseek_v32`, `deepseek_v4`, `kimi_audio`). Integrating `gigatoken` as an experimental tokenizer mode (`--tokenizer-mode gigatoken`) provides: - **Experimental Integration**: Allows vLLM users to evaluate and benchmark the new GigaToken engine against standard HuggingFace/Mistral tokenizers. - **Performance Optimization**: Enables fast text-to-token ID encoding and detokenization during input preprocessing and API serving. - **Explicit, Opt-In Interface**: Users can explicitly opt into `gigatoken` acceleration without altering default tokenization behavior for standard users. - **Zero Overhead**: `gigatoken` is lazy-loaded only when `tokenizer_mode="gigatoken"` is explicitly invoked, preventing unnecessary binary imports for default users. ## Proposed Change. ### A. Tokenizer Backend Wrapper Create [gigatoken.py](file:///data/inference/vllm/vllm/tokenizers/gigatoken.py) implementing the `TokenizerLike` protocol ([protocol.py](file:///data/inference/vllm/vllm/tokenizers/protocol.py)): ```python # SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 from collections.abc import Sequence from pathlib import Path from typing import Any, overload from transformers import BatchEncoding from vllm.tokenizers.hf import CachedHfTokenizer from vllm.tokenizers.protocol import TokenizerLike class GigaTokenTokenizer(TokenizerLike): """Tokenizer wrapper for Stanford's gigatoken accelerated backend (https://github.com/marcelroed/gigatoken).""" def __init__(self, tokenizer: TokenizerLike) -> None: self._tokenizer = tokenizer @classmethod def from_pretrained( cls, path_or_repo_id: str | Path, *args, trust_remote_code: bool = False, revision: str | None = None, download_dir: str | None = None, **kwargs, ) -> "GigaTokenTokenizer": try: import gigatoken except ImportError as e: raise ImportError( "The 'gigatoken' package is required when tokenizer_mode='gigatoken'. " "Please install it via 'pip install gigatoken' or 'pip install vllm[gigatoken]'." ) from e base_tokenizer = CachedHfTokenizer.from_pretrained( path_or_repo_id, *args, trust_remote_code=trust_remote_code, revision=revision, download_dir=download_dir, **kwargs, ) accelerated_tokenizer = ( gigatoken.wrap_tokenizer(base_tokenizer) if hasattr(gigatoken, "wrap_tokenizer") else base_tokenizer ) return cls(accelerated_tokenizer) def encode( self, text: str, truncation: bool | None = None, max_length: int | None = None, add_special_tokens: bool = True, ) -> list[int]: return self._tokenizer.encode( text, truncation=truncation, max_length=max_length, add_special_tokens=add_special_tokens, ) def decode( self, ids: Sequence[int] | int, skip_special_tokens: bool = False ) -> str: return self._tokenizer.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=skip_special_tokens) # Delegations for bos_token_id, eos_token_id, pad_token_id, vocab_size, is_fast, etc. ``` ### B. Tokenizer Registry Mapping Register `"gigatoken"` in `_VLLM_TOKENIZERS` map within [registry.py](file:///data/inference/vllm/vllm/tokenizers/registry.py#L41-L47): ```python _VLLM_TOKENIZERS = { "deepseek_v32": ("deepseek_v32", "DeepseekV32Tokenizer"), "deepseek_v4": ("deepseek_v4", "DeepseekV4Tokenizer"), "gigatoken": ("gigatoken", "GigaTokenTokenizer"), "hf": ("hf", "CachedHfTokenizer"), "kimi_audio": ("kimi_audio", "KimiAudioTokenizer"), "mistral": ("mistral", "MistralTokenizer"), } ``` ### C. Model Configuration Type Extension Add `"gigatoken"` to `TokenizerMode` in [model.py](file:///data/inference/vllm/vllm/config/model.py#L86-L88): ```python TokenizerMode = Literal[ "auto", "hf", "slow", "mistral", "deepseek_v32", "deepseek_v4", "inkling", "gigatoken" ] ``` ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. @WoosukKwon @zhuohan123 @simon-mo @youkaichao ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: KV offload event path refactor — provenance-carrying events and key-only removals
author: Change72
body:
### Motivation.

> Code references are pinned to `main` at
> `3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f`; implementation starts from
> current `main`.

[#48679](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48679) added self-describing KV-offload events as an initial implementation. This RFC finishes the event-path refactor in two PRs.

Today, `OffloadKey` contains only `(block_hash, group_idx)` ([base.py:23-41](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py#L23-L41)), and a raw `OffloadingEvent` has no request context ([base.py:153-159](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py#L153-L159)). The tracker therefore builds the full event payload at scheduler lookup/store time and keeps it until eviction ([events.py:78-114](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/events.py#L78-L114)).

```text
lookup / prepare_store
        |
snapshot full payload in a global map
        |
async store / promotion completion
        |
BlockStored
        |
keep part of the snapshot until removal
```

This has two problems:

- Async promotion and secondary-tier completions can lose the request provenance needed to build a full `BlockStored`. Promotions already retain `ReqContext` through `PendingPromotion` and `TransferJob` ([manager.py:62-68](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py#L62-L68), [manager.py:469-490](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py#L469-L490)), but raw events do not carry it.
- Full removal metadata stays in vLLM from store until eviction. That lifetime can be much longer than the request, especially for persistent tiers.

### Proposed Change.

#### Scope map

| PR | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| **PR 1 — stored-event provenance** | Carry request context through existing async store, cascade, and promotion paths. Build `BlockStored` only when the raw stored event is translated. |
| **PR 2 — key-only removal** | Emit only the chunk key in `BlockRemoved`, remove vLLM's long-lived removal table, and move chunk expansion/owner cleanup to the router. |

This is the scope agreed in [#49506](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49506#issuecomment-5263904604). `OffloadKey`, single-key admission, and worker transfer reshaping are not part of this RFC.

#### PR 1: stored-event provenance

```text
Request + KV-group geometry
            |
     ReqContext event state
            |
   existing async job paths
            |
CPU / FS / OBJ completion
            |
OffloadingEvent(key, ReqContext)
            |
      full BlockStored
```

The implementation will:

- Keep `OffloadKey = (block_hash, group_idx)`.
- Attach request-scoped event state to `ReqContext`, which already supports typed per-request state ([base.py:90-104](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py#L90-L104)).
- Lazily resolve an event key to its full-chunk or partial-tail position when the stored event is translated.
- Carry the exact `ReqContext` through CPU, FS, OBJ, cascade, and promotion completion.
- Generate per-block `extra_keys`, matching GPU events ([kv_events.py:50-76](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f/vllm/distributed/kv_events.py#L50-L76)).
- Keep placeholder events for external work, unsupported cache shapes, and token-mutating request paths whose hashes are not safe yet.
- Keep only a small detached CPU removal record for PR 2 compatibility. It contains chunk hashes and group index, never `Request` or `ReqContext`.

The normal lifetime is bounded by existing owners:

```text
RequestOffloadState -> GPU store completion
TransferJob / PendingPromotion -> secondary or promotion completion
raw OffloadingEvent -> event translation
```

Ownership moves with the work: request state -> pending job -> raw stored event ->
event translation. Failure and shutdown release their owned context; reset drains
in-flight tier work and preserves any still-valid queued secondary stored event
until translation. A synchronous failed tier submission unwinds the job and its
primary-tier pin. Each job keeps the exact context object, so request-ID reuse
cannot bind old work to a new request. PR 1 does not add a new refcount or retain
request state until storage eviction.

[#51614](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51614) is now merged and provides the KV-group block-granularity base used here.

#### PR 2: key-only removal

For one offload chunk:

```text
chunk members = [H0, H1]
chunk key     = H1

vLLM:   BlockRemoved([H1])
router:  find H1's chunk -> remove that owner from H0 and H1
```

PR 2 will:

- Send only the removed chunk key and group.
- Delete vLLM's detached removal-expansion table.
- Let the router own `chunk key -> members` and member ownership.
- Define CPU reset/restart cleanup for the producer owner scope.
- Land with the matching router contract and implementation in [Dynamo #11930](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/11930). vLLM and router will move together; no compatibility window is planned.

FS/OBJ deletion, TTL cleanup, and shared-storage global invalidation remain out of scope.

### Observable behavior.

- PR 1: locally initiated promotions and secondary stores can emit full `BlockStored` payloads instead of placeholders.
- PR 1: stored events include per-block `extra_keys`; plain-text events may carry explicit `None` entries.
- PR 2: `BlockRemoved` changes from expanded block hashes to one chunk key.

PR 1 does not change `OffloadKey`, manager admission, batching, worker transfers, or the public KV-event schema.

### Out of scope.

- Single-key `prepare_store`, `OffloadReject`, and k-way admission ordering.
- Worker transfer reshaping; [#44865](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44865) owns that work.
- Adding `chunk_idx` to `OffloadKey`.
- Request-side medium/locality filtering; [#48123](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48123) owns that API.
- Fixing token-mutating request paths. [#49377](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49377) tracks stale `Request.block_hashes`; PR 1 keeps their event payloads as placeholders until their hash and offload state are safe.
- FS/OBJ deletion events and shared-storage global invalidation.

### Implementation order.

1. PR 1: stored-event provenance, based on current `main`.
2. PR 2: key-only removal plus the matching Dynamo owner-index change.

### Feedback Period.

The design discussion is complete. Implementation review should focus on event parity, promotion coverage, context cleanup on every terminal path, and the vLLM/router lockstep contract for PR 2.

### CC List.

@orozery @ronensc @jthomson04

### Any Other Things.

| Related work | Relationship |
| --- | --- |
| [#43468](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43468) | Introduced self-describing offload events and expanded removals. |
| [#51614](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51614) | Merged KV-group block-granularity fix used by PR 1. |
| [#49377](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49377) | Tracks stale request hashes after token truncation. |
| [Dynamo #11930](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/11930) | Router-side chunk ownership and key-only removal consumer. |

AI assistance was used to trace the event lifecycle, prepare this RFC, and implement tests. All code links were verified against `main` at `3d204dfdaaf09d67d49c7855630ef949754e0f8f`.

- [x] I searched for relevant issues and asked the documentation chatbot.

title: [RFC] Persistent, in-place drafting attention metadata for full-CUDA-graph MTP/spec-decode
author: chanh
body:
## Summary

Profiling **Step-3.7-Flash** (`Step3p5` MTP drafter, `num_speculative_tokens=2`) on H100 shows the GPU **idling on the host during the MTP draft phase** — `Self CPU time ≈ Self CUDA time`, and ~25% of the decode timeline is GPU-idle-waiting-for-kernel-launch (nsys `GAP_PERCENTAGE`/`LONG_GPU_WAITING_FOR_KERNEL_LAUNCH`). A torch profile attributes it to a swarm of tiny host-driven ops per step (`aten::copy_` ×12.7k, decomposed RMSNorm, MoE dispatch) around the draft loop.

**Root cause:** the draft *forwards* are already CUDA-graphed (`set_forward_context(cudagraph_runtime_mode=…)`), but inside the multi-step draft loop (`llm_base_proposer.py` ~L657–712, `step3p5.py` L385–440) **each speculative step reconstructs attention metadata on the host** via `build_per_group_and_layer_attn_metadata → metadata_builder.build_for_drafting(...)`, plus per-step position/slot-mapping recompute. That host-side construction serializes CPU↔GPU *between* the graphed forwards and starves the GPU.

## Why the existing fast path doesn't apply

`constant_draft_positions=True` (Gemma4, `gemma4.py:47`) skips the per-step rebuild, but its docstring states it assumes *all draft steps predict from the same position*. **MTP is sequential** — `step3p5._update_positions_dependent_metadata` advances `positions + 1` and recomputes slot_mappings each step — so the rebuild is currently **required for correctness**. The fast path is not applicable to sequential MTP/EAGLE drafting.

## Proposal — persistent, in-place drafting attention metadata

Make the whole draft loop GPU-side and full-cudagraph-capturable *even under dynamism* by reusing the pattern main-decode already uses (persistent metadata buffers updated in place):

1. **Pre-allocate** the drafting attention-metadata object + its tensors once at max padded shape (persistent input/hidden/position/slot_mapping buffers already exist).
2. Per draft step, **update the metadata tensors in place on GPU** (`positions += 1`, recompute `slot_mapping` via the existing kernel, adjust `seq_lens`) instead of constructing a new metadata object on the host.
3. **Absorb dynamism** (rejected tokens, variable seq_lens) via pad-to-max + `PADDING_SLOT_ID` masking (already partially present).
4. **Capture the draft loop under full cudagraph** so the graphed forwards fire back-to-back with no host stall between them.

New backend hook, alongside `build_for_drafting`:
```python
def update_for_drafting_inplace(self, md, common_attn_metadata, draft_index) -> None: ...
```
implemented first for **FlashAttention-3** (the backend Step-3.7 uses), then extendable to other backends.

## Expected impact

Removes the per-step host metadata rebuild + copies from the critical path → the GPU stops waiting during MTP. (The separate ~32% TP all-reduce cost seen on H100-**NVL** is a *topology* issue — custom all-reduce is correctly disabled on bridged-pair GPUs; it disappears on NVSwitch H100 — and is out of scope here.)

## Scope & correctness

Cross-backend (start with FA3). **Correctness-critical** — spec-decode failures are silent, so validation must confirm **mean acceptance length is unchanged** (~2.28 for this config) and output parity vs. the current path, before this leaves draft.

Draft PR: _to follow / see linked PR_.

title: [RFC]: Speculative recompute fallback for slow remote KV cache loads
author: Lin-z-w
body:
### Motivation.

Remote KV cache loading usually completes much faster than local recomputation. However, a rare slow Mooncake `get` may keep a request waiting for up to approximately 60 seconds before returning a failure.

For these outliers, continuing to wait may be more expensive than recomputing the KV cache locally. This RFC proposes a soft-timeout fallback that reduces tail latency without changing the normal remote KV loading path.

### Proposed Change.

Introduce an optional soft timeout for remote KV cache loads, for example 5 seconds.

The proposed flow is:

1. Allocate KV blocks `A` and start loading the remote KV cache into them.
2. If the load finishes before the soft timeout, use `A` normally.
3. If the soft timeout expires:
   - Remove the load from the request's critical path.
   - Keep `A` reserved and unavailable to the block allocator.
   - Allocate a physically different set of KV blocks `B`.
   - Remap the request to `B` and recompute its KV cache locally.
4. Let the original remote load continue in the background.
5. When the original load completes, ignore its result for the request and release `A`.

If additional KV blocks cannot be allocated, vLLM should retain its existing wait or failure behavior.

The feature should initially be opt-in, with configurable limits for:

- The soft timeout.
- The maximum quarantined HBM capacity or number of fallback requests.

The normal fast path remains unchanged. Additional HBM and computation are used only when a remote load exceeds the soft timeout.

Correctness requires that `A` must not be returned to the allocator while the original transfer may still access it. A logical timeout alone must not be treated as proof that the underlying transfer has completed.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

This RFC focuses only on reducing request latency through early recomputation. RDMA cancellation and transport-level recovery are out of scope.

This proposal is not equivalent to reducing Mooncake's existing timeout from 60 seconds to 5 seconds. The old destination blocks must remain isolated until the corresponding transfer is known to have completed.

The main expected trade-off is lower tail latency at the cost of temporary HBM usage and duplicate computation for slow outliers.

title: [RFC]: Enable full CUDA graphs for MoRIIO READ mode via async KV-load gating
author: edwinlim0919
body:
### Motivation.

MoRIIO supports two KV-transfer modes for P/D disaggregation:
- WRITE (producer pushes KV to the decode node): decode runs with FULL CUDA graphs.
- READ (decode pulls KV from the prefill node): decode runs with PIECEWISE CUDA graphs with #48534.

READ is forced to piecewise because it posts per-layer RDMA reads at the start of the decode forward and must block per layer until that layer's KV has landed before running that layer's attention. That barrier (wait_for_layer_load) is a Python wait that runs between attention layers. A FULL CUDA graph captures the whole forward as one replayable graph with no host code in the middle, so on replay the barrier is silently skipped. Attention then races ahead of KV that has not arrived yet, producing garbage decode output that worsens with concurrency. #48534 makes the barrier real (correctness) and sets requires_piecewise_for_cudagraph = True, which downgrades the decode engine to PIECEWISE.

PIECEWISE pays per-op kernel launch overhead on every decode step. We want READ decode to run under full CUDA graphs for best performance, matching WRITE.

A full-CUDA-graph READ-mode pull connector implementation already exists for reference. vLLM's NIXL pull mode is also READ-based (decode pulls KV), yet it runs under full CUDA graphs with no per-layer barrier. It achieves this with an async KV-load gate:
    - get_num_new_matched_tokens returns async = True
    - The request parks in WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS (blocks are allocated but forward not allowed yet)
    - the request is promoted to RUNNING only after the whole KV has landed (per-request done_recving) --> KV READ no longer within forward pass
    - By the time the decode forward runs, all KV is already resident, so the forward needs no mid-graph wait (fully CUDA-graphable)

MoRIIO WRITE already uses exactly this gate on its consumer side (async whole-request completion), which is why WRITE decode is full-graph. READ chose a synchronous contract (async = False, request goes straight to RUNNING, reads consumed within the same forward), and that is what forces the mid-forward barrier and the piecewise downgrade.


### Proposed Change.

Make MoRIIO READ adopt the same async-load gate that MoRIIO WRITE and NIXL PULL mode use.
(1) get_num_new_matched_tokens (READ): return async = True
    - request parks in WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS
(2) Put reads outside of the forward path
    - start_load_kv already runs every step, including the no-forward path (kv_connector_no_forward), so reads for a           parked request get posted without a forward
    - Report per-request completion via get_finished → done_recving (_pop_done_transfers already computes per-request completion but currently discards it on the READ path)
(3) wait_for_layer_load reverts to a no-op.
    - The barrier added in #48534 is no longer needed as the KV is fully present before the decode forward runs
(4) requires_piecewise_for_cudagraph → False for READ, restoring full CUDA graphs.


Tradeoff
- Async-gating trades a one-time latency for a per-step saving: the request waits for the whole KV to land before its first decode step, instead of overlapping reads with the forward. Because start_load_kv posts reads a step ahead and runs every step, request N's reads overlap other requests' decode compute, so at steady-state concurrency the pipeline bubble is largely hidden. WRITE and NIXL already accept this trade, and full CUDA graphs remove per-op launch overhead on every subsequent decode step.


Relationship to #48534
#48534 is the correct fix for the current piecewise design: it makes the barrier real so READ produces correct output today, and explicitly marks READ as requiring piecewise. This RFC proposes the longer-term design in which the barrier becomes unnecessary (KV load gated before forward), enabling full CUDA graphs for READ decode. 

Suggested sequencing: land #48534 first (correctness now), then implement this RFC to recover full-graph performance.


### Feedback Period.

Hi, @tjtanaa @AndreasKaratzas @Rohan138 , I would greatly appreciate it if you can take a brief look at this RFC, since it describes how to enable full cudagraph mode on decode with MORIIO.

This is related to the discussion we had earlier this week in the AMD SIG meeting, where we discussed how to enable to full cudagraph for the best performance.

Thank you!!!

title: [RFC]: Expose narrow EPLB extension hooks for out-of-tree accelerators
author: freyfwt
body:
### Motivation.

Out-of-tree accelerators need to supply EPLB operations without replacing upstream coordination or patching global policy and communicator factories. This proposal exposes a small set of overridable operations on the components that already own them.

Implementation: #49700. Router class replacement is already supported by #51006 through concrete `PluggableLayer` registrations. The proposal uses that existing router mechanism and ordinary `EplbState` subclassing; it introduces no backend object or additional registry.

### Proposed Change.

#### Ownership and configuration

`EplbState` owns load aggregation, scheduling, cross-rank coordination and the background worker. Each existing `EplbModelState` owns its maps, expert buffer, pending transfer result and consumption protocol. An OOT integration supplies an `EplbState` subclass through its worker/controller and selects its model-state subclass through `model_state_cls`.

`Platform.supports_eplb()` declares capability. When EPLB is enabled, `check_and_update_eplb_config(parallel_config)` resolves platform defaults and validates policy/communicator names and supported combinations. Built-in platforms preserve their existing choices and async communicator restrictions. Numeric constraints remain in `EPLBConfig`.

The selector aliases remain `Literal` types for built-in names, while fields also accept platform-defined strings. An omitted policy is represented by `None` until the platform selects its default; explicit choices must be preserved. No supported-name getter interfaces are proposed.

#### State extension boundaries

- `create_policy()` selects the policy used by the state. The default reuses the built-in policy table and its class-based calling convention; an OOT subclass may supply its own policy instance.
- `create_model_communicator()` constructs a model's communicator. The default reuses the existing factory, including communicator-owned buffer handling.
- `rebalance_experts(model_state, ...)` receives model identity and the existing planning inputs in both synchronous and asynchronous paths. Its result remains a CPU integer physical-to-logical placement tensor.
- `model_state_cls` selects an `EplbModelState` subclass without a factory or registry. The existing `_commit_eplb_maps()`, `_commit_eplb_maps_for_layer()` and `_move_to_workspace()` functions become methods on that existing model-state class.
- Full-model commits, including Sentinel recovery, call the model instance's `_commit_eplb_maps()`. Async workspace consumption calls its `_commit_eplb_maps_for_layer()` before clearing the pending result and recording consumption. Device subclasses submit routing-table updates through these methods; no manager commit wrapper or callback is needed.

The upstream caller keeps the weight-move → map/device update → result acknowledgement sequence. Commit work must be submitted in the foreground stream's dependency order before acknowledgement. This contract does not require a host-wide or whole-stream synchronization per commit. A commit exception prevents acknowledgement; already installed weights or maps are not rolled back.

#### Router ownership and compatibility

Registered concrete router subclasses own expert mapping, load recording and their layer state. This RFC adds no `map_and_record` field, layer-state factory, or vendor branch in the base router. Existing model-specific classes and explicitly selected implementations retain their contracts unless the plugin registers a compatible replacement through the existing mechanism.

Built-in algorithms, topology selection, window semantics, transfer scheduling and fallback behavior remain outside this change. No `EplbPlan`, `EplbPolicyState`, `EplbRebalanceContext` or `EplbTopology` type is introduced.

#### Independent follow-ups

Async worker shutdown is a separate lifecycle concern, already addressed by the open #56854. This proposal does not add a stop event, interruptible-event API or shutdown stream barrier. Downstream integrations must preserve their existing resource-completion and teardown guarantees until they can adopt an upstream lifecycle implementation.

EP-aware initial placement, explicit transfer-source plans and sparse changed-layer execution remain separate requirements. Existing work such as #49572 and #51883 should be evaluated before proposing overlapping changes; these references do not establish that the open PRs satisfy every downstream requirement.

#### Risks and acceptance

The principal risks are unintended built-in selection changes, mismatched weight/map state, buffer reuse before a device update is submitted, and loss of model-specific router behavior. Acceptance requires targeted configuration and fallback tests, equivalent default planning results in both paths, successful weight/map commits, and failure ordering that withholds acknowledgement. A paired OOT integration must also run real-device component and checkpoint-backed migration/shutdown tests. CPU mocks alone do not establish device correctness.

### Feedback Period.

Feedback is requested on the revised ownership boundaries and compatibility contract.

### Any Other Things.

This revision supersedes the earlier comprehensive-backend, `transfer_layer_fn`, layer-state `map_and_record`, and separate `on_layer_committed` proposals. It preserves the goal of one upstream EPLB control plane while limiting #49700 to configuration and state override boundaries. Concrete commands, results and remaining hardware qualification belong in the implementation PR descriptions.

AI assistance was used to prepare this revision.

- [x] Related issues and open implementation PRs were checked; this updates the existing RFC and PR.

title: [RFC]: Support router-driven mixtures of multiple LoRA adapters
author: navyanshmahla
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM currently supports serving one LoRA adapter per request and supports LoRA weights for MoE base-model experts. It does not support router-driven mixtures of multiple LoRA adapters within one request, token, or layer.

This blocks inference for adapter-MoE approaches such as X-LoRA ([Buehler and Buehler, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07148)), MixLoRA ([Li et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15159)), and Riemannian MoE-LoRA ([Sun et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15828)) where the serving-time forward form is:

$$\text{base}(x) + \sum_i \text{gate}_i(x) \times \text{LoRA}_i(x)$$

The goal is to add serving support for multiple active LoRA adapters whose contributions are selected or weighted by a router.

## Current Behavior

Today, `LoRARequest` represents a single adapter, and runtime LoRA metadata maps tokens to one LoRA id. Existing fused MoE LoRA support is for applying LoRA to MoE model experts, not for treating LoRA adapters themselves as routed experts.

### Proposed Change.

Add an experimental multi-adapter LoRA routing path with these stages:

1. Add internal data structures for representing multiple active LoRA adapters for one request.
2. Add a reference implementation that computes weighted adapter mixtures in PyTorch for correctness.
3. Add optimized kernels / Punica integration after the semantics are validated.
4. Add docs, examples, and benchmarks.

Initial supported mode:

- Inference only.
- Same base model.
- Multiple already-loaded LoRA adapters.
- Per-token or per-layer routing weights supplied by an internal router interface.
- No training support.
- No optimizer support.
- No promise of supporting every MoE-LoRA paper in the first version.

## API Sketch

Possible internal representation:

```python
@dataclass
class LoRARoutingRequest:
    adapters: list[LoRARequest]
    routing_mode: Literal["dense", "topk"]
    top_k: int | None
```

### Feedback Period.

I would like to keep the RFC open for feedback for at least one week.

During that period I am mainly looking for maintainer feedback on:

  - whether this belongs in vLLM core or should start as an experimental path
  - whether the first implementation should keep the API internal
  - whether the proposed staged PR plan is acceptable
  - which LoRA/runtime/kernel maintainers should review the follow-up PRs

I plan to open a small draft prototype PR alongside this RFC so reviewers can   inspect the proposed internal data-model direction while discussion is ongoing. I will not treat the prototype API as final until the RFC feedback is addressed.

### CC List.

I'm not sure who the right owners are for this area. Reviewers familiar with LoRA serving, MoE runtime/Punica Kernels would be very helpful. 

### Any Other Things.

I plan to open a small draft prototype PR shortly after this RFC so maintainers can review the concrete internal data-model direction while the design is being discussed. Also, I am using AI code assistance for planning and code drafting and I will disclose that in follow-up PRs. Not to mention, I will personally review every changed line and run the relevant tests before requesting review.

title: [RFC]: Native Disaggregated Pull-Based Queue Worker Interface and Heuristic Pull Router
author: aojea
body:
### Motivation.

We propose adding a native, additive **Disaggregated Pull-Based Queue Worker interface** (`vllm.entrypoints.pull_worker.worker`).

This feature enables workers to initiate gRPC streaming connections **outward** to a central queue server, explicitly pulling tasks via credit grants (`TaskGrantRequest`) only when GPU execution slots and KV cache blocks are available. This replaces traditional push-based HTTP proxies that push requests to vLLM workers.

1. **Multi-Hardware / Heterogeneous GPU Support**: Clusters increasingly contain a mix of GPU types with varying VRAM capacities (e.g., 80GB A100s alongside 24GB RTX 4090s) and specific LoRA adapters. Push routers struggle to route large context prompts safely, risking OOMs on smaller GPUs. In a pull-based model, workers naturally filter and pull only tasks that fit their specific hardware capacity and capabilities, seamlessly enabling efficient heterogeneous cluster utilization.
1. **Multi-Zone, Multi-Region and Multi-Cloud Topology Awareness:** In enterprise Kubernetes deployments, worker nodes span availability zones and regions. Traditional push routers lack topology awareness, pushing requests across cloud regions and incurring cross-zone data egress costs and latency spikes. Pull workers can automatically report node topology labels (e.g., `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) via `WorkerStatus`. The central heuristic router steers tasks to same-zone workers, eliminating cross-zone egress costs and optimizing inter-region routing.
2. **Natural Backpressure (Zero OOMs):** Push routers estimate load via active HTTP connections, often overwhelming worker KV block allocation during bursty traffic and causing OOM crashes. Pull workers grant work strictly when KV cache memory is available.
3. **Zero-Drift Prefix Cache Locality:** Workers report active radix tree block hashes (`active_prefix_hashes`). Central heuristics match system prompt prefixes to warm workers before granting tasks, eliminating prompt prefill overhead.
4. **No Ingress Load Balancer Needed:** Pull workers pull directly from the central queue server, eliminating the need for NGINX/Envoy load balancers in front of GPU worker nodes (Those are still needed in front of the Queue Workers but can also be replaced by the cloud providers or north-south loadbalancers directly).

### Proposed Change.

We propose adding a native, additive Disaggregated Pull-Based Queue Worker interface (`vllm.entrypoints.pull_worker.worker`) and an official example reference implementation (`examples/heuristic_pull_router/`)

This change is purely additive. **It does not modify any core vLLM engine files or existing HTTP push endpoints**, ensuring zero instability for existing push-based deployments.

Extensibility is achieved via a gRPC interface (`queue.proto`). Users can write custom queue implementations in any language simply by implementing the proto interface.

Telemetry is pluggable. Workers report a `WorkerStatus` message split into two categories:

* **Core Metrics:** Essential safety data (e.g., num_running_reqs, free_gpu_kv_blocks).

* **Extended Metrics:** Opt-in data containing custom telemetry. Users can inject custom hardware or software state (e.g., Kubernetes zone labels, active LoRA adapters) into the custom_metrics maps via a custom StatLoggerBase plugin, allowing the central router to execute complex business logic without altering the vLLM core.

**Reference:** https://github.com/aojea/vllm/tree/vllm_pull

* `vllm/entrypoints/pull_worker/`: The native pull-worker executable and stat-logger.
* `vllm/entrypoints/pull_worker/proto/`: The queue.proto interface contract.
* `examples/heuristic_pull_router/`: The reference implementation (stateless gRPC server, Redis backend, and pluggable BasePolicy heuristic interface).
* `tests/entrypoints/pull_worker/`: Comprehensive unit and end-to-end integration tests.

title: [RFC]: Back-pressure detection for KV cache offloading tiers
author: bnellnm
body:
### Summary

vLLM's KV cache offloading framework (CPU DRAM, local NVMe, shared storage) does not detect or respond to bandwidth saturation on secondary tiers. When a tier is saturated — whether from concurrent eviction, excessive store operations, or high IOPS — the system continues dispatching load/store jobs that pile up, further degrading bandwidth for actual serving loads. This RFC proposes adding back-pressure detection to secondary offloading tiers and a response strategy to mitigate the impact on serving performance.

### Motivation

When secondary tiers (disk, shared storage) reach bandwidth saturation, three failure modes emerge:

1. **Unbounded job pileup**: Load/store operations continue to be issued to saturated tiers with no feedback. Pending jobs accumulate, increasing latency for all subsequent operations including loads for imminently-scheduled requests.

2. **No load/store prioritization: Under contention, background store operations compete equally with load operations. Serving latency suffers because stores consume bandwidth needed by loads.

3. **Saturated-Tier bottleneck: In the case when multiple secondary tiers are specified, all tiers receive the same amount of stores. The CPU blocks are protected from eviction, when the stores are in progress and are released only when the slowest tier has completed the store. Here the slowest tier becomes the bottleneck for the entire system. Further, we observe CPU tier running out of memory, preventing further offloads.


### Proposed Change.

### Phase 1 (this RFC): Back-pressure detection with store dropping

The initial implementation adds back-pressure detection to secondary offloading tiers and a single response policy: **drop store (write) requests** to a tier that is under pressure. No load prioritization, tier rerouting, or load-vs-recompute decision is included in this phase.

#### 1. Back-pressure detection in the offloading tier manager

Back-pressure detection could live at three levels:

1. **vLLM scheduler** — too intrusive; the scheduler should not need to understand tier-specific pressure signals
2. **Offloading tier manager** (`TieringOffloadingManager` / `OffloadingConnectorScheduler`) — has visibility into pending job counts across all tiers without requiring tier-specific cooperation
3. **Individual secondary tiers** (`SecondaryTierManager` implementations) — would require every new tier to implement a back-pressure mechanism, increasing the integration burden

This RFC places detection at **level 2, the offloading tier manager**. The manager already tracks pending store and load jobs per tier. It can derive back-pressure state from this bookkeeping without requiring changes to the `SecondaryTierManager` interface or individual tier implementations.

The signal should be:

- **Lightweight** — amortized across scheduler steps, not per-block
- **Non-blocking** — no synchronous I/O to compute

Several approaches to detecting back-pressure were considered:

1. **Measure store completion rate** — time completed store operations and compute a throughput EMA. When the observed rate drops below a configurable threshold, the tier is considered under pressure. This is minimally intrusive: it uses information already available when the manager processes job completions, requires no changes to tier implementations, and no OS-level metrics.

2. **Monitor pending job queue depth** — track the number of in-flight store jobs per tier and trigger when a high-water mark is exceeded. Simpler than rate-based detection but less responsive to gradual degradation — a deep queue may be normal for a high-bandwidth tier.

3. **Query OS/device-level I/O metrics** — read disk queue depth or I/O utilization from `/sys/block/` or equivalent. Provides the most direct signal but is platform-specific, requires filesystem-level knowledge the manager shouldn't need, and adds OS coupling.

4. **Tier-reported pressure** — have each `SecondaryTierManager` expose an `is_under_pressure()` method. Most accurate per-tier but increases the integration burden for new tiers (rejected for the same reason detection was placed at level 2).

This RFC proposes **approach 1 (store completion rate)** as the primary detection mechanism. It is the least intrusive, works uniformly across tier types, and degrades gracefully — a tier that stops completing stores will be detected as slow regardless of the underlying cause (disk saturation, network congestion, PVC eviction interference).

#### 2. Tier Manager response: drop stores to slow tiers

When a store to the CPU primary tier completes, `TieringOffloadingManager` cascades the blocks to all secondary tiers. This makes the tiering manager the natural intervention point — it can check per-tier pressure state and skip the cascade for any tier that is under pressure, silently dropping the secondary-tier store when a tier is slow.

Blocks that would have been stored are left in the CPU primary tier (subject to normal LRU eviction). Loads from the pressured tier continue normally. This is the only policy in Phase 1.

The threshold should be configurable with a sensible default. A hysteresis mechanism (high-water mark to activate, low-water mark to deactivate) prevents oscillation.

#### 3. Metrics and observability

- Back-pressure state per tier (active/inactive) exposed via Prometheus gauge
- Dropped store count per tier exposed via Prometheus counter

title: [RFC]: Per-layer online quantization configuration
author: fxmarty-amd
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM online quantization currently provides coarse-grained controls for applying quantization to `linear` and `moe` layers, plus an `ignore` list for excluding exact layer names or regex patterns:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a0c092ee72c0dcefbb3b3e74f97ac62d842e5f4b/vllm/config/quantization.py#L79-L94

This works well when a user wants to quantize a broad class of modules, but it becomes unnatural when we want to:

- only quantize layers whose names match a pattern, or
- use different online quantization schemes for different layer-name patterns.

The current workaround is to select a broad quantization mode and then carve out everything else with a long exclusion list.

For example, PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49313 uses a configuration like:

```bash
--quantization-config \
'{"linear":"fp8_per_channel","ignore":["lm_head","re:.*embed_tokens.*","re:.*mlp\\.gate$","re:.*expert.*","re:.*kv_b_proj.*"]}'
```

This is difficult to read, easy to get wrong, and model-specific in ways that are not obvious from the command line.

Another example is PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32238, which handled `kv_b_proj` quantization through hard-coded model logic instead of a standard user-facing configuration mechanism.

This matters more as partially quantized models become common (e.g. Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek V3), while other components remain good candidates for online quantization. Easily testing the effects of quantization on certain layers only directly through vLLM is valuable, as well as giving the deployment option.

Users should be able to describe that mixed policy directly instead of relying on negative matching patterns or model-specific code paths.

### Proposed Change.

Add a per-layer online quantization mapping to [`QuantizationConfigArgs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a0c092ee72c0dcefbb3b3e74f97ac62d842e5f4b/vllm/config/quantization.py#L80).

The mapping keys are exact layer names or regex patterns using the same `re:` convention as `ignore`, and the values are either:

- online quantization schemes from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a0c092ee72c0dcefbb3b3e74f97ac62d842e5f4b/vllm/config/quantization.py#L115, or
- the same `{"weight": ..., "activation": ...}` option existing for `linear`/`moe` keys.

Proposed CLI shape:

```bash
vllm serve <model> \
  --quantization-config.online '{"re:.*self_attn.*":"fp8"}'
```

without the need of a global `--quantization` flag.

Equivalent Python API shape:

```python
from vllm import LLM

llm = LLM(
    "<model>",
    quantization_config={
        "online": {
            "re:.*self_attn.*": "fp8",
            "re:.*kv_b_proj.*": "mxfp4",
            "re:.*shared_experts.*": "mxfp4",
        },
    },
)
```

Layers that do not match any entry would keep the behavior they would have had without the `online` mapping: they remain unquantized.

The initial scope should be limited to the same module families already handled by online quantization, i.e. `linear` and `moe`.

Implementation details:

- If the provided config is not compatible with the checkpoint, an error would be raised.
- `quantization_config.online` would be a mapping from exact layer name or `re:` regex pattern string to online quantization scheme.
- Invalid regex patterns would raise error or warning.
- If more than one pattern matches the same layer, vLLM would raise an error.
- vLLM would raise an error if `quantization_config.online` and `quantization_config.ignore` collide.
- `--quantization-config.online` would take precedence over `--quantization`/`--quantization-config.linear`/`--quantization-config.moe`.

Example use cases:

```bash
# Quantize only MLA projection layers with MXFP4.
vllm serve <model> \
  --quantization-config.online '{"re:.*kv_b_proj.*":"mxfp4"}'

# Use FP8 for attention linears and MXFP4 for shared experts.
vllm serve <model> \
  --quantization-config.online \
  '{"re:.*self_attn.*":"fp8","re:.*shared_experts.*":"mxfp4"}'
```

A user who wants to quantize only layers matching `re:.*kv_b_proj.*` can say that directly, instead of selecting a broad linear quantization scheme and excluding embeddings, gates, experts, heads, and other unrelated modules.

Implementation questions to resolve during review:

- Should the field be named `quantization_config.online` or something else? Should a different API be used?

### Feedback Period.

Proposed feedback period: one week.

### CC List.

@mgoin @kylesayrs @vkuzo @bowenbao @hangy-amd @dllehr-amd @fanxingran @zhaolin-amd

### Any Other Things.

This RFC is intended to cover API design only, and does not propose new quantization kernels or new quantization formats.

Related:
- #32412: Original online quantization API discussion.
- #32029: Online quantization roadmap.
- #31028: Quark vLLM plugin supports this feature in https://github.com/amd/Quark/tree/release/0.12/examples/online_quantization

title: [RFC]: Deprecate the FlexAttention backend
author: yewentao256
body:
### Motivation.

FlexAttention is no longer selected by default on ROCm and ranks behind TritonAttention on CUDA.

It has a lot of test coverage and is not used in practice, and sometimes breaks CI like https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/46531

**TritonAttention** now covers the standard FlexAttention use cases, including FP32, encoder-only, non-causal, sliding window, multimodal prefix, batch invariance, and Unlimited-OCR R-SWA.

Removing FlexAttention would eliminate roughly 1,900 lines of backend-specific implementation and tests, while reducing reliance on private PyTorch FlexAttention APIs.


### Proposed Change.

- Now: Mark `FLEX_ATTENTION` as deprecated.
- v0.29.0/v0.30.0: Remove the backend implementation, enum entry, Flex-specific configuration fields, and tests.
