The Phase 1 prototype has completed same-machine, single-GPU, TP=1 sleep/wake validation. Both public modes, `full` and `minimized`, have passed real CRIU/CUDA capture and restore. Two additional internal resource ablations were tested earlier for engineering comparison only and are not part of the user-facing interface.

### Test Environment
- GPU:  single GPU exposed inside the container
- Model: Qwen3-8B, BF16
- Topology: TP=1, PP=1, DP=1, single API server
- Engine: non-eager, `max_model_len=8192`, `max_num_seqs=16`, `gpu_memory_utilization=0.50`
- Software: PyTorch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0, CRIU 4.1 `20c6014e1`
- Storage: model, compilation cache, CRIU images, and snapshots all on tmpfs
- Snapshot config: `page_cache + optimistic`, skip SHA-256 computation for large files on restore
- Sampling: 6 runs per group, first run as warmup, last 5 runs used for statistics. Times reported in the table are medians.

`minimized` was run independently in three groups, totaling 15 steady-state runs. L3 restore time is measured from the `/wake_up` request to the first non-empty token received in a fixed streaming request, with final response content confirmed correct.

### Performance Results

| L3 Policy | Runs | Checkpoint Time | Restore Time | Artifact Size |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `minimized` | 15 | 2.837 s | **5.948 s** | 4.251 GiB |
| `full` | 5 | 27.242 s | 22.990 s | 49.659 GiB |

Baseline results from the same batch:

| Path | Runs | Sleep | Wake / Start | First Inference |
|----|----|-----|------------|---------------|
| Fresh Engine | 5 | — | 35.396 s to `/ready` | 0.054 s |
| CuMem L1 | 5 | 0.340 s | 0.407 s | 0.044 s |
| CuMem L2 | 5 | 0.047 s | 2.907 s | 0.049 s |

### Restore Breakdown

Phase-by-phase timing for `minimized`:

| Phase | Median |
|-----|------|
| CRIU restore | 1.861 s |
| CUDA restore-TID discovery | 0.335 s |
| CUDA restore action | 0.553 s |
| CUDA unlock | 0.021 s |
| Provider total | 2.810 s |
| Worker restore | 3.147 s |
| Post-restore TTFT | 0.014 s |

### Correctness and Resource Results
- All 30 formal L3 runs restored successfully and passed fixed semantic checks.
- Model page residency rate was 100% before every restore.
- Engine `read_bytes` delta was 0 for all runs.
- Across 30 `HIBERNATED` checks, project process HBM and full-GPU HBM were both 0 MiB.
- Ruff and Python 3.10 mypy passed.
- Snapshot tests: `75 passed`.
- CLI parser tests: `3 passed, 30 deselected`.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

## Discussion Topics
1. **Snapshot boundary.** This proposal preserves the frontend and only saves/restores EngineCore. #51360 saves the entire initialized process tree. We would like to discuss which scenarios each approach is best suited for, and the trade-offs around HTTP lifecycle, restore adoption, and persistent overhead.
2. **User interface.** Should Engine Snapshot be integrated as a new sleep level within `sleep/wake`, or exposed as a standalone `snapshot create/restore` interface? Which lifecycle and state definitions can be shared between the two entry points?
3. **Future evolution.** This proposal plans to progress through cross-machine 1→N, single-machine multi-GPU, and multi-node multi-GPU. We would like to discuss whether this roadmap aligns with the community's plans, which scenarios should be prioritized, and what additional considerations are needed for cross-machine and distributed restore.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Extended online quantization roadmap
author: fxmarty-amd
body:
### Motivation.

Continuation of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32029.

Online quantization API is now relatively stable at https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online and documented at https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/quantization/online/.

This RFC summarizes and motivates proposed features that would be helpful to make online quantization to be more flexible and more widely compatible with models, including pre-quantized ones.

### Proposed Change.

### 1. [done - partially] Support activation quant key override

Implemented in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51808.

This is necessary to dispatch on specific linear/moe backends that can be picked only through the `activation_quant_key` (see e.g. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c4e969294ecab9ffefb995b734303f13f62b723f/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/mxfp4.py#L441-L445)

### 2. [done] Targeted online quantization configuration based on user patterns

Implemented in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51285, RFC in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50281.

The goal is simply to extend the UI to support e.g. `--quantization-config.targets '{"re:.*o_proj.*":"mxfp8"}'`, e.g. to target a single layer similar to e.g. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc9f845ddc54c1df38fdbce5afe03f9fd15813bd/vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py#L935-L948 (that is currently hard-coded and may be causing accuracy issues if done silently https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48051), or e.g. `--quantization-config.targets '{"re:.*shared_expert.*":"fp8_per_block"}'` to enable fused shared expert.

### 3. [done] Support online quantization with partially pre-quantized checkpoints

Implemented in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51392.

This is necessary to combine online quantization with already partially quantized checkpoints, which is notoriously the case recently. This is e.g. useful to test the accuracy/speed tradeoff of quantizing certain additional layers, or useful to e.g. release a single model compatible with fused shared expert / unfused shared expert.

This has e.g. been requested in separate PRs:
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48983
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49313

### 4. [done] Requantize already-quantized layers to different precision (different weight quant key)

Implemented in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55684

This is similar to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28291 & https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29328 on sglang side.

This idea here would be to allow loading through a certain quantization method, dequantize and override the quantization method on request.

This has e.g. been requested in:
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48427
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51274

### 5. Adopt `online/*` API for Humming online quantization, torchao online quantization

Currently, Humming (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/34556) and torchao (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32133, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/23014) have their own online quantization logic:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/93eea4f665a0a6a188fd52b37f4a18bc37315f62/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/humming.py#L268-L277

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/340b7e4909f14ff33943ab6ac7955191e1b8b4ff/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/torchao.py#L383-L389

In contrary proposed online quantization for AMD/Quark in vLLM that intended to plug similarly in existing quant method was rejected: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/31028 - so we ended up [having a plugin](https://github.com/amd/Quark/tree/release/0.12/examples/online_quantization) (and eventually adopting upstream `online/*` API now).

These torchao/humming logics could be moved to use the online quantization frontend.

cc @jerryzh168 @kylesayrs @jinzhen-lin

One month

title: [RFC]: fp8_ds_mla KV cache on pre-SM89 (Ampere) GPUs via software-dequant TritonMLA decode
author: nickus
body:
### Motivation

MLA models (DeepSeek family, Kimi-K3) on Ampere fleets (RTX 3090 / A100) can only run bf16 KV today: `--kv-cache-dtype fp8*` is rejected below SM89. The `fp8_ds_mla` packed layout (656 B/token/layer vs 1152 bf16) is storage-only — the query stays bf16 — so it does not need native fp8 arithmetic at all. Enabling it on Ampere is **1.75× context per card**.

### What already works upstream (verified on sm_86)

- the CUDA cache writer (`*_ds_mla_insert`) is ungated in CMake, and its PDL blocks are no-ops below SM90;
- chunked-prefill dequant (`cp_gather_and_upconvert_fp8_kv_cache`) is ungated, and `_compute_prefill_context` already dispatches on `fp8_ds_mla`;
- `MLAAttentionSpec.real_page_size_bytes` already returns 656 for this layout.

### The one gap

TritonMLA decode reads a contiguous 576-wide bf16 row and does not list `fp8_ds_mla` in its supported cache dtypes.

### Proposal

1. A Triton decode path reading the packed 656-byte row with in-kernel fp8e4m3→fp16 bit-math dequant (~220-line kernel, no new CUDA).
2. Carve `fp8_ds_mla` out of the SM89 kv-cache-dtype gate **for TritonMLA only**. No Hopper/Blackwell path changes.

### Evidence in hand

- kernel test suite 12/12, CPU-runnable via `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` (CI-friendly);
- cosine vs bf16: 0.9999967;
- greedy outputs identical to bf16, including under pipeline parallelism (PP=2);
- measured end-to-end on RTX 3090.

### Alternatives considered

- Status quo: bf16-only KV on Ampere — the 1.75× context stays on the table.
- Enabling the plain-fp8 KV path below SM89: rejected — that path genuinely needs native fp8 query math.

Happy to submit the PR if the direction is acceptable.

---

title: [RFC]: First-class agentic inference support in vLLM
author: franciscojavierarceo
body:
# RFC: First-class agentic inference support in vLLM

## Motivation

The [vLLM Agentic API project](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api) has completed an MVP supporting Codex and Claude Code with vLLM as the inference engine. It is a high-performance Rust runtime for the capabilities these clients need beyond token generation: stateful continuation, tool loops, web search, MCP, streaming, and Responses/Messages compatibility.

Agentic workloads are increasingly important to llm-d and the broader serving community. The question is how vLLM and Agentic API should evolve together as these workloads become more stateful and operationally complex. Emerging capabilities such as [Computer History](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/customization/computer-history) show how agentic systems are beginning to use persistent activity, search, and external context to resume work and understand what happened across tools.

vLLM already supports Responses and Messages APIs, an optional in-process Responses store, and MCP/tool-server integrations. Agentic API builds on that foundation with a broader runtime for stateful continuation, tool loops, web search, vendor-neutral integrations, and the operational needs of agentic inference workloads. These capabilities are complementary, but vLLM does not currently plan to pursue the full Agentic API scope in its existing serving surface.

How should vLLM and Agentic API evolve together to support this next generation of agentic inference workloads?

## Proposed change

We propose that vLLM make agentic inference a first-class supported capability by integrating more tightly with Agentic API. The project’s MVP provides a working starting point for stateful Responses and Messages APIs, tool orchestration, and vendor-neutral integrations. The options below describe different ways to bring those capabilities into the vLLM ecosystem; this RFC seeks agreement on the desired integration model and the boundaries that should remain stable.

### Goal

Agentic API aims to provide a vendor-neutral integration layer connecting agentic clients to databases, third-party APIs, and external tools while preserving and optimizing vLLM’s inference capabilities. It should also provide llm-d with practical Responses API and Messages API solutions that externalize conversation state and orchestration without forcing hard affinity to the engine that served an earlier turn.

### Scope and boundary

The boundary is intentional: vLLM Core focuses on model execution, scheduling, batching, tokenization, rendering, parsing, and structured decoding; Agentic API focuses on state, external integrations, tool orchestration, and client compatibility. The goal is to make these capabilities more tightly integrated and accessible through the vLLM ecosystem.

### Desired outcome

The goal is for the vLLM ecosystem to expose a first-class agentic inference experience by building on vLLM’s existing Responses, Messages, response-store, and MCP/tool-server support and integrating the broader capabilities provided by Agentic API. This RFC seeks alignment on how Agentic API and vLLM should become more tightly integrated to reach that goal.

## Options

These options are not mutually exclusive. A first-class boundary could be the near-term step before deciding whether to merge or formally package Agentic API with vLLM.

| Option | Description | Proposed change | Main tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Merge** | Move Agentic API into vLLM Core. | Merge the code, consolidate APIs and tests, and document the agentic serving experience in vLLM. | One project and release process, but vLLM takes on persistence, integrations, and workflow orchestration. |
| **2. Remain separate** | Continue with today’s architecture and independent evolution. | Improve documentation, publish a dedicated Agentic API website or landing page, and clearly document how it integrates with vLLM. | Clear boundaries, but leaves the broader agentic workload experience outside vLLM’s existing serving surface and risks capability gaps and compatibility drift. |
| **3. Official dependency** | Keep a separate repository, but officially distribute or depend on Agentic API for Responses and agentic inference. | Add supported packaging and version compatibility, vLLM documentation and examples, and a maintained integration path. | Better integration, but tighter versioning and packaging coupling. |
| **4. First-class runtime boundary** | Keep the repositories separate while defining supported interfaces, compatibility guarantees, and shared tests. | Establish shared contracts, conformance tests, release coordination, and cross-linked documentation or landing pages. | Preserves flexibility, but requires sustained coordination. |

## Key questions

1. How should vLLM extend its existing Responses, Messages, response-store, and MCP/tool-server support to provide a broader agentic inference experience?
2. What should agentic applications, including coding harnesses, be able to rely on from the vLLM ecosystem?
3. Which responsibilities should remain separate even if the projects are distributed together?
4. What interfaces and tests should vLLM, Agentic API, and llm-d share?

## Additional context

- [vLLM Responses API and Tool Calling lookahead (#34857)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/34857)
- [vLLM session-centric KV-cache orchestration (#48501)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48501)
- [vLLM Agentic API Codex CLI integration (#54)](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/issues/54)
- [vLLM Agentic API response-store semantics (#14)](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/issues/14)
- [vLLM multi-turn Responses API support (#33089)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/33089)
- [vLLM Rust frontend / Anthropic Messages RFC (#47753)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47753)
- [llm-d-router session-centric KV lifecycle orchestration (#1979)](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/1979)
- [llm-d-router external Responses state store (#1104)](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/1104)
- [llm-d-router Session Control Protocol (#2003)](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/2003)
- [llm-d-router agentic routing profiles (#1867)](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/1867)

## Recommended direction

The long-term goal should be for vLLM to provide a first-class agentic serving experience that builds on its existing Responses, Messages, response-store, and MCP/tool-server support and adds the orchestration and integrations needed by real agentic workloads.

The immediate goal is tighter integration between Agentic API and vLLM Core so that vLLM’s support for agentic workloads is visible and accessible throughout the ecosystem. The options above provide several paths to that outcome, from merging the projects to establishing an officially supported dependency or first-class integration contract.

## CC list

@robertgshaw2-redhat @noobHappylife @maralbahari @tjtanaa @ashwing

title: [RFC]: support rl feature : weight checker
author: shiyuan680
body:
### Background

In RL training workflows such as PPO, GRPO, and DPO, the training side
periodically transfers model weights to the inference/rollout engines.

A weight update may fail because some tensors were not transferred, only part
of the distributed engines received the update, or the transferred tensor
contents were corrupted.

Weight Checker provides a development-only verification mechanism based on
per-tensor SHA-256 checksums. It verifies that inference weights restored or
transferred after a reset exactly match the original inference weights.


The three actions that weight_checker depends on:

* **compare**: Recompute the current SHA-256 values Gang compare them with the snapshot, returning `match` + `mismatches`
* **checksum**: Return the current per-tensor SHA-256 values 
* **reset**: Randomize the weights, to set up detection of whether a later weight update was correct

### Motivation.

In the RL training loop: `start_weight_update → update_weights* → finish_weight_update`, we need to confirm that **after the training side pushes/synchronizes the Actor weights to the rollout inference engine, the weights held by the engine are indeed consistent with what we intended to push**.

Before the training loop begins, check the correctness of the weight-update function to avoid off-policy training crashes.


### Proposed Change.

Add a development-only `POST /weight_checker` endpoint with three actions:

- `checksum`
  - Computes per-tensor SHA-256 checksums.
  - The first `checksum` in a verification cycle stores the result as the
    comparison baseline.
  - Subsequent `checksum` calls return current checksums without replacing the
    existing baseline.
- `reset`
  - Randomizes every tensor covered by Weight Checker.
  - Does not modify the stored baseline.
- `compare`
  - Computes the current checksums and compares them with the stored baseline.
  - Returns `match` and `mismatches`.
  - Clears the baseline after comparison.

### Overall Architecture

Add a new `POST /weight_checker` endpoint to the vLLM dev router, which obtains the per-tensor SHA-256 values via the engine-side `compute_weight_checksums()`, and maintains a process-level state object on the server for storing and comparing snapshots:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Router as dev/rlhf/api_router.py
    participant Engine as Engine/Core Client
    participant Worker as GPU Worker(s)
    participant Trainer

    Note over Client,Worker: Weight-update verification cycle

    Client->>Router: POST /weight_checker {"action":"checksum"}
    Router->>Engine: compute_weight_checksums_all()
    Engine->>Worker: collective_rpc(compute_weight_checksums)
    Worker->>Worker: Hash persistent parameters/buffers
    Worker-->>Engine: dp/pp/tp-qualified SHA-256 checksums
    Engine-->>Router: checksums from all engines
    Router->>Router: Store baseline if no baseline exists
    Router-->>Client: checksums, baseline_created=true

    Client->>Router: POST /weight_checker {"action":"reset"}
    Router->>Engine: reset_weights()
    Engine->>Worker: collective_rpc(reset_weights)
    Worker->>Worker: Randomize checksum-covered tensors
    Worker-->>Engine: ok
    Engine-->>Router: ok
    Router-->>Client: status=reset

    Note over Trainer,Worker: Reload or transfer original inference weights

    Trainer->>Engine: start_weight_update
    Trainer->>Engine: update_weights
    Engine->>Worker: Write inference weights
    Trainer->>Engine: finish_weight_update

    Client->>Router: POST /weight_checker {"action":"checksum"}
    Router->>Engine: compute_weight_checksums_all()
    Engine->>Worker: collective_rpc(compute_weight_checksums)
    Worker-->>Engine: Current SHA-256 checksums
    Engine-->>Router: checksums from all engines
    Router->>Router: Preserve existing baseline
    Router-->>Client: checksums, baseline_created=false

    Client->>Router: POST /weight_checker {"action":"compare"}
    Router->>Engine: compute_weight_checksums_all()
    Engine->>Worker: collective_rpc(compute_weight_checksums)
    Worker-->>Engine: Current SHA-256 checksums
    Engine-->>Router: checksums from all engines
    Router->>Router: Compare with baseline and clear baseline
    Router-->>Client: match=true, mismatches=[]
```

**Core logic (using RL weight-update verification as an example):**

```
1. checksum
   - Compute original inference-weight checksums.
   - Save them as the baseline.

2. reset
   - Randomize all checksum-covered inference tensors.

3. reload or transfer inference weights
   - start_weight_update
   - update_weights*
   - finish_weight_update

4. checksum
   - Compute the transferred inference-weight checksums.
   - Do not replace the original baseline.

5. compare
   - Compare current checksums with the original baseline.
   - Expected result: match=true and mismatches=[].
   - Clear the baseline after comparison.
```

###  Test case design

| Test group | Functional points covered | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API | Snapshot creation and replacement; compare state handling; checksum stability and snapshot isolation; sleep/wake and generation consistency; invalid-action handling; server health; reset and weight-update verification | P0 |
| TP| Checksum and comparison behavior with tensor parallelism enabled | P1 |
| EP| Checksum coverage of locally owned expert weights with expert parallelism enabled| P1 |

title: [RFC]: Extensible GEMM Epilogue Contracts for Residual, Norm, and Gated Activation Fusion
author: calvin-fei
body:
### Motivation. vLLM has mature linear-kernel selection and several compiler fusion passes, but the kernel interface and the graph-fusion interface do not yet share one typed contract for fusing a producer GEMM with adjacent residual, normalization, scaling, quantization, or gated-activation work. Today a provider is generally selected to produce the linear output, after which model code or a compilation pass applies downstream operations. This leaves two recurring gaps: 1. a provider that can evaluate a valid epilogue while accumulators are still in registers cannot advertise that capability through the same selection path; and 2. correctness constraints around reduction domains and tensor-parallel collective boundaries are encoded in one-off fused modules/patterns instead of one fail-closed contract. This RFC proposes an optional `GemmEpilogueSpec` understood by linear-kernel providers and compiler rewrites. It is not a request to fuse every decoder block or to require one backend. A provider may accept a spec only when it can implement the exact shape, dtype, reduction, aliasing, and distributed semantics; otherwise vLLM uses the existing unfused path. The initial target is the common Transformer structure in which GEMMs are interleaved with residual addition, RMSNorm-style normalization, scaling/quantization, and SwiGLU-like gated activations. Diffusion/omni models are a downstream consumer, but the abstraction belongs in vLLM's kernel boundary if it is sufficiently generic. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. Design principles - Optional and fail closed: existing kernels and model paths are unchanged without a matched spec. - Typed semantics, not arbitrary Python callbacks in the hot path. - Provider-neutral: CUTLASS/CuTe DSL, Triton, FlashInfer, vendor plugins, or native code may implement a capability. - Compiler-aware: a graph pass may request a spec only after matching a proven graph. - TP-aware: a row-parallel partial sum cannot be normalized as though it were the complete tensor before all-reduce. - Numerically explicit: accumulation dtype, cast points, reduction dtype, and output/alias semantics are part of the contract. - Measured enablement: a valid fusion is not automatically faster for every shape/batch. #### 2. Proposed types Illustrative API: ```python class EpilogueOp(Enum): BIAS = "bias" RESIDUAL_ADD = "residual_add" ROW_SCALE = "row_scale" RMS_NORM = "rms_norm" STATIC_QUANTIZE = "static_quantize" SILU_MUL = "silu_mul" class CollectiveBoundary(Enum): NONE = "none" PRE_COLLECTIVE_PARTIAL = "pre_collective_partial" POST_ALL_REDUCE_COMPLETE = "post_all_reduce_complete" @dataclass(frozen=True) class GemmEpilogueSpec: ops: tuple[EpilogueOp, ...] accumulation_dtype: torch.dtype output_dtype: torch.dtype reduction_dtype: torch.dtype | None collective_boundary: CollectiveBoundary auxiliary_inputs: tuple[str, ...] outputs: tuple[str, ...] mutates: frozenset[str] class MMLinearKernel(...): @classmethod def can_implement_epilogue( cls, config, spec: GemmEpilogueSpec ) -> tuple[bool, str | None]: ... def apply(self, layer, x, bias=None, *, epilogue=None, **kwargs): ... ``` The final interface may use specialized subtypes rather than an enum list. The important property is that supported compositions are explicit and inspectable. #### 3. Compiler/provider flow ```mermaid flowchart LR Graph["FX/model graph
GEMM + adjacent ops"] Match["Semantic pattern match
shape, alias, reduction, TP boundary"] Spec["Build GemmEpilogueSpec"] Select["Existing linear-kernel selector"] Cap{"Provider can implement
this exact spec?"} Fused["Provider fused GEMM + epilogue"] Fallback["Existing GEMM
+ existing separate ops"] Verify["Debug/CI reference checks
and benchmark gate"] Graph --> Match --> Spec --> Select --> Cap Cap -->|yes| Fused --> Verify Cap -->|no| Fallback ``` Graph matching remains in compilation/model integration. Kernel providers do not parse arbitrary FX graphs. Providers receive a normalized, validated spec. #### 4. Correct placement around tensor parallelism ```mermaid flowchart TD Col["Column-parallel GEMM
output shard is semantically complete
for shard-local eligible epilogues"] Row["Row-parallel GEMM
rank-local partial sums"] AR["Tensor-parallel all-reduce"] Full["Complete output tensor"] Post["Residual / norm / gated op
when reduction domain is complete"] Col --> Post Row --> AR --> Full --> Post ``` Some operations can run on a shard; others require the full hidden dimension or the globally reduced value. The pattern matcher must encode the mathematical reduction domain. A provider cannot accept `POST_ALL_REDUCE_COMPLETE` work on a rank-local partial accumulator. An implementation may eventually fuse all-reduce plus a post-collective epilogue through a communicator/provider that supports it, but that is a separate capability. This RFC must not move normalization across a collective merely to make a kernel shape convenient. #### 5. Initial supported compositions Start small and evidence-driven. Candidate specs: - GEMM + bias; - GEMM + row scale; - GEMM + static output quantization; - GEMM + residual add when aliasing and broadcast semantics are simple; - paired gate/up projections + SiLU-multiply where the provider exposes a joint output contract; and - post-all-reduce residual/RMSNorm only through an existing correctly placed fused collective capability. RMSNorm inside a GEMM epilogue is valid only if the provider can compute the full required row reduction correctly. A tiled GEMM that sees only part of the normalized dimension must reject the spec or use a proven multi-tile reduction scheme. #### 6. Integration with current kernel selection The current `MMLinearKernel` selection lifecycle already separates: - hardware support; - whether a kernel can implement a layer configuration; - parameter processing; and - execution. Add epilogue capability after ordinary layer compatibility. `--linear-backend` continues to constrain providers. A selected backend may still reject a particular epilogue and execute the ordinary linear path; no new backend should be selected solely because it claims a fusion unless the existing priority/benchmark policy allows it. The contract should also be visible in debug logs/metrics: requested spec, selected provider, rejection reason, and fallback path. #### 7. Numerical and aliasing contract Every supported spec declares: - GEMM accumulation dtype; - when the accumulator is cast; - epsilon and reduction dtype for normalization; - whether residual is read before an output write; - exact broadcasting rules for weights/scales/bias; - output dtype(s), including optional dual output; - allowed non-contiguous inputs; and - mutation/alias behavior for `torch.compile` fake/meta implementations. Tests compare against an independent high-precision reference as well as the existing unfused path. A fusion may be numerically closer to the high-precision reference while not bitwise equal to bf16 eager execution; that must be represented by a declared tolerance and model-level gate, not silently treated as exact. #### 8. Validation matrix Unit/kernel tests: - multiple `M/N/K`, including small decode and larger prefill batches; - bf16/fp16/fp8 inputs and supported accumulation/output dtypes; - contiguous and declared non-contiguous layouts; - bias/residual broadcast cases; - alias/mutation checks under eager and `torch.compile`; - negative tests for unsupported reduction domains/spec orderings; - TP world sizes 1/2/4 with a distributed reference; and - graph pass fallback when no provider accepts the spec. End-to-end tests: - at least one autoregressive decoder block; - one diffusion/omni Transformer consumer if the abstraction is shared downstream; - compilation enabled/disabled; and - output/accuracy gates appropriate to the model. #### 9. Benchmark and enablement policy For each provider/spec/shape regime report: - kernel latency and achieved compute/bandwidth; - kernel launch count; - HBM bytes when measurable; - end-to-end latency/throughput; - compile/capture compatibility; - peak workspace memory; and - numerical results. Enable only where end-to-end evidence supports it. A fusion can regress low-batch execution because fixed scheduling/collective overhead outweighs saved launches. The selector/config may need shape-regime gating rather than a universal boolean. #### 10. Alternatives considered - **Keep adding one-off fused modules.** Fast for a single pattern but duplicates capability, fallback, and correctness logic. - **Rely only on compiler-generated fusion.** Valuable and should remain the first option, but does not expose provider-specific GEMM epilogues or distributed placement semantics uniformly. - **Allow arbitrary Python epilogue callables.** Hard to validate, serialize, select, and support across providers. - **Put the abstraction only in vLLM-Omni.** Diffusion is a motivating consumer, but linear-kernel selection and several relevant fusion passes are upstream vLLM concepts. #### 11. Phased plan 1. Agree on the typed spec and rejection/fallback behavior. 2. Implement one minimal existing capability (for example bias/static scaling) through the contract without changing defaults. 3. Connect one compiler pattern and add debug observability. 4. Add distributed-boundary negative/positive tests. 5. Benchmark one residual/norm or gated-activation composition. 6. Let downstream vLLM-Omni/SGLang work evaluate additional providers separately. ### Feedback Period. At least one week. ### CC List. No specific CC requested; feedback from linear-kernel, compilation, distributed, and quantization maintainers would be valuable. ### Any Other Things. Relevant code and discussions: - vLLM linear-kernel interface and providers: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear - `MMLinearKernel` base contract: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/base.py - Existing all-reduce/RMSNorm compilation fusion: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/allreduce_rms_fusion.py - Hardware-agnostic model-definition RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/44219 - vLLM-Omni diffusion kernel optimization RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/3186 - vLLM-Omni diffusion operator-boundary RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/5582 - SGLang CUTLASS dynamic epilogue investigation: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/30809 ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Rank-Skew-Aware Collective Attribution for Tensor-Parallel Serving
author: calvin-fei
body:
### Motivation. Tensor-parallel traces often report a large amount of GPU time inside all-reduce or another collective. That observation alone does not identify the cause. The interval may contain: - useful data transfer limited by the interconnect/backend; - rank-arrival skew, where an early rank waits for a slower peer; - host dispatch or graph-launch skew before the collective; - additional copies/registration imposed by a selected communicator; or - a correctness failure in which ranks issue different collective sequences. These causes require different remedies. Replacing a collective kernel cannot fix time dominated by peer arrival, while reducing host skew cannot raise a genuinely saturated bandwidth ceiling. vLLM has communicator benchmarks and several collective implementations, but it does not expose a common, request/layer-correlated attribution workflow that combines production traces, a message-size-matched zero-skew baseline, and controlled skew injection. This RFC proposes an opt-in profiling facility and offline report that classify collective cost as transfer-dominated, arrival-skew-dominated, mixed, or inconclusive. It complements, but does not duplicate, TP consensus/deadlock work such as #48720: that RFC detects/recoveries collective-sequence failures; this RFC attributes performance when execution is correct. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. Goals - Assign a stable logical ID to sampled TP collectives. - Record per-rank arrival/enqueue and completion evidence without adding a synchronizing collective to the measured hot path. - Run the same operator/message sizes in an isolated calibration benchmark. - Inject controlled rank delay to learn latency sensitivity to skew. - Produce a causally conservative classification with confidence/evidence. - Point optimization work toward host scheduling, batching/parallel policy, overlap, or communicator/backend changes based on the classification. #### 2. Non-goals - Always-on per-collective production tracing. - A new collective implementation. - Automatically changing NCCL algorithms from one trace. - Treating `collective_duration - arrival_skew` as an exact transfer time. - Detecting/recovering mismatched collective sequences (covered by separate reliability work). #### 3. Trace record Illustrative schema: ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) class CollectiveTraceRecord: run_id: str request_class: str step_id: int layer_id: str collective_ordinal: int group_name: str rank: int world_size: int op: str shape: tuple[int, ...] dtype: str payload_bytes: int backend: str execution_mode: str # eager / compile / cuda_graph host_enqueue_ns: int gpu_begin_ns: int | None gpu_end_ns: int | None ``` `(step_id, layer_id, collective_ordinal, group_name)` must be derived from control flow shared by all ranks, not assigned by a rank-local counter that can silently diverge. Trace artifacts are merged after the run. The profiler must not call an extra all-gather/barrier around each measured collective, because that would manufacture or hide the skew being measured. #### 4. Three-source attribution ```mermaid flowchart TD Prod["Sampled production/profile run
per-rank arrival and collective spans"] Base["Isolated calibration
same op, size, dtype, topology, backend"] Inject["Controlled skew sweep
delay one rank by known intervals"] Join["Join by collective signature"] Features["Derived evidence
arrival spread, zero-skew floor,
throughput headroom, skew sensitivity"] Classify{"Conservative classifier"} Wait["Arrival-skew dominated
reduce host/rank imbalance"] Transfer["Transfer dominated
backend/topology/overlap candidate"] Mixed["Mixed
optimize both / change parallel plan"] Unknown["Inconclusive
collect more evidence"] Prod --> Join Base --> Join Inject --> Join --> Features --> Classify Classify --> Wait Classify --> Transfer Classify --> Mixed Classify --> Unknown ``` Evidence sources: 1. **Production arrival spread.** Difference between earliest/latest rank enqueue/readiness for the same logical collective, after clock calibration where needed. 2. **Zero-skew calibration curve.** Latency/throughput distribution for the exact op, payload, world size, topology, backend, and registration mode under synchronized inputs. 3. **Skew-injection curve.** Repeat calibration while delaying selected ranks by controlled intervals. This establishes how the backend's observed span changes when arrival skew is known. The report should not claim an exact decomposition if clocks or execution mode cannot support it. It can still classify when multiple independent measurements agree. #### 5. Clock and execution-mode handling Same-node phase 1 can use a shared host monotonic clock source plus CUDA/CUPTI timestamps, with startup/end calibration and explicit uncertainty. Multi-node support must estimate clock offsets/drift or rely on profiler data with a documented cross-node time base. CUDA graphs require special handling because Python wrappers run at capture rather than each replay. Supported choices include: - graph-node/CUPTI/Nsight evidence correlated to a deterministic collective ordinal; - sampled eager/compile runs for arrival instrumentation plus a separate graph-mode calibration; or - backend profiler callbacks that execute on replay. The report must label evidence as capture-time or replay-time and must not reuse capture timestamps as though they describe every replay. #### 6. Instrumentation modes Proposed modes: - `off` (default): no records or extra state; - `trace`: short, explicitly profiled run with detailed sampled records and NVTX ranges; - `aggregate`: optional low-rate sampled summaries if a provider can supply replay-safe timestamps without synchronization; and - `calibrate`: isolated communicator benchmark plus optional skew sweep. Instrumentation belongs near `GroupCoordinator`/device-communicator dispatch so custom all-reduce, pynccl, symmetric-memory, and platform providers emit the same schema. High-level `tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce()` can add request/layer context without owning timing. #### 7. Derived report For each collective signature, report: - call count and total payload bytes; - per-rank enqueue spread distribution; - observed collective span/duration distribution; - calibrated zero-skew p50/p95 and achieved bandwidth; - hardware/topology bandwidth ceiling when available; - skew-injection response curve; - backend/algorithm/registration and graph mode; - classification and confidence; - missing evidence/clock uncertainty; and - suggested next experiment, not an automatic configuration change. Example decision logic (thresholds to be validated, not hard-coded by this RFC): - observed latency near zero-skew calibration and bandwidth near measured ceiling -> transfer-dominated; - observed excess latency tracks arrival spread and injected-skew curve while zero-skew calibration has headroom -> arrival-skew-dominated; - both arrival spread and zero-skew transfer cost are material -> mixed; - mismatched op IDs/call counts -> stop performance attribution and route to correctness/consensus diagnostics; - otherwise -> inconclusive. #### 8. Optimization routing The report maps classifications to candidate work: | Classification | Candidate next steps | | --- | --- | | Arrival-skew dominated | profile host dispatch/pre-collective compute, remove rank-asymmetric work, reduce tiny collective fragmentation, evaluate smaller TP | | Transfer dominated | evaluate backend/algorithm/topology, fusion, overlap, payload/layout, or a different parallel axis | | Mixed | address largest source first; rerun attribution after each change | | Inconclusive | improve clock/replay instrumentation or collect a longer isolated trace | This table is guidance, not an auto-tuner. #### 9. Validation Synthetic tests: - zero injected skew with payload sweep; - fixed delay on one rank and alternating delayed rank; - compute imbalance before a collective; - bandwidth saturation with large payloads; - many small collectives dominated by launch overhead; - custom all-reduce registered/unregistered buffers; - eager, compile, and CUDA-graph replay where supported; and - intentionally mismatched collective IDs to verify handoff to reliability diagnostics. Correctness/safety tests: - `off` adds no hot-path allocation or thread; - profiler emits no additional measured-group collectives; - trace collection cannot change collective order; - bounded buffers drop samples with a counter rather than blocking execution; - artifacts exclude prompt/output tensor contents by default; and - profiler teardown works after request cancellation/error. #### 10. Benchmark plan Use the existing device-communicator benchmark as the calibration entrypoint where possible. Add: - exact production payload list import; - controlled pre-call delay per rank; - output JSON matching the trace schema/signature; - at least two TP world sizes and small/large payload regimes; and - comparison across the communicator(s) available on the test topology. Then run one representative model in trace mode and verify that the tool's classification matches the synthetic regime introduced before selected layers. #### 11. Alternatives considered - **Use only Nsight time inside NCCL.** It identifies where time is observed, not why peers entered at different times. - **Use only an isolated NCCL benchmark.** It gives a ceiling/floor but cannot show whether production ranks arrive together. - **Subtract arrival spread from duration.** Collective protocols overlap waiting and transfer nonlinearly; the result is not a reliable exact decomposition. - **Insert barriers around each collective.** This destroys the phenomenon under measurement and adds overhead. - **Reuse the TP consensus guard.** Collective-count health is valuable but does not quantify healthy-run transfer versus skew cost. #### 12. Phased plan 1. Define schema and add skew injection/output JSON to the communicator benchmark. 2. Add `trace` instrumentation for eager same-node TP behind an explicit profiler option. 3. Build the offline join/classification report with uncertainty. 4. Validate against synthetic known-skew and bandwidth regimes. 5. Add compile/CUDA-graph replay evidence. 6. Consider multi-node clock calibration and low-rate aggregate mode separately. ### Feedback Period. At least one week. ### CC List. No specific CC requested; feedback from distributed, observability, benchmark, and CUDA-graph maintainers would be especially useful. ### Any Other Things. Relevant code and discussions: - High-level TP communication operations: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/communication_op.py - Group/device communicator dispatch: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/parallel_state.py - Custom all-reduce implementation: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/device_communicators/custom_all_reduce.py - Device communicator benchmark: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_device_communicators.py - Complementary TP consensus/deadlock RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48720 ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Hybrid SSM models and last-block-replay with SpecDec and APC enabled
author: roikoren755
body:
### Motivation.

Long name, I know, but it should explain the issue we're facing.
Currently, when running a model with EAGLE-like speculative decoding (EAGLE/MTP/DFlash/DSpark) and APC enabled, on prefix cache match, vLLM needs to re-run the last full block of the cached prefix, as the drafter needs access to the first uncached token's EAGLE intermediate states.
This is usually fine for pure attention models, where a block consists of ~16 tokens. For hybrid SSM/attention models, however, each block may contain thousands of tokens (for Nemotron 3 Nano in TP1 it's 4224 tokens per block), and re-running a block can really hurt performance.

This RFC aims to offer a few different possibilities for properly solving this issue.

### Proposed Change.

We came up with three different ideas, and have working prototypes of them, and are actively working on a fourth one, initially rejected as too wasteful, but it might turn out to be the simplest. The ideas can potentially compliment each other, too, and work in unison, which may lead to better performance. We'll validate that once we land on an agreed path forward. The exception here are the last two ideas, both looking at caching the intermediate EAGLE states, just in differing ways.

From least to most involved, the ideas are:

- Partial match block promotion
  - Building on top of @ZJY0516 's work in [#45702](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45702).
  - First prefix cache hit will re-run last full block, up to `prefix-match-unit` tokens from the end of the block.
  - The SSM state at that point will get promoted, and saved to the prefix cache as a new block.
  - Subsequent matches can match on the new block, and only re-run the last `prefix-match-unit` tokens, with COW so that the prefix cache remains valid in the partial block.
  - Partial block granularity is not limited to "`prefix-match-unit` tokens from the end", specifically, but rather any multiple of `prefix-match-unit` can become a promotion junction.
- Next-token receipt on cached blocks
  - Each cached block will store additional information on the token that was generated following it.
  - If the prefix cache is hit, with the uncached token matching the first token that will be computed, the full prefix cache can be used, without any re-computation needed.
  - Still not sure on this point, but we're working to verify it as well.
- Cache boundary EAGLE states
  - After determining an SSM cache block's size, it is rounded up in number-of-tokens terms for the KV cache, and any diff is used as padding in the SSM view of the block.
  - We can take advantage of that, and before rounding up, append enough memory to the SSM cache for a single token's worth of EAGLE states.
    - For Nemotron 3 Nano in TP1, for example, 5,376 bytes are needed for the EAGLE states, which fits inside the existing `all`-mode APC's padding.
  - These states can then be used in conjunction with the cache, and eliminate the need to re-compute that block altogether.
  - This solution can add quite a lot of code complexity, surrounding different parallelization schemes.
    - With PP, for example, the SSM cache the EAGLE states are written to might belong to a rank that doesn't hold the drafter model.
- Sparse EAGLE cache
  - This is the newly revived idea, and is not fully fleshed or tested yet.
  - Building on top of the existing `HiddenStateCacheSpec`, adapting it for our needs.
  - Only cache states at block boundaries, packing multiple such states into a single cache page and sharing them across requests.
  - Requires somewhat complex bookkeeping:
    - Coupling states with the right prefix
    - Evicting states only when corresponding prefix cache blocks are evicted
    - Consolidating sparse pages as states get evicted

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@benchislett @ZJY0516 @yewentao256 @Naveassaf @amitz-nv @amirkl94 @shaunkotek 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Derive KV offload save sources from prefix-cache records
author: Dao007forever
body:
### Motivation.

Two related changes are proposed for KV connector save paths:

1. Derive offload sources from prefix-cache records for every KV-cache group instead of resolving a physical block positionally from a connector-owned copy of the request block table.
2. For connectors using this path, allow saving only when prefix caching is enabled and produces validated content keys.

Together, these make one correctness argument cover both systems: if the GPU prefix cache says a physical block holds a particular prefix hash, KV offload may save that block under that key.

This is narrower than the general offloading architecture in #19854 and the multi-tier design in #38260. It concerns how a save identifies the bytes belonging to a content key.

Several public fixes expose parts of the same invariant:

| PR | Relevant invariant |
|---|---|
| #51358 | Save exact core-selected Mamba boundary states rather than resolving them positionally |
| #51766 | Preserve running-request Mamba CoW ownership after external hits |
| #52372 | Keep GPU blocks referenced while asynchronous Mooncake store jobs read them |
| #43468 | Publish self-describing offload events |
| #44784 | Make MTP/EAGLE offloading lifecycle safe |
| #46972 | Store interior chunk-boundary blocks under MTP/EAGLE |
| #48596 | Save final blocks and prevent reuse races |
| #49671 | Defer request finalization until the final store completes |

These changes are useful and should be kept. The RFC asks whether the underlying save-source contract should be made content-addressed across cache groups so correctness does not depend on connector-specific exclusions and positional bookkeeping.

#### Root cause

A positional save typically has this shape:

```python
block_idx = start // block_size
block_id = block_ids_per_group[group_idx][block_idx]
```

That is valid only while logical position to physical block is a stable, total mapping.

It holds for a conventional full-attention block table. It does not generally hold for hybrid cache managers:

- Mamba managers may null and free superseded interior state blocks, relocate speculative scratch blocks, and move a durable partial-tail hash to a CoW destination.
- Sliding-window attention releases head-prefix blocks as the window advances.
- A connector-side mirror or append log does not necessarily observe in-place nulling, freeing, reuse, or CoW movement.

A stale physical ID can therefore refer to another request's live bytes while the save still uses a valid prefix hash. Deduplicating backends can preserve that bad value because a later correct save sees the key as already present.

Per-group exclusions contain known cases but leave the same trap for the next hybrid layout. The desired invariant is stronger: the source block and content key should come from the same cache transition.

### Proposed Change.

#### 1. Record save candidates at prefix-cache insertion

Every path that makes a block reachable under a hash funnels through `BlockPool._insert_block_hash`, including the operations used by:

- `cache_full_blocks` for block-aligned boundaries;
- `cache_partial_block` for sub-block entries;
- `move_block_hashes` for CoW re-pointing.

When recording is armed for a cache group, produce a self-contained entry such as:

```text
(request_id, group_id, block_id, num_tokens, block_hash/content_key)
```

The connector consumes those records instead of reconstructing either the physical source or content key from positional request snapshots.

Recording at the cache insertion boundary has several useful properties:

- It inherits the prefix cache's reachability, retention, and null filtering.
- A recycled block fails closed: reuse resets or replaces its hash binding, so a stale record can be rejected before pinning.
- Full attention, sliding-window attention, and Mamba use the same handoff contract.
- The request ID becomes a routing/lifecycle label rather than the source of truth for content identity.

Durability remains a property of the producer transition. Two examples:

- An append-only attention block or an off-table checkpoint whose model write has completed can be recorded when its hash is inserted.
- A live Mamba partial-tail block must not be offered while the next forward can overwrite it. Record the durable CoW destination when the hash is re-pointed instead.

Before accepting a record, verify that the block still holds the recorded hash. Once accepted, pin the physical block and release it only after all required ranks report the store attempt terminal. Success, deduplication, pressure drop, cancellation, and failure are all terminal for lifetime purposes; a failed save remains a future cache miss rather than a reason to retain an unbounded pin.

Recording should be explicitly armed by a producer connector and scoped per cache group so unused records cannot accumulate.

#### 2. Saves become record-driven; loads remain positional

A load asks where incoming bytes should be written. The request's newly allocated block table is the correct destination address, so loads should remain positional.

A save asks which physical block currently holds the content named by a key. That is a content lookup, so saves should be record-driven.

This distinction also makes pinning and retry semantics explicit:

- The connector pins exactly the blocks it accepts.
- A preempted request's unaccepted records can be dropped.
- Accepted records survive request completion or preemption as long as the hash binding remains valid.
- Retry can be bounded within a handoff without keeping unrelated later blocks pinned behind a token watermark.

#### 3. Require prefix caching for the record-driven save path

With prefix caching disabled, no prefix-cache hash binding exists to validate a save record. The record-driven path should therefore not save.

This is intended as a correctness rule for connectors migrated to this path, not an assumption that every existing offload implementation already follows it. The standard `OffloadingConnector`, `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`, LMCache integrations, and other connectors that maintain their own content index need an explicit decision: adopt the same validated record contract, provide an equivalent independent invariant, or remain on their current path temporarily.

#### 4. Migration

A staged migration can remain independently revertible and gated per group:

1. Move Mamba saves to record-driven handoffs, building on the exact-state and lifetime work in #51358.
2. Re-measure correctness, store coverage, streaming latency, and prefix-hit behavior.
3. Move sliding-window groups. This is a correctness step because head-prefix entries are mutable.
4. Move full-attention groups, then remove the positional save-source path and its per-group exclusions.
5. Revisit token-watermark state such as `_saved_offset`; self-contained handoffs may make range-based resume/retry bookkeeping unnecessary.

Full attention is last because its table is genuinely append-only today. Moving it is primarily a uniformity and code-deletion argument.

#### Expected benefits

- One correctness argument: a save is valid only while the prefix cache validates the content-key-to-block binding.
- Unified handling for full attention, sliding-window attention, and Mamba.
- No latent correctness dependency on a connector's stale block-table mirror.
- Well-defined pin/release behavior across asynchronous stores, preemption, failure, and request completion.
- Less connector-specific machinery: positional source resolution, save masks used only for exclusions, and eventually range-watermark retry state can be removed.

#### Open questions

1. What resume behavior must remain for any positional saver while migration is incomplete, and what should replace `_saved_offset`?
2. KV events are currently emitted from particular aligned-save paths. Should events be emitted directly from accepted/completed records so moving a group does not suppress publication?
3. Should `OffloadingConnector`, `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`, LMCache, and other positional savers adopt the same record type immediately or in separate follow-ups?
4. #51358 already provides exact Mamba handoffs, pinning, cross-rank completion watermarks, and fail-closed behavior. Should its emission site carry a self-contained content key and become the first implementation of this more general contract?
5. Should prefix caching be required globally for saving, or should connectors with an independently validated content index implement an equivalent capability/interface?
6. How should sub-block boundaries be represented so the record is self-describing across groups with different physical block sizes?

### Any Other Things.

The closest existing RFCs are #19854 and #38260. This proposal does not replace either one; it tightens the save-source identity and lifetime contract within those architectures.

Public implementation context: #51358, #51766, #52372, #43468, #44784, #46972, #48596, and #49671.

AI assistance was used to draft this RFC.

title: [RFC]: Adaptive prefill token budget based on scheduling pressure
author: TimoSaemann
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM exposes `max_num_batched_tokens` (MBT) as a static scheduling configuration. For long-context workloads, however, we observe that the latency-optimal token budget depends on the current scheduling pressure.

Under low scheduling pressure, a large MBT can improve prefill execution efficiency and reduce end-to-end latency. As concurrent prefill and decode work increases, a smaller prefill budget can become preferable by limiting prefill interference with active decoding.

This means that no single static MBT is optimal across changing load regimes.

We investigated this behavior across multiple models, workloads, and NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 5090, A100, and H100), including kernel-level profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute. Based on these observations, we developed Prefill-Pressure Adaptive Scheduling (P-PAS), a lightweight policy that adapts the amount of prefill work admitted by the scheduler.

Across the main load sweep, P-PAS reduced average end-to-end latency by 8.5% relative to fixed MBT 2k and by 11.3% relative to fixed MBT 16k.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15171

Implementation, benchmarks, raw results, and profiling traces:
https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm

### Proposed Change.

Add an optional adaptive prefill-budget policy to the V1 scheduler.

The evaluated P-PAS policy uses scheduler state that is already available.
Let:

- `N_p` be the number of running and waiting prefill requests
- `N_d` be the number of running decode requests
- `N_th` be a prefill-pressure threshold
- `B_max` be the normal prefill token budget
- `B_cap` be the reduced prefill token budget

The policy is:

```text
if N_p >= N_th and N_d > 0:
    prefill_budget = B_cap
else:
    prefill_budget = B_max
```

For the experiments in the paper:

```text
N_th  = 2
B_max = 16384
B_cap = 2048
```

The global scheduler token budget remains unchanged. The adaptive budget only limits the aggregate amount of prefill work admitted within a scheduler iteration.

The current implementation is a small modification of the vLLM V1 scheduler and can be enabled or disabled without changing the standard scheduling behavior when disabled.

I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and make the policy/configuration interface consistent with the maintainers' preferred design.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

A working implementation for vLLM 0.22.1 is available in the repository linked above. If there is interest in this direction, I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and prepare a PR.

title: [RFC]: DeepSeek-V4 Performance Optimization on ROCm (Phase Two)
author: shen-shanshan
body:
## Motivation

> Continue working on phase one: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41820.

DeepSeek-V4 introduces CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention, `compress_ratio=4`), HCA layers, and a large MoE backbone. A side-by-side trace comparison of the vLLM decode path against vLLM-ATOM on ROCm shows that vLLM still leaves measurable performance on the table. The gaps cluster into three areas:

1. **Unfused mHC kernels.** vLLM runs `mhc_post` and `mhc_pre` as separate kernels, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` as two kernels, while ATOM fuses each pair into a single kernel (`mhc_fused_post_pre` and `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`). Every extra kernel launch on the decode critical path costs launch latency and cache/register thrash.
2. **Serial execution where overlap is possible.** ATOM forks auxiliary HIP streams to run compressor GEMMs (CSA pre-attention), SWA KV insertion (HCA), and the MoE router/shared experts concurrently with the main stream. vLLM executes all of these serially.
3. **Slower attention support kernels.** ATOM replaces the vLLM CSA top-k selection kernels and the post-attention batched GEMMs (`torch.mm` + `manual_unroll`) with dedicated optimized kernels (e.g., `batched_gemm_bf16_kernel`).

An earlier attempt at closing gap #2 — PR #51794, which enables three-stream overlap for CSA pre-attention — is currently a draft: the overlapped region itself is faster when there is no bubble, but some ranks see a much slower tail all-reduce due to inter-rank latency jitter. The un-optimized kernels running in the parallel streams contend for hardware resources and desynchronize ranks. This suggests the correct order of work is: **replace the kernels with ATOM's optimized versions first, then enable stream overlap on top of them.**

## Proposed Change

Port the ATOM-optimized decode path into vLLM's ROCm DeepSeek-V4 implementation, using the ATOM trace as the reference for each change. The work is organized per module:

### CSA:

- [x] **Fuse mHC kernels:** merge `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` into `mhc_fused_post_pre`, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` into `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`. #52737 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse SWA q/kv RMSNorm and q FP8 group quant:** #53540 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse main-compressor and indexer-compressor projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53838 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Pre-attention three-stream overlap:** Before the input GEMMs, fork three HIP streams: (1) **default stream**: fused wqa+wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert; (2) **aux stream 0**: main-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → compress kernels (compressed KV cache write); (3) **aux stream 1**: indexer-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → K-cache write. After the join, the indexer weights GEMM, the indexer q-side (wq_b + fused q RoPE+quant), the sparse indexer op (top-k selection), and the MLA attention run serially on the main stream. Each aux stream is a self-contained chain starting from `hidden_states`, so no fine-grained cross-stream dependencies are required. **This item stays disabled (draft) until the kernels in the parallel streams are replaced with ATOM's**.
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50866 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51794 @shen-shanshan 
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54571 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61378 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Support MXFP4 indexer:**
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56834 @LiuYinfeng01
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60834 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63669 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Remove MQA temporary fix:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55808 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Replace top-k kernels:** between `gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` and the core `sparse_attention`, replace the vLLM top-k implementation with ATOM's fused sparse-indexer kernels. #52882 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Support FP8 attention output projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54894 @LiuYinfeng01 

### HCA:

- [x] **Pre-attention two-stream overlap:** for `c128a` layers (which have no indexer), run the main KV compression concurrently with SWA token insertion on an auxiliary stream. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56853 @shen-shanshan 

### MoE:

- [x] **Router and shared-experts dual-stream overlap:** run the router computation concurrently with the shared experts on a second stream, then join before the routed experts. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56098 @mawong-amd 
- [x] Enable AITER heterogeneous fused MoE:
  - [x] TP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53161 @Fangzhou-Ai 
  - [ ] DP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54134 (not needed now, prefer to use dual-stream MoE for DP) @LiuYinfeng01
- [x] Enable mega MoE: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59685 @micah-wil

- [x] Prefill optimization:
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54855 @jiacao-amd  
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58405 @ZhengGong-amd

  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63002 @shen-shanshan
