title: [RFC] Adaptive spin grace + bounded arch waits (aarch64 WFET, x86 WAITPKG) for shm_broadcast
author: randomvariable
body:
## Problem

`SpinCondition` in `shm_broadcast.py` busy-loops with `sched_yield` for a
fixed grace period after each successful read before a reader transitions to
the poll/sleep path. Two problems follow:

1. The grace is a compile-time constant (`busy_loop_s=1` at
   `SpinCondition.__init__`). Real message cadence in serving varies over
   ~4 orders of magnitude (sub-ms during decode, multi-second when idle), so
   no single fixed value is right.
2. On aarch64, the optional `spinloop` native extension degrades to a plain
   `yield` busy-poll — the x86 path has MONITORX/MWAITX (AMD) but there is
   no aarch64 equivalent, and x86 Intel parts have WAITPKG
   (UMONITOR/UMWAIT) with no equivalent wired either.

The consequence on integrated CPU+GPU packages (e.g. DGX Spark-class GB10,
or any SoC where the CPU and GPU share a thermal/power envelope): during
idle-adjacent decode the mp executor's shm_broadcast readers pin performance
cores at 100% for the duration of the fixed grace on every poll cycle,
heating the SoC and stealing power/thermal headroom from the GPU. The same
class of issue applies to the writer side: `acquire_write` yields in a tight
loop while waiting for ALL readers to consume a block.

## Proposed change

Draft implementation: #52917

1. **Adaptive spin grace (readers and writers, Python).** Derive the spin
   grace from an exponential moving average of observed inter-event
   intervals: `grace = clamp(B*B/T_ema, MIN_GRACE, MAX_GRACE)` where `B` is
   a latency budget (default 1ms). The relation is chosen so that the
   pivot `grace == B` sits exactly at `T_ema == B`: traffic arriving at
   budget-rate spins for the budget, faster traffic spins longer (toward
   MAX), slower traffic parks sooner (toward MIN). Monotonically decreasing
   in `T_ema` — slower traffic never increases spin — and hard-bounded by
   MIN/MAX regardless of estimate staleness. Env tunables
   (`VLLM_SHM_BROADCAST_ADAPTIVE_*`) for budget/min/max/alpha; an explicit
   `busy_loop_s` pins a fixed grace for debug/opt-out.
2. **Bounded arch waits in the native fallback (C).**
   - aarch64: FEAT_WFxT (`WFET`) wait on an absolute CNTVCT deadline,
     runtime-gated on `HWCAP2_WFXT`, capped by remaining timeout and a
     50µs per-wait budget. Encoded via `.inst` so baseline armv8 builds
     are unchanged.
   - x86: Intel WAITPKG (`UMONITOR`/`UMWAIT`), runtime-gated on
     CPUID.7.EDX[5], Intel-only by design (AMD parts keep their existing
     MONITORX/MWAITX bounded wait from #36517; older Intel keeps
     `_mm_pause`). Encoded via `.byte` (SDM encodings) so assemblers
     without WAITPKG mnemonics still build.
   - Writer `acquire_write` parks in doubling steps (50µs→1ms cap) once
     its adaptive grace expires, instead of yielding indefinitely.

## Hardware coverage

Architecture facts: FEAT_WFxT was introduced in Armv8.7-A and is mandatory
only from Armv9.2-A; WAITPKG is Intel-only (AMD exposes MONITORX/MWAITX
instead — already wired). So:

- Cores implementing pre-8.7 architecture (Altra/Neoverse-N1,
  Graviton2-3's Ares/V1) cannot have FEAT_WFxT — they keep `yield`.
- Cores in the 8.7–9.1 window (e.g. Neoverse V2 in Grace/Graviton4,
  AmpereOne) MAY implement it; support is per-implementation, which is why
  the runtime `HWCAP2_WFXT` probe — not a hardware list — decides.
  Verified present on GB10 (Cortex-X925/A725).
- The adaptive grace works everywhere and is the load-bearing fix for
  fleet-wide idle CPU burn; the arch waits improve the power profile of
  the wait itself exactly where the probes fire.

## Alternatives

- Fixed lower grace (e.g. 2ms): helps idle, hurts burst wake latency — the
  inverse relation is the minimal fix that adapts to both regimes.
- Blocking waits only: removes spin cost but adds a poll-wake latency floor
  to every burst; the adaptive grace keeps the spin fast-path exactly when
  it pays.
- Per-process env tuning alone: doesn't change with phase; the EMA tracks
  it automatically with no config surface.

## Related

- #36517 added the spinloop ext (x86 AMD monitorx only).
- DPDK's `rte_wait_until_equal_*` WFE series is the same pattern for
  packet-processing polling loops.

title: [RFC]: Internal State Checkpoints for Mamba Align Mode
author: ZJY0516
body:
# [RFC]: Internal State Checkpoints for Mamba Align Mode

## Motivation.

`mamba_cache_mode="align"` stores recurrent states at reusable Mamba block boundaries. Today a state can only be committed at the end of a model forward, so a prefill that crosses its last reusable boundary must be split:

```text
forward [0, 7680)  -> cache state@7680
forward [7680, 8000) -> running state@8000
```

The second call repeats the full model only to obtain an intermediate recurrent state. A checkpoint-capable recurrent kernel can do both in one call:

```text
forward [0, 8000)
  -> checkpoint state@7680
  -> running state@8000
```

This RFC adds `support_internal_checkpoint` to `MambaSpec` and derives checkpoint states from the scheduled prefill range. The optimization is enabled only when support is explicitly declared; all other configurations keep the current split behavior.

## Examples

Notation:

```text
B       Mamba block size
CP@N    checkpoint after token N
RUN@N   private running state after token N
```

### Aligned prefill

For `B=4`, a six-token prefill can cross the reusable boundary at position 4 in one model forward:

```text
tokens       [0-------------4-----6)

forward      [0-------------------6)
state         ZERO ---> CP@4 ---> RUN@6
```

### Non-final chunk

For `B=4` and `prompt_len=20`, a scheduler chunk ending at 10 does not need to be clipped to 8:

```text
prompt       [0-----------------------------20)
chunk        [0-------------8-----10)
forward      [0-------------------10)
state         ZERO ---> CP@8 ---> RUN@10
```

### Chunk ending on a Mamba boundary

A chunk ending at 12 needs no internal checkpoint:

```text
chunk        [0-------------------12)
forward      [0-------------------12)
state         ZERO -------------> RUN@12
```

### Resume from an partial state

A request resuming from `state@6` can continue to 14 in one forward; it does not first stop at 8:

```text
chunk        [6------------12----14)
forward      [6------------------14)
state         state@6 --> CP@12 --> RUN@14
```

### Partial prefix caching

Assume `B=4`, `prefix_match_unit=2`, and `prompt_len=23`. A single prefill forward ending at 23 retains three states:

```text
state@20    last Mamba boundary
state@22    prompt's final prefix-match boundary
state@23    final running state
```

```text
forward [0, 23): ZERO --> CP@20 --> CP@22 --> RUN@23
```

`state@22` is retained only because the prompt ends at 23. An intermediate chunk ending at 23 for a longer prompt would not create this partial-cache entry.

### Orthogonality with speculative decoding

Internal checkpoints apply only to prefill rows. Speculative state allocation applies only to decode rows. A mixed batch keeps the two paths separate:

```text
prefill row P  --> prefill metadata --> CP@4, RUN@6
decode row D   --> spec metadata    --> D0, D1, D2
```

Neither path changes the other's position or ownership rules. Their memory requirements are only additive:

```text
total state pages = prefill state pages + speculative decode pages
```

EAGLE may already affect `cacheable_end` through existing prefill cacheability rules, but internal checkpoints add no EAGLE-specific scheduling or allocation logic.

## Proposed Change.

### 1. Capability in `MambaSpec`

Add the capability to `MambaSpec`:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MambaSpec(KVCacheSpec):
    ...
    support_internal_checkpoint: bool = False
```

The default is `False`. Internal checkpoints are enabled only if every `MambaSpec` across all cache groups and pipeline stages reports support. Otherwise vLLM uses the existing split path.

### 2. Scheduler behavior and checkpoint derivation

The scheduler still outputs only the scheduled token range. When every `MambaSpec` supports internal checkpoints, `_mamba_block_aligned_split` may let an eligible prefill cross its last reusable Mamba boundary instead of clipping there. No new `SchedulerOutput` field is needed.

The required state positions are determined by the existing cache policy:

```python
required_positions = {step_end}

mamba_boundary = (step_end // mamba_block_size) * mamba_block_size
if mamba_boundary > 0:
    required_positions.add(mamba_boundary)

if step_end == prompt_len:
    partial_tail = (prompt_len // prefix_match_unit) * prefix_match_unit
    if partial_tail < prompt_len:
        required_positions.add(partial_tail)

```

Positions that coincide are stored once. A partial-prefix state is retained only at the prompt's final prefix-match boundary; intermediate chunks do not create partial-cache entries. The metadata builder treats required positions strictly inside the query as checkpoints and `step_end` as the final state. Decode rows do not enter this path, so speculative decoding adds no checkpoint condition and requires no scheduler side channel.

Checkpoint positions come from existing Mamba and prefix-cache boundaries, which already satisfy the kernel chunk-size requirement. No separate checkpoint-alignment field is needed.

### 3. Block allocation

The KV cache manager allocates incrementally after the scheduler has chosen the current prefill chunk. It applies the cache-retention rule above and allocates one physical block for each required state that is not already backed:

```python
required_positions = get_required_mamba_state_positions(request, step_end)
num_new_blocks = count_unbacked(required_positions) + num_cow_blocks
```

For example:

```text
prompt_len=23, step_end=21 -> state@20, state@21
prompt_len=23, step_end=23 -> state@20, state@22, state@23
```

If a required state already exists from an earlier chunk, no new block is allocated for it. A shared block that must remain cacheable adds a copy-on-write block.

This calculation does not inspect `support_internal_checkpoint`. Without support, the scheduler reaches the positions through separate forwards; with support, one forward produces them together. The resulting block IDs use the existing request block-table update, so `SchedulerOutput` needs no new field.

`MambaSpec.max_memory_usage_bytes()` accounts for the maximum number of simultaneously resident states, but blocks are not eagerly allocated when the request arrives.

### 4. Testing

- Scheduler tests: supported and unsupported layers plus aligned and unaligned prefill starts.
- Cache-manager tests: prefill-page capacity, CoW, preemption, and ownership; existing speculative-page tests remain independent.
- Metadata tests: mixed rows and absolute-to-relative offset conversion.
- Kernel tests: compare one forward with checkpoints against sequential forwards at the same boundaries; check tokens, checkpoint states, and final state.
- Integration tests: one-forward prefill, partial hits, KV connectors, and mixed prefill/speculative batches.
- Model evaluation and performance results: output parity, TTFT, prompt throughput, memory, and forward count.


### Alternatives considered

**Add checkpoint positions to `SchedulerOutput`.** Rejected because they are uniquely determined by existing sequence lengths, query lengths, cache geometry, and row masks.

## Feedback Period.

Ten calendar days after posting. The main review questions are:

1. Is `MambaSpec` the right place to expose this capability?
2. Is deterministic worker-side derivation sufficient for every supported prefill path?
3. Is the worst-case additional align-mode state capacity acceptable in admission accounting?

## Any Other Things.

- [RFC #45702](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45702) covers partial cache hits and copy-on-write.
- [#50372](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50372) optimizes FlashInfer GDN final-state I/O but does not provide internal checkpoints.
- [#52789](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52789) Support internal prefill checkpoints for Mamba prefix caching


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Experimental Recirculation for causal decoder models
author: mihir-s-05
body:
## Motivation

[Recirculation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17981) improves a pretrained decoder without changing weights by norm-matching a deep residual-stream activation, mixing it into an earlier residual boundary, and rerunning the upper layers. The first pass supplies the current token's logits; the rerun overwrites its upper-layer KV entries so later tokens attend to the recirculated representation.

This RFC proposes experimental vLLM support for that execution pattern. A working implementation is available at [mihir-s-05/vllm@`e32222290`](https://github.com/mihir-s-05/vllm/commit/e3222229016064f47b47b43d2234bc56a0498923).

## Proposed change

### Configuration

Accept a validated `recirculation_config` through `--hf-overrides`:

```json
{
  "source_layer": 11,
  "destination_layer": 4,
  "alpha": 0.15,
  "beta": null,
  "ramp_tokens": 10,
  "wavefront": true
}
```

The parser is engine-level, validates the full grammar before deciding whether a configuration is an identity, and supports both ordinary `[tokens]` positions and text-token `[dimensions, tokens]` MRoPE positions.

### Model capability boundary

The scheduler, pending recurrent-state buffer, KV-slot remapping, and CUDA-graph specialization are shared engine features. Residual-decoder implementations opt in with a capability interface and a common decoder mixin. This prevents an unreviewed model subclass from inheriting support accidentally while allowing family-specific state snapshot/restore logic.

The current adapters cover:

- serial and wavefront: Gemma 3/4, Llama/Llama 4, Mistral/Mixtral, Qwen 2/3/3 MoE, GLM-4 MoE, MiniMax-M2, MiMo-V2, Step-3.5;
- serial only: DeepSeek V2/V3/V3.2, GLM-4.7-Flash, GPT-OSS, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3-Next, and Qwen 3.5 dense/MoE.

DeepSeek-V4 hyperconnections, multimodal wrappers, diffusion/non-causal backbones, pipeline parallelism, and Model Runner V2 are not enabled.

### Execution semantics

Serial execution runs the normal decoder stack, returns its final hidden state for logits, mixes the source and destination residuals, restores family-specific recurrent state where needed, and reruns layers above the destination. The rerun overwrites upper-layer KV state.

Wavefront execution preserves the same token dependency while batching the previous token's recurrent upper stack with the current token's normal upper stack. After a one-token warmup, each upper attention layer overwrites the previous token's KV entry before the current token consumes it. The current implementation limits this path to one sequence and one scheduled token, FlashAttention, no prefix caching, and no DP/DCP/SP/PP.

Prefill with a one-token threshold is exact tokenwise recurrence. Larger chunks are an explicit blockwise quality/throughput approximation.

### Recurrent and MoE families

MoE routing remains part of each rerun: Recirculation changes the residual entering the upper stack, so experts may be selected differently. No model-specific expert script is required.

Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 need an additional rule because their convolution/GDN states update in place. Their adapters snapshot active state slots before the normal upper pass and restore them before the recurrent rerun. They remain serial-only because the current two-token FlashAttention wavefront cannot represent those recurrent state transitions.

All speculative configurations, including EAGLE/DFlash auxiliary hidden-state extraction, are rejected initially. Supporting them requires an explicit definition for draft-token recurrence and auxiliary-state ownership.

## Validation

All results below were collected on an RTX 3080 10 GB after rebasing onto current `main`.

- Focused regression suites: 76 passed.
- Repository pre-commit stack passed, including Ruff, formatting, Markdown, mypy 3.10, import rules, SPDX, and CUDA API checks.
- No-download GPU matrix: all 20 documented families generated with four-layer BF16 dummy models through real attention/MoE/recurrent kernels.
- MRoPE ramping: Qwen 3.5 dense and MoE passed with `ramp_tokens=10`.
- Compiled Gemma 3 dummy comparison:
  - no-op was bit-identical to baseline;
  - serial and wavefront produced identical token IDs;
  - maximum serial/wavefront selected-token log-probability difference was `1.235e-4`.
- Real `google/gemma-3-1b-pt`, compiled BF16, the same 16 fixed C4 windows (16,368 scored tokens):
  - baseline perplexity 19.1576, mean prefill latency 7.9496 s;
  - wavefront perplexity 16.9613, mean prefill latency 8.4007 s;
  - 11.46% lower perplexity and 5.67% higher mean prefill latency on this small sample.

The branch contains the commands, harnesses, model/config revisions, window hashes, and a compact RTX 3080 result table. Dummy elapsed times are treated only as compatibility evidence because they include startup and JIT work.

## Alternatives considered

- **Gemma-only implementation.** Simpler initially, but duplicates identical residual-stack logic across families and cannot coordinate scheduling/KV semantics centrally.
- **Automatic support for every decoder subclass.** Rejected because recurrent state, hyperconnections, per-layer embeddings, and attention backends require explicit capability review.
- **Serial execution only.** Correct but leaves avoidable upper-stack launch/dispatch overhead; retained as the compatibility path while wavefront is opt-in.
- **Speculative decoding with undefined auxiliary semantics.** Rejected until recurrence over draft blocks and auxiliary hidden states is designed and tested.

## Feedback period

At least one week. The main questions are:

1. Is a model capability interface plus shared residual-decoder mixin the right abstraction boundary?
2. Should experimental Recirculation remain an `hf_overrides` feature or gain a first-class engine argument?
3. Are the initial restrictions appropriate for an experimental merge?
4. What additional real-weight model-family evidence should be required before broadening the opt-in list?

## AI assistance disclosure

OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, review fixes, regression harnesses, and benchmark analysis. The reported results were measured on the stated hardware, and the branch includes reproducible commands and tests.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched for relevant issues and pull requests using `recirculation`, `residual stream recurrence`, `looped transformer`, and `recurrent depth`; no duplicate proposal was found.
- [x] Reviewed the project documentation and contribution requirements.

title: [RFC]: V1/V2 Weight Reload with Streaming Quantization Units
author: new-TonyWang
body:
## Motivation.

vLLM weight reload currently has to bridge two different representations:

```text
checkpoint tensor
  -> model name mapping and TP/EP sharding
  -> fusion, padding, transpose, and layout conversion
  -> quantization or repack
  -> PWAL and derived state
  -> serving tensor
```

A received checkpoint tensor therefore cannot always be copied directly into the current runtime parameter. Runtime weights may already be fused, shuffled, packed for a backend, or accompanied by derived MLA/MoE state. CUDA Graphs and backend objects can also retain storage addresses, so reload must preserve parameter identity and `data_ptr()`.

The existing layerwise approach makes correctness depend on layer boundaries, tensor order, and element-count accounting. It also retains too much checkpoint-format data when online quantization waits for a whole layer or model, especially for MoE weights.

This RFC asks for feedback on a reload lifecycle with two explicit scopes and on a shard-aware quantization contract that releases temporary input as soon as the smallest independently quantizable unit is complete.

## Proposed Change.

### Lifecycle and invariants

Reload follows `drain -> update -> resume`; hot-swapping while requests execute is out of scope.

```text
START
  drain requests
  restore only shape-changing parameters to checkpoint shape
DATA*
  receive checkpoint-format shards
  call native model.load_weights()
  let param.weight_loader copy, transpose, repack, or quantize
FINISH
  run selective PWAL for restored shape-changing layers
  refresh derived state
  validate manifest coverage
  resume requests
```

The design preserves `data_ptr()`, reuses native model loaders and TP/EP routing, does not use layerwise meta rematerialization, and fails closed on unsupported dtype conversion or incomplete coverage.

### V1: matching dtype and checkpoint format

V1 assumes the sender provides the dtype and checkpoint format expected by serving:

- BF16 -> BF16 dense/MoE: direct native-loader copy;
- block FP8 -> block FP8: direct copy when scale/layout match;
- per-tensor FP8 dense: transpose/copy as required;
- per-tensor FP8 MoE: restore checkpoint shape, load, then run scale requantization, kernel shuffle, and derived-scale refresh;
- pre-quantized GPTQ/AWQ/Marlin: restore checkpoint shape, load checkpoint format, then repack;
- MLA: load base tensors and refresh `W_UK_T`, `W_UV`, or backend-specific quantized derivatives.

Shape-changing PWAL must use `resize_ + copy_` instead of replacing graph-visible storage.

### V2: online quantization

V2 keeps the same lifecycle but permanently attaches online quantization to parameter loaders during `create_weights`:

- BF16 -> block FP8, MXFP8/MXFP4, per-group, or per-channel formats can quantize each logical shard eagerly when the scale domain is contained in that shard;
- BF16 -> per-tensor FP8 for fused QKV or MoE w1/w3 retains only the shards sharing one serving scale, then requantizes and releases them as soon as coverage is complete;
- NVFP4 and other formats declare their smallest valid dependency closure through the quantization method;
- a serving quantization configuration without a matching online loader is rejected.

Pre-quantized checkpoints remain V1 paths; V2 is specifically for trainer-to-serving dtype conversion.

### Quantization units and sharded transport

A `QuantizationUnit` is the smallest set of logical shard keys whose scale domain and layout dependencies are complete. The quantization method declares unit keys, staged slots, and finalization; a shard-aware wrapper around the model's existing loader reports actual `(parameter, local expert, shard id)` arrivals. Completion uses key-set coverage, never tensor count, byte count, or transport-bucket boundaries.

Only cross-shard units allocate staging lazily. Per-block, per-group, per-channel, and non-fused per-tensor paths consume the received shard directly. Fused per-tensor paths retain unmatched shards, finalize immediately when their peers arrive, and release staging after the CUDA event completes.

Transport may send one sharding at a time and pack records across parameters, experts, or layers. Each record carries its logical unit identity and TP/EP/expert/shard coordinates. Backpressure is based on bytes retained by incomplete quantization units. A bucket is a communication unit; it is not a model-completion or quantization-completion boundary.

### Backend boundary and failure semantics

Fine-grained units are enabled only when the quantization backend can finalize them independently. Backends requiring layer-wide shuffle, padding, or conversion fall back to selective PWAL at `FINISH`.

Requests are drained, so eager in-place writes are not externally visible during the update. In-place updates do not provide rollback. If coverage, conversion, or finalization fails, the worker must not resume serving; the update must be completed or the worker reloaded/restarted. Preserving the old model after failure would require a full shadow copy and is outside this scope.

### Complete V1/V2 scenario matrix

| Scenario | Scope | Start | Receive (`weight_loader`) | Finish |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BF16 dense/MoE with a BF16 trainer | V1 | None | `copy_` | None |
| Block FP8 with an FP8 trainer | V1 | None | `copy_` | None |
| Per-tensor FP8 dense with an FP8 trainer | V1 | None | transpose + `copy_` | None |
| Per-tensor FP8 MoE with an FP8 trainer | V1 + PWAL | Restore checkpoint shape | Copy checkpoint-format values | Scale requantization, kernel shuffle, and `_g1_alphas` refresh |
| MLA models such as DeepSeek V2/V3/R1 and Kimi K3 | V1 + derived state | None | Copy `kv_b_proj` | Refresh `W_UK_T/W_UV`; MXFP4/FP8 backends use their corresponding re-quantization path |
| Pre-quantized INT4/Marlin checkpoint | V1 + PWAL | Restore checkpoint shape | Copy GPTQ/AWQ-format values | Marlin repack |
| Block FP8 serving with a BF16 trainer | V2 | None | Online loader performs per-block quantization + `copy_` | None |
| Per-tensor FP8 serving with a BF16 trainer | V2 | None | Online loader plus fused-parameter unit buffer | Finalize only unified-scale units not completed eagerly |
| NVFP4 serving with a BF16 trainer | V2 | Backend dependent | Online loader plus the smallest required closure buffer | Layout shuffle or derived-state refresh when required |
| BF16 trainer with low-precision serving but no online loader | Reject | None | Raise `ValueError` | None |

### Complete quantization-unit matrix

| Granularity/parameter | Smallest processing unit | Cross-shard buffer | Processing point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-block: Block FP8, MXFP4, MXFP8 | One logical shard, processing its internal blocks independently | No | Quantize when the shard arrives |
| Per-group: GPTQ/AWQ group | A logical shard containing complete groups | No | Convert or quantize when the shard arrives |
| Per-channel: INT8/SmoothQuant | A logical shard containing the complete row/column scale domain | No | Quantize when the shard arrives |
| Per-tensor FP8, non-fused parameter | Complete local tensor shard | No | Compute the local tensor scale and quantize on arrival |
| Per-tensor FP8 fused QKV | Q/K/V shards sharing one serving scale | Yes | Quantize after all paired shards arrive |
| Per-tensor FP8 fused MoE `w13` | One expert's w1, w3, and corresponding scales | Yes | Requantize with a unified scale after both halves arrive |
| MoE w2 | One expert's w2 and scale | No | Process the serving slice on arrival |
| Layer-wide activation scale | All expert/layer contributions covered by the scale | Yes | After the dependency set completes, usually at `FINISH` |
| MLA-derived `W_UK_T/W_UV` | One MLA layer with all base tensors updated | Not a transport buffer | `refresh_derived_state()` |

For the per-expert FP8 reference path, the quantization method declares these units:

| Unit | Required keys | Staged values | Finalize |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-tensor `w13[e]` | Expert e's w1/w3 weights and scales | `[2I, H]` weight and `[2]` scale | Requantize both halves with `max(s1, s3)` and write `w13[e]` |
| Block `w13[e]` | Expert e's w1/w3 weights and block scales | None | Checkpoint format is already serving format; the loader writes directly |
| `w2[e]` | Expert e's w2 weight and scale | None | The non-fused parameter is written directly |
| Static `input_scale` | Input scales from all experts | One scalar per expert | Take the layer-wide maximum at `FINISH` |

The quantization method exposes the unit keys, staged parameter specifications, and finalize callback. The loader wrapper maps global expert ids to local expert ids and reports `(parameter, local expert, shard id)` keys. For staged slots, the tracker lazily creates one checkpoint-format slab per `(parameter, local expert)` and exposes it through an expert-dimension broadcast proxy, allowing the original loader to keep its TP narrowing, expert indexing, padding, and fusion behavior. The quantization method declares the slab shape and dtype because runtime parameters may already have different shapes. Finalization deletes both slab and proxy immediately. Unit finalization shares the same quantization function as cold loading.

### Backend applicability

Fine-grained unit support is declared by the quantization method and backend, not inferred from dtype. Per-tensor FP8 MoE can finalize `w13` per expert for Triton and batched-Triton on non-FNUZ platforms. FlashInfer, Marlin, AITER, and DeepGEMM paths that require layer-wide shuffle, padding, or backend-owned conversion fall back to selective PWAL at `FINISH`. A backend must not advertise per-expert units if any serving-format value depends on data outside the unit.

### Relationship to existing RFCs and PRs

- #48312 defines the broader weight-reload correctness taxonomy. This RFC proposes a concrete V1/V2 lifecycle and quantization/transport design within that correctness space.
- #48920 proposes a shared `WeightLoadSession` across initial load and reload. This RFC is narrower: drained runtime weight reload, dtype/quantization routing, selective PWAL, and early quantization-unit release.
- #48478 defines graph-storage safety requirements; this RFC preserves storage and treats unsupported backend paths as fail-closed.
- Draft PR #51378 explores whole-model checkpoint-schema restoration. This RFC proposes a materially different lifecycle that restores only shape-changing parameters and avoids whole-model meta rematerialization.

Relevant open issues and PRs were searched before submission. The proposal is intended to consolidate the lifecycle and memory design discussion rather than duplicate the existing correctness trackers.

## CC List.

Maintainers and contributors working on RL weight transfer, model loading, online quantization, MoE backends, and CUDA Graph storage are invited to review.

## Any Other Things.

This RFC is documentation-first. Implementation should be split by scope and backend only after the contracts are agreed. A support claim requires cold-load equivalence, manifest/coverage failure tests, stable parameter identity and `data_ptr`, and relevant hardware validation.

AI assistance was used to audit the existing reload paths, analyze the design alternatives, and draft the RFC. I reviewed the proposal and am responsible for defending it end to end.

- [x] I searched existing RFCs and related issues before submitting this proposal.

title: [RFC]: A conformance suite for KV-cache key partitioning
author: Tejasvichand
body:
### Motivation.

Over the last five months, at least ten separate defects have been filed in which a dimension that must partition the KV cache keyspace failed to do so in some tier or on some path. Each was found independently, reported separately, and fixed locally. All ten are still open.

They are not ten bugs. They are one missing invariant, observed ten times.

| Dimension | Tier / path where it was dropped | Report | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cache_salt` | chunked embeddings preprocessing | — | #47696 |
| `cache_salt` | Harmony tool turns (Responses API) | — | #51818 |
| `cache_salt` | HF3FS external cache keys | — | #51748 |
| `cache_salt` | LMCache free / lock path | #44096 | #44097 |
| `cache_salt` | LMCache MP fallback adapter | #40040 | #40041 |
| `cache_salt` vs LoRA name | block-hash extra keys, no domain separation | #44701 | #44706 |
| LoRA identity | LMCache MP external key | #44250 | #45549 |
| LoRA version | prefix cache after same-name reload | #42125 | — |
| `prompt_embeds` content | LMCache external key | #42119 | — |
| `cache_salt` charset | vLLM / LMCache contract mismatch | — | #51444 |

The consequence is the same in almost every row: two requests that must not share KV blocks share them anyway, and the only external symptom is a cache hit that should have been a miss. #47696 and #51748 both describe cross-tenant reuse reachable from a normal API call.

**Why the existing tests do not catch it.** There is good coverage of this property — it is just all local. `tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py` asserts different salts miss at the `KVCacheManager` level, and five of the fixes above ship their own new test file: `test_harmony_continuation_cache_salt.py`, `test_hf3fs_connector.py`, `test_lmcache_mp_connector.py`, `test_lmcache_mp_fallback_adapter.py`, `test_cache_salt_validation.py`.

Each proves one path is correct today. None constrains the next path. The core test also constructs `Request` objects directly, so it begins after the plumbing that actually keeps breaking. Adding a sixth local test file alongside the next fix will not change the rate.

### Proposed Change.

State the invariant explicitly and back it with a parametrized conformance suite.

> If two requests differ in any dimension that is required to partition the KV cache keyspace, they must not reuse each other's blocks — in every cache tier the request touches, reached through every entrypoint that accepts that dimension.

Dimensions today: `cache_salt`, LoRA identity, LoRA version, `prompt_embeds` content. Tiers: in-engine block hash, external connectors (LMCache MP, HF3FS, native offload), and the lookup/free path. Entrypoints: chat completions, completions, responses (including multi-turn and tool turns), pooling and embeddings (including the chunked path), Anthropic messages.

The suite would be parametrized over `dimension x tier x entrypoint`, asserting from outside the engine — `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, or the prefix-cache counters — rather than from hand-built `Request` objects, so a value lost anywhere between HTTP and the hasher is caught.

One detail worth building in from the start: **every isolation assertion needs a matching positive control.** A test that only asserts "different salt, no reuse" passes when prefix caching is broken outright, and passes when the salt is plumbed nowhere and nothing ever hits. The paired assertion — same salt, reuse does occur — is what makes the negative meaningful. A cross-tenant hit and a same-tenant hit are indistinguishable from outside unless both are pinned.

Longer term the same invariant would be better served by a single shared key construction that every tier is required to call, so a new connector cannot re-derive keying by hand. That is a larger change and I am not proposing it here; the suite would at least make a violation loud.

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@dr75 @russellb

### Any Other Things.

I have been measuring prefix-cache timing isolation on v0.26.0 from the server-side `vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds` and `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` counters, which is how I ran into the positive-control problem above — an early run of mine was silently invalid because nothing proved the uncached arm was actually uncached.

Happy to write the suite if there is interest, and happy to scope it smaller first `cache_salt` across entrypoints only, if a full matrix is too much for one PR. Guidance on where it should live (`tests/v1/e2e/`, `tests/entrypoints/`, or a new `tests/v1/core/conformance/`) would help.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Opt-out control for individual startup kernel warmups
author: YongfengX
body:
### Motivation.

`kernel_warmup()` (vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py:98-215) runs a fixed warmup sequence from `Worker.compile_or_warm_up_model` (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:728), just before CUDA graph capture. Per the module docstring (kernel_warmup.py:3-7) the sequence exists for JIT'ed kernels. Some entries are already individually controllable — `VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip` (:162-166), `kernel_config.enable_cutedsl_warmup` (:149), `kernel_config.enable_flashinfer_autotune` (:176-183) — and `kernel_config.enable_jit_warmup` (:110) is an all-or-nothing gate for the registry. But the set is ad hoc, and some entries have no switch at all: `qwen_triton_warmup` (:126) sits outside every gate.

We maintain an out-of-tree hardware platform plugin for a non-CUDA accelerator, which redirects the GDN ops to an AOT-compiled kernel library. With no JIT to hide, the warmup is pure startup cost for us — and the dummy inputs upstream builds for the reference Triton kernels do not satisfy our AOT kernels' host-side argument validation. Concretely, `_warm_fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update_kernel` (vllm/model_executor/warmup/qwen_triton_warmup.py:203-241) builds `initial_state` as a rank-2 tensor (:216-220) and passes it at :235. The reference Triton path never notices, since it only reads `initial_state.stride(0)` (vllm/third_party/flash_linear_attention/ops/fused_sigmoid_gating.py:231) and forwards the tensor as a raw pointer (:253). Our kernel requires rank 4 and rejects it, so engine startup fails.


### Current workaround.

Our plugin monkeypatches the private `qwen_triton_warmup._warm_fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update_kernel` into a no-op. It depends on a private symbol and breaks on any upstream refactor, which is what prompted this RFC.


### Proposed Change.

One generic opt-out axis, rather than a new env var per warmup. Two sketches:

**A — named warmups + skip list.** Give each entry in `kernel_warmup()` a stable name and add e.g. `VLLM_SKIP_KERNEL_WARMUPS=qwen_triton,deep_gemm`. This mirrors `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS` (vllm/envs.py:1716-1724, consumed at kernel_warmup.py:218-234), which is already a comma-separated name skip list.

**B — platform hook.** `current_platform.get_skip_kernel_warmups() -> set[str]`, consumed where `KernelConfig.set_platform_defaults` (vllm/config/kernel.py:285-311) already calls `current_platform.get_default_ir_op_priority` (vllm/platforms/interface.py:1299). A platform knows whether its kernels are JIT or AOT, so a plugin can declare this itself instead of asking operators to set env vars.

The two compose: B supplies the default, A lets a user override it. Default behaviour is unchanged — an empty skip list or an unimplemented hook runs every warmup exactly as today. Purely additive and backward compatible.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Sleep Mode Tensor Ownership and Recovery
author: Ronald1995
body:
# Sleep Mode Tensor Ownership and Recovery

This RFC describes a correctness issue in the current sleep-mode allocation
boundaries and proposes ownership and recovery rules for tensors that outlive
model and KV-cache initialization. It is motivated by a similar issue found in
vLLM Ascend ([vllm-ascend PR #13352](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/13352)).

## Summary

vLLM sleep mode places model initialization and KV-cache initialization inside
tagged device memory pools. The allocator records a tag for each underlying
allocation, not the semantic role of every tensor backed by that allocation.
Consequently, every device tensor created while a tagged pool is active inherits
the sleep policy for that tag, even if the tensor is actually persistent runtime
metadata, a kernel constant, a synchronization buffer, or derived model state.

This is mostly benign for level-1 sleep and model weights because all allocations
tagged `weights` are copied to host memory. It is unsafe for allocations tagged
`kv_cache`, which are intentionally discarded. On wake-up, the same virtual
addresses are mapped to new physical memory, but discarded contents are not
restored. A CUDA graph can therefore replay successfully using stable pointers
while reading corrupted constants or indices.

Level-2 sleep has an additional variant of the problem. Parameters are expected
to be reloaded and registered model buffers are explicitly saved and restored,
but plain tensor attributes are neither reloaded nor restored. A level-2
sleep/wake/reload cycle can therefore leave model constants, kernel metadata, or
synchronization workspaces corrupted.

This RFC proposes:

1. Restrict the `kv_cache` memory-pool scope to actual discardable cache backing
   allocations.
2. Define explicit ownership and recovery requirements for every persistent
   device tensor.
3. Represent static model tensors as registered buffers or host/Python values,
   rebuild derived weights after reload, and explicitly reset stateful kernel
   workspaces.
4. Add deterministic remap poisoning tests so fresh zero-filled pages cannot
   hide missing recovery logic.

## Motivation

### Current allocation scopes

Model loading currently runs as one `weights` allocation scope in
[`GPUWorker.load_model`](../../vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py). KV-cache
initialization similarly runs as one `kv_cache` allocation scope:

```python
with self._maybe_get_memory_pool_context(tag="kv_cache"):
    self.model_runner.initialize_kv_cache(kv_cache_config)
```

`initialize_kv_cache` performs substantially more work than allocating KV-cache
storage. Depending on the model runner and backend, it can also construct:

- attention metadata builders;
- persistent block-table and scheduler metadata;
- speculative-decoding and adaptive-verification state;
- Mamba or GDN state-cache metadata;
- connector state;
- CUDA-graph-safe constants and index buffers.

Those objects survive initialization and are read on later model executions.
Their tensors nevertheless receive the `kv_cache` tag solely because of when
they were allocated.

### Allocator behavior

[`CuMemAllocator`](../../vllm/device_allocator/cumem.py) records each allocation
handle, its virtual address, and the allocator's current tag. Sleep behavior is
selected per allocation:

| Sleep mode | `weights` allocations | `kv_cache` allocations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level 1 | Copy to host, then unmap and release | Unmap and release without backup |
| Level 2 | Unmap and release without backup | Unmap and release without backup |

Wake-up recreates physical memory at the original virtual address. If an
allocation has a host backup, vLLM copies it back. Otherwise, the allocation has
valid storage and a stable address but no preserved contents.

The distinction between virtual-address stability and value preservation is
important for CUDA graphs. Stable addresses keep captured pointer arguments
valid; they do not restore a scale, index sequence, sentinel, or lock value at
that address.

### Observable failure

A minimal example is a persistent attention scale created in the KV-cache
scope:

```python
with allocator.use_memory_pool(tag="kv_cache"):
    kv_cache = torch.empty(cache_shape, device="cuda")
    scale = torch.tensor([3.0], device="cuda")
```

After level-1 sleep and wake-up:

- `kv_cache.data_ptr()` is unchanged and its old contents are intentionally
  gone;
- `scale.data_ptr()` is also unchanged;
- the value `3.0` is gone even though `scale` is not KV cache;
- a captured graph can replay without an invalid-pointer error but calculate a
  different result.

The likely manifestations depend on the tensor:

- zero or incorrect attention output from a corrupted scale;
- incorrect block lookup from a corrupted `arange` or block-table prefix;
- incorrect sparse-attention bounds or top-k selection;
- a hang or intermittent failure from a corrupted lock or synchronization
  sentinel;
- model-specific accuracy loss from a corrupted embedding or preprocessing
  constant.

## Why This Has Not Caused Widespread Accuracy Failures

Several existing properties limit exposure without making the ownership model
safe:

1. Level-1 sleep preserves every allocation tagged `weights`, including tensors
   that were accidentally included in the scope.
2. Actual KV-cache contents are intentionally disposable. Sleep aborts or drains
   requests and clears request-dependent caches before new work is accepted.
3. Most persistent attention metadata is a workspace that is fully overwritten
   for each batch before it is read.
4. Common configurations use backends that overwrite their metadata, while many
   confirmed nonzero constants occur in optional RSWA, sparse MLA, ROCm Aiter,
   XPU, or model-specific paths.
5. Fresh physical memory is commonly observed as zero-filled. This turns the
   problem into feature-specific deterministic corruption rather than arbitrary
   process-wide corruption, and can make zero-initialized workspaces appear
   correct by accident.
6. Existing wake-up hooks already repair FP8 KV-cache scales and MRV2 block-table
   layout tensors.
7. Current end-to-end sleep tests primarily use small dense-attention models and
   therefore do not exercise the affected metadata.

These factors explain the limited blast radius but are not correctness
guarantees.

## Confirmed Risk Inventory

The following inventory is based on a static scan of vLLM commit
`41f179b57aa8ab6f634f508128ce1f1efadd0eb1`. A tensor is listed as confirmed when
it is retained after its allocation scope and a consumer can read it without a
complete preceding rewrite.

### KV-cache scope

| Component | Persistent tensor | Failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static Sink Attention | fixed sink block IDs in `block_table_with_sink` | wrong cache blocks selected |
| FlashAttention R-SWA | `persistent_rswa_window_tensor` | wrong recurrent sliding-window bound |
| FlashMLA Sparse | `topk_tokens_tensor`, `max_model_len_tensor` | wrong sparse selection bounds |
| DSA indexer | `offsets_buffer`, `arange_buffer` | wrong decode expansion and padding indices |
| ROCm Aiter FlashAttention | `scale` | wrong K/V scaling |
| ROCm Aiter MLA | `paged_kv_last_page_len` initialized to ones | invalid page metadata |
| ROCm Aiter Sparse MLA | `max_model_len_tensor`, `qo_indptr`, `paged_kv_last_page_len` | invalid sparse decode metadata |
| XPU Sparse MLA | `topk_tokens_tensor`, `max_model_len_tensor` | wrong sparse selection bounds |

Examples can be found in:

- [`static_sink_attention.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/static_sink_attention.py)
- [`flash_attn.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py)
- [`flashmla_sparse.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashmla_sparse.py)
- [`indexer.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py)
- [`rocm_aiter_fa.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_aiter_fa.py)
- [`rocm_aiter_mla.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/rocm_aiter_mla.py)
- [`rocm_aiter_mla_sparse.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/rocm_aiter_mla_sparse.py)
- [`xpu_mla_sparse.py`](../../vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/xpu_mla_sparse.py)

Other attention, Mamba, input-batch, connector, and speculative-decoding
workspaces are conditionally risky. Most are currently overwritten before use,
but they depend on an implicit invariant that is not expressed by the allocator
or component interface. Out-of-tree backends and connectors can introduce the
same issue during registration or initialization.

### Weights scope and level-2 reload

The following classes retain plain device tensor attributes that are not
parameters or registered buffers:

- Gemma3n router and embedding scales;
- Conformer relative positional encodings;
- Voxtral mel filter banks;
- Ernie VL visual token ID tensors;
- OpenPangu's zero-valued sink tensor;
- TRT-LLM and FlashInfer MoE activation constants and fake scales;
- Cutlass MoE stride tensors;
- Humming kernel lock buffers;
- MiniMax Lamport all-reduce flags, layout metadata, negative-zero sentinels,
  and device pointer arrays.

Examples can be found in:

- [`gemma3n.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/models/gemma3n.py)
- [`conformer_encoder.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/models/conformer_encoder.py)
- [`voxtral.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/models/voxtral.py)
- [`ernie45_vl.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/models/ernie45_vl.py)
- [`openpangu.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/models/openpangu.py)
- [`fused_moe/experts`](../../vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts)
- [`humming.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/humming.py)
- [`lamport_workspace.py`](../../vllm/model_executor/layers/minimax_rms_norm/lamport_workspace.py)

Some derived DFlash weights are plain attributes but are already rebuilt by
model-specific `load_weights` hooks. They are not currently confirmed failures,
although their recovery contract should be made explicit and tested.

## Goals

1. Ensure that no persistent non-KV tensor is silently discarded by level-1
   sleep.
2. Make level-2 recovery requirements explicit for parameters, buffers, derived
   weights, kernel constants, and stateful workspaces.
3. Preserve CUDA-graph pointer stability where required.
4. Keep actual KV-cache and recurrent-state backing allocations discardable.
5. Provide a deterministic test mechanism that fails before missing recovery
   logic reaches an end-to-end model test.
6. Define a contract that also applies to out-of-tree attention backends,
   connectors, and hardware plugins.

## Non-Goals

1. Preserve active request KV-cache contents across sleep.
2. Make level-2 wake-up automatically reload model parameters. The caller still
   controls weight reload or replacement.
3. Persist CUDA state across process termination.
4. Change scheduler pause, abort, or drain semantics.
5. Guarantee that every scratch allocation is zeroed. Scratch buffers may remain
   uninitialized if their owner fully writes them before every read.

## Proposed Tensor Ownership Model

Every device tensor that survives initialization must belong to one of the
following classes.

| Ownership class | Sleep behavior | Recovery requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discardable cache backing | Unmap without backup | New requests must not read old contents |
| Model parameter | Level 1 host backup; level 2 discard | Reload before execution after level 2 |
| Static model buffer | Restore after both levels | Register as a model buffer or rematerialize from host/Python data |
| Derived weight | Rebuild after parameter reload | Explicit post-reload hook |
| Persistent runtime metadata | Keep outside discardable pool or restore in place | Explicit owner and wake hook |
| Scratch workspace | May be discarded | Complete write/reset before first read |
| Stateful synchronization workspace | Discard only with explicit reset | Restore sentinels, counters, layouts, and pointer arrays in place |

The classification is semantic and belongs to the component that owns the
tensor. Allocation time must not be used as a proxy for ownership.

### Required invariants

1. A tensor in a discardable allocation must either be discardable itself or be
   fully rewritten before its first post-wake read.
2. Recovery must be in place for tensors referenced by CUDA graphs. Replacing a
   Python tensor object after capture is not sufficient unless all captured
   graphs are rebuilt.
3. Level-2 parameter reload must be followed by rebuilding every derived tensor
   that snapshots or repacks those parameters.
4. Synchronization buffers must restore protocol-specific initial state, not
   merely zero memory.
5. Plugins that allocate persistent device tensors during KV registration must
   obey the same ownership contract.

## Proposed Design

### 1. Narrow the KV-cache allocation scope

Split KV-cache initialization into preparation, allocation, and binding phases:

```python
prepared = model_runner.prepare_kv_cache(kv_cache_config)

with worker._maybe_get_memory_pool_context(tag="kv_cache"):
    kv_cache_tensors = model_runner.allocate_kv_cache(prepared)

model_runner.bind_kv_cache(prepared, kv_cache_tensors)
```

Only actual cache backing allocations should occur in
`allocate_kv_cache`. Attention builders, block tables, connector objects,
speculator state, and fixed metadata should be constructed outside the pool.

The exact method split can differ between MRV1 and MRV2, but both must enforce
the same boundary. The existing KV-zero metadata initialization already follows
this principle by running outside the pool.

Small persistent metadata allocated outside the custom pool remains resident
during sleep. This is preferable for correctness and usually negligible beside
model and KV-cache storage. A future recoverable metadata tag can be introduced
if measurements show that this memory is material.

### 2. Add explicit component recovery hooks

Components that own state which must be reset after discarded storage is
remapped should implement a narrow lifecycle contract, for example:

```python
class SleepAwareTensorOwner(Protocol):
    def post_wake_up(self, discarded_tags: set[str]) -> None: ...

    def post_weights_reload(self) -> None: ...
```

The model runner should maintain an explicit registry of such owners rather
than discover them through arbitrary Python object traversal. Recovery order
must be deterministic:

1. remap selected allocator tags;
2. restore host-backed allocations and registered model buffers;
3. reload model parameters when requested by the caller;
4. rebuild derived weights;
5. reset persistent runtime and synchronization state;
6. permit scheduling and CUDA-graph replay.

This hook is a fallback for state that cannot be moved outside a discardable
pool. Narrowing the allocation scope remains the primary fix.

### 3. Use model buffers and host values for static model tensors

Static tensors owned by an `nn.Module` should use
`register_buffer(..., persistent=False)`. The current level-2 worker path saves
and restores `named_buffers`, including non-persistent state-dict buffers.

Scalar constants should remain Python values when kernels do not require a
device pointer. Small ID lists should remain host tuples or tensors and be
materialized on the destination device when needed.

Non-module kernel implementations should register persistent tensors on their
owning layer. Keeping the only reference on a quantization or kernel helper
object bypasses the existing model-buffer recovery path.

### 4. Rebuild derived weights after reload

Models and quantization methods that cache concatenated, stacked, repacked, or
otherwise derived tensors must expose an idempotent post-reload operation. This
operation must update captured storage in place or explicitly invalidate and
recapture CUDA graphs.

Existing model-specific behavior, such as DFlash fused KV-buffer rebuilding,
should be routed through the common lifecycle and covered by level-2 tests.

### 5. Reset synchronization state explicitly

Lock buffers and distributed workspaces require protocol-aware recovery.
Examples include:

- zeroing Humming locks;
- restoring Lamport negative-zero sentinels;
- resetting Lamport rotation counters;
- restoring layout constants;
- recreating device pointer arrays from current stable virtual addresses.

These operations must complete before any kernel or captured graph can consume
the workspace.

## Alternatives Considered

### Back up the entire KV-cache tag

This preserves accidentally tagged tensors but also copies the full KV cache to
host memory, defeating the memory and latency goals of level-1 sleep.

### Zero every discarded allocation on wake-up

Zeroing makes behavior deterministic but does not restore nonzero scales,
`arange` indices, top-k values, sentinels, or pointer arrays. It can also hide
missing ownership declarations for zero-initialized state.

### Add only backend-specific wake hooks

Hooks can repair the currently known tensors, but every new backend or connector
can reintroduce the issue. Hooks are useful for protocol state; they are not a
substitute for a correct allocation boundary.

### Introduce a third recoverable metadata tag

A `persistent_metadata` tag backed up at both sleep levels is viable for larger
metadata that should be reclaimed. It adds policy and allocation complexity,
and allocation-level tagging still requires clean scope boundaries. This RFC
therefore proposes pool exclusion first and leaves the additional tag as a
future optimization.

### Recapture every CUDA graph after wake-up

Recapture avoids stale pointer and value assumptions but significantly increases
wake latency and still does not define how eager execution state is restored.
It should be required only when a component cannot restore captured storage in
place.

## Test Strategy

### Deterministic remap poisoning

Tests must not assume that freshly mapped memory is nonzero. A test helper should
wrap `create_and_map`, fill every new mapping with a known byte such as `0xA5`,
and then allow the normal CPU-backup restoration to run:

```python
original = cumem.create_and_map

def create_map_and_poison(handle):
    original(handle)
    _, size, ptr, _ = handle
    cumem.libcudart.cudaMemset(ptr, 0xA5, size)
```

Host-backed weights are overwritten with their saved bytes after poisoning.
Discarded KV allocations retain the poison. A persistent tensor passes only if
it was outside the discarded allocation or its owner restored it.

The helper must be isolated in a fresh subprocess because `CuMemAllocator` is a
singleton and keeps allocator pools alive.

### Test 1: allocator ownership reproducer

Extend [`tests/basic_correctness/test_mem.py`](../../tests/basic_correctness/test_mem.py)
with a minimal allocation-level test:

1. allocate a known byte tensor under `weights`;
2. allocate a fake KV tensor and unrelated metadata tensor under `kv_cache`;
3. record all virtual addresses;
4. run level-1 sleep and poisoned wake-up;
5. assert that all addresses are stable;
6. assert that the weight is restored;
7. assert that both KV and unrelated metadata contain poison.

This test documents the allocator contract. It does not assert that the
allocator should infer tensor ownership.

### Test 2: CUDA-graph precision reproducer

Capture a graph that multiplies an input by a nonzero scale allocated in the
`kv_cache` pool. After poisoned sleep/wake, replay the graph and verify that:

- graph replay succeeds;
- the scale pointer is unchanged;
- the output is wrong before recovery;
- the output matches the reference after the owner's wake hook or after moving
  the scale outside the pool.

This is the smallest test demonstrating that pointer stability can turn a
memory-lifecycle bug into silent accuracy corruption.

### Test 3: level-2 recovery classification

Construct a toy module containing:

- one parameter;
- one `persistent=False` registered buffer;
- one plain tensor attribute.

Run poisoned level-2 sleep/wake, simulate parameter reload, and restore
`named_buffers`. Verify that the parameter and buffer recover while the plain
attribute remains poisoned. The permanent regression version should convert the
plain attribute to a buffer and require all three values to recover.

### Test 4: real backend regression

At least one CUDA backend test must instantiate an actual metadata builder in
the real initialization scope and verify values after sleep/wake. FlashMLA
Sparse is a suitable first target because
[`test_sparse_mla_backends.py`](../../tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py)
already has compact builder fixtures.

Platform-specific tests should then cover:

- FlashAttention R-SWA and Static Sink Attention on CUDA;
- ROCm Aiter FlashAttention and MLA metadata;
- XPU Sparse MLA metadata;
- DSA indexer offsets and padding indices.

Each test should check tensor contents or kernel output, not only shape and
allocation validity.

### Test 5: targeted end-to-end generation

The existing dense tiny-model sleep test remains useful but is insufficient.
Add end-to-end tests only where a small model exercises a confirmed affected
path. Compare deterministic tokens or logits before and after sleep, and include
multiple cycles to expose incomplete reset logic.

Model-affecting changes must also run the relevant evaluation suite described in
the contribution guidelines.

## Migration Plan

### Phase 1: establish deterministic failures

1. Add the poison helper and allocator contract test.
2. Add CUDA-graph scale and level-2 classification tests.
3. Add one real affected backend test that fails before the fix.

### Phase 2: correct allocation boundaries

1. Split MRV1 KV preparation, allocation, and binding.
2. Split MRV2 KV preparation, allocation, and binding.
3. Move attention builders, block tables, connectors, and fixed metadata outside
   the `kv_cache` pool.
4. Verify that only cache backing allocations carry the `kv_cache` tag.

### Phase 3: migrate persistent owners

1. Repair the confirmed KV-scope inventory.
2. Convert static model constants to buffers or host/Python values.
3. Register non-module kernel constants on owning modules.
4. standardize derived-weight rebuild hooks.
5. add Humming and Lamport protocol resets.

### Phase 4: enforce the contract

Add a debug-only allocation audit using `TorchDispatchMode` or equivalent
instrumentation during tagged scopes. Record tensor creation stacks with weak
references and report surviving tensors at scope exit. The report should include
the tag, size, allocation range, owner type, and creation location.

This audit should be available to backend and plugin authors without enabling it
in production by default.

## Compatibility and Performance

### CUDA graphs

Moving persistent metadata outside the discardable pool preserves its virtual
and physical storage across sleep, so existing captured pointers remain valid.
In-place recovery hooks preserve addresses for the remaining state. Components
that replace storage must explicitly invalidate captured graphs.

### Memory reclamation

Some small metadata allocations will remain resident during sleep. Their size
should be measured and reported separately from weights and cache backing. If
the retained memory is significant for a backend, that backend can use a future
recoverable metadata tag rather than the discardable KV tag.

### Fragmentation

Narrower scopes can change allocation grouping and fragmentation. Validation
must record peak model-load memory, available KV-cache memory, memory freed by
sleep, and wake latency before and after the change.

### Platform behavior

CUDA, ROCm, and XPU allocators differ in mapping and initialization behavior.
The ownership contract is platform-independent: discarded contents must never
be consumed without recovery. Poisoning tests should use the platform's memory
set operation and should not rely on observed zero-fill behavior.

### Out-of-tree components

Attention backends, connectors, and hardware plugins must not allocate
persistent metadata inside a callback documented as a discardable cache
allocation phase. If unavoidable, they must register a sleep-aware owner and
restore state in place.

## Open Questions

1. Should recoverable runtime metadata receive a dedicated allocator tag, or is
   keeping it resident sufficient for all supported configurations?
2. Should the sleep-aware lifecycle be a new protocol or an extension of the
   existing model-runner/backend interfaces?
3. Should level-2 wake-up reject execution until parameter reload and all
   post-reload hooks have completed?
4. How should plugins declare and validate persistent tensor ownership without
   exposing allocator internals?
5. Should the debug allocation audit become a CI mode for selected backend
   initialization tests?

## Acceptance Criteria

The proposal is complete when:

1. only discardable cache backing allocations receive the `kv_cache` tag;
2. all confirmed persistent constants survive or are restored after poisoned
   level-1 sleep/wake;
3. all registered buffers, derived weights, locks, and synchronization state
   satisfy their level-2 recovery contract;
4. CUDA graphs produce the same result before and after sleep/wake;
5. targeted CUDA, ROCm, and XPU tests cover their affected backends;
6. sleep memory reclamation and wake latency do not regress materially;
7. backend and plugin documentation states the persistent tensor ownership
   requirements.




## Implementation PR series (MRV2-only scope change)

The implementation from #53344 has been split into five focused PRs. The KV-cache allocation-scope change is intentionally limited to Model Runner V2; this series does not change the MRV1 model-runner implementation.

| PR | Scope | Dependency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #53508 | Restrict the MRV2 `kv_cache` pool to cache backing allocations and add deterministic allocation/CUDA Graph reproducers | Independent |
| #53507 | Register static model-owned runtime tensors as non-persistent buffers | Independent |
| #53509 | Register and rebind derived modular-MoE runtime buffers after layerwise weight reload | Independent; foundation for #53510 |
| #53510 | Reset Humming reload state, rebind locks, and reset locks after wake-up | Depends on #53509 |
| #53511 | Reset MiniMax Lamport workspace protocol state in place after wake-up | Depends on #53510, transitively #53509 |

Dependency graph:

```text
#53508  (independent)
#53507  (independent)
#53509
  └── #53510
        └── #53511
```

Recommended merge order:

1. #53508 and #53507 can merge independently in any order.
2. Merge #53509.
3. Merge #53510 after #53509.
4. Merge #53511 after #53510.

The original combined implementation PR #53344 is superseded by this series.

title: [RFC]: Optimization: Take over a partial-hit block instead of CoW copy when ref_cnt == 1
author: THUqliu
body:
### Motivation.

In `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py`, when a request has a partial block hit in the KV cache, the cache manager always performs the following operations:
1. Increments the reference count of the partial block by 1.
2. Allocates a new block.
3. Copies the content from the partial block into the newly allocated block.

If the cache manager checks the reference count of the partial block and finds that `ref == 1`, it indicates that no other requests are using this block and no new tokens will be appended to it. In this case, the partial block can be safely reassigned to the current request directly.

This optimization would:
- **Reduce block allocations**: Eliminate the need to allocate one new block per partial-hit request.
- **Eliminate redundant copies**: Avoid the memory copy operation from the partial block to the new block.


### Proposed Change.

I propose the following change:
In allocate_new_blocks(), before triggering CoW for a partial-hit block, we first check the partial block's ref_cnt == 1. If true, the block has no other related requests and will receive no future token appends. We can skip the new block allocation and the pending copy. Because source partial block has been added in req_to_block in function add_local_computed_blocks(), if no other requests use the partial block, we can just assign it to current request.

Current behavior:
```
if request_id in self._partial_hit_reqs:
    block_idx, source_block = self._partial_hit_reqs.pop(request_id)
    cow_block = self.block_pool.get_new_blocks(1)[0]
    self._apply_cow(request_id, block_idx, source_block, cow_block)
    self.new_block_ids.append(cow_block.block_id)
    cow_blocks.append(cow_block)
```

Proposed：
```
if request_id in self._partial_hit_reqs:
    block_idx, source_block = self._partial_hit_reqs.pop(request_id)
    if source_block.ref_cnt == 1:
     #This partial block is exclusively used by the current request and will not receive new tokens from others, we can directly assign it to the current           #request without copying
        pass
    else:
        cow_block = self.block_pool.get_new_blocks(1)[0]
        self._apply_cow(request_id, block_idx, source_block, cow_block)
        self.new_block_ids.append(cow_block.block_id)
        cow_blocks.append(cow_block)
```

I have a working prototype and am running benchmarks to validate the improvement. Feedback and reviews are welcome.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Experimental Recirculation for causal decoders
author: mihir-s-05
body:
### Motivation.

[Recirculation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17981) is an inference-time method
that changes a pretrained causal decoder's effective depth without changing
its weights. A normal pass produces logits and a deep residual-stream state.
That state is norm-matched, mixed into an earlier residual boundary, and the
upper stack is run again. The rerun overwrites upper-layer KV entries so later
tokens attend to the recirculated representation.

The design question for vLLM is broader than adding a branch to one model's
`forward`: cache ownership, scheduler behavior, CUDA-graph shapes, model
capability negotiation, and recurrent state must agree on the same semantics.
This RFC asks whether vLLM wants that behavior as an experimental engine
feature with explicit model-family opt-in.

This proposal supersedes author-closed RFC #53178. That issue was closed before
feedback and received no maintainer comments; it should not be interpreted as
either approval or rejection. This proposal narrows the initial code review to
the core engine and Gemma 3, with other model families reviewed separately.

### Proposed Change.

### Algorithm and cache invariant

For destination layer `d` and source layer `s`, where
`0 <= d < s < num_hidden_layers`, one scheduled token block executes as:

```text
normal pass: layers 0 ... d ... s ... N
                  |       |
                  |       +-- source residual
                  +---------- destination residual

mix: norm_match(source, destination) * alpha + destination * beta

rerun: mixed residual -> layers d+1 ... N
```

The normal pass's final hidden state supplies logits. The rerun replaces the
block's upper-layer cache state; lower-layer cache entries are unchanged. A
one-token block implements tokenwise Recirculation. Larger prefill blocks are
an explicit blockwise approximation: their logits come from the normal pass,
and their recirculated cache affects later blocks.

### Experimental configuration and capability boundary

The initial implementation accepts a validated dictionary through
`--hf-overrides`, avoiding a stable public CLI contract while the feature is
experimental:

```json
{
  "recirculation_config": {
    "source_layer": 11,
    "destination_layer": 4,
    "alpha": 0.15,
    "beta": null,
    "ramp_tokens": 10,
    "wavefront": true
  }
}
```

Validation covers unknown or missing fields, layer ordering, coefficient
ranges, identity configurations, ramping, and both ordinary and MRoPE token
positions. An open question is whether maintainers prefer a first-class
configuration object before merge.

Engine code detects an explicit `SupportsRecirculation` capability. Models opt
in through a shared residual-decoder mixin and declare the modes they support;
unreviewed subclasses and wrappers fail closed. Families may override layer
execution, residual materialization, finalization, or non-KV state handling
without duplicating the scheduler and cache protocol.

### Execution paths

The serial compatibility path runs the normal stack, records the source and
destination boundaries, returns the normal final state for logits, and reruns
the upper stack from the mixed residual. Ordinary attention KV entries are
overwritten at the same token positions. Hybrid recurrent models must instead
snapshot and restore affected convolutional or recurrent state before the
rerun.

An optional two-token wavefront batches the previous token's recirculated
upper pass with the current token's normal upper pass after a one-token warmup:

```text
row 0: previous token's recirculated upper pass
row 1: current token's normal upper pass
```

At every upper attention layer, row 0 first replaces the previous token's KV
entry and row 1 then consumes the same effective cache as serial execution.
The engine owns the pending residual, positions, attention metadata, remapped
slot mappings, and a dedicated two-row upper-stack CUDA graph.

The first wavefront implementation is limited to one sequence, one scheduled
token, FlashAttention, and no prefix caching or distributed parallel modes.
Other compatible configurations use the serial path.

### Safety boundary

The initial implementation targets Model Runner V1 and rejects explicit V2
selection. It also rejects speculative decoding and auxiliary hidden-state
extraction, pipeline parallelism, non-causal or diffusion backbones,
DeepSeek-V4 hyperconnection state, unreviewed wrappers, and parallel modes
whose state ownership has not been defined. Speculative decoding would need a
separate definition of which pass owns draft blocks, cache writes, and
auxiliary states.

MoE routing is recomputed during the upper rerun. A mixed residual may select
different experts; the proposal does not replay fixed routing decisions.

### Staged rollout

Implementation is split into dependent, scoped PRs:

1. Core engine/configuration and Gemma 3.
2. Ordinary residual dense and MoE adapters.
3. DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM DSA adapters.
4. Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 recurrent-state adapters.
5. MiniMax-M3 sparse-attention adapters.
6. Kimi Linear and reviewed wrapper delegation.

Each family opts in only after its residual, cache, and non-KV state semantics
are reviewed and tested; support is not inferred from model configuration.
Kimi-K3 AttnRes is excluded because its residual-bank mapping requires a
separate design decision.

Serial Recirculation intentionally adds upper-stack compute and cache writes.
Wavefront execution reduces dispatch overhead, not mathematical work. No
universal quality or performance claim is proposed: each adapter must provide
correctness tests and appropriate real-model evidence.

### Feedback Period.

Fourteen calendar days, with no code PR until a maintainer indicates that the
core direction is worth reviewing. Main questions:

1. Is explicit capability negotiation plus a shared residual-decoder mixin the
   right boundary?
2. Should Llama and Mistral accompany Gemma 3 in the core PR or follow it?
3. Is V1-only experimental support acceptable, or should this wait for V2?
4. Are the wavefront invariant and initial restrictions convincing?
5. Should configuration use `hf_overrides` or a first-class interface?
6. What real-model evidence should be required for later adapter classes?

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

- Paper: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17981>
- Superseded author-closed RFC: #53178
- Superseded author-closed draft PR: #53179

The local prototype has exercised baseline, identity, serial, and wavefront
generation on an RTX 3080 using dummy weights through eager and compiled engine
paths, FlashAttention 2, CUDA graphs, and slot mapping. A cached Gemma 3 1B
sanity check over 1,020 scored tokens measured compiled perplexity `36.9618`
for baseline, `32.5482` for serial, and `32.2460` for wavefront. This was a
small fixed sample, not a standardized benchmark, and must be rerun on the
final rebased PR head.

Core acceptance requires parser and mixing tests, adapter cache/state tests,
serial/wavefront equivalence tests, direct runner and slot-mapping coverage,
and at least one real-weight comparison on the final PR head. Large Kimi,
MiniMax-M3, GLM-5, and similar checkpoints have not received local real-weight
validation; synthetic tests are not a substitute, so those follow-up PRs need
fresh model evidence or maintainer-approved provider validation.

### AI assistance disclosure

OpenAI Codex provided non-trivial assistance with implementation, code review,
test development, local validation, branch decomposition, and this RFC draft.
The human submitter remains responsible for reviewing, understanding, and
defending every proposed change and reported result.
