title: [RFC]: First-Class, Orchestrator-Agnostic KV Hint Envelope for Agentic Workloads
author: karen-sy
body:
> [!NOTE]
Please review alongside companion PR #53423 .
> 

## Motivation
RFC #51428   proposes a router-initiated “KvHint” surface as a first-class construct for e2e programmatic KV management between vLLM and an orchestrator (such as Dynamo). This RFC proposes a concrete implementation of this hint protocol, such that it is extensible, expressive, and durable: the protocol is compatible with various orchestrators, enables semantics-free expression of various types of hints (e.g. fetch, share, …), and guarantees durability via typing and versioning.

Today, integrations (such as [Dynamo PR #13134](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13134)) prototype vLLM KV hints via indirect, untyped plumbings, such as `SamplingParams.extra_args` and `kv_transfer_params`. KvHints instead provides a typed, versioned request contract within vLLM which can be accessed by routers, schedulers, cache managers, and KV connectors:
```
Router / control plane
  -> KvHintsEnvelope
  -> vLLM request ingress
  -> EngineCoreRequest.kv_hints
  -> Request.kv_hints
  -> scheduler-visible metadata
```

## Proposed API
### Canonical Types
The canonical transport types – `KvHintsEnvelope`, `KvHintAction` – should be broadly accessible and live outside any specific cache manager or connector:
```
vllm/v1/kv_hints/
  __init__.py
  protocol.py

KvHintsEnvelope
KvHintAction
```

### Typed Envelope Contents
A `KvHintsEnvelope` requires:
1. A `protocol_version`
2. A `message_id`
3. A list of `KvHintAction` objects 

Each `KvHintAction` contains:
1. `action_id`
2. `action_version`
3. `action_type`
4. An action-specific JSON payload

The envelope and action fields are typed. The payload remains opaque to the transport layer and is validated by the vLLM component implementing that action type. Action-specific payload types should be introduced with their implementations.


## Example of a KvHintsEnvelope
The following uses `kv.fetch` to illustrate the envelope. (Defining the kv.fetch payload or semantics is out of this RFC's scope; future vLLM feature work should define the scheduling / G1<->G2 mechanisms.)
```
# a KVHintsEnvelope for the fetch KvHintAction 
{
  "protocol_version": "0.1",
  "message_id": "msg-123",
  "actions": [
    {
      "action_id": "a1",
      "action_type": "kv.fetch",
      "action_version": "1.0",
      "payload": {...}
    }
  ]
}
```
> [!NOTE]
> This RFC does not define a closed set of `action_type` values. Each action type, including its payload schema, validation, and execution semantics, should be introduced with its implementation; `kv.fetch` above is illustrative only. See #51428 for a few possible examples of KV hints and their semantics.
>

## Additional Durability Guarantees
1. Envelope and action versions evolve independently. 
2. Required schema changes bump the relevant version; optional additions and new action types do not require an envelope-version bump.
3. Every V1 request-construction path should pass either a `KvHintsEnvelope` or `None`. Requests without hints retain existing behavior. Orchestrators, such as Dynamo, construct or deserialize the canonical envelope at vLLM ingress.
4. Future vLLM components implementing an action (e.g. scheduler, connector) should skip unsupported action versions or invalid payloads without preventing other supported actions in the envelope from being processed. Raw ingress adapters should reject unsupported envelope versions.

## KvHints Propagation 
KvHints are request metadata, not sampling parameters. They should be available explicitly throughout the V1 request path:

```
Schema:
  vllm/v1/kv_hints/protocol.py
    - KvHintsEnvelope
    - KvHintAction
```
Then, as the orchestrator and vLLM execute policy-driven KV management, these KvHints become the clean transport layer:
```
Runtime propagation:
  Dynamo policy produces implementation-specific hints
    -> orchestrator-side vLLM adapter constructs KvHintsEnvelope
    -> vLLM request ingress receives KvHintsEnvelope
    -> AsyncLLM.generate(kv_hints=...) or equivalent
    -> InputProcessor.process_inputs
    -> EngineCoreRequest.kv_hints
    -> Request.kv_hints
    -> scheduler-visible metadata

(Future work should implement additional propagation steps for hint execution:
  scheduler -> KVCacheManager / KV connector(s) for G1 and G2+)
```

## Related Work
#### vLLM - Agentic KV management
- **The aforementioned [main RFC (#51428)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/51428) defines the broader KV orchestration policy and execution model which contextualizes this RFC work**
- [vLLM #48048](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48048) - merged first-class session_id request plumbing.
- [vLLM #51381](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51381) - open session_id tagging on GPU KV events.
- [RFC #52113](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52113) is concurrent work which proposes an application-facing `agent_hint` schema and possible execution mechanisms. Future adapters may lower such `agent_hint` fields into the generalized `KvHintsEnvelope` protocol.

#### Dynamo - Agentic KV management
- [Dynamo PR #11695](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/11695) initial prototype of router → vLLM Kv Hints. Does not yet use first-class KV hint construct; see [Dynamo #13134](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13134) below.
- [Dynamo PR #13134](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13134) prototypes the router-side typed contract for KvHints and integration path. This is fully consistent with the KvHint API introduced in this RFC (though it will be updated to use the vLLM `KvHintsEnvelope` instead of `SamplingParams.extra_args["kv_transfer_params"]["kv_hint"] `once our PR lands.)
- [vLLM PR #53624](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53624) Dynamo team's KVCR is an example consumer of this KvHint protocol.

title: [Rust Frontend][RFC] Add Qwen3-ASR WebSocket `/v1/realtime`
author: TanNgocDo
body:
Part of the Rust frontend parity roadmap in #44280.

## Motivation

The Rust frontend does not implement the Python speech-to-text WebSocket
`/v1/realtime` API tracked in #44280. This issue tracks a Qwen3-ASR-first
implementation over the existing EngineCore streaming-input protocol.

## Scope

- WebSocket `/v1/realtime` taking base64 PCM16, 16 kHz, mono audio.
- One resumable engine request per transcription turn, streaming
  `transcription.delta` and one terminal `transcription.done`.
- Qwen3-ASR through a model-specific adapter. Voxtral and unknown model
  families fail closed; Voxtral needs its own frame construction, waveform
  positioning, and token-feedback policy, so it is a follow-up.
- Auth exactly as Python has it: the existing optional Bearer check on upgrade,
  enforced only when `--api-key` or `VLLM_API_KEY` is set.

## Design summary

Three reusable seams land before the endpoint:

1. Resumable open, continuation, finish, and abort in the engine client,
   wrapped by the LLM facade ([#53454](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53454)).
   A session ends once the closing sentinel has been sent and every submitted
   segment has stopped, counted client-side as one `finish_reason` per segment
   — the bookkeeping `OutputProcessor.process_outputs` does with
   `input_chunk_queue`. `EngineCoreOutputs.finished_requests` cannot serve as
   that signal: engines populate it only under data-parallel internal load
   balancing, so a single-engine server never sends it for a normal finish.
2. A sample-native audio entry point reusing chat multimodal preprocessing
   without a WAV round-trip.
3. WebSocket upgrade support in the server lifecycle.

**PR 4** then lands the protocol, socket actor, audio buffering, Qwen adapter,
Bearer check on upgrade, connection limits, graceful drain, metrics, and
integration tests as one unit, because a route without that hardening is not
safe to expose.

## PR series

- [x] [#53454](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53454) — Resumable streaming sessions in engine-core-client and Llm facade
- [ ] Sample-native realtime audio preprocessing
- [ ] WebSocket upgrades in the Rust server lifecycle
- [ ] Qwen3-ASR `/v1/realtime` (after the above)

Each PR says `Part of #<this issue>`; only the final endpoint PR may close this
issue. Roadmap #44280 stays open.

## Validation

### Resumable sessions (engine-core client + llm facade)

- Mock-engine resumable coverage where the mock reports only segment stops and
  never `finished_requests`.
- Both completion orderings: last stop after the sentinel, and sentinel after
  the last stop.
- Existing one-shot client behavior unchanged.
- `GenerateRequest.resumable` reaches the wire; `Llm::generate_streaming` /
  `SegmentSink` integration tests pass.

### Endpoint (closes this issue)

- Disconnect/abort, connection-cap, and shutdown-drain tests.
- WebSocket upgrades over plain TCP and TLS.
- With an API key configured, an upgrade without a valid Bearer returns 401
  before accept; without one, the endpoint is open.
- A real Qwen3-ASR engine accepts the Rust prompt and `mm_features`.
- Recorded-stream transcript, delta boundaries, and `transcription.done`
  cadence match Python.
- Time to first delta within 1.1× Python p50 on the same fixture and hardware.

## Non-goals

- Reimplementing EngineCore streaming-input scheduling.
- Realtime text or speech generation.
- Voxtral parity through Qwen-shaped segmentation or preprocessing.
- Auth mechanisms Python lacks (subprotocol tokens, query-string tokens,
  post-connect auth).

## Related material

- Roadmap: #44280
- Python reference: `vllm/entrypoints/speech_to_text/realtime/`
- Docs: `docs/serving/online_serving/speech_to_text.md#realtime-api`

title: [RFC]: Generalize Connector Metrics
author: Srinivasoo7
body:
### Motivation.

`KVConnectorBase_V1.build_prom_metrics()` (`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/base.py:703`) is already a generic extension point any KV connector (NIXL, Mooncake, MoRIIO, the offloading connector, etc.) can implement it to register and update its own Prometheus metrics. But the base class it returns, `KVConnectorPromMetrics` (`kv_connector/v1/metrics.py:109`), gives almost nothing beyond a constructor: `observe()` is `raise NotImplementedError`, so every connector that wants Prometheus metrics has to hand-write Gauge/Counter/Histogram creation, per-engine labeling, and update logic from scratch.

The offloading connector already solved this once. `vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py` defines `OffloadingMetricMetadata` / `OffloadingCounterMetadata` / `OffloadingGaugeMetadata` / `OffloadingHistogramMetadata`, declarative metric definitions consumed by a shared registration path and `get_connector_metric_definitions()` (`kv_offload/tiering/offloading/metrics.py`) plus `build_metric_definitions()` hooks on every tier and policy (used directly by #51240's admission policies, and by my own metrics PRs #45957/#47666/#47679/#48798) build on it. It works well and is now used across multiple sub-components of one connector. Nothing about the pattern is offload-specific, it's just declarative Prometheus registration, but it's currently namespaced and located as if it were.

I checked whether other connectors duplicate this: `nixl_connector.py` doesn't implement `build_prom_metrics()` at all today, i.e. it has no Prometheus metrics of its own — it would be a natural next adopter, and would otherwise have to reinvent the same declarative pattern rather than reuse it, purely because the reusable version currently lives under `kv_offload`.

### Proposed Change.

### 1. Move the declarative metric-metadata types to the connector-agnostic module

Relocate `OffloadingMetricMetadata` and its `Counter`/`Gauge`/`Histogram` subclasses from `vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py` into `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py`, renamed to drop the offload-specific prefix (e.g. `PromCounterMetadata`, `PromGaugeMetadata`, `PromHistogramMetadata`), alongside `KVConnectorPromMetrics`. Keep `Offloading*` as thin deprecated aliases in `kv_offload/base.py` for one release to avoid a breaking import change for any out-of-tree tier/policy implementations.

### 2. Give `KVConnectorPromMetrics` a default, metadata-driven `observe()`

Add a `build_metric_definitions() -> dict[str, PromMetricMetadata]` hook to `KVConnectorPromMetrics` (mirroring the one `SecondaryTierManager` and `TieringAdmissionPolicy` already have), and implement a default `observe()` that registers each declared metric on init and updates it from the stats payload by name, exactly the mechanism the offloading connector's registration path already does. Connectors that need genuinely custom recording logic can still override `observe()` directly, same as today; this only removes the boilerplate for the common case (which is every current offloading sub-component, and would be the common case for any future connector metrics too).

### 3. Migrate the offloading connector to be the reference consumer, not a special case

Update `get_connector_metric_definitions()` and the tiering `build_metric_definitions()` hooks to use the relocated, renamed types. This is a rename/relocate, not a behavior change, Prometheus metric names, label semantics, and aggregation (counter=sum, gauge=latest, histogram=accumulate) stay identical, so no dashboards or alerts on existing `vllm:kv_offload_*` metric names break.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@markmc @orozery 

### Any Other Things.

Scope: this is a refactor/generalization of existing, working machinery, not a new metrics system. It deliberately does not try to solve #39979's broader OTel/per-request tracing ask (different problem: that RFC is about request-level tracing granularity, this one is about connector-level Prometheus registration boilerplate) or #51639's generic control RPC (orthogonal transport concern). Filing this separately rather than folding it into either avoids scope creep on RFCs that are already large.

Risk: relocating types out of `kv_offload/base.py` touches an import path used by every existing tier and policy implementation (`fs`, `obj`, `p2p`, `admission/*`), so the deprecated-alias period matters — this should land as a pure rename PR before any new connector adopts the generalized path, to keep the diff reviewable.

title: [RFC]: Reconcile Backpressure Admission
author: Srinivasoo7
body:
### Motivation.

Two open RFCs currently propose overlapping mechanisms for the same problem a secondary offloading tier becoming slow/saturated and the system needing to react:

- **#50031** (Back-pressure detection for KV cache offloading tiers, @bnellnm): Phase 1 proposes detecting tier saturation via an EMA of *store completion rate*, with high/low water marks, and responding by silently dropping cascade stores to the pressured tier. Metrics: a per-tier back-pressure gauge and a dropped-store counter.
- **#51240** (Tiering Admission Policy Design, @orozery): defines a `TieringAdmissionPolicy` interface and ships `CascadeBackpressurePolicy`, which detects saturation via an EMA of *submission-to-completion wall-clock latency*, with the same high/low water-mark hysteresis pattern, and responds by rejecting (`should_admit` → `False`) cascade jobs to the pressured tier before they're submitted.

These are the same mechanism EMA-based tier saturation detection with hysteresis, gating cascade stores built on two different signals (throughput vs. latency) and two different integration points (manual check inside the cascade path vs. a policy hook that's already wired into `create_store_job()`). #51240 is newer, already has an implementation, and reuses the metrics infrastructure from #48798 (`TieringMetricsTracker`, `OffloadingGaugeMetadata`). Left unreconciled, #50031's Phase 1 will either land as a second, parallel back-pressure mechanism, or someone will have to redo it as a `TieringAdmissionPolicy` anyway duplicated review and implementation effort on both sides.

This RFC proposes closing that gap explicitly, and since #51240 only covers Phase 1 of #50031's scope extends the `TieringAdmissionPolicy` framework to also cover #50031's stated Phase 2/3 concerns (load-vs-store prioritization, multi-tier bottleneck avoidance), which #51240 does not yet address.

### Proposed Change.

### 1. Reconcile detection signal

Adopt `CascadeBackpressurePolicy`'s wall-clock latency EMA (submission → completion) as the canonical signal, since it captures queue wait time in addition to raw transfer time a tier with a deep backlog but fast individual transfers is still "under pressure" from the scheduler's point of view, which #50031's throughput-only EMA would miss. Retain #50031's exact metric names (`back-pressure gauge`, `dropped-store counter`) as the public Prometheus surface, but wire them through `CascadeBackpressurePolicy.build_metric_definitions()` (already the extension point #51240 defines) rather than a separate manual instrumentation path.

Concretely: `CascadeBackpressurePolicy` publishes
- `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_backpressure_active{tier}` (gauge, already proposed)
- `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_cascades_dropped{tier}` (counter, already proposed at the manager level in #51240 the two just need to be confirmed as the same counter #50031 asked for)

### 2. Cover #50031's Phase 2/3 scope as additional `TieringAdmissionPolicy` implementations

#50031 explicitly scopes back-pressure *response* beyond store-dropping:

- **Load/store prioritization under contention** not a `should_admit` decision (loads aren't gated by `CascadeBackpressurePolicy` today; only cascades and promotions are). Propose a `LoadPriorityPolicy` that isn't an admission gate at all, but a job-ordering hook consulted by the tier manager's submission queue a new, narrower interface (`order_pending(jobs) -> jobs`) alongside `TieringAdmissionPolicy`, since prioritization and admission are logically distinct decisions (this RFC's main open question see below).
- **Saturated-tier-as-bottleneck when multiple secondary tiers are configured** (#50031's failure mode 3: CPU blocks pinned until the *slowest* tier completes) this is a `CompositePolicy` composition question, not a new mechanism: `CascadeBackpressurePolicy` already gates cascades per-tier, so the CPU-blocking-until-slowest-tier problem is really about pin/release semantics in the manager (already flagged in #51240 as "Pin Lifecycle (Manager, not Policy)"), not the policy layer. Propose scoping pin release to only the *admitted* tiers for a given block, so a store rejected by `should_admit` for tier B doesn't hold the CPU pin waiting on tier B.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@orozery @bnellnm @varun-sundar-rabindranath @tlrmchlsmth @rajkiranjoshi


### Any Other Things.

Open question: should load prioritization live in a new `TieringLoadOrderingPolicy` interface (kept separate from `TieringAdmissionPolicy` since it reorders rather than rejects), or should `TieringAdmissionPolicy` grow an optional `priority(job) -> int` hook used only by loads? Leaning toward a separate interface, conflating "should this run" with "in what order should these run" makes `CompositePolicy` composition ambiguous (what does AND-ing two priority functions mean?)

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Secondary Tier Usage Metrics
author: Srinivasoo7
body:
### Motivation.

#43763 asks whether `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` will support disk/SSD tiers. The answer is: a different, newer connector already does `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/manager.py` (`FileSystemTierManager`) is a working disk-backed secondary tier, and `obj/manager.py` covers object storage, both integrated into the same `TieringOffloadingManager` used for CPU-primary offloading. That issue can be closed with a pointer to the existing tiering framework rather than treated as unimplemented.

But looking at what those secondary tiers actually expose today surfaces a real, unaddressed gap. `TieringMetricsTracker` (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/metrics.py`, from #48798) tracks per-tier read/write bytes, transfer time, failures, and active promotion/cascade counts but there is no per-tier **capacity/usage** signal. The primary (CPU) tier has one `PRIMARY_WRITE_USAGE_PERC` / `PRIMARY_READ_USAGE_PERC` gauges (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/base.py`) built in #47666. Secondary tiers have none. `FileSystemTierManager` in particular has no capacity or quota accounting at all; it writes to `root_dir` with no size bound and no way to know how full it is.

This matters more than a missing metric: #51240's `TieringAdmissionPolicy` framework is designed to gate stores/promotions on tier state, but today the only signal available to an admission policy is latency (`CascadeBackpressurePolicy`'s EMA) there is no way to write an admission policy that says "stop cascading to disk, it's 95% full," because no component tracks that. Disk/object tiers are also the ones most likely to actually fill up in practice (unlike CPU DRAM, which is bounded by `num_primary_blocks` and already tracked).

### Proposed Change.

### 1. Capacity accounting per secondary tier

Add an optional `capacity_bytes` config to `SecondaryTierManager` (default `None` = unbounded, preserving current behavior for tiers like shared network storage where "capacity" isn't meaningful). When set, each tier implementation is responsible for tracking bytes written under management for `FileSystemTierManager` this means accounting during `submit_store`'s existing eviction path (the docstring at `SecondaryTierManager.submit_store` already documents "evicting blocks if capacity is needed," so the eviction logic exists; it just isn't instrumented).

### 2. Usage gauge, following the existing primary-tier pattern exactly

Add to `TieringMetricsTracker`, mirroring `PRIMARY_WRITE_USAGE_PERC`:

```
vllm:kv_offload_tiering_secondary_usage_perc{tier}
```

Published via each tier's existing `build_metric_definitions()` / `get_stats()` hooks (`SecondaryTierManager`, `base.py:328-334`) no new extension point needed, this is exactly the mechanism #51240 already uses for policy-specific metrics. Tiers without capacity accounting configured simply don't register the gauge, rather than emitting a meaningless value.

### 3. Feed it to admission policies

Once the gauge exists, add a `SecondaryTierCapacityPolicy(TieringAdmissionPolicy)` (same file layout #51240 proposes: `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/admission/capacity.py`) that rejects cascades to a tier once usage crosses a high-water mark, composable via `CompositePolicy` alongside `CascadeBackpressurePolicy`. This is the piece that makes disk/object tiers safe to enable without risk of silently filling the underlying volume.

### 4. Close #43763

Comment linking to the `fs`/`obj` tier managers as the existing answer, and reference this RFC as the follow-up for making them production-safe (capacity visibility was the real gap, not disk support itself).

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@orozery @ivanium

### Any Other Things.

Scope check: this RFC only adds accounting + a gauge + one admission policy. It does not propose an eviction policy for secondary tiers (LRU/LFU on disk) that's a larger design question (does eviction differ per tier type? is it delegated entirely to the tier implementation, as it partially is today?) better left to a separate RFC if the usage gauge surfaces a real need for it.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: SM90 Exact Fused DSA Prefill Indexer
author: fxfxfxfxfxfxfxfx
body: ### Motivation. We propose an optional SM90 backend for vLLM's `SparseAttnIndexer` prefill path. It computes FP8 scores and exact TopK in one CUDA kernel without materializing the full score tensor or intermediate candidates in HBM. The first implementation PR targets only the H64, D=128, topk=2048, single-GPU FP8 prefill path used by DeepSeek V3.2. The existing path remains the default. H32 support will follow in a separate PR. The current vLLM prefill indexer follows this high-level flow: ```text gather K -> fp8_fp4_mqa_logits -> materialize logits -> top_k_per_row_prefill ``` At long context lengths, writing and reading the full logits tensor and the extra kernel boundary become significant. In our current H20 matrix, the `H=1M, B=32, Q=512` case has a 508.25 MiB peak score chunk and materializes 64.03 GiB of scores over one indexer call, while the final TopK index output is 128 MiB. The goal is to replace only the score + TopK stage and eliminate full-score HBM materialization without changing downstream Sparse MLA attention. ### Proposed Change. #### Scope and integration The new backend plugs into the existing `sparse_attn_indexer()` prefill branch: ```text existing Q quantization, KV-cache insert, and chunk metadata | v cp_gather_indexer_k_quant_cache | v SM90 fused score + exact TopK | v existing topk_indices_buffer ``` The first PR is intentionally limited to: - SM90a, validated separately on H20, H800, and H100; - the DeepSeek V3.2 FP8 prefill path; - H64, D=128, and topk=2048; - single-GPU execution without DCP or PCP; - INT32 output shaped `[M, 2048]`, with unspecified order. Decode, KV-cache layout, K gather, and Sparse MLA attention remain unchanged. The proposed configuration is: ```python attention_config.indexer_prefill_backend = "default" | "sm90_exact" ``` `default` preserves the existing vLLM implementation. `sm90_exact` explicitly enables the experimental backend. Selecting `sm90_exact` reports a clear initialization error when GPU, dtype, H/D/topk, DCP/PCP, or shared-memory requirements are not met. Rows shorter than topk use the existing short-sequence path and `-1` sentinel rule. A row exactly equal to topk returns all valid indices without reading Q/K. DCP is excluded because the current DCP merge consumes both local TopK scores and indices, while this kernel outputs indices only. #### Kernel design The current H64 kernel uses a one-query-per-CTA pipeline: ```text TMA K/K-scale double buffer -> 4 WGMMA math warp groups (256 keys/round) -> generation-tagged shared-memory score ring -> FP32 ordered-bit histogram/radix cutoff -> running Top-2048 and final indices ``` The main implementation parameters are: - 768 threads per CTA; - four WGMMA math warp groups; - two TMA stages; - 12,544 scores per selection group and two ring slots; - 704 threads participating in the final drain; - 80 registers per thread; - 232,448 bytes of dynamic shared memory and 1,024 bytes of static shared memory; - zero stack and local-memory usage in the production cubin. Shared-memory usage gives one CTA per SM on H20. H20, H800, and H100 share one SM90a source, while eligibility and performance are validated separately on each device instead of maintaining SKU-specific implementations. The prototype uses runtime NVCC for iteration speed. The upstream version will retain only the selected production variant and use vLLM's static CUDA build, with no first-request JIT compilation. #### Exactness contract `exact` means that the selector computes an exact cutoff for the FP32 scores produced by the fused kernel. For a valid interval, let `c` be its 2048th-largest score. A valid output must: - contain 2048 unique indices from the valid interval; - include every index with `score > c`; - include no index with `score < c`; - fill the remaining positions from indices with `score == c`. Output order and the specific choice among cutoff ties are unstable and are not part of the API contract. This matches unordered TopK set semantics. The score expression is arithmetically equivalent to the current FP8 indexer, but WGMMA and DeepGEMM may use different floating-point reduction orders. Validation must therefore separate selector exactness relative to the fused scores from numerical error and model outputs relative to the latest vLLM backend. This RFC does not claim bitwise equivalence between those score producers. #### Related work - **Current vLLM:** materializes full logits in HBM before TopK and serves as the current baseline. - **[#52696](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52696):** materializes FP16 logits and uses native FP16 TopK, reducing the size of the logits tensor without removing its HBM round trip. - **[#48726](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48726) and the [LiteTopK paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11976):** target SM100 with tcgen05 and online candidate filtering, and also include LiteDSA attention work. - **This proposal:** targets SM90 with TMA/WGMMA, keeps scores on chip, performs exact cutoff selection, and changes only the prefill indexer. This proposal has a different architecture, selector, and submission scope from #48726, so it should be reviewed as an independent backend rather than appended to that PR. #### Preliminary results The following preliminary operator-level results use one NVIDIA H20 with synthetic FP8 inputs and fixed H64, D=128, and topk=2048. The benchmark matrix contains 665 shapes: - history KV lengths: 4K, 6K, 8K, 12K, 16K, 24K, 32K, 48K, 64K, 96K, 128K, 192K, 256K, 384K, 512K, 640K, 768K, 896K, and 1M; - batch sizes: 1, 4, 16, 32, and 128; - query lengths: 8, 64, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, and 8192. The vLLM baseline is vLLM 0.27.1's `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` with FP32 scores, followed by `top_k_per_row_prefill`. Both paths use the same shapes and mathematical boundaries, but were measured in independent runs. The following speedups are preliminary operator-level comparisons, not paired regression results. Current results: - 1.3918981x geometric-mean speedup over vLLM 0.27.1 FP32 DeepGEMM + TopK across all 665 shapes; - faster than vLLM in 604 of 665 shapes; - 58 of 58 current correctness cases passed; - zero sampled DeepGEMM cutoff deficit. The figure shows four representative shapes covering `B=1/32`, `Q=512/8192`, and 4K--1M history. The 1.3918981x value is calculated from the complete 665-shape matrix, not inferred from these four curves. These results only justify upstream evaluation. The baseline is still vLLM 0.27.1's FP32 synthetic operator path, and the vLLM and fused-kernel results come from independent runs. Latest-main, H800/H100, real-model, CUDA Graph, and end-to-end TTFT validation are still pending. #### Compatibility and scope PR 1 excludes decode, H32, DCP/PCP, FP4/MXFP4, LiteDSA attention, and experimental selector variants. It does not change the default backend or introduce a new KV-cache format. H32 changes the Q layout, WGMMA epilogue, shared-memory budget, and thread-role balance. It will be submitted separately for GLM-5.1/5.2 after the interface and validation method are established. #### Test plan Before requesting implementation review, the PR will provide: - a cutoff oracle built from a test-only fused-score output, requiring 100% TopK set equality for unique scores and the contract above for ties; - random and real-model inputs, all-equal and cutoff-dense scores, extreme gates, ragged and unaligned rows, `0/K`, and multiple ring generations; - custom-op schema, FakeTensor, output mutation, CUDA Graph, multiple streams, dispatcher error/bypass, and compute-sanitizer coverage; - paired H20, H800, and H100 comparisons against latest main's default path, a forced FP32 path, and #52696 if still relevant; - separate reporting for score+TopK latency, full indexer latency, peak HBM, and end-to-end TTFT; - real DeepSeek V3.2 prefill, MRCR/NIAH, and standard accuracy tasks. We propose an implementation evidence floor of at least 1.10x indexer-stage geometric-mean speedup over the target validation matrix and at least 3% TTFT improvement in two long-context configurations. #### Implementation plan 1. **PR 1: H64 / DeepSeek V3.2.** Production H64 kernel, static CUDA build, custom op, prefill dispatcher, tests, and benchmarks only. 2. **PR 2: H32 / GLM-5.1/5.2.** Reuse the reviewed interface and test contract, with separate tuning and validation. Before submission, we will remove experimental selector branches, retain one production implementation, and add SPDX headers, MIT provenance, source commits, and a human-review record. #### Core request for comments We would like maintainer feedback on one decision: **would vLLM accept the H64 SM90 fused prefill indexer first as an opt-in experimental backend, with H32 in a separate PR after the interface and validation method are established?** ### Feedback Period. one week. ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. AI assistance was used for investigation, implementation experiments, and RFC drafting. The human submitter will review the RFC, code, and test results before requesting maintainer review. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
speedup_claims: 10x indexer-stage geometric-mean speedup over the target validation matrix and at least 3% TTFT improvement in two long-context configurations

title: [RFC]: Apply MoE weight transformations at disk streaming time instead of materializing raw tensor
author: wjabbour
body:
### Motivation.

Quantized MoE model weight loading is two phases today:

1) **load**: streamed from disk -> VRAM
2) **convert**: reshape the weights and re-write to VRAM

For this brief period, memory utilization will peak as both weight matrices are resident.

Current flow, one expert's weight, start to finish:

1) Tensor streamed from disk and TP-sharded straight into its VRAM parameter slot — [`RoutedExperts._load_w13`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6a9c69fa851389dcf1ee5d3a2363e27af665d26d/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/routed_experts.py#L477)
2) Once all experts have streamed in, the oracle picks a backend for this layer — [`select_wna16_moe_backend`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6a9c69fa851389dcf1ee5d3a2363e27af665d26d/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/int_wna16.py#L199)
3) `process_weights_after_loading` hands the *entire* `(E, ...)` tensor to the oracle for conversion — [`CompressedTensorsWNA16MoEMethod.process_weights_after_loading`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6a9c69fa851389dcf1ee5d3a2363e27af665d26d/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/compressed_tensors/compressed_tensors_moe/compressed_tensors_moe_wna16.py#L507-L515)
4) Backend-specific quantization remapping + `.contiguous()` materializes the converted copy — e.g. the TRITON path's transpose/repack — [`convert_to_wna16_moe_kernel_format`, TRITON branch](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6a9c69fa851389dcf1ee5d3a2363e27af665d26d/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/int_wna16.py#L1657-L1663)

Step 1 is already per-expert and memory-conscious. Steps 3-4 run once, on the whole `(E, ...)` tensor, only after every expert has finished step 1 — that's where the transient peak comes from.

### Proposed Change.

Since the expert weight transformations performed for these different backends typically operate independently per expert tensor, these expert tensors could be transformed at disk streaming time — running steps 3-4 per-expert, immediately after that expert finishes step 1, instead of once on the whole tensor at the end. This reduces peak startup memory utilization.

## Goals
- TP-sharding is unaffected: sharding happens before conversion.
- No change to the resulting kernel-facing tensor layout.

## Rollout
`moe_weight_conversion_strategy={bulk,streamed}`, default `bulk`.

A similar pattern to the `safetensors-load-strategy` knob:

```
vllm serve <model> --safetensors-load-strategy=eager
```

Same pattern proposed here: `--moe-weight-conversion-strategy={bulk,streamed}`, opt-in initially, defaulting to today's `bulk` behavior.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Happy to take this on if you think it would be helpful

title: [RFC]: Decouple draft-model parallelism from the target model (PCP/DCP + speculative decoding)
author: LucasWilkinson
body:
## Motivation

vLLM supports context parallelism for the target model (PCP, #25749, and DCP), but speculative decoding currently assumes the drafter uses the same parallel mapping as the target. Two in-flight PRs take different approaches to PCP + MTP:

- #53427 (@pisceskkk) keeps the target PCP-sharded but runs a fully replicated drafter on every PCP rank over the global batch. This is simple and works for any drafter with no PCP awareness, at the cost of repeating long-prefill draft compute and KV writes on every rank.
- #53653 (@GirasoleY) keeps the MTP draft prefill PCP-sharded, restoring global order only at sampling boundaries. This performs better on long prefills and supports the GLM-5.2 sparse-MLA path, but each speculative method needs its own PCP adaptation.

We probably want both eventually:

1. A drafter that hasn't implemented PCP/DCP (ngram, DSpark, EAGLE, suffix decoding, new methods) should still work when the target uses context parallelism, by consuming the global batch.
2. A drafter that has a sharded implementation (MTP today) should run sharded and skip the redundant compute.

The same question comes up for DCP: e.g. Kimi K3 (MLA, so DCP makes sense for the target) paired with a GQA draft model. There it probably makes sense to disable DCP for the draft model, since GQA already shards KV heads across TP and DCP would just add latency.

We already let the draft model diverge from the target config in some places: `draft_tensor_parallel_size` (draft TP=1 under target TP=N), and the per-draft `moe_backend` / `attention_backend` overrides in `SpeculativeConfig`. This RFC proposes generalizing that into a separate drafter parallel config so we don't accumulate ad-hoc per-method special cases in the model runner.

## Proposed Change

Give the draft model its own parallel config instead of implicitly inheriting the target's: `SpeculativeConfig` grows a `draft_parallel_config` (subsuming the existing `draft_tensor_parallel_size` field), where each parallelism size is initially restricted to 1 or the target's value. Defaults are per-method (e.g. MTP inherits the target's PCP size; methods without a sharded implementation default to 1) and can be overridden via `--speculative-config`. A drafter validates the config it is handed at startup and fails with a clear error if it can't execute it.

Note this does not mean different process groups or rank placement. The drafter still runs on the same ranks as the target; a draft size of 1 just means that group is treated as replication for the drafter, the same way draft TP=1 under target TP=N works today. No new distributed groups are needed.

## Alternatives considered

- Replicated-only (#53427 alone): simplest and works for every method, but gives up long-prefill draft perf and scales draft KV memory with CP size.
- Sharded-only (#53653 alone): best perf where implemented, but every drafter has to be individually adapted to PCP before it works at all, so new and niche speculative methods would silently lose CP support.
- Arbitrary drafter parallelism (any TP/CP/EP per draft model with its own process groups and rank placement): much bigger change to distributed init and scheduling, and nothing on the table needs it. The proposed config keeps the drafter on the target's ranks and restricts each size to 1 or the target's value, and we can relax this later if a use case shows up.

## Open questions

1. CUDA graph support: #53427 validates PIECEWISE (with #53515); #53653 currently requires eager. What do we commit to for each path, and should supported graph modes depend on the drafter parallel config?
2. Should the global-vs-sharded choice ever be dynamic (e.g. global for short-prefill batches, sharded for long), or is a static per-run choice enough?
3. Sparse-MLA indexer: #53653 distinguishes PCP-expanded target slot mappings from replicated-draft mappings. Does that distinction belong in the attention backend interface or the PCP manager?
4. Does the scheduler need to know the drafter's effective CP degree for token budgeting, or can this stay contained in the runner?

## Feedback Period

~2 weeks.

## CC

@pisceskkk @GirasoleY @LucasWilkinson

## Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues and PRs (#25749, #53427, #53653, #53515).

title: [RFC]: Allow the DSA Indexer to Use Context Parallelism Independently
author: fxfxfxfxfxfxfxfx
body: ### Motivation. > **RFC scope.** This RFC requests architectural feedback on allowing the DSA Indexer and Sparse MLA to use different parallel contexts. It does not propose a complete scheduling policy or optimized cross-rank communication system. The first implementation would exercise this capability only through a fixed Indexer-CP configuration while preserving the existing Sparse MLA execution path and today's default behavior. DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) has two sequential stages: 1. The Indexer scans the history-wide index cache and selects global Top-K token positions. 2. Sparse MLA reads only those positions from the latent KV cache. vLLM currently derives both stages' parallel rank, group, and world size from the same Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) configuration. Enabling DCP for the Indexer therefore also enables it for Sparse MLA. The two stages do not benefit equally from this coupling. The Indexer scans a compact cache over the full history, so its work grows with history length and can be divided across ranks. Sparse MLA reads a fixed Top-K from a much larger latent KV cache, so using more ranks adds partial-output/LSE merging and consumes ranks that could otherwise serve independent requests. Our preliminary operator benchmarks on 2x NVIDIA H20 report CP2 latency speedup as `T(DCP=1) / T(DCP=2)`. Each panel fixes batch size and query length; the x-axis is history length. The Indexer obtains substantially higher CP2 speedup than Sparse MLA across most long-context `Q>1` shapes, while both stages regress at `Q=1` because communication and launch overheads dominate. *Figure 1. CP2 latency speedup on 2x NVIDIA H20. Teal is the Indexer; red is Sparse MLA using the same BF16 KV precision across TP1 and CP2. A value above 1.0 is a latency improvement, and 2.0 is ideal linear scaling. `Q=1` denotes decode. The anomalous Indexer regions in this figure use paired random-input TP1/CP2 reruns.* The proposed path therefore initially targets only long-context `Q>1` execution. This RFC asks vLLM to stop requiring the DSA Indexer and Sparse MLA to use the same parallel context. It intentionally proposes only one concrete new mode: > Run the Indexer with a fixed CP group, then run Sparse MLA locally on the request-owning data-parallel rank. The key observation is: > DSA turns attention into a small dense read over the index cache followed by a large sparse read over the latent KV cache. The two reads should not be required to use the same parallel group. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. Remove the shared-group assumption `SparseAttnIndexer` and sparse MLA backends should receive separate internal parallel contexts. The exact type should align with the ongoing [Per-Layer Parallelism Policy RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42659), but the sparse-attention interface must not assume that these values are equal: ```text indexer_parallel_context sparse_mla_parallel_context ``` For all existing configurations, both contexts resolve to today's DCP group. This keeps current behavior unchanged. This RFC does not propose a general per-state placement framework. It only leaves an explicit extension point so that a DSA backend can select a different group for its Indexer. #### 2. Implement one fixed Indexer-CP mode The first opt-in implementation uses a fixed single-node topology: - Attention is deployed with data-parallel request ownership. - Each request has one owner rank. - The owner stores the request's full latent KV cache. - The request's compact Indexer cache is sharded across a fixed Indexer CP group. - The owner sends the Indexer query to that group. - Each helper computes local Top-K candidates. - The candidates are merged and the global Top-K indices are returned to the owner. - The owner executes Sparse MLA locally without Sparse MLA CP. ```text request owner fixed Indexer CP group | | |--------- query + metadata ---------->| | | local index scans |<----------- global Top-K ------------| | | local Sparse MLA over owner-local latent KV ``` Only query metadata, new Indexer keys, and Top-K candidates cross ranks. The large latent KV cache is not migrated or repartitioned at the stage boundary. The implementation may initially use existing NCCL/PyTorch communication. It must use groups created during initialization, preserve global token indices, and handle empty helper work. An optimized transport is not required by this RFC. #### 3. Limit initial routing and fallback The new path is selected only when all of the following are true: - The model uses the supported DSA Indexer and sparse MLA backend. - Execution is single-node with a supported fixed group. - Query length is greater than one. - The request's latent KV cache fits on its owner rank. Otherwise, vLLM uses the existing local or coupled-DCP path. Unsupported configurations must fail clearly after the new mode is explicitly selected; they must not silently use an inconsistent cache layout. #### Non-goals The first RFC and implementation do not include: - Dynamic CP degree selection. - Per-request rank resizing. - A goodput-aware scheduler. - Latent-KV migration or dynamic request-owner migration. - Multi-node execution. - A new generic collective or DeepEP-like communication backend. - Changes to the existing coupled-DCP implementation. - A claim that Sparse MLA should never use CP. These may be considered separately after the fixed path demonstrates an end-to-end benefit. ### Feedback Period. Two weeks after the RFC is posted. ### CC List. ### Any Other Things. #### Correctness and evaluation Correctness tests should compare the new path with DCP=1 and existing coupled DCP for: - Global Top-K indices and model outputs. - Causal boundaries and Top-K ties. - Uneven query counts and empty helper work. - Indexer-cache append and global token-index mapping. - Repeated execution without stale communication buffers. Performance evaluation should use the same hardware, precision, kernels, memory limit, and request workload for: 1. DPA with local Indexer and local Sparse MLA. 2. Existing coupled DCP. 3. Fixed Indexer CP with owner-local Sparse MLA. The operator breakdown should report Indexer scan, query dispatch, Top-K merge, and Sparse MLA latency. The end-to-end evaluation should report TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and goodput under explicit latency SLOs. The single-GPU baseline must use the best available Indexer backend. In particular, the proposed [SM90 fused DSA prefill Indexer backend](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53563) could reduce the available benefit from Indexer CP and should be included when available. #### Relationship to existing RFCs - [Per-Layer Parallelism Policy #42659](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42659) is the preferred home for resolving parallel contexts. This RFC adds the narrower requirement that two stages inside DSA may consume different contexts. - [Shared Context Parallelism #50127](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50127) may later optimize Indexer query, key, and Top-K exchange. This RFC does not depend on that optimized path. - [Dynamic Context Parallelism #29295](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/29295) addresses dynamic collaboration across DP ranks. This RFC uses only a fixed group and does not resize it per request. - [Data Parallel Attention and Expert Parallel MoEs #16037](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/16037) provides the request-owned attention mode in which owner-local Sparse MLA runs. #### Open questions 1. Should the two contexts be represented directly by #42659's parallel plan, or by a small nested sparse-attention plan? 2. Can the existing DP/EP execution order safely support a fixed cross-DP Indexer operation, including empty ranks, or is an explicit synchronization point required? 3. Should the first implementation reuse an existing DCP collective path or a Shared-CP object when both are available? #### Requested feedback 1. Is removing the shared parallel-context assumption from DSA an acceptable extension to vLLM's attention interface? 2. Is a fixed, single-node Indexer-CP/Sparse-MLA-local implementation an appropriate first scope? ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Progressive block handoff for NIXL Push
author: yimdev
body:
### Motivation.


`NixlPushConnector` currently starts transferring a remote-prefill request's
KV cache after the producer finishes the request. With chunked prefill, earlier
chunks may already contain complete logical blocks that will not be modified
again, but those blocks still wait for the final chunk before transfer starts.

The current critical path is:

```text
finish all P prefill compute
  -> transfer all request KV
  -> mark D ready
  -> run the first D decode step
```

Progressive Push publishes immutable logical block ranges while P continues
prefill, so earlier transfers overlap later computation:

```text
P: compute chunk 1 -> compute chunk 2 -> ... -> compute final chunk
                       ||                  ||
NIXL:             WRITE earlier KV -> WRITE later KV -> commit
```

D still reads its local paged KV and does not become schedulable until the
whole request is committed. This proposal does not introduce remote attention
or partial-KV decode.

### Separate settlement from WRITE submission

A completed scheduler step is an opportunity to advance the immutable
frontier, not a requirement to issue a NIXL WRITE. Sending one WRITE per
prefill chunk would couple transfer granularity to scheduler configuration and
increase descriptor construction, submission, polling, and GPU/NIC contention.

The mechanism therefore separates four events:

- **settlement:** a prefill model step completed successfully;
- **publication:** newly immutable logical block ranges became visible;
- **transfer:** one or more published ranges were coalesced into a WRITE;
- **commit:** all final data for the request epoch was transferred.



### Proposed Change.


Add an opt-in, capability-gated progressive handoff path to
`NixlPushConnector`.

### Core flow

1. D allocates destination blocks and sends the existing Push registration in
   a group-native form.
2. After a P model step completes and scheduler state is settled, the
   connector receives the grouped block table and settled-token count.
3. A layout/export policy seals newly immutable, complete logical block
   ranges. The connector does not infer immutability from a model name.
4. P establishes CUDA producer-memory visibility before publishing those
   ranges to the Push writer.
5. The writer matches source and destination ranges by request epoch, group
   ID, and logical position. It coalesces pending ranges and issues bounded
   NIXL WRITEs.
6. Intermediate WRITE completion advances transfer progress only. It never
   makes D ready.
7. The terminal update publishes the remaining partial tail and forces a final
   flush. After all request-local WRITEs complete, every producer rank sends
   one idempotent commit.
8. D becomes ready only after every expected producer commit and the existing
   control-token conditions are satisfied.

### Sequence diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Router
    participant D as D scheduler/worker
    participant P as P scheduler/model
    participant W as P Push writer
    participant K as D KV memory

    R->>D: Start request early
    D->>D: Allocate destination blocks
    D-->>W: PUSH_REG(grouped destination runs)
    R->>P: Start chunked prefill

    P->>P: Complete and settle chunk N
    P->>P: Seal immutable full blocks
    P->>W: Publish ranges after CUDA visibility fence
    W->>W: Coalesce pending ranges

    par Continue prefill
        P->>P: Compute later chunks
    and Transfer earlier KV
        W->>K: NIXL WRITE(coalesced ranges)
        K-->>W: WRITE completed
        Note over W,D: Intermediate completion does not make D ready
    end

    Note over P,W: Settlement may repeat without submitting a WRITE
    P->>P: Complete and settle final chunk
    P->>W: Publish final range and partial tail
    W->>K: Flush remaining WRITE
    K-->>W: All WRITEs completed
    W-->>D: PUSH_COMMIT(request epoch)
    D->>D: Wait for all producer ranks
    D->>D: Mark request ready
    D->>D: Run first decode step
```

### Group-native protocol boundary

The publication unit is an immutable logical range:

```text
(request_epoch, group_id, start_logical_block, end_logical_block)
```

Registration records carry a stable group ID, runtime block size, and
destination runs with explicit logical positions. Transfer progress is tracked
per group as monotonic `sealed`, `posted`, and `completed` frontiers.

The writer lowers logical ranges into physical NIXL descriptors using the
existing P/D mapping and memory registration. The existing Push group
registration, writer thread, descriptor builder, and watchdog are reused;
there is no second registration transport.

Intermediate WRITEs do not signal request readiness. Readiness is represented
only by the final, idempotent commit barrier.

### Correctness invariants

For a published range in a request epoch:

1. model execution will not write its bytes again;
2. its logical-to-physical mapping remains fixed until WRITE completion;
3. its source blocks remain pinned while NIXL may read them;
4. every alias of the same backing bytes crosses the same immutable boundary;
5. non-terminal partial blocks are not published;
6. published ranges are monotonic, non-overlapping, and idempotent;
7. the CUDA producing stream is visible before the writer can post the range.

Cancellation suppresses commit and drains outstanding handles before block
release. Preemption stops publication and resumes through a new epoch or the
existing whole-request path; it does not reuse the interrupted progressive
epoch.

D must wait for the final tail, all WRITE completions, every producer-rank
commit, and the existing first-token/control condition. Intermediate progress
cannot satisfy this barrier.

### Batching

The writer coalesces adjacent published ranges until
`progressive_push_min_bytes` is reached. It initially allows at most one
request-local progressive WRITE in flight. Final settlement flushes all
remaining ranges regardless of size.

For example:

```text
WRITE group=0 logical=[0, 16)
WRITE group=0 logical=[16, 40)
FINAL WRITE group=0 logical=[40, 51)
COMMIT request_epoch=0
```

The final WRITE transfers only data not already posted. If the threshold is
never reached before final settlement, the mechanism intentionally degenerates
toward the existing whole-request WRITE.

### Capability boundary and extension

The initial data path targets the simplest useful structure:

- CUDA-direct NIXL Push;
- one causal full-attention KV group with a contiguous block table;
- compatible P/D layouts and block sizes;
- same-TP producer and consumer, PP1;
- chunked prefill enabled;
- prefix caching and speculative decoding disabled.

This is sufficient for the initial Hunyuan3 path and a Qwen3-0.6B local
regression setup. Unsupported configurations retain whole-request Push.
Eligibility depends on cache structure and runtime configuration, not the
checkpoint name.

The protocol is group-native even when the first enabled layout has one group.
Future DeepSeek V4 support can add layout-specific policies for:

- multiple groups and per-group block sizes;
- independently advancing immutable frontiers;
- packed backing conflict domains and alias deduplication;
- physical transfer planning for non-contiguous group runs.

The request-level commit already spans every group and producer rank, so those
extensions do not replace the registration/publication/WRITE/commit state
machine.

### Control-plane requirement and fallback

D registration must arrive before P finishes, otherwise no transfer can
overlap prefill. A router therefore starts D allocation and registration early
using the existing Push coordinates. The connector does not reimplement
router dispatch.

If the feature is disabled, the capability gate fails, registration arrives
too late, or progressive state cannot be used safely, the request uses the
existing whole-request Push path. Progressive failures must not expose partial
KV as ready.

### Configuration

The initial public controls are deliberately small:

```json
{
  "progressive_push": true,
  "progressive_push_min_bytes": 16777216
}
```

`progressive_push` defaults to `false`. The byte threshold controls WRITE
coalescing; adaptive thresholds and cross-request batching are outside this
proposal.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

## Small-model prototype validation

The current implementation was tested only as a basic framework and mechanism
check with the small `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` model. Baseline and progressive modes
ran sequentially on the same two NVIDIA B300 GPUs with TP1/PP1, 
Prefix caching and speculative decoding were disabled, 2,048-token
prefill chunks(max-num-batched-tokens 2048,max-num-seqs 1), 16-token KV blocks, early D registration, and a 16 MiB WRITE
threshold. Each cell contains 20 concurrency-one measurements and reports the
observed average and maximum; no percentile interpolation is used.

`off -> on` means whole-request Push followed by progressive Push. The handoff
tail is measured from completion of the P response to completion of the D
response.

| Prompt | Total avg off -> on (ms) | Avg gain | Total max off -> on (ms) | Max gain | Tail avg off -> on (ms) | Avg gain | Tail max off -> on (ms) | Max gain |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 62.0 -> 51.8 | 16.5% | 106.1 -> 90.9 | 14.4% | 36.1 -> 35.0 | 2.9% | 78.6 -> 75.0 | 4.5% |
| 4K | 96.6 -> 86.1 | 10.9% | 180.9 -> 104.9 | 42.0% | 46.1 -> 43.4 | 5.9% | 100.6 -> 59.5 | 40.9% |
| 16K | 480.4 -> 412.7 | 14.1% | 612.2 -> 428.3 | 30.0% | 93.6 -> 28.0 | 70.1% | 229.6 -> 30.8 | 86.6% |
| 32K | 1,531.9 -> 1,410.2 | 7.9% | 1,588.7 -> 1,463.6 | 7.9% | 150.7 -> 31.3 | 79.2% | 206.6 -> 38.8 | 81.2% |
| 64K | 5,541.1 -> 5,281.8 | 4.7% | 5,817.0 -> 5,308.4 | 8.7% | 297.4 -> 34.4 | 88.4% | 574.0 -> 43.2 | 92.5% |
| 80K | 8,106.3 -> 7,854.4 | 3.1% | 8,160.2 -> 7,885.4 | 3.4% | 360.7 -> 37.5 | 89.6% | 413.2 -> 50.9 | 87.7% |

All 240 measured requests produced matching P and D output tokens, and the
token also matched between baseline and progressive modes at every prompt
length. At 16K--80K, average handoff-tail latency fell by 70.1%--89.6%, showing
that earlier WRITEs overlapped later prefill work.

These results are only a simple validation of the initial implementation with
a small TP1 model. They are not a production performance claim.

title: [RFC]: PCP-Sharded O-Projection Weights
author: pisceskkk
body:
### Motivation.

In the current prefill context parallel (PCP) design, every PCP rank stores the same TP-local `o_proj` weights. This redundant replication consumes significant HBM on large MLA models.

The proposal further shards each TP-local `o_proj` weight across the PCP group to reduce persistent HBM usage, then selects the computation flow according to the batch composition. Prefill and mixed batches asynchronously reconstruct the full TP-local weight and overlap the all-gather with attention computation, while decode-only batches compute with the resident PCP-local weight shards and all-reduce the partial projection outputs across the PCP group.

The feature is opt-in through `--enable-pcp-o-proj-tp`. A draft implementation is available in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53422.

### Proposed Change.

### Design goals

- Reduce persistent O-projection weight residency by distributing each TP-local shard across PCP ranks.
- Preserve the numerical contract of the existing row-parallel O-projection in both prefill and decode.
- Hide prefill weight reconstruction behind attention work through an explicit, model-owned prefetch point.
- Provide a representation-aware extension point for quantized weights whose physical layout requires custom reconstruction.

### Weight layout and checkpoint loading

For an O-projection weight `W[N, K]`, TP rank `t` normally owns a contiguous input-dimension shard of width `K / T`. With PCP O-projection TP enabled, PCP rank `p` owns:

`W_local[t, p] = W[:, (t * P + p) * K / (T * P) : (t * P + p + 1) * K / (T * P)]`

Here `T` is the TP size and `P` is the PCP size. Each rank therefore persistently stores `1 / P` of its original TP-local O-projection shard. The checkpoint loader addresses the shard with flattened rank `t * P + p` and flattened size `T * P`, so the checkpoint format remains unchanged.

### Phase-specific execution

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Build global batch metadata] --> B{global_has_prefill}
    B -->|Prefill or mixed batch| P0[Q and KV normalization]
    P0 --> P1[Explicit O-proj prefetch hook]
    P1 --> P2[Launch asynchronous PCP weight all-gather]
    P1 --> P3[Q projection, RoPE, indexer, PCP KV exchange, and attention]
    P2 --> P4[Full TP-local O-proj weight ready]
    P3 --> P5[Wait at O-proj consumption point]
    P4 --> P5
    P5 --> P6[O-proj GEMM with full TP-local weight]
    B -->|Decode batch| D0[Attention output]
    D0 --> D1[Slice input dimension by PCP rank]
    D1 --> D2[O-proj GEMM with resident PCP-local weight]
    D2 --> D3[PCP all-reduce partial outputs]
    P6 --> Z[Preserve existing TP reduction semantics]
    D3 --> Z
```

For prefill and mixed batches, the model explicitly calls `o_proj.prefetch_full_weight_if_needed(global_has_prefill)` after attention normalization. The asynchronous PCP all-gather reconstructs the full TP-local weight while Q projection, RoPE, indexer work, PCP KV communication, and main attention execute. O-projection waits for the collective only at its consumption point. PCP ranks own different token partitions in this phase, so the reconstructed weight is applied locally and no PCP output reduction is required.

For decode, the weight remains PCP-sharded and no weight all-gather is launched. Each rank slices the attention output along the O-projection input dimension, multiplies it by the resident local weight, and participates in a PCP all-reduce to produce the complete output. The existing TP reduction behavior remains unchanged.

### Collective ordering and prefetch placement

The scheduler establishes the batch-level `global_has_prefill` value before PCP partitioning. Every PCP rank therefore makes the same phase decision and enters the same collective sequence. The current MVP uses DCP equal to 1, which keeps this decision independent of decode-context partitioning.

The prefetch call is owned by the attention module because it has the earliest reliable point at which normalization has completed and enough attention work remains to hide the collective. Generic MLA invokes the hook after `kv_a_layernorm(kv_c)`, while DeepSeek V3.2 modular attention invokes it after `fused_norm_rope`. A GLM-4.7 PCP4TP1 trace recorded all 47 layer-level weight all-gathers completing before FlashAttention, with a minimum 1.02 ms margin to attention start and a median 3.68 ms margin to the O-projection GEMM.

### Linear-layer weight switching

`RowParallelLinear` manages two logical O-projection states: the resident PCP-local representation and the reconstructed TP-local representation. Prefill switches the linear method to the reconstructed tensors after the asynchronous gather completes, executes the projection, and restores the resident representation. Decode directly consumes the resident representation after slicing its input.

A weak shared buffer pool provides full-weight reconstruction storage so compatible layers can reuse a single-layer allocation. The buffer remains part of peak and ready-state memory accounting even though persistent per-layer parameter residency is reduced; a workspace lease and reuse policy is planned to make this lifecycle explicit.

### Quantization extension through `TPWeightSwitchMixin`

`TPWeightSwitchMixin` separates the phase-switching state machine from method-specific tensor representation. A quantization method declares which tensors are sharded, how a full representation is allocated and gathered, which tensors remain replicated, and how local tensor references are restored after execution.

The initial adapters cover unquantized linear weights and ModelOpt W4A4 NVFP4 with a CUTLASS-compatible post-load layout. For NVFP4, the packed `weight` tensor is gathered directly. The `128x4`-swizzled block scale is converted to its logical ordering, gathered through `uint8` bit views, and reassembled into the kernel-facing layout. Replicated `input_global_scale_inv`, `weight_global_scale`, and `alpha` values remain unchanged. Additional physical layouts can implement the same mixin contract with representation-specific shard and reconstruction rules.

### Performance summary

The current implementation was measured on four NVIDIA H20 GPUs with GLM-4.7-Flash, 32,768 input tokens, 1,024 output tokens, and concurrency 1, 8, and 16. The ranges below summarize enabled-versus-disabled deltas across those concurrency levels.

| Topology |       TTFT delta |       TPOT delta | Throughput delta |
| -------- | ---------------: | ---------------: | ---------------: |
| PCP4TP1  | +0.15% to +0.36% | +4.93% to +7.51% | -6.06% to -4.55% |
| PCP2TP2  | -0.45% to +2.88% | +5.45% to +7.55% | -6.43% to -4.52% |

The prefill overlap keeps TTFT broadly stable in this workload. Decode adds one PCP input slice and one PCP all-reduce per O-projection, which accounts for the measured TPOT and throughput cost and is the primary performance optimization target.

### Theoretical PCP8 weight-memory benefit

The following calculation assumes TP1, PCP8, DCP1, a compatible O-projection representation, and one reusable full-weight buffer for a single layer. It covers model-weight residency and excludes communication workspace, staging, allocator fragmentation, KV cache, activations, and runtime overhead. With combined TP degree `T`, the local O-projection, full-weight buffer, and per-rank saving shown here each divide by `T`.

| Model/checkpoint       | Shardable O-proj (GiB) | PCP8 local O-proj (GiB) | Per-rank persistent saving (GiB) |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------: | ----------------------: | -------------------------------: |
| GLM-5.2 BF16           |                 14.812 |                   1.852 |                           12.773 |
| GLM-5.2 FP8            |                  7.408 |                   0.926 |                            6.388 |
| DeepSeek-V4 Flash-Base |                  1.375 |                   0.172 |                            1.172 |
| DeepSeek-V4 Flash      |                  1.375 |                   0.172 |                            1.172 |
| DeepSeek-V4 Pro-Base   |                  6.782 |                   0.848 |                            5.825 |
| DeepSeek-V4 Pro        |                  6.782 |                   0.848 |                            5.825 |

The theoretical benefit is a reduction in persistent O-projection parameter residency. Converting that reduction into process-level available HBM requires the full-weight buffer, communication workspace, and staging allocations to share an explicit and reusable workspace lifecycle.

### Feedback Period.

~ two weeks

### CC List.

@LucasWilkinson @GirasoleY 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_
