- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Using Helion for Selected vLLM CustomOps
author: yushangdi
body: ### Motivation. **TL;DR** 1. We propose to use Helion by default for some CustomOps. 2. We show that Helion kernels have superior performance compared to the CUDA kernels in vLLM. Across broad shape sweeps, the three Helion kernels we benchmarked achieve 1.382–1.785x geomean speedups on H100, 1.556–1.804x on B200, and 1.022–1.427x on MI350X. On Qwen3-8B-FP8, this translates to 2.59%–3.49% higher end-to-end throughput on H100, 3.77%–7.44% on B200, and 3.41%–8.76% on MI350X across the tested concurrency levels. 3. We propose to let vLLM take a permanent Helion dependency. [Helion](https://github.com/pytorch/helion) is a Python-embedded DSL that compiles PyTorch-like kernel code to lower-level DSLs, such as Triton. As demonstrated in the PyTorch blog post [Portable vLLM Model Inference Kernels in Helion](https://pytorch.org/blog/portable-vllm-model-inference-kernels-in-helion/), kernels under `vllm/kernels/helion/` are competitive with—and often faster than—their CUDA counterparts in vLLM, delivering end-to-end gains on Qwen3 FP8 models running on H100 and B200 GPUs. We have also observed end-to-end gains on AMD MI350X GPUs. This RFC proposes an integration model for **using Helion kernels in vLLM CustomOps when CUDA graphs are enabled.** The initial rollout will cover the following kernels: 1. `per_token_group_fp8_quant` 2. `silu_and_mul_per_block_quant` 3. `rms_norm_per_block_quant` The earlier Helion kernel-authoring RFC, [[RFC]: Add Helion integration in vLLM (#32219)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32219), remains the design reference for implementing and registering kernels. This RFC proposes the following additional integration changes: 1. **Make Helion a pinned vLLM dependency.** 2. **Use Helion by default for some CustomOps.** **Comparison with Helion integration in SGLang.** Helion is integrated into [SGLang as an optional backend for Kimi Delta Attention](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/main/python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/helion). Like the integration proposed here, it uses pre-tuned Helion configs and requires no runtime autotuning. The main difference is that SGLang provides separate kernel implementations and fixed configurations for decode and prefill workloads; our integration uses a single kernel implementation for each CustomOp and selects among pre-tuned configurations based on the input shape range. In SGLang, for Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct (TP=2, 2xGB200), we observe a geomean 5.04%–5.27% improvement in tok/s compared to the default kernels. ## Performance When measuring performance, we used a single config for each Helion kernel on H100 and up to six configs for each Helion kernel on B200. ### Standalone Kernel Performance with Extensive Shape Sweeps on H100 and B200 A sweep uses physical dimensions from public model configurations and TP-local dimensions for TP sizes 1, 2, 4, and 8. The shape matrix includes RNJ1, Gemma 3 (270M through 27B), dense and MoE Qwen3 variants, MiniMax-M2, DeepSeek-V3, and Kimi-K2. - H100 artifact: - B200 artifact: #### H100 #### B200 | Kernel | Number of shapes | | --- | ---: | | `per_token_group_fp8_quant` | 1,173 | | `rms_norm_per_block_quant` | 255 | | `silu_and_mul_per_block_quant` | 918 | **Smaller number of configs used by each Helion kernel.** Higher performance gains are possible with additional configurations. For example, the existing configuration set achieves a 2.313x geomean speedup (range: 1.54–3.57x) for `rms_norm_per_block_quant`. In this RFC, we intentionally trade some performance for a smaller, more manageable configuration set—**at most six configs** for each Helion kernel. Users seeking further performance improvements can autotune the Helion kernel for their specific workloads. ### End-to-End Model Performance on Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 with Helion CustomOps #### H100 Settings: - Linear backend: DeepGEMM with float32 ceiling E8M0 scales - Input/output lengths: 512/600, with EOS ignored - Concurrency: 8, 16, 32, and 64 - Per observation: one full-concurrency warmup wave, then four measured waves | Concurrency | Native tok/s | Helion tok/s | Helion vs. native | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 8 | 1,273.46 | 1,317.89 | +3.489% | | 16 | 2,352.54 | 2,432.04 | +3.379% | | 32 | 4,008.54 | 4,129.85 | +3.026% | | 64 | 6,292.87 | 6,455.52 | +2.585% | #### B200 Settings: - Linear backend: CUTLASS. We do not use the DeepGEMM linear backend for the B200 experiments because it does not use all three kernels. - Input/output lengths: 512/600, with EOS ignored - Concurrency: 8, 16, 32, and 64 - Per observation: one full-concurrency warmup wave, then four measured waves | Concurrency | Native tok/s | Helion tok/s | Helion vs. native | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 8 | 1,804.0 | 1,938.1 | +7.44% | | 16 | 3,135.6 | 3,296.8 | +5.14% | | 32 | 5,633.5 | 5,992.3 | +6.37% | | 64 | 9,159.9 | 9,505.6 | +3.77% | ### Proposed Change. The proposed integration is prototyped in . If this RFC is accepted, we will submit the changes as a series of polished PRs. - **[existing]** `@register_kernel` exposes a kernel as `torch.ops.vllm_helion.`. - **[existing]** `ConfigManager` loads checked-in Helion configurations from `configs//.json`. - **[existing]** Each kernel's deterministic `pick_config()` chooses one pre-tuned config. There is no runtime autotuning. - **[new]** Helion kernels being used will JIT-compile a selected variant during CUDA-graph capture. - **[new]** Gate CustomOp routing to Helion kernels with `VLLM_USE_HELION_KERNELS`, defaulting to `1`. Setting it to `0` falls back to the alternative `torch.ops._C` CUDA kernel. The runtime behavior is: | Condition | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Supported op during CUDA-graph capture | Helion | | `VLLM_USE_HELION_KERNELS` feature disabled | Same as current | | No CUDA graph | Same as current; compiled routing pass is not installed | | Unsupported platform (no Helion config file for it) | Same as current | | Op executed outside CUDA-graph capture | Same as current | ### Routed Custom Op vLLM defines `torch.ops.vllm_helion.routed_`. Its schema and mutation contract match the corresponding Helion op. Its implementation is conceptually: ```python def routed_impl(*args): if torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing(): return helion_op(*args) # torch.ops.vllm_helion. return native_op(*args) # torch.ops._C. ``` During CUDA-graph capture, the Helion launch is recorded; replay executes the recorded kernel without re-entering the Python dispatcher. Outside capture, the same routed op calls the native implementation. If either the Helion op or the native op is unavailable—for example, because the native build does not contain the CUDA op or the platform has no Helion configs—the routed op is not registered. ### Direct Call `per_token_group_fp8_quant` has a direct eager call site in `QuantFP8.forward_cuda`. Conceptually, we write: ```python if ( VLLM_USE_HELION_KERNELS and not torch.compiler.is_compiling() and x.is_contiguous() and torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing() ): # This calls the routed custom op registered above. return helion_per_token_group_fp8_quant(...) return native_per_token_group_fp8_quant(...) ``` The `not torch.compiler.is_compiling()` condition short-circuits before the capture check while Dynamo is tracing. The compiled graph therefore still contains the native quant op, allowing RMSNorm/quant fusion to match normally; the post-grad routing pass handles any supported op that remains afterward. Only genuinely eager execution being captured into a CUDA graph takes the direct Helion path. ### Handling the `torch.compile` Path Some models still use `torch.compile` by default, and we integrate Helion into them by using a post-grad Inductor pass in the compiled path. The routed Helion custom ops are inserted into the `torch.compile`d graph through the Inductor pass. We add an additional post-grad FX pass, `HelionFusionRoutingPass`. It retargets direct calls to these native ops and remaining `auto_functionalized` wrappers whose inner target is a native op. Running it last therefore preserves vLLM's existing fusion, lowering, functionalization, and copy-elimination behavior. ### Extending Support to AMD Although this RFC initially targets NVIDIA sm90 and sm100, the same integration can support AMD GPUs by adding platform-specific tuned configurations. On ROCm, `torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing()` reports the HIP stream-capture state, allowing the routed custom op to work without platform-specific logic. The AMD results below demonstrate the resulting performance gains. **Helion compared with the corresponding AITER kernels on MI350X:** Artifact: The RMSNorm gains are concentrated in large-token, wide-hidden shapes rather than spread uniformly across the matrix: | Shape regime | Number of shapes | Geomean | | --- | ---: | ---: | | hidden <= 4096, all token counts | 153 | 1.001x | | hidden > 4096, tokens <= 256 | 70 | 1.005x | | hidden > 4096, tokens >= 272 | 32 | **1.169x** | **End-to-End Model Performance on Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 on MI350X** | Max concurrency | Prompts | AITER output tok/s | Helion output tok/s | Throughput change | AITER TPOT (ms) | Helion TPOT (ms) | TPOT change | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 8 | 64 | 1,358.20 | 1,463.29 | +7.74% | 5.580 | 5.432 | -2.65% | | 16 | 128 | 2,589.50 | 2,816.32 | +8.76% | 5.892 | 5.633 | -4.40% | | 32 | 512 | 4,489.52 | 4,642.60 | +3.41% | 6.641 | 6.387 | -3.82% | | 64 | 512 | 8,479.87 | 8,840.22 | +4.25% | 7.459 | 7.160 | -4.01% | ### Feedback Period. 2 weeks ### CC List. @xiaohongchen1991 @zou3519 ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Native Text Watermarking Support
author: TQCB
body: # Motivation Text watermarking for LLMs is a process by which we perturb the output of a model in such a way that is detectable after generation. This process allows us to test whether a sequence of text is consistent with a watermarked generation process after the fact. Watermarking is a necessary functionality in vLLM, because: - It has become an important part of responsible LLM deployment - It has become required by regulation by certain entities, to support provenance and transparency requirements (see [EU AI Act, Article 50(2)](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/) and [California SB 942](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB942)) - It is a modification of the sampling process, which cannot be modified by downstream consumers Watermarking cannot be left as an out-of-tree functionality (such as `CustomLogitsProcessor`) because: - Not all watermarking schemes are simple "logit biasers": some (such as gumbel-max) require adjust the sampling process itself - Some schemes require access to the final output distribution of the model (after top-p, temperature...) and this is not currently possible with a `CustomLogitsProcessor` - Production-ready implementations of watermarking will require support for speculative-decoding, which will potentially require adjustments to rejection sampling and other core behaviours of vLLM - Watermarking will only become more ingrained with the generation process as techniques evolve and complexify # Proposed Change We propose the implementation of native vLLM watermarking during sampling, using techniques such as Gumbel-max or SynthID-Text. This change is drafted in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54053, and we recommend you treat it as a technical support to this RFC. ## Desiderata 1. Non-distortion - the watermark should not alter the expected output distribution of a model over keyed generations, nor rely on metadata attached to an output. 2. Detectable - the watermark should be reliably detectable using inexpensive techniques, to allow for large-scale scoring. ## Proposed Algorithm We propose an initial implementation using the [Gumbel-max algorithm (Aaronson and Kirchner, 2023)](https://simons.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/2024-10/LLM24-2%20Slides%20-%20Scott%20Aaronson.pdf) which has multiple desirable qualities: - Single-token non-distortion (can be adjusted for single-sequence non-distortion using repeated-context deduplication) of the model's output distribution, see G.3 of [SynthID-Text Appendix](https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-024-08025-4/MediaObjects/41586_2024_8025_MOESM1_ESM.pdf) - Fast, relative to other schemes - Unintrusive to implement, as it does not require access to significant parts of the model or request state - Good detectability, using inexpensive methods - May be updated to support speculative sampling This algorithm uses a pseudo-random function (PRF) to create a deterministic keyed vector of uniform-random values `r_k ~ U(0, 1)`. At each position, we them sample `argmax_x r_k(x) ^ 1/p(x)`. The Gumbel-max identity allows us to structure our sampling by a key `k` without changing the expected distribution `p` over `k`. Given a sequence of text of unknown provenance, we can then recalculate `r_k` for each token, and `score = sum_t -log(1 - r_t)` over our sequence. Under the null, `score` follows `Gamma(n, 1)`, so we have a length-adjusted p-value: this can be used with a threshold to classify a sequence as watermarked. ## Implementation The implementation is divided into two independent components: generation and reference detection primitives. ### Watermarked generation The initial implementation will support Model Runner V2 and Gumbel-max watermarking. Speculative decoding is out of scope initially, but may be supported with dual-key approaches: see [He et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12456) and [Sander et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.01428) Watermarking is configured at engine startup: ```python @dataclass class WatermarkConfig: algorithm: Literal["gumbel"] key: int context_width: int = 4 ``` as well as a `SamplingParams` change that allows requests to control whether watermarking is applied: ```python @dataclass class SamplingParams: watermarking: bool | None = None ``` This allows for us to deploy an engine with watermarking configured, but to disable it on a per-request basis when unnecessary, such as internal or none-human-facing use. The sampling pipeline remains unchanged until final token selection: ```text model logits | existing penalties and constraints | temperature, min-p, top-k and top-p | final token selection | watermark disabled → existing random sampler watermark enabled → configured Watermarker ``` A shared `Watermarker` interface will define the algorithm-specific final selection. The initial `GumbelWatermarker` replaces the ordinary random draw with the keyed Gumbel-max draw. Greedy requests remain ordinary greedy sampling, as they cannot be watermarked. This isolates watermarking from the model runner and allows us to extend support to additional algorithms, such as SynthID-Text and more advanced forms of Gumbel-max sampling (dual-key generation for example). ### Detection primitives Basic detection does not require model weights or inference (although more advanced techniques that do this may be considered). vLLM will expose reusable detector primitives that expect token IDs: ```python detector = GumbelWatermarkDetector( key=key, context_width=context_width, ) result = detector.detect(token_ids) ``` The result contains the aggregate score, p-value, number of scored tokens, and threshold-based classification. Shared detector logic handles context construction, repeated-context deduplication (necessary for p-value calibration), score aggregation, and thresholding. Concrete implementations will provide the token-level scoring and the corresponding p-value if available, if not then an aggregate score. These implementations will serve as references for downstream implementations of detection services. A full detection endpoint would need to handle multiple tokenizers, multiple keys, additional algorithmic optimizations to the detection algorithms (entropy-weighting, early-fusion), and hinted search. These all fall outside the scope of vLLM and thus are not being proposed here. We would suggest having a small, minimal example of a detection server in `examples/` to serve as documentation, and to further expose the detection primitives to downstream users. ### Implementation plan While the code required to implement this proposal is minimal, it is critical that we thoroughly verify its behaviour. We must ensure that: - Watermarked sampling is not significantly slower than normal sampling: this can be evaluated using E2E latency and throughput benchmarks, as well as micro-benchmarking of the samplers. This is heavily dependent on the chosen algorithm (both the watermarking scheme, and the PRF), we expect throughput degradation of O(0.3% for 1B models, 0.1% for 30B+ models) for Gumbel-max sampling and O(1% - 0.5%) for SynthID-Text (see Table 4 of [TextSeal](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12456)) - Watermarked sampling does not significantly distort the quality of an expected output of a model: this is mathematically proven theoretically but remains dependent on certain aspects of key generation and context handling, it will be empirically validated with evaluations - Watermarked generations are reliably detectable: we will provide TPR@FPR and detection power across lengths and generation entropies to accompany the baseline detection algorithm, but we expect downstream consumers to optimize their own algorithms as there is a large cost-quality tradeoff to explore that will differ by provider (as well as false-positive calibration) ### Note on diversity Note that while watermarked generation may induce a loss in diversity over a sequence (single-token non-distortion) or multiple sequences (single-sequence non-distortion), most methods that would be considered for production watermarking do not produce a _catastrophic_ loss of diversity (determinism, given a fixed key and input). The proposed Gumbel-max algorithm, given its simplicity, does exhibit this behaviour. If this RFC is accepted, we expect to add multiple other watermarking schemes. These schemes may employ techniques that restore diversity: - Repeated-context deduplication - Tournament sampling with randomly sampled candidates - Random-tape methods - Dual or multi-key methods - Gated watermarking (random, or conditional on entropy, or conditional on context) - Speculative decoding See Results section below for results. ### Additional points of discussion #### Choice of PRF Many watermarking schemes rely on a keyed PRF to guide generation, making the choice of such a function important to the behaviour of the algorithm. There are certain qualities we desire in our PRF: 1. Stability over time: a torch/triton update should not break a `(k, WM_k(output))` pair (see [Philox](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2063384.2063405), which otherwise would be an excellent candidate) 2. Fast on GPU: many PRFs are only available in CPU form (see [SipHash](https://www.aumasson.jp/siphash/siphash.pdf)), which would require us to maintain an internal GPU/triton implementation 3. Good statistical properties: the PRF must have good uniformity in its output, independence across inputs and no structure; most PRFs have this as a principal objective already 4. [optional] Cryptographically secure: it may be desirable for the `(context, key) -> pseudorandom value` mapping to be indistinguishable from a fresh random function, as it protect from attackers predicting keys from context, predicting values from unseen contexts, or generating strongly watermarked text without the key. We can also suppose that some deployments may require FIPS compliancy As we cannot ensure that every PRF is suitable to every use, we propose a modular PRF system to allow easy extension to new PRFs. This will allow us to implement a PRF that aligns with points 1, 2 and 3 while downstream consumers may extend the system to use PRFs with other qualities (such as FIPS compliance). Here are some candidates for a suitable PRF: | Candidate | 1. Stable | 2. Fast on GPU | 3. Statistical quality | |---|---:|---:|---:| | HMAC-SHA-256 | Yes | No | Yes | | Philox (PyTorch) | No, due to API | Yes | Yes | | SipHash-2-4 | Yes | No existing impl. | Yes | | TextSeal integer hash | Yes* | Yes* | Yes** | _* Assuming we maintain a frozen internal implementation_ _** Its statistical properties have no public analysis compared to the alternatives_ For an initial implementation, we propose an internal version of the Philox algorithm, that can be maintained as stable. It is high-performance and well-established for PRFs (supported by NumPy and used by PyTorch for CUDA RNG). [HMAC](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/224/ipd) is a potential contender, as it is also well-established, cryptographically secure and can be FIPS compliant (unlike Philox), but even an optimized GPU implementation may not be fast enough as the algorithm itself is much heavier. ```python def philox4x32-10-v1(key, context, token) -> uint32 -> uniform float ``` ## Results - Model: Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B - Dataset: GSM8K - top_p=1.0, max_tokens=256 - Watermark: Gumbel-max, Philox PRF, context width 4 ### Performance All ran on H100, median of 3 runs Config | Total output token/s/gpu | Delta v. baseline ---|---|--- Baseline | 11,056.947 | 0.000% Watermarked | 10,985.863 | -0.643% BSZ | p20 (ms) | Median (ms) | p80 (ms) | Peak temporary memory (MiB) ---|---|---|---|--- 1 | 0.037568 | 0.039088 | 0.040640 | 0.003906 8 | 0.038176 | 0.038800 | 0.039968 | 0.023926 32 | 0.042400 | 0.042544 | 0.042880 | 0.090332 256 | 0.254432 | 0.254960 | 0.256000 | 0.715820 ### Quality Evals were run and averaged over 8 watermark keys. Accuracy: Variant | T=0.7 | T=1.0 ---|---|--- Main | 42.88% | 27.63% PR, watermark off | 43.31% | 26.06% PR, watermark on | 44.00% | 27.63% Variance, min-max range and SD for each config: T | Main | PR (wm=off) | PR (wm=on) ---|---|---|--- 0.7 | 39.5–49.0%, 2.9 pp | 40.0–50.0%, 3.0 pp | 38.5–47.5%, 2.5 pp 1.0 | 23.5–31.0%, 2.2 pp | 23.5–31.0%, 2.4 pp | 25.5–30.0%, 1.8 pp Output length: Temperature | PR (wm=off) | PR (wm=on) | Difference | 95% CI ---|---|---|---|--- 0.7 | 117.70 | 121.59 | +3.89 tokens | [+0.93, +6.88] 1.0 | 137.37 | 155.60 | +18.23 tokens | [+13.98, +22.50] Fraction reaching `gen_length=256` limit: Temperature | PR (wm=off) | PR (wm=on) ---|---|--- 0.7 | 7.38% | 10.81% 1.0 | 16.25% | 32.94% This Gumbel-max implementation's single-token non-distortion does not guarantee non-distortion over a keyed sequence, we can see this here with a change in generation length. See "Note on diversity" above for solutions. ### Diversity _See "Note on diversity" section for notes on output diversity for this implementation of Gumbel-max._ This form of Gumbel-max watermarking exhibits a catastrophic collapse in diversity. ### Detectability All numbers use a threshold of `p<=0.01`, so a 1% FPR, and are averaged over 8 watermark keys. Watermarked GSM8K response detection: Temp. | Positive rate ---|--- 0.7 | 42.13% 1.0 | 84.17% Unwatermarked GSM8K response detection: Config | Temp. | Positive rate ---|---|--- Main | 0.7 | 1.154% Main | 1.0 | 1.139% PR | 0.7 | 1.172% PR | 1.0 | 1.135% TPR@FPR by sequence length (`Unknown Key` refers to having to evaluate the watermark score over 8 keys, and applying a Bonferroni correction to the p-value): ## References and ressources For key algorithms, definitions: - Gumbel-max: https://simons.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/2024-10/LLM24-2%20Slides%20-%20Scott%20Aaronson.pdf - Random tape Gumbel-max: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.15593 - SynthID-Text - Paper: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08025-4#MOESM1 - Appendix: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-024-08025-4/MediaObjects/41586_2024_8025_MOESM1_ESM.pdf - TextSeal: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12456 For the choice of PRF: - Philox's Random123 algorithm - Paper: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2063384.2063405 - Code: https://github.com/DEShawResearch/random123/blob/main/include/Random123/philox.h - HMAC: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/224/ipd For further reading: - Speculative decoding considerations: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.20418v1 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.01428

title: [RFC]: Elastic EP support in Model Runner V2
author: almogtavor
body:
### Motivation

Elastic EP is listed under "TBD features" in #47172, this RFC is for related decisions discussion.

Today `--enable-elastic-ep` lands in `_get_v2_model_runner_unsupported_features()`, so vLLM quietly goes back to the V1 model runner, and forcing `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` just raises. That is fine while MRV2 is opt-in per model. #53183 makes it the default, and then elastic EP is the thing keeping a deployment on V1.

Some of it is already wired. #37488 gave MRV2 an `EPLBController` that exposes `eplb_state`, `eep_eplb_suppressed` and `setup_eplb_from_mapping`, which is what `ElasticEPScalingExecutor` reaches for, and MRV2's `_dummy_run` already takes `skip_eplb` and `is_profile`.

### Proposed Change

Three things in the scaling path assume the V1 runner (with suggestion for each).

1. **Block tables**: `warm_and_capture` saves `worker.model_runner.input_batch.block_table`, clears it so the dummy MoE forward cannot write dummy slot mappings into live KV blocks, then puts it back. MRV2 has no persistent `input_batch` at all, it builds one per step on `execute_model_state` and drops it at the end.

My suggestion is to skip this on MRV2 rather than port it. MRV2 already keeps the persistent per-request block ids in `BlockTables.block_tables` and the per-step gather destination in `input_block_tables`, and `_dummy_run` goes through `prepare_dummy_attn()`, which only touches the second one. So the thing the V1 code is protecting never gets written, and the guard has no work to do. The alternative is saving and restoring `runner.block_tables` anyway for symmetry, which copies every block table on each scale for nothing, but I would rather be told than guess.

2. **CUDA graphs**: `_release_cuda_graphs` checks `isinstance(model_runner.model, CUDAGraphWrapper)` and empties `concrete_cudagraph_entries`. MRV2 never wraps the model, it captures through `CudaGraphManager`, so neither branch fires and the function falls straight through to the compile reset without dropping a single graph.

That is worse than it sounds, because of what runs right after. `warm_and_capture` releases graphs before re-warming precisely because growing the MoE workspace reallocates the buffer, and every graph captured against the old one still holds a pointer into it, see [elastic_execute.py#L726-L729](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c71f6f8a81d3d3c49a045c8b88eed36366cc7d92/vllm/distributed/elastic_ep/elastic_execute.py#L726-L729). On MRV2 those graphs would survive the scale and get replayed against freed memory. A `release_graphs()` on `CudaGraphManager` covers it: clear `graphs`, mark it uncaptured so `dispatch()` falls back to eager, leave `_capture_descs` so `needs_capture()` still knows what to redo.

3. **DP world size**: `GPUModelRunner` copies `dp_size` and `dp_rank` out of `parallel_config` when it is built, and `CudaGraphManager` copies `dp_size` too. Elastic EP rewrites those fields in place on every reconfigure, so after a scale the old ranks are still sizing their DP collectives for the previous world. V1 does not hit this because `coordinate_batch_across_dp` takes `parallel_config` and reads the size at call time. Reading through `parallel_config` in both places is the smallest fix I can see.

additionally: `_release_cuda_graphs` raises on `UBatchWrapper` with "DBO is not yet supported in elastic EP", and DBO for MRV2 is being added separately in #50945 and #51700, so whoever does this should agree with them on what that guard turns into.

### Feedback Period

_No response_

### CC List

@njhill @Etelis @tzulingk

### Any Other Things

What I actually want to know is whether this is wanted. #47172 puts elastic EP in the bucket of things where the complexity and utility tradeoff is still open, so it is possible the answer is that these deployments should just stay on V1, and that is a fine answer.

If it is wanted, is an RFC plus staged PRs the right shape here, the way DBO went from #50738 into #50945 and #51700?

Elastic EP is also still moving, #44994 is reworking the communicator path, so I would rather not build further against it without someone saying the target is stable enough to aim at.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] Config-driven AITER auto-enable instead of a manual opt-in?
author: wjabbour
body:
Small idea I wanted to float, not a concrete proposal yet.

`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER` defaults to False, and per #31653 that's intentional -- not every config is supported, so the safe default wins for end users. Makes sense.

What I noticed digging around: most of the individual AITER sub-toggles (`_MOE`, `_LINEAR`, `_RMSNORM`, `_MLA`, `_MHA`, etc.) already default True, and individual backends already do their own capability checks (GPU arch, package presence). So a lot of "is this even possible" self-determination already exists -- it's just all still gated behind one manual master switch that has no awareness of which model/config is actually running.

Idea: what if there were a maintainer-curated table (keyed on something like model architecture / dtype / quant scheme / TP-PP shape / GPU arch) that vLLM updates once a specific combo is confirmed correct and has real test coverage -- and AITER auto-enables for any config that matches, no user opt-in required? Users would never need to know AITER exists as a separate construct; they'd just get the fastest verified-safe path for their actual setup.

Open questions I don't have answers to:
- What's the right key shape for the table?
- Where would it live -- a static data file in-tree, PR-reviewed like anything else?
- Does `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER` stick around as a manual override for people who want to force an unconfirmed combo at their own risk?
- Is this ROCm/AITER-specific, or would a similar pattern make sense for other backend-specific opt-in flags?

Curious if this resonates with anyone who's thought about this more, or if there's a reason it wouldn't work that I'm missing.

title: [RFC]: TreeWY: Tree Speculative Decoding for hybrid (GDN) models
author: sneha5gsm
body:
### Motivation.

Hello!
I recently explored speculative decoding for hybrid models (Qwen 3.5 model series) in vLLM and the recurrent-state memory bottleneck in the current implementation. With `mamba_cache_mode="all"`, a draft of `N` positions needs `N+1` full state snapshots per sequence per layer. On Qwen3.5-397B that is 90 MiB/seq i.e. 360 MiB for a depth-3 chain and ~1.2 GiB for a `[2,2,2]` tree (14 nodes), out of the same budget as the KV cache. To alleviate the recurrent-state memory bottleneck, my current implementation reconstructs the accepted state on commit rather than snapshotting it, using the WY/UT representation of the gated delta rule: one strictly-lower-triangular solve over the verify window gives every draft node's output, and any node's continuation state rebuilds from a small per-node stash. I extended it to support **tree** speculative decoding on GDN-based Qwen hybrids. Here's the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20961) related to the study. It has the memory analysis at both model scales, and the serving sweep.

I see that [ReplaySSM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47572) does something similar for part of this.
I benchmarked ReplaySSM against my implementation on Qwen3.5-35B, and ReplaySSM is the more performant one for chain speculative decoding in hybrid models. It also is broader in terms of model support. Kudos to the team!

Where the two designs diverge: ReplaySSM and my current implementation solve the same triangular system on the same corrected inputs. The two kernels differ in one predicate: an index comparison where mine loads an explicit ancestor mask, so a commit becomes an ancestor-masked reduction rather than a cursor move. That is what makes a tree reachable.

Here's the [current implementation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...sneha5gsm:vllm:treewy-gdn-spec-decode), for reference.

Draft trees are not a throughput win yet: acceptance rises monotonically with width (from 3.23 to 3.44 on Spec-Bench) but throughput falls at every width. The cause is CUDA graph capture: a branching verify step cannot be fully captured today. Tree speculative decoding (width > 1) needs a non-causal ancestor mask on the softmax layers which leads to a fallback to PIECEWISE. 



 

### Proposed Change.

I would like to support tree speculative decoding for hybrid models in vLLM.

Since this relates to the ReplaySSM contribution, I am happy to collaborate with the ReplaySSM team to further support it for tree speculative decoding in hybrid models.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@Johnny-Liou 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Backend-stable stateless RNG for Gumbel sampling
author: freyfwt
body:
# Motivation

Model Runner V2 Gumbel sampling currently depends on Triton/Philox helpers for uniform generation. For cross-backend portability and reproducibility, it is useful to have a small stateless integer mixing path whose output depends only on `(seed, position, token_id)` and is implemented identically across supported backends.

The main requirement is not bitwise compatibility with Philox, but preserving the target categorical distribution and avoiding measurable correlation-induced sampling bias.

Related implementation PR: #51367.

This also overlaps with the PRF discussion in #53916, but this RFC is scoped to the ordinary Gumbel sampler rather than watermarking.

# Proposed Change

Use a fixed Murmur3 x86_32-style mixing path keyed by request seed, token position, and vocabulary offset:

```text
(seed, position, token_id) -> 32-bit mixed value -> centered uniform -> Gumbel noise
```

For fp32, construct the centered uniform from the full 32-bit source value as `(x + 0.5) / 2^32`, using two exact 16-bit integer-to-fp32 conversions for backend portability. For fp64, combine two domain-separated 32-bit outputs and retain 53 bits.

The existing Philox helpers remain available for other sampling utilities.

# Correctness Requirements

1. The integer mapping should be deterministic and stable across backends.
2. Uniform construction must retain sufficient tail resolution for Gumbel-max; truncating to 24 bits is not acceptable.
3. Joint outputs across token IDs / positions / seeds must not show detectable correlation that biases categorical sampling.
4. Seeded non-greedy token sequences may change, but the target sampling distribution should remain unchanged within statistical error.

# Validation

For the implementation in #51367:

- 32-bit uniform reconstruction matched correctly rounded fp32 on 2M random uint32 values: 0 mismatches.
- Pairwise token-output correlation, byte/bit tests, and position-serial tests were consistent with random noise.
- Sampler-level Monte Carlo found no detectable categorical bias after the 32-bit fix.
- In a vocab=129,280 tail-stress test with 100k draws, the corrected 32-bit path produced z=-1.18 at logit gap 18 and z=-1.09 at gap 20; the earlier 24-bit prototype produced z=-5.89 and z=-5.16, respectively.

GPU CI, accelerator distribution tests, and performance measurements remain required before merge.

# Feedback Period

No fixed deadline; feedback is welcome while #51367 is under review.

title: [RFC]: Privacy-safe runtime incident snapshots for fatal EngineCore failures
author: jackLei0901
body:
### Motivation.

When EngineCore dies, an operator can often see that serving stopped but cannot recover the short sequence of scheduler, KV-cache, and worker state that led to the failure. Existing metrics, traces, logs, `/health`, exit status, and `dump_engine_exception()` each cover part of the incident, but none provides one bounded, privacy-reviewed pre-failure history at the EngineCore fatal boundary.

I tested which evidence could remain external and which required an EngineCore-owned producer. On a single RTX 4090 with vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev1103+g7ca49fbe4`, a bounded external process sampled health, process state, GPU memory, and public metrics while I injected paired lifecycle failures:

| Scenario | What the external recorder observed | Top-level exit |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Intentional API-server `SIGTERM` | `process_exit` | 0 |
| EngineCore `SIGKILL` | `/health` reached 503, then `process_exit` | 0 |
| One-shot `execute_model` CUDA OOM | request 500; `/health` 503, then connection refusal | 0 |

The external recorder preserved when health or process state was lost, but it could not identify the internal fatal kind or stage, and it could not reliably distinguish intentional shutdown from abrupt EngineCore loss. The uniform exit code 0 did not distinguish the cases either; that is the separate lifecycle defect tracked by #48966. The CUDA OOM was a deterministic one-shot source-level injection, not an organic allocator-exhaustion result. The tested build predates the launcher fix proposed in #52178: that PR addresses the exit-code/restart contract, while this RFC addresses the missing-evidence contract.

This boundary experiment supports two complementary producers, not a choice in which one replaces the other. An external observer can remain available when an internal thread stalls or a process disappears; an EngineCore-owned recorder can add a typed trigger and iteration context for failures that reach a fatal handler, as the injected CUDA OOM did. A separate TP fault-injection run observed worker-loss propagation through the executor. Direct EngineCore `SIGKILL` is instead a negative boundary case: the killed process cannot publish its own artifact, and v1 does not claim otherwise. The experiment does **not** prove that the resulting internal artifact improves diagnosis. That utility must be established with real artifacts and issue uptake.

The proposed v1 is an opt-in experimental preview. It retains a strict aggregate projection of the most recent completed EngineCore iterations and writes one small, versioned JSON artifact on a fatal EngineCore failure. It does not record prompts, generated text, token IDs, request IDs, sampling parameters, block IDs, structured-output schemas, paths, environment dumps, exception messages, or arbitrary object representations. When disabled, it allocates no ring and computes no statistics solely for this feature.

The immediate consumer is an operator or external orchestrator deciding what evidence to collect next and whether the first fault domain is scheduler/KV pressure, model execution, worker/executor loss, or local persistence. The artifact may inform existing restart, routing, rebalancing, and capacity decisions; it does not execute remediation or claim a final line-level root cause.

A [provider-internal study of 156 high-severity LLM inference incidents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07424) classified approximately 60% at the inference-engine layer and documents traffic routing, node rebalancing, and capacity changes among practical mitigations. This supports the layer and consumer workflow, not a claim that this fatal-only v1 covers 60% of incidents.

The external boundary harness is now a runnable, independently maintained [vLLM Runtime Reliability Lab](https://github.com/jackLei0901/vllm-runtime-reliability-lab). Its current evidence validates bounded external capture and failure isolation, plus a [single-GPU health-green no-progress boundary experiment](https://github.com/jackLei0901/vllm-runtime-reliability-lab/blob/b5f99d3/experiments/vllm-zmq-event-backpressure/STAGE1_R3_RESULT_2026-09-16.md) on #53859: with a paused KV-event consumer, token progress stopped while `/health` remained 2xx and an external stack located EngineCore in `Queue.put()`; the same-base #53883 arm preserved progress by dropping event batches. This establishes a bounded external observation capability under a deterministic trigger. It does not validate the proposed internal Snapshot, reliable event delivery, the reported DP-wide consequence, or a general production no-progress detector. Cross-process correlation remains a future gate. The full internal schema, provenance records, pilot limitations, fault-injection results, test plan, resource rationale, historical coverage protocol, prior-art audit, and longer evolution path are in the revision-pinned [evidence and design appendix](https://gist.github.com/jackLei0901/10840b4c04f434efc012918ac51dac12/8355ab2bdabcc5c3c399c19541812e4a98f69bb7). This issue keeps only the information needed to decide whether the v1 ownership boundary is appropriate.

### Proposed Change.

#### v1 contract

```text
completed EngineCore iteration
  -> typed allow-listed projection
  -> fixed-size in-memory ring

fatal EngineCore handler
  -> typed trigger {kind, stage, exception type}
  -> idempotent capture_once()
  -> bounded local JSON write
  -> original exception still propagates
```

EngineCore owns three internal responsibilities without adding a public plugin API:

- `IncidentRecorder`: safe projection, local sequence, bounded ring, and recorder-health counters;
- `TriggerContext`: fatal kind/stage, incident ID, and idempotent capture;
- `IncidentWriter`: encoding, size enforcement, atomic publication, and bounded failure handling.

The recorder is single-writer: `record()` is called only from the EngineCore busy loop after a model-executing iteration completes. It performs no file I/O, IPC, blocking synchronization, or cross-rank communication on the normal path. Projection or append failure must not alter inference; the last valid ring remains available and dropped production is counted when possible.

The initial fatal call sites are the model-execution error path and the outer EngineCore process exception path. `capture_once()` prevents nested handlers from emitting duplicate artifacts. Normal SIGTERM, SIGINT, and graceful shutdown do not trigger a fatal snapshot. Existing logs remain responsible for the human-readable traceback.

The proposed configuration is deliberately small:

```text
--runtime-incident-snapshot-dir PATH   # unset = disabled
--runtime-incident-history-size 256
--runtime-incident-max-files 4
```

Each EngineCore writes to a feature-owned rank-local subdirectory. Startup validates the directory, removes stale feature-owned temporary files, and rotates completed artifacts before accepting work. If it cannot maintain the configured cap, the recorder is disabled for that process and emits a warning; rotation is never attempted from the fatal path.

#### Artifact and privacy boundary

The top-level v1 object contains only:

```text
schema_version, component_type, created_at, incident_id,
trigger, runtime, config, history[], recorder, writer
```

History is aggregate, not per-request. It may include the local sequence, time relative to the trigger, running/waiting counts, KV-cache utilization, aggregate prefill/decode counts and tokens, iteration/model-execution timing already available in process, preemption delta, and model-executed/dummy flags. An unavailable value is `null`, never a fabricated zero.

`runtime` is limited to the vLLM version/commit, an ephemeral engine-instance hash, and DP/TP/PP shape. `config` is limited to typed execution-shape fields such as dtype, quant_method, model architecture, sequence/batch limits, KV-cache allocation controls, eager mode, and attention backend. It contains no hostname, device serial, PID, model path, CLI dump, or environment dump.

The included JSON Schema is normative and uses `additionalProperties: false` at every object boundary. The implementation must construct typed projections and must not call generic `__dict__`, `repr()`, or recursive dump helpers. A standing CI canary test places unique sensitive values in request and configuration locations and asserts that neither artifact keys nor bytes contain them.

The writer performs one bounded synchronous local write because a daemon thread may not finish before process exit. It encodes only allow-listed fields, drops oldest history if needed to remain at or below 256 KiB, creates a unique `0600` temporary file (`O_EXCL`, and `O_NOFOLLOW` where supported), and publishes with `os.replace()`. A feature-created directory uses mode `0700`. v1 does not call `fsync()`. Any encode, write, or replace failure produces only a bounded warning and never replaces or suppresses the original fatal exception.

An enabled recorder emits one readiness log and exposes monotonic appended/dropped health totals through an existing stats path; it introduces no thread or transport solely for self-observability. Successful publication emits `incident_id` in the fatal log and filename for correlation. The exact Prometheus spelling should follow the naming direction resolved by #51186 rather than establish a competing convention.

#### Scope and failure boundaries

v1 covers fatal state observable inside EngineCore. API-server, authentication, request-parsing, and other frontend failures that never reach EngineCore are out of scope. Timeout/no-progress detection is also out of scope because it requires a separate progress definition, threshold, false-positive policy, and distributed coordination contract. The external lab may investigate that separate problem without expanding this RFC's v1 contract.

An in-process recorder cannot publish after SIGKILL, system/cgroup OOM kill, native process crash, or a hard hang before a fatal handler runs. That is a structural limitation, not something writer retries can fix. The typed projection should remain transport-neutral so a later supervisor-owned or shared-memory recorder can reuse it, but crash-resilient transport, DP aggregation, NCCL/GPU artifacts, automatic upload, stable fleet signatures, and remediation are not part of v1.

For TP, a worker failure propagated through the executor may produce one EngineCore artifact containing `tp_size`; exception strings are never parsed for rank identity. For DP, each rank may eventually write a rank-local artifact, but v1 performs no failure-time collective or merge.

#### Acceptance gates

The feature should not move into EngineCore merely because the design is complete. vLLM previously added automatic crash input dumps in #8305 and removed them in #12582 after reporters did not attach the output; #13407 later restored a narrower V1 metadata dump. To avoid repeating that maintenance-without-usage outcome, I propose the following order:

1. Keep the published external lab independent and use it to validate the observer boundary, non-interference, overhead, and failure-injection method. Its external schema is not evidence that the proposed EngineCore fields are useful.
2. If EngineCore ownership is acceptable in principle, build a small **out-of-tree internal preview** instrumented at the fatal boundary and publish its schema/privacy, bounded-retention, writer-non-interference, fault-injection, single-GPU/TP=2, and enabled/disabled overhead results.
3. Run the frozen 15??0-case historical schema-coverage audit over resolved public vLLM incidents. It uses no invented Snapshot values and can measure only whether proposed fields address documented blocking questions??ot diagnostic accuracy or time saved.
4. Collect real internal-preview artifacts where possible and record whether an artifact changed the next diagnostic action or avoided a reproduction.
5. Only then open an upstream implementation PR. Release it as opt-in preview and review public uptake after two releases or about six months; simplify, externalize, or remove it if valid artifacts do not inform diagnosis.

The earlier author-run pilot is intentionally weak evidence: one KV-pressure/preemption case gained useful ordered context, while abrupt worker loss and a reported forward-pass CUDA OOM did not show an incremental first-domain benefit over existing logs. That negative result narrows the expected value to sequence-dependent incidents. A four-reviewer blinded drill remains desirable but is no longer an open-ended prerequisite; difficulty recruiting reviewers is not itself evidence for or against utility.

Proposed implementation budgets are a 256-iteration default, a 256 KiB artifact cap, four files per EngineCore rank, enabled append P99 below 10 microseconds in a host microbenchmark, and less than 0.5% TPOT/throughput impact in interleaved decode-heavy tests. These are acceptance targets, not measured upstream results, and the history size must be revisited using the wall-clock window retained by a real per-iteration recorder.

#### Primary decision

**Does vLLM want an opt-in, bounded EngineCore incident recorder that captures only allow-listed aggregate state on fatal failures, or should it remain an out-of-tree/downstream tool because local diagnostic persistence is outside EngineCore's ownership?**

If EngineCore ownership is acceptable in principle, secondary details such as reuse of #52061, synchronous local write without `fsync()`, coordination with #47368, and the internal writer seam can be resolved before an implementation PR. If it is not, the external lab will continue under its separate `external-runtime-observation-v1` contract; the proposed internal schema will remain a research artifact rather than being presented as external evidence.

### Feedback Period.

I propose a two-week feedback period after this concise revision. I will not open an upstream EngineCore implementation PR until a maintainer confirms that the ownership boundary is acceptable. Work on the out-of-tree preview and evidence collection does not depend on that approval.

### CC List.

Suggested focused CC: @njhill for EngineCore/lifecycle ownership and @tedzhouhk for coordination with #52061.

### Any Other Things.

A duplicate-work search was performed on 2026-08-28 and is documented in the pinned appendix. The proposal is adjacent to, but does not duplicate, #52061 (per-iteration metrics transport), #53550 (Prometheus distributions), #48292 (iteration-detail logging), #47364/#47368 (privacy in the existing recursive crash dump), #51186 (OTel metric naming), or #52178/#48966 (fatal exit semantics).

Relevant design precedents include the [PyTorch ProcessGroupNCCL Flight Recorder](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/unstable/flight_recorder_tutorial.html), its [cross-rank analysis and stated CPU main-thread-stack gap](https://pytorch.org/blog/flight-recorder-a-new-lens-for-understanding-nccl-watchdog-timeouts/), its [sequence-ID limitation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/125173), [SGLang's detection-only NCCL RAS proposal](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/32928), [Java Flight Recorder configurations](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/jfapi/flight-recorder-configurations.html), and [Crashpad's handler separation](https://chromium.googlesource.com/crashpad/crashpad/+/main/doc/overview_design.md). PyTorch's missing distributed CPU-stack view is a candidate for the external lab's future correlation work, not part of this fatal-only v1. These precedents inform bounds and extension seams; they are not evidence that this specific artifact is useful in vLLM.

AI assistance was used for drafting, code and document review, and test-harness iteration. The proposal, source boundaries, claims, and submission decisions were reviewed by the author.

title: [RFC]: Reduced sampling for tensor-parallel decoding
author: hzx55906
body:
### Motivation.

Tensor-parallel vocabulary projection produces one vocabulary shard per TP rank. The current sampling path gathers all shards before selecting the next token, resulting in `O(B × V)` communication per sampling step.

This is unnecessary for several common workloads:

- Greedy decoding only needs the global argmax.
- Bounded top-k sampling only needs the global top-k candidate set.
- Greedy speculative verification only needs one target argmax per position.

This RFC proposes a generic reduced sampling path that avoids full-vocabulary communication when possible and safely falls back otherwise.

### Proposed Change.

Add an opt-in flag:

```text
--enable-reduced-sampling
```

The feature is disabled by default and initially requires:

- Model Runner V2.
- Tensor parallel size greater than one.
- Standard vocab-parallel logits heads.
- The built-in sampler.

### Local-logits capture

While `model.compute_logits()` runs, the common `LogitsProcessor` may skip the TP gather and expose:

- Shard-local logits.
- Global vocabulary size.
- The shard's starting global token ID.
- Local padded vocabulary size.

Local logits are accepted only when exactly one standard projection is captured and the returned Tensor matches the captured result.

Models with missing metadata, added vocabulary, multiple projections, or unsupported postprocessing use the normal full-logits path. This avoids adding `compute_logits_local()` to individual model files.

### Greedy sampling

Each rank computes its local maximum and global token ID. The ranks gather only these candidate pairs and select the global maximum.

```text
Full logits: O(B × V)
Reduced:     O(B × TP)
```

### Bounded random sampling

For finite top-k sampling, each rank gathers its local top-k values and global token IDs. Global top-k/top-p filtering and Gumbel sampling then run on the combined candidates.

```text
Full logits: O(B × V)
Reduced:     O(B × K × TP)
```

The reduced path is used only when its communication payload is smaller than gathering the local full-vocabulary logits.

Random requests with explicit seeds fall back because the reduced candidate positions do not preserve the existing full-vocabulary Gumbel RNG mapping.

### Speculative decoding

Reduced speculative verification is supported when:

- All target requests are greedy.
- Draft sampling is greedy.
- Synthetic conditional rates are disabled.
- The built-in rejection sampler is used.

A Triton kernel compares draft tokens with the reduced target argmaxes and returns the accepted prefix, first rejected target token, or bonus token.

Probabilistic target or draft sampling continues to use the existing full-vocabulary rejection sampler.

### Fallback policy

Fallback is evaluated for the whole sampler batch. Full logits are used when any active request needs:

- Logit bias, allowed-token filtering, bad words, or penalties.
- Thinking budgets, `min_p`, grammar, or structured output.
- Logprobs, explicit logprob token IDs, NaN counting, or distribution replay.
- Random sampling without bounded top-k or with an explicit seed.
- Probabilistic speculative decoding.
- Unsupported model/head metadata.
- Candidate communication that would not be smaller.

The configuration is rejected for Model Runner V1, TP=1, batch-sharded sampling, LoRA, diffusion models, and custom samplers.

### Correctness and limitations

For unique maxima, reduced greedy sampling returns the same global argmax as the full-logits path.

For bounded random sampling, the global top-k candidate set is preserved unless exact logits ties occur at the cutoff. The current full path may retain all cutoff ties, while reduced sampling selects exactly K local candidates. Handling these ties through detection or fallback remains an open question.

Random reduced sampling targets the same distribution outside tie cases but does not guarantee bit-for-bit equality with every existing backend.

The capture mechanism detects out-of-place model postprocessing. An out-of-tree model that mutates the same Tensor in place may require a future explicit local-logits API.

### Alternatives considered

- Model-specific `compute_logits_local()`: rejected as the primary design because it requires changes across model families.
- Batch-sharded sampling: retained as a separate, mutually exclusive strategy.
- Always gathering top-k candidates: rejected because large K can communicate more data than full logits.
- Probabilistic speculative reduction: deferred because exact rejection sampling requires complete probability distributions.

### Rollout and validation

1. Introduce the feature behind an opt-in flag.
2. Validate greedy and speculative exact-match behavior on TP=2+.
3. Validate random sampling distributions and every fallback condition.
4. Measure latency, throughput, NCCL traffic, and peak memory.
5. Add observability for reduced-path hits and fallback reasons.
6. Consider broader support or default enablement only after validation.

### Feedback Period.

Proposed period: August 29, 2026 through September 12, 2026.

### CC List.

TODO: Add Model Runner V2, sampler, speculative decoding, and distributed communication maintainers.

### Any Other Things.

Prototype PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54332

The implementation does not modify individual model files and retains full logits as the correctness and peak-memory fallback.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Data integrity and I/O liveness for the filesystem KV offload tier
author: zdtsw
body:
### Motivation.

The filesystem secondary tier (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/`) is a data path with no integrity verification and no bound on how long a single I/O operation may take. #49328 established the partial-keep contract this builds on: a failed load marks its own cached lookup verdict a miss and reports how many blocks loaded before the failure, so earlier blocks survive. Two gaps remain on top of that:

1. **No data integrity verification.** Block contents written to the filesystem tier are never checksummed. `_load_block` detects a file shorter than `block_size` and deletes it, so truncation is caught. What is not caught is content that is the right length and the wrong bytes: bit rot on the storage device, a partially rewritten file, or a block written by an instance whose layout differs in a way the `FileMapper` path hash does not capture. Such a block is copied into the primary tier and consumed as attention KV, producing wrong logits with no error signal anywhere in the system.

2. **No deadline on filesystem I/O.** `batch_store_block` and `batch_load_block` run as a single pool task per job with no deadline. A stalled NFS mount, hung FUSE filesystem, or a device in error recovery blocks that pool thread indefinitely. The pool is bounded at `n_read_threads` + `n_write_threads` (16 + 16 by default), and read-priority threads fall back to the store queue and vice versa, so ~32 stuck operations stall all tiering traffic in both directions. This is the tier-side half of the problem reported in #49829: that issue bounds how long the scheduler waits on a `HIT_PENDING` block, but nothing bounds the write it is waiting for.

Two smaller gaps follow from the same code path:

1. **Stale temporary files are never reclaimed.** `_store_block` writes to `<dest>_<random>.tmp` and `os.replace` it, cleaning up the temp file if the write raises. If the engine dies between the two (OOM kill, SIGKILL, node preemption), the temp file survives with nothing that will ever remove it. On a long-lived shared PVC these accumulate without bound.

2. **No errno-based error classification.** Both the C and Python I/O paths already surface `errno` (`PyErr_SetFromErrnoWithFilename` in `csrc/fs_io.cpp`), and partial progress is already reported (`exc.num_succeeded` -> `JobResult.successful_keys`, added in #49328). Nothing consumes the errno. A transient `ESTALE` on an NFS remount is treated identically to a permanent `ENOSPC`: the remaining keys in the batch are marked a miss and recomputed.

These matter most on shared or network filesystems (NFS, POSIX PVCs), which the tier explicitly supports: `FileSystemTierManager` documents cross-instance cache sharing over a common `root_dir`.

### Proposed Change.

Four changes, each independently. Every one of them touches both I/O implementations: `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/io.py` is a pure-Python fallback, and `csrc/fs_io.cpp` (built as `vllm.fs_io_C`) is the path actually taken whenever the extension imports. 

### 1. Block-level checksum validation
**What:** Compute a CRC32C over each block when storing it to the filesystem tier, persist it with the block, and verify it on load. A mismatch deletes the file and marks the key a miss rather than returning corrupt KV.
**Design:**
- **Placement, given O_DIRECT.** The tier prefers `O_DIRECT` and falls back to buffered I/O only where the probe fails, so block payloads must stay length- and offset-aligned. A 4-byte trailer appended to the payload breaks that alignment for every block. Two viable options, and choosing between them is the main open question for this item:
  - *Padded trailer:* store the checksum in a full logical block appended after the payload, keeping the payload aligned. Costs one extra device block (512 B or 4 KiB) per file, where a file holds `blocks_per_chunk` blocks. This overhead is the main argument for the sidecar.
  - *Sidecar directory:* keep checksums in a separate file keyed by the same hash. Preserves the payload byte-for-byte, but loses the single-rename atomicity that `os.replace` gives today.
- **Verification point.** `_load_block` reads via `os.readv` directly into the primary tier's memoryview slice, so a block cannot be verified before it lands there. Verification happens after the read and before the key is reported as a successful load, and a mismatch is reported through the existing `num_succeeded` partial-keep path so preceding blocks in the batch are still kept.
- **On-disk format versioning.** `FileMapper._compute_base_path` derives the storage directory from a SHA-256 of `FileMapper.fields`. Enabling checksums changes the on-disk format, so it must add a field there. Without it, a cache directory written before the upgrade is read as if it carried checksums, and every block fails verification. This is a one-line change and the reason the item touches `file_mapper.py`.
- **Algorithm.** CRC32C is hardware-accelerated on x86 (SSE 4.2) and ARM (CRC extension) and is straightforward to implement in `csrc/fs_io.cpp` alongside the existing I/O, which avoids adding a Python dependency for the fast path.
- **Config:** `checksum_blocks: bool = False` as a `FileSystemTierManager` kwarg, plumbed through the tier config dict that `SecondaryTierFactory.create_secondary_tier` splats into the constructor. Defaulting to off keeps the change inert until the storage-overhead and throughput numbers are on the table.
- **Metric:** `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_checksum_failures`, labeled by tier. Existing counters in this subsystem are unsuffixed (`..._cascade_job_failures`, `..._promotion_job_failures`); `vllm:kv_offload_cpu_evictions_total` is the sole `_total` user, so this follows the local majority.

### 2. I/O deadline for filesystem jobs
**What:** Give each enqueued filesystem job a deadline. When it expires, report the job as failed to the tiering manager so the scheduler stops waiting, and account for the fact that the worker thread may still be blocked.
**Design:**
- Add a monotonic deadline to `JobState` at enqueue time. A periodic check in `DualQueueThreadPool.get_finished()` (the pool's own method; the tier-level API is `get_finished_jobs()`) publishes expired jobs to `_finished_q`.
- **Reconciling a reaped job is the core problem, not the timer.** `JobState.task_done` publishes a job when `_completed == _n_tasks` and decrements `_inflight_jobs` there. If the reaper publishes a job and its stuck task later completes, the job is published twice and `_inflight_jobs` goes negative, which breaks the `wait_idle()` that `drain_jobs()` and `shutdown()` depend on. The proposal is a terminal flag on `JobState`: the first publisher wins, the second is dropped, and `_inflight_jobs` is decremented exactly once. Reviewers should push on this part first.
- **Interrupting the I/O.** A blocked `os.write`/`os.readv` cannot be interrupted from Python, and the C path releases the GIL for the entire batch with no cancellation check, so a flag polled between blocks only works if `csrc/fs_io.cpp` grows one. Even then it cannot preempt a syscall already blocked in the kernel. The honest scope is: the deadline unblocks the *scheduler* promptly; the thread stays stuck until the filesystem returns. `p2p/manager.py::_reap_unbound_stores` is the in-tree precedent for this shape.
- **Config:** `io_timeout_seconds: float | None = None` (off by default) as a `FileSystemTierManager` kwarg.
- **Metric:** `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_io_timeouts`, labeled by tier and direction.

### 3. Stale temporary file cleanup
**What:** Reclaim `*.tmp` files left behind by a crashed engine.
**Design:**
- **A blind sweep at startup is not safe.** `FileSystemTierManager` documents cross-process cache sharing over a common `root_dir`, and `FileMapper` is constructed with `parallel_agnostic=True`, which forces `rank` to 0 for qualifying models. Multiple live instances therefore write into the same directory. Deleting every `*.tmp` at init would delete another running instance's in-flight temp files. The temp suffix is `_<random>.tmp` with no owner encoded, so ownership cannot be recovered from the name.
- Proposal: delete only temp files whose mtime is older than a conservative threshold (default 1 hour), which no in-flight write can plausibly reach. The `.o_direct_probe_<random>.tmp` files from `probe_o_direct` are covered by the same rule.
- Alternative worth discussing: encode the writing instance's identity in the temp suffix so a sweep can skip files belonging to a live PID. More precise, but does not help across containers or nodes, which is the deployment this tier targets.
- **Config:** `cleanup_stale_tmp_after_seconds: float | None = 3600.0`.

### 4. Transient error classification and retry
**What:** Use the `errno` already surfaced by both I/O paths to distinguish retryable from terminal failures, and retry the retryable ones once or twice before falling back to the existing partial-keep path.
**Design:**
- Classify: `EAGAIN`, `EIO`, `ESTALE`, `ETIMEDOUT`, `EINTR` retryable; `ENOSPC`, `EPERM`, `EACCES`, `ENOENT` terminal. `ENOENT` on load is an ordinary miss, not an error, and must not be retried. The open PR #52838 takes the same shape one layer up, dropping a failed store but escalating a failed load, and is worth keeping consistent with.
- Retry the failing block only, not the batch. `exc.num_succeeded` already identifies where the batch stopped, so a retry resumes there.
- Bound retries so they cannot extend a job past the item 2 deadline; a retry budget without a deadline reintroduces the unbounded wait this RFC is trying to remove. This is why this item lands last.
- **Metric:** `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_io_retries`, labeled by tier, direction, and errno.

### Out of scope: tracked in other threads
The following are deliberately excluded so this RFC does not duplicate or pre-empt work already under discussion. All are open issues rather than merged or in-flight changes, so none of the four items above depends on any of them landing.
- **Tier health tracking and circuit breaking.** Two RFCs already build per-tier gating: #50031 detects saturation from an EMA of store completion rate and drops cascade stores; #51240 defines a `TieringAdmissionPolicy` ABC and ships `CascadeBackpressurePolicy`, detecting saturation from an EMA of submission-to-completion latency and rejecting jobs in `should_admit`. #53485 exists to reconcile the two and argues #51240's hook is the integration point, since it is already wired into `create_store_job()`. An error-rate breaker is a different *signal* — a tier failing fast with `EIO` is not saturated, and neither EMA would trip — but it is the same *decision*, and `TieringAdmissionPolicy.on_completed(job, result)` already receives `JobResult.success`. It therefore belongs as a policy implementation under #51240 once that lands, not as a separate `health.py` and not as a section of this RFC. Metrics from items 1, 2, and 4 are what such a policy would act on.
- **Bounding how long the scheduler waits on an in-flight write.** #49829: `TieringOffloadingManager.lookup()` returns `HIT_PENDING` with no deadline and the scheduler re-polls in a hot loop, so a stalled write defers requests until the client timeout. Item 2 bounds the write itself. The two are complementary and neither subsumes the other.
- **Reclaiming leaked shared-memory segments after a crash.** #54002: `SharedOffloadRegion` never unlinks `/dev/shm/vllm_offload_<engine_id>.mmap`, and on Kubernetes `/dev/shm` survives container restarts, so a crash wedges the pod in CrashLoopBackOff. Same failure class as item 3 (an artifact outliving the process that made it) but a different artifact, a different owner, and a much sharper impact.
- **Recovering primary-tier ref-counts after a crash.** Not needed, and worth stating so reviewers do not ask. `CPUPrimaryTierOffloadingManager` inherits its block index and `ref_cnt` bookkeeping from `CPUOffloadingManager`, built in memory in `__init__` with no restore-from-disk path, and `SharedOffloadRegion` keys its backing file on `engine_id`, so a restarted engine gets a fresh region rather than reattaching to the old one. In-flight transfer state is therefore gone, not stale. The old region itself does leak, but that is the memory-reclamation problem in #54002, not a ref-count problem.

### Summary table
items are numbered in the order they should be merged, and the motivation list above uses the same numbering.
| Item | Needs a `csrc/fs_io.cpp` change | Priority |
|------|-------------------------------|----------|
| 1. Checksum validation | Yes | High — silent corruption has no error signal today |
| 2. I/O deadline | Yes, for a cancellation point | High — pool starvation stalls both directions |
| 3. Stale tmp cleanup | No | Medium — unbounded growth on shared PVCs |
| 4. Transient retry | Yes | Low — needs item 2's deadline to bound the retry budget |

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@varun-sundar-rabindranath 

### Any Other Things.

- Scope is the filesystem tier only. The P2P tier already has abort-on-timeout, abort-ack timeout, and `_reap_unbound_stores` in `p2p/manager.py`. The object store tier (`tiering/obj/`) would benefit from items 1 and 4 but is left out to keep each PR reviewable.
- Item 1 changes the on-disk format. Existing caches are not migrated: the `FileMapper` field change moves checksummed caches to a new directory, and operators enabling the flag start with a cold tier.
- Each PR adds unit tests for both the C and Python I/O paths. The existing `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_fs_tier.py` covers both and is the pattern to follow. Fault injection for items 2 and 4 needs a stub that blocks or returns a chosen errno, since a real stalled mount is not reproducible in CI.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: fp8_e4m3 KV cache on the QSA path — working patch, one machine, looking for corroboration
author: Nanetnounou
body:
## TL;DR

The QSA path of `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` refuses any KV dtype other than bf16. Most of
the machinery for fp8 is already in vLLM — only the **read** side of the QSA Triton
kernels was missing. Wiring it up roughly doubles the KV pool.

Measured on **one** GB10 (DGX Spark, sm_121):

| | bf16 | fp8_e4m3 | |
|---|---|---|---|
| KV pool | 780 638 tokens | **1 399 848** | ×1.79 |
| Max concurrency @ 262144 tok/req | 2.98× | **5.34×** | +79 % |
| Needle-in-a-haystack, 5 depths | — | **5/5** | |
| Decode, single stream, 100k ctx | — | 32.0 tok/s | no regression |

A working diff is here: https://gist.github.com/Nanetnounou/2e6486dd033bf077a9b8fdfcb6e1f7c8 (against vLLM `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`). **This is not a merge request yet** — see *What is not
tested* below. Posting it as an RFC because the interesting part may be the four
non-obvious integration points, and because a single machine is thin evidence.

## The problem

On a single 128 GB unified-memory box this model is attractive, but the KV pool
binds: at 262144 tokens per request the engine sustains ~3 concurrent requests, so
admission closes as soon as a queue forms — the normal regime under load, not an
incident.

`--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` fails with:

```
NotImplementedError: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next QSA requires a BF16 main KV cache
```

## What already worked

The change is small because most of it exists already:

| Piece | Before |
|---|---|
| `get_kv_cache_spec` passes `kv_quant_mode` | wired |
| `_k_scale` / `_v_scale` registered | wired |
| Quantised allocation | core |
| KV **write** via `reshape_and_cache_flash` | dtype-aware |
| KV **read** in QSA Triton kernels | **missing** |

The guards were doing the right thing: refusing rather than reading incorrectly.

## The four things that were not obvious

Sharing these because they are what cost the time, and none is visible from
reading the QSA sources alone.

1. **The cache is allocated as `uint8`**, not `float8_e4m3fn`. It needs
   `.view(torch.float8_e4m3fn)` before the kernel — exactly what `triton_attn.py`
   already does for unified attention. Without it, the kernel converts the
   *integer* rather than decoding the float.

2. **The block selector reads a different cache.** `qsa_mqa_paged` operates on the
   indexer's `raw_key_cache`, a separate tensor that follows the same dtype.
   Reinterpreting only the main cache left the selector reading bytes as floats,
   so it picked essentially arbitrary blocks. Outputs then diverged **from the
   first token** while the decode path was correct and the engine looked healthy.
   This was by far the hardest to find.

3. **Shared memory.** `_cast_kv_tile` materialises an fp32 tile, doubling shared
   memory for K and V. The kernel requested 106496 bytes against sm_121's 101376
   and failed to start. Halving `block_n` under quantisation fits.

4. **A guard inherited from `FlashAttentionImpl`** rejects a quantised cache
   because *its* kernels cannot read it on this device. QSA does not use them — it
   calls `qsa_sparse_paged_attention` in Triton and only inherits the surrounding
   plumbing.

## What the patch does

Reuses `_cast_kv_tile` from `triton_unified_attention.py` in both QSA kernels
rather than writing a second dequantisation; reinterprets `uint8` for both the
main and the indexer cache; halves `block_n` under quantisation; relaxes the
dtype guards. Inert in bf16 — `KV_QUANT_MODE` is a `constexpr`, so the branch is
compiled out.

89 added / 12 removed, across two files — [diff](https://gist.github.com/Nanetnounou/2e6486dd033bf077a9b8fdfcb6e1f7c8).

## On throughput — we do not claim a win

At typical context lengths the KV is a small fraction of the bytes read per token
compared with the active weights (this is an MoE: 6 B active of 176 B), so halving
it saves roughly 1–4 %. Decode measured 34.4 / 35.1 / 32.0 tok/s at 4k / 32k /
100k context: flat. The gain is **capacity**, not speed, and the numbers are given
to show absence of regression only.

## What is NOT tested

Being explicit, because this is the weak part:

- **One machine, one architecture** (sm_121). The AMD QSA owner carries the same
  guards and was left untouched.
- **No long-run soak.** On this same model a prefix-caching bug once booted fine,
  served ~105k reused tokens, then died on an illegal memory access. Twenty
  minutes of tests say nothing about two hours.
- **bf16 no-op not verified on a live engine** — only on synthetic tensors. The
  claim that the patch is inert in bf16 is reasoned, not measured end to end.
- **Prefix-cache hit vs miss not compared** under fp8.
- **fp8_e4m3 only**, per-tensor scales only. nvfp4 would be separate work: there is
  no Triton dequantisation to reuse for it in-tree (the only NVFP4 KV path is in
  the FlashInfer backend), and it needs 4-bit unpacking with nested fp8 scales.

Those tests are being run; results will be posted here. If the patch is useful,
they should land before any merge request.

## What would help

- Anyone with a second sm_121 box: does the pool roughly double for you too?
- Anyone on other hardware: does the guard removal hold, or does something else
  break first?
- Maintainers: is reusing `_cast_kv_tile` across model-specific kernels the
  intended direction, or is a QSA-local helper preferred?

## Prior art

The same idea was implemented independently for SGLang on a two-node setup, which
was a useful signal that a quantised KV is viable on this architecture at all.
That work upcasts K/V to fp32 in-kernel; this patch keeps vLLM's own convention
(`_cast_kv_tile` scales in fp32 and returns at the query dtype) so the QSA path
stays aligned with the rest of the tree.

title: [RFC]: Weight version attribution for RL rollouts and Background survey
author: ShuoleiWang
body:
_Revision 2 (2026-09-28): re-anchored on #48305 §3.8 after #48306 closed; spans are always returned; no request-level scalar; KV provenance is out of scope; corrected the `keep`/`clear_cache` description._

## Motivation

vLLM reports one engine-wide weight-version label (`/weight_info`, #49040), but it does not say which weights produced a given output.

#48305 §3.8 ("Per-Request Weight Provenance") asks for exactly that, at token granularity:
- contiguous `[start, end)` ranges of generated tokens;
- each range tagged with the version used by the model computation;
- together covering every output token and its logprob exactly once;
- a defined contract for streaming, speculative decoding and DP.

This RFC is the design for that item, and it asks for decisions on the points §3.8 leaves open.

### Requests straddle weight updates

`docs/training/async_rl.md` describes `pause(mode="keep")` → update → `resume` as the typical async RL flow. A kept request produces tokens from the old weights before the pause and from the new weights after it. `keep` has two KV variants:

| `pause(mode="keep", ...)` | Running requests after resume |
|---|---|
| `clear_cache=True` (default) | Preempted ([`_finish_pause` → `_reset_caches()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d6cce94fd4221e6f5547e1c00ca5e0c92ab52d6c/vllm/v1/engine/core.py#L874-L879)). On resume their KV is recomputed with the new weights, or loaded from a KV connector that kept an old copy (#57970). |
| `clear_cache=False` | The KV computed with the old weights is kept, and new tokens attend to it. |

The `/pause` docstring still says `clear_cache` is ignored under `keep`. #57970 (draft) fixes the docs, and #57810 fixes that docstring.

Nothing tells the caller where the boundary fell.
