The official example infers it by sleeping five seconds after pausing and then counting streamed tokens ([`rlhf_async_new_apis.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d6cce94fd4221e6f5547e1c00ca5e0c92ab52d6c/examples/rl/rlhf_async_new_apis.py#L111-L117)).

Requests admitted during the pause wait in the queue and are then served entirely by the new weights (#51476; #51488 keeps that behavior for `keep`).

prime-rl, SkyRL and PipelineRL use `keep` on their async update paths and retain KV by default, and so does NeMo-RL when in-flight weight updates are enabled. #58041 describes the same setup for GLM-5.3 with P/D.

### Existing signals are not enough

Take request R. It generates tokens `[0, 57)` under v7, the weights become v8, and it generates `[57, 128)` under v8.

- `/weight_info` returns v8, the engine's label at query time.
- Draft #53199 records v7, the label at admission. For a request that waited in the queue across the update, that label names weights that produced none of its tokens.
- The controller knows which version it dispatched. It does not know which version was live on a given replica when a token was sampled. Delayed or failed replica updates, DP, P/D and `keep` all break that link, and the fact is gone once the step is over.

Only the engine can record this. Today, token-level attribution requires patching vLLM, and each patch uses its own encoding:
- PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-rl#2957 (a closed prototype): version segments on the `/inference/v1/generate` choice.
- ServiceNow/PipelineRL#150 (`fast-llm` branch): a per-token version appended to each OpenAI chat logprob token string.
- OpenPipe/ART: its own `policy_token_spans`.

Other frameworks record coarser versions on the client side: request start and end versions on chat responses in NVIDIA-NeMo/RL#4146 (draft), and a version-keyed `cache_salt` in SkyRL.

### What this is, and is not

The span shape is SGLang's `weight_versions` (sgl-project/sglang#35926, consumed by radixark/miles#1891), so frameworks can share one parser. On top of that shape, this RFC adds a native output-attribution contract to vLLM, with the capture point, the boundary definition, delivery (final output only, including aborts) and `n > 1` written down and tested.

The metadata is a filtering, masking and audit signal:
- **Freshness filtering by the oldest version.** GLM-5 records `(w0, …, wk)` per response and drops it when `current − w0 > τ`.
- **Token-level staleness masking**, as in DeepSeek-V4.1 §5.2.2 and areal-project/AReaL#1722.
- **Per-segment replay** of `routed_experts` and `sampling_mask` for samples that span checkpoints (DeepSeek-V4.1 §5.2.1). This needs the offsets, not just a list of versions.
- **Auditing** partial fleet updates.

It is not an off-policy correction; that stays on rollout logprobs, `routed_experts` and `sampling_mask`. Freshness thresholds, global version assignment and update coordination stay with the RL controller.

A span names the target weights that ran a step. It does not certify which weights computed the KV that the span's tokens attended to:
- With `keep` and `clear_cache=False`, the spans after a boundary attended to KV retained from the older version.
- Salting requests with the weight version (`cache_salt`) prevents new requests from reusing prefix-cache blocks across versions. It does not refresh KV that a kept request already holds.
- P/D version skew and external KV tiers belong to #48312 (cache coherence).

## Proposed Change

### Output

The final output of every output sequence carries `weight_versions`, a list of spans over its output tokens. There is one span per version, so the size grows with updates, not tokens:

```json
"weight_versions": [
  {"version": "v7", "start": 0,  "end": 57},
  {"version": "v8", "start": 57, "end": 128}
]
```

| Case | `weight_versions` |
|---|---|
| No update while the request ran | `[{v7, 0, n}]` |
| Running when a `keep` pause starts, like R (either `clear_cache` value) | `[{v7, 0, 57}, {v8, 57, 128}]` |
| Admitted during the pause | `[{v8, 0, n}]` |
| No output tokens | `[]` |

It is always returned on `CompletionOutput` and on `/inference/v1/generate` choices. OpenAI chat and completions return it on each choice only when the request asks for it, like `return_token_ids`.

### Contract

1. **Coverage.** Each output sequence, including each `n > 1` child, has its own list. Spans are half-open ranges over output-token indexes (prompt excluded), contiguous and in generation order, and together cover every returned token and logprob exactly once. Adjacent spans with the same label merge; A → B → A gives three spans. `routed_experts` rows use their own coordinates and must be converted before slicing.
2. **Capture.** `version` is the label of the target weights whose forward pass sampled the token: under DP, the label of the engine that ran the request; under P/D, the decode instance's label. It is stamped when the step is scheduled, so in-flight steps keep their label. It does not say which weights computed the KV that the token attended to.
3. **Boundaries.** A new span starts when the engine's committed label changes: after a successful update that carries a label, or after `update_weight_version`. The label changes in the same EngineCore call that finishes the update. Failed and draft-only updates leave it unchanged; keeping a partially updated model from serving is #48312's job. Any request that crosses a change gets one span per version, whatever the pause mode: `wait` drains running requests, not preempted ones. LoRA adapters swapped without a pause are not covered until adapters have versions (#48297).
4. **Delivery.** Only on the final output, including aborted ones. Streaming sends it on the last chunk, with offsets over the whole output; streaming-input sessions send it at the end of each input chunk.
5. **Labels.** Opaque strings set by the caller; vLLM never orders them. There is no request-level scalar: `[0]` is the first token's version and `[-1]` the last, and neither is necessarily the oldest. An engine argument sets the initial label; `"default"` means unknown. §3.8's `model_id` (the served model or LoRA adapter) cannot change within a sequence, so it stays at the sequence level.

### Implementation

EngineCore stamps its label on each scheduled step, and every finish path (Python, the Ray client, the Rust server) passes the new label into the finish call. The scheduler attaches the label to `EngineCoreOutput` only when it changes for a request, and `OutputProcessor` turns those change points into spans on the final output. The Rust engine-core client decodes `EngineCoreOutput` too, so its protocol struct changes in the same PR; Rust frontend responses and gRPC follow under #44280. This reuses the transport of #53199, but records the label of the step that ran rather than the label at admission, per `CompletionOutput` rather than per request.

## CC List.

@aoshen02

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Direct Weight Reload for RL Training
author: aoshen02
body:
> **Revision 2 (2026-10-27).** Rewritten after validating direct reload on 17 flagship families.
>
> Rev 1 classified the 88 PWAL implementations so that most modules would skip post-load processing on reload. That skip caused silent errors: MLA absorbed weights went stale, and loaders that bypass tracking were missed. Rev 2 drops the skip, so every module reruns cold-start post-load processing.
>
> Rev 1 is in the edit history. #59502 was closed in favor of this design.
>
> **Update (2026-10-27, later).** The work is split into PRs and the PR stack is validated on DeepSeek-V4.1, MiniMax-M3.1, Muse Spark and gpt-oss (Validation → PR stack). Derived tensors now go through `refill_derived` instead of widening `replace_parameter`, so F6 is dropped.

## TL;DR

After a weight update, the engine must serve exactly what a cold start on the new checkpoint would serve, and the cold-start CUDA graphs must stay valid. `VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct` does this with three rules:

1. **View back.** At begin, each tensor is reinterpreted in its own storage as its checkpoint layout: the shape, stride and dtype recorded at cold start. Nothing is allocated.
2. **Rerun cold start.** The model's own `load_weights` writes the new bytes in place. At finish, every module reruns its cold-start post-load processing (PWAL), then the model-level hooks run. Nothing is skipped, so correctness equals cold start by construction.
3. **Derived state stays at its address.** Some tensors that a kernel or CUDA graph reads are derived from the weights: kernel constants, `1/a_scale`, absorbed MLA weights, decode copies. They are written back into their existing storage: parameters with `replace_parameter`, buffers and plain attributes with `refill_derived`, and the constants of MoE experts objects (rebuilt on every rerun) are kept on the layer with `keep_constants`. There is no generic pinning and no kernel refresh API: the code that derives a value keeps its address.

## Lifecycle

```text
cold start: load_weights -> record each tensor's checkpoint layout -> PWAL -> capture CUDA graphs
update:
  begin   view every tensor back to its checkpoint layout (same storage)
  load    model.load_weights(bucket) for each bucket, written in place
  finish  rerun PWAL for every module, then model-level hooks
```

The RL-facing API is unchanged: `start_weight_update`, then any number of `update_weights` calls, then `finish_weight_update`, over NCCL, IPC or disk.

## Contract for trainers

- Send checkpoint-format tensors under their checkpoint names, exactly as a checkpoint on disk would hold them.
- Send every module whose post-load processing changes its layout (quantized weights, transposes, swizzles). An unsent module keeps its post-processed bytes, which the rerun then treats as checkpoint bytes and processes again: tensors stay bit-identical in shape, but values are wrong.
- Modules without such processing may be left out, for example DeepSeek-V4.1 Engram embedding tables, Qwen3.8 PLE tables, and MTP layers the trainer does not train. The target never loads MTP layers, and a draft model is touched only in a draft update session.
- DeepSeek-V4.1: the Engram tables may be left out, but `engram.wkv` (weight and scale) must be sent. It is an FP8 block-scaled linear whose post-load processing changes its layout; leaving it out costs about 3 GSM8K points with every tensor shape intact.

## Tracker

PRs, families and follow-ups are tracked in [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54477#issuecomment-6450991360).

## Validation

Each run does same-weight updates, 3 per run, and checks two things:

- every tensor matches the pre-update state (diff 0);
- GSM8K before and after the update matches (chat API for chat models).

| Family | Format | GSM8K pre → post | Time per update |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | MXFP4 MoE + MLA, Engram not sent | 0.905 → 0.906 | 17 s |
| Kimi-K3 | BF16, TP8 × 2 nodes | 0.951 → 0.948 | 105 s |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next | block FP8 | 0.969 → 0.976 | 33 s |
| GLM-5.3-Flash | block FP8 + MLA | 0.916 → 0.921 | 12 s |
| MiniMax-M3.1 | NVFP4 (compressed-tensors) | 0.946 → 0.949 | 11 s |
| Nemotron-3.5-Lightning | NVFP4 (ModelOpt) | 0.851 → 0.848 | 4.3 s |
| Nemotron-3.5-Lightning | BF16 hybrid Mamba | 0.858 → 0.857 | 0.9 s |
| gpt-oss-120b | MXFP4 + SWA | 0.940 → 0.934 | 2.5 s |
| Beam | NVFP4 | 0.945 → 0.945 | 17 s |
| Gemma-4 | BF16 | 0.948 → 0.948 | 0.9 s |
| Ling-3 | BF16 MoE | 0.908 → 0.900 | 9 s |
| Hy4-preview | TP8 × PP2, 4 nodes | 0.901 → 0.910 | 4.7 s |
| Muse Spark | vendor image | 0.948 → 0.956 | — |
| Inkling | BF16, 1.77 TB | 0.889 → 0.892 | 4.0 s |
| MiMo-V2.6 | fused FP8 qkv | 0.917 → 0.920 | 8 s |
| Step-5 | NVFP4 | 0.923 → 0.930 | 14 s |
| dots3 | FP8 MLA + vision + audio | 0.952 → 0.952 | 9 s |

**PR stack.** The same checks on #57733 + #62407 + #58382 + aoshen02/vllm#179 + aoshen02/vllm#180 (+ aoshen02/vllm#175 for Muse), 3 updates per run, every tensor fingerprinted after each update:

| Family | Format | GSM8K pre → post | Tensors changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | MXFP4 MoE + MLA, Engram tables not sent, `engram.wkv` sent | 0.909 → 0.904 | 0 / 1709 |
| MiniMax-M3.1 | MXFP8 + NVFP4 experts | 0.951 → 0.951 | 0 / 3148 |
| Muse Spark | NVFP4, NVIDIA nightly | 0.815 → 0.839 | 0 / 3311 |
| gpt-oss-120b | TRTLLM MXFP4 | 0.938 → 0.936 | 0 / 796 |

- MiniMax-M3.1 runs on the vendor image `vllm/vllm-openai:minimax-m31-flash`: its NVFP4-expert checkpoint needs #63232, which is not merged.
- Muse Spark sampling is not deterministic: pre and post differ on about 110–130 questions each way in every run, including runs with no update effect (98 lost / 130 gained here).
- CuteDSL NVFP4 MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B NVFP4), layerwise reload: 0.832 → 0.039 without PR 5, 0.840 → 0.844 with it.

**New-weight check (perturbation).** The trainer scales checkpoint tensors by 1.01 and publishes them, and a second engine cold-starts on the same perturbed checkpoint. Every parameter, buffer and tensor attribute of the updated engine is bit-identical to the cold-started one for these classes:

- BF16 dense and hybrid;
- FP8 block + MLA (GLM-5.3), where the absorbed `W_UK`/`W_UV` follow `kv_b_proj`;
- NVFP4;
- MXFP4 + SWA (gpt-oss-120b);
- FP8 MLA + vision MoE (dots3).

## Known limitations

- Sharded RDT refuses direct mode, because its init dry run begins an update without finishing it.
- `draft_lm_head_quantization` is refused at cold start in direct mode until F7.
- A cold start from pre-processed (IPC weight-cache) weights records no checkpoint layout, so direct updates are refused.
- Online quantization is not supported until F8.

AI assistance was used in drafting this RFC; the authors reviewed every claim against the code and the runs.

title: [RFC]: Batch invariance for speculative decoding needs to cover the forward pass (M=1 vs M=k+1)
author: Leonccaa
body:
### Motivation.

At temperature 0, enabling speculative decoding can change the generated sequence relative to plain decoding. This is already reported for ngram spec decode in #41758, and #52522 proposes batch-invariant support for speculative decoding — but scoped to the sampling layer (RNG streams, request ordering, preemption recovery).

We ran a multi-day forensic campaign driving a 125B hybrid linear-attention/MoE model with a native MTP head (TP4, FP16) toward bitwise verify↔decode parity. Our finding: on our stack the dominant cause is **forward-pass arithmetic**, not sampling. The target model's verification pass computes rows with `M = k+1`, plain decode computes the same rows with `M = 1`, and **nothing in the current stack guarantees those two produce identical bits**. Real text contains decision points whose top-2 logit margin sits at ULP scale; one 1-ULP difference in one operator flips such a token, and greedy decoding turns that flip into a permanently divergent trajectory. Visible symptom on one of our workloads, purely from this effect: draft acceptance ~100% → 72%, decode ~110 → 89 tok/s.

**The invariant being violated:** given the same checkpoint, the same input and the same runtime/load configuration, the target model's verify pass over rows `[t..t+k]` must reproduce, bit for bit, what plain `M=1` decode would produce at each of those positions.

We are filing this because the mechanisms below are hardware- and method-generic, and because our experience says model-level point-mitigation does not converge. We deliberately do **not** propose a design.

#### Taxonomy of sources (each observed and isolated with bitwise evidence)

**Class A — kernel-level M-dependent reductions.** The same kernel produces different bits for the same logical row depending on how many rows were launched.
- Split-K GEMMs: partial-sum combination order follows launch geometry, which includes M.
- Explicit M-conditioned reduction configuration: we found a norm implementation selecting a 1024-wide reduction for M=1 and 512-wide for M>1 — a literal per-M topology branch.
- Hand-written F16 GEMM, M=5 vs 5×(M=1), random weights: ~92–114 of 20480 elements differ by 1–2 ULP.

**Class B — compiler/fusion topology.** `torch.compile`/Inductor generates reduction schedules **per shape specialization**.
- The native decomposition of an op (a gated RMSNorm, in our case) is fused differently inside an M=1 graph than inside an M=k+1 graph, producing sparse 1-ULP output differences from bitwise-identical inputs.
- **Opaque custom ops act as fusion barriers.** Registering an extra, numerically no-op custom op into only one engine's graph changed *neighbouring* arithmetic by 1 ULP; making both engines' graphs structurally identical restored bitwise equality. Graph structure — not just op semantics — is part of the numerical contract.
- Instrumentation participates in this: adding dump/trace ops changes fusion topology, so naive tracing perturbs the very difference under measurement.

**Class C — execution-form asymmetry between engines.** Spec-enabled engines route parts of the model through different execution forms than non-spec engines.
- An auto-gate keyed on "speculative config is present" moved a whole attention-block family to an opaque/eager path on the spec engine while the non-spec engine kept the compiled path → divergence at **prefill layer 0**, before any speculative token exists.
- The reverse leak also occurred: an opaque wrapper unconditionally instantiated in the non-spec engine moved the *non-spec* baseline trajectory. Which modules run compiled vs eager has to be treated as part of each engine's frozen contract.

**Class D — configuration-activated members.** Which of the above actually express depends on deployment configuration, so a fix validated in one configuration silently loses coverage in another.
- Quantization admission (a path accepted vs rejected) swaps whole kernel families in and out.
- **Load strategy is numerically non-neutral:** switching checkpoint loading between prefetch and mmap/lazy changed the greedy trajectory from token 0 with identical checkpoint bytes — not by corrupting data, but by shifting mapped addresses, allocation order and compile/capture timing, which re-rolls every Class A–C die.

#### Why model-level point-mitigation does not converge (empirical)

We closed a long series of individual members with pre/post bitwise evidence (top-k tie-break determinism, per-row replays of specific projections, norm dispatch admission, symmetric op placement, fixed-topology reduction reimplementations). Observed dynamics:

1. **The divergence point migrates instead of closing.** Across successive true fixes, the index of the first divergent token moved 14 → 2 → 14 → 10. Every real fix exposes the next member earlier or later, and each spec depth k, plus boundary prompt lengths (4/5/6 tokens), exercises *distinct* compile specializations with distinct expressing members.
2. **Gates lie in both directions when fed synthetic data.** Random-weight kernel probes over-predicted expression (kernel red, engine mute). Mild synthetic samples under-predicted it (operator gate green, real checkpoint red). Only per-instance gates on real checkpoint weights were trustworthy — and two layer instances sharing one kernel and one shape can still disagree, because expression is value-dependent.
3. **Replicating compiled arithmetic is a treadmill.** Matching Inductor's generated reduction means cloning exact codegen parameters (XBLOCK / R-block / warps / output tiling) per shape, it breaks on multi-output subgraphs with alias/buffer contracts, and any compiler upgrade invalidates it.

After closing every member that expressed at production shapes, we reached 16/16 greedy-token parity at 1K/4K contexts with acceptance restored to 81% and the expected spec speedup back — but residual 1-ULP members remained reachable at boundary shapes, each costing several full-model runs to localize. We stopped and documented those as known differences. That end state is operationally usable; it is a workaround, not a solution.

#### Gap relative to existing work

- #41758 is the symptom class, on a completely different model/method/hardware combination (Qwen3-0.6B, ngram, A100) — which is what convinced us this is systemic rather than a property of our stack.
- #52522's scope (sampling, RNG streams, preemption recovery) is necessary but not sufficient: none of Classes A–D live in the sampling layer.
- The `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` kernel work is the right neighbourhood, but its axis is batch composition across requests. Speculative decoding adds the `M=1 ↔ M=k+1` axis for the *same* logical row, which is the axis we found unguarded.

### Proposed Change.

What we are asking for is a **scope decision, not an implementation** — we have no design to offer here, and we think ours would be the wrong one: every mitigation we built lives at the model/site level, and the campaign above is our evidence that this level cannot hold the invariant durably.

The change we would like considered: treat **forward-pass batch invariance across M for a fixed logical row** as a first-class contract at the kernel and compilation layer, in the same way `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` treats batch composition today, and extend the batch-invariant spec-decode effort (#52522) to cover it rather than stopping at the sampling boundary.

Questions we think are worth settling before anyone writes code:

1. Is forward-pass M-invariance considered in scope for #52522, or is it a separate workstream?
2. Should verify↔decode bitwise parity be an explicitly documented guarantee under a batch-invariant mode (with the cost that implies), or an explicit non-guarantee — so that users stop treating greedy-output changes under spec decode as a bug in their own configuration?
3. If it becomes a guarantee, does it cover the compilation layer as well as kernels? Class B and Class C say that guaranteeing only kernels is not enough: fusion topology and per-engine execution form change results on their own.

We are happy to contribute evidence, reproduction methodology and measurements to whatever direction maintainers choose. Details in the appendices below.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@SAKETH11111 (#41758), @andakai (#52522), and anyone working on `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` kernels or the spec-decode verification path.

### Any Other Things.

Everything below is offered as raw material for anyone continuing this investigation on their own stack. Each item exists because the naive version misled us first.

#### Appendix A — attribution methodology that survived

1. **Route-hit proof before interpretation.** Before trusting any A/B, prove the code under test actually executed (one-shot entry probes checked in logs). Note that logging inside compiled regions can be silenced by `torch.compiler.is_compiling()` guards — probe at admission time or outside the graph. Several of our early "fixes" were no-ops because the gate meant to admit them evaluated false on the spec engine; two others passed reduced gates and then regressed the full model. Arms without route-hit proof must be marked INVALID, never "no effect".
2. **Per-instance operator gates on real checkpoint weights.** Extract each layer instance's actual weights from the loaded engine and compare `op(k rows stacked)` against `k × op(1 row)` bitwise, per instance, for M = 1..8, plus padded-M variants. Per (1) above, do not substitute random weights. Our final inventory ran ~1,500 such comparisons across two operator families to certify zero expression at production shapes.
3. **Observation neutrality.** Under full CUDA graphs, naively saving intermediates returns capture-aliased garbage, and inserting dump ops changes fusion topology. The only neutral mechanism we found was copying from persistent, pre-registered graph buffers present identically in both arms, snapshotted after the step. Validate neutrality by checking that the instrumented run still reproduces the uninstrumented token sequence.
4. **Anchor gates.** Before comparing anything across arms: assert `input_ids` bitwise-identical, and pin both arms by full commit tuple. Every code snapshot silently spawns a new numerical baseline (Class B), so "matches the previously recorded golden output" is only meaningful when you name the build that produced that golden.
5. **Execution-form bisection.** Forcing both engines into the same form (both eager, or both compiled) is a cheap diagnostic: it collapses Class C entirely and leaves A/B isolated. In our case, unifying a single op's implementation across forms made all 48 layers' block outputs bitwise-equal over a 1024-token prefill — one op's fusion boundary accounted for the entire asymmetry.
6. **Fragile tokens are detectors, not evidence.** A token position with a ULP-scale top-2 margin is a sensitive tripwire, but different perturbations flip it to *different* tokens, so token-level observation cannot attribute cause. Attribution has to happen at the first divergent tensor, walked layer by layer.

#### Appendix B — measured signatures per class

- **Class A:** hand-written F16 GEMM, M=5 vs 5×(M=1), random weights: ~92–114 of 20480 elements at 1–2 ULP. The same kernel, gated per-instance on real checkpoint weights across 140+ instances × M=2..8: **zero** expression — fully latent on that checkpoint. This contrast is exactly why synthetic probes mislead.
- **Class B (fusion):** gated-RMSNorm decomposition under Inductor, M=1 vs M=2, bitwise-identical inputs: 1 FP16 element of 10240 differs, |Δ| = 7.63e-6, deterministic across reruns (a topology property, not a race). Generated reduction for the M=1 specialization: XBLOCK=1, R0_BLOCK=2048, 16 warps over a 128-element row — parameters that change per shape specialization.
- **Class B (barrier asymmetry):** one numerically no-op custom op registered into a single engine's graph → downstream layer outputs differ at 1 ULP across ~2.3M elements; symmetric registration → bitwise equal.
- **Class C:** spec-engine-only eager routing of an attention-block family → divergence present from prefill layer 0, before any speculative token exists.
- **Class D:** load-strategy flip (prefetch ↔ mmap/lazy) alone changed the greedy trajectory from token 0, with identical checkpoint bytes.
- **End-to-end:** first divergent token index migrated 14 → 2 → 14 → 10 across successive true fixes; acceptance ~100% → 72% and decode ~110 → 89 tok/s while members were expressing; after closing all members expressed at production shapes, 16/16 greedy-token parity at 1K and 4K with 81% acceptance and the expected speedup restored.

#### Appendix C — minimal reproduction recipe (any model, mainline vLLM)

1. **Symptom:** temperature 0, fixed prompt, spec decode on vs off, compare full token sequences (this is #41758's setup; any spec method works).
2. **First split:** compare the two configurations' **prefill** logits for the same prompt, bitwise. If they already differ, you have Class C/D — engine construction, execution form or configuration asymmetry — before speculation is even involved.
3. **Core check:** for an accepted prefix, compare the target model's verify-pass logits at position t (computed with M=k+1 rows) against plain decode logits at the same position (M=1). Any bit difference is Class A/B expressing. Walk layers to the first divergent tensor using pre-registered buffers (Appendix A.3).
4. **Shape axes that expose members:** tiny prompts (4/5/6 tokens — compile-specialization boundaries), prompts straddling block/graph-capture boundaries, and each spec depth k separately (each k is its own specialization).
5. **Configuration axes:** load format, quantization on/off, CUDA graph mode, `custom_ops` selection (native decomposition vs custom kernel), TP size. Each combination re-rolls which members express.

#### Environment

Observed on SM70/V100 ×4 (TP4), FP16 activations, a 125B hybrid linear-attention/MoE model with a native MTP head, full+piecewise CUDA graphs, `torch.compile`/Inductor. The SM70 software stack made expression *frequent*, but every mechanism above — split-K reductions, per-shape Inductor codegen, fusion barriers, spec-keyed execution-form gates, load-order sensitivity — exists on current hardware and mainline code paths.

Searched existing issues before filing; the closest are #41758 (symptom) and #52522 (adjacent scope), both linked above.

title: [RFC]: Preemption victim-selection extension point (least-computed-first as the first built-in)
author: shivasathishs-rp
body:
### Motivation.

When the V1 scheduler has to preempt a request to free KV cache, it does so by recompute: `_preempt_request` in `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` resets the victim's `num_computed_tokens` to zero, and those tokens are computed again when the request resumes. This means the choice of which running request to evict directly decides how much compute a preemption throws away.

Neither of the current policies takes that into account. FCFS evicts the last request that was admitted, using `self.running.pop()`. PRIORITY evicts `max(running, key=(priority, arrival_time))`. Both ignore how much work a request has already done, so the scheduler can evict a request that has already prefilled several thousand tokens in order to admit a tiny one, and all of that computed KV is discarded.

I measured how much this costs. I call it the recompute tax, defined as recomputed tokens divided by total token compute. The numbers are in the Evaluation section below. The short version is that under KV pressure the tax is large, reaching about 79 percent in a forced offline sweep and 10 to 23 percent in realistic online serving, and a victim-policy ablation shows that the victim choice by itself accounts for roughly half of it. That half is something we can recover today with a policy that only looks at current state.

### Proposed Change.

I want to line this up with the Extensible Scheduler Plugin Framework in #51608 rather than propose something beside it. That RFC defines the QueueSort, Filter, and Score extension points, and it says explicitly that preemption remains a separate decision, deferring a preemption extension point to its phase 5. This RFC proposes the concrete design for that deferred point.

There are two parts.

The first part is an interim built-in that is already implemented in PR #53723 (open). It adds a `preemption_victim` setting that is orthogonal to the existing `policy` setting, which controls admission order.

- `SchedulerConfig.preemption_victim: Literal["fcfs", "lcf"] = "fcfs"`, with a matching CLI flag `--preemption-victim`.
- The default `"fcfs"` leaves the current behavior exactly as it is.
- `"lcf"` evicts the running request with the least sunk compute. LCF and PRIORITY share a single remove-and-restore path that is covered by tests, and the FCFS fast path through `pop()` is left untouched.

The second part is the actual ask. I would like to promote victim selection to a pluggable extension point under #51608, which is what its phase 5 anticipates. The interface would follow the read-only-feature contract that #51608 sets out, where a plugin receives read-only features owned by the scheduler rather than the scheduler's internal mutable objects.

```python
def select_victim(view: RunningView) -> RequestID: ...
# RunningView exposes read-only per-request features:
#   request_id, num_computed_tokens, num_cached_tokens,
#   arrival_time, priority, num_scheduled_tokens
```

The built-in policies `fcfs` and `lcf` would be the first implementations. The enum is the interim surface, and the plugin interface is the durable one.

One detail matters for correctness. The obvious key, `num_computed_tokens`, over-counts the real cost. When prefix caching and chunked prefill are on, some of a victim's computed tokens can be recovered from the cache on resume and are never actually recomputed. The key that reflects the true recompute cost is the number of computed tokens that are not cacheable, which is `num_computed_tokens - num_cached_tokens`. This RFC proposes that refined key. The key in #53723 today is `num_computed_tokens`, which is a conservative first version, and I will update it.

Fairness needs attention too. Because LCF evicts the request with the least sunk compute, it tends to pick requests that were only just admitted, so under sustained pressure a request could be preempted again and again and never make progress. Admission order still comes from FCFS or PRIORITY, so fairness at intake is unchanged, but the victim side needs a guard. I propose a per-request counter of consecutive preemptions, and once a request has been preempted more than a threshold K, it is protected from being chosen again and the tie-break moves toward older requests with more sunk compute. K would be configurable, and the default would be set high enough that the guard rarely fires under normal load. Measuring the worst-case starvation bound is part of the validation plan.

Finally, I would like to expose two Prometheus counters, `vllm:wasted_recompute_tokens_total` for the tokens discarded by preemption and `vllm:preemptions_total` for the number of preemptions, so that operators can see both the tax and the fact that LCF trades a few more but much cheaper preemptions.

### Evaluation.

I ran these on the Qwen2.5 family (0.5B, 7B-Instruct, 14B, and 32B) with ShareGPT prompts on A100 GPUs. The 7B model runs on a single GPU, and 14B and 32B run with tensor parallelism. The offline runs force KV pressure through `num_gpu_blocks_override`, and the online runs use `vllm bench serve` with a sweep over arrival rate. Wasted recompute is logged inside `_preempt_request` before the reset.

| Setting | Regime | Recompute tax (baseline) | LCF effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Offline 0.5B, 300 reqs, seed 12345 | KV = 2800 of 4200 blocks | 0 percent, no preemption | not applicable |
| Offline 0.5B | KV = 1600 | 32.2 percent | wasted tokens down 59 percent |
| Offline 0.5B | KV = 800 | 57.9 percent | down 40 percent |
| Offline 0.5B | KV = 400, forced worst case | 78.8 percent | down 43 percent, from 623,948 to 354,882 tokens; per-preemption waste falls from 415 to 261 |
| Online 7B, 800 prompts, heterogeneous (`--random-range-ratio 0.5`) | under KV pressure | 10 to 23 percent | total wasted down 24 to 30 percent, and 35 to 41 percent per preemption, with throughput and latency unchanged |
| Online 7B, fixed 512-token input | under KV pressure | 10 to 23 percent | aggregate waste is unchanged, but the tail improves: mean TTFT down 24 percent, p99 down 21 percent, and goodput 6.4 times higher at a 0.05x KV cap |
| Scale 14B and 32B with tensor parallel | under KV pressure | 15 to 22 percent | wasted down 20 to 29 percent |
| Victim design-space ablation | under KV pressure | not applicable | the ordering is LCF better than LIFO, better than Random, better than most-computed-first, and victim choice alone is about 51 percent of the tax |

A few honest caveats. The 79 percent offline figure is an upper bound under forced pressure and does not represent normal load. In the fixed-length online case LCF does not reduce aggregate waste but gives a clear tail and goodput win, while under heterogeneous load it reduces waste directly. I have not yet quantified run-to-run variance with confidence intervals, and that is on the validation list.

### Alternatives considered.

I considered keeping only FCFS and PRIORITY and doing nothing about the victim key, but that leaves about half the tax on the table under pressure. I considered a clairvoyant policy such as SRPT or Gittins that is aware of remaining output length, but that needs output-length prediction, so I am treating LCF as the non-clairvoyant baseline that ships today and leaving the question of whether a predictive victim belongs in scope open for discussion. I considered avoiding recompute entirely through KV offload or swap rather than changing the victim, but that is a heavier and orthogonal change, and V1 is recompute-only by design, so victim choice is the change that costs no new infrastructure and still composes with offload later. I also measured most-computed-first and random victims, and both are strictly worse, as the ablation row shows.

### Rollout and validation.

1. Land the interim enum built-in in #53723, default off, with FCFS unchanged.
2. Add the `wasted_recompute_tokens` and `preemptions_total` metrics.
3. Refine the victim key to computed-minus-cacheable and re-run the offline and online sweeps.
4. Add the fairness guard as a consecutive-preemption cap and measure the starvation bound.
5. Define and implement `select_victim(RunningView)` under the #51608 phase 5 extension point, and move `fcfs` and `lcf` onto it.
6. Gate on validation: p99 TTFT and TPOT together with preemption-count deltas and run-to-run variance, correctness parity so the FCFS path is unchanged, and coverage with prefix caching and chunked prefill both on and off.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@yewentao256 and @chaunceyjiang, who authored the scheduler plugin framework in #51608.

### Any Other Things.

The reference implementation is PR #53723, which is open. I have the full per-run logs and the victim design-space ablation and can link them if that is useful.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] I searched existing issues and RFCs, including #51608 for the scheduler plugin framework, #45558 and #45561 for the priority victim key, and #49675 for zero-progress preemption, and none of them defines a preemption victim extension point.

title: [RFC] Organize the Python package by architectural domain
author: xiaoyanzi191
body:
vLLM's Python source currently mixes public interfaces, request processing,
runtime state, hardware mechanisms, and shared infrastructure at the package
root. This makes the source difficult to navigate and obscures ownership
boundaries for new contributors.

This RFC proposes organizing the Python package around four conceptual and
physical domains:

```text
vllm/
├── frontend/      # public interfaces, serving, request/output processing
├── runtime/       # inference-run state and policy
├── backends/      # platform, compiler, compute, distributed mechanisms
└── foundation/    # config, environment, logging, utilities, integrations
```

The experiment physically moves 42 package entries and rewrites internal
imports to canonical paths. Generated compatibility shims preserve legacy
imports. Leaf modules use `sys.modules` aliases; package roots lazily delegate
attributes to avoid eager imports and circular dependencies.

The proposal deliberately keeps `vllm/v1`, `vllm/model_executor`,
`vllm/models`, `vllm/third_party`, and `vllm/vllm_flash_attn` in place because
their runtime, registry, feature-probe, or compiled-extension paths require
separate designs.

Compatibility checks cover the public root API, CLI and plugin entry points,
dynamic model/attention registries, old/new object identity, focused unit
tests, and local Qwen3-0.6B inference. No behavioral difference was observed
on the tested surface; this is not a claim of exhaustive equivalence across
all optional hardware backends.

A Draft PR implements the experiment for review. The intended outcome of this
RFC is feedback on domain boundaries and whether any part should proceed as
smaller staged PRs.

This is not a duplicate of RFC #17419: that RFC concerns kernel library and
packaging separation, while this proposal covers Python source ownership and
legacy import compatibility. The compute-kernel directory is the only partial
overlap.

AI assistance disclosure: OpenAI Codex assisted with source inventory,
mechanical moves, compatibility-shim generation, testing, and documentation.
The human submitter remains responsible for reviewing and validating the
change.

title: [RFC]: Per-KV-cache-group prefix-cache retention, with a hit-min exemption for hit-inert EAGLE sliding-window draft groups
author: nood-co1
body:
### Motivation.

**Summary.** On hybrid models that carry an EAGLE-style sliding-window draft group (DFlash/DSpark-shaped drafters), that group hashes `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) + 1` block ids at *every* prefix-cache boundary and frees them *cached* onto the protected tail of the one LRU that all groups share, while — once it is exempted from the hit `min` — contributing nothing to the reconciled hit length. On a GLM-5.3-Flash deployment this one group spends 87% of the prefix cache and caps coexisting conversations at ~50K tokens each. A per-group retention interval, combined with exempting such hit-inert groups from the hit `min`, restored ~4× the coexisting-conversation capacity with the fine hit grid kept for the target model's groups, and a third party reproduced 99.95% cached across alternating 120K conversations. All numbers below are **deployment evidence from a vLLM fork**, not upstream verification; the code reading is against upstream `main` @ `22df3a3`. This RFC asks for agreement on the policy before any code is posted as a PR.

**Where the cost comes from (upstream `main` @ `22df3a3`, verified).**

- `--prefix-cache-retention-interval` (`vllm/config/cache.py:156-158`, `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:530`) reaches the coordinator as one scalar, `KVCacheCoordinator.retention_interval` (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:158`), and is handed unchanged to every manager at both `cache_blocks` sites (`:306-326` base, `:740-768` hybrid).
- Everything below the coordinator is already per group: `SingleTypeKVCacheManager.cache_blocks(..., retention_interval=None)` (`vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:432-436`), and each `reachable_block_mask` interprets it against its own block size and window (`:485-`, `:1010-`, `:1472-`).
- A sliding-window group needs `need = _contiguous_blocks_for_hit(window, block_size, use_eagle)` contiguous blocks at every retained boundary (`:898-908`, `:1028`); a full-attention group needs one block per boundary. Those SWA blocks are freed by `remove_skipped_blocks` -> `_remove_blocks_in_range` -> `BlockPool.free_blocks` (`:632`, `:605`), and because they are hashed they go to `blocks_to_evict_last` / `append_n`, the LRU *tail* (`vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:723-747`). Full-attention blocks stay allocated until request end; Mamba align-mode state blocks may also be freed mid-request (`single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:1529-1557`), but a 3584-token Mamba group frees one id per segment where the draft group frees 33. The group with the least reusable state gets the most eviction protection.
- `HybridKVCacheCoordinator.find_longest_cache_hit` folds every attention group, EAGLE draft group included, into the reconciled hit (`kv_cache_coordinator.py:770-903`, `curr_hit_length = _new_hit_length` at `:871`). So giving the draft group a sparser retention on `main` today would shorten everyone's hit — which is why the fork below carries a `min` exemption first.

**Measured (deployment evidence: GLM-5.3-Flash, 2× DGX Spark, TP=2, DFlash2 draft k=7; vLLM fork `0.1.dev20051+g487ecf187`; GLM-5.3-Flash support upstream is #53906).** Groups: MLA block 3584, four Mamba "align" groups at 3584, one EAGLE sliding-window draft group with window 2048 / block 64, scheduler block 3584; one `BlockPool` of 643 block ids (642 usable; derived from the logged `max_concurrency`, see *Any Other Things*).

| group | block ids per cached 3584-token segment (dense retention) |
|---|---:|
| full attention (MLA) | 1 |
| Mamba × 4 | 4 |
| **draft sliding window** | **33** (`cdiv(2047, 64) + 1`) |
| total | 38 |

Two conversations of `S` segments coexist only while `642 >= 43·S` (each of B's segments pops 38 ids while A's cached draft tail contributes 33 back), i.e. `S <= 14.9`. Measured on a clean server: 14 segments OK / 17 evicting; pair ladders at 45K / 56K / 66K tokens hit 99% / 0% / 0%.

Raising the single global `--prefix-cache-retention-interval` to 14336 restored the ladder to 99 / 98 / 97 / 96% at 45K / 56K / 66K / 80K — but it bought that capacity by coarsening *everyone's* retention grid: a diverging sub-agent prefix then hit only 45% of a ~29K prompt instead of landing on the 3584 grid.

With per-group retention — retention `0` (reachable-boundary tails only) on the draft group, dense for MLA/Mamba — and the draft group exempted from the hit `min`, the per-segment cost drops to 5 ids (+33 per turn boundary), projected `S <= 54` (~195K tokens per conversation) with the 3584 hit grid kept. Independent reproduction by a third-party tester on a different 2× DGX Spark deployment (`max_model_len=524288`, `max_num_seqs=4`), two distinct 120K-token conversations alternated A -> B -> A -> B:

```
A cold             cached      0 / 119,995   TTFT 174.522s
A warm             cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.581s
B cold             cached      0 / 119,995   TTFT 174.392s
B warm             cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.590s
A return after B   cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.567s
B return after A   cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.567s
```

99.95% cached on every return, where the same shape previously evicted the parked conversation. Sources: https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks/pull/83 (per-group retention; the tester's receipt above is in its comments) and https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks/pull/84 (fine-grained hits, tested together). Those are recipe overlays on a fork; nothing there applies to `main` as-is.

### Proposed Change.

Three parts, in this order. The ask is agreement on 1 and 3 before any of the code is posted as a PR.

1. **Exempt hit-inert sliding-window groups from the reconciled hit `min`, with an explicit per-group lookup/consumption contract.** A sliding-window group is *hit-inert* when (a) it is EAGLE-annotated (`KVCacheGroupSpec.is_eagle_group`), so its hit length is not needed to bound the target's; (b) its window is shorter than `_cache_hit_alignment_tokens`, so its cached tail is only ever consultable at an alignment boundary; and (c) sparse retention is actually reachable for it: `need < alignment_tokens // block_size` (otherwise `reachable_block_mask` returns dense anyway, `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:1027-1053`), `block_size` divides the alignment, and `extra_retained_tokens == 0` (it separately affects admission/retention sizing, `vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py:694-730` / `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:888-895`; nonzero values require separate handling or exclusion).

   The group is still looked up. If its own hit reaches the candidate boundary, its blocks are consumed as today — that is how the retained boundary tail keeps a conversation's own follow-up turn warm. If its hit is *shorter*, it must neither shorten `curr_hit_length` nor inflate `longest_hit_length`, and its per-group result must be an explicit "no reusable blocks; allocate a fresh window", not the empty list the current lookup would return: today `find_longest_cache_hit` initialises empty per-group results (`kv_cache_coordinator.py:795-800`), fills them only for `attention_groups` (`:815-874`), and `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` passes them straight to allocation (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py:228-294`), so an empty draft result cannot reuse a retained tail. This is the same per-group-boundary concern #53786 raises for SWA fine-grained hits, and it is the part that needs design agreement.

   **Unproven risk, stated plainly:** final outputs are protected by target verification, but the drafter's *acceptance* depends on the window's KV being valid. Whether a newly allocated window block is zeroed depends on `needs_kv_cache_zeroing` (`single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:88-94`); the design must guarantee the window is recomputed during prefill of the uncached remainder rather than read stale, and the acceptance dip while it refills has only been measured on the fork (decode-rate control within noise), not upstream. It is free whenever the remainder is at least one window — the diverging-prefix / new-turn case. #50457 (all-sliding DFlash drafter with prefix caching, PR) is in this area and may be the right home.

2. **Resolve the retention interval per KV cache group.** `KVCacheCoordinator` gains `retention_interval_by_group: tuple[int | None, ...]`, resolved once in `__init__` and indexed at both `cache_blocks` sites. The manager API is untouched (already per call). With the identity resolution behaviour is byte-identical, which the accompanying tests pin. The seam patch is ready and rebased on `22df3a3` — `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py` +37/−4, tests +72: https://github.com/nood-co1/vllm/tree/feat/per-group-prefix-cache-retention (commit https://github.com/nood-co1/vllm/commit/b9f82ae0f946039be1e96084ef15399e8cf2e07c). It is deliberately *not* opened as a PR: on its own it is plumbing with no user-visible effect, and it is only safe to use once part 1 exists.

3. **Policy:** resolve `retention_interval = 0` for groups that satisfy part 1's predicate, i.e. cache only the reachable-boundary tails (`SlidingWindowManager.reachable_block_mask`, `retention_interval == 0` branch), and the configured value for every other group. A genuine SWA target model (window spanning the alignment, or a group still inside the `min`) is unchanged. A user override can come later if wanted; the default should not need one.

Offered as a follow-up PR (parts 1–3 together, or 2 first if maintainers prefer the decomposition) once the policy is agreed.

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@rchalamala (#50457), @RichApple123 (#54397), @Suppressor72 (#53786 has the same DFlash2 all-sliding drafter shape), @woosebastian (#48532, eviction order in the shared pool).

### Any Other Things.

**Related work, and why this is not a duplicate** (`gh pr list` / `gh issue list --state open --search` for "per-group retention", "retention interval", "sliding window prefix cache eviction", "EAGLE draft prefix cache", 2026-09-01; titles verified with `gh` the same day):

- Issue [#48435](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48435) — hybrid-SWA prefix caching collapses under multi-session round-robin on Gemma-4 (eager-freed SWA tails recycled tail-first). Same LRU mechanism seen from the other side: there the SWA group *is* the target's own attention, its tails are needed for the hit, and losing them zeroes the hit. This RFC targets the case where the SWA group is a drafter whose hit is not needed; the eviction-order remedy for #48435 is different and the two compose.
- PR [#50457](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50457) — all-sliding DFlash drafter with prefix caching (open). Part 1 belongs near it.
- PR [#54397](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54397) — fine-grained SWA hits (draft). Orthogonal (lookup granularity, not retention or eviction).
- PR [#51886](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51886) — retention interval for `OffloadingConnector`; PR [#52747](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52747) — docs for the existing flag; PRs [#53803](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53803), [#53479](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53479), [#53945](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53945) — which Mamba checkpoints are materialized. None make the coordinator's retention per group.
- Issues [#53670](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53670), [#53786](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53786) — EAGLE last-block drop and SWA fine-grained hits on Qwen3.8/3.5 hybrids with DFlash2 drafters; same deployment shape, different costs.
- PR [#48532](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48532) — per-group eviction order in deferred block free (same pool, different path).

**Caveats.** All measurements are deployment evidence from a fork on GLM-5.3-Flash, which is not yet in `main` (#53906); the block-id arithmetic uses code paths that exist unchanged on `main` (`SlidingWindowManager.reachable_block_mask`, `BlockPool.free_blocks`). The pool size (643 ids) is derived from the logged `GPU KV cache size` / `max_concurrency` figure rather than logged directly — filed separately as a small observability request. The ~195K-per-conversation projection is from the capacity model (`642 >= 2C − D`), which predicted every measured row's sign and order but ran ~25% optimistic at retention 7168; the 120K × 2 reproduction above is the measured point.

Submitted by nood-co1 on behalf of Blockbrain Labs (https://x.com/blockbrain_labs, GitHub org blockbrain-ai); drafted with AI assistance (Claude, with an independent adversarial review pass by OpenAI Codex folded in) and reviewed by the submitter, who checked every `file:line` against `22df3a3`.
