title: [RFC]: fp8 KV cache support for Inkling on SM100-family GPUs
author: drkm-eng
body:
### Motivation.

Inkling and Inkling-Small serve with a bf16 KV cache only. `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` fails at JIT warmup: the cache is allocated as uint8, nothing in the Inkling stack reinterprets it as an fp8 dtype, and both kernel backends assert on the dtype.

KV memory is the binding constraint for long context on memory-limited deployments. fp8 halves attention KV bytes across the stack (7,168 to 3,584 bytes/token/rank at TP4: the 7 full-attention layers at 1,024 bytes/token/layer; the 35 sliding-window layers hold only their 512-token window, so they do not scale with context). The realized pool gain depends on serving settings, because the per-request pool charge is dominated by the bf16-pinned conv-state admission reserve, which this change cannot touch. Measured through vLLM's own `get_kv_cache_configs` at the same memory budget:

| max_model_len | max_num_batched_tokens | pool gain (fp8 vs bf16) |
|---|---|---|
| 8,192 | 16,384 | +5.9% |
| 131,072 | 16,384 (serve default) | +8.6% |
| 131,072 | 2,048 | +28.1% |
| 1,048,576 | 16,384 | +27.9% |
| 1,048,576 | 2,048 | +73.1% |

The 1M configuration was validated live, not just modeled: two servers booted at max_model_len 1,048,576 measured +73.06% pool capacity against the +73.1% prediction, with capacity for 24 concurrent 1M-token requests under fp8 vs 14 under bf16 (vLLM's logged maximum concurrency), and cold-prefill TTFT at 0.84x bf16 at 1M. Kernel-level attention speedups reach 1.45x and grow with KV length.

### Proposed Change.

Two PRs, sequenced. The kernel PR merges first; the wiring PR references it; a follow-up bumps the vendored pin.

1. tml-fa4 kernel PR (vllm-project/tml-fa4#4): plain per-tensor fp8 e4m3 Q/KV support in the Blackwell sheared-bias forward kernel. 4 files, +148/-27, based on current main (b206834, the exact commit vLLM vendors). It adapts closed PR vllm-project/tml-fa4#1 and fixes a correctness bug in it: with fp8 P pre-scaled by 2\*\*8, the lazy-rescale slack that guarantees zero P clipping is log2(448) - 8 = 0.807, but that PR set rescale_threshold=4.0. Attention bias makes sub-threshold row-max jumps routine, clipping P (six deterministic test failures, 0.3-0.7 abs error, root cause proven by zero-bias diagnostic and three-arm bisection: threshold=0 fixes, max_offset=0 fixes, ex2-tuning-off does not). We ship rescale_threshold=0.75, chosen to guarantee the invariant with margin for compiler reassociation. The empirical failure onset sits between 1.5 and 2.0 with monotonic dose-response beyond it.

2. vLLM wiring PR: `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` for Inkling. 8 files, +596/-35 across two commits (the feature, plus a clean NotImplementedError for quantized KV dtypes on the ROCm path; non-test delta ~260 lines). Runtime-validated on v0.28.0; cherry-picks cleanly onto main as of 2026-08-28 (4c6c9d5).

3. Follow-up after (1) merges: bump the tml-fa4 GIT_TAG in cmake/external_projects/tml_fa4.cmake.

Design summary:

- Quant-on-store. K/V are already computed in fp32 inside the fused qkvr_prep store kernels; with fp8 active they are multiplied by the reciprocal scale, clamped to the e4m3 finite range (+/-448), and stored as e4m3. Write-path cost is -1.3% to +2.0% vs the bf16 store (median ratio 1.01); the added multiply+clamp+convert is offset by halved write bytes.
- Scales. Per-tensor, per-layer k_scale/v_scale, default 1.0, loaded from checkpoint tensors `model.llm.layers.<i>.attn.{k,v}_scale` through the standard loader path with no flags. Q is quantized with a static per-tensor scale after qkvr_prep.
- Kernel read path. The shipped sheared kernel takes fp8 Q/KV directly and adds no descale parameters; both descales are per-tensor scalars applied at the vLLM wrapper (fa4_rel_attention.py). The QK descale is folded into softmax_scale, so scores are descaled before the relative position bias is added and the bias term stays exact; the V descale is applied as a post-hoc multiply on the kernel output, which is linear in V. The fold sits outside the backend branch and is path-independent: the CuTe score-mod fallback receives the same folded softmax_scale and output multiply, since neither vendored varlen entry exposes descale parameters.
- Gating. SM100-family e4m3 only; a clear error is raised elsewhere. ROCm gains no fp8 path: quantized KV dtypes are rejected at layer construction (second wiring commit); non-quantized dtypes are untouched.
- Conv state stays bf16. It is pinned to model dtype, unaffected by kv_cache_dtype; conv-cache stores are untouched and verified bit-identical to the bf16 run.
- Load-time warning. If fp8 KV is enabled and the checkpoint carries v_scale tensors for fewer layers than run quantized (coverage-checked at model level from the loader's return value, since unity values are legitimate in a calibrated checkpoint), a warning names the measured failure mode; loaded scales are validated finite and positive.
- CI. New tests live under tests/models/inkling/ and are picked up by the existing B200 Inkling Buildkite entry (key inkling-unit-tests-b200); no CI config change.

### Evidence Summary

Serving measurements on B200 (SM100), vLLM v0.28.0, TP4, two identical 4-GPU servers (bf16 vs fp8), greedy, paired prompts. Kernel-level numbers are from a separate single-B200 host. The full evidence document with per-run artifacts and the pre-registered gate scorecard will be attached to the wiring PR.

| axis | result |
|---|---|
| kernel correctness | 160/160 tests across the three test files this change touches: both backends, fp8 x {sheared, scoremod} x scale sets x rel extents, atol/rtol 0.15 vs a dequantized-input fp32 reference, plus spec/warmup/gate tests |
| kernel latency | fp8 faster in 18/20 cases; best 1.45x (batched decode, kv=64K, b=32); worst regression +2.6% |
| long-context logprobs (book-length docs, longest 121K scored tokens, noise-free paired design, production path) | on the stable documents (5/10; the replication-unstable documents, four high-PPL and one at PPL 14, are excluded from certification because they amplify replication noise, see evidence doc), every position bucket within +/-0.71% PPL on both fp8 configs; deepest bucket (64K-128K) ~0.1%; median across all 10 docs +0.21% (unity) / +0.16% (calibrated); top-1 agreement rises with depth; no error compounding |
| GSM8K / MMLU (n=14,042) / IFEval / HumanEval | parity on all four on the score-mod path, paired McNemar per sample; GSM8K and MMLU repeated at parity on the production sheared path |
| tool calling, 500-call replay | 475 vs 474 pass, McNemar p=1.0; 100% JSON- and schema-valid on both arms; 50/50 negatives correctly silent |
| needle-in-a-haystack (custom paired single-needle test, substituted for the pre-registered RULER suite; no multi-needle or aggregation coverage) | 120/120 both dtypes to 120K; at the 1M boot, 27/27 paired retrievals including needles ~950K tokens behind the query |
| capacity, live 1M boot | +73.06% measured vs +73.1% predicted; 24 vs 14 concurrent 1M-token requests |
| TTFT, cold single request | 0.96x at 256K, 0.91x at 512K, 0.84x at 1M (fp8 faster, monotonic in context) |
| serving throughput | parity within +/-1.1% up to 32K contexts; +2.2% total tok/s and -2.3% TTFT at 100K prefill; two exceptions: decode-workload median TTFT +10.2% (143.7 to 158.3 ms, p99 improves) and mid-workload median TTFT +2.7% |

Known limitation: MATH-500 regresses at unity scale.

- -4.2pt mean (41.9 to 37.7, triplicate runs per arm, run-level p 0.05-0.10; direction consistent across all 9 cross-run pairings). Every other task in the battery is at parity.
- Mechanism, measured: V outliers clip at unity scale, concentrated in the global attention layers (max |V| = 1,272 vs e4m3 max 448; the worst global layer clips ~1 in 1,100 V elements). K never clips anywhere. Global layers carry long-range information, consistent with the deficit surfacing only on long-derivation math.
- Remedy: calibrated v_scale recovers about half the deficit (37.7 to 39.7 mean; the best calibrated run, 41.0, comes within 0.8pt of the weakest bf16 run at 41.8, while the best unity run reaches only 39.4) at no cost elsewhere (GSM8K 83.55% on the calibrated server, center of the healthy band). Per-layer calibration of this checkpoint touches 14 of 42 layers, all v_scale, no k_scale.
- The wiring PR ships the coverage-checked warning. A standalone calibration utility exists: it hooks the fused store sites, measures real per-layer K/V ranges, derives clip-free per-layer scales, and writes them into the checkpoint for the existing loader. llm-compressor cannot calibrate this model because its HF-side observers never see Inkling's post-norm/post-conv fused store sites.

### Related Finding

The conv-state admission reserve that mutes the capacity gain at serve defaults is a separate, dtype-independent accounting behavior: tiny-window SlidingWindowSpec conv state is charged a per-request in-flight reserve that reaches 84% of per-request blocks. It affects any KV compression on hybrid conv models, not just this change. Filed separately as vllm-project/vllm#54703; it is referenced here to explain the sensitivity table above.

### Feedback Requested

1. Calibration tool placement. The documented KV-scale pathway is out-of-tree calibration via llm-compressor, which cannot observe this model's fused store sites (K is stored post-rms-norm and post-conv inside a fused kernel). Our prepared default: keep the utility out-of-tree and add a short Inkling section to docs/features/quantization/quantized_kvcache.md (drafted, ready to include). Alternatives if preferred: land it under examples/, or upstream the flow into llm-compressor as the long-term home.
2. Unity-scale serving behavior. Given the measured MATH-500 regression at unity scale, should serving an fp8 KV checkpoint without v_scale tensors warn (current behavior) or refuse unless explicitly opted in? The warning matches the existing unity-scale warning convention in BaseKVCacheMethod.process_weights_after_loading; we kept that precedent and would want a strong reason to diverge from it for one model.
3. ROCm scope. This proposal gates fp8 KV to SM100-family e4m3; the ROCm path rejects quantized KV dtypes at layer construction with an explicit NotImplementedError (included in the wiring PR, with a CPU test). A tracking issue for ROCm parity is drafted and ready to file if wanted.
4. Checkpoint scale schema. The emitted tensor names are in vLLM's canonical post-remap form and an opt-in flag records kv_cache_quant_algo=FP8 so kv_cache_dtype="auto" resolves to fp8 for downstream consumers. Any objection to that convention for this model?

### Feedback Period.

At least one week. Two weeks preferred: reproducing the end-to-end evidence requires B200 hardware.

### CC List.

Quantization: @mgoin @robertgshaw2-redhat @tlrmchlsmth @yewentao256 @pavanimajety @zyongye. Attention: @LucasWilkinson @MatthewBonanni. Inkling: @mikekg. @WoosukKwon authored vllm-project/tml-fa4#1, which the kernel PR adapts.

### Any Other Things.

- AI assistance disclosure: AI was used to implement, benchmark, debug, and document this work. The human submitter has reviewed every changed line and can explain and defend the implementation. Commits carry Co-authored-by trailers alongside Signed-off-by, per the contributing guide.
- Per the contributing guide's threshold, this RFC is optional (the wiring PR's non-test delta is ~260 lines); it is posted alongside the PRs (the wiring PR stays in draft) to collect design feedback, primarily on the questions above.
- Two pre-registered gates failed as written and are disclosed in the evidence document's scorecard. The top-1 agreement gate (>=99% short / >=97% long) was ill-posed: the bf16-vs-bf16 control arm itself scores 88.2-90.5% under prefix perturbation, and fp8 agreement is within ~1pt of that control in every bucket. The zero-KV-clip-at-unity gate failed on V (pooled 2.2e-5; K exact 0): this is the V-clipping mechanism behind the MATH-500 deficit described above. The scorecard also records that RULER was replaced by the custom paired single-needle NIAH noted in the evidence table, and the canonical-evaluator GSM8K cross-check was not run (its pre-registered bound is a <=1.0pt delta; within-harness deltas: 0.83pt on the sheared path, inside that bound; 1.82pt on the score-mod path, outside it, fp8-favored).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: The dynamic-SD K decision is a batch-keyed array index — agreeing on its shape before more signals arrive
author: seongyun1104
body:
### Motivation.

On current `main` (`504bb8b0c3`) the dynamic-SD K decision is one array index:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:1321-1324
if self.dynamic_sd_lookup is not None and len(num_scheduled_tokens) > 0:
    num_spec_tokens_to_schedule = self.dynamic_sd_lookup[
        len(num_scheduled_tokens)
    ]
```

The key is batch size, and that choice is fixed in four places, not one:

- `validate_and_normalize_dynamic_sd_schedule` unpacks entries as
  `(range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens)` (`dynamic/utils.py:37`)
- `build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup` returns `list[int]`, a dense
  `batch_size -> K` table (`dynamic/utils.py:77-81`)
- the scheduler indexes it by `len(num_scheduled_tokens)` (`sched/scheduler.py:1322`)
- since #50488, two capture-planning sites read the same dense table
  (`worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:219`, `config/vllm.py:2067`)

The decision site is not short of information — `schedule()` has the request set
in hand, so per-request `num_computed_tokens`, acceptance history and queue
depth are all in scope. They are simply not read. Whatever a proposal wants K to
depend on, it currently has to widen that tuple everywhere, or bypass the
schedule entirely.

**Six different signals are being proposed for this one decision right now.**
Batch size is what ships. Beyond it:

| signal | where |
|---|---|
| context length | #48944 (mine), widening the tuple to `(bs, ctx) -> K` |
| token entropy | #54082, gating K between 0 and K at runtime |
| marginal gain | LibraSpec, [2608.08721](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08721) |
| expert activation cost | EcoSpec, [2607.12696](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12696) |
| step-wise efficiency (entropy-controlled length) | SparseSpec-L, [2607.27735](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27735) |
| learned verification payoff | Hybrid Verified Decoding, [2606.01019](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01019) |

Two of those papers converge on the same criterion. SparseSpec-L states it
directly: *"extending the speculation horizon can reduce rather than improve
speedup when the marginal acceptance probability falls below the relative
drafting cost."*

I am not asking for any of them to be adopted. I am asking whether the K
decision should keep being a batch-keyed array index, given that the next six
proposals all need it not to be.

> **Update, 2026-09-07 — prior art I should have cited, and a seventh signal.**
>
> **#38038** (`Dynamic SD scheduler decides`, draft, opened 2026-03-24) already
> answers the question this RFC asks, and I did not find it before posting. It
> adds `vllm/v1/spec_decode/dynamic/manager.py` —
> `DynamicSpeculativeDecodingManager`, which picks K by maximizing
> `goodput = acceptance_length / ITL` over a profiled `batch_stats[bs][K] -> ITL`
> table, refreshes its per-position acceptance rates from live
> `SpecDecodingStats` after a warmup period, and interpolates between measured
> batch sizes and K values. It is a policy object, not an array index, and it is
> the most developed K controller in the tree.
>
> It is also keyed on batch size alone: `step(batch_size) -> int`, and the
> companion `generate_config.py` sweeps `(batch_size, K)` on a fixed dataset to
> produce `{batch_size: {num_drafts: median_itl_ms}}`. ITL is context-dependent,
> so in that design context is a constant of the profiling run rather than an
> input to the policy.
>
> That is the sharpest form of what this RFC is asking about, and it points the
> question at the maintainers more than at me: the one component here that was
> built as a policy rather than a table still cannot express a context-dependent
> K, and it has been dormant since 2026-05-07. Whether that is the intended
> destination for this decision is exactly what I do not know.
>
> Separately, a seventh signal has since been proposed and implemented:
> **#54801** adds `num_speculative_tokens_per_seq_len` as a second table
> consulted only when the batch-size table is unset, prompted by **#54691**,
> which reports speculation becoming a net loss at 185k context and states that
> no per-sequence-length hook exists today. I have commented there rather than
> restate it here. That is two new entries to the table above in the six days
> since this was opened, which is the part I would ask maintainers to weigh.

### Evidence I can offer, with its limits.

I ran the (batch, ctx) case, so the numbers below are about that one signal.
Full provenance, including what I have withdrawn, is in a
[ledger](https://github.com/seongyun1104/depthchart/blob/931ff25/EVIDENCE_LEDGER.md);
the per-cell working is in a
[companion note](https://github.com/seongyun1104/depthchart/blob/931ff25/POLICY_INTERFACE.md).

**1. The win localises to a single cell.** Position-balanced 2 trials, cache
wiped per launch, cold-start burn, 3 warm-up discarded + 3 measured per cell,
c=256, per-arm stdev at most 1.72 %, Gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-FP8 with its assistant
drafter on one H100 NVL. A batch-only schedule `[[1,64,3],[65,128,1],[129,512,0]]`
against a (bs, ctx) schedule that differs from it in exactly one cell — at
bs ≥ 129 and ctx ≥ 769, K=3 instead of K=0:

| ctx | batch-only | (bs, ctx) | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|:-:|
| 400 | 1875.6 | 1890.7 | 1.01× |
| 900 | 1453.5 | 1874.6 | 1.29× |
| 1900 | 1416.6 | 1848.2 | 1.30× |
| 4000 | 1232.8 | 1680.4 | 1.36× |

The ctx=400 tie is the design working: there both schedules select K=0. The
mechanism is narrow and worth stating plainly — **at high batch a batch-only
schedule has to turn speculation off, and context is what tells you when to turn
it back on.**

The distinct-K set is `{0, 1, 3}` for both schedules, so this costs no extra
CUDA graphs; graphs are keyed on K, and the K values are the same ones.

**2. A cost model over the same interface gets that cell wrong.** I also have a
producer that derives the schedule from a stated cost model rather than typing
it — `K* = argmax_K E_accept(K) / (F(ctx) + K·M(bs))`, the same marginal-utility
shape LibraSpec and SparseSpec-L arrive at. Run with the coefficients it ships,
sweeping only the acceptance prior across 0.35–0.75 (the campaign observed
44–47 % in the K=3 tier), it selects **K=0 at the high-batch tier at every
context**. It reproduces the batch-only schedule and would not have found the
cell worth 29–36 %.

That gap closes under recalibration — the per-context coefficient has to be
roughly an order of magnitude larger relative to the per-batch one — not under a
change of functional form. I am reporting it because it is the honest state of
that producer: a stated model, uncalibrated, currently disagreeing with my own
measurement.

**3. What I have not established.** One model pair, one hardware configuration,
one concurrency, four context points, one differing cell. I have not calibrated
the cost model on hardware. I have not attributed the DSD baseline tax to its
terms — the 2×2 design for that is written and unrun. And the sharpness of the K
optimum at low batch did not clear its own pre-registered bar (#48627, and see
the ledger); the result above is at c=256, which is a different regime.

### Proposed Change.

**None yet — this asks for a decision, not a design.** I have a stake here
(#48944 is the ctx-axis version) and I would rather the shape be agreed before
more signals arrive than argue for mine.

The question is where the K decision should live:

1. **Keep it batch-keyed** and let each new signal negotiate its own widening.
   Predictable, and the dense array stays trivially cheap. #50488 has just made
   this the assumption in two more places, so this is the status quo by default
   rather than by decision.
2. **Let the schedule declare its own key set**, so `(bs, ctx)` and any later
   key are the same kind of object to the consumers. This is what #48944 does
   for one extra key; generalising it is a small change to the validator, the
   lookup and the three read sites.
3. **Separate the decision from the schedule**, so that a table, a cost model,
   or a runtime controller are interchangeable producers of K. Two producers
   already exist behind one schedule in my branch, which is the minimum evidence
   for this being more than speculative generality — but two is also the
   minimum, and I would not argue for it on that basis alone.

What I think matters more than which option: **nothing in the engine currently
measures the quantity these policies need.** Acceptance is exported in aggregate,
but per-`(batch bucket, ctx bucket, K)` draft and verify latency, first-rejection
position, committed tokens per verification, and K-keyed graph hit/miss are not.
My cost model missed the cell above because its coefficients were guesses; there
is no way to stop them being guesses from inside vLLM today. If only one thing
comes out of this thread, that telemetry is the one I would pick, and it is
independent of which option above wins.

I have opened #54748 for the smallest piece of it, so this is not a request for
someone else to do the work: steps the schedule sends to K=0 build no
`SpecDecodingStats` at all, so a schedule that has correctly stopped speculating
under load is indistinguishable from speculative decoding not running. That PR
adds a step counter keyed on the selected K and is deliberately independent of
everything proposed here.

### Feedback Period.

No deadline. I will not open a PR against any of the three options without
agreement here first.

### Any Other Things.

Related: RFC #48627 (the ctx axis specifically, with its evidence section
corrected on 2026-09-01), PR #48944, #54082, #49986, #49548, #48494.

Prior art on the ctx dependence itself: MagicDec
([blog](https://infini-ai-lab.github.io/MagicDec-part1/), paper
[2408.11049](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11049)) proposes choosing speculation
amount as a function of sequence length; TurboSpec/SmartSpec
([2406.14066](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14066)) is the batch-adaptive
predecessor of the schedule API this RFC is about.



> **Update, 2026-09-13 — this RFC left out the controller that actually shipped, and with it in view the question gets sharper.**
>
> My 2026-09-07 update said of #38038 that *"whether that is the intended destination for
> this decision is exactly what I do not know."* It is answerable, and I should have
> answered it here rather than leaving it open: the destination was **#47808**
> (`[Spec Decode] DSpark confidence-scheduled verification`, merged 2026-08-12), which
> added `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/adaptive_verification.py`. RFC #48627 cites it;
> this RFC does not, which makes the Motivation section above read as though the dense
> `batch_size -> K` array were the only controller in the tree. It is not, and the
> omission is mine.
>
> **#38038 and #47808 are the same author's two answers to this RFC's question.** Both are
> @LucasWilkinson's. Both choose a speculation budget by maximizing goodput. Both price
> context once, before serving, and then hold it fixed.
>
> | | #38038 (open, draft, dormant since 2026-05-07) | #47808 (merged 2026-08-12) |
> |---|---|---|
> | objective | `acceptance_length / ITL` | estimated accepted tokens / cost |
> | cost table keyed on | `batch_stats[bs][K] -> ITL` | `num_reqs`, `num_target_tokens` |
> | context | constant of the profiling run | constant of the profiling run |
>
> For #47808 that is visible in three places. The budget is a goodput argmax
> (`adaptive_verification.py:342`):
>
> ```python
> draft_budget = int(np.argmax(num_tokens_to_estimated_accepted_tokens / costs))
> ```
>
> `costs` is assembled from two profiled curves, neither of which carries a context axis —
> `set_initial_cost_curves` builds `draft_curve` keyed on `s.num_reqs` and `verify_curve`
> keyed on `s.num_target_tokens`:
>
> ```python
>         costs = (
>             draft_cost_ms[len(req_ids)]
>             + verify_cost_ms[
>                 num_non_draft_tokens_total : num_non_draft_tokens_total
>                 + max_draft_budget
>                 + 1
>             ]
>         )
> ```
>
> And context enters exactly once, in `batches_to_profile`, held fixed across every sample:
>
> ```python
>                 yield {
>                     "num_tokens": num_tokens,
>                     "context_len": envs.VLLM_ADAPTIVE_VERIFICATION_PROFILE_CONTEXT_LEN,
>                 }
> ```
>
> That env var defaults to 8192. Its comment in `envs.py` states the consequence directly:
> *"Raise it for long-context deployments, where step cost is dominated by attention over
> a much larger KV cache than the default assumes."* The feature documentation says the
> same thing to operators: *"Deployments serving much longer contexts may want to raise it
> so the profiled step reads a more realistic amount of cache."*
>
> So context is not absent from the shipped controller. It is a **deployment-wide scalar
> set before serving**, not an input the policy reads per step — which is the distinction
> this RFC exists to ask about, and I had been asking it against the weaker example.
>
> To be precise about scope, since it would be easy to overstate: adaptive verification
> does not choose K. Drafting still happens at the scheduled length; it chooses how much
> of the already-drafted block to verify, scoring every (request, position) slot by
> survival probability and admitting the best until the budget is spent. So the array
> index above is still the K decision. But "should a table, a cost model, or a runtime
> controller produce the budget" is not an open question in the way I framed it — a cost
> model shipped in August, and 41 open PRs reference it today.
>
> **The question I would actually ask, now:** the person who owns this decision has
> implemented it twice, three months apart, in two subsystems, and both times context was
> priced once at startup rather than read as an input. @LucasWilkinson — is that a
> deliberate boundary?
>
> It is a real question and either answer is useful to me. If it is deliberate, then
> #48944 and #54801 are both arguing against a decision that has already been made twice
> by the person best placed to make it, and the honest thing is for me to say so on my own
> PR. If it is not deliberate, then the natural place for a context term is
> #47808's cost curves rather than the config tuple I have been widening — a smaller and
> better-located change than the one I have been proposing.
>
> I have no measurement on the adaptive-verification path and am not claiming one.
>
> ---
>
> Two smaller corrections while I am here.
>
> **Coordinates in the Motivation section have drifted.** Refreshed against `main`
> (`fa1b3b1922`): the scheduler index is now `sched/scheduler.py:1393-1397` (was
> `:1321-1324`); the capture-planning reads are `worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:246` (was
> `:219`) and `config/vllm.py:2282` (was `:2067`). `dynamic/utils.py:37` and `:77-81` are
> unchanged, and the quoted block itself is unchanged.
>
> **One piece of external evidence has arrived.** In #54691, @hongboshi1234 measured a
> break-even acceptance surface on B300 / TP8 / DCP-8 with Kimi-K3 and a DFlash drafter —
> different vendor, model family and drafter from mine — by forcing every draft to be
> rejected and comparing per-token latency against no speculation. For any achievable
> accept length in (1.91, 3.51), the resulting pays / does-not-pay region cannot be
> produced by a context rule and a batch rule consulted separately: (2k, B=8) pays, so
> neither rule fires there; (32k, B=8) does not pay, so the context rule must fire at 32k;
> but then (32k, B=1) would be switched off, and it pays. My own result has the opposite
> sign — speculation switched back *on* at high batch when context is long — and the same
> non-separable shape. Two measurements is not many, but they are independent, and the
> second was not looking for this. I checked their proposed *mechanism* and it does not
> hold, which I have said in that thread; the surface stands, the explanation for its
> magnitude is open.


> **Update, 2026-09-20 — walking back one phrase, and a constraint that applies to either answer.**
>
> No answer yet on the question above, which is a fair outcome for a question nobody asked
> for. Two things are worth putting in the record regardless of who decides, because both
> narrow the decision rather than argue for a side.
>
> **First, a correction to my own 2026-09-13 update.** I wrote that a context term in
> #47808's cost curves would be *"a smaller and better-located change"* than widening the
> config tuple. I had not checked that, and having checked it, "better-located" holds but
> **"smaller" does not**. `self.cost_tables` is a pair of 1-D `np.ndarray`
> (`adaptive_verification.py:151`), built by `build_cost_tables_from_curves` (`:81-129`),
> which stitches three regimes together: a step function below the cudagraph capture limit
> where execution pads to the next captured size, linear interpolation above it where
> nothing pads, and linear extrapolation past the last profiled point. A context axis means
> reproducing all three per context slice, and the cudagraph discontinuity is a function of
> token count rather than context, so the axes do not separate cleanly. Profiling would
> also multiply: `batches_to_profile` currently yields
> `(capture_sizes + tail_sizes) × _PROFILE_REPLAYS`, with context pinned to one env value.
>
> **Second, the part that matters more, because it is not a preference.** Wherever the
> context term lives, the same question has to be answered, and I had not noticed that it
> is invariant to the choice.
>
> `get_num_tokens` computes one cost vector for the whole batch:
>
> ```python
>         draft_cost_ms, verify_cost_ms = self.cost_tables
>         costs = (
>             draft_cost_ms[len(req_ids)]
>             + verify_cost_ms[num_non_draft_tokens_total : ...]
>         )
> ```
>
> But a batch holds requests at many different context lengths. Indexing a context-keyed
> cost table requires collapsing them to a single number — and that is exactly the question
> benchislett put to me on #48944 on 2026-07-21:
>
> > *"It's not clear to me what is the right way to aggregate sequence length across a
> > batch. I feel like mean or max … makes more sense than median"*
>
> which #48944 currently exposes as `ctx_agg: Literal["median", "mean", "max"]`.
>
> So the aggregation question is **not** an artifact of the schedule-table design I have
> been proposing. It is a property of putting context into a per-batch budget decision at
> all, and it lands on the shipped controller identically. Whoever decides where the
> context term belongs — including deciding that it belongs nowhere — is deciding this too.
>
> I am noting it rather than answering it. My own answer to benchislett did not hold up:
> I retracted the benchmark evidence for the `mean` default on 2026-09-10 on #48944, because
> two of the four scenarios I had cited turned out to be controls. The knob names a real
> decision; the measurement I offered for its default does not survive, and I would not want
> that distinction lost if someone picks this up.
>
> **Third, a correction I owe on the telemetry ask above.** The Proposed Change section
> says *"nothing in the engine currently measures the quantity these policies need"* and
> picks that telemetry as the one thing worth taking from this thread. Half of that is
> wrong, and I should not have written it without looking harder.
>
> #50919 (`[MRV2] Worker-Level Timings`, open since 2026-08-03, +929/-7) exports exactly
> the latencies I said were missing:
>
> ```
> vllm:worker_spec_decode_proposer_time_seconds   labels: phase, num_requests
> vllm:worker_model_execute_time_seconds          labels: phase, num_model_tokens
> vllm:worker_step_time_seconds                   labels: phase, num_model_tokens
> ```
>
> So draft time and verify time are measured. What survives, and is sharper than what I
> originally wrote, is the **keying**. `WorkerTimingStats` carries `iteration_index`,
> `phase`, `num_model_tokens`, `num_requests`, and the prefill/decode token and request
> splits. It carries no KV context length and no selected K, and the `num_*_tokens` fields
> are query tokens for the step rather than cache depth.
>
> Those are the same two keys as the cost curves in #47808: `draft_curve` keyed on
> `s.num_reqs`, `verify_curve` on `s.num_target_tokens`. And #50919's own stated purpose
> is *"establish reliable statistics for introspective profiling-based tuning such as
> adaptive verification"* — so the instrument is being built to tune the policy, and the
> two share a key set that excludes context.
>
> That is the thing I would now put in place of my original ask. A profiling-driven policy
> cannot discover a dependence on an axis its instrumentation does not record. If context
> is deliberately out of scope for this decision, then this is all consistent and I should
> stop. If it is not deliberate, the cheapest place to find out is a context bucket on the
> proposer timing, long before anything needs to change in a schedule or a config tuple.
>
> I am not raising this on #50919 itself. It is a draft, and I have an open PR that
> benchislett holds review authority over, so a request there for the axis I happen to be
> arguing for would read as exactly what it would be.
>
> **Fourth, something merged after I drafted the rest of this, which changes the scope of
> the question rather than my answer to it.**
>
> #52228 (`[Model Runner V2] Acceptance estimation for adaptive verification`) merged on
> 2026-09-14 as `3bb0a03f35`. Two things about it are worth recording here.
>
> It removed the gate confining adaptive verification to DSpark. `SpeculativeConfig` used
> to raise `"Adaptive verification only supported with DSpark"`, and `DSparkSpeculator`
> additionally required a checkpoint with a trained confidence head. The new
> `OnlineAcceptanceEstimator` predicts per-position acceptance from draft logits that any
> drafter already materializes, so the trained head became an optimization rather than a
> precondition. The controller this thread has been asking about is therefore no longer a
> DSpark feature; on main it is the general adaptive-verification path.
>
> And it makes the shape of the decision visible in a way it was not before, because the
> two sides of the ratio in `get_num_tokens` are now keyed differently from each other.
>
> The benefit side is per-slot. `adaptive_verification.py:314, 326-328`:
>
> ```python
>         scores = np.sort(survival_probability[valid])[::-1]
>         ...
>         num_tokens_to_estimated_accepted_tokens = np.concatenate(
>             ([num_sampling_requests], num_sampling_requests + np.cumsum(scores))
>         )
> ```
>
> `survival_probability` is each request's own running product of per-position
> confidences, so the b-th admitted draft slot contributes `scores[b-1]` expected accepted
> tokens and that quantity belongs to an identifiable request.
>
> The cost side is not. Its marginal term is
> `verify_cost_ms[T+b] - verify_cost_ms[T+b-1]`, a function of the batch's total token
> count, identical no matter which request the slot belongs to. So the descending sort is
> the right admission order exactly when every draft slot costs the same to verify, which
> is what a table keyed on `s.num_target_tokens` encodes.
>
> This refines what I wrote above rather than repeating it. I said the batch-to-scalar
> aggregation question is invariant to where the context term lives. That still holds for
> a **batch-keyed** cost table, which is what both #48944 and #47808 have. What #52228
> shows is that the aggregation is forced by the table's keying and not by pricing context
> as such — because the benefit side prices per slot and never needs a batch reduction at
> all. I had been treating the aggregation as intrinsic. It is not; it is a consequence of
> the shape I picked, and of the shape the shipped cost table picked.
>
> One detail I want to state plainly because it removes the most reasonable objection.
> Per-request KV depth is not unavailable at this decision — it is already read there, at `:322-325`, above the cost expression at `:329`:
>
> ```python
>         num_sampling_requests = np.count_nonzero(
>             self.req_states.num_computed_tokens_np[slots] + num_non_draft_tokens
>             >= self.req_states.prefill_len.np[slots]
>         )
> ```
>
> `num_computed_tokens_np[slots]` is gathered for exactly the requests being priced, used
> to count how many have finished prefill, and not consulted again. So "context is not
> modelled in the cost table" is not a statement about what the scheduler can see.
>
> There is also a timing asymmetry now. The acceptance coefficients refit online every
> 100 steps for the life of the process (`acceptance_estimator.py:330`). The cost curves
> are fitted once, during startup capture — `set_initial_cost_curves` has a single caller,
> `model_runner.py:1044` — at one context length taken from
> `VLLM_ADAPTIVE_VERIFICATION_PROFILE_CONTEXT_LEN`, whose own comment in `envs.py` reads:
>
> > Raise it for long-context deployments, where step cost is dominated by attention over
> > a much larger KV cache than the default assumes.
>
> I am quoting that because it states the dependence better than I have been stating it,
> and because it shows the current answer is not that context does not matter — it is that
> context is an operator-set constant. That is a coherent position. It is the position I
> am asking whether anyone intends.
>
> To be careful about what I am not claiming: the acceptance estimator is **not** context-
> blind. Its feature is computed from the drafter's forward pass over the real prefix, and
> the code says so — *"It scores the draft distribution, not the token drawn from it, so
> it is a function of the prefix alone."* Context reaches the benefit side implicitly,
> through the drafter's own confidence. What is pooled is the fit: one global slope, with
> intercepts keyed on draft position only. Whether that pooling holds across context
> regimes is a question I can state but have not measured, and I would rather leave it
> stated than dress it up.
>
> One note on that pooling, since it stopped being only my reading of the code. #57533
> was opened on 2026-09-18 against the estimator, from a different direction: request-
> specific sampling transforms are applied on the target but not on the draft, so
> accept/reject labels from those requests were being folded into worker-wide coefficients
> that then size verification for unrelated later requests. That is not my question and it
> does not answer it — it concerns which observations are admissible, not which regimes a
> single fit is expected to span. I raise it only because it establishes that the fit being
> shared across heterogeneous requests is load-bearing rather than incidental, which
> otherwise I would be asserting on my own.
>
> Absent a decision here I am going to go and measure the boundary rather than keep arguing
> its shape, and I will report what comes back whichever way it falls. This RFC does not
> need a reply for that to happen.

title: [RFC]: Custom all-reduce for XPU
author: recutita
body:
### Motivation.

On 2x Intel Arc Pro B70, TP=2 runs at **61.4% of a single card** (17.5 vs 28.5 tok/s, Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ INT4, eager, no spec decode). Communication volume is not the reason: decode moves 1.29 MB/token over a link measured at 28.6 GB/s, so roughly 45 µs of wire time against a 47 ms step.

The cost is per *invocation*, not per byte. Each collective issues 85 to 91 Level Zero API calls regardless of message size, and a 0-byte `barrier()` costs the same 88 calls and 41.9 µs as a 10 KiB all-reduce. 24 of those calls are `zeDeviceGetCommandQueueGroupProperties`, a static device property that is re-queried every time. Decode issues 129 collectives per token, so this is paid 129 times per token with nothing to amortise it against.

There is a second, independent cost. The collective is synchronous on the host: `dist.all_reduce` blocks the calling thread for its full duration (measured, issue time equals completion time), so in eager mode the host stalls for 129 x 17 to 56 µs per token.

<details>
<summary>Measurements</summary>

2x Intel Arc Pro B70, PCIe Gen5 x8 (28.65 GB/s H2D measured), 600.3 GB/s VRAM read. `vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:nightly-7c5dc571` (unpatched upstream, vLLM 0.28.1rc1.dev199, vllm-xpu-kernels 0.1.14.1), Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ INT4, `--enforce-eager --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 1`, 300 tokens x2.

**Level Zero calls per collective** (2 ranks, bf16, torch profiler):

| call | per collective | note |
|---|---|---|
| `zeDeviceGetCommandQueueGroupProperties` | 24.00 | invariant across 10 KiB / 100 KiB / 1 MiB and `barrier()` |
| `zeEventQueryStatus` | 24 to 33 | completion spin; 173 at 1 MiB |
| `zeMemGetAllocProperties` | 13.00 | invariant |
| others | ~28 | |
| **total** | **85 to 91** | a single matmul costs 8.96 |

**Host cost** (10 KiB all-reduce, 2 ranks):

| | latency | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| `dist.all_reduce` (oneCCL) | 56.0 µs | 98.2 µs |
| `barrier()` (0 bytes) | 41.9 µs | |

CPU exceeds latency for oneCCL because a spin thread burns a second core.

**End-to-end**, TP=2, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.45`:

| | tok/s | vs TP=1 |
|---|---|---|
| TP=1 (util 0.90) | 28.48 | 100% |
| TP=2 oneCCL | 17.49 | 61.4% |

**Profile** (50 tokens, rank 0): `vllm::all_reduce` accounts for 2422 ms of a 9.10 s window over 6450 calls, which is 129 per token. Both ranks are symmetric within 2%, so this is not straggler skew. Device (`kernel`) time drops from 1780 to 1126 ms as expected for TP=2, while host `cpu_op` time rises from 7489 to 13327 ms.

</details>

### Proposed Change.

Add an opt-in XPU device communicator that bypasses oneCCL for `all_reduce`, following the shape of `custom_all_reduce.py` (CUDA, #2192) and `quick_all_reduce.py` (ROCm, #19744):

* Level Zero IPC gives each rank direct access to the peer's device buffer. dma-buf FDs are exchanged once at init over a UNIX socket (`SCM_RIGHTS`) and cached.
* Reduction is one-shot, as CUDA does for `world_size == 2`.
* The rank handshake happens **inside the kernel** via flags in IPC-shared device memory, so the host enqueues and returns (CUDA's `Signal` / `RankSignals`). Above 128 KiB the kernel's PCIe read (~12 GB/s) loses to the copy engine (~28 GB/s), so larger messages take a host-synchronised path instead.
* Single opt-in flag, **default off**. Degrades from device-sync to host-sync to oneCCL on any failure, with both ranks agreeing before switching.
* Scope: `all_reduce` only, `world_size == 2`, single node. Everything else goes to oneCCL.

Measured effect with the linked Draft PR: **17.5 to 28.5 tok/s (+62.9%)**, which puts TP=2 at parity with a single card. With MTP speculative decoding (built into Qwen3.5/3.8), **30.8 to 47.3 tok/s (+53.7%)**, which puts TP=2 5.5% ahead of a single card. Per-collective host cost drops from 56.0 to 6.8 µs.

### Would fixing oneCCL be better?

For the first half of the problem, yes. The 24 redundant property queries are an oneCCL/UR issue, and fixing them there would benefit every XPU user including ones not on this path. I would rather that happened. But it does not address the second half. `dist.all_reduce` blocking the host is why CUDA and ROCm both carry their own implementations, and making oneCCL cheaper does not remove it.

### Alternatives considered

* **Host shared-memory staging** instead of IPC: works and needs no C++ extension, but at 1 MiB it is indistinguishable from oneCCL (296.0 vs 294.8 µs), and it cannot move the handshake off the host. Dropped.
* **A wrapper around an existing library**, as `aiter_custom_all_reduce.py` does for AMD: I could not find such a library for XPU.

### Feedback Period.

No deadline on my side. The Draft PR is there to try; I will keep it rebased while this is open.

### CC List.

@mayuyuace @chaojun-zhang @jikunshang @xinyu-intel @YizhouZ

### Any Other Things.

A Draft PR with a working implementation is open at #54768 . It is 578 lines of Python excluding kernels, which is over the 500 LOC threshold in CONTRIBUTING, hence this RFC.

I am an external contributor with a pair of B70s as my only test hardware, so the scope above (all_reduce, world_size == 2, single node) reflects what I can verify rather than what the design could cover.

I found no prior or in-flight work on this in either repo. If I missed something, please point me at it.

## AI assistance


The investigation and the linked implementation were done with Claude Code (Opus 5 directing and measuring, Fable 5 implementing), with the human author choosing the problem and scope, rejecting conclusions the data did not support, and reviewing the result. The measurements above were produced and cross-checked in that loop; details are in the PR.

title: [RFC]: GDS kv offloading
author: effi-ofer
body:
## Motivation

vLLM KV cache offloading persists KV cache blocks from device (GPU, TPU, etc) to slower storage (CPU memory, NVMe, object stores) and loads them back on demand. We intend to add GDS (GPUDirect Storage) as a primary tier alongside CPU offloading. 

A large part of this work involves the refactoring of the existing cpu offloading.  Specifically, the `OffloadingWorker` interface passes logical device block IDs to workers, which then internally resolve them to device pointers. This duplicates tensor layout logic in every worker implementation. As part of our GDS implementation, we refactor the worker interface so that device pointer resolution happens once (at the `OffloadingConnectorWorker` boundary) and workers receive pre-resolved device pointers.

To further facilitate code reuse, we also introduce `FSOffloadingWorker`, an abstract base for file-based device offloading, so that different filesystem backends (GDS/cuFile, POSIX, NIXL, etc.) can be added without duplicating logic.

## Goals:

- GDS supports both read and write
- GDS supports canonical and TP agnostic
- GDS supports cross layout. Traditional per-layer contiguous layout might require a bounce buffer.
- Maximize code reuse between cpu offloading and gds offloading

## High level design

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        Scheduler Process                             │
│  **Shown for completeness, we do not change this process.**             │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │           OffloadingConnectorScheduler                         │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  │  • Decides which blocks to offload/load                       │  │
│  │  • Constructs DeviceLoadStoreSpec (block_ids, group_sizes, ...)  │  │
│  │  • Calls manager.prepare_store()                              │  │
│  │        → OffloadingLoadStoreSpec (polymorphic)                 │  │
│  │          resolved to CPULoadStoreSpec or FSLoadStoreSpec       │  │
│  │  • Packs into TransferJob(src_spec, dst_spec)                 │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  └───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                              │                                       │
│                              │ TransferJobs serialized into           │
│                              │ OffloadingConnectorMetadata            │
└──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               │  IPC (scheduler → worker process)
                               ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         Worker Process (Device)                       │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │           OffloadingConnectorWorker                             │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  │  • Receives TransferJobs containing DeviceLoadStoreSpec           │  │
│  │  • Holds CanonicalKVCaches (device tensor references)          │  │
│  │  • Maps: DeviceLoadStoreSpec → DevicePointers                 │  │
│  │  • Calls worker.submit_store(job_id, device_ptrs, dst_spec)    │  │
│  │  • Calls worker.submit_load(job_id, src_spec, device_ptrs)     │  │
│  │  • Polls worker.get_finished() for completion                  │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                │                                      │
│                                │ submit_store / submit_load           │
│                                ▼                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    OffloadingWorker (ABC)                       │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  │  submit_store(job_id, device_ptrs: DevicePointers,             │  │
│  │               dst_spec: OffloadingLoadStoreSpec) -> bool       │  │
│  │  submit_load(job_id, src_spec: OffloadingLoadStoreSpec,        │  │
│  │              device_ptrs: DevicePointers) -> bool              │  │
│  │  get_finished() -> list[TransferResult]                        │  │
│  │  wait(job_ids: set[int]) -> None                               │  │
│  │  shutdown() -> None                                            │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  ├────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │                        │                                       │  │
│  │  CPUOffloadingWorker   │   FSOffloadingWorker (ABC)            │  │
│  │                        │       │                               │  │
│  │  • Device ↔ CPU DMA    │       ├── GDSOffloadingWorker         │  │
│  │                        │       │   (cuFileWrite/Read)          │  │
│  │                        │       ├── PosixOffloadingWorker       │  │
│  │                        │       │   (pread/pwrite, future)      │  │
│  │                        │       └── NIXLOffloadingWorker         │  │
│  │                        │           (NIXL, future)              │  │
│  │                        │                                       │  │
│  └────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Worker Class Hierarchy

```
OffloadingWorker (ABC)
│
├── CPUOffloadingWorker
│   • Device ↔ CPU pinned memory DMA
│   • Receives: DevicePointers + CPULoadStoreSpec
│   • Resolves CPU block_ids → CPU tensor pointers internally
│   • Executes: swap_blocks_batch on device stream
│
└── FSOffloadingWorker (ABC)
    • Device ↔ filesystem (common orchestration)
    • Receives: DevicePointers + FSLoadStoreSpec (keys)
    • Groups pointers per key, resolves keys → file paths via FileMapper
    • Manages thread pool, completion tracking, file handle lifecycle
    • Delegates actual I/O to subclass abstract methods
    │
    ├── GDSOffloadingWorker
    │   • cuFileWrite / cuFileRead (device-direct DMA to NVMe)
    │   • Registers device buffers with cuFileBufRegister at init
    │   • No CPU bounce buffer — true zero-copy
    │
    ├── PosixOffloadingWorker (future)
    │   • pread / pwrite with CPU bounce buffer
    │   • Works on any POSIX filesystem
    │
    ├── NIXLOffloadingWorker (future)
    │   • NIXL FILE→VRAM transfers
    │
    └── CUDAFileOffloadingWorker (future)
        • cuFile async API (stream-ordered)
```

## Component Interactions (Store Path)

```
 OffloadingConnectorScheduler          OffloadingConnectorWorker
 ─────────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────────
 1. Selects blocks to offload
 2. device_spec = DeviceLoadStoreSpec(
        block_ids=[0,1,2],
        group_sizes=[3],
        block_indices=[0])
 3. dst_spec = manager.prepare_store()
        → OffloadingLoadStoreSpec (polymorphic)
          e.g. CPULoadStoreSpec(block_ids=[5,6,7])
          or   FSLoadStoreSpec(keys=[key0, key1, key2])
 4. Packs TransferJob
                    ──── IPC ────►     5. Receives TransferJob
                                       6. device_ptrs = resolve_device_pointers(
                                              device_spec, self.kv_caches)
                                       7. worker.submit_store(
                                              job_id, device_ptrs, dst_spec)
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
                                       CPUOffloadingWorker:
                                         • src = device_ptrs.ptrs (device addrs)
                                         • dst = resolve CPU block_ids
                                               → CPU tensor pointers
                                         • swap_blocks_batch(src, dst, sizes)

                                       ── OR ──

                                       GDSOffloadingWorker (via FSOffloadingWorker):
                                         • Groups device_ptrs per key
                                         • For each key:
                                           path = file_mapper.get_file_name(key)
                                           cuFileWrite(dev_ptr, size, file_offset)
```

## Component Interactions (Load Path)

```
 OffloadingConnectorScheduler          OffloadingConnectorWorker
 ─────────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────────
 1. Identifies blocks to load
 2. device_spec = DeviceLoadStoreSpec(
        block_ids=[10,11,12],
        group_sizes=[3],
        block_indices=[0])
 3. src_spec = manager.prepare_load()
        → OffloadingLoadStoreSpec (polymorphic)
          e.g. CPULoadStoreSpec(block_ids=[5,6,7])
          or   FSLoadStoreSpec(keys=[...])
 4. Packs TransferJob
                    ──── IPC ────►     5. Receives TransferJob
                                       6. device_ptrs = resolve_device_pointers(
                                              device_spec, self.kv_caches)
                                       7. worker.submit_load(
                                              job_id, src_spec, device_ptrs)
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
                                       CPUOffloadingWorker:
                                         • src = resolve CPU block_ids
                                         • dst = device_ptrs.ptrs (device addrs)
                                         • swap_blocks_batch(src, dst, sizes)

                                       ── OR ──

                                       GDSOffloadingWorker (via FSOffloadingWorker):
                                         • Groups device_ptrs per key
                                         • For each key:
                                           path = file_mapper.get_file_name(key)
                                           cuFileRead(path → dev_ptr, size, offset)
```

## FSOffloadingWorker Internal Design

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FSOffloadingWorker (ABC)                                         │
│                                                                  │
│  Owned state:                                                    │
│  • file_mapper: FileMapper          (key → path resolution)      │
│  • block_size_factor: int           (device blocks per file)     │
│  • thread_pool: ThreadPoolExecutor  (async I/O submission)       │
│  • transfers: dict[job_id, _Transfer]  (in-flight tracking)      │
│                                                                  │
│  submit_store(job_id, device_ptrs, dst_spec):                       │
│    1. Groups device_ptrs into per-key chunks                        │
│       (using group_block_counts + group_data_ref_counts)         │
│    2. For each key in dst_spec.keys:                             │
│       • Builds ops: list[(dev_ptr, size, file_offset)]           │
│       • Submits to thread pool: self.write_block(path, ops)      │
│    3. Records futures in _Transfer for completion tracking       │
│                                                                  │
│  submit_load(job_id, src_spec, device_ptrs):                        │
│    (mirror of submit_store)                                      │
│                                                                  │
│  get_finished() / wait() / shutdown():                           │
│    (common future-based completion tracking)                     │
│                                                                  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Abstract methods (subclass implements):                    │  │
│  │                                                            │  │
│  │  write_block(path, ops: list[(dev_ptr, size, offset)])     │  │
│  │  read_block(path, ops: list[(dev_ptr, size, offset)])      │  │
│  │  init_backend(kv_caches)  ← optional setup (buf register) │  │
│  │  shutdown_backend()       ← optional cleanup               │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │                              │
         ▼                              ▼
┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐
│  GDSOffloadingWorker │    │  PosixOffloadingWorker   │
│                      │    │  (future)                │
│  init_backend:       │    │                          │
│    cuFileDriverOpen  │    │  write_block:            │
│    cuFileBufRegister │    │    os.pwrite(fd, buf,    │
│                      │    │      offset)             │
│  write_block:        │    │    (with CPU bounce buf) │
│    fd = open_for_gds │    │                          │
│    h = HandleRegister│    │  read_block:             │
│    cuFileWrite(...)  │    │    os.pread(fd, size,    │
│    HandleDeregister  │    │      offset)             │
│    os.close(fd)      │    │    cudaMemcpy → GPU      │
│                      │    │                          │
│  read_block:         │    └──────────────────────────┘
│    fd = open_for_gds │
│    h = HandleRegister│
│    cuFileRead(...)   │
│    HandleDeregister  │
│    os.close(fd)      │
│                      │
└──────────────────────┘
```


## TP agnostic related changes

To enable larger IO when reading or writting TP agnostic data, we propose writing TP agnostic data in the following order: layer, head, chunk. This is a change from the way TP agnostic data is writen today, which is: block, head, layer.

## Access mode

Introduce access mode offloading connector parameter which can be read, write, or readwrite (which is the default). This facilitates multi-connector setup using multi-tier and gds, where the multi tier writes to the file system and the gds connector reads.  We suggest enabling access mode for the multi-tier fs secondary connector and gds.

## Key Design Decisions

1. **Changes are resticted to the worker** - we avoid making changes in
   the scheduler or to the multi-tier logic. An exception can be made for
   introducing a write_only mode to the multi-tier secondary storage.

2. **`DeviceLoadStoreSpec` stays at the scheduler level** — the scheduler thinks
   in block IDs. Resolution to device pointers happens once at the
   `OffloadingConnectorWorker` boundary via `resolve_device_pointers()`.

3. **Code reuse** - a prime goal of this work is to avoid code duplication
   between the cpu offloading and gds offloading

4. **`FSOffloadingWorker` as ABC** — common file-based offloading logic
   (key→path mapping, per-key pointer grouping, thread pool, completion
   tracking) lives in the base class. Subclasses implement only
   `write_block`/`read_block`.

---

### Proposed Change.

two weeks

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@Etelis @orozery @dannyharnik @maheshrbapatu


### Any Other Things.

This RFC intends to include the work described in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48504.

title: [RFC]: Truncate mode for `thinking_token_budget`
author: walterbm-cohere
body:
### Motivation.

`thinking_token_budget` currently enforces the budget by forcing the logits of
`reasoning_end_str` (e.g. `</think>`) once the reasoning block reaches the budget, then
letting the model continue with the answer. That make sense for general serving but is not ideal for RL
rollouts:

- The forced tokens are not sampled from the policy, so they are off-policy tokens in the
  trajectory and their logprobs are polluted by the 1e9 logit override.
- There is no signal that the budget was hit; the response finishes with the usual
  `finish_reason="stop"`.
- RL trainers typically want an over-budget sample to end right there, be marked as
  truncated (`finish_reason="length"`), and free its KV cache instead of generating an answer

### Proposed Change.

Add an engine-wide flag to `ReasoningConfig`:

```python
thinking_budget_action: Literal["force_end", "truncate"] = "force_end" # keeps current behavior as default
```

```bash
vllm serve ... --reasoning-config '{ ... "thinking_budget_action": "truncate"}'
```

With `thinking_budget_action=truncate`:

- The budget is enforced in the scheduler, not the sampler. A small tracker on
  `Request` (reasoning start position, reasoning token count) is updated per output token
  in `_update_request_with_output`, using the start and natural-end token ids already
  derived by `ReasoningConfig.initialize_token_ids`. Prompt-resident reasoning tokens
  are counted at request creation, as the current implementation does.
- `check_stop` add one conditional branch next to the `max_tokens` check: when the count reaches
  the budget the request is finished with a new `RequestStatus.FINISHED_THINKING_BUDGET`,
  mapped to `FinishReason.LENGTH`, with `stop_reason="thinking_token_budget"`. No new
  `FinishReason` value, so API and Rust DTOs are unchanged.
- The sampler-side engines are disabled at construction in this mode
  (`maybe_create_thinking_budget_state_holder` returns `None`; V2 `ThinkingBudgetState`
  is constructed disabled). No token is ever forced.
- Speculative decoding and async scheduling need no special handling: the existing
  per-token stop loop already trims tokens after a stop, and the one-step lag is the same as
  for `max_tokens`.

List of affected files (probably): `vllm/config/reasoning.py`, `vllm/v1/request.py`,
`vllm/v1/core/sched/utils.py`, one condition each in `gpu_input_batch.py` and
`gpu/sample/thinking_budget.py`, docs in `reasoning_outputs.md`, unit tests in
`tests/v1/core` and an e2e case in `test_thinking_token_budget.py`.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

🤚 happy to contribute this feature if accepted! I already have a working implementation
