- Our recipe forces `--moe-backend aiter_triton_mxfp4_bf16`, which resolves to `AiterW4A16ExpertsMonolithic` -> Triton `moe_gemm_a16w4`. That path takes **heuristic** kernel configs (`get_kernel_config_triton/gluon`), and AITER ships no gfx950 `a16w4` tuned dispatch tree (only `a8w4/DEFAULT.json`). None of the configs above apply to us.
- Meanwhile the ROCm oracle, under `moe_backend=auto`, explicitly prefers the other one for this routing method: *"DeepSeek-V4 on ROCm: prefer AITER FlyDSL MoE (better perf + accuracy after shuffle/TP-offset fixes), with Triton-unfused as fallback"* (`oracle/mxfp4.py:690-701`).
- And `benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_moe.py` cannot tune our backend even if we wanted to: its dtype choices are `auto`, `fp8_w8a8`, `int8_w8a16`, `int4_w4a16` - no MXFP4 mode (`benchmark_moe.py:1075`).

Proposal, in order: A/B `auto` / `aiter` against the forced `aiter_triton_mxfp4_bf16` on gfx950 and fix the recipe if FlyDSL wins, since tuned configs already exist for it; then add an MXFP4 mode to `benchmark_moe.py` so the Triton `a16w4` path can be tuned at all; then upstream gfx950 `a16w4` configs.

Note #56543 (DNM) proposes the opposite for the same code path -- pinning `backend="triton"` for both AITER W4A16 MoE GEMMs on gfx942/gfx950 -- so the A/B result above is worth reconciling against it before either lands.

---

## 5. Prefill top-k combine falls back to Torch

`deepseek_v4_1/amd/rocm.py:175-186` uses ordinary Torch indexing because the Triton kernel inherited from V4 "can issue an out-of-bounds access for V4.1's mixed prefill metadata" on gfx950. Prefill-only and small tensors, but it is a known-missing gfx950-safe kernel and TTFT has room.

Addressed by #56638, which re-enables `_combine_topk_swa_indices_kernel` with the three unsafe behaviours fixed in place. It also notes the fallback is not merely slow: `repeat_interleave` on a tensor syncs to the host, so the Torch path cannot be graph-captured at all.

---

## 6. DSA sparse indexer

Not in the original write-up, and on a newer nightly it is the second-largest block of the decode step after the MoE GEMMs. Splitting it out of the single "indexer/topk" bucket a category summary produces, at 131k context, MoE on the CK a8w4 path:

| | conc 1 | conc 4 | conc 16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| mqa logits (fp8 paged) | 0.148 | 0.405 | 1.534 |
| candidate mask | 0.048 | 0.133 | 0.464 |
| candidate select | 0.059 | 0.072 | 0.118 |
| topk per row | 0.485 | 0.527 | 0.838 |
| **indexer total** | **0.741** | **1.138** | **2.954** |
| **share of step** | **4.1%** | **6.2%** | **11.4%** |

The composition inverts with concurrency: at 1 the top-k dominates and is launch-bound, at 16 the MQA logits GEMM does. Full detail and method in [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56506#issuecomment-5647767775).

### 6.1 Candidate mask sized by the workspace, not the context

`apply_candidate_mask` receives the `[rows, max_model_len]` logits workspace unsliced, so its grid was 1024 programs per row when ~128 have work, and cost tracked rows while ignoring context. Columns at or past a row's `end` are never read: `top_k_per_row_decode` bounds its scan by the same ends, which is also why the no-candidate path skips the mask entirely and reads the same workspace safely.

Addressed by #56628: 2.7x / 4.3x / 6.0x on the kernel at concurrency 1 / 4 / 16, gsm8k 0.9727 / 0.9719.

### 6.2 `next_n` is spent on program count instead of the GEMM tile

The largest single item at concurrency 16 (1.534 ms/step, 5.9% of the step) is `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits`. AITER launches `grid = batch * next_n * SplitKV`, so with DSpark 5-token MTP the kernel issues six independent M=32 MFMAs per K block where one M=192 would do.

Its own M-scaling, measured at constant K traffic, is monotone: per unit of work M=64 is 1.27x more efficient than M=32, and M=128 is 1.53x. We sit at the worst point of that curve.

Filed as [ROCm/aiter#5477](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/5477). It has to be an AITER change -- the kernel is 2213 lines of hand-scheduled Gluon, `next_n` is not a constexpr there, and a plain-Triton reimplementation of the same algorithm runs 2.2x slower, so the call site cannot reach it.

Two things ruled out on the way, recorded so nobody repeats them. The `grid = batch * next_n * SplitKV` shape looks like it streams K `next_n` times, but building both variants in Triton shows the shared-K version requests 5.2x fewer HBM bytes and is *slightly slower* -- the re-reads are already absorbed by cache. And `VarCtxSchedule`, the persistent-grid variant that looks made for our ragged contexts, is 1.7x slower.

### 6.3 gfx950 decode top-k tunings are unreachable at `index_topk = 512`

`csrc/libtorch_stable/sampler.cu` has two gfx950-specific configurations and both are gated on `topK == 1024`; this model sets 512, so every decode falls to the generic `multipleBlocksPerRowConfig = 10` path. The trace confirms it: `vllm::topKPerRowDecode<512, true, true, false>`. Asking the op for `topK = 1024` is *faster* than 512 at our shapes despite twice the output (0.0508 vs 0.0632 ms at concurrency 16), so the gate looks like tuning rather than a correctness bound. Worth roughly 0.2 ms/step; needs a C++ rebuild to confirm, and I would rather know whether the `== 1024` is deliberate first.

The other three routes are closed on ROCm: `cooperative_topk` and `persistent_topk` both accept `topk_tokens` of 512 but are gated on `is_cuda()`, and AITER's decode top-k is excluded twice in `_get_aiter_top_k_kernel` (by `compress_ratio <= 1` for five of the eight indexer layers, and by the 64k compressed-length bound for the rest). That bound also computes a different quantity in the FULL and non-FULL branches -- `max_model_len` undivided versus `max_seq_len // compress_ratio` -- which should be reconciled even though fixing it unlocks nothing here.

### 6.4 FP4 MQA logits

AITER ships `flydsl_pa_mqa_logits_fp4` and variants. Four things sit in the way: `dsa_indexer_uses_fp4()` raises unless `is_device_capability_family(100)`; `forward_hip` asserts `not self.use_fp4_cache`; there is no FP4 indexer K-cache insert on ROCm (the unfused path asserts, and AITER's `indexer_k_quant_and_cache` has no FP4 mode); and the kernel wants a pre-swizzled `q_scale`.

Sizing this was initially done by traffic accounting -- halve the K read, halve the kernel -- and that is wrong. At `next_n = 6` this kernel is not HBM-bandwidth bound: doubling `heads` doubles the compute at constant K bytes for only 1.5x the time, and removing 5.2x of the K reads changes nothing. So FP4 remains worth having for the memory footprint, but should not be sized as a decode-time win until measured. Accuracy is the larger risk either way, since the indexer picks which 512 tokens attention sees.

---

## 7. MXFP8 dense-linear path

Not in the original write-up, and after #56503 it is the largest block of the decode step outside the MoE and the indexer. The dense projections (MLA `fused_wqa_wkv` / `wq_b` / `wo_a` / `wo_b`, the indexer projections, the compressor, and the shared-expert MLP) are MXFP8 and run `RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel`.

Method, since it bounds what these numbers support: rank-0 graph-captured decode traces at 131k context, MoE on the CK a8w4 path, `ROCPROFILER_QUEUE_INTERPOSITION=0`, eight decode steps sampled after all lanes are confirmed decoding by client-side SSE counting. Figures are summed kernel durations divided by steps. That basis is inflated -- at concurrency 1 it sums to 17.4 ms/step against a client-measured unprofiled step of 12.9 ms -- so **only launch counts and relative composition should be read as load-bearing**, not absolute times. Where a claim needs an absolute number it comes from a separate graph-replay microbenchmark, noted inline.

Where the step goes, at concurrency 1 and 32:

| group | c1 | c32 | launches/step (c32) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| sparse indexer | 1.05 | 6.14 | 146 |
| MoE experts (CK a8w4) | 1.20 | 5.92 | 92 |
| long tail of small elementwise ops | 4.11 | 4.96 | 880 |
| **MXFP8 weight dequant (per step)** | **2.15** | **4.47** | 360 |
| MXFP8 linear (quant + GEMM) | 2.13 | 3.98 | 397 |
| MLA attention core | 0.89 | 3.16 | 142 |
| BF16 Tensile GEMMs | 1.23 | 2.73 | 163 |
| TP all-reduce | 0.73 | 2.72 | 98 |
| mHC / hyper-connection | 2.05 | 2.57 | 460 |
| MoE sort / route / quant | 1.45 | 1.82 | 229 |

The step still issues **2,850 launches at concurrency 1 and 3,064 at 32**, of which 89% and 75% respectively are shorter than 10 us. The dispatch-bound thesis in the Motivation survives #56503; it just moved.

### 7.1 The MXFP8 weight is dequantized on every forward

`RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel.apply_weights` needs `K % 128 == 0` for `tl.dot_scaled`, and where that fails it rebuilds a BF16 copy of a constant weight per step:

```python
w_bf16 = dequant_mxfp8_to_bf16(layer.weight, layer.weight_scale)
out = torch.nn.functional.linear(x2d, w_bf16).to(x.dtype)
```

On V4.1-Flash this fires on the shared expert's row-parallel `down_proj`, whose K is sharded while `gate_up`'s stays at 5120: `moe_intermediate_size` 2304 gives 576 at TP4 and 288 at TP8, neither divisible by 128, so TP4 and TP8 pay it on every layer while TP1 and TP2 never see it.

`dequant_mxfp8_to_bf16` is six pointwise kernels with an FP32 intermediate, so it is far off what the bytes justify -- about 97 us per layer in these traces. The `exp2_kernel_vectorized4` launch count is an unambiguous fingerprint for it: 43.4 per step at concurrency 1 and 45.9 at 32, one per layer, flat in concurrency because the work is weight-sized. Summed over the signature kernels it is 2.09 -> 4.33 ms/step, a steady 11-12% of kernel time at every concurrency measured.

Addressed by #56560, which converts once in `process_weights_after_loading` and dispatches on the weight's element size, as `EmulationMxfp8LinearKernel` already does. Reported at 4.6% / 2.3% lower median TPOT at concurrency 1 / 8 with `exp2_kernel_vectorized4` going to exactly zero, and 0.11 GiB more weight memory per rank. Its only failing check is the `pre-run-check` label gate, not a test.

### 7.2 The activation quant is a separate launch per GEMM

`_mxfp8_dot_scaled_linear` calls `mxfp8_e4m3_quantize` and then the GEMM, so the pair `_kernel.kd` -> `_mxfp8_linear_kernel.kd` is the most frequent back-to-back chain in the step: 187.2 occurrences at concurrency 1 and 198.2 at 32, and adjacency is 100% -- every quant launch is immediately followed by its GEMM. The quant kernel is dispatch-floor rather than work: it moves 92 KB at M=6 (11 ns of traffic at 8 TB/s) and its marginal cost measures 4.4 us, matching the 4.15 us the trace attributes to it. AITER's `per_1x32_mx_quant_hip` measures 2.05 us against the Triton kernel's 2.04 us on the same shape, so swapping implementations is not the lever.

**The obvious fix does not work.** Folding the quant into the GEMM prologue -- recomputing the per-32 E8M0 scale in registers inside the K-loop and feeding `tl.dot_scaled` directly -- is numerically correct and **0.28-0.89x**, i.e. up to 3.5x slower. It is not the redundant work across N-tiles, which is the intuitive explanation: sweeping N from 16 to 1280 (grid_n 1 to 80) holds the ratio flat at 0.41-0.45x, so it is just as slow when the activation is quantized exactly once. The in-register quant adds 26 us on top of a 12 us GEMM to save a 4.4 us launch, against roughly 0.3 us of actual arithmetic, and a ~100-config tile sweep got no further than 0.71x. That gap is how Triton lowers the reshape-and-reduce on gfx950, not something tuning reaches. Recorded so nobody repeats it.

**The producer side works.** Asking the trace what *produces* these activations: `aiter::add_rmsnorm_quant_kernel` immediately precedes the quant 78.6 times per step at concurrency 1 and 83.1 at 32. That kernel already normalizes and quantizes, so folding the MX quant into it costs no redundant work. AITER supports this today in principle -- `rmsnorm2d_fwd_with_add_dynamicquant` routes a 1-byte E8M0 scale plus a `group_size` to the HIP `add_rmsnorm_quant`, which is exactly the format `tl.dot_scaled` consumes.

It was blocked by one arithmetic detail. The kernel picks `thread_data_size` from the hidden size and then asserts `group_size % thread_data_size == 0`; hidden 5120 lands in the `n <= 6144` band at `thread_data_size = 24`, and 32 does not divide 24, so it aborts. Confirmed across the ladder: 1024, 2048, 4096 and 6272-8192 all accept group 32, and only 5120 and 6144 -- the two `tds=24` sizes -- are rejected. This is a latent AITER bug rather than a missing feature, since the existing `per_1x32` MXFP4 test path hits it too; it survived because the test's default `-n` sweep skips that band entirely.

Fixed by [ROCm/aiter#5480](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5480), which mirrors the group-aware config selection the `n <= 8192` branch already uses into the `n <= 6144` band, reusing instantiations that branch already relies on. It is strictly additive: `group_size == 0` and multiples of 24 keep today's config. With it, hidden 5120 emits MXFP8 matching a reference MX quantizer on 99.7% of block scales, within one E4M3 ULP dequantized, residual bit-exact, and AITER's own MXFP4 test passes at 5120 and 6144 where it previously aborted.

Worth **1.49x at M=8 rising to 1.77x at M=256** on the norm-plus-quant pair (2.2 us and 4.1 us saved per occurrence, graph-replay latency with the replay floor amortized over 64 copies per graph). At step level that is ~175 us at concurrency 1 and ~343 us at 32, so about **1% of kernel time** -- less than the quant kernel's full 4.5%/2.2% share, because the fused norm is itself ~0.9 us more expensive than the plain one and only ~80 of the ~190 quant calls have this producer. It also removes ~80 of the 2,850-3,064 launches per step.

Still open: the vLLM side needs an op returning the norm's `(fp8, E8M0 scale)` pair and a `RocmDotScaledMxfp8LinearKernel` entry point that accepts a pre-quantized activation instead of quantizing internally. And the remaining ~107 quant calls per step have different producers -- `elementwise_kernel_manual_unro

title: [RFC]: Streaming prompt prefill for overlapping upstream generation and downstream prefill
author: xu-jia-ming
body:
### Motivation.

Some serving pipelines generate a request's prompt incrementally before the full prompt is known. One important case is chained or multi-stage generation, where an upstream model produces tokens that become part of a downstream model's prompt.

Today, the downstream request generally cannot begin prefill until the full prompt has been materialized and submitted. This creates avoidable latency: upstream generation and downstream prefill are serialized even when the downstream engine could already process the prefix tokens that are available.

This RFC proposes adding streaming prompt prefill support so a request can accept additional prompt tokens after submission, prefill them incrementally, and only enter decode after the prompt is finalized.

This is related to, but different from, output streaming. The goal is not to expose decode output early. The goal is to let prompt prefill make progress while the prompt is still being produced.

A prototype implementation is available in PR #53733:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53733

### Proposed Change.

Add a V1 engine/scheduler flow for streaming prompt requests:

- Submit a request as a streaming-prompt request with an initial prompt prefix.
- Allow the client to append prompt token IDs while the request is still in prompt-processing mode.
- Allow the client to finalize the prompt.
- Prevent decode/sampling output from being exposed before finalization.
- Let the scheduler run prefill-only steps for unfinished streaming prompts.
- Resume normal decode once the request is finalized and all prompt tokens have been processed.
- Track prompt-processing metrics so callers can observe how much incremental prefill has completed.

The prototype PR currently implements this across:

- request state
- scheduler output/state transitions
- async engine APIs
- core client routing
- GPU model runner request-state updates
- tests for scheduler behavior, async engine behavior, cached request appends, invalid inputs, and output suppression before finalization

The intended benefit is lower end-to-end latency for pipelines where prompt construction is incremental, especially when downstream prompt prefill can overlap upstream token generation.

The current PR intentionally keeps the behavior conservative:

- streaming prompt requests do not expose sampled output before finalization
- unsupported sampling configurations are rejected
- appended prompts are checked against max model length
- cached/rescheduled requests propagate appended prompt tokens into worker state before the next forward pass

Open questions for maintainers:

- Is this API shape acceptable for V1, or should the append/finalize surface live elsewhere?
- Should this be limited to token IDs only, or should text-level append be supported later?
- Are there scheduler fairness concerns for prefill-only streaming prompt work?
- Should metrics be exposed through the current helper API or integrated into a broader request-status API?
- Are there additional constraints needed for distributed / DPLB execution paths?

### Feedback Period.

One to two weeks, or whatever timeline maintainers prefer. Feedback on the API shape and scheduler semantics would be especially helpful before further expanding the implementation.

### CC List.

Potentially relevant areas: scheduler, V1 engine, disaggregated serving / prefill-decode pipelines.

### Any Other Things.

Prototype PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53733

The PR is currently rebased on latest main and includes local validation results in the PR discussion. The goal of this RFC is to discuss whether the feature direction and API semantics are acceptable, not to bypass normal PR review.

title: [RFC][KV Offload]: Align sliding-window restore coverage with MTP-retained history
author: jacklin78911-collab
body:
### Motivation

Native KV offload can report a sliding-window prefix hit and then try to load an older chunk that was never included in that hit. I reproduced both `Chunk ... not found in cache` and `Chunk ... is not ready for reading` through the real Python offload scheduler, CPU manager, and GPU block allocator classes, without concurrent eviction or any GPU kernel execution.

The trigger is `SlidingWindowSpec.extra_retained_tokens > 0`. `get_kv_cache_configs()` sets this to `num_speculative_tokens - 1` for multi-module MTP. That field extends the history retained by the block manager, but offload lookup and the producer's reachable-store mask still use the attention window without that extension.

This RFC asks whether the offload contract should cover the entire retained interval. My proposed first fix is to make lookup and store coverage match the existing allocation contract. The alternative—allocating only the attention-required interval on an external hit—needs a separate proof that later MTP replay and caching cannot read or publish the omitted history.

Source inspected and exercised: upstream main at [`fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748).

### Reproduced failure

A small hybrid layout is sufficient:

- Full-attention group: 64 tokens per block.
- Sliding-window group: 16 tokens per block, attention window 32, extra retained history 3.
- One block per offload chunk, 16 tokens per hash, 65-token prompt, zero local cache hits.
- CPU cache contains the full-attention prefix and SWA chunks 2 and 3. SWA chunk 1 is independently missing, pending, or ready.

At the 64-token hit boundary, attention needs history starting at token `64 - 32 + 1 = 33`, within SWA chunk 2. The actual allocator retains history starting at `64 - 32 + 1 - 3 = 30`, within chunk 1.

| Extra history | Chunk 1 | Reported hit | Allocated SWA offsets | Load result |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 0 | missing / pending / ready | 64 | 2, 3 | succeeds |
| 3 | missing | 64 | 1, 2, 3 | `not found in cache` assertion |
| 3 | pending | 64 | 1, 2, 3 | `not ready for reading` assertion |
| 3 | ready | 64 | 1, 2, 3 | succeeds |

The missing chunk does not require an eviction race. For this hybrid layout, the real `_reachable_store_block_mask()` returns `[False, False, True, True]` at the 64-token boundary even with extra history enabled: the producer's filter itself omits chunk 1.

This is a bookkeeping reproduction, not a full model-serving reproduction. The prompt hashes and config objects are synthetic; `OffloadingConnectorScheduler`, `CPUOffloadingManager`, `BlockPool`, `FullAttentionManager`, and `SlidingWindowManager` are the actual implementations. No scheduler or allocator function is mocked. The target SWA descriptor is populated directly to isolate the retention contract; the probe does not instantiate an MTP drafter.

### Code path

1. [`get_kv_cache_configs()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py) tags sliding-window specs for multi-module MTP.
2. [`SlidingWindowManager.get_num_skipped_tokens()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py) subtracts `extra_retained_tokens`. Initial local-block adoption pads fewer null slots; external allocation therefore allocates the older retained block too.
3. [`get_sliding_window_size_in_chunks()` / `load_window_size_in_chunks()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py) omit that extension. Lookup reports 64 matched tokens without checking chunk 1.
4. `update_state_after_alloc()` starts from the first fresh non-null block, including chunk 1. [`CPUOffloadingManager.prepare_load()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/manager.py) then correctly rejects the unavailable chunk.
5. `SlidingWindowManager.reachable_block_mask()`, used by offload store filtering, also derives coverage from `sliding_window` alone.

### Proposed change

Keep the current allocator and MTP retention semantics. Make native offload coverage include every chunk that those semantics cause an external restore to read:

1. Derive offload lookup coverage from the retained interval, including partial-chunk alignment. Apply the same interval to the in-flight-load conflict check and relevant recency touches.
2. Extend the producer's offload store mask to supply that interval. Changing the lookup window alone would turn affected restores into misses because the producer can still omit the required chunk.
3. Keep the current outcomes: a missing required chunk shortens/rejects the hit; a pending required chunk defers lookup; a complete hit can be allocated and loaded. Preserve the existing `prepare_load` assertions.
4. Keep the actual model attention window, wire format, cache keys, and transfer ownership unchanged. No new user option is needed for an internal correctness contract.

The invariant is: **every chunk consumed by an admitted restore must be covered by the confirmed lookup, and every required chunk must be reachable through the corresponding producer store policy.**

A diagnostic baseline expands only the offload coverage descriptor from window 32 to 35 while preserving the real allocator's original `window=32, extra=3` spec. With this expansion, the mask becomes `[False, True, True, True]`; a missing chunk produces zero hits, a pending chunk defers, and a ready chunk restores 64 tokens successfully. All six `extra=0` controls are unchanged across the two modes. The script below checks all 12 combinations.

This descriptor substitution is an experiment, not the proposed production implementation. Production code should express offload coverage explicitly rather than changing a model's attention window. Wider coverage also has a cost: this example stores/loads three SWA chunks instead of two. It needs measurement, not an assumption that extra history is free.

### Validation before a PR

- Protect the confirmed missing/pending/ready behavior and zero-extra controls in the existing offload scheduler suite.
- Exercise a producer-to-consumer replay using actual store selection, CPU completion, lookup, and allocation; check that demanded keys were offered for storage.
- Cover chunk factors greater than one, unaligned hybrid hit boundaries, EAGLE tail handling, and in-flight loads with the same coverage invariant.
- Validate real multi-module MTP outputs and acceptance, plus cache bytes/hit rate and end-to-end latency on a prefix-reusing workload. These model/performance results have not been run and are not claimed here.

### Related work and duplicate check

Searched open PRs and issues for `extra_retained_tokens`, offload + retained history, multi-module + offload, and offload window/load coverage on 2026-09-13.

- #55818 addresses sliding-window allocation scaling and preserves extra retention; it does not align offload lookup/store coverage.
- #52287 addresses store windows moved by EAGLE's volatile-tail pop. This reproduction has no EAGLE pop.
- #56486 addresses a pending flag left behind by an invalid suffix. This reproduction has a complete reported hit and a later load failure.
- #54914 reports a similar load assertion under DSpark. I have not reproduced that deployment or established this mechanism as its cause; this RFC does not claim to resolve it.

### Feedback period

One week. The main decision is whether native offload should restore the entire retained interval, as proposed here, or whether initial external-hit allocation should distinguish retention-only history from the history required to resume. The latter must also preserve MTP replay and cache-publication correctness.

### Reproducer and environment

The 12-case diagnostic was executed with Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, the pinned Python source above, and existing precompiled extensions in WSL Ubuntu 24.04. No GPU kernels or model inference were executed. This is not validation on the repository's current PyTorch 2.13 dependency matrix.

Save the following as `retained_window_probe.py` in an installed checkout and run `.venv/bin/python retained_window_probe.py`. It writes a JSON result beside the script and checks the expected outcomes, including the two assertions in the unmodified path.

<details>
<summary>Executable 12-case diagnostic</summary>

```python
"""Exercise real offload lookup/allocation with MTP's retained SWA history."""

import json
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import torch

from vllm.distributed.kv_transfer.kv_connector.v1.offloading.scheduler import (
    OffloadingConnectorScheduler,
)
from vllm.v1.core.block_pool import BlockPool
from vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_manager import KVCacheBlocks
from vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_utils import BlockHash
from vllm.v1.core.single_type_kv_cache_manager import (
    FullAttentionManager,
    SlidingWindowManager,
)
from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import (
    FullAttentionSpec,
    KVCacheConfig,
    KVCacheGroupSpec,
    SlidingWindowSpec,
)
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.base import OffloadingKVEventsConfig
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.cpu.manager import CPUOffloadingManager


def probe(extra: int, older_state: str, expanded_coverage: bool = False):
    kv_spec = SlidingWindowSpec(
        block_size=16,
        num_kv_heads=1,
        head_size=1,
        dtype=torch.float32,
        sliding_window=32,
        extra_retained_tokens=extra,
    )
    full_spec = FullAttentionSpec(
        block_size=64,
        num_kv_heads=1,
        head_size=1,
        dtype=torch.float32,
    )
    groups = [KVCacheGroupSpec(["full"], full_spec), KVCacheGroupSpec(["swa"], kv_spec)]
    manager = CPUOffloadingManager(num_chunks=8)
    spec = SimpleNamespace(
        config=SimpleNamespace(
            groups=tuple(
                SimpleNamespace(group_id=i, tokens_per_block=g.kv_cache_spec.block_size)
                for i, g in enumerate(groups)
            )
        ),
        tokens_per_block=(64, 16),
        tokens_per_hash=16,
        blocks_per_chunk=1,
        offload_prompt_only=True,
        kv_events_config=OffloadingKVEventsConfig(
            enable_kv_cache_events=False, self_describing_kv_events=False
        ),
        get_manager=lambda: manager,
    )
    config = SimpleNamespace(
        speculative_config=None,
        cache_config=SimpleNamespace(
            enable_prefix_caching=True, prefix_cache_retention_interval=None
        ),
        parallel_config=SimpleNamespace(world_size=1, decode_context_parallel_size=1),
    )
    sched = OffloadingConnectorScheduler(
        spec,
        config,
        KVCacheConfig(num_blocks=32, kv_cache_tensors=[], kv_cache_groups=groups),
    )
    if expanded_coverage:
        # Diagnostic only: expand the offload coverage descriptor, preserving the
        # real GPU allocator's spec. This is not a production model patch.
        coverage_spec = replace(
            kv_spec, sliding_window=32 + extra, extra_retained_tokens=0
        )
        group = sched.config.kv_group_configs[1]._replace(
            sliding_window_size_in_chunks=(32 + extra + 15) // 16,
            kv_cache_spec=coverage_spec,
        )
        sched.config = sched.config._replace(
            kv_group_configs=(sched.config.kv_group_configs[0], group)
        )
    req = MagicMock()
    req.request_id = "replay"
    req.kv_transfer_params = None
    req.num_tokens = req.num_prompt_tokens = 65
    req.block_hashes = [BlockHash(f"block{i}".encode()) for i in range(4)]
    req.skip_reading_prefix_cache = False
    sched.on_new_request(req)
    state = sched._req_status[req.request_id]
    state.update_offload_keys()
    full_keys, keys = (g.offload_keys for g in state.group_states)
    ready = full_keys[:1] + keys[1 if older_state == "ready" else 2 :]
    store = manager.prepare_store(ready, state.req_context)
    assert store is not None
    manager.complete_store(store.keys_to_store, state.req_context)
    if older_state == "pending":
        assert manager.prepare_store([keys[1]], state.req_context) is not None
    external, async_load = sched.get_num_new_matched_tokens(req, 0)
    pool = BlockPool(32, enable_caching=True, hash_block_size=16)
    managers = [
        cls(
            kv_cache_spec=g.kv_cache_spec,
            block_pool=pool,
            enable_caching=True,
            kv_cache_group_id=i,
            scheduler_block_size=64,
        )
        for i, (cls, g) in enumerate(
            zip((FullAttentionManager, SlidingWindowManager), groups)
        )
    ]
    store_mask = sched._reachable_store_block_mask(
        sched.config.kv_group_configs[1], 0, 4, 4, ()
    )
    record = dict(
        extra_retained_tokens=extra,
        older_state=older_state,
        expanded_coverage=expanded_coverage,
        hit_tokens=external,
        async_load=async_load,
        swa_store_mask=store_mask,
    )
    if external:
        for m in managers:
            m.add_local_computed_blocks(req.request_id, [], 0, external)
        for m in managers:
            m.allocate_external_computed_blocks(req.request_id, 0, external)
        blocks = managers[1].req_to_blocks[req.request_id]
        record["allocated_offsets"] = [i for i, b in enumerate(blocks) if not b.is_null]
        try:
            sched.update_state_after_alloc(
                req,
                KVCacheBlocks(tuple(m.req_to_blocks[req.request_id] for m in managers)),
                external,
            )
        except AssertionError as exc:
            record["error"] = str(exc)
        else:
            record["load_jobs"] = len(sched._jobs)
            for job in sched._jobs.values():
                manager.complete_load(job.keys, state.req_context)
    return record


if __name__ == "__main__":
    records = [
        probe(extra, older, expand)
        for expand in (False, True)
        for extra in (0, 3)
        for older in ("missing", "pending", "ready")
    ]
    for r in records:
        if r["extra_retained_tokens"] == 0 or r["older_state"] == "ready":
            assert r["hit_tokens"] == 64 and r["load_jobs"] == 1, r
        elif r["expanded_coverage"]:
            assert r["hit_tokens"] == (0 if r["older_state"] == "missing" else None), r
            assert "error" not in r, r
        else:
            assert r["hit_tokens"] == 64 and "error" in r, r
    output = json.dumps(records, indent=2)
    Path(__file__).with_suffix(".json").write_text(output + "\n")
    print(output)
    print("All 12 diagnostic cases matched their expected outcomes.")
```

</details>

### AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with issue/PR searches, source inspection, the reproducer, execution, and this RFC. This is a design discussion with a verified bookkeeping failure, not a reviewed production patch or a claim of completed model validation.

title: [RFC] CLI configuration without runtime initialization
author: matteso1
body:
# CLI configuration without runtime initialization Updated September 24. Code references use main `7a9406690ebe`. The CLI already gets types, defaults and help from config. The problem is that reading those definitions imports runtime code, and building the parser constructs config objects with platform-dependent defaults. Even `vllm --version` builds the serve parser first. I propose keeping the config classes and `get_kwargs`, while separating **describing arguments** from **constructing their values**. Build only the requested command's parser. For nested config defaults, use the existing JSON conversion path during parsing instead of constructing config to print help. Keep platform extensions before parsing, where they can still register flags. This replaces the generator and separate declaration layer from #56884. The intended result is a responsive CLI with fewer incidental imports. A serving-startup improvement would need a separate measurement. ## Current structure Config owns field definitions and validation. `get_kwargs()` derives argparse settings from those fields. Registration adds flag names, aliases and CLI overrides. `EngineArgs` receives the parsed values, resolves model- and hardware-dependent settings, and constructs runtime config. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Config fields"] -->|"types, defaults, docs"| K["get_kwargs"] K --> A["Argparse"] O["Flag names and
CLI overrides"] --> A A --> E["EngineArgs"] E -->|"resolve inputs"| R["Runtime config
and validation"] ``` `EngineArgs` mirrors fields and maps them back into config, but removing that repetition does not remove the import cost. [`get_kwargs`][kwargs] is already the connection between config and the parser. ### A scheduler option, end to end `--max-num-batched-tokens` has three different defaults for a reason: | Stage | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `SchedulerConfig` | Integer, default 2048, bound `ge=1`. Its docstring says the default is mainly for testing. | | CLI / `EngineArgs` | `None` means the user has not selected a value. An explicit value uses the human-readable integer converter. | | Engine configuration | Resolve an unset value using the device, serving/offline context and model settings; then construct `SchedulerConfig`. | For H100/H200-class GPUs, the initial choices are 8192 tokens for serving and 16384 for offline use, before further model-dependent adjustments. Replacing the CLI's `None` with the field's 2048 would change behavior. The parser also accepts zero; the `ge=1` check runs when `SchedulerConfig` is constructed. [Declaration][scheduler], [registration][scheduler-flags], [runtime defaults][batch-defaults]. ## Work that help triggers There are both import-time and parser-construction costs: ```mermaid flowchart TD S["CLI startup"] --> P["Package initialization"] P --> ENV["env_override"] --> T["Torch"] S --> CMD["Import commands;
build every parser"] CMD --> API["Serving implementation"] --> F["FastAPI"] CMD --> CFG["arg_utils / config imports"] CFG --> DEP["Torch, Transformers,
OpenAI"] CMD --> PARSE["Build serve arguments"] PARSE --> PL["Load general plugins"] PARSE --> HOOK["Platform hook
and device choices"] PARSE --> FACT["Construct config defaults"] FACT --> PLATFORM["Resolve current platform"] HOOK --> PLATFORM PLATFORM --> RT["Platform / backend imports"] ``` Importing `vllm.config.scheduler` still executes `vllm.config.__init__`. Both the package and individual config modules therefore need cheap imports. Some dependencies are small declarations stored in heavy packages; others are functions used only during runtime construction. Moving the declaration or importing the function at its use site removes the dependency without duplicating config. [Command loading][cli-main], [config exports][config-init], [one quantization import][quantization]. The parser adds two less obvious dependencies: - `_compute_kwargs()` visits every field and calls its default factory. A trace of ordinary top-level and serve help reached `DeviceConfig.__post_init__` and `CompilationConfig.__post_init__` through `get_kwargs(VllmConfig)`. - `AsyncEngineArgs.add_cli_args()` loads general plugins and calls `current_platform.pre_register_and_update(parser)`. Plugins can register types or flags. The choices for `--mm-processor-device` also read `current_platform.device_type`. Moving imports does not remove these calls. [Factories][kwargs], [plugin and platform hooks][async-args], [device choices][device-choices]. ### Why lazy field lookup is insufficient Skipping unused fields avoids constructing `DeviceConfig` for the aggregate config. But `--compilation-config` is an exposed field. Its factory still constructs `CompilationConfig`, whose post-init chooses a compile backend and applies Torch-version-dependent settings. The current help prints the resulting configuration, including those settings. [Flag registration][compilation-flag], [initialization][compilation-init]. The observed path is: ```text build serve parser → get_kwargs(VllmConfig) → default_factory() → CompilationConfig.__post_init__() → platform and compiler defaults ``` Nor can we simply replace every nested config with a dictionary: [the parser contract][compilation-test] includes returning a real `CompilationConfig` for both omitted and explicit inputs. Explicit JSON values already construct and validate nested configs during parsing. ## Proposed boundary ```mermaid flowchart TD CLI["Command selection"] --> P["Build selected parser"] C["Existing config
field metadata"] --> P B["Platform metadata
and extension hooks"] --> P P --> H["Help:
no default construction"] P --> V["Convert supplied values"] V --> D["Convert omitted defaults"] D --> N["Return typed Namespace"] N --> E["EngineArgs resolves
model / device settings"] E --> R["Runtime config / engine"] ``` **Command and package loading.** Command modules remain the registry, with cheap names, descriptions and dispatch methods. Only the selected command builds its full parser. Separately, `import vllm` should stop importing Torch as a side effect. Environment settings that must precede Torch stay early; version-specific patches must still run before vLLM uses their targets. This needs both import orders checked. **Field lookup.** Make `get_kwargs()` a lazy mapping over the existing fields. Looking up a flag computes that field's parser metadata; an unused field does no factory work. Cache metadata and keep caller mutations isolated, as today's deep copy does. This avoids a second, hand-maintained list of exposed fields. **Nested config defaults.** For a field whose factory is exactly its config class, use `default="{}"` with the existing JSON converter. Argparse already converts string defaults during parsing. Help can describe `{}` as “use the config defaults,” while a successful parse still returns the real config object. Explicit values use the same converter as today. [Argparse's default conversion][argparse-default]. A focused check with the current `CompilationConfig` converter supports this: constructing the small parser and printing help made zero calls to its post-init; omitted input made one and returned a config equal to today's default. Explicit empty/non-default JSON, invalid input, repeated parses and `parse_known_args` behaved as expected. Config was imported normally before this check; it establishes the conversion mechanism, not Torch-free help. This changes the displayed default in help and generated argument docs from an initialized config dump to `{}`, and moves default construction into parsing. Repeated parses also receive fresh config objects. Literal defaults and deliberate `None` overrides stay intact. Apply this only where empty JSON is equivalent to the declared constructor; it uses Pydantic's JSON path, and a custom factory must not silently become `{}`. Nested subparsers and direct `parser.get_default()` callers still need qualification. No new deferred-value framework is needed for the demonstrated case. The ordering change needs an explicit check: today these factories run before the platform's parser hook; under this proposal they run after it. An extension that changes config state could therefore affect the result. Factory failures also move into argparse's error handling. Those cases need a comparison before changing a field, even if its successful default value matches. `CompilationConfig()` still leaves settings such as compilation mode to later engine setup; parsing does not resolve every runtime default. **Platform and plugin behavior.** Preserve host-specific choices and pre-parse extension hooks. I would have platform selection expose the chosen built-in backend's identifier and device type without loading its implementation class. Share those small declarations with the runtime platform, so the parser does not maintain a second set of choices. Use the same selection rules for both, including explicit CPU selection and out-of-tree platform precedence. Do not broaden accepted device values merely to avoid detecting the platform. Enabled extensions retain their registration path and may import runtime libraries. A later no-argument platform hook cannot replace a hook that adds flags to a parser. Built-in side effects also need care: ROCm's hook sets an environment variable. Its setup must remain before the operations that depend on it. [Platform selection][platform-selection], [hook contract][platform-hook], [ROCm setup][rocm-hook]. **Pydantic and runtime types.** Config already uses Pydantic dataclasses. The shared `@config` decorator builds a schema, and its utility module itself imports Torch for value normalization. `ModelConfig.dtype` and `LoRAConfig.lora_dtype` accept Torch dtype objects as well as specific strings; `DeviceConfig.device` skips Pydantic validation but performs runtime normalization in post-init. [Decorator and utilities][config-utils], [model dtype][model-dtype], [LoRA dtype][lora-dtype], [device config][device]. Those contracts must survive making the declarations cheap to inspect. A focused proof should describe the fields with Torch blocked, then check the existing accepted/rejected inputs and normalization under normal runtime imports. Replacing an annotation with `Any` does not establish that. Python callers constructing config directly should keep their current behavior. The exact type adapter remains an implementation question, rather than a reason to add a parallel schema. The strict import target is ordinary built-in `--help`, `--version` and `serve --help=all`, with extensions disabled and without explicit nested config values. A supplied JSON config can invoke runtime validation before a later help flag; a third-party extension can load its backend. Neither should be silently bypassed to satisfy an import test. ## Prior work and alternatives [#41518](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41518) establishes that the import cleanup can make full help substantially cheaper: a matched rerun on its August base reduced the median from **3.51 s to 0.28 s**, with identical help output. It moves imports to use sites, builds a selected parser, reads built-in device types through a small lookup, and limits aggregate default evaluation to named fields. Its parser platform hook runs only when an out-of-tree platform plugin is present; general plugin loading remains. Those mechanisms need a current-main compatibility audit. Where its code is reused, Netanel will remain a co-author. The Pydantic-settings work in [#42136](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42136) concerns environment-variable definitions and validation. It is useful precedent for deriving behavior from declarations, but does not by itself remove config imports or runtime factories from this parser. | Alternative | Why I would not use it here | | --- | --- | | Generate CLI definitions or help | Introduces an artifact that must track config; it does not resolve runtime defaults or plugin contracts. | | Separate `config_specs` / inherited base | Our prototype added machinery while the serve parser still imported the config package. Moving fields also lost the existing field-docstring check. | | Add CLI metadata to existing fields | Could reduce registration boilerplate later. It does not remove imports, constructors or platform hooks by itself. | ## Implementation and review I would land this in small pieces after agreement on the boundary: selected-command loading, package initialization, then config import chains and default handling. The local command-loading prototype is evidence for the first piece; it does not implement the full design. A fresh-process import check can tighten with each change. It should track the heavy package families still permitted for each command, rather than brittle exact module counts. Compare help, parsed values, errors and effective runtime config against the same base. Any deliberate help-default change should have an explicit before/after example. Keep coverage for enabled plugins and nested config inputs alongside the import check. Linux serving checks must cover both model runners, registration, Torch patches and config hashes. The main tradeoff for review is the runtime-default boundary: **show the declared config input in help, then construct its value through the existing converter during parsing, preserving typed arguments and pre-parse extensions.** I recommend that over calculating a host-specific config dump just to print help. If that boundary is acceptable, the first implementation can stay small without committing us to a generator or a second set of config definitions.
Measurements, current-source probes and limits Historical timings used macOS arm64, Python 3.12.13, Torch 2.11, fresh processes, warm files and `VLLM_PLUGINS=''`. They used a shared environment with source overlays, not rebuilt wheels. Times include Python startup. | Source | Three runs (seconds) | Median | | --- | --- | --- | | Main `711fc55c` | 3.3338, 3.3554, 3.3862 | 3.3554 s | | #41518 base `7ca49fbe` | 3.4444, 3.5068, 3.7607 | 3.5068 s | | #41518 head `b8bc7028` | 0.2816, 0.2805, 0.2788 | 0.2805 s | The matched historical pair had one excluded warm-up per arm. All six measured runs exited 0 and produced identical 124,918-byte help, SHA256 `cb276189432cbc3759ab104c9b664808579a25667b8bd7120568999722df5b9e`. The `711fc55c` row is a separate baseline, not that pair's control. A separate probe on the historical head passed full help with Torch, Transformers, FastAPI and OpenAI blocked. This does not establish runtime or extension compatibility. On September 24, eleven CPU-only subprocess probes used clean main `7a940669` and its local command-loading child `8e6e6789`. These instrumented runs observed calls, not performance. Loaded vLLM Python paths and hashes were recorded; the shared generated version module was tracked separately. Top-level, serve and benchmark help on main all loaded the four heavy package families and constructed config defaults. A temporary synthetic platform plugin added an integer flag; a general plugin logged registration. The comparison preserved version/help stdout, accepted the custom integer before serve help, and rejected an invalid value with exit 2. Parser-hook calls changed as follows: | Invocation | Main | Command-loading prototype | | --- | --- | --- | | `--version` | serve, launch-render, run-batch | none | | serve help with custom flag | serve, launch-render, run-batch | serve | | `bench latency --help` | serve, launch-render, throughput, run-batch | throughput | Both versions still discovered the platform. General-plugin registration still ran for selected serve and benchmark help. Benchmark help still built the throughput parser within the selected benchmark tree. This qualifies one synthetic extension and top-level command selection; it does not prove every extension works or that all unselected nested parsers are avoided. Raw stderr was not byte-identical: imports emitted process/address-specific macOS native-library warnings. The CLI error line matched. The separate string-default fixture used the existing `CompilationConfig` converter after normal imports. Omitted input and explicit `{}` each constructed one equal config; a non-default input preserved its backend and capture sizes; invalid input exited 2. Help constructed none. Repeated parses returned equal but distinct objects with distinct mutable option dictionaries. `parse_known_args` also returned a typed config. This is a proof for one field, not a change to the full parser. No current-main full-help speedup is claimed. Integration of the default change and Torch-free type validation remain unimplemented. CUDA/ROCm behavior, installed Linux behavior and serving need qualification for those changes. These measurements do not establish a serving-startup improvement.

title: [RFC]: Return `routed_experts` on the terminal streaming chunk
author: ryanliang10000-cmyk
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM already supports surfacing MoE routing data to clients via the
`routed_experts` field when the server is started with
`--enable-return-routed-experts`. This is useful for MoE research, routing
analysis, expert-load/utilization studies, distillation, and debugging expert
selection.

Today this only works for **non-streaming** responses:

- `CompletionResponseChoice.routed_experts` (`/v1/completions`)
- `ChatCompletionResponseChoice.routed_experts` (`/v1/chat/completions`)

On the **streaming** path (`stream=True`) the routing data is dropped entirely.
The streaming choice protocols
(`CompletionResponseStreamChoice`, `ChatCompletionResponseStreamChoice`) have no
`routed_experts` field, and the serving code never populates one. As a result,
any client that relies on streaming — which is the common case for interactive
and low-latency serving — cannot obtain routing data at all, and must fall back
to a separate non-streaming request to get it. This is an inconsistency in the
public OpenAI-compatible API: the same feature flag produces different response
capabilities depending only on `stream`.

This inconsistency is worth an RFC because it changes the public streaming
response schema, and because there are a few reasonable design points (where to
attach the data, per-chunk vs. terminal-only) that are easier to settle up front
than to change after clients depend on them.


### Proposed Change.

Return `routed_experts` on the **terminal streaming chunk** (the chunk that
carries `finish_reason`) for both the completion and chat-completion endpoints,
matching the non-streaming format byte-for-byte.

Rationale for terminal-only (not per-token):

- Routing data is only *materialized on the finished output*. It is concatenated
  in the output processor at finish time, so there is no per-token routing
  payload available on intermediate chunks anyway.
- Attaching it to the terminal chunk keeps the per-token hot path untouched — no
  extra serialization/encoding work per streamed token, and no bandwidth cost on
  every chunk.
- The terminal-chunk value is identical to the non-streaming response, so
  streaming and non-streaming clients get the same bytes for the same
  (greedy-decoded) request.

Concretely:

1. **Protocol** — add an optional `routed_experts: str | None = None` field to:
   - `CompletionResponseStreamChoice`
   - `ChatCompletionResponseStreamChoice`

   Same format and semantics as the existing non-streaming
   `*.routed_experts` field (base64-encoded `numpy` payload).

2. **Serving** — in the streaming loops of `OpenAIServingCompletion` and
   `OpenAIServingChat`, when the finished `output.routed_experts` is available,
   base64-encode it (`numpy2base64`) and set it on the choice for the terminal
   chunk. On all non-terminal chunks it is naturally `None` (routing data is not
   yet materialized), so no per-token work is added.

3. **Behavior when the flag is off** — the field stays `None`, exactly like the
   non-streaming path, so there is no behavioral change for users who do not set
   `--enable-return-routed-experts`.

4. **Tests** — add streaming tests for both endpoints asserting that:
   - non-terminal chunks omit `routed_experts` (it is `None`), and
   - the terminal chunk's `routed_experts` matches the non-streaming response
     byte-for-byte under greedy decoding (`temperature=0`).

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC] Exact single-session HOT continuation for hybrid Mamba models
author: KonnyakuMatcha
body:
# Exact single-session HOT continuation for hybrid Mamba models

## Motivation

Hybrid Mamba/attention models (e.g. Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 35B-A3B) keep two kinds
of state: per-token KV blocks for full attention, and one recurrent state per
sequence for GDN/Mamba layers.

For a single sequential agent session, the next turn usually appends only a
small user/tool tail. General prefix caching can reuse token blocks, but for
hybrid recurrent state it must reconstruct or replay the recurrent state at a
shared boundary. This RFC discusses a narrow exact-successor path called HOT
(Hot Ongoing Transfer): a completed turn hands its live state directly to the
next request.

This is an RFC, not a PR. It was prepared with assistance from OpenAI Codex.

## Proposed Behavior

1. A completed request returns a server-issued `continuation_handle`.
2. The next turn sends only the new tail plus that handle.
3. The scheduler validates the handle, model/session fingerprint, and the
   exact token boundary.
4. On a hit, full-attention block ownership and the latest Mamba state slot
   are transferred to the successor.
5. On a miss, eviction, or invalid/expired handle, the request either falls
   back to full prefill through a lightweight token chain or returns HTTP 400;
   it never silently prefills only the tail.

## Relationship to Existing Work

This overlaps with several existing directions, so the main question is
whether it should exist as a separate mode.

- **#55697 / #55873 / #55875 / #55876**:
  application-directed shared-prefix checkpoints. They target 1-to-N
  producer/consumer reuse through a declared prefix marker.
  HOT targets an exact sequential successor with a server-issued handle and
  does not require a shared prefix.
- **#52959**: internal Mamba-align checkpoints inside one forward pass.
  HOT transfers the latest materialized state slot across requests and could
  potentially build on that primitive later.
- **#45702**: fine-grained hash-based partial prefix reuse.
  HOT is handle-based and exact, with no hash/block lookup. Its fallback path
  benefits from the same partial-cache infrastructure.

## Current Prototype

Branch: https://github.com/KonnyakuMatcha/vllm-HOT/tree/hot-continuation
Design draft:
https://github.com/KonnyakuMatcha/vllm-HOT/blob/hot-continuation/docs/design/hot_continuation_rfc.md

Implemented in the prototype:

- one checkpoint per session, keyed by `continuation_handle`
- full-attention block ownership transfer and Mamba state-slot transfer
- capacity/TTL bounded checkpoint registry
- lightweight token-chain fallback when a block checkpoint is evicted
- invalid/expired handle returns HTTP 400
- multi-session e2e token-equivalence tests

Not implemented:

- async scheduling
- speculative decoding
- KV connectors
- multimodal inputs
- PP > 1

## Evaluation

Target model: `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4`, TP=2 on RTX 5090 pairs.

Correctness:

- single-session natural-EOS token equivalence: verified
- multi-session token equivalence up to 8 concurrent sessions: verified
- shared-prefix + checkpoint eviction + token-chain fallback: verified
- invalid/expired handle: HTTP 400

Concurrent TTFT benchmark (4 independent sessions, ~5.1k-token context each,
3 turns, `max_tokens=8`):

| Mode | Turn 1 | Turn 2 | Turn 3 | Steady mean |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| HOT | 1453.3 ms | 417.2 ms | 181.4 ms | 299.3 ms |
| Prefix | 1501.0 ms | 561.3 ms | 291.2 ms | 426.3 ms |

HOT steady-state TTFT was about 29.8% lower in this workload.
A separate full-latency run measured 570.6 ms vs 930.8 ms steady mean.

For comparison, #55697 reports 48.6% TTFT reduction and +110% QPS for a
1-to-9 shared-prefix workload. The numbers are not directly comparable; HOT
covers independent long contexts with one exact sequential successor.

## Known Limitations

- HOT currently requires `async_scheduling=False`.
  - A relaxed experimental async path passed a single-session 3-turn test but
    failed a 2-session 6-turn token-equivalence test.
  - Async support needs a request-level drain/commit-fence or state rollback
    transaction, not just a boundary adjustment.
- The prototype still uses env variables; upstream should use formal config.
- No producer-consumer shared checkpoint support yet.

## Questions

1. Is exact single-session HOT sufficiently distinct from #55697 to be a
   separate RFC/PR, or should it be folded into #55873/#55875/#55876?
2. Is a server-issued `continuation_handle` acceptable, or should this use an
   in-prompt marker / `session_id` style interface?
3. Should the first upstream contribution be only the ownership-transfer
   primitive, with API and async scheduling as follow-ups?
4. What is the preferred fallback contract for invalid/expired handles:
   HTTP 400, or client-resend-full-history?

title: [RFC]: Add Watchdog for Engine and Worker Monitoring
author: wenjinhust
body:
### Motivation.

Hangs and deadlocks in vLLM V1 are notoriously hard to diagnose. When the engine core process or a worker process stops making progress — for example due to a deadlock in collective communication (NCCL), an infinite wait on a synchronization primitive, a stuck device kernel, or a scheduler bug — the process usually stays alive but silent: no exception, no traceback, no signal. Operators are left with an opaque production incident; diagnosing it requires reproducing the hang, attaching a debugger (e.g. `py-spy`), or sending a signal manually, none of which is always possible in production.

There is no automatic mechanism to capture what every thread is doing *at the moment* progress stops. A watchdog that detects "no progress for N seconds" and automatically dumps all-thread stack traces would turn a previously opaque hang into an actionable diagnostic artifact (e.g. "the engine has been stuck in `all_reduce` for 10 minutes").

This RFC proposes adding such a watchdog to vLLM V1, integrated at the two places where hangs are most commonly observed: the engine core process and the worker processes.

### Proposed Change.


## 1. New `vllm/utils/watch_dog.py` — the `WatchDog` class

A lightweight watchdog implemented as one background daemon thread per process:

- **Heartbeat model.** External callers call `feed()` to refresh a `time.monotonic()`-based heartbeat timestamp. A single float assignment is atomic in CPython, so `feed()` is safe to call from any thread and costs almost nothing.
- **Monitor loop.** The daemon thread wakes every `_check_interval` seconds (default **10 s**, implemented as a wait on the stop event so `stop()` wakes it immediately). If the heartbeat has not been refreshed for more than `_timeout` seconds (default **300 s**), it triggers a stack dump.
- **Stack dump.** `dump_stack(reason)` appends a numbered entry (`Call stack dump #<n> ... due to <reason>`) to a per-process log file `<user home>/vllm/dump/VLLM_STACK_DUMP_for_<name>_<pid>.log`, containing all-thread stack traces captured via `faulthandler.dump_traceback(all_threads=True)`.
- **De-duplication.** Consecutive timeouts without an intervening `feed()` produce only one dump — the watchdog tracks the last logged timeout (`_last_timeout_log`) and only dumps when the current timeout post-dates the last feed. This avoids spamming the log file while the process remains hung.
- **API.** `feed()` / `dump_stack(reason)` / `start()` / `stop()` / `set_name(name)` / `set_logger(logger)`, plus a process-wide singleton `get_watch_dog()`. `start()` is idempotent (never spawns a second monitor thread); `stop()` joins the thread and is safe to call before `start()`.
- The dump file name embeds the watchdog name and the PID, so each process (engine, every worker) gets its own file.

## 2. New `vllm/utils/safe_fs.py` — hardened file/directory helpers

Stack traces can contain sensitive data (request contents, model details), so the dump file and its directory are created with basic hardening against local symlink attacks:

- `get_user_root_dir()` — the per-user vLLM runtime directory (`~/vllm`).
- `prepare_private_dir(path)` — creates the directory with mode `0700`, verifies it is a real directory owned by the current user, and refuses symlinked path components.
- `safe_open_file(path, mode)` — opens with `O_NOFOLLOW | O_APPEND` and file mode `0600`, refusing symlinked files instead of following them.

## 3. Integration points

- **EngineCoreProc** (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py`):
  - Creates a watchdog named `engine_<engine_index>` and starts it after initialization.
  - Feeds it while draining the input queue and before each engine step (`_process_engine_step`).
  - `input_queue.get()` now uses `timeout=5` so the queue-drain loop stays responsive to the watchdog; the original blocking semantics are preserved by continuing the loop when `block=True` and the queue is empty.
  - The shutdown signal handler dumps all thread stacks for diagnosis before shutting down.
- **WorkerProc** (`vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py`):
  - Creates a watchdog named `worker-<rank>` and starts it after worker initialization.
  - Feeds it before **and after** executing every worker RPC method — the post-call feed protects the output serialization/enqueue path, which can itself run close to the timeout.
  - The worker signal handler dumps all thread stacks on shutdown signals.
- **MessageQueue.acquire_read** (`vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_broadcast.py`):
  - Feeds the watchdog while spin-waiting for a block to be written by the producer. Readers legitimately busy-wait here for long periods, so without feeding, the watchdog would raise false timeout alarms.


### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@njhill @WoosukKwon @youkaichao @robertgshaw2-redhat @mgoin @tlrmchlsmth @houseroad @yewentao256 @ProExpertProg 

### Any Other Things.

- **Scope.** This first version targets the engine core process and the `multiproc` executor workers. Other executors (e.g. Ray-based) and other long-lived processes can adopt the same `WatchDog` class later — the class itself is executor-agnostic.
- **Configurability.** The timeout (300 s) and check interval (10 s) are currently hard-coded module constants. Making them configurable (e.g. environment variables such as `VLLM_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT`) is follow-up work and feedback on naming is welcome.
- **CPU-side only.** `faulthandler` captures Python/C thread stacks; it does not include device-side (GPU/NPU) state. Device-side diagnostics remain out of scope.
- **Performance.** `feed()` is a monotonic clock read plus a float assignment; the 5-second input-queue timeout adds no measurable overhead and no benchmark regression is expected.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Request level text and derender output on `/inference/v1/generate`
author: hickeyma
body:
### Motivation.

The disaggregated serving path in vLLM is render → generate → derender. `/render` turns an OpenAI request into a `GenerateRequest` (#36166). `/inference/v1/generate` runs it on the GPU tier and returns token IDs (#22817, #24261).
`/v1/chat/completions/derender` and `/v1/completions/derender` turn the result back into an OpenAI response (#42729).
This works well for batch and RL traffic where the caller already holds the complete `GenerateResponse`.

Latency sensitive interactive traffic in prefill/decode (P/D) deployments is a poor fit. Streaming derender (#47161) is a stateless per chunk translator, so every SSE chunk from generate costs the client another HTTP round trip:

- One `POST` per chunk with the client echoing `stream_state` back on each call.
- On the parsing path the full `chat_request` is re-sent with every chunk.
- Parser state is rebuilt by replaying all output tokens each chunk. #50550 documents this as O(n³) character work over a generation and defers caching it.

All of this lands on the TPOT critical path and for parsed output the cost grows with response length. A benchmark
of the streaming derender PRs measured it (1×A100-40G, Qwen3-8B, hermes + qwen3 parsers, main plus #50550, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56851#issuecomment-5685698033). At matched load, detokenize and parse on the derender tier cost ~9× the in-process CPU, and E2E p50 rose 15% on multi-thousand-token reasoning outputs. Tokens-in / text-out in a single call already works on the main server (`/v1/completions` accepts token IDs in `prompt`). The gap is specific to deployments whose wire format is `GenerateRequest`.

**Tokenizer availability is per pool. Detokenization is already per request.** Only one of these is a launch time decision:

| | Granularity | Where it's decided today |
|---|---|---|
| Tokenizer loaded | per pool, at launch | `--tokens-only` sets `skip_tokenizer_init` |
| Detokenize this request | per request | `SamplingParams.detokenize`, default `True`. `GenerateRequest.sampling_params` is a full `SamplingParams`, so it's on the wire today. |

The only thing that makes detokenization look launch level is `--tokens-only` overriding the request value. A generate server launched with `--enable-scale-out` and without `--tokens-only` already runs a `FastIncrementalDetokenizer` for every request. The handler then builds the response from `output.token_ids` only and throws `output.text` away.

**P/D makes request level the natural grain:**

- **Only the terminal leg's output reaches the client.** Proxies run the prefill leg with `max_tokens=1` and keep only `kv_transfer_params`. Decode recomputes the last prompt token to sample the first output token itself.
- **Decode already has everything detokenization needs.** `GenerateRequest.token_ids` carries the full prompt and the detokenizer primes its `DecodeStream` from it. No detokenizer state crosses the P→D boundary.
- **State lives with the live request.** `RequestState` owns the detokenizer and is popped on finish and on abort/disconnect. There's no session registry or eviction. That's the property #47161 couldn't get on the stateless derender tier which has no live request to hang state on.
- **No new pool flavor.** P/D fleets already run prefill and decode pools with different launch configs. Prefill pools stay `--tokens-only`. Decode pools load a tokenizer.

This also continues #22817's original design, which says *"We can make `Detokenization` step optional in the `AsyncLLM`"* and sketches a service mapping `GenerateRequest` → `ChatCompletionResponse`.

### Proposed Change.

#### 1. A request-level `output_mode` field

Add a top level field to `GenerateRequest`:

```python
output_mode: Literal["tokens", "text", "derender"] = "tokens"
```

It's a new field rather than a reuse of `sampling_params.detokenize`. That field defaults to `True`, so keying response content off it would change every existing response on tokenizer loaded servers. It's also an engine field and response shape is a serving concern.

| Level | Response adds | Equivalent today | Server needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tokens` (default) | nothing, unchanged behavior | `/inference/v1/generate` | nothing |
| `text` | detokenized `text`, resolved logprob tokens | `/v1/completions/derender` | tokenizer |
| `derender` | `content`, `reasoning`, `tool_calls` | `/v1/chat/completions/derender` | tokenizer, parser config, per request parser context |

#### 2. Response shape

One response class per level with `GenerateResponse` as a union discriminated on `output_mode` (open question 1, suggested by @DarkLight1337):

```python
class GenerateTokensResponse(GenerateResponseBase):
    output_mode: Literal["tokens"] = "tokens"
    choices: list[GenerateTokensChoice]

class GenerateTextResponse(GenerateResponseBase):
    output_mode: Literal["text"]
    choices: list[GenerateTextChoice]

class GenerateDerenderResponse(GenerateResponseBase):
    output_mode: Literal["derender"]
    choices: list[GenerateDerenderChoice]

GenerateResponse = Annotated[
    Annotated[GenerateTokensResponse, Tag("tokens")]
    | Annotated[GenerateTextResponse, Tag("text")]
    | Annotated[GenerateDerenderResponse, Tag("derender")],
    Discriminator(output_mode_or_tokens),  # missing tag -> "tokens"
]
```

The choices follow the same pattern:

| Level | Choice adds | Stream choice adds | `logprobs` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tokens` | nothing | nothing | token ID form (#57574 - implemented in #58181) |
| `text` | `text: str` | `text: str` (delta) | resolved token strings (section 5) |
| `derender` | `message: ChatMessage` | `delta: DeltaMessage` | resolved token strings (section 5) |

- **Shared fields stay in the base classes.** `GenerateResponseBase` holds `request_id`, `usage`, `prompt_token_ids`, `mm_placeholders`, `metrics`, `kv_transfer_params` and `ec_transfer_params`. The choice base holds `index`, `finish_reason`, `token_ids`, `routed_experts` and `sampling_mask`. The stream response and stream choices split the same way.
- **The response echoes `output_mode`.** It's what the union discriminates on and it makes every response and stream chunk self-describing. For existing clients this is one new field on `tokens` responses and nothing else changes.
- **A missing `output_mode` means `tokens`.** `GenerateResponse` is also parsed as input by `/derender` (`DerenderChatRequest.generate_response`) and existing clients don't send the field. A plain discriminated union rejects a missing tag, so the discriminator is a callable that falls back to `"tokens"`. The trade-off is that the OpenAPI schema shows a `oneOf` without a discriminator mapping.
- **Mode-specific fields are required, not optional.** `text` is `str` on a text choice and `message` is `ChatMessage` on a derender choice, so callers don't need `None` checks. It also removes the need to exclude unset `text` / `message` / `delta` fields by hand, since the `tokens` classes don't have them.
- **`logprobs` is typed per level.** That answers the question of `choice.logprobs` changing type with `output_mode`. Each level declares its own type.
- **`derender` doesn't carry the raw `text`** which matches `/derender`. `message` / `delta` are the same types `/derender` and `/v1/chat/completions` emit, so the parity check compares field for field.
- **Python code that constructs `GenerateResponse` moves to `GenerateTokensResponse`** because `GenerateResponse` becomes a type alias rather than a class.

Example decode-leg request and stream chunk:

```json
{"token_ids": [151644, 872, ...], "sampling_params": {"max_tokens": 512},
 "stream": true, "output_mode": "text", "kv_transfer_params": {...}}
```

```json
{"request_id": "...", "output_mode": "text",
 "choices": [{"index": 0, "token_ids": [9707], "text": " Hello"}]}
```
#### 3. Parser context for the `derender` level

Parsers are built per request from context `GenerateRequest` doesn't carry today. An audit of `adjust_request` overrides (Open Q2) found that none of them need the prompt and parsers read only a few request fields at parse time. So the request carries a slim context instead of the full `ChatCompletionRequest`:

```python
parse_context: ParseContext | None = None  # used only when output_mode="derender"
```

| Field | Used for |
|---|---|
| `tools`, `tool_choice`, `parallel_tool_calls` | parser construction, extraction, assembly |
| `include_reasoning` | `parse_delta`, assembly |
| `chat_template_kwargs` (after server defaults) | parser construction, Nemotron V3 |
| `history_tool_call_cnt` (int) | Kimi-style tool call IDs. Replaces `messages` |

`/render` builds it from the request and sets it on the returned `GenerateRequest`. Only `output_mode="derender"` reads it. The rest comes from fields the generate server already has:

- **Decode flags.** `adjust_request` changes `skip_special_tokens` and `spaces_between_special_tokens` for many parsers. They're already in `sampling_params` and the engine decodes with them.
- **Structural tag.** hy_v4 reads it at parse time. It comes from `sampling_params.structured_outputs`.
- **Logprob settings.** `logprob_token_ids` is in `sampling_params.logprob_token_ids` and `top_logprobs` is in `sampling_params.logprobs` (`None` when `logprob_token_ids` is set, `-1` passes through). The parse request gets `logprobs`, `top_logprobs` and `logprob_token_ids` filled in from these, so the `top_logprobs` cut (#59518) and Poolside's streaming match the main endpoint.
- **Prompt.** `token_ids` is the prompt. It gives the initial reasoning state and the prefix for parsers that need one (`set_prompt_token_ids`, the `hf` parser from #58604) or when `parse_context` fails validation.

So the generate server never re-runs `adjust_request`. Everything it changes for sampling is already in `sampling_params`.

- It's sent once per request, not once per chunk as with streaming derender. The prompt isn't sent a second time as `messages`.
- The parser reads the engine's own text (`output.text`), not a second decode of the token IDs. That's the same text the `text` level returns, so `skip_special_tokens`, `spaces_between_special_tokens` and stop strings are applied once, by the engine, with the post `adjust_request` values. Phase 2 reuses the parse and message assembly code from `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat` but not its decode step.
- `/derender` works differently. It gets the client's request as sent to `/render` before `adjust_request` and on the parser path it always keeps special tokens. That's by design and documented in `derenderer.md` (#42729). Use `output_mode="derender"` when it matters.
- Out-of-tree plugin parsers get a `ChatCompletionRequest` built from the context with `messages=[]`. A plugin that reads other request fields won't see them. The plugin docs should say so.
- Parsing runs on the renderer's executor which has `renderer_num_workers` threads (default `1`). It runs once per request and decode pools do no prompt tokenization, so contention is low but the pool size caps concurrent `derender` calls.
- Without `parse_context`, a server with a reasoning or tool parser configured returns **400** (section 6). Batch `/derender` falls back to plain detokenization instead which can mix reasoning or tool call markup into `message.content`. Streaming derender already fails closed for parser configured models. Clients that want plain text use `text`. On a server with no parser, `derender` without `parse_context` puts the plain text in `message.content`.

#### 4. Streaming

- **`text`**: `text` carries each chunk's delta from the request's existing incremental detokenizer (`RequestOutputKind.DELTA`). No extra state.
- **`derender`**: one `Parser` per choice, created when the request starts and kept for its lifetime. This is the same way `/v1/chat/completions` streams today. It's fed the engine's text delta, the same delta the `text` level returns, so batch and streaming parse the same text (section 3). There's no replay, no `stream_state` and no per chunk `chat_request`.
- **End of stream**: at `text` and `derender` levels, the stream emits a chunk whenever the engine output carries new text or a `finish_reason`, even with no new token IDs. That covers the final output the engine produces on an abort which has no token IDs but can flush text held back for stop string matching. The generate stream skips outputs with no new token IDs today (on `main`, #53187 only keeps them while prompt metadata is pending), so `tokens` streams already drop a finish only chunk. #47933 fixed that for `tokens` by emitting the terminal chunk when `finish_reason` is set. Phase 1 (#58588) also emits chunks that carry only new text.

#### 5. Logprobs

At `text` and `derender` levels, logprob entries carry decoded token strings and `bytes`, as `/derender` produces, instead of the `token_id:N` placeholders generate emits today. The tokens level shape follows #57574 (implemented in #58181).

Dense logprobs are the expensive case. At `top_logprobs=20` the benchmark measured 355 µs per logprob-bearing token and 0.83 of a frontend core within 1.2× of the GPU's token rate. On a tokenizer loaded server that cost is already paid at the `tokens` level: `LogprobsProcessor` decodes every top-k token whenever `sampling_params.detokenize` is true and generate then discards the strings. Clients that want wide logprobs off the decode host send `output_mode="tokens"` with `detokenize: false` (which rules out `stop` strings) or use a `--tokens-only` pool. The Phase 1 docs should say so.

#### 6. Validation (fail loud)

- `output_mode != "tokens"` on a server without a tokenizer → **400**. Today's no-op detokenizer returns `""`, so a naive implementation would return empty text with a 200 for any request routed to a `--tokens-only` pool.
- `output_mode != "tokens"` with `sampling_params.detokenize` explicitly `false` → **400**.
- `parse_context` without `output_mode="derender"` → ignored because `/render` always sets it. Unknown fields are logged and ignored at those levels.
- `derender` with `stream: true` → supported since Phase 3 (#63103).
- `output_mode="derender"` without `parse_context` on a server with a reasoning or tool parser configured → **400**, rather than falling back to plain text that may contain reasoning or tool call markup.

**Rollout note:** `GenerateRequest` is a plain pydantic `BaseModel`, so servers without this change ignore `output_mode` and return tokens only with a 200. Clients should check that `output_mode` in the response matches the request. Older servers don't return it.

#### 7. Role agnostic P/D usage

The field has no behavior tied to pod role or `kv_transfer_params`. The same decode pod may serve some requests decode only and others after a remote prefill, so role keyed behavior would differ across those paths.
