Orchestrators set `output_mode` and `parse_context` on the terminal leg only. If they reach a tokenizer free prefill pool anyway, the 400 above surfaces the misconfiguration.

For llm-d: the coordinator builds the prefill request from scratch, so it needs no change. `parse_context` is ignored on the prefill leg. The cost is every rendered request carries the tools list.

#### 8. Decoupling `--tokens-only`

A decode pool needs the generate API surface *with* a tokenizer. `--tokens-only` currently does four jobs:

| Job | Where | Proposal |
|---|---|---|
| Skip tokenizer init | [arg_utils](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/362a64b21d5038691c929521478b63dcb4828e58/vllm/engine/arg_utils.py#L2385-L2386) | keep |
| Force `detokenize=False` | [factories](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/362a64b21d5038691c929521478b63dcb4828e58/vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/factories.py#L61) → [serving](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/362a64b21d5038691c929521478b63dcb4828e58/vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py#L249-L250) | keep |
| Register `/abort_requests` | [api_router](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/362a64b21d5038691c929521478b63dcb4828e58/vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/api_router.py#L77) | serve `/inference/v1/abort_requests` wherever generate is served, behind `--api-key`. Keep the unauthenticated `/abort_requests` on `--tokens-only` only (open question 4) |
| Imply scale-out endpoints | [factories](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/362a64b21d5038691c929521478b63dcb4828e58/vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/factories.py#L73) | keep |

A decode pool then runs `--enable-scale-out` with a tokenizer and without `--tokens-only`.

#### 9. Parity and shared code

The inline path and `/derender` must produce identical output or clients get different text depending on deployment.

- Both go through the same `Parser` code, with no parallel copy.
- Extend the round-trip parity test (#48617, streaming added in #57922) to assert `generate(output_mode=X)` matches `derender(generate(output_mode="tokens"))` for `text` and `derender`, batch and streaming.
- Streaming derender returns resolved logprobs since #55029, so the streaming logprob checks can run now.
- For parsers whose `adjust_request` changes the decode flags (Hermes with tools, Kimi K3, the `hf` parser and others), `/derender` can differ from the inline path. That's by design (#42729, `derenderer.md`). The inline `derender` level isn't affected because it parses the engine's text. The #60082 parity tests cover it with Hermes and tools.
- A logprobs case with `logprob_token_ids` set, so the inline path keeps every candidate the way the coupled endpoint does (#59518).
- **Stop strings.** Inline levels follow the engine's stop handling, like `/v1/completions` and `/v1/chat/completions`: a matched stop string is cut from the text unless `include_stop_str_in_output` is set. Token IDs keep every generated token, so decoding them in `/derender` brings the stop string back, plus anything after it in the same token. For requests with `stop`, the test asserts inline output matches the coupled endpoint and that `/derender` output starts with the inline text and differs only after it. The `tokens` leg has to run on a tokenizer-loaded server, since `--tokens-only` rejects `stop` with a 400 (#57058). The Phase 2 (#60082) inline path parses the engine's text which is already truncated, so it needs no extra stop handling (section 3). `/derender` only accepts `output_mode="tokens"` responses and returns a 400 for anything else. Decoding a text response's token IDs again would bring back a stop string the engine already cut.
- **End of stream.** Tests cover a final chunk carrying only buffered text or only a `finish_reason`, including after an abort (section 4).

#### 10. Rust frontend

The Rust frontend serves generate over HTTP and gRPC and both need the change. The protocol should be agreed here once and mirrored in both with the Rust frontend owners.

**HTTP.** `rust/src/server/src/routes/inference/generate/types.rs` mirrors `GenerateRequest` / `GenerateResponse`. It takes `output_mode`, `chat_request`, `text`, `message` and `delta` to also mirror the per level response types. For example, with a `#[serde(tag = "output_mode")]` enum that defaults to `tokens` when the tag is missing. The proto keeps optional fields. A proto `oneof` doesn't fit because every level carries `token_ids`.

**gRPC.** `rust/proto/inference.proto` (`Inference.Generate` / `GenerateStream`, enabled with `--grpc-port`) already serves most of the `text` level. It accepts `token_ids` and `kv_transfer_params` and returns decoded `text` on every `SequenceOutput` because `ResponseOptions.output_text` defaults to `true`. That's the reverse of HTTP generate where `tokens` is the default. gRPC shapes responses with per-field `ResponseOptions` flags rather than one mode, so the levels map onto flags:

| Level | gRPC today | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `tokens` | `output_text: false`, `output_token_ids: true` | none |
| `text` | `output_text: true` (default) | resolved logprob tokens |
| `derender` | not supported | `DerenderOptions` on `ResponseOptions`, `ParsedOutput` on `SequenceOutput` |

Proposed additions. All are new fields or messages, so they're wire compatible:

```proto
message ResponseOptions {
  ...
  // Set for the derender level. output_text stays independent.
  // Set it false to drop the raw text.
  optional DerenderOptions derender = 9;
}

message DerenderOptions {
  // Parse context (section 3).
  ParseContext parse_context = 1;
}

message SequenceOutput {
  ...
  // Set for the derender level. The full message in Generate, a delta in GenerateStream.
  optional ParsedOutput parsed = 11;
}

message ParsedOutput {
  optional string content = 1;
  optional string reasoning = 2;
  repeated ToolCall tool_calls = 3;
}

message ToolCall {
  uint32 index = 1;
  string id = 2;         // first delta for this index only when streaming
  string name = 3;       // first delta for this index only when streaming
  string arguments = 4;  // full JSON in Generate, a fragment in GenerateStream
}
```

- **Logprobs.** Sampled and candidate logprobs carry token IDs only. `CandidateTokenInfo.TokenInfo` already has `text = 4` and `token_bytes = 5` commented out. The `text` level fills them and adds the same for the sampled token, matching section 5.
- **Finish reason.** `FinishInfo.FinishReason` gains `TOOL_CALLS` for the `finish_reason` rewrite `/derender` does when tool calls were emitted.
- **Parser context.** `ParseContext` is a typed message with the section 3 fields. `tools` and `chat_template_kwargs` stay `google.protobuf.Struct`, the same way `kv_transfer_params` does.
- **Validation.** Section 6's 400s become `INVALID_ARGUMENT`. The no-tokenizer case doesn't come up because the Rust frontend doesn't support `--tokens-only` or `--skip-tokenizer-init` yet and always loads a tokenizer.
- **Streaming.** `GenerateStream` stays server streaming. Parsing runs with the request, so the client has nothing to send after it and bidirectional streaming isn't needed (Alternatives, item 7). `GenerateStream` forwards every decoded event without filtering on new token IDs, so the end of stream gap in section 4 may not apply here. The section 9 tests should confirm it.
- **Parity.** The `derender` level on both Rust surfaces uses the Rust parsers in `rust/src/parser` and depends on the Rust `/derender` work, which has stalled: #53223 closed unmerged on 2026-09-17 and the draft follow-ups #53418 / #53419 haven't moved since 2026-09-10. The Rust `derender` level needs someone to pick that stack back up. The section 9 parity tests also run against the Rust frontend so Rust and Python produce the same output.
- **Release.** The proto change ships with a `vllm-proto` version bump in the same PR, checked by `cargo-semver-checks` (see `rust/proto/README.md`).
- **Out of scope.** `vllm serve --grpc` uses the external `smg-grpc-servicer` package with its own proto.

#### 11. Phasing

| Phase | Scope | PR(s)
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `output_mode` field, `text` level (batch and streaming), logprob resolution, validation, `/inference/v1/abort_requests`, `/derender` rejecting non `tokens` input, docs, latency benchmarks (section 12) | #58588 (merged) |
| 2 | `derender` level, batch: `parse_context` on `GenerateRequest`, `message` on the choice, parsing the engine's text with the parse and assembly code from `/render` (section 3) | #60082 (merged) |
| 3 | `derender` level, streaming: request-scoped parsers, `delta` on stream choices, parity CI extension, latency benchmarks (section 12) |  #63103 (merged) |
| — | Rust frontend mirror, tracked with the Rust frontend owners | #44280 ([comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/44280#issuecomment-6600404082)) |

#### 12. Latency benchmarks

The CPU numbers above don't cover latency. The Phase 1 and Phase 3 PRs report TTFT and TPOT for:

- inline `text` / `derender` against generate plus streaming derender, across concurrency levels and response lengths.
- `tokens` requests on the same pod, with and without `text` or `derender` traffic mixed in.

**Phase 3 results** (#63103): @shimib ran these on one A100-40G, [Qwen3-8B](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63103#issuecomment-6407286233) and [Qwen3-VL-8B](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63103#issuecomment-6446448022), over 16,000 requests with zero errors. Output tokens matched within 2%. The runs compare tokens only (G), tokens plus a per-chunk `/derender` call (B) and inline `output_mode: "derender"` (D).

- **TTFT:** D is 85–150 ms faster than B at p50 and 14–35 ms behind G. That holds for text, tool calls, reasoning and images.
- **TPOT:** D is within 0.5 ms of G. It streams token by token with ITL close to G and B only keeps its TPOT by batching tokens which means clients get text in bursts.
- **Mixed traffic:** G and D on one worker don't affect each other, except under heavy reasoning load.
- **Heavy reasoning load (~1.9k tok/s through the Qwen3 parser):** D's TPOT p95 rises 6 ms and colocated `tokens` requests lose about 10–23 ms of TTFT because parsing runs on the API server event loop.

**Not measured:** E2E latency and `--api-server-count` as a way to reduce the heavy reasoning cost. It should help because it scales the parsing but that hasn't been tested.

#### Alternatives considered

1. **Streaming derender as-is (#47161).** Keeps the GPU tier tokenizer free but puts a round trip and echoed state on every chunk, plus replay for parsed output. It stays the right tool for stateless postprocessing (RL, batch, gateways that own postprocessing). This RFC complements it and doesn't replace it.
2. **The gateway composes generate + derender.** The per chunk hop moves from client to gateway rather than going away. Holding state in the gateway instead means reimplementing postprocessing there.
3. **Server-side derender sessions keyed by `request_id`.** Rejected in #47161 (Option B) over session lifecycle, eviction and memory. The derender tier has no live request to attach state to. The generate server does.
4. **Token IDs on `/v1/chat/completions`.** Complementary, not a replacement. Chat only takes token IDs through `kv_transfer_params["prompt_token_ids"]` (#48145) and #55771 proposes a first class `prompt_token_ids` field. That serves routers that already use the OpenAI format and tokenize to pick a replica. It doesn't serve orchestrators on the generate format because a render produced `GenerateRequest` carries resolved `SamplingParams` that don't map back onto OpenAI request fields without resolving. They would therefore have to support two wire formats. The reverse holds too. `output_mode` doesn't help OpenAI format routers because they'd need a `/render` hop, `--enable-scale-out` on the engines and a wrap into `chat.completion`, even at the `derender` level.
5. **Run the coupled OpenAI server on decode pools.** Decode pods leave the generate protocol with the same
   two format problem as (4).
6. **Reuse `sampling_params.detokenize` as the switch.** It defaults to `True`, so every existing response on a
   tokenizer loaded server would grow text and token only clients would pay for detokenization by default.
7. **gRPC bidirectional streaming derender** (suggested by @andylolu2 on slack). The client opens one bidi stream to the derender tier, sends the parser context once, then forwards each generate chunk. The parser lives on the stream until it closes. That removes the echoed `stream_state`, the per chunk `chat_request` and replay. It also answers the lifecycle and eviction objections behind (3) because state lasts exactly as long as the stream. It doesn't remove the hop though. Every chunk still passes from the generate stream through the derender stream on the TPOT path and clients would need gRPC next to the HTTP generate format. If a derender replica fails mid stream, the parser state goes with it and the client has to reconnect and replay. A WebSocket would give the same stream lifetime on the HTTP stack. This complements the RFC rather than replacing it. It fits #57571 as an alternative to the parser cache for consumers that want a tokenizer free GPU tier.

#### Costs and risks

- **CPU on the decode host.** Detokenization and parsing run in the API server process, not the engine core. They don't block the scheduler but they use host CPU. `text` adds little on a tokenizer loaded server because detokenization already runs there today. Parsing and logprob resolution are the new work. In the benchmark, with the GPU saturated, the in-process frontend stayed under 0.25 of a core for chat, reasoning and tool-calling traffic (24–144 µs per token), at least 3.5× headroom over the GPU's token rate. That was one A100 and a faster GPU narrows the gap.
  `--api-server-count` scales the frontend if it becomes the limit. Dense logprobs are the exception (section 5). Opt-in per request bounds the cost to the traffic that asks for it.
- **Parser config drift.** Decode pools need the same `--reasoning-parser`, `--tool-call-parser` and `--enable-auto-tool-choice` as the render tier. That's the same obligation the derender tier already has.
- **Two call sites for postprocessing.** Mitigated by shared `Parser` code and the parity CI in section 9.
- **Security.** The inline path postprocesses engine produced tokens bounded by the request's resolved limits. It doesn't accept caller supplied output token IDs the way `/derender` does, so it doesn't need `/derender`'s explicit bounds checks. `parse_context` is caller supplied. `tools`, `tool_choice` and `chat_template_kwargs` need the same validation as on the chat and derender endpoints.

#### Open questions

1. ~**Response shape.**~ RESOLVED. An extended generate format with `text` / `message` / `delta` (proposed) or return `ChatCompletionResponse` / `ChatCompletionStreamResponse` directly for `output_mode="derender"`? The latter is a drop-in for existing `/derender` consumers but the endpoint's response schema would then depend on a request field and the generate only fields would need a home. *Feedback so

title: [RFC]: Per-position target token logprobs for prefill scoring
author: aoshen02
body:
### Motivation.

**Status:** Draft

#### Summary

Add an inference/scoring-only interface that lets the caller specify a different set of target token IDs for each input position. The model returns only the logits or logprobs of those tokens at the corresponding positions.

The primary use case is Top-K scoring for On-Policy Distillation (OPD):

1. The student rollout records its own Top-K token IDs and logprobs at every response position.
2. The teacher runs a single forward pass over the full prompt plus the student response.
3. At each position, the teacher gathers only the candidate IDs supplied by the student and returns their logprobs (or logits).

The logical candidate tensor has shape `[batch, sequence_length, K]`. The number of candidates may differ between positions, so the implementation needs to support ragged lists.

#### Background

The existing `SamplingParams.logprob_token_ids` lets each request specify one fixed set of token IDs. This fits classification, label scoring, and similar workloads, where every scored row of a request uses the same candidates.

The OPD Top-K access pattern is different. The candidate sets of a single response may be:

```text
position 0: [A, B, C]
position 1: [B, D, E]
position 2: [A, F, G]
```

Taking the global union of the IDs across all positions and applying that union at every position gives correct results, but produces a large amount of unneeded data. With response length `R`, `K` candidates per position, and global union size `U`:

```text
data actually needed:              O(R × K)
global-union intermediate result:  O(R × U)
worst case:                        O(R² × K)
```

Each position should therefore carry only the candidate IDs it actually needs.

This RFC defines only the generic scoring capability; it does not prescribe how candidate sets are produced. Candidates may come from:

- student Top-K;
- teacher Top-K;
- the union/intersection of student and teacher Top-K;
- a caller-defined candidate set.

#### Goals

- Score arbitrary token IDs at each position during prompt/prefill scoring.
- Return only the IDs the caller requested and their values, without producing a full-vocabulary host/HTTP payload.
- Support raw logits and normalized logprobs, following the existing `logprobs_mode` semantics.
- Keep the existing request-wise `logprob_token_ids` behavior unchanged.
- Support continuous batching and ragged lists whose candidate count differs by position.
- Define causal alignment explicitly: the candidates at position `t` correspond to "predicting the token at position `t` from the prefix before position `t`".

#### Non-goals

- Implementing OPD or any distillation loss in vLLM.
- Deciding whether to use student Top-K or teacher Top-K.
- Changing token sampling or forcing the model to output a particular token.
- Returning full-vocabulary logits by default.

### Proposed Change.

#### Proposed interface

Add an engine-level parameter, tentatively named `logprob_token_ids_positions`:

```python
SamplingParams(
    max_tokens=0,
    logprob_token_ids_positions=[
        [],          # nothing requested at this position
        [101, 202],  # candidate IDs for this position
        [7, 8, 9],
    ],
)
```

The exact wire name can be settled by the API maintainers. The key semantics are that every scored input position has its own set of candidate IDs. For multiple requests in a batch, each request has its own position-aligned list.

The result should keep both IDs and values, preserving the candidate order passed by the caller:

```text
position 0: ids=[],          values=[]
position 1: ids=[101, 202],  values=[...]
position 2: ids=[7, 8, 9],   values=[...]
```

The first causal position may keep an empty/placeholder entry for compatibility with the existing prompt-logprob output convention. Callers can restrict the returned range with `logprob_start_len`.

#### Execution model

1. The model runs one normal prompt/prefill forward over the supplied prompt and response token IDs.
2. The logits processor applies whatever normalization is configured.
3. A GPU gather reads

   ```python
   logits[position, candidate_ids[position]]
   ```

   or the corresponding logprobs.

4. Only the IDs and values of the ragged candidates are copied to the output.

For an OPD teacher request, prompt positions use empty lists, each response position carries the student's candidate IDs, and the teacher generates no new tokens (`max_tokens=0`).

Note: the teacher still has to run the forward over the full prompt+response. This interface only avoids returning token scores that are not needed; it does not compute hidden states for the response alone.

#### Compatibility and limitations

- The existing `logprob_token_ids` remains the fast path for "one fixed set of IDs per request".
- The initial implementation should support prompt/prefill scoring only; the decode path can be extended later if there is a clear need.
- Candidate IDs must be bounds-checked against the vocabulary.
- Behavior for duplicate IDs must be defined: either keep duplicates stably or reject them.
- The output must preserve the candidate order passed by the caller.
- HTTP/OpenAI-compatible exposure can be discussed separately later; nested lists add parameter-validation and serialization cost.

#### Implementation roadmap

##### M1: Prefill request-wise fixed-ID scoring

First, support one fixed set of candidate IDs per request (the global union):

```python
prompt_logprob_token_ids=[101, 202, 303]
```

This is intended only for `max_tokens=0` prefill/scoring requests. The teacher runs the forward over the full input and gathers this set of IDs at every scored position. This stage reuses the existing request-wise token state and GPU gather path, and focuses on validating the output format, the logits/logprobs semantics, and position alignment under chunked prefill.

M1 is implemented in #54335.

##### M2: Prefill per-position sparse scoring

Add an interface with an independent candidate list per position:

```python
prompt_logprob_token_ids_positions=[
    [], [101, 202], [7, 8, 9],
]
```

The first version is still limited to prefill/scoring, `max_tokens=0`, and non-streaming requests. Decode-time per-position candidates, speculative/beam search, multimodal inputs, prefix cache, and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint are not supported yet. It supports multi-request batches, ragged candidate lists, and chunked prefill. Chunked prefill must carry each chunk's absolute start position so that logits rows stay aligned with candidate positions; otherwise the request must be rejected explicitly rather than silently returning misaligned results.

Internally, the first version can use a fixed-width `[num_rows, max_k]` candidate tensor plus a mask and restore ragged lists at output time; a fully packed sparse tensor is not required.

### Feedback Period.

At least one week.

### Any Other Things.

#### Related implementations

Miles's OPD implementation has a path compatible with older SGLang: it first takes the global union of the candidate IDs across all positions, then queries through the request-wise `token_ids_logprob`. For example, when the per-position candidates are `[A, B]`, `[C, D]`, and `[A, E]`, it sends the fixed list `[A, B, C, D, E]`; the teacher returns the logprobs of these five tokens at every position, and Miles then filters out the entries each position actually needs. This path requires no server-side change but returns unneeded data, at `O(R × |U|)` scale (`U` being the union).

The optional `token_ids_logprob_positions` path instead sends a candidate list per position, and the teacher gathers only each position's own IDs, reducing the response from dense `O(R × |U|)` to sparse `O(R × K)`. Both paths compute the same result; they differ only in how candidates are transmitted and in the gather range.

SGLang's `top_logprobs_num` can already return the IDs and values of the natural Top-K at every position; its older `token_ids_logprob` is a request-wise fixed ID list. This RFC aims to support both "per-position candidate selection" and "gathering by specified IDs" in vLLM.

#### Open questions

- Should the parameter be named `logprob_token_ids_positions`, or something else?
- Should raw logits reuse the existing `logprobs_mode`, or should a separate scoring result be introduced?
- Should only the engine API be provided at first, without exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint?
- What is the most efficient representation of ragged candidates for CUDA graphs and TP/DP attention?
- Should position alignment use empty lists, or an explicit start offset / packed `(position, IDs)` pairs?

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Add NCP-OLMo support and NCP DFlash speculative decoding
author: LuckySJTU
body:
### Motivation.

[NCP-ArchPreview](https://huggingface.co/collections/ArchSpace-Collection/ncp-archpreview) is a decoder-only language-model family that places token-level encoder and decoder towers around a chunk-level high-level model (HLM). Its public Hugging Face checkpoints use the `NCPOlmo3ForCausalLM` architecture and `ncp_olmo3` model type.

Supporting this architecture in vLLM requires more than registering a conventional decoder. The token towers can use vLLM attention and block tables, but the HLM also owns request-local state: an incomplete encoder fragment, per-layer HLM states and K/V tensors, selected concepts, and routed decoder features. That state must remain associated with request IDs across scheduler row reordering, completion, refill, chunked prefill, and recompute preemption. Prefix caching is not correct unless the corresponding HLM snapshot is cached with the token prefix.

The public Stage 2 v1 model also has a matching [NCP DFlash checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/ArchSpace-Collection/NCP_ArchPreview_dolma3_8.9B_Stage2_DFlash2_NCPFlash). Existing vLLM DFlash infrastructure is oriented around other target architectures. NCP DFlash additionally needs target-feature capture from routed decoder layers, request-owned proposal context, and transactional rollback/replay of the hierarchical target state after rejection.

I searched open vLLM issues and pull requests for NCP-OLMo, `NCPOlmo3ForCausalLM`, NCP-ArchPreview, ConceptLM, and NCP DFlash. I did not find an implementation of this model family. The related DFlash issues and PRs cover generic or other-model behavior; they do not implement NCP's hierarchical request-state contract.

Reference implementations prepared for discussion:

- [Target-model backend](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...LuckySJTU:vllm:dev/ncp-archpreview)
- [DFlash extension stacked on the target backend](https://github.com/LuckySJTU/vllm/compare/dev/ncp-archpreview...dev/ncp-archpreview-dflash)

### Proposed Change.

I propose landing the work in two pull requests after RFC feedback.

#### 1. NCP-OLMo target backend

The first PR would:

- register `NCPOlmo3ForCausalLM` and document all non-DFlash checkpoints in the public NCP-ArchPreview collection;
- load standalone Hugging Face checkpoints, validating the published architecture contract and mapping split Q/K/V and gate/up tensors into vLLM's fused parameters;
- implement the token encoder, chunk-level HLM, routing/product-codebook path, and token decoder while using regular vLLM `Attention` layers for token-tower KV blocks;
- keep HLM state keyed by request ID, with explicit add/remove/reorder/refill/release and recompute-replay behavior through the V2 model-state lifecycle;
- fail closed on unsupported checkpoint variants, prefix caching, tensor or pipeline parallelism, quantized checkpoints, and CUDA graph capture in the first version; and
- add public examples, model documentation, dummy-weight registry coverage, weight-contract tests, and HF-versus-vLLM correctness tests.

The initial target scope is deliberately narrow: TP=1, PP=1, eager execution, and no prefix caching. Token-tower KV remains managed by vLLM, while dense HLM state stays request-owned outside the block manager.

#### 2. NCP DFlash extension

The stacked PR would reuse vLLM's `method="dflash"` integration while adding an NCP-specific speculator and state contract:

- validate and bind the public DFlash checkpoint to its matching Stage 2 v1 target;
- capture the configured target decoder features and load the draft during normal model initialization;
- cache proposal-side context K/V by request ID, project only newly committed suffixes, and prune state on completion or preemption;
- derive proposal width from the active decode batch after completion/refill, without mutating checkpoint configuration;
- trim variable-width proposal suffixes before target verification and reject invalid internal holes; and
- transactionally truncate or restore/replay token, HLM, routed-feature, and draft-cache state after rejection.

The correctness-first default is `sequential_exact`. `intra_chunk_exact` may widen proposals only inside the current safe HLM chunk. A cross-chunk `segmented_kv_approx` mode remains explicit and experimental because proposal-side conditioning and batched target numerics may differ even though target verification remains authoritative.

The initial implementation keeps NCP-specific behavior gated by the public DFlash checkpoint contract. Generic DFlash and non-DFlash speculators retain their existing defaults.

#### Validation completed

- Clean source builds passed for both branches.
- Target tests: 55 passed; registry dummy-weight initialization passed and was not skipped.
- NCP DFlash tests: 88 passed.
- Public Stage 1 and Stage 2 v1 checkpoints passed HF-versus-vLLM greedy-token and top-k-logprob checks and batched-versus-sequential parity.
- Stage 1 passed chunked-prefill, recompute-preemption, continuous refill, and request cleanup checks with more queued requests than `max_num_seqs`.
- The public NCP DFlash checkpoint passed target-only token parity, continuous-refill parity, same- and cross-chunk rollback tests, and a recompute-preemption test that both increased the preemption counter and preserved target tokens, text, and top-k logprobs.
- All 17 non-DFlash checkpoint configs in the public collection matched the accepted contract and exposed the same 842 weight keys.

The following is a short synthetic one-H200 snapshot with greedy decoding, seed 42, three repetitions, and medians. It is included to characterize the current trade-off, not as a universal serving-throughput claim.

| Active batch : configured width | Target-only tok/s | Exact tok/s (speedup, acceptance) | Experimental adaptive tok/s (speedup, acceptance) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1:8 | 27.05 | 29.19 (1.079x, 89.10%) | 51.68 (1.910x, 49.46%) |
| 2:8 | 47.25 | 47.95 (1.015x, 89.10%) | 70.69 (1.496x, 49.46%) |
| 4:4 | 79.45 | 75.15 (0.946x, 89.10%) | 102.21 (1.286x, 68.04%) |
| 8:2 | 120.86 | 117.31 (0.971x, 89.10%) | 135.29 (1.119x, 80.67%) |

For a continuous-refill case with 16 requests and `max_num_seqs=8`, target-only reached 68.11 tok/s; exact mode reached 66.39 tok/s (0.975x, 79.37% acceptance); and experimental adaptive mode reached 81.17 tok/s (1.192x, 68.45% acceptance). Both speculative modes produced the exact target-only token sequences in this test.

#### Alternatives considered

- **Out-of-tree plugin:** this would isolate the model code, but the required V2 request-state lifecycle, model-runner feature capture, and DFlash proposal/rollback integration are not exposed as a stable plugin surface.
- **Replay the full HLM state every step:** simpler, but it discards incremental state and substantially increases repeated work.
- **Store HLM state in the token KV block manager immediately:** attractive longer term, but it requires a separate cache payload and copy-on-write contract; treating token KV alone as sufficient would make prefix hits incorrect.
- **Ship only the widest DFlash mode:** rejected because correctness should be the default and the wider cross-chunk mode has a distinct, explicitly experimental state contract.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is an in-tree model implementation appropriate, or should vLLM first expose additional out-of-tree hooks for request-owned model state and model-specific speculators?
2. Is the proposed two-PR split (target backend, then stacked DFlash support) the preferred review boundary?
3. Should the NCP DFlash settings remain typed fields in `SpeculativeConfig`, or move under a method-specific nested configuration?
4. Is fail-closed prefix caching acceptable for the first PR while a joint token/HLM cache contract is designed separately?

### Feedback Period.

At least one week, or longer if maintainers want the request-state and speculative-decoding design split into separate RFCs.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

The implementation and validation were AI-assisted. The submitting human reviewed the changes and validation evidence and can defend the design. Before opening either PR, the branches will be rebased onto the then-current `main`, the relevant test matrix will be rerun, and the PR descriptions will include exact test commands/results, model-evaluation evidence, non-duplication rationale, and the required AI-assistance disclosure.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Windowed Hidden-State Collection for vLLM Rollouts
author: vx120
body:
# RFC: Request-Scoped Hidden-State Capture Windows

## Motivation

Some applications need hidden states for only a bounded range of generated tokens. Capturing and exporting hidden states for an entire generation adds memory traffic, device-to-host copies, and serialization work for tokens the application does not need.

vLLM should support request-scoped, position-aware hidden-state capture so a request can collect a selected window, such as response positions `[1000, 2000)`, without exporting hidden states before or after that window.

## Goals

* Capture hidden states for a fixed token-position window on a per-request basis.
* Support batches whose requests are at different points in their windows.
* Avoid hidden-state export and associated copies outside the requested window.
* Preserve existing behavior and the fast path when capture is not requested.
* Support speculative decoding, tensor/pipeline parallelism, and CUDA Graphs where the relevant execution path supports selective capture.

## Non-goals

* Avoiding the model's normal internal activation computation.
* Returning full-sequence, all-layer activations as a substitute for selective capture.
* Defining application-specific storage or training behavior.

## Proposed API

Add an optional per-request capture configuration. The exact public API shape can follow vLLM's request conventions; the following illustrates the required semantics:

```yaml
hidden_state_capture:
  mode: fixed
  coordinate: response
  start: 1000
  end: 2000
  layer_ids: [1, 8, 16]
```

* `start` is inclusive and `end` is exclusive; `0 <= start < end`.
* `response` is the default coordinate system. A response offset `r` maps to the hidden position used to predict response token `r`; for prompt length `prompt_len`, this is absolute position `prompt_len - 1 + r`.
* `absolute` may be provided for callers that already work with absolute sequence positions.
* The requested layer selection should be explicit and validated by vLLM.
* When the option is absent or disabled, request behavior remains unchanged.

## Design

### Per-request capture state

The engine should create immutable capture metadata when it accepts a request and propagate it through scheduling to the worker execution path. It must be associated with the request rather than stored in a process-global switch or passed through unsupported fields in public sampling parameters.

Each request follows this state machine:

```text
DISABLED → ARMED → CAPTURING → FINISHED
```

* `DISABLED`: no capture was requested.
* `ARMED`: capture was requested, but the request has not reached the window.
* `CAPTURING`: scheduled token positions overlap the requested window.
* `FINISHED`: all requested positions have been processed; request capture state and buffers are released.

### Selective export

The runtime should derive selected rows from the active batch's request IDs and token positions. Only rows inside the requested window may be gathered, combined across selected layers, copied to CPU, or returned to the caller. Requests in `ARMED` or `FINISHED` state must not retain or export hidden-state tensors.

Capture state must remain request-local when requests share a batch. The implementation should not register and remove PyTorch hooks on every decode step; the per-request selection should govern export in the normal execution path.

After the final requested position has been processed, capture for that request must finish and release its buffers. Later decode steps must not produce hidden states for it, even if generation continues.

### Output and alignment

For each request with captured rows, return the hidden states together with metadata equivalent to:

```text
hidden_positions
hidden_window_start
hidden_window_end
layer_ids
request_id
```

`hidden_positions` is authoritative. The returned positions may be a subset of the requested window because generation can stop early or execution can fragment the capture. If a request ends before entering its window, return no hidden-state payload for it.

### Execution compatibility

Selective capture must not enable global `output_hidden_states=True` or silently force eager execution. vLLM should validate whether the active model runner and execution mode can provide the required mapping from scheduled rows to request IDs and sequence positions. If a requested combination is unsupported, return a clear capability error rather than silently exporting full-sequence states or ignoring the request.

## Observability

Expose metrics sufficient to measure capture overhead and effectiveness:

```text
vllm/hidden_capture_requests
vllm/hidden_capture_rows_planned
vllm/hidden_capture_rows_captured
vllm/hidden_capture_bytes_copied
vllm/hidden_capture_copy_ms
```

Benchmark decode throughput before, during, and after the capture window. With the same model, batch size, sequence lengths, and speculative-decoding settings, median throughput outside the window should be no more than 3% below the baseline with hidden-state capture disabled.

## Test plan

* Unit tests for response-relative and absolute position conversion, inclusive and exclusive window boundaries, and requests with different prompt lengths.
* Tests for requests ending before, inside, and after the window, and for mixed batches containing `ARMED`, `CAPTURING`, and `FINISHED` requests.
* Tests that returned hidden rows match `hidden_positions` and that no rows are copied or returned after capture finishes.
* Integration tests for request metadata propagation through the serving, scheduler, and worker paths.
* Compatibility tests for eager and CUDA Graph execution, speculative decoding, tensor/pipeline parallelism, prefix caching, and supported hardware backends.

title: [RFC]: Plain-Python watermarking performance regression benchmark
author: SyaOtiLan
body:
### Scope

Address the speed-regression item in [#56105](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56105), following [the preference for plain Python benchmarks/tests](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56105#issuecomment-5676111413). This proposal does not depend on perf-eval or add a generic assertion framework.

### Proposed first version

- Add a focused Python benchmark in vLLM, reusing existing serving-benchmark utilities where practical.
- Compare watermarking off and on with the same model, hardware, engine options, prompts, input/output lengths, concurrency and sampling settings. Keep temperature nonzero: the tracker notes that temperature zero deactivates watermarking. Verify that the enabled configuration actually exercises watermarking; matching seeds does not imply matching generated tokens.
- Start with one supported TP=1 configuration using default compiled execution and a fixed, recorded watermark key. Use fixed-length requests for this controlled overhead measurement; quality and detectability evaluation remain separate.
- Warm up each condition, run repeated measurements in alternating off/on order, and retain per-run results and environment metadata. Report output throughput, TTFT, TPOT, completed-request counts, and relative overhead. Do not treat failed or incomplete requests as valid performance samples.
- Add the automated regression check against an agreed workload-specific overhead budget after validating measurement noise on its intended GPU runner. The tracker's example of 1% is a candidate requirement to confirm, not a threshold established by the earlier generic assertion smoke test.

### Scope boundaries

No new quality/detection scorer or full compatibility matrix in this change. Quantization, speculative decoding and multi-GPU cases can be added as supported configurations are agreed. No new CI job is assumed by this proposal.

### Decision needed before implementation

Which existing GPU job and model should the initial regression check target, and should the tracker's example 1% overhead be its acceptance criterion?

title: [RFC]: Split scale-out into owned components (Renderer / Frontend / Generation) with dedicated launch commands
author: hickeyma
body:
### Motivation.

#55176 replaced `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS` with `--enable-scale-out` for plain `vllm serve`. During review, @sagearc proposed a cleaner long term model for scale-out: instead of one server exposing an ad-hoc set of endpoints gated by flags (`--enable-scale-out`, `vllm launch render`, `--tokens-only`), split scale-out into components that each own their endpoint surface. This would mean a Renderer, a Frontend and a Generation component. This RFC is that follow up, split off from #55176 so it didn't block landing that PR.

It also handles the `--tokens-only` deprecation raised in the same thread: `--tokens-only` today forces `skip_tokenizer_init`, forces the scale-out and Cohere render routers on, sets a no-op `force_no_detokenize` and registers `/abort_requests`. A `vllm launch tokens` command (the counterpart to the existing `vllm launch render`) was proposed as its replacement, deprecating `--tokens-only`.

See the [review comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55176#pullrequestreview-5170631409) that raised this.

### Proposed Change.

1. **Components own their endpoints.** Each scale-out role gets a dedicated launch surface instead of one server with overlapping flags:
   - **Renderer** (`vllm launch render`, already exists): preprocessing, OpenAI compatible endpoints and derender (postprocessing, tokens back to an OpenAI response). 
   - **Generation** (new, replaces `--tokens-only`, proposed as `vllm launch tokens`): `/inference/v1/generate` plus request abort. Don't force `skip_tokenizer_init`. Local decoding is common and useful and without a tokenizer:
     - Structured outputs are rejected outright (`vllm/sampling_params.py:1071`, `"Structured outputs requires a tokenizer so it can't be used with 'skip_tokenizer_init'"`).
     - `stop` strings are silently ignored (`IncrementalDetokenizer.from_new_request` falls back to the base class with no tokenizer `vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py:43,57` which never calls `check_stop_strings`).
     `--skip-tokenizer-init` should stay a separate, opt-in flag on this launch mode, not something it implies.
   - **Frontend**: scheduling / request routing. Needs clarification. Does this mean routing that already lives outside vLLM (the llm-d EPP or Dynamo router role) or something to be added inside vLLM? Note `/v1/models` is currently registered on every server, including the render server (`vllm/entrypoints/launchers/api_server/routers.py:26`), so "owns" should be read as *primary owner*, not *exclusive*.

2. **Move `/abort_requests` under a guarded prefix.** It's currently only registered under `--tokens-only` (`vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/api_router.py:77`) and sits outside `GUARDED_PREFIX = ("/v1", "/v2", "/inference", "/cohere")` (`vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py:11`). This means `--api-key` does not protect it today. Generation is a natural point to move it under `/inference/v1/` so it inherits API key protection.

3. **Decide what "`vllm serve` orchestrates components" means.** Two different sized changes are both consistent with the framing:
   - `vllm serve` spawns and manages separate component processes (bigger change) **OR**
   - one process that mounts every component's routers as it effectively does today (smaller change, closer to current behavior with `--enable-scale-out`)

4. **`--tokens-only` deprecation.** Introduce `vllm launch tokens` as the pair to `vllm launch render` covering what `--tokens-only` does today (minus the forced `skip_tokenizer_init` per point 1). Deprecate `--tokens-only` with a removal path once the replacement lands. `force_no_detokenize` is currently a no-op without a tokenizer and undesirable with one (loading the tokenizer is the point of local decoding on this component). Decide whether it's dropped entirely or kept for a different purpose.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@DarkLight1337 @sagearc

### Any Other Things.

**Related:**

- PR #55176  which triggered this RFC
- Derender work under RFC #47161 (postprocessing side of the Renderer component)

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Programmable KV Cache: Composable Policies for Agentic Serving
author: zhhangBian
body:
## TL;DR

This RFC defines a provider-neutral Programmable KV Cache abstraction in which routers supply session lifecycle and placement intent, composable engine policies propose retention, movement, and quota actions against a shared pressure snapshot, and the engine provides unified resource approval and completion contracts above existing connectors.

## Motivation

Agentic applications are not one continuous generation. A task can:

1. generate one model response;
2. call an external tool and pause;
3. create several child agents from the same context;
4. complete or abandon a branch;
5. resume on the same or another engine.

During a pause, the KV is often the most valuable prefix for the next request, yet it may have no active request reference and enter an ordinary LRU eviction order. During spatial contention, a non-critical request can consume capacity and evict a critical-path prefix. The next turn needs to load an external copy or recompute the context if no usable copy is available.

The [vLLM AgentX post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx) describes representative traffic: a median of 43 turns per session, a median 142K-token input and 444-token output, prefix-cache hit rates above 96%, and subagents in 44% of sessions. These patterns require a cache policy that can combine lifecycle information with local resource state.

## Existing foundations and related RFCs/PRs

### 1. Identity and events: associating multiple requests

[Identity RFC #48049](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48049) separates session_id from request_id: the former persists across calls; the latter retains per-request output, cancellation, and scheduling semantics. Its implementation [#48048](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48048) is merged and supplies typed session identity through the request path.

[Event PR #51381](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51381) is merged. It adds the triggering session_id to GPU BlockStored and supports full reporting of prefixes hit by the current request. [#54325](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54325) is also merged and corrects SimpleCPU offload event metadata and tier labels. These report cache activity; they do not automatically provide a complete session↔block index. [#50732](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50732) still proposes BlockInactive to distinguish active references from reclaimable cache; inactivity does not mean session completion.

[#48501](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48501) extends this direction with session-centric orchestration, continuation_id coordinates, event attribution, and publisher epochs. Logical coordinates help upper layers interpret cache activity, but must remain distinct from content hashes and physical copies. The first session triggering an event is not the exclusive owner of shared content.

### 2. Programmatic KV: existing actions, indexes, and execution boundaries

[#51428](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/51428) is the overarching architecture proposal. It defines Share, Prefetch, Demote, Pin, and Retain, and explicitly allows engine acceptance, clipping, deferral, and rejection. It considers both engine-local SessionPrefixIndex and external orchestrator resolution, including many-to-many associations, cache-hit membership, and bidirectional outcomes.

This establishes important foundations. We do not claim engine authority or action results as unique additions. The remaining contract is how multiple local policies use common observations, produce executable plans, share finite capacity, and connect those plans to existing connectors.

[#52113](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52113) starts from application events. It proposes agent_hint, a SessionAwareManager (SAM), parent/child sessions, TTLs, and context management. SAM owns detailed associations and updates block metadata through a guarded KVCacheManager interface; the proposal also discusses a remote SPM adapter and a direct connector-capability direction. It provides a broader lifecycle model than a retention parameter and already recognizes remote observation and completion.

The coordination question is not whether a separate manager is valid. It is whether agent_hint and KvHintsEnvelope become competing ingress contracts, whether SAM and another session index duplicate tracking, and whether concrete fields, timers, or adapters unnecessarily constrain the public interface.

### 3. Retention: expressing value over token ranges

[#37003](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/37003) proposes token-range priority/duration to distinguish shared prefixes, tool-wait contexts, and lower-value tails. Its implementation [#38514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/38514) remains open. It keeps the existing LRU and adds a priority queue and TTL handling for annotated blocks, with retention_scope semantics.

Its strength is separating cache priority from request scheduling priority and directly addressing victim order. Its scope is primarily GPU retention; it does not independently choose request-free prefetch timing, a retention backend, or competition with future request capacity. This RFC adopts range/priority/TTL semantics, permits replacement algorithms as policy implementations, and retains independent declarations for different sessions’ lifetimes.

### 4. Common envelope: unified ingress without rebuilding transport

[#53421](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53421) defines KvHintsEnvelope and KvHintAction. The envelope carries protocol_version, message_id, and actions; actions carry identity, type, version, and payload. [#53423](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53423) remains open and provides Python/Rust typed plumbing and kv_hints propagation. Its description includes public HTTP/gRPC fields, but it neither defines nor executes individual actions.

That is an intentional transport boundary. We reuse it and define the cache-operation, policy-input, and result contracts above it. A second envelope is unnecessary; the absence of an executor is not a defect in the transport PR.

### 5. Dynamo: global indexing, hint production, and external execution

[Dynamo DEP #13279](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/13279) proposes a router-side SessionPrefixIndexer, separating session/frontier/shared-ancestor structure from FlashIndexer residency observations. Known matches and newly stored content update logical relations; Removed/Cleared update residency rather than deleting task lineage. It remains a proposal.

[Dynamo #13134](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13134) is merged and provides typed hints with a transitional engine bridge through kv_transfer_params.kv_hint, to be aligned with vLLM kv_hints. It demonstrates extensible router-produced inputs, not engine execution of every proposed action.

[KVCC #11673](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/11673), the [KVCR project](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/kvcr), and the open [vLLM adapter #53624](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53624) address pooled caches and external execution. An adapter keeps storage and transfer in an independent backend; it should not also be the only implementation of all engine GPU retention, request-capacity, and policy-composition decisions.

### 6. Agentic API and agentic router: how application state reaches the engine

[agentic-api #195](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/pull/195) is a draft for Messages server-managed cache state, covering affinity, checkpoints, retention, and branches while preserving the conversation-stateless public Messages contract. Its boundary is explicit: Agentic API derives trusted logical coordinates and lifecycle intent, llm-d selects the worker, and vLLM resolves and executes physical KV operations.

[#52567](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52567) discusses the broader vLLM/Agentic API relationship and links [llm-d-router #1979](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/1979) on session-centric orchestration, [#2003](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/2003) on session control, and [#1867](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/1867) on agentic routing profiles. These represent the agentic-router role here: cross-request task interpretation, affinity, and global routing, rather than another cache allocator.

There is a substantive tradeoff. Router-led approaches centralize semantics and reduce engine application awareness. However, a wholly policy-unaware engine cannot autonomously exploit immediate demand and capacity changes. We retain router ownership of global decisions while permitting local policies to act on reusable runtime information. Hard session affinity and migratable shared KV are also different capabilities and are not bound to one interface here.

### 7. SGLang and cross-system semantics

[SGLang #27574](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27574) uses a similar router-to-engine taxonomy with tiered storage, cross-engine sharing, and Mooncake-related retention. It demonstrates that these requirements extend beyond vLLM. Action meanings can align without making SGLang’s internal session structure or a backend lease a mandatory vLLM implementation.

## Concrete contribution of this RFC

**We propose an engine policy interface separate from connectors, with a complete contract from observation and proposals through composition, resource approval, and completion.**

Existing work already provides session identity, logical cache actions, a common envelope, and backend execution paths. We define the local decision boundaries between those pieces so different algorithms can run in one engine without each adding another set of fields, session managers, and resource accounts.

| Addition                           | Concrete contract proposed here                              | Value to consumers                                           |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Common observations                | Reclaimable capacity, valid Pins, in-flight reservations, request growth, and backend capabilities in one view | Retention, movement, and quota policies can use the same facts |
| Composable policy interface        | Policies propose; a replaceable composer produces one plan; the engine approves resources | Identical prefetches coalesce and competing operations cannot independently spend the same capacity |
| Two inputs, one execution boundary | Explicit router actions and runtime signals enter the same planning/execution flow | Orchestrated and autonomous local policies coexist without mirroring instantaneous scheduler state in the router |
| Control across request lifetimes   | Resolve explicit prefixes and retain, demote, or prefetch after a request completes | Tool waits and branch completion have executable semantics without synthetic inference requests |
| Resource and completion contract   | Distinguish proposal, receipt, approval, in-flight work, and availability; define resource holders and release | Adapters have explicit inputs/outputs and observed benefits follow actual completion |
| Request/KV cooperation             | Demand observations and request-score proposals usable by quota examples | More optimization space without prescribing a queue, preemption, or partitioning algorithm |

For example, two policies request the same 8 GiB prefix on the same GPU, with only 10 GiB available for new work. This design coalesces them into one 8 GiB reservation. If they target different prefixes, some work must be selected, clipped, or deferred. The envelope can carry both requests, but does not determine that engine resource decision. **The common arbitration and execution interface is the contribution, not the action names themselves.**

These numbers illustrate capacity accounting. Benefits of the common implementation still need evaluation; observation, indexing, composition, and backend adapters also consume CPU, memory, and engineering effort.

## Goals

The RFC provides:

- logical KV targets based on BlockHash, Session, Continuation, and logical token ranges;
- session-to-logical-block associations, parent/child lineage, and multiple branches;
- common semantics for Retain, bounded-TTL Pin, Prefetch, Demote, Share, Evict, and Release;
- a pressure snapshot readable by engine policies;
- composition of multiple policy proposals with one engine-level resource decision;
- optional admission, agent-class quota, and request-score extensions;
- connector capability advertisement, asynchronous movement, and completion results;
- observation contracts for association, residency, inactivity, action results, restart, and event gaps;
- useful degradation when no router or no particular connector is present.

## Proposed Change

### Responsibility boundaries

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R["Router: global intent and logical index"] --> H["KvHintsEnvelope: signals and actions"]
  A["Direct application"] --> H
  H --> P["Policies: retention, movement, optional quota and score"]
  V["Pressure snapshot: capacity, demand, in-flight work"] --> P
  P --> C["Replaceable composition policy"]
  C --> E["Engine: validation, unified approval and accounting"]
  E --> B["Local KV manager / BlockPool"]
  E --> K["KV connector"]
  K --> M["Mooncake / CPU / other KV backends"]
  B --> O["Residency, associations, results and recovery"]
  K --> O
  O --> R
```

This RFC uses the following boundary:

| Component           | Owns                                                         | Does not own                                                 |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Router/orchestrator | Global worker selection, cross-engine placement, task/branch relations, lifecycle intent | Whether this engine can allocate space or whether a local copy still exists |
| Engine policy       | Local target resolution, capacity/reference checks, final local feasibility of retention, admission, and movement | Cluster routing and backend-specific transfer                |
| Connector           | Remote lookup, copy/move, tier selection, asynchronous completion, backend errors | Global session policy and request ordering                   |

A router directive is a request, not a resource grant. The engine may accept, clip, defer, reject, or report a missing target. If it reports that a bounded-TTL Pin is active, it must honor the accepted target layer and duration; a best-effort receive path must not silently revoke an accepted guarantee.

Request and KV scheduling are allowed to cooperate: a policy can read waiting demand and provide a request score proposal. The RFC does not replace the waiting queue or preemption algorithm.

### From envelope to execution: interface responsibilities

These are conceptual interfaces, not fixed Python classes or RPC signatures. They define what each participant can observe, what it returns, and which boundary changes resource state.

| Responsibility        | Input                                             | Output                                                      | Allowed effect                                               |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Receive and normalize | KvHintsEnvelope and optional request context      | Logical actions and runtime information                     | Record and correlate input; a signal does not automatically allocate memory |
| Resolve targets       | Hash / session / continuation / range             | Explicit content boundaries, known copies, missing portions | Do not infer a current physical block from an obsolete session name |
| Observe runtime       | Engine, KV manager, and connector state           | Read-only PolicyView / pressure snapshot                    | Supply facts and labeled estimates, not capacity grants      |
| Propose policy        | Runtime information, targets, shared observations | Retention, movement, quota, or score proposals              | Do not mutate allocators/queues or start backend transfers   |
| Compose proposals     | Policies plus explicit actions                    | Consistent pending KVPlan                                   | Coalesce duplicate intent and arbitrate local policy competition |
| Approve in engine     | KVPlan and current state                          | Accepted scope/reservation or deferral/rejection            | Sole approval boundary for physical capacity and operation holds |
| Execute backend       | Approved targets, space, and requirements         | In-flight state and completion                              | Use existing managers/connectors without expanding approved scope |
| Complete and report   | Completion, failure, or target changes            | Availability, released resources, events, queryable results | Update actual residency for subsequent router/policy decisions |

Conceptually:

    inputs = normalize(envelope, optional_request_context)
    targets = resolve(inputs.targets)
    view = observe_engine_and_backends()
    proposals = [policy.propose(inputs, targets, view) for policy in policies]
    plan = composer.combine(inputs.explicit_actions, proposals, view)
    approved = engine.validate_and_reserve(plan)
    executor.submit(approved)
    # Later completion: register usable content, release resources, report.

Explicit actions still need engine approval. The composer can arbitrate competition, but cannot silently convert a caller’s GPU Pin into CPU Retain. Allowed clipping or unsupported guarantees must be reflected in the result.

### What the core records express

| Record                     | Content                                                      | Distinction                                                  |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| KVTarget                   | Logical selector, branch/range, cache compatibility context  | No externally stable physical block ID                       |
| WorkloadSignal             | Pause, resume, completion, parent/continuation, optional importance/resume time | Fact or prediction, not resource authorization               |
| ProtectionDeclaration      | Target, declarant, Pin/Retain, priority, lifetime, target tier | Session association alone does not imply Pin                 |
| KVProposal                 | A policy’s suggested action, rationale, resource demand, or score | May be dropped by composition or deferred by the engine      |
| KVPlan                     | Pending actions and dependencies, such as cold completion before GPU reclamation | Does not mean execution succeeded                            |
| ApprovedOperation / Result | Actual approved scope, execution stage, result               | Correlated to message_id/action_id; physical resources charged once |

Implementations can extend or adapt existing records; these do not require a second public wire schema.

## Terminology and logical model

### Logical content, association, and residency

These are separate:

- **Logical content:** a reusable prefix identified using the compatible model, cache salt, KV group, and BlockHash.
- **Association:** a session or continuation may use the prefix; one logical block can be associated with multiple sessions.
- **Residency:** the engines, GPUs, CPU tiers, disks, or remote stores holding valid copies.

Removing a GPU copy does not remove the session association. Ending one session does not authorize deletion of a prefix still used by another.

### Session and continuation

A Session represents task-level lifecycle. A Continuation represents an explicit continuation or branch boundary inside that task. It may be generated by an upper layer and carried as opaque metadata; it does not replace BlockHash as the cache identity.

### Active references and policy protection

- **Active reference:** a request or transfer reference required for correctness. A replaceable policy cannot revoke it arbitrarily.
- **Retain:** a relative eviction priority, optionally bounded by a TTL; it may yield under pressure.
- **Pin:** a bounded-TTL strong protection. Once accepted, it is excluded from ordinary eviction within the accepted target layer or valid-copy scope. Its effective result reports the accepted layer/scope and TTL.
- **Prefetch reservation:** destination capacity held before a request arrives; it counts against the engine’s current capacity.

## Control protocol

### KvHintsEnvelope

The RFC reuses the typed KvHintsEnvelope and request field kv_hints from [RFC #53421](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53421) and [PR #53423](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53423). The envelope carries:

    KvHintsEnvelope(protocol_version, message_id, actions[])
    KvHintAction(action_id, action_type, action_version, payload)

The same envelope can accompany an inference request or arrive through a control entry point while no generation is active. This makes retention, demotion, and prefetch during tool pauses ordinary capabilities, without synthetic inference requests. HTTP, gRPC, and internal utility paths are not prescribed here.

Signals and commands may share the envelope, but their semantics differ:

- a command asks the engine to attempt a specific operation;
- a signal reports tool waiting, a branch transition, importance, or an estimated resume time, leaving the policy to decide what operation is useful.

This RFC defines the meaning and resource contract above the envelope. It does not fork the transport format.

### Target addressing

The portable interface should support:

- **BlockHash:** the router or connector already knows a logical hash;
- **Session:** operate on associated content, optionally qualified by an explicit continuation and half-open logical token range;
- **Active RequestRange:** operate on a cache range belonging to a still-active request.

Continuation and range qualify a logical target rather than introducing physical addressing. A whole-session operation covers its relevant branches. Historical branch or range operations bind to an explicit continuation/prefix boundary, not an implicitly changing “latest” branch. Token-range retention does not delete text from model input.

Selectors identify logical content. The engine resolves them to group-specific cache entries and current residency.

### Action semantics

| Action   | Meaning                                                      |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Retain   | Add a relative priority, optionally with a TTL; equal priorities use LRU |
| Pin      | Provide bounded-TTL strong protection; the target can be GPU, CPU, remote, or at least one valid copy |
| Prefetch | Prepare KV at a target engine/tier before expected use, including CPU-to-GPU preparation before resume; do not report availability before completion |
| Demote   | Confirm a valid colder copy; once active references and valid GPU Pins permit reclamation, invalidate the GPU hash and make its space reusable |
| Share    | Ensure a valid copy at a target engine; do not implicitly remove the source |
| Evict    | Remove a selected engine/tier residency when active references and valid Pins permit |
| Release  | Remove a session/continuation Pin/Retain declaration without deleting unrelated copies |

A Retain TTL expires the declaration’s priority; it does not require immediate deletion. Independent session declarations remain independent: if A’s high priority expires while B’s lower priority remains valid, B’s protection remains. A layer’s Pin protection ends only when all valid Pin declarations for that layer have expired or been released.

A declaration with a TTL starts when it becomes effective. Only an explicit update renews it; a cache hit does not renew it implicitly. Every Pin acceptance or renewal is bounded, and the engine may clip, defer, or reject requests beyond its capability or capacity. A valid GPU Pin prevents ordinary demotion; a cold-tier Pin permits reclamation of the GPU copy. Retain without a TTL remains an evictable priority bias.

A shared block’s effective priority is the maximum among still-valid declarations. A’s high priority must not be combined with B’s longer TTL into a stronger declaration. Expiration or release affects only the corresponding declaration. Bytes remaining on the GPU after demotion are not a registered cache hit.

Share does not implicitly delete its source. A migration explicitly handles the source after the destination is valid; copy completion alone does not authorize revoking source references or protection.

### Agentic lifecycle

A parent session remains logically hot throughout a task: its associations remain valid and its cache is valuable, but all KV need not remain on the GPU. Tool pauses may trigger Demote to a cold tier, followed by Prefetch before the expected resume. Misprediction or insufficient capacity is handled through the existing load/recompute paths.

One LLM request returning a tool call does not end the task. Parent-task completion releases associations and protection declarations for the entire task tree, including the parent session, without deleting content shared with other tasks or revoking active references. Waiting for an unknown future user reply after task completion returns to ordinary cache policy.

## Engine policies: observation, composition, and resource approval

### 1. PolicyView supplies facts, not a fixed algorithm

| Observation                                            | Producer                                        | Policy use                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| GPU/cold-tier capacity, occupancy, reclaimable cache   | KV manager and connector                        | Determine whether protection/movement consumes scarce resources |
| Active references, valid Pins, in-flight reservations  | Engine operation/resource records               | Exclude capacity already committed or not currently reclaimable |
| Incremental demand from waiting/running requests       | Scheduler and KV manager                        | Estimate whether movement creates useful capacity for requests |
| Admitted requests’ remaining unallocated growth        | Engine observations or optional capacity policy | Avoid treating committed future demand as unlimited spare space |
| Backend hits/unknown state, queues, transfer estimates | Connector                                       | Estimate recovery cost and completion time                   |
| Session, continuation, tool state, importance          | Router/application and optional local index     | Relate content location to task value                        |

Physical facts, estimated demand, and policy commitments must be distinguishable. A maximum output budget is an upper bound, not a prediction of actual use. The view requires neither a complete DAG nor one sampling interval or memory layout.

### 2. Policies return composable proposals

Policies and connectors are registered independently. Policies may propose:

- Retain/Pin declarations for a logical range;
- Prefetch, Demote, or Share based on expected use;
- capacity guidance for an agent class;
- request-score recommendations.

They do not directly execute backend work or remove blocks from the free queue. Engine/KV-manager paths own physical mutation, so replacement algorithms can change without duplicating lifecycle handling.

The composer first removes duplicate work, then arbitrates retention versus movement, destinations, quotas, and request demand. Shared Pin/Retain declarations preserve independent lifetimes; this is a defined protection rule, not arbitrary score weighting. Composition of heuristic advice remains replaceable and does not assume equal score scales.

### 3. Approval is a separate engine decision

Before execution, the engine rechecks content, protection, active references, and current capacity instead of trusting an earlier snapshot. Approval identifies the actual scope and reservation. Failure returns missing, unsupported, deferred, or rejected as appropriate.

Data may be referenced by a task and participate in a transfer simultaneously, but physical capacity is charged once. GPU allocations, pending destination reservations, and a quota example’s logical cost shares are not independent sources of space. Completion/cancellation release operation resources through their records; removing a proposal cannot reclaim memory still accessed by a transfer.

### 4. Request/KV cooperation boundary

KV policies consume request demand and growth information; scheduler extensions can consume request scores. They share facts without allowing cache plugins to reorder the waiting queue or choose preemption victims directly.

Dynamic quota is an example enabled by the interface: a request belongs to at most one agent class, shared content can be apportioned across logical session references, and physical copies are counted once. A quota limit is not guaranteed space. Borrowing, over-quota handling, and ordering remain example-policy choices. TokenCake-like algorithms can integrate without imposing one partitioning model on every deployment.

## SessionPrefixIndex: functions, placement, and updates

The RFC first defines the questions the index answers, then where information belongs. The router

title: [RFC]: [FS Offloading][ThreadPool] Updates to Thread Pool
author: varun-sundar-rabindranath
body: ### Motivation. ## Introduction This RFC proposes updates to the `thread_pool` in the filesystem (FS) KV cache offloading subsystem (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/`). The FS tier has two optimization targets: - **TTFT** — how fast a waiting request can be loaded and scheduled - **CPU KV cache space** — reducing promotion failures by freeing CPU KV blocks quickly Loads and stores serve these targets differently. **Loads** are unbounded in size and affect both targets. **Stores** are bounded by the engine forward pass and benefit only CPU KV cache space. The current thread pool treats them symmetrically — this RFC argues that is sub-optimal and proposes a differentiated policy across job ordering, batching, work stealing, and disk type (local SSD vs. remote NFS). ## Loads and Stores Are Not the Same Store jobs are tied to **running requests**: each store is bounded by the engine's forward pass, making stores relatively short and predictable in duration. Load jobs are tied to **waiting requests**: a load can bring in an arbitrary amount of data from the FS tier, making them unbounded in size and duration. ### Prefill Task Distribution ### Decode Task Distribution ## Workloads Are Not the Same ### Prefill Benchmark Data ``` Time range : 11:19:51 – 11:31:31 Total seconds : 701 Store-only secs : 164 (23.4%) # seconds where only stores were submitted Load-only secs : 1 (0.1%) # seconds where only loads were submitted Mixed secs : 536 (76.5%) Idle secs : 0 (0.0%) Store jobs : 4611 (24399 blocks total) Load jobs : 3106 (73625 blocks total) ``` ### Decode Benchmark Data ``` Time range : 12:04:04 – 12:15:44 Total seconds : 701 Store-only secs : 277 (39.5%) # seconds where only stores were submitted Load-only secs : 27 (3.9%) # seconds where only loads were submitted Mixed secs : 257 (36.7%) Idle secs : 140 (20.0%) Store jobs : 1915 (11914 blocks total) Load jobs : 1703 (38688 blocks total) ``` Prefill workloads generate significantly more concurrent load and store jobs than decode workloads. During prefill, KV blocks are produced rapidly and both loads (for prefix cache hits) and stores (to offload blocks) contend for disk bandwidth simultaneously. Decode workloads are not as intensive. Once a request enters the decode phase, its KV blocks no longer need to be offloaded. This gives the system natural breathing room — periods where the thread pool handles exclusively loads or exclusively stores, rather than both at once. ## Disks Are Not the Same This RFC considers two disk types, corresponding to the existing `Locality` abstraction used by the offloading tiers: `LOCAL` (SSD) and `REMOTE` (NFS). For `LOCAL` SSDs, mixing reads and writes significantly degrades read throughput. FIO benchmarks, with 1MB files (left) and 32MB files (right), on SSD A modest 75%/25% read-write mix reduces read bandwidth drastically. Batching both reads and writes together drives the effective mix toward 50-50, hurting TTFT. Reads serve both optimization targets while writes serve to help only CPU KV cache space — and writes are bounded by the engine forward pass while reads are not. For `REMOTE` NFS, this read-write interference does not apply. For these reasons the thread-pool needs to treat loads vs stores differently. ### Proposed Change. ## Proposal ### Batching Policy | Disk Type | Load (read) batching | Store (write) batching | |---|---|---| | `LOCAL` (SSD) | `n_read_threads` | 1 | | `REMOTE` (NFS) | `n_read_threads` | `n_write_threads` | ### Job Ordering **Load jobs:** use two queues, alternated on every get(): - **FCFS** (First-Come-First-Served) - **Shortest Job First** *Rationale:* Batching concentrates all read threads on a single job, maximizing disk bandwidth for that job and minimizing its TTFT. The downside is that smaller jobs arriving later get stuck behind larger ones. Alternating with "Shortest Job First" breaks this starvation — small jobs are cheap to dispatch and quickly free CPU KV cache space. **Store jobs:** use a single queue: - **Shortest Job First** *Rationale:* Unlike loads, stores have only one optimization target: freeing CPU KV cache space.
