Processing the smallest stores first is a greedy strategy that frees space as quickly as possible. ### Work Stealing Read threads **may** steal store jobs — stores are short and the cost of a read thread handling one is low. Store threads: There are 2 ways to handle store thread work-stealing, 1. **should avoid** stealing load jobs. Because load jobs are batched across multiple threads, a stolen load job pulls several store threads into the job, leaving no threads available to handle incoming store work and locking up CPU KV cache space. 2. Store jobs, if allowed to steal from loads, should steal only a small quanta at a time so it can come back to check any arrival of store jobs. This will make the implementation a bit more complicated, but might be worth it. I have a branch here with these policies implemented https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...neuralmagic:vllm:varun/allioc-batch-pr?expand=1 - look at file `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/fs/policy.py` ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. @dannyharnik @orozery @Etelis @tlrmchlsmth @bnellnm ### Any Other Things. This RFC came out of the batching work in the PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49225 ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Checkpoint-aware cache eviction and segmented recomputation for hybrid models
author: warriorsniu
body:
### Motivation.


#### Background

Hybrid models such as Qwen3.5 interleave Full Attention (FA) layers with recurrent GDN/Mamba layers. vLLM stores FA KV blocks and recurrent states in different cache groups, while a prefix is reusable only when all required groups can resume from compatible token boundaries.

Internal recurrent-state checkpoints make it possible to resume GDN/Mamba computation from selected boundaries. However, checkpoint creation alone does not coordinate the eviction order of those checkpoints with the FA blocks around them. Under mild KV-capacity pressure, a multi-turn request may therefore lose only a small tail of physical cache but still need to recompute nearly its entire private context on the next turn.

#### Problem

FA blocks and recurrent checkpoints become evictable at different times and in different directions:

- A request normally releases its unreferenced FA blocks together at request completion. Native release preserves the continuous left prefix and therefore exposes the right side of the request to eviction first.
- In align-mode GDN/Mamba execution, a newer recurrent state replaces an older state while the request is still running. Unless explicitly retained as a checkpoint, the older state becomes evictable first, producing a left-to-right checkpoint order.

The shared eviction queue can consequently contain a mixture of FA tail-first and recurrent-state head-first order. The problem is not whether FA or Mamba should have a globally higher eviction priority. The problem is that the physical range evicted from one cache group no longer matches the range that all cache groups must recompute.

Consider a completed request divided by recurrent checkpoints:

```text
token order:  FA0 | checkpoint1 | FA1 | checkpoint2 | FA2 | checkpoint3
```

If pressure evicts only a few FA blocks at the tail of `FA2`, the next turn cannot simply recompute those blocks: it must also reconstruct recurrent state from `checkpoint2` through `checkpoint3`. If pressure instead evicts only `checkpoint3`, the same recurrent interval must be recomputed even though most FA blocks remain resident. In both cases, evicting roughly one block can require recomputing an entire checkpoint interval.

A global FA head-first policy would protect recent cache but damage reusable shared prefixes. This RFC instead proposes checkpoint-delimited segments with the following request-local eviction order:

```text
FA2 (head-first) -> checkpoint3 -> FA1 (head-first) -> checkpoint2
                 -> FA0 (head-first) -> checkpoint1
```

With this order, FA blocks immediately to the left of a checkpoint become evictable before that checkpoint. A partial eviction creates one explicit missing interval whose length is close to the amount of FA state evicted. If the checkpoint and a later FA suffix remain resident, segmented recomputation repairs only that missing interval.

#### Goal

This RFC proposes three coupled changes:

1. Release completed-request blocks in checkpoint-aware segment order.
2. Detect a missing middle FA interval followed by a resident FA suffix and compatible recurrent checkpoint.
3. Recompute only the missing interval, then reuse the resident suffix and resume from the checkpoint.

The goal is to align physical eviction with required recomputation and preserve later-turn cache hits under mild KV-capacity pressure. The first cold turn is not the optimization target.

#### Scope

The initial scope is a hybrid cache containing FA and GDN/Mamba groups in `mamba_cache_mode="align"`, with prefix caching enabled. It covers checkpoint-aware release and middle-interval recomputation. Other hybrid layouts, external-KV gaps, arbitrary non-contiguous model execution, and model-kernel changes are out of scope.


### Proposed Change.


#### Terminology

Token positions increase from left to right. A `-` denotes resident cache, while a blank interval denotes evicted FA blocks:

```text
FA segments      : |          Segment0          |          Segment1          | 
FA blocks        : -----------------------------------------------------------
Mamba blocks     : -----------------------------------------------------------
Mamba checkpoints: |                            |                            |
                                          checkpoint1                   checkpoint2
Resident FA cache: -----------------------------              ----------------
                   |                            |             |              |
                   0                       repair_start   repair_end   resume_checkpoint

Execution         : <--------- reuse ----------><-- repair --><--- reuse --->
Recurrent resume  :                                                        checkpoint
```

The first line describes the request before eviction. The `Resident FA cache` line describes the same request when its next turn arrives: `[0, repair_start)` remains a native continuous hit, `[repair_start, repair_end)` has been evicted, and `[repair_end, resume_checkpoint)` is still resident behind the gap.

- A **checkpoint** is a cached recurrent state at token boundary `T` from which all required GDN/Mamba groups can continue execution.
- An **FA segment** is the FA interval between adjacent checkpoint boundaries, or the prefix/suffix outside the first/last checkpoint.
- `repair_start` is the end of the native continuous cache hit. `[0, repair_start)` is already reusable.
- `repair_end` is the beginning of the resident FA suffix and the end of the interval that must be repaired.
- `resume_checkpoint` is the compatible recurrent boundary at the end of that resident FA suffix.
- A **segmented recompute plan** contains these three boundaries plus temporary references to the resident blocks required by the second lookup.

Every useful plan satisfies:

```text
repair_start < repair_end < resume_checkpoint
```

The request recomputes `[repair_start, repair_end)`, reuses `[repair_end, resume_checkpoint)`, and resumes recurrent execution at `resume_checkpoint`. Its total locally reused tokens are:

```text
repair_start + resume_checkpoint - repair_end
```

Within an FA segment, **head-first eviction** means that lower-token-position blocks enter the eviction queue before higher-token-position blocks.

#### Overview

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Request finishes] --> B[Collect resident checkpoints]
    B --> C[Partition FA blocks at checkpoint boundaries]
    C --> D[Release blocks in segmented order]
    D --> E[Later request arrives]
    E --> F[Run native continuous-prefix lookup]
    F --> G{Resident suffix and compatible checkpoint?}
    G -->|No| H[Use native recomputation path]
    G -->|Yes| I[Build read-only repair candidate]
    I --> J{Native token and KV budgets admit repair?}
    J -->|No| K[Keep request waiting and retry later]
    J -->|Yes| L[Retain suffix and checkpoint]
    L --> M[Recompute missing interval]
    M --> N[Run native lookup again]
    N --> O[Reuse suffix and resume at checkpoint]
```

The design has three coupled parts: track replayable checkpoint boundaries, release blocks in checkpoint-aware order, and consume the resulting resident suffix through segmented recomputation.

#### 1. Track replayable checkpoints

`MambaManager` records recurrent states together with exact token boundaries. A boundary is usable only when every required recurrent cache group has a resident compatible checkpoint at that position. Incomplete boundaries use native fallback behavior.

The shared-prefix-boundary checkpoint is retained while its producing request is alive so align-mode state rotation cannot place it into the free queue prematurely. The latest running checkpoint may also hold a temporary request-lifetime reference. Other observed checkpoints are not permanently pinned and participate only while their blocks and hashes remain resident.

The proposal does not reserve capacity for every historical checkpoint. It preserves the checkpoint needed to establish shared-prefix reuse, changes the release order of blocks that have become evictable, and temporarily retains only the resident blocks selected for an admitted repair.

#### 2. Build a checkpoint-aware eviction order

For the following layout:

```text
FA0 | checkpoint1 | FA1 | checkpoint2 | FA2 | checkpoint3 | FA3
```

the order from earliest to latest eviction is:

```text
FA3 -> FA2 (head-first) -> checkpoint3 -> FA1 (head-first)
    -> checkpoint2 -> FA0 (head-first) -> checkpoint1
```

The rightmost uncheckpointed FA suffix is released first. Checkpoint-delimited segments are then processed from right to left. Within a segment, FA blocks are released in increasing token order, followed by the checkpoint at the segment's right boundary. The checkpoint remains useful until the FA interval needed to reach it has already become the repair interval.

This policy does not change total cache capacity, admission capacity, or the global block-pool eviction mechanism. It only controls the order in which one completed request contributes blocks to that mechanism.

Let `B` be the number of released FA blocks and `K` the number of complete checkpoint boundaries. Sorting boundaries and assigning blocks to segments by binary search costs `O(B log K + K)` time and `O(B + K)` temporary storage. This work occurs on request release, not on ordinary decode-only scheduling steps.

#### 3. Detect a recoverable resident suffix

After native lookup returns a continuous hit ending at `repair_start`, the coordinator performs a read-only probe:

1. Find the farthest compatible recurrent checkpoint `resume_checkpoint` not beyond the request's cacheable prompt.
2. Search backward in the FA cache for the longest contiguous resident suffix ending at that checkpoint.
3. Set `repair_end` to the beginning of the resident suffix.
4. Accept the plan only when `repair_start < repair_end < resume_checkpoint` and every required recurrent group contributes the checkpoint.

The resulting layout is:

```text
[0, repair_start)                    native continuous hit
[repair_start, repair_end)           missing FA interval to recompute
[repair_end, resume_checkpoint)      resident FA suffix to reuse
resume_checkpoint                    resident recurrent checkpoint
```

If no compatible checkpoint exists, the suffix is empty, the interval is already continuous, or a required group is absent, the request follows native recomputation.

Candidate discovery must not change cache recency. The selected suffix and checkpoint are touched and retained only after the scheduler selects the request and native KV allocation succeeds. A request that cannot fit is left waiting and may be probed again against current cache state.

#### 4. Perform two-phase segmented recomputation

The initial implementation reuses native continuous prefill and lookup rather than passing a gapped block table to the model runner:

1. Native prefix lookup establishes `repair_start`.
2. After native token and KV-block budgets admit the request, retain the resident suffix and recurrent checkpoint.
3. Schedule normal prefill only for `[repair_start, repair_end)`; chunking and concurrency remain governed by native scheduler budgets.
4. Wait until the final asynchronous repair step has completed and `num_in_flight_tokens` reaches zero.
5. Retain the newly produced FA blocks, release repair-only allocations, reset the request to prefix lookup, and prepend it to the waiting queue.
6. Run native lookup again. The repaired interval and resident suffix now form a continuous FA hit through `resume_checkpoint`, and the recurrent group provides the matching checkpoint.
7. Once native allocation owns the cache-hit references, release temporary repair retention and continue from `resume_checkpoint`.

Only tokens that were actually reused are reported as cache hits. Tokens in `[repair_start, repair_end)` are recomputed and are not counted as cached. Unlike an earlier prototype, this design has no separate global repair slot: a repair is prefill work and therefore uses the existing scheduler token budget and KV-block allocation path.

#### Proposed internal APIs

The names below match the current prototype. They are internal interfaces, but their responsibilities should remain separated during review.

| Component | Proposed function | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MambaManager` | `_record_checkpoint(request_id, block, block_hash, num_tokens, pin, retain)` | Record an exact replay boundary and maintain request-lifetime ownership where required. |
| `MambaManager` | `pop_blocks_and_checkpoints(request_id)` | Remove request bookkeeping and return ordinary recurrent blocks separately from resident checkpoint entries. |
| `KVCacheCoordinator` | `pop_blocks_in_eviction_order(request_id)` | Define the generic release hook that returns blocks in intended eviction order. |
| `HybridKVCacheCoordinator` | `pop_blocks_in_eviction_order(request_id)` | Intersect checkpoint boundaries across recurrent groups, partition FA blocks, and produce segmented release order. |
| `FullAttentionManager` | `find_cache_suffix_ending_at(block_hashes, end_length, ...)` | Find the contiguous resident FA suffix ending at a checkpoint. |
| `HybridKVCacheCoordinator` | `find_segmented_recompute_plan(block_hashes, max_cache_hit_length, repair_start)` | Return a three-boundary repair candidate and the resident blocks it depends on. |
| `HybridKVCacheCoordinator` | `get_repaired_prefix_blocks(request_id, repair_end, excluded_ids)` | Collect newly cacheable FA blocks produced by interval repair. |
| `KVCacheManager` | `prepare_segmented_recompute(request, repair_start)` | Probe and store a read-only repair candidate without touching cache blocks. |
| `KVCacheManager` | `discard_unscheduled_segmented_recompute(request_id)` | Discard a stale candidate that was not selected. |
| `KVCacheManager` | `defer_segmented_recompute(request_id)` | Discard a candidate after allocation failure while preserving retry diagnostics. |
| `KVCacheManager` | `complete_segmented_recompute_interval(request)` | Retain repaired FA blocks and prepare the request for native lookup. |
| `KVCacheManager` | `finish_segmented_recompute(request_id)` | Release temporary retention after native lookup owns the hit blocks. |
| `KVCacheManager` | `release_segmented_recompute(request_id, clear_deferrals)` | Clean up repair state on abort, preemption, finish, fallback, or shutdown. |
| `Scheduler` | `_complete_segmented_recompute_if_ready(request)` | Enforce the async completion barrier and requeue the request for its second lookup. |

The recovery state is represented by:

```python
@dataclass
class SegmentedRecomputePlan:
    repair_start: int
    repair_end: int
    resume_checkpoint: int
    retained_blocks: list[KVCacheBlock]
    retention_acquired: bool = False
    ready_for_lookup: bool = False

    @property
    def cached_tokens(self) -> int:
        return self.repair_start + self.resume_checkpoint - self.repair_end
```

#### Scheduler integration

The feature augments three existing scheduler lifecycle paths rather than replacing the scheduler:

| Path | Added behavior | Hot-path effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waiting-request admission | After native lookup, probe a segmented plan and cap scheduled prefill at `repair_end`. | Only waiting requests with a recoverable gap enter repair. |
| `Scheduler.update_from_output()` | After the repair interval has no in-flight tokens, finalize it and requeue the request for native lookup. | One completion check for requests with repair state. |
| Request release | Return blocks through `pop_blocks_in_eviction_order()`. | Sorting and segmentation occur only when request blocks are released. |

Ordinary decode scheduling does not search checkpoints, partition FA blocks, or construct repair plans.

#### Concurrency and lifecycle safety

Repair work is admitted through native request token and KV-block budgets. Multiple repairable requests may make progress when those budgets permit; the feature does not add a separate repair queue, lock, or serialized repair slot.

Read-only probes do not touch blocks. Retention is acquired only after the request is selected and allocation succeeds, preventing repeated probe-touch-release cycles from perturbing LRU order. If allocation fails, the candidate is discarded and the waiting request can be evaluated again later.

Under asynchronous scheduling, a repair cannot reset its request while `num_in_flight_tokens` is nonzero. The second lookup occurs only after the final repair model step has completed and its cache writes are visible.

Abort, ordinary preemption, request finish, failed second lookup, and scheduler shutdown release all temporary references. Request-lifetime shared-boundary retention is also released when the request is freed. These paths must not leak block references or leave stale repair state.

#### Feature gate and compatibility

The prototype uses one default-off feature gate, `VLLM_HYBRID_CACHE_SEGMENTED_REUSE`, for checkpoint tracking, shared-boundary retention, checkpoint-aware release, and segmented recomputation. A production CLI or `CacheConfig` field may replace the environment variable after the public configuration surface is reviewed.

When the gate is disabled, the additional checkpoint and repair state is not used and scheduling follows native behavior. Unsupported cache layouts fall back to native behavior even when the gate is enabled.

#### Alternatives considered

##### Preserve only the latest checkpoint

Keeping the latest checkpoint can help an adjacent turn, but it does not align that checkpoint with FA eviction and cannot consume a resident suffix after an earlier FA gap appears.

##### Globally evict FA blocks head-first

Global head-first eviction protects recent cache at the expense of shared prefixes. It also creates gapped FA layouts that native continuous-prefix lookup cannot consume without segmented recomputation.

##### Keep native mixed release order

Independent FA and recurrent release can evict a small physical range while forcing an entire checkpoint interval to be recomputed. This is the mismatch targeted by the RFC.

##### Pin all checkpoints

Permanently pinning all checkpoints changes effective capacity and admission semantics. This proposal retains only request-lifetime boundaries needed for correctness of shared-prefix reuse and blocks used by an admitted repair.

##### Implement arbitrary gapped execution in the model runner

A general gapped block-table execution interface could avoid the second lookup, but it requires broader scheduler, worker, and kernel changes. Two-phase repair reuses existing continuous-prefill and prefix-lookup paths. Its interval representation should remain compatible with the direction explored in PR #32785.

#### Preliminary evaluation

We ran a default-off/default-on comparison with vLLM's multi-turn serving benchmark using Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8 on two NVIDIA L20 GPUs, TP=2, native `AsyncScheduler`, `mamba_cache_mode="align"`, eight concurrent conversations, three LLM requests per conversation, an approximately 8K-token cross-conversation shared prefix, an approximately 30K-token private first-turn context, and a 276,390-token KV capacity. Both variants enabled the same intermediate-prefix retention policy; the proposed variant additionally enabled checkpoint-aware ordering and segmented repair.

Because the first turn is a compulsory cold prefill, the primary comparison uses turns 2 and 3:

| Later-turn metric | Retention baseline | Proposed behavior | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Token-weighted prefix-cache hit rate | 29.05% | 88.18% | +59.13 pp |
| Uncached prompt tokens | 438,400 | 73,024 | -83.34% |
| Mean TTFT | 23.56 s | 6.09 s | -74.14% |
| Mean TPOT | 319.77 ms | 302.25 ms | -5.48% |
| Mean request latency | 64.17 s | 44.48 s | -30.68% |
| Completion window | 194.77 s | 147.13 s | -24.46% |
| Request throughput | 0.0821 req/s | 0.1087 req/s | +32.38% |

The retention baseline's token-weighted hit rate fell from 39.10% on turn 2 to 19.07% on turn 3. The proposed path remained at 87.80% and 88.56%, respectively. The much larger TTFT reduction than TPOT reduction is consistent with avoiding repeated prefill rather than accelerating decode kernels.

These are preliminary results from one short A/B run with diagnostics enabled. They demonstrate that the path is exercised and that later-turn reuse can improve under the targeted pressure, but they are not a general performance claim.

#### Validation plan

Before implementation review, we plan to provide:

- Feature-disabled parity with upstream `main`.
- Deterministic token-by-token output equivalence between segmented recovery and cold recomputation.
- Unit coverage for eviction order, shared-prefix-boundary lifetime, incomplete checkpoint boundaries, multiple recurrent groups, partial FA boundaries, and native fallback.
- Lifecycle coverage for allocation deferral, retry, abort, preemption, asynchronous completion, request finish, and shutdown.
- Cache-accounting checks proving that repaired tokens are not reported as hits.
- Multi-turn serving results under no pressure and mild-to-high KV pressure, with per-turn cached tokens, TTFT, TPOT, latency, throughput, recomputed tokens, and zero-hit requests.
- CPU microbenchmarks for release-time ordering and admission-time suffix lookup.

#### Success criteria

- No output-correctness difference from cold recomputation for supported deterministic cases.
- No block-reference leak or invalid request transition across retry, abort, preemption, finish, and asynchronous execution.
- Feature-disabled behavior and performance remain consistent with upstream behavior.
- Under the targeted multi-turn pressure workload, later-turn cache hits and TTFT improve without a material TPOT regression.
- Request-release ordering and admission lookup add no work to ordinary decode-only scheduling steps.

### Feedback Period.

One week from RFC publication.

### CC List.

@yewentao256 @ZJY0516 @s3woz @heheda12345 @ivanium @ywang96 @njhill

### Any Other Things.


#### Relationship to existing work

- [RFC #45702: Partial Cache Hits for Hybrid Models](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45702) discusses finer-grained hybrid prefix hits and request-boundary recurrent states. It does not define coordinated eviction for checkpoint-delimited FA segments.
- [RFC #52959: Internal State Checkpoints for Mamba Align Mode](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52959) and its implementation provide recurrent checkpoints. This proposal builds on those checkpoints and aligns their eviction with FA recovery.
- [PR #32785: Segmented prefill for gapped external KV cache hits](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32785) explores segmented prefill for gaps reported by an external KV connector. This RFC targets gaps created by local hybrid-cache eviction and should reuse a common segmented-range representation where practical.

#### Proposed implementation sequence

1. Rebase the prototype onto the latest upstream `main` and rerun the strict feature-disabled/feature-enabled reproduction.
2. Submit checkpoint-aware request-release ordering, shared-boundary lifetime management, segmented recomputation, and lifecycle tests as one default-off Draft PR because none independently consumes the intended cache layout.
3. Split out only a prerequisite segmented-range abstraction if it can be shared with PR #32785 or its successor.
4. Complete correctness evaluation and repeated no-pressure/pressure benchmarks before discussing default enablement.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Retain MRV2 DBO CUDA graph replay under DP imbalance through real-token staging
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation. I am investigating eager fallback under imbalanced DP decode workloads with MRV2 DBO, building on #51700 and the original RFC #50738. For example, with per-rank token counts [63, 97] and a 128-token FULL CUDA graph, each captured microbatch has a capacity of 64 tokens. On the smaller rank, the first microbatch contains 63 real tokens and one padding token, while the second contains only padding. The existing guard: ```python 2 * min_tokens < descriptor.num_tokens ``` therefore rejects the microbatched graph and falls back to eager execution across the DP group. I would like to investigate whether FULL CUDA graph replay can be retained by redistributing real tokens within each rank's existing captured input layout, without moving requests between DP ranks. The motivation is to avoid unnecessary eager fallback while preserving graph-visible addresses, physical capacities and collective ordering. The additional staging, metadata updates and output restoration introduce overhead that must be evaluated against the benefit of retaining graph replay. ### Proposed Change.

Introduce real-token staging before CUDA Graph replay.

Instead of placing all 63 real tokens in the first microbatch and leaving the second microbatch empty, redistribute the real tokens across the two captured regions.

For example:

Captured region | Existing layout | Proposed layout -- | -- | -- Rows 0–63 | 63 real + 1 padding | 32 real + 32 padding Rows 64–127 | 64 padding | 31 real + 33 padding

The proposal would reuse the existing graph capacity while ensuring that both microbatches contain real tokens.

The implementation must preserve token-to-request mappings, positions, attention metadata, KV-cache indexing, MoE dispatch/combine mappings, and output ordering.

The existing eager fallback should remain available for unsupported or unsafe cases.

The intended scope is limited to eligible decode workloads where the redistribution can be performed safely.

### Feedback Period. At least one week. I would appreciate early design feedback before proceeding with a production-ready implementation. Benchmark results and profiling evidence will be added as they become available. ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things.

1. Throughput

Higher is better.

Seed | Config | Duration (s) | Requests/s | Output tokens/s | Total tokens/s -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- 1 | E | 271.24 | 3.7752 | 1932.90 | 2416.13 1 | G | 261.34 | 3.9183 | 2006.16 | 2507.70 1 | A | 237.66 | 4.3086 | 2206.01 | 2757.51 2 | G | 263.42 | 3.8873 | 1990.29 | 2487.86 2 | A | 237.45 | 4.3125 | 2208.02 | 2760.03

Median E2E latency improves by 11.36% and 12.52% relative to G.

### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Retain MRV2 DBO CUDA Graph replay under DP imbalance through real-token staging
author: algebra-MCX
body: ### Motivation. I am investigating eager fallback under imbalanced data-parallel (DP) decode workloads with MRV2 DBO, building on #51700 and the original RFC #50738. Consider a 128-token FULL CUDA Graph with two microbatches, each having a capacity of 64 tokens. For DP ranks with token counts [63, 97], the smaller rank's second microbatch contains only padding. The existing guard: 2 * min_tokens < descriptor.num_tokens rejects the microbatched graph and falls back to eager execution across the DP group. This preserves correctness but potentially sacrifices CUDA Graph replay even when the real tokens could be redistributed across the existing captured input layout. The goal is to retain FULL CUDA Graph replay without changing the captured graph shape or the number of microbatches. ### Proposed Change. Introduce real-token staging before CUDA Graph replay. Instead of placing all 63 real tokens in the first microbatch and leaving the second microbatch empty, redistribute the real tokens across the two captured regions. The proposal would reuse the existing graph capacity while ensuring that both microbatches contain real tokens. The implementation must preserve token-to-request mappings, positions, attention metadata, KV-cache indexing, MoE dispatch/combine mappings, and output ordering. The existing eager fallback should remain available for unsupported or unsafe cases. The intended scope is limited to eligible decode workloads where the redistribution can be performed safely. Preliminary Benchmark Results I compared three configurations: E: Original implementation, eager execution. G: Original implementation, CUDA Graph enabled. MLA uses FULL_DECODE_ONLY in practice, and fallback still occurs. A: Proposed DeepSeek adaptation with CUDA Graph and real-token staging. Environment Each run completed all 1,024 requests with zero failures. Each measured run processed 131,072 input tokens and 524,288 output tokens. ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Scheduler-Aware Multi-Tier KV Caching for vLLM with MORI-UMBP
author: charxwu
body:
## Motivation

vLLM's GPU prefix cache is bounded by accelerator memory. CPU offloading can extend capacity within an engine, while an external KV store can preserve and reuse prefixes across engines, DP ranks, nodes, and engine restarts. The open [vLLM UMBP feature request](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48191) tracks this need for AMD deployments.

MORI-UMBP provides an AMD-focused storage path with HIP-visible GPU-buffer registration, NUMA-aware host DRAM, MORI-IO RDMA, SSD backends, tier-placement policy, and scheduler-visible KV location and hit metadata. Integrating it into vLLM provides several concrete benefits:

- **Shareable capacity:** standalone UMBP places the node-local KV pool in a separate process so DP ranks and model instances can share DRAM. This also allows round-robin traffic to reuse KV across DP ranks.
- **Direct GPU-to-store movement:** grouped ranged operations move between registered vLLM KV buffers and UMBP without requiring a connector-owned contiguous host staging copy.
- **Cache lifetime independent of the engine:** standalone storage survives worker restart or rolling upgrade, avoiding a complete host-cache warm-up.
- **Global placement and routing:** distributed UMBP can use cluster-wide capacity and location information instead of making every placement or eviction decision from one rank's local view.
- **Replication-aware storage:** byte-identical TP replicas can share one object identity in shared storage, while rank-sharded data retains distinct shard identity. Writer election can additionally reduce duplicate traffic when every reader can reach the elected writer's object.
- **Layer-wise overlap:** grouped ranged I/O, batched offload, and per-layer completion allow later-layer KV loading to overlap earlier-layer compute.
- **Tiered capacity:** UMBP can extend the same object namespace from DRAM to SSD and optional UMBP-owned HBM without adding medium-specific branches to the vLLM connector.

The initial integration should not require a redesign of vLLM's connector API. `MooncakeStoreConnector` provides a useful structural precedent: one `KVConnectorBase_V1` implementation dispatches to scheduler-side lookup/planning and worker-side registration/transfer logic.

`UMBPStoreConnector` follows that vLLM-facing structure while keeping UMBP semantics behind `IUMBPRuntime`. Embedded mode is worker-private and masterless; standalone mode shares a node-local service; distributed mode uses Master routing, peer-owned slots, MORI-IO, and heartbeat-acknowledged publication. Identity, layout, metadata, completion, preemption, and failure-to-recompute remain common across all three modes.

## Proposed Change

### Summary

This RFC proposes adding one vLLM V1 `UMBPStoreConnector` backed by MORI-UMBP. It follows the proven scheduler/worker organization of `MooncakeStoreConnector` while keeping UMBP-specific lookup, transfer, and publication semantics behind `IUMBPRuntime`.

The connector supports embedded, standalone, and distributed UMBP modes without duplicating vLLM-facing code. All modes share replication-aware object identity, KV layout, grouped/layer-wise transfer planning, metadata, job lifecycle, pinning, completion, and failure-to-recompute behavior; only runtime topology and data movement differ.

Implementation proceeds through small PRs, beginning with the shared connector framework and embedded mode, then adding standalone and distributed runtimes. A broader backend-neutral connector for UMBP, Mooncake, and other stores is recorded as an open architectural discussion and does not block UMBP delivery.

### Goals

- Add one vLLM V1 `UMBPStoreConnector` following the existing `KVConnectorBase_V1` scheduler/worker lifecycle.
- Support embedded, standalone, and distributed UMBP modes through one shared connector framework.
- Select the UMBP runtime mode at connector initialization without changing scheduler/worker connector code.
- Use vLLM content-derived block hashes, never physical GPU block IDs, as the basis of persistent object identity.
- Make object identity replication-aware per KV-cache group:
  - sharded TP data keeps a logical shard/rank component;
  - byte-identical TP replicas use one shared object key when the selected runtime storage is shared by those ranks;
  - private embedded pools retain the physical copy needed by each process, even if their logical key is identical.
- Avoid redundant writes only when the runtime can prove that one writer's object is visible to every rank that will read it. Key deduplication and writer election are separate optimizations.
- Keep KV layout planning, connector metadata, transfer job state, pinning, completion, and recomputation logic common across all modes.
- Use UMBP ranged Put/Get operations for non-contiguous GPU KV regions.
- Support both bulk and layer-wise execution through the shared framework: submit grouped asynchronous range operations, wait only for the layer about to execute, and batch completed-layer offloads.
- Register vLLM GPU KV allocations once and pass registered GPU regions directly to UMBP/MORI-IO without connector-owned contiguous staging.
- Treat missing, evicted, timed-out, stale, or partially transferred objects as cache misses and safely recompute them.
- Keep UMBP transport, routing, and publication details out of vLLM scheduler, model-runner, and attention code.
- Incubate through `kv_connector_module_path` against a pinned vLLM revision before considering upstream registration.

### Architecture

![vLLM and MORI-UMBP architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charxwu/vllm/b6827f6b9ad236a7806f1e60fe739494eb81a7ed/docs/assets/vllm-umbp-architecture-v2.svg)

_Figure 1. `UMBPStoreConnector` bridges vLLM's scheduler and worker lifecycle to UMBP's control and data planes._

vLLM owns request scheduling and GPU KV blocks. `UMBPStoreConnector` maps vLLM's scheduler/worker lifecycle onto UMBP control and data operations. UMBP owns routing, transfer, publication, and storage-tier policy.

![Shared UMBP connector and three runtime modes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charxwu/vllm/b6827f6b9ad236a7806f1e60fe739494eb81a7ed/docs/assets/vllm-umbp-connector-v6.svg)

_Figure 2. Shared connector code sits above `IUMBPRuntime`; embedded, standalone, and distributed implement only mode-specific operations._

All modes share connector identity, metadata, layout, pinning, completion, and failure behavior. Only the runtime implementation changes.

`IUMBPRuntime` exposes lookup, direct GPU-buffer registration, grouped load, per-layer wait, batched store, publication, and shutdown operations. Runtime handles receive UMBP keys and transfer plans rather than vLLM request or attention objects.

The shared identity planner classifies each cache group as rank-sharded or rank-replicated. It retains shard identity for different bytes and collapses the TP key component for byte-identical replicas only when runtime visibility allows those ranks to share one stored object.

For layer-wise loading, the worker submits grouped range operations before model execution. `wait_for_layer_load(layer_name)` waits only for ranges needed by that layer, allowing later-layer transfer to overlap earlier-layer compute. Bulk mode remains a valid implementation that reports all layers ready together.

The four related capabilities have separate meanings:

- **Layer-wise loading** controls readiness and overlap: each attention layer waits for only its own KV.
- **Grouped ranged multi-buffer I/O** describes many non-contiguous K/V ranges in one UMBP submission instead of creating a contiguous staging object.
- **Batched offload** combines multiple completed blocks or layers to reduce submission, RPC, and synchronization overhead.
- **Direct GPU-buffer registration** registers vLLM KV allocations once so local copy or MORI-IO can access GPU memory without a connector-owned host copy.

These capabilities require an UMBP-specific worker/runtime adapter. The current `MooncakeStoreConnector` explicitly leaves `wait_for_layer_load()` and `save_kv_layer()` as no-ops, so its bulk lifecycle cannot simply be copied for this path. Current MoRIIO code implements per-layer wait/save hooks. LMCacheMP exposes the same vLLM hooks and batched retrieval, but its current `wait_for_layer_load()` and `save_kv_layer()` are also no-ops; it is not evidence of equivalent per-layer readiness semantics.

Mode-specific behavior is confined below this boundary:

- **Embedded:** worker lookup bridge, private masterless client, local ranged transfers, immediate visibility.
- **Standalone:** node-local service lookup and transfer, shared same-host ownership, no cluster Master or RDMA requirement.
- **Distributed:** Master lookup/routing, peer slot operations, MORI-IO RDMA, and heartbeat-acknowledged global visibility.

### Compatibility

The initial integration targets a deliberately narrow compatibility range:

- vLLM V1 against one pinned revision while `KVConnectorBase_V1` remains experimental;
- decoder-only MHA/GQA models using a supported paged KV-cache layout;
- PP size 1;
- TP size 1 initially, followed by TP size 2 or greater before the shared framework is considered complete;
- full, hash-aligned KV blocks;
- replication-aware object identity per cache group: rank-sharded bytes retain shard identity, while byte-identical replicas may share one key in a shared runtime;
- bulk all-layer transfer as the fallback path;
- layer-wise loading for attention backends and UMBP runtimes that support grouped ranged I/O and per-layer completion;
- `kv_producer`, `kv_consumer`, and `kv_both` roles;
- embedded mode with DRAM;
- standalone mode with a node-local service and DRAM;
- distributed mode with DRAM and MORI-IO RDMA.

Objects are reusable only when the model identity, model revision, KV dtype, block size, attention layout, TP/PP topology, cache-group description, and object-layout version match. These fields are included in the key namespace so an incompatible object becomes a miss rather than being loaded.

MLA, hybrid attention/Mamba, heterogeneous KV-cache groups, PP greater than 1, SSD policies, and UMBP-owned HBM are follow-up extensions. Replication-aware identity is part of the initial framework even when the first model matrix does not exercise every replicated layout. Unsupported layout or layer-wise capability combinations must fail during initialization or explicitly fall back to bulk transfer.

### Test Plan

#### Shared connector tests

- [ ] Verify deterministic keys and namespace isolation, including distinct identities for TP-sharded bytes and collapsed keys for byte-identical replicas when runtime visibility permits sharing.
- [ ] Verify replication-aware storage scope: private embedded pools retain one physical copy per process, while shared runtimes can deduplicate a replicated object.
- [ ] Verify writer election independently from key deduplication and disable it unless every reader can reach the elected writer's object.
- [ ] Verify KV-layout extraction, grouped non-contiguous range construction, and scheduler/worker metadata round-trip.
- [ ] Verify consecutive-prefix matching, TP-rank completeness, and failure-to-recompute behavior.
- [ ] Verify block pinning, preemption, per-key completion, and safe GPU block reuse.
- [ ] Verify the layer-wise pipeline end to end: one-time GPU registration, grouped load submission, per-layer readiness, later layers remaining in flight, and batched offload.
- [ ] Run the same runtime contract suite against fake, embedded, standalone, and distributed runtimes, and verify that changing `mode` does not change connector metadata, key format, range layout, or error semantics.

#### Embedded mode

- [ ] Verify repeated-request prefix reuse, byte-identical KV restoration, and output equivalence with recomputation.
- [ ] Verify eviction between lookup and load, asynchronous save completion, and safe GPU block reuse.
- [ ] Verify grouped/layer-wise local ranged I/O without Master, RDMA fabric, or external storage service.

#### Standalone mode

- [ ] Verify two workers or engines reuse objects through one node-local service, including replicated TP ranks consuming one stored object.
- [ ] Verify concurrent-client behavior and namespace isolation.
- [ ] Verify disconnect, restart, timeout, and eviction degrade to a miss or explicit load error followed by recomputation.

#### Distributed mode

- [ ] Verify a block produced on one node is reused on another through Master routing, peer slot resolution, MORI-IO, and direct GPU registration, with byte-identical restoration.
- [ ] Verify TP completeness and sharded-versus-replicated identity across nodes.
- [ ] Verify stale routes, remote eviction, peer/RDMA failure, and Master timeout/restart degrade safely to recomputation.
- [ ] Verify a store is not globally visible before heartbeat publication is acknowledged.
- [ ] Verify grouped ranged I/O and per-layer completion over the distributed path.

#### Performance

- [ ] Measure cold/cache-hit TTFT, lookup latency, load/store latency, and effective bandwidth for every mode.
- [ ] Measure asynchronous-save overhead, CPU utilization, and hit behavior under eviction.
- [ ] Measure standalone local-IPC contention and distributed local/remote transfer, NIC scaling, and Master/publication overhead.
- [ ] Compare with normal vLLM recomputation and the relevant existing connector.

### PR Roadmap

The PRs are ordered so that the common framework lands before mode-specific runtime implementations:

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add shared UMBPStoreConnector core and IUMBPRuntime contract**
  - Add the `KVConnectorBase_V1` role dispatcher, shared scheduler/worker components, connector metadata, replication-aware key/layout planning, `IUMBPRuntime`, configuration validation, and fake-runtime unit tests.
  - Define bulk and layer-wise transfer-plan contracts here so later modes do not need to change connector metadata.
  - This PR implements the common connector layer shown above; it does not include embedded, standalone, or distributed runtime implementations.

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add embedded mode**
  - Add worker-private, masterless DRAM storage, scheduler-to-worker lookup, local ranged Put/Get, direct GPU-buffer registration, completion, and failure-to-recompute coverage.

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add standalone mode**
  - Connect scheduler and workers to a node-local UMBP service so multiple engines can share one DRAM pool.
  - Cover local IPC, service lifecycle, namespace isolation, and replicated-TP key deduplication within the service's visibility scope.

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add distributed mode**
  - Add Master lookup/routing, peer slot allocation and resolution, MORI-IO RDMA, heartbeat-acknowledged publication, and distributed failure handling.

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add SSD tier support**
  - Enable file/io_uring and SPDK-backed capacity tiers through UMBP policy, including DRAM-to-SSD offload, promotion, eviction, and tier metrics.
  - Keep medium selection below `IUMBPRuntime`; the connector key and metadata remain unchanged.

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add cache-aware routing**
  - Publish UMBP-owned and engine-local KV placement events and expose scheduler-visible hit/capacity information.
  - Allow a router to prefer an engine or node that can reuse the longest prefix without putting routing policy inside `UMBPStoreConnector`.

- [ ] **[UMBP][vLLM] Add layer-wise KV loading**
  - Submit grouped ranged multi-buffer loads before model execution and make `wait_for_layer_load(layer_name)` wait only for the current layer.
  - Add batched offload, direct registered-GPU paths, transfer/compute overlap validation, and bulk-mode fallback.

### Open Discussion: Backend-Neutral Connector Interface

The current `KVConnectorBase_V1` API standardizes lifecycle hooks, but each storage integration still generally implements its own connector class, scheduler component, worker component, metadata, lookup tracking, completion, preemption, and error handling. UMBP, Mooncake, NIXL, and other offloading connectors therefore repeat a substantial amount of structure.

A possible future vLLM abstraction is:

```text
KVConnectorBase_V1
        |
        v
StorageBackendConnector
  shared scheduler/worker lifecycle
  canonical metadata, key, range plan, pinning, completion
        |
        v
IStorageBackend
  Capabilities | Lookup | RegisterBuffers
  Load | Store | Wait | Publish | Close
        |
        +-- UMBPBackend
        +-- MooncakeBackend
        +-- FutureBackend
```

The comparison to a dynamic library is conceptual: the same connector code is initialized with one backend implementation selected by configuration. It does not require a C/C++ shared library and does not imply runtime hot-switching.

Compared with implementing one complete connector per storage system, this could:

- eliminate repeated scheduler/worker forwarding and metadata scaffolding;
- centralize prefix, TP-completeness, pinning, preemption, and failure-to-recompute fixes;
- provide one conformance suite for storage backends;
- add a storage system through one backend implementation rather than another complete `KVConnectorBase_V1` implementation;
- select UMBP, Mooncake, or another backend without changing connector code.

The unresolved risk is whether one interface can preserve optimized behavior across different stores. UMBP and Mooncake differ in key limits, allocation ownership, scatter/gather support, replication, publication, cancellation, and per-key errors. The abstraction could become too weak for optimized paths or too large with optional capabilities.

The current lookup lifecycle is another constraint: `get_num_new_matched_tokens()` returns only `(token_count, load_async)` and does not carry an opaque lookup/reservation plan into `update_state_after_alloc()`. Reservation-based stores may need a generic prepare/commit/abort external-match lifecycle.

This discussion does not block `UMBPStoreConnector`. The proposed shared UMBP core and `IUMBPRuntime` boundary provide concrete implementation experience that can later inform a backend-neutral vLLM interface.

Questions to resolve:

1. Which semantics belong in generic vLLM code versus a storage backend?
2. Can UMBP and Mooncake satisfy the same contract without losing optimized transfer or publication behavior?
3. Which backend capabilities are mandatory, and which can use safe defaults?
4. Should a backend expose one factory or separate scheduler/worker handles?
5. Should vLLM add an opaque external-match plan with prepare, commit, and abort operations?

## Feedback Period

The proposed feedback period is at least one week after this RFC is posted to the vLLM community. The architecture and first PR boundary should be agreed before implementation begins; mode-specific details can continue to evolve in their corresponding PRs.

## CC List

@hongxiayang @tjtanaa @vllmellm @TianDi101

## Any Other Things

### References

- [MORI repository](https://github.com/ROCm/mori)
- [SGLang MORI-UMBP RFC](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27898)
- [vLLM MoRI UMBP offloading support feature request](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48191)

title: [RFC] Model console logging configuration as CLI/serve configuration
author: markmc
body:
##### Problem

This is a logging-focused offshoot of [#25700](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/25700). vLLM's ordinary console logging is configured primarily through environment variables, with related CLI fields spread across other configuration classes. The settings are therefore not represented by one typed configuration and cannot all be supplied, validated, or documented consistently through the CLI and `--config` YAML.

##### Proposal

Introduce a typed `LoggingConfig` on `VllmConfig` for vLLM-managed console logging. Expose the complete object as `--logging-config` JSON, as individual dotted CLI arguments, through `--config` YAML, and through Python configuration.

Start with the three existing environment-backed settings needed to establish the model:

- `configure_logging`, defaulting from `VLLM_CONFIGURE_LOGGING`
- `log_level`, defaulting from `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL`
- `pylogging_config_file`, defaulting from `VLLM_LOGGING_CONFIG_PATH`

For example, the following forms are equivalent:

```bash
vllm serve MODEL --logging-config '{"log_level":"DEBUG"}'
vllm serve MODEL --logging-config.log_level DEBUG
vllm serve MODEL --log-level DEBUG
```

and in a serve configuration file:

```yaml
logging-config:
  log_level: DEBUG
```

`--log-level` should be a convenience override for `log_level`. The pre-existing `--log-config-file` should remain as a legacy override for `pylogging_config_file`.

Configuration precedence should be:

```text
--log-level / --log-config-file > --logging-config CLI > --config YAML > compatibility environment variable > default
```

`pylogging_config_file` remains an advanced escape hatch for supplying a complete Python `logging.config.dictConfig` JSON file; it is not a vLLM configuration file mirroring CLI arguments. A custom `dictConfig` is authoritative over `log_level` for its logger, handler, and formatter settings, and requires `configure_logging` to be enabled. A CLI-supplied file must configure vLLM, Uvicorn, and subprocess logging consistently.

Prototype implementation: [#57205](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57205).

##### Suggested first implementation slice

- [ ] Add `LoggingConfig` to `VllmConfig` with `configure_logging`, `log_level`, and `pylogging_config_file`.
- [ ] Expose the object as `--logging-config` JSON and dotted CLI arguments.
- [ ] Add `--log-level` as a convenience override and retain `--log-config-file` as a legacy override.
- [ ] Support the same model through `--config` YAML and Python configuration.
- [ ] Retain the existing environment variables as compatibility defaults with the precedence above.
- [ ] Apply the resolved configuration after argument parsing and propagate it consistently to vLLM, Uvicorn, and child processes.
- [ ] Make consumers use the effective logger configuration rather than rereading `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL`.
- [ ] Preserve the existing default text output and custom-`dictConfig` behavior.
- [ ] Add parsing, precedence, post-import reconfiguration, and subprocess coverage.

##### Follow-up checklist

- [ ] Decide whether and when to deprecate the legacy `--log-config-file` alias.
- [ ] `VLLM_LOGGING_STREAM` -> `log_stream` / `--log-stream`
- [ ] `VLLM_LOGGING_PREFIX` -> `log_prefix` / `--log-prefix`
- [ ] `VLLM_LOGGING_COLOR` and standard `NO_COLOR` behavior -> `log_color` / `--log-color`
- [ ] Existing `enable_log_requests` / `--enable-log-requests`
- [ ] Existing `max_log_len` / `--max-log-len`
- [ ] Existing `enable_log_outputs` / `--enable-log-outputs`
- [ ] Existing `enable_log_deltas` / `--enable-log-deltas`
- [ ] Existing `log_error_stack` / `--log-error-stack`
- [ ] Define how future built-in logging fields interact with an explicitly supplied Python `dictConfig`.
- [ ] Document and test CLI/YAML/environment/default precedence.
- [ ] Verify propagation to the API server, engine core, workers, Uvicorn, and offline/library entry points where applicable.

##### Scope

This issue covers configuration of the Python logging that normally emits to the console, plus generic request-log policy. It does not attempt to collect every setting whose name happens to contain "log".

For example, `--disable-log-stats`, `VLLM_LOG_STATS_INTERVAL`, and `--aggregate-engine-logging` belong with engine statistics; `log_balancedness` belongs in `EPLBConfig`; and `VLLM_TRACE_FUNCTION` is a separate debugging probe. Similar feature-specific controls should remain with their owning domain configuration.

##### Related future settings

New logging features should extend this model rather than add more standalone environment variables. Examples include:

- `--log-file PATH` for the file-output request in [#31863](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31863)
- `--log-format {text,json,otel-json}` for built-in structured profiles
- a process-prefix policy for [#28582](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/28582)
