title: [RFC][ROCm]: Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) for DeepSeek-V4 hybrid SWA + compressed KV cache
author: edwinlim0919
body:
### Motivation.

## Motivation

DeepSeek-V4 is MLA-based (1 latent KV head), so under TP, every rank stores a full replica of the KV cache. This means TP8 spends ~8x the KV memory than technically required, leading to reduced HBM headroom. DCP removes this replication by sharding the KV cache along the sequence dimension. On agentic workloads with huge sequence lengths (comprising mostly of prefill work) and heavy cache pressure, aggregate KV capacity is the dominant lever for being able to fit many requests in the cache and achieve high throughput. DP-attention also solves this problem, but can suffer from very high latency, especially when a single GPU is computing a large uncached prefill.






### Proposed Change.

## Scope / Hardware

Primary target is **ROCm on MI355X (gfx950)**. All development and validation runs on an 8xMI355X node. The ROCm/AITER leg is the focus of this work. Most of the work is vendor-neutral in nature (scheduler geometry, ownership/layout math, compressor Triton kernels, merge collectives, etc.), but we focus on MI355X for validation and performance optimization. The NVIDIA/FlashMLA attention leg is transplanted from #44573 directly, however we have no NVIDIA hardware to validate it.


## Current State

#44573 (DCP) and #43809 (PCP) by @baonudesifeizhai implemented DSV4 CP for the NVIDIA/FlashMLA path in May/June, however both are inactive since June and predate the mainline DCP framework consolidation. The merged K3 DCP stack from #51705 (decode-LSE) and #53598 (per-group cache geometry) provides the framework upon which this line of PRs is being built. However, no DSV4 model-specific support in vllm/models/deepseek_v4/ currently has the necessary DCP wiring. Additionally, mainline's DCP support currently does not support deduplication for DSV4's SWA/compressed groups.


## Proposal

We are implementing DSV4 DCP as a new PR series on top of the current main and with ongoing efforts to support DCP on other models such as Kimi-K3. Current draft PRs are here (WIP draft: <TODO>), and focuses on transplanting the validated #44573 mechanisms to the currently merged framework. The overall structure of the ongoing contribution is detailed below:

1) Interleaved position ownership with logical block tables, so prefix caching works on sharded DSV4 groups. Needs design alignment with the #53598 geometry (see below).
2) Compressor under DCP: per-rank partial softmax-pool stats -> 1 all-gather/all-reduce merge -> owner-masked cache insert.
3) Sink-free local attention returns LSE, cross-rank merge via mainline collectives such as dcp_a2a_lse_reduce / cp_lse_ag_out_rs, attn sink applied only once after merge has completed.
4) ROCm leg: LSE return + deferred sink for DSV4 sparse split-K/ragged Triton kernels, Triton topk twin for CuteDSL-only indexer merge, DCP wiring for DeepSeekV4ROCMAiterMLAAttention.forward_mqa. Validation on 8xMI355X (gfx950).
5) interleave=1 only initially, to adhere to the sparse-indexer gate. Future work could involve allowing other interleaving degrees if there is potential performance benefit.


## Asks

1) **Cache Geometry**: we are extending dcp_world_size_for_kv_cache_spec to respect the supports_context_parallel flag. Is the current design compatible with the AMD roadmap for hybrid cache DCP? cc @tjtanaa @YukioZzz @okorzh-amd 
2) **AITER**: the gfx950 OPUS sparse prefill (pa_sparse_prefill_opus) returns output only without LSE. For the initial implementation, DCP>1 prefill falls back to the triton ragged path, which can be detrimental for performance. Otherwise, we may run into the issue of double counting attn sink for DCP>1. We can prototype and contribute this, once the initial implementation is finished and validated.
3) @baonudesifeizhai we are building on your #44573/#43809 work with co-authored credit on transplanted commits. Happy to collaborate if you're still interested.

### Feedback Period.

We are requesting a feedback period of ~1-2 weeks, as implementation is already underway. 

### CC List.

cc @tjtanaa @YukioZzz @okorzh-amd 


### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.






## Design update (v2): 2026-09-22
After looking at the relative cache sizes, we decided to drop the #44573 shard-every-cache design. DSV4's SWA cache and compressor state rings are constant-size per request, and is not worth the tradeoff of sharding those in our opinion. v2 only shards the two MLAttentionSpec groups (compressed KV + indexer K), which is already sharded in the mainline and ongoing PRs. This makes the same design decision as the ongoing work in #56738.

Status update:
scheduler geometry (hybrid coordinator whitelist) -> DONE (#57382 
CP-aware compressed/indexer slot mappings -> DONE (#57239)
per-group worker block-table geometry -> DONE (#57239)
indexer top-k merge -> IN PROGRESS
attention wiring -> TODO
ROCm kernel LSE changes -> TODO

## Related work

- #44573 / #43809 : the original DSV4 DCP/PCP implementations (mechanism reference, design superseded per above)
- #51705 / #53598 : the merged K3 DCP foundation this builds on
- #56738 : DSV4.1 DCP on Model Runner V2 (NVIDIA FlashMLA, no prefix caching) -> complementary scope, same cache-placement design
- #57832 / #57840 / #57909 : MiniMax-M3 context-parallel indexers on ROCm
- #57858 / #57859 : candidate-only DSA indexer scorers on gfx950 -> composes with DCP shard-restricted scoring
- #56834 : ROCm mxfp4 indexer cache (DCP=1 gated; layout coordination needed if combined with DCP later)

title: [RFC]: Share KV transfer planning primitives across KV connectors
author: CAICAIIs
body:
### Problem

KV transfer connectors answer the same planning questions in different places:

1. What kind of state is each cache group: attention, SSM, or other?
2. What concrete spec does each layer use, and is it MLA?
3. What byte layout does a registered cache tensor expose?
4. Which peer ranks own each shard?
5. What source/destination byte ranges should a block transfer copy?

The first two questions are already duplicated in NIXL, MooncakeConnector, and MoRIIOConnector. The remaining questions are mixed with connector-specific layouts, transport metadata, and completion accounting. Sharing all of that at once would spread the current NIXL design and increase the blast radius of future changes.

### Boundary

Share a primitive only when two connectors need the same question answered from the same inputs and the result is connector-independent.

The shared layer may consume `KVCacheSpec`, `KVCacheConfig`, `KVCacheSpecKind`, and transfer-group metadata. It returns classification or plain rank/region/byte descriptions. It must not depend on a connector package or produce transport handles, descriptor IDs, wire messages, notification state, or storage-specific layouts.

The five planning areas are:

| Area | Shared result | Current owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classification | group transfer class, per-layer spec type and MLA flag | framework / transfer-planning module |
| Region geometry | block and region byte layout | connector until Stage 2 |
| Peer shard relation | remote ranks, split/replicate relation, reader count | connector until Stage 3 |
| Region pairing | producer/consumer region matches and validation | connector until Stage 3 |
| Transfer plan | ordered byte ranges and coalescing | connector until Stage 4 |

`KVCacheConfig.transfer_groups` and `transfer_group_ids` already define which groups participate in external transfer. A second participation wrapper is not part of the shared API.

### Stages

1. **Classification: #57309**

   `v1/transfer_planning.py` owns `TransferClass`, `transfer_class`, `is_attention_spec`, `is_ssm_spec`, `get_representative_spec`, and `get_representative_spec_type`. The framework exposes the class-level `KVCacheSpecKind` lookup. NIXL and MooncakeConnector use these helpers. `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` is classified by all of its layers; mixed transfer classes fail closed, and MLA remains a per-layer property. NIXL's wrapped Mamba speculative-block handling is covered as a compatibility fix.

   MoRIIO is intentionally not changed in this PR. Its layer map, MLA check, hybrid scheduler rules, and layout code stay connector-local until its own follow-up has a concrete shared primitive to adopt.

2. **Region geometry**

   Define a connector-independent region description from registered tensor layout, spec, kernel block size, and peer geometry. Start after the geometry contract and the relevant Mooncake baselines are settled. Related work: #53078, #55523, #57952, and #56261.

3. **Peer shard relation and region pairing**

   Define rank ownership, split/replicate rules, reader counts, and fail-closed pairing validation. Keep NIXL's descriptor and notification projections connector-local.

4. **Transfer plan**

   Define ordered source/destination byte ranges and coalescing rules. Keep handles, wire metadata, block lifetime, and completion accounting connector-local.

5. **Connector adoption**

   Adopt the stable primitives in Mooncake and MoRIIO where their layouts and validation rules match. Do not force a connector to use an abstraction that does not fit its storage model.

### Invariants

- NIXL descriptor geometry, descriptor IDs, notification counts, and wire formats stay unchanged in every stage.
- Each stage updates all of its adopting connectors in the same change and adds contract tests for the shared result.
- Connector-specific abstractions remain local until a second connector needs the same primitive.
- A new shared primitive requires an update to this boundary and a test matrix before code migration.

### Related work

- #53078: Mooncake heterogeneous-TP transfer for hybrid GDN/Mamba.
- #55523: Mooncake mixed GQA/MLA transfer regions.
- #57952: Mooncake packed hybrid/MLA regions.
- #56261: Mooncake request-local grouping reuse.
- #58362: Mooncake physical block-size bug with mixed KV group sizes. This is separate from Stage 1 and is not fixed by #57309.

title: [RFC]: Asymmetric P/D Deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash
author: gz944367214
body:
## Summary. DeepSeek-V4.1's bounded-replay structure creates an opportunity to make Prefill/Decode disaggregation substantially more asymmetric. Today, a Prefill worker still loads the full 40-layer model even though, after layer 20, only the final 128 prompt tokens need to be processed. This keeps almost half of the model weights resident on P for a small decoder-layer workload whose MoE utilization is likely poor. This RFC proposes moving that final 128-token window entirely to the Decode worker: - For a prompt of length `N`, P computes only `[0, N-128)` and transfers the resulting prefix KV state. - D computes `[N-128, N)` as its first full-model step and samples the first output token. - The request then continues through normal speculative decode with `q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens`. This asymmetry has two main benefits. - First, P would load only the causal encoder plus the minimal layer-20 KV/Indexer projection path, potentially removing close to half of its transformer-layer weights; a key target is fitting a production Prefill replica on one B300 GPU. - Second, moving the decoder-layer work to D increases the computational intensity of that work by executing it as part of D's much larger token batches, improving utilization relative to processing the 128-token replay on P. The execution model on D also becomes simpler than layer-local decoder replay. D never needs separate encoder and decoder token batches: ```text first D step: all L0-L39 process the same 128 prompt tokens later D steps: all L0-L39 process the same 1 + num_spec_tokens tokens ``` The trade-off is that each newly admitted request contributes 128 bounded-prefill tokens to a D step, which can temporarily increase the Decode token count and affect ITL (TPOT). This incremental cost is expected to be modest for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash: its light KV cache permits large Decode batches, and DSpark also makes each Decode batch process many tokens. Against that baseline, adding 128 tokens when a new request is admitted is a relatively small increase. This RFC is a design proposal for discussion. I do not currently plan to implement it, and there is no prototype or benchmark result yet. Implementation ownership is open. ## Proposed Change. ### Model placement and token ownership ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Prompt: N tokens] I -->|Prefix: N-W tokens| P I -->|Final window: W tokens| D subgraph P[Prefill worker: partial model] PE[Causal encoder L0-L19] PK[Minimal L20 Main-KV / Indexer
projection path] PE --> PK end subgraph D[Decode worker: full model] BR[First step: bounded prefill
L0-L39, q_len = W] FT[Sample first output token] ND[Later steps: speculative decode
L0-L39, q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens] BR --> FT --> ND end P -->|Prefix Main / Indexer KV| D ``` For prompts no longer than `W`, P performs no model forward and D processes the complete prompt. Conceptually, P would retain: - embeddings and complete layers L0-L19; - the minimal layer-20 projections needed to produce its canonical C1 Main KV and Indexer K; and - the state required by the KV connector handoff. P would not retain the complete layer-20 attention/MoE path, layers 21–39, final normalization, or the LM head. ### Request flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Prefill worker participant D as Decode worker P->>P: Run prompt prefix [0, N-W) P->>P: Produce prefix Main/Indexer KV P->>D: Send prefix KV D->>D: First step: run final W prompt tokens D->>D: Sample first output token D->>D: Later steps: normal speculative decode ``` Moving first-token generation to Decode is intentional. To minimize changes to the P-node scheduler, the P-node can compute the entire prompt (N tokens) instead of (N−W) tokens, since W is generally much smaller than N and the resulting redundant computation is negligible. ### Uniform Decode execution Decode has two full-model step shapes: ```text new request, first step: q_len = W active layers = L0-L39 later speculative decode steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens active layers = L0-L39 ``` The first step is a bounded prefill using the transferred prefix state. After sampling, the request joins normal speculative decoding. This avoids changing the token set after layer 20. The attention history differs by cache group, but the query rows do not: - prefix-cacheable Main/Indexer groups read the transferred prefix state; - SWA groups are rebuilt locally over the replay window, following the mechanism in #56227; and - every layer executes the same `W` query rows in the first D step. If bounded-prefill requests and ongoing decode requests are scheduled together, their request-level `q_len` values differ. This step is a non-uniform batch and may fallback to piecewise cudagraph. ## Why This May Help. ### Smaller Prefill replicas Prefill node no longer needs the complete decoder stack or LM head. This is expected to remove close to **`half of the weights`** from each Prefill node. The exact saving depends on embeddings, KV pools, connector buffers, CUDA graphs, and allocator headroom. For DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash, savings map straight to GPUs: tiny KV cache + offloading make Prefill HBM weight-bound, so halving transformer weights nearly halves the Prefill GPU count. A key target is fitting one production Prefill replica on a single B300 GPU. ### Avoid a low-density late-decoder tail on P The bounded replay contains at most 128 tokens per new request. Running it on P produces a small decoder-layer token workload and low arithmetic intensity because Prefill batchsize is usually small. In this proposal, D executes the final window as an ordinary full-model bounded-prefill step. It can batch multiple newly admitted requests and coordinate them with the larger Decode workload to get a **`higher arithmetic intensity`**. ### Simpler, unified model execution The split is by workers and token ranges, not by layer ranges within a forward: - P runs the entire model (encoder + layer-20 KV/Indexer projection path) on the prompt, using the same workload throughout each step—no workload reset between encoder and decoder layers. - D runs the entire model (encoder + decoder) on the bounded final window or normal decode workload. This makes the execution architecture **`simpler and more uniform`**, while naturally accommodating Chunked Prefill, Prefix Caching, and Context Parallelism. ### Cost and Trade-offs. The main cost is a larger first step on D: ```text new request, first step: q_len <= 128 later steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens ``` Potential costs include: - D must support both bounded-prefill and speculative-decode shapes. - Admission bursts may increase ITL/TPOT for running requests. - Mixing both request types in one scheduler iteration may require piecewise CUDA graphs or eager fallback. This is likely **`acceptable`** for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash because its compressed KV cache permits a **`large Decode batch`**, and steps admitting new requests are usually a small fraction of all Decode steps. This requires measurement. ## Relationship to Existing vLLM Work. This proposal builds on, but is different from, two open vLLM PRs. ### #56227: encoder-side SWA bounded replay [#56227](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56227) already provides much of the required runtime behavior: - after a local or KV-connector prefix hit ending at `H`, the scheduler rewinds the final window; - the worker recomputes `[H-W, H)` locally; - Main/Indexer KV remains cached or transferred, while SWA is rebuilt locally; and - `Request.replay_start` and attention metadata floor the replay window. This PR is nearly orthogonal to the current RFC and provides sound logic for the P node's execution. ### #56752: decoder-side SWA bounded replay [#56752](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56752) compacts the batch after layer 20 so layers 21–39 process only each request's trailing window. That design still performs one forward in which different layer ranges process different token sets: ```text L0-L20: full prompt rows L21-L39: trailing W rows ``` This RFC proposes a different deployment boundary: ```text P: [0, N-W), L0-L19 and L20's KV/Indexer projection path D: [N-W, N), through all L0-L39 ``` Within a Decode step, every layer processes the same rows. There is no layer-20 compaction boundary, internal gather/scatter, or replay-layer sub-batch. ### Feedback Period. ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Layer-Wise Mixed-Precision KV Cache
author: meenchen
body:
Status: Draft for discussion. Scope: a four-part vLLM implementation stack (logical dtype, packed allocation, ModelOpt integration, and CPU offloading) plus a separate proposed manager-block optimization. Cache calculations below evaluate the full design including that optimization; none of the four PRs enables it.

## Summary

Allow a model to use different KV-cache formats in different attention layers, initially full FP8 K/V and full NVFP4 K/V. Preserve each layer's logical encoding through dispatch and allocation, and support both attention-only models and hybrid attention/Mamba models using existing attention kernels and the heterogeneous cache-packing infrastructure already used by DeepSeek V4.

This is **layer-wise** mixed precision. FP8 K with NVFP4 V inside the same layer is a separate feature and is not enabled by this RFC.

## Motivation

Layers can have different sensitivity to KV quantization. A checkpoint should be able to retain FP8 in selected layers and use NVFP4 elsewhere, without requiring a model-wide format or changes to attention kernels.

Two runtime assumptions make this difficult:

- Physical tensor dtype alone does not fully describe the KV encoding or scales.
- Legacy hybrid allocation couples attention block sizing to recurrent-state page sizes. Adding attention formats with different byte sizes can increase alignment requirements, padding, and prefix-cache block granularity.

The proposal separates logical encoding from physical page allocation. It enables quality/memory trade-off experiments; it does not prescribe the optimal layer recipe or claim an accuracy improvement for every model.

## Proposed Change

```text
ModelOpt checkpoint recipe       Explicit global KV dtype override
             |                                  |
             +----------> Effective per-layer dtype
                                      |
                          AttentionSpec.cache_dtype
                              /                 \
                 Backend dtype dispatch     Exact cache-page specs
                          |                         |
                 Existing FP8/NVFP4 kernels  Packed block-pool allocation
```

### 1. Preserve Logical Dtype

Add `AttentionSpec.cache_dtype` and the generic `QuantizationConfig.get_kv_cache_dtype(prefix)` hook, defaulting to `None`. Preserve logical dtype and quantization mode during spec merges, and reject conflicting formats.

FlashInfer uses an explicit global KV dtype first, then a concrete per-spec dtype. An ambiguous quantized spec fails clearly instead of guessing its encoding. Existing unquantized behavior and skip-layer precedence are retained.

### 2. Reuse DeepSeek V4 Cache Packing

DeepSeek V4 already needs caches with different page sizes, such as MLA, indexer, and sliding-window caches. vLLM's existing infrastructure represents those pages separately and packs compatible layers into cache groups. We reuse that mechanism for pages whose sizes differ because of FP8/NVFP4 encoding.

| Existing mechanism | Reuse for layer-wise mixed precision |
|---|---|
| `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` | Retain each layer's exact spec and page size within a compatible group. |
| `_get_packed_kv_cache_groups()` | Group layers by compatible cache behavior, without requiring identical page sizes. |
| Block-outer allocation and per-layer offsets/strides | Place FP8 and NVFP4 pages side by side and expose each layer's view to its existing kernel. |
| Shared block pool | Size rows for the widest packed group; a block ID belongs to one group at a time. |

Here, "uniform type" means compatible token-slot requirements, not necessarily the same encoding or byte size. Attention and Mamba state still retain their distinct cache semantics; we do not merge them into one attention spec.

The packed-group builder and core allocator are reused without changes in this stack. The additions preserve per-layer dtype, enable a compatible layout, avoid premature page-size unification, and consume checkpoint recipes. This does **not** reuse DeepSeek's model-specific compression algorithm, attention kernels, or token-selection policy.

Add a default-disabled `has_layerwise_kv_cache()` capability. When supported, reuse `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` and block-outer allocation to pack exact per-layer attention and state-cache pages. Bypass legacy hybrid page-size unification only for compatible configurations; incompatible layouts retain the existing aligned-page fallback.

The shared pool row must fit the widest packed group. Exact per-layer sizes therefore remove per-layer padding, but **do not eliminate pool-row slack**. Wrapped Mamba specs must still initialize the Mamba SSU backend.

The current implementation keeps the manager block equal to the supported kernel page: P64 in the validated FlashInfer NVFP4 configuration. The full design additionally considers larger manager blocks containing multiple P64 kernel pages, as described below. These larger blocks require a separately validated subpage layout; they are not currently supported merely by setting a larger `--block-size`.

### 3. Enable ModelOpt Recipes

Consume schema-v1 `kv_cache_quantized_layers` metadata, resolve attention-layer prefixes, and map FP8 to `fp8_e4m3` and NVFP4 to `nvfp4`. Validate invalid or incomplete recipes and preserve legacy metadata handling.

With `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, use the checkpoint recipe. An explicit global dtype overrides it. Weight quantization remains independent of the KV recipe. Producer-side support is tracked in [Model-Optimizer #2272](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer/pull/2272).

### 4. Preserve Packed Layouts for CPU Offloading

The built-in `OffloadingConnector` normally requests `LBHNC`, which can bypass packed hybrid allocation and select padded pages that cannot be split into supported kernel pages. For configurations advertising `has_layerwise_kv_cache()`, let the allocator select the compatible layout instead. Ordinary non-layerwise configurations keep their existing layout requirement; HiSparse retains its explicit requirement.

Reuse the existing packed-row CPU transfer path to preserve quantized attention payloads, scales, and recurrent-state bytes without format conversion. This supports store/reload with the same model, recipe, and parallel topology. It still transfers the complete backing row, including unused space; it does not implement compact CPU slots, new transfer kernels, or manager-block optimization.

### 5. Proposed Manager-Block Optimization (Separate Follow-Up)

Exact per-layer sizes alone do not resolve shared-pool slack. Size the manager block so several small attention pages fit the allocation size needed by a state group, while keeping attention kernel pages at P64. Attention and state groups still own separate pool blocks; this does not co-locate a live state and attention payload in the same row.

The design estimate evaluates manager-block multiples of 64 through 1,024 tokens, scores the complete request footprint at the configured maximum sequence length, and selects the smallest candidate within 1% of the minimum. Production candidates must first pass backend, subpage-layout, and cross-group validation. For the Nano example below, the estimate selects 448 tokens: seven P64 attention pages require 525 KiB, closely matching a 521-KiB Mamba state.

This is the intended optimization on top of the core stack, not a claim that the current PRs implement it. Before enabling it, validate multiple physical pages, kernel-block IDs, per-layer scale/stride indexing, prefix-cache boundaries, CUDA graphs, and end-to-end generation. The manager/prefix boundary is 448 tokens in this example, not 64; kernel page size alone does not establish cache-hit granularity.

## Compatibility and Limits

- No new kernels, extension ABI changes, or asynchronous compression manager.
- Infrastructure hooks default to disabled; only ModelOpt integration activates this feature in the proposed stack.
- Existing backend hardware, format, head-size, and layout restrictions apply.
- The CPU-offload follow-up covers the built-in connector on a fixed model, recipe, and topology. NIXL prefill/decode transfer, LMCache, secondary tiers, and cross-topology canonical offloading remain unvalidated.
- MLA spec metadata is preserved, but mixed-format MLA serving is not validated or claimed as supported by these experiments.
- The implemented intermediate path uses a P64 manager block; the stacked design can use a larger manager block while retaining P64 kernel pages. Actual prefix reuse also depends on cache-group and recurrent-state constraints. No measured cache-hit-rate gain is claimed.
- The recorded P64-only Nano configuration remains state-row dominated. The stacked calculation addresses that slack, but its projected memory reduction is not a measured serving-capacity result.

## Memory Accounting: Same Mixed Recipe

For Nano TP4 with three FP8 K/V layers, three NVFP4 K/V layers, and 23 Mamba layers, compare **legacy aligned allocation** against **the full stacked design: exact-page packing plus manager-block optimization**, keeping logical dtypes fixed. These are CPU allocator-source/design estimates, not GPU peak-memory measurements. The control retains recipe support but disables the layout preference and hybrid-alignment bypass; unmodified upstream cannot consume the recipe.

MiB per rank per request; waste = allocation minus useful payload:

| Tokens | Useful Payload, Both | Legacy Allocation | Legacy Waste | Stacked Allocation | Stacked Waste |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4,096 | 28.09 | 35.06 | 6.97 | 28.71 | 0.62 |
| 16,384 | 42.15 | 63.75 | 21.60 | 42.55 | 0.40 |
| 131,072 | 173.40 | 315.56 | 142.16 | 173.80 | 0.40 |

Accounting includes quantized attention payload/scales and two resident Mamba states per layer, following `align`-mode request budgeting. Waste includes per-layer page padding, last-block token rounding, and unused shared-pool row space. It excludes weights, graphs, activations, metadata, prefix sharing, inactive cached requests, and transient extra states. The 128K row is a sizing projection, not a validated serving run.

Legacy unification produces 2,176-token FP8 blocks and 1,088-token NVFP4 blocks. The stacked estimate selects a 448-token manager block for all three lengths, while kernel pages remain P64. The attention group fills a 525-KiB row; state-owned rows leave only 4 KiB of slack each. Estimated allocation is `525 KiB * (ceil(tokens / 448) + 46)`, with the 46 state rows accounting for two states across 23 layers.

For transparency, the **current P64-only intermediate implementation** still estimates 55.97 / 153.65 / 1,065.40 MiB allocation and 27.88 / 111.50 / 892.00 MiB waste at these lengths. Its attention-owned rows reserve 521 KiB for 75 KiB of payload. Those are not the full stacked-design results and must not be presented as memory savings.

The replay uses grouping/spec source at `513d810e82` and the historical optimizer's candidate/tie-break policy at `287e63a837`. Ten accounting tests pass, including candidate selection and byte conservation. P64 groups/page sizes match the recorded GPU snapshot; the 448-token layout is a design projection, not validated tensor views or an end-to-end runtime. Both legacy-control serving validation and stacked-layout validation remain outstanding.

## Expected Benefits

- **Quality flexibility:** retain higher precision in sensitive layers while compressing less sensitive layers. Actual quality depends on the recipe and requires model-specific evaluation; no accuracy scores are disclosed here.
- **Smaller attention payloads:** avoid forcing every layer to use the higher-precision format. Overall capacity gains depend on allocator layout and state-cache requirements.
- **Infrastructure reuse:** extend an existing heterogeneous-cache mechanism rather than introduce a ModelOpt-specific allocator or new attention kernels.
- **Serving compatibility:** retain existing compile, CUDA graph, and backend execution paths, with explicit dtype overrides and layout fallback behavior.

## Validation

Unit/regression coverage includes dtype merges and precedence, recipe parsing, exact page offsets and strides, multiple physical pages, fallback layouts, and wrapped-Mamba dispatch. The September 16 rebased stack passed 185 tests on GB300. A subsequent typing-only fix passed local mypy checks for all three PRs and full upstream pre-commit for PR 1; those GPU suites were not rerun for that fix.

Earlier TP4 serving smokes passed on Qwen3.8-27B (7 FP8 + 9 NVFP4 attention layers) and Nano v3 (3 FP8 + 3 NVFP4), with CUDA graph capture and 512-token generation with finite logprobs. These are pre-rebase functional smokes, not benchmark-accuracy results or a fresh validation of the current heads.

Earlier Nano serving measurements showed broadly comparable throughput to homogeneous FP8 and NVFP4 under the tested workloads, with a latency regression in one long-context, low-concurrency case. All formats used the same packed allocator: this does not establish zero overhead or compare the allocator against unmodified upstream allocation. Detailed experimental figures are intentionally omitted from this RFC.

The CPU-offload follow-up passed 541 focused regression tests (one ROCm-only skip), plus Nano TP4 cache round trips with FULL and PIECEWISE graphs and 512-token generation. Cold, CPU-reloaded, and fully recomputed outputs matched exactly within each successful process. Default unpatched offloading reproduced the padded-page startup failure; explicit `BLHNC` and the patched default both enabled reloads. Strict cross-process comparison matrices still failed because cold outputs varied across some independent launches, including unpatched no-offload controls. Reload transparency is validated for the tested configuration; full cross-launch reproducibility is not. These are functional checks, not benchmark-accuracy claims.

Before final integration, rerun serving smokes on the final rebased stack, retain explicit coverage of homogeneous formats and unsupported-layout fallback, and investigate the observed cross-launch cold-output variability separately from CPU reload correctness.

## Rollout and Discussion

The implementation is organized as four dependent PRs:

1. [#56155: Logical per-layer dtype](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56155).
2. [#56156: Packed heterogeneous allocation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56156).
3. [#56116: ModelOpt integration](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56116).
4. [#59265: CPU offloading for packed layer-wise KV cache](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59265) (draft; depends on #56116).

Manager-block optimization and validated P64 subpage addressing remain a separate proposed follow-up, outside these four PRs. No PR is linked for that optimization; it is included only in this RFC's design-level memory estimates. The CPU-offload PR does not change those estimates or reduce backing-row slack.

The main review questions are whether the generic hooks and fallback policy are appropriate, how to validate larger manager blocks without changing kernel pages, and what additional backend coverage is needed before expansion. The full stack must pass memory, prefix-reuse, CUDA graph, and serving validation before its projected savings are claimed as runtime results.

title: [RFC]: Bound frontend drain latency for bulk aborts and long non-streaming completions
author: aoshen02
body:
> **Revision 2026-10-07.** This RFC was rewritten around a model of where the time and > memory of an RL `pause(mode="abort")` go, and the PR stacks that follow from it. The previous > text is preserved verbatim in a comment below and in > [`history-original-rfc.md`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479/history-original-rfc.md); its GPU evidence is > summarised in §9. Long derivations, full tables and reproduction commands are on the fork > branch [`aoshen02/vllm@rfc57479/docs`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/tree/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479), together with the > measurement harness ([`harness/`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/tree/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479/harness)). # 0. TL;DR An RL trainer pauses generation with `POST /pause?mode=abort` before a weight update, and then needs every partial rollout back. With long outputs and top-k logprobs, the default `/inference/v1/generate` response is several GB per request. Both frontends spend most of the post-pause time building and serialising it. The Python frontend can also run out of memory before the pause. We model the cost per (position, top-k slot) entry, derive which terms dominate, and propose two independent PR stacks, one per frontend. Each stack has one default-format change (same bytes as today) and one opt-in compact format for RL. **Workload:** 32 non-streaming requests in flight, 16,384 input tokens, 245,760 output tokens each, top-128 logprobs, aborted together. DP8 with one mock engine per rank and the real `DPCoordinatorProc`; EP8 is engine-side and not modelled by the CPU mock. Times are seconds from the pause until the client has parsed every response. Memory is the frontend peak RSS: per process for Python (32 API servers on one node), total for Rust (one process). | n = 32, DP8 | Base `0fd2e8d503` | Python stack | Rust stack | |---|---|---|---| | **Default format** (bytes identical to base) | Python: **FAIL**, node memory floor after ~8 min at 36 GiB per process [S2]

Two Rust changes with mock-only gains are kept as backup branches and are not proposed (§4). # 1. Problem and scope **The operation.** In RL training the rollout manager calls `pause(mode="abort")` on every API server before each weight sync. Engines abort the running requests and the frontends return each partial completion with `finish_reason="abort"`. The trainer cannot start the update until it has all partials, so the time from the pause to the last parsed response is on the critical path of every training step. The pause/resume API is from RFC #32103. **The workload.** It is the shape of our production RL rollout: - 245,760 output tokens per request, top-128 logprobs, 16,384-token input, non-streaming; - DP8 EP8, n = 32 per frontend node in the main cells and bs = 256 in the cohort cells; - `ignore_eos`, no stop strings, no prompt logprobs. **What RL needs from each response:** the output `token_ids`, and for every position the top-k token ids and their float32 logprobs. It does not need text, decoded token strings, the sampled slot or ranks. **Out of scope:** - **R3 (routed experts):** deferred by the submitter. The default `routed_experts` path is unchanged. - **Streaming:** RL here uses non-streaming requests. Streaming default responses are unchanged; the compact format rejects `stream: true` with 400 in Rust. Python compact streaming lives only in the out-of-tree plugin. - Engine-side pause semantics and DP consensus are unchanged. # 2. Theoretical model Each term below is derived first, then checked against a measurement. All constants are measured on GB200 nodes (Grace CPU). Full derivations are in [`theory.md`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479/theory.md). ## 2.1 Data volume One request carries P = 245,760 positions, each with k + 1 = 129 (token id, logprob) entries: the sampled slot plus top-128. That is P × 129 = **31,703,040 entries per request**. **Default JSON.** Each entry is a JSON object with a token string and a float: - Rust renders 3,408,730,749 B per request, i.e. **107.5 B per entry** [S6]. - Python renders 2,199,627,310 B per request, i.e. **69.4 B per entry** (70,388,073,920 B for 32 requests) [S7]. - The two frontends' default schemas differ. Each frontend's bytes are identical to its own base (§3). - So n = 32 moves **109.1 GB** (Rust) or **70.4 GB** (Python) through the frontend, the network and the client parser. **Compact (RL) format.** It sends only the top-k block as two base64 little-endian arrays, `int32[P×k]` ids and `float32[P×k]` logprobs. The sampled ids stay in `choices[0].token_ids`: - raw arrays: 245,760 × 128 × (4 + 4) B = 251,658,240 B; - base64 (× 4/3): 335,544,320 B; - the JSON `token_ids` list and the envelope add 1,498,903 B, about 6.1 B per id. That gives **337,043,223 B per request**, measured on the reference payload with sha256 `1a5360f0…` [S6]; harness bodies are 337,043,485 B [S7]. Compact is **10.1×** smaller than the Rust default and **6.5×** smaller than the Python default. An n = 32 cell moves 10.79 GB. **Wire floor.** The client NIC is 200 Gb/s, i.e. 25 GB/s. The minimum transfer time is: - n = 32: compact 0.43 s, Python default 2.8 s, Rust default 4.4 s; - bs = 256: compact 3.5 s, Python default 22.5 s, Rust default 35 s. ## 2.2 Python object model **Base storage.** Base `LogprobsProcessor` creates a `Logprob` object per entry while consuming engine output. The default renderer then builds a pydantic model per entry, dumps it to dicts and encodes JSON. For one request on the base-path bench [S13]: | Quantity | Base | Per entry | |---|---|---| | Live GC-tracked objects at the abort | 32,316,015 | ≈ 1.02 per entry | | RSS after consumption | 9.12 GB | ≈ 288 B | | Consumption (pre-pause, on the output-processing loop) | 376.7 µs per position (92.6 s per request) | ≈ 2.9 µs | | Build + render after the abort | 134.7 s (≈37 s of it gen-2 GC [S22]) | ≈ 4.2 µs | | Peak memory (VmHWM) | 39.4 GB | ≈ 1.24 KB | Bench memory figures here are the kernel kB counters divided by 10⁶ (so "39.4 GB" is 39.4 × 10⁶ KiB ≈ 40.3 × 10⁹ B ≈ 37.6 GiB); per-entry byte figures derived from them are therefore about 2.4% low. This explains the failures seen at scale: - **Memory.** The 36 GiB per process at n = 32 DP8 is the default storage of the requests on the busiest server [S2][S8]. At bs = 256 the stack without P3 reached 30–75 GiB per process and tripped the node memory floor [S8]. - **CPU after the pause.** About 127–135 s of single-threaded CPU per request is spent after the abort [S12][S13]. In base it runs on the server's event-loop thread, so it also blocks the `/pause` reply when `/pause` lands on a busy server: 132–145 s in base [S1][S11][S12]. **Array storage without the object-free render is slower.** The ablation [S12] stored engine rows as arrays (T2) and kept the legacy renderer. Consumption dropped from 373 to 0.34 µs per position, but the legacy renderer then had to materialise every `Logprob` after the abort: **148 s per request, against 127 s in base**, of which 94 s is materialisation. Server-ready time rose from 157–411 s to 433–453 s. **Storage and render must therefore ship together** (P3), never storage alone. **With P3** (same bench, same body sha `e663245f53`) [S13]: | Quantity | P3 | |---|---| | Consumption | 0.335 µs per position | | Build + render | 4.44 s | | Peak memory | 5.6 GB | | Live objects at the abort | 613,313 | With `VLLM_GENERATE_ARRAY_LOGPROBS=0`, P3 is at parity with base (+0.15% consumption, +0.19% build + render). ## 2.3 Time model **Python, default format.** Each API server builds its large responses one at a time, on one GIL-bound thread. The last response is therefore ready about `c × (requests on the busiest server)` after the pause. A fit over 9 bs = 256 default-format runs (wide client) [S9] gives: ``` all_parsed ≈ 30.7 s + 4.62 s × busiest (R² = 0.958) ``` - **The slope matches the directly measured build CPU** of 4.40–4.43 s per request on a single server (P3 and the in-tree reference alike) [S9]. - **The intercept** is transfer, client parse, and the first response's own consumption and build. - **Re-fit on the current P3.** The round-24 P3 builds responses without an executor and is faster. Re-fitted on 14 L4 runs of dp-round12, the model is `40.9 s + 2.65 s × busiest` (R² 0.92) [S24]. The busiest server still explains the cell. - **Base has the same shape** with c ≈ 120–135 s. At n = 32 [S12], server-ready was 157 s with 1 request on the busiest server, 270–280 s with 2 and 411 s with 3. dp-round3 found the same shape( with 5.4 s spacing) for the earlier in-tree build [S11]. **Rust, default format.** Rust renders on a multi-threaded request runtime, so the n = 32 responses render concurrently. The render cost is therefore not multiplied by a per-server count: | Per-response render cost (one 245,760 × 129 response, one core) [S6] | | |---|---| | Base: eager serde tree, then `axum::Json` | 6.77 s, and the whole tree in memory | | R-A: streamed writer | 1.10 s (4.48 µs per position) | | R-B compact (245,760 × 128): encode + render | 0.141 s (1 run, final tip [S26]); 0.125 s (median of 3) before the int32 check | After R-A, n = 32 default is bound by transfer and client parse: 109.1 GB at the client's ≈6 GB/s parse rate is ≈18 s, measured on loopback [S15]. That is consistent with 20.7 s from the pause [S4]. **Compact (both frontends).** Server time to the first byte is ≈0.01 s (Rust); Python has the last response headers out at 0.06–0.10 s (Python) [S14][S12]. An n = 32 cell then splits as follows [S14]: - **Wire:** 0.46–0.59 s against the 0.434 s floor. - **Client:** 1.16–1.33 s of client CPU after the last byte (sha256 plus strict validation on 8 cores). So **the frontend is no longer the bottleneck for RL compact**: 1.80–1.85 s is client and network time. ## 2.4 Distribution model (which server gets which request) This term only matters for Python, where each server builds its large responses serially (§2.3). Rust runs one process per node, and its requests are spread by the DP load balancer. Three ways to assign requests to k API servers were measured at DP8 in dp-round12 [S24]. All three used the same tree (the Python stack plus #58278's listener lines) and a client that opens one connection per request: - **S, shared accept socket (today).** All servers inherit one listening socket, and whichever event loop calls `accept()` first wins. With one connection per request this is **tighter than random**, because an idle server tends to win the accept race. - **R, independent `SO_REUSEPORT` listeners (#58278).** The kernel hashes each new connection to a server **uniformly at random**. - **RR, deterministic round-robin.** Each server listens on its own port, and the client sends request i to server i mod k. This is a harness option, not a proposed change. **Expected busiest server under uniform random assignment** of m requests per server over k servers [S24]: | Load | m | k | Monte Carlo mean [5th / 50th / 95th pct] | m + sqrt(2 m ln k) | Round-robin | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | L1 | 1 | 32 | 3.53 [3 / 3 / 5] | 3.63 | 1 | | L4 | 4 | 64 | 9.31 [8 / 9 / 11] | 9.77 | 4 | | L16 | 16 | 16 | 23.1 [20 / 23 / 27] | 25.4 | 16 | **Measured** [S24]. Each value is the busiest server's request count (median) and the all-parsed time, median [min–max]: | Load | S shared | R `SO_REUSEPORT` | RR round-robin | |---|---|---|---| | L1: 32 requests, 32 servers, default | 2; **21.2** [20.5–21.6] s | 3.5; **22.2** [20.0–30.6] s | 1; **22.0** [21.8–22.0] s | | L4: 256 requests, 64 servers, default | 8; **61.6** [59.6–64.4] s | 10; **66.2** [59.8–69.0] s (+8%) | 4; **51.0** [50.2–51.8] s (**−17%**) | | L16: 256 requests, 16 servers, default | 18.5; **101.8** [99.9–103.7] s | 23; **117.1** [110.0–124.2] s (+15%) | 16; **102.1** [92.6–111.7] s | | RL-lean, 256 requests, 64 servers | 8.5; **4.23** s | 9; **4.14** s | 4; **4.29** s | Run counts: 6 / 6 / 3 at L1, 6 / 6 / 2 at L4, 2 / 2 / 2 at L16, and 6 / 6 / 2 for RL-lean. **Reading the results:** - R lands on the random expectation: busiest 3.5 / 10 / 23, and a per-server sd of 1.95 against the binomial 1.97. S lands below it: busiest 2 / 8 / 18.5, sd 1.46. - Because the busiest server sets the finish time, **R is slower than S at every default-format load**. Our earlier expectation that R would beat S at high load was wrong for clients that open one connection per request. - Only deterministic assignment reaches the per-server mean, and it is 17% faster than S at L4. - At L1, RR is equal to S. - At L16, the RR median equals S's, with more run-to-run spread (92.6–111.7 s at an identical busiest count of 16). - RL-lean is unaffected: 4.1–4.3 s in all three arms. That cell is bound by the client and the network, not by per-server work. - Peak memory per process is lowest with RR: 6.85 GiB at L4, against 7.38 (S) and 7.86 GiB (R). **When #58278 helps.** Independent listeners fix a real problem: **one greedy worker when clients send many requests over a few long-lived keep-alive connections**. That is the case in #58278's own benchmark, and in the original RFC's two-process client (§9). They do not balance load in general. With one connection per request, the shared queue already balances better than random. We therefore **recommend gating #58278 behind an option** for deployments whose clients reuse connections, rather than making it the default. Assignment that actually balances needs a deterministic policy, for example round-robin over per-worker ports or a least-loaded router; this is open item §8. The larger lever is still to make `c` small, which P3 does (a few seconds instead of 127+ s per request). Assignment only changes the multiplier. ## 2.5 Ingest model (pre-pause) The frontend must also keep up with engine output **before** the pause. **Real rate.** A real engine emits 1 token per request per step. At 25–50 tokens/s per sequence, DP8 serving 256 sequences in total is about **6–13 k outputs/s** (256 × 25–50 tokens/s) [S10]. **Frontend capacity.** Measured with the mock at real granularity (1 token per step, int32 ids) [S10]: | Frontend | Ingest | Headroom over the real rate | |---|---|---| | Rust, one process | ≥150–160 k outputs/s | **≈12×** (11.7–12.4×) | | Python, 64 processes | ≥73–77 k outputs/s | **≥5×** | Both figures are lower bounds, limited by the mock. **Consequences:** - **Granularity does not change post-pause results.** Every post-pause metric (all parsed, pause, HWM, bytes) was equal between 1,024-token and 1-token steps [S10]. - **Two Rust changes are backups, not PRs.** Wire decode (decoding logprobs straight from msgpack bytes) and parallel output decode speed up ingest only. With the fast mock they gave: - wire decode: consumption 14.5 → 10.2 s at n = 32; - parallel decode: 0.81 → 1.27 M positions/s at DP8 [S17][S18][S4]. Real engines do not approach these rates, so neither change shows a gain with a real engine. - **The next Rust ingest limit** is the single ZMQ PULL receive task, at ≈1 core and ~2.4 GB/s [S25]. It is far above the real rate. ## 2.6 Client parsing ceiling The client is part of the critical path. **Our measurement client** is client v3: native Rust, 8 cores, sha256 plus full semantic validation [S15]. It parses: - default JSON at ≈6 GB/s (Rust ×32: 109.1 GB in 18.14 s, loopback); - compact at ≈9.6 GB/s (87.3 GB in 9.09 s). **Cohort cells are client-bound.** At bs = 256, RL compact takes 10.9 s with this client and 4.2–4.7 s with a 64-thread "wide" client, against a 3.5 s wire floor [S2][S7]. **Real trainers** decode base64 with numpy, at a rate we have not measured. A Python JSON parser of the default format would be far slower than 6 GB/s, which makes the 6.5–10× smaller compact body matter even more. ## 2.7 DP pause consensus cost **Real engines.** The pause is a two-phase DP consensus. The all-reduce runs only when `step_counter % 32 == 0`, and idle ranks run real dummy forwards. A real DP pause can therefore take up to ~32 forward steps: **≈0.3–1.6 s at 10–50 ms per step** [S10]. **The mock** takes 20–70 ms for this step, so absolute pause numbers in this RFC at DP > 1 are understated by that amount. The cost is engine-side and identical for both frontends, so no frontend comparison changes. **In base Python** the dominant pause cost is different: `/pause` waits behind a busy event loop, which took 132–145 s (§2.2). After the stacks, `/pause` returns in 0.04–0.18 s with the mock [S7]. ## 2.8 Memory model Frontend bytes held per position at k = 128, and why: | Representation | Bytes per position | Evidence | |---|---|---| | Engine row on the wire (int32 ids, f32 logprobs, int64 rank) | ≈1,040 B (≈1,099 B with msgpack framing) | [S10] | | Python base: one `Logprob` per entry | ≈37 KB after consumption, ≈160 KB at the build peak | 9.12 GB / 39.4 GB per request [S13] | | Python P3: engine rows in numpy blocks, object-free render | 5.6 GB peak per request (rows plus the joined 2.2 GB body) | [S13] | | Rust base: eager `ChatLogProbs` tree plus the full JSON buffer | ≈6–7 GiB per request (199–222 GiB for n = 32) | [S2][S3][S17] | | Rust R-A: decoded rows, streamed render in 64-position chunks through a 2-chunk channel | 14.47 GiB for n = 32: the body is never materialised | [S4] | | Compact (both): the base64 body itself, built while consuming | ≈1,371 B (337 MB per request) | [S5][S6] | **Streaming render (R-A).** A task on the request runtime writes 64-position chunks into a channel bounded at 2 chunks, so memory per in-flight default response is O(chunk) instead of O(body). That is the 199–202 → 14.47 GiB drop at DP8 [S2][S3][S4] (215–222 GiB with the eager toggle at DP1 [S17]). **Segment presize (R-B).** The compact body is a list of ≤1 MiB base64 segments. - Growing each segment by doubling left freed intermediate blocks in the allocator: 14.83 GiB at n = 32. - Reserving each segment once at 1 MiB, and shrinking the last one, gives **11.86 GiB, i.e. −3.0 GiB**, with identical bodies and overlapping times (1.81 vs 1.85 s, ABBA) [S5]. **Python per process.** P3 bounds a server's peak at about one large build in flight. A second build thread overlaps the build's GIL-free 10–15%, at +4 GiB per busy server [S9]; see §8. # 3. Methodology The full setup and commands are in [`methodology.md`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479/methodology.md). **Engine mock and topology.** - **Engines.** One CPU mock engine process per DP rank. It speaks the real EngineCore ZMQ/msgpack protocol, using vLLM's own `MsgpackEncoder` and its aux-frame rules. - **Coordinator.** It implements the engine side of the DP coordinator protocol (stats, wave complete, `START_DP_WAVE`, stale waves, lockstep dummy steps, two-phase pause), and it runs against the **real `DPCoordinatorProc`**. - **Routing.** Outputs are routed by `client_index`, as real engines do. This matters: Rust deploys one process per server, because every Rust process reports `client_index` 0, so all Rust numbers here use that one-process deployable topology [S19]. - **Nodes** (GB200 nodes cn01–cn04): - engines on cn02; - Python with 32 API servers per node (n = 32 cells: cn02 only; bs = 256: cn02 and cn03); - Rust as one process with 32–64 request threads; - the client on cn04. - **Python topology:** no independent listeners in the stack arms (§2.4). **Cells** (`final-validation.sh`) [S2]: | Cell | What it runs | |---|---| | `n32-def`, `n32-rl` | n = 32, default and compact format | | `cohort-rl-v3`, `cohort-rl-wide`, `cohort-def-wide` | bs = 256, 8-core and 64-thread client | | `wf-paced` | The full RL cycle: lognormal output lengths, paced engine, pause at 10 s, 5 s sleep, resume, resubmit the partials | **Fairness rules.** - Fresh services in every cell. - ABBA ordering for each A/B. - Same nodes, topology and client in both arms. - Concurrency, lengths and top-k are never changed to gain speed. - Failures (timeouts, memory floor) are kept as results. - A node lock file serialises all benchmark jobs on the shared allocation, and every run snapshot is a node-local `git archive` verified with `tar -d`. **Byte identity.** - **Rust:** every default body sha256 equals base (`572252e6…`, 3,408,730,749 B), whether the payload is decoded from wire bytes or built directly. Compact is pinned at `1a5360f0…` [S6]. - **Python:** responses carry `created`, so the sha varies per run. Its checks are: - 27 golden `/inference/v1/generate` scenarios through the real router and `OutputProcessor`, byte-identical to base; - the base-path bench sha `e663245f53`; - per-request byte-length lists that are identical across arms [S7][S13]. **Mock fidelity** [S10]. 17 behaviours were compared with the real `EngineCoreProc`, `DPEngineCoreProc`, `Scheduler`, `Sampler` and `DPCoordinatorProc`. There are two material differences: - **Granularity.** The real engine emits 1 token per step with int32 ids; the mock emitted 1,024 per step with int64 ids. An A/B shows that no post-pause metric changes. - **DP pause.** The DP pause is understated (§2.7). No GPU was used for this RFC's top-128 numbers. The conclusions hold because each optimisation removes per-entry frontend work after the engine has already accepted the abort. That work does not depend on the engine being real, and the one engine-dependent term (ingest) has ≥5–12× headroom. # 4.
