- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Pluggable KV connector metrics on the Rust frontend via connector metrics descriptor
author: grYe99
body:
<!-- proposed title: [RFC]: Pluggable KV connector metrics on the Rust frontend via connector metrics descriptor -->

### Motivation.

[vllm-project/vllm#52755](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52755) added Rust frontend Prometheus metrics for **Nixl** and **Mooncake**. But other KV connectors still have no metrics on that frontend, including the in-tree **Offloading**, **HF3FS**, and **HiSparse** connectors and all **third-party** connectors.

On the Python frontend this already works without hardcoding each connector: a shared plugin asks the configured connector for its metrics, and the connector owns registration and observation. If we repeat the Nixl/Mooncake pattern in Rust, adding a typed decode and observe branch for each connector inside the frontend, it does not scale, and it cannot cover connectors whose code never lands in the vLLM tree.

The Rust frontend cannot reuse the Python plugin path, because it runs in a separate process from EngineCore and cannot import connector Python classes. Connector stats reach it only as a field in the scheduler stats sent from EngineCore. Stats from any connector other than Nixl and Mooncake currently have no matching Rust type and are dropped.

What is missing is a way for KV connectors other than Nixl and Mooncake, both in-tree and out-of-tree, to expose their metrics on the Rust frontend, without the frontend adding code for each connector. The Python frontend already has this property.

### Proposed Change.

This RFC proposes a generic way to observe KV connector Prometheus metrics on the Rust frontend, for connectors other than Nixl and Mooncake, including the in-tree builtins (Offloading, HF3FS, HiSparse) and third-party connectors. Nixl and Mooncake keep their existing typed path unchanged.

We introduce a **metrics descriptor**: a small, self-describing document that a connector attaches to its stats. It carries what the Rust frontend needs to register Prometheus metrics: metric names, types, help text, histogram buckets, and where each metric's values sit in the stats payload. When the Rust frontend is enabled, the first stats payload from a connector includes the descriptor, and Rust registers the metrics once. Later payloads carry only values, which Rust records into the registered metrics. `GET /metrics` only renders the Rust-side registry and never calls into connector Python. On the Python frontend the descriptor is not attached, so that path has no extra cost.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  EC[EngineCore connector stats] --> RF[Rust frontend]
  RF --> D{Connector?}
  D -->|Nixl / Mooncake| T[Existing typed path]
  D -->|Other| S[Descriptor-driven path]
  S --> P1[First payload carries descriptor: register once]
  S --> P2[Later payloads carry values only: record]
  P1 --> P[Prometheus /metrics]
  P2 --> P
  T --> P
```

#### How the Rust frontend handles descriptors

The Rust frontend keeps each registered descriptor under its `connector_id`. When a payload with a descriptor arrives, it registers that connector's metrics and records the values in the same payload. Later value-only payloads are matched to the registered descriptor: a single connector's stats map to its one descriptor, and under MultiConnector each child's stats are matched by the child's class name. If stats arrive from a connector that has never sent a descriptor (for example, a connector that has not adopted this mechanism), the frontend logs one warning and ignores them. It does not fail, and other connectors' metrics are unaffected.

#### What ships in vLLM

vLLM ships the generic Rust-side registration and recording, a shared Python helper that attaches the descriptor only on the Rust frontend and only once, and descriptors for the in-tree Offloading, HF3FS, and HiSparse connectors. The builtins derive their descriptors from the same definitions their Python Prom metrics use, rather than from a separately maintained file. Third-party descriptors live in the third-party packages.

#### How third-party KV connectors adopt this mechanism

A connector that already reports Prometheus metrics on the Python frontend (via `KVConnectorStats` and `build_prom_metrics()`) needs only a few additions to expose the same metrics on the Rust frontend. The in-tree builtins serve as references: **HiSparse** (`hisparse/stats.py`) is the smallest example, **HF3FS** covers histograms, and **Offloading** derives the descriptor from existing metric metadata.

**1. A single source of metric definitions.** Each metric is declared once, with its Prometheus name, type, help text, and (for histograms) buckets. Both the Python Prom metrics and the descriptor are built from that declaration. HiSparse uses a small tuple table; Offloading reuses its existing metadata classes. This avoids a second hand-maintained copy that can drift.

**2. Information Rust cannot infer.** Python Prom code knows how to apply each value because it is code. Rust sees only the descriptor, so each metric entry also has to state:

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| `name`, `type`, `documentation`, `buckets` | Same as the Python Prom metric (`type` is `counter`, `gauge`, or `histogram`) |
| `samples_path` | The key in the connector's stats dict (`KVConnectorStats.data`) that holds this metric's values |
| `sample_kind` | How the values are applied: add one integer, add the sum of a list, add a float, set a gauge, or observe each list element into a histogram |

The descriptor also carries a `connector_id`, which should be the connector class name; MultiConnector uses the same name as the key when nesting child stats.

**3. Attaching the descriptor during serialization.** The connector's stats class returns its data from `to_dict()` through the shared helper, and strips the descriptor key when stats are rebuilt from the wire (`__post_init__`). The helper handles gating: it attaches the descriptor only when the Rust frontend is enabled, and only on the first emit. No new RPC, environment variable, or config file is required.

**4. Guaranteeing a first emit.** Rust can register the metrics only after it has seen one payload that carries the descriptor. A connector that may stay silent for a long time after startup should emit one zero-valued snapshot early (HiSparse does this on its first empty poll).

**5. Verification.** With `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1` and some traffic, the connector's metric names should appear on `/metrics`, with values matching a Python frontend run.

One current limit: every metric must be declared in the descriptor up front, so a metric that a connector only creates later at runtime has to be included in the descriptor from the start.

### Any Other Things.

#### Non-goals

- Moving Nixl and Mooncake to the descriptor path. They keep their existing typed path.
- Printing connector stats in the Rust frontend's periodic log line, as the Python frontend does today.
- Labels derived from payload contents. Metric labels stay fixed (per engine), so connectors cannot add arbitrary label values at runtime.

#### Implementation

Implementation, tests, and end-to-end results: #58563

#### AI assistance

This RFC was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed and revised by the author, who is responsible for the design.

title: [RFC]: KV cache grouping for hybrid models with speculative drafters
author: LucasWilkinson
body:
**Status:** Draft · **PRs:** #58207 (group size), #58380 (prefer `BLHNC`, stacked on #58207)

## TL;DR

Speculative drafters on hybrid models add a small KV cache bucket of their own, which breaks vLLM's KV cache grouping heuristic in two ways:

- **Too many groups (Qwen3.5 / 3.6 + DFlash):** a one-layer drafter bucket forces **one group per layer**: Qwen3.5-27B goes from 4 to 70 groups (#49730), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 4 to 46. Each group rebuilds attention metadata every step, so DFlash loses much of its speedup; forcing fewer groups today costs KV cache capacity.
- **Full attention padding (MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash):** the 5-layer drafter bucket sets the group size, which doesn't divide the target's 9 full attention layers, so a full attention padding layer is allocated for the whole context (#58175). Kimi-K3 + DSpark has the same problem: its 5-layer drafter bucket pads the 24 MLA (full attention) layers, with 20 groups.

Checked and unaffected (identical grouping with and without these PRs): GLM-5.3-Flash + DFlash2, MiniMax-M3 + DSpark, DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark.

A two-part proposal fixes both:

| part | problem | fix | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 · #58207** | small drafter buckets force per-layer KV groups, or full attn padding | pick the group size by worst-case padding **bytes**; `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` (default 3) | 46 → **17** groups, **+54%** tok/s @c=1, **+36%** @c=32 | 11 → **7** groups, no full attn padding, KV capacity 5.76M → 5.96M |
| **2 · #58380** | `LBHNC` forces padding when drafter bytes/token ≠ target's | prefer `BLHNC` when the backends can run it and it avoids full attn padding or needs fewer groups | **5** groups, no padding, 7.53M tokens (> main's 7.42M); Triton only today | stays `LBHNC` at 7 groups (`BLHNC` would need 12 and has no full attn padding to remove) |

The parts are complementary: part 2 picks the path; part 1 is the fallback path (§5).

---

## 1. Background

**Motivation.** Enabling DFlash on Qwen3.5-27B raises the number of KV cache groups from 4 to **70**. Without a drafter, its 64 layers (48 GDN + 16 full attention) form 4 groups of 16; with DFlash, every layer gets its own group (64 target + 6 drafter). The drafter adds a one-layer full attention bucket, and the grouping heuristic falls back to one group per layer (#49730). Every group rebuilds its attention metadata each step, and GDN (linear attention) metadata builders are expensive, so this becomes per-step host overhead and DFlash runs well below its expected speedup; the effect is larger on Qwen3.5-4B. Forcing a larger group size recovers the throughput but, with today's grouping, costs KV cache capacity.

A drafter can also cost KV cache capacity rather than speed. MiMo-V2.5 + its DFlash drafter has buckets `[9 full, 39 SW, 5 drafter SW]`: the drafter bucket is the smallest, so the group size becomes 5, and the 9 full attention layers get a padding layer that grows with context (#58175 reports ~10% more KV capacity once it's removed). Kimi-K3 + its DSpark drafter behaves the same way (Case 3).

Related reports:

| report | model | groups | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| #49730 | Qwen3.5-27B / 4B + DFlash (H100) | 4 without DFlash → 70 with (one per layer) | DFlash ITL much slower than expected; forcing gs=16 recovers ~10% tok/s on 27B but shrinks KV capacity 216k → 141k tokens |
| #51742 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (H200) | 46 | `build_attn_metadata` ~31 ms/step vs ~6 ms at 10 groups; output tok/s ~2× at c=1 with fewer groups |
| #52297 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | — | one GDN `build()` takes ~900 µs and is repeated per group |
| #58175 | MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash | 11 | 1 full attn padding layer; removing it gives +10.57% KV capacity (their setup); +8.4% in ours (5.76M → 6.25M) |
| this RFC | Kimi-K3 + DSpark (`RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark`, TP4) | 20 | 1 MLA (full attn) padding layer; #58207: 17 groups, no MLA padding, +0.37% KV capacity |
| #42505, #46462 | Qwen3.5 / 3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | — | DFlash slower than expected / than baseline at higher concurrency; not root-caused, likely related |

This RFC's own measurement (§4.1): Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash on B300 goes from 460 → 733 tok/s at c=1 when the 46 groups drop to 17.

### 1.0 Terms

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| bucket | all layers whose KV cache specs merge (same attention type and shape) |
| group / `group_size` (gs) | a KV cache group shares one block table; buckets are split into groups of `group_size` layers |
| page | one layer's slice of a block; its size is that layer's bytes/token × block size |
| padding | layer slots in a group with no layer behind them; allocated but never written |
| manager vs kernel block | the KV manager allocates *manager* blocks; attention kernels may need them split into smaller *kernel* blocks |
| `LBHNC` | layer-outermost `KVCacheLayout` (today's default): every page is resized to one size, each group gets `group_size` pages per block |
| `BLHNC` | block-outermost `KVCacheLayout`: a block is one contiguous run of per-layer pages, so pages of different sizes share a block. `LBNHC`/`BLNHC` group the same way as `LBHNC`/`BLHNC` |

### 1.1 Buckets, groups, padding

```
Legend:  F/f = target/DRAFTER full attn   S/s = target/DRAFTER sliding window   M = mamba/GDN
         ▓ = full attn padding (grows with context, up to max_model_len)
         ░ = SW / mamba padding or idle page (bounded by window / state)

drafter full-attn group, group_size = 5 (one physical block):
│ f │ ▓ │ ▓ │ ▓ │ ▓ │   4 of 5 pages never written

every group's block has the same byte size (block IDs are shared across groups)
```

| cost | grows with | note |
|---|---|---|
| per-step metadata | # groups | one block table + builder call per group; GDN builders are expensive |
| KV capacity | padded slots × bytes/request | full attn slot: up to `max_model_len` tokens; SW / mamba slot: bounded |

### 1.2 Bad cases

```python
group_size = min(bucket sizes)                       # main
if max(bucket sizes) < 1.5 * min(bucket sizes):
    group_size = max(bucket sizes)
```

The heuristic sizes groups from bucket **counts** only. A drafter adds a small bucket of its own, which breaks it in the ways below. Each group is drawn as `[ ]` with one letter per layer slot.

#### Case 1: Qwen3.5 / 3.6 + DFlash: a one-layer drafter bucket forces one group per layer

Qwen3.5-27B + DFlash (4 → 70 groups), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (4 → 46), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B + Eagle3 (4 → 41). Per-step metadata overhead grows with the layer count.

```
Qwen3.6 alone:     buckets [30 M, 10 F]              gs = 10  →  4 groups
Qwen3.6 + DFlash:  buckets [30 M, 10 F, 5 s, 1 f]    gs = min(30, 10, 5, 1) = 1

bucket                   layers   groups on main (one layer each)
target mamba/GDN    M      30     [M][M][M][M][M][M][M][M][M][M] … [M]   30
target full attn    F      10     [F][F][F][F][F][F][F][F][F][F]         10
drafter SW          s       5     [s][s][s][s][s]                         5
drafter full attn   f       1     [f]   ← smallest bucket sets gs = 1     1
                                                                        ────
                                        metadata builds per step:        46
```

With #58207: Qwen3.6 + DFlash 17 groups, Qwen3.5 + Eagle3 9 groups.

#### Case 2: MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash: the drafter's bucket doesn't divide the target's

MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash. The 5-layer drafter bucket is the smallest, so it sets gs=5, and the 9 full attention layers get a padding slot that grows with context.

Why full attention padding is the one that matters: a padding slot costs whatever a real layer of that type would hold for each request.

| padding slot | holds per request | MiMo-V2.5, per slot |
|---|---|---|
| full attention | every token of the context | 2.5 KiB/token × 256k tokens ≈ **640 MiB** (≈ 2.5 GiB at 1M) |
| sliding window | only the window (128 tokens), plus tokens in flight | 5 KiB/token × 128 ≈ **0.6 MiB** (≈ 41 MiB worst case with 8k in-flight tokens) |

So one full attention padding slot wastes as much as hundreds of sliding-window slots, and it keeps growing with context length.

```
main    gs = 5 → 11 groups
  F  [FFFFF][FFFF▓]              ← full attn padding
  S  [SSSSS] ×7 + [SSSS░]
  s  [sssss]

#58207  gs = 9 → 7 groups
  F  [FFFFFFFFF]                 ← no full attn padding
  S  [SSSSSSSS░] ×4 + [SSSSSSS░░]
  s  [sssss░░░░]
```

#### Case 3: Kimi-K3 + DSpark: same as Case 2, with MLA

Kimi-K3 has 69 KDA (linear attention) and 24 MLA (full attention) layers; the DSpark drafter (`RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark`) adds 5 sliding-window layers. The drafter bucket sets gs=5, which doesn't divide 24, so an MLA padding slot is allocated for the whole context.

```
L = KDA (linear attention)

main    gs = 5 → 20 groups
  L  [LLLLL] ×13 + [LLLL░]
  F  [FFFFF] ×4 + [FFFF▓]        ← MLA (full attn) padding
  s  [sssss]

#58207  gs = 6 → 17 groups
  L  [LLLLLL] ×9 + [LLLLL░] ×3
  F  [FFFFFF] ×4                 ← no MLA padding
  s  [sssss░]
```

Served (Kimi-K3-pruned75, same 93 layers, TP4): KV capacity 4.76M → 4.78M tokens at 131k context. #58380 keeps `LBNHC` here.

---

## 2. Part 1 · #58207: group size by worst-case padding bytes

Replace the [min / 1.5×-max heuristic](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b3a87b2d04e6439e2a1aef0cbf9ca65328076c86/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py#L1547-L1558) with a search over group sizes that minimizes **worst-case padding bytes** per request, bounded below so groups can't explode:

```python
lo = max(smallest bucket, min(min_kv_cache_group_layers, largest bucket))
group_size = argmin over gs in [lo, largest bucket] of
    (Σ padding_slots(bucket, gs) × spec.max_memory_usage_bytes(vllm_config), num_groups(gs))
```

Padding is costed in bytes, so full attention padding (which grows with `max_model_len`) is avoided in favor of bounded sliding-window / mamba padding. The lower bound keeps groups from exploding: never below the smallest bucket, and never below `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` (default 3), so a one-layer drafter bucket can't force one group per layer.

```
Qwen3.6 + DFlash, gs = 3 → 17 groups (each bucket padded independently)
  M  [MMM] ×10    F  [FFF][FFF][FF▓][FF▓]    s  [sss][ss░]    f  [f▓▓]
```

## 3. Part 2 · #58380: prefer `BLHNC`

In `BLHNC` a block is one contiguous run of per-layer pages, so pages of different sizes share a block instead of being padded to one size. The widest non-state bucket sets the block; mamba / SW groups split to fit it. #58380 prefers these layouts when specs have mixed page sizes **and** every backend runs each attention block unsplit, since packed blocks can't be split into smaller kernel blocks:

| backend (B300) | kernel block sizes | can use `BLHNC` |
|---|---|---|
| Triton | any multiple of 16 | yes |
| FlashInfer | 16 / 32 / 64 | no |
| FlashAttention hd256 (FA4) | 128 | no |

**`BLHNC` cost check:** `BLHNC` is not always better (MiMo below: 7 → 12 groups), so #58380 also computes both groupings from the specs and picks `BLHNC` only if the `LBHNC` grouping would pad full attention, or `BLHNC` needs fewer groups.

Each row below is a separate group; rows align because every block is the same size:

```
Qwen3.6 + DFlash: 5 groups, 12-page blocks
full-attn ×1   │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │   f   │   10 target + drafter (2 pages): no padding
mamba ×3       │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ M │ ░ │ ░ │   10 GDN states each, 2 idle pages
drafter sw ×1  │   s   │   s   │   s   │   s   │   s   │ ░ │ ░ │   5 layers × 2 pages, 2 idle pages

MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash under `BLHNC` (not picked by the cost check): 12 groups, 9-page blocks
full-attn ×1   │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │ F │   9 full pages: no padding
SWA ×10        │   S   │   S   │   S   │   S   │ ░ │   4 layers × 2 pages, 1 idle page (one group has 3)
drafter SW ×1  │  d d d d d  (1.6 pages each)  │ ░ │   5 layers × 64 KiB = 8 pages, 1 idle page
```

## 4. Results by model and layout

### 4.1 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (1× B300)

| plan | groups | padding / request @256k | KV capacity | tok/s c=1 / c=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 46 | 0 | 7.42M | 460 / 4654 |
| #58207 | 17 | 3.05 GiB (full attn) | 5.19M | 733 / 6495 |
| **#58380** (Triton, `BLHNC`) | **5** | **58 MiB** | **7.53M** | **746 / 7463** |

### 4.2 MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash (TP2)

| plan | groups | padding / request @256k | KV capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 11 | 726 MiB (incl. 1 full attn layer) | 5.76M |
| #58175 | 18 | **90 MiB** | **6.25M** |
| #58207 | **7** | 469 MiB | 5.96M |
| `BLHNC` (#58380 doesn't pick it) | 12 | 266 MiB | 6.10M |

Padding is worst case (8192 in-flight tokens). Full attn padding grows with context, so `BLHNC` wins outright for Qwen3.6; MiMo has none, so it's a trade between groups and bounded bytes.

### 4.3 Qwen3.6 + DFlash: `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` sweep

![min-kv-cache-group-layers sweep](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LucasWilkinson/vllm/af4013a3827d250b266c6e48b1fc124880523780/pareto_min_layers.png)

| `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` | gs | groups | KV capacity | padding/req @256k | c=1 | c=32 | with #52297 ² c=1 / c=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (= main) | 1 | 46 | 7.42M | 0 | 460 | 4654 | 653 / 5735 |
| 2 | 2 | 24 | 6.42M | 1.02 GiB (+17%) | 684 | 5711 | 716 / 6247 |
| **3 (default)** | 3 | 17 | 5.19M | 3.02 GiB (+50%) | 710 | 6339 | 727 / 7100 |
| 4 | 5 | 10 | 4.80M | 4 GiB (+67%) | 726 | 6676 | 758 / 6865 |

² #52297 (open PR) computes GDN attention metadata once per step instead of per group, making extra groups cheaper.

### 4.4 Qwen3.6 + DFlash: `BLHNC` vs `LBHNC`

![BLHNC vs LBHNC](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LucasWilkinson/vllm/f52d0d4bb0b941fff5dbc5834f62d865db084188/pareto_packed.png)

## 5. How the two parts fit together

**Defaults after both PRs merge** (default backends, no `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT`). Padding is per request at 256k context (worst case, 8192 in-flight tokens):

| model (B300 backend) | main today | after #58207 + #58380 |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6 + DFlash (FlashInfer/FA) | `LBHNC`, 46 groups, no padding | `LBHNC`, **17** groups, 3.05 GiB padding (full attn) |
| Qwen3.6 + DFlash (`--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`) | `LBHNC`, 46 groups, no padding | **`BLHNC`, 5** groups, 58 MiB padding |
| MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash (FA) | `LBHNC`, 11 groups, 726 MiB padding (640 MiB full attn) | `LBHNC`, **7** groups, 469 MiB padding (no full attn) |
| Kimi-K3 + DSpark (TP4) | `LBHNC`, 20 groups, 1 MLA padding layer | `LBHNC`, **17** groups, no MLA padding |
| MiMo-V2.6 + MTP (FA) | `LBHNC`, 6 groups, 203 MiB padding (SW) | unchanged |
| Qwen3.5 + Eagle3 (FlashInfer/FA) | `LBHNC`, 41 groups, no padding | `LBHNC`, 9 groups, 4 drafter full attn padding slots |
| GLM-5.3-Flash + DFlash2, MiniMax-M3 + DSpark, DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark | unchanged | unchanged |
| single page size (Gemma3, gpt-oss, Llama4, Qwen3.5, …) | unchanged | unchanged |

**Recommendation:** land #58207 first (helps every layout/backend), then #58380. `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT` / connector preferences still win.

---

## 6. Alternatives considered

Other open PRs that change this heuristic, and what each gives for Qwen3.6 + DFlash:

| PR | approach | Qwen3.6 + DFlash | shortcoming |
|---|---|---|---|
| #51742 | ignore one-layer buckets when taking the min | gs=5, 10 groups | pads the drafter's full attn layer with 4 slots that grow with context |
| #58175 | shrink gs to a divisor of the full attn bucket sizes (targets MiMo) | gs=1, 46 groups | doesn't help drafters |
| #49472 | minimize padding + number of groups, counted in layers | gs=5, 10 groups | a padded full attn layer counts the same as a sliding-window one, so it pads full attn |

Other approaches:

- **Bigger `block_size` for the lone drafter group** (same bytes, fewer layers): prefix-cache hits align to the LCM of group block sizes, so hits get ~5× coarser for every group.
- **Only forbid one layer per group (`group_size ≥ 2`) and minimize padding:** still 24 groups for Qwen3.6 + DFlash, and over-splits models with cheap padding (Gemma3-27B 7 → 31 groups).
- **Absolute cap on the number of groups:** the right cap depends on the backend (GDN vs FlashAttention metadata cost).
- **Drafter-aware sizing** (size groups from target buckets, pad the drafter): worst case when the drafter has a full attention layer, and drafter layers can only be identified heuristically at grouping time.
- **Separate KV pool for drafter layers:** removes the constraint entirely, but is a much larger allocator change.
- **#58345 (rescale sliding-window blocks for `BLHNC`):** on main (since #53007) sliding-window layers already use the full attention block size when the backend allows it (group block sizes 262144 ×3, 592, 592); when it doesn't, rescaling would need kernel-block splitting, which `BLHNC` can't do.

---

## 7. Open questions

1. **Default `--min-kv-cache-group-layers`:** 3 (17 groups, −30% KV capacity on Qwen3.6 + DFlash) or 4 (10 groups, +2–5% tok/s, −35%)? Should it depend on whether the model has GDN layers?
2. **`BLHNC` with FlashInfer / FlashAttention:** re-page inside the kernels (as #55219 / #57169 do for sparse MLA), or stop inflating the block size for block-outermost layouts (but then few GDN states fit per block)?
3. **FlashAttention drafter block size:** the 128-only FA4 hd256 kernel block is derived from the *target's* head size and applied to a hd128 drafter, causing `No common block size for 592` on main unless `--block-size 128` is set. Fixed separately by #58630.
4. **Validation:** #58380 switches mixed-page-size models to `BLHNC` when the cost check passes on capable backends; needs accuracy and throughput validation beyond DFlash and MiMo.

---

## 8. Methodology

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 --max-num-seqs 32 --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 128 \
  --mamba-cache-dtype bfloat16 --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16 [--min-kv-cache-group-layers N] \
  [--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN] \
  --speculative-config '{"model":"z-lab/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash","method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7}'
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 --dataset-name hf --dataset-path openai/gsm8k --hf-split test \
  --num-prompts max(32, 8*C) --max-concurrency C --num-warmups 2*C
```

| item | value |
|---|---|
| hardware | 1× B300 per run (MiMo: TP2, `max_model_len` 1M) |
| runs | single; noise ~2–3% (repeated gs=5) |
| interactivity | 1000 / p99 TPOT |
| acceptance length | 5.1–5.2 in all Qwen runs |
| `--block-size 128` | needed on all variants, including main: FlashAttention's 128-only FA4 hd256 kernel block is derived from the target's head size and also applied to the hd128 drafter, which otherwise fails with `No common block size for 592` |


---

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to run the experiments and draft this RFC; I have reviewed its contents.

title: [RFC]: Hardening /v1/messages (Anthropic API) for Claude Code across model families
author: robertgshaw2-redhat
body:
### Motivation

Claude Code can run against vLLM through the Anthropic Messages endpoint (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` → `/v1/messages`). Claude Code's agentic loop is a demanding client of that endpoint:

- It sends every request with ~25 tools, many with large nested JSON schemas.
- It uses interleaved thinking with parallel tool calls.
- It sends inline `role: "system"` messages that change every turn.
- It sends side queries (title generation, the auto-mode permission classifier) with `stop_sequences` and small `max_tokens` budgets.
- It recovers from context overflow based on the error it gets back.

This issue audits the current converter (`vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/`) and the HF chat templates of the major open model families against real Claude Code traffic. We found:

- several gaps that affect every model family;
- a set of model-specific breakages, some of which return **400 on Claude Code's default requests**.

Many of the small fixes already have open PRs, often more than one per problem. This issue gathers them so they can be deduplicated and prioritized, and it proposes the pieces that have no owner yet.

**How we checked**

- We captured `/v1/messages` traffic from Claude Code 2.1.281 through a logging proxy (~50 requests covering main-loop turns, title generation and the auto-mode classifier).
- We replayed synthetic Claude Code-shaped conversations through `AnthropicServingMessages.to_chat_completion_request` → `chat_utils` post-processing.
- We rendered the result with the current HF templates, and with `mistral_common` / the DeepSeek Python encoders / Harmony where applicable.

Items marked *(unverified)* were not reproduced at runtime.

**Observed request shape (from captures)**

| Field | Values seen |
|---|---|
| `system` | List of text blocks with `cache_control`. The first is the `x-anthropic-billing-header` line. |
| `messages` | Contains inline `role: "system"` messages at non-leading positions (e.g. a `<total_tokens>` update each turn). |
| `thinking` | `{"type":"adaptive"}`, `{"type":"adaptive","display":"omitted"}`, `{"type":"enabled"}`, `{"type":"disabled"}`, or absent |
| `output_config` | `{"effort":"high"}`; title generation adds `format: json_schema` |
| `context_management` | `{"edits":[{"type":"clear_thinking_20251015","keep":"all"}]}` |
| `max_tokens` | `32000` (main loop), `2112` (classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]`), `64` (stage-1 classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</severity>"]`) |
| `tool_result` | `is_error` is set on most results. Content is a string or a list of text/image blocks. User turns often carry extra text blocks (system reminders) after the tool results. |

---

### Part 1: Converter / API gaps (all models)

| # | Gap | Location | Impact | Existing work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Inline system messages are always hoisted into the leading system prompt.** `_detect_merge_inline_system` is called with the CLI `--chat-template` value, which is `None` by default, so it returns `True` for every deployment that uses the model's own template. Claude Code sends a changing inline system message every turn, so the leading system text changes every request. | `serving.py:142,152,248-257` | **Prefix cache misses on the whole conversation, every turn.** Also changes semantics: mid-conversation instructions become part of the global system prompt. | #53393, #48874, #41114, #46710; PRs #53501, #56520, #52978, #47681 (competing approaches) |
| 2 | **The `thinking` request field is silently dropped.** `AnthropicMessagesRequest` has no `thinking` field and pydantic ignores extras. `output_config.effort` → `reasoning_effort` then forces `enable_thinking=True` (`chat_completion/protocol.py:585`). Anthropic's default when `thinking` is absent is *off*, but we use the template default, which is usually *on*. | `protocol.py:121` | Side queries (title generation, classifier) reason and spend their `max_tokens` budget before answering. `display: "omitted"` is ignored. | PRs #58613, #53058 |
| 3 | **Stop strings are matched against reasoning text.** `check_stop_strings` runs over the full detokenized output. | `v1/engine/detokenizer.py:130` | The classifier's `</block>` / `</severity>` can match inside `<think>` and end the request with no verdict. | #51669 (related) |
| 4 | **Context-overflow errors are not in Anthropic's format.** vLLM returns "This model's maximum context length is …". Claude Code decides whether to auto-compact or retry with a smaller `max_tokens` based on Anthropic's context-limit error messages *(exact strings unverified)*. Claude Code always sends `max_tokens=32000`, so a 128k-context deployment rejects prompts once they pass ~99k tokens. | `renderers/params.py:357,499` | Long sessions fail hard instead of compacting. | none found |
| 5 | **Unknown content-block types reject the whole request (422).** `AnthropicContentBlock.type` is a closed `Literal`. `document` (PDFs from the Read tool), `search_result`, `tool_addition` / `tool_removal` and server-tool blocks all fail. Once one is in the history, every later request in the session fails. | `protocol.py:41` | Session becomes unrecoverable. | #57324, #46790; PRs #45653, #57693, #46797, #47747, #47877 |
| 6 | **Images in a `tool_result` become a separate `user` message** inserted between tool messages. | `serving.py:445-455` | Gemma 4 silently drops later tool results. Mistral returns 400 (`Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user'`). DeepSeek-V3.2 raises. MiniMax-M3 and Gemma 4 could render the image inside the tool message natively. | none found |
| 7 | **`tool_reference` produces an extra tool message, and the first one is empty.** | `serving.py:457-465` | 400 on Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 (`Unexpected item type in content`) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (`No tool calls but found tool output`). Python repr rendered on MiniMax. | #52489; PRs #52498, #52610 |
| 8 | **User text after `tool_result`s in the same turn becomes a separate trailing `user` message.** Templates that keep reasoning only after the last user message then drop the current tool loop's reasoning. | `serving.py:306` | Interleaved thinking lost mid-loop on GLM-4.7/5/5.1/5.2, Qwen3.5/3.6, MiniMax-M2.x and DeepSeek-V3.2. | none found |
| 9 | **`is_error` on `tool_result` is dropped.** | `serving.py:408-445` | The model cannot tell failed tool calls from successful ones. | none found |
| 10 | **System blocks are joined with `""`.** | `serving.py:257` | Prompt text runs together, e.g. `…for Claude.You are…`. | none found |
| 11 | **Malformed tool-call arguments crash non-streaming** (`json.loads` → 500). | `serving.py` (`messages_full_converter`) | Hard failure on a single bad generation. | PRs #57244, #52519 |
| 12 | **Error envelopes and types don't match Anthropic's.** FastAPI 422s are not wrapped in Anthropic's error format. Stream errors use `internal_error` instead of `api_error` / `overloaded_error`. Mid-stream upstream errors are replaced with "Invalid data format received". | `api_router.py`, `serving.py` | Client retry/backoff logic doesn't fire correctly. | PRs #58023, #46162 |
| 13 | **`x-api-key` is not accepted** by `--api-key` auth. | `serve/middleware/authenticate.py` | Requires `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` instead of `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. | PRs #51675, #51588 |
| 14 | **No `ping` or early `message_start` during long prefills** (100k+ token prompts). | `serving.py` (`message_stream_converter`) | Idle-timeout risk through proxies and load balancers *(unverified)*. | none found |
| 15 | **Tool-call id collisions/format.** vLLM-generated ids are reused across turns for some parsers (e.g. Kimi `functions.X:0`). | | See Kimi below. | PR #35667 |

---

### Part 2: Model / template-specific findings

The common thread: every family uses **different names and values** for thinking and effort. Examples: `enable_thinking`, `thinking`, `thinking_mode`, `low_effort`, `thinking_budget`, and effort sets such as `{low,high}`, `{none,high}` or `{xhigh,medium,low}`. Passing `output_config.effort` straight through as `reasoning_effort` therefore gives inconsistent behavior, and 400s on several families.

| Family | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3.8** (27B, Flash-Next, 2.4T) | The template raises `Unexpected reasoning effort high. Supported types are xhigh (default), medium, and low.` Claude Code sends `high` by default, so **every default Claude Code request returns 400**. 2.4T also raises `Disabling thinking is not supported.` | confirmed |
| **Qwen3.5 / 3.6** | Keep reasoning only after the last user message (item 8). 3.6 supports `preserve_thinking`, which vLLM never sets. The system-first guard is hidden only by item 1. | confirmed |
| **Qwen3.5 / Qwen3-Coder** | Historical arguments rendered with `\| string` produce Python `True`. Qwen3-Coder renders nested `anyOf` lossily. | confirmed (template-side) |
| **GLM-5.2 / 5.3** | Effort is mapped as `'high' if effort == 'high' else 'max'` (5.2), or only `{low,high}` is recognized (5.3), so `low`/`medium` become **Max**. 5.3 cannot disable thinking: the generation prompt is always `<think>`. `glm47_moe` parser switches to content-only when `enable_thinking=False`, so a naive disabled-thinking mapping would leak reasoning into `content`. | confirmed |
| **MiniMax-M3** | The template's `thinking_mode` (`enabled`/`disabled`/`adaptive`) maps 1:1 to Anthropic `thinking.type`, but vLLM never sets it. The template has no branch for non-leading system messages, so they are silently dropped once item 1 is fixed. | confirmed |
| **MiniMax-M2.x** | Reasoning is dropped before the last user message (item 8). | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V3.1** | The stock HF template does `'<｜tool▁sep｜>' + arguments`, but `chat_utils` has already turned arguments into a dict, so rendering raises `TypeError` on any history containing a tool call. It also never renders `tools`. Workaround: `examples/tool_chat_template_deepseekv31.jinja`. | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V3.2** (encoder) | `drop_thinking = messages[-1]["role"] == "user"` drops the current loop's reasoning (item 8). The strict tool-ordering check breaks on items 6 and 7. A non-merged inline system message has no role token and lands inside `<think>`. | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1** | V4 is fine. V4.1 raises on `effort: "medium"` (accepts low/high/xhigh/max). | confirmed |
| **Kimi K2-Thinking / K2.5 / K2.6** | The template renders only the tool-call **id**, never the tool name (`<\|tool_call_begin\|>{{ id }}`). Any id not generated by Kimi on vLLM (`toolu_…`, `chatcmpl-tool-…`, after `/model` or a resumed session) loses the tool name. Thinking uses `thinking`, not `enable_thinking`. | confirmed |
| **Kimi K3** | Only low/high/max effort are accepted, so `medium` / `xhigh` return 400. Tool-result matching is robust to foreign ids. | confirmed |
| **gpt-oss (Harmony)** | `max` / `xhigh` effort raise. Reasoning cannot be disabled. Images are dropped. Each inline system message becomes a new developer message. JSON Schema → TypeScript is lossy: `anyOf`+enum, `allOf`, `$ref` and `const` become `any`, and `additionalProperties` maps become `{}` (affects Claude Code's `AskUserQuestion` / `Workflow` tools). | confirmed |
| **Mistral / Devstral** | `validate_request_params` allows only `{none, high}` effort, so Claude Code's other values return 400. Devstral-Small-2 and Devstral-2 raise `think tokens are not available for this tokenizer` whenever the history contains a thinking block. `truncate_tool_call_ids` works but logs a WARNING per historical tool call on every request. | confirmed |
| **Gemma 4** | Later tool results are lost when a user message is inserted (item 6). The template renders `anyOf` as an empty type, renders enums only for strings, and renders map-typed objects as fake properties (hits `AskUserQuestion`). | confirmed |
| **Nemotron v3** | The template reads `low_effort`, which vLLM never sets, so effort has no effect. Thinking cannot be disabled via the Anthropic API. | confirmed |
| **Seed-OSS** | Thinking is controlled only by `thinking_budget` (default unlimited). The default tool rendering is Python signatures that drop nested types and enums; `use_json_tooldef` fixes this but is off by default. Historical arguments use Python repr. | confirmed |

---

### Proposed Change

Suggested priority order:

1. **Per-model thinking/effort mapping layer.** Map Anthropic `thinking.type` (+ `budget_tokens`) and `output_config.effort` onto each model's native switch (`enable_thinking`, `thinking`, `thinking_mode`, `low_effort`, `thinking_budget`) and clamp to the levels that model accepts. Treat absent `thinking` as disabled only where the model can actually disable it. This extends #58613 and #52738, and removes most of the 400s above.
2. **Inline system handling that preserves the prefix.** Keep inline system messages in place, or fold them into the adjacent user turn when the template requires system-first (as proposed in #53393). Never hoist them into the leading system block. Detect the template requirement against the *resolved* tokenizer template, not the CLI flag.
3. **Converter structure fixes.**
   - Keep tool-result images inside the `tool` message.
   - Emit one merged user message per Anthropic user turn, so the trailing text doesn't cut off reasoning.
   - Mark `is_error` (e.g. an `Error:` prefix).
   - Join system blocks with `\n\n`.
   - Emit a single `tool_reference` message.
4. **Error compatibility.**
   - Translate context-overflow errors to Anthropic's messages so Claude Code can auto-compact or reduce `max_tokens`.
   - Degrade unknown content blocks to text instead of failing with 422.
   - Use Anthropic error types and envelopes throughout.
5. **Model-specific fixes.**
   - Rewrite Kimi tool-call ids to `functions.{name}:{idx}`.
   - Drop historical reasoning for Mistral tokenizers without `[THINK]`.
   - Add a schema-normalization pass (flatten `anyOf`/`$ref`) for Harmony, Gemma 4 and Seed-OSS.
   - Evaluate stop strings against content only, not reasoning.
6. **Regression coverage.** Add a small Claude Code-shaped fixture (captured request shapes, no user content) to `tests/entrypoints/anthropic/`, rendered through the converter for each supported template family.

~2 weeks.

title: [RFC]: Shared JSON Schema structure for structured-output checks and transformations
author: equiluxe
body:
This RFC describes the target design. Illustrative interfaces below are not implemented APIs.

## Motivation

The core problem is that vLLM's pre-compilation JSON Schema checks and configuration-driven transformations lack a shared schema-aware structural model. Several recurse through arbitrary dictionaries and lists, so they can mistake property names or literal JSON values for schema keywords, or treat an unreferenced `$defs` entry as an active constraint. Some type-specific checks also require an explicit `type`, although JSON Schema assertions can apply without one. Patching these cases one walker at a time is whack-a-mole: the next keyword or consumer can repeat the same mistake. These consumers need one shared account of schema boundaries, reference reachability, and type applicability.

Concrete motivating cases include:

- A property named `patternProperties`, or the same key inside `const`, incorrectly triggers the [Guidance feature gate](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa94450b743766d466021a40e5b5f5f5746c92b9/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_guidance.py#L50-L73) ([bug #58694](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58694)).
- With `disable_additional_properties=True`, the [Guidance transformation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa94450b743766d466021a40e5b5f5f5746c92b9/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_guidance.py#L37-L48) inserts `additionalProperties: false` into an object inside `const`, changing the allowed value ([bug #58695](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58695)).
- String assertions can bypass xgrammar checks when `type` is omitted; [#57550](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57550) tracks this bug, and open [#57592](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57592) proposes a scoped fix with related traversal changes.
- An unreferenced `$defs` entry can change backend selection even though it does not constrain the generated value (also reproduced in [bug #58694](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58694)).

For a concrete Guidance case, this valid schema has a property **named** `patternProperties`; it has no `patternProperties` keyword:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "patternProperties": {"type": "string"},
    "n": {"type": "number", "multipleOf": 3}
  },
  "required": ["patternProperties", "n"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

On upstream `main` at `fa94450b74` (September 25, 2026), the Guidance gate reports it unsupported and `auto` selects Outlines. The original schema rejects `{"patternProperties":"x","n":7}`, while the resulting Outlines regex accepts it; the Guidance matcher rejects it.

Separately, with `disable_additional_properties=True`, Guidance inserts `additionalProperties: false` into a literal object under `const` or `enum` when that object has a `properties` member. Its matcher then accepts the changed literal, which the original schema rejects. These are local request-validation and matcher/regex reproductions, without model generation.

The proposal is a shared **schema-document layer** used by checks and transformations. Backend grammar compilers remain responsible for producing grammars.

## Proposed Change

The target is a shared schema document used by backend checks and configuration transformations before grammar compilation. The [fork-only Draft demo PR](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/pull/1) is a proof of concept that makes the design discussable through a code diff. It does not propose that diff as the fix and is marked **Do Not Merge**. The contract below defines the intended behavior, including requirements the prototype does not implement.

The shared document has these contracts. Each code excerpt is from the [fork-only Draft demo PR](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/pull/1) at commit `a83751a1` and illustrates only the stated part of the target design.

#### Schema/data boundary

`properties` is a name-to-schema map, `allOf` is a list of schemas, and `additionalProperties` holds a schema. `const`, `enum`, and `default` hold ordinary JSON values. Structural traversal visits nodes inside recognized schema-bearing keywords; it does not treat a property named `patternProperties` or an object inside `const` as a schema.

Keyword roles depend on the dialect of each schema resource, not on a single universal keyword table. The document obtains that dialect from `$schema` or a documented caller default; an embedded `$id` resource may declare another dialect. Ordinary unknown fields remain opaque and preserved. If a declared dialect requires a vocabulary this layer cannot interpret, capability analysis reports incomplete.

The demo recurses into recognized schema-bearing keywords and stores other values without parsing them as schemas. [Code](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/schema_document.py#L200-L210):

```python
elif keyword in _SCHEMA_SINGLE:
    subschemas[keyword] = _parse_node(value)
else:
    values[keyword] = _copy_value(value)
```

The demo uses a fixed `2020-12` keyword table and does not inspect `$schema`. It also treats legacy `additionalItems` as schema-bearing under `2020-12`, although [that dialect replaced it with `items`](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core#section-10.3.1.2) and treats it as an unknown keyword; dialect-specific roles remain target work.

#### Lossless representation

Boolean schemas and generic schema objects preserve the original child-container shapes. There is no second independently mutable raw tree. Without a transformation, `SchemaDocument.parse(schema, dialect).export() == schema` for JSON-valued inputs. Parsing does not mutate caller input or silently treat malformed structural values as absent. A present but invalid keyword value is not treated as an omitted keyword by derived analysis, even though structural parsing is separate from full schema-validity checking. Transformations use immutable nodes or controlled edits that keep keyword order, source locations/indexes, and derived caches consistent. Existing accepted dialect and legacy forms, including tuple-valued `items`, need an explicit normalization or round-trip contract.

The demo exports boolean nodes directly and reconstructs object keywords in their original order. [Code](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/schema_document.py#L213-L230):

```python
if isinstance(node, BoolSchema):
    return node.value
exported: dict[str, Any] = {}
for keyword in node.order:
    if keyword in node.values:
        exported[keyword] = _copy_value(node.values[keyword])
```

This demonstrates the representation for the prototype's accepted forms; compatibility across existing dialects and legacy forms has not been established. The demo exposes mutable keyword dictionaries, so edits outside its narrow transformation method can leave export order or derived caches stale.

#### Two traversals

`walk_all_schema_nodes()` includes definitions and schema-valued annotations for structural inspection and controlled whole-document edits. `walk_potential_constraints()` starts at the root and follows only edges that may affect the generated instance under the relevant dialect, plus resolved references. Schema-bearing does not imply instance-applicable: Draft 2020-12 [`contentSchema`](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-validation#section-8.5) is a content annotation by default, and [`then`/`else`](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core#section-10.2.2) have no effect without `if` in the same schema object. An unused `$defs` schema is preserved without changing semantic capability checks. Reachability is conservative, not a satisfiability proof.

References remain edges, with cycle tracking and explicit coverage for local pointers, `$id` scopes, and anchors. Dialect-specific reference rules, including [Draft-07's treatment of `$ref` siblings](https://json-schema.org/draft-07/json-schema-core#section-8.3), govern which edges apply. Unresolved or unsupported cases are reported as incomplete; remote schemas are not fetched automatically. Source locations support diagnostics such as `#/properties/code`; the full pointer index can be built only when references or diagnostics require it.

The demo's capability walk skips unused definitions, follows local references, and tracks visited nodes. [Code](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/schema_document.py#L349-L367):

```python
visited.add(id(node))
yield node
if isinstance(node, GeneralSchema):
    _push_children(pending, node, include_definitions=False)
    target = self._local_reference(node)
    if target is not None:
        pending.append(self.nodes[target])
```

The demo resolves only root-local JSON Pointers; `$id` scopes, anchors, and remote references remain incomplete. It also follows `contentSchema` and orphan `then`/`else` as if they could constrain the generated value; the target walk must distinguish these edges. A pointer-yielding walk exists, but the backend gates do not yet return source locations.

#### Derived assertions

The document keeps explicit `type` separate from type-specific assertions. A schema such as `{"pattern": "^[a-z]+$", "maxLength": 3}` still constrains string instances while allowing non-strings. A backend checks string features unless string is definitely excluded; it does not infer or insert `type: string`. One schema node owns the data and exposes numeric, string, array, and object behavior; these do not require four separately allocated views or another mutable tree. Scalar, list-valued, and omitted types use the same applicability rules. Backend profiles own their capability rules; no general entailment solver is required.

In the demo, omitted `type` leaves string instances possible, so the [Xgrammar check](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py#L265-L281) can inspect string-specific keywords without inserting a type. [Code](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/schema_document.py#L68-L71):

```python
def may_be_string(self) -> bool:
    types = self._explicit_types
    return types is None or "string" in types
```

The demo currently treats an explicit invalid `"type": null` as if `type` were omitted. The target distinguishes absence from an invalid value and reports invalidity or incomplete analysis under its validation policy.

#### Safe preparation

Transformations edit eligible schema nodes in a new document; they never edit literal JSON values such as `{"const": {"properties": {"status": "ok"}}}`. Guidance's `disable_additional_properties=True` may add `additionalProperties: false` to an object schema, but this is a configuration-driven semantic rewrite, not necessarily a monotone restriction. For example, `{"not":{"properties":{"x":{"const":1}}}}` rejects `{"x":1,"extra":2}`; adding `additionalProperties: false` inside `not` makes that value valid. `if` and `oneOf` also have non-monotone cases. Which contexts the configuration rewrites is an explicit compatibility decision, not something structural traversal decides automatically.

Each candidate backend starts from the unmodified parsed document. Conceptually, it prepares its own copy, checks that prepared schema and configuration, and, if selected, compiles that same prepared schema and configuration.

The demo copies the document and visits only `GeneralSchema` nodes, including definitions; literal JSON inside `const` and `enum` remains opaque. [Code](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/schema_document.py#L391-L410):

```python
prepared = SchemaDocument(deepcopy(self.root), self.dialect)
pending = [prepared.root]
nodes: list[GeneralSchema] = []
while pending:
    node = pending.pop()
    if isinstance(node, GeneralSchema):
        nodes.append(node)
        _push_children(pending, node, include_definitions=True)
```

[Guidance applies](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_guidance.py#L62-L71) its `additionalProperties` change to these nodes. The demo does not select eligible contexts within that set, so `not`, `if`, and schema-valued annotations can also be rewritten. Candidate preparation, capability checks, and actual compilation do not yet share one end-to-end prepared result.

#### Routing boundary

A check reports a reason, schema location, backend, and one of **known unsupported**, **analysis incomplete**, or **no known issue**. A definite unsupported feature remains reportable even if another branch is incomplete; otherwise incomplete analysis must not become **no known issue**. The last state is not proof of complete backend support.

Routing handles incomplete analysis explicitly and preserves existing validation/fallback behavior unless a separate policy change is reviewed. Ordinary JSON, tool parameters, and structural-tag inner schemas use this schema path while retaining their outer protocol handling. Parsing and analysis run during preparation/compilation, outside the per-token masking path.

The demo's feature gate still returns a Boolean, so this contract is not implemented. [Code](https://github.com/equiluxe/vllm/blob/a83751a1a89082ffe11642918405fe6a66a7d833/vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_guidance.py#L41-L51):

```python
document = SchemaDocument.parse(schema)
return any(
    isinstance(node, GeneralSchema) and node.pattern_properties is not None
    for node in document.walk_potential_constraint_nodes()
)
```

When traversal reaches an unsupported reference form, it raises `IncompleteSchemaAnalysis`; routing does not yet handle a distinct incomplete result or return a reason and location. `False` means no known issue in this gate, not proof of backend support. Tool and structural-tag paths are also outside this demo.

Backend grammar compilation, runtime matcher state, a full instance validator, exact satisfiability/type inference, and a new default fallback order are outside this proposal. Benchmark preparation against today's path on representative schemas: parsing, traversal, candidate-specific rewrites, export, and allocations, especially when multiple backend candidates inspect one schema. Measure that separately from grammar compilation before deciding whether caching is useful.

### Adoption

Adoption does not require a complete JSON Schema parser up front. Start with the smallest schema-aware reader needed by one consumer: recognize the schema-bearing positions and application edges it uses, leave the caller's schema untouched, and report **analysis incomplete** for dialects, references, or structures it cannot safely analyze. Extend coverage only as consumers need it. Each small, consumer-backed PR should state the behavior it changes or preserves, protect unrelated backend routing and accepted schema forms, and include targeted regressions. Independent bug fixes can be reviewed while the shared interface is discussed. The exact order, dependencies, and code split belong in those PRs; this RFC defines the shared end state and its compatibility boundaries.

For example, first compare a narrow Guidance check against the existing check **in tests only**, so serving still uses the old decision. Test unchanged cases for equivalence and give each intended behavior change its own regression. A later PR can switch that one consumer while preserving the old decision whenever analysis is incomplete (illustrative pseudocode, not a proposed API):

```python
# First PR: compare only schemas expected to keep the current decision.
for unchanged_schema in unchanged_cases:
    analysis = analyze_guidance_subset(unchanged_schema)
    if analysis.status != ANALYSIS_INCOMPLETE:
        assert (analysis.status == KNOWN_UNSUPPORTED) == legacy_guidance_gate(
            unchanged_schema
        )

# Later PR: migrate one consumer; leave global routing policy unchanged.
analysis = analyze_guidance_subset(schema)
if analysis.status == ANALYSIS_INCOMPLETE:
    return legacy_guidance_gate(schema)
return analysis.status == KNOWN_UNSUPPORTED
```

An incomplete result never means "supported"; it preserves the existing decision until that schema form is covered. This keeps each structural addition reviewable without changing every backend, schema entry point, or fallback rule at once.

### Test contracts and real backend behavior

Use an independent validator on the **original schema**, not our AST, as the semantic oracle. For a supported test case with no configuration-driven schema rewrite:

```python
original = deepcopy(schema)
document = SchemaDocument.parse(schema, dialect=DRAFT_2020_12)
assert document.export() == original
assert schema == original

Draft202012Validator.check_schema(original)
oracle = Draft202012Validator(original)  # independent of our parser
matcher = compile_via_vllm(document, backend, config=no_schema_rewrite_config)
for value in ["abc", "abcd", "ABC", 123, None]:
    expected = oracle.is_valid(value)
    assert accepts_complete_json(matcher, value) == expected
```

`accepts_complete_json` creates fresh matcher state and checks the whole serialized value **and legal termination/EOS**, not just prefix acceptance. This is test pseudocode, not a production validation layer.

The test plan includes:

- Structural round trips and non-mutation: boolean schemas, property names, opaque data, unknown fields, nested schemas, escaped pointers, and cycles. Dialect cases include 2020-12 `additionalItems`, Draft-07/2020-12 `$ref` sibling behavior, and invalid explicit keyword values distinct from omission.
- Constraint traversal: unused definitions, schema-valued content annotations, orphan `then`/`else`, active conditional branches, and referenced definitions.
- Curated cases from the [JSON Schema Test Suite](https://github.com/json-schema-org/JSON-Schema-Test-Suite), targeted positive/negative regressions, and bounded generated instances. Pin dialect, backend versions, serialization policy, and `format` assertion behavior; [python-jsonschema does not enforce formats by default](https://python-jsonschema.readthedocs.io/en/stable/validate/).
- Separate transformation contracts: equivalence for lossless operations; independently specified acceptance and rejection effects for configuration-driven rewrites, including preservation of literal values and non-monotone `not`/`if`/`oneOf` contexts.
- Integration checks for explicit/automatic backends, actual routing and compilation, and supported JSON/tool/tag entry points. Output-affecting fixes also need model smoke tests; length-truncated output is not a successful schema-valid generation.

Unsupported cases should test diagnostics and routing, not demand universal backend acceptance. Differential tests increase confidence but do not prove correctness for arbitrary schemas, and compilation success alone does not prove that all assertions are enforced.

### Alternatives and tradeoffs

- **Only share a walker:** sufficient for read-only checks, but transformations and export also need a common structure contract. A walker remains a reasonable alternative if it preserves the same schema/data boundary and offers a safe transformation interface.
- **Rely only on backend compilation:** avoids duplicated checks, but cannot address vLLM's own data traversal/transformation bugs or compilers that warn and ignore constraints. Prefer reliable backend-native diagnostics wherever available.
- **Build a complete semantic AST:** more uniform in theory, but expands review scope and duplicates backend work. General/boolean nodes with derived behavior for actual consumers cover the proposed contract. Evaluate existing dialect/reference utilities before implementing a new resolver.

The main costs are another representation, dialect/reference maintenance, and preparation overhead. The preparation benchmark above makes these costs visible alongside routing and correctness changes.

### Feedback requested

1. Is a structural document/AST justified by the check **and transformation** use cases, or would a schema-aware visitor with a safe transformation interface be a better shared contract?
2. Which dialect/legacy forms and reference behaviors must this layer support? How should routing handle incomplete analysis when backend-native validation cannot cover it?
3. Which capability rules belong in vLLM, and which should be replaced by backend-native diagnostics?
4. Which schema contexts should `disable_additional_properties` rewrite, given that a rewrite below `not`, `if`, or `oneOf` can admit values the original schema rejects?

## Feedback Period

September 25 through October 2, 2026 (at least one week). Discussion can continue until the core scope questions have received maintainer feedback.

## CC List

Structured-output maintainers and authors of overlapping changes are invited to comment. No one is explicitly mentioned in this issue.

## Any Other Things

- [#48416](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48416) established scalar/list type handling. Preserve that behavior and its tests when extracting shared analysis.
- [#57592](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57592) overlaps omitted-type handling, schema-aware traversal, and local references; coordinate and reuse its work rather than submit a competing fix. [#57594](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57594) updates a backend capability gate; that remains backend policy, not parser behavior. Recheck overlapping work before each implementation PR.
- xgrammar already has an internal schema parser ([v0.2.7 source](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/blob/v0.2.7/cpp/json_schema_converter.cc)). This proposal does not replace it. Prefer upstream diagnostics for unsupported or dropped constraints, and remove vLLM compatibility rules when a supported dependency provides a tested replacement. That upstream work need not block vLLM-local structural fixes.

AI assistance: this RFC was prepared with OpenAI Codex. The pinned local reproductions above are reported as such; no production AST implementation is claimed.

title: [RFC]: Universal Triton kernel autotuning at warmup
author: giuseppegrossi
body:
### Motivation.

Rescope of my initial PR#48980 to a more universal approach.

vLLM runs many Triton kernels whose launch parameters (`BLOCK_*`, `num_warps`, `num_stages`) are shape-, device-, and dtype-dependent. Today these parameters are chosen in three different ways:

1. **`@triton.autotune`** (~50 call sites): Triton times a candidate list lazily the first time it sees each new key, during `profile_run`.
2. **Offline JSON tables** (fused MoE, W8A8 block FP8, LoRA, Mamba `selective_state_update`): a config is looked up by `(shape, device, dtype)`. When no file matches, the kernel silently falls back to a hard-coded heuristic default.
3. **Plain `@triton.jit`** (~500 call sites): not tunable automatically.

The gap is category (2). vLLM only bundles a curated set of shapes and devices. When someone serves a model + accelerator combination that isn't in the table, the kernel quietly uses the heuristic default, which can be significantly slower. The only workaround today is to run a standalone
`benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_*.py` script by hand and drop the result into `VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER`.  Furthermore, users need to maintain many config files for various architectures (including new ones) and would instead like an easy out of the box solution that just picks the right configurations for **all** the kernels being used in the serving model.

FlashInfer already solves the analogous problem with `--kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune`, which tunes at kernel warmup for the model actually being served. There is no equivalent for Triton. This RFC proposes one.

### Proposed Change.

Add an opt-in flag, `--kernel-config.enable_triton_autotune` (default `False`), modeled on `enable_flashinfer_autotune`. When enabled, during kernel warmup — after the model is loaded and the KV cache is allocated, but **before** CUDA graph capture — vLLM tunes every Triton config-table kernel that the served model will actually use **but that has no config yet**, and persists the result to a local cache that later startups reuse without re-tuning. Scope is intentionally limited to category (2) above (kernels that read a JSON config table).

A "family" is one config table / lookup function, not one kernel. Each table implements a small interface:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TuningItem:
    table: str        # which table this belongs to
    shape: Hashable   # e.g. (headdim, dstate, dtype, nheads, ...)
    bucket: int       # the varying dimension, e.g. effective batch size

class TunableConfigTable(ABC):
    name: ClassVar[str]

    @abstractmethod
    def pending_items(self, worker) -> list[TuningItem]:
        """Items the served model will look up that have no config yet."""

    @abstractmethod
    def tune(self, item: TuningItem) -> dict | None:
        """Benchmark one item on scratch buffers; None if nothing valid."""

    @abstractmethod
    def commit(self, results: dict[TuningItem, dict]) -> None:
        """Persist results and clear the table's lookup caches. Runs on all ranks."""
```

Every rank must reach every collective and every rank must end up with identical configs (so captured CUDA graphs match across TP/PP ranks). The loop:

1. Each rank computes its own `pending_items` (shapes are per-rank, e.g. after TP sharding, but contain nothing rank-specific like a device index).
2. `all_gather_object` the union of pending items.
3. Deterministically sort the union and shard it `items[rank::world_size]` so each item is tuned exactly once.
4. Each rank tunes its slice; failures are caught so they never skip a collective.
5. `all_gather_object` the results; **every** rank calls `commit`, so all ranks write the same files and clear the same caches.

This runs from `kernel_warmup()` right after the `process_local_only` early return, so it always executes on the normal startup path on every rank and before `capture_model`.

### Persistence

- Results are stored under `VLLM_TRITON_AUTOTUNE_CACHE_DIR` (default `$VLLM_CACHE_ROOT/triton_autotune/triton=<version>/<table>/`), reusing each table's existing on-disk JSON schema (keyed by `shape/device/dtype`) so the same files are also usable via `VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER`.
- The config loader gains one extra lookup path (user folder → autotune cache → bundled default), so a second startup finds the tuned file and skips tuning.
- `VLLM_TRITON_AUTOTUNE_FORCE=1` re-tunes even when a config already exists.
- Curated bundled configs are respected by default; tuning only fills gaps.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@hongxiayang @vanshbhatia-amd @tdoublep 

### Any Other Things.

### AI assistance
This RFC was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed and revised by the author, who is responsible for the design.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Native span pooling for contextual chunk embeddings
author: LinzeShi
body:
## Motivation

Retrieval applications often index paragraphs separately. Encoding each paragraph in isolation loses cross-paragraph context: “its maintenance team” may refer to a company named in an earlier paragraph. [Late chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04701) encodes the document first, then pools token representations within each chunk.

vLLM already returns token embeddings. For suitable models, an application can disable token normalization with `use_activation=False`, export the representations and pool them correctly outside the worker. This proposal adds a native way to return only the requested chunk vectors, with a shared request contract and worker-side aggregation.

The existing [long-text embedding feature](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/22280) splits an oversized input into independent forwards and combines their outputs into one document vector. Here, multiple chunk vectors come from one shared document encoding, within the model's context limit. The algorithm is established; the proposed contribution is its integration into vLLM's pooling path.

## Proposed change

Add an opt-in span-pooling task, tentatively named `span_embed`, through `LLM.encode` and the existing `/pooling` endpoint. The default embedding APIs keep their current behavior.

### Request semantics

For the first release, use the existing token-ID input path. Each request contains one complete, unpadded token sequence and one or more ordered, non-overlapping ranges. This makes the worker's input unambiguous and avoids introducing a second server-side tokenization path.

Illustrative request; the task and `token_spans` field are proposed:

```json
{
  "model": "span-enabled-encoder",
  "task": "span_embed",
  "input": [101, 2023, 2003, 1037, 7953, 1012, 102],
  "add_special_tokens": false,
  "token_spans": [[0, 4], [4, 7]]
}
```

Token IDs are illustrative; callers must use the served model's tokenizer and pinned revision.

- Ranges are zero-based and half-open: `[start, end)`. They refer to the exact submitted token sequence. Reject empty, reversed, overlapping or out-of-bounds ranges, and enforce a server-side span-count limit.
- All input tokens provide context. Only tokens within each range participate in its mean. Special tokens and instructions are included if their positions are selected; the engine never silently includes or excludes them.
- Require `add_special_tokens=false` and reject request/config options that would truncate, pad, rewrite or split this input. Ordinary internal batch padding is not part of the sequence or its ranges. Oversized inputs fail validation.
- Return one `[K, D]` matrix in the existing pooling response, where row `i` corresponds to input span `i`. Count input tokens once per document. Concurrent requests remain independently batched by the engine.

Ship a text-to-token example with the first release so users can start from text and paragraph boundaries. It uses the same pinned tokenizer as the deployment, tokenizes the complete model input once, and sends those exact IDs with the resolved ranges. It rejects boundaries inside a token. The late-chunking reference example follows the paper's convention of including prefix tokens in the first chunk and suffix tokens in the last. A content-only example must be identified as a different convention. A text/character-span server API can follow once this operation is established.

### Shared implementation, explicit model support

Implement the reduction once in the common pooler layer:

```text
full-document model forward
  -> span means, accumulated in FP32
  -> validated model-specific embedding head
  -> K output vectors, copied from the worker
```

The head includes the supported projection, dtype conversion and normalization in the model's verified order. We must not move nonlinear transformations across the mean or assume that exported token embeddings always equal raw hidden states.

Start with an explicitly enabled bidirectional MEAN-pooling model. `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1`, at the revision pinned by existing vLLM tests, is the initial integration candidate; its HF compatibility constraint remains in place. MiniLM provides inexpensive reference coverage. Additional models reuse the reducer but require validation of their head and input conventions. Unsupported models fail before scheduling. LAST/CLS models are not automatically enabled.

The integration covers:

1. Pooling request/offline input validation and typed `token_spans` in `PoolingParams`.
2. Task registration, parameter defaults, model capability reporting and `DispatchPooler` selection. A compatible head must explicitly support the new task; existing heads must not advertise support globally.
3. Request metadata transport and batch slicing, preserving the association between each request's ranges and hidden states through reordering and task grouping.
4. Reduction before worker output copying, using the existing variable-row pooling output. Extend existing pooling tests and examples.

This uses the current scheduler and model forward path. Initial encoder targets keep their existing restrictions on prefix caching and chunked prefill. Documents must fit a full supported context. Automatic segmentation, cross-window context, decoder models and multimodal inputs are outside the first release.

### Alternatives and related work

A correct token-export/client-pooling path is the first baseline. An IO processor can also aggregate outputs before the HTTP response, although token-level worker output has already been produced. A custom model pooler combined with a plugin can perform aggregation inside the worker too.

The argument for native support is a reusable contract and validated model integration, rather than requiring separate model wrappers. Plugins are a legitimate alternative: [#37344](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/37344#issuecomment-4080081406) recommended them for custom span-shaped outputs. I would like feedback on whether this use case warrants a native task.

This differs from existing multi-head embedding output and late-interaction scoring. It also differs from [#56916](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56916), which concerns capturing hidden states during response generation. External demand exists, for example [TEI #434](https://github.com/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference/issues/434); vLLM users' models and workloads would help establish the priority here.

### Validation and delivery

A local CPU probe combined a real MiniLM encoder with vLLM's pooler/head components on four documents and eleven spans. The component results matched direct reference calculations. This is feasibility evidence, not an end-to-end implementation or a performance result.

Implementation acceptance should cover:

- Numerical agreement with a fixed-revision HF reference using identical token IDs, ranges and head semantics, including special-token selection.
- Online/offline agreement, mixed-length and mixed-task batching, invalid inputs, context limits and unchanged existing embedding results.
- Comparison with correctly configured token export plus client pooling: worker-output bytes, host memory and end-to-end latency at matched workloads. A worker-side plugin can establish whether native integration adds any overhead, rather than assuming it must be faster.
- A representative retrieval comparison with independent-chunk encoding, reporting gains and regressions. [Subsequent evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16974) finds task-dependent effects; this is an optional capability, not a universal retrieval upgrade.

Reducing output from `N × D` to `K × D` values does not reduce the full-document attention cost or establish an end-to-end speedup.

I propose three implementation steps: the shared reducer and offline reference tests; online request integration plus the text-to-token example; then end-to-end validation and documentation for the first supported model. I would like to drive the implementation and maintain this path.

## Feedback period

Initial feedback through October 2, 2026; discussion can continue afterward. The main questions are whether native support is preferable to a plugin, whether the token-range contract is suitable, and which initial model/workload users would actually deploy. Task naming and exact field placement can be settled in review.

## CC list

cc @noooop @DarkLight1337. I would appreciate your thoughts on the pooling API and whether this belongs in core or a plugin.

title: [RFC] RL Weight Update Roadmap
author: aoshen02
body:
Goal: make repeated trainer → vLLM weight updates correct and efficient across supported models and transports.

Correctness drives the refactor: the failures tracked below include layerwise reload changing graph-visible storage or leaving derived weights stale. Direct reload is the safer path for eligible models; other models need a verified fallback.

Done when repeated A→B→A updates match cold-start results on every claimed model, transport and reload path.
