title: [RFC]: [Spec decode] KV-cache pool collapse when a draft model introduces a new cache spec type (hybrid GDN + DFlash): diagnosis, mitigation dead-ends, and a working dedicated-draft-pool POC
author: ZZXX-bit
body:
### Motivation.

The unified hybrid KV-cache pool assumes that all attention layers can be grouped by their KV-cache spec type and that **every request draws blocks from every group**. This assumption breaks when a speculative-decoding draft model registers attention layers whose spec type no target layer has: the draft's spec type fragments grouping, inflates per-request block demand, and the scheduler's usable KV pool collapses — even though the draft itself needs very little memory.

We hit this end-to-end with a real deployment: a 27B hybrid model (48 linear-attention/GDN layers + 16 full-attention layers) served with a DFlash draft (`num_speculative_tokens=7`) whose 5 attention layers are sliding-window (window 2048, non-causal). On vLLM 0.30 (same on 0.29):

| Setup | no draft | with draft | collapse |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2×RTX 5090 32GB (tp2) | 369,121 tokens / 22.53x concurrency @16k | 33,530 tokens / **2.05x** | **11.0x** |
| A800 80GB (tp1) | 455,717 tokens / 27.81x | 142,137 tokens / **8.68x** | 3.2x |

On the 32GB setup `blocks_per_request` goes 14 → 86 @16k; c=8 throughput drops 21% and c=16 OOMs the engine. The draft's *actual* KV need is ~42 MB/request (2048-token window × 5 layers) — the loss is pure pool bookkeeping: 4 → 16 groups (the uniform-page-size unifier adds "padding layers, may waste at most 25% KV cache memory") plus every request paying blocks to the draft group.

Every lighter mitigation fails empirically:

- serving the draft with full attention instead of sliding window: **no recovery** (137,346 vs 139,907 tokens) — the extra *spec type* itself, not the window, causes fragmentation;
- the grouping heuristics of PR #58207 (ported to 0.30): +4% / −12% — noise-to-negative; GCD-based grouping (#56445): gcd(16, 48, 5) = 1, falls back;
- `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`: engine crash (GDN specs cannot be unified).

Draft acceptance is healthy in all configurations (EAL ≈ 2.7–3.5), so the draft is fine — the pool model is the bottleneck. We believe the right fix is the direction RFC #58638 points at: **give the draft model its own dedicated cache pool** instead of forcing it into the unified hybrid pool. A working POC (~400 lines, 3 files) confirms it: main pool restored to no-draft equivalence, acceptance unchanged, c=8 QPS +19.6% / TPOT −20.8%, c=16 from "cannot run" to parity.

### Proposed Change.

Keep draft-model attention layers **out of the unified hybrid pool** and give the speculator a small, self-managed cache:

1. **Exclude draft layers from the main pool.** The speculator tags the layers it loads (same convention as the existing `kv_sharing_target_layer_name` exclusion in `get_kv_cache_spec`). The main KVCacheConfig then becomes *identical* to the no-draft config — grouping, page sizes, and `num_blocks` all recover.
2. **Draft-owned pool in `DraftModelSpeculator`.** Build a single-group homogeneous `KVCacheConfig` from the draft layers' specs + a dedicated tensor + `BlockTables`, sized deterministically: `num_blocks = max_concurrent_draft_reqs × ceil(window / page) + margin`. For our draft (2048-token window, 5 layers, 128 concurrent requests): 385 blocks ≈ 6.1 GiB.
3. **Budget accounting.** Subtract the draft pool bytes from available KV memory before the main pool is sized (worker + scheduler see the same number). The draft pool is a startup reservation: not scheduler-managed, no prefix caching for draft KV in v1.
4. **Static ring block table.** Fill each request-slot row with a wrapped pattern (`entry[j] = base + j % ring_blocks`) and refresh it per step by one gather on `idx_mapping`. This is equivalent to `SlidingWindowManager`'s ring for all reads (attention kernels index the page table by absolute page number; ring capacity ≥ window ensures no stale reads; slot reuse across requests is safe because a request fully overwrites its window before reading it) — **zero allocation/lifecycle code** in the scheduler.
5. **Handle the profiling-phase double init.** `initialize_kv_cache` runs once during memory profiling and the teardown resets layer bindings (`clear_layer_kv_caches` → empty 1-D tensor); the real init must re-bind draft tensors, and a repeated `set_attn` must restore repointed state. This should be covered by tests.

POC results (A800 80GB, tp1, v0.30; DFlash drafting math untouched):

| metric | no draft | draft, unified pool | draft, **dedicated pool** |
|---|---|---|---|
| main-pool groups | 4 | 16 | **4, structurally identical to no-draft** |
| main-pool num_blocks | 751 | — | **486, proportional to its (smaller) memory share, same per-block cost** |
| EAL (acceptance) | — | 2.73 | **3.18 / 3.19** (c=8 / c=16) |
| QPS, 400 production-like reqs, 0 errors | c=8: 0.897 / c=16: 1.282 | (OOM @c=16 on 32GB) | **c=8: 1.073 (+19.6%) / c=16: 1.227 (−4.3%)** |

Scope for a first PR: single homogeneous draft spec group; tp>1 / DCP / PCP and prefix-cached draft KV are follow-ups. Alternatives considered: grouping-heuristic fixes (measured above — cannot recover once a third spec type exists) and spec unification (impossible for GDN+sliding). We are happy to open the PR and add unit tests for the ring block-table math and the rebind semantics.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [RFC][KV Connector] NIXL support for shared in-flight prefix loads
author: NolenLiang
body:
Propose a NIXL follow-up to #57418 so concurrent rollout requests can share an in-flight KV prefix load. The parent provides shared allocation, reference counting and receive-failure handling. This follow-up adds NIXL compatibility checks and producer-lease coordination.

### Why this is useful

The [cold 1P+1D baseline](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57418#issuecomment-5884091617) reproduces repeated prefix transfers at concurrency 4. At concurrency 8, existing decode prefix caching already reduces the bytes transferred. The opportunity depends on requests overlapping an unfinished load.

### Proposed scope and behavior

Start with opt-in NIXL pull, direct GPU buffers, TP1/PP1/CP1, one full-attention cache group and prefix caching. Enable it with `enable_shared_prefix_loads=true`. Host staging, bidirectional transfer, speculative decoding and encoder inputs are outside the initial scope.

- Keep the owner's full READ. Share only complete blocks before the last request token and give each follower a private writable tail.
- Require matching prefix hashes, producer engine/endpoint, block geometry and leased physical source-prefix blocks. Each sibling must have a distinct producer lease.
- Release unused follower leases through notification without another READ. Keep the owner's destination and heartbeat alive until the READ completes, including after cancellation.
- Reuse the parent's failure propagation and local recomputation. Followers must not reread through released leases.

Unsupported configurations or producer metadata missing `remote_block_size` use independent loads. The connector interface adds a slicing capability, a metadata-only compatibility check and notification after successful attachment. Existing connector defaults preserve the parent's exact partial-prefix behavior.

### Implementation and validation — status updated October 11, 2026

The implementation is in [draft PR #59343](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59343), now at `376f6836b497b59ce556b24c568683a9773ce235`. It incorporates parent #57418 at `acc247941a7bd7eb41cebde9a97eb89dbddc3a52` and main snapshot `fcae5c98870ff2c20659731dce7ba3a3ff0d48aa`. The queue integration follows the parent's KV-holding waiting queue and KV-fetch stages, avoiding a duplicate queue pop.

**Current-source validation: 790 distinct focused tests passed**, including lifecycle/heartbeat (109), offloading/prefix caching/failure recovery/admission (649), selected NIXL worker cases (30), and HMA cases (2). All applicable pre-commit hooks passed on 19 changed files. The published source tree matches the tested tree. [Commands, environment limits and logs](https://github.com/NolenLiang/vllm/blob/c4f6bfdd11c2718f767b85c82ed2af8314dd8135/pr-rebase-evidence/20261011/README.md). These focused regressions use mocked transport boundaries; they are not new GPU peer-transfer acceptance results.

The original `529d597` prototype and September 29 archive are historical snapshots. Candidate `e6e362a` recorded the following prior validation; those results retain their original revision attribution:

- 186 distinct compute tests passed, including unsupported-configuration fallback, admission cleanup, heartbeat, polling exceptions and native disconnect/release retry. Applicable changed-file pre-commit hooks and the separate Python 3.12 mypy check passed locally.
- 12 real peer-failure trials passed on candidate `e6e362a`: recompute/fail policies, 16384/16385-token prompts, three repetitions. Event replay checked native in-progress status around peer termination, disconnect, handle release, core failure propagation, destination reclamation and recovery on the same D process after P restarted.
- A repeated untraced off/on/on/off comparison completed 120 measured groups, 520 D requests and 64 correctness outputs. Text and finish reasons matched; maximum token-logprob error was 0.00709399 against a 0.01 tolerance.
- At four siblings, 4096/4097-token cases reduced four transfers to one and payload by 75%. Eight-sibling median payload was unchanged with ordinary prefix-cache reuse; timing drift prevents a stable latency claim.
- Earlier source snapshots separately passed cancellation, real-in-progress polling-exception and heartbeat-crossing probes. Those results remain attributed to their actual snapshots. Default-background-progress heartbeat crossing remains inconclusive.

These are recorded results from the PR; the October 11 status update did not independently rerun the GPU experiments. The workload uses two GB200 GPUs on one node and is GRPO-shaped serving, not a trainer integration. Payload is connector telemetry, not NIC wire bytes.

### Remaining work

- Preserve previous GPU results as historical evidence. Verify cancellation/failure/reclamation paths affected by the adaptation on the final source when suitable hardware is available. The previous dual-GB200 environment is no longer accessible; no final-source hardware result is claimed.
- Obtain human review and personal test execution for the new adaptation, maintainer review and upstream CI. Earlier upstream pre-commit was skipped after a contributor-eligibility precheck failure; no successful upstream CI run is claimed for the new source.

Would this connector interface and initial scope fit #57418's direction?

AI assistance: Codex assisted implementation, tests, measurements and this status update. The prior candidate's human review is recorded in the PR; review and personal test execution of the October 11 adaptation remain outstanding.

title: [RFC]: Modular read strategies and custom parameters for /v1/systemone and /v1/decisions
author: Timiku
body:
> **Update 2026-10-07:** With #59299 now brings structured decisions into the API server (`/v1/systemone`, next-token reads), and #60465 adds OpenAI's Decisions format at `/v1/decisions` on top of it. This RFC no longer proposes its own endpoint design. It now proposes two additions on top of those PRs: read strategies (backends) that are modular, and a request block for custom parameters on both endpoints. The earlier version is in this issue's edit history.

### Motivation.

Typed decisions are questions about a piece of text that come back as a probability for every option, not as generated text: yes / no, a pick from a set of choices, or a score. #59299 serves them on `/v1/systemone` with a next-token read on generative models, and #60465 serves OpenAI's format on `/v1/decisions` over the same core. Two model-specific reads exist outside it so far:

- #57250 (merged) serves DiffusionGemma canvas reads through an example server.
- #58429 (open) adds Laya encoder reads through pooling, on the same example wire.

#59299 already has a `ReadStrategy` class and says a diffusion strategy is coming, and that other decision models "may wish to ship their own". Two things are still missing for that to work:

- *A new strategy can't be added from outside, or chosen per request.* `select_read_strategy` maps a model architecture to one built-in strategy for the whole server. A new decision model (an encoder, a diffusion model, a finetuned classifier head) needs a core edit, and a request can't pick a different read or pass it options.
- *Neither endpoint takes parameters beyond its published format.* `/v1/systemone` follows Jev's request and `/v1/decisions` follows OpenAI's, which refuses unknown fields. There is no place for a per-request calibration temperature, a strategy choice and its options, or the diagnostics a strategy wants to return. #59299 notes that calibration is uncalibrated for now and that how to make it pluggable is not yet planned.

I've been running both pieces in an out-of-tree package on vLLM v0.30.0, with three backends behind one interface. With the next-token read and one temperature fitted at startup, Qwen3.8-27B INT4 matches Jev's hosted service on the easy and hard splits of JevBench (public), and on its speed score:

| | easy | standard | hard | speed score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Logit read, Qwen3.8-27B INT4 | 1.000 | 0.931 | 0.730 | 83.0 |
| Jev hosted | 1.000 | 0.986 | 0.730 | 83.3 |

**This RFC proposes making the read strategy modular and letting both endpoints accept custom parameters, on top of #59299 and #60465, so that new decision models plug in without core changes and callers can tune and inspect a read without breaking either published format.**

### Proposed Change.

I have designed a demonstration patch with docs and benchmark results here: https://github.com/Timiku/v1-decisions-vllm. It follows OpenAI's format on `/v1/decisions` and Jev's on `/v1/systemone`, and works where OpenAI leaves behaviour open. The differences are listed in its README. On Qwen3.8-27B INT4, the OpenAI Python SDK reads its responses unchanged, and the two endpoints return identical probabilities on all 231 JevBench public questions.

#### 1. Modular read strategies

- **A registry for strategies.** A strategy registers by name, directly or through an entry point (e.g. `vllm.decision_strategies`), and lists the architectures it serves. The server picks the one that claims the served model's architecture, with an operator override (flag or env var), and next-token as the fallback. This replaces the fixed mapping in `select_read_strategy`.
- **A small surface.** A strategy reads scores per option for a question; the server keeps everything else (prompt rendering, softmax and temperature, typed answers, limits). In my package that is one class with `read(question, request_id)` and an optional `read_many` for several questions that share a prefix. The canvas read (#57250) and the encoder read (#58429) fit in it as two more strategies.
- **Per-request choice and options.** A request may pick any loaded strategy and pass it options, validated by that strategy's own model, e.g. for next-token: the read mode (`exact` with `logprob_token_ids`, or the plain top-k list), and for canvas: the number of samples.
- **Strategy diagnostics.** Whatever a strategy reports (raw option logits, label mass, which read ran) comes back in the response's custom block, with the same shape on every strategy.

#### 2. Custom parameters on both endpoints

- **One block, the same on both endpoints**, for what neither format has a field for: calibration temperature, strategy and strategy options, seed, and how much diagnostic detail to return. On `/v1/decisions` an OpenAI SDK client sends it through `extra_body`, and a client that never sends it gets a plain OpenAI response. In my package it is called `extra`.
- **The answers carry the same block**, with the strategy's diagnostics and an audit record (served model, input hash, prompt version, the T applied and where it came from, tokens, cached tokens).
- **Custom question types on both endpoints.** #59299 already has a question-type registry. A registered type is accepted on both endpoints next to the format's own types and returns its own answer fields.
- **Calibration as a parameter.** A per-request temperature on top of a server default. Fitting that default at startup is optional and could come later.

#### Implementation roadmap

Separate PRs, each after its base lands:

1. Strategy registry, entry point and per-request strategy choice and options (after #59299).
2. The custom-parameter block on `/v1/systemone` and `/v1/decisions`, with per-request temperature and diagnostics (after #60465).
3. Encoder and canvas reads as strategies, unifying #58429 and #57250 (after the diffusion strategy #59299 mentions, or together with it).

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

#### Open questions

1. Name and shape of the block: one `extra` object on both endpoints as in my package, or vLLM's usual top-level extra fields? A single object keeps `/v1/decisions` free of fields OpenAI might add later.
2. Is an entry point for strategies OK, or should it start with built-ins plus a registry only?
3. Should per-request strategy choice be on by default, or opt-in by the operator?

#### Out of scope

- A separate endpoint or wire format: #59299 and #60465 cover those.
- Training or fine-tuning. Everything above runs on stock weights.

#### Disclosure

AI assistance was used in the research, building, and review of the demonstration code, as well as proofreading this RFC. I am responsible for the design of the API and have reviewed the tests' methodology and outputs.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: MoRIIO WRITE failure handling and safe KV block reclamation
author: yuzhouo7
body:
### Motivation.

MoRIIO WRITE can leave decode requests waiting with KV blocks allocated when the producer disappears (#59114). A receive timeout should fail the request, but should not by itself authorize block reuse. This RFC proposes using the scheduler's existing delayed-free path to separate request failure from eventual block release, and asks what event can safely authorize that release when no completion arrives.

In #59114, I reproduced the failure three times with four requests per run. After killing the prefill instance, clients timed out after approximately 400 seconds. Decode KV usage remained at 11.0998%, above its idle baseline, for another 295–388 seconds.

This shows failure to recover during the observation window. Block ownership was not traced, so it does not establish a permanent leak, a specific leaked block count, whether writes remained in flight, or whether late writes corrupted reused blocks.

The correctness concern is separate from that observation: a timeout tells D to stop waiting, but does not establish that the old transfer can no longer write its destination.

The initial scope is MoRIIO WRITE. Transparent retry, broader P/D failover, READ-mode changes, and connector-wide redesign are out of scope.

### Proposed Change.

Keep request failure and authorization to reuse blocks separate.

#### Receive lifetime

Pending receive tracking should remain independent of the client request. Client abort or disconnect should not discard the mapping or disable tracking for an unfinished receive.

The receive-wait watchdog should be disarmed when the receive completes, not when the request finishes. A request that has received its KV and is still decoding should no longer be subject to it.

A timeout should be reported once for a live request. If the client has already cancelled, cleanup should continue without producing another terminal outcome. Internal receive/block tracking should remain until safe termination or verified recovery.

Timeout detection and cleanup should continue after client disconnect and without new traffic.

#### Lifecycle and ownership

In `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`, `finish_requests()` can already make a `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` request terminal while `delay_free_blocks` keeps its blocks allocated. I propose using that path as the starting point rather than introducing connector-owned block allocation.

On timeout, the request should reach an error/terminal path while block release remains delayed. Receive/block tracking should remain available for later completion or recovery. Reporting request failure must not itself authorize block reuse.

There are three separate questions:

- **Request fate:** whether the request is still waiting or has failed/cancelled. Later transfer events must not revive a terminal request.
- **Transfer safety:** whether the old transfer can still write the affected blocks. Timeout, cancellation, and request failure do not establish safe termination.
- **KV validity and allocation:** whether the received KV is usable for decode and when its blocks may be reused. Safe termination does not make partial or failed KV valid.

The connector interface allows a failed receive to report load errors together with `finished_recving`, so `finished_recving` does not necessarily mean that KV transfer succeeded. However, processing it may allow the scheduler to release blocks.

For retained blocks, `finished_recving` or another release-authorizing scheduler input should not be emitted until safe transfer termination is established. A late `write_done` may complete cleanup only if its completion semantics establish that condition. It must not revive the request or release blocks twice.

Recomputation must follow the same boundary: it must not start on memory that the old transfer may still modify.

#### Failure and reclamation

Block reuse requires a no-further-writes guarantee covering both already-submitted writes and later submissions from the old transfer/session.

The relevant writers are those that could target the affected blocks, including participating ranks with such access. If D cannot establish that all of them are covered, reuse remains unauthorized.

Without that guarantee, the affected blocks should remain retained and recovery should be treated as required.

One conservative option is to end the affected request, retain its blocks, and pause new P/D admission to that D instance after a receive timeout whose safe termination cannot be established. Admission would resume after verified recovery. This could stall the entire D instance after one failure, so it is an option for discussion rather than a fixed policy.

If this policy is chosen, the admission enforcement point also needs to be defined.

Verified recovery must establish the no-further-writes guarantee before retained blocks return to the allocatable pool. If recovery uses a reset, its teardown must provide that guarantee. The appropriate recovery scope—transfer, connection, or engine—is still open. This RFC does not propose a new MoRI fencing API.

Isolated blocks still consume physical capacity. Accounting may distinguish normal request occupancy from failure-isolation occupancy, but isolated blocks must remain unavailable for allocation.

#### Alternatives

Immediate free after timeout bounds retention but does not provide the required safety guarantee. Retaining affected blocks until verified safe termination avoids premature reuse and may allow other requests to continue if block isolation is reliable. Pausing admission to the affected D instance until verified recovery is more conservative but sacrifices that instance's availability.

### Feedback Period.

One week initially.

### CC List.

@ErliCai @amirakb89 @inkcherry @KuntaiDu @tjtanaa

### Any Other Things.

#### Related Work

- #59058 preserves WRITE receive mappings after consumer abort so late completion can still reach cleanup.
- #58962 adds the WRITE consumer watchdog and timeout lifecycle. This RFC separates the decision to stop waiting from the conditions that authorize subsequent block reclamation.

Follow-up changes should build on these PRs rather than introduce a competing timeout implementation.

#### Validation

Planned validation uses deterministic CPU tests for lifecycle bookkeeping, followed by GPU/RDMA fault injection for transport-safety claims:

- Normal completion, including a request that has finished receiving KV but is still decoding.
- Client abort followed by late completion.
- Producer loss with and without client abort, including cleanup after disconnect with no new traffic.
- Late or duplicate activity after timeout, checking that terminal requests remain terminal, unsafe memory is not used for recomputation, and blocks are not released twice.
- Block ownership and data integrity, including a multi-rank transfer where only one participating rank fails.

These are validation goals, not completed results for this design. CPU bookkeeping tests cannot establish the RDMA no-further-writes guarantee.

#### Questions

1. From the description of ROCm/mori#670, my current reading is that it adds producer-side failure reporting, rejects later submissions on degraded endpoints, and makes retry parameters configurable. I have not found a documented consumer-side guarantee there covering both already-submitted writes and later writes from the old transfer/session. Does an existing teardown operation provide that guarantee, and at what scope: transfer, connection, or engine?

2. Can `finish_requests()` plus `delay_free_blocks` carry "receive timed out, request failed, blocks not reusable yet," or does timeout handling need an additional scheduler-facing failure signal? What receive tracking and later release events are needed so that `finished_recving` is not emitted until safe termination is known?

3. When safe reclamation cannot be established, what recovery scope should we use: transfer, connection, or engine? Should the first-cut policy pause new P/D admission to the affected D instance, or can block isolation support continued service safely? Where should that admission decision be enforced?

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Weight Reload Refactor
author: hao-aaron
body:
> **Revisions**
> - **Rev 3 (2026-10-19), current.** Design changes from rev 2:
>   - DIRECT modules run PWAL once at finish; only MODULEWISE modules run it as they complete.
>   - One `refresh()` tree walk replaces `register_refresh`, `refresh_model()` and `post_load_setup()`. MLA absorption moves into the attention layer's `refresh()`, so no PWAL reads another module.
>   - `reload_safe` flags on every post-load component (quant methods, kernels, attention layers and impls), checked once at `init_weight_transfer_engine`. `SupportsReload` becomes a marker.
>   - Coverage at finish (failing an update with a missing shard) is deferred. Completion stays.
> - Rev 2 (2026-10-17): direct loading by default with modulewise fallback, arrival units, opt-in core, one PR per family. Responses to the rev 1 review are [below](#user-content-responses-to-review).
> - Rev 1 (2026-09-30): layerwise with first-touch materialization, element counting, full integrity first. Full text is in the edit history.

## PR Tracker

```
PR 1 fixes + harness ─► PR 2 post-load contract ─► PR 3 core (opt-in) ─► family PRs (Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, Nemotron) ─► flip default ─► delete layerwise
                                                              └──────► RDT / nccl_m2n (separate design) ─────────────────────────────────┘
```

- [ ] **PR 1: Reload fixes on main, refit harness** (#61287)
  - Fixes on today's path: gpt-oss Quark and fused-BF16 experts through the param loader; loader routing for colpali, colqwen3/3.5, nano_nemotron_vl, nemotron_parse, pixtral, voxtral; KV-scale dtype on reload; FlashInfer device bmm scales; online block-FP8 QuantFP8 op; DeepSeek-V3.2 indexer pairing state on `self`.
  - Refit-equals-fresh harness and tests.
- [ ] **PR 2: Post-load contract, no behavior change** (#60931)
  - The `refresh()` tree walk, `reload_safe` flags, the `SupportsReload` marker, the reload-safety check and `check_reload_support`.
  - MoE kernels built once, with weight-derived values refreshed in place: FP8, MXFP4, NVFP4, CT/Quark FP8, online FP8/INT8/MXFP8.
  - Cold start runs the same refresh walk and stays bitwise identical to main. Build-once applies only under the core; layerwise keeps main's rebuild.
- [ ] **PR 3: Reload core, opt-in** (`VLLM_RELOAD_CORE=1`)
  - DIRECT / MODULEWISE per module, arrival units and completion, post steps, slim integrity, the `collective_rpc` fix.
  - Benchmark: sync time and peak memory against layerwise.
- [ ] **PRs 4…N: one per supported family**: move weight-derived model-level work into `refresh()`, add `SupportsReload`, audit model-local loaders, add a refit case on the core.
  - [ ] Qwen
  - [ ] GLM
  - [ ] DeepSeek
  - [ ] Kimi
  - [ ] Nemotron
- [ ] **Flip the default** to the core. `VLLM_RELOAD_LEGACY=1` selects layerwise.
- [ ] **RDT / `nccl_m2n`** (separate design).
- [ ] **Delete layerwise**, one release after the flip and after the RDT / `nccl_m2n` track.

## TL;DR

RL frameworks update a running engine through `start_weight_update` → `update_weights` → `finish_weight_update`. The NCCL and IPC transports, and `reload_weights` from a path, all feed checkpoint-format tensors to the model's own `load_weights` under **layerwise reload**. Layerwise works for every quantization method, but:

- **Memory.** It buffers incoming tensors until a module is complete. Under NCCL broadcast that includes other ranks' TP rows and every expert the rank doesn't own.
- **Stale state under CUDA graphs.** PWAL rebuilds kernel objects, and values they derive (MoE alphas, `1/a1_scale`, FlashInfer KV scales) move while captured graphs keep reading the old addresses.
- **Silent failures.** Completion is inferred from element counts, writes other than `aten.copy_` are invisible, and a failed update can resume serving half-updated weights.

After an update, the engine must serve exactly what a fresh load of the same checkpoint would, with the cold-start CUDA graphs still in place and bounded extra memory. This RFC proposes a reload core built on four decisions:

1. **`load_weights` is the contract.** Every transport ends by passing checkpoint-named tensors to `model.load_weights`. Neither transports nor RL frameworks touch quant methods, kernels or module internals.
2. **Write in place when the live bytes can hold the checkpoint tensor (DIRECT).** Otherwise fall back to MODULEWISE: layerwise without GPU buffering or element counting. The choice is made per module, from metadata.
3. **PWAL is the only checkpoint → kernel transform, and kernels are built once.** After an update PWAL rewrites the same tensors in place, and `refresh()` hooks, found by walking the module tree, recompute derived state.
4. **DIRECT costs no extra memory for weights.** MODULEWISE scratch is only this rank's partition of a module, freed as soon as it completes.

The core lands opt-in and purely additive. Supported families convert one PR at a time, then the default flips and layerwise is deleted a release later.

**Scope.** We officially support and validate five families: Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Nemotron. Other models can opt in the same way; until they do, they get a warning, not a guarantee.

## Goals and non-goals

**Goals**

- A fresh-load-equivalent engine after every successful update, with CUDA graphs reused.
- One contract for every transport that feeds `load_weights`: IPC, NCCL (packed or not) and disk.
- Peak extra memory bounded by the per-rank scratch of the MODULEWISE modules open at once, and zero for DIRECT modules.
- Fail loudly before any write when an update can't be done correctly. A failed update never silently resumes serving.

**Non-goals**

- Rollback, and inverse transforms from kernel layout back to checkpoint layout.
- Partial (sparse or delta) writes into kernel layouts.
- Sharded RDT and `nccl_m2n`. They write into storage without calling `load_weights` on every update, so they get a separate design and stay on layerwise until then.
- Coverage: proving at finish that every module received its weights. Deferred (see [Loading](#user-content-3-loading-arrival-units-and-completion)).
- Improving layerwise. It stays the default until the flip and is then deleted.

## Proposed design

"Module" means any `nn.Module` that directly owns loadable tensors (a `QKVParallelLinear`, a `RoutedExperts`), not a decoder layer.

### 1. External API

The RL-facing calls are unchanged, on `LLM`, `AsyncLLM` and the HTTP router: `pause_generation` → `start_weight_update` → `update_weights` (any number of times) → `finish_weight_update` → `resume_generation`. A transport is correct if it delivers the same name/tensor pairs a checkpoint on disk would.

**Failure contract.**

- A failed start, update or finish raises on the caller. vLLM aborts the update, puts the original tensor objects back, and marks the engine dirty, because DIRECT modules may hold half-written bytes.
- While dirty, `resume_generation` refuses, so requests queue instead of reaching a corrupted model. The next successful full update clears the flag; a sparse update can't. With multiple ranks, every rank agrees before resuming.

**Kept internal.** Frameworks never see the DIRECT / MODULEWISE choice, when PWAL runs, quant-method hooks, `SupportsReload`, or the core's environment flags. `check_reload_support()` (`GET /check_reload_support`) returns the reload-safety report (§5), so frameworks can read it at startup.

### 2. Pre-processing: DIRECT and MODULEWISE

Every weight loader writes into a tensor shaped like the checkpoint, so each module needs such a target.

- **DIRECT (new).** If the live bytes can hold the checkpoint tensor, they are the target. The loader writes straight into live memory, and PWAL transforms it in place at finish. Nothing is allocated for the weights.
- **MODULEWISE (fallback).** On a module's first write, the core materializes checkpoint-layout scratch and the loader writes into it directly. When the module's expected units are in (§3), PWAL runs, the results are copied into the live tensors, and the scratch is freed. Only modules still receiving data hold scratch.

**Deciding whether scratch is needed.** Right after the model is constructed, `record_metadata_for_reloading` snapshots every param and persistent buffer as a meta tensor, keeping its class and `__dict__` (so `weight_loader`, `input_dim` and so on survive). That snapshot is the per-rank partition in checkpoint layout, from `create_weights`, before any PWAL. At `start_weight_update` the core compares it with the live tensor:

| Target | When | Extra memory |
|---|---|---|
| As-is | Live tensor matches the snapshot exactly and owns its storage | 0 |
| View | Different shape or stride, but the live bytes are large enough, aligned, and not shared | 0 |
| Scratch | Anything else: online quant (BF16 in, FP8 live), tensor subclasses, released params | The module's per-rank shard in checkpoint dtype |

A module is DIRECT when every tensor is as-is or a view; otherwise the whole module is MODULEWISE, so PWAL always sees one consistent layout. The decision follows from what PWAL actually did to the tensor, never from a quant method's claim. One exception keeps the big weights DIRECT: a small scale that PWAL shrinks gets a temporary **side buffer**. In per-tensor FP8 MoE the checkpoint `w13_weight_scale` is `[E, 2]` and PWAL reduces it to `[E]`; only that scale is buffered, and `w13_weight` / `w2_weight` are still written in place.

| Module | Path |
|---|---|
| Unquantized; block FP8; MXFP4 / NVFP4 weights; most MoE, shuffled or not | DIRECT, as-is |
| Per-tensor FP8 linear (`[K,N]` live vs `[N,K]` checkpoint) | DIRECT, view |
| Per-tensor FP8 / NVFP4 MoE | DIRECT, scales in side buffers |
| Online quantization (BF16 checkpoint, FP8 or MXFP8 live) | MODULEWISE |
| torchao subclasses, kernel-held opaque weights | MODULEWISE |

Two rules keep DIRECT safe: no forward runs between start and finish (start checks the engine is paused), and a DIRECT module's PWAL runs only at finish, after every module has landed. `VLLM_RELOAD_DIRECT=0` forces MODULEWISE everywhere. GPU incoming tensors are never buffered; CPU incoming tensors for a MODULEWISE module wait in host memory and are replayed into scratch once its units are in.

### 3. Loading: arrival units and completion

The core needs to know when a module is complete, for correctness (PWAL on a half-written module corrupts it) and for memory (MODULEWISE scratch can only be freed after landing). The trainer can't say: it sends checkpoint names in any order and batching, and doesn't know how vLLM fuses them (q, k, v into `qkv_proj`).

**Why not count elements.** Layerwise compares elements `copy_`'d with the module's size. Shared scale slots and duplicate shards over-count, so PWAL fires early on partial data. Padding under-counts, so scratch is held until finish. Writes other than `aten.copy_` are invisible.

**Count loader calls instead.** The core wraps every `weight_loader`; each call becomes a key `(module, tensor, shard, checkpoint name)`, with `shard` read from the loader's own arguments (`"*"`, `"q"`, `("w1", 7)`). A dry run of `load_weights` over metadata only gives each module its expected count per key. Each call decrements its key, and a module is complete when all counts reach zero.

- Counting writes, not names, matters: the shared MoE loader turns one fused `experts.gate_up_proj` name into 2E calls, and under EP each rank declines the experts it doesn't own, so the expected counts differ per rank and must be observed from the real loaders.
- Expected counts come from, in priority order: trainer metadata (sent at `init_weight_transfer_engine` when `send_weight_metadata` is on), the checkpoint's safetensors headers, or the keys observed during the cold load.
- Loaders usually need nothing. A loader that skips another rank's data calls `report_declined()`.
- An unexpected key warns and that module completes at finish (correct, costs memory). A key arriving more often than exact metadata declares raises. A call after its module completed raises.

**How each path uses it.** MODULEWISE: counts reaching zero trigger PWAL, landing and freeing scratch. DIRECT: only "touched" matters; at finish PWAL runs on every touched DIRECT module in tree order, and an untouched one is skipped (its bytes are already kernel layout).

**Coverage (deferred).** Finish doesn't yet check that every count reached zero. Callers are assumed to send the whole model; a module never sent keeps its old weights, and a DIRECT module sent only in part would get PWAL over mixed bytes. The counts are exactly what the coverage check will read once it lands.

### 4. Post-processing: PWAL and refresh

**When PWAL runs.** Each module has one PWAL, the one cold start calls: its quant method's, or the attention layer's own.

| Module | PWAL runs |
|---|---|
| MODULEWISE | As soon as the module completes, so its scratch is freed early |
| DIRECT | At finish, if touched |
| Declared `pwal_at_finish` | At finish, on every rank, in tree order |
| Declared `none` | Never: the loader already wrote kernel layout (as #60096 does for MegaMoE) |

The declaration is `reload_post_step` on the quant method. `none` is opt-in, listed by the reload-safety report, and needs a refit test. No PWAL needs `pwal_at_finish` today; it stays for future cross-module or EP-collective cases.

**Collectives.** Some PWALs run collectives: online FP8 amax over TP or the MoE group, static FP8 / NVFP4 MoE input scales over EP under EPLB, MLA with DCP. We assume every rank in a group receives data in the same order, which holds for NCCL broadcast, so ranks of a TP group complete a MODULEWISE module at the same point. EP is the exception (see [Known issues](#user-content-known-issues)).

**Build once.** Rebuilding kernel objects or derived tensors after cold start leaves captured graphs reading freed or stale storage. Kernels are built at cold start and reused on update (`FusedMoEMethodBase.reuses_kernel()`), derived tensors are registered buffers filled in place, and values computed from weights are recomputed by `refresh()`.

**Refresh: one hook, found by walking the tree.** After every PWAL and landing, one function walks the model children first, calling `quant_method.refresh(module)` and then `module.refresh()` wherever defined. It replaces `register_refresh` (the MoE runner's fused gate and KDA's merged conv just define `refresh()`), `refresh_model()` (the model class defines `refresh()`, reached last), and the derived half of attention PWAL (MLA `W_UK_T` / `W_UV` move into the attention layer's `refresh()`). A kernel's internal chain (quant config → prepare/finalize → experts) stays inside `quant_method.refresh`. Cold start and core finish call the same walk; layerwise is unchanged.

Rules for a refresh:

1. It reads only params and buffers, not another object's derived tensors.
2. It writes only derived tensors it declared, in place, allocated on the first call (at cold start, before graph capture).
3. It is idempotent.
4. It runs on every rank, unconditionally, never skipped because a module wasn't touched (MLA with DCP all-gathers inside absorption).

Setup that isn't derived from weights (compiling, memory placement) stays where it is; it only has to be harmless to rerun if an update reruns it.

### 5. Reload safety: `reload_safe` and `SupportsReload`

Each post-load protocol is a promise by a different author. Before the first update, the engine checks that every piece of this model, with this quantization and serving config, has made it.

**Each author stamps their own code.** `reload_safe` flags go on `QuantizeMethodBase` (default False; may be a property to veto a backend branch), on the kernel bases (MoE prepare/finalize and experts, the linear kernel bases), on `AttentionLayerBase`, and on `AttentionImplBase` (default True). A flag covers that author's code, including its `refresh()`, and nothing it delegates to. Runtime-chosen components (the kernel a method's oracle picked, the attention impls the selector picked) carry their own flags, so the check ANDs the objects actually in use. The model author vouches only for model code (module classes, `load_weights`, the model's `refresh()`) by implementing the marker `SupportsReload`; that code is trusted, not inspected, and refit tests prove the values.

**The check** runs once at `init_weight_transfer_engine`, after cold start: one pass over `named_modules()` checking the root for `SupportsReload`, each quant method AND the kernel it built, and each attention-like layer with a PWAL AND its impls. Each finding is SAFE, UNSAFE (names the module, component and reason) or UNVERIFIED (no marker).

**Enforcement**, refusing only what is known wrong:

- UNSAFE components are refused on the core under CUDA graphs and warned in eager mode.
- UNVERIFIED and the layerwise path only warn.
- `VLLM_RELOAD_ALLOW_UNSAFE=1` turns refusals into warnings (generalizes `VLLM_RELOAD_ALLOW_UNSAFE_MOE`).
- `start_weight_update` keeps its runtime checks for what can change after init: live tensor signatures and kernel objects replaced since the last update.

**Why a model's own PWAL is never called on reload.** Quant-method and attention PWALs have one job, converting their own tensors, so they can be rerun. A model's or submodule's own PWAL is arbitrary code that mixes weight-derived work, one-time setup and code that only works once. Reload can't tell these apart, so it calls none of them; the contract asks model authors to move weight-derived work into `refresh()`.

**Opting in.** PR 2 opts in everything known safe today (unquantized linear and embedding, the KV-cache method, the MoE backends in today's safe lists, `Attention`, `MLAAttention` and their default impls, the kernel bases they use). Anything new starts at False. To opt in a quant method, follow `Fp8MoEMethod`: always transform, build the kernel only if it doesn't exist, keep derived values in registered buffers that `refresh()` recomputes, set `reload_safe`, add a refit case.

### 6. Integrity (slim, in PR 3)

1. **Pause check.** The engine core refuses `start_weight_update` unless no step can run: `PAUSED_ALL`, or `PAUSED_NEW` with no requests left.
2. **Abort and dirty on failure.** Any exception aborts the session (original objects back, loaders unwrapped, scratch freed), sets the dirty bit and re-raises. A new start aborts a leftover session.
3. **No resume while dirty.** `EngineCore.resume_scheduler` (also called by `wake_up`) refuses while any worker is dirty. New requests queue rather than being rejected, which hung offline DP `generate()` on the prototype.
4. **Clearing.** The next successful non-sparse update clears the bit.
5. **`collective_rpc` after a one-rank failure.** `MultiprocExecutor.collective_rpc` now reads every expected reply before raising, so stale replies don't leak into the next call. Not gated by the flag.

Full integrity (auto-pause, serve guard, module sets on the API, structured reload report) is a follow-up.

### 7. What the opt-in flag gates

With `VLLM_RELOAD_CORE` unset, none of these run and layerwise behaves as on main:

| Place | Gated behavior |
|---|---|
| `start_reload` / `finish_reload` | Choose layerwise |
| Cold load | Key observation and the name-tracking wrapper |
| `init_weight_transfer_engine` | The dry run over trainer metadata |
| `reload_weights` | The safetensors header dry run |
| Engine core | The pause check and slim integrity |
| PR 2's reload-side behavior | Build-once, strict landing, refusal of UNSAFE components |

Sharded RDT and `nccl_m2n` call the layerwise entry points directly, so they stay on layerwise before and after the flip.

## Peak memory

Extra GPU memory of an update is at most: the transport's receive buffers (packed NCCL defaults to 2 × 1 GiB), DIRECT side buffers (scales only), the scratch of MODULEWISE modules open at once (each this rank's shard, about one module when the trainer sends in module order), and PWAL's own temporaries (the same as cold start).

Kimi K3 estimate (93 layers, 896 routed experts in 92 MoE layers, MXFP4 routed experts, everything else BF16), peak extra memory per GPU from the routed experts, on top of the transport buffers:

| Case | Path | EP = 8 | EP = 16 | EP = 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MXFP4 checkpoint, MXFP4 serving | DIRECT, as-is | ≈ 0 | ≈ 0 | ≈ 0 |
| Online quantization (BF16 checkpoint) | MODULEWISE, one layer open | 6.9 GiB | 3.4 GiB | 0.86 GiB |
| Layerwise today, MXFP4 checkpoint | One layer materialized | 1.8 GiB | 0.92 GiB | 0.23 GiB |
| Layerwise today, online quantization | One layer of BF16 | 6.9 GiB | 3.4 GiB | 0.86 GiB |

This assumes layer-ordered sends; if the trainer interleaves layers, every partly sent MODULEWISE module holds its scratch (worst case all 92 layers, 317 GiB per GPU at EP = 16).

Measured on the prototype (single GB200, Qwen3-30B-A3B, peak over baseline):

| Model | Core | Forced MODULEWISE | Layerwise |
|---|---|---|---|
| BF16 | 0.64 GiB | 2.32 GiB | 2.62 GiB |
| FP8-block | 1.29 GiB | 1.75 GiB | 2.10 GiB |
| Online FP8 | 2.85 GiB | 2.85 GiB | 3.18 GiB |
| NVFP4 | 0.59 GiB | 1.48 GiB | 1.47 GiB |

Sync time hasn't been measured on the code this plan lands; PR 3 reports it for the core, forced MODULEWISE and layerwise, over packed NCCL from a sharded trainer.

## Known issues

- **Host-float scales baked into CUDA graphs.** The KV-cache method also keeps q/k/v scales as Python floats (`_k_scale_float`), which some decode paths pass as kernel arguments, so captured graphs bake them in and no in-place refresh changes them. The core refuses a change only for impls declaring `float_scales_in_decode` (FlashInfer). K3's CuTe DSL MLA decode reads them without declaring it, as do the native FlashInfer decode wrapper, DCP decode and attention + output-quant fusion. Fix options: detect any changed `_*_scale_float` and refuse under graphs, or make them 0-dim device tensors. RL checkpoints usually keep KV scales fixed.
- **A collective PWAL in a MODULEWISE module under EP.** Ranks decline different experts, so they can complete the same module at different points; a PWAL collective over the EP group could hang. It doesn't arise today: the EP collectives (input scales under EPLB) belong to static FP8 / NVFP4 MoE, which are DIRECT and run at finish. The fallback is `pwal_at_finish`, at the cost of holding that module's scratch.
- **MoE methods not declared `reload_safe`** are refused on the core under graphs: NVFP4 on B12x, MXFP8 on Triton, MXFP4 on FlashInfer CUTLASS, online MXFP4.
- **DeepSeek-V4 with FlashInfer MoE-EP experts** keeps weights in a FlashInfer object that graphs likely read; it needs an in-place refill API.
- **Level-2 sleep** frees all GPU memory and restores only registered buffers; off-registry constants come back as garbage until registered (#60009). `sleep(2)` followed by `wake_up()` also resumes before weights are reloaded.
- **EPLB.** `build_expert_params_mapping` uses the initial placement, so a reload after a rearrangement may write each expert into its startup slot. Not reproduced yet; needs a regression test and an update gate (#59063).
- **Validated only at small scale.** A full-size Kimi K3 / DeepSeek-V4 refit in graph mode (EP ≥ 2, DeepGEMM MegaMoE) is pending.

## Relation to RFC #54477 and #58382

[RFC #54477](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54477) (Selective Weight Reload) and its PR #58382 share this RFC's goals: stable `data_ptr()`s, `load_weights` as the only router, kernels built once, derived state refreshed in place, and explicit failure semantics. #58382's direct mode (loaders write live params; finish checks nothing moved) is this RFC's DIRECT-as-is case.

| | #54477 / #58382 | This RFC |
|---|---|---|
| Live layout ≠ checkpoint layout | Loader-side quantization, or explicit staging | View, side buffer or MODULEWISE scratch, chosen automatically |
| Transform on reload | Per-method refresh hooks | PWAL itself, the same code cold start runs |
| Derived state | `refresh_derived_state()` per method | `refresh()` found by the tree walk |
| Failure | Terminal | Dirty bit: paused until a successful full update |

We'd like one shared implementation of the refresh contract and the reload-safety check.

## Responses to review

| Comment | Response |
|---|---|
| **@aoshen02 1: staging should be the exception.** | Adopted in rev 2. DIRECT is the default; MODULEWISE only when live bytes can't hold the checkpoint tensor, chosen automatically from the snapshot. |
| **@aoshen02 2: completion from element counts is fragile.** | Adopted. `CopyCounter` is replaced by counting loader calls against expected counts observed from metadata. Coverage at finish is deferred in rev 3; the counts are what it will read. |
| **@aoshen02 3: reload runs a different PWAL branch; loader first; latency unmeasured.** | Reload runs the same PWAL as cold start. A module whose loader writes kernel layout declares `none` (#60096 does this for MegaMoE). PR 3 reports sync time and peak memory against layerwise. |
| **@ShuoleiWang 1: dirty clears on an empty finish.** | Dirty clears only on a successful non-sparse update on the core. |
| **@ShuoleiWang 2: required keys per name, not per shard; duplicate shards.** | Keys are per shard and per local expert. A key arriving more often than exact metadata declares raises. Missing-shard detection at finish comes with coverage (deferred). |
| **@ShuoleiWang 3: `refresh_derived_state` misses attention; sparse NCCL patches.** | The refresh walk runs on every module on every update, touched or not, attention included. Session-less sparse patches are unchanged and correct only where live layout equals checkpoint layout; sparse updates are refused while dirty. |

## Prototype and validation

**Rev 1** ([`hao-aaron/vllm:modulewise-reload-clean`](https://github.com/hao-aaron/vllm/tree/modulewise-reload-clean)) validated the modulewise mechanism on 4× GB200: about 25 configurations reloaded bitwise equal to a fresh load in graph mode with zero pointer changes, across dense, MLA, Mamba hybrid, FP8 / NVFP4 / MXFP4 MoE backends and online quantization, over NCCL, IPC and sharded RDT.

**Rev 2** ([`hao-aaron/vllm:reload-direct-modulewise`](https://github.com/hao-aaron/vllm/tree/reload-direct-modulewise)), built as a GPU-gated stack: reload unit and integration suites, refit-equals-fresh cases, online cold start, tiny real-format family checkpoints and all nine MoE backend matrix suites pass, also with MODULEWISE forced everywhere; weight-transfer (127) and sharded RDT (219) suites pass; an end-to-end weight-sync audit passes on Qwen3-0.6B and OLMoE. Shadow mode (keys recorded next to `CopyCounter`) found the counter completing `RoutedExperts` early in 16 of 16 layers on OLMoE static FP8, and 3 early and 3 never-complete modules on tiny K3; the keys were right in each case.

## PR plan

**Why this order.** Model-by-model alone multiplies per-model reload paths with no shared contract. Core-first with the default on day one would silently serve stale state for models that still finalize inside `load_weights` or keep derived state in plain attributes. So: a general core, opt-in; then one family at a time; then flip.

**Principles.**

- The core is purely additive until the flip; with the flag unset no core code runs.
- Structural PRs first, model conversions last; family PRs can land in any order before the flip.
- Every intermediate commit passes the reload unit, weight-transfer and sharded RDT suites and the refit cases enabled so far. Cases failing on main start as `xfail(strict=True)`.

| PR | Scope | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fixes on today's path, refit harness (#61287) | main |
| 2 | Post-load contract: refresh walk, `reload_safe`, `SupportsReload`, build-once MoE, reload-safety check. No behavior change | 1 |
| 3 | The core, opt-in: paths, arrival units, post steps, slim integrity, `collective_rpc` fix, benchmark | 2 |
| 4…N | One per supported family | 2, 3 |
| Flip | Core becomes the default; gated by the refit and weight-transfer suites with the core on | all above |
| Delete | Layerwise, `CopyCounter`, `weight_loader_numel` and the flag, one release after the flip and the RDT / m2n track | Flip |

**Supported families.**

| Family | Candidates | Known conversion work |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen | Qwen3 dense and MoE; Qwen3.5 / Next | None known for Qwen3 |
| GLM | GLM-4.x MoE; GLM-5-Next | KDA merged conv weight → `refresh()` |
| DeepSeek | V3 / V3.2 (MLA); V4 / V4.1 with MTP and DSpark | mHC broadcast → `refresh()`; remove finalize-in-`load_weights` |
| Kimi | K2; Kimi-Linear (KDA); K3 with DSpark | DSpark stacks → `refresh()`; KDA side copies |
| Nemotron | Nemotron-H / Nano (Mamba hybrid) | To be checked |

#60096 and #60064 load MegaMoE experts and DeepSeek-V4.1 mega attention straight into kernel layout, so those have no post-load step left.

**Follow-ups.** Coverage at finish, full integrity, per-expert completion for online MoE if the benchmark shows it matters, and kernel-format (runtime-layout) updates.

**De-risking.** Shadow mode (done on the prototype), a loader audit per family, fault injection (drop or duplicate a shard, reorder, stop mid-update), property tests over random batching (refit equals fresh over 1000+ seeds), forced MODULEWISE as a required CI stage, flag-off equivalence until the flip, and end-to-end weight-sync audits at each step of the sequence.

## Open questions

1. **#54477 / #58382 authors:** can we share one refresh contract and reload-safety check?
2. **Rollout:** is opt-in → per-family validation → flip → delete the right path, and is one release between flip and deletion enough?
3. **Integrity scope:** is slim integrity enough for PR 3?
4. **Send order:** should the trainer helpers enforce layer-ordered sends, or only document them? MODULEWISE peak memory depends on it.
5. **Drafters:** should EAGLE / MTP / DSpark drafters update with the main model or stay frozen? Until decided, they warn.
