title: [RFC]: Opt-in return of the last hidden state at sampled positions, per request (Model Runner V2)
author: aminry
body:
### Motivation.

A growing class of deployments puts a small trained head on top of a served model: a linear probe, a per-task classifier over a fixed label set, a calibration layer.
Such a head needs two things from one forward pass: the model's scores for a few tokens, and the hidden state those scores were computed from.
vLLM returns the first (logprobs, `logprob_token_ids`) but not the second.

Today there are two ways to get it, and both are costly:

1. **A second engine in pooling mode** (`LLM.encode` with last-token pooling).
   It holds a second copy of the weights, and it runs a different runner and kernels, so its hidden state is not the one the generate engine's scores came from.
   In our deployment (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, FP8, RTX PRO 6000), the label readout computed from the pooling engine's state picked the same top label as the generate engine's own readout on 97.3% of 150 Banking77 items (100% of 100 CLINC items), with a median largest probability difference of 0.016.
2. **A model class that overwrites reserved logit columns with the hidden state**, read back through `allowed_token_ids` and logprobs (`h_j = lp_j - lp_0`).
   It works, but it is a workaround: the sampler allows at most 1,024 ids per request, so a 2,048-dimensional state takes three requests sent one at a time (identical requests batched together are not the same forward on FP8 MoE stacks), which costs a median 113 ms per question, against 35 ms for one request that returns the labels and the state with this change (RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q).
   It also makes a text generation that samples a reserved id meaningless, so the class can never be the default.
   This is what [Decisio](https://github.com/aminry/decisio), the open project this RFC comes from, runs today ([design note](https://github.com/aminry/decisio/blob/main/docs/design/hidden-state-readout.md)).

The same need comes up elsewhere, always in its narrow form (the last layer, at the positions tokens are sampled from):
- #48743 (open): inline return of extracted hidden states; commenters ask for "the narrow version: final-layer hidden state in the generation response", for example for on-policy distillation in TRL (the final hidden state is a cheap exact substitute for the full-vocabulary distribution);
- #18176 (closed): the last layer's last-token hidden state for inference verification (TopLOC);
- #24288, #6165, #4435 (closed): general requests.

Earlier proposals were declined or superseded for reasons this RFC is designed around:
- hot-path cost and complexity for everyone (#15434, #18176): here, the engine flag is off by default, and with it off the model runner holds no state and does no work;
- serialisation size and the risk of large payloads (#18176): here, the output is one `hidden_size` vector per generated token, only for requests that ask, only on engines that allow it;
- general layer or prompt extraction (#24288, #33118): that is served by the hidden-states extraction connector (#33736), and this RFC does not touch it.

**Open proposals in the same area, and how this differs.**

| | This RFC | #57185 | RFC #56916 / #57736 | #48743 (with #33736) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Returned | the tensor `compute_logits` received for each generated token, one row per token | the final hidden state at the last prompt position (the state the first output token is predicted from), one vector per request | hidden-state rows for the output tokens in a requested window, optionally auxiliary layers | auxiliary-layer hidden states captured by the extraction connector, returned inline |
| Requests | any length, `n > 1`, stop tokens; rows with the final output | one generated token, `n = 1`, non-streaming | response-relative or absolute windows | connector parameters |
| Models | any Model Runner V2 generation model | native Qwen2 and Qwen3.5 | not limited | models with auxiliary-hidden-state support |
| API | a typed `SamplingParams` field, a `CompletionOutput` field, an engine flag | `kv_transfer_params` / `extra_args` | a capture plan on the request | KV connector configuration |
| Size (library) | about 150 lines, no new abstraction | a larger change across the Python and Rust frontends | a new capture module through the stack | the connector, plus inline return |

The use case here (a head reading the scores and the state of the same forward, for every generated token, on any model) is not covered by #57185, which returns the prompt's final state for one-token requests on two model families, nor by the windowed capture of #56916, which targets rollout collection and adds a capture plan and its lifecycle.
This RFC proposes the smallest standalone version; if maintainers prefer one of those as the vehicle, its semantics (the exact `compute_logits` input, every generated token, a typed output) could be folded into it instead.

### Proposed Change.

**API.**
- Engine: `enable_return_last_hidden_states: bool = False` on `ModelConfig` (`--enable-return-last-hidden-states`, `LLM(..., enable_return_last_hidden_states=True)`).
  Excluded from the compile hash: it does not change the forward.
- Request: `SamplingParams.return_last_hidden_states: bool = False`.
  Rejected at validation (`VLLMValidationError`) when the engine flag is off, so it can never be silently ignored.
- Output: `CompletionOutput.last_hidden_states: torch.Tensor | None`, shaped `[len(token_ids), hidden_size]`, CPU, in the model's dtype, one row per generated token, returned with the final output (as `routed_experts` and `sampling_mask` are).
  Row `i` is exactly the tensor the model's `compute_logits` received for generated token `i`: for most decoder models, the last layer's output after the final norm.

**Semantics.**
- Exact: rows are gathered from the same `hidden_states` and `logits_indices` that `sample()` passes to `compute_logits`, with no recomputation.
- Rows follow the tokens the request keeps: sliced in the scheduler to `len(new_token_ids)`, so stop tokens, `max_tokens` and `n > 1` behave like logprobs.
- Partial prefill chunks produce no row, as they produce no token.

**Memory and lifetime.**
- The engine core serialises each step's rows with the rest of `EngineCoreOutputs`; rows above `VLLM_MSGPACK_ZERO_COPY_THRESHOLD` (256 bytes, so every row of a real model) travel as auxiliary zmq frames, and the frontend's `MsgpackDecoder` (`share_mem=True`, frames received with `copy=False`) decodes them as zero-copy `torch.frombuffer` views of those frames.
- Those views live only in the request's `RequestState` chunk list, which is dropped with the request state when it finishes.
- The tensor handed to the user is `torch.cat` of the chunks, a new allocation even for a single chunk, so it never aliases a transport frame and can be kept after the engine shuts down.
- This is the pattern `routed_experts` already follows (zero-copy ndarray chunks, `np.concatenate` on finish).

**Scope and restrictions (initial).**
Model Runner V2 only, generation models only, and refused at start-up with speculative decoding, pipeline parallelism or context parallelism, which have not been validated.
These mirror `return_sampling_mask` and `enable_trace_replay`, and can be lifted with tests.
Tensor parallelism and batch-sharded sampling need nothing: the gather reads the full, replicated `hidden_states` with the batch's global logits indices.

**Implementation** (about 150 lines of library code, no new abstraction; the path already used by `prompt_token_id_logprobs_dict`):
- `GPUModelRunner` (MRV2): a set of request ids that asked (created only when the flag is on; maintained in `add_requests` and `_remove_request`); after `sample()`, `gather_last_hidden_states()` gathers their logits rows into `ModelRunnerOutput.last_hidden_states: dict[str, Tensor]`;
- `AsyncOutput`: a non-blocking device-to-host copy of that dict on the output copy stream, like `prompt_token_id_logprobs_dict`;
- `Scheduler.update_from_output`: slices each request's rows to its kept tokens into `EngineCoreOutput.new_last_hidden_states` (appended last for `array_like` compatibility);
- `OutputProcessor`: accumulates the chunks and concatenates them on finish; `RequestOutput.add` keeps them through aggregation;
- `SamplingParams.verify` and `VllmConfig`: the validation and the guards above.

**Cost.**
- Flag off: no allocation and no GPU work; a few falsy checks per step (the runner's `None` set, the output's `None` field).
- Flag on, no request asking: the same checks on an empty set.
- Per asking request and generated token: one row gather on the main stream and `hidden_size x dtype` bytes copied to the host and serialised (4 KiB for a 2,048-dimensional bf16 model, 16 KiB at 8,192), against about 12 bytes per top logprob entry.
- Measured on our deployment (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B FP8, one RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q, the v0.30.0 backport, 250 single-question requests, alternating order): a median 35.0 ms without the output and 35.2 ms with it (per-request difference: median 0.12 ms, p10 -0.10, p90 0.45).
  The three-request workaround it replaces: a median 112.9 ms per question on the same card.

**Status.**
The implementation is in #59543 (against main), with tests, docs and an example; a backport to v0.30.0, for deployments pinned to it, is on [this branch](https://github.com/aminry/vllm/tree/rfc/return-last-hidden-states-v0.30.0) for reference.

### Alternatives considered

1. **Pooling engine or `LLM.encode` after `generate`** (the status quo): a second pass, a second weight copy or no shared prefix state on hybrid models, and different kernels, so the state does not match the scores (above).
2. **The hidden-states extraction connector (#33736), with inline return (#48743)**: the right tool for multi-layer and prompt-token extraction for spec-decode training.
   For this use it needs a speculative-decoding method and a KV connector, needs the model's auxiliary-hidden-state support (EAGLE-3-capable models or the Transformers backend), captures auxiliary layers rather than the final-norm output (see the question on #33118 about the last hidden state), and routes through storage or connector parameters.
   This RFC is complementary: it covers only the last layer at sampled positions, through the generate output.
3. **The reserved-logit-column model class** (what we run today): no vLLM change, but three sequential requests per question at `hidden_size = 2,048`, float32 rounding at the normaliser's magnitude, and a class that cannot serve ordinary generation.
4. **Processing inside the engine** (a hash, as suggested on #18176, or a user head applied in the worker, as suggested on #24288): it returns less data but needs a plugin interface in the sampling path; for heads trained offline on the same states, the raw state is what training needs, and it is only `hidden_size` values per token.
   A processing hook could be layered on this output later.
5. **An `extra_args` key instead of a field**: no schema change, but the request would pass validation on engines that cannot serve it; a typed field lets `verify` reject it.
6. **Per-step (streaming) delivery**: more useful for long streamed generations; returning with the final output matches `routed_experts` and `sampling_mask` and keeps the output processor change to a few lines.
   Could follow if wanted.

### Test plan

Unit (CPU):
- `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_update_from_output_routes_last_hidden_states_by_request`: rows routed per request by id, cut to kept tokens, none for requests that did not ask, kept on the finishing step;
- `tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py::test_last_hidden_states_are_accumulated_until_finish` (DELTA and FINAL_ONLY), `::test_last_hidden_states_do_not_alias_transport_buffers` (a row sent through the real msgpack encoder and decoder; zeroing the received frames after the request finishes leaves the returned rows unchanged) and `::test_last_hidden_states_survive_output_aggregation`;
- `tests/test_sampling_params.py`: rejected without the engine flag, accepted with it, the flag alone changes no request;
- `tests/config/test_last_hidden_states_config.py`: every guard, the flag reaching `ModelConfig`.

GPU end to end (`tests/v1/sample/test_last_hidden_states.py`, `facebook/opt-125m`):
- one row per generated token, CPU, model dtype, `hidden_size` wide;
- rows follow stop tokens and `n = 2`;
- rows times the output embedding reproduce the engine's own raw logits (`logprobs_mode="raw_logits"`);
- asking changes no other output: within one batch (the same prompt asked for twice and not asked for once) and across runs of the same batch asked for by some, all or none of its requests, equal token ids, and logits and rows within four fp16 ULPs.
  Not bit for bit, because neither holds on every GPU regardless of who asks: with CUDA graphs, an identical batch repeated moved one row by 3 ULPs between runs on an RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q (eager runs bit-identical; the moved row matched no other row, so nothing was misrouted), and on an RTX 4090 one of three identical sequences in a batch differed from the other two by one fp16 step in 1 of 30 batches, with all three asking.
  Earlier versions of this test asserted bit equality and failed for exactly these reasons.
- No host synchronization in the hot path: the GPU file passes with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`, and a deliberate blocking copy added to the gather fails it (a positive control).

Verified on our deployment before this RFC (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B FP8, the v0.30.0 backport, on two cards: an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition and an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q; 1,400 production items, one question each):
- flag off, or flag on and unused: label log-probabilities bit-identical to stock v0.30.0 in all 9 runs (1,400 of 1,400 each);
- flag on, every request asking: in separate processes, 4 of 5 runs bit-identical to stock, and one run moved 2 of 1,400 items by one bf16 step of one logit with the same top option, which is within the platform's measured run-to-run drift (stock was bit-identical in 4 of 4 runs of its own; 1 of 4 against 0 of 4 on that card is not distinguishable, p = 1.0); within one process, 5 asking passes alternating with 5 non-asking passes were all bit-identical to stock, and the returned states were equal across the asking passes.
  The output's path is a read (the rows are gathered after sampling from the tensor `compute_logits` received); our candidate for the one cross-process move, not tested, is the output's extra allocations changing allocator state, and with it a kernel's selection or workspace;
- same response: label probabilities recomputed from the returned state (`softmax(bf16(h @ W_labels^T))`) match the response's own within 3.0e-8 on all 1,400 items, with the same top option;
- against the reserved-column workaround on 250 items: within 3.1e-8 (median 0), the same top option on all 250.

The implementation on current main, on an RTX 4090 (installed with `VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1`): the GPU file 4 of 4 in every run (three runs with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`, then ten runs and one more with the check for the final version of the test); the positive control fails with the sync error; the example runs with the check on.
Existing suites run with the patch: `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`, `tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py`, `tests/test_sampling_params.py`, `tests/v1/engine/test_engine_args.py`.
No new failures, on CPU and on three cards, on main and on v0.30.0: every failure in the patched runs also occurs on the unpatched code (in our environments, two pipeline-parallel scheduler tests on main, multimodal scheduler tests whose model inspection fails on a `transformers` import on v0.30.0, and `test_stop_token` with the ungated tokenizer we substitute for the gated Llama one).

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

No individual CC; I would be grateful for triage to the Model Runner V2 and output-processor owners.

### Any Other Things.

Consumer example in the patch: `examples/generate/last_hidden_states_offline.py` (label scores plus a linear head on the same forward, in one request).
The motivating consumer is [Decisio](https://github.com/aminry/decisio), which serves typed decisions from a frozen open model and reads such heads on every request.

AI assistance: this RFC and its implementation were prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code). I have reviewed the change and the verification and am responsible for both.

title: [RFC]: Fast-Track Merging for Model Optimization PRs
author: benchislett
body:
# [RFC]: Fast-Track Merging for Model Optimization PRs

### Motivation.

Frontier coding models have become extremely proficient at inference model optimization and efficient GPU kernel development. The frequency of new vLLM PRs is rapidly increasing, and is outpacing reviewer bandwidth.
Powered by fully autonomous optimization loops (e.g. "autoresearch"), optimization development can be scaled horizontally across a wide range of models, hardware architectures, and deployment scenarios.

The potential speedups are extremely large, but careful steps must be taken to ensure that vLLM's code quality, usability, and reliability is not sacrificed in the process -- this is why we have a comprehensive review process. Striking a balance between contribution barriers and performance upside is critical.

The fundamental goal of the fast-track is to merge PRs faster, with the same standard of quality. The way to achieve this is by systematically verifying aspects that ordinarily require manual reviewer verification (correctness, performance, no risk of breaking other workloads, etc.). By focusing on a subset of PRs whose changes are strictly contained to an isolated module (namely, the "model forward pass") we can tailor guardrails to decrease reviewer involvement while maintaining a high bar for stability.

### 1. Proposed Change.

I propose a relaxation of the review and merge requirements, limited to cases where changes are contained, comprehensively validated, and provably limited to explicitly validated deployment scenarios.

The remainder of the RFC details the following:
1. Process changes we can make to more efficiently merge "safe" optimization PRs
2. How we can systematically ensure that an eligible PR is "safe to merge"

#### 1.1: One-Touch Merge ("LGTM")

Reviewers often need to revisit PRs multiple times throughout review: one pass to leave comments, another pass to approve and enable CI, additional passes to rerun/retry CI, and possibly a final force-merge request must be made.

For contained model optimizations, much of this can be prevented:
- If no comments are required, a single reviewer action approves the PR and starts an automated procedure to merge: CI runs and executes an automated procedure of rebase and retry until the PR goes in (up to 3 times) or a fallback force-merge is automatically requested. 
- If only trivial edits or conflict resolution are requested, a reviewer may submit a "conditional approval" on the requested changes. After the changes are made the automated merge procedure begins. The "conditional approval" persists through rebase, conflict resolution, acceptance of reviewer-suggested edits, and changes localized to tests/, provided the changes preserve the approved behavior. An amount of trust is delegated to the contributor in the event of a conditional approval.

The CI runs should hopefully not be an obstacle in these cases as changes should be contained to localized files/directories which will mitigate the range of detected test cases.

In cases when a maintainer decides nontrivial changes are needed, the maintainer closes or demotes the PR and the contributor is responsible for updating and re-opening or re-requesting review.

#### 1.2: Primary-Maintainer Merge

One common issue that blocks merge is when the primary maintainer of a feature makes a small PR to update an aspect of that feature which they themselves have the most expertise with. In such cases it can be difficult to find a dedicated second reviewer who can confidently approve the changes.

To resolve this I propose we permit core committers to merge their own PRs, provided they follow the validation and isolation requirements of the fast-track specification below.

#### 1.3: Priority Review

I propose that eligible fast-track PRs be automatically labelled as such, and that maintainer review is prioritized towards fast-track PRs. This will involve slack integration, an automated tracking dashboard, and escalation when fast-track-eligible PRs are "stale" for more than N=7 days.

Because fast-track model optimizations are targeted towards a specific model (or small family of models), there should be a small set of assigned reviewers who can be held more directly responsible for triaging fast-track PRs. This burden will be opt-in, but should not be too heavy as triaging fast-track PRs should be very easy by design.

#### 1.4: PR Template

Similar to the [PR-Checklist](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57084) change which updated the PR template, there will be a dedicated template for fast-track PRs which formalizes the requirements and streamlines review. PR will follow the RFC within a few days.

### 2. Validations and Confidence

#### 2.1: Isolation of Code Changes

The primary risk of merging code tailored to optimize one use-case is impact to other deployments. Performance regressions, breaking other features, or correctness violations are all common side-effects of a seemingly harmless change.

The first pillar of raising confidence in safety is _isolation_: limiting code changes to a specific deployment scenario.

I propose the initial prototype require that fast-track changes be limited to "flat model" subdirectories (e.g. all diff is within a folder such as `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia`). 

#### 2.2: Bounded Impact on Deployments

Optionally, changes can be further gated programmatically (e.g. a kernel fusion only enabled at small input sizes). The more isolated a change is, the smaller the potential impact. By placing rigid bounds on the changes, we can limit the impact to a very small set of deployment scenarios which can be tested explicitly.

Naturally, limiting the scope in this way also reduces the net improvement per PR: other excluded scenarios might benefit from the changes as well. This may also increase code duplication and redundancy. However, it creates a clear path toward improving stability and scalability as we accelerate the pace of optimizations with coding agents.

[TensorRT-LLM has merged a design](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/19056) which isolates/replicates model code for each model, hardware, and parallelism triple (e.g. gpt-oss TP1 on SM103). This is a fairly extreme flavor of replication, but it highlights an architectural direction we can move towards for if the initial results from vLLM's flat-model design prove sufficiently maintainable.

#### 2.3: Explicit Validation of Affected Deployments

Once an isolated and bounded deployment is established for a contribution, what remains is to run sufficient validations against a representative set of configurations.

Since reviewers are still involved in the process, there is some flexibility in the extent of validation: some changes might warrant testing every parallelism configuration or testing on multiple hardwares, while others might be sufficient with only a single parallelism/HW configuration. If a contribution is not sufficiently validated, reviewers may request additional validation and approve conditionally (see 1.1) or they may demote the PR from the fast-track and/or close it as necessary. Submissions following the fast-track accept a higher evidence standard and a higher risk of reviewers closing low-quality PRs wholesale without discussion.

To codify expectations, I propose the following requirements:

- **E2E Correctness Evaluation:**
  - `GSM8k` and `GPQA-Diamond` be run for all proposed model optimizations
  - A long-context benchmark such as `MRCR v2 256K (8-needle)` and/or a long-generation benchmark such as `AIME25`/`AIME26` (pass@1 avg1) should be included when changes affect sensitive token-mixing operations such as FMHA or SSM.
  - A "hard" correctness benchmark such as `AIME25`/`AIME26` (pass@1 avg4+) or `HLE` or `TerminalBench (any)` should be included when changes include a "high correctness risk factor": low-level CUDA C++ or PTX/SASS or equivalent, or new communications kernels for which race conditions cannot be ruled out by formal verification.
  - All correctness evaluations should use at least "high" reasoning effort, where supported. All evaluations should compare against a known "good" baseline, either referencing official vendor reported numbers or those from a vLLM reference run. Running your own baseline on the vLLM main branch to compare against is acceptable. Measured scores should exceed or match the reference within one percentage point (absolute delta, after accounting for run-to-run variance).
  - Correctness validation runs should ensure that the deployment scenario is reproduced. For example, if adding a small-batch fusion, GSM8k should run at a correspondingly low batch size (to trigger the change and contribute coverage to the diff).
- **Kernel Correctness Evaluation:**
  - New kernels should be exhaustively validated for correctness on a broad range of inputs. This includes multiple possible input shapes as well as input distributions.
    - If bit-exactness is not maintained, it should be justified and validated with a strict tolerance.
    - If quantization or lossy optimizations are used, this is considered a "high correctness risk factor" and warrants additional E2E validation (see above).
  - For low-level CUDA kernels, include [compute-sanitizer](https://developer.nvidia.com/compute-sanitizer) tests such as `memcheck`, `racecheck`, and `synccheck` sanitization are required where applicable.
  - Note, committed tests should be a small subset of validation performed during development. These should exist strictly for regression checks, not for comprehensive reproduction. We do not want to run exhaustive correctness testing in CI every time we make a model change.
- **Performance Evaluation:**
  - PRs should include a "headline" speedup on a specified "target" workload. This is required but not sufficient for performance validation.
  - Performance change should also be swept across the range of bounded-affected-workloads: multiple concurrencies should be benchmarked almost always, as well as high/low sequence length when applicable. Any throughput or latency regression exceeding 1% for any measured configuration is unacceptable and disqualifies the PR from the fast-track.
    - For MoE models, ensure real prompts (such as speed-bench throughput_8k) are used so that expert balance is realistic. 

### Feedback Period.

Feedback period will continue for 12 days, ending on Oct 13. @benchislett will request maintainer review and open a candidate PR with a reference implementation of the proposed design. 

### CC List.

@njhill @LucasWilkinson @yewentao256 @WoosukKwon @mgoin @vllm-project/vllm-committers @xinli-sw 

### Discussion Areas

1. Do we want to further solidify the requirements from sec. 2.3 into a structured requirement matrix? Or do we want to leave it flexible for reviewers to decide on a per-PR basis if validation is sufficient?
2. How strict should we be about isolating code changes? Are minor one-liner integration patches in core files acceptable, or do we require rigid file-structure-based guarantees about isolation? Can we build static linting tooling (possibly AI powered) that can enforce or verify that changes are limited to the claimed workloads?
3. Is committer self-merge a good idea, or is it too permissive?
4. How much control are we comfortable delegating to automated verification systems, versus committer judgement? Should we be more/less aggressive in automating merge workflows?

title: [RFC]: Modular and Extensible APIs & Execution Surface for Orchestrator-Driven KV Hint Policies
author: karen-sy
body: **TL;DR:** - We propose a common KvHints Primitives set (`COPY_TO`, `MOVE_TO`, `SET_PRIORITY`) from which various user-defined KVHints (such as Retain, Prefetch, P2P Transfer) can be composed. - We present a concrete API surface and implementation surface for vLLM to execute each KvHint primitive. - We explicitly preserve the option for G2+ cache owner backends (such as Dynamo KVCR) to define and execute their own hint taxonomy, in which vLLM treats the KvHintEnvelope as an opaque transport envelope to a separate hint execution runtime. > [!NOTE] Please review alongside companion PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59714 which implements **G1 Retain** with the proposed API / Execution surface proposed by this RFC. > ## Motivation Our RFC #51428 establishes the roadmap for orchestrator (e.g. Dynamo)-driven KV management. RFC #53421 (PR #53423) provide the typed envelope and request propagation. The next gap is the consumer interface: which component interprets an action, what effect it promises, and where execution enters existing vLLM machinery. This distinction matters especially when a connector has its own policy runtime. For example, a G2+ cache manager backend such as KVCR (#53624) can maintain its own catalogue of KV policies’ definitions and implementation contracts; on the other hand, other cache backends or G1-only consumers (such as Mooncake #57103) may prefer to opt-in to a vLLM-native catalogue of KV policies with built-in operational semantics. An API surface for agentic KV policies must disambiguate between those paths without risking competing semantic definitions and/or conflicting KV policy execution paths. Concretely, this RFC aims to resolve these three questions: 1. **Q: What exactly can an orchestrator communicate to vLLM to do via KvHintEnvelopes?** 1. **CASE 1: A KvHintEnvelope whose hint type is interpretable by vLLM**, such as `vllm.copy_to`, `vllm.move_to`, `vllm.set_priority`, will be executed by vLLM (and if applicable, an offloading backend such as Mooncake which subscribes to this contract). Concretely, actions targeting G1 execute beside the core vLLM cache manager; actions requiring G2+ involvement use the configured connector and its completion path. 1. This is compatible with a concurrent RFC #57103 from the Mooncake team. That RFC also positions vLLM engine-side approval and operation lifecycle above connector-side storage and transfer work. 2. **CASE 2: A KvHintEnvelope whose payload is owned by a non-subscribing backend**, such as by KVCR, will be opaquely passed to that backend’s hint execution runtime, which should manage its own hint payload validation, policy meaning, and backend-owned memory state. 1. See https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53624 and https://github.com/ai-dynamo/kvcr. 2. A backend operation that needs cache allocation, publication, or reclamation on HBM still uses vLLM-controlled G1 operations through its integration. 2. **How should backend-owned KV policy semantics coexist with vLLM-owned KV policy semantics?** 1. We position a Dispatch interface at the KvHintEnvelope ingress layer, which determines whether the hint should be interpreted by vLLM’s policy layer or by a backend. 3. **After resolving the above, what should otherwise independent features standardize for best modularity?** 1. A common Action interface lets retention and prefetch implementations share addressing, dispatch, and outcome conventions while keeping their execution machinery separate. At a high level, our proposal for vLLM's KvHint definition and execution surface is: (1) `kv_hints/actions.py` defines the action contracts. (2) At request+KvHintEnvelope ingress, `kv_hints/dispatch.py` validates vLLM-owned action definitions against the contracts, and (3) dispatches them to the appropriate executor, immediately or at a registered lifecycle point within the request path. ## System Overview: Modes of vLLM KvHint Policy Execution The architecture separates payload interpretation from resource authority. G1 denotes the framework’s GPU KV cache; G2 denotes the configured offload/shared-cache tier. A transfer backend can also move directly between GPUs without storing a G2 copy. ## Action Primitive: Copy, Move, Priority Our goal is to provide KvHint primitives which are modular, composable, and semantically unambiguous. As such, instead of hardcoding a taxonomy of policy goals (e.g. RETAIN, PREFETCH, SHARE, DEMOTE) which may contain overlapping principles and/or implementation strategies — consider the intuitive similarity between a “RETAIN” and “PIN”, for example — we propose that vLLM codify the concrete building blocks of these policy implementations. Specifically, we propose three action primitives: `COPY`, `MOVE`, `PRIORITY`. Here is a simplified contract signature: ``` COPY_TO(target_blocks, src, dst, **kwargs) MOVE_TO(target_blocks, src, dst, **kwargs) SET_PRIORITY(target_blocks, location, value, ttl_seconds, **kwargs) ``` ### COPY_TO Definition: Copy the targeted blocks in `src` into `dst` Example uses: - **Prefetch** blocks of a worker from a higher tier to lower tier: `COPY_TO(target_blocks, src=(Worker1, G2), dst=(Worker1, G1))` - **P2P copy** of blocks between two workers’ HBM (potentially via G1 → G2 → G2 → G1, owned by Mooncake): `COPY_TO(target_blocks, src=Worker1, dst=Worker2)` ### MOVE_TO Definition: Move the targeted blocks in `src` into `dst`. Example uses: - **Demote** blocks from a lower tier to higher tier to free memory: `MOVE_TO(target_blocks, src=(Worker_1, G1), dst=(Worker_1, G2))` ### SET_PRIORITY Definition: Set or clear an eviction-priority declaration for the selected copies. Higher values favor retention; lower values favor earlier eviction. `value = null` removes the named declaration. Clearing a declaration does not remove data and does not override another declaration. Example uses: - **Retain** blocks in HBM: `SET_PRIORITY(target_blocks, G1, 10, 60.0)` ## Action targets and dispatch Proposed wire names are `vllm.copy_to`, `vllm.move_to`, and `vllm.set_priority`, each with `action_version = "1.0"`. Each supported `(action_type, action_version)` has one registered consumer; conflicting registrations are rejected. Dispatch preserves the envelope’s per-action failure isolation. ```markdown # Example KvHintEnvelope of prefetch via COPY_TO KvHintEnvelope{ "protocol_version": "0.1", "message_id": "msg-123", "actions": [ { "action_id": "a1", "action_type": "vllm.copy_to", "action_version": "1.0", "payload": {"target_blocks": [0,1,2,3,4], "src": ("Worker-A", "DRAM") "dst": ("Worker-A", "HBM") } } } ] } ``` `src`, `dst`, and `location` identify the owning engine, memory tier, and configured backend where applicable. Executors resolve local targets against current state; remote validation requires the participating backend or engine. Missing targets and partial affected scope must be explicit and must not expand the request. ## Where the interface lives ``` vllm/v1/kv_hints/ protocol.py # existing envelope/action wrappers actions.py # proposed typed vLLM action contracts dispatch.py # proposed consumer/executor routing vllm/v1/core/ kv_cache_priority.py # proposed native G1 executor/state block_pool.py # allocator and lifetime integration vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/ offloading/actions.py # proposed COPY_TO handler offloading/scheduler.py # existing offload orchestration offloading/worker.py # existing transfer execution mooncake/store/ # future supported Store actions vllm/v1/kv_offload/ # existing offload managers/workers ``` - `actions.py` defines payload types, static validation, and result meaning. It must not import schedulers, allocators, or backend runtimes. - `dispatch.py` resolves the registered consumer and configured executor, passes request context, and preserves action/job correlation. It does not maintain another copy of allocator state or implement eviction and transfer algorithms. - `core/kv_cache_priority.py` owns live declarations, expiry, overlap resolution, limits, and victim ordering. This state belongs beside allocation because it must remain correct during cache hits, freeing, reuse, invalidation, and reset even when no new hint arrives. Queue details can remain private to that module. - `block_pool.py` retains small integration points for victim selection and block lifecycle transitions. `kv_cache_manager.py` may expose the lookup/context an executor needs, but it should not parse wire payloads. A scheduler lifecycle hook can apply request-completion actions before releasing request references; this introduces no new request ranking or admission policy. - Connector handlers own backend-specific lowering and asynchronous jobs. Existing offload managers, worker transfer paths, and completion aggregation remain the execution machinery. G1↔︎G2 transfer does not imply a KVCR dependency: the configured offloading connector may supply it. SimpleCPUOffload is a separate implementation and would need its own handler if supported. ## Example policies and execution paths The examples show policy goals expressed through vLLM primitives or backend-owned hints, with interpretation and execution assigned to their respective owners. ### RETAIN in G1 via SET_PRIORITY (#59714) ```mermaid flowchart LR D["`**Dynamo policy** RETAIN prefix during a tool pause SET_PRIORITY(prefix, G1, priority, TTL) Apply at request completion`"] I["`**vLLM action interface** Decode and dispatch`"] E["`**vLLM native G1 executor** Resolve copies; install declaration Manage expiry and overlapping claims`"] P["`**vLLM block pool** Preserve active references Select victims; clear state on reuse`"] D -->|KvHintsEnvelope| I I -->|request completed| E E -->|victim order| P P -.->|lifecycle| E classDef dynamo fill:#f0ebfc,stroke:#8b75b5,color:#182638; classDef vllm fill:#eaf2ff,stroke:#6b91bd,color:#182638; classDef backend fill:#e7f4ec,stroke:#73a186,color:#182638; class D dynamo; class I,E,P vllm; ``` | Component | vLLM implementation modules | | --- | --- | | Action interface | `v1/kv_hints/actions.py`, `v1/kv_hints/dispatch.py` | | Native G1 executor | `core/kv_cache_priority.py`, `core/block_pool.py` | *Result: priority installed. Blocks remain evictable under pressure.* During a tool pause, favor the session’s prefix by assigning a bounded G1 priority. Apply the declaration at successful request completion, before releasing request references. Numeric priority biases eviction; it does not guarantee residency. The G1 actions branch and PR #38514 provide implementation examples. Their lifetime and ownership rules must be reconciled with the selected `SET_PRIORITY` contract. ### PREFETCH G2→G1 via COPY_TO ```mermaid flowchart LR D["`**1. Dynamo router** Send PREFETCH KV hint before resume COPY_TO(G2 → G1)`"] I["`**2. vLLM action interface** Decode and dispatch`"] E["`**3. vLLM offloading executor** Reserve G1 destination; transfer Hold buffers until transfer completes`"] C["`**4. vLLM completion** Publish loaded copies for lookup Release transfer protection safely Report ready(scope) or failure to Dynamo`"] D -->|KvHintsEnvelope| I I -->|COPY_TO| E E -->|load finished| C classDef dynamo fill:#f0ebfc,stroke:#8b75b5,color:#182638; classDef vllm fill:#eaf2ff,stroke:#6b91bd,color:#182638; classDef backend fill:#e7f4ec,stroke:#73a186,color:#182638; class D dynamo; class I,E,C vllm; ``` | Component | Python modules | | --- | --- | | Action interface | `v1/kv_hints/actions.py`, `v1/kv_hints/dispatch.py` | | Offloading executor | `offloading/actions.py`; `offloading/scheduler.py` reserves G1; `offloading/worker.py` + `kv_offload/` transfer bytes | *Result: accepted prefix is usable in G1. Normal cache eviction applies.* Before a session resumes, use COPY_TO(G2 → G1) to stage its offloaded prefix in the GPU cache. Completion means the accepted scope is loaded and registered for reuse. This is compatible with the direction of PR #58198, which demonstrates request-free G2->G1 prefetch through `OffloadingConnector`. Our proposed implementation can reuse core portions of its machinery (destination reservation, async transfer, event publication) and integrate `KvHintEnvelope` + `COPY_TO` processing onto it. ### PREFETCH through Mooncake: vLLM-owned COPY_TO ```mermaid flowchart LR D["`**Dynamo — resume on B** PREFETCH prefix from shared Store COPY_TO(H, Store G2 → B G1, backend=Mooncake)`"] I["`**vLLM B — action interface** Interpret and dispatch`"] E["`**vLLM B — Store connector executor** Resolve Store keys Reserve G1 via KVCacheManager Submit transfer; hold buffers`"] M["`**Mooncake runtime** Resolve backend copies Transfer bytes or report failure Own Store and transport state`"] C["`**vLLM B — publish and complete** Register usable G1 copies Report actual completed scope Submitted does not mean ready`"] D -->|KvHintsEnvelope| I I -->|typed COPY_TO| E E -->|Store read into approved buffers| M M -->|connector completion| C C -.->|Action result — proposed feedback plumbing| D classDef dynamo fill:#f0ebfc,stroke:#8b75b5,color:#182638; classDef vllm fill:#eaf2ff,stroke:#6b91bd,color:#182638; classDef backend fill:#e7f4ec,stroke:#73a186,color:#182638; class D dynamo; class I,E,C vllm; class M backend; ``` | Component | Python modules | | --- | --- | | Action interface | `kv_hints/actions.py`, `kv_hints/dispatch.py` | | MooncakeStoreConnector executor | Proposed `mooncake/store/actions.py`; transfer submission through `mooncake/store/worker.py` | *Proposed control lifecycle (compatible with #57103); reuses the existing Store data path. vLLM owns COPY_TO; Mooncake supplies G2 storage and transfer.* Before resume on B, Dynamo requests PREFETCH through COPY_TO(H, Store G2 → B G1, backend=Mooncake). vLLM owns target resolution, GPU allocation, and destination readiness; Mooncake supplies storage and transfer. Proposed `mooncake/store/actions.py` lowers the action into connector keys and buffers, then reuses worker execution and completion. ### Remote prefix reuse: KVCR-owned kv.fetch We briefly describe how KVCR-owned `kv.fetch` works in this system. For details, please visit the `ai-dynamo/KVCR` repository, as well as the KVCR tiering adapter in the vLLM repo. 1. Dynamo sends kv.fetch(source_control_endpoint=A, block_hashes=H, mode=copy) to B. vLLM forwards it to KVCR without COPY_TO interpretation. submit_hint validates the supported payload and records the source; it does not move data. 2. On a later read, vLLM supplies framework DRAM destinations through deliver. KVCR resolves sources, acquires claims or framework pins, and transfers bytes. vLLM loads completed data into G1 and controls GPU readiness. ## Implementation scope, open questions **Implementation order (generally in dependency order):** - Typed actions, dispatch in `v1/kv_hints` - vLLM-owned, G1-only hints with minimal BlockPool / lifecycle hooks, i.e. a G1 Retain via `PRIORITY` - vLLM-owned, offloader-integrated hints, i.e. a G2→G1 prefetch via `COPY` **Validation should cover:** - Hint parsing: unknown-action isolation, stale/missing logical targets, overlapping declarations and expiry, partial copy scope, and failure/cancellation during transfer. - Memory safety: referenced-block safety, block reuse/reset, a copy must never become discoverable before successful publication, and no path may reclaim memory still accessed by a request or DMA. **Open questions:** - **How/where to emit asynchronous (i.e. not attached to a request) KV Hints,** and how vLLM should handle it. One idea is for the orchestrator to “piggyback” the hint onto the earliest possible next request. - **Implementation surfaces in vLLM for more time-sensitive hints.** For example, the Continuum paper’s hint policy generates the retain hint *during* response generation, as soon as the response is detected to contain a tool call. In order for vLLM to generate and execute hints *within the request path*, not only receive hints from Orchestrator, more conditional callbacks would have to be added to the engine core (e.g. to the scheduler for this Retain type). - **Addressing information staleness and persisting session-centric KV block view in vLLM.** The orchestrator emits KvHintEnvelopes based on its current understanding of the engine’s KV block residency state. There is risk of this information being stale; in order for vLLM to be able to verify e.g. “this set of block ids, which the KvHintEnvelope claims belongs to session-1 and must be evicted in Worker 1, are indeed in Worker 1”, vLLM requires a persistent indexer of block-to-session associations. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/51428 calls this the `SessionPrefixIndexer`, and an analogous structure is implemented in Dynamo https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13807. **cc list** @ishandhanani @oandreeva-nv @mkhazraee @ziqifan617 @vMaroon @franciscojavierarceo @zhhangBian @ivanium @zhewenl @njhill ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Handle empty responses in synthetic acceptance benchmarks
author: whx-sjtu
body:
### Motivation.

Agentic performance tests using synthetic speculative acceptance can generate tokens while delivering no usable response data to the benchmark client. Synthetic acceptance can accept draft tokens that normal verification would reject. The resulting output may degenerate into channel or tool framing, which detokenization and model-specific parsing can remove. AIPerf then rejects the request with:

```text
InvalidInferenceResultError: No responses with actual content were received from the server
```

Here, “empty” means that the client receives no recognized text, reasoning, or tool-call data across the response. An empty `message.content` alone, or an individual metadata-only SSE event, is not sufficient: [AIPerf recognizes reasoning and tool-call data too][aiperf-chat], and its [record validation][aiperf-validation] requires at least one response containing actual data.

Current vLLM supports `rejection_sample_method="synthetic"` with exactly one of `synthetic_acceptance_rates` or `synthetic_acceptance_length`. These settings control acceptance decisions, but do not define a corresponding output-presentation policy. The shared output processor still detokenizes the generated IDs, checks stop conditions, and passes text and original token IDs to serving for parsing. See the [configuration][config], [sampler][sampler], and [output processor][output-update].

Synthetic acceptance is useful for measuring inference performance at a controlled acceptance rate; the generated text is not suitable for evaluating model quality. However, a response with no usable data prevents clients from completing the benchmark and collecting content-based timing metrics. This RFC proposes two ways to handle output in that mode.

### Proposed Change.

Both options apply only when the effective `rejection_sample_method` is `"synthetic"`. Use that mode to select the behavior: 

Both options preserve real generated token IDs, model computation, internal context/KV state, acceptance metrics, and stop checks. Ordinary serving retains its existing behavior. The intended use is text-based throughput testing and recorded agentic workloads that do not depend on meaningful generated answers or actual tool execution.

#### Option 1: Return decoded text without model-specific output parsing

For synthetic acceptance requests, add a serving-layer branch that delivers the existing decoded text directly as ordinary response content:

```text
real generated token IDs
  -> existing detokenization and stop checks
  -> decoded text
  -> content / delta.content
```

For `/v1/chat/completions`, this branch would skip output-side reasoning and tool-call extraction for both streaming and non-streaming responses. Keep prompt rendering and engine processing intact. Parser implementations remain unchanged; synthetic responses simply take a different presentation path. `/v1/completions` already exposes decoded text without chat reasoning/tool extraction and would not need that routing change.

This is a smaller serving-layer change. It preserves the decoded text, avoids losing framing-only output to model-specific parsers, and does not require a new presentation policy in the shared `OutputProcessor`.

Its limitation is that it only addresses content removed during parsing. If detokenization already produces an empty string—for example, because all generated IDs are skipped special tokens—bypassing parsers cannot recover nonempty text. It also exposes malformed framing as ordinary content, so behavior remains dependent on the generated sequence and tokenizer. It cannot provide a general nonempty-output guarantee for synthetic benchmarks.

The response is raw benchmark text, not parsed reasoning or a valid tool call. This mode should not claim to satisfy requests that require a specific tool call or structured response.

#### Option 2: Render explicit placeholder text after stop checks

For synthetic acceptance requests, replace the delivered text with the literal `"synthetic "` once per generated output token ID. Keep real detokenization and stop checks, then apply the replacement when constructing `CompletionOutput`:

```text
real generated token IDs
  -> existing detokenization and stop checks
  -> existing delta/cumulative token-ID selection
  -> "synthetic " * len(selected_output_token_ids)
  -> content / delta.content
```

Thread an internal presentation policy through `AsyncLLM` and `LLMEngine` into `OutputProcessor` and its request state. Generate the placeholder in [`RequestState._new_completion_output()`][output-build], after selecting the delta or cumulative IDs. This gives offline text output and the supported HTTP endpoints the same presentation rule.

Two implementation boundaries matter:

- **Keep stop matching on real text.** vLLM checks stop strings inside [`detokenizer.update()`][detokenizer]. Substituting text before that check would change termination. Retain real decoding and stop matching, including their computational cost, and replace only the delivered text afterward.
- **Do not parse placeholder text together with original control-token IDs.** vLLM parsers consume IDs as well as text. For example, [the base thinking parser][thinking-parser] drops a single reasoning control token by ID even if the accompanying text is nonempty. Synthetic chat responses therefore need an explicit ordinary-content presentation branch; replacing `output.text` alone is insufficient.

The output rules would be:

| Concern | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Streaming | Emit one fragment per newly delivered generated ID, preserving batching and stream intervals. Do not repeat text for final or usage-only events with no new IDs. |
| Cumulative/final output | Emit one fragment per accumulated generated ID, including accepted draft and recovery/bonus tokens. |
| Special and stop tokens | An ID counted in the output receives a fragment even if ordinary decoding would hide its spelling. Actual stop detection still uses the original token/text path. |
| Stop buffering | Real stop processing remains active, but placeholder delivery follows delivered IDs and does not wait for the real-text buffer to flush. |
| Usage | Preserve real token counts; do not retokenize the placeholder to calculate completion usage. |
| Zero-token/error results | Do not fabricate tokens for zero-token results, prefill events, cancellations, or failed requests. |
| Token-only requests | Preserve intentional `detokenize=False` and tokenizer-free behavior; these requests are outside the text-presentation contract. |

This option makes text delivery independent of degenerate token spellings and clearly identifies the result as synthetic. For a successful supported text response containing generated IDs, it provides nonempty content even when ordinary detokenization or parsing would remove all visible text.

The tradeoff is a change to the shared output layer as well as serving. Initial support should cover offline text, `/v1/completions`, and `/v1/chat/completions`, including streaming and non-streaming. Other adapters need explicit capability checks before their requests reach the engine. Required/named tool calls, schema-constrained output, and API logprob-to-visible-text correspondence need a separate contract; initially reject such combinations rather than imply that placeholder text satisfies them. Raw IDs and logprob values can remain available for offline diagnostics of the actual generated sequence.

Placeholder text changes response size and the timing of visible content, and bypassing model-specific parsing changes CPU work. These effects need measurement. AIPerf should use [`--use-server-token-count`][aiperf-count-flag] with server-provided usage: a placeholder fragment is not necessarily one token when re-encoded. If a multi-turn client appends the returned text to its next prompt, later prompt lengths and prefix-cache behavior can also change; use fixed replay inputs or account for that difference.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_
