title: [RFC]: Octave KV, a native 3-bit KV cache for AMD GPUs
author: JartX
body:
PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774

### Proposal to improve performance

## Where this comes from

We serve Qwen3.8-27B (GPTQ W4A16) on boxes with four RX 7900 XTX, 96 GB in
total, with tensor parallel 4 and MTP. Our users send long prompts: whole
repositories, long documents, agent sessions that run for hours. With an fp16
KV cache and 8 GB per GPU for it, a box holds about 446k tokens, so one long
request fills it.

On ROCm today the options below 8 bits are TurboQuant, UltraQuant (#57057,
gfx950 only) and KVarN (#46613, CUDA-first). We tried TurboQuant first, since
it is merged and its idea (random rotation plus a Lloyd-Max codebook) is the
right one. On our hardware three things got in the way:

- With MTP on (`qwen3_next_mtp`, k=3) every preset produced garbage, and
  GSM8K fell to around 1%. Without MTP it was correct.
- Its multi-token path copies between host and device per layer, so it
  cannot be captured in CUDA graphs.
- Its Triton kernels are slow on RDNA3. At 380k tokens the first token took
  621 s, against 371 s with fp16.

So we wrote our own backend: same family of ideas, a few changes to the
format, and every kernel in HIP. Against TurboQuant on the same hardware it
comes out ahead on all three things we care about. It holds as many tokens or
more at each size: at about 200 bytes per slot the two hold 2.07M and 2.05M
tokens, and our 216-byte format holds 6% more than TurboQuant's 230-byte one.
It loses less: 2.5× less excess NLL at 380k at the same size, and GSM8K
stays at fp16 level (91.8-92.4 against 89.8). And it is faster: per layer at
380k, decode is 4.6× faster, MTP verification 11×, a prefill chunk takes
30% less time, and the first token of a 380k prompt arrives 2.1× sooner.

We have run it in production since October 2, 2026, and we would like to
propose it upstream. We would also like it to be more than an RDNA3 side
project: one compressed KV format for the whole AMD line, with a short
written contract that says what each architecture needs to implement. That
is the part where we most need your opinion, and AMD's help.

## Why it matters for AMD

The KV cache is usually what limits how many long requests a GPU can serve,
and on AMD it has been the hardest part to shrink: the options below 8 bits
were built for CUDA or fall back to Triton. A native compressed cache changes
that, and at any scale, because the saving is a ratio of bytes. In the same
memory it holds 4.7× more tokens than fp16 and 2.4× more than fp8 or int8,
whether that memory is a 24 GB 7900 XTX or a 192 GB MI300X. The cost is small:
no measurable change on GSM8K, and a next-token NLL increase of about 0.001
nats at 380k that stays flat as the context grows.

The smaller cache is also faster. At long context attention is limited by
memory bandwidth, so reading 4.7× fewer bytes is where most of the 4× decode
speedup comes from, as long as the kernels read the packed cache directly
instead of expanding it first. On our four 7900 XTX that turned a box that
held one long request into one that serves about four at 512k, with decode at
127 tok/s at that length.

With the kernels this tight, attention stops being the part of the step that
grows with the context. With fp16 at 380k, attention took over the decode
step and generation fell to 2.7 tok/s. With Octave KV, going from 128k to
512k (four times the context) only takes decode from 153 to 127 tok/s; most
of the step is the rest of the model again, the same weights and all-reduce
you pay at short context. Prefill shows the same thing: at 100k all the
backends we tried are within 8% of each other, because the GEMMs and the
all-reduce dominate. Long context stops being a special, expensive case and
becomes close to the normal one.

Getting this much out of the hardware makes AMD GPUs, consumer cards and
Instinct alike, more competitive for long-context serving. We think a native
compressed cache is one of the pieces that can make AMD a first choice for
long-context serving rather than an alternative: the capacity gain holds on
every card, and on the one we could measure, long context costs close to what
short context does. We would like every ROCm user to have it without writing
their own kernels, which is why we want the format to cover the whole line.
We have now measured speed on two architectures: RDNA3 and, since October 20,
MI300X, where Octave KV holds about twice the tokens of AITER's fp8 cache at
the same speed (see "MI300X" under Numbers).

## What it is

`ROCM_OCTAVE` is an attention backend for the full-attention layers. You turn
it on with the cache dtype, `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3` (or
`octave_k3v4`, `octave_k3v3_compact`). The name comes from the 3-bit codes:
each one indexes an eight-level codebook.

Each (token, KV head) is stored as one packed slot. Before quantizing we flip
signs at random and apply a Walsh-Hadamard rotation, which makes the
coordinates close to Gaussian, so a fixed Lloyd-Max codebook for N(0, 1) fits
any model without calibration. The kernels apply the codebook with one
`v_perm_b32` per four codes. Each vector gets one scale (four on the blocked
K layout), chosen so that `x · x̂ = |x|²`. We started with a least-squares
scale and it was clearly worse: it shrinks every vector a little, the softmax
gets flatter, and NLL at 380k came out 2-3× higher.

The three formats differ in how they treat K. V is always rotated over the
whole head:

| Cache dtype | K | V | Bytes per slot (head 256) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | whole head rotated, 3-bit | 3-bit | 196 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 4 blocks of 64: RoPE block 4-bit, the rest 3-bit | 3-bit | 216 |
| `octave_k3v4` | as above | 4-bit | 248 |

For reference, `turboquant_3bit_nc` is 198 bytes, `turboquant_k3v4_nc` 230,
int8 per-token-head 520 and fp16 1024.

Decode, MTP verification and prefill all read the packed cache directly;
there is no dequantized copy of the prefix. MTP verification was the case we
cared most about: the query tokens of one request share every K/V read, and
the whole decode path is captured in CUDA graphs. The backend has its own
metadata builder, which computes the per-query maps on the device without
host syncs.

## Written for the GPU

Most of the speed does not come from the format, it comes from writing each
kernel for what an AMD GPU does well, instead of going through Triton. A few
examples from the RDNA3 kernels:

- The codebook costs nothing. Each code is an index into an eight-entry
  table, and one `v_perm_b32` turns four codes into four int8 values. Nothing
  is dequantized to fp16 in memory; the cache stays packed until it is in
  registers.
- The products run on the matrix units straight from those codebook values.
  In prefill, QK is an int8 WMMA with one scale per 64-dim block applied
  afterwards; in decode the values go into fp16 WMMA with a constant offset
  that is removed in the softmax. PV uses fp16 WMMA with the V scale folded
  into the probabilities. The portable tier does the same with
  `v_dot4_i32_iu8` (`v_dot4_i32_i8` on gfx9).
- In decode, the query tokens of one request (the 4 tokens of an MTP
  verification, for instance) share every K/V tile, so verifying 4 tokens
  costs almost the same as decoding 1. Pairs of lanes share matrix fragments
  through a DPP swap.
- In prefill, 8 loader waves unpack 16-token tiles into double-buffered LDS
  one tile ahead of 16 compute waves, and the compute waves synchronize on LDS
  only, so the loaders' global reads stay in flight. The GQA heads of one KV
  head share every tile.
- Nothing waits for the host: the metadata is computed on the device, and the
  whole decode path, MTP included, is captured in CUDA graphs.

This is also why the backend is per architecture. The same ideas map to MFMA
and wave64 on CDNA, but the kernel that gets the most out of a MI300 is not
the one that gets the most out of a 7900 XTX. On MI300X (gfx942), for
instance:
- QK runs on the int8 MFMA with the query split into two int8 halves.
- V is widened to fp16 with a single `v_perm` that turns each codebook byte
  into an exact fp16 denormal, which the MI300 MFMA keeps.
- The decode is compiled with its accumulators in VGPRs so it keeps two waves
  per SIMD.

## The reference and the tests

The PyTorch reference in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/rocm_octave.py` defines the
byte layout, and every kernel is tested against it. There is no Triton
fallback on purpose. If an architecture is missing a kernel the backend
refuses to start and says which one, instead of running slowly without
anyone noticing.

## Numbers

Everything below was measured on 4× RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ
W4A16, TP4, 8 GB of KV cache per GPU, `--max-num-seqs 6`,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 2048`, CUDA graphs on. Only the cache dtype changes
between rows.

### Capacity and quality

GSM8K uses `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py` (chat, thinking off, 500
questions, temperature 0.6, no MTP so that TurboQuant is correct; the noise
is about ±1.2 points). NLL is the next-token NLL over a single 380k-token
document.

| KV cache | Bytes | KV tokens | GSM8K | NLL over fp16 at 380k |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 1024 | 445,825 | 91.8 | — |
| `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | 230 | 1,790,625 | 89.8 | +0.00155 |
| `turboquant_3bit_nc` | 198 | 2,053,571 | — | +0.00368 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 248 | 1,678,832 | 91.4 | +0.00086 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 216 | 1,897,520 | 92.4 | +0.00125 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 196 | 2,068,468 | 91.8 | +0.00150 |

GSM8K cannot tell Octave KV from fp16. The NLL is where the formats separate.
At the size of `turboquant_3bit_nc`, the compact format loses 2.5× less, about
what `turboquant_k3v4_nc` loses with 34 more bytes. The blocked formats also
stay flat as the context grows; TurboQuant's error grows with it.

### Speed

Per layer, one TP4 shard (6 query heads, 1 KV head) at 380k tokens of
context, with `benchmarks/attention_benchmarks`:

| | fp16 | `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | `octave_k3v3_compact` | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode, 1 token | 2370 µs | 2565 µs | 563 µs | 614 µs |
| MTP verify, 4 tokens | 48.8 ms | 6.65 ms | 0.58 ms | 0.62 ms |
| prefill, 2048-token chunk | 125.6 ms | 86.6 ms | 60.8 ms | 63.9 ms |

End to end with `vllm bench serve` (cold prefix, different seed per length,
MTP on), time to first token:

| | fp16 | `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | `octave_k3v3_compact` | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100k | 61.5 s | 59.9 s* | 57.2 s | 56.7 s |
| 380k | 371 s | 621 s | 297 s | 300 s |

\* The first TurboQuant request at 100k took 155 s, probably a Triton compile
for new shapes; we report the second one.

At 100k the prefill is dominated by the model's GEMMs and all-reduce, so the
attention backend matters less. At 380k decode with MTP runs at 152 tok/s
with `octave_k3v3_compact` against 2.7 tok/s with fp16.


### Sparse attention: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (update, Oct 7)

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (`qwen4_exp`) uses sparse attention (QSA) in its
full-attention layers: each token attends to the 2048 positions an indexer
picks. The PR now has a sparse decode that reads the packed cache through
those top-k indices, so Octave KV can be the main KV cache there too.

4x RX 7900 XTX, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GPTQ W4A16 (asymmetric, g32), TP4, fp16,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 512`, no prefix caching. NLL from
`prompt_logprobs` over 12 documents of ~8k tokens, split at position 2048
(where top-k starts to drop tokens), and over 24 short documents. Nats over
fp16; mean NLL repeats to about ±0.003 nats between runs.

| KV cache | KV tokens | NLL pos >= 2048 | NLL pos < 2048 | NLL short |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 47,409 | 1.0856 | 1.6707 | 1.1788 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 155,930 | +0.0395 | +0.0851 | +0.0708 |
| `octave_k3v3` + fp16 window | 155,930 | +0.0163 | noise | +0.0085 |

This model is much harder on a 3-bit cache than the 27B. The protocol is not
the same as the 380k NLL above, but the gap is clear. Looking at real Q/K, its
attention is far sharper: the spread between median and p99 logits is 6-9
nats, the last 64 tokens take 35-80% of the attention mass in most layers,
and the first 4 take 15-40% in a few. When a few tokens carry most of the
mass, their quantization error is not averaged out over many others. Both
halves contribute (quantizing only V costs more than quantizing only K), and
giving K 4 bits did not move the result.

The window keeps the first 4 and the last 64 tokens in fp16 as well, in small
tables keyed by cache slot (~18 MB per layer, no change in capacity), and an
exact kernel adds them to the sparse decode as one more split. It removes
most of the loss. It lives in the QSA path only for now; see step 4 of the
plan and question 4.

These numbers come from our fork: the fp16 port of QSA and two fixes to the
RDNA3 W4A16 MoE path for compressed-tensors checkpoints go in separate PRs.

### MI300X (update, Oct 20)

AMD lent us an MI300X, and the PR now has native gfx942 kernels: MFMA
prefill and an MFMA decode. Everything else is shared with RDNA3.

1× MI300X, Qwen3.8-27B W4A16 (compressed-tensors, int4, group 32; to reproduce, [`cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4) is a public checkpoint with the same scheme and architecture, so KV token counts will differ only slightly), TP1, fp16, MTP k=3,
`--max-model-len 131072`; only the cache dtype changes between rows.
- GSM8K: chat, thinking off, 200 questions.
- NIAH: 16 look-alike keys in one 126k document, asked at 32k, 64k and 126k
  (28 questions).
- Speed: `vllm bench serve` with random prompts.
- The fp8 row is AITER's flash attention, forced with
  `--attention-backend ROCM_AITER_FA`. Without it vLLM picks `ROCM_ATTN` even
  with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`.

| KV cache | KV tokens | GSM8K | NIAH | decode at 126k | TPOT 1 user, 8k / 32k / 100k | 16 users, 8k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` | 7,014,973 | 98.0 | 28/28 | 52 tok/s | 15 / 18 / 16 ms | 221 tok/s |
| `octave_k3v4` | 6,391,547 | 97.5 | 28/28 | 52 tok/s | 15 / 15 / 19 ms | 226 tok/s |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 7,446,005 | 97.0 | 28/28 | 50 tok/s | 16 / 18 / 16 ms | 211 tok/s |
| fp8, `ROCM_AITER_FA` | 3,597,048 | 97.0 | 28/28 | 50 tok/s | 15 / 17 / 16 ms | 235 tok/s |
| fp16, `ROCM_ATTN` | 1,952,899 | 97.0 | 28/28 | 6 tok/s | 22 / 45 / 108 ms | 120 tok/s |

NIAH in detail. The haystack is vLLM's own Python source, tokenized and cut
to 126k tokens. 16 keys are inserted every ~7.7k tokens, each a line such as
`# PROJECT KEY Aldebaran: WK3DEGZD`, with star names as look-alike labels
and random 8-character values. The same document is then cut at 32k, 64k
and 126k, which hold 4, 8 and 16 keys. For each key present the model is
asked, thinking off, to answer only that key's value; an answer counts if it
contains the exact value. Keys sit between 3% and 95% of the context. We
also check whether an answer returns another key's value: none did.

| KV cache | 32k (4 keys) | 64k (8 keys) | 126k (16 keys) | another key's value returned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| fp8, `ROCM_AITER_FA` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |
| fp16, `ROCM_ATTN` | 4/4 | 8/8 | 16/16 | 0 |

The task is easy for this model at 128k, so all rows saturate. It shows that
the 3-bit cache loses no retrieval up to the model's served window here,
not that it beats fp8. The harder test is the 800k curve in the RFC, where
the keys start to blur only past 640k, from the model and not from the cache.

`vllm bench serve` in detail. Random prompts (`--dataset-name random`),
512 output tokens with `--ignore-eos`, `--seed 0`, no prefix reuse. Runs:
- 6 prompts at 8k, 4 at 32k and 3 at 100k, one at a time;
- 64 prompts at 8k with 16 concurrent.

No request failed. Each cell is median TTFT / median TPOT / output tok/s.
Random tokens give MTP a low acceptance, so TPOT is higher than on real
text, the same for every row.

| KV cache | 8k, 1 user | 32k, 1 user | 100k, 1 user | 8k, 16 users |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` | 1.55 s / 15.3 ms / 51.3 | 5.99 s / 18.1 ms / 33.4 | 20.2 s / 15.6 ms / 17.9 | 3.34 s / 62.1 ms / 221 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 1.55 s / 15.4 ms / 52.4 | 6.06 s / 15.3 ms / 35.8 | 20.2 s / 19.2 ms / 17.1 | 3.95 s / 57.0 ms / 226 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 1.57 s / 16.2 ms / 50.2 | 6.73 s / 17.6 ms / 32.4 | 20.1 s / 15.6 ms / 17.9 | 3.27 s / 57.2 ms / 211 |
| fp8, `ROCM_AITER_FA` | 1.57 s / 15.2 ms / 49.3 | 5.53 s / 17.1 ms / 34.1 | 18.6 s / 16.2 ms / 19.0 | 3.29 s / 49.9 ms / 235 |
| fp16, `ROCM_ATTN` | 1.64 s / 22.5 ms / 36.8 | 5.78 s / 44.6 ms / 16.9 | 23.1 s / 108.4 ms / 6.2 | 7.26 s / 112.4 ms / 120 |

Without MTP, to compare with UltraQuant, which needs bf16 here:

| KV cache | 8k, 1 user | 32k, 1 user | 100k, 1 user | 8k, 16 users |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3` (fp16) | 1.57 s / 51.9 ms / 18.2 | 5.28 s / 52.2 ms / 16.0 | 19.1 s / 52.6 ms / 11.1 | 10.9 s / 82.0 ms / 157 |
| `ultraquant_4bit` (bf16) | 1.84 s / 58.5 ms / 16.1 | 6.24 s / 66.0 ms / 12.8 | 20.3 s / 87.5 ms / 7.9 | 14.0 s / 94.5 ms / 135 |

Without MTP the Octave TPOT is flat at ~52 ms from 8k to 100k: on gfx942 the
step is the W4A16 GEMMs, and attention adds almost nothing as the context
grows.

On one MI300X that is 53 concurrent requests of 128k with `octave_k3v3`,
against 27 with fp8 and 15 with fp16. For one request Octave KV runs at
AITER's speed, and per layer its decode is faster from 32k on (65 vs 103 µs
at 128k). AITER is still ahead with 16 users at 8k and in time to first token
at 100k (18.6 vs 20.2 s), which points at our prefill over a cached prefix.

We also ran UltraQuant (#57057) on the same setup, in bf16 as it requires.
On gfx942 its FlyDSL decode is not used (it is written for gfx950 and does
not cover 6 query heads per KV head), so it runs its Triton fallback:
- With MTP k=3 the output was not usable: GSM8K 1.0%, NIAH 0/28, answers
  repeating their first characters.
- Without MTP it is correct: 7,730,626 tokens, GSM8K 98.0, NIAH 28/28.
  `octave_k3v3` without MTP holds 9,437,184 tokens and decodes at 19.0 vs
  10.4 tok/s at 126k.

This says nothing about UltraQuant on gfx950, which is the hardware it was
written for.

### In production

We switched two boxes from int8 per-token-head to `octave_k3v3` (it is still
called `splitq_k3v3` in our fork). On the same image and flags, checked on a
local copy before switching:

| | int8 per-token-head | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|
| KV cache tokens | 961,194 | 2,142,148 |
| Decode step, 1 / 2 / 4 users, short context | 15.91 / 18.05 / 23.02 ms | 16.19 / 18.41 / 23.26 ms |
| MTP acceptance | 67.6-68.2% | 67.6-68.0% |

At short context we pay 1-2% per step, probably the fixed cost of the
rotations (we have not profiled it). What we gain is capacity, and speed at
long context. Both boxes now serve 512k-token contexts, with room for about
four such requests at once.

One thing that will surprise other users of hybrid models: vLLM sizes the
scheduler block so that one attention page matches one GDN state page. A
smaller KV slot makes the block longer, 1,584 tokens with int8 and 3,792 with
`octave_k3v3`. Flags that must be a multiple of the block, such as
`--prefix-cache-retention-interval`, have to follow it or the engine will not
start, and the prefix cache becomes coarser: the next turn of a conversation
can recompute up to one block.

### How far the context goes

We were curious whether the 3-bit cache would be what limits context, so we
raised `max_model_len` to 820k and built one document from vLLM's own source
code, with 16 look-alike keys ("CLAVE DEL PROYECTO <star>: <8 chars>") every
50k tokens. At each length we asked for every key present. The model was
trained to 262k and we did not scale RoPE:

| Context | Keys retrieved | Decode with MTP |
|---|---|---|
| 128k | 3/3 | 153 tok/s |
| 256k | 5/5 | 140 tok/s |
| 512k | 10/10 | 127 tok/s |
| 640k | 13/13 | 107 tok/s |
| 800k | 13/16 | 95 tok/s |

At 800k the model starts to answer three of the keys with the most recent
one. It confuses them, it does not produce garbage. This is one document and
an easy task, so we read it as an upper bound, but it suggests the format is
not the bottleneck: retrieval holds until the model itself starts to blur.

## A contract per architecture

Most of the backend is portable HIP that runs on wave32 and wave64 alike: the
cache store, the split-KV reduce, the rotation and a dot4 decode. What each
architecture has to add is one native prefill kernel and, if it wants to be
fast, a decode on its matrix instructions. Following the review on the PR,
Octave is built and selected only on the architectures it has been validated
on, gfx1100 and gfx942, and each new one is added once it passes the tests
and an end-to-end run. This is where things stand:

| Target | GPUs | Decode | Prefill |
|---|---|---|---|
| gfx1100 (RDNA3) | RX 7900 XTX/XT/GRE, PRO W7900/W7800 | WMMA | WMMA, in this PR |
| gfx942 (CDNA3) | MI300X/MI325X | MFMA | MFMA, in this PR |
| gfx1101-1103 (RDNA3) | RX 7800/7700/7600, PRO W7700/W7600 | — | same kernels as gfx1100, not yet validated |
| gfx1150/1151 (RDNA3.5) | Ryzen AI 300, Ryzen AI Max (Strix Halo) | portable | missing; same WMMA as RDNA3, so probably only wider guards |
| gfx1200/1201 (RDNA4) | RX 9070/9060, Radeon AI PRO R9700 | portable | missing; needs a port of the WMMA kernels to the gfx12 layout |
| gfx950 (CDNA4) | MI350X/MI355X | portable | missing; the gfx942 kernels plus the new FP8/FP4 MFMA |
| gfx90a (CDNA2) | MI210/MI250X | portable | missing; a new kernel on MFMA |

"Portable" means the shared HIP kernels would compile there, but the backend
is not built or selected on those targets until they are validated; the test
suite runs the portable decode next to the native one on gfx1100 and gfx942.

A new kernel can be HIP or FlyDSL. FlyDSL looks like a good fit for CDNA, and
it would add a runtime dependency, which is one of our open questions below.
Whatever the language, it keeps the signature of `octave_prefill`, passes
`tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py` against the reference, and is
is added to the CMake guard, `_kernel_tier` and `supports_compute_capability`. For every new path we also break
the kernel on purpose once and check that the tests catch it.

The backend states what it does not support, and vLLM rejects it at startup:
head sizes other than 256 for now, sliding windows, ALiBi, sinks, soft-cap,
and bidirectional attention over image tokens. One limit depends on the
tensor-parallel size rather than on the model: the decode handles 1, 2, 4, 6
or 8 query heads per KV head on each GPU, so Qwen3.5-122B needs TP 4 or more.

This is what we would like to ask AMD for, if the direction makes sense to
you:

1. A review of the format and the contract, as a common basis for compressed
   KV caches on ROCm.
2. Help with gfx950 and the RDNA4 port. gfx942 is done, thanks to the MI300X
   AMD lent us. We are happy to review against the tests and to help with
   the format side.
3. Running `test_rocm_octave.py` on the AMD CI runners.
4. Access to a gfx1151 and a gfx1201 machine, which we cannot test today.

## Models

Today the kernels need head size 256 with 64 RoPE dims, which is the
Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 / 3.6 / 3.8 family, dense and MoE. We run Qwen3.8-27B,
and since October 7 also Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, whose sparse attention (QSA)
uses Octave KV as its main cache through a sparse decode (see "Sparse
attention" above). The 35B-A3B, 80B-A3B, 9B and 4B models of that family have
the same shape but we have not run them.

Most other models use head size 128. Those with partial RoPE (GLM-4.5/4.6,
MiniMax-M2) fit the blocked layout as it is, and those with full RoPE (Llama,
Qwen3, Mistral and others) can use the compact layout, which does not care
about RoPE. Templating the kernels on head size is our next step. We also
tried Gemma 4 26B-A4B; it does not start on gfx1100 even with Triton and fp16,
because of its 512-dim heads, so it would need its own kernels.

## Plan

1. This PR: the backend, the three formats, the shared kernels, and the
   decode and prefill for RDNA3 (gfx1100) and MI300X (gfx942), for head size
   256.
2. Head size 128, validated on models that fit our boxes
   (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, and GLM-4.5-Air if it fits).
3. The rest of the AMD line, following the contract, hopefully with AMD.
4. Keeping the first and the last tokens in fp16. On real Q/K/V of the 27B,
   keeping the first 16 and the last 256 cuts the attention error of the
   compact format from 14.6% to 5.9%. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next it is not
   optional: keeping the first 4 and the last 64 takes the NLL cost from
   +0.040 to +0.016 nats after position 2048, and from +0.071 to +0.009 on
   short documents (Oct 7, see "Sparse attention"). A first version lives in
   the QSA path of the PR. It is not specific to this backend, so we would
   still rather design the general mechanism with you than grow it inside
   one.

## Questions for you

1. Is a backend tied to one attention shape acceptable for a first PR (as the
   MLA backends are), with head size 128 as a follow-up?
2. Is "native kernels only, fail at startup otherwise" the right policy for a
   ROCm-only backend, or would you rather have a slow portable prefill?
3. Would a FlyDSL dependency be acceptable for the CDNA kernels, and how
   should it be declared?
4. Should the fp16 window from step 4 be a general KV-cache mechanism in
   vLLM?
5. On hybrid models, should flags tied to the block size (like the
   retention interval) be given in tokens and rounded by vLLM instead of
   being rejected?

## Related work

TurboQuant (#38479) gave us the starting point. We differ in the V quantizer
(Lloyd-Max instead of uniform min/max), the norm-preserving scale, the
RoPE-aware K blocks, and in reading the packed cache in every phase with
native kernels. The compact layout rotates the whole K head at 3 bits like
`turboquant_3bit_nc`, which makes the comparison direct; we have not isolated
which of the differences matters most.

Other related work: UltraQuant (#57057, FP4 with FlyDSL on gfx950, built on
TurboQuant), KVarN (#46613 / #46812, Triton, int4 K / int2 V), #43835 (HIP
int8/int4 per-token-head for CDNA), #40396 (a Triton decode for TurboQuant on
MI300X), #53231 (TurboQuant for Gemma 4 on ROCm) and #59132
(`ROCM_SEGMENTED_ATTN`, Triton attention for RDNA with fp16/bf16 KV, which
covers many of the shapes we reject).

We used AI assistance to write kernels, tests and this text: Claude, and
Qwen3.8-27B itself, served on these same boxes, so the model helped build the
cache it now runs on. Every number here was measured on the hardware
described, and I have reviewed the code and can answer for it.

cc @tjtanaa @dllehr-amd @hongxiayang @AndreasKaratzas @BowenBao @mgehre-amd
(ROCm) · @LucasWilkinson @MatthewBonanni (attention backends) · @sighingnow
(Qwen models, since these kernels target the Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 attention shape)

title: [RFC]: Bounded prefix reuse for target-token prefill scoring
author: LinzeShi
body:
### Motivation.

Allow target-token scoring requests to reuse the context before their first scoring position. When several responses share a long prompt, the teacher can reuse its KV cache for that prompt and compute every requested response score.

[#56860](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56860) and [#56984](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56984) added per-position token candidates. [VIME #467](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/pull/467), currently under review, adds an optional path that uses this API for OPD teacher scoring. These requests submit the complete context and student response, but need scores only for the response.

Scoring requests skip prefix-cache reads by default. Explicitly setting `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False` allows a cache hit to extend past a required scoring position. KV blocks contain attention state, not the scores for skipped positions, so the result can be incomplete. This proposal bounds the hit at the scoring boundary, using the existing cache lookup interface.

The target workload is repeated scoring with substantial shared context, such as document QA or text requests containing long instructions and tool descriptions. The benefit depends on context length, response length, and when requests arrive. The prototype results below show a clear gain on long document inputs and a smaller gain on short math prompts.

### Proposed Change.

#### Request behavior

Use the existing parameters and response format. For a response following `P >= 1` context tokens:

```python
SamplingParams(
    max_tokens=1,
    prompt_logprob_start=P - 1,
    prompt_logprob_token_ids=[[token] for token in response_token_ids],
    skip_reading_prefix_cache=False,
)
```

The model input is `context_token_ids + response_token_ids`. `max_tokens=1` follows the current request lifecycle; the caller discards the generated token. The separate [scoring-only lifecycle proposal](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56860#issuecomment-5971319472) can later use the same cache boundary with `max_tokens=0`.

| Request | Cache behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Scoring request with the option omitted or set to `True` | Keep the current no-read default. |
| Explicit `False` with an eligible target-token scoring request | Reuse local KV up to the first scoring position. |
| Ordinary `prompt_logprobs` also requested, zero scoring rows, or a configuration outside the enabled scope | Recompute the input through the existing scoring path. |
| Request without target-token scoring | Keep existing behavior. |

Existing validation determines whether a scoring request is supported. Python and Rust frontends preserve the same omitted/`True`/`False` semantics; candidate order, padding, normalization, and serialization stay unchanged.

Let `S` be `prompt_logprob_start` (zero when omitted), `N` the input length, and `H` the number of cached prefix tokens. Cache lookup uses:

```text
max_cache_hit_length = min(S, N - 1)
H <= S
```

The cache supplies positions `[0, H)`. Scoring row `j` uses the model output at position `S + j`, so position `S` must be computed. For OPD, this is the last context position, which predicts the first response token.

For example, `P=2048` gives `S=2047`. With 16-token cache alignment, the maximum hit is 2032 tokens. The coordinator rounds down to an available aligned prefix. This cap applies even when a previous complete request, including its response, is cached. The suffix still attends to the entire preceding context through KV.

#### Implementation and scope

The engine resolves the policy per request and applies it at three points:

1. **Admission:** derive the effective skip-read flag and scoring cap before connector `on_new_request` handling. Store them on the request without modifying the caller's `SamplingParams`.
2. **Lookup:** pass the cap through `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` to the existing coordinator. Retain existing block allocation, reference counting, and scheduling order.
3. **Resume:** retain the original cap across prefill chunks and reapply it after preemption. Rebuild any discarded partial scoring state from the capped restart position, using the worker's existing absolute row indices.

The initial path uses Model Runner V2, text token IDs, one full-attention KV group, ordinary block-aligned local caching, fixed unquantized weights and KV, non-streaming output, and `max_tokens=1`. It includes chunked prefill and preemption during prefill.

Single-GPU execution and standard tensor parallelism (TP) use the same scheduler lookup. The scheduler distributes the capped execution plan to the workers; no separate TP cache algorithm is needed. The prototype has been tested at TP=1, TP=2, and TP=4 for cache boundaries, score assembly, preemption, and numerical agreement. These tests use Qwen3-0.6B; VIME's Qwen3-32B TP=4 teacher remains a separate deployment check.

Other cache paths retain full recomputation for these scoring requests: connectors/offload and P/D, hybrid or sliding-window state, partial-block reuse, multimodal or embedding inputs, LoRA, speculative decoding, resumable input sessions, auxiliary-output capture, other distributed topologies, and larger generation budgets. Their effective no-read policy covers both local and external cache hits.

The change belongs in request admission, `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py`, and scheduler resume handling. The scoring worker continues to assemble results by absolute position and reject incomplete buffers. Existing cache identity, cache salt, and weight-update invalidation rules remain in effect. Candidate IDs select scores and do not change KV identity.

#### Prototype results

A process-local lookup-cap prototype ran on Qwen3-0.6B, revision `c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca`, with vLLM `97bd8c74ebf12c3d847fb59f24966a83bf6f6920`. It used RTX 4090 GPUs, BF16, Model Runner V2, eager execution, synchronous scheduling, 16-token cache blocks, and at most four concurrent requests.

Inputs were four [DAPO math](https://huggingface.co/datasets/zhuzilin/dapo-math-17k) prompts and four document QA prompts from [LongBench Qasper](https://huggingface.co/datasets/zai-org/LongBench/tree/5e628be450b7e67fb7ae6e201bd6d8f7056f7672). Qwen3-0.6B generated four responses per prompt. Math contexts contained 142–209 tokens and responses 437–1024 tokens; 10 of 16 responses reached the 1024-token generation limit. Document contexts contained 2933–3944 tokens and responses 13–58 tokens; none reached the limit. Input contexts were not truncated.

The following TP=1 results use batch-invariant mode. Each group starts with an empty cache. Six alternating baseline/prototype repetitions replay the same tokens. Ratios divide the sum of the four per-prompt median times without reuse by the corresponding sum with reuse.

| Workload | Prefill token budget | Four requests together | Staggered requests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Short math prompts | 512 | 1.12x | 1.12x |
| Short math prompts | 2048 | 1.09x | 1.01x |
| Document QA | 512 | 3.82x | 3.82x |
| Document QA | 2048 | 3.12x | 1.80x |

Staggered replay targets 20 ms between arrivals, admitting requests at engine-step boundaries. Times include cache creation and one generated token. They measure the teacher-scoring stage on this small sample, not a training speedup or a production arrival trace. Ordinary BF16 runs showed the same workload pattern; at budget 512, document QA cold-group speedups were 3.73x at TP=2 and 3.72x at TP=4, each against its own uncached baseline.

At TP=1/2/4, controlled batch-invariant comparisons matched the uncached scores elementwise for all 32 generated responses, six boundary cases, and forced preemption at budget 512. Ordinary BF16 reuse comparisons had maximum absolute logprob differences of 0.21–0.28 on the generated responses; changing the uncached batch also produced differences. Independent Transformers full-forward checks on eight responses supported the intended next-token alignment, but were not numerically identical to vLLM: in batch-invariant mode, both cached and uncached vLLM paths had the same differences from that reference, with maxima of approximately 0.345–0.409 across the tested configurations. Per-response mean absolute differences were below 0.045 nats with the intended alignment and above 16 nats when shifted by one row, supporting the expected row alignment.

The prototype exercises the cache cap. Request admission, configuration fallback, and frontend integration remain implementation work.

Benchmark scripts and recorded results are available in [my fork](https://github.com/LinzeShi/vllm/blob/a3ee20187a82e3ea6220e4831cf402216df8bc02/benchmarks/opd_prefix_reuse/README.md).

#### Validation

Extend the existing cache, scheduler, scoring, and frontend suites:

| Area | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Boundary and outputs | `S=0`, block edges, cached responses extending past `S`, different suffixes and candidate IDs; verify actual adopted KV length, first and last score rows, candidate order, `-1` padding to `-inf`, empty outputs, and simultaneous ordinary prompt scores. |
| Lifecycle and fallback | Chunked prefill, forced preemption after scoring starts, cancellation, fresh request IDs, cache-salt isolation, and connectors offering an external hit. Verify complete scores and the no-read fallback; cover eager and standard async/CUDA graph execution. |
| Frontends and defaults | Matching Python/Rust request behavior; unchanged defaults and ordinary generation. |
| Numerics | Compare with the uncached scorer and an independent full-forward next-token reference. Use batch-invariant controls, following [#60056](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60056), alongside ordinary BF16 runs with batch and prefill-shape controls. Select tolerances for the model, backend, and comparison being tested. |
| Tensor parallelism | Convert the TP=1/2/4 prototype checks into regression tests against the production implementation. |

Extend the real-input replay with more prompts, the intended teacher model, and recorded VIME arrivals. Record the dataset revision, chat template, actual token lengths, generation settings, and truncation. Replay the same tokens with and without reuse, including cold single requests, cold groups, staggered arrivals, unrelated prompts, and cache pressure. Use at least two prefill scheduling budgets and report group latency, throughput, computed tokens, and cache hits. Compare each execution mode against its own baseline; these measurements cover the teacher-scoring stage.

Update the existing oversized-hit regression to expect complete target-token scores, and keep a worker-level check that an incomplete scoring buffer is still rejected. Experiment-only replay scripts stay outside the upstream feature diff.

#### Delivery

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Real-input prototype]
    B[Request policy and bounded lookup]
    C[Lifecycle and numerical validation]
    D[VIME opt-in integration]
    A --> B --> C --> D
```

| Step | Deliverable | Dependency | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Real-input cache-cap prototype and TP=1/2/4 measurements | Existing scoring API | @LinzeShi |
| 2 | Request policy, lookup cap, and CPU regression coverage | Step 1 | @LinzeShi |
| 3 | Frontend, lifecycle, numerical, and TP regression coverage; intended-teacher replay | Step 2 | @LinzeShi |
| 4 | VIME opt-in for validated teacher configurations and versions | Validated engine support | @LinzeShi |

The prototype measurements for step 1 are complete. The next deliverable is the vLLM implementation and its regression tests. VIME integration follows as a separate change, preserving the existing OPD loss and default scoring mode. VIME enables reuse only with a compatible teacher version; older teachers keep the existing no-read path.

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@aoshen02 @njhill @Isotr0py

### Any Other Things.

#### Related work

- [Earlier discussion in #8268](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/8268#issuecomment-2612758200) proposed reusing context before the requested scoring suffix. This proposal applies that boundary to the current per-position scoring API.
- [#56860](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56860) and [#56984](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56984) provide the scoring API. The `max_tokens=0` follow-up addresses request lifecycle; the cache cap is independent of it.
- [#42245](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42245) discusses ordinary prompt scores missing after cache hits. This proposal reuses positions before the requested scores begin.
- [#45221](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45221) covers auxiliary-output storage. This proposal uses existing KV and requires no stored scores or hidden states.
- [#48312](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48312) covers cache correctness after weight updates. This proposal operates within the existing invalidation contract.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]:Ownership boundaries for externally orchestrated checkpoint and restore
author: leeZardNav
body:
### Motivation.

**The use case.** Start a vLLM replica from a checkpoint of a warm server instead of a cold load. On a cluster, the replica that restores is rarely the one that was captured. It runs in a new container, often on another node.

**System context.** [Snapshot](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot) is a Kubernetes-native system that checkpoints and restores GPU workloads from outside the process:

- A node agent captures the whole container, CPU and GPU memory, with [CRIU](https://criu.org) and [cuda-checkpoint](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-checkpoint).
- Snapshot stores the image and restores it into a new container on a compatible node.
- The privileged work stays in the node agent. vLLM runs unprivileged and never links CRIU.
- vLLM doesn't need to know it runs on Kubernetes.

In the rest of this RFC, Snapshot is the orchestrator. It can't make a running server safe to capture. Only vLLM can drain its requests, let go of its GPU-to-GPU links, and decide what stays in GPU memory. After the restore, only vLLM can rebuild those links and start serving again.

**The gap.** vLLM already has most of the parts: `pause_generation()`, `sleep()` and `wake_up()`, and the communicator hooks `checkpoint_prepare()` and `checkpoint_restore()` from [#46877](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46877). What it lacks is a contract for who starts a capture, how vLLM says it is safe to capture, and how it hears it may resume. Without one, each orchestrator wraps `vllm serve` in its own application, and other proposals define that contract differently (see Any Other Things).

**Deployments differ.** They differ in what they can afford to keep in GPU memory and what code of their own they need to run around a capture. The contract needs a default that works with no configuration, a few settings for the common choices, and a place for a deployment's own code.

This RFC proposes that contract: how the orchestrator talks to vLLM, what vLLM does once it gets the signal, and how a deployment configures and extends that behavior. It adds no orchestrator code to vLLM.


### Proposed Change.

#### Ownership

**What vLLM owns.** vLLM gets itself ready for a capture, on its own at startup or when a caller asks. It drains its requests, clears its caches, lets go of its GPU-to-GPU links, and releases what the deployer configured it to release. Once that's done, it reports itself as `prepared`, which means it is now safe to capture. After the restore, when the orchestrator tells it to resume, it rebuilds what it released and returns to serving on its own. Its existing `/health` tells the platform when to route traffic to it.

**What the orchestrator owns.** The orchestrator polls vLLM's status until it reads `prepared`, then captures, stores and restores the container. It holds the privileges and runs CRIU, the CUDA checkpoint and the node compatibility checks. Apart from an optional request to get ready, its only message to vLLM is the signal that vLLM may resume.

#### Boundary 1: how the orchestrator talks to vLLM

vLLM adds three routes for checkpointing:

- `POST /checkpoint/prepare` asks vLLM to get ready for a capture.
- `GET /checkpoint/status` tells whether vLLM is `prepared`, and returns 503 when it isn't.
- `POST /checkpoint/resume` tells vLLM to go back to work after the restore.

All endpoints return 200 on success, 401 when the server has an API key and the call doesn't carry it, and 409 when the call conflicts with the current state. Any other error returns 500.

Everything is opt-in behind one flag, shown here as `--enable-checkpoint`. All names in this RFC are placeholders. Without the flag, nothing changes. A policy's prerequisites keep their own flags, such as `--enable-sleep-mode` for the default offload-weights, and startup fails if one is missing.

**Who initiates.** Getting ready is separate from capturing. vLLM can get ready on its own at startup, or a caller can ask it while it's serving. Either way, the orchestrator only watches for `prepared` and doesn't need to know which one happened.

- **vLLM itself, at startup.** With a startup option, vLLM prepares as soon as it is loaded and warm, before serving any request. This is the common case: capture once, then start every replica from that checkpoint.
- **A caller, while serving.** `POST /checkpoint/prepare` asks a running server to get ready. The caller can be the orchestrator, an operator, or a script.

vLLM never calls the orchestrator. It only publishes its state.

**Readiness.** `GET /checkpoint/status` answers one question: is vLLM `prepared`, meaning safe to capture. The orchestrator polls it until the return is 200. This is separate from serving readiness. While vLLM isn't serving, inference routes and `/health` return 503, so the platform takes it out of rotation. The prepare and resume calls return 200 as soon as vLLM accepts them, without waiting for the work to finish. `GET /checkpoint/status` shows when prepare is done, and `/health` shows when resume is. A failure after the response is logged, and the status body carries the error.

**Resume.** After the restore, the orchestrator calls `POST /checkpoint/resume` on a fresh connection. Apart from the optional prepare, it's the only message the orchestrator sends.

The status and resume routes keep working while vLLM is prepared, even though inference routes return 503. All three routes work without `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`.

vLLM handles one lifecycle call at a time: repeating prepare or resume while it is running or already done has no extra effect, and calling one while the other is running returns 409. A prepare that arrives while vLLM is serving always starts a new cycle, so a caller should check the status before retrying one.

#### Boundary 2: what vLLM does behind the routes

**Prepare** (default, configuration in the next section):

1. Stop admitting requests, finish those in flight, and clear the prefix, multimodal and encoder caches, with `pause_generation(mode="wait")`.
2. prepare supported communicator workspaces for checkpointing with `checkpoint_prepare()` ([#46877](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46877)).
3. Release what the checkpoint shouldn't carry, per the configured policy. By default vLLM calls `sleep(level=1)`, which moves the weights to CPU memory and discards the KV cache.
4. Run the deployment's own pre-capture code, if any (user custom code).
5. Report `prepared` and wait.

**Resume** reverses it. vLLM refreshes values that may differ on the new node, then runs the deployment's own post-restore code, if any (user custom code). Then it reloads what was released, rebuilds fresh links with `checkpoint_restore()`, resumes scheduling and reopens admission. It reports nothing further and returns to healthy on its own.

#### Configuration and extension

A default covers the simple case, settings cover the common choices, and a deployment's own code covers the rest.

**What survives.** The deployer picks a policy with one setting.

| Policy | Kept in the checkpoint | Released before capture |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `offload-weights` (default) | Weights, in CPU memory | KV cache, and weights from GPU memory, as `sleep(level=1)` |
| `resident` | Weights, KV cache, and the prefix, multimodal and encoder caches | Nothing |
| `keep-weights` | Weights | KV cache, with a release option no sleep level offers today |
| `reload-weights` | Neither | Weights and KV cache, as `sleep(level=2)`. Weights reload after restore, as in [#51360](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51360) |

Every policy except `resident` clears the prefix, multimodal and encoder caches in prepare step 1. In-flight requests never survive, because prepare drains them first.

**Extension.** A deployment that keeps `vllm serve` can supply its own hooks as a Python class, given by its full import name, the way `--worker-extension-cls` works today. Its `before_capture()` runs at prepare step 4 and its `after_restore()` at the start of resume. They run in addition to the configured policy, so a deployment can add its own logic without wrapping the entry point or giving up the default. A typical use is reloading credentials or a gateway address after a restore on another node.

**Settings.** Each is a serve argument with a matching environment variable, so a deployment can turn this on without changing its command.

| Setting | Controls | Default |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `--enable-checkpoint` | The `/checkpoint/*` routes and the lifecycle | Off |
| `--checkpoint-at-startup` | Preparing once loaded and warm | Off |
| `--checkpoint-policy` | What survives, from the table above | `offload-weights` |
| `--checkpoint-hooks` | The full import name of the hooks class, such as `mypkg.hooks.SnapshotHooks` | None |
| `--checkpoint-prepare-timeout` | How long draining may take before prepare fails | No limit |

#### Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller (optional)
    participant V as vLLM
    participant O as Orchestrator
    alt at startup
        V->>V: load and warm up
    else while serving
        C->>V: POST /checkpoint/prepare
    end
    V->>V: drain, clear caches, release links, apply policy
    loop until prepared
        O->>V: GET /checkpoint/status
    end
    V-->>O: prepared
    O->>O: capture and store
    O->>O: restore into a new container
    Note over V: from here, this is the restored copy
    O->>V: POST /checkpoint/resume
    V->>V: reload per policy, rebuild links, reopen admission
    Note over V: serving again, /health returns 200
```

#### Failure scenarios

If prepare fails, such as a hook error or a drain that times out, vLLM stays unhealthy and never reports `prepared`, so nothing is captured. The error is logged and shown in the status body, and the platform replaces the replica. If the capture fails, the platform replaces the source. If resume fails, vLLM logs the error, shows it in the status body, and stays unhealthy. The deployment's controller can then replace the replica or start one cold. If the orchestrator never captures or never resumes, vLLM stays `prepared` and unhealthy until the orchestrator or the platform replaces it.

**Initial scope.** One serving container, including multiple API processes and local TP, PP and DP. Remote engines, Ray and elastic EP come later.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@galletas1712 @matteso1

### Any Other Things.

**Related work.** This RFC doesn't replace any of these. It proposes the contract they could share.

| Work | State | How it relates |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| [#34303](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/34303), CUDA checkpoint/restore RFC | Open | In its Tier 2, vLLM runs CRIU itself. Here the orchestrator does, and vLLM only prepares and resumes |
| [#51360](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51360), `vllm snapshot` | Merged | In-process capture on one host. Could share the policy API |
| [#54940](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54940), container snapshot with CRIU | Open | Similar HTTP lifecycle, but vLLM copies device memory to host and back through a device plugin. Here cuda-checkpoint captures GPU memory from outside |

**Prototypes.**

- [galletas1712/vllm#1](https://github.com/galletas1712/vllm/pull/1) implements both boundaries: HTTP prepare, resume and status for the Python and Rust frontends, and a pluggable policy API that `vllm snapshot` also uses.
- With [galletas1712/vllm#2](https://github.com/galletas1712/vllm/pull/2), it ran end to end with ai-dynamo/snapshot on one T4, including a restore into a new pod. Multi-GPU and multi-API-process configurations haven't run yet.
- A file-signaled version of the same lifecycle captured stock `vllm serve` with ai-dynamo/snapshot on a single A10G and restored it into a new pod that served completions. The only addition to the deployment was one environment variable.


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Improving MooncakeConnector
author: wangxiyuan
body:
# [RFC]: Improving MooncakeConnector

MooncakeConnector is the built-in P/D disaggregation KV direct-transfer connector in vLLM. Its underlying Mooncake TransferEngine supports pluggable transports (RDMA/TCP/Ascend direct, etc.), making it **the primary path for P/D disaggregation on non-CUDA platforms**. Its engineering quality directly determines the usability of P/D disaggregation on those platforms. There are currently 20+ open issues in the vLLM repo pointing directly at MooncakeConnector, with crash/hang/leak and data-corruption reports making up the largest share.

## Motivation.

<details>

**Transfer and protocol**

1. **Single transfer mode**: push only — no pull path and no mode configuration; the decode side cannot pull on demand at its own scheduling pace.
2. **Redundant metadata**: the full KV region table of the decode node is rebuilt and re-sent with every request batch, and the prefill side re-aligns it every time — layout information that never changes during the engine lifetime sits on the per-request critical path.
3. **Fragile discovery**: the HTTP bootstrap server runs inside a prefill-side worker process and is affected by that process's GIL; the query side has a hard-coded timeout with no retry, the register side once blocked producer startup indefinitely, and under external DP LB all workers register as dp_rank 0.

    Refs: #58543 (query-side timeout), #55114 (registration blocking), #51531 (dp_rank)

4. **Questionable transfer correctness with no debugging means**: two independent reports reproduce `dst != src` after RDMA WRITE (concentrated on large descriptors), and the connector lacks a verified-transfer debug mode (per-descriptor verification / deferred confirmation) to tell whether the fault is in the connector or in the TransferEngine.

    Refs: #42395, #44238

**Robustness**

5. **Broken failure propagation**: failures in worker threads / the side channel / bootstrap are not propagated to the scheduler; requests hang with no terminal error visible to the client.

    Refs: #55870, #50425, #57530

6. **Preemption timing window**: request preemption (including the `reset_prefix_cache` path that preempts outside `schedule()`) races with in-flight KV transfers; the prefill side only has a 480s expire fallback, with no delay-free / state-retention protocol. The timing is more complex with PP > 1.
7. **Block-size semantics defect**: the `cache_config.block_size` collapsed across KV groups by `min()` is treated as the physical transfer block size, so hybrid models crash on the first P2P transfer; the hybrid Mamba/GDN path is bug-dense.

    Refs: #58362, #49537, #54392

**Feature coverage**

8. **Incomplete parallelism support**: neither DCP nor PCP is supported; there is no design for KVPP or for transfers where the draft model and the main model use different parallelism strategies; pipeline parallelism (PP) itself — running the prefill and decode stages of one request across PP ranks with in-flight KV handoff between stages — is not supported either, and interacts with the preemption window above. Hetero-TP (P/D sides with different TP degrees) is likewise not yet supported.

    Refs: #53205

9. **Incomplete HMA / new-model coverage**: the connector subclasses `SupportsHMA`, but end-to-end P2P disaggregation is not validated — and in places not implemented — for the wave of hybrid-memory-allocator models it is meant to serve (Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, and newer variants such as GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash). These models stress exactly the paths where the connector is bug-dense today: heterogeneous KV groups with mixed block sizes (item 7), Mamba/GDN and sliding-window groups, per-group layouts, and multi-group `request_finished` semantics. There is no per-model conformance matrix telling users which of these models work over P2P PD today.

10. **Missing ecosystem integrations**: no layerwise (transfer cannot overlap with compute); no rd2h (remote KV landing directly in host memory); no integration with pooling/offload/hiSparse features at all.

**Quality infrastructure**

11. **Insufficient observability**: a stats container exists but there are no Prometheus metrics; `cached_tokens` is reported with wrong semantics.

    Refs: #47136

12. **Poor platform portability**: the registration interface's layout/alignment assumptions cannot parameterize platform differences (e.g., Ascend's 2MiB alignment and register-region count limits), which forced vllm-ascend to maintain a 4,290-line forked connector plus 5 variants, drifting on two fronts.
13. 
</details>

## Proposed Change.
**Phase 1 — Robustness and correctness**
- Failure spine (worker / side-channel / bootstrap failures propagate to the scheduler, fail-or-recompute decision, terminal error to the client; design in #57530):
    - [ ] #57529 (failure ledger)
    - [ ] #55220, #55217 (fail-closed commit manifests, endpoint-neutral region keys)
    - [ ] #55297 (recompute after load failures)
    - [ ] #59028 (state cleanup for re-admitted requests)
    - [ ] #62668 (keep readiness waits out of transfer slots)
    - [ ] #61006, #50565 (stale completion handling)
    - [ ] #49796 (reject duplicate transfer_id, KV-cache leak)
    - [x] #59347 (suppress completion for empty pulls)

- Bootstrap reliability: configurable query timeout + bounded retries, dp_rank registration fix:
    - [x] #58919 (registration retry, landed on main)
    - [ ] #55763 (same-topic PR, still open)
    - [ ] #55137 (bootstrap registration hang on timeout)
    - [ ] #50464 (LookupKeyServer/Client close wired into teardown)

- Block-size semantics and hybrid groups (port of the vllm-ascend-validated fix; Mamba/GDN convergence):
    - [ ] #58525 (use physical KV-group block size — upstream port)
    - [ ] vllm-ascend#17414 (ascend-side fix, open)
    - [ ] #59592 (reject mismatched block sizes in the handshake)
    - [ ] #55097 (drop NULL_BLOCK_ID pairs after P/D alignment)
    - [ ] #53078 (hetero-TP for hybrid GDN/Mamba)
    - [ ] #55523 (mixed-TP GQA + indexer cache, MiniMax-M3)
    - [ ] #50208 (preserve HMA region strides)
    - [x] #60712 (Mamba cache mode `none` for capacity-only workers)
    - [x] #61012 (EAGLE replay boundary for sliding-window tails)

- Preemption protocol (audit exposure outside `schedule()`; `handle_preemptions`-style hook / delay-free protocol; PP > 1 timing; reduce decode-side recompute):

title: [RFC]: TPSP Fusion Design
author: hlin99
body:
### Motivation.

# RFC: TPSP Fusion Design

## 0. Goal

TPSP decomposes AllReduce into ReduceScatter (RS) + AllGather (AG), fusing RS/AG with adjacent compute (Norm, routing, GEMM) to hide communication behind computation. This brings roughly **10% TTFT improvement on long prefills**, which is especially valuable for today's agentic workloads where long-context prefill is common.


## 1. TPSP Design Principles

- **Conditionally enable TPSP based on measured performance:** A model may be compatible with TPSP without benefiting from it. Auto-profiling should identify the workload-specific crossover point, disable TPSP below it where overhead outweighs the gains, and enable it above it.
- **Enable TPSP model by model:** TPSP changes model execution structure, so models should opt in individually until the approach is sufficiently established. Models not enabled for TPSP should continue using the existing path, with no TPSP-induced change in behavior or performance.
- **Require device-side kernel support:** TPSP relies on fused kernels that may be model- and device-specific. If the required kernel is unavailable on a device, TPSP should automatically be disabled and the existing path used.
- **Share the auto-profiling framework while allowing platform-specific tuning:** Provide common profiling logic that platforms can override or extend to account for their hardware characteristics. The profiling process should complete in about 60 seconds.

---

## 2. Dense Architecture

Two fusion sites per decoder layer: **o_proj** (after attention) and **down_proj** (after MLP).

**Site A — o_proj → RS → Norm → AG**
```
            ┌────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────┐
hidden ───► │ o_proj │──►│ micro-chunk   │──►│  Norm   │──►│ AllGather │──► hidden [full,H]
[full,H]    │ (GEMM) │   │ ReduceScatter │   │(+resid) │   │           │     → gate/up_proj
            └────────┘   └──────────────┘   └─────────┘   └───────────┘
```
Per micro-chunk: `GEMM → partial`, `RS(partial) → reduced`, `Norm(reduced+residual)`, `AG(norm) → full hidden`.

**Site B — down_proj → RS → (next layer's) Norm → AG**
```
            ┌───────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────┐   ┌───────────┐
hidden ───► │ down_proj │──►│ micro-chunk   │──►│ Norm (Layer L+1!)    │──►│ AllGather │──► hidden [full,H]
[full,H]    │ (GEMM)    │   │ ReduceScatter │   │ pulled forward early │   │           │     → Layer L+1 attn
            └───────────┘   └──────────────┘   └─────────────────────┘   └───────────┘
```
Layer L+1's pre-attention norm is pulled into Layer L's RS output, so AG feeds directly into the next layer with no standalone norm in between.

**Notes:** RS accumulation uses peer-visible buffers with a generation-tagged completion signal; Norm fuses "sum partials + residual + LayerNorm/RMSNorm" in one pass; chunk `m+1`'s GEMM overlaps with chunk `m`'s RS/Norm/AG. AG's physical delivery mechanism is an implementation detail, out of scope here.

---

## 3. MoE Architecture (TP MoE only)

Same two fusion sites as dense, but site ① interleaves with **routing**, and site ② interleaves with **expert permutation**.

**Site ① — o_proj → RS → Norm → Top-K/Softmax → AG + Expert Permute**
```
            ┌────────┐   ┌──────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────────┐
hidden ───► │ o_proj │──►│  RS  │──►│Norm(+resid) │──►│ router  │──►│ top-k/softmax  │
[full,H]    │ (GEMM) │   │      │   │  [shard,H]  │   │ logits  │   │  (per shard)   │
            └────────┘   └──────┘   └────────────┘   └─────────┘   └───────┬───────┘
                                          │                                  │ (expert_id, weight)
                                          ▼                                  │
                                    ┌───────────┐                            │
                                    │ AllGather │◄───────────────────────────┘ (overlaps)
                                    │hidden_norm │
                                    └─────┬─────┘
                                          ▼
                                 ┌─────────────────┐
                                 │ Expert Permute    │──► grouped_hidden ──► Group GEMM
                                 └─────────────────┘
```
Routing is computed at shard granularity **before** AG, so permutation index work overlaps with the AG transfer instead of blocking on it.

**Site ② — Group GEMM → (Expert Unpermute + RS) → (next layer's) Norm → AG**
```
            ┌────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌───────────┐
grouped   ─►│ Group GEMM │──►│ Expert Unpermute + RS     │──►│ residual + Norm(L+1)  │──►│ AllGather │──► hidden [full,H]
hidden      │(per-expert │   │ (weighted sum to token   │   │   pulled forward      │   │           │     → Layer L+1
            │    FFN)    │   │ order, fused w/ cross-   │   │                       │   │           │
            │            │   │ rank reduction)          │   │                       │   │           │
            └────────────┘   └─────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘   └───────────┘
```
Unpermute and RS are **fused into one step**, not sequential: as each expert's output is scattered back to token order, it is simultaneously accumulated across ranks.

**Dense vs. MoE:**

| | Dense | MoE |
|---|---|---|
| Fusion sites | 2 | 2 (more complex) |
| Pre-AG work | none | top-k/softmax at shard granularity |
| GEMM type | standard | Group GEMM (variable per-expert batch) |
| Reordering | none | permute + unpermute (fused with RS), overlapped with comm |
| Load balancing | n/a | uneven expert load needs padding/capacity policy |

**Notes:** Group GEMM needs variable per-expert batch support; routing math stays high-precision regardless of main dtype; both sites reuse the same RS/AG signaling as dense.

---

## 4. Implementation Plan

| Stage | Goal |
|---|---|
| 1 https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60571 or https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62385 | BF16 Dense |
| 2 | BF16 MoE |
| 3 | FP8/FP4 Dense |
| 4 | FP8/FP4 MoE |
| 5 | TPSP as default modeling |

- **Stage 1/2** implement the Section 1/2 architectures as-is, on dense/MoE models respectively.
- **Stage 3** inserts Quantize just before AG on a quantized dense model, keeping RS in higher precision: `GEMM → RS (high prec) → Norm → Quantize (fp8/fp4+scale) → AG (low-bit) → next GEMM`.
- **Stage 4** layers Stage 3's quantization point onto the Stage 2 MoE pipeline using a quantized MoE model; routing stays unquantized.
- **Stage 5** makes fusion the default: unified op registration, automatic graph rewriting of `proj → AllReduce → Norm` patterns, fallback to standard AllReduce when constraints/thresholds aren't met, numerical parity tests, broader model coverage, and performance benchmarking.

### Proposed Change.

- Model Integration
- C++/CUDA operators and kernels
- Auto-profiling and tuning
- Platform backends

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Strcutured Outputs Not Respected When Reasoning Implicitly Ends
author: yzong-rh
body:
### Motivation.

I want to start a discussion on how implicit reasoning end can break structured ouptuts + spec decode.

### Background

For structured outputs, we only apply constrained decoding after reasoning ends. This is to allow models to reason while constraining the user-visible content.

At each decode step, the scheduler roughly calls:
1. `StructuredOutputManager.validate_tokens` to validate the draft tokens need constraining and trim any grammar-invalid tokens
2. `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask` to create bitmasks for the draft tokens that need constraining
3. `StructuredOutputManager.accpet_tokens` to advance grammar FSM over the constrained tokens

These three methods rely on a `StructuredOutputManager._get_constraint_start` helper to identify when reasoning ends. It returns `reasoning_end_index + 1`

### Implicit Reasoning Ends

Reasoning end is usually marked by a special token (e.g. `</think>` for GLM 5.3). However, reasoning can also end implicitly when the model starts emitting content or tool call without closing reasoning first (e.g. `<think> ... <tool_call>` instead of `<think> ... </think><tool_call>`). This presents challenges for strcutured output constraint start detection.

### Issues with Implicit Reasoning Ends

Currently, `StructuredOutputManager._get_constraint_start` assumes all reasoning end markers are explicit. For example, given `prefix <tool_call> suffix`,
1. `StructuredOutputManager.validate_tokens` doesn't validate the `<tool_call>`
2. `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask` creates bitmasks for `suffix` only
3. `StructuredOutputManager.accpet_tokens` advances grammar FSM over accepted `suffix` + bonux token only.

This leads to two issues:
- I1: `<tool_call>` may not be grammar valid, yet it is unconditionally accepted
- I2: if a model is required to make a tool call, it will be forced to generate duplicate `<tool_call>` because the grammar isn't aware of the first one #59608

### Fix attempt: Adjust `_get_constraint_start` for implicit reasoning end markers. 

A simple fix seems to be to make `_get_constraint_start` return `reasoning_end_index` instead of `reasoning_end_index + 1` for implicit reasoning end markers. `_get_constraint_start` still returns `reasoning_end_index + 1` for explicit reasoning end markers.

Given `prefix <tool_call> suffix`,
1. `StructuredOutputManager.validate_tokens` now validates `<tool_call> suffix`
2. `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask` creates bitmasks for `<tool_call> suffix`
3. `StructuredOutputManager.accept_tokens` advances grammar FSM over the accepted `<tool_call> suffix` and bonus token.

This seems to fix both issues:
- I1: `<tool_call>` is validated and rejected if grammar-invalid
- I2: grammar is aware of `<tool_call>`, not duplicate emission needed

However, the fix is subtly incorrect: spec decode changes the target model's output distribution:
- the drafter proposes `prefix <tool_call> suffix`
- structure outputs sees `<tool_call>` and determines that constraint should start
- but the target model could reject `<tool_call>`, it could choose to continue reasoning
- but structured ouputs forces a grammar-valid token to be sampled
Constraint start was determined by the drafter's output, before target model can accpet or reject it.

This was implemented in my intial attempt and in #59629

### Correct fix: Distinguish between `grammar_start` and `constraint_start`.

Make `_get_constraint_start` return a tuple of `grammar_start, constraint_start`. For explicit reasoning end markers, `grammar_start == constraint_start`. For implicit end markers, `grammar_start < constraint_start`.
1. `StructuredOutputManager.validate_tokens` validate from `grammar_start`
2. `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask` is aware of tokens from `grammar_start` but only emit bitmasks from `constraint_start`
3. `StructuredOutputManager.accept_tokens` validate from `grammar_start`

Given `prefix <tool_call> suffix`,
1. `StructuredOutputManager.validate_tokens` validates `<tool_call> suffix`
2. `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask` creatse bitmasks for `suffix` only
3. `StructuredOutputManager.accept_tokens` advances grammar FSM over the accepted `<tool_call> suffix` and bonus token.

This fixes both the issues without affecting the target model's output distribution.

This was implemented in #59627 and merged.

### Remaining Issues

The fix is currently limited to engine-based parsers. It also doesn't account for implicit multi-token reasoning end markers (e.g. deepseek_v4) or text-only reasoning end markers (e.g. inkling).

There's also one more fundamental issue that remains: we can still sample implicit reasoning ends even when they are not grammar-valid.

For example, suppose the grammar disallows tool calls, the drafts are `reasoning_prefix reasoning_suffix`.
1. `StructuredOutputManager.validate_tokens` doesn't validate anything since reasoning has not ended
2. `StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask` doesn't constrain anything
3. Target model rejects `reasoning_suffix`. Since there's no constraint, it can sample `<tool_call>`.
4. `StructuredOutputManager.accept_tokens` attempts to advance grammar FSM over `<tool_call>` and fails

This is unavoidable when a reasoning end marker can also be part of the grammar:
- We must not constrain any reasoning end marker because it forces the model to end reasoning, changing the output distribution
- We must constrain any token that's part of the grammar.
We can't satisfy both requirements with implicit reasoning ends

### Proposed Change.

As I see it, the only way to avoid this is disallow implicit reasoning markers. SGLang has a feature `--enable-strict-thinking` that "Blocks model-specific excluded tokens (e.g., tool call markers) during reasoning. Requires a grammar backend that supports token filtering." https://docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/server_arguments

I see two ways to implement this:
1. Global implementation that reads a model's implicit reasoning end marker and disallow them during sampling
    - Con: Doesn't work for models with multi-token reasoning end markers. Additional logic to maintain.
2. Per-model structural tags (via the structural tags registry)
    - Con: Reliance on xgrammar, doesn't work with other backends

Questions for maintainers:
1. Do we want to add a `--enable-strict-thinking` feature to cover the reamining edge case?
2. If so, do we prefer a global implementation or per-model structural tags?
3. If not, do we have preferences on how to address remaining edge cases (multi-token / text only reasoning end, non engine-parsers)


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_
