title: [RFC][Experimental]: Model- and platform-customized KV cache planning
author: ivanium
body:
**Status:** draft · **PRs:** #53558 (builder, model hook, checks), wangxiyuan/vllm#2 (Qwen3.8 and Kimi-K3 hooks, golden plans) · **Related:** #58638 (grouping with drafters), #42449 / #61452 (KV cache spec refactor) This RFC updates the design of #44276 ("Model customized KVCache Planning"). The design changed substantially during review of #53558, so we track it here as a separate RFC; #44276 keeps the earlier discussion. Design doc with comments: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZnTISAsNuP9qNsbpF4FIPGPsYd_5TbdaBTrVhpW0N4A/edit?tab=t.v32av17qd6tq ## TL;DR We currently heavily rely on a heuristic-based KV cache grouping method in core, `get_kv_cache_groups()`, for every model. The heuristic still works so far, but new hybrid models, drafters, cache precisions and platforms will likely add further complexities to this method. Some examples: quite a few new models changed it (DSV4, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DSV4.1-Flash); a drafter can re-cut a whole model (Kimi-K3 + DSpark: 4 → 20 groups); and vllm-ascend monkey-patches about 680 lines of vLLM to use its own DSV4 plan. This RFC proposes an **experimental** pluggable `KVCacheConfigBuilder` API, which lets models and platforms own their KV cache plan, while core keeps the planning flow and checks every plan: | part | who | what | where | | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | | builder | platform | overrides grouping and placement | #53558 | | grouping hook | model | returns the model's KV cache groups | #53558 | | checks | core | rejects a malformed plan at startup, from any source | #53558 | | golden plans | tests | one readable plan file per model | wangxiyuan/vllm#2 | The APIs are experimental: their signatures can change, in particular when #61452 changes the KV cache group data structure. Non-goals: for models where the existing heuristic already works well, we don't change anything. The API is mainly for (1) new model and speculator support and (2) platform customization for now. --- ## 1. The problem Currently, we heavily rely on the heuristic-based `get_kv_cache_groups()` in vLLM core for all models, especially recent hybrid models. We see these issues. ### 1.1 Models Recent models, such as DSV4, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DSV4.1-Flash, have complex architectures: 1. More than three types of `KVCacheSpec`: full attention / MLA, SWA, linear attention / Mamba state, circular buffer, etc. 2. Different precisions for layers. DSV4 has an fp8 main KV cache, but the indexer cache can be fp4 or fp8. This is not only a memory question: precision changes the page size, and the page size decides the grouping. On DSV4.1-Flash, an mxfp4 indexer changes the plan from 7 groups to 9, although the SWA layers did not change: ``` packed layout: block size = widest group (main MLA + indexer pages) fp8 indexer: block 135,168 B → 8 SWA pages fit → 40 SWA layers / 8 = 5 groups mxfp4 indexer: block 114,688 B → 6 SWA pages fit → 40 SWA layers / 6 = 7 groups ``` 3. Different speculators. A drafter can use MLA or GQA, with or without SWA. In many cases its layers cannot merge with the target layers, so they form a new bucket. The heuristic sizes all groups by the smallest bucket, so a small draft bucket re-cuts every target group: ``` Kimi-K3: buckets [69 KDA, 24 MLA] group size 24 → 4 groups Kimi-K3 + DSpark: buckets [69 KDA, 24 MLA, 5 SWA] group size 5 → 20 groups ``` For many models, like Kimi-K3, Qwen3.5/3.6 and MiMo-V2.5, adding a DSpark/DFlash drafter blows up the groups from a few to 20 or more (Qwen3.5-27B + DFlash: 70). Each group prepares its own attention metadata every step, so this eats much of the drafter's speedup. #58638 has the measurements and improves the heuristic for these cases. ### 1.2 Features Additionally, there are new features that make KV cache grouping and planning more complex: 1. Different KV cache layouts: block-major or layer-major, for example. The layout is chosen before grouping and selects the grouping algorithm (block-major packs pages of different sizes into one block; layer-major first makes all page sizes equal). So a grouping decision depends on a placement decision. 2. HiSparse, which optionally keeps the indexer KV in GPU HBM but offloads the main attention KV. It adds layers that the model does not have and a second (host) memory pool, and today it is a separate branch inside the heuristic. 3. Speculators that add a hidden-state cache. This exists: the hidden-state extraction method adds one hidden-state cache layer, and the heuristic has a special case to keep it in its own group. ### 1.3 Parallelism and P/D In addition, we need to handle different parallelism, and P/D with heterogeneous TP: * TP can partition some specs but not others (like MLA). Each spec must declare this correctly; a missing declaration once changed a drafter's grouping (#59733). * P/D disaggregation with heterogeneous TP requires the same KV cache grouping on P and D: NIXL sends block IDs as one list per group and pairs the lists by position. This is implicitly assumed today, but not enforced: the NIXL compatibility hash does not include the grouping. With custom plans, P and D can more easily end up with different plans, for example when one side runs a platform builder and the other does not. ### 1.4 Why one heuristic does not scale All of these create uncertainties for the heuristic. They also make day-0 model support harder: a new model must modify the heuristic to match the grouping plan it has in mind, while being careful not to break other models. In practice, DSV4, Kimi-K3, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DSV4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash each changed core planning, and most of them needed follow-up fixes. The heuristic now has checks by model name, and it finds draft layers by guessing from layer positions. This also makes adding speculators tricky: a speculator can silently change the KV cache grouping plan and add a high metadata preparation cost. In other words, the KV cache grouping plan is implicit and error-prone. It is also hard for other (non-NVIDIA) platforms to use their own KV cache grouping and allocation plans. For example, vllm-ascend uses a different plan for DSV4-Pro (it groups layers into tuples and pads SWA pages to the MLA page size), and it has to monkey-patch vLLM to make that plan work. ## 2. Goals vLLM core: 1. Hooks that allow platforms and each model to customize KV cache planning. Platform overrides come at a higher priority. The APIs are general enough to cover all the cases above. 2. vLLM core stays stable and robust. 1. Stable: a day-0 model does not need to modify the core heuristic to get a new grouping plan, and all its changes stay in the model's directory. 2. Robust: vLLM core detects a malformed custom plan and rejects it at startup. Platforms and models: 1. The grouping logic is simple and intuitive. A model can directly define its groups and their roles (e.g., "full", "SWA1", "SWA2", "compressor state"). 2. The logic stays in Python to be generic. A static, structured form of each plan (YAML) is generated for humans and agents to read: the "golden" KV cache plan. 3. Tests check whether a commit, for example a new speculator, changes a grouping plan. The change becomes explicit in review instead of a silent regression. Non-goals: worker-driven allocation (#42449); several memory pools in the builder interface (HiSparse stays in core); custom schedulers, prefix-cache coordinators or admission rules. ## 3. Design ### 3.1 Overview Core keeps one planning flow, and no plugin can change it. Plugins make only two decisions: how to group the layers, and how to place a list of groups in memory for a given number of blocks.

*Figure 1: Core runs the planning flow and calls the builder for grouping and placement. The gold box is future work.* The flow, once at startup: merge the specs of all workers → group → check → project the groups onto each PP stage → find the number of blocks (block-count override, automatic max model length, admission check) → place each worker's KV cache → reduce all ranks to the same number of blocks. Memory profiling at startup uses the same builder. Keeping the flow in core matters, because the steps after grouping (PP projection, memory accounting, the block-count override, cross-rank agreement) must behave the same for every model and platform. vllm-ascend's patches today copy and change parts of this flow; with the builder, they only make the two decisions. PP also needs nothing new: core projects any plan onto the stages, whatever its source. ### 3.2 Platforms: the builder A platform selects a builder class (`Platform.get_kv_cache_config_builder_cls`). The builder has two methods: ```python class KVCacheConfigBuilder: def get_kv_cache_groups(self, vllm_config, kv_cache_spec) -> list[KVCacheGroupSpec]: ... def get_kv_cache_config_from_groups(self, vllm_config, kv_cache_groups, num_blocks) -> KVCacheConfig: ... ``` The default builder calls the model hook if the model has one, else the core heuristic. A platform builder that overrides grouping has priority; it reaches the model hook only through `super()`. Core finds the bytes per block by asking the builder to place one block, so a platform with a different placement does not need to compute memory separately. A plan that depends on the hardware belongs here. vllm-ascend's DSV4 plan is one: its grouping (layer tuples, padded SWA pages) and its placement depend on each other, so both decisions should come from one shared function in the builder. vllm-ascend#18359 moves the Ascend plans into a builder and removes most of the patches. ### 3.3 Models: the grouping hook A model class can implement `SupportsKVCacheGrouping` and return its groups directly: ```python class SupportsKVCacheGrouping(Protocol): @classmethod def get_kv_cache_groups(cls, vllm_config, kv_cache_spec) -> list[KVCacheGroupSpec]: ... ``` The model author knows the architecture, so the hook states the intended grouping instead of hoping the heuristic finds it. Two examples: **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.** Its 48 layers repeat a period of 4: three GDN (linear attention) layers and one QSA layer. A QSA layer has three caches: the main cache, a compressed key cache and a raw key ring. One replicated PLE state also exists. The hook returns 6 groups: | group | layers | why apart | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | GDN, position 0 | layers 0, 4, …, 44 | one group per position in the period | | GDN, position 1 | layers 1, 5, …, 45 | | | GDN, position 2 | layers 2, 6, …, 46 | | | PLE state | layer 1 | replicated across TP, the GDN state is sharded | | QSA raw key ring | layers 3, 7, …, 47 | scratch ring, not prefix-cached | | QSA main + compressed keys | layers 3, 7, …, 47 | share one block table | This is the same plan the heuristic gives today; the hook makes it explicit, so a change in the heuristic cannot change it. **Kimi-K3 + DSpark.** The hook groups the target layers as if there were no drafter, and puts the 5 draft layers in a group of their own: 4 + 1 groups instead of 20. This is only an example. The better fix is in the core heuristic, which RFC #58638 and its PRs (#58207, #58380) improve for drafters. The point is that a hook can unblock a model first, without waiting for a core change, and the hook can go away when core catches up. Three rules for hook authors, learned from these two hooks: 1. **Group in the layout's terms.** On a layer-major layout, all groups must have one page size. The first Kimi-K3 hook made the page sizes equal for target and draft layers separately, so the plan had two page sizes, and core rejected it at startup. The hook can reuse core's helpers: make page sizes equal over all layers first, then split. 2. **Work on any subset of layers.** During startup profiling, a worker calls the hook with only its own PP stage's layers. 3. **Keep the hook a function of the config and the specs.** Then the golden plan (§3.5) captures its behavior. ### 3.4 Checks Core checks every plan right after grouping, from any source (heuristic, model hook, platform builder), and stops startup with an error that names the problem: 1. Every layer is in exactly one group. 2. For a group whose layers have different specs, the group's spec describes exactly the group's layers. Placement problems also stop startup: core places one block with the builder before it computes the number of blocks, so a plan that the layout cannot hold fails there (this is how the first Kimi-K3 hook failed). Core cannot check more than the structure. It cannot compare a group's spec with the merge of its layers' specs, because core itself changes specs during grouping (it pads pages and changes block sizes). And it cannot judge whether a valid plan is a good plan, for example whether 20 groups are too many. That is the job of the golden plans. ### 3.5 Golden plans Each model has one plan file that shows its KV cache grouping in a readable form. A GPU script starts the real engine for each case (real model config, dummy weights), records the plan through the platform builder and the model hook, and checks that every worker received its part. The script writes the file; nobody edits it by hand. A PR that changes a grouping includes the new plan, so reviewers see the change as a diff. Part of the Kimi-K3 plan: ``` cases: tp1: {structure: tp1, groups: 4} tp4: {structure: tp1, groups: 4} tp1-dspark: {structure: tp1-dspark, groups: 5} structures: tp1-dspark: - kind: MambaSpec layers: ['language_model.model.layers.{0-88:4}.self_attn'] # ... two more MambaSpec (KDA) groups and one MLA group, as in tp1 - kind: SlidingWindowSpec sliding_window: 2048 layers: ['model.layers.{93-97}.self_attn.attn'] ``` A plan records only the grouping decision: which layers share a block table, the spec type of each group, and flags that are not default (for example, eagle group or host memory). Every grouping source produces exactly this, so one format covers all of them. The file has no bytes, block sizes, page sizes or block counts. A file lists each distinct plan once and maps cases to it (above, `tp1` and `tp4` share one plan), and it writes layer ranges compactly (`{0-88:4}` is layers 0, 4, …, 88). CPU tests read only the plan files and check two rules across cases: tensor parallelism does not change the grouping, and a speculator keeps the target grouping. These rules are policies, not laws. A precision change, for example, changes the grouping on purpose (§1.1). So each known exception is listed with its reason, for example DSV4.1 + DSpark. For now, a plan is a reviewed snapshot, not a formal spec, for three reasons: 1. **The plan depends on inputs the file does not record.** The grouping depends on page sizes, and page sizes depend on the GPU, the attention backend and the KV cache layout. The current plans come from GB200; Hopper can give different plans. A formal spec would have to name these inputs, and the file would no longer be simple. 2. **The format follows an experimental API.** #61452 will change the group data structure, and a versioned schema now would freeze choices that will change. 3. **Nothing regenerates the plans yet.** No CI job runs the GPU script, so a plan can drift from the code. As a first step, each case should record the layout it was made with, because the layout selects the grouping algorithm. A versioned schema and a CI job that regenerates the plans on GPUs (first optional, then gating) are future work. ## 4. Future work - **Core knows the draft layers.** The worker knows which layers belong to the drafter, but sends core only the specs. If it also sent the draft layer names, core could group target and draft layers apart by default (as the Kimi-K3 hook does today) and mark eagle groups exactly, instead of guessing from layer positions. - **Explicit P/D grouping match.** When a model or platform customizes the grouping, P and D can compare their plans when they connect, and reject a mismatch. This would also be the first reader of plans outside the tests, which is the point where a versioned plan format becomes necessary. - **Golden plans in CI.** Regenerate the plans on GPUs in CI, first as an optional step, then as a gate once its runtime and stability are known. ## 5. Alternatives considered | alternative | why not | | :---- | :---- | | Only improve the heuristic (#58207, #58380) | Helps every model and should land, but platforms still cannot use their own placement, and each new model still has to fit one shared heuristic. | | A role per layer instead of full groups (core builds the groups from the roles) | It hides layout details from the hook, but it is less direct and less general than stating the groups, and core would still decide the final grouping. | | A YAML file as the model's input | YAML cannot see spec properties (TP replication, precision) or draft layers, which exist only at runtime. YAML is the right output, not input. |

title: [RFC]: Request-scoped auxiliary decision heads on a shared generative backbone
author: sylvanus4
body:
**Question for maintainers:** can vLLM support request-scoped auxiliary decision readouts inside an existing generation
engine, consumed through the current Decisions / ReadStrategy interfaces, without running an auxiliary branch for
ordinary generation requests?

## Motivation.

Some deployments pair a generative model with a small decision model on the same backbone: a retrieval/evidence gate in
RAG ("answer, retrieve more, or abstain"), a router, a guard. When the decision model is a trained head, or a few
adapted layers, on that backbone, serving it as a second engine loads the backbone twice and splits the GPU, even
though most of the computation is shared.

vLLM now covers the API side well: `/v1/systemone` (#59299) and `/v1/decisions` (#60465) are merged, read strategies
are being made modular (#59365), and D3 decision models (#61565) are served through a read strategy on the classify
task. What is still missing is in the engine:

- `NextTokenStrategy` reads label tokens through the LM head, so a decision is only as good as the model's next-token
  distribution over label words. A trained decision head cannot be used this way.
- `D3Strategy` runs on the pooling runner (`task = "classify"`), which by design does not generate in the same engine.
- Per-request last hidden states (RFC #59542, PR #59543, open) let a client apply its own head to the final hidden
  state. A head that reads an intermediate layer, or a short branch of decoder layers with its own adapter, cannot be
  applied client-side.

We run such a deployment out of tree: **ECP-SB v0.1.0**, a vLLM plugin that serves a 27B Qwen3.5-family model for
generation and, from the same engine and the same single weight load, a 3-way evidence gate. The gate re-runs the last 4
decoder layers (44-47) with a LoRA-merged MLP and an fp32 head ([code](https://github.com/ThakiCloud/ecp-shared-backbone-vllm),
Apache-2.0; [weights](https://huggingface.co/ThakiCloud/ECP-SB-27B-Research)). To fit the current engine it needs three
workarounds:

1. gate requests are recognised by a **token signature** at the end of the prompt;
2. the branch runs on **every scheduled token of every step**, whether or not a gate request is in the batch;
3. the head's fp32 logits are **bit-packed into extra columns of the hidden-state tensor**, and `compute_logits`
   overwrites the LM logits with `-inf` except three label tokens.

This RFC proposes the engine piece that removes those workarounds. It does **not** propose a new decisions API.

**Disclosure.** The gate model behind that deployment is a research model and misses its own safety target (pooled
unsupported-answer rate 6.5% vs a 5% target). It illustrates the serving pattern and is not a recommendation to use it
as a safety control. Its port to vLLM 0.31 also failed our own frozen mixed-traffic generation criterion (1/64
token-divergent vs a 0/64 stock-vs-stock floor in that run). We report that result as recorded and do not revise it.

## Proposed Change.

Two layers. The first is the core of this RFC; the second only connects it to the existing APIs.

### 1. Engine: per-request auxiliary readouts in the generate runner (Model Runner V2)

```python
llm = LLM(model, enable_aux_readouts=True)          # engine flag, default False
sp = SamplingParams(max_tokens=1, aux_readouts=["evidence_gate"])
out = llm.generate(prompt, sp)[0].outputs[0]
out.aux_readouts["evidence_gate"]                     # float32 tensor [len(token_ids), 3]
```

- A readout is returned for each generated token, at the row its logits were computed from (the same rows as
  #59543). The decision-only shape is `max_tokens=1`.
- Requests that do not set `aux_readouts` get `None` and are otherwise unaffected.
- With the flag off, requests that set `aux_readouts` are rejected, and the runner holds no readout state and does no
  readout work.

Model interface:

```python
@runtime_checkable
class SupportsAuxReadout(Protocol):
    supports_aux_readout: ClassVar[Literal[True]] = True
    aux_readout_dims: ClassVar[dict[str, int]]     # name -> width
    aux_readout_stateful: ClassVar[bool] = False   # readout keeps per-request state across steps

    def set_aux_readout_rows(self, rows: torch.Tensor | None) -> None: ...
    def compute_aux_readouts(self, hidden_states: torch.Tensor, rows: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: ...
```

Per step:

1. Before the forward, the runner passes the row indices of the scheduled requests that asked, or `None` when none
   did. **`None` means the model must do no readout work.**
2. After the forward, if rows were passed, the runner calls `compute_aux_readouts` and gathers the result per request,
   `[num_rows, sum(widths)]` float32, with columns sliced to each request's names.

What a readout reads is up to the model. A head on the final hidden state is a few lines. A branch of decoder layers
with its own KV/recurrent state is also possible (our case), and the engine stays unaware of it.

Engine semantics in the prototype:

- **Steps with readout rows run without CUDA graphs** (`need_eager`). Steps without readout rows dispatch as before.
  - A decision request with `max_tokens=1` lives only in prefill steps. In our 27B workload those steps were above the
    CUDA graph capture size and ran eagerly anyway (see Validation).
  - Open question: excluding readout steps only from FULL graphs, and keeping PIECEWISE, would cover small readout
    steps. The prototype has this behind an experiment switch, but it is **not validated** yet.
- **`aux_readout_stateful = True`** makes readout requests skip prefix-cache reads, because a cached prefix never built
  the readout's own state.
- Rejected at start-up, as in #59543: the V1 runner, non-generate runners, speculative decoding, PP, and CP.
- **Transport and serialization** follow #59543:
  - `ModelRunnerOutput.aux_readouts: dict[req_id, Tensor]`;
  - `EngineCoreOutput.new_aux_readouts`, appended last;
  - accumulated by the output processor and split by name into `CompletionOutput.aux_readouts`.

  Readouts are float32 tensors on the default msgspec path. **No insecure (pickle) serialization is needed.** One of our
  earlier diagnostic runs set `VLLM_ALLOW_INSECURE_SERIALIZATION=1`, but only so that the test harness could call
  `LLM.apply_model` with a Python function to read branch counters. The mixed-traffic run below uses default
  serialization throughout. Its counters come from a log written by the model, behind an environment variable.

The prototype is about 300 library lines across 13 files: a protocol, a registry field, a config flag and validation,
a `SamplingParams` field, a runner hook, and transport.

### 2. Decisions: one read strategy, no API change

A read strategy for models that declare readouts would:

- send `max_tokens=1, aux_readouts=[name]`;
- map the readout's columns to the question's options, the way `D3Strategy` maps codes;
- return `QuestionRead` as usual.

`/v1/systemone` and `/v1/decisions` stay as they are. It would be one entry in `READ_STRATEGIES` today, or one plugin
under the registry #59365 proposes. This step is optional and comes after the engine piece.

### Relationship to existing work

| Work | Relationship |
|---|---|
| #59299 `/v1/systemone`, #60465 `/v1/decisions` (merged) | Unchanged and reused. This RFC adds no endpoint or wire format. |
| #59365 modular read strategies (open) | Complementary. A readout-backed strategy is one more backend for that registry. This RFC does not depend on the registry's design. |
| #59542 / #59543 last hidden states (open) | Same opt-in pattern and the same transport path. We would rather share one per-request auxiliary output channel than add a second one. Hidden states suit client-side heads on the final layer. Readouts suit model-defined heads, including intermediate-layer branches, and return a few floats per token instead of `hidden_size`. |
| #61565 D3 on the classify task (merged) | Unchanged. That path is pooling. This one stays a generate-runner output, so decisions and generation share one engine, which also addresses the "one engine, one task" concern raised in #12249 / #40804. |
| #33736 `extract_hidden_states` | Different goal (export for drafter training). Our model reuses its custom-op-in-graph pattern for the layer-44 capture. |

## Validation.

**Prototype on vLLM nightly `49cb2bb`, Model Runner V2, one B200.** Three engines ran on the same build:

- stock;
- the v0.1.0 workaround (branch every step);
- readouts.

**Tiny real-architecture Qwen3.5.** 8 layers, hybrid GDN/full attention, and a random LoRA + head branch on layers 2-5.
There were 4 gate items and 8 generation prompts. These numbers check the plumbing, not model quality.

- **vLLM-side GPU test:** passes, 8/8 cases. The first version had one bug (an unhashable field in the model-info
  record), which is now fixed.
- **Readout vs the v0.1.0 path:** max |Δ log p| 1.8e-6, with 0/4 decision flips.
- **Generation with the feature on but unused vs stock:** 0/8 token-divergent.

**27B.** Qwen3.8-27B bf16 with the published gate, 256 gate items and 64 RAG generation prompts. Settings were identical
across engines: max_num_seqs 64, CUDA graphs on, no prefix caching, no chunked prefill.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Readout vs the v0.1.0 path, same weights | max \|Δ log p\| 1.7e-4; 0/256 decision changes under the frozen threshold rule |
| Gate branch work when no request asks (counter in the model) | 0 calls after load, after 64 generation-only requests, and during all throughput runs |
| Generation, feature on but unused, vs stock | 0/64 token-divergent, max logprob gap 0 |
| Generation-only throughput vs stock, batch 1 / 8 / 32 / 64, median of 3 | v0.1.0 branch-every-step: −7.3% / −7.7% / −7.8% / −7.7%. Readouts: +0.3% / −0.3% / −0.2% / −0.3% |
| GPU memory after load | 151.8 / 150.8 / 151.9 GiB (stock / v0.1.0 / readouts) |
| Readout of a request alone vs inside a mixed batch (64 generation + 256 readout requests) | 0/256 decision changes; 1/256 items moved by more than .01 in probability (max .016) |

The throughput numbers are three repeats from one setup on one GPU. They are not a general serving-throughput claim.
Zero branch calls also does not mean zero added cost: the model still copies the layer-44 input inside the compiled
graph on every step. The remaining difference of about 0.3% is not attributed.

The first 27B run also found **4/64 generation sequences that changed when readout requests shared the batch**. We ran
a matched control on the same build and inputs. Each condition was repeated 3 times in a rotated order, and stock was
also run in a second process.

| Condition | Engine | Traffic in one `generate` call |
|---|---|---|
| A | stock | 64 generation requests |
| B | stock | 64 generation + 256 plain 1-token requests (same token ids as the readout requests) |
| C | readouts | 64 generation requests (feature unused) |
| D | readouts | 64 generation + 256 readout requests |
| E | readouts | 64 generation + 256 plain 1-token requests |

| Comparison | Token-divergent sequences out of 64 (repeats 1 / 2 / 3) |
|---|---|
| D vs E: same engine and batch, only `aux_readouts` differs | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| B vs A: stock, plain requests join the batch | 5 / 4 / 4 |
| D vs C: readout requests join the batch | 4 / 4 / 4 |
| D vs B: readout engine vs stock, same traffic | 1 / 0 / 0 |
| Identical repeats of one condition (A, B, C, D, E) | at most 1 |

- **The 4/64 is a batch-composition effect that stock shows too.** The same four prompts change at the same token
  positions in stock when the plain requests join (B vs A) as when readout requests join (D vs C).
- **The repeat-to-repeat 1/64 is stock's own run-to-run variation.** It is always one prompt, flipping at token 16, and
  it appears in stock repeats, in a second stock process, and once in a readout-engine repeat.
- **Readout decisions agreed with the v0.1.0 path:** 0/256 changes in every repeat.
- **The branch ran only in the readout runs** (34 calls per D run) and never during C or E.
- **CUDA graph status was checked from a model-side log.** Every readout step, and every matching step in E, ran without
  CUDA graphs: they carry thousands of prefill tokens, above the capture size.

What this does and does not establish:

- We found **no generation change attributable to readouts**: in this experiment, readout requests changed co-batched
  generation exactly as plain requests of the same shape did.
- Our pre-registered rule still returns **INCONCLUSIVE**, not PASS. It requires a zero stock-vs-stock floor, and stock
  was not repeat-stable here (1/64). We keep that verdict as recorded.
- **Generation equivalence under mixed traffic is therefore not established in general.** Readout steps small enough
  for a CUDA graph (short prompts, or readouts during decode) were not exercised, so the eager fallback was not tested
  on steps where it changes the execution mode.
- The v0.1.0 workaround on vLLM 0.28 passed its frozen deployment criteria (generation-only 2/64 vs a 1/64 stock
  floor). Its vLLM 0.31 port failed them, as noted above. Those runs used the older stack and V1 runner and are not
  re-judged here.

## Phased plan

1. **[Core] Per-request auxiliary readouts (MRV2).** This is the first PR, kept minimal:
   - flag and validation, the `SamplingParams` field, and the runner hook with rows / `None`;
   - transport, shared with #59543 if that lands first;
   - the stateless reference test: an OPT-125m head whose readout must equal the engine's own raw logits of three
     tokens, and "no readout work when nobody asks".

   No stateful branches, intermediate-layer capture, or decisions integration in this PR.
2. **[Model] `SupportsAuxReadout` docs and a stateless in-tree example.** Plus `aux_readout_stateful` and its
   prefix-cache rule, with a test.
3. **[Frontend] A readout-backed read strategy** for `/v1/systemone` and `/v1/decisions` (optional).
4. **Follow-up RFC.** Running a stateful branch on only the asking requests' tokens (today it runs on all tokens of an
   asking step), and a CUDA graph policy for small readout steps.

## Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

## CC List.

@mmastrac (#59299 structured decisions), @Timiku (#59365 read strategies), @aminry (#59542 / #59543 hidden states)

## Any Other Things.

Open questions:

1. One channel for raw hidden states (#59543) and readouts, or two fields? We lean to one container with typed entries,
   and would align with #59543 rather than compete with it.
2. Is a model-owned branch with its own KV/GDN state acceptable as an in-tree pattern? Or should in-tree examples stay
   stateless while stateful branches remain plugins?
3. Readout steps and CUDA graphs: is forcing eager acceptable for a first version? Or should readout steps only be
   excluded from FULL graphs from the start?

Not proposed: a new endpoint or wire format, changes to generation logits, training, or official support for our
specific model.

Disclosure: this RFC and the prototype were prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code). The numbers come from committed
experiment ledgers. The prototype code has not yet had a full line-by-line human review. That review, the
`pr-checklist`, and the required `Co-authored-by` / DCO trailers will come before any PR.

title: [RFC]: PD disaggregation + RL lifecycle (pause, sleep, abort) tracking
author: aoshen02
body:
### Motivation.

RL training on PD disaggregation pauses, sleeps, aborts and resets the cache around every weight update. On main (`ce49c47`), only 8 of 27 lifecycle cases pass with MooncakeConnector on GB300. The rest block a pause for 480 s, wedge D, or return 500.

**Tracker:** https://claude.ai/artifact/5yU9HihNDSW86B1oZFL2mc


### Proposed Change.

Merge in this order:

- [x] #59625 Mooncake sleep mode
- [x] #60572 Drain async KV loads in a wait pause
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#86 Answer every pull and free dropped transfers promptly (R1–R3)
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#87 Release transfer-held KV before a cache reset (R4)
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#88 Stop the decode stream when its prefill fails (R5)
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#104 Let P recompute KV that a cache reset dropped (optional, like SGLang's rebootstrap)

The fork PRs will be opened here one at a time. With all of them, the matrix passes 27 of 27.

Related: #59055 (sleep-mode memory).

title: [RFC]: Module layout for the Mooncake P2P KV connector
author: CAICAIIs
body:
### Motivation.

`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_connector.py` holds the whole Mooncake P2P connector in one module. On `main` it is 3077 lines:

| Concern | Lines |
| --- | --- |
| Module header, constants, `ReqId`/`TransferId` | 1–107 (107) |
| Region geometry and planning (`TransferRegion`, expand/align/coalesce/validate, `group_concurrent_contiguous`) | 110–606, 2997–3011 (512) |
| Wire structs (`MooncakeXferMetadata`, `MooncakeXferResponseStatus`, `MooncakeXferResponse`) | 608–657 (50) |
| Request metadata (`PullReqMeta`, `SendBlockMeta`, `MooncakeConnectorMetadata`) | 661–714 (54) |
| Facade (`MooncakeConnector`) | 717–903 (187) |
| Scheduler (`MooncakeConnectorScheduler`) | 906–1204 (299) |
| Worker (`MooncakeConnectorWorker`, 41 methods) | 1207–2994 (1788) |
| Bootstrap helpers and event loop | 3014–3077 (64) |

Three things make this a problem now:

1. **A second mode exists.** #61974 adds `mooncake_pull_connector.py` (956 lines), `transfer_plan.py` (264) and `compat.py` (129). It shares the request metadata, the wire structs, registration/discovery and completion accounting with the push connector, but which parts of the 1788-line worker it depends on is only visible by reading both files.
2. **Unrelated concerns land in the same class.** #59825 (layout once per peer), #57952 (packed region coalescing) and #59347 (suppress completion for empty pulls) each edited the same `MooncakeConnectorWorker`, whose methods span registration, discovery, bootstrap querying, region preparation, transfer, layout caching, completion accounting, expiry and stats.
3. **Sibling Mooncake connectors are already per-concern.** `mooncake/store/` has `connector.py`, `data.py`, `protocol.py`, `scheduler.py`, `worker.py`, `coordinator.py`, `metrics.py`; `ec_transfer/ec_connector/mooncake/` has `metadata.py`, `scheduler.py`, `worker.py`, `transfer.py`, `state.py`, `control.py`. The P2P connector is the one left as a single module.

### Proposed layout.

Split by concern, with no change to behavior or wire formats.

| Module | Contents | Why there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `metadata.py` | `ReqId`, `TransferId`, `PullReqMeta`, `SendBlockMeta`, `MooncakeConnectorMetadata`, the compatibility factors and `MOONCAKE_CONNECTOR_VERSION` | Everything a side tells its peer about a request, including the digest that gates the handshake |
| `protocol.py` | `MooncakeXferMetadata`, `MooncakeXferResponseStatus`, `MooncakeXferResponse`, the pull protocol marker and its `Layout`/`Request`/`Done`/`Response`/`Ack` structs | Both wire formats in one place, so they can be compared |
| `transfer_plan.py` | Existing file from #61974, which already holds the pull-side plan builder. S3 adds the push-side region geometry; the symbol list is in Planning module below. #53205 later adds the DCP mapping | The single canonical planning module for both directions, and the outbox for #57373 stages 2–4 |
| `base_worker.py` | Registration and the `_kv_layout_id` it mints, bootstrap registration and query, peer discovery, side-channel plumbing, the completion state both modes share (`reqs_need_send`, `finished_sending_reqs`, `finished_recving_reqs`, `_failed_recv_reqs`, `_invalid_block_ids`), the expiry sweep, stats | The machinery both modes need, unchanged from today |
| `push_worker.py` | `send_kv_to_decode`, `_prepared_transfer_regions`, `_layout_by_peer`, `_acked_layout_peers`, the byte counters (`sent`, `sending`, `resolve_need_send`) | Only the prefiller's respond-to-pull path touches these |
| `pull_worker.py` | The pull protocol handlers, reader accounting (`_handed_out_readers`, `_done_readers`, `_handed_out_at`, `_resolve_expected_readers`, `_mark_reader_done`), reader-side completion | The reader set has no meaning in push mode |
| `scheduler.py` | `MooncakeConnectorScheduler` | Both modes share it; written to be subclassed (see #62504) |
| `connector.py` | `MooncakeConnector` and `MooncakePullConnector` facades | The registration entry points |
| `bootstrap.py` | `should_launch_bootstrap_server`, `get_mooncake_bootstrap_addr`, `get_mooncake_side_channel_port`, `_async_loop` | Stateless helpers used by the worker and by tests |

`mooncake_utils.py` keeps the bootstrap server and the registration payload. `mooncake_connector.py` stays as a re-export module (see Compatibility).

Three decisions worth naming:

- **One canonical planning module, named `transfer_plan.py`.** #61974 already ships that file with the pull-side plan builder and imports five names from `mooncake_connector.py`. S3 adds the push-side geometry to it rather than creating a second planning module.
- **The worker splits into base plus one file per direction**, cut by use rather than by name: the row above already assigns each piece of state to the file that owns it.
- **Both wire formats live in `protocol.py`, not unified.** The push handshake carries the decoder's address book and the pull protocol the prefiller's; merging them changes the format.

### Planning module (S3).

Every symbol involved has one home:

| Symbol | Defined today | Defined after S3 | Imported after S3 by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_SHARED_REGION_GROUP_ID`, `TransferRegion` | `mooncake_connector.py` | `transfer_plan.py` | push worker, pull worker, scheduler, shim, tests |
| `_block_ids_for_region`, `_can_coalesce_block_transfers`, `group_concurrent_contiguous` | `mooncake_connector.py` | `transfer_plan.py` | `transfer_plan.py` itself, worker, tests |
| `_get_tp_ratio`, `_expand_transfer_regions`, `_compute_sender_transfer_plan`, `_validate_asymmetric_region_lengths`, `_align_transfer_regions`, `_coalesce_contiguous_transfer_regions`, `_has_opaque_packed_row`, `_pp_mismatch_hides_packed_layers`, `_get_tensor_dense_flag` | `mooncake_connector.py` | `transfer_plan.py` | push worker, tests |
| `ReqId` | `mooncake_connector.py` (S1: `metadata.py`) | `metadata.py` | `transfer_plan.py` imports it from `metadata.py` |
| `TransferPlan`, `ReadRequest`, `_kernel_block_ids`, `_drop_mamba_placeholders`, `plan_read_block_descriptors` | `transfer_plan.py` | unchanged | pull worker |

After S3 the file imports `ReqId` from `metadata.py` and nothing else from the package, never imports `protocol.py`, and holds no runtime state: every function is pure over its arguments. #53205 adds direction-neutral DCP mapping and block-ownership filtering to the same file, which is the kind of content it exists to hold.

### Worker contract (S4).

State and its owner, as of `main` plus #61974:

| State | Owner | Invariant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kv_caches`, registered region table, `_kv_layout_id` | base | written once in `register_kv_caches`; `_kv_layout_id` is odd, never 0, and a re-register mints a new one |
| `_remote_agents`, `_peer_connectors` | base | one entry per `(engine_id, tp_rank, pp_rank)`, never dropped while the peer is alive |
| `reqs_need_send: dict[TransferId, SendBlockMeta]` | base | present from `record_send_reqs` until completion or expiry; `expire_time` never moves later |
| `finished_sending_reqs`, `finished_recving_reqs` | base | emptied only by `fetch_finished_*`; a request id appears at most once between drains |
| `_failed_recv_reqs`, `_invalid_block_ids` | base | one entry per failed decode-side request or block, drained in `get_finished` |
| `_prepared_transfer_regions` | push | keyed by the full peer meta in `_prepare_transfer_regions` (host, port, tp size/rank, pp size, `kv_caches_base_addr`, `block_lens`, `kv_block_lens`, registered layer names/indices/group indices, shared group ids, row offsets); no cap; cleared on re-register |
| `_layout_by_peer` | push | keyed by `_peer_layout_key`: `(remote_hostname, remote_port, remote_tp_rank, remote_pp_size, remote_tp_size, layout_id)`; LRU capped at `_MAX_PEER_LAYOUTS` (1024); filled only after a pull that carried a layout; cleared on re-register |
| `_acked_layout_peers` | push, held on the decode side | prefill addresses that echoed the current `_kv_layout_id`; cleared on re-register |
| `SendBlockMeta.sent`, `.sending` | advanced by push | `sent + sending <= need_send`; a transfer completes when `sent == need_send` |
| `_peer_layouts` | pull | the reader's cached `MooncakePullLayout` per prefill address; dropped on a layout mismatch and on a peer restart |
| `_handed_out_readers`, `_done_readers`, `_handed_out_at` | pull | the two reader sets are disjoint and `_mark_reader_done` moves a reader from the first to the second; completion at `len(_done_readers[k]) >= need_send`; `_send_idle` releases only when nothing is handed out or after `VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` |

Hooks that differ per direction, and nothing else:

| Concern | Push | Pull |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Send completion | write-response accounting over `sent`/`sending` | `MooncakePullDone` per reader, compared against `need_send` |
| Sizing `need_send` | `resolve_need_send`: number of remote ranks that will read the blocks, times the remote PP size when PP differs | `_resolve_expected_readers` from the request topology; rejects a reader whose topology disagrees |
| Expiry | sweep in the base over `reqs_need_send` by `expire_time`, gated by `_send_idle`; the base `_send_idle` is `sending == 0` | pull overrides `_send_idle` to check `_handed_out_readers` and `_handed_out_at` |
| Reader failure | not applicable | releases the prefiller's blocks and fails the reader |

A deployed connector has one role: `is_kv_producer` and `is_kv_consumer` both come from `kv_role`, so at most one is true, and each facade instantiates one worker class rather than composing two objects. The cases below that set both flags are tests exercising both paths in one process, which is why the shared state belongs in the base.

Behaviour that has to survive the split, with the test that pins it today:

| Scenario | Test |
| --- | --- |
| Both flags set on one instance | `test_send_kv_to_decode_*`, `test_heterogeneous_pp_*`, `test_kv_producer*` in `test_mooncake_connector.py` |
| Scheduler-side abort | `test_scheduler_request_finished` |
| Worker-side completion timeout | `test_worker_get_finished_timeout` |
| Empty transfer | no direct unit test; the empty block list is created in `update_state_after_alloc` and again in `request_finished`, and suppressed in the completion path (#59347), so S4 keeps those call sites together |
| Prefix hit releasing the prefiller | `test_pull_releases_the_producer_on_a_local_prefix_hit` |
| Producer abort failing the reader | `test_producer_abort_fails_the_reader` |
| Producer timeout failing the reader | `test_producer_timeout_fails_the_reader` |
| Reader failure releasing the producer | `test_reader_failure_releases_the_producer` |
| Expiry while a reader is mid-read | `test_expiry_skips_transfers_a_reader_is_still_reading` |

### Invariants.

- **Wire formats stay unchanged, guarded in two layers, neither a captured snapshot.** For review, `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_wire_format.py` (landed with S1 in #62255) states the push contract as data: the ordered `(field, type, required-or-default)` list from `msgspec.structs.fields()`, the struct configuration that shapes the encoding (`omit_defaults`, `tag`, `tag_field`, `array_like`, `forbid_unknown_fields`), and the status values. A reorder, a renamed key, a changed type or default, a dropped `omit_defaults` or a changed status value fails there, and the failing row is the diff. Byte snapshots catch the same but nobody can read them, and every deliberate change turns into pasting new bytes. At runtime the compatibility hash refuses a P/D pair whose wire differs. The pull structs get the same tables in #61974's rebase, the bootstrap payload in S2. The re-export of the moved names needs no test: every Mooncake suite imports from `mooncake_connector.py`.
- **Behavior stays identical**: registration and retries, discovery, timeouts, expiry, failure reporting, completion accounting and stats, with the state invariants above holding after every step.
- **S1, S2, S3 and S5 are definition-site moves plus import updates.** S4 moves method bodies, verbatim except where the Worker contract requires a hook to differ; S4 lists each method whose body is not carried over and what was extracted.
- **Every step leaves the existing suite green with assertions unchanged**, apart from import paths.
- **Module boundaries are an import DAG, not a line count.** After S5 the allowed in-package edges are `protocol.py` → `metadata.py`; `transfer_plan.py` → `metadata.py`; `scheduler.py` → `metadata.py`; `bootstrap.py` → nothing in-package; `base_worker.py` → `metadata.py`, `protocol.py`, `transfer_plan.py`, `bootstrap.py`, `mooncake_utils.py`; `push_worker.py` and `pull_worker.py` → `base_worker.py` plus that set; `connector.py` → workers and scheduler. Forbidden: `metadata.py` → `protocol.py`, `transfer_plan.py` → `protocol.py`, `push_worker.py` ↔ `pull_worker.py`, any worker → `connector.py`, any new module → `mooncake_connector.py`. A unit test parses the package's imports and fails on an edge outside the set.

### Non-goals.

- Promoting region geometry or the transfer plan into a shared layer; that is #57373 stages 2–4, and this RFC gives those pieces a defined outbox.
- Changing the failure model; the ledger in #57529 replaces the current accounting afterwards.
- Metrics work (#56939), which lands on the facade and the stats module.
- Deduplicating the address book structs of the two protocols, which changes the wire format.
- Any behavior or mixed-pair semantics change; #61974 defines those.

### Migration.

| Step | Content | Requires merged first | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | `protocol.py` and `metadata.py` (about 160 lines moved), plus the push wire tables | nothing | Very low. Landed as #62255 |
| S2 | `bootstrap.py`, then `scheduler.py` | #57309 | Low |
| S3 | Push-side geometry into the existing `transfer_plan.py` | #61974 | Low; the natural starting point for #57373 stage 2 |
| S4 | Worker becomes `base_worker.py` + `push_worker.py` + `pull_worker.py` | #61974, #57529 | Medium: the only step that moves bodies and extracts hooks |
| S5 | Facades into `connector.py`, registry repointed, `mooncake_connector.py` becomes a re-export | #56939 | Low |

Data first, then the stateless helpers and the scheduler, then planning in the file #61974 creates, then the worker, which needs both modes on `main` before the base/mode boundary means anything, then the facade and the registry path. Each step rebases on `origin/main` when it starts and waits for the PRs above instead of absorbing them.

### Compatibility.

`mooncake_connector.py` stays as a re-export module. Two things pin the path: `KVConnectorFactory` registers `MooncakeConnector` against it (and #61974 registers `MooncakePullConnector` the same way), and `kv_connector_module_path` imports a module path and looks the class up by name, so a deployment can pin an in-tree module even though the option is documented for out-of-tree connectors. S5 gives the module an `__all__` covering every name it exports today, in the shape `nixl/scheduler.py` and `nixl/worker.py` already use. Removing it is a separate change after at least one release, with a note in `docs/features/mooncake_connector_usage.md`.

### Validation.

- After every step, the Mooncake unit suites plus `pre-commit` and `mypy` pass. As of #62255 that is seven files and 429 tests, against 424 on `main` at `34ac4f96a`; #61974 adds 24 more.
- The wire tables and the import-DAG test keep passing after every step.
- One test asserts both registered names still construct their connectors.
- Before and after S4 and S5, a same-host P/D smoke run on an H20 node with a dense and a hybrid model, comparing the pull output, the push output and a non-disaggregated baseline character by character.

### Related work.

| Item | Relation | Effect on this plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [#57373](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57373) | Defines what may leave the connector package and in which stages | `transfer_plan.py` is its outbox for stages 2–4 |
| [#57309](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57309) | Stage 1 of #57373, edits the same module | S2 waits for it |
| [#61974](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61974) | Adds the pull connector, `transfer_plan.py`, `compat.py` | S3 and S4 wait for it; its wire structs and hash stay there |
| [#57529](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57529) | Adds the failure ledger | S4 waits for it; accounting moves to the ledger afterwards |
| [#56939](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56939) | Prometheus metrics on the facade and the stats module | S5 waits for it |
| [#62504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62504), [#53205](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53205) | Layerwise WRITE variant with a scheduler subclass; DCP head-group mapping and block filtering, plus a wire change | S4 keeps `push_worker.py` and `scheduler.py` subclassable; S3 takes the DCP mapping; the wire tables and the compatibility hash are edited in whichever PR merges second |

### Feedback Period.

2 weeks.

### CC List.

@NickLucche, @robertgshaw2-redhat, @ZJY0516, @ivanium, @zhewenl, @staryxchen

### Any Other Things.

The split is mechanical and can be reviewed step by step; if reviewers prefer fewer steps, S2 and S3 can be merged into one change because they only move pure functions.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Add Single-Process In-Memory Engine Mode for Low-Tier Sandbox Environments (Colab T4 / Jupyter)
author: ragulk143
body:
### Motivation.

With the deprecation of the older V0 engine backend, the modern V1 architecture enforces a distributed, multi-process topology by default. When initializing `LLM(...)` inside single-GPU, memory-constrained sandboxes—such as standard Google Colab (Tesla T4 profiles) or strict enterprise Jupyter notebook nodes—the engine consistently experiences initialization timeouts and process handshake deadlocks:

```text
RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {}
```

This occurs because the core engine orchestrates separate background processes (`EngineCore`, `ModelExecutor`) and relies on a socket-based `SyncMPClient` to manage IPC network handshakes. In sandboxed cloud environments or browser-based notebooks, these multi-process loops fail to synchronize cleanly due to restricted loop configurations, firewalled internal sockets, and Triton/CUDA graph compilation latency spikes on legacy hardware.

#### **Why addressing this benefits the vLLM Ecosystem:**
* **Democratizes AI Prototyping:** It allows students, independent researchers, and engineers to safely prototype structured decoding schemas (JSON/Regex templates), prompt optimization pipelines, and agentic workflows on free, universally accessible hardware.
* **Accelerates Open-Source Contributions:** It simplifies the developer onboarding lifecycle by removing heavy multi-process infrastructural requirements during rapid local unit testing and quick debugging iterations.


### Proposed Change.

I propose introducing an **In-Process / Single-Threaded Driver Runner** fallback option. We can expose a straightforward runtime configuration flag, such as an environment variable (`VLLM_RUNTIME_SANDBOX=1`) or an initialization flag (`local_stub=True` in the Engine Config parameters).

When this configuration path is explicitly activated by the user:
1. **Bypass IPC Handshakes:** The engine initialization pipeline entirely skips spawning independent background OS processes via the standard process manager framework.
2. **Unified Main-Thread Execution:** The `Frontend`, the sequence scheduler, and the single-GPU `ModelExecutor` are instantiated sequentially inside the **Main Process thread**.
3. **Direct In-Memory Pipeline:** Token arrays, request updates, and KV-cache block instructions are passed natively via standard Python object references instead of serializing/deserializing them over virtual IPC network sockets.

#### **Performance & Feature Integrity Design Constraints:**
* **Zero Production Performance Impact:** The proposed single-process loop is strictly opt-in. The core production code path utilizing multi-process, multi-GPU topologies remains 100% untouched and unaffected.
* **100% Core Feature Parity:** This modification purely refines the orchestration layer. Core optimizations—such as **PagedAttention** block allocation, iteration-level **Continuous Batching**, **Guided Decoding** token masks, and **Multi-LoRA serving**—remain completely intact and execute exactly as designed, just within a single process space.


### Feedback Period.

Standard one-week community review period to discuss viability, architectural constraints, and potential entry-point implementation strategies with the core maintainers.


### CC List.

/cc @vllm-project/co-maintainers


### Any Other Things.

I am happy to work on a prototype for this single-process execution path. If the core maintainers agree that this is a valid direction for the V1 sandbox experience, I can set up a fork, create a draft PR, and test the in-memory client architecture within a Google Colab environment to verify feature parity.


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: [V1 Scheduler][KV Offload] Eliminate 1.0–1.8s Re-Queueing Stall for Completed Async KV Pulls via Front-of-Queue Re-Admission
author: cheng-hsiang-chiu
body:
### Motivation. ## Motivation & Problem Summary When running vLLM V1 (`main`) with asynchronous KV cache pulling—such as `OffloadingConnector` configured with `TieringOffloadingSpec` (`CPUPrimaryTierOffloadingManager` + `p2p` secondary tier over RoCE RDMA) or remote KV connectors (`NixlConnector`, `MooncakeConnector`)—there is a **5×–7× gap** between **hardware KV transfer latency** and **end-to-end pull latency on a busy destination pod (`WaitingQueueSize >= 1`)**: - **Idle Destination Pod (`WaitingQueueSize == 0`)**: On `NVIDIA H200` GPUs with `200 Gbps` RoCE v2 RDMA (`mlx5`), pulling a `49,152`-token cached prefix (`1.82 GB` on `openai/gpt-oss-120b`; `4.83 GB` on `Qwen3-30B-A3B`) takes only **`207.6 ms` (`20 ms` fixed + `3.8 µs/token`)** on Monolithic and **`282.6 ms` (`24.8 ms` fixed + `5.3 µs/token`)** on Disaggregated P/D—**`8.6×` to `10.0×` faster** than local GPU prefill recomputation (`1,874 ms` to `2,280 ms`). - **Busy Destination Pod (`WaitingQueueSize >= 1`)**: When the exact same P2P pull executes on a destination pod with concurrent traffic, OLS calibration across multi-turn agentic workloads reveals **two large scheduler re-admission stalls**: 1. **Stage 1 Re-Queue Stall (`transferFixedMs` = `419 ms`, up `21×` from `20 ms` idle)** while waiting in `self.waiting` during and after `Secondary Tier (P2P) -> Primary Tier (CPU RAM)` promotion. 2. **Stage 2 Re-Queue Stall (`requeueMs` = `637 ms` on Monolithic / `1,410 ms` on Disaggregated P/D)** while waiting in `self.kv_holding_waiting` (`KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING`) after `Primary Tier (CPU RAM) / Remote -> GPU HBM` (`WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`) completes. Over **`80%` of the wall-clock time of a loaded KV pull (`1,056 ms` to `1,829 ms` of queueing delay vs. `~200 ms` of actual wire + PCIe transfer)** is spent waiting to be re-admitted by the V1 scheduler *after* the KV cache blocks have already arrived. --- ## Root-Cause Analysis (Against `vllm` `main`) Consider a destination pod receiving **Request `R`** (`48,000` cached prefix tokens on a remote peer + `256` uncached suffix tokens) alongside **Cold Request `C`** (`49,000` uncached tokens). ``` [ R arrives at Destination Pod ] │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Queue 1: self.waiting (Holds 0 GPU HBM blocks) │ │ • Hop 1 runs here: Remote Peer ──(RoCE RDMA)──► Local CPU Primary Tier │ │ • TieringOffloadingManager.lookup() returns RETRY / HIT_PENDING │ │ -> get_num_new_matched_tokens() returns (None, False). │ │ • Scheduler.schedule() (L1041–L1046) calls skip_request(self.waiting) │ │ and continues scanning younger requests, admitting Cold Request C │ │ into self.running (L1408) for a 6-step, 49K-token cold prefill. │ │ • STALL 1: When Hop 1 finishes in _complete_promotion() (L456–L496): │ │ (a) R is NOT moved to the head of self.waiting, and │ │ (b) primary_tier.complete_write() drops ref_cnt from -1 to 0 (L485, L834),│ │ leaving R's promoted CPU chunks evictable before R is re-scanned! │ └───────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘ │ Scheduler eventually re-scans R -> allocates 48K GPU HBM blocks (L1313) │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Queue 2: self.kv_holding_waiting (Holds 48K GPU HBM blocks = 1.8–4.8 GB!) │ │ • Hop 2 runs here: Local CPU Primary Tier ──(PCIe DMA)──► Local GPU HBM │ │ • R sits in self.kv_holding_waiting with status = WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS. │ │ • STALL 2: When Hop 2 finishes in _update_from_kv_xfer_finished() (L3318), │ │ R enters stage KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING (L3319). R already holds │ │ 1.8–4.8 GB of locked GPU HBM and only needs 256 tokens (~10 ms) of │ │ compute, yet R is starved of token_budget by C's multi-chunk cold prefill │ │ in self.running (L712–L943) and sits behind unready requests in │ │ self.kv_holding_waiting! │ └───────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Queue 3: self.running (GPU Execution) │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` ### Fault 1 (Stage 1 — `self.waiting`): No Front-of-Queue Promotion & Unpinned CPU Chunks After `_complete_promotion()` In [`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py) and [`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py): 1. **Leapfrogging & Scan Breakage in `self.waiting`**: - When `TieringOffloadingManager.lookup()` (`tiering/manager.py#L584-L666`) initiates a secondary-to-primary promotion via `_initiate_promotion()` (`#L677-L729`), it returns `LookupResult.HIT_PENDING` (`#L653`) or `LookupResult.RETRY` (`#L665`). - In [`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py) (`_maximal_prefix_lookup`, `#L766-L775`), both `HIT_PENDING` and `RETRY` set `defer_lookup = True`, so `get_num_new_matched_tokens()` (`#L1109-L1171`) returns `(None, False)`. - In `Scheduler.schedule()` (`scheduler.py#L1041-L1046`), `if ext_tokens is None:` calls `skip_request(request_queue)` and `continue`, allowing younger cold requests (`C`) behind `R` in `self.waiting` to be popped (`#L1406`) and admitted into `self.running` (`#L1408`). - Meanwhile, if any request `A` ahead of `R` in `self.waiting` fails block allocation (`new_blocks is None` at `scheduler.py#L1332-L1339`), the `while token_budget > 0:` loop executes **`break`** (`#L1339`) and stops scanning `self.waiting` before ever reaching `R`—even if `R`'s promotion into CPU RAM has already completed! 2. **Unprotected CPU Eviction Window (`ref_cnt == 0`) Right After `_complete_promotion()`**: - In `TieringOffloadingManager._complete_promotion()` (`tiering/manager.py#L456-L496`), as soon as the `secondary -> primary` transfer completes, lines `484–489` call: ```python if successful_keys: self.primary_tier.complete_write( successful_keys, transfer_job.req_context, True, ) ``` - As explicitly noted in `TieringOffloadingManager.prepare_store()` (`tiering/manager.py#L833-L848`), `_process_finished_jobs()` (`#L842`, or the background `vllm_offload_tier_poll` thread in `poll_tiers()` at `#L420`) transitions those promoted chunks from `ref_cnt = -1` to **`ref_cnt = 0` ("making it evictable for the first time")** *before* `R` is re-scanned by the scheduler and pins them via `prepare_load()` (`#L757-L776`). - Consequently, a running request calling `prepare_store()` (`#L848`) can immediately evict `R`'s freshly pulled P2P chunks from `primary_tier` while `R` is still waiting in `self.waiting`! ### Fault 2 (Stage 2 — `self.kv_holding_waiting`): Starvation in `KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING` Behind `self.running` Cold Prefill Chunks & Unready Requests In [`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py): Once `R` is re-scanned in `self.waiting` and hits in the CPU primary tier (`load_kv_async = True`), `Scheduler.schedule()` allocates `48,000` tokens of **GPU HBM `KVCacheBlocks` (`1.82–4.83 GB`)** (`#L1313`), sets `request.status = RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` (`#L1386`), and calls `skip_request(request_queue)` (`#L1403`), which places `R` into `self.kv_holding_waiting` (`#L962-L963`, `#L1464`). When the worker finishes the GPU DMA copy (`_update_from_kv_xfer_finished`, `scheduler.py#L3300-L3327`): - Line `3318` adds `req_id` to `self.finished_recving_kv_req_ids`, and line `3319` transitions `R`'s metric stage to **`KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING`**. - At this point, `R` is **already holding `1.82–4.83 GB` of populated GPU HBM blocks** and only needs **`256` uncached suffix tokens (`~10 ms`)** to complete prefill and emit its first token (TTFT). - Yet `R` remains stuck in `KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING` for `637–1,410 ms` due to two bottlenecks in `Scheduler.schedule()`: 1. **`self.running` Multi-Chunk Cold Prefill Starvation (`scheduler.py#L712-L943`)**: `Scheduler.schedule()` always schedules `self.running` (`#L712`) **before** `self.kv_holding_waiting` (`#L970`). Unless `long_prefill_token_threshold` (`#L678`, default `0`) is set, an in-progress cold prefill chunk (`request.is_prefill_chunk == True`) in `self.running` consumes **100% of `token_budget` (`max_num_scheduled_tokens`)** at `#L765` / `#L911`. When execution reaches `while token_budget > 0:` for `self.kv_holding_waiting` at `#L967`, **`token_budget == 0`**! Thus `R` sits starved in `self.kv_holding_waiting` step after step—locking gigabytes of GPU HBM—waiting for `C` to finish all of its cold prefill chunks in `self.running`. 2. **No Front-of-Queue Prepending in `self.kv_holding_waiting` (`scheduler.py#L3313-L3320` & `#L3266-L3281`)**: When `_update_from_kv_xfer_finished()` (`#L3318`) marks `R` as `KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING`, `R` stays at its existing position inside `self.kv_holding_waiting` behind older requests whose `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` transfer is still in flight (or behind a request in `self.kv_holding_waiting` whose suffix allocation fails and triggers `break` at `#L1339`). --- We are happy to submit a PR if this direction looks good to the maintainers! ### Proposed Change. ## Proposed Solution: Mechanism 1A & Mechanism 1B Both stalls can be eliminated cleanly using the existing `self.waiting` and `self.kv_holding_waiting` queues (`RequestQueue.remove_request` + `RequestQueue.prepend_request` in [`vllm/v1/core/sched/request_queue.py#L39-L52`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/core/sched/request_queue.py#L39-L52)): ### Mechanism 1A: Front-of-Queue Promotion in `self.waiting` & CPU Read-Pinning on `_complete_promotion()` (4 Files) #### File 1: [`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py) (`TieringOffloadingManager`) 1. **In `TieringOffloadingManager.__init__()` (`~L300`) — Add tracking sets for newly promoted requests and pinned CPU keys**: ```python self._newly_promoted_req_ids: set[str] = set() self._promoted_pins: dict[str, tuple[list[OffloadKey], ReqContext]] = {} ``` 2. **In `TieringOffloadingManager._complete_promotion()` (`#L456-L496`) — Pin promoted CPU chunks (`ref_cnt: 0 -> 1`) and record `req_id` when promotion finishes**: ```python if successful_keys: self.primary_tier.complete_write( successful_keys, transfer_job.req_context, True, ) if transfer_job.req_context is not None: req_id = transfer_job.req_context.req_id # 1. Pin promoted chunks in CPU primary tier (ref_cnt: 0 -> 1) # so prepare_store() (#L848) cannot evict them before R is scheduled: self.primary_tier.prepare_read(successful_keys, transfer_job.req_context) prev_keys, _ = self._promoted_pins.get( req_id, ([], transfer_job.req_context) ) prev_keys.extend(successful_keys) self._promoted_pins[req_id] = (prev_keys, transfer_job.req_context) # 2. Record that req_id finished its secondary -> primary promotion: self._newly_promoted_req_ids.add(req_id) ``` 3. **In `TieringOffloadingManager.prepare_load()` (`#L757`) and `on_request_finished()` (`#L1036`) — Release the temporary read-pin once `prepare_load()` claims the chunks for GPU DMA (or if the request is aborted)**: ```python # At the start of prepare_load(self, keys, req_context) and on_request_finished(self, req_context): pinned = self._promoted_pins.pop(req_context.req_id, None) if pinned is not None: pinned_keys, pinned_ctx = pinned self.primary_tier.complete_read(pinned_keys, pinned_ctx) ``` 4. **Add `pop_newly_promoted_req_ids()` to `TieringOffloadingManager` (after `has_pending_work` at `#L1117`)**: ```python @override def pop_newly_promoted_req_ids(self) -> set[str]: # Ensure any finished secondary -> primary jobs are harvested first: self._maybe_process_finished_jobs() if not self._newly_promoted_req_ids: return set() promoted = self._newly_promoted_req_ids self._newly_promoted_req_ids = set() return promoted ``` #### File 2: [`vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py) (`OffloadingManager` Base Interface, `#L648`) Add a default no-op method on the base `OffloadingManager` class so non-tiered managers don't break: ```python def pop_newly_promoted_req_ids(self) -> set[str]: return set() ``` #### File 3: [`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading_connector.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading_connector.py) & [`offloading/scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py) (and can call `self.connector.pop_newly_promoted_req_ids()`: - In **`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/base.py`** (`KVConnectorBase_V1`, `#L688`): ```python def pop_newly_promoted_req_ids(self) -> set[str]: return set() ``` - In **`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading_connector.py`** (`OffloadingConnector`, `#L255`): ```python def pop_newly_promoted_req_ids(self) -> set[str]: assert self.connector_scheduler is not None return self.connector_scheduler.pop_newly_promoted_req_ids() ``` - In **`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py`** (`OffloadingConnectorScheduler`, `#L2017`): ```python def pop_newly_promoted_req_ids(self) -> set[str]: self._acquire_step() return self.manager.pop_newly_promoted_req_ids() ``` #### File 4: [`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py) (`Scheduler.schedule()`, right before `#L712`) In `Scheduler.schedule()` right before **Line `712`** (`# First, schedule the RUNNING requests.`), pop newly promoted request IDs (`self.connector.pop_newly_promoted_req_ids()`) and move each matching request in `self.waiting` to the **very front of `self.waiting`**: ```python # [INSERT BEFORE LINE 712 of vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py] if self.connector is not None: promoted_reqs: list[Request] = [] for req_id in self.connector.pop_newly_promoted_req_ids(): req = self.requests.get(req_id) if req is not None and req in self.waiting: self.waiting.remove_request(req) self.deferred_waiting.discard(req) req.priority = -100 # Top of heap in PriorityRequestQueue promoted_reqs.append(req) for req in reversed(promoted_reqs): self.waiting.prepend_request(req) # Index 0 in FCFSRequestQueue ``` --- ### Mechanism 1B: Front-of-Queue Prepending in `self.kv_holding_waiting` & Short-Suffix Priority Over `is_prefill_chunk` *(Note: Mechanism 1B is 100% self-contained in [`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py) in `~25 LOC` and applies universally to **all** async V1 KV connectors—including `OffloadingConnector`, `NixlConnector`, and `MooncakeConnector`.)* 1. **Immediate Head Prepending in `_update_from_kv_xfer_finished()` (`scheduler.py#L3313-L3320`) / Start of `schedule()`**: When a request in `self.kv_holding_waiting` finishes receiving remote KVs (`self.finished_recving_kv_req_ids`), immediately run `_update_waiting_for_remote_kv(req)` (`#L3214`), transition `req.status` to `WAITING`/`PREEMPTED` (`#L3277-L3280`), and prepend `req` to the **very front of `self.kv_holding_waiting`**: ```python def _promote_finished_recving_to_front(self) -> None: if not self.finished_recving_kv_req_ids: return ready_reqs: list[Request] = [] for req_id in list(self.finished_recving_kv_req_ids): req = self.requests.get(req_id) if req is None or req.status != RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS: continue self._update_waiting_for_remote_kv(req) req.status = ( RequestStatus.PREEMPTED if req.num_preemptions else RequestStatus.WAITING ) self.kv_holding_waiting.remove_request(req) self.deferred_waiting.discard(req) req.priority = -100 ready_reqs.append(req) for req in reversed(ready_reqs): self.kv_holding_waiting.prepend_request(req) ``` 2. **Drain `KV_FETCH_COMPLETED_WAITING` Requests Before In-Progress Cold Prefill Chunks (`request.is_prefill_chunk` in `self.running`, `#L712-L943`)**: When `self.kv_holding_waiting` has ready requests at its head (which already hold gigabytes of allocated GPU HBM and only need their uncached suffix tokens to finish prefill), do not let `request.is_prefill_chunk` in `self.running` consume 100% of `token_budget` ahead of them: - **Pass 1**: Schedule running decode requests (`not request.is_prefill_chunk` in `self.running`) so decode ITL/TPOT is completely unaffected. - **Pass 2**: Drain ready requests (`status in (WAITING, PREEMPTED)`) at the head of `self.kv_holding_waiting`. - **Pass 3**: Schedule in-progress cold prefill chunks (`request.is_prefill_chunk` in `self.running`) and `self.waiting` with the remaining `token_budget`. --- ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. ## Expected Quantitative Impact | Latency Component of a Loaded `49,152`-Token P2P Pull | Current `vllm` `main` | With Mechanism 1A + 1B | Mechanism | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- | | **1. RoCE v2 RDMA Wire Transfer** | `187 ms` *(Mono)* / `258 ms` *(P/D)* | `187 ms` / `258 ms` | Hardware wire speed | | **2. Stage 1 Stall + CPU Staging (`transferFixedMs`)** | `419 ms` | **`~65 ms`** *(PCIe H2D copy only)* | **Mechanism 1A**: Front-of-queue promotion in `self.waiting` + CPU read-pinning in `_complete_promotion()` | | **3. Stage 2 Queue Re-Admission (`requeueMs`)** | `637 ms` *(Mono)* / `1,410 ms` *(P/D)* | **`~15 ms`** *(1 engine step)* | **Mechanism 1B**: Head prepending in `self.kv_holding_waiting` + priority before `is_prefill_chunk` | | **4. Suffix Prefill Compute (`256` tokens)** | `10 ms` | `10 ms` | Tensor Core prefill compute | | **Total Loaded P2P Pull TTFT** | **`1,253 ms` (Mono)**
**`2,097 ms` (P/D)** | **`277 ms` (`4.5×` faster)**

title: [RFC]: Improve MTP configuration warning
author: nfm-corti
body:
### Motivation.

Hi,

currently, the MTP warning is rather aggressive:
```
(APIServer pid=1) WARNING 10-20 07:22:23 [speculative.py:1375] Enabling num_speculative_tokens > 1
will run multiple times of forward on same MTP layer,which may result in lower acceptance rate
```

Most production deployments will run with `MTP >= 3` and more typically `MTP = 5`. This is even more true considering that this is what many of the official vLLM recipes recommend. 

### Proposed Change.

Having a warning that highlights a risk without concrete recommendations on what to do, feels like an unnecessary papercut. I have a few ideas an would like to know what people think:
1. Reduce the level to `INFO`
1. Improve the message to point at `https://recipes.vllm.ai/` and to mention the draft acceptance rate metric with a target between 60 - 80%.
1. If we keep warning as the level, increase the threshold to `5`
