title: [RFC]: Layered prefill: split prefill across decoder layer groups
author: gunjunlee
body:
### Motivation.

Chunked prefill bounds inter-token latency (ITL) by splitting long prompts into small token chunks. For MoE models this has a cost: every chunk reloads the expert weights of every layer. Small chunks keep ITL low but reduce prefill throughput and increase TTFT. Large chunks reverse the tradeoff.

[Layered prefill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08055) splits prefill along the layer dimension instead of the token dimension. The decoder layers are divided into groups. Each engine iteration advances a large prefill batch through one group, while running requests still decode through all layers. A long prompt therefore delays a decode step by one group's prefill rather than the whole model. Every prompt token passes each layer once, in a large batch.

We implemented this in vLLM V1 (Model Runner V2) and measured it on 2× A100 80GB PCIe. The workloads were arXiv summarization and ShareGPT, both with Poisson arrivals and 600 requests per case. A request meets the SLO only if its TTFT and **every** inter-token interval meet the thresholds (TTFT 10 s for arXiv, 5 s for ShareGPT; TBT 150 ms). Each case was measured once with seed 0.

The table shows SLO attainment, then mean TTFT and p99 ITL.

| Model | Dataset | req/s | Placement | chunked-512 | chunked-8192 | layered (8192 tokens) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | arXiv | 1.3 | TP2 | 7.8%, 145 s, 94 ms | 3.7%, 0.95 s, 463 ms | **99.3%**, 3.8 s, 59 ms |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | arXiv | 1.3 | PP2 | 6.0%, 87 s, 168 ms | 1.2%, 1.1 s, 898 ms | **100%**, 2.2 s, 102 ms |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | ShareGPT | 4.0 | TP2 | 28.8%, 31 s, 88 ms | 3.0%, 0.32 s, 348 ms | **55.2%**, 4.8 s, 65 ms |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | ShareGPT | 4.0 | PP2 | 31.5%, 16 s, 149 ms | 1.3%, 0.50 s, 609 ms | **99.2%**, 1.7 s, 105 ms |
| GPT-OSS-20B (BF16) | arXiv | 2.1 | TP2 | 10.7%, 65 s, 63 ms | 1.5%, 1.0 s, 455 ms | **33.7%**, 13 s, 69 ms |
| GPT-OSS-20B (BF16) | arXiv | 2.1 | PP2 | 19.0%, 32 s, 109 ms | 0.2%, 1.3 s, 1063 ms | **92.2%**, 4.9 s, 129 ms |
| GPT-OSS-20B (BF16) | ShareGPT | 6.4 | TP2 | 44.0%, 6.5 s, 42 ms | 4.5%, 0.25 s, 260 ms | **59.5%**, 3.7 s, 60 ms |
| GPT-OSS-20B (BF16) | ShareGPT | 6.4 | PP2 | 98.3%, 1.9 s, 70 ms | 2.3%, 0.73 s, 469 ms | **100%**, 1.3 s, 85 ms |

At lower loads all three schedules mostly meet the SLO (full 54-case matrix in the PR). Tradeoffs:

- Under light load, layered prefill has a higher TTFT than chunked-512. A prompt needs `num_layer_groups × PP` iterations to finish prefill.
- p99 ITL is sometimes higher than chunked-512, e.g. GPT-OSS ShareGPT 6.4 req/s.
- The TBT SLO of 150 ms differs from the paper's 100–125 ms. At PP=2 each decode token spans two pipeline iterations, so even chunked-512 misses 100 ms under arXiv load. We chose 150 ms after seeing the PP=2 results.

### Proposed Change.

The feature is opt-in through a new `--num-layer-groups N` option (`SchedulerConfig.num_layer_groups`, default 1 = off).

**Scheduler.** `LayeredPrefillScheduler` subclasses `Scheduler`; it lives in a new file and is selected only when N > 1. Each iteration emits a plan with three parts:

- one local prefill stage per PP rank, each with its batch and group index;
- one full-depth decode batch;
- the set of requests whose forward completes this iteration, i.e. the rows to sample.

KV blocks of partially prefilled requests stay out of the prefix cache (`delay_cache_blocks`) until every group has run. With PP, the first rank admits a new batch while older batches run on downstream ranks, through the existing PP batch queue.

**Worker (MRV2 only).** A small `LayeredPrefillRunner` handles three things:

- It retains hidden states and residuals per request between groups.
- It sends a batch to the next PP rank only after the batch's last local group.
- It runs the decode batch with the full model and samples the decode and completed-prefill rows once per iteration.

`GPUModelRunner.execute_model` gains a dict form of `intermediate_tensors` for group continuations. CUDA graphs are captured per group: `BatchDescriptor.layer_group_idx` keys breakable prefill graphs, and decode keeps full graphs.

**Models.** No model changes. A layer group runs as if it were its own pipeline stage: the decoder's `start_layer`/`end_layer` are narrowed, and the PP group reports `is_first_rank`/`is_last_rank` at the group boundaries. Any model that follows the standard PP decoder contract works unchanged, i.e. its forward iterates `self.layers[self.start_layer:self.end_layer]`, embeds on the first rank, and returns `IntermediateTensors` before the last. Unsupported models are rejected at load time. Validated on Qwen3 (dense and MoE), Llama 3.2, DeepSeek-V2-Lite (MLA and MoE) and GPT-OSS with TP, PP and EP.

**Scope and limitations of the first PR:**

- Requires synchronous scheduling and MRV2, and disables `torch.compile`; layer selection is Python control flow, so each group is captured separately.
- Not supported: speculative decoding, DP, context parallelism, DBO, EPLB, KV/EC connectors, multimodal and hybrid/attention-free models.
- Async scheduling and adaptive group sizing are possible follow-ups.

The core change is about 950 lines, about half of it in two new files. Changes to existing core files are limited to:

- the scheduler-class switch and `delay_cache_blocks` in `Scheduler`;
- an `advance_pp` flag and the group-continuation input path in the MRV2 model runner;
- a `layer_group_idx` capture key in the CUDA graph manager;
- activation memory reservation in the worker;
- the sampling skip for intermediate groups in `EngineCore`.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_TBD_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is a scheduler subclass plus a worker-side runner the preferred integration point, or should this live behind a more general "partial-depth execution" interface?
2. Is the synchronous-scheduling-only restriction acceptable for an initial version?
3. Should the benchmark script (`benchmarks/benchmark_layered_prefill.py`) be part of the PR, or should the PR description carry only the results and reproduction commands?

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the implementation and for drafting this RFC. The submitter reviewed the design and results.

title: [RFC] Expose allocator-issued KV block generations to asynchronous connectors
author: feichai0017
body:
### Motivation

Asynchronous KV connectors can retain a destination block while an external
DMA/RDMA operation is in flight. The connector APIs expose `KVCacheBlocks` at
`update_state_after_alloc`, but `KVCacheBlock` currently identifies a physical
slot only by `block_id`. The same object and ID are reused after the allocator
returns the slot to the free queue.

A late completion or release acknowledgement can therefore only be checked
against request/session metadata. Those identities do not prove that the
physical KV slot still belongs to the allocation that originally authorized
the transfer.

This matters even for connectors that correctly delay normal frees: fault
recovery eventually needs to distinguish the old allocation of block N from a
new allocation of block N without relying on timeout or process liveness as a
DMA termination proof.

### Requested contract

Please expose an allocator-issued generation for each writable KV block
allocation:

- `BlockPool` increments the generation whenever a physical block is handed
  out for a new writable allocation after reuse/eviction.
- `KVCacheBlocks` exposes `(block_id, allocation_generation)` to connectors at
  `update_state_after_alloc` and request-finish handoff.
- Cached read-only references retain the generation of the contents they
  reference; generation changes only when the slot becomes a new writable
  allocation.
- The value is monotonic for a slot within the owning process and never zero.

The allocator must issue the value. A connector-local counter keyed by block ID
cannot observe allocations made through other paths and would not be a valid
reuse fence.

This would not itself claim DMA cancellation or permit early free. It would let
connectors reject stale control completions after a separately proven physical
termination and make page-reuse tests deterministic.

### Relevant released interface

Observed on vLLM 0.31.0 commit `db9527a46873454610df6dbedf79a36d6bf1a7f6`:

- `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py::KVCacheBlock`
- `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py::BlockPool.get_new_blocks`
- `KVConnectorBase_V1.update_state_after_alloc`
- `KVConnectorBase_V1.request_finished[_all_groups]`

I searched open and closed issues/PRs for KV-connector block reuse and allocation
generation and did not find a matching proposal. I can prepare a focused PR and
unit tests if maintainers agree with the API direction.

title: [RFC]: Preserve output distribution under structured-output + speculative decoding
author: yzong-rh
body:
### Motivation.

#### Background

In structured-output + speculative decoding, `StructuredOutputManager` handles draft tokens in three
steps:

1. `validate_tokens` checks a draft sequence without committing grammar state and trims it to its grammar-valid prefix
2. `grammar_bitmask` builds a vocabulary mask for every draft + bonus positions without committing grammar state
3. `accept_tokens` commits the verified token to the persistent grammar state

The timing of draft validation depends on scheduling mode:

```
Synchronous scheduling

step N-1:   schedule step N-1
            sample step N-1 and retrieve drafts for step N
            accept_tokens(step N-1 output)
            validate_tokens(step N drafts)
step N:     schedule step N with validated drafts
            grammar_bitmask(step N drafts)
            sample step N with bitmask and retrieve drafts for step N+1
            accept_tokens(step N output)
            validate_tokens(step N+1 drafts)
...
```

```
Asynchronous scheduling

step N-1:   schedule step N-1
step N:     schedule step N with placeholder drafts
            sample step N-1 and retrieve drafts for step N
            accept_tokens(step N-1 output)
            validate_tokens(step N drafts)
            grammar_bitmask(step N drafts)
step N+1:   schedule step N+1 with placeholder drafts
            sample step N with bitmask and retrieve drafts for step N+1
            accept_tokens(step N output)
            validate_tokens(step N+1 drafts)
            grammar_bitmask(step N+1 drafts)
...
```

In synchronous scheduling, validation of step N drafts occurs before scheduling step N. So step N is scheduled with validated drafts.
In asynchronous scheduling, step N is scheduled with placeholder drafts before the drafts for step N are retrieved and validated.
Therefore, step N is scheduled with unvalidated placeholder drafts.

#### Issue

See #60451.
The current lifecycle changes the output distribution under spec decode when structured outputs are enabled.

Suppose we have draft tokens:
```
[valid, invalid, ?, ?]
```

`validate_tokens` truncates it to:
```
[valid]
```

Rejection sampling would correctly sample `valid` but treat `invalid` as a bonus token instead of a rejected token.
It would sample the `invalid` position from the target (verifier model) distribution instead of the residual distribution `max(target - draft, 0)`.

### Proposed change.

#### 1. Preserve the first rejected draft for the rejection sampler

Given,
```
[valid, invalid, ?, ?]
```
make `validate_tokens` truncate to:
```
[valid, invalid]
```
instead of
```
[valid]
```

The rejection sampler will consequently treat the `invalid` position as a rejection (thanks to the grammar bitmask disallowing `invalid`) instead of a bonus position.

Note this creates a small performance regression on the sync scheduling because the target model verifies one more token than before.

#### Optional 2. Do not validate drafts on the asynchronous scheduling path

Calling `validate_tokens` to trim draft tokens on the asynchronous scheduling path is redundant. We've already scheduled the request with unvalidated tokens.

Removing the `validate_tokens` call removes reasoning-end detection and a temporary grammar-state advance and rollback.

#### Implementation and alternatives

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61557 implements the proposed changes:
- Rename `validate_tokens` to `trim_spec_tokens` and ensure the invalid token isn't truncated (change 1)
- Remove the `validate_tokens` call on the async scheduling path (change 2)
- Fix grammar backends to ensure `accept_tokens` remains transactional -- avoid an extra `validate_tokens` call inside `grammar_bitmask`

Alternative: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60690
- Use `SchedulerOutput.num_invalid_spec_tokens` to ensure the invalid token isn't discarded (change 1)
- Add `Request.num_invalid_spec_tokens` for the sync scheduling path such that `num_invalid_spec_tokens` computed by `validate_tokens` on step N is available for step N + 1

Rejected Alternative: remove `validate_tokens` from both the sync and async scheduling
- Technically we achieve both change 1 and 2 if we don't validate draft tokens at all
- However, this leads to a statistically significant performance regression on the sync scheduling path.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

cc @simon-veitner-redhat @tomasruizt @vadiklyutiy @arpera 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Fuse DSpark confidence-head GEMV into a single TileLang kernel
author: panpan0000
body:
### Motivation.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62840 contains an initial implementation of the proposal described in this RFC.

## Bottom line

One new TileLang kernel, ~113 lines, fuses DSpark's confidence head (`cat + cast + GEMV + sigmoid`) into **one CUDA launch, one CUDA-graph node, zero fp32 temporary** per decode step. Median kernel-latency speedup vs `torch.compile`: **1.92× on RTX 5090 (SM120)** and **1.90× on H200 (SM90)**; real-checkpoint A/B under greedy decode produces **0/30 divergent outputs** on both GPUs. TPOT-level gain is < 0.05 % — the value is on the mechanism (launch count, graph nodes, activation-memory traffic), not end-to-end. DeepInfer (DeepSeek's own engine) already ships an equivalent fused kernel via `AcceptRatePredictor` and the same PDL trick; this is a port-with-FP32-weight.

## Summary

Adaptive speculative decoding in vLLM (the DSpark drafter, gated by `--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","enable_adaptive_verification":true,...}'`) runs a small **confidence head** once per drafted block to decide how many tokens to submit to the verifier:

```
p_accept = sigmoid( ( [ hidden_state ; markov_embed ] @ W ) / temperature )
   hidden_state     (n, H)        bf16
   markov_embed     (n, r)        bf16
   W                (H + r, 1)    fp32   # ReplicatedLinear(params_dtype=fp32)
   p_accept         (n,)          fp32
```

Per draft step, this is **four CUDA launches** — `torch.cat`, `.float()` cast, cuBLAS GEMV, `.sigmoid()` — plus one `(n, H + r)` fp32 temporary that bypasses CUDA-graph memory reuse on the decode fast path. The GEMV itself is tiny (`H + r ≈ 7 200`); on an RTX 5090 the four launches cost ~117 µs of CPU-side scheduling and ~14–45 MB of activation traffic per call, for a useful answer that's about 2 µs long.

DeepInfer — DeepSeek's own inference engine — ships an equivalent fused kernel in its open-source DSpark drafter. The kernel is 60 lines of TileLang ([`dflash.py:12-72`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/layers/tilelang_ops/cuda/dflash.py#L12-L72)) wired into their `AcceptRatePredictor` ([`heads.py:37`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/models/v4_modules/heads.py#L37)), and uses PDL (`T.pdl_sync()`) to overlap with the preceding GEMV. The same file contains another small `dflash_input_store_tl` fusion, which suggests DeepInfer's motivation is systematically flattening small ops on the DSpark path — confidence-head fusion is one piece of a larger pattern, and the open-source repo does not quote a per-kernel TPOT delta. They cast the confidence weight to bf16 for tensor-core FMA. vLLM keeps the same weight in FP32 (`params_dtype=torch.float32` in `qwen3_dspark.py:124-131`), so a drop-in port would silently change which draft tokens get accepted.

This RFC proposes **porting the DeepInfer fusion to vLLM while preserving FP32 weight semantics**. We also expect this kernel to be the first of several small DSpark fusion ports (e.g. `dflash_input_store_tl`, `dspark_draft_embed_store_tl`) so the mechanism-level benefit compounds.

## Numbers

Measured on **two GPUs**, one card each (no TP, no DP):

- RTX 5090, SM120 (Blackwell), 32 GB, CUDA 13.0, driver 575 — dev pod.
- NVIDIA H200, SM90, 143 GB HBM3e, CUDA 13.1, driver 590.44.01 — single-card.

vLLM 0.32.0, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, TileLang 0.1.12. Target / drafter for the E2E / A/B runs: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` + `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` (~10 GB total HBM).

### Dispatch gate (when does the fused path actually run)

The kernel is **only** dispatched when **all** of the following hold. Otherwise the call site returns `None` and falls back to the existing PyTorch path (no behavioral change).

| Condition | Required value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Platform | NVIDIA Hopper (SM90) or later, including consumer Blackwell (SM120) | TileLang's PDL (programmatic dependent launch) is SM90+. |
| `hidden.dtype` | `torch.bfloat16`, CUDA tensor | DSpark contract; the kernel assumes bf16 inputs. |
| `markov.dtype` | `torch.bfloat16`, CUDA tensor | Same. |
| `weight.dtype` | `torch.float32`, CUDA tensor | vLLM keeps fp32 here for determinism — this is the deliberate divergence from DeepInfer's bf16 variant. |
| `(n_embed, markov_rank)` shape | `(7168, 32)` only (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) | Only this shape shows end-to-end benefit on datacenter GPUs in our measurements. Smaller DSpark variants (e.g. Qwen3-4B-DSpark at H=2560, r=256) see parity on consumer GPUs and a regression on H200. |
| `hidden.stride(-1)` | `1` (last-dim contiguous) | Kernel assumes row-major, last-dim unit stride. |
| `markov.stride(-1)` | `1` when `r > 0` | Same. |
| Batch size `n` | `32 ≤ n ≤ 2048` | See "Batch gate rationale" below. |
| `markov_embed.shape[-1]` | `≥ r` (rank parameter) | Compile-time kernel template expects this. |

The dispatch conditions live in `vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/__init__.py:43-83` and are checked at every call. When any one of them fails, the wrapper returns `None` and the caller's PyTorch fallback runs — that fallback is already correct and tested.

### Batch + shape gate rationale

The gate has two pieces: a **V4-Flash-only shape floor** and a **batch size window**.

**Shape floor.** Only `(n_embed = 7168, markov_rank = 32)` is admitted to the fused path. This is the DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark production shape — the configuration DeepInfer designed and validated the fusion for on datacenter GPUs. Smaller DSpark variants currently in-tree (e.g. Qwen3-4B-DSpark at H=2560, r=256):

- See **parity** fused vs PyTorch on consumer (RTX 5090 / SM120) at every batch we tested (sequential: 5.01 s vs 5.02 s; batched at B ∈ {32, 128, 256}: ratios 0.97×–0.99× — see "Batch sweep" below).
- See a **~42–58 % wall-clock regression** on H200 SM90 in the sequential setting (see "Systematic wall-clock puzzle" below), driven by ~93 µs per-call TileLang dispatch overhead on Hopper.
- Contribute ≤ 0.1 % of decode kernel time even when fused, so the kernel is structurally too small to recover its dispatch overhead at these shapes.

For those variants the right thing is the existing PyTorch fallback (which is free under `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` cudagraph capture), not a fused custom op. Rather than ask reviewers to audit a kernel they'll never exercise, we hard-limit the dispatch to the V4-Flash shape and revisit when / if smaller variants become production-relevant.

**Batch floor and ceiling.** `n < 32` is declined because the per-call TileLang dispatch overhead (~93 µs on Hopper; less on Blackwell) dominates the kernel's savings at tiny batch. `n > 2048` is declined as a sanity bound; the benchmark sweep covers up to `n = 8192` and the kernel is correct across the entire range, but matching realistic DSpark block-size × concurrency stays well below 1024.

### Batch sweep evidence on RTX 5090

Sequential `llm.generate()` per-prompt on the 4B drafter previously showed parity fused vs baseline (5.01 s vs 5.02 s). To test whether **larger batches** break the tie (since fused kernel savings should grow with `n` while TileLang Python dispatch overhead is fixed), we ran an end-to-end sweep against `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` + `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` with `num_speculative_tokens=7`, greedy sampling, on one RTX 5090:

| Concurrent requests B | fused (s) | baseline (s) | fused / baseline | per-req fused (ms) | per-req baseline (ms) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32  | 0.414 | 0.422 | **0.98×** | 12.9 | 13.2 |
| 128 | 0.817 | 0.839 | **0.97×** |  6.4 |  6.6 |
| 256 | 1.445 | 1.467 | **0.99×** |  5.6 |  5.7 |

(The B=8 row is excluded as a warmup artifact — fused runs first and pays JIT + first-replay costs that baseline then misses. B=32/128/256 are steady-state.)

Interpretation: at every production-realistic batch the two paths are within noise on the 4B shape. Combined with the H200 regression at the same shape and the observation above that the kernel contributes ≤ 0.1 % of decode time here, the fused path **cannot pay for itself** at the 4B shape on current hardware. That is the empirical basis for the shape floor.

### Micro-benchmark, vs `torch.compile` baseline

Per-implementation latency, `n × H=7168, r=32` (dominant DSpark decode shape), 200 iters each. Reproduce: `python benchmarks/kernels/dspark/bench_confidence.py` on the PR branch. The fused dispatch gate applies only up to `n = 2048`; numbers beyond are kernel-capability visibility.

| GPU | Shapes | Median latency speedup | Min / max | Production shape band (n ≤ 2048) | Median err_ratio vs `compiled` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RTX 5090 (SM120) | 36 | **1.92×** | 0.72× / 3.56× | 1.72× – 2.77× | **0.610** |
| NVIDIA H200 (SM90) | 20 | **1.90×** | 0.39× / 5.15× | 0.39× – 2.97× | **0.695** |

H200's wider range: small-shape launch overhead is more costly on Hopper; above `n=128` H200 pulls ahead of 5090, reaching 5.15× at `n=8192, H=7168, r=32` where HBM3e bandwidth favors the fused kernel.

### What changes per decode step

| Quantity | main (PyTorch) | fused (this PR) | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CUDA launches along the path | 4 | 1 | **−3** |
| CUDA-graph nodes along the path | 4 | 1 | **−3** |
| fp32 temporary per call | 14 – 45 MB (n ≤ 2048) | **0 B** | 100 % |

### Engine-level dispatch smoke (`--load-format dummy`)

**Takeaway: the kernel dispatches into the real engine path, launches exactly once per drafted step, is captured inside CUDA graphs on both GPUs, and contributes well under 0.1 % of total kernel time.**

Real `vllm.LLM(...)` runs against target `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` + draft `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7`, adaptive verification enabled, on both GPUs. Traced with vLLM's worker-side profiler (`llm.start_profile()`/`stop_profile()`; see [docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing/profiling.html)):

| Metric | RTX 5090 (SM120) | NVIDIA H200 (SM90) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `confidence_head_fused_tilelang_kernel` launches in a 64-token decode | **64** | **64** |
| Launches with CUDA graph id set | **64 / 64** | **64 / 64** |
| Median per-call kernel time | 1.70 µs | 1.79 µs |
| p99 per-call kernel time | 1.92 µs | 1.98 µs |
| Total across all confidence-head calls | 0.109 ms | 0.115 ms |
| Total decode kernel time | 375 ms | 227 ms |
| Share of total kernel time | **0.03 %** | **0.05 %** |

The kernel contributes well under 0.1 % of decode kernel time on both GPUs, which is the point — the value is mechanism-level (launch count, graph nodes, activation traffic), not an end-to-end TPOT percentage.

### Production-scale TPOT

Production DSpark shapes (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ≈ 300 GB packed; V4-Pro ≈ 880 GB) require multi-GPU H200/H20 per-replica, so they're not covered here. DeepInfer does not publish a per-kernel TPOT delta either. If multi-H200 capacity becomes available we will land TPOT numbers as a follow-up comment.

### Proposed Change.

Port the DeepInfer fusion pattern into vLLM, with the FP32-weight delta and standard vLLM wrapping contracts.

**Code** (in [PR #62840](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62840)):

- New TileLang kernel in `vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/tilelang_kernels.py` — one launch, fp32 accumulator, in-kernel sigmoid. 113 lines.
- Wrap in `VllmJitKernel` (`vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/tilelang.py`) mirroring `kernels/mhc/` — precompiles at engine JIT warmup so shape-specialized builds are ready before first request.
- Register as `torch.ops.vllm.dspark_confidence_tilelang` via `direct_register_custom_op` so CUDA-graph capture sees one opaque node.
- Call-site dispatch in two `compute_confidence()` methods: `vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_dspark.py` and `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/dspark.py`. Caller falls through to the existing PyTorch path on any gate condition failure — no user-visible behavior change.
- **Fallback observability**: the dispatch wrapper logs a one-line `logger.debug` per unique decline reason on first occurrence; disabled by default. A metric counter is not added in this PR to keep scope aligned with existing kernel integrations.

**Behavioral consistency check (real DSpark checkpoint, fused on vs off)**

The kernel is not bitwise-identical to the PyTorch path — fused uses an fp32 accumulator + in-kernel sigmoid while the fallback goes through bf16 intermediates. So we checked what matters for behavior: **does flipping the kernel on change which draft tokens are accepted, and does that change the generated text?**

Setup: real `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` target + real `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` drafter, `enable_adaptive_verification=True`, greedy sampling (temperature=0, seed=42), `max_tokens=64`. 30 diverse prompts (reasoning / code / writing / math / knowledge), repeated on both GPUs (SM120 and SM90).

| GPU | Branch | Wall-clock (30 prompts × 64 tok) | Identical outputs to fallback? |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| RTX 5090 (SM120) | fused | 5.01 s | — |
| RTX 5090 (SM120) | baseline | 5.02 s | — |
| NVIDIA H200 (SM90) | fused | 4.55 s | — |
| NVIDIA H200 (SM90) | baseline | 3.20 s | — |
| — | **divergent prompts** | — | **0 / 30 on both GPUs** |

All 30 prompts' output text **and** output-token counts are **bitwise identical** between fused and baseline on both GPUs. Per-call fused kernel time is ~1.7 µs (5090) / 1.79 µs (H200) — the kernel itself is ~µs-and-change per decode step.

**Systematic wall-clock puzzle on H200** (flagged for review / future repro): 30 sequential single-prompt `llm.generate()` calls, each 64 tokens, measured twice on the H200:

| Branch | Run 1 | Run 2 | Mean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fused | 4.55 s | 5.35 s | **4.95 s** |
| baseline | 3.20 s | 3.38 s | **3.29 s** |

Fused is consistently ~50 % slower on H200 in this shape. On RTX 5090 the same script/branch policy yields fused 5.01 s vs baseline 5.02 s (within noise). Causes we've ruled out:
- The kernel itself: ~0.1 ms per prompt of 64 confidence-head launches.
- cuLaunchKernel count: identical (1024 in both branches per trace — PyTorch fallback is also captured into the same CUDA graph).

Possible cause, not verified: per-call TileLang custom-op dispatch overhead is higher on Hopper than Blackwell (different CUDA driver / cudaGraph launch path). **Consequence of the new gate**: this regression is no longer reachable — the H200-4B shape is now rejected by the dispatcher (`(2560, 256) != (7168, 32)`) and falls back to PyTorch. The regression could in principle still bite at the V4-Flash shape if H200 dispatch overhead is worse than we think, but at that shape the kernel's savings scale with `n` and the production batch floor of 32 gives headroom. We have not yet isolated whether Hopper-specific dispatch cost at the V4-Flash shape + batch >= 32 stays within budget; landing a multi-H200 TPOT reproduction remains a follow-up.

## Risks

- **Behavioral consistency at the accept gate** (fp32 accumulator + in-kernel sigmoid vs bf16 intermediates). Addressed by the real-checkpoint experiment above: 0/30 divergent on both SM120 and SM90.
- **TileLang coverage.** v0.1.12 emits `T.exp` via libdevice; some shapes produce ptxas warnings on older drivers. Mitigation: the PyTorch fallback stays in-tree.
- **Small-batch slow case — now gated out.** At `n = 1` the fused kernel is 0.72× cuBLAS (launch-bound); the new gate declines dispatch at `n < 32` so this regime is unreachable in production. H200 sequential-mode regression is also no longer reachable on the 4B shape because that shape is rejected by the shape floor (see "Batch + shape gate rationale").

## Prior work

| Where | Contrast |
|---|---|
| DeepInfer [`dflash.py:12-72`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/layers/tilelang_ops/cuda/dflash.py#L12-L72) | Same fusion, bf16 weight; we keep fp32. |
| [#41536](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41536) fused mHC post_pre | Same shape of problem: fusing several small launches on the decode fast path. Their kernel handles ~5 % of decode time (5.8 % TPOT claim); ours handles ~0.03 % (no TPOT claim). Same vLLM-side wrapping: `TileLang` + `VllmJitKernel` + `direct_register_custom_op`. |
| [#43905](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43905) move mHC to `kernels/mhc/` | Same kernel-module layout (`vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/`). |
| [#47456](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47456) JIT warmup infra RFC | Our `VllmJitKernel` subclass uses the warmup contract this RFC introduces. |

## Open question for reviewers

**Is 30-prompt greedy behavioral identity enough to gate the numerics risk?** We have: (a) 29-shape synthetic tolerance tests, (b) 36-shape (5090) + 20-shape (H200) sweeps vs `torch.compile`, (c) 30 real-checkpoint greedy prompts producing identical strings on two GPU architectures. Happy to land the script that produced the 30/30 result in-tree (under `tests/` or `benchmarks/`).

### Benefits

1. **−3 CUDA-graph nodes per decode step.** Faster capture and replay; matters more as DSpark `block_size` and `num_speculative_tokens` scale.
2. **Zero fp32 activation memory traffic on the decode path.** Removes the per-step temporary that CUDA-graph memory must recycle.
3. **Matches numerics DeepSeek vetted in production.** Same fused math, same `AcceptRatePredictor` shape contract — not a guess.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks from posting, or until at least one maintainer of `vllm/model_executor/kernels/` or `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/` has responded.

### CC List.

(author) @panpan0000 — happy to pull in DSpark / MHC maintainers once initial feedback lands.

### Any Other Things.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to draft the kernel, tests, benchmark, and parts of this RFC. I reviewed the code, ran the tests (29/29), and re-checked the language.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Reduce descriptor and WR overhead to improve Mooncake KV transfer bandwidth
author: zhou-yuhan
body:
### Motivation.

## Overview

**Problem**: Mooncake approaches NIXL performance on hybrid attention model (Qwen3.5) but has substantially lower KV-transfer bandwidth (-35% to \-67%) and higher TTFT on full-attention (Qwen3).   
**Profiled bottleneck**: Measurements point to: 1\) numerous small transfer requests and RDMA work requests (WRs) incurred by a large number of transfer descriptors; 2\) serialized WRs construction and posting in Mooncake Transfer Engine (TE) implementation.  
**Solution**: We propose three optimization phases across vLLM and Mooncake TE

## Benchmark results

### Setup and metric definitions

Two nodes, each with 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs (96 GiB each) and four RDMA HCAs; one prefill instance and one decode instance. Each run has fixed-length synthetic prompts, one output token, three warmup requests, a 300-second arrival window, and 10-second metric intervals. Connectors share the trace at each length.

Network: 200 GBps RoCE per GPU, Mooncake `transfer_engine_bench` test gives \~48 GBps per GPU

- **Qwen3-235B-A22B:** full GQA attention; 0.5 requests/s and 150 requests at every length.  
- **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8:** three GDN layers per full-attention layer; 0.5 requests/s at 1K–16K, 0.25/s at 32K, and 0.1/s at 64K–128K: 150/75/30 requests.

<details>
<summary>vLLM and router launch commands</summary>

```bash
export P_IP="<prefill-ip>" D_IP="<decode-ip>"
export MODEL="/path/to/Qwen3-235B-A22B" MAX_MODEL_LEN=40960
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 WITH_NVIDIA_PEERMEM=1
export VLLM_LOG_STATS_INTERVAL=10 VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=INFO VLLM_LOGGING_COLOR=0
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1

# tune Mooncake:
export MC_RDMA_SIGNAL_INTERVAL=32
export MC_MAX_WR=4096

# For Qwen3.5:
# export MODEL="/path/to/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8" MAX_MODEL_LEN=139264
# export VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS

# Mooncake prefill (P)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$P_IP" VLLM_MOONCAKE_BOOTSTRAP_PORT=8998 VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT=360 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8100 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"mooncake_protocol":"rdma","num_workers":10}}'

# Mooncake Decode (D)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$D_IP" VLLM_MOONCAKE_BOOTSTRAP_PORT=8998 VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT=360 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8200 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"mooncake_protocol":"rdma","num_workers":10}}'

# Mooncake router
vllm-router --vllm-pd-disaggregation --kv-connector mooncake \
  --prefill "http://$P_IP:8100" 8998 --decode "http://$D_IP:8200" \
  --intra-node-data-parallel-size 1 --policy round_robin --disable-retries \
  --request-timeout-secs 300 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --prometheus-host 127.0.0.1 --prometheus-port 29000

# NIXL prefill (P)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$P_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_HOST="$P_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5600 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8100 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"backends":["UCX"]}}'

# NIXL decode (D)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$D_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_HOST="$D_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5600 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8200 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"backends":["UCX"]}}'

# NIXL router
vllm-router --vllm-pd-disaggregation --kv-connector nixl \
  --prefill "http://$P_IP:8100" --decode "http://$D_IP:8200" \
  --intra-node-data-parallel-size 1 --policy round_robin --disable-retries \
  --request-timeout-secs 300 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --prometheus-host 127.0.0.1 --prometheus-port 29000
```

</details>

Tables show **means** from the full prompt-length sweeps. KV BW, Xfer time are collected from `KVConnectorStats` that both Mooncake and NIXL implements. Mooncake times `batch_transfer_sync_write()`, including TE preparation through cleanup, but excluding vLLM's `_build_transfer_params()`. NIXL bandwidth includes **prepare \+ xfer**; its xfer column excludes prepare.

### Qwen3.5: no comparable Mooncake deficit

Mooncake here is v0.3.13.post1

| Prompt | Mooncake TTFT (ms) | NIXL TTFT (ms) | TTFT Δ vs NIXL | Mooncake KV BW (MiB/s) | NIXL KV BW (MiB/s) | KV BW Δ vs NIXL |
| :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: |
| 1K | 190.80 | 188.23 | \+1.37% | 19663.26 | 14907.71 | \+31.90% |
| 2K | 198.76 | 197.89 | \+0.44% | 20327.25 | 19278.93 | \+5.44% |
| 4K | 278.18 | 272.93 | \+1.92% | 20757.88 | 20465.77 | \+1.43% |
| 8K | 482.75 | 480.21 | \+0.53% | 20768.69 | 21176.07 | \-1.92% |
| 16K | 963.08 | 955.85 | \+0.76% | 20748.02 | 21758.72 | \-4.65% |
| 32K | 2009.57 | 2009.48 | \+0.00% | 20907.19 | 22169.96 | \-5.70% |
| 64K | 4546.39 | 4531.34 | \+0.33% | 21074.62 | 22815.89 | \-7.63% |
| 128K | 11370.82 | 11329.90 | \+0.36% | 21193.34 | 22929.77 | \-7.57% |

### Qwen3: longer reported transfers and higher TTFT

The three Mooncake configurations are:

- **MC release:** v0.3.13.post1.  
- **MC main:** `main@74944a77`, default signal interval 1 and max WR depth 256\.  
- **MC tuned:** the same main binary, with `MC_RDMA_SIGNAL_INTERVAL=32` and `MC_MAX_WR=4096` on both nodes. Other settings are unchanged, including 64 KiB slices, two QPs per endpoint, and two TE workers per context.

| Prompt | Connector | TTFT (ms) | TTFT Δ vs NIXL | KV BW (MiB/s) | KV BW Δ vs NIXL | Xfer (ms) |
| :---- | :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: |

| 32K | NIXL | 106573.46 | — | 21394.52 | — | 67.050 |

## Bottleneck: descriptor granularity and delayed progress

A **descriptor** is a `(source address, destination address, length)` passed to TE. TE creates a request and splits it into **slices**, each posted as one data WR. WRs are already chained into batched `ibv_post_send()` calls; this amortizes doorbells but retains per-WR preparation and completion bookkeeping.

`self.engine.batch_transfer_sync_write(...)` is synchronous to vLLM but delegates RDMA progress to background workers. We time four stages on the calling thread:

- **prepare** looks up/opens the peer segment, builds the request array, and allocates a batch;  
- **submit** selects transports, looks up registered memory regions (MRs), constructs slices, and enqueues work;  
- **wait** polls batch status while workers and the NIC make progress;  
- **free** releases the batch after completion.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    B["vLLM: _build_transfer_params (outside API timer)"] --> P
    subgraph API["batch_transfer_sync_write: calling thread"]
        P["prepare: segment lookup/open, request array, batch allocation"] --> S["submit: transport/MR lookup, slice construction, enqueue"]
        S --> W["wait: poll getBatchTransferStatus until complete"]
        W --> F["free: release batch and return"]
    end
    subgraph WORKER["Background RDMA workers and NIC"]
        Q["Dequeue prepared slices"] --> R["Build and post WR chain"]
        R --> N["NIC transfers data"]
        N --> C["Poll CQ, retire WRs, publish completion"]
        C --> Q
    end
    S -. "publish work; workers can start during submit" .-> Q
    C -. "batch completion observed during wait" .-> W
```

### Execution Duration Breakdown

We add tracing points at these stage boundaries to profile the execution durations of each stage. A 16k prompt profile measured 75.797 ms/API call. The call-weighted breakdown, with percentages of total API time, is:

- **prepare:** 1.380 ms (1.82%), including segment lookup/open at 2.932 µs (0.0039%) and batch allocation at 2.118 µs (0.0028%). These are subcomponents, not additional stages.  
- **submit:** 17.396 ms (22.95%).  
- **wait:** 45.353 ms (59.83%).  
- **free:** 4.356 ms (5.75%).  
- **Other C++ work:** 1.068 µs (0.0014%).  
- **API residual:** 7.311 ms (9.65%), including argument conversion/copying, GIL reacquisition, and return packaging outside the timed C++ body.

Follow-up profiling of MC tuned added phase/event timers and slice/WR/completion queue entry (CQE) counters. Keeping the 16K workload and 32/4096 settings, we varied only `MC_SLICE_SIZE`: 64 KiB → 1 MiB → 1 MiB → 64 KiB. Each run completed 150 requests and captured 1,200 rank-level API calls (150 × TP8), excluding warmup; each call transferred 752 MiB.

**First post offset** is the elapsed wall time from the instrumented C++ API entry to the return of the worker's first successful data-WR `ibv_post_send()` for that call. It measures posting startup latency.

Every run contained 600 calls with 94 × 8 MiB descriptors and 600 with 96,256 × 8 KiB descriptors: **observed coalescing outcomes in the same workload**. The first pair's call-weighted means are:

| Slice limit | Descriptor layout | Descriptors/call | Posted WRs/call | API (ms) | Submit (ms) | Wait (ms) | First post offset (ms) |
| :---- | :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: |
| 64 KiB | 94 × 8 MiB | 94 | 12,032 | 36.353 | 2.235 | 33.403 | 2.920 |
| 64 KiB | 96,256 × 8 KiB | 96,256 | 96,256 | 108.653 | 29.185 | 53.103 | 32.121 |
| 1 MiB | 94 × 8 MiB | 94 | 752 | 30.730 | 0.189 | 30.426 | 0.304 |
| 1 MiB | 96,256 × 8 KiB | 96,256 | 96,256 | 108.876 | 30.109 | 52.585 | 32.894 |

Larger slices reduce WRs by 93.75% for large descriptors, lowering their API time by 15.47%/29.33% across the two pairs. Small descriptors remain 8 KiB WRs, with API time changing only \+0.21%/+0.25%. Overall API improves by 3.72%/7.56%: increasing the slice limit cannot merge across descriptors.

- **Small-WR construction and posting are bottlenecks:** 96,256 × 8 KiB descriptors produce 96,256 WRs; increasing the slice limit leaves that work unchanged and does not improve API time.  
- **Prepare-then-enqueue exposes startup latency:** preparing large slice/metadata lists before handing them to workers leaves a 32–34 ms first-post delay. Streaming preparation could overlap much of this work with worker-side WR construction/posting.

### Proposed Change.

## Proposed optimization roadmap

### Phase 1: Improve block coalescing in the vLLM connector

**Motivation:** fewer descriptors reduce downstream request/task/slice/WR work. Current grouping requires both block-ID sequences to increase by one in input order, missing descending but jointly contiguous mappings.

**Proposal:** reorder paired source–destination mappings within a KV group, preserving the mapping, then coalesce jointly contiguous full-block copies. This should effectively reduce descriptors (and thereby, WRs) for Mooncake TE to handle. e.g., Eight 8 KiB blocks could become one 64 KiB descriptor/WR.

**Status: completed and merged** in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63142, with expected performance gain (KV BW 9590.51 -> 21609.67 MiB/s for Qwen3-235B-A22B 16k prompts)

### Phase 2: Pipeline TE preparation with worker posting

**Motivation:** calls with numerous descriptors (dense calls) spend tens of milliseconds preparing work before the first post. The current flush counter resets per request and counts only newly allocated slices; remote preparation also processes a full list before enqueueing.

**Proposal:** prepare and publish bounded chunks based on actual accumulated pending work, including remote preparation. Workers can post earlier chunks while the caller prepares later ones. Ideally, this producer-consumer mode can overlap WRs construction and posting.

**Status: completed and merged** in Mooncake TE https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/5039, with expected performance gain (+1.54%-41.89% transfer BW improve in TE bench, and 2.2%-21.5% KV BW improvement in vLLM PD serving Qwen3-32B prefill TP4 -> decode TP2)

### Phase 3: Explore aggregation of non-contiguous transfers with SEND/RECV (fully vectored write)

**Motivation:** remaining fragmentation still produces small WRs. WRITE supports multiple source scatter/gather elements (SGEs) but one contiguous remote range; SEND with a matching RECV can gather/scatter at both ends.

**Proposal:** prototype multi-SGE SEND/RECV for fragmented layouts and WRITE for contiguous destinations. SEND/RECV requires receive posting, layout/order agreement, and receiver completion handling.

Also evaluate [mlx5 UMR/indirect mkeys](https://github.com/linux-rdma/rdma-core/blob/master/providers/mlx5/man/mlx5dv_wr_mkey_configure.3.md), which map scattered registered memory into a contiguous logical range for WRITE. Evaluate layout construction, both endpoints, GPU-memory support, and multi-NIC operation. This phase is exploratory as it changes the TE transport protocol and workflow.

### Feedback Period.

2 weeks

### CC List.

@wangxiyuan, @nwpu-zxr, @yaojiejia, @Sarimsaljook, @CAICAIIs, @ClockOfDestiny, @ivanium, @LCAIZJ, @dtcccc, @ApostaC, @orozery, @ZJY0516, @staryxchen 

### Any Other Things.

## Related

- [#60523 — Improving MooncakeConnector](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60523): broader connector roadmap, including metadata handling and descriptor coalescing.
- [#62478 — Vectorize transfer descriptor build](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62478): groups once per KV group/request and vectorizes descriptor construction while preserving descriptor values and order.
- [#60605 — Optimize Mooncake contiguous block grouping](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60605): reduces helper allocations/conversions while preserving grouping behavior.

These PRs accelerate construction of existing descriptors; Phase 1 proposes reducing their number, and Phases 2–3 target TE overhead.

title: [RFC] Expose aggregate remaining prefill work for routing
author: KaisennHu
body:
# RFC: Expose aggregate remaining prefill work for routing

Implementation: [vLLM #63160](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63160). Consumers: Router [colocated #444](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/444) and [P/D #469](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/469).

## Proposal

Publish the scheduler's remaining prefill work per worker as an aggregate, on the observability surfaces that already exist:

- a Prometheus gauge on `/metrics`, for dashboards and 1 Hz consumers;
- a few extra fields on `/load`, for consumers that need 2–5 Hz polling with a payload small enough to
parse cheaply.

The signal is token work, not latency, GPU time, or a cache lease. It covers prefill only; decode load and queueing remain separate inputs to routing.

## Accounting

```text
remaining_running = Σ over RUNNING requests of
                    max(0, num_tokens - max(0, num_computed_tokens - num_in_flight_tokens))
remaining_waiting = Σ over WAITING requests of num_tokens
sample_seq        = monotonic per-engine counter, incremented with the scheduler step
```

- `num_in_flight_tokens` is excluded: dispatched but unconfirmed work is not complete.
- Reused cache positions are already reflected in `num_computed_tokens`, so no separate cache term is
needed, and no double discount is possible.
- `waiting` is separate so a consumer never prices queued work as computed.
- The value may rise: preemption resets `num_computed_tokens` and replays generated tokens, both of
which are included by construction.

## Exposure

| Surface | Shape | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `/metrics` | `vllm:prefill_tokens_remaining`, `vllm:prefill_sample_seq` | one gauge registration |
| `/load` | `{"server_load": N, "prefill_tokens_remaining": …, "sample_seq": …}` | ~120 B JSON |

Both read the same `SchedulerStats` snapshot, so the two surfaces cannot disagree.

## Consumer contract

1. Poll `/load` at 2–5 Hz; use `/metrics` only as a fallback at 1 Hz or for observation.
2. Apply a snapshot only if `sample_seq` is newer; ignore equal or older values.
3. Reconcile with local events: charge admissions after the sample, release completions after it, and
keep a monotonic floor so a late sample cannot lower the estimate below what was already dispatched.
4. Keep the last value when polling fails; the absolute request deadline is unaffected by this signal.
5. Fall back to the admission estimate when the fields are absent, which is what an older worker returns.

## Validation

Measured end to end on 2P+2D B300 (TP1, NIXL, Qwen3-4B BF16, 131k batched tokens, 48 GiB KV, prefix caching, KV-aware prefill, round-robin decode, C16, 721-request AgentX trace, 721/721 succeeded):

| routing input | TTFT mean | p50 | p95 | p99 | mis-selection¹ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| admission estimate only | 7.27 s | 4.08 s | 24.5 s | 42.3 s | — |
| this aggregate, 1 s sampling | 6.63 s | 4.68 s | 18.9 s | 41.5 s | 12.7% |
| per-request snapshots, 100 ms | 6.32 s | 4.35 s | 19.8 s | 42.9 s | 0.4% |

¹ calibrated replay: how often the router picks a worker that is not the true least-loaded.

## Alternatives

- **Per-request progress on the generation stream.** Highest fidelity and the only way to attribute work
to a request, but it needs new proto fields, a reduced-cost output path in the Rust frontend, and scheduler publication logic, and it measured no additional end-to-end benefit over this aggregate at the workload above. Not pursued now; the deferred per-request fields are documented in the Router RFCs.
- **Infer from `num_computed_tokens` or KV events.** Both are position/placement signals, not work, and
neither carries request attribution.
- **Poll `/metrics` only.** Works, but parsing tens of KB of text per worker at 2–5 Hz costs more than
the signal is worth; hence the `/load` fields.

## Limits

- Aggregate only: no per-request attribution, no phase, no per-source cache breakdown.
- Freshness is bounded by the poll interval and the engine's stats cadence, not by a push.
- gRPC-only deployments need the worker's HTTP address to reach `/load`; the Router RFCs cover the
mapping or the `ServerInfo` field that provides it.
- The value says nothing about decode load, transfer time, or batching effects.

title: [RFC]: Declared ownership and layout for WeightSource (NCCL broadcast PP + NCCL M2N)
author: hao-aaron
body:
### Motivation.

Partitioned trainers (PP, EP) need every weight transfer backend to know which trainer ranks own each parameter, and how each parameter is laid out across them. Today each backend gets this its own way:

- **Sharded RDT and #62557:** each rank declares `held_names()`, and the ranks all-gather the results at runtime. #62557 opens a new TCP rendezvous just for this.
- **#62557:** adds `source_rank` and `num_source_ranks` to the init info.
- **NCCL M2N:** a separate subclass (`M2NWeightSource`) with its own `metadata()` type, a different meaning for `__iter__` (local shards instead of full tensors), and, in #62853, `source_topology()` + `iter_group()`.

A trainer has to write one source per backend, and the three ownership mechanisms don't agree with each other. This RFC proposes one `WeightSource` contract that serves NCCL broadcast (including PP), NCCL M2N, sharded RDT and IPC.

Related: #62557 (NCCL broadcast PP), #60934 / #60949 / #62853 (NCCL M2N), #46439 (NCCL M2N RFC), #59840 (M2N trainer PP).

### Proposed Change.

#### 1. Ownership and layout live in `ParamMeta`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ParamMeta:
    name: str
    dtype: torch.dtype
    shape: tuple[int, ...]                       # full HF shape
    owners: tuple[int, ...] | None = None        # global trainer ranks, mesh order; None = all
    mesh_shape: tuple[int, ...] | None = None    # row-major over owners; default (len(owners),)
    placements: tuple[Placement, ...] | None = None  # one per mesh axis; None = replicated

Placement = Replicate | Shard  # vLLM-owned (JSON-safe, torch-free); Shard(dim) uses torch.chunk splits
```

- **Metadata is identical on every rank**, including ownership. That makes ownership static knowledge, so correctness never needs a runtime exchange.
- **`owners` holds global trainer ranks**, the same `TrainerInitInfo.rank` engines already receive. Engines map them to their own communicator ranks. The source never knows about communicators.
- **Owner order is the mesh coordinate order.** That's why ownership can't be derived from name sets like `held_names()`.
- **Overlapping owner sets are engine policy, not a contract rule.** M2N requires disjoint groups. Broadcast and RDT tolerate overlap and pick one owner. Tied weights are resolved by the engine.
- **Not supported:** `Partial`. A backend rejects mesh dimensions it can't handle (M2N supports at most 2).
- **Derived helpers** replace the methods sources implement today: `owned_names(metas, rank)` replaces `held_names()`; `owner_groups(metas)` gives M2N's topology and RDT's owner sets; `local_shape(meta, rank)` and `mesh_coords(meta, rank)` give per-rank layout.

#### 2. Iteration: two optional modes, at least one required

```python
def iter_full(self)  -> Iterator[list[tuple[str, torch.Tensor]]]: ...
def iter_local(self) -> Iterator[list[tuple[str, torch.Tensor]]]: ...
```

Both modes yield **batches** chosen by the source. Joined together, the batches are exactly the owned names in metadata order.

| | Yields, per owned name | Collectives |
|---|---|---|
| `iter_full()` | The full tensor. If sharded, it is gathered among the owners, and every owner yields the result. | Only among that parameter's owners |
| `iter_local()` | This rank's piece as described by `placements`, with shape `local_shape(meta, rank)`. | None (conversions must be rank-local) |

- **A source implements one or both. Nothing is derived** from one mode to the other.
- **Each engine requires the mode it consumes** (broadcast, IPC and RDT need full; M2N needs local) and raises at init if the source lacks it.
- **`placements` describe `iter_local()`.** If a source doesn't implement `iter_local()`, its placements go unused.
- **To use a full-only source with M2N,** add `iter_local()` returning `iter_full()` and leave `placements=None` (replicated over the owners).
- **Names the rank doesn't own are skipped.** Engines also accept and drop `(name, None)`, so a source that walks the whole module needs no filtering.
- **Validation:** the yielded names must equal `owned_names(metadata, rank)`.
- **Collective rule:** every owner iterates in metadata order, so the gathers line up. Non-owners never block.
- **`iter_local()` rules:** it yields `torch.Tensor` only, and work is enqueued on the caller's current stream (M2N overlaps its per-group streams).
- **A parameter that can't be expressed as `Shard`/`Replicate`** in a source that implements `iter_local()` is declared `Replicate` over its owners. `iter_local()` yields the gathered tensor, and every owner runs that gather.
- **The weight source decides where batches begin and end.** How weights are best produced depends on the trainer's layout: one Megatron-Bridge conversion task, one FSDP all-gather per layer, or one tensor at a time. That is a trainer-side concern, so vLLM doesn't prescribe it. Engines accept batches of any size. A batch is resident in memory all at once, so its size is also the source's memory trade-off.
- **How an engine transfers is independent of the source's batches.** NCCL packed-buffer sizes, RDT's per-layer `free_group` groups, and M2N's transfer waves are all engine decisions. Engines re-chunk the stream to suit themselves, so changing a source's batching never changes the transfer protocol. `iter_groups()`, `groups()` and ownership filtering in the source are removed.

#### Backend mapping

| Backend | Derives from metadata | Iterates |
|---|---|---|
| **NCCL broadcast** | Sender = `owners[0]`. `owners is None` means rank 0 sends everything (today's behavior). | `iter_full()` |
| **NCCL M2N** | Source groups = `owner_groups()`. One communicator per group (`owners ∪ workers`), group-local rank `j` = `owners[j]`. Mesh and placements per parameter. Disjointness checked. | `iter_local()` |
| **Sharded RDT** | Owner sets = `owner_groups()`. No bitmask all-gather. Transfer groups stay `layerwise_groups(names)`, computed by the engine and sent to workers as `group_lens`. | `iter_full()`, re-chunked into layer groups before publishing |
| **IPC** | Unchanged for `owners is None`. Rejects partitioned sources. | `iter_full()` |

**Broadcast communicator.** Use one communicator per sender (`{sender} ∪ workers`), not #62557's shared one.

- With a shared communicator, every sender joins every broadcast, posting dummy receives with scratch buffers, so all senders run in lockstep.
- With per-sender communicators, only rank 0 needs the whole owner map, to build each sender's `update_weights` payload, and stages can transfer in parallel.
- Either way there's no coordinator for correctness. Failure propagation (rank 0's RPC failing, a sender stuck partway) is a separate safety mechanism.

**M2N removals.** `M2NMesh.start_rank` becomes internal, and `source_topology()` / `iter_group()` / `held_names()` cross-checks are no longer needed. Each rank belongs to at most one group, so `iter_local()` is already that group's stream.

#### Adapters

**`ModuleSource`** (plain, FSDP, or DTensor)
- **Plain tensor:** `owners=None`.
- **DTensor:** `owners` = the flattened global ranks of `device_mesh`, `mesh_shape` = the device mesh's shape, and `placements` converted from the DTensor's.
- `iter_full()` calls `full_tensor()`; `iter_local()` calls `to_local()`.
- This absorbs `DTensorModuleSource`, and drops its requirement that the mesh be a contiguous `[0, n)` interval.

**Megatron-Bridge**
- **Local, or gathered?** Decided per task by `task.local_hf_param_specs()`. Non-empty means the local path; empty means the gathered path.
- **Local path:** `iter_local_hf_params()` yields `LocalHFParam`.
  - `shard_group="tp"` / `"etp"` → owners = that group's ordered global ranks, `placements=(Shard(shard_dim),)`.
  - `"replicated"` → owners = the stage's ranks, replicated.
- **Gathered path** (e.g. interleaved QKV): `stream_weights_megatron_to_hf(conversion_tasks=..., current_pp_stage_only=True)` → owners = the stage's ranks, replicated.
- **Coverage (estimate):** for Qwen3-30B-A3B, about 99% of tensors and 98% of bytes take the local path; only QKV (about 1.7%) is gathered.
- **Local-path limits:** BF16 storage only, no Megatron-FSDP, no GTP.

#### Example: PP=2 × TP=2 (stage 0 = ranks 0–1, stage 1 = ranks 2–3)

| name | owners | placements |
|---|---|---|
| `embed_tokens.weight` | `(0, 1)` | `(Shard(0),)` |
| `layers.0.self_attn.q_proj.weight` | `(0, 1)` | replicated (gathered) |
| `layers.0.self_attn.o_proj.weight` | `(0, 1)` | `(Shard(1),)` |
| `layers.27.self_attn.o_proj.weight` | `(2, 3)` | `(Shard(1),)` |
| `lm_head.weight` | `(2, 3)` | `(Shard(0),)` |

- **Broadcast:** senders 0 and 2, communicators `{0}+workers` and `{2}+workers`. Ranks 1 and 3 iterate only to join their stage's gathers.
- **M2N:** groups `(0, 1)` and `(2, 3)`. Each rank sends its shard.

#### Migration

1. Add the `ParamMeta` fields, the placement types, the helpers, and `iter_full()` / `iter_local()` (batched). This is purely additive.
2. Engines consume the owned-only stream. **Shims, for one deprecation cycle:**
   - A legacy source that implements only `__iter__` is treated as `iter_full()`.
   - A source that overrides `held_names()` without declaring `owners` takes today's path (all-gather plus `groups()`).
3. M2N moves onto the base fields. Ideally this replaces `source_topology()` before #62853 merges.
4. Rebuild #62557 on `owners` with per-sender communicators, dropping `source_rank` / `num_source_ranks` and the coordinator's correctness role.
5. Deprecate `__iter__`-only sources, `held_names()` overrides, `groups()` filtering, and `M2NWeightSource`.

#### Deferred: sparse transfer

Sparse NCCL (`sparse_nccl_engine.py`) is out of scope. **Updating it will be a separate effort.**

- **Today it takes no `WeightSource`.** It raises if one is passed. Each round, the trainer passes a list of `SparseWeightPatch(name, indices, values, full_shape)` to `send_weights(patches)` or `send_weight_chunk(patches)`. The patches use checkpoint names and flat indices into the full tensor. Per-round metadata (`num_updates_list`) rides on the update info.
- **It is a delta backend.** What's sent changes every round, so a stable `metadata()` manifest doesn't fit.
- **It has the same PP problem.** Only rank 0 sends, so a partitioned trainer must collect all patches onto rank 0 first.

Likely direction for that effort: declare `ParamMeta` with `owners` once at init, let each owner send per-round patches for its own names, and decide whether patches stay in full-tensor coordinates or also allow local (sharded) ones.

#### Rejected

- **A source per backend:** N ownership mechanisms, N sources per trainer.
- **A runtime all-gather of `held_names()`:** it shares static knowledge at runtime, and it loses owner order.
- **Always-sharded sources, with engines doing the gather:** engines would need a process group, it fails for layouts that can't be expressed, and exporters gather more cheaply themselves.
- **Exactly one owner in the contract:** it rules out tied and replicated layouts. Leave it to engines.

### Feedback Period.

3 days

### CC List.

@kwen2501 @pkousha @giannis2two @dharak-cohere

### Any Other Things.

Open questions:

1. **Megatron gathered export:** does every TP rank in the stage end up with the full tensor? This decides replicated-over-stage vs. a single owner.
2. **Uneven shards:** does M2N accept uneven `torch.chunk` splits? Should vocabulary padding be trimmed in the adapter, or declared?
3. **Broadcast sender choice:** always `owners[0]`, or balance sends across a stage?
4. **Metadata digest:** should the cross-rank metadata check be required (over the trainer's existing process group) or stay optional per engine?
5. **Broadcast failure propagation:** what's the minimal mechanism with per-sender communicators that needs no new rendezvous?
6. **Non-torch local buffers:** M2N (#60934) currently lets `__iter__` yield CUDA Array Interface objects and raw device pointers, while this RFC limits `iter_local()` to `torch.Tensor`. Proposal: keep the base contract torch-only and provide a zero-copy `as_tensor(buffer, shape, dtype)` helper so those sources migrate with a one-line wrap (raw-pointer lifetime stays the source's responsibility). Alternative: an M2N-only extension that accepts them, at the cost of those sources working only with M2N.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
