title: [RFC]: MoRIIO transfer contract: safe KV reclamation and bounded failure for P/D (READ and WRITE)
author: tjtanaa
body: ### Motivation. The MoRIIO KV connector moves KV between prefill (P) and decode (D) instances over MoRI-IO, in READ mode (decode pulls) or WRITE mode (prefill pushes). It works on the happy path. Its failure paths, though, have no shared rule for *when KV memory may be reused*. Each path decides for itself, and several of them free memory that RDMA may still read or write: - **Wrong output with no error.** In READ mode, prefill frees a request's blocks after a fixed 60 s if decode hasn't released them. Decode may still be queued, or already reading. It then reads another request's KV, and MoRI reports success ([`moriio_connector.py#L1680-L1684`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio/moriio_connector.py#L1680-L1684)). - **Freeing under live DMA.** A READ batch is judged FAILED on its first failed status while sibling reads are still pending. Decode releases prefill and recomputes into its own blocks ([`moriio_engine.py#L877-L893`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio/moriio_engine.py#L877-L893)). A WRITE finalize failure frees the source blocks and tells decode nothing ([`moriio_engine.py#L617-L622`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio/moriio_engine.py#L617-L622), [`#L219-L225`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio/moriio_engine.py#L219-L225)). - **Hangs and stalls.** A WRITE consumer has no receive deadline on main. One bad message kills the notify listener ([`moriio_engine.py#L992-L998`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio/moriio_engine.py#L992-L998)). Every wait calls MoRI `wait_all(30 s)`, which sleeps to its deadline on xGMI ([`moriio_engine.py#L911-L920`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio/moriio_engine.py#L911-L920)). - **Leaks and broken peers.** Dead or replaced peers are never torn down, and MoRI's `DeregisterRemoteEngine` only erases a map entry ([`backend_impl.cpp#L1175-L1178`](https://github.com/ROCm/mori/blob/2d4c3e2748b9329b2e0fc90e12f449231b4691ed/src/io/rdma/backend_impl.cpp#L1175-L1178)). - **The scheduler can't help.** On a failed load, the scheduler frees the request's blocks and recomputes ([`scheduler.py#L3307-L3313`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L3307-L3313)). That is correct only if DMA into them has stopped, and the connector has no way to say "failed, but not safe yet". These share one root cause: **"the wait ended" is treated as "the memory is free."** Two existing efforts already attack the symptoms: - [ROCm/mori#759](https://github.com/ROCm/mori/issues/759) tracks 12 framework-side gaps with owners and PRs. - #59382 argues for separating "fail the request" from "reuse its blocks" for WRITE timeouts. This RFC proposes the **single contract** those fixes should follow, so each PR can be checked against one rule instead of re-deciding it. It covers both modes, both sides, and large xPyD. These evaluations are designed based on vLLM main da180ef (2026-10-23) and ROCm/mori 2d4c3e2. ### Proposed Change. ### Summary Adopt one transfer contract for MoRIIO, implemented by a per-worker **transfer ledger** inside the existing connector, plus one small scheduler API (**allocator hold**). In short: 1. **Reclaim only on proof.** Memory a peer could touch is reused only when `reclaimable(x) = sealed(x) ∧ E_x ⊆ F_x`: nothing new can be posted, and every possible accessor is proven quiet. Timers, epochs and failure reports never free memory. 2. **Report now, reclaim later.** A failure reaches the scheduler at once and the request fails or recomputes in **fresh** blocks. Unproven memory waits in a counted allocator hold. 3. **Grant before access.** Decode **CLAIMs** an OFFER before any DMA. A lease frees only an *unclaimed* OFFER. 4. **Every wait is bounded**, with three exits: a positive message, a negative message and peer-down. 5. **MoRI-IO requirements are stated** as guarantees T1–T9. vLLM runs a conservative profile until each one exists, so nothing waits on a MoRI release. ### Goals - No KV memory is reused while any RDMA/xGMI operation may still touch it, in READ or WRITE, on prefill or decode. - Every failed transfer ends as a reported failure within a bound. `kv_load_failure_policy` (`fail` / `recompute`) then applies unchanged. - One state machine and one message protocol for both modes, including heterogeneous TP and DCP (multiple readers or writers per request). - Bounded resource use at large xPyD: peers, sessions, QPs, in-flight bytes, credits and held bytes. - Measurable: every timer, hold and failure is a metric. - No change for other connectors unless they opt into the allocator hold. ### Architecture MoRIIO P/D transfer architecture _Figure 1. Each instance runs the same connector. Control messages go over the existing ZMQ side channel; KV bytes go over MoRI-IO. Decode initiates RDMA READ and prefill initiates RDMA WRITE._ The router picks one P and one D per request and copies prefill's OFFER into the decode request. A request's KV never goes to more than one D instance. With heterogeneous TP or DCP, several workers on each side still take part, so reader and writer counts come from a layout plan fixed at CLAIM time. MoRIIO connector layers _Figure 2. vLLM hooks stay as they are. Inside the connector, one ledger per worker owns all transfer state, and an execution adapter runs every MoRI call. Below the transport contract, MoRI-IO's current status per guarantee is shown._ - **Transfer ledger (one owner per worker).** It is the only code that mutates transfer state, and it consumes events from the scheduler hooks, the execution adapter, the control link and timers. It replaces about 20 shared dicts guarded by one lock across three threads today. - **Execution adapter.** MoRI's batch submit blocks on `future.get()` ([`executor.cpp#L226`](https://github.com/ROCm/mori/blob/2d4c3e2748b9329b2e0fc90e12f449231b4691ed/src/io/rdma/executor.cpp#L226)), and several bindings hold the GIL. So calls run on a bounded queue with bounded native threads. An op is registered as an accessor *before* it is enqueued. A stalled or exhausted adapter withdraws admission and recovers. - **Instance coordinator.** It commits CLAIMs for all workers of an instance, so a binding is all-or-nothing. ### Transfer contract | Id | Rule | |---|---| | I1 | **Reclaim only when provably quiet** (`reclaimable(x)`). | | I2 | **Outcome is separate from reclamation.** Every worker reports every transfer exactly once, as soon as the outcome is known. A failure goes in both `finished_recving` and `failed_recving`. | | I3 | **Every wait has three exits:** positive, negative, peer-down. | | I4 | **Timers escalate, they never free.** The one exception is an OFFER nobody has claimed. | | I5 | **Messages are idempotent, ordered and epoch-checked.** Replays answer only while the grant is live. | | I6 | **Reader and writer counts come from the plan bound at CLAIM.** | | I7 | **One owner per worker.** Queued native work already counts as an accessor. | | I8 | **Everything is bounded.** Hitting a cap means waiting or refusing, never growing. | | I9 | **Behaviour is gated by its proof** (activation profile, below). | Failure: report now, reclaim on proof _Figure 3. Every failure signal seals the attempt. The outcome goes to the scheduler at once. The memory is freed only when every accessor is proven quiet; otherwise it waits in an allocator hold released per participant._ | Accessor | Proof of quiescence | Not proof | |---|---|---| | Local ops | every op registered before enqueue has retired; for a MoRI batch, every op on every QP it was spread over (T1) | one ERR status; a later SUCCESS; zero posted statuses while work is queued | | Remote initiator (READ: each decode reader; WRITE: each prefill writer) | its own fenced DONE/ABORT; or the local QPs to that peer moved to ERR with their flushes drained (T3) | missed heartbeats; a new epoch or HELLO; a passive receiver's ACK | | xGMI importer | its fenced DONE/ABORT, or the exit of that exact process | a HELLO from its successor | ### Lifecycle and CLAIM Transfer lifecycle _Figure 4. Per (attempt, worker). Inside the shaded region a peer may touch the memory. Every way out of it ends at a reclaimable close or in a hold._ CLAIM rules: 1. **Frozen binding.** The first committed CLAIM binds the OFFER to one (consumer engine, epoch, attempt, layout, mode). Duplicates get the same answer while the grant is live; conflicting claims get `CLAIM_REJECT{bound}`. 2. **One commit point.** The producer's instance coordinator commits after every owning worker confirms. A partial refusal rejects, and the confirmed workers drop their reservation immediately. 3. **Serialized with expiry.** Exactly one of commit or lease end wins. A late CLAIM gets `CLAIM_REJECT{expired}`, and decode recomputes. 4. **Every worker learns the binding,** including workers with zero planned peers. 5. **Rejection holds nothing.** Decode releases unexposed destinations, backs off with jitter after `retry_after`, and stops at an absolute deadline (recompute or error). Oversized requests are refused at once. In READ mode the CLAIM round trip happens while the request is still queued, so it is off the transfer's critical path. ### Protocol and liveness READ and WRITE message flows _Figure 5. The side that posts the DMA drains it before sending a fenced DONE, so one message means "fenced" on both sides._ - **Envelope:** one msgpack map `{v, k, src:[engine, epoch, worker], dst, cg, seq, ack, x, a, pd, b}` on the existing ZMQ channel, with per-link sequence numbers, cumulative acks and a 1 s retransmit. - **HELLO** negotiates the protocol and planner versions and exchanges a shard descriptor (model hash, layers, cache kind per group, KV heads, backend layout, dtype, parallel layout). A mismatch is refused with the field named (mori#759 gap 12). - **Messages:** HELLO, PING, RENEW, CLAIM / CLAIM_OK / CLAIM_REJECT, READ_DONE / READ_ABORT, WRITE_DONE / WRITE_ABORT, CANCEL / CANCEL_ACK, RELEASE, REVOKE / REVOKE_ACK, BYE. - **Ports:** one formula from the flat worker index (`dp_local, pp, pcp, tp`) is used for both bind and dial. There are four liveness signals, kept apart: | Signal | Carried by | On loss | Reclaims? | |---|---|---|---| | Native heartbeat | libzmq `ZMQ_HEARTBEAT_*` (I/O thread, no GIL) | SUSPECT: no new CLAIM to that peer | no | | Semantic renewal | RENEW, batched per instance pair | lease end: unclaimed freed, claimed revoked | only unclaimed | | Worker progress | PING progress counters, engine worker monitor | DOWN: revoke and fail attempts | no | | MoRI peer failure | `pop_peer_failure()` / `session.alive()` (ROCm/mori#716) | DOWN for that teardown domain, initiator side | no; a QP error event is not a drained flush | An epoch change, a deregister or a re-handshake marks the old incarnation DOWN. It never releases that incarnation's memory. ### Core change: allocator hold This is the only change outside the connector, and it needs scheduler maintainers' review. `finish_requests()` + `delay_free_blocks` (as discussed in #59382) keeps blocks, but it ties them to the request and has no per-worker release. Block ids are shared across TP workers, and `KVOutputAggregator` counts receive completions only. So we propose: ```python # On a failed receive whose quiescence is unproven, in one scheduler operation: hold_id = kv_cache_manager.quarantine(request, attempt, participants) # detaches the blocks from the request and drops their prefix-cache hashes; # the request then fails or recomputes into FRESH blocks. # Later, once per participant (e.g. each TP worker) that proves quiescence: kv_cache_manager.release_quarantine(hold_id, participant) # the last participant drops the hold's reference through BlockPool.free_blocks. ``` - Holds have their own identity, so a late or duplicate release never touches another attempt's blocks. - Holds cover every KV cache group (hybrid models, mori#759 gap 8). - Held blocks count against capacity and are exported as a metric. Crossing a threshold (5% per worker to start) triggers the drain sequence: fail readiness, keep holds, then a controlled restart with a fleet-wide cap. - The connector reports held participants through a new optional `KVConnectorOutput` field. Connectors that don't set it behave exactly as today. Release aggregation sits next to the salvage path added in #56430. ### MoRI-IO requirements and activation profile MoRI is pinned to the version in the ROCm container, so every guarantee has a conservative stand-in in vLLM. We'll track the library asks under ROCm/mori#759 and #732. | # | Guarantee | mori 2d4c3e2 | vLLM until then | |---|---|---|---| | T1 | Whole-batch terminal: every op, on every QP, reaches one outcome; terminal means the NIC won't touch memory again (mori#759 gap 1) | one aggregate status; flush on QP error undocumented | ERR is unproven: hold | | T2 | Bounded waits drive progress | `WaitFor(t)` sleeps on polled backends | poll `WaitFor(0)` per step | | T3 | Real teardown scoped to the shared QP domain (mori#759 gap 7, mori#815) | `DeregisterRemoteEngine` erases a map entry | hold on DOWN; refuse new peers at the cap | | T4 | Passive-side liveness for WRITE targets | none | liveness signals above | | T5 | Completion with data at the target | `PopInboundTransferStatus`, unused | WRITE_DONE message | | T6 | xGMI exporter limits documented | undocumented | importer rule above | | T7 | `prepare_for_compute` per backend and rail | none | configuration not supported | | T8 | Completion drain (finished ids in one call + eventfd) | none | full per-status accounting, admission capped | | T9 | Optional scoped memory-window revocation | none | off | Each behaviour switches on only when its gate is met. For example, "reclaim after an error outcome" needs T1 on that backend, and "recompute while old DMA is uncertain" needs the allocator hold. A build with today's MoRI is correct but conservative: after a peer dies it may hold blocks until a restart. ### Bounds for large xPyD | Bound | When it's hit | |---|---| | Peer instances K per side, so active pairs A ≤ min(P·K, D·K, P·D) | `HELLO_REJECT{peer_cap}`; bounded reroutes, then a capacity error | | Native sessions and QPs | evict an idle, quiet teardown domain with a real teardown, or refuse | | In-flight ops, bytes and adapter queue depth | wait; never post past the cap | | Destination credits (both modes) | allocation waits; credits stay charged through holds | | Claimed-but-queued source bytes | `CLAIM_REJECT{source_budget, retry_after}` | | `_reqs_to_send`, unmatched messages, terminal ids | capped, epoch-keyed, expired with a metric (mori#759 gaps 9 and 10) | With instance-scope renewal, heartbeats scale with active instance pairs (2A per second) rather than worker pairs. ### Compatibility - The control protocol is versioned at HELLO. A v2 worker refuses a v1 peer with a clear error (open question 1). - `kv_transfer_params` gains a versioned `moriio` sub-map that carries the OFFER. - `defer_timeout` maps to the lease and `recv_abort_timeout` to the watchdog (open question 3). - No change for other connectors unless they adopt the allocator hold. ### Test Plan Every unit and E2E test is parameterized over all ROCm attention backends the model supports: - `TRITON_ATTN`, `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN`, and `ROCM_AITER_FA` with `VLLM_ROCM_SHUFFLE_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT=0/1`; - `TRITON_MLA` and `ROCM_AITER_MLA`; - `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE`; - the model-pinned backends. **Ledger (CPU)** - [ ] Randomized interleavings of scheduler, op, message, timer and liveness events; I1–I9 checked after every step - [ ] Competing and duplicate CLAIMs; expiry racing commit; zero-peer workers report - [ ] P0 confirms, P1 refuses: P0's reservation is gone by the next tick - [ ] Budget cycle (source 1, destination 1, two requests) finishes with no watchdog firing - [ ] Multi-QP batch with one QP failed: partial completion never authorizes reuse - [ ] One of two writers aborts: failure reported now, destination held until the other retires - [ ] Cancel after enqueue, before the native call starts: the task is removed with proof it never ran, or its memory is held **Allocator hold (CPU)** - [ ] Failed receive then immediate recompute: old blocks held, retry uses fresh blocks, prefix cache never returns them - [ ] TP2, one worker still has DMA in flight: the hold stays until it reports - [ ] Late or duplicate release for an old `hold_id` leaves the new attempt untouched **Fault injection (GPU, single node over xGMI, and RDMA where supported)** - [ ] Kill prefill or decode mid-transfer, in both modes - [ ] Decode stops renewing while a read is in flight: no free before proof - [ ] Failed status injected mid-batch (ROCm/mori#731 fault injector) - [ ] Bad message to the listener: the listener survives, the request fails cleanly - [ ] Poison check: a reused block is never read or written by an old transfer **Performance** - [ ] No TTFT/ITL regression on the happy path (CLAIM is off the critical path in READ) - [ ] Status-handling CPU per transfer stays within budget at real model shapes - [ ] Heartbeat, renewal and session counts stay bounded at 16P×16D ### PR Roadmap Land the open PRs that already keep blocks, amend the ones that free too early, then stack the contract PRs. The full PR-by-PR mapping is in the migration plan._ 1. **Land now** (already consistent with the contract): #62473 (READ release to every holder), #60743 (listener bind failure), #59058 → #60852 (WRITE abort ownership), #58962 (WRITE consumer watchdog, reporting through `failed_recving`), #50674 (bounded pending-ACK buffer). 2. **Amend, then land:** - #62552: keep blocks when the posted-write wait fails. - #56465: count its hold. - #60693: split it into handshake timeout, settle-before-free and sleep mode, and choose one sleep design with #62832. - #62457 and #62474: feature work; rebase on the above. 3. **Close or fold in:** #51301 (a longer timer that still frees), #32291 (folds into C6's port formula). 4. **Contract PRs:** - **C1** `KVConnectorStats` for MoRIIO. - **C2** non-blocking whole-request polling (`WaitFor(0)`). - **C3** negative paths (mori#759 gaps 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9). - **C4** the core allocator hold, in parallel. - **C5** ledger + execution adapter on today's wire protocol. - **C6** protocol v2: HELLO, CLAIM, lease, liveness (gaps 2, 7, 12). - **C7** bounds and drain. 5. **MoRI-IO, in parallel:** T1, T2, T3 (with #815), T8, and GIL release in the session and registration bindings. C1–C5 change behaviour inside each process only, so they roll out without a coordinated P/D upgrade. C6 is the first change on the wire. ### Open Discussion 1. Refuse v1 peers, or support a mixed-version window? 2. Should the allocator hold be a general `KVCacheManager` API that NIXL and Mooncake can also use? NIXL has the same lease-under-reader gap (#20139) and no decode deadline (#59872). 3. Keep `defer_timeout` / `recv_abort_timeout` as aliases, or rename them `lease_s` / `watchdog_s`? 4. Should the CLAIM coordinator live on prefill worker 0 or in the scheduler process? 5. **READ source rule.** A READ never writes prefill's memory, so prefill could free its source once each reader commits not to consume (a fenced DONE, an ABORT, a REVOKE_ACK, or a reported failure with the destination held), instead of waiting for proof that its reads have stopped. A partitioned decode is then covered by the lease (decode consumes only reads that completed before its grant deadline). Prefill would never need a hold in READ mode. Is that relaxation acceptable? ### Feedback Period. Two weeks. The first PRs on the roadmap don't depend on the open questions and can be reviewed in parallel. We'd like agreement on the contract (rules, CLAIM and the allocator hold) before the ledger PR lands. ### CC List. @simondanielsson @TianDi101 @inkcherry @vllmellm @kliuae @BadrBasowid ### Any Other Things. ### References - ROCm/mori#759, framework-side RAS for MoRI-IO (gap list and owners); #732 (library-side fault work); #731 (fault injector); #716 (peer failure reporting); #815 (`no-qp-rebuild`) - vLLM #59382 (RFC: MoRIIO WRITE failure handling and safe reclamation), #58962 (WRITE consumer watchdog), #59058, #57705 (merged), #60808 (merged), #62473, #61726 (merged), #56430 (merged) - NIXL references: #56104 (sibling handles), #59872 / #59874 (decode deadline), #59873 (heartbeats as activity), #20139 (lease under an active reader) - Code: [`moriio/`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/moriio), [`scheduler.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/da180efbcddcfbb211acc8a22ea55d8dfeb3f943/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py), [ROCm/mori `src/io`](https://github.com/ROCm/mori/tree/2d4c3e2748b9329b2e0fc90e12f449231b4691ed/src/io) All code findings above come from reading the pinned revisions; none were run. Each one gets a fault-injection test before its fix lands. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Use session Agent Hints to reuse prompt tokens and block hashes
author: RichealYoung
body:
### Motivation.

A typical agent sends the conversation again after adding a reply, tool result, or new instruction. APC can reuse the corresponding KV blocks, but the service still has to tokenize the prompt and construct block hashes before it can find those blocks. These CPU costs grow with the conversation, even when most of its KV is already cached.

The session hint gives the service a straightforward place to look for reusable input: one recent request from the same session. The client continues to send the complete request, so the service can check the actual content. This gives the existing session hint another practical use: reducing repeated input-processing work.

### Proposed Change.

Use the existing `session_id` Agent Hint to reduce repeated input tokenization and block-hash construction across agent turns. The frontend and EngineCore would each save one recent input per session, check whether the next input matches, and reuse the matching work.

Both stages would be opt-in, with separate CPU memory budgets. The first version supports text-only Chat Completions with the checked Qwen3 tokenizer configuration. This is a proposed use of the session identity discussed in the [Q4 roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61024) and [session-aware hints RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52113).

## How a request would be processed

The implementation follows the two stages of input processing:

1. **Tokenization in the frontend.** Apply the chat template to obtain the final prompt text. Look up the saved candidate using `(cache_salt, session_id)`. If the text is unchanged, reuse its token IDs. If a prefix matches, reuse tokens up to a safe boundary and tokenize the remaining suffix. Otherwise, tokenize the complete prompt.
2. **Block hashing in EngineCore.** Pass the complete token list to EngineCore. It compares the list against its own saved candidate, reuses hashes for matching complete blocks, and computes the rest with the existing block hasher.
3. **KV-cache lookup and execution.** Process the resulting request through the existing KV-cache lookup and scheduler. Saving token IDs and hashes does not keep physical KV blocks alive.

Each stage can save the current input as its next candidate, subject to its memory budget. The frontend's candidate and EngineCore's candidate do not need to come from the same request.

### Why select only one candidate per session?

An agent conversation often extends a recent input. We use that relationship to try one candidate rather than search a collection of previous prompts. This keeps candidate selection and the amount of history per session simple.

A session ID does not tell us which request is the next request's parent. Concurrent branches can replace each other's saved candidates, and requests routed to different workers may not find the same history. The content checks still determine what can be reused; an unhelpful candidate reduces the hit rate rather than making its tokens valid.

This is a tradeoff. A broader prefix index or segment cache may find reuse that a single candidate misses. We have not measured superiority over those alternatives. The proposal is to use an available hint for a simpler candidate-selection policy, not to require hints for all tokenization caching.

In the tested workload, successful reuse saved about 33 ms per request with one output token. New-session misses added 1.52 ms on average; head-rewrite measurements did not establish a clear latency change. Whether this pays off overall depends on the workload's reuse rate.

### Why does EngineCore check tokens again?

Tokenization happens in the frontend, while block hashes are constructed in EngineCore. Letting each stage check its own candidate means their histories can be replaced or cleared independently.

Trusting a frontend match result could remove EngineCore's token-prefix comparison. It would also require a way to identify the corresponding EngineCore history and handle replacement, reset, and requests already in flight. The proposed first version keeps the complete token list and the second comparison, avoiding that additional cross-process protocol.

### Where is partial token reuse safe?

Appending text can change how a tokenizer splits the end of an existing text prefix. A matching string prefix is therefore insufficient on its own.

For the supported Qwen3 tokenizer configuration, safe boundaries occur immediately after complete added tokens. These are strings registered as individual tokens, including the chat template's control markers. The supported configuration recognizes them before normalization and ordinary text tokenization. Text on either side is processed independently, so changes in the remaining suffix cannot alter the token IDs through the shared marker.

The frontend records where these safe boundaries occur in both the prompt text and token list. It chooses the last boundary within the matching text prefix. If none is available, it tokenizes the complete prompt.

This depends on the exact tokenizer configuration and encoding methods. The token cache checks both during initialization. A tokenizer update or custom encoding method can disable reuse until its behavior is checked. The first version intentionally limits support rather than assuming that every model's control tokens provide the same guarantee.

## Memory, concurrency, and fallback

The token and hash histories have separate configurable CPU memory budgets, exposed by `--session-token-cache-mb` and `--session-hash-cache-mb`. Both default to zero. When space is needed, each cache evicts older entries.

Saved candidates are snapshots: cache-owned copies of the token IDs, hashes, and metadata needed for reuse. A request can finish reading an old snapshot after another request replaces it. That snapshot continues to count toward the budget until its readers release it. Space is reserved before making cache-owned copies or building boundary metadata. If the reservation fails, the request continues without saving a new candidate.

Clearing or closing a cache prevents requests already in progress from restoring history based on the old cache state. Concurrent publication does not establish conversation ancestry; it only selects the next candidate.

Unsupported inputs use the existing computation path. Initial token reuse excludes explicit input truncation, padding, token offsets, multimodal and embedding inputs, LoRA, and KV-transfer connectors. Hash reuse has separate eligibility checks and can be enabled independently.

A miss is not free: matching and saving a new candidate add work on top of full computation. Those costs are included in the measurements below.

## How this relates to existing work

Tokenization reuse already has direct precedents. The proposed contribution is the session-hint-based candidate policy and its use across frontend token reuse and EngineCore block-hash reuse.

| Related work | Relationship to this proposal |
|---|---|
| [Incremental prompt encoding #47583](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47583) | Reuses a previous prompt encoding after checking a text prefix. This overlaps our frontend work. |
| [Segmented encoding #45514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45514) | Splits prompts around delimiters for parallel encoding and optional segment reuse. |
| [Bounded segment caching #61335](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61335) | Caches reusable tokenized segments in HF renderers. Boundary handling and compatibility checks are relevant to our frontend. |
| [Responses Session Store #56963](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56963) | Stores conversation history and accepts incremental API inputs. Our proposal continues to receive the complete request and checks its content. |

[Dynamo](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/frontend-crates/blob/main/tokenizers/src/cache/l1.rs) and [SMG](https://github.com/smg-project/smg/blob/main/crates/tokenizer/src/cache/mod.rs) also implement tokenization-prefix caches. Research including [Delta Tokenizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19801) and [TokTier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29678) addresses incremental tokenization and reuse.

We would prefer to share compatible frontend boundary and encoding logic with existing work where practical. The design question is whether session-selected candidates and the EngineCore hash stage fit alongside those caches, and where that shared logic should live. Adding another general tokenizer-cache framework is not the goal.

## What the experiments show

Real-model tests used Qwen3-0.6B on an RTX 2080 Ti, approximately 16K-token text prompts, one output token per request, and one request in flight at a time. APC, AsyncScheduler, chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, and output detokenization remained enabled.

Each case used 12 randomized request pairs across two server runs. Requests in each pair went to the same instance: one used a session hint to enable token and hash reuse; the other performed full computation without the hint. Paired requests had the same physical KV-cache hit count.

| Scenario | Mean E2E change, 1 output token |
|---|---:|
| Unchanged prompt | −32.95 ms |
| Chat history extended | −33.38 ms |
| New session | +1.52 ms |
| Head rewrite | +0.41 ms |

Negative values mean lower request latency. The unchanged prompt repeats the saved text exactly; the growing conversation adds an assistant reply and the next user message. New sessions have no saved candidate, and head rewrites modify the beginning of the prompt. Reuse reduced latency on unchanged and growing prompts in both server runs; new sessions showed an increase. The head-rewrite measurements did not establish a clear latency change. Full paired results and uncertainty estimates are retained in the reproduction materials.

Most of the full-path savings came from token reuse. With one output token, hash-only reuse reduced mean E2E latency by 2.3–3.3 ms on the tested hit cases against full computation in the same instance. The [implementation branch](https://github.com/RichealYoung/vllm/tree/codex/agent-hint-session-prefix-main-20261023) and [reproduction materials](https://github.com/RichealYoung/vllm/releases/tag/session-prefix-reader-materials-20261023-002) provide the full results and comparison methods, including the token-only configuration.

Correctness checks passed on the pinned upstream main: 86 CPU tests and 332 real-model serving requests across all four token/hash reuse configurations. We compared complete input token IDs and block hashes against full computation, and checked generated outputs against the baseline. Real-model lifecycle tests also passed in all four configurations, covering concurrent branches, cancellation, and cache reset. Four separate shutdown and fault-handling tests passed with the separate shutdown fix described in the reproduction materials. Correctness checks ran separately from latency measurements.

## Integration cost and next steps

The implementation adds two bounded CPU histories, safe-boundary metadata, and a small C++ helper for string/token comparisons and boundary processing through public CPython APIs. That helper avoids doing the full scan one Python element at a time, but it adds native build and maintenance work. Copies and history updates remain part of the request cost.

The current evidence supports discussing an opt-in implementation for long, highly reusable inputs. Misses cost extra. The initial implementation supports one checked Qwen3 tokenizer configuration with fixed Transformers and tokenizers versions. We would keep those tradeoffs visible rather than enable the feature by default.

Follow-up work would extend tokenizer coverage, test more GPUs and representative agent workloads, and reduce the remaining CPU cost of prefix matching and cache updates.

## Feedback requested

- Is session-hint-selected token and block-hash reuse an appropriate scope for an opt-in vLLM feature?
- Should the frontend reuse boundary and encoding logic from an existing tokenizer-cache proposal, and where should the session-candidate policy live?
- Is independent EngineCore token verification the right initial tradeoff, given the extra comparison and the protocol coordination it avoids?
- Is a Qwen3-only initial version acceptable, or should broader tokenizer support be required before integration?

### Feedback Period.

At least one week; feedback remains welcome while the implementation is under review.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Implementation: https://github.com/RichealYoung/vllm/tree/codex/agent-hint-session-prefix-main-20261023

Reproduction guide and evidence: https://github.com/RichealYoung/vllm/releases/tag/session-prefix-reader-materials-20261023-002

Companion implementation: [Draft PR #63361](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63361).

title: [RFC]: Keep per-request token lists out of EngineCore garbage collection
author: gcanlin
body:
### Motivation.

Each `Request` in EngineCore holds its prompt twice as Python `list[int]`: `prompt_token_ids` and the copy `_all_token_ids`. CPython's cyclic GC visits every element of every tracked list, so each gen-0/gen-1 collection costs O(tokens of the requests that arrived since the previous collection). Long prompts make these pauses long. Under DP the cost multiplies, because all ranks run in lockstep and a pause on any one rank stalls the whole group.

Observed on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, P/D disaggregated, decode DEP8 on 8×B200. Workload: AgentX traces, average ISL ~135K tokens, ~100 running requests per rank. GC timed with `gc.callbacks` over 840 s:

| per decode EngineCore | collections | avg pause | max pause |
|---|---|---|---|
| gen-0 | ~500 | ~20 ms | ~110 ms |
| gen-1 | ~45 | ~150 ms | ~350 ms |
| gen-2 | 0 | – | – |

- That is only ~2% of each rank's time, but the pauses land on different ranks at different steps, so the group pays roughly 8 × 2% ≈ 17%. This matches the decode GPUs' idle time (83% utilization; ~5.6 ms of a 33 ms step).
- In nsys, the late rank's worker sits between `execute_model` calls with no CUDA activity, waiting for its EngineCore.
- Workers are unaffected: their pauses are under 1 ms.

Repro (CPU only): 20 requests with two 135K-int lists each give a 20.9 ms gen-0 collection.

#### Related: #63306

#63306 calls `gc.freeze()` after any scheduling step that admits new requests. On GB300 DEP4 it removes 38–57 ms gen-2 passes (decode step −1.7%). It is cheap (O(1)) and helps.

- **No leak found on the scheduler path.** We ran the real `Scheduler` through admit → schedule → output → finish for 1,920 requests. The frozen object count stays flat (84–85 beyond the startup heap), and an `unfreeze()` + `collect()` at the end finds 0 cyclic garbage; the same loop without freezing also produces none. Paths outside the scheduler (KV connectors, structured output, aborts) were not covered.
- **Coverage on disaggregated decode.** On a decode instance, new requests first wait in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`, which keeps them out of `scheduled_new_reqs`. Their lists stay in the young generations until they are scheduled and can be traversed in the meantime. Freezing when new requests arrive would cover this.
- **The cost is hidden, not removed.** The lists remain `list[int]`, about 9× the memory of int32 storage, and can be traversed once before the freeze.

### Proposed Change.

**A. Untrack token lists (small, short term).** In `Request.__init__`, call `PyObject_GC_UnTrack` (via ctypes, or a tiny C helper) on `prompt_token_ids`, `_all_token_ids` and `block_hashes`.

- These lists only ever hold ints or bytes, which cannot form reference cycles. CPython already untracks tuples and dicts of atomic values for the same reason; it just never does it for lists.
- The lists stay lists: `append`, `extend`, slicing and `==` are unchanged, and appending does not re-track them. Prefix hashes are unaffected.
- No leak risk, about 10 lines.
- Microbenchmark: gen-0 20.9 ms → 0.0 ms. End-to-end A/B pending.
- Caveats: CPython-specific; the lists must never hold other object types (needs a comment and a test).

**B. Compact token storage (larger, long term).** Store token ids as `array('i')` or numpy in `Request`. A small `array('i')` subclass whose slices and `copy()` return lists keeps most call sites unchanged and works directly with numpy and torch. With 100 live requests × 2 × 135K tokens: gen-0 180 ms → 0.03 ms, process RSS 1,117 → 604 MB.

- Same GC effect, and ~9× less memory: about 36 B → 4 B per token, roughly 1 GB per decode EngineCore at 100 × 130K tokens.
- A plain `array('i')` is not a drop-in: slices become arrays, `array == list` is always False, `list + array` raises, and msgspec cannot encode arrays (KV events). The subclass covers slices, `copy()` and equality; the rest needs small fixes at the call sites.
- Touches `request.py`, `ConstantList`, `block_pool` events, `scheduler` (sessions, PP and v1 paths), `sched/output.py`, scheduler-side connectors (Mooncake store, LMCache, HF3FS, offloading, NIXL), structured output and tests.
- Block hashing is unaffected: tokens go through `tuple()` before hashing.

A complementary mitigation for DP (no API change): disable automatic GC in DP EngineCores and run `gc.collect(1)` every N steps on the DP-aligned `step_counter`, so the remaining pauses overlap across ranks. Measured on the deployment above, 15-min A/B: per-user tok/s p10/p50 78/91 → 96/104, ITL p50 10.9 → 9.6 ms, output tok/s per GPU +3.9%.

title: [RFC]: Reduce CPU overhead in Model Runner V2 for long-context P/D serving
author: gcanlin
body:
### Background

Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with P/D disaggregation (2P1D on 16x B200: prefill 2x DEP4, decode DEP8; AgentX traces with ~130K-token prompts at 2,048 concurrent sessions), the GPUs often sit idle waiting for the host: decode was ~17% idle and prefill 15-17% idle. Most of it is per-request host work that grows with prompt length (Python lists of token and block ids, GC traversal of them, pickling), and under DP lockstep one rank's stall stalls every rank. The changes below took decode GPU busy from ~83% to ~95%.

### Track

- [ ] #59908 — sends new requests' token ids to the workers as int32 arrays. It was the only decode-side change in our A/B: ITL mean 14.0 -> 9.0 ms (-36%), per-user tok/s p50 68 -> 112, decode GPU idle 32% -> 18% (nsys); output tok/s per GPU +15.5% together with the prefill-side changes of that run.
- [ ] #63438 — builds on #59908 for block ids: ships them as int32 arrays and stages them without Python lists. On top of #59908: block-table write p99 5.7 -> 0.4 ms, decode GPU busy 90.9% -> 94.6%, per-user tok/s p10 / p50 +3% / +2%.
- [ ] #63363 — keeps per-request token lists out of EngineCore GC; int32 token ids plus GC on the same step on every DP rank: decode per-user tok/s p10 / p50 +21% / +16%, ITL p50 10.9 -> 9.4 ms, output tok/s per GPU +3.9%.
- [ ] #63441 — emits one `BlockRemoved` per KV cache group per allocation instead of one per evicted block. With KV events on, prefill loading most of each prompt from Mooncake spent 5-7% of each EngineCore's main thread in this path (py-spy); event cost per evicted block 1,613 -> 717 ns (micro-benchmark), end-to-end A/B pending.
- [ ] #63454 — opt-in `sha256_int32` prefix-cache hash: hashes each block's token ids as raw int32 bytes straight from the request's int32 buffer (stacked on #62702) instead of pickling one Python int per token. Decode engine input thread 18.3 -> 10.6 ms per new request (it holds the GIL the engine loop needs); per-user tok/s p10 / p50 +8% / +10%, ITL p50 9.2 -> 8.4 ms, output tok/s per GPU +2.2%.

title: [RFC]: Select the MRV2 DBO microbatch count per step within an allocated capacity
author: algebra-MCX
body:
> **Status: draft.** Recording the direction for early feedback; the design and evidence below are still incomplete.

### Motivation.

MRV2 DBO always splits a step into two microbatches (`ubatch_size` is either 2 with `--enable-dbo` or a fixed user value). #57177 keeps that count fixed and only redistributes real tokens across the captured regions. This RFC records the follow-up I split out of #57184: choosing how many microbatches a step uses, per step, within an allocated capacity, while keeping FULL CUDA Graph replay.

Two observations motivate it:

- Under DP imbalance, the right count depends on the smallest rank's real tail, not only on the padded descriptor. A fixed count either leaves microbatches empty (falling back to eager) or leaves overlap unused when every rank has enough tokens.
- A count that is fixed at startup cannot follow the load, while capturing every count for every bucket is too expensive. A bounded set of captured counts, selected through the existing DP synchronization, sits between the two.

I want to be upfront about the evidence. On 8x H200 (DeepSeek-V2-Lite BF16, DP8/EP8, NIXL EP, `batched_triton`, imbalanced loads `[63,97,80x6]`), my prototype ran FULL graphs with two microbatches throughout, and serving was never validated at three or more. On that workload NIXL DBO ON is also still slower than DBO OFF (about 7.8k vs 12.9k output tok/s). #63485 removes a large part of that gap, the static 8192-token dispatch capacity, and needs to be re-measured first. So this RFC asks whether the direction and the interfaces are acceptable before I propose code or performance claims.

### Proposed Change.

1. **Config capacity.** An explicit `ubatch_size` keeps priority. An automatic mode computes an upper bound on how many microbatches can be allocated (per-microbatch NIXL/shared-expert resources, workspace). The bound is a capacity, not the count used by every step.
2. **Runner active count.** `UBatchRunner` separates the allocated capacity from the count used by the current step, through prepare, the thread barrier, capture and output merging.
3. **Captured variants.** For each eligible bucket, capture CUDA graph variants for the eligible active counts through the normal capture API.
4. **DP-synchronized selection.** Factor microbatch descriptor selection out of the DP collective code into one entry point. All ranks select the same captured count from the synchronized per-rank real-token counts. If no captured count fits, use a smaller count, then eager two-way DBO.
5. **Real-tail threshold.** A rank only participates in a count if its real tail per microbatch passes a threshold, so microbatches are not made of padding. This is wired to the automatic config and CLI and documented.

Fixed-count behaviour stays the default. Unsupported layouts keep the current fallback.

Split branches on my fork, one per step above (stacked on the #57177 staging work and the NIXL per-microbatch resources): [`12-microbatch-capacity`](https://github.com/algebra-MCX/vllm/tree/small/pr57184-12-microbatch-capacity), [`13-active-microbatch-count`](https://github.com/algebra-MCX/vllm/tree/small/pr57184-13-active-microbatch-count), [`14-graph-active-counts`](https://github.com/algebra-MCX/vllm/tree/small/pr57184-14-graph-active-counts), [`15-isolate-dp-selection`](https://github.com/algebra-MCX/vllm/tree/small/pr57184-15-isolate-dp-selection), [`16-auto-dp-selection`](https://github.com/algebra-MCX/vllm/tree/small/pr57184-16-auto-dp-selection), [`17-enable-auto-dbo`](https://github.com/algebra-MCX/vllm/tree/small/pr57184-17-enable-auto-dbo).

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks. I'll keep the split PRs as drafts until there is agreement on the direction.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Related: #57177 (real-token staging under DP imbalance), #57184 (original prototype), #51700, #50738.

Already submitted from the same split, independent of this RFC: #63372, #63476, #63485.

Open questions:

- Should the active count live in `UBatchRunner`, or should DBO stay two-way, with more microbatches as a separate execution mode?
- Is a bounded set of captured counts per bucket acceptable for graph memory and capture time, or should variants be opt-in?
- Is "same count on every DP rank, chosen from synchronized real-token counts" the right contract, or should ranks be allowed to differ?

title: [RFC]: Bring vLLM's development cost back to linear: a small core with owned, independently tested components
author: aijanai
body:
### Motivation.

Every new model, kernel, platform or quantization method in vLLM lands in the same tree, the same review queue and the same CI. Because components import each other directly, the cost of a change grows with the number of pairs that can interact, not with the number of components: development cost grows much faster than the codebase. The symptoms are already tracked separately: review backlog (#58253, #59665), stalled kernel packaging split and multi-hour builds (#17419), unversioned extension points that break out-of-tree code (#57566, #62187).

The goal of this RFC is to bring that cost back to linear: each component is owned, reviewed, tested and built on its own, against a small core with stable contracts, so adding the N+1-th model or backend costs the same as the first.

Measured coupling today (pruning upstream down to 8 models, CUDA sm_12x only, no LoRA):

- 230 modules we wanted to drop had to be restored because the core imports them unconditionally.
- Engine entry points statically reach 65% of all modules, including model-specific packages (e.g. the speculative proposer base imports `deepseek_v4` and `minimax_m3`; sparse MLA backends import `deepseek_v2`).
- The pruned build crashed at startup because `get_quantization_config` imports every quantization method eagerly.

### Proposed Change.

Split vLLM into a small engine core plus independent components (models, kernels, platforms, quantization, KV transfer, speculative decoding, serving), as separate repos or at least as independently owned and tested modules. Kubernetes did this with SIGs, OWNERS files, versioned interfaces (CSI, out-of-tree cloud providers) and a staging/publishing model; we propose the same shape:

1. **Ownership**: each component has owners and its own review path (OWNERS/CODEOWNERS per directory), complementing #58253.
2. **Versioned contracts**: the core never imports a component; components register and are loaded lazily by name. Contracts (model, attention backend/KV spec, quantization, KV connector, speculator, platform) get a version, a deprecation window and a conformance suite.
3. **Enforced boundaries**: an import-boundary check in CI, warning first, blocking once the current violations are fixed.
4. **Scoped CI and builds**: a change in a component runs that component's tests plus the conformance suites, not the whole matrix.
5. **Tiers**: core-maintained, community-maintained, out of tree, with explicit criteria to move between them.

Incremental path: ownership first (no code change), then lazy registries and import-boundary check, then versioned contracts, then scoped CI and repo/package splits (#17419). Each step is useful on its own.

This extends #42770, which already makes the model runner model-agnostic, to every component.

### Feedback Period.

2-3 weeks.

title: [RFC]: Lossless 12-bit storage for BF16 dense weights to speed up memory-bound decode
author: JimmyToluene
body:
### Motivation.

At small batch, decode is bound by memory bandwidth, so every byte of weights read per step costs time. Many low-bit checkpoints still keep their dense layers in BF16, including attention projections, linear-attention projections, the LM head and MTP heads. 

NVFP4 MoE checkpoints are one example. In Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4, these BF16 tensors are the largest share of the bytes each decode step reads. Users who keep them in BF16 for accuracy have no lossless way to read fewer bytes.

The BF16 exponent carries much less information than its 8 bits: about 2.6 bits, the same observation DFloat11 makes. In this model's dense weights, the 15 most frequent exponents form one contiguous range and cover 99.9–99.98% of the values. 

That allows a **fixed-length** 12-bit format. Each value can be decoded on its own, so decoding fits inside the GEMV and needs no separate decompression pass.

### Proposed Change.

An opt-in storage for eligible unquantized linear layers and LM heads. Weights are converted at load time, and checkpoint is unchanged.

**Format** (per tensor):
- An 8-bit `sm` per value: the sign and the 7 mantissa bits, unchanged.
- A 4-bit index per value: the exponent minus a per-tensor base, in the range 0–14. Index 15 is an escape that decodes to +0, because padded rows are all zeros.
- Values whose exponent falls outside the 15-wide window (0.02–0.11% here) are stored row-wise as CSR exceptions and added back exactly.
- The result is 12 bits per value, 75% of BF16.
- Every tensor is verified bit-exact against the original at conversion.
- A tensor stays in BF16 if any 32-row block holds more than 2048 exceptions. This keeps the exception path from turning serial.

**Kernels**:
- **Decode, M ≤ 16**: a Triton GEMV decodes each tile to BF16 in registers and runs `tl.dot`. Exceptions are added in fp32 before the single final rounding, and there is no intermediate BF16 matrix. When a shape gives too few row blocks, the GEMV splits along K.
- **Prefill, M > 16**: row chunks are decoded into a shared 84 MB BF16 scratch buffer and multiplied with cuBLAS. The result is bit-identical to cuBLAS on the original weights.
- **Eligibility**: at least 15M elements, and K a multiple of 256. Small or short-K matrices were slower than the existing kernels, so they are left unchanged.

**Integration (open question, see below)**: in our prototype, a `LinearMethodBase` wrapper replaces `UnquantizedLinearMethod` on eligible modules after load, and a matching method replaces it on `ParallelLMHead`. It is enabled by an environment variable and covers one model family (Qwen4Exp, including its MTP drafter). The prototype is about 470 lines, plus 16 GPU tests.

**Results**: one DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121, 273 GB/s), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4, MTP k=3, single stream. 100 BF16 tensors were converted (6.95 GB to 5.23 GB, 0.038% exceptions); 2 tensors stayed in BF16 under the exception guard.

| GEMV, M=4 | Existing path | 12-bit |
|---|---|---|
| linear-attention in_proj 16384×2560 | 334 µs | 269 µs (1.24×) |
| LM head 248320×2560 | 5.14 ms | 4.06 ms (1.27×) |
| out_proj 2560×6144 | 130 µs | 104 µs (1.24×) |
| attention qkv 13952×2560 | 285 µs | 231 µs (1.23×) |

| End to end | Before | 12-bit |
|---|---|---|
| Decode steps/s | 14.8–15.0 | 16.5–16.7 (+11%) |
| Prose, T=0, tok/s | 32.9 | 37.1–38.1 |
| Code, T=0, tok/s | 48.5 | 53.5–54.8 |
| 19K-token cold prefill TTFT | 7.29–7.69 s | 7.58 / 7.73 s |
| Teacher-forced \|Δlogprob\| vs the BF16 server (mean / p99) | 0.0337 / 0.37 (two BF16 runs) | 0.0336 / 0.38 |

The stored weights are bit-exact. The decode GEMV results differ from the BF16 path only in summation order: they are within about 1 BF16 ulp of an fp32 reference, as with any change of GEMV kernel.

**What did not work**: our first version encoded zeros as exceptions. The 12 zero padding rows of one fused matrix then put 122,880 exceptions into a single row block, and decode ran about 20× slower. The +0 escape, vectorized exception handling, the per-block guard and the size filter came out of that.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@mgoin @gau-nernst @stecasta

### Any Other Things.

**Related work and how this differs**:
- [DFloat11](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11651) (NeurIPS 2025) entropy-codes the exponent with variable-length codes, about 11 bits per value, and decompresses to BF16 on the GPU. It targets capacity: running models that would not fit otherwise.
- [ZipNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05239) targets storage and transfer.
- This proposal trades about one bit per value for a fixed-length layout that the GEMV can decode in registers. The aim is decode speed on bandwidth-bound hardware.
- #20003 asked for DFloat11 support and was closed for inactivity without discussion.

**Questions for maintainers**:
1. Is a lossless weight-storage option in scope for vLLM core?
2. If so, where should it live: a quantization method, a model-agnostic post-load transform, or a flag such as `--weight-storage`?
3. Should it also apply to the BF16 parts of mixed-precision checkpoints (FP8/NVFP4 models with BF16 dense layers)?
4. We have only measured GB10. Batch-1 decode on H100/H200 is also bandwidth-bound, but the gain there is unmeasured. Is anyone able to try it?

If there is interest, we would open a PR with the kernels, the conversion and the tests, generalized beyond Qwen4Exp.

**AI assistance**: this RFC and the prototype were developed with AI assistance (Claude); the measurements are from our own runs on one DGX Spark.

title: [RFC]: Attention Backend Test Suites
author: tjtanaa
body:
### Motivation.

Attention backends are where kernels, the metadata builder, the model runner, the KV-cache manager and the backend selector meet. Most backend bugs come from the contracts between those parts, not from inside a kernel:
- a declared feature that the kernel silently ignores;
- a batch order the builder does not expect;
- a KV dtype the selector accepts but the cache write rejects;
- a layout or CUDA graph mode that nobody exercises.

Today each backend's tests are written ad hoc. They mostly compare outputs on a few shapes, so a fallback kernel or a dropped feature still passes. Coverage also can't be compared from one backend to another, and reviewers have no shared bar for what a backend PR should prove.

Trying the standard on one backend showed the gap. ROCM_AITER_FA had no failing tests, yet a suite built to the standard found seven backend defects that tests did not catch:
- wrong results under model runner v2;
- logits soft cap, sinks and ALiBi dropped in prefill/extend;
- shuffle-layout configs that crash at the first decode;
- non-causal fp8 decode raising an error;
- a declared KV dtype that the cache write rejects;
- an unusable KV layout listed as supported;
- a capability flag that went stale after an env change.

It also found an AITER kernel addressing bug.

### Proposed Change.

Adopt a written test standard for attention backends, kept in two forms: a document for people, and an agent skill (`.agents/skills/attention-backend-testing/`) that authors and reviewers can follow. The full text is in the Google Doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/11AUaJvNDP2iRow112ej1Uc4zd8LMAnTCRZdGNSObJPo/edit?usp=sharing

What the standard requires:

1. **Every dispatch path is tested.** Each branch of `forward`, `build`, the capture and drafting builds and the KV-update hooks gets a test. The test asserts which kernel ran (via a kernel spy) and checks the output against a float32 reference. Every declared feature is run through every phase (prefill, extend, decode, spec decode, mixed), every head size and every KV dtype.
2. **Declarations are tested both ways.** What a backend declares must run, and what it doesn't declare must be rejected by the selector with a reason.
3. **Shapes come from real models.** Head sizes, GQA ratios, windows, sinks and per-rank shapes are taken from flagship-model HF configs, together with their deployed TP/DP/EP/PP/PCP/DCP layouts. Pre-merge runs a covering set; nightly runs the full product.
4. **The runtime is exercised through dummy-weight models.** Each model is cut to its smallest repeating layer block and run through `LLM` in every CUDA graph mode, with model runner v1/v2, async scheduling, fp8 KV and spec decode. Prompt logprobs are compared with a reference backend under identical settings, using a calibrated tolerance and a negative control.
5. **One layout and one set of CI steps for every backend.**
   - Layout: `tests/v1/attention/backends/<backend>/` (capabilities, metadata builder, dispatch, KV cache, correctness, CUDA graph, workspace) plus `tests/v1/e2e/attention/`.
   - CI: sharded Buildkite steps, perf configs whose results are compared with the merge base, and a review checklist.
6. **Land the suite first, then the fixes.** The suite PR registers every known defect as a strict xfail in `known_defects.py`. Each fix is its own small PR that deletes its registry entry, so the fix has to prove itself.

**An implementation has been attempted** on MI350X:

| Backend | PRs | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |

**Other open PRs that overlap the ROCM_AITER_FA fixes:**
- #63676 (model runner v2 batch order): #63542 is an equivalent fix to the same splitter, and #59098 fixes the same bug from the MRV2 sort side.
- #63677 (soft cap, sinks, ALiBi in prefill/extend): #60487 fixes the sink double count in chunked-context extend, one part of it.
- #63678 (shuffle-layout guards): #46847 (shuffled sliding-window decode) and #45144 (MTP under the shuffle layout) add support for some configs it refuses.

Whichever fix lands, its entry in the suite's `known_defects.py` is deleted with it, so the suite checks that fix.

The ROCM_AITER_FA PRs are open upstream. The other three suites are on the fork for now, and their upstream PRs will be linked here when they open.

**CI cost** (ROCM_AITER_FA, measured):
- About 1 GPU-hour per PR that touches the backend: around 15 minutes of wall time on 6 sharded MI355 jobs, with the engine runs dominating.

title: [RFC] M-gated HPC-Ops dual-BF16 router GEMM for fp32 MoE router weights on SM90
author: new-TonyWang
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**RFC: Add an M-gated HPC-Ops dual-BF16 router GEMM tier for fp32 MoE router weights on SM90**

#### Prior work

- #49277 (feature request, stale) and PR #49312 by @lengrongfu (opt-in HPC BF16xFP32 router GEMM, currently stalled). This RFC proposes the same kernel but a different dispatch design, driven by new kernel-level measurements; see "Relationship to PR #49312" below.
- Kernel: [`Tencent/hpc-ops`](https://github.com/Tencent/hpc-ops) `gemm_bf16xfp32` ([src/gemm/sm90/gemm.cu](https://github.com/Tencent/hpc-ops/blob/main/src/gemm/sm90/gemm.cu)), dual-BF16 decomposition of fp32 weights, SM90 GMMA warpgroup kernel with split-K.

#### Motivation

MoE models with fp32 router weights (MiniMax-M2/M2.5/M3, DeepSeek-V3, HunYuan-V3, ...) fall back to cuBLAS FP32 `F.linear` in `GateLinear` whenever the batch is too large for the specialized small-M kernels:

- Tier 2 `fp32_router_gemm`: 5 fixed (H, E) shapes, M ≤ 32
- Tier 3 `ll_fp32w_gemm` (cuteDSL): any shape, M ≤ 32
- Tier 4 `bf16x3` (exact): SM100 only

So on SM90 (H20/H100/H200), fp32-weight routers with M > 32 run on plain cuBLAS FP32. HPC-Ops' dual-BF16 kernel can close part of this gap — but only part of it, and the boundary matters.

#### New evidence: kernel-level benchmark (H100 + H200, hpc-ops @ main)

We benchmarked `gemm_bf16xfp32` (persistent `split_flag` workspace, fp32 output) vs cuBLAS FP32 (`F.linear`, TF32 off — the current fallback) on 6 router shapes × M ∈ [1, 4096], with correctness checked against both an exact same-activation fp32-weight reference and a full-fp64 reference. Full tables in the appendix.

**Correctness (vs exact fp32-weight, same bf16 activation):**

- Row-absmax-normalized max error: **2e-6 ~ 1.8e-5** across all cells.
- Top-8 expert selection agreement: **100% in 63/66 (shape, M) cells, worst 99.95%**.
- The ~1.5-2% top-8 divergence vs full-fp64 comes entirely from bf16 activation quantization, which the existing bf16-input tiers (`ll_fp32w_gemm`, bf16x3) share.

**Performance — the effective range is M ≥ ~1024, with a shape-dependent crossover:**

Crossover = smallest M where the HPC kernel beats cuBLAS FP32 (H200; H100 tracks it almost exactly):

| shape (K, N) | crossover M | speedup @M=1024 | @M=2048 | @M=4096 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (8192, 256) | ~512 | 2.03x | 2.65x | 3.03x |
| DeepSeek-V3 (7168, 256) | ~1024 | 1.82x | 2.02x | 2.80x |
| (5120, 256) | ~1024 | 1.65x | 2.44x | 2.70x |
| MiniMax-M2 (3072, 256) | ~1024 | 1.08x | 1.93x | 2.45x |
| MiniMax-M3 (6144, 128) | ~1024 | 1.16x | 1.68x | 1.93x |
| Qwen3-30B (2048, 128) | ~2048 | 0.73x | 1.10x | 1.90x |

Concretely:

- **M ≤ 512: always slower** on every shape (0.48x-0.96x vs cuBLAS FP32). Never dispatch to the HPC kernel here.
- **512 < M < 1024: only the largest-K shape wins** ((8192, 256) crosses at ~512).
- **M ≥ 1024: wins on all router shapes we tested** (1.08x-2.03x at M=1024, growing with M), except the smallest shape Qwen3-30B (2048, 128), which needs M ≥ 2048.
- **M ≥ 2048: universal win** (1.10x-2.65x), up to 3.03x at M=4096.

So a single conservative dispatch threshold of **M ≥ 2048 is never wrong** on H100/H200; per-shape thresholds of M ≥ 1024 for K ≥ 3072 recover most of the win region. On H20 the fp32:bf16 compute ratio is much worse, so the crossover should move left — H20 data pending.

Representative timings:

| shape (K, N) | M | cuBLAS fp32 (us) | hpc (us) | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V3 (7168, 256) | 32 | 18.3 | 25.8 | 0.71x |
| DeepSeek-V3 (7168, 256) | 512 | 54.4 | 56.8 | 0.96x |
| DeepSeek-V3 (7168, 256) | 2048 | 161.9 | 80.2 | 2.02x |
| DeepSeek-V3 (7168, 256) | 4096 | 302.6 | 108.2 | 2.80x |
| (8192, 256) | 4096 | 356.5 | 117.7 | 3.03x |
| Qwen3-30B (2048, 128) | 512 | 16.4 | 34.1 | 0.48x |

Two structural reasons for the small-M loss:

1. Small-M router GEMM is memory-bound (time ≈ weight bytes / bandwidth), and the dual-BF16 split reads exactly as many bytes as the fp32 original (2 × 2B). It only saves tensor-core compute, which is not the bottleneck at small M.
2. Fixed per-call overheads: the upstream entry point allocates a `[split_k, m, n]` fp32 scratch per call, and the split_k=8 path adds a spin-wait reduction pass — a flat ~26us floor at M ≤ 64 vs cuBLAS FP32's 13-20us.

#### Proposed change

Add a new tier to `GateLinear.forward`, checked after the exact bf16x3 tier and before cuBLAS/F.linear:

1. **Static eligibility** (`allow_hpc_router_gemm`): unquantized fp32 weight, no bias, bf16 activation, `out_dtype == fp32`, CUDA SM90, `has_hpc()`, `N % 64 == 0`, and **not** batch-invariant mode. Off by default behind a kernel-config flag (e.g. `kernel_config.enable_hpc_router_gemm`).
2. **Runtime M-gating inside a custom op**: dispatch on `x.shape[0] >= threshold`, where the threshold comes from the measured per-shape crossover (M ≥ 1024 for K ≥ 3072 shapes, M ≥ 2048 otherwise; a single conservative 2048 works everywhere on H100/H200 — see the crossover table above). Because vLLM drops Dynamo guards on `num_tokens`, this branch must live in a `direct_register_custom_op`-registered op with a fake impl — the same pattern as the existing `fp32_router_gemm_dispatch` and `rocm_bf16x3_router_gemm_dispatch`.
3. **Weight pre-split in `process_weights_after_loading`** (mirroring the ROCm bf16x3 `_GateLinearMethod` pattern): build `w_high`/`w_low` once as non-persistent buffers, plus a per-layer split-flag workspace. This also fixes the buffer-identity concern across weight reloads: PWAL re-runs on reload, so stale splits cannot survive, and CUDA-graph-captured addresses stay stable because the buffers are never reallocated in `forward`.
4. **SM100 keeps preferring the exact bf16x3 tier** — the HPC kernel is non-exact and SM90-only upstream, so it must not preempt the exact path.
5. On shapes already claimed by Tier 2 (`fp32_router_gemm`), extend that dispatch op's M > 32 fallback to the HPC path instead of `F.linear` (or leave as-is in v1; open to maintainer preference).

#### Relationship to PR #49312

PR #49312 integrates the same kernel but dispatches unconditionally when statically eligible. Reviewers observed an e2e throughput regression on a decode-heavy workload (+11.39% reported by the author turned out to be a regression on re-measurement) and asked for full benchmark logs and `lm_eval` accuracy. Our kernel-level data explains the regression directly: always-on dispatch routes small-M decode batches to a kernel that is ~0.5-0.7x the speed of cuBLAS FP32 there. The M-gated design in this RFC is specifically intended to resolve that objection. We also plan to run `lm_eval` on a fp32-router model (MiniMax-M2 or DeepSeek-V3) comparing gate-on vs gate-off as part of the PR evidence. Happy to either revive #49312 with these changes in cooperation with @lengrongfu, or carry a fresh PR — whichever the maintainers prefer.

#### Feedback period

Two weeks.

#### CC list

@lengrongfu @yewentao256

#### Any other things

- H20 is the kernel's primary target upstream and its fp32:bf16 compute ratio is much worse than H100/H200, so the M-crossover should move left there. We will add H20 measurements before proposing a default threshold.
- HPC-Ops is tuned for H20 upstream. Our H100/H200 numbers show the current tuning leaves performance on the table on these parts (e.g. the ~26us small-M floor and per-call scratch allocation). We will keep analyzing the kernel to see whether H100/H200-specific tuning (tile/split-K configs, persistent workspace, SM count utilization) can move the crossover down and lift the large-M speedup further.
- Upstream constraints to encode in the eligibility check: bf16 activation only, N % 64 == 0, SM90 (SM100 untested upstream), contiguous inputs.
- AI assistance was used for benchmarking and drafting; all numbers are from actual H100/H200 runs.

### Alternatives

- Keep the status quo: SM90 fp32-weight routers with M > 32 stay on cuBLAS FP32.
- PR #61903 (cuteDSL bf16x3 on Hopper) would cover the same niche with exact numerics if it lands and performs; the HPC kernel would then only matter where bf16x3-Hopper is slower or for the H20 card class. Worth benchmarking both before deciding.

### Appendix: benchmark tables

Columns: `fp32_us` = cuBLAS FP32 (TF32 off); `bf16_us` = single-pass cuBLAS BF16 (lower-bound reference); `hpc_us` = `gemm_bf16xfp32` with persistent workspace; `vs_fp32` = speedup vs cuBLAS FP32; `wrel` = row-absmax-normalized max error vs exact fp32-weight/same-activation reference; `topk8_w` = top-8 agreement with that reference; `topk8_fp64` = top-8 agreement vs full-fp64 (gap is bf16 activation quantization).
