title: [RFC]: Tiered MoE Expert Offload with Lookahead Expert Scheduling (LES) for single-GPU Intel XPU (dGPU: VRAM ↔ Host RAM, iGPU: Memory ↔ SSD)
author: wyc55069407
body:
## Motivation.

### Summary

We propose opt-in, isolated MoE expert offload for **one Intel GPU**. The design is the one we built and measured in our POC prototype on Intel GPUs. It has two hardware variants:

| Variant | Hardware | Tiers |
|---|---|---|
| **dGPU** | Arc Pro B-series, e.g. B70 32 GB | **2 tiers:** VRAM ↔ pinned host RAM (host RAM must hold every expert not in VRAM; decode never reads the SSD) |
| **iGPU** | Panther Lake, 32 GB unified memory | **2 tiers:** GPU-visible system memory ↔ local NVMe SSD |

**Building blocks**
- **One global expert pool shared by all MoE layers.** Hot experts stay resident. Each slot holds one whole expert.
- **A per-expert pointer table.** The MoE kernel reads every expert wherever it currently lives: a VRAM slot, a pinned host slot read in place over PCIe, or a unified-memory slot on the iGPU.
- **Frequency-aware residency.** LFRU eviction and asynchronous promotion. Decode is warm-started from prefill routing.
- **Lookahead Expert Scheduling (LES).** OpenBMB/ModelBest's scheduling idea for MiniCPM-V 4.7. While layer L computes, layer L+1's experts are predicted by applying layer L+1's router to layer L's hidden state, and then loaded ahead of need. This is the scheduling core of the design (see "Lookahead Expert Scheduling" below). We apply it with a per-platform budget that fits Intel GPUs.

Computation always follows the real router output, so the path is **lossless**.

**Decode and prefill use different strategies**

| Phase | Priority | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| **Decode (TPOT)** | **Primary goal.** Stay as close as possible to all-resident TPOT. | Pool hits are read in place. dGPU resolves expert locations on the device, with no host sync, inside a FULL XPU graph. iGPU fetches misses from SSD with a multi-threaded reader, plus a 1-expert-per-layer LES prefetch from SSD. |
| **Prefill (TTFT), with chunked prefill** | **Secondary goal.** Bound the TTFT penalty. | Stream a full per-layer expert image into a double-buffered arena, one layer ahead, overlapped with the previous layer's compute. Prefill never evicts decode residency. |

**Scope** (deliberately narrow)
- single GPU;
- `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` and `MiniCPM-V-4.7-35B-A3B` (same `qwen3_5` MoE backbone: 40 layers, 256 experts, top-8);
- **INT4 W4A16** and **FP8** formats, limited to those the XPU MoE path already supports;
- `max_num_seqs ≤ 8`;
- **enabled on XPU only.** Other platforms get a startup error and no behaviour change (see §1, "Platform scope and isolation policy");
- default-off. When disabled, the existing path is unchanged.

### Why: offload decides whether the model runs on client GPUs

Each routed expert has 3 × 2048 × 512 = 3.1 M parameters. There are 40 × 256 of them.

| Weights | Per expert | All routed experts | Whole model |
|---|---|---|---|
| INT4 W4A16, group 128 | ~1.55 MiB | ~15.5 GiB | ~19 GB |
| FP8 | ~3.0 MiB | ~30 GiB | ~35 GB |

| Device | INT4 | FP8 |
|---|---|---|
| Arc Pro B70, 32 GB | Fits; offload frees VRAM for KV, context and concurrency | **Does not fit**: offload decides whether it runs |
| 16–24 GB dGPU | **Does not fit / tight** | Does not fit |
| Panther Lake laptop, 32 GB shared with the OS | **Tight** once OS and KV are counted | Does not fit |

We position this as **capacity extension for client, workstation and edge single-GPU deployments at low concurrency (≤ 8)**. It is not a serving-throughput feature, which matches the position agreed in the #38256 discussion.

### Why expert residency works here (and when it does not)

**When residency does not help.** Expert caching cannot help when the resident set is a small fraction of all experts and routing is close to uniform. The hit rate then roughly equals the resident fraction. Community reports in the #37190 discussion (large multi-GPU MoE models, a few GiB of cache) are in that regime.

**Our regime is different.** It rests on **capacity**, not routing skew:
- The resident pool holds most experts: 60% on the iGPU, and VRAM + host covering 100% on the dGPU.
- Decode also has strong token-to-token reuse of experts.

Measured hit rates:

| Model / platform | Resident fraction | Measured hit rate (decode) | Uniform-routing expectation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B**, Panther Lake iGPU, 4-bit experts, LRU | 60% of experts | **97.5%** (expert miss 2.48%) | ~60% | Our POC; MTP k=2, 1024 output tokens |
| ″ LFRU | 60% | **97.5%** (miss 2.47%) | ~60% | ″ |
| ″ LFRU, 5-turn chat, fixed 2100 MHz | 60% | **96.8%** (weighted miss 3.16%); 97.0% with 1-expert LES prefetch | ~60% | ″ |
| ″ LRU | 80% | **99.35%** (miss 0.65%) | ~80% | ″ |
| **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B**, Arc Pro B70 (60% in VRAM, rest in host RAM) | 60% VRAM | VRAM hit **90% → 98% → 99.9%** over requests 1–3 with prefill-heat seeding (72% → 84% → 89% without) | ~60% | Our POC |
| **MiniCPM-V-4.7-35B-A3B**, phones/tablets (flash), LES | per-layer windows | LES prepares **> 80% of the required experts in advance** in most scenarios | — | OpenBMB/ModelBest MiniCPM-V 4.7 release |

**Notes on the data**
- "Expert miss" counts misses per routed (token, expert) lookup. Per MoE-layer call (any miss in the layer), the rate is 14.7% at a 60% pool and 4.0% at an 80% pool.
- On the iGPU the remaining cost is dominated by the fixed per-layer path (readback plus lock), not by misses. Going from a 60% to an 80% pool cut misses about 4× but barely moved TPS (§17).
- We will publish the same statistics in-tree for both models:
  - per-layer routing entropy,
  - token-to-token expert reuse,
  - hit rate vs pool size, for text-only and image+text prompts.

### Prior art in vLLM

| PR / Issue | What it does | Gap this RFC addresses |
|---|---|---|
| #34535 `--cpu-offload-params` (merged) | Static UVA offload by parameter name | Every token reads offloaded experts over PCIe. No residency, no SSD tier. |
| #29941 prefetch offloader (merged) | Whole-layer async prefetch on a CUDA side stream | Layer granularity only. |
| #62054 (merged 10-22), #62060 (open) | Host-resident experts read once per step; large prefill steps staged into VRAM | No device-side residency. We share the "stage for prefill" idea. |
| #38256 / #37190 GPU expert cache + LFRU (open) | Per-layer slot cache, sync H2D, torch.compile split graphs only | Review concerns were CUDA graphs, invasiveness and bs=1 positioning. No disk tier. Addressed in §15. |
| #56177 shared expert pool (open) | Device planner, pool shared across layers | CUDA/NVFP4 only. No disk tier, no XPU. Same pool-across-layers direction as ours. |

**Relation to the existing offloaders.** This is **not a parallel offload stack**.
- It is a new **expert-granularity backend of the existing `OffloadConfig` / offloader framework**: `--offload-backend expert`, next to `uva` and `prefetch`.
- It reuses existing pieces:
  - UVA host views (`get_accelerator_view_from_cpu_tensor`, #34535) for the pinned host tier;
  - the side-stream / event / static-buffer pattern of the prefetch offloader (#29941) for staging;
  - the "stage host experts for large prefill steps" idea of #62060.
- It adds what those cannot express:
  - per-expert residency driven by routing;
  - a device-side location table that keeps decode inside FULL graphs;
  - an SSD tier for unified-memory iGPUs.

**Building on community results from #38256 / #37190.** We adopt and credit these:
- **Use a contract that keeps quantization scales aligned with ids.** #37190 found that remapping `topk_ids` alone leaves FP8 scales indexed by global id, so output is wrong from the first token. The fix moved to the `expert_map` contract (yasinyaman, in #37190). Our pointer table carries a per-expert scale pointer for the same reason.
- **Expect the union of active experts to grow fast with concurrency.** From C = 1 to C = 32, unique experts grew 15.3× while aggregate throughput grew 4.2× (CRPONCELET, in #38256). This is why we cap concurrency at 8 and position the feature as capacity extension.
- **Capacity and placement matter more than a tiny per-token cache.** On GB300, the hottest 73% of experts took 98.7% of selections. Frequency-based static placement gave +73% at C1, while a cache of only 3× top_k reached an oracle hit rate of just 0.68 (jmeadlock, in #38256). Our design follows that: a large resident pool (60–100% of experts), warm-started from routing frequency.
- **Zero-copy reads from host memory beat slot copies where the link allows it.** On unified memory, reading host memory directly was 4.3× faster than copying into slots at C = 8 (yasinyaman, in #37190). This matches our in-place host reads (dGPU) and shared-USM pool (iGPU).

### Lookahead Expert Scheduling (LES): the idea this RFC builds on

LES was published by OpenBMB/ModelBest with the MiniCPM-V 4.7 on-device release, in `llama.cpp-omni`. It ran a 35B-A3B MoE model from flash storage on phones and tablets. Its principles:

1. **Predict without training.** Layer L+1's router is applied to layer L's post-attention hidden state, and its top-k gives layer L+1's likely experts. This costs one small GEMV and needs no extra model or calibration.
2. **Load ahead, overlapped with compute.** Predicted experts that are not resident are fetched while layer L, and then layer L+1's attention, are computing.
3. **Stay lossless.** Computation always uses the real router output. A wrong prediction costs bandwidth, never accuracy. A real miss is still loaded on demand.
4. **Never block the critical path on prefetch.** Do not wait for in-flight prefetches, and drop new prefetch work while the loader is busy.
5. **Decode only.** Prefill touches nearly every expert per layer, so it streams instead of predicting.

LES itself targets Apple unified memory and flash. The model there has a long per-layer time, so a deep prefetch window (8 experts per layer) fits.

**This RFC carries the LES principles to Intel GPUs inside vLLM.** The prefetch budget is set by measurement on our POC:
- **Panther Lake iGPU:** per-layer decode time is about 0.8 ms and one SSD read is 0.5–0.8 ms, so we prefetch **1 expert per layer**. That is worth about 5 points of decode throughput (§17).
- **B70 dGPU:** host-tier experts are read in place over PCIe, so there is no SSD latency to hide. On B70 our POC measured prefetch at about −1% for AR decode (warm and cold); it only helped the cold first request with MTP (+3.7–4.1% at 8K, +0.5% at 32K), and speculative decoding is out of scope here. **This RFC does no prefetch on dGPU**, which keeps the dGPU graph path plain: FULL XPU graph for decode, no breakable graph.

Around LES, we add tiering, a global expert pool and device-side residency. These were validated on Intel GPUs in our POC (§5–§7).

### Key design principle

> **Offload is a weight provider behind `RoutedExperts`, not a new MoE algorithm.**
> The fused-MoE math is unchanged. The kernel only learns *where* each expert's weights are.

---

## Proposed Change.

### 1. Scope

**Supported**

| Area | Supported |
|---|---|
| Platform | XPU, 1 device: Xe2 dGPU (B-series), Xe3 iGPU (Panther Lake) |
| Models | `Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM` backbone: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and MiniCPM-V-4.7-35B-A3B, decoder MoE only |
| Weights | Only formats the XPU MoE path already supports²: **INT4 W4A16** (symmetric group-wise: GPTQ sym, AutoRound, compressed-tensors W4A16 sym), **online FP8** (bf16 checkpoint + `--quantization fp8_per_tensor` / `fp8_per_block`)¹, and **serialized block-FP8** (128×128) |
| Concurrency | `max_num_seqs ≤ 8` |

**Rejected at startup with a clear error**
- any non-XPU platform (`Platform.supports_expert_offload()` is `False`);
- TP, PP, DP or EP greater than 1;
- any model outside the allow-list;
- any format the XPU MoE path does not already support;
- `max_num_seqs` above 8;
- on dGPU: VRAM pool + host-RAM cap smaller than all experts (the error states the required host RAM);
- speculative decoding, EPLB, LoRA on experts, online weight reload.

¹ Recent vLLM main rejects plain `--quantization fp8` on a bf16 checkpoint.
² This RFC adds no quantization formats. Asymmetric INT4, AWQ zero points and GPTQ `desc_act` / `g_idx` are out of scope.

**Non-goals**
- no CPU computation of experts;
- no lossy expert substitution;
- no vision-encoder offload (vision tower, projector, shared expert and dense layers stay resident);
- no KV offload;
- no scheduler or attention changes;
- no silent downgrade;
- no remote storage;
- no writes back to disk;
- no dGPU configuration where host RAM cannot hold the non-resident experts (refused at startup, no SSD fallback on dGPU in v1);
- no enablement on CUDA, ROCm, CPU or other platforms in this RFC.

#### Platform scope and isolation policy

**Enabled on XPU only; every other platform is guaranteed no regression.** This follows the pattern vLLM already uses for platform-specific features (ROCm AITER, the XPU MoE and attention backends).

**How the gate is expressed (no `is_xpu()` in shared code)**
- A new platform capability method, `Platform.supports_expert_offload() -> bool`, defaults to `False` in `vllm/platforms/interface.py`. `XPUPlatform` returns `True`.
- `OffloadConfig` validation checks it once. On any other platform, `--offload-backend expert` fails at startup with `expert offload is only supported on XPU`. There is no silent fallback.
- All other platform-specific behaviour (USM allocation, copy-engine streams, the SYCL topology query) sits behind `xpu_ops.py` and the XPU platform class. The generic modules (pool bookkeeping, LFRU, IO pool, predictor) have no platform branches.
- The new kernel variant lives only in `vllm-xpu-kernels`. No CUDA or ROCm kernel is touched.

**Every touch point in shared vLLM code**

| File | Change | Est. LOC | When the feature is off |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vllm/platforms/interface.py` | `supports_expert_offload()` returning `False` | ~5 | Never called |
| `vllm/platforms/xpu.py` | Returns `True`; topology query | ~15 | Never called |
| `vllm/config/offload.py` | `expert` backend literal and `ExpertOffloadConfig` sub-config, included in `compute_hash` | ~50 | Default value; hash unchanged for existing configs |
| `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py` | `--offload-expert-*` flags | ~30 | Defaults only |
| `vllm/model_executor/offloader/base.py` (`create_offloader`) | Lazily import and construct the expert backend | ~10 | Branch not taken; the new package is never imported |
| Fused-MoE layer construction | Select `OffloadedRoutedExperts` through the existing `routed_experts_cls` seam | ~10 | Same class and the same `forward` as today |
| `vllm/config/vllm.py` | iGPU mode: auto-enable breakable graphs (`VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH`), same pattern as the per-architecture auto-enable; dGPU mode: `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`. User can override both | ~10 | Unchanged |
| `XPUExperts` / `XpuFusedMoe` (PR 0) | Forward `expert_map`; refresh weight references | ~30 | XPU-only file; bit-identical output for existing XPU models |

Everything else is new files: `vllm/model_executor/offloader/expert/` and the tests.

**No-regression guarantees we will demonstrate in the PRs**
- Default off. When off, the new package is not imported and the fused-MoE layer object graph is identical to today's.
- Existing `vllm-xpu-kernels` ops and binaries are bit-identical; the variant has a new op name.
- No change to CUDA/ROCm kernels, to the scheduler, to attention, or to the default compilation config.
- No new dependencies. The bookkeeping unit tests are device-free Python. Kernel and end-to-end tests run in the existing XPU CI. The CUDA/ROCm CI needs no new jobs.
- A test asserts that a non-XPU platform rejects `--offload-backend expert`.

**Other platforms later.** The interfaces are platform-neutral: the pointer-table kernel contract, the `RoutedExperts` subclass and the offloader backend. A platform opts in by implementing the capability method and a pointer-table MoE kernel. That is explicitly out of scope here; CUDA already has #34535, #29941 and #62060.

### 2. Architecture

```
 Global expert pool (all layers)          Pointer table  table[L][E] → {w13, w2, scales…}   (device memory)
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ dGPU: VRAM slots + pinned host slots │◄┤ entry points at: VRAM slot | pinned host slot │
 │ iGPU: shared-USM slots               │◄┤ (dGPU) or unified-memory slot (iGPU)          │
 └──────────────────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 iGPU only: NVMe expert store (canonical copy, per-expert kernel-layout records)

 decode, layer L:  router_L → top-k ids ─► resolve (hits++, pointers)  ─► XPU fused-MoE(ids, table[L])
                         └─ iGPU only: gate_{L+1}·h_L → top-1 prediction ─► next-layer SSD prefetch (IO pool)
 prefill, layer L: arena[L%2] = full layer image (assembled one layer ahead) ─► unchanged grouped GEMM
```

**New package `vllm/model_executor/offloader/expert/`**

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `manager.py` | `ExpertOffloadManager`. Owns the global pool, the tiers, the pointer table, LFRU/promotion and the prefill arena. One per process. |
| `routed_experts.py` | `OffloadedRoutedExperts(RoutedExperts)`. The layer allocates no device expert weights. A host-row weight loader feeds the manager. `forward_modular` calls the pointer-table kernel. Selected via the existing `routed_experts_cls` seam, like `SubstitutedRoutedExperts`. |
| `store.py` | `HostExpertPool` (dGPU pinned USM, lazy chunks) and `DiskExpertStore` (iGPU record files) |
| `io_pool.py` | Persistent multi-threaded SSD reader, iGPU (§7) |
| `prefill_arena.py` | Double-buffered per-layer image and its assembly (§9) |
| `prefetch.py` | Next-layer predictor and SSD prefetch, iGPU (§8) |
| `xpu_ops.py` | The only module with XPU-specific calls: fixed-shape resolve / table-apply / gather custom ops (`mutates_args` declared), the MoE eager-break op (`@eager_break_during_capture`), USM allocation, copy-engine stream |

### 3. Platform modes: iGPU 2-tier (memory ↔ SSD) vs dGPU 2-tier (VRAM ↔ host RAM)

Storage media differ between the two platforms, so the miss path, the LES prefetch path and the prefill path differ too. The mode is chosen once at startup. Each platform has **exactly one mode**; there is no capacity-dependent sub-mode.

**Detection**
- The SYCL device query `sycl::info::device::host_unified_memory` (the same query our POC uses), exposed through `XPUPlatform`.
  - `true` → **iGPU mode** (memory ↔ SSD).
  - `false` → **dGPU mode** (VRAM ↔ host RAM).
  - Override: `--offload-expert-topology {auto,igpu-ssd,dgpu-host}`.
- **dGPU requires full coverage:** VRAM pool + host-tier cap ≥ all experts. Otherwise startup fails and the error states the host RAM needed. The requirement is modest: at the default 60% VRAM pool, the host tier holds ~6 GiB of INT4 or ~12 GiB of FP8 experts.
- The resolved mode is printed in the startup line.

**Why there is no dGPU SSD fallback.** Our POC had one, for hosts too small to cover all experts. It is left out of v1 to keep the design small:
- it needs a third tier, the expert store and the IO pool on dGPU, plus `O_DIRECT` and bounce buffers (buffered reads let the kernel reclaim the pinned host tier: 0.3 tok/s in the POC);
- it needs host-side miss detection, so decode could not stay in one FULL XPU graph and would need the breakable graph again;
- the B70 results in this RFC (−15% TPS, +7% TTFT, lossless) were measured with VRAM + host RAM covering every expert, with no SSD involved;
- its target is rare: a workstation dGPU without the ~6 GiB (INT4) or ~12 GiB (FP8) of free host RAM the exclusive host tier needs at the default 60% VRAM pool.

If host RAM is short, startup fails and states the required size. A dGPU SSD tier is listed under "Later".

**Behaviour by storage medium**

| | **iGPU: memory ↔ SSD** | **dGPU: VRAM ↔ host RAM** |
|---|---|---|
| Resident pool | Global pool in **shared USM** (system DRAM; CPU-writable, GPU-readable) | Global pool in **VRAM** |
| Second tier | **SSD expert store**: every non-resident expert, read **during decode** | **Pinned host pool**, exclusive with the VRAM pool, grown lazily. Loaded from the checkpoint at startup, **no SSD at runtime** |
| Where a decode miss lives | SSD | Pinned host memory |
| Who detects misses | Host (one top-k readback per MoE layer) | **Device** resolve kernel, no host sync |
| Miss read path | IO pool, buffered read **directly into the shared-USM slot** | **No copy**: the kernel reads the host slot in place over PCIe |
| Decode waits for misses | Yes, per layer | No |
| Hot experts reach the pool by | LFRU replacement on miss | **Async promotion** from device hit counters (every 4 steps, ≤ 32) |
| **LES prefetch** | **SSD → 40-slot reserve** in shared USM, by the IO pool threads, issued inside the MoE eager break | **None** (host experts are already read in place) |
| LES default / width | **On, P = 1**, issued after the layer's own fetch | — |
| Prefill source for the full-layer image | **Whole layer read from SSD** by the IO pool, one layer ahead | VRAM D2D + up to 128 H2D staged on the **copy engine** + in-place host reads |
| Page cache | Buffered (free DRAM acts as an implicit tier) | n/a |
| Graph mode (decode) | **Breakable XPU graph**: MoE is an eager break, the rest of the layer is captured | **FULL XPU graph** |
| Graph mode (prefill / mixed) | Breakable XPU graph, MoE eager break | **Eager** (`FULL_DECODE_ONLY`); the engine thread issues copy-engine staging directly |
| New pieces needed | Expert store, IO pool | Host pool, promotion |

### 4. Global pool and the MoE kernel

**Pool layout**
- One pool of `S` slots shared by all 40 MoE layers. Each slot holds one whole expert (`w13`, `w2`, scales).
- All MoE layers of the target models have identical expert shapes and formats, so slots are uniform and any slot can hold any (layer, expert).
- Default size: `--offload-expert-gpu-fraction` = 0.6 of all experts, same as the POC.
- Hot layers naturally take more slots than cold layers. There is no per-layer quota.

**Constraint**
- At ≤ 8 sequences × top-8, a decode step touches at most 64 experts per layer, all of which must be addressable in the same step.
- The pool capacity is checked against this at startup.

**Kernel contract: a per-expert pointer table (`vllm-xpu-kernels`)**
- The xe_2 grouped GEMM addresses expert *e* as `base + e × stride`, inside a persistent work-stealing loop.
- We add a **new op variant** that takes `expert_ptr_table[E, P]`: int64, in device memory, the slice for the current layer, indexed by **logical** expert id.
  - `P` pointers per expert cover the weights, scales and bias planes.
  - The pointer arithmetic is one block outside the K-loop, so the variant replaces it with a table load: about 25 lines of device code, ~300–450 LOC including bindings and tests.
  - The variant has a new op name and a template flag that defaults off. **Existing kernels and binaries are bit-identical.**
- **Routing (`remap_hidden_states`, `rows_per_expert[256]`) is unchanged.**
  - There is no `topk_ids` rewrite.
  - A residency change is a device-side write into the table, which is graph-safe.

**Why pointers rather than gathering experts into a contiguous tensor**
- In our POC, gathering the 8 active experts into contiguous scratch cost **2.1–3.2 ms per layer**, while the MoE compute it fed took **0.87 ms**. End to end that was 13–23% slower.
- Reading pooled experts in place through per-expert pointers was 1.39× faster in the kernel and bit-exact.

**Prefill does not use the variant.** It runs the existing grouped GEMM on a contiguous per-layer image (§9).

### 5. Tiers and residency

**dGPU: VRAM ↔ host RAM**
- **VRAM pool.**
  - The global pool.
  - Allocated during loading, so `gpu_memory_utilization` profiling counts it before the KV cache is sized. The prefill arena is counted the same way.
- **Pinned host tier.**
  - An **exclusive** second tier: each expert lives in exactly one of the VRAM pool or the host tier.
  - Filled during weight loading, after `process_weights_after_loading` (so online-FP8 experts are stored already quantized). There is no expert store on dGPU.
  - Grown **lazily** in 64-slot chunks, never as one up-front multi-GB pinned allocation.
  - Capped at `min(--offload-expert-host-gb, MemAvailable − OS reserve)` and at the driver's pinned limit. The cap sticks after the first allocation failure.
- **Full coverage is required:** every table entry points at either a VRAM slot or a pinned host slot. **Decode never reads the SSD.** If the cap cannot hold the non-resident experts, startup fails (§3).
  - Host-tier experts are read **in place over PCIe** by the kernel.

**iGPU: memory ↔ SSD**
- The pool lives in **shared USM** in system memory: CPU-writable and GPU-readable.
- The SSD expert store backs everything else. There is no separate host tier, since the "host" memory is the same DRAM.

**Eviction**
- LFRU, `score = freq / (age + 1)`, with **a single victim chosen on demand**.
- Slots touched in the current step, and slots pinned by a prefill in flight, are never evicted.
- In our POC, batch eviction from a stale snapshot raised the miss rate from 3.45% to ~5%.

**dGPU asynchronous promotion**
- Every N decode steps (default 4), device hit counters are read back. Up to M (default 32) hot host-tier experts are promoted over the coldest VRAM-pool experts.
- Promotion runs at step boundaries on the copy engine, using a three-point protocol:
  1. D2H of the victim;
  2. table → host copy, then H2D;
  3. table → VRAM.
- The table never points at bytes that are not yet present. Errors roll back and are counted.

**Warm start from prefill heat**
- Per-expert selection counts from the prompt are rescaled to a prior of about 64 decode tokens.
- They are added to frequency **without refreshing recency** (refreshing it caused about 250 extra swaps per request) and seed up to 4096 placements before the first decode step.
- In the POC, host-served decode lookups on dGPU fell from 28 / 16 / 11% (requests 1–3, no seeding) to **10 / 2 / 0.1%**.
- On the iGPU, the hottest experts per layer are fetched into the pool.

**Cross-request persistence.** Pool, table and heat live for the whole process.

### 6. Decode path (TPOT: the primary goal)

**dGPU.** Fully on the device, with no host sync.
1. Router → top-k ids.
2. **Resolve:** a tiny fixed-shape kernel counts hits per (layer, expert) for promotion. The table slice for layer L is passed to the kernel as is.
3. The pointer-table fused MoE reads VRAM experts locally and host experts over PCIe in place.
4. Promotion runs between steps, on the copy engine (§5).

There is no prefetch on dGPU (§8), so the whole decode step is one FULL XPU graph.

**iGPU**
1. Router → top-k ids → **one device→host readback per MoE layer.** An SSD miss has to be served by a host thread; on unified memory this readback is cheap.
2. **Claim, under the residency lock:**
   - a hit uses its slot;
   - a miss picks an LFRU victim, marks it `PENDING` and emits a read job;
   - jobs are de-duplicated per slot.
3. **Read, without the lock.** The IO pool (§7) reads every miss of the layer in parallel, **directly into its pool slot**, which is shared USM on the iGPU. Decode waits until the layer's misses have landed.
4. **Publish, under the lock.** `PENDING → READY` (or roll back), and the table entries are updated.
5. The pointer-table fused MoE runs.
6. Next-layer LES prefetch from SSD, issued **after** the layer's own fetch (§8).

Steps 1–6 run inside one eager-break op (§10). The attention and dense parts of the layer stay captured.

**On the iGPU the bottleneck is the fixed per-layer cost, not misses.**
- In the POC, raising the pool from 60% to 80% cut misses by about 4× but barely moved TPS.
- The fixed per-layer cost (readback plus lock) dominates. This is why claim/read/publish holds the lock only around bookkeeping.

### 7. Multi-threaded IO and the expert store (iGPU only)

The dGPU mode does not use either component.

**Persistent reader pool** (`--offload-expert-io-threads`, default 4, max 16)
- The calling thread executes job 0 itself, which saves one hand-off (~0.1 ms). Jobs 1..n fan out to the workers over a channel, and the caller waits for its batch.
- Each worker caches file handles for the lifetime of the store. Reopening per miss dominated miss latency.
- A caller that needs a slot another thread is still reading waits on a generation condition variable, then re-claims.
- Read failures are returned as errors and never panic a worker. If spawning the threads fails, a single-threaded path is used.

**Expert store**
- **Record files:** one per layer, `layer_NNN.experts`.
  - A 4 KiB header: magic, layer, number of experts, dtype and record length per projection, padded length, CRC32.
  - Then one record per expert, `[w13 | w2 | scales]`, **in the final kernel layout** (after online quantization and relayout), padded to 4 KiB, at offset `4096 + e × padded_len`.
  - One miss = one aligned read with **no conversion**. Records are always read whole; in our POC a split read was slower than one full read.
- **Manifest:** a format version plus a geometry/quant hash. Written **last**, so a crash during conversion triggers a rebuild, and any mismatch regenerates the store.
- **A separate, derived copy.** The store is a separate copy of the routed experts in kernel layout. The checkpoint is never modified.
  - Users never repack checkpoints by hand. For online FP8, the quantized bytes do not exist in any checkpoint.
  - Disk footprint is about one copy of all routed experts: ~15.5 GiB for INT4 W4A16 or ~30 GiB for FP8 (plus < 4 KiB of padding per record). This is in addition to the checkpoint.
  - Startup checks the free space and fails with the required size if it is short.
- **First-boot builder, streamed per layer.**
  - It runs inside weight loading, one MoE layer at a time: the expert weight loader collects a layer's expert rows from the checkpoint; when the layer is complete, the same

title: [RFC]: Define a graceful-draining contract for external Kubernetes controllers
author: raravind007
body:
### Motivation

Hi vLLM maintainers,

I'm developing a reference inference-aware drain plugin for NVIDIA NVSentinel, which detects GPU faults and coordinates Kubernetes node remediation.

References:
- NVSentinel proposal: https://github.com/NVIDIA/NVSentinel/issues/2124
- Reference implementation: https://github.com/raravind007/nvsentinel-vllm-drain-plugin

The NVSentinel maintainers have expressed interest in including this implementation as a reference plugin.

vLLM already provides native graceful-shutdown functionality:
- PR #34730 introduced `--shutdown-timeout`, allowing in-flight requests to finish during SIGTERM-driven shutdown.
- RFC #24885 explored broader shutdown semantics, including distributed serving and KV transfers.
- PR #43208 proposed adding graceful-shutdown guidance to vLLM's Kubernetes deployment documentation. It received an approving review but was subsequently closed unmerged, leaving the proposed guidance unpublished.
- llm-d documents a Kubernetes shutdown pattern combining `--shutdown-timeout`, `preStop`, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.

These are valuable capabilities. However, I'm looking for guidance on the supported contract between vLLM and external orchestration systems that need to coordinate draining before initiating termination.

For example, during GPU fault remediation, a controller may need to stop new request admissions, allow existing generations to finish, determine whether the serving instance is safe to terminate, and then initiate Kubernetes eviction.

The controller also needs bounded deadlines because hardware faults may make graceful completion impossible.

### Proposed Change

I'd like to propose clarifying and documenting a graceful-draining contract for external Kubernetes controllers, ideally using existing vLLM capabilities wherever possible.

The intended lifecycle is:
1. Stop admitting new inference requests.
2. Allow already admitted requests to complete.
3. Expose a reliable indication that the serving instance is quiescent.
4. Allow the external controller to initiate eviction.
5. Use native `--shutdown-timeout` as an additional safeguard during SIGTERM-driven termination.

This RFC is initially about defining and validating the operational contract, not necessarily introducing a new API.

#### Questions for maintainers

**1. Reliable quiescence detection**

Can `vllm:num_requests_running == 0` and `vllm:num_requests_waiting == 0` reliably indicate that all admitted inference requests have completed?

In particular, do these metrics cover streaming responses through final delivery to the HTTP client, or can the metrics reach zero while a response is still being transmitted?

Would another existing API or metric provide a stronger completion guarantee?

**2. Admission control before SIGTERM**

The reference plugin currently uses Kubernetes readiness gates to remove pods from normal Service routing.

However, readiness changes alone do not guarantee that new requests cannot arrive through existing connections or external gateways.

We also considered vLLM's `/pause` functionality, but it appears intended to suspend active generation rather than reject new requests while allowing existing generations to finish.

Is there an existing supported mechanism for this admission-control behavior before SIGTERM, or would it require additional API functionality?

**3. Interaction with native shutdown**

Would you recommend combining external pre-termination quiescence with a nonzero `--shutdown-timeout` as defense in depth?

Are there important race conditions or lifecycle interactions when a controller observes quiescence before initiating Kubernetes eviction?

**4. Distributed and disaggregated serving**

For tensor-parallel, pipeline-parallel, or disaggregated prefill/decode deployments, can an individual serving pod independently establish that it is safe to terminate?

Could outstanding KV transfers or worker activity require coordination beyond the API server's request metrics?

**5. Scope of the supported contract**

Would documenting the expected behavior of existing metrics, shutdown mechanisms, and request admission be sufficient?

Or would a dedicated drain/readiness API provide a more reliable integration point for external orchestration systems?

### Feedback Period

I'd suggest an initial feedback period of two weeks.

### Any Other Things

The current NVSentinel plugin:
- Uses a Kubernetes readiness gate to remove a pod from normal Service routing.
- Polls running and waiting request metrics over a confirmation window.
- Initiates eviction through the Kubernetes Eviction API, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets.
- Applies bounded deadlines and fault-severity-aware fallback behavior.

I'm planning to validate this approach against native vLLM graceful shutdown, including streaming workloads.

The goal is to avoid duplicating existing vLLM functionality while providing reliable integration guidance for Kubernetes-native systems such as NVSentinel.

I'd appreciate feedback on whether the proposed contract can be implemented entirely using existing interfaces, and whether there are known correctness gaps in the current approach.

Thanks!

title: [RFC / Performance] How LLM Agent Context Compaction Collapses Automatic Prefix Caching (APC)
author: yansu202511
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Many long-horizon LLM Agent frameworks perform context compaction (summarization) to prevent context window overflow. In our production runs (~81k context), we observed that compaction caused a severe prefill stall (TTFT stalled at 206.9s), collapsing vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) hit rate down to 10.1%.

Root Cause:
Agent frameworks often strip older archive checkpoints from the prompt to "keep the window lean". This drops an early message and shifts all subsequent tokens, causing APC prefix matching to fail right after the system prompt (token 8,886). 73k tokens had to undergo full re-prefill.

The Proposal & Benchmark:
By ensuring the compaction request's message prefix is token-identical to normal conversation turns, APC hit rate immediately recovered to 99.6%:
- Cache Hit Rate: 10.1% -> 99.6%
- Cached Tokens: 8,192 -> 144,165
- Re-prefilled Tokens: 72,986 -> 627 (116x reduction)
- TTFT: 206.9s -> 3.1s (66x faster)

We propose adding guidelines/warnings in vLLM docs regarding APC-friendly prompt construction for Agent builders.

### Alternatives

Explicit cache control breakpoints can help, but keeping the prefix token-identical in the request builder is the cleanest, zero-overhead solution.

### Additional context

Full methodology, de-identified logs, and 2-second model-free reproduction script:
https://github.com/yansu202511/cache-alignment-findings

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Context-length-bounded FULL decode CUDA graphs in Model Runner V2
author: eppaneamd
body:
### Motivation.

Model Runner V2 captures every FULL decode CUDA graph with attention metadata `max_seq_len = max_model_len`, so the graph is valid for any context it replays. Any host-side decision made from `max_seq_len` during capture is therefore made for the longest context and frozen into the graph.

Some models skip work when every context in a step is short, but cannot do so in FULL decode graphs:

- GLM-5-Next's sparse indexer: when all contexts fit `index_topk` (2048 on GLM-5.3-Flash), its top-k is every causal token, so the q projection, head-weight projection, q quantization, paged-MQA logits and top-k are dead work.
- DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1's indexers already skip this work in eager steps, but guard the shortcut with `not torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing()` (#52492), so FULL decode graphs never take it.

The rule from #52492 and #59709, no capture-time shortcut that a replay can invalidate, is right. What is missing is a FULL graph whose capture-time `max_seq_len` is smaller and still bounds every replay.

### Proposed Change.

1. **Declare.** A module sets `cudagraph_seq_len_bound: int | None`. The runner collects the distinct values below `max_model_len` from `model.modules()`.
2. **Capture.** Each FULL decode graph gets one copy per bound, captured with `max_seq_len = bound` in every backend's metadata.
3. **Dispatch.** `BatchExecutionDescriptor` gains `max_seq_len`, matched like `max_query_len`. A decode step whose contexts all fit a bound replays the copy (tightest first); any other step replays the default graph. The step's bound comes from the CPU arrays `prepare_inputs` already uses (no device read).
4. **Rule for modules.** Skip only work that `max_seq_len <= bound` makes dead, decided from the metadata the module receives, and only while a FULL graph is being captured.
   - Not in a PIECEWISE capture: that capture runs on the dummy batch's metadata.
   - Not in eager steps, including the warm-up run before each capture: the warm-up must compile and autotune everything its capture runs. Otherwise a cold start can compile or autotune inside the capture, which fails (seen in the reference implementation's first commit under breakable `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`).

Invariant: **the `max_seq_len` a FULL graph is captured with is an upper bound on every context of every batch it replays** (`max_model_len` for default graphs, the bound for copies). Host decisions made from it at capture hold for every replay.

Scope: off under PCP/DCP; opt-out `CompilationConfig.cudagraph_specialize_seq_len`. PIECEWISE-only deployments, mixed FULL graphs and micro-batched (DBO) graphs get no copies. Steps that cross the bound mid-request switch to the default graph.

#### Evidence

- Reference implementation: #63758 (mechanism + GLM-5-Next's indexer). GLM-5.3-Flash MXFP4, 2x MI355X, TP2, one image per request:
  - `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`: output throughput +2.32 % (SE 0.44 pp) at concurrency 16-64, +12.3 % at 4. Text rows that cross or exceed the bound are within noise. GSM8K unchanged. Cost: one extra graph per capture size and bound (graph memory 0.79 → 1.07 GiB per rank, KV cache −0.03 %).
  - Breakable `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`: +4.50 % (SE 1.92 pp) at concurrency 16-64.
- Second user, a follow-up PR stacked on the reference implementation: DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1 (V4.1-Flash gets bounds 512 and 1025 from compress ratios 1 and 2).
- Prior art: SGLang selects a dense or sparse DSA decode graph on `max_kv_len <= index_topk` (`python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/graph_variants.py`).

#### Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Why not |
|---|---|
| Kernels read a device-side bound and exit early (or graph conditional nodes) | The q-side GEMMs are library GEMMs with no such predicate; every kernel on every platform would need it. |
| Eager segment around the indexer inside FULL graphs | One graph break per sparse-attention layer (not measured). |
| `ForwardContext` flag set during bounded captures | Repeats what `max_seq_len` carries; every forward-context producer must leave it unset correctly. |
| Model-interface method or attention-builder attribute | One declaration per model class that re-derives per-layer facts; a shared builder would capture copies for models that skip nothing. |
| Serve with `max_model_len <= bound` | No code, but only for deployments capped at the bound. |

#### Open questions

1. **#62749** records FULL decode metadata builds keyed on batch shape, with `max_seq_len = max_model_len`. A step sent to a copy would match a build recorded for the default graph. Whichever lands second either adds `max_seq_len` to that key or keeps bounded steps on the eager build. Which is preferred?
2. **DP.** The bound is per rank, not in the DP sync: a copy has its default graph's token and request counts, which is all ranks agree on, and `max_seq_len`-dependent work is already rank-local in eager steps. A max-over-ranks row would make ranks switch together, at the cost of one long-context rank disabling the copies for all. Untested with DP > 1.
3. **Default on or opt-in.** Default on in the implementation, like `cudagraph_specialize_lora`.

### Feedback Period.

At least one week. The reference implementation stays a draft until then.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Not measured: NVIDIA, TP 1/4/8, DP > 1. Model Runner V1 graphs are unchanged. A search of open PRs found none that keys decode graphs on context length.

title: [RFC]: Pluggable pipeline-parallel transport, and a path to out-of-process (elastic) PP stages
author: yanyinglin
body:
### Motivation.

Pipeline parallelism in vLLM assumes a fixed group. All stages are ranks of one
`torch.distributed` world, they start together, and `send`/`recv` between them
never fail. Every stage also holds the KV of every request in flight. This fits a
single node or a static multi-node job. It does not fit two deployment shapes we
run in production-like settings:

1. **Stages as independent processes/pods.** Each stage is its own process with
   its own lifetime, and stage replicas join, leave or die while the service keeps
   running (spot/preemptible GPUs, rolling upgrades, scaling one stage without
   restarting the others). The neighbour a stage talks to becomes a routing
   decision, not a rank.
2. **Different transports between stages.** Lightweight point-to-point libraries such as
   Mooncake Transfer Engine, NIXL or UCX move the hidden states. They come with
   their own membership and retry logic, which a NCCL p2p group cannot provide.

More generally, PP traffic does not need NCCL. Between two stages it is
point-to-point, one direction per hop, and small per step (the hidden states
of the scheduled tokens plus residuals, typically a few hundred KB to a few MB
for decode). NCCL brings properties that PP does not use and that get in the
way of the two shapes above: a communicator whose membership is fixed at
creation, a collective bootstrap that all ranks must join, and failure
semantics where one dead peer poisons the communicator (abort and rebuild
the group). A lightweight point-to-point library is a better fit for this hop:
UCX (tag send/recv or one-sided RDMA, GPUDirect when available), NIXL,
Mooncake Transfer Engine, or plain TCP/ZeroMQ for small deployments. These
connect peers lazily, let a peer join or leave without touching the others,
and report a dead peer as an error on that endpoint. NCCL should stay the
default; the point is that it should not be the only option.

We built such a system (Connex, Apache-2.0) on a vLLM fork. It runs each PP stage
as an independent engine, uses a pluggable inter-stage communicator, and hands
requests over without client-visible errors when a downstream replica dies (it
recomputes the requests whose KV the new replica does not hold). We would like to
ship it as an out-of-tree plugin instead of a fork. While rebasing we found that
nearly all of the fork's diff is code that should stay out of tree. Only a few
seams are missing upstream.

RFC #50853 (Workstream B) already proposes making the PP state transport an
explicit, declarative module (`PPTransport`, `ForwardPayload`,
`DeferredResultPayload`). This RFC asks that the module be **replaceable by a
plugin**. It also proposes the small set of hooks that out-of-process stages need
on top of that.

### Proposed Change.

**Phase 1: replaceable PP group (small, no behaviour change).**
Add `ParallelConfig.pp_group_cls` / `--pp-group-cls`: the qualified name of a
`GroupCoordinator` subclass that `initialize_model_parallel` uses for the PP group
only. It is constructed with the same arguments. A plugin overrides
`isend_tensor_dict` / `irecv_tensor_dict` (and, for MRV2, the sampled-token
broadcast) to move inter-stage tensors over its own transport. The TP/DP/EP
groups and the rest of the engine stay unchanged. This works the same way as
`--worker-cls` / `--worker-extension-cls` and needs no new registry. A draft PR is
ready (about 30 lines + test + docs). If #50853 lands a `PPTransport` owner, the
same knob should select that class instead, and we are happy to follow that shape.

**Phase 2: out-of-process stages (needs discussion).** These are the hooks the
fork adds today. We list them so maintainers can say which ones belong upstream.

| Need | Today in the fork | Proposed upstream shape |
|---|---|---|
| A PP group whose size is not the `torch.distributed` world (each stage process has world size = TP size) | `ExternalPPGroupCoordinator` with `rank_in_group = stage_idx` | allowed by Phase 1 if `initialize_model_parallel` accepts a PP group from the plugin and does not derive PP from world ranks; `ModelConfig.get_layers_start_end_indices` should read the PP rank/size from the PP group (or a `pp_rank` override) instead of `parallel_config.rank` |
| Layer range per stage | `--pipeline-layer-range` | already possible with `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION`, once rank/size come from the PP group |
| Stage 0 schedules; stages 1.. run a receive-compute-send loop with no scheduler | custom `execute_external_pipeline_step` in the model runner and a loop in the worker | out of tree through `--worker-cls` plus a custom executor (`distributed_executor_backend=<class>`). One question: should a downstream worker be allowed to build attention metadata from a received step description (block ids, positions, seq lens) rather than from a `SchedulerOutput`? |
| KV held on a downstream stage, and recompute after failover | runtime patches to model runner + scheduler | (a) a scheduler-side way for a plugin to rewind a running request to `num_computed_tokens = 0` and drop its last sampled token (a "re-prefill" API, close to what preemption-by-recompute already does), and (b) a per-request KV query/release on workers. We think (b) belongs in the KV connector API (`KVConnectorBase_V1`), next to `get_finished` and `request_finished`. |
| Finished-request propagation to downstream stages | piggy-backed on the step dict | plugin-side, no upstream change |

Non-goals: no new transport implementation in tree. No change to the default
NCCL path or to CUDA-graph behaviour. No elastic membership logic in vLLM.

### Feedback Period.

2 weeks.

### CC List.

PP / MRV2 PP owners and the authors of #50853; KV connector owners for the
KV-held / re-prefill question.

### Any Other Things.

- Related: #50853 (MRV2 PP completion, Workstream B transport abstraction),
  #58329 (KV pipeline parallel), #27584 / #22799 (attention-FFN disaggregation,
  also stage-to-stage hidden-state transport), #20323 (Elastic EP, the
  stateless-group machinery in `vllm/distributed/stateless_coordinator.py`).
- Plugin code that would use these hooks (https://github.com/HeterInfra/connex): `connex/pp` (engine-neutral step
  protocol, routing, handover rules) and `connex/adapters/vllm`.
- Developed with AI coding assistance; all changes were reviewed and tested by the author.

title: [RFC] [DSV4.1] [Engram]: Share immutable host-backed Engram tables across independent instances
author: foraxe
body:
## Motivation: Engram host offload alone is not enough. 

* Engram host offload saves accelerator memory, but independently launched serving instances can still keep separate copies of the same large immutable tables.
* This is particularly expensive for prefill/decode deployments with different TP layouts. Sharing inside one instance's DP group does not eliminate these cross-instance copies.
* Additionally, when deployed with KVcache Pool (such as Mooncake), DRAM fragments will lead to engine OOM. 

We propose separating **table ownership and physical placement** from
**the instances that perform lookups**. A persistent owner publishes one table
generation. Independent workers attach the head ranges they need and run lookup
kernels against device-accessible mappings of that backing. Selected rows and
model activations remain local to each worker.

This proposal targets host-backed tables on supported direct-access domains.

## Proposed Change

### Two aspects
* engram sharing across workers.
* engram sharding to distribute the engram across nodes.

### Data path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[Immutable checkpoint] -->|load once| O[Persistent table owner]
    O --> H[Physical host table backing]
    O -. generation / metadata / mapping handles .-> P[Independent prefill workers]
    O -. generation / metadata / mapping handles .-> D[Independent decode workers]
    H -->|device loads via local mapping| PK[Prefill lookup + dequantization]
    H -->|device loads via local mapping| DK[Decode lookup + dequantization]
    P -. attach at startup .-> PK
    D -. attach at startup .-> DK
    PK --> PH[Selected rows in local HBM]
    DK --> DH[Selected rows in local HBM]
```

Handle exchange and attachment happen at startup. Once attached, this path
does not send IDs to an owner service or fetch rows through per-request RPC,
RDMA copy APIs, or full-table staging. Loads still move bytes through the
memory hierarchy and consume interconnect bandwidth. Existing local row
buffers, model collectives, prefetch scheduling and P/D KV transfer remain.

## Proposed common semantics

1. **Immutable published generation.** Identify the checkpoint revision, tensor
   keys, row counts, widths, quantization format, scale encoding and generation.
   Publish only after loading and any backend-required visibility fence finish.
   A config/index hash alone is not a full weight-content integrity check.
2. **Layout-independent backing.** Consumers choose row/head ranges for their
   own TP layout. Physical table ownership is independent of DP/TP process-group
   membership; attachment must also work for an independent DP=1 instance.
3. **Explicit direct-access capability.** A provider establishes stable local
   device-accessible views and reports its actual reachability/placement limits.
   Metadata-only parameters, contiguous tensor views and chunk pointer tables
   are distinct representations; a tensor-shaped descriptor is not evidence
   that its CPU address can be dereferenced.
4. **No consumer table initialization or overwrite.** Attached parameters must
   not allocate full replicas, randomize owner storage, or copy checkpoint
   tensors into it. Preserve strict loading checks for unrelated weights.
5. **Mapping lifetime includes asynchronous work and graphs.** Retain backing,
   mappings and address tables while kernels or graph replays can reference
   them. Synchronize outstanding reads before detaching.
6. **Conservative ownership.** A normal owner drain stops new attachments and
   waits for live consumers. A disconnected control socket is insufficient
   proof that device access has stopped. No transparent owner failover is
   promised; forced teardown requires all consumers of that generation gone.

Read-only is the consumer contract. Backends should apply hardware read-only
permissions where supported; the reference implementation does not establish
a universal hardware-enforced isolation guarantee.

## Where this fits in vLLM

The following integration points are based on main commit
`6fe3d447ac6429ef13aff117744d0298e28879ed`:

| Area | Current behavior | Proposed change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EngramConfig` | Local host/device storage and DP sharing | Explicit opt-in external shared generation; validate incompatible settings |
| `ParallelEngramEmbedding._allocate_weights()` | Allocates local or DP-shared storage | Attach published storage instead of allocating a table replica |
| Weight loading and tracking | Loads checkpoint head slices into parameters | Exclude externally supplied table weights before materialization where possible; account for validated external parameters |
| `ParallelEngramEmbedding._storage()` and lookup | Gets accelerator views and launches lookup | Use stable imported views; keep platform address representation in its backend |
| Hash/head routing | Depends on local/DP storage topology | Derive routing from shared placement without requiring cross-instance process groups |
| Shutdown | Storage lifetime follows model/process | Release external mappings only after pending reads and graphs stop |

These are integration requirements, not a proposed final Python ABI. In
particular, overriding allocation alone is insufficient: default weight loading
can overwrite shared storage, and DP routing can introduce unwanted collectives.
The existing loader's `is_unused_checkpoint_weight` mechanism is a candidate
for excluding table-only safetensors shards. Mixed shards and different loader
strategies still need a precise loading contract; a no-op weight loader alone
does not prove the absence of transient full-table materialization.

A first implementation should make the smallest useful storage/lifecycle seam
and use the existing platform extension mechanisms. It should not require a
new generic distributed-memory framework, MemFabric imports in common model
code, or changes to unrelated model execution paths. Public configuration names
and provider selection remain open for maintainer discussion.

## Backends and portability

The common feature is **shared ownership plus direct mapped reads**, rather
than a particular VMM function or global-address format.

| Mechanism | Suitable role | Scope / limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registered shared host memory | Node-local provider | Independent processes can map one local backing; no cross-host promise |
| Native driver VMM and shareable handles | Reference mechanism for capable fabrics | Allocation/export/import/map/access APIs and handle lifetimes are platform-specific |
| Ascend MemFabric BM GVA | Working Ascend provider | Resolves logical GVA to local NPU addresses; BM runtime and reachable A3 topology required |
| CUDA host-NUMA VMM / EGM | Candidate NVIDIA provider | Documented host-memory and fabric mapping mechanism; deployment must validate support, IMEX and permissions |

NVIDIA documents remote host-NUMA allocation sharing through EGM using
`cuMemCreate`, FABRIC export/import and local VA mapping on supported NVLink
systems. Fabric sharing also requires appropriate IMEX access. This establishes
a plausible second implementation, not a benchmark or compatibility claim for
this proposal. Ordinary CUDA UVA and local IPC alone do not establish remote
host-DRAM reachability.

References: [CUDA EGM](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/extended-gpu-memory.html),
[CUDA VMM](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/virtual-memory-management.html).

## Ascend implementation and measured case study

[vllm-ascend #19528](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/19528)
implements this ownership model. The original native VMM version is preserved
on the [tested VMM backup branch](https://github.com/foraxe/vllm-ascend/tree/backup/engram-shared-host-vmm-20261022).
Its allocation/export/import/map implementation was subsequently replaced by
MemFabric BM, while preserving independent owner/consumer semantics and the
native gather/dequantization data path. This backend replacement is practical
evidence that the common feature need not depend on either API.

The current GVA run used four A3 servers in one physical supernode, 64 NPUs:
three DP4/TP4 prefills and one DP8/TP2 decoder. One owner held two real checkpoint
tables in four host backing objects. All 64 workers attached 128 layer views.
Both native per-instance host offload and shared GVA completed 1440/1440
requests without errors. Table backing fell from about **824 GiB to 208 GiB**,
saving **616 GiB / 75%**. Consumers had no large POSIX table replicas and
contributed zero local table allocation capacity.

| Prompt bucket | Concurrency | Native QPS | Shared GVA QPS |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0–10K | 96 | 3.979 | 4.181 |
| 10–20K | 108 | 4.133 | 4.172 |
| 20–40K | 120 | 3.773 | 3.832 |
| 40–80K | 64 | 2.038 | 2.034 |
| Cache-hit dataset | 92 | 4.024 | 4.089 |

This was one sequential A/B, with a 700-token cap, original EOS/sampling,
24 warmups and prefix-cache reset per case. Paired request hashes and input
token counts matched. Results support broadly unchanged throughput, not a
stable speedup or whole-model output equivalence. Both runs missed the 20–40K
TTFT target of 7s: native 8.007s, GVA 8.182s. The memory figures count table
backing, not total RSS or HBM. Framework validation used leaf-module overlays
on a pinned runtime and a repaired MemFabric wheel.

The Ascend path also exposed a backend initialization-order constraint:
AICPU metadata initialization had to precede remote BM imports for successful
decode graph capture on the tested stack. This belongs in backend preparation,
not in a vendor-neutral Engram contract. Active-graph owner failure and complete
model-quality evaluation remain open. Ascend INT8/FP32 storage is not the same
encoding as upstream CUDA's MXFP8/E8M0; sharing requires matching formats.

## Roadmap alignment

This extends the Engram work in [DSv4.1 #57448](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57448) and the disaggregated-serving direction in [Q4 roadmap #61024](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61024) to sharing tables across independent instances. [Ascend roadmap #16375](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/issues/16375) provides the implementation context.

## Relationship to existing work

- [#62359](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62359): changes backing to
  host-NUMA cuMem within the existing DP-sharing group. Complementary NVIDIA
  allocation work; the proposal here adds independent-instance ownership.
- [#57023](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57023): external Mooncake
  storage with IDs submitted to a background read path and packed rows read
  into registered CUDA destinations. The external-table loading concerns
  overlap; the direct-mapped lookup mechanism differs. Reuse compatible seams.
- [#57195](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57195): shared host lookup
  for SP token owners. Its row/head-layout changes can be useful independently;
  cross-instance ownership does not by itself eliminate every TP/SP collective.
- [#61553](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61553): PCP/shared-storage
  integration. Coordinate topology and shared-placement semantics.
- Ascend [#16689](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/16689) and
  [#16544](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/16544) are preceding
  VMM/native host-offload contributions; #19528 extends independent ownership.

No existing PR identified in this review implements this exact combination of
independent owner lifetime, TP-independent attachments and direct mapped reads.
That is a scoped duplicate-work assessment, not a claim to invent memory sharing.

## Delivery and validation

- [x] Ascend native VMM and replacement GVA implementations with preserved source.
- [x] Real cross-server GVA lookup/graph checks and full 3P1D comparison.
- [x] Review current vLLM source and related open PRs before proposing a seam.
- [ ] Agree on the narrow shared-generation and loading contract with maintainers.
- [ ] Implement the common integration and adapt the Ascend provider.
- [x] Test identity/format mismatches, no table overwrite/materialization, different
      consumer layouts, safe detach, and unchanged ordinary storage behavior.
- [x] Add a real serving-entry test and model evaluation for the upstream change.
- [x] Prototype a CUDA provider on supported EGM hardware; separately report its
      capability probes, correctness, physical backing and serving performance.

A second backend is useful validation of the design, but an RFC should not
require claiming an unimplemented universal backend. The initial scope excludes
automatic placement, caches, mutable tables, transparent failover and changes
to P/D KV transfer.

cc @jianzs  @QwertyJack 

## Feedback requested

1. Is an independently owned, immutable table generation the right scope for
   cross-instance sharing?
2. Which existing extension point should expose storage attachment and external
   weight accounting, coordinating with #57023 and #62359?
3. What minimum second-platform evidence should precede merging a common seam,
   versus discussing the RFC with the existing Ascend evidence?

## Feedback Period

At least one week. Feedback on scope and integration points is welcome before implementation of the common vLLM changes.

## Any Other Things

AI assistance was used to prepare this proposal. Related open issues and PRs were searched before submission; the overlapping work and proposed differences are listed above.

title: [RFC]: Disaggregated pre/post-processing for pooling IO Processor plugins
author: kon-pap
body:
### Motivation.

IO Processor plugins (`vllm/plugins/io_processors`) allow pooling models to accept and return arbitrary data. One example is TerraTorch with Prithvi-EO-2.0 for geospatial segmentation. For these models, `IOProcessor.pre_process()` (decoding, tiling and normalising large rasters) and `post_process()` (stitching tiles back and encoding the output) are CPU-heavy. They often take longer than the forward pass itself.

Today all three stages run in the `vllm serve` process that owns the GPU. As a result:

- the GPU waits while pre-processing and post-processing run on the CPU;
- adding CPU capacity for processing means adding more GPU replicas;
- the work cannot be placed on cheaper GPU-less nodes.

vLLM already separates rendering from inference for generative models (`vllm launch render`, `scale_out/render` and `scale_out/derender`). It also already moves data between instances for P/D with `KVTransferConfig` and for encoder disaggregation with `ECTransferConfig`. This RFC proposes applying the same two ideas to pooling with IO Processor plugins:

- pre-processing and post-processing run on GPU-less render instances that scale on their own;
- the GPU instance only runs inference;
- tensors move between instances through a pluggable connector, and requests carry only references to them.

**Measurements** (TerraTorch Prithvi-EO-2.0 segmentation, using the implementation described below):

- **Inference is a minority of request time.** On a monolithic deployment, inference takes only 11–31% of end-to-end time. Pre-processing accounts for 31–37% and post-processing for 33–55%. Inference's share falls as images grow from 1 to 100 tiles.
- **Monolithic deployments saturate early because of CPU/GPU interference** (1 tile per request, 16 CPU workers in both setups):

  | At 80 req/s | Monolithic (16 workers) | Disaggregated (8 pre + 8 post) |
  |---|---|---|
  | Throughput | ~45 tiles/s (plateaus at ~40 req/s) | ~79 tiles/s (still scaling) |
  | Mean latency | ~1.7 s | ~0.34 s |
  | GPU utilization | ~45% | ~84% |

### Proposed Change.

All of the following is opt-in. Existing endpoints and default behaviour do not change.

**1. Three-stage request flow**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Router
  participant PRE as Preprocess (vllm launch render)
  participant INF as Inference (vllm serve)
  participant POST as Postprocess (vllm launch render)

  S->>PRE: POST /pooling/preprocess (IOProcessorRequest)
  PRE-->>PRE: IOProcessor.pre_process + render
  PRE-->>PRE: put_data(mm item), put_metadata(request state)
  PRE->>S: [GeneratePoolingRequest{data_ref, metadata_ref}]
  S->>INF: POST /pooling/inference (one per item)
  INF-->>PRE: get_data(data_ref)
  INF-->>INF: encode()
  INF-->>INF: put_data(output tensor)
  INF->>S: GeneratePoolingResponse{output_data_ref, metadata_ref}
  S->>POST: POST /pooling/postprocess (all responses)
  POST-->>INF: get_data(output_data_ref)
  POST-->>PRE: get_metadata(metadata_ref)
  POST-->>POST: update_request_metadata + IOProcessor.post_process
  POST->>S: IOProcessorResponse
```

Endpoints:

| Endpoint | Server | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /pooling/preprocess` | `vllm launch render` | Runs `IOProcessor.pre_process()` and rendering. Returns one `GeneratePoolingRequest` per item. |
| `POST /pooling/inference` | `vllm serve` | Fetches the pre-processed `MultiModalKwargsItem` and runs `encode()`. Returns a `GeneratePoolingResponse` that references the output tensor. |
| `POST /pooling/postprocess` | `vllm launch render` | Fetches the outputs and request metadata, then runs `IOProcessor.post_process()`. |

The router that fans requests out across the three stages lives outside vLLM. We have a working proxy implementation.

**2. Protocol: references, not payloads**

New models: `DataRef` (`object_id` plus `locator`), `MetadataRef`, `GeneratePoolingRequest`/`GeneratePoolingResponse` and `PostProcessPoolingRequest`.

- The `object_id` of the pre-processed item reuses its `mm_hash`. The inference output is stored as `<mm_hash>:<served_model_name>:output`.
- Data is keyed by object and metadata by request, so one data object can serve requests whose metadata differs.
- When no connector is configured, the same endpoints carry the payloads inline as base64 msgpack. Stages can therefore be split without shared storage, which is useful for debugging and small deployments.

**3. `IOTransferConfig` / `--io-transfer-config`**

This mirrors `KVTransferConfig` and `ECTransferConfig`:

- `io_connector` selects the connector;
- `io_role` is one of `io_producer`, `io_consumer` or `io_both`;
- `io_connector_extra_config` holds connector-specific settings;
- `io_connector_module_path` loads an out-of-tree connector.

**4. IO connector framework (`vllm/distributed/io_transfer`)**

- `IOConnectorBase` defines `put_data`, `get_data`, `cleanup_data`, `put_metadata`, `get_metadata` and `cleanup_metadata`, each with an async variant.
- A lazy-loading factory and process-wide state create the connector once per process, as the EC and KV transfer state modules do. Both servers shut it down on exit.
- On render instances, blocking connector calls run on a dedicated thread pool (`max_io_threads`), so they do not take renderer workers.
- Two reference backends:
  - `IOExampleConnector` uses a shared filesystem, such as a Kubernetes PVC.
  - `IOP2PConnector` uses ZMQ ROUTER/DEALER, is pull-based and sends tensor buffers as zero-copy frames.
- Serialization uses the existing `MsgpackEncoder`/`MsgpackDecoder` and `msgspec`. No new dependencies are added.

**5. IOProcessor plugin hooks**

`get_request_metadata()` and `update_request_metadata()` are added with no-op defaults. Plugins use them to export state saved during `pre_process` (for example tiling layout or geo-referencing) and restore it on a different post-processing instance. Existing plugins need no changes.

**Implementation plan**

A working implementation exists, about 2.6k LOC across six self-contained commits. Depending on feedback, we would split it into a series of PRs:

1. `IOTransferConfig` and the IOProcessor metadata hooks (small, no behaviour change)
2. Disaggregated pooling protocol models and tensor serde
3. IO connector framework with `IOExampleConnector` (`IOP2PConnector` could follow separately)
4. The `/pooling/inference` endpoint
5. `/pooling/preprocess` and `/pooling/postprocess` on the render server, plus docs and an example

Each PR would include unit tests for its part: connector round trips, config validation and the routes with a mock IO processor.

**Open questions for maintainers**

1. Is `vllm/distributed/io_transfer` the right home? Should it share more infrastructure with `ec_transfer`? Both move per-item multimodal data between instances, but the payloads and lifecycles differ.
2. Is it acceptable to add the new routes under `/pooling/*`, or should they live under a scale-out namespace next to `render`/`derender`?
3. Should `IOP2PConnector` be in-tree, or should only the filesystem reference connector ship in-tree, with others loaded through `io_connector_module_path`?
4. How should we cover this in CI? Tests can use the filesystem connector and a dummy IO processor plugin on CPU.

**Current limitations**

- Only full three-stage disaggregation is supported. Partial setups, such as co-locating inference and post-processing, are not.
- Each prompt must contain exactly one `image` item. This is enough for TerraTorch, and other inputs are rejected with a 400 error.
- `IOP2PConnector` still needs performance tuning under high load.



### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@noooop @DarkLight1337 @aoshen02 @christian-pinto 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Consistent semantics for drafted, verified and accepted spec decode tokens
author: tomasruizt
body:
## Summary vLLM reports how many draft tokens were drafted and accepted during speculative decoding (SD). With adaptive verification (AV) and structured outputs (SO), it is no longer clear what `drafted` means. We propose three clear definitions, one invariant that always holds, and to report all three metrics when using SD. | Count | Meaning | | --- | --- | | **Drafted** | Draft tokens proposed by the drafter. | | **Verified** | Draft tokens the target model ran a forward pass on. | | **Accepted** | Draft tokens the target model accepted. | Invariant: `drafted >= verified >= accepted`, in total and at every step. This RFC grew out of reviewing #58340, and discussions with @benchislett and @yzong-rh. ## Problem AV skips some draft tokens to save target compute. SO drops grammar-invalid draft tokens, before the forward pass in sync scheduling, and after it in async scheduling. See [appendix A](#Appendix) for details. Today, `num_draft_tokens` counts the draft tokens that passed the grammar check. This is neither the number of proposed tokens nor the number of verified tokens: - **It is not "proposed tokens".** Grammar-invalid draft tokens are subtracted, but draft tokens skipped by AV are kept. - **It is not "verified tokens".** Async scheduling subtracts grammar-invalid draft tokens, even though they were included in the target forward pass. On top of that, `verified` is not reported. If we add it without changing `drafted`, the invariant can be violated (async scheduling + SO + AV). Sync and async scheduling also count `num_spec_steps` differently (#56977). ## Proposal 1. **`drafted` means proposed by the drafter.** It includes grammar-invalid draft tokens and draft tokens skipped by AV. 2. **`verified` means included in the target forward pass.** With AV, the model runner reports it. Otherwise, the scheduler computes it. 3. **`num_spec_steps` counts the same way in sync and async scheduling.** It counts the engine steps in which the drafter proposed draft tokens for the request (Prometheus: `num_drafts`), even if all of them are grammar-invalid. The mean acceptance length stays `1 + accepted / num_spec_steps`. 4. **Report `verified` everywhere** `drafted` and `accepted` are reported ([appendix C](#appendix)). A client should use `drafted` to judge the drafter, `verified` to measure target compute, and the mean acceptance length to estimate the speedup. See [appendix B](#appendix) for the alternatives we considered, and [appendix E](#appendix) for edge cases. ## Worked examples All examples use `k = 4`. The last column shows today's `drafted` count. | Case | What happens | `drafted` | `verified` | `accepted` | `drafted` today | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | AV | Drafter proposes 4, target verifies the first 3, accepts 2 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | | Sync scheduling, grammar rejects last 2 draft tokens | Only 2 draft tokens in the target forward pass, target accepts 1 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 2 | | Async scheduling, grammar rejects last 2 draft tokens | All 4 in the target forward pass, last 2 masked, target accepts 1 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 2 | | Async + AV, grammar rejects last 2 draft tokens | Target verifies the first 3 (the 3rd is invalid), accepts 1 | 4 | 3 | 1 | 2 (less than `verified`) | | Sync scheduling, grammar rejects all 4 draft tokens | No draft tokens in the target forward pass | 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 (step skipped) | The acceptance rate (`accepted / drafted`) is the same for sync and async scheduling (1/4). Only `verified` differs, which reflects the real difference in compute. ## Impact on users and clients - Without SO, `drafted` and `accepted` do not change, and `verified` equals `drafted` unless AV is on. - With SO, `num_draft_tokens` goes up and `draft_acceptance_rate` goes down, the same way in sync and async scheduling. Dashboards and benchmarks that compute `accepted / drafted` (e.g. AIPerf, Datadog) will show lower rates. - The mean acceptance length only changes in sync scheduling, when all draft tokens of a step are grammar-invalid. - There is no flag for the old behavior. We will note the change in the release notes and update the docs. See [appendix D](#appendix) for details on client compatibility. ## Open questions 1. Is `accepted / drafted` the right default for `draft_acceptance_rate`, or should we also expose `accepted / verified` as its own field? See [appendix F](#appendix) for arguments. 2. Should draft tokens skipped by AV lower the acceptance rate? They were not rejected by the target, but a better drafter could have produced higher-confidence draft tokens. As proposed, they count in `drafted`, so they do lower it. ## Appendix
A. Background: AV and SO **Adaptive verification.** The drafter proposes `k` tokens, but the target only verifies a prefix of them, chosen by a confidence score. This saves target compute when the later draft tokens are unlikely to be accepted. AV is only available in the V2 model runner (MRV2), not in the V1 model runner (MRV1). The skipped draft tokens were proposed, but never verified. **Structured outputs.** A grammar (e.g. a JSON schema) constrains the output. A draft token that violates the grammar can never be accepted. When vLLM checks the grammar depends on the scheduling mode: - **Sync scheduling** checks the draft tokens against the grammar before the forward pass. Invalid draft tokens are dropped and never included in the target forward pass. - **Async scheduling** launches the forward pass first and checks the grammar on the CPU in parallel, to keep the GPU busy. Invalid draft tokens are included in the target forward pass, then masked out before sampling, so they are always rejected. Without AV, the scheduler computes `verified` as `min(scheduled draft tokens, proposed draft tokens)`. This counts grammar-invalid draft tokens in async scheduling (included in the target forward pass), and drops them in sync scheduling (not included).
B. Alternatives considered - **`drafted` means "sent to verification".** This would not penalize the drafter for grammar-invalid tokens, although a better drafter would have proposed valid ones. It also clashes with the domain language: AV skips draft tokens without verifying them, but "drafted but not verified" would become a contradiction. - **Rename `drafted` to `proposed`.** The two words mean the same thing, and a rename breaks existing dashboards and clients. It also does not solve the problem, since we would still need `verified`. - **Only add `verified`.** The smallest change, but `verified` can then be larger than `drafted`, violating the invariant (see [Problem](#problem)).
C. Where each count is reported | Surface | `drafted` | `verified` | `accepted` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Prometheus | `vllm:spec_decode_num_draft_tokens` | `vllm:spec_decode_num_verified_tokens` (new) | `vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens` | | Periodic log line | `Drafted:` | `Verified:` (new) | `Accepted:` | | Per-request metrics | `num_draft_tokens`, `per_step_drafted` | `num_verified_tokens`, `per_step_verified` (new) | `num_accepted_draft_tokens`, `per_step_accepted` | | `vllm bench serve` | yes | new | yes | | Rust frontend | yes | new | yes | `verified` is always reported, even when it equals `drafted`, so the output format does not depend on the config. This adds two Prometheus counters (one of them per position).
D. Client compatibility - Clients that use `drafted` to estimate target compute should use `verified` instead. - AIPerf's per-request adapter keeps working. It ignores new fields, and all of its consistency checks still hold. Its docs say vLLM subtracts grammar-invalid draft tokens, which would need an update. - The new Prometheus counter name contains neither `num_draft_tokens` nor `num_drafts`, so parsers that match metric names by substring (like `vllm bench serve`) do not double count.
E. Edge cases - **Async draft tokens enter the target forward pass before the grammar check.** The forward pass for step N starts while the CPU still validates the draft tokens against the grammar. So invalid draft tokens cost target compute, even though they can never be accepted. This is why they count as `verified` on that path. - **Padding slots count only if the target runs a forward pass on them.** When `ngram_gpu` finds fewer than `k` matches, MRV2 fills the empty slots with the last sampled token and verifies them, so they count. MRV1 pads with `-1` and removes those slots before the forward pass, so they don't. Exception (pre-existing): with MRV1 and without SO, the scheduler doesn't see the removed slots and still counts all `k`. - **All draft tokens grammar-invalid (sync).** No draft tokens are scheduled, but the drafter did propose them. The step now counts in `num_spec_steps`, with 0 accepted. #56977 considers counting such steps a bug.
