| 256 MB | 4 of 9 rounds lost all 768 / 1 of 3 rounds lost all 768 / 3 of 3 rounds lost all 768 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| 384 MB | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |

1. **A's loss is all-or-nothing.** What A loses is the cache segment. When a shared system-prompt block is evicted between prefill and the first fetch, every request referencing it misses all 128 system-prompt blocks at once. In a 256 MB pool, offload alone turned 0/9 failed rounds into 4/9. The engine stays healthy and every HTTP response is 200; the loss shows up only when the trainer fetches.
2. **A's loss is not recoverable.** The rows of hit blocks exist only in the pool; the engine never had them.
3. **A's safe threshold has no provable bound.** Above it the pool still evicts (20–40k keys per round), but there is always a dead object to evict first. The threshold depends on the whole KV hierarchy and on the trainer's read pattern.
4. **What B loses here is only delivery**, a few rows per request rather than whole batches, and B dedup needs a smaller pool (0-loss threshold B 192–224 MB, A 256–320 MB). B still has the rows in EngineCore when a put fails, so the loss can be turned into backpressure.

### 2. B's delivery with the #64380 protocol

With hard-pinned delivery objects, bounded writer queue, retry on no-space, and an in-flight trajectory cap, B's delivery lost nothing in 431 long runs (28,736 samples, 243,212 requests, 86.16 M rows content-checked, 2,462 weight-sync resets), including two- and four-engine shared pools, replica and master failures under Mooncake HA, speculative decoding and TP2. Cost: −1% throughput vs. R3 off. Details and the failure cases that motivated each rule are in #64380.

This is available to B only: B can release delivery objects as soon as the trainer has consumed them, because the cache segment no longer lives in the pool.

### 3. Memory cost

- A pool writes ≈ 384 B × (unique prompt tokens + 2 × response tokens); decoded rows are written once as `r3-tail` and once per completed block. Measured: GRPO 32×16, P=2048, R=1024 predicted 424 MB, measured 424.5 MB. A's pool must also hold the cache segment for as long as the KV may hit.
- B adds host pinned memory = KV token capacity × bytes/token, ~0.4% of KV bytes for Qwen3-30B. Measured host layer per engine: 109 MB (Qwen3-30B), 151 MB (Qwen3.6-35B), 176 MB (gpt-oss-20b), 298 MB (DeepSeek-V2-Lite). GPU KV capacity change ≤ 0.04%. The offload tier stores the R3 layer too (same ratio). B's pool holds only in-flight deliveries and is released after consumption.

**B spends ~0.4% of the KV hierarchy to guarantee "if the KV hits, the rows exist".** Larger aux outputs scale linearly:

| aux | bytes/token | / Qwen KV | B host layer (270k tokens) |
|---|---|---|---|
| R3 Qwen3-30B | 384 | 0.39% | 0.09 GiB |
| R3 DeepSeek-V3 | 464 | 0.47% | 0.11 GiB |
| indexer top-2048 int32 × 1 layer | 8 KB | 8.3% | 2 GiB |
| indexer top-2048 int32 × 61 layers | 500 KB | 508% | 121 GiB |

Putting the cache segment in an LRU pool does not reduce the capacity it needs (section 1); it only makes loss silent.

### 4. Performance

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Throughput, Mooncake delivery, vs. R3 off | GRPO +1%, P8192 +1%, agent −3% | GRPO +1%, P8192 −5%, agent −2% |
| Prefill TTFT, 8k, no hit | 166 → 180 ms | 165 → 166 ms |
| One request hitting an 8k prefix | +4.1 ms | +5.2 ms |
| 16 GRPO siblings hitting an 8k prefix | +18–35 ms | +67 ms |
| Trainer fetch | 2.5–2.8 GB/s | 3–28 GB/s |

B's measurable disadvantage: hit rows are copied from the host layer through the GPU at the prompt's last step (~3 MB per sibling). The rows are already in host memory, so EngineCore can read them by slot at request end instead. Not implemented yet.

### 5. Row provenance without batch invariance

With block-hash sharing across requests (A), the first writer's rows are returned to every request hitting that hash. Without batch invariance, the same block computed in different batches can route differently: in GRPO, 34–42% of siblings had ~0.3% of their prompt rows differ from the KV they actually used (0.07–0.1% across engines). B returns the rows stored next to the KV the request actually used. With batch invariance the difference is 0.

### 6. Failure modes

| Case | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Pool under pressure | Returned keys dangle (54% of requests in a 128 MB pool); engine healthy, HTTP 200 | Cache segment unaffected; delivery backpressures (#64380) |
| Engine reads an evicted object | EngineCore exits (boundary blocks, stop/streaming, P→D tail) | The engine never reads the pool |
| Writer process exits (embedded segment) | Every engine sharing the prefix exits | Only that writer's unconsumed deliveries are lost |
| Loss recoverable? | No | Delivery retries; rows stay in EngineCore until written |

### 7. Feature coverage

B guarantees that rows **live as long as the KV wherever the KV goes**, but every component that moves KV must handle one host-resident layer next to device-resident layers. A must make keys and block hashes agree across engines and handle partial blocks.

B was validated with self-consistency checks (each cached row compared with the row of the request that computed the block; "0" = 0 mismatched rows). A was evaluated only for sections 1–6.

| Scenario | A (#57968) | B |
|---|---|---|
| Local prefix caching, preemption, ngram spec decode, sleep/wake + `reset_prefix_cache` | not evaluated here | 0 (Qwen3-30B BI, Qwen3.6 hybrid, gpt-oss-20b, DeepSeek-V2-Lite MLA) |
| Hybrid models (Gated DeltaNet, sliding window) | not evaluated here | 0; requires a block-outer KV layout so the R3 layer joins the full-attention group |
| `OffloadingConnector`, `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`, `MultiConnector` | works; loses rows under pool pressure (section 1) | 0 |
| `MooncakeStoreConnector` | not evaluated here | 0, including two instances over RDMA and a restarted instance reading old keys |
| P/D, `NixlConnector` (pull) | D reads P's rows from Mooncake; not evaluated here. #62056 / #45419 instead stitch P's rows in the proxy | 0 (1P1D, heterogeneous TP both ways, MLA). The NIXL producer side must split DRAM / VRAM descriptors |
| P/D, `MooncakeConnector` | as above | 0 with BI; without BI, mismatches only in positions D recomputes |
| P/D, NIXL push, MoRIIO, `LMCacheConnectorV1`, `LMCacheMPConnector` | not evaluated here | rejected at config time |
| PP | #61897 stitches rows across stages, then stores whole rows | each stage caches its own layers (PP2, PP2 + offload: 0); rows stitched at request end with #61897's `AuxOutputAggregator` |
| PP + P/D (NIXL), DCP / PCP > 1 | not evaluated here | rejected at config time |
| TP, DP | not evaluated here | 0. Host layer currently allocated on every TP rank |

## Proposal

1. **Adopt B for the cache segment.** "KV hit ⇒ rows exist" holds by construction across every KV tier, with no second LRU to coordinate. A's failure mode is silent, all-or-nothing and unrecoverable; avoiding it needs a pool sized against the whole KV hierarchy with no provable bound, and hard pinning does not help because nothing knows when to release a block-hash object.
2. **Deliver per #64380.** Session-scoped block keys give A's dedup without A's cache-segment problem.
3. **Before merging B:**
   - read hit rows from the host layer in EngineCore instead of a GPU round trip;
   - allocate the host layer on one TP rank only;
   - a failed delivery never exits EngineCore (bounded retry, then mark the request's rows failed).
4. **Land the orthogonal work regardless of this decision:** capturer init before KV profiling, explicit capture row layout, #61086 (batched incremental transfer), the collection half of #61897 (stage stitching, which B depends on).

## Open questions

1. **Connector burden:** every KV connector must support a host-resident layer or reject R3 at config time. Explicit capability flag, or a deny list?
2. **#62920 (per-request opt-out):** blocks written by opted-out requests have no R3 rows. We propose that a hit requires R3 to be present (otherwise recompute).
3. **Host memory at indexer-replay scale** (up to 121 GiB per engine for 61 layers): per-layer opt-in, or a GPU-resident option?

title: [RFC]: Large-page KV cache allocator: one KV cache group per spec
author: ivanium
body:
**Status:** draft · **Implementation:** two stacked PRs to follow (PR1 opt-in, PR2 large pages only) · **Related:** [#62100](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62100) (pluggable KV cache planning) ## TL;DR vLLM requires every KV cache group to have the same page size in bytes. For hybrid models, this one rule is the source of most of the grouping complexity in core: layer-count grouping, page padding, raised block sizes, `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs`, and a second hash granularity (`hash_block_size`). Each new hybrid model, drafter or cache precision tends to need another special case. This RFC proposes to remove the rule. The KV cache pool becomes a set of equal **large pages**. A page belongs to one KV cache group at a time, and the group cuts it into blocks of its own size. Then grouping becomes trivial: **one group per `KVCacheSpec`**, with one block size for every prefix-cacheable group. Block ids stay affine (block `b` is kernel row `b * R`), so attention kernels and slot mapping keep their upstream form. KV cache capacity stays within 1% of main on the models we checked. The motivation is simpler code, not memory. ## 1. Background Main stores the KV cache of each group in per-layer tensors that several groups share. A block id `b` addresses page `b` of every layer in its group, and one tensor can back one layer from each group. This sharing works only if all groups have the same page size in bytes. Core enforces this rule (`assert len(page_sizes) == 1`) and makes models satisfy it in three ways: - **Group by layer count.** Layers of the same type are split into groups of equal size, so that each shared tensor holds one layer per group. - **Raise the block size.** A narrow attention page grows in tokens until it is as wide as the widest page, for example a Mamba state. - **Pad pages.** A page that still does not match is padded up to the widest page. When different groups then have different block sizes, prefix caching hashes at a smaller common granularity (`hash_block_size`) and scales hits back up. ## 2. Problem **The grouping is byte arithmetic, not model structure.** On Kimi-Linear-48B (TP4; 20 KDA layers, 7 MLA layers), one KDA state is 561,152 bytes. To give MLA the same page size, main raises the block size to 512 tokens (512 × 1,152 B = 589,824 B) and pads every KDA state by 5.1%. The 20 KDA layers become 3 groups because the MLA group has 7 layers. The model has two kinds of KV cache, but main runs four groups with 512-token blocks. **Small changes re-cut the whole plan.** On DSV4.1-Flash, a change of the indexer precision from fp8 to mxfp4 changes the plan from 7 groups to 9, although no SWA layer changed ([#62100](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62100) has the details). A drafter can do the same (Kimi-K3 with DSpark: 4 groups become 20). **The workarounds add concepts that every component must understand.** `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` merges layers of one type with different sizes into one spec. `hash_block_size` and `prefix_match_unit` add a third token granularity next to the scheduler block size and the group block size. Platforms override `_align_hybrid_block_size`, and models declare custom grouping through `SupportsKVCacheGrouping`. [#62100](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62100) makes the grouping pluggable, so a model or platform can own its plan. That moves the heuristic out of core, but it keeps the equal-page rule that makes a heuristic necessary. ## 3. Goals and non-goals Goals: - One KV cache group per `KVCacheSpec`. Same-spec drafter layers join the target model's group. - One block size `B` for all prefix-cacheable groups, so that a block hash means the same tokens in every group. - No page padding, no block-size raise for byte reasons, no sub-block hashing. - Kernel addressing, slot mapping and block tables keep their upstream form. - KV cache capacity close to main, with a bounded loss. Non-goals: - Higher KV cache capacity. Capacity is a constraint, not the motivation. - A new eviction policy. LRU over cached blocks stays. - Changes to attention kernels, apart from 64-bit offsets where a pool can exceed 2 GiB per view. ## 4. Design

*Figure 1. Kimi-Linear-48B, TP4. Left: main pads every KDA state to the 512-token MLA page and runs four groups over shared per-layer tensors. Right: the pool is a set of 32.1 MiB large pages. Each page belongs to one group. The KDA group fits 3 blocks in a page, and the MLA group fits 64 blocks of 64 tokens.* **Groups.** The planner makes one group for each distinct `KVCacheSpec` (after normalization) and kernel block size. A group's block holds the data of all its layers for `B` tokens, or one state for a state-based spec. On Kimi-Linear, the KDA block is 20 layers × 561,152 B = 10.7 MiB, and the MLA block is 7 layers × 64 tokens × 1,152 B = 504 KiB. **Block size.** `B` is the least common multiple of the model's hard constraints (ring capacity, Mamba checkpoint alignment, DCP), raised to at least 64 tokens and then to the next size that every layer's attention kernel supports. An explicit `--block-size` is used as given, also below 64, if it is feasible. Groups that are not prefix-cacheable (rings, bounded-replay SWA, state pools) keep their own size. **Large pages.** The pool is `N` pages of `S` bytes. Page 0 holds every group's null block. A page has exactly one owner group at a time; when all blocks of a page are free, the page returns to the shared free list and any group can take it. Ownership changes over time, so a block id is unique only within its group, and every component identifies a block as `(group_id, block_id)`. **Page size.** `S` is the smallest multiple of any group's block size that satisfies two conditions: it is at least the largest block, and its demand-weighted waste is at most 2%. Waste is the page tail that a group cannot fill, weighted by how many blocks of each group one max-length request needs. The planner also checks that one max-length request fits on every rank. On Kimi-Linear, `S` = 3 KDA blocks = 32.1 MiB; the MLA group uses 64 blocks of a page and loses a 1.9% tail. The 2% bound is the only tuning constant.

*Figure 2. Affine block ids. Block `b` of a group starts at byte `b × block_bytes` of the pool, so the kernel row is `b × R`. An id that crosses a page end belongs to no page and is never allocated (a hole). The page owner decides which group's ids are live on that page.* **Affine block ids.** Block `b` of group `g` occupies bytes `[b × block_bytes_g, (b + 1) × block_bytes_g)` of one pool buffer. Each layer gets one strided view over that buffer, with the stride equal to the group's row size. Thus the kernel row of block `b` is `b × R_g`, where `R_g` is the number of kernel blocks in one manager block. There is no lookup table and no second address formula. When `S` is not a multiple of a group's block size, the id that crosses a page end is a hole. The pool never allocates holes, and admission uses the minimum number of blocks per page. **Rank-uniform geometry.** `S` and each group's row size are equal on all ranks; a group's row is its maximum over ranks. Therefore all TP and PP ranks, and both sides of a P/D pair, agree on block ids and page boundaries. Startup asserts this. **Allocation.** A group takes a block from the first source that has one: 1. A free block on a page that the group already owns. The fullest page goes first, so that pages empty and return to the free list. 2. A free page with no cached blocks. 3. The older of two candidates: the group's least recently used cached block, or the oldest page in the free list. If the page wins, the pool evicts the cached blocks of all groups on that page. **Admission.** `can_allocate` checks a request against free pages with a closed form, independent of the order in which groups then allocate. For each group, the uncovered demand is the demand minus the group's free blocks. This gives a lower and an upper page count, depending on how many cached blocks the group can reuse. The request is admitted if the free pages cover the sum of the upper counts minus the smallest slack (upper minus lower) of any group. A naive per-group sum is not sound, because one group's allocation can consume pages that another group counted. Models with one block per page per group take a scalar fast path. **Prefix caching.** Every prefix-cacheable group hashes at `B`. Cache hits, KV events and connector transfers use whole blocks. Partial-block hits at a finer granularity are removed. **Workers and connectors.** Workers allocate one buffer for the pool and bind per-layer views. Zeroing, copy-on-write, warmup and CUDA graph capture use the affine ids. Connectors receive per-group geometry (`kernel_rows_per_block`, `row_bytes`) and address blocks as `(group_id, block_id)`. NIXL sends the geometry in its handshake and rejects peers with a different version or geometry. ## 5. Costs **Single-owner pages strand free blocks.** A page returns to the free list only when all its blocks are free. In CPU replays of multi-turn traffic with 4 to 8 GiB of KV cache, prefix hit rates were 5 to 6 points below an ideal LRU over the same bytes (Kimi-Linear, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). Smaller pages would reduce the gap, but the largest state sets the minimum page size. **Page tails.** By construction, the demand-weighted tail is at most 2%. On Kimi-Linear, the branch has 473.28x maximum concurrency at 32K tokens against 472.24x on main. Main pads each KDA state by 5.1%; the branch loses 1.6% (demand-weighted) to page tails. **A coarser default block size.** Dense models move from 16-token blocks to 64-token blocks unless `--block-size` is set. Capacity does not change, but prefix hits round down to 64 tokens. A connector configured with a block size that is not a multiple of 64 now fails at startup. **Compatibility.** The NIXL handshake version changes, so P and D instances must upgrade together. In PR2, external connectors that read the KV layout (LMCache, FlexKV, UMBP) need a matching release. Models that declare custom grouping (`SupportsKVCacheGrouping`) lose that hook. ## 6. Rollout **PR1: opt-in allocator.** PR1 adds `--kv-cache-allocator large_page`. The default stays `uniform_page`. PR1 contains the planner, the page-owning block pool and admission, worker views, kernel changes for 64-bit offsets, NIXL and SimpleCPU offload. A platform opts in through `Platform.support_large_page_kv_cache()`. Startup rejects the unported cases: other connectors, NIXL host buffers, HiSparse and FlexAttention. PR1 has 7 commits: +3.4k/−0.6k lines in `vllm/` and about the same again in tests. **PR2: one allocator.** PR2 makes large pages the only allocator. It ports the other platforms, every in-tree connector (Mooncake, Offloading, LMCache, HF3FS, MoRIIO, UMBP, FlexKV) and HiSparse. Then it deletes the equal-page path: `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs`, `hash_block_size`, `prefix_match_unit`, page padding and the layer-count grouping. PR2 has 10 commits, one per area. Over the two PRs, `vllm/` gains 6.9k lines and loses 10.6k. We propose to merge PR1 first and run it opt-in on the hybrid models for one release, then merge PR2. **Validation.** At an earlier revision of the branches, GSM8K accuracy matched main on DSV4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Kimi-Linear-48B, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and MiniMax-M3. NIXL P/D and SimpleCPU offload runs also passed GSM8K. The current revision adds affine ids and the 2% page rule. It passes the unit tests and CPU replays of the planner and the block pool, but GPU end-to-end runs are not done yet. ## 7. Alternatives **Keep the equal-page rule and make grouping pluggable ([#62100](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62100)).** This lets a model or platform fix its own plan, but each new model still needs a plan, and core still needs `hash_block_size` for mixed block sizes. The two proposals compose: with one group per spec, a planner override is needed only for placement, not for grouping. **Pack unequal pages into one block slot ([#64307](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64307), [#56156](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56156)).** These proposals give one block id a slot that holds every group's page at its exact size, so padding goes away. One block id still spans all groups, so the layer-count grouping and `hash_block_size` stay. This RFC removes the shared block id instead. **Per-group pools with fixed sizes.** A static split of memory between groups is simple, but the right split depends on the workload. A wrong split wastes memory that the other group needs. Shared large pages move memory between groups at run time. **Pages smaller than the largest state.** A state that spans several smaller pages would reduce stranding. It needs a block to map to more than one page, which breaks affine ids and puts a lookup back into every kernel. We think the stranding cost does not justify that today. ## 8. Open questions ~1. **Default block size.** Is 64 tokens the right floor for dense models, or should the floor apply only to hybrid models?~ 2. **Performance.** Kimi-Linear now hashes 8 times more blocks per request (64-token instead of 512-token blocks). The per-step cost at the current revision is not yet measured on GPU. At an earlier revision, a prefill-heavy GLM-5.2 HiSparse workload was 4.7% slower than main. 3. **Release order of external connectors.** Should PR2 wait for LMCache and FlexKV releases, or merge with those connectors gated off? 4. **Prefix caching.** Need to balance eviction of blocks from the same group, or a large page from another group. AI assistance (Claude) was used to prepare this RFC and the code.

title: [RFC]: Load plan — an engine-neutral API for sharded weight transfer
author: hao-aaron
body:
# Motivation.

Weight transfer engines that move sharded bytes themselves (`nccl_m2n`, sharded RDT/NIXL) need to
know, for every tensor the trainer sends, **which part this rank needs** and **where in live memory
it goes**. `load_weights` can't tell them: it takes full tensors and shards them internally.

Today each engine works this out on its own by reaching into reload internals:

- **NCCL M2N** (#51520, #60934, #62853, #60949, #63216) matches parameter names
  (`resolve_parameter_destinations`) and uses a hand-written hook for experts
  (`resolve_sharded_weight_target`). Anything else is a full tensor through `load_weights`.
- **Sharded RDT** (#43375) bakes an op chain with `FakeRDTTensor` in a layerwise meta dry run and
  scatters on background threads. The dry run keeps it off direct reload (#64336).

Two merged or in-flight pieces make one shared answer possible:

- **#63215 / #63256**: every `WeightSource` declares its tensors once in `ParamMeta` (HF name,
  dtype, shape, owners, placements), identically on every trainer rank.
- **#54477** (direct reload): each update views every tensor back to its checkpoint layout in its
  own storage, `load_weights` writes in place, and post-load processing (PWAL) reruns at finish.
  Storage never moves.

**Goals.** One `plan_loads(model, metadata)` for every engine; the model's loaders stay the only
source of truth for sharding; results equal a cold start, checked byte for byte in CI; anything
the plan can't express falls back to `load_weights`.

**Non-goals for now.** Online quantization, EPLB, per-update subsets of names, rollback, staging
buffers in vLLM, coordinating failures across trainer ranks, draft models (a draft update session,
`start_draft_weight_update`, keeps calling `load_weights`).

# Proposed Change.

## 1. Assumptions

Planned loading builds on direct reload and requires `VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct`:

- Every update sends every name the sender declared at init.
- View-back gives each target its checkpoint shape, stride and dtype in its own storage, so a
  destination is almost always contiguous.
- PWAL reruns once at finish and keeps addresses (#54477 PR 5: `replace_parameter`,
  `refill_derived`, `keep_constants`). Storage never moves (#62407; checked by #54477 F2).
- Module state a loader sets while the plan is traced (an attribute, a flag, a cache,
  `requires_grad`, a `.data` rebind) is harmless or needed, so the bake keeps it instead of
  restoring it. This may not hold for every model today.

## 2. Wire format: HF tensors

The sender sends HF tensors under HF names, in the target's dtype. Routed experts may come either
way, and the plan follows whatever the sender declares:

- **per expert**, as Hub checkpoints store them: `experts.E.{gate,up,down}_proj.weight`;
- **transformers v5 fused**, as v5 model classes hold them: `experts.gate_up_proj` `[E, 2I, H]`
  (gate rows, then up rows) and `experts.down_proj` `[E, H, I]`.

gpt-oss (`[E, H, 2I]`, gate/up interleaved) and Llama4 (`[E, H, 2I]`, transposed) keep their own
loaders. FSDP2 on v5 models works as is (`ModuleSource` declares `gate_up_proj` as `Shard(0)`).
Megatron users gather over expert TP and emit HF tensors, because Megatron's local
`[gate_shard; up_shard]` isn't a `Shard`/`Replicate` of `[E, 2I, H]`:

```python
parts = all_gather(fc1_local, group=etp_group)          # etp x [2*I/etp, H]
yield f"{prefix}.experts.{e}.gate_proj.weight", torch.cat([p.chunk(2)[0] for p in parts])
yield f"{prefix}.experts.{e}.up_proj.weight", torch.cat([p.chunk(2)[1] for p in parts])
```

## 3. The plan

When a tensor goes through `load_weights`, the loaders decide which part this rank keeps and where
those bytes land. We trace the loaders once, on the first update after `start_reload` (so the trace sees the checkpoint layout direct reload itself applied), and record that for every tensor declared at init. The
record is the plan: a sharded loading API. `load_weights` takes full tensors and shards them
itself; the plan tells an engine up front which shard each rank needs and where it goes.

```python
plan = plan_loads(model, metadata)                     # once, after the first start_reload

plan.get_boxes(name) -> tuple[Box, ...] | None
    # parts of the HF tensor this rank needs; None: nothing (other PP stage, non-local expert,
    # tied alias the loader skips). Box = half-open (start, stop) per dim.
plan.get_dest(name) -> list[tuple[Box, torch.Tensor]] | None
    # (part of a box, live tensor) pairs; copying each part into its tensor is exactly what the
    # loader would have written. None: fallback, so send the full tensor and call load_weights.
```

Example, TP2 rank 0: `get_boxes("…k_proj.weight")` is rows `[0, K/2)`, and `get_dest` maps that
box to the `[K/2, H]` slice of `qkv_proj.weight` after the `q_proj` rows. Under expert TP,
`gate_up_proj` has two boxes (gate shard, up shard), each mapped to its half of `w13`.

**Destinations are built once.** `plan_loads` creates each destination tensor directly on the
target's storage, in the checkpoint dtype. Storage never moves, so engines may keep these tensors
for the plan's lifetime, with two limits: write through them only between `start_reload` and
`finish_reload`, and never read them between updates (they hold kernel-format bytes then). If
storage ever moved, #54477 F2's address check fails at finish and the engine re-plans.

The plan is keyed by wire name, not by vLLM parameter: fused parameters like `qkv_proj` and `w13`
appear only as destinations, never to a transport. It does no communication and holds no engine
policy. Its internal fields are in §11.

## 4. Building the plan

**View rule.** A name is direct only if every destination byte is a copy of one incoming byte:

- only view ops on source and destination (`narrow`, slicing, `view`, `reshape`, `transpose`,
  `permute`, `chunk`, `unbind`, …), plus `.to()` calls that change neither dtype nor device;
- exact dtype at each `copy_`. `src.view(dtype)` is a bit reinterpret and allowed (loaders already
  do this for E8M0 → `uint8`). A cast is not: BF16 bytes copied into FP16 are not a conversion.

Casts, arithmetic, dequantization, repetition and reductions make a name a fallback.

**What any chain of views turns into.** Every view op is an offset, a shape and strides over the
same memory, and chaining views gives another one. So however a loader combines views, the trace
reduces each write to: a **box** of the HF tensor, and a **destination tensor** whose strides say
where each box element lands. Example: the loader does `P.copy_(W.t())` with `W` `[4, 6]` and `P`
`[6, 4]` contiguous. `W[i, j]` lands in `P[j, i]`, at address `4j + i`, so the destination is
`P.as_strided((4, 6), (1, 4))`: shaped like the box, with the transpose folded into its strides.
Copying the box into it writes exactly what the loader wrote.

This works for any chain of views as long as two things hold:

1. the source side picks a rectangular box: `narrow`, slices with step 1, integer indexing,
   `chunk`, `unbind`;
2. every other op on either side is a true view: `transpose`, `permute`, `view`, a `reshape` that
   doesn't copy, `flatten`, `unflatten`, `squeeze`, `unsqueeze`.

If a loader splits a box dimension and sends the parts to unrelated places, the destination has the
box's dimension split (for example `6` → `(2, 3)`). The box's elements are still in the same
row-major order, so an engine just reshapes its data before copying.

These break the rule and make the name a fallback: slices with a step (gpt-oss's interleaved
gate/up, `[..., ::2]`), `expand` or broadcasting (one value to many places), index lists and
masks (a gather), a `reshape` that has to copy, and `diagonal` or overlapping `as_strided`.

**Refusals.** `plan_loads` refuses layerwise mode, online-quantized modules, EPLB, and whatever
#64336 already refuses. It also refuses when a required name is missing, using #54477 F2's
required set (cold-start names minus `is_unused_checkpoint_weight` and
`VLLM_DIRECT_RELOAD_EXCLUDE_REGEX`); F2 alone would only catch it at finish.

**The bake.** `TraceTensor` (today's `FakeRDTTensor`, moved into the reload core) runs the model's
`load_weights` over all declared names at once, on meta stand-ins that share one base per real
storage, so tied weights alias exactly as in the model.

- `copy_` into a target is the only recorded write.
- An unsupported op marks the name as a fallback and the bake continues. A value read (`.item()`,
  `bool()`) can't continue: that name falls back and `load_weights` resumes with the names after
  it, so every name is traced once.
- Constant writes into targets (`fill_`, `zero_`) are ignored: PWAL owns all padding (§6).
- Module state a loader sets while tracing stays on the model (§1). For state that depends only
  on the name's metadata (dtype, shape) this is exactly right: every update under the plan sends
  the same metadata, so the state the bake's loader run leaves on the model holds for every
  update, provided PWAL does not reset it. #54477 PR 6's
  `fp8_rows` (which rows arrive as FP8) and MiMo-V2's `fp8_weight_loaded` / `requantize_rows` are
  the cases (L7).

**Checks.** A fallback name that writes nothing when loaded alone needs another tensor in the same
call, so the plan is refused ("move the combine into PWAL", §5). Writes must not overlap in
storage, since direct writes land in any order.

**Report.** `plan_loads` logs each name as direct or fallback, with the reason, the bytes, and a
fix hint where there is one ("send as FP32 to make this direct").

## 5. Loader contract for RL target models

Planned loading targets the models used for RL: the #54477 families (DeepSeek-V4.x, GLM-5.x,
Kimi-K3, MiMo-V2, Qwen3.x, MiniMax-M3, Nemotron, gpt-oss, Gemma-4, Ling, HY-V4, dots3, Step-5,
Muse Spark, Inkling, …). Their loaders follow three rules; other models get fallbacks or refusals.

1. **No cross-name state.** Each checkpoint tensor loads on its own as it arrives (nothing is held
   or deferred), in any order and any split across calls. Combining tensors (FP8 weight + scale → BF16, max over experts) happens in PWAL,
   as #54477 PR 6's `Fp8DequantLinearMethod` does.
2. **Write parameters only with `copy_`.**
3. **Set no state that PWAL or the forward reads.** PWAL learns that new weights arrived from
   `start_reload`, not from loaders. The one exception is state fixed by the update metadata, which
   the bake sets once (§4, L7).

## 6. Padding is rewritten by PWAL on every update

Some parameters have padding that holds a constant, not checkpoint data (MoE sizes rounded up for a
kernel, vocab rounded to 64, attention-sink heads padded to the TP size). Today loaders write it.
On the direct path the loader doesn't run, and view-back leaves the previous update's
post-processed bytes in the padding. Some kernels read it: #64352 found 96 stale padded expert
parameters on gpt-oss-20b after an NCCL sync.

**Requirement: PWAL rewrites all padding on every update.** That is safe on every path: loaders
never read padding, PWAL runs before the next forward on every rank, rewriting a constant gives
the same bytes, and cold start takes the same path. Loaders may keep writing their constants; the
bake ignores them.

How PWAL knows the regions is a per-case implementation choice:

| Padding | Read by a kernel? | How PWAL fills it |
|---|---|---|
| MoE padded TP / hidden round-up (weights 0, scales 1) | yes | the loader records the region once at cold start (`mark_padding`, #64352); `fill_padding` at the top of PWAL writes it |
| gpt-oss MXFP4 round-up | yes | same, finishing #64352's remaining `zero_()` sites |
| Inkling experts | yes | same |
| DeepSeek-V4 shared experts | yes | the loader writes a narrowed destination instead of `torch.cat` with zeros on the source (which today makes the whole shared MLP a fallback); then the same |
| GLM5-Next NoPE `kv_a` rows | yes | the dequantize-on-finish PWAL zeroes them (#54477 PR 6) |
| vocab rows, attention-sink heads, Kimi-K3 KDA | no / no / probably not | that module's PWAL fills from sizes it already knows (`org_vocab_size`, head count, `padding_size`) |
| unquantized TRT-LLM MoE | yes | already in PWAL (`_zero_intermediate_padding`) |

Recording where the geometry is tricky (per expert, per TP shard inside `w13`) keeps it out of
PWAL code. Where it's a one-liner, PWAL just fills.

**One change to #64352.** `fill_padding` currently runs only if the loader set
`_padding_pending`, which never happens on the direct path. It must run unconditionally. That
breaks layerwise reload, so it lands as X1 (Tracker).

Loaders must also not read their destination: after view-back it holds post-processed bytes. The
one loader that decides from it, the compressed-tensors MoE `input_scale` equality check, is
dropped. Loaders built with `composed_weight_loader` read it only to transform what they just wrote
(`param.copy_(fn(param))`); the bake marks those names fallbacks, and X4 moves the transforms.

## 7. Engine API

| Call | Status |
|---|---|
| `plan_loads(model, metadata)`, `plan.get_boxes(name)`, `plan.get_dest(name)` | new |
| `start_reload` / `finish_reload` / `abort_reload` | unchanged (#64336); don't take the plan |
| `model.load_weights([(name, buf)])` | unchanged, for fallbacks |
| `record_delivered(model, names)` | #54477 F2, for names written directly |

```python
start_reload(model)
for meta in source.metadata:                        # any order; collective engines fix one
    dest = plan.get_dest(meta.name)
    if dest is not None and engine_can_write(dest):
        for box, tensor in dest:
            transport_write(box, tensor)
        record_delivered(model, [meta.name])        # once those bytes are complete
    else:
        buf = torch.empty(meta.shape, dtype=meta.dtype, device=device)
        transport_fill_full(buf)
        model.load_weights([(meta.name, buf)])
finish_reload(model)                                # coverage (F2), padding, PWAL, address checks
```

**Rules for engines.**

1. **Completion is the engine's job.** Record a name, or call `load_weights` on it, only once its
   bytes are complete and visible to the current stream. Nothing in the API tracks streams.
2. **Direct or fallback, decided by the engine.** `get_dest` returns `None` only when no engine
   could write the name directly. Otherwise each engine checks the pairs against what its
   transport can do, once when the plan is built (the destinations never change):
   - an engine that receives into its own buffer and copies (RDT) can write any pairs: its check
     is `dest is not None`;
   - M2N writes straight into model memory with one `reshard`, so it needs exactly one pair whose
     tensor is contiguous and box-shaped:
     `len(dest) == 1 and dest[0][1].is_contiguous() and dest[0][1].shape == box_shape(dest[0][0])`.

   A name that fails the check goes through `load_weights` as a full tensor. Whether that's
   acceptable is the engine's policy (M2N keeps its per-parameter `allow_full_fallback`). An engine may describe buffers to its transport
   as any dtype of the same size (E8M0 as `uint8`).
3. **Order is free.** Collective engines fix one order and check it in their own init agreement.
4. **Quiesce before starting over.** No transfer may still be writing into model memory when the
   engine calls `start_weight_update` again (§8).
5. **Re-plan** when the sender's metadata changes or F2 reports moved storage. Engines register
   only their own buffers, never model memory.

## 8. Failure handling

vLLM guarantees one thing: **after any failure, an engine can always start over.** A transfer that
died halfway, an update the engine abandoned, a `finish_reload` that failed partway through PWAL:
in every case, calling `start_weight_update` (`start_reload`) again views every tensor back to its
checkpoint layout, and a full sync from there gives the same weights as a cold start. #64336 tests
this (`test_retry_after_aborted_update_matches_cold_start`). The plan keeps no per-update state,
so it never needs resetting.

Until that full sync finishes, the model is pending (`direct_reload_pending`, #64336) and must not
serve. Refusing to serve while pending is a #64336 follow-up this RFC depends on. There is no
rollback to the previous weights: that would double weight memory, and the trainer can resend.

**Everything else is the engine's concern:** detecting the failure, aborting or re-initializing its
transport, whether and when to retry, and agreeing on the outcome across trainer ranks.

## 9. Engines on the plan

**Sharded RDT.** At init it sends `get_boxes` for every name to the trainer, so the trainer packs
each rank's boxes, and registers its own receive buffer with NIXL. Per group: one NIXL read into
that buffer, then `copy_` into each `get_dest` tensor. Several writes per name are just several
copies, so expert TP and Mamba2 segments still move only box bytes. The dry run and background
threads go away, and RDT can use direct reload.

**NCCL M2N** (a proposed integration; the M2N maintainers own it). At init, inside M2N's existing
agreement rounds:

1. each worker checks, per name, that its destination is a single contiguous box-shaped tensor
   (§7 rule 2), and tests a fixed list of candidate layouts (every 2-D factorization of the N
   workers, each axis `Replicate` or `Shard(d)`, at most one sharded axis) against its own boxes;
2. the workers AND their results over the metadata group, so a name is direct only if it is direct
   on every rank (a `reshard` is collective, so all ranks must take the same path); the first
   common candidate is the layout; none means fallback;
3. the layouts go to the trainer as per-parameter meshes (as #63216's `auto_dst_mesh`), followed by
   the existing complete-plan agreement.

Example, DP2 × TP2, `q_proj.weight` `[8, H]`: ranks hold rows `[0,4)`, `[4,8)`, `[0,4)`, `[4,8)`.
`(Replicate, Shard(0))` on `(2, 2)` matches every rank; `(Shard(0), Replicate)` matches only ranks
0 and 3, so ranks can't pick locally. Experts under EP4 give `Shard(0)` on `(1, 4)`.

Per update, M2N `reshard`s direct names into their `get_dest` tensor and fallbacks into a full
buffer for `load_weights`. For a strided single box (#54477 PR 6's FP8-in-BF16 rows) it
may receive into its own buffer and copy, as RDT does. Known M2N fallbacks, all transport limits:
expert TP, Mamba2 segments, vocab not a multiple of 64 (only step3's 128815 among public
RL-family vocabs checked), k/v replication with DP > 1. Destination PP stays refused until the
library supports meshes over part of the communicator.

Replaced: `resolve_parameter_destinations`, `M2NDestination`, name matching, `run_trace`, and
#60949's `resolve_sharded_weight_target`.

NCCL broadcast, IPC and disk keep calling `load_weights` and need no plan.

## 10. Relation to other work

- **#54477** is the base. The lifecycle is unchanged; this adds `plan_loads` and its lookups, the
  loader contract, and unconditional padding fills. It replaces #54477's batched per-expert loading follow-up with L1
  below.
- **#63215 / #63256** describe the sender's layout; the plan describes the receiver's.
- **#60949** first showed the logical `[E, 2I, H]` expert transfer. The bake covers it without
  per-module code and adds direct writes, quantized experts, and no dependence on layerwise reload.
- **#63216** (`auto_dst_mesh`, `allow_full_fallback`) carries over into the M2N integration.

## 11. Internal representation of the plan

Not API: engines only call `get_boxes` and `get_dest`. This is the trace's output, what the CI test
compares across ranks, and what the checks run on.

```python
Box = tuple[tuple[int, int], ...]          # half-open (start, stop) per dim, in HF tensor coords

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LoadPlan:
    entries: dict[str, Entry]                    # per declared name, in metadata order
    dests: dict[str, list[tuple[Box, Tensor]]]   # live tensors built at plan_loads; not data

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Entry:
    name: str
    shape: tuple[int, ...]                 # from ParamMeta
    dtype: torch.dtype
    boxes: tuple[Box, ...] | None          # what this rank needs; None: nothing
    writes: tuple[Write, ...] | None       # where it goes; None: fallback

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Write:
    src: Box                               # part of one of entry.boxes
    module: str                            # target tensor by name
    tensor: str
    dst: Region

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Region:                              # as_strided arguments, relative to the target's
    offset: int                            #   storage_offset, in checkpoint-dtype elements
    shape: tuple[int, ...]
    stride: tuple[int, ...]
```

`Region.shape` is the shape of its `src` box (or that shape with some dimensions split), and any
view ops the loader applied on either side live in `Region.stride` (§4).

`get_boxes` reads `entries[name].boxes`; `get_dest` returns `None` for a fallback, else
`dests[name]`, one `(w.src, tensor)` pair per write.

Examples (TP2, rank 0):

| Name | `boxes` | `writes` |
