title: [RFC]: Checkpoint-internal paging for hybrid recurrent state
author: kang-dongwook
body:
## Motivation.

Hybrid models can lose prefix-cache reuse opportunities when a useful recurrent checkpoint is unavailable. Reusing a prefix requires both the attention key/value (KV) cache and the recurrent state after the same number of tokens. If requests share a prefix but its recurrent checkpoint was never saved or has already been discarded, the server must resume from an earlier available checkpoint or recompute from the start.

The inspected upstream hybrid path ties the attention block size to the size of a complete recurrent state. At commit [fa3b9d137721](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/fa3b9d1377219247060d3c8b49eae199c9e7e154), [_align_hybrid_block_size()](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa3b9d1377219247060d3c8b49eae199c9e7e154/vllm/platforms/interface.py#L945) increases the number of tokens in an attention block until its page size is at least as large as the Mamba state. align is the Mamba caching mode whose basic rule saves state when a scheduler step ends at a block boundary. In this mode, the alignment path also sets the Mamba block size to the same number of tokens as the attention block. This makes the state size a constraint on the ordinary block and checkpoint spacing, even when a workload would benefit from smaller intervals.

Upstream already supports some checkpoints inside a physical block, with restrictions on where they can be produced. A smaller prefix_match_unit enables finer prefix matching, but does not save a recurrent state at every matching position. Existing paths support checkpoints near the end of a prompt, internal prefill checkpoints on supported backends, and conditional checkpoints at shared-prefix junctions. Internal checkpoint positions must also satisfy the backend's export alignment. With prefix_match_unit set, the [checkpoint grid](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa3b9d1377219247060d3c8b49eae199c9e7e154/vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/abstract.py#L116) uses the least common multiple of that unit and the backend alignment, so both requirements are satisfied.

S1 would let the shared cache pool use smaller pages by spreading one recurrent state across several pages. This is the S1 organization described in [Native Dual Pools or Shared Paging? Memory Organization for Concurrent Hybrid LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15755). The port would remove the need for one attention allocation unit to accommodate an entire recurrent state. It would use that flexibility to explore smaller block and checkpoint intervals while keeping the backend's alignment requirements.

The intended benefit is more useful prefix reuse and better use of the shared cache budget. A checkpoint closer to the end of a shared prefix can reduce repeated prefill computation, while smaller attention allocation units can reduce unused space in partially filled blocks. The evaluation would test whether these effects improve throughput and latency after paying for checkpoint storage, copying, and page lookup.

## Proposed Change.

### State representation and kernel access

Each recurrent checkpoint would remain one logical state, with a mapping to all pages that store it. The mapping would contain an ordered list of state-space model (SSM) member-page IDs and one convolution-state page ID. A member page stores part of the SSM state, and the pages may be far apart in physical memory. The supported state shape, data type, and kernel alignment would determine the page size and member count.

The page planner would allow a shared physical page to be smaller than a complete recurrent state. In the S1 path, attention block sizing would be based on the selected page size and backend alignment, while each recurrent checkpoint would reserve the full set of pages needed for its SSM and convolution states. The planner would account for those member pages and the actual layer-group allocation layout when computing memory capacity.

Recurrent decode kernels would use the page mapping directly when reading and updating state. For each part of the SSM state, the kernel would find its page and then access the required position within that page. Source and destination mappings would be explicit so that an update writes to the intended state. Both the state of a running request and a saved checkpoint would use this representation.

Prefill could initially assemble the required state in a contiguous temporary buffer. This would let existing prefill kernels consume the initial state while the port adds support for the new storage format. The evaluation would include the extra copying and temporary memory, including the work needed to write resulting states back into pages.

### Cache-manager support for multi-page checkpoints

The cache manager would be extended to manage several physical pages as one recurrent checkpoint. A cache lookup would resolve the checkpoint identifier to its complete page mapping and check that every required state component is available. The existing prefix match would still identify one token boundary, with attention data and recurrent state available at that same boundary.

Allocation and copy operations would use the checkpoint's full page mapping. Allocation would obtain the required SSM and convolution pages and register them under one checkpoint identifier. Copy operations would follow the source and destination page lists to transfer the complete state. This would also support copy-on-write, where a request copies a shared checkpoint before modifying its own state.

Reference tracking and page reclamation would account for every page belonging to a checkpoint. A request using a checkpoint would protect all of its pages. Before a page is reassigned, the manager would invalidate any cached checkpoint that refers to its current contents. This requires tracking the relationship between member pages and their logical checkpoint.

The cache manager and memory planner would count physical pages separately from logical checkpoints. A checkpoint could occupy several pages while still representing one saved state at one token boundary. Memory accounting would charge the actual allocated pages, mapping buffers, and temporary workspace, counting shared pages only once. The main integration points would be `MambaSpec`, page-size planning, `MambaManager`, `BlockPool`, and runner metadata.

The first prototype would retain upstream's checkpoint-generation, retention, and admission policies while adapting their storage operations. The proposal changes how states are stored and managed. Smaller block sizes could change the resulting checkpoint intervals, so those settings would be recorded in comparisons.

### First implementation

The first implementation would be an optional Falcon-H1/Mamba2 path on one CUDA GPU. It would use tensor parallel size 1, one documented backend and data type combination, and eager execution without CUDA graphs. Turning the feature off would retain the existing representation, and explicitly requesting an unsupported combination would produce a clear error.

Broader execution support would follow validation of the initial path. CUDA graphs, speculative decoding, distributed execution, and cache offload or transfer would need to preserve the page mappings and checkpoint ownership rules. These combinations would remain unavailable for the new representation until their relevant paths are implemented and tested.

S2 convolution-slot packing would be evaluated as a separate extension to S1. S1 gives each checkpoint a dedicated convolution page, which can leave substantial space unused. S2 would place several small convolution states in one shared page and reduce that waste when the slots are sufficiently occupied. Its benefits and the effects of sharing a page would be measured separately from S1.

### Evaluation

Validation would check that paged storage preserves state computation and correct checkpoint reuse. The prototype would compare paged and contiguous state on the same inputs, then check that lookup, copying, page reuse, and execution resumed from a checkpoint behave correctly. These checks would cover both the recurrent kernels and the cache manager.

Performance evaluation would compare S1 with current upstream at the same usable cache-memory budget. The primary comparison would use the same model, backend, data types, and execution mode. The baseline would use suitable settings for upstream's existing prefix-reuse and checkpoint-retention features. Measurements would cover memory use, reused prefix tokens, throughput, and latency, including the additional storage, copying, and page-access costs. S1 can increase the allocated bytes per checkpoint because it still stores the full state and rounds allocations to pages. The comparison would therefore judge the overall serving benefit after those costs. Detailed workloads and test procedures would be chosen after feedback on the proposed design.

### Related approaches

Separate page sizes for different cache groups provide another way to handle unequal state sizes. [#55196](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55196) discusses that direction together with state quantization. S1 would retain a shared allocation unit and let a recurrent state occupy several units. A comparison with separate pools would help assess the value of flexible capacity sharing against the cost of page lookup.

Producing intermediate checkpoints during prefill complements the proposed storage format. [#52959](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52959) discusses generating those checkpoints within a prefill forward. S1 could store the resulting states once their producer and copy paths understand the page mapping.

Current block-outer packing combines whole layer-state regions of different sizes within a block layout. The inspected Mamba binding still exposes each recurrent state as a contiguous payload. S1 would add a mapping inside that state so that its parts can occupy independently allocated pages.

### Feedback requested

Feedback would be most useful on whether to prototype this representation and where it should fit in vLLM. The main questions are:

1. Is checkpoint-internal paging worth prototyping alongside current packing, fine-grained checkpoint reuse, and per-group page-size approaches?
2. Where should the mapping from a logical state to its member pages live: the existing Mamba manager, a general cache abstraction, or a backend-specific prototype?
3. Is the proposed single-GPU Mamba2 path a useful first target, and which compatibility requirements should accompany that first implementation?


## Feedback Period.

I propose an initial feedback period of two weeks after posting. Discussion can continue longer if the design changes substantially or maintainers need more evidence.


## CC List.

There are no initial CC recipients.

## Any Other Things.

The paper provides an existing research prototype and scoped S1 kernel checks. The implementation proposed here would adapt that approach to the cited upstream code. Performance measurements for this upstream port are still needed.

End-to-end continuation remains a validation requirement for the upstream port. The paper reports output divergence in retained-state serving experiments, as well as variability in a condition without cross-request retained-state reuse. The cause remains unresolved. Controlled continuation tests would investigate these observations before the port is considered ready for use.

## Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Accept already-decoded images over NIXL in the vllm-rs gRPC API
author: KrishnanPrash
body:
### Motivation. A gRPC client of vllm-rs often decodes images before it sends them: to route by image content, to validate them, or to send one image to several workers. Today it must send the encoded file anyway, and vllm-rs decodes it again on the request path, one image after another. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["gRPC client"] -->|"data_uri / raw_bytes
(encoded PNG, JPEG)"| T subgraph S["vllm-rs"] T["media tracker
(llm-multimodal)
decodes each image
on the CPU"] --> P["resize, normalize,
patchify"] end P -->|pixel_values| E["engine"] ``` On Qwen3.8-27B (1 x GB200), a request with 8 full 1920x1080 PNGs has a TTFT of 426 ms with `data_uri` and 337 ms when vllm-rs reads the decoded pixels instead (-21%; -9% to -19% at 1.2 to 4.2 req/s). A single new image or a small JPEG shows no change, because prefill hides the decode. ### Proposed Change. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph CL["gRPC client"] A["encoded image"] D["decoded pixels,
registered with NIXL
(host DRAM)"] end subgraph S["vllm-rs"] T["media tracker
decodes on the CPU"] --> J["merge in
request order"] V["validate nixl_ref"] --> R["NIXL reader
(reused buffers,
64 MiB pool)"] R --> J J --> P["resize, normalize,
patchify"] end A -->|"data_uri / raw_bytes"| T D -->|"nixl_ref: agent metadata,
address, height, width, channels"| V D ==>|"pixels, one-sided
NIXL READ"| R P -->|pixel_values| E["engine"] ``` `nixl_ref` images skip the decode. NIXL reads run while vllm-rs decodes the encoded images of the same request, and a merge puts all images back in request order. Model preprocessing and the encoded path do not change. - Add `NixlRef` to the `MediaItem.source` oneof: NIXL agent metadata, the address of 8-bit pixels in the client's host memory, and height, width, and channels. `GetModelInfo.supports_nixl_ref` reports support. - vllm-rs reads the pixels with a one-sided NIXL READ (the pull model of the NIXL KV connector), then runs its normal resize, normalization, and patchify. The client replaces only the decoder. - The proto states the pixel contract: EXIF orientation applied, 16-bit samples narrowed as vllm-rs narrows them, first frame of an animation, and a 30 s window after a request ends during which the client keeps the memory registered. - Opt-in: the `nixl-media` cargo feature and `--enable-grpc-nixl-media`. The server connects to the agent that a request names, so the feature is for trusted peers only (docs/usage/security.md). - The new `oneof` variant goes into the unreleased `vllm-proto` 0.7.0 on `main`. It breaks Rust callers that match on `Source`. Out of scope: the Python frontend PR: #64601 ### Feedback Period. One week. ### CC List. None yet.

title: [RFC]: Direct layerwise and chunk-wise KV WRITE with Mooncake
author: nwpu-zxr
body:
## Motivation

We propose an opt-in `MooncakeLayerwiseConnector` that transfers completed KV ranges from prefill (P) to decode (D) during prefill execution. The goal is to reduce the transfer tail exposed after prefill by overlapping direct Mooncake WRITEs with subsequent layer computation.

The ordinary request-level push path waits for the prefill handoff before sending the cache. When D has already allocated its destination blocks, completed layers and complete blocks from earlier prefill chunks could be transferred sooner. This opportunity depends on D admission and destination readiness; early transfer cannot remove that dependency.

This proposal develops the direct-transfer work discussed in [#60523](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60523) and [#61567](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61567). The implementation is available in [#62504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62504). The design below describes commit `5d91a490f94a7df9c1ff67b43ba6ad46a7f6c1b1`.

The intended benefit is a shorter exposed transfer tail, not a demonstrated speedup. More device events, smaller transfer batches, reduced cross-layer coalescing, and producer graph restrictions may offset the overlap. End-to-end measurements are part of the acceptance criteria.

## Proposed Change

### 1. An opt-in connector sharing the Mooncake implementation

Register `MooncakeLayerwiseConnector` as a separate connector with fixed producer and consumer roles. Both peers select this connector. Reuse Mooncake's transport, bootstrap, registered-region representation, TP routing, address planning, and scheduler completion/failure interfaces.

The new connector owns incremental request progress, layer readiness, per-destination scheduling, and completion coverage. Small shared hooks allow it to preserve cache identities during registration and use per-spec physical block ratios. Address planning is exposed as a synchronous helper usable by background executors. The connector reuses the shared receive path, which settles every contacted peer before reporting receive completion after a failure. This receive-failure behavior is already present in the rebased upstream baseline.

There is no new transport or Store dependency. D continues to wait for the complete required handoff before execution. This proposal does not pipeline D's forward with partially received layers.

### 2. Transfer lifecycle and execution ownership

The design separates three owners:

| Owner | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Model thread | Apply scheduler snapshots; track request, layer, and destination progress; record device events; submit immutable transfer tasks; publish completion. |
| Background executor | Build source/destination addresses; wait for the producing device event; check the send budget; issue synchronous Mooncake WRITE; return progress or errors. |
| Control loop | Receive D-ready messages; validate/cache peer layouts; queue destinations; own sockets and send completion responses. |

For each scheduled prefill chunk, the scheduler snapshots the current transfer-group block tables, scheduled token endpoint, prompt length, request ID, and transfer ID. Worker state must be initialized before any layer hook runs. The implementation sets `has_sync_kv_loads` on producer scheduling metadata to obtain this ordering; it does not make P perform a remote KV load.

After a layer's KV writes are submitted, `save_kv_layer()` records a device event and marks that layer's range available. The executor may prepare addresses before the event completes, but must wait for the event before reading source memory. This assumes all relevant KV writes are ordered on the fenced compute stream, including independent caches associated with the same transformer layer.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Decode worker
    participant C as P control loop
    participant P as P model thread
    participant E as P transfer executor
    D->>C: Ready: destination blocks, layout, receive budget
    C->>P: Queue validated destination
    P->>P: Initialize chunk snapshot before forward
    P->>P: Compute layer and record readiness event
    P->>E: Snapshot eligible block ranges
    E->>E: Plan addresses and wait for event
    par Later layers compute
        P->>P: Continue forward
    and Ready KV transfers
        E->>D: Direct WRITE
    end
    P->>E: wait_for_save drains current step
    E-->>P: Transfer results
    Note over P,D: Repeat for later chunks if present
    P->>C: Schedule final success or failure response
    C-->>D: Completion with cache-layer coverage
    Note over D: Execute only after all required peers settle successfully
```

For steps with prefill work, `wait_for_save()` drains submitted batches and the currently available work before the step returns. Steps without prefill work drain in `start_load_kv()`; `wait_for_save()` returns without processing them again. Pending destination batches prevent a new submission wave until they settle. Independent destinations within a wave can execute concurrently.

This is deliberately bounded within a scheduler step. Incremental progress persists across chunks, but outstanding DMA does not intentionally span steps. The design therefore gives up overlap between one chunk's transfer and the next chunk's compute in exchange for a simpler source-lifetime boundary.

### 3. Cache semantics determine what can be sent

Layer identity alone is insufficient. Each cache name retains its own transfer-group identity, block mapping, and sent progress, even when multiple caches belong to one transformer layer.

| Cache semantics | Transfer policy |
| --- | --- |
| Append-only full-attention / MLA KV | Send newly completed blocks at layer readiness across prefill chunks. Send the final partial block only when that layer's final chunk is ready. |
| Sliding-window cache | Send the final requested window after final-layer readiness. Preserve logical positions and skip destination null slots without compacting source positions. |
| Windowed `FullAttentionSpec` | Populate the whole requested suffix managed by the full-attention allocator, including blocks needed for valid prefix-cache publication. |
| Mamba / GDN state | Transfer final resident state slots, preserving state semantics rather than expanding them as token blocks. Initially require equal P/D TP sizes. |
| Circular buffer | Transfer the final resident pages; do not multiply storage by prompt length. Initially require equal P/D TP sizes. |

For append-only KV with group block size `B`, intermediate publication ends at `floor(available_tokens / B)`. Final publication may extend to `ceil(prompt_tokens / B)`. D's block list represents its required suffix, so the mapping must account for already cached prefix blocks.

For example, with `B = 16`, a 70-token prompt, and D already caching the first 32 tokens, D needs logical blocks 2–4. At 50 available tokens, only block 2 can be sent: block 3 is still partial. At final readiness, blocks 3 and 4 can be sent, with block 4 carrying the final valid tail. These are logical block positions; physical block IDs differ between P and D.

Each attention group's logical blocks expand into kernel blocks using that group's own ratio. Recurrent and circular-buffer pages use a ratio of one. An independent indexer cache remains a separate cache component and must be ready before the hook that publishes it.

### 4. Layout handshake and topology

D advertises cache names, group identities, registered regions, semantic signatures, block-size information, and worker identity. Worker identity includes engine, TP rank, PP rank, and PCP rank so equal TP ranks in different stages or replicas cannot alias.

P aligns regions by cache identity, checks semantic compatibility, and reuses Mooncake's TP address-routing checks. Different P/D PP partitions are matched through overlapping cache names. D contacts the applicable P stages and verifies that successful responses collectively cover its required cache names.

Peer layouts and alignment results are cached. Later ready messages can omit the full address table; a cache miss requests a full layout resend. Transfer snapshots retain references to the destination layout so LRU eviction cannot invalidate queued work.

The initial implementation boundaries are:

- Heterogeneous PP partitions and the TP mappings accepted by the shared Mooncake planner.
- PCP only with explicit `pcp_cache_mode: replicated` and complete cache replicas. Only P replica zero is advertised as a source and sends data; D replica identities remain distinct. This does not gather sharded PCP caches.
- DCP equal to one.
- Matching peer logical/kernel block sizes and compatible per-cache semantics, payloads, and layouts. No dtype conversion or cache transposition.
- Individually attributable cache regions. Opaque packed rows that lose writer identity are rejected.

These are implementation boundaries, not a validated cross-product of models and parallel configurations.

### 5. Completion, late readiness, and failures

Early copy completion does not finish the P request. P publishes the scheduler's send-completion notification only after the normal terminal handoff and safe transfer completion, or terminal error cleanup. Active prefill requests remain active even if their currently available ranges have already been copied.

A destination succeeds only after all of its required cache components reach the handoff endpoint. D aggregates peer results and cache-name coverage. A failure remains sticky; a later successful peer cannot turn an incomplete handoff into success. Failed receives use the existing scheduler failure policy rather than exposing partial KV to decode.

Planning failures discard all planned entries for the affected request while retaining unrelated healthy requests in the same batch. A transport-batch exception fails the requests depending on that batch. P drains all submitted destination batches before permitting completion or block release. On D, each contacted peer settles its own receive obligation before aggregate receive completion is reported.

For late D-ready messages, P retains completed prefill state and the final device fence. Empty scheduler steps drain available transfers in `start_load_kv()`, even without another forward. Completion polling does not submit new transfers. If P has become fully idle and no new scheduler step runs, a late-ready message may remain queued until scheduling resumes or D times out. An idle-worker wakeup mechanism is deferred.

D provides a relative receive-time budget. P uses a local monotonic deadline and checks `layerwise_send_timeout_margin_s` before submission and again after the device wait. The default margin is 10 seconds. This avoids comparing P/D wall clocks and rejects near-expiry requests without cancelling unrelated requests.

The margin is a conservative admission check, not transport cancellation or a renewable lease. It does not prove that an already-issued WRITE cannot outlive D's receive timeout. Delayed control messages, long-running WRITEs, peer failure, and destination reclamation require explicit fault testing and review before claiming robust timeout safety. Completion ACK delivery failures are currently logged; a stronger delivery/retry contract remains a discussion point.

### 6. Configuration and execution limits

Producer configuration fragment:

```json
{
  "kv_connector": "MooncakeLayerwiseConnector",
  "kv_role": "kv_producer",
  "kv_connector_extra_config": {
    "layerwise_send_timeout_margin_s": 10
  }
}
```

D uses the same connector with `kv_role: kv_consumer`. Existing model, bootstrap, and transport configuration is still required. For PCP greater than one, explicitly configure `pcp_cache_mode: replicated` on both peers and verify that the runtime actually supplies complete replicas.

P requires eager or PIECEWISE execution so Python layer hooks run; FULL graphs on P are rejected. D retains its whole-receive scheduling boundary. Producer PD requests should use `max_tokens=1`. Role switching, `kv_both`, sleep/storage replacement, chunked-local attention, sharded PCP, and DCP are outside the initial scope.

### 7. Alternatives and changes from the earlier proposal

[#61567](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61567) explored completed-chunk sending and final-chunk layerwise sending. The implementation chooses per-layer publication across chunks with a step-end drain.

| Alternative | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- |
| Ordinary request-level WRITE | Preserves coarse batching and simpler scheduling, but starts after request readiness. |
| Completed-chunk transfer spanning steps | Can overlap with later chunks and retain cross-layer coalescing, but needs allocator-backed retention across preemption and subsequent steps. |
| Final-chunk-only layerwise transfer | Limits incremental state, but leaves earlier chunk KV unsent until the final forward. |
| Current per-layer, per-chunk proposal | Sends eligible KV earlier with a bounded step lifetime, at the cost of Python hooks, more submissions, and blocking step-end drains. |
| Group several ready layers | May amortize submission overhead while delaying transfer start; should be evaluated before adding a tuning interface. |

Two choices need explicit review because they differ from #61567: using the synchronous-load scheduling flag to initialize producer state, and allowing host-side blocking at the step-end drain. A dedicated pre-forward producer hook may express the first requirement more clearly. Removing the drain would require a separate lifetime design; merely keeping a Python task reference does not pin allocator blocks.

### 8. Follow-up roadmap

The first planned extension after the initial implementation is **decode context parallelism (DCP) support**. The initial scope remains DCP=1; this milestone will extend layerwise WRITE to DCP-sharded decode caches.

- Define the supported P/D TP and DCP combinations and carry the required topology and cache-sharding information in the peer handshake.
- Map each logical KV range to its destination DCP owner and local physical offsets, accounting for the cache's token distribution and per-group block semantics. Preserve incremental chunk progress and final-tail handling.
- Extend completion aggregation and failure handling to cover every required destination shard before D executes or either side releases transfer-owned storage.
- Validate payload placement and model outputs with DCP greater than one, including block/chunk boundaries, prefix-cache hits, concurrent requests, and failed or delayed destination shards. Measure end-to-end performance under matched configurations before making performance claims.

The detailed topology and model support matrix will be specified in the DCP follow-up design. Other feature milestones will be planned later based on community feedback and validation results; no additional feature commitments are made in this RFC.

## Feedback Period

Two weeks from publication.

Feedback is particularly requested on:

1. Is a separate opt-in connector with shared Mooncake planning/registration hooks the right integration boundary?
2. Is the step-end drain an acceptable initial tradeoff, and what workloads should establish its value?
3. Should producer initialization use a dedicated metadata/pre-forward hook instead of `has_sync_kv_loads`?
4. What transport lifetime guarantee or lease/cancellation mechanism is required when WRITE outlives D's receive budget?
5. Should the first supported scope be narrowed to append-only KV until state/window and heterogeneous-topology tests are complete?

## Any Other Things

### Validation and acceptance

The [implementation PR](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62504) reports Ascend functional runs with P eager, D FULL_DECODE_ONLY, and CP disabled:

| Model and configuration | Reported functional evidence |
| --- | --- |
| DeepSeek-V3.1, P TP8 / D TP8, MTP off | Short and multi-chunk requests; output token sequences matched ordinary Mooncake PD. |
| GLM-5.2, P TP8 / D TP8, MTP off | Short and multi-chunk requests with main KV and independent indexer caches. |
| GLM-5.2, P TP8/MTP1 / D DP2×TP4/MTP3 | Seven requests completed, including long and concurrent requests; both D replicas served traffic and all three draft positions accepted tokens. |

These results establish bounded functional evidence, not general numerical accuracy or a performance improvement. The implementation includes host-logic tests with mocked device events/transport and device-independent mapping tests. The five device-independent mapping tests, Ruff lint/format checks, and diff checks pass at the referenced commit. A full connector unit rerun, GPU accuracy/performance, and broader model/topology coverage remain pending.

Before presenting the implementation as ready for merge, the proposed acceptance work is:

- **Mapping and payload correctness:** test `B-1`, `B`, and `B+1` boundaries, multi-chunk tails, cached prefixes, independent cache components, null window positions, recurrent state slots, and circular-buffer wraparound. Compare transferred valid payloads and first-consumption state against the source.
- **Lifecycle and failure safety:** exercise early/late D readiness, no-forward steps, preemption and re-admission, cancellation while WRITE is active, one failed destination alongside healthy destinations, peer timeout, lost ACK, and repeated block reuse. Demonstrate that no live transfer accesses reclaimed pages.
- **Integration:** run real-device comparisons with ordinary Mooncake PD, verify actual connector transfers, and record exact revisions, layouts, graph modes, topology, token outputs and suitable numerical comparisons. Cover both runner hook ordering and integration with the shared receive-failure path.
- **Performance:** compare ordinary and layerwise WRITE under equal eager/PIECEWISE settings, then compare against the ordinary production graph configuration. Measure TTFT distributions, throughput, exposed transfer tail, transfer/event/submission counts, CPU overhead, and retained KV bytes. Include single-chunk and multi-chunk prompts, concurrent requests, and forced late readiness. Device/transfer traces must demonstrate overlap; repeat runs and report variability.

### Related work

- [#60523](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60523): broader Mooncake roadmap.
- [#61567](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61567): earlier direct early-transfer design and lifetime discussion.
- [#62504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62504): implementation proposed here.
- [#61974](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61974): decode-initiated direct READ; a different transfer direction.
- [#51978](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51978): Store-side layerwise transfer and Session API integration; a different data path.

### Implementation references

- [Layerwise scheduler, worker, control loop and connector](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5d91a490f94a7df9c1ff67b43ba6ad46a7f6c1b1/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_layerwise_connector.py)
- [Device-independent block mapping](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5d91a490f94a7df9c1ff67b43ba6ad46a7f6c1b1/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/layerwise_mapping.py)
- [Shared Mooncake planning, registration and receive completion](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5d91a490f94a7df9c1ff67b43ba6ad46a7f6c1b1/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_connector.py)

title: [RFC]: Integrating LeapQuant into vLLM — INT8 Quantization of GDN/KDA Linear Attention Recurrent States
author: lihaoyang-amd
body:
# Title

[RFC]: INT8 recurrent-state quantization for GDN/KDA linear attention (LeapQuant)

# Field: Motivation.

#### Summary

[LeapQuant](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.38166) (arXiv:2609.38166) stores the recurrent state of GDN/KDA layers in INT8, at about 1.19 bytes per element instead of 4 for FP32. It re-quantizes the state only once every 16 tokens, and handles outliers with 4 FP16 compensator tokens and per-row smoothing. It needs no training and no calibration data.

This RFC proposes adding LeapQuant to vLLM as a quantized checkpoint format for ReplaySSM. It reuses the record ring buffer, cursors, and flush mechanism of #62004, and replaces only the checkpoint storage format and the work done at flush time (called *fold* below). The feature is off by default. Phase 1 covers standard (non-speculative) decode for GDN; phase 2 adds KDA.

#### Why

- **Bottleneck.** Most layers of hybrid models such as Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.8, Kimi-Linear, and GLM-5.3-Flash are GDN or KDA. Every decode step reads and writes the whole FP32 state; for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next that is about 3 MB per request per layer, independent of context length. At large batch sizes this step is bound by memory bandwidth.
- **The existing options are not enough.** `--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype` offers only float32, float16, and bfloat16. Storing a BF16 state at every step hurts long reasoning: in the paper, Qwen3.5-9B drops from 87.9 to 72.1 on AIME, and on Qwen3.8 we measured GPQA 1.7 points lower with twice as many truncated answers. Per-step INT8 or FP8 collapses outright (AIME 7.1 and 14.6).
- **What LeapQuant achieves.** In the paper, the average over 12 model–task pairs at 8 bits equals FP32 (75.5 vs 75.5), the state is 3.4× smaller, kernels are 2.05–3.70× faster on average, and end-to-end inference is 1.47× faster on average (NVIDIA GPUs). Prefix-cache state checkpoints shrink by the same factor. We reproduced the paper's decode setup for Qwen3.5-9B on MI355X: decode steps are 1.08–1.26× faster, in line with the paper's 1.02–1.23× on B200 (see §2.2 under Proposed Change).
- **Fits the upstream roadmap.** Per-window quantization is structurally ReplaySSM's "checkpoint + replay of recent records" plus a quantization step. The ReplaySSM RFC #49232 lists "Quantized SSM-state format" and "More SSM types: KDA" as mid-term items, and neither has started. This RFC proposes a concrete design for both.

# Field: Proposed Change.

#### 1. Goals and non-goals

Goals:

- Support the LeapQuant INT8 state for standard decode of GDN models (Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Next, Qwen4Exp/Qwen3.8), with no measurable accuracy difference from FP32.
- Work with `--mamba-cache-mode align` prefix caching, CUDA graphs, and TP.
- Implement the kernels in Triton so they run on both CUDA and ROCm (MI355X).
- In phase 2, support KDA models (Kimi-Linear, GLM-5.3-Flash).

Non-goals for phase 1:

- Speculative decoding and MTP (the RecoverSSM path).
- Mamba2 and other SSM types. Quantized Mamba2 checkpoints are covered by #52962.
- 6-bit, 4-bit, and MXFP4 (STEPQuant) formats, which need a separate RFC.
- Transferring LeapQuant state through KV connectors or offloading.

#### 2. Existing work

**2.1 Upstream vLLM**

Merged:

| PR | What it does | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| #48018 | ReplaySSM standard decode for Mamba2; adds `--use-replayssm` and `--replayssm-buffer-len` (default 16) | Reused as-is; the buffer length is the paper's window p |
| #49909 | ReplaySSM uses the backend-default dot precision on ROCm | Precedent for ROCm compatibility |
| #51855, #63045 | KDA RecoverSSM for Kimi-K3, speculative decoding only | Reference for the KDA record layout, but KDA still has no standard-decode ReplaySSM |
| #62141 | AMD CI runs the ReplaySSM tests on MI355 | A ROCm CI path already exists |
| #35753 | Stochastic rounding of the Mamba state | Incompatible with LeapQuant; must be rejected at startup |

In progress:

| PR | What it does | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| #62004 | ReplaySSM standard decode for GDN (Qwen3.5). Records (k, d, g) live in the paged block, per-row flush flags are computed on the host, and align mode forces a flush at block boundaries. The PR's results cover only H100 and B300 | **Direct base.** LeapQuant replaces only its checkpoint format and flush logic |
| #52962 (draft, stacked on #55688) | Quantized Mamba2 checkpoints; adds `--replayssm-state-dtype {auto,fp8,int8,nvfp4}` and `--replayssm-checkpoint-mode`. Built on FlashInfer/CuTe DSL, NVIDIA only | Config naming should align with it |
| #63176 | When a running request is skipped for a step, its unflushed ring records are dropped | Correctness prerequisite |
| #58863, #61309, #56466 | RecoverSSM (MTP) for Qwen GDN, and its prefix caching | Basis for future speculative-decoding support |
| #61245 | Allocates the Kimi-Linear KDA state according to `--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype` | Needed in the KDA phase |
| #40012, #26301 (drafts, inactive for months) | Per-step INT8/FP8 state for Mamba2 | The per-step approach, which the paper shows does not work for long GDN reasoning |
| #61124 | SketchSSM (Mamba-2, needs a calibration file) | Similar idea, no conflict |
| #63032 | `--monokernel` decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on ROCm (1–16 rows) | Reads the state cache in place, so it is incompatible with the new layout; the two must be mutually exclusive |

**2.2 Our prototype (ROCm, MI355X)**

- **Kernels:** about 1,200 lines of Triton covering GDN/KDA decode, a cross-layer fold (reconstruction, power iteration, smoothing, INT8 quantization), quantization and dequantization for prefill, prefix-cache checkpoint writes, and record replay.
- **Validation tools:** a PyTorch reference; kernel correctness checks, including a NaN regression test and a check that the same input run 200 times gives identical results; prefix-cache checks; flush-race checks; and long-reasoning evaluation (AIME, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, with per-question paired tests). All of these can become vLLM tests.

All numbers below were measured on the prototype system. Kernel numbers carry over directly; end-to-end numbers depend on the serving framework's scheduling and must be re-measured once the feature is in vLLM.

*Qwen3.5-9B with the paper's configuration*

One MI355X, TP1, BF16 weights, CUDA graphs on, prefix caching off. The baseline reads and writes the FP32 state every step; ReplaySSM uses an FP32 checkpoint and 16 records; LeapQuant uses p=16 and r=4.

Decode steps (paper Figure 8): context 4K, 1,024 output tokens, one round of equal-length requests per concurrency level. The metric is the mean ITL, flush steps included, over the window in which every request is decoding. Each mode ran once on each of two GPUs and the results were averaged; the two GPUs differ by at most 3%.

| Concurrency | FP32 | ReplaySSM | LeapQuant | Paper, B200 (LeapQuant) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | 6.64 ms | 6.29 ms (1.06×) | 6.16 ms (1.08×) | 1.02× |
| 128 | 13.07 ms | 11.86 ms (1.10×) | 11.15 ms (1.17×) | 1.13× |
| 512 | 39.15 ms | 34.04 ms (1.15×) | 31.10 ms (1.26×) | 1.23× |

Kernels (paper Figure 7): one GDN layer with 32 v heads, 16 q/k heads, and d_k = d_v = 128. Speedups over the FP32 kernel:

| Batch size | ReplaySSM | LeapQuant | LeapQuant decode kernel alone (no fold) | Paper, B200 (LeapQuant) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | 0.82× | 0.50× | 2.0× | 1.59× |
| 128 | 1.36× | 1.30× | 3.6× | 2.22× |
| 512 | 1.65× | 2.77× | 4.7× | 2.68× |

- The decode-step speedup matches the paper, but most of it comes from ReplaySSM itself: LeapQuant is only 2–9% faster than ReplaySSM.
- At batch size 512 the kernel matches the paper; at small batch sizes it falls well behind. The fold runs as a separate launch that takes about 0.03–0.07 ms regardless of batch size, whereas the paper fuses the fold into the layer kernel. Summed over the 24 GDN layers of Qwen3.5-9B, with one fold launch for all layers, LeapQuant reaches 1.63×, 2.58×, and 3.05×, and ReplaySSM 1.22×, 1.54×, and 1.76×.
- In the same 24-layer measurement, per-window BF16 (ReplaySSM with a BF16 checkpoint) reaches 1.69×, 2.51×, and 2.87×, about as fast as LeapQuant. LeapQuant's advantage over it is therefore memory (1.19 vs 2 bytes per element), not speed.
- State memory per request: FP32 51.5 MB, ReplaySSM 57.9 MB, LeapQuant 22.9 MB (−56%). With the same memory settings, the KV cache holds 7.8% more.
- Absolute throughput is not comparable: FP32 reaches 13.1k tok/s at concurrency 512, against about 18k read from the paper's B200 figure, on different hardware and a different framework.

*Larger models*

| Metric | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (TP2, GDN) | Kimi-Linear-48B (TP1, KDA) |
|---|---|---|
| Linear-attention kernels (all layers, per step, B=512) | 12.02 → 5.20 ms (2.31×) | 9.45 → 5.08 ms (1.86×) |
| Decode step time | 1.08–1.13× faster (concurrency 128–512) | 1.03–1.12× faster (concurrency 32–512) |
| State memory per request | 57.9 → 25.7 MB (−56%) | 43.4 → 25.1 MB (−42%) |
| Accuracy vs FP32 | AIME 95.6 vs 95.6, GPQA 91.6 vs 90.4, GSM8K on par | AIME and MMLU-Pro on par; GPQA about 2 points lower in all three runs |

Issues found and fixed in the prototype, which a vLLM implementation must handle too:

- Heads whose state is exactly low rank underflow during the fold and produce NaN.
- On ROCm, the fold and record replay were nondeterministic because they mixed vectors reduced from a tile with separately loaded vectors.
- At flush time, several programs of the same launch read and wrote the same record row, which caused a race.

Known limitations:

- No speculative decoding.
- The fold does not overlap with memory reads. On Qwen3.8 it takes 43% of LeapQuant's GDN time (at most 7% in the paper), and the impact is larger at small batch sizes (see the kernel table above).
- KDA's per-channel FP32 gate records take 5.6 MB per request.

#### 3. Design

The core idea is **LeapQuant = ReplaySSM + a quantized checkpoint**. Everything from #62004 is reused: the record ring buffer, the per-row cursors and flush flags, the paged layout, and the forced flush in align mode. Only three things change:

1. **Checkpoint format.** The FP32 state `[HV, K, V]` is replaced by an INT8 residual `[HV, K, V]`, FP32 per-value-channel scales `[HV, V]`, FP32 per-key-row smoothing factors `[HV, K]`, and r=4 FP16 compensator tokens (`[HV, K, r]` and `[HV, V, r]`). With K = V = 128, each head takes 19,456 bytes, 30% of FP32. Like the records, these tensors are stored as extra state in the paged block.
2. **Flush becomes fold.** When a window is full, the state is reconstructed in FP32. Power iteration fits the rank-r compensator term, which is subtracted from the state; the remainder is smoothed per row and quantized to INT8.
3. **Decode readout.** The output is computed directly from the dequantized residual, the smoothing factors, the compensator tokens, and the records in the window, without materializing the state. Compensator tokens take the same rank-1 update path as real records.

Other parts:

- **Prefill:** the state is dequantized to FP32 on read, passed to the existing `chunk_gated_delta_rule`, and folded once at the end on write-back. No fusion in phase 1.
- **Prefix caching (align):** align mode saves state only at block boundaries, and #62004 forces a flush on the step that completes a block. The record buffer is therefore empty at every checkpoint: saving copies only the tensors above, and restoring needs no record replay.
- **TP:** each head is quantized independently, so sharding by head works without cross-device communication.
- **Configuration (to be discussed):** align with #52962 by adding `--replayssm-state-dtype leapquant`, which requires `--use-replayssm`. If #52962 has not landed first, this proposal introduces the field. The window length reuses `--replayssm-buffer-len` (default 16). The compensator rank r is fixed at 4 and not exposed for now.
- **Rejected at startup:** speculative decoding, stochastic rounding, `--monokernel`, non-GDN/KDA layers, and KV connectors or offloading that transfer the mamba state. There is no silent fallback.

#### 4. Remaining work

Upstream prerequisites:

1. Help #62004 land, and validate it on MI355X: run its kernel tests and end-to-end parity tests, and add ROCm launch configs to `replayssm_config.py`.
2. Help #63176 land.
3. Settle the config naming with the authors of #52962.

Kernels, in `vllm/third_party/flash_linear_attention/ops/` and following the kernel–runtime contract of #62004:

4. Port the prototype's GDN decode, fold, quantization, and dequantization kernels to that contract, keeping the three fixes listed in §2.2.
5. Tune on CUDA (H100, B200); the prototype was tuned only on MI355X. `tf32x3` is CUDA-only (see #49909, #63918). With large state pools, address offsets must be 64-bit, or the pool size must be bounded at startup.

Integration:

6. Compute the state shapes and dtypes in `mamba_utils.py`. A block mixes INT8, FP16, and FP32 tensors, the page size must align with the attention page, and the memory profiler must account for these tensors.
7. Dispatch to the LeapQuant kernels in the GDN mixer (`qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py`), and wire up `qwen3_5.py`, `qwen3_next.py`, and `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/{nvidia,amd}`. #62004 wires up only Qwen3.5.
8. Reuse the cursors and flush flags in the metadata builder (`gdn_attn.py`), and decide what launches the fold (see §8).
9. Handle dequantization and quantization in prefill and chunked prefill, and prefix caching in align mode.
10. KDA (phase 2): vLLM has no standard-decode ReplaySSM for KDA yet; Kimi-K3 has only RecoverSSM for speculative decoding. An FP32 version comes first, then LeapQuant on top. Kimi-Linear lives in `vllm/models/kimi_k3` and GLM-5.3-Flash in `vllm/models/glm5next`; both have AMD and NVIDIA implementations, and both need wiring.

Tests and evaluation:

11. Unit tests:
    - Kernels: compare against the PyTorch reference over multiple windows, including zero, tiny, and exactly low-rank states, and run repeated-determinism tests on a GPU under load.
    - Builder: cursors, flushes, preemption, skipped steps, and re-anchoring in align mode.
    - End to end: TP1 and TP2, with matching outputs on prefix-cache hits and misses. LeapQuant is not bit-identical to FP32, so end-to-end tests use a logprob tolerance plus a GSM8K threshold.
12. Offline accuracy: run AIME, GPQA, and MMLU-Pro with the paper's settings and per-question paired tests. **Add a ReplaySSM + FP16/BF16 checkpoint baseline (per-window 16-bit).** In Table 2 of the paper, per-window BF16 is already near-lossless (AIME 87.8 vs 87.9), and in the prototype's kernel tests it is as fast as LeapQuant (§2.2). LeapQuant's advantage over it is mainly memory (1.19 vs 2 bytes per element), which needs data to back it. So far this baseline has only kernel numbers; end-to-end throughput, memory, and long-reasoning accuracy are still missing.
13. Performance: extend `benchmarks/replayssm/e2e_decode_speedup.py` to compare FP32, ReplaySSM FP32, and ReplaySSM FP16/BF16. The prototype has been measured on MI355X with the configurations of the paper's Figures 7 and 8 (§2.2). The vLLM version needs re-measuring on MI355X and H100/B200, plus the end-to-end throughput of the paper's Figure 9, which replays GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA with the original model's input and output lengths.
14. Documentation: the feature, the supported models and platforms, and a note that it changes model outputs.

#### 5. Safety and security

- **Off by default:** when disabled, the code path is byte-for-byte unchanged, and the new kernels are imported only when enabled.
- **Unsupported combinations fail at startup** (list in §3), so nothing silently degrades into wrong results.
- **Numerical safety:** the prototype hit NaN on heads whose state was exactly low rank, which turned the output into a string of "!!!!". Every normalization in the fold must first scale by the maximum absolute value and zero out negligible components, and the regression tests must stay.
- **Memory safety:** every new side buffer needs bounds checks. Triton address offsets must not overflow 32 bits; upstream has fixed a similar bug before (#55730, a KDA RecoverSSM pointer overflow).
- **Concurrency and determinism:** when several programs of one launch read and write the same records, their order must be well defined. Tests should run the same input 200 times on a GPU with other load, because races rarely show on an idle GPU.
- **Request isolation:** when a block is recycled, the new request's scales, smoothing factors, compensator tokens, records, and cursors must all be overwritten before their first read. Otherwise the new request reads the previous request's leftover state, which corrupts its output and can leak context from another request. Upstream has had stale-state bugs of this kind (#56524, #63776).
- **State format across instances:** cached state must carry a format identifier (format, r, p, record dtype). Until KV connectors and offloading support the format, these combinations are rejected, so FP32 and LeapQuant states are never mixed.
- **No new dependencies:** only Triton, with no calibration files, no external data loading, and no new deserialization surface.

#### 6. Implementation plan

| Phase | Content | Depends on | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Alignment | Post this RFC and link it from #49232; agree on the config and kernel contract with the ReplaySSM and #52962 authors; ask the paper authors about their release plans | – | Config form and fold placement agreed |
| 1. Prerequisites | Validate #62004 on MI355X and add ROCm configs; help #63176 land | #62004 | All GDN ReplaySSM FP32 tests pass on ROCm |
| 2. GDN | PR-1: kernels and unit tests, not yet wired into models. PR-2: config, layout, builder, prefill, prefix caching, model wiring, end-to-end tests, and docs | Phase 1 | Unit tests pass on CUDA and ROCm; no significant drop in per-question long-reasoning comparisons; faster step time than ReplaySSM FP32 at B≥128; state memory reduced by more than 50% |
| 3. KDA | PR-3: standard-decode ReplaySSM for KDA (FP32). PR-4: KDA LeapQuant with FP16 gate records | Phase 2 | Kimi-Linear evaluated with the paper's settings, confirming whether the ~2-point GPQA drop is real |
| 4. Optimization and extensions | Overlap the fold with memory reads and fuse prefill; speculative decoding together with RecoverSSM; KV connector support | Phases 2 and 3 | Evaluated separately as needed |

#### 7. Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Upstream dependencies have not landed: #62004 is in review, #52962 is a draft, and interfaces may change | Keep LeapQuant's changes in separate kernel files and a single format value to limit rebases; agree on the contract early |
| Duplicate work: the paper's implementation is built on vLLM and may also be upstreamed, and the ReplaySSM roadmap lists a quantized state format | Post the RFC first and loop in the relevant authors to coordinate. This proposal can contribute a Triton implementation, ROCm support, KDA support, and prefix-caching validation |
| Limited speed gains: on Qwen3.5-9B decode steps are 1.08–1.26× faster, but only 2–9% faster than ReplaySSM, and kernel speed matches per-window BF16; on Qwen3.8 they are only 8–13% faster (GDN is about 20% of the FP32 step); on Kimi only about 1% faster than per-step BF16, with a larger state than BF16 | Position the main benefit as "FP32-level accuracy with less memory than BF16", backed by long-reasoning accuracy, memory, and concurrency data; fuse the fold into the layer kernel to help small batches; measure on CUDA, where lower-bandwidth GPUs gain more |
| Accuracy: GPQA on Kimi-Linear is about 2 points lower in all three runs, and accuracy has been validated on only 3–4 models | Off by default; document the validated models; evaluate with per-question paired tests |
| Platform differences: the kernels were tuned only on MI355X, and the paper's NVIDIA numbers come from TileLang kernels | Measure on both platforms; use per-platform launch configs if needed |
| Complex state lifecycle: preemption, skipped steps, chunked prefill, prefix caching, CUDA graphs, and TP interact | Reuse and extend the builder tests of #62004; turn every issue found in the prototype into a regression test |
| Maintenance cost: Model Runner V1 is being removed (#63373) | Support Model Runner V2 only |

#### 8. Open questions

1. Configuration: `--replayssm-state-dtype leapquant`, or a separate flag? Should r be exposed?
2. Where should the fold run: inside the decode kernel for rows that flush (as #62004 does), as a separate launch before each layer's decode, or as one launch across all layers (as the prototype does, which needs a cross-layer pointer table)? Benchmarks should decide.
3. For KDA, should an FP32 standard-decode ReplaySSM land first, with LeapQuant added on top?
4. What accuracy criteria should the end-to-end tests use (logprob tolerance, GSM8K threshold)?

# Field: Feedback Period.

One week from posting.

# Field: CC List.

@askliar (#49232, #52962) @Johnny-Liou (#62004) @hnover-nv (ReplaySSM) @tdoublep (hybrid models) @mjkvaak-amd (#63032)
@dllehr-amd 
# Field: Any Other Things.

- LeapQuant paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38166
- ReplaySSM blog: https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/

title: [RFC]: Single Batch Overlap (down GEMM ↔ combine) for DeepEP LL
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation.

**I (@algebra-MCX) propose to integrate Single Batch Overlap (SBO) for the DeepEP low-latency path, once the required kernel arguments exist upstream, and would be glad to work on the vLLM-side implementation and validation if maintainers are open to it.** This revisits [#34963](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/34963) (closed as stale) and the prototype [#29211](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/29211) (closed as abandoned because it depended on two unmerged forks). This issue records what has changed, what is still blocking, and a vLLM-side plan that does not pin a fork.

SBO targets decode batches that are too small for DBO to pay off (the crossover studied in [#64100](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64100)). With one batch there is no second microbatch to hide the all-to-all. SBO instead lets the DeepEP LL combine start sending each expert's rows as soon as the down GEMM has finished them, coordinated through a shared signal tensor.

#### Current vLLM behavior

At `dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068`, without DBO, on an async prepare/finalize (DeepEP LL, NIXL EP):

| Phase | Current behavior | Overlap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dispatch | [`_prepare`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1276-L1306) calls the receive hook immediately | none |
| Expert down GEMM | [`fp8_m_grouped_gemm_nt_masked`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/batched_deep_gemm_moe.py#L471) finishes completely before combine starts | none |
| Combine | [`_finalize`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1457-L1488) sends, runs shared experts (`MK_INTERNAL_OVERLAPPED`), then receives | shared experts |

So the shared-expert half of SBO already exists. The missing part is down GEMM ↔ combine send.

#### Upstream kernel status (checked 2026-10-30)

| Component | Status |
| --- | --- |
| DeepEP `main` (`f6aa38fe06`, 2026-10-21) | no `src_signals` / signal-aware combine |
| DeepEP [#249](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/249), [#388](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/388) (computation/communication overlap) | open, conflicting |
| DeepGEMM `main` (`5081f8513a`, 2026-10-20) | masked GEMM has no signal output |
| DeepGEMM [#183](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/pull/183) (SBO: down GEMM with combine send) | open, conflicting |
| SGLang | ships its own packaged forks (`sgl-deep-ep`, `sgl-deep-gemm`) whose `low_latency_combine` takes `overlap`, `src_signals`, `src_signal_expect_value` |

vLLM's DeepEP LL integration does not depend on these forks, and #29211 showed that pinning forks is not a mergeable path.

### Proposed Change.

**Phase 0 – kernels (prerequisite, outside vLLM).** Help land a signal-aware LL combine and a signal-producing masked FP8 grouped GEMM upstream (DeepEP #249/#388, DeepGEMM #183 or successors). vLLM work does not start merging until a released upstream version exposes them.

**Phase 1 – vLLM, opt-in, Hopper, DeepEP LL + DeepGEMM masked FP8.**

1. Capability check, no fork pin: enable SBO only when the installed DeepEP/DeepGEMM expose the signal arguments; otherwise keep today's path unchanged. Opt-in flag, default off.
2. Per layer step, allocate a zeroed `int32` signal tensor of `num_local_experts × ceil(max_tokens_per_rank / block_m)` from existing workspace (graph-capturable, no per-step `torch.zeros`).
3. Down GEMM runs with `num_sms - comm_sms` SMs and increments the signal per finished block; combine is launched on the existing aux stream with `overlap=True`, waits on a start event, and sends rows whose signal reached the expected value.
4. Shared experts move to the dispatch window (between dispatch send and receive hook), because the combine window is now taken by the down GEMM.
5. DBO interaction: a step uses either DBO or SBO, never both. The first version disables SBO whenever the step is microbatched.

Out of scope for phase 1: NIXL EP (`nixl_ep` 1.5 has no signal argument), FlashInfer CuteDSL / Blackwell (the #34963 path), DeepEP HT/v2, BF16 masked GEMM.

#### Completion criteria

- [ ] Upstream DeepEP and DeepGEMM releases expose the signal interfaces; vLLM requires no fork.
- [ ] With SBO off or unsupported, the code path and outputs are unchanged.
- [ ] Unit tests: capability detection, signal sizing, SM split, shared-expert placement, DBO exclusion.
- [ ] DeepSeek-V3/R1 FP8, DP/EP decode on H200: identical outputs/logprobs with SBO on and off; FULL CUDA graph capture and replay.
- [ ] `vllm bench serve` TPOT/throughput, plus a trace showing combine sends overlapping the down GEMM, across batch sizes below and around the DBO crossover.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks; implementation waits for the Phase 0 kernels regardless.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is a capability-detected, opt-in integration acceptable once released upstream kernels expose the arguments?
2. Should vLLM wait for DeepEP/DeepGEMM `main`, or accept a released tag that includes the change?
3. Is shared experts in the dispatch window the preferred placement when SBO is on?

No implementation, GPU run or performance result exists yet. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: DBO support for FlashInfer NVLink all-to-all backends (single-node H200/B200 first)
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation.

**I (@algebra-MCX) propose to add DBO support for the FlashInfer NVLink all-to-all backends (`flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`, `flashinfer_nvlink_two_sided`), starting with single-node H200/B200, and would be glad to work on the implementation and validation if maintainers are open to it.**

These backends are vLLM's NVLink-native EP path, but `--enable-dbo` cannot be combined with them today. Users of these backends lose the option to overlap the all-to-all with the other microbatch's compute, which DeepEP and NIXL EP users already have.

#### Current vLLM behavior

At `dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068`:

| Layer | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Config | On CUDA, [`use_ubatching`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/config/vllm.py#L2196-L2220) allows only `deepep_low_latency`, `deepep_high_throughput` and `nixl_ep`. |
| Modular kernel | Both prepare/finalize classes keep the default `supports_async() == supports_dbo() == False`, so [`_prepare`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1258) and [`_finalize`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1447) would assert under DBO. |
| Per-step state | One-sided stores [`runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided.py#L99) on the instance; the two-sided manager owns a [single workspace](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/distributed/device_communicators/all2all.py#L707-L710). Two microbatches in flight would share both. |

(The DBO rejection in `flashinfer_moe_ep.py` belongs to the SM100/103 FlashInfer MoE EP megakernel and is out of scope here.)

#### Hardware: GB200 is not required for the first slice

From static reading of FlashInfer 0.7.2 and the vLLM source above (not yet run on H200):

| Aspect | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| Memory sharing | `MnnvlMemory` falls back from FABRIC handles to POSIX file descriptors when the device has no fabric cluster, so a single NVSwitch node works. |
| Kernels | The default `backend="trtllm"` (legacy) kernels have no Python architecture gate; the MNNVL comm JIT module targets SM 9.x/10.x. Only the opt-in `backend="cake"` requires SM 10.0/10.3. |
| Multi-node | Needs FABRIC handles (MNNVL, e.g. GB200 NVL72). Out of scope for the first slice. |
| CI | These backends' kernel tests already run on `b200-k8s`. |

### Proposed Change.

**Scope of the first slice:** single node, DP/EP over NVLink, CUDA, eager DBO (prefill and decode). FULL CUDA graph DBO, multi-node MNNVL and `backend="cake"` come later.

1. **Execution model.** The FlashInfer APIs used here do not expose a send/receive hook pair, so follow the existing synchronous pattern of [`naive_dp_ep._comm_region`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/naive_dp_ep.py#L145-L173): under DBO, yield and run dispatch/combine on the comm stream, then switch back. `supports_dbo()` returns True; `supports_async()` stays False so shared-expert placement is unchanged.
2. **Per-microbatch state.** Index per-step state (`runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`, dispatch handles/metadata) by `dbo_current_ubatch_id()`. Allocate one FlashInfer workspace per microbatch so two in-flight collectives never share buffers or completion flags.
3. **SM budget.** Run the comm-stream kernels within the existing DBO comm-SM budget, and confirm that a spinning receive cannot starve the peer microbatch's sender (deadlock check).
4. **Config.** Add the two backends to the CUDA DBO allow-list only after (1)–(3) pass.

Out of scope: changing FlashInfer kernels, async hooks inside FlashInfer, SBO ([#64776](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64776)).

#### Completion criteria

- [ ] DBO off: code path and outputs unchanged for both backends.
- [ ] Unit tests: per-microbatch state indexing, workspace ownership, `supports_dbo`, config allow-list.
- [ ] 2× and 8× H200 (and B200 if available), DP/EP, eager DBO: identical outputs/logprobs with DBO on/off for one MoE model (e.g. DeepSeek-V2-Lite and a DeepSeek-V3-class model); no hang across repeated steps with uneven microbatches.
- [ ] Note: four tests in `tests/distributed/test_mnnvl_alltoall.py` skip without `SYS_PTRACE` in `CapEff`; validation must run them on a host where they execute, and skips are not counted as passes.
- [ ] `vllm bench serve` throughput/TPOT with DBO on/off, plus a trace showing the all-to-all overlapping the peer microbatch's compute.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is the synchronous comm-stream pattern (as in `naive_dp_ep`) acceptable for these backends, or should vLLM wait for FlashInfer send/receive hooks?
2. Should per-microbatch workspaces live in the all2all manager or in the prepare/finalize objects?
3. Is a single-node H200/B200 qualification sufficient for the first slice, with GB200 MNNVL as a follow-up?

No implementation, GPU run or performance result exists yet. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Hybrid KV Backend: Eliminating Disk Restore Pipeline Bubbles Without CPU Memory Bloat
author: silence-breaker
body:
## Insight
While SimpleCPU ( #49644 ) already uses dedicated 2-buffer double-buffering for pure disk-to-GPU streaming, it operates in a single tier that completely discards CPU DRAM caching. Conversely, Native Tiering preserves CPU L 1 caching but suffers from an all-or-nothing staging design: it attempts to materialize the entire secondary SSD prefix into host DRAM prior to GPU transfer, directly causing memory exhaustion ( #62931 ) and forcing destructive capacity truncation ( #62932 ) .

My core architectural insight is that **with maintained CPU DRAM caching, tiered restoration can be fully pipelined to eliminate transmission bubbles without dedicating extra memory or materializing secondary prefixes in CPU DRAM**:

1. **Zero-Expansion Staging via Ephemeral Credit Leases:**
   Instead of allocating dedicated persistent staging buffers (as in SimpleCPU) or expanding host memory to hold multi-gigabyte prefixes (as in Native Tiering) , this design dynamically borrows a tiny sliver of existing rows from `SharedOffloadRegion` on-the-fly . Leased slots are recycled immediately across waves and returned to the shared pool, allowing arbitrarily large SSD prefixes to be restored without increasing host DRAM footprint .

2. **Absorbing the Initial SSD Bubble with L 1 Hits:**
   Due to physical bandwidth asymmetry ($B_{\text{H2D}} \gg B_{\text{SSD}}$), initiating the first SSD read introduces a multi-hundred-millisecond latency bubble where the GPU H 2 D engine sits completely idle . Our pipeline schedules existing CPU L 1 hits to drain directly to GPU during this exact window. By the time the first SSD wave arrives in host memory, the L 1 portion is already populated in HBM, eliminating the initial read bubble from critical-path latency.

3. **Steady-State Asynchronous Overlap:**
   Throughout subsequent waves, the pipeline overlaps the asynchronous NVMe read of Wave $N+1$ (via PCIe Upstream Rx) with the H 2 D DMA transfer of Wave $N$ (via PCIe Downstream Tx). Because H 2 D duration is significantly shorter than NVMe read time, GPU copy latency is completely hidden behind storage I/O, sustaining peak SSD throughput into the final GPU allocations with near-zero transmission stalls .

```
Required KV Prefix
    │
    ├──► [L1 DRAM Hits] ───────── (Direct H2D via PCIe Tx) ──────────┐
    │                                                                 ▼
    └──► [L2 SSD Blocks] ──► [Pinned Buffers A/B] ──► (Wave H2D) ──► [Final Unified GPU Allocation]
          (Async O_DIRECT     (Reused dynamically;
           via PCIe Rx)        Zero CPU materialization)
```

This also removes the requirement that the selected prefix fit in CPU memory before loading. Issue [#62931](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62931) reports that limitation in native tiering; [#62932](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62932) proposes capacity truncation. Here, SSD blocks can stream even when total restore bytes exceed CPU capacity, provided GPU admission succeeds.

## Pipeline Model

Consider one worker restoring $n \ge 1$ equal cold blocks with two load buffers:

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| $b$ | Cold-block bytes |
| $r$ | SSD read service time per block, approximately $b/B_{\mathrm{SSD}}$ |
| $g$ | H2D service time per cold block, approximately $b/B_{\mathrm{H2D}}$ |
| $H$ | CPU-hit bytes |
| $h$ | Total hot-copy time, approximately $H/B_{\mathrm{H2D}}$ |

Use effective service times; the bandwidth expressions omit syscall, submission, and coordination overhead. Assume disk reads and H2D can overlap, while hot and cold copies share one effective H2D resource.

The ideal cold-only pipeline takes:

$$
T_{\mathrm{cold}} = r + (n-1)\max(r,g) + g
$$

Its H2D idle budget is:

$$
W = T_{\mathrm{cold}} - ng
  = r + (n-1)\max(r-g,0)
$$

For an SSD-bound path ($r>g$), this includes the initial read bubble $r$ and $n-1$ later bubbles of $r-g$.

```text
Example timing: r = 4g; each character represents g.

Interval         initial read   next read      next read      drain
SSD              [rrrr]         [rrrr]         [rrrr]
Cold-only H2D    [....]         [c...]         [c...]         [c]
Hybrid H2D       [hhhh]         [chhh]         [chhh]         [c]

r = SSD read work   c = cold H2D   h = hot H2D   . = idle
Hot copies occupy available bubbles only while hot data remains.
```

With ideally divisible hot work and priority for ready cold blocks:

$$
T_{\mathrm{hybrid}}^{\mathrm{ideal}}
= T_{\mathrm{cold}} + \max(0,h-W)
$$

Thus **$h \le W$ is the ideal budget condition for hiding hot-copy work**. Hiding everything in the *first* bubble requires the stronger condition $h \le r$. If $r \le g$, only the initial bubble remains; if there are no cold blocks, restore reduces to the CPU-hit path.

For illustration, $r=1$ ms, $g=0.25$ ms, and $n=128$ give $T_{\mathrm{cold}}=128.25$ ms and $W=96.25$ ms. An 8 ms hot transfer fits the cumulative budget but not the first bubble. These are model inputs, not measurements.

**Scheduling implication:** submit hot hits in bounded batches that fit the available slack; avoid queuing one large hot copy ahead of ready cold data. Worker-local interleaving must preserve buffer reuse and cold-stream progress. Separate CUDA streams alone do not provide this behavior.

The equation is an ideal reference, not a latency guarantee. Finite copy batches, read jitter, shared host-memory bandwidth, GPU contention, and submission overhead can reduce usable slack. PCIe full duplex does not imply zero contention or unchanged decode ITL.

Also, $T_{\mathrm{cold}}$ covers only SSD misses: a disk-only baseline must read and transfer the hot bytes too. The expected benefit combines **avoided SSD reads** with **overlapped hot copies**.

## Pipelined Restore Lifecycle

The lifecycle orchestrates two disjoint transfer flows into a single unified GPU allocation without expanding static host memory footprints. It operates entirely as a bounded restore path; the store path remains governed by existing Tiering/SimpleCPU mechanisms.

### Dynamic Staging Accounting

Rather than statically partitioning host DRAM into dedicated buffer pools, the pipeline utilizes ephemeral credit leases from the primary tier (`SharedOffloadRegion`):

```text
Host DRAM (SharedOffloadRegion)
+───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
| CPU Hot-Cache Entries (L1 Hits)                               |
|   (Dynamic capacity available for caching and staging)        |
+──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────+
                               │ Leased on-demand (Max S bytes)
                               ▼
                [ Buffer Slot A ]  [ Buffer Slot B ]
                (Ephemeral Staging Credit, returned after H2D)
```
- **Lease on Admit:** When a restore plan is admitted, the worker leases at most 2 physical row slots for double-buffering.
- **Return on Step:** As soon as a slot completes its H2D transfer, its lease credit is immediately released back to the primary pool, eliminating persistent memory bloat.

## Preliminary Experiments

| Platform / condition | Configuration |
| --- | --- |
| Hardware | NVIDIA A100 40GB , Samsung 990 PRO NVMe SSD |
| Model | Qwen3-4B, BF16, full attention |
| Host KV budget | DRAM and Hybrid: 2 GiB each, including Hybrid's staging buffers. SimpleCPU SSD: two slots per direction, 9 MiB payload, no hot cache. |
| Storage | 4 GiB KV file per disk backend, ext4, `O_DIRECT` |
| Engine | Eager mode, 1.5 GiB GPU KV cache, 16-token blocks, 256-token prefill batches |
| Workload | 4,097 input and 64 output tokens; greedy sampling; concurrency 1 and 2 |
| Cache control | GPU KV reset before each warm batch; zero measured GPU prefix hits |
| Repetitions | Three processes per backend and scenario; 12/24 warm requests at concurrency 1/2 |

TTFT is measured from submission to the first streamed token through `AsyncLLM`, excluding HTTP transport. Output throughput is generated tokens divided by measured batch duration, excluding seeding and reset overhead; it is not saturation throughput. `C` denotes concurrency.

| Reusable KV working set | Backend | TTFT p50, C=1 (ms) | TTFT p50, C=2 (ms) | Output tok/s, C=1 | Output tok/s, C=2 |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1.125 GiB, 2 prefixes | SimpleCPU SSD | 193.4 | 347.9 | 41.2 | 65.7 |
| 1.125 GiB, 2 prefixes | DRAM | 91.1 | 151.4 | 46.2 | 84.4 |
| 1.125 GiB, 2 prefixes | Hybrid | 104.3 | 181.6 | 45.5 | 83.4 |
| 2.25 GiB, 4 prefixes | SimpleCPU SSD | 191.5 | 400.6 | 41.6 | 64.2 |
| 2.25 GiB, 4 prefixes | DRAM | 386.2 | 426.2 | 34.5 | 64.8 |
| 2.25 GiB, 4 prefixes | Hybrid | 106.0 | 208.8 | 40.6 | 71.8 |

The smaller working set gives both DRAM and Hybrid 100% host hits; Hybrid still has hot-path overhead relative to DRAM. Under capacity pressure, Hybrid restores 88.38% of tokens from host and 11.62% from SSD, while DRAM hits 55.47%/77.73% at C=1/2 and recomputes the rest.

Cold-start medians pool six fresh processes per backend across both scenarios, measured before seeding. The second metric is the first request after model readiness, with all KV caches empty.

| Backend | Process launch to ready (s) | First KV-empty request TTFT (ms) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| SimpleCPU SSD | 24.074 | 792.7 |
| DRAM | 25.088 | 788.5 |
| Hybrid | 25.095 | 784.1 |

The longer startup of DRAM and Hybrid plausibly reflects host-cache initialization: SimpleCPU allocates only about 9 MiB of streaming slots, whereas both DRAM and Hybrid configure 2 GiB of host buffers, requiring allocation and memory registration. Their startup times are nearly identical. Without phase-level timing, this remains a hypothesis rather than a measured attribution.

Hybrid's cold TTFT is only 4.4 ms below DRAM and 8.6 ms below SimpleCPU, much smaller than the observed run-to-run variation. Shared-GPU contention and first-request execution overhead can affect these measurements. Since the KV caches are empty, neither hot hits nor SSD restore overlap explains this difference; these samples do not establish a cold-TTFT advantage for Hybrid.

These preliminary results combine avoided SSD reads, cache-policy effects, and transfer scheduling. 

## Scope and integration
| Existing area | Expected integration |
| --- | --- |
| SimpleCPU disk backend and offload helpers | Reuse buffers, files, slot management, and I/O; support hot/cold interleaving and completion/error handling. |
| Native offloading connector and tiering managers | Translate keys to source slots, combine CPU/disk transfers, and track request lifetime. |
| Configuration and scheduling hooks | Account for CPU buffers and GPU reservations; expose opt-in settings. |
| Existing tests, metrics, and docs | Validate correctness, overlap, memory bounds, and regressions. |


## Open question
1. Is worker-local CPU-hit interleaving over the existing disk backend the right integration point?
2. What batching/arbitration policy best exploits measured slack without delaying ready cold blocks or decode?
