title: [RFC]: Bounded load/save admission for Mooncake Store
author: shaoyuyoung
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch


## Motivation

A cache hit can still turn into recomputation if the connector cannot admit the load. In the canonical Mooncake Store connector used by our deployment, loads and saves have separate execution threads but share a byte budget and a pending-job limit. A save can occupy that budget while a load needed by a waiting request is rejected.

The observations below come from the downstream `Dsv41StoreWorker` at [bytedance-iaas/vllm@802e387][worker], used with a DRAM-only Store and PP2/PCP4 prefill on H20. The [upstream Store worker][upstream-worker] has a different implementation. This RFC asks for feedback on the admission policy before adapting it for upstream; the first prototype would use the downstream connector where the problem has been reproduced.

Today, admission charges the entire job:

```text
pending_jobs < max_pending_jobs
pending_bytes + job_bytes <= max_inflight_bytes
```

The transfer then runs in smaller RPC batches, but holds the full reservation until the job ends. For example, with a 256 MiB budget, a pending 192 MiB save causes a 120 MiB load to be rejected. The same load is admitted when the save is absent. A CPU-only check using the original admission methods and a parked executor reproduces this behavior. It also reproduces rejection when job slots are exhausted even though bytes remain available.

During a 70-minute production observation on November 4, 2026, we recorded 818 load-admission skips and 222 save-admission skips. L2 reuse supplied about 11% of prefill input tokens over that window. The skips are worker-operation counts, not unique requests. The current counters do not distinguish write/read contention from read/read contention, oversized jobs, slot exhaustion, or an unhealthy backend. They establish a reason to investigate, but do not yet quantify the recoverable tokens or expected speedup.

I propose admitting aligned transfer batches, keeping waiting work in a bounded connector queue, and reserving some transfer capacity for loads. Saves would retain a way to make progress under sustained reads. The policy would be opt-in. GPU/RDMA and end-to-end results are still pending.

### Alternatives

_No response_

title: [RFC]: [Draft] Split FusedMoEQuantConfig into static schema and runtime state
author: bnellnm
body:
# Fused MoE Static and Runtime Quantization Configs

**Status:** Proposal / RFC

**Date:** 2026-11-03

## Summary

Split `FusedMoEQuantConfig` into two objects with different lifetimes:

* `FusedMoEQuantSchema` is an immutable, tensor-free description of the
  quantization scheme owned by a quantization method. It contains
  [`QuantKey`](vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/quant_utils.py)
  values for both activation GEMMs and both expert weight GEMMs, plus only the
  role metadata and GEMM1 activation parameters that are not derivable from
  those keys, as well as the backend-selected scale-layout and MX-alignment
  fields.
* `FusedMoEQuantConfig` remains the runtime object. It contains the loaded
  weights, scales, zero points, biases, and other tensor-valued parameters.
  During the compatibility stages it also holds temporary references to static
  metadata; those references are removed once they are no longer needed.

The existing external interface is preserved through properties. Callers keep
using the current names such as `quant_dtype`, `block_shape`, `a1_scale`, and
`w1_bias`; they do not read dataclass fields, `_a1`/`_w1` descriptors, or the
new static reference directly.

`FusedMoEQuantSchema` is the only static quantization type. Selection consumes
only the schema's role keys; after choosing the backend, the quantization method
finalizes the backend ABI fields (`is_scale_swizzled`, `is_scale_transposed`, and
`mx_alignment`) by constructing a new immutable schema value for kernel
construction.

Schema construction, backend selection, ABI finalization, and modular kernel
construction happen in each quantization method's `__init__`, before weights are
loaded. This proposal does not add a setup hook or change the
`RoutedExperts.__init__` sequence. `process_weights_after_loading` transforms
tensors, constructs the runtime `FusedMoEQuantConfig`, and retains it on the
quantization method for execution. The runtime config is passed explicitly to
the already-built kernel on each invocation; the kernel and experts do not own
or cache it. Post-load processing no longer selects a backend, constructs a
kernel, or mutates the quantization schema.

The split gives the system one explicit ordering:

```text
quant method __init__: static schema keys -> select backend
                     -> construct kernel (kernel finalizes schema ABI)
weight loading       -> transform weights -> build runtime config
                     -> pass at execution
```

## Motivation

### Current state

`FusedMoEQuantConfig` currently combines two kinds of information:

* Static information: quantized dtypes, group shapes, symmetry, scale layout,
  activation constants, and derived predicates such as `is_block_quantized` or
  `use_fp8_w8a8`.
* Runtime information: weight scales, activation scales, global scales,
  zero points, biases, Triton `PrecisionConfig`s, and now, in some paths, the
  weights themselves.

This conflation affects the whole setup flow:

1. A quantization method selects a backend from `QuantKey`s during
   construction.
2. Weights and scales are loaded.
3. `process_weights_after_loading` transforms tensors and builds
   `FusedMoEQuantConfig` from the loaded parameters.
4. Only then can the modular kernel be constructed.
5. Some expert implementations run their own `process_weights_after_loading`
   after the kernel has been constructed.
6. Wrappers such as `FusedMoEModularMethod` may replace the kernel's
   implementation during post-load processing.

The kernel is therefore built at the end of a long, implementation-specific
post-load sequence even though all inputs needed to choose and construct it are
available at model setup. At the same time, backend selection often happens in
the quantization-method constructor, before dimension rounding. One decision is
therefore split across the two extreme ends of model setup, which makes both
orderings accidental.

### Problems

#### Kernel construction depends on loaded tensors

Many expert constructors read `quant_config` tensor fields. Examples include
scale-derived buffers in FlashInfer CuteDSL, scale-processing setup in TRT-LLM,
and the emulation experts that rewrite the quant config. Consequently the
kernel cannot be constructed until after loading.

#### Post-load ordering is implicit and fragile

The required order differs by quantization method and expert. Some experts need
the kernel to exist before their post-load hook runs. Others must transform
scales before the quant config is built. Others cause the kernel to be rebuilt
or swapped. This creates ordering dependencies between unrelated objects and
makes adding a backend or an expert easy to get wrong.

#### The quant config is mutable shared state

Several experts modify the config after construction, for example by clearing
scales or changing the effective weight dtype. This means the object does not
describe a stable contract: the same config can mean different things before and
after a hook runs. It also complicates weight reloads, CUDA graph capture, and
reasoning about which tensors a captured kernel will read.

#### Backend execution policy can differ implicitly

An emulation backend may be selected from the checkpoint scheme
(`kInt4Static32`, for example) but execute a different effective scheme
(unquantized weights). Today that difference is represented by mutating the
config. It should instead be an explicit execution policy of the selected
backend or expert, with the schema left unchanged.

#### Oracles and quant methods duplicate derivation logic

Oracles consume selection keys, quantization methods build a second config with
the same dtype and shape information, and kernel classes derive predicates from
that config again. Keeping one canonical static description removes this
duplication.

#### Kernel construction is split across model setup and weight loading

Some quantization methods select a backend in `__init__`, while others select
one during `process_weights_after_loading`. Stage 4 centralizes schema
creation, backend selection, and modular kernel construction in each
quantization method's `__init__`; the kernel constructor owns ABI finalization.
It deliberately leaves the
`RoutedExperts.__init__` sequence and dimension-rounding behavior unchanged.

## Goals

* Provide one immutable static quantization contract for modular MoE kernels.
* Use the schema for selection through its key roles, then have the kernel
  constructor finalize its backend-specific ABI fields without introducing a
  second configuration type.
* Make `QuantKey` the canonical representation of quantization type, scale
  semantics, and symmetry inside that contract.
* Construct prepare/finalize and expert kernels in each quantization method's
  `__init__`, before weights are loaded, without changing
  `RoutedExperts.__init__`.
* Keep all loaded tensors in one runtime config. A reference to the static
  contract may exist during migration, but it is not part of the final runtime
  payload contract.
* Define a deterministic post-load sequence that produces a validated runtime
  config for execution.
* Eliminate post-construction mutation of quantization scheme fields.
* Preserve the existing external `FusedMoEQuantConfig` API with properties and
  methods rather than exposing new fields.
* Make oracle selection and kernel construction testable without allocating
  real quantized weights.
* Land the work in independently reviewable stages: first introduce the static
  config behind the existing API, then migrate internal consumers incrementally.

## Proposed Design

### API compatibility rules

The split is an internal representation change first. External code should
continue to interact with `FusedMoEQuantConfig` through the current properties
and helper methods.

* Dataclass fields are private. Cross-module access uses `@property` methods or
  explicit methods, never `_schema`, `_a1`, `_w1`, or role-descriptor members.
* Existing property names and semantics are preserved. Runtime properties
  delegate static questions to `FusedMoEQuantSchema`; they do not ask
  callers to learn a new vocabulary.
* Static-only consumers eventually take `FusedMoEQuantSchema` directly. They do
  not reach through a runtime config to obtain it.
* The compatibility guarantee for schema-derived runtime properties lasts only
  while `_schema` is present. It is removed after all callers use the schema
  directly.
* New properties and methods are additive in Stage 1. Constructor and factory
  signature changes are deferred to Stages 2a-3.
* Any unavoidable exception is implemented as a compatibility property or
  helper with a documented removal plan, not as direct member access.

### Static quantization description

The static side adds one immutable schema and one role descriptor. The
quantization method creates the schema in `__init__`, before weight loading;
selection consumes its role keys, after which the schema's backend ABI fields
are finalized by constructing a new immutable value. Its dataclass fields are
internal to `config.py`; external consumers use the properties described below:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FusedMoEStaticQuantDesc:
    """Static description of one activation or weight role."""

    # The complete quantization description. Do not duplicate fields from it.
    key: QuantKey | None = None

    # Supplemental layout metadata only when key is absent or key's scale group
    # shape cannot represent the required alignment, e.g. GPTQ activation
    # alignment. This must be None when key already supplies the same shape.
    alignment_shape: GroupShape | None = None

    # Presence flags are part of the kernel ABI and are not 100% derivable from
    # the key: symmetry does not, by itself, guarantee a zero point is present.
    has_bias: bool = False
    has_zero_point: bool = False

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        assert self.alignment_shape is None or self.key is None or (
            self.alignment_shape != self.key.scale.group_shape
        ), "alignment_shape must not duplicate key.scale.group_shape"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FusedMoEQuantSchema:
    """Static quantization and kernel-ABI description for one MoE layer."""

    a1: FusedMoEStaticQuantDesc
    a2: FusedMoEStaticQuantDesc
    w1: FusedMoEStaticQuantDesc
    w2: FusedMoEStaticQuantDesc

    is_scale_swizzled: bool = True
    is_scale_transposed: bool = False
    mx_alignment: int = 0

    gemm1_alpha: float | None = None
    gemm1_beta: float | None = None
    gemm1_clamp_limit: float | None = None
```

The schema has separate `a1`/`a2` and `w1`/`w2` roles so it can represent
different quantization for each GEMM. `w1` denotes the fused gate/up weight
(`w13`); `w2` denotes the down projection. Most current kernels require
`a1 == a2` and `w1 == w2`. Initial builders preserve that restriction by using
one activation key for both activation roles and one weight key for both weight
roles. A backend that later supports mixed schemes can consume the distinct
roles without changing the schema type.

#### Oracle selection inputs

Oracles receive `FusedMoEQuantSchema` and select using only its role keys.
Selection-specific policy such as `allow_vllm_cutlass`, user backend overrides,
and platform checks remain explicit arguments to, or internal policy of, the
concrete oracle; they are not schema fields.

The initial single-key oracle adapters use the schema's common `activation_key`
and `weight_key` properties. Those properties raise when `a1 != a2` or
`w1 != w2`, so a single-key adapter cannot silently choose one role. An oracle
is widened to the role-specific keys when it actually supports mixed schemes.

#### Backend ABI fields

`is_scale_swizzled`, `is_scale_transposed`, and `mx_alignment` are not derivable
from `QuantKey` and depend on the selected backend. The initial schema supplies
defaults for selection; after the backend is chosen, the kernel constructor
finalizes these fields in a new immutable schema value and stores it as the
kernel's canonical schema. Selection must not inspect these fields.
Prepare/finalize, experts, and the kernel's `quant_schema` use that finalized
value.

### Runtime quantization description

Keep the existing name, but make the object a tensor payload. During Stages 2a-3
it retains a transitional reference to the static schema so that existing
properties can keep delegating to static information. The layout below shows
that intermediate shape:

```python
@dataclass
class FusedMoEQuantTensors:
    """Tensor-valued parameters for one activation or weight role."""

    scale: torch.Tensor | PrecisionConfig | None = None
    alpha_or_gscale: torch.Tensor | None = None
    zp: torch.Tensor | None = None
    bias: torch.Tensor | None = None


@dataclass
class FusedMoEQuantConfig:
    """Runtime quantization state for one MoE layer."""

    # Transitional compatibility reference; removed when static questions no
    # longer need to be answered through the runtime config.
    _schema: FusedMoEQuantSchema

    # Weights are part of the runtime state in the target design.
    _w1_weight: torch.Tensor
    _w2_weight: torch.Tensor

    _a1_tensors: FusedMoEQuantTensors = field(default_factory=FusedMoEQuantTensors)
    _a2_tensors: FusedMoEQuantTensors = field(default_factory=FusedMoEQuantTensors)
    _w1_tensors: FusedMoEQuantTensors = field(default_factory=FusedMoEQuantTensors)
    _w2_tensors: FusedMoEQuantTensors = field(default_factory=FusedMoEQuantTensors)

    @property
    def quant_schema(self) -> FusedMoEQuantSchema: ...

    @property
    def w1(self) -> torch.Tensor: ...

    @property
    def w2(self) -> torch.Tensor: ...

    @property
    def a1_scale(self) -> torch.Tensor | None: ...

    @property
    def w1_scale(self) -> torch.Tensor | None: ...

    @property
    def g1_alphas(self) -> torch.Tensor | None: ...

    @property
    def w1_bias(self) -> torch.Tensor | None: ...
```

The `_schema` member and `FusedMoEQuantConfig.quant_schema` accessor are bootstrap
compatibility mechanisms, not part of the final runtime contract. Remove them
once no call site needs the runtime config to answer static questions. After that
cleanup, static-only consumers read `FusedMoEQuantSchema` directly and the
runtime config contains only loaded tensor state.

The property list above is illustrative, not exhaustive. The existing
accessors such as `quant_dtype`, `weight_quant_dtype`, `is_quantized`,
`is_per_act_token`, `per_act_token_quant`, `per_out_ch_quant`, `block_shape`,
`is_block_quantized`, `is_per_tensor`, `is_scale_swizzled`,
`is_scale_transposed`, `mx_alignment`, `a1_scale`, `a2_scale`, `w1_scale`,
`w2_scale`, `a1_gscale`, `a2_gscale`, `w1_zp`, `w2_zp`, `w1_bias`, `w2_bias`,
`w1_precision`, `g1_alphas`, `g2_alphas`, `gemm1_alpha`, `gemm1_beta`,
`gemm1_clamp_limit`, the `use_*` predicates, `ocp_mx_scheme`, `config_name`,
`scale_shape`, and `batched_scale_shape` retain their names and meaning.

Static predicates are implemented once on `FusedMoEQuantSchema`; while the
compatibility reference exists, the runtime config delegates to them through its
existing properties. No caller outside `config.py` reads `_schema`,
`_a1_tensors`, `_w1_tensors`, or the role descriptors. New internal code must
use properties or explicit methods. Existing private accesses such as
`quant_config._w1.scale = ...` are migration debt and are removed when the
corresponding expert moves to the static API.

The runtime config is constructed only after all weight and scale
transformations are complete. Its construction validates that tensor presence,
dtype, and shape agree with the static contract. The quantization method retains
the runtime config for its layer and passes it explicitly to kernel execution. A
runtime config without weights is not a valid input to a modular kernel. Unit
tests or benchmarks that only need static quantization information must use
`FusedMoEQuantSchema`, not a partially populated runtime object.

Shape validation must be backend-aware. Swizzled or transposed scales use a
physical layout that may differ from the logical `QuantKey` shape. The shared
validator checks logical dtype and presence; the backend's construction helper
checks the kernel's canonical schema ABI fields before the runtime config is
used.

Once built, the runtime object is treated as immutable even though its fields
contain mutable tensors. Reload and weight-replacement paths construct a new
runtime object; they do not patch fields in place. Kernels and experts receive
the runtime object per invocation and must not retain it across calls.

During migration, the legacy `make()` helpers may continue to return a runtime
config with absent weights so existing monolithic and test call sites keep
working. That compatibility form is incomplete and is not a valid input to
modular-kernel execution.

### Backend selection and execution policy

Selection sees the schema's role keys and must not inspect its backend ABI
fields. After choosing the backend, the quantization method creates the finalized
schema used for kernel construction. The original selection input is not
mutated. Selection may additionally depend on `FusedMoEConfig`, platform
capabilities, a user backend override, or oracle-specific policy such as
`allow_vllm_cutlass`.

An emulation backend may dequantize those parameters at load time or on the fly.
That is an execution policy of the selected expert, not a second quantization
scheme. For example, the int4 emulation path retains the int4 weight keys in the
schema so selection and construction know what storage the quant method owns;
the selected emulation expert dequantizes the runtime tensors and applies an
unquantized compute path. During migration, such an expert may expose an
internal execution view for the shared unquantized base class, but it must not
clear fields on the schema or mutate a shared runtime config during
construction.

If an online quantization method changes the stored format before kernel
execution, it builds the schema for that final stored format before selection.
The source checkpoint method remains a separate object.

### Quantization-method construction API

`FusedMoEMethodBase` keeps its existing constructor lifecycle. The explicit API
adds the schema and repurposes the runtime builder:

```python
class FusedMoEMethodBase:
    def fused_moe_quant_schema(self) -> FusedMoEQuantSchema:
        ...

    def get_fused_moe_quant_config(
        self, layer: "RoutedExperts"
    ) -> FusedMoEQuantConfig | None:
        """Collect final weights and transformed scales after loading."""
```

Each concrete quantization method constructs a transient `quant_schema` in
`__init__`, selects the backend and experts class, and constructs
prepare/finalize plus the expert kernel through its oracle. The oracle's kernel
constructor finalizes the schema's ABI fields internally and stores the
canonical schema on the kernel. All of this completes before the constructor
returns and before weight loading starts. No new model-setup hook is added, and
`RoutedExperts.__init__` remains unchanged. Backend selection therefore uses the
`FusedMoEConfig` available at quantization-method construction; a post-rounding
revalidation phase is outside this proposal.

The existing `get_fused_moe_quant_config` is repurposed as the runtime builder.
Its existing name, signature, and optional return remain unchanged for
compatibility; a non-`None` result must now contain the complete final tensor
payload. It is the only method allowed to collect that payload.

### Kernel and oracle APIs

The target interfaces are:

```python
class MoEKernelOracle(ABC):
    def select_backend(
        self,
        moe_config: FusedMoEConfig,
        quant_schema: FusedMoEQuantSchema,
    ) -> tuple[BackendT, type[FusedMoEExperts] | None]: ...

    def make_kernel(
        self,
        moe_config: FusedMoEConfig,
        quant_schema: FusedMoEQuantSchema,
        backend: BackendT,
        experts_cls: type[FusedMoEExperts],
        routing_tables: RoutingTables | None = None,
    ) -> FusedMoEKernel: ...
```

`select_backend` and `make_kernel` remain separate in the initial stages so that
selection can be tested independently and `make_kernel` owns schema
finalization. A later stage may combine both operations into one oracle routine
once schema finalization and experts-class resolution are fully owned by the
oracle; that consolidation is not required for this refactor.

Concrete oracles no longer build `FusedMoEQuantConfig`; that is the
quantization method's responsibility. Oracles consume the schema for both
selection and kernel construction. `make_kernel` finalizes the schema ABI fields
internally and stores the canonical schema on the kernel; a quantization method
reads `kernel.quant_schema` if it needs the schema beyond construction. The
current single `weight_key` / `activation_key` signature can remain temporarily
as an adapter over the schema's common key properties; it must use `w1` (the
`w13` weight) and reject schemas where `w1 != w2` until each oracle API accepts
both weight keys explicitly.

The target API invariant is stricter than "pass static data when convenient":
`FusedMoEQuantConfig` must not appear in any constructor signature, any
`maybe_make_prepare_finalize` or `make_*_moe_kernel` signature, or an oracle's
`make_kernel` signature. The runtime object appears only in
`get_fused_moe_quant_config` and execution-time `prepare`/`finalize`/`apply`
methods that need the loaded tensors.

Experts and prepare/finalize implementations take static configuration during
construction:

```python
class FusedMoEExperts:
    def __init__(
        self,
        moe_config: FusedMoEConfig,
        quant_schema: FusedMoEQuantSchema,
        ...,
    ): ...


class FusedMoEKernel:
    def apply(
        self,
        ...,
        quant_config: FusedMoEQuantConfig,
    ): ...

    def apply_monolithic(
        self,
        ...,
        quant_config: FusedMoEQuantConfig,
    ): ...
```

Prepare/finalize constructors likewise take static information only. Any tensor
needed by dispatch is passed to `prepare`/`finalize` at execution time from the
runtime config argument.

During Stages 3-6, kernel execution validates that
`quant_config.quant_schema == self.fused_experts.quant_schema`.
Structural equality is used rather than object identity so a reload may recreate
an equal immutable schema; unequal schemas are always rejected. The config is an
execution argument, not kernel state, and the kernel forwards it to
prepare/finalize and the experts for that invocation.

Prepare/finalize implementations continue to receive the runtime config as an
argument to `prepare`; their constructors receive only static data.

In the target design, `FusedMoEKernel.apply` and `apply_monolithic` accept the
runtime config and read weights from it. During migration they may keep explicit
`w1` and `w2` arguments, but the kernel must assert that those tensors are the
same objects as `quant_config.w1` and `quant_config.w2`. The explicit arguments
are removed in the final stage.

### Quantization-method lifecycle

The following is the target lifecycle after Stage 4. Stages 1-3 preserve the
current construction timing and introduce the static contract and the
execution-time runtime argument.

```text
Quantization method construction
  -> construct transient FusedMoEQuantSchema
  -> select backend and experts class
  -> construct prepare/finalize, experts, and FusedMoEKernel
     (kernel finalizes and stores the canonical schema)

Weight loading
  load parameters

process_weights_after_loading
  -> quant method transforms/replaces weights and scales
  -> optional expert tensor-only post-load hook(layer, static)
  -> quant_method.get_fused_moe_quant_config(layer)
  -> validate runtime tensors and static contract
  -> retain runtime config on the quantization method
  -> keep_constants()

Forward
  -> quant method passes the runtime config to the kernel
  -> kernel forwards it to prepare/finalize and experts
```

Nothing in `process_weights_after_loading` may:

* change `quant_schema`;
* replace `experts_cls` or the selected backend;
* construct a new kernel merely because weights were loaded; or
* mutate schema or its ABI fields.

If a topology change such as elastic EP requires a different kernel, that is a
separate explicit reconfiguration step and not part of ordinary weight loading.

Construction completes before weight loading begins. All later stages operate
on the existing kernel and produce only runtime tensor state.

Parameter replacement and EPLB need special care because the runtime config
holds weight references. A path that replaces parameter storage must rebuild the
runtime config before graph capture or the next execution. A path that reorders
weights in place may reuse the runtime config only if it keeps the same tensor
objects.

### Field ownership

| Current field or property | New owner | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FusedMoEQuantDesc.dtype` | static | `QuantKey.dtype`; no stored field |
| `FusedMoEQuantDesc.shape` | static | `QuantKey.scale.group_shape`; no stored field except non-representable `alignment_shape` |
| symmetry implied by quant method | static | `QuantKey.symmetric`; no stored field |
| `quant_dtype`, `weight_quant_dtype` | static | Key-derived legacy projections; no stored field |
| `is_quantized`, `is_per_act_token`, `per_out_ch_quant`, `block_shape` | static | Derived properties; no stored fields |
| `use_fp8_w8a8`, `use_int8_*`, `use_*_w4a*`, `ocp_mx_scheme` | static | Derived properties; no stored fields |
| `config_name`, `scale_shape`, `batched_scale_shape` | static | Derived methods; no stored fields |
| `is_scale_swizzled`, `is_scale_transposed` | static | Schema ABI fields, finalized after backend selection |
| `mx_alignment` | static | Schema ABI field, finalized after backend selection |
| `gemm1_alpha`, `gemm1_beta`, `gemm1_clamp_limit` | static | Snapshot of `FusedMoEConfig` activation parameters |
| bias presence, zero-point presence | static | Known before selection; not derivable from the key |
| `scale`, `alpha_or_gscale`, `zp`, `bias` | runtime | Loaded tensors or `PrecisionConfig` |
| `w1`, `w2` | runtime | Canonical weight handles for the layer |

## Consequences

### Benefits

* Kernel selection and construction become deterministic and testable without
  weights.
* Post-load processing has one clear output: transformed tensors plus a
  validated runtime config.
* Expert constructors no longer capture scale tensors that may later be
  replaced.
* Config mutation disappears, which simplifies reloads and graph capture.
* Oracles consume one canonical schema for selection and construction instead of
  re-deriving it.
* Backend-specific ABI parameters are finalized in the schema by the kernel
  constructor after selection without introducing a second configuration type.

### Costs and risks

* Static and runtime configuration can become inconsistent unless runtime-config
  construction validates presence, dtype, and shape.
* `QuantKey` does not encode every current quirk. Bias/zero-point presence and
  legacy alignment-only shapes need the small role metadata described above.
  The Triton `PrecisionConfig` representation is handled by a derived property
  or backend-specific static adapter, not by adding a parallel scale-kind field.
* Weight reload must rebuild the runtime config after parameter replacement.
  Kernels and experts must not retain runtime tensors across invocations.

## Migration Plan

The work lands in stages that track the branch series. Stage 1 introduces the
data model without changing external behavior or constructor signatures.
Stages 2a-6 migrate internal consumers to the split API and remove runtime state
from construction.

Each stage changes only the named interfaces, keeps current behavior elsewhere,
and is independently testable. Quantization methods with special post-load
behavior may remain on the transitional path until Stage 5, but they must not
add new constructor dependencies on runtime tensors.

| Stage | Branch or scope |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `quant-config-refactor-1`: introduce the static config behind the existing API |
| 2a | `quant-config-refactor-2`: construct schemas and migrate oracle selection |
| 3 | `quant-config-refactor-3`: make the runtime config an execution argument; constructors retain only the static schema |
| 4 | `quant-config-refactor-4`: move modular kernel construction into the quantization method `__init__` |
| 5 | Normalize special execution policies and reconfiguration |
| 6 | Remove compatibility scaffolding |

After all stages, the target invariant is that runtime configs are absent from
construction:

* `FusedMoEQuantConfig` must not appear as a parameter type in any `__init__`
  outside `config.py`. Stage 3 replaces the constructor parameter with
  `FusedMoEQuantSchema`.
* It must not appear in `maybe_make_prepare_finalize`, `make_*_moe_kernel`, or
  oracle `make_kernel` signatures.
* It must not appear in `make_*_moe_quant_config`; static builders replace the
  static portion of those helpers.
* The runtime object is constructed only by `get_fused_moe_quant_config` and
  appears at execution time only in `prepare`/`finalize`/`apply` paths that
  genuinely consume loaded tensors.

### Stage 1: Introduce the static config behind the existing API

This stage is intentionally narrow. The goal is to make the static description
available and authoritative for existing derived properties while leaving the
current call graph intact.

* Add `FusedMoEQuantSchema` and `FusedMoEStaticQuantDesc`.
* Add `_schema` to `FusedMoEQuantConfig` as a transitional compatibility
  reference and expose it through the `quant_schema` property. Do not
  make callers access the field.
* Keep every existing `FusedMoEQuantConfig` constructor, helper, and property
  name. `make()` and `make_*_moe_quant_config()` build th

title: [RFC]: A KV compatibility identity, enforced on NIXL and P2P transfers and readable by routers
author: vMaroon
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM transfers KV between engines over NIXL (prefill to decode) and the P2P offload tier (engine to engine). Each checks compatibility once per peer connection. NIXL hashes the vLLM version, model path, dtype, KV shape, attention backend, cache dtype and speculative factors ([metadata.py#L150-L215](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/metadata.py#L150-L215)). P2P compares the block length, the hash seed and a fingerprint of the offload run config: model path, KV dtype, parallel sizes, KV groups ([session.py#L647-L654](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/session/session.py#L647-L654), [file_mapper.py#L64-L73](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/v1/kv_offload/file_mapper.py#L64-L73)); the page layout joins only with `canonical_layout`, off by default.

Neither check covers what the KV is computed from. Weights are identified by path, so a new checkpoint at the same path passes. Quantization and `hf_overrides` are not checked, and on P2P neither are the model dtype and page layout. The code identity is the whole `vllm_version`, which changes with every commit (2,036 in the 30 days to 2026-11-03), or on P2P nothing. A passing check uses the received pages silently.

One example of where this bites is in rolling updates. Old and new engines serve the same prompts, a cache-aware router pairs them, and the only separator is deployment labels, which block safe sharing (a rebuild that leaves the model alone) and miss unsafe cases (new weights under an old label). Weights can also change at runtime through `reload_weights`, `update_weights`, `add_lora` and `sleep`/`wake_up` ([gpu_worker.py#L688](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py#L688), [#L1790](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py#L1790)), with no re-check.

### Proposed Change.

This is a request for the capability; the design follows as a separate RFC.

`kv_identity`: one value per engine. Equal values mean the engines compute the same KV bytes for the same token ids, up to floating-point rounding order. Requirements:

1. Equal only when the weights, the loaded configuration and the code that computes and stores the KV are the same; otherwise different. A false "same" is the failure to prevent; a needless "different" costs cache warmth.
2. Unchanged by code outside the KV path: API server, scheduler, sampling, logging. Precedent: the compile cache keys on the source files Dynamo traced, by content ([decorators.py#L639-L654](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/compilation/decorators.py#L639-L654), [backends.py#L1064-L1091](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/39dbf51839/vllm/compilation/backends.py#L1064-L1091)).
3. Exposed with its components (weights digest, configuration factors, code files, libraries), so a mismatch names its cause.
4. A factor in the NIXL hash and in the P2P fingerprint, and a label on `vllm:cache_config_info`, so routers pair prefill with decode and name a `remote_kv_source` only among equal engines.
5. Recomputed on a runtime weight change, with sessions dropped or transfers refused until then.
6. Keeps today's heterogeneous pairing: NIXL TP ratios, P2P parallelism-agnostic layouts, prefill and decode engines that differ in compile mode and limits. Those change rounding order and placement only.
7. Startup cost on the order of the load, with no second read of the checkpoint.

Checked already: the KV of a fixed probe prompt cannot be the identity, since its bits vary with TP size and GPU generation and a tolerance cannot separate a small weight change from kernel noise. The version string splits on every commit, while about 9% of commits touch a given model's forward-path files. A content hash of the files executed during an engine's first forward is deterministic across processes and moves only when one of those files changes (CPU build; the GPU check across TP sizes and compile modes is pending).

Questions:

1. Is "same bytes up to rounding order" the right contract, keeping cross-TP and cross-hardware pairing in scope?
2. Which configuration fields belong to the KV contract? Our reading: `ModelConfig` minus `max_model_len`, cache dtype, KV layout, attention backend, draft model.
3. Tens of seconds of startup cost by default, or opt-in?
4. Metrics label, endpoint, or both?
5. On a runtime weight change: drop live sessions, or refuse new transfers until the value is recomputed?

### Feedback Period.

One week, then the design RFC.

### CC List.

@NickLucche @ApostaC @orozery @liranschour

### Any Other Things.

None.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: SM90 DeepGEMM MegaMoE for DeepSeek V4
author: new-TonyWang
body:
## Motivation

vLLM's current DeepGEMM MegaMoE backend is SM100-only (its support check hard-requires device capability 100), and all SM100 formats rely on Blackwell features (TMEM, UTCCP, MX datatypes). Hopper (SM90) has no megakernel path.

DeepSeek V4 ships two routed-expert precisions:

- `expert_dtype="fp4"` (Flash): MXFP4, served by the existing SM100 path.
- `expert_dtype="fp8"` (Flash-Base): FP8 e4m3 + float32 block (128, 128) scales, which needs no Blackwell hardware.

Hopper clusters running Flash-Base currently fall back to the multi-kernel DeepEP + grouped-GEMM path. This RFC reserves the SM90 megakernel work to close that gap.

## Proposed Change

Two coordinated PRs:

1. **DeepGEMM (upstream)**: `Add SM90 MegaMoE by cooperative` ([deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#360](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/pull/360)) — the `fp8_mega_moe` fused kernel; continue optimizing in place.
2. **vLLM (this RFC)**: adapt `fp8_mega_moe` into the existing `DeepGemmMegaMoEExperts` path.

vLLM-side integration reuses the existing MegaMoE machinery:

- Add an SM90 FP8 weight format (`kernel="fp8_mega_moe"`) to `MegaMoEWeightFormat`.
- Relax `check_deep_gemm_mega_moe_supported` for SM90 on this format only.
- Reuse `prepare_megamoe_inputs` for FP8 staging and top-k repack.
- Reuse `MegaMoEActivation` (`swiglu`, clamp 10) for DeepSeek V4.

DeepSeek V4 shapes satisfy the kernel constraints: `hidden=7168` (multiple of 256), `intermediate_hidden=2048` (multiple of 128, `2048/128 <= 64`).

## Feedback Period

One week.

## CC List

@mpdfdfl

## Any Other Things

Validation: DeepGEMM unit tests (`test_mega_moe_sm90.py`), vLLM layer parity against the unfused DeepEP + grouped-GEMM path, model-level smoke on a Flash-Base checkpoint, and perf via `bench_mega_moe_sm90.py` (defaults to the V4 shape) against the DeepEP V1/V2 baseline.

title: [RFC]: Token-id parity with the Python frontend as a tested contract for the Rust frontend
author: waynehacking8
body:
### Motivation.

I propose a CI test that checks the Rust frontend's token ids against the Python frontend's on a fixed corpus, with the divergences already on main listed and pinned. #65757 implements it. What I need from maintainers is listed at the end.

When the Rust frontend tokenizes a prompt differently from the Python frontend, no test fails, and often nothing visible fails either: wrong ids decode to the same text, so the endpoints return normal-looking results while the model sees a different input. Three tokenizer bugs reached main with no failing test:

- #63467: fastokens 0.2.1's thread-local split cache gave a prompt different ids when it shared a prefix of 4 KiB or more with the previous prompt on the same thread and diverged inside a whitespace run. Fixed in fastokens 0.3.4 (crusoecloud/fastokens#78); the Rust frontend moved to 0.3.5 in #63707.
- The truncation cut fixed in #63707: the `tokenizers` fallback applied `tokenizer.json`'s `truncation` block, "silently cutting prompts for such a checkpoint when fastokens couldn't load it".
- Hy3's carriage return (crusoecloud/fastokens#88, open): Hy3's vocabulary has no token for byte 0x0d, so fastokens, the default Rust backend for that file, fails to encode any text containing `\r`, so the request errors, where Hugging Face tokenizers drops the byte.

Each was found by hand, after release. The existing tests that run against the Rust frontend check request fields, behaviour and ordinary prompts, not ids on edge-case text. #44280 accepts some differences from the Python frontend, but token ids change the model's input, so I'd treat them as outside that allowance. It has no item for this; it would fit under its testing and compatibility infrastructure section.

### Proposed Change.

- Contract, on this corpus: for each covered tokenizer and every case, `Tokenizer::encode` on each Rust backend returns exactly the Python frontend's ids. A difference already on main is listed with its input, its cause, an upstream link once one exists, and the exact outcome it produces. A listed case that changes outcome or matches Python again fails the test, so the list stays current.
- Production default: each file is also loaded through the constructors `vllm-text` calls, so a change of default backend (for example to fastokens for `tiktoken.model`, as draft #51027 proposes) shows up in the test.
- Reference: the ids come from the Python frontend's own tokenizer path, are committed as snapshots, and are regenerated by a script that never downloads weights.
- Corpus and coverage: 31 cases (whitespace runs, tabs, CRLF and lone CR, Unicode edge cases, special tokens, and shared prefixes over 4 KiB) on 8 tokenizers. Seven cover the tokenizer pipelines of the 35 recipes that default to the Rust frontend, and one is a published file with a 512-token truncation block. Every backend that can load each file runs: fastokens (vLLM's default Rust backend for `tokenizer.json`) and the `tokenizers` fallback, or riptoken (the default for `tiktoken.model` files) and tiktoken-rs.
- Maintenance: the snapshots are regenerated, from a vLLM install, when the Python-side tokenizer pins, `get_tokenizer` or the encode kwargs change, or a recipe changes tokenizer; nothing checks their freshness automatically. I'll maintain them and the test.

What #65757 finds and catches:

| What | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Divergences on main | 2, both pinned: Hy3 on fastokens (6 cases with `\r`), Kimi K3 on riptoken (7 cases with long space runs) |
| Same test with #63707 (the fastokens 0.3.5 bump and the truncation fix) reverted | 7 of 8 tokenizer tests fail: the split cache on Qwen3.5, GLM-5.2 and Muse Spark, and the truncation cut on the 512-token file and, once the test adds a truncation block, on every other `tokenizer.json` (details in #65757) |

The Kimi K3 divergence is new and affects production today. riptoken 0.3.0 emits a long run of spaces as the same tokens as tiktoken in reverse order. When the run ends in a newline, tab or CRLF, it also splits the final spaces-plus-character token in two, so it returns one more id. tiktoken-rs, loaded from the same file, matches Python. There is no upstream report yet; I'll file one with riptoken.

CI cost: the test runs in the existing Rust Frontend Cargo step, which triggers on any change under `rust/`, so every bump of a Rust tokenizer crate reruns it; Python-side changes don't. It downloads about 100 MB of pinned tokenizer files on a cold cache, as the `vllm-chat` roundtrip tests already do for seven of the eight repos. Worst observed time with a cold cache and a debug build: 20.1 s for the slowest parity test, against nextest's 120 s limit.

Rollout:

1. Land #65757 with the two pinned divergences.
2. A Rust tokenizer dependency bump that changes ids fails the step; the bump then fixes the cause or pins the new divergence with an upstream link.
3. A recipe that switches to the Rust frontend with a new tokenizer pipeline adds one snapshot in the same PR.
4. When fastokens#88 is fixed and the pin moves, the Hy3 entry goes; the riptoken entry gets an upstream report and the same treatment.

What I need from maintainers:

1. Agreement in principle that Rust tokenizer dependency bumps are gated on this test, as in rollout step 2.
2. A review of #65757.
3. Is `vllm-tokenizer`'s `tests/` the right home, or should this sit with model loading in `vllm-text`?
4. Are Hub downloads in the cargo step acceptable here? Like the roundtrip tests, the test fails when the Hub is unreachable and the files aren't cached.
5. Is the Python frontend the reference even where it drops a byte (Hy3), and may a pinned divergence on a default backend merge? I'd say yes to both, and leave default switches (the `tokenizers` fallback for Hy3, tiktoken-rs for Kimi K3) to separate PRs.
6. Is manual snapshot regeneration enough, or should a periodic job check the snapshots against the current Python frontend?

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

None.

### Any Other Things.

Out of scope: `encode_ordinary` (which the Kimi K3 and `glm5_next` renderers call), decoding, logprob token strings, chat templates, parsers, and `vllm-text`'s file selection and load-time fallbacks. Most of #63917's items have claimants, and the render-parity issues (#64431 to #64433, #65114 to #65116) cover rendering. fastokens picks its scanner kernel per CPU, so each CI runner tests the kernel it gets.

This change was prepared with AI assistance.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [ ] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

I searched the issues (the related ones are linked above); I haven't asked the docs chatbot.

title: [RFC]: Add a Tree Speculative Decoding Framework
author: drslark
body:
### Motivation Tree-based speculative decoding is an active research direction, with recent work such as [EAGLE-4](https://github.com/eagle-hq/EAGLE-4) and [SpecPilot](https://github.com/StargazerX0/SpecPilot) exploring tree-based drafting and verification. By covering multiple candidate continuations, tree methods can substantially improve draft acceptance and increase the number of tokens accepted per target verification step. However, upstream vLLM lacks a unified, reusable tree speculation framework, making these methods difficult to implement and evaluate. ### Proposed Change Build tree speculative decoding support incrementally: 1. **Introduce tree interfaces in the model runner and attention layers.** Define common tree metadata and interfaces for tree proposals, verification, and accepted-path commitment, including KV cache and drafter state updates. 2. **Add attention backend support progressively.** Enable tree attention in individual backends, starting with static trees. Each backend should explicitly declare its supported capabilities. 3. **Support dynamic tree verification.** Handle trees with varying topology and node counts across requests and decoding steps, enabling adaptive expansion and pruning. After the shared interfaces are established, steps 2 and 3 can proceed in parallel. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Step 1: Tree interfaces
Model runner and attention layers"] B["Step 2: Attention backend support
Enable tree attention progressively"] C["Step 3: Dynamic tree verification
Support varying topology and node counts"] A --> B A --> C ``` Existing chain speculative decoding should remain compatible throughout these stages. ### Validation Validate attention isolation, verification correctness, and cache consistency. Compare end-to-end latency, throughput, accepted tokens per verification step, and memory overhead against autoregressive and chain speculative decoding.

title: [RFC]: Deprecate and remove the torchao reload decorator in favor of reload_weights
author: aoshen02
body:
### Motivation.

`model.load_weights(...)` on a torchao-quantized model that has already been loaded has its own reload path: `support_quantized_model_reload_from_hp_weights` (`model_loader/reload/torchao_decorator.py`, added in #26327 and moved in #32133). After the first load, `set_torchao_reload_attrs` sets `model._do_torchao_reload`. From then on, `AutoWeightsLoader.load_weights` runs `initialize_layerwise_reload` and `finalize_layerwise_processing` around the call, so the high-precision weights are quantized again.

That path has been superseded:

- **`reload_weights` already covers torchao.** `llm.collective_rpc("reload_weights")` and the weight-transfer engines reload torchao models through the shared reload lifecycle, which handles online quantization. `tests/quantization/test_torchao.py::test_reload_weights` exercises it. Inside that lifecycle the decorator is switched off: `initialize_layerwise_reload` sets `_do_torchao_reload = False`. So the decorator only runs when user code calls `model.load_weights` directly on a loaded model.
- **The code marks itself for removal.** At its call site in `model_loader/utils.py`: "Needed for torchao model reloading via model.reload_weights. @kylesayrs @jerryzh168 this can be removed if callers move to `reload_weights`".
- **It is a third reload lifecycle with its own state.** `_do_torchao_reload` and `_original_do_torchao_reload` are saved and restored in `reload/layerwise.py` and `distributed/weight_transfer/sharded_rdt_engine.py`.
- **It is not a complete reload.** By its own docstring, it assumes every weight arrives in one `load_weights` call, so it cannot serve bucketed RL weight updates. It also does not run the model-level post-load hooks that every other load and reload path now ends with (`finalize_model_weights`, #64357, #57678), so state a module derives from its weights is not rebuilt.
- **No known users.** The only caller in the repository is the reload step at the end of `test_online_quant_config_dict_json`. The torchao docs do not mention it. I found no RL framework that reloads torchao-quantized vLLM models this way: verl uses torchao only for training-side optimizers.

### Proposed Change.

- Now: log a one-time deprecation warning when the decorator triggers, pointing to `reload_weights`.
- After a one-month feedback period (by 2026-12-05) with no objections: remove `support_quantized_model_reload_from_hp_weights`, `set_torchao_reload_attrs`, the `_do_torchao_reload` / `_original_do_torchao_reload` handling in layerwise reload and the sharded-RDT engine, and the direct `model.load_weights` reload step in `test_online_quant_config_dict_json`.
- torchao quantization itself is unchanged. Loading and `reload_weights` keep working.

Migration: replace

```python
llm.apply_model(lambda model: model.load_weights(weights))
```

with `llm.collective_rpc("reload_weights")` (optionally with `weights_path`), or a weight-transfer engine for RL updates.

### Feedback Period.

One month, until 2026-12-05. If you rely on reloading torchao models through `model.load_weights` directly, please comment with the use case.

### CC List.

@jerryzh168 @kylesayrs @hao-aaron

### Any Other Things.

Part of RFC #54477 (one finish for every load and update path).

title: [RFC]: Switch Rust regex engine for response parsing
author: Rocketknight1
body:
### Motivation.

Hi! Matt from the Transformers team at HF here. I see there's a Rust implementation of the response parsing feature (in `rust/src/parser/src/unified/hf/`), but it uses the standard `regex` crate which doesn't support lookaround. However, a lot of regexes in response parsing do use lookarounds, and they're quite hard to avoid, and this makes it hard to add templates to models because the model owners don't want to break vLLM support ([example](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/discussions/68))

Note that this only applies to Rust, the Python code uses Python's `regex` which does support lookarounds!

### Proposed Change.

Could we move the regex engine to something else? For example, I think `PCRE2` supports lookarounds and partial matching. Regexes might need a couple of changes to work in `PCRE2` but we these can be implemented fairly straightforwardly. Of course, if anyone has other ideas, I'm open to suggestions!

title: [RFC]: Compute-free prefix KV lookup-and-pin for router-driven peer KV reuse
author: briefgaming
body:
### Motivation.

KV-aware routers such as the vLLM router (`kv_aware` policy) keep an index of which worker holds which prefix blocks, built from KV events. When the worker with the best prefix hit (A) is busy, the router would like to send the request to a less loaded worker (B) and have B reuse A's cached prefix over NIXL instead of recomputing it.

Issue https://github.com/vllm-project/router/issues/424 and PR https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/509 seeks to have worker B transfer kv from worker A.

Doing this with stock vLLM is a 3-request flow:

1. Router → A: the prefix only, `kv_transfer_params: {do_remote_decode: true}`, `max_tokens=1`. A keeps the blocks under a lease (`kv_lease_duration`, 30 s by default) and returns their ids.
2. Router → B: the prefix plus A's params, `do_remote_prefill: true`, `max_tokens=1`. B pulls the blocks and caches them.
3. Router → B: the real request, which hits B's local prefix cache.

This works, but it has two problems the router can't fix.

**Problem 1: A computes on a miss, and nothing can stop it.** The router's index is eventually consistent. A can evict the prefix just before step 1 arrives, while its `BlockRemoved` event is still in flight. Step 1 then becomes a normal prefill on A: the busy worker we were trying to unload recomputes the prefix, just to export it. No request option says "serve this only from the prefix cache, otherwise refuse", and `cached_tokens` in the response arrives after the work is done.

**Problem 2: The pull is all-or-nothing.** The NIXL connector pulls blocks for B's whole prompt (`nixl/pull_scheduler.py`). B can't take a prefix from A and compute the rest itself, so a partial hit on A can't be used, and the real request can't carry the pull. That is why step 2 exists.

### Proposed Change.

**1. Lookup-and-pin with no compute.** An engine-side operation that takes a prefix as vLLM block hashes and:

- looks it up in the prefix cache (`BlockHashToBlockMap`, which already indexes cached blocks by hash) without scheduling any compute
- pins the longest cached run under a lease, reusing the existing `kv_lease_duration` / delayed-free mechanism;
- returns the pinned block ids and the hit length in tokens (0 on a miss), in a form a NIXL peer can pull from.

**2. B calls it in a single request.** The router sends one request to B with a peer hint (A's address plus the prefix block hashes). B's connector calls lookup-and-pin on A over the connector's existing side channel, pulls whatever A pinned, and computes the rest. This needs a new connector-to-connector contract. We prefer it to the router calling A because:

- **No extra HTTP request on the critical path.** A request through A's API server goes through the kernel network stack, HTTP parsing, tokenization and scheduler admission before A looks at its cache. A connector-to-connector lookup skips all of that.
- **A's cache is checked when B is about to pull.** The router's index can point at blocks A has already evicted. A lookup on A at pull time is the source of truth: B pulls only what A still has and computes the rest.

The alternative, where the router calls lookup-and-pin on A and then sends B the real request with A's params, also avoids A's compute, but adds an HTTP round trip and depends on the lease holding until B pulls.

**3. Partial remote prefix.** B pulls a remote prefix of length k and computes tokens k..n locally in the same request, instead of asserting. This removes the warm-up request and makes partial hits usable. Without it, the system could be limited to full-prefix hits.

### Feedback Period.

One week

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Alternatives considered:

- **Stock 3-request flow.** Works today, but wastes A's compute on a stale-index miss and costs an extra round trip.
- **Router-side guards only.** Plan only on GPU-tier hits and measure the miss rate. Reduces the waste but can't remove it.
- **Shared external KV store** (e.g. LMCache or the offloading connectors). Avoids the peer request, but needs extra infrastructure and a second copy of the KV.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is a compute-free lookup-and-pin acceptable in the scheduler, or should it live entirely in the KV connector?
2. Is a connector-to-connector lookup-and-pin call (B asks A directly) acceptable, or would you rather expose it as an API that the router calls?
3. Is partial remote prefix plus local suffix compute on the NIXL roadmap, or open for contribution?

title: [RFC][HiSparse] Selective shared KV offloading for DeepSeek V4.1
author: Etelis
body:
We tested keeping the shared KV pools owned by layers **2 and 20** on CPU,
with selected rows fetched into a GPU cache during decode. The model keeps
its existing indexers; indexer K and sliding-window state stay on GPU.
Pools **8 and 14** stay on GPU. When space is needed, reclaim clean
CPU-backed copies before evicting GPU-only cached prefixes.

![Shared pools and proposed CPU/GPU placement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Etelis/vllm/d17dfa931fb647f6383fa92d79a3b4cb416762bd/docs/assets/dsv41-hisparse/layer-map.png)

Feedback on that integration would be welcome.

title: [RFC]: Text sessions on /v1/realtime with streaming-input prefill
author: AshutoshRautela
body:
### Motivation.

`/v1/realtime` is transcription only today. It accepts `input_audio_buffer.*` events and works only for models that implement `SupportsRealtime`. Voice agents that run ASR separately and use a text LLM can't use it.

These agents get the user's words incrementally while the user is still speaking. With streaming input (`StreamingInput`, resumable requests), the engine can prefill those words before the turn ends. When the turn is committed, only the last few tokens are left to prefill before decoding starts. vLLM has this engine support, but the server has no text API for it. Today a client has to write its own websocket server around `AsyncLLM`, or run another serving layer.

This RFC proposes text sessions on `/v1/realtime` in `vllm serve`. vLLM-Omni tracked streaming input for Qwen3-Omni in [vllm-project/vllm-omni#1951](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/1951). This RFC covers text LLMs in vLLM itself.

### Proposed Change.

Add text sessions to `/v1/realtime` for generative text models. Audio transcription keeps its current behavior.

**Protocol.** These are OpenAI Realtime events, except `input_text.*`, which mirrors `input_audio_buffer.*` because the OpenAI protocol has no text buffer.

- Client:
  - `session.update` (`instructions`, `tools`, `tool_choice`)
  - `conversation.item.create` (`message`, `function_call_output`)
  - `conversation.item.delete`
  - `input_text.append`, `input_text.commit`, `input_text.clear`
  - `response.create`, `response.cancel`
- Server:
  - `session.updated`
  - `conversation.item.added`, `conversation.item.done`, `conversation.item.deleted`
  - `response.created`
  - `response.output_item.added`, `response.output_item.done`
  - `response.output_text.delta`, `response.output_text.done`
  - `response.function_call_arguments.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.done`
  - `response.done`
  - `error`

**Serving.**

1. Register the route when the model supports `generate`, next to the current `realtime` task path. The session picks the text or transcription flow from the model's supported tasks.
2. Render the conversation with the existing chat serving code (chat template, tools, `chat_template_kwargs`). Text sessions then behave like `/v1/chat/completions`.
3. Keep one resumable request per turn:
   - Each `input_text.append` sends only the new prompt tokens as a `StreamingInput` chunk with `max_tokens=1`.
   - `response.create` sends the last chunk with the real sampling params.
   - If a new render no longer extends the tokens already sent (for example, the template changed earlier tokens), abort the request and start a new one from the full prompt.
4. Stream the answer through the chat completions output path, so reasoning parsers, tool call parsers, and structured outputs work as they do in chat.

**Scope of the first PR.**

- Text input and text output.
- Function tools.
- Reasoning output.

**Out of scope.**

- Audio output.
- Server VAD.
- Turn detection.
- Mixing audio and text input in one session.

**Dependencies.** Streaming input sessions need per-chunk structured outputs ([#57685](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57685)). Without that fix, tool calls and `response_format` break on the answer chunk.

**Expected benefit.** We ran an end-to-end voice agent benchmark (ASR, LLM, TTS) with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, using a 5000-token prompt with prefix caching off. The streaming mode used a websocket server around `AsyncLLM` with `StreamingInput`, and the chat mode used `/v1/chat/completions`. LLM TTFT is measured from the end of the user turn to the first token.

| Parallel streams | Chat LLM TTFT (ms) | Streaming LLM TTFT (ms) | Chat avg E2E latency (ms) | Streaming avg E2E latency (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 252 | 24 | 944 | 707 |
| 2 | 256 | 26 | 1004 | 726 |
| 4 | 243 | 26 | 972 | 734 |
| 8 | 260 | 30 | 984 | 758 |
| 16 | 268 | 34 | 1005 | 769 |
| 32 | 327 | 51 | 1158 | 846 |

Streaming prefill moves prompt processing into the time the user is speaking, when the engine is otherwise idle for that session. With chat completions, TTFT grows with the prompt, because the whole prompt is prefilled after the turn ends. With prefix caching on, earlier turns are reused, so chat completions only prefill the new turn and the gap shrinks. Streaming still removes that last prefill from the critical path.

The other benefit is the API. One websocket carries the whole conversation, the server keeps the context, and tools and reasoning work as they do in chat. Clients don't need to resend the full history on each turn.

**Open questions.**

1. Are `input_text.append` / `commit` / `clear` acceptable names, or should text use `conversation.item.create` with a partial flag?
2. Should text sessions live under `entrypoints/speech_to_text/realtime/`, or move to a shared `entrypoints/realtime/` with transcription and text handlers?
3. Should the held request be capped (idle timeout, max held sessions) to protect other traffic?

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@njhill @NickLucche

### Any Other Things.

We're happy to implement this after feedback, in PRs of a few hundred lines each: the protocol and text flow first, then tools and reasoning.

AI assistance was used to draft this RFC. The numbers come from our own benchmark runs.

title: [RFC][ROCm]: Batch-invariant kernels for Kimi-K3.1 on MI355X (KDA, DSA/indexer, MXFP4 MoE, LoRA, all-reduce)
author: indianspeedster
body:
## Motivation

`VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` works on ROCm since #52231, but Kimi-K3.1 (hybrid KDA linear attention + DSA sparse MLA, MXFP4 routed experts, LoRA) is not batch-invariant on MI355X with it alone. In RL, this mode is what lets the rollout's token log-probs match the trainer's exactly ("true on-policy"). On NVIDIA GB300 this already works for Kimi-K3.1 via a set of overlays (Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl); this issue tracks the ROCm counterparts so they can land in vLLM, in small PRs.

Tracking parent: #27433 ("AMD support").

## What breaks on ROCm today (Kimi-K3.1, TP8 + EP8, MI355X)

Found by bisection with a full-model batch-size sweep (same prompt alone vs. inside batches of 1..128):

| Component | Source of batch variance |
|---|---|
| KDA (linear attention) | decode and prefill take different kernels; in mixed batches decode rows go through the prefill path; FLA kernels autotune per shape; KDA state slots can be written twice under CUDA-graph replay after wake |
| DSA indexer | decode logits are computed differently from prefill; top-k tie order |
| Sparse MLA | FlyDSL path only above a token threshold; split-K count follows the number of query rows |
| Routed experts (MXFP4) | AITER CK / FlyDSL MoE choose tiles and splits by token count |
| AttnRes (block residual mix) | first diverging tensor in the full-model probe |
| TP all-reduce | custom all-reduce changes algorithm with message size |
| EP combine | rank partials summed in arrival order |
| Dense LoRA (punica expand) | two BF16 roundings (`bf16(bf16(delta) + base)`) |
| Dense BI matmul at decode M | correct, but on ROCm uses 128x128x64 at every M (no gfx950 entries in the tuned table), so decode is slow |

## Proposed changes (one PR each, all gated on `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`; default path unchanged)

- [ ] **BI matmul: gfx950 tile table** (#66628) for `batch_invariant` (small-M buckets; BLOCK_K kept at 64 so the K-reduction order and the bits are unchanged; every entry bitwise-equal to the default config at every tested M)
- [ ] **LoRA: single-rounding expand epilogue** (#66651) under BI (`bf16(fp32(delta) + fp32(base))`); platform-independent
- [ ] **DSA / indexer BI for Kimi-K3.1 on ROCm**: decode logits computed like prefill (row-bounded kernels), deterministic top-k, sparse MLA with one KV split, no FlyDSL dispatch in BI mode, allow the AITER FA MLA prefill in BI mode (related: #65278)
- [ ] **AttnRes BI** (#66718) (`models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/attn_res.py`)
- [ ] **KDA BI**: pinned FLA `chunk_kda` configs; a decode path that is bitwise equal to the chunk (prefill) form so a token's result does not depend on batch composition; CUDA-graph-capturable decode; KDA state-slot write dedup (last write wins) (related: #42960, #48613 for GDN)
- [ ] **BI two-stage custom all-reduce** for ROCm, bitwise equal to the 1-stage reduction
- [ ] **BI MXFP4 routed-expert MoE**: kernel proposed to AITER as an opt-in deterministic mode (fixed K order, no shape-dependent split), selected by vLLM under BI; includes expert LoRA
- [ ] **Ordered EP combine** (rank-order mode; MoRI side + vLLM flag)
- [ ] **Tests**: batch-size sweep + full-model gate in `tests/v1/determinism` for a ROCm Kimi-K3.1 config

## Evidence so far (out of tree, 2 nodes x 8 MI355X, vLLM rollout + Megatron trainer, LoRA r32 on all modules incl. experts)

- GRPO with `rollout_probs_diff_max == 0` at every step: 30-step run, 3,840 / 3,840 samples, 11,893,214 tokens, max abs diff 0 (checked per token, not only the batch max).
- Cost of BI at NVIDIA's published Kimi-K3.1 RL shape (256 samples/step, 2048 prompt / 6144 response, DAPO-Math-17k), same nodes, crossed design, 3 steps per arm: rollout **+1.0%**, whole RL step **-2.9%** vs. BI off.
- Kernel-level gates: each change above is bitwise-checked against its reference across batch sizes 1..128 before use.

The code is currently out-of-tree plugins + patches (verl draft PR verl-project/verl#8574). We'd like feedback on the split above, especially where maintainers prefer the MoE kernel to live (AITER vs. vLLM) and how KDA BI should be structured relative to the GDN work.

cc @mawong-amd @AndreasKaratzas @yewentao256 @aoshen02

title: [RFC]: P/D disaggregation for continuous RL rollouts (S1): order-free, seconds-long weight-update pauses
author: BeichenHuang
body:
### TL;DR

- **Problem.** Fully-async RL frameworks (prime-rl in production on NIXL) update weights with `pause(mode="keep", clear_cache=False)` on every P and D engine. On main, a P pause waits until D has read P's exports (31 s on NIXL, the lease), and a paused D stops renewing leases, so a pause longer than the lease frees KV that D will still read.
- **Proposal (variant A).** Three scheduler-side structures: a transfer ledger (P1), a pause table keyed by mode (P2), and zero-compute stepping while transfers are live (P3). S1 needs no connector code. About +400/-44 lines outside tests, in 3 PRs, plus a small Mooncake fix (step M).
- **Measured** on H20, 1P1D: S1 matrix 8/8 on NIXL and Mooncake (main: NIXL 4/8). P pause 0.9–1.7 s, D pause 0.03 s, 0 lease expiries, including 45 s pauses. No cost without a pause.
- A glue variant that does not touch `vllm/v1/core/` was built and measured for comparison. It needs a 300 s grace knob to pass and is not proposed.
- **Asks:** the decisions below, and review of steps 1–3.

### Decisions requested.

1. **A D-only pause holds P's exports** (open question 4). With A, P keeps a paused D's unread exports for as long as D is paused. With D paused alone and P still serving, P's KV fills up (measured: 99.4% KV usage, 0 running) until D resumes. Main expires those exports after the lease and keeps serving. Should the default be "hold" with an opt-in cap, or a cap?
2. **A keep pause no longer waits for D**, for every caller. #59670 does this behind a flag. Is it acceptable as the default?
3. **`resume()` during a pending pause fails that pause** ("Resumed before the pause completed", HTTP 500), instead of returning a late 200 for a pause that never held.
4. **An abort pause drops retained exports** instead of waiting for D to read them. What the connector is told about the drop is open question 1.
5. **Paused engines keep stepping with zero compute** while the ledger has live transfers. A keep pause then guarantees no *model* execution, not an idle KV cache (open question 2).
6. **The transfer ledger lives in `vllm/v1/core/sched/`** and is used with every connector. It replaces the current inference `len(requests) > running + waiting`.

### Scope: S1 only.

#62150 tracks three ways an RL framework pauses P/D engines to update weights. **This RFC is about S1 only.** S2 and S3 will get their own RFCs. Here we only check that the S1 structures do not make them worse and that they can be reused for them: the "S2/S3 probes" and the "What the other #62150 scenarios reuse" table below. A passing S2/S3 probe means the S1 change did not break that case, not that S2 or S3 is solved.

| | Scenario | Call sequence | In-flight requests and prefix cache | Users | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S1** | **Continuous (fully-async) rollout** | `pause(mode="keep", clear_cache=False)` on every P and D, in any order → broadcast weights → `update_weight_version` → `resume` | Keep their KV and continue under the new weights. New rollouts carry a `cache_salt` with the policy version. The cache is never reset. | prime-rl (production, NIXL); miles `in_place` is equivalent | P0, **this RFC** |
| S2 | Synchronous drain | `pause(mode="wait"\|"abort", clear_cache=True)` → [`sleep` → wake weights → update → wake KV, if colocated] → `reset_prefix_cache` → `resume` | Finished (`wait`) or aborted (`abort`). The engine is empty during the update; blocks are reclaimed. | verl, SkyRL (Mooncake), NeMo-RL, miles sync mode | P0, separate RFC |
| S3 | Retract | `pause(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)` → update → `resume` | Kept, but their KV is invalidated and recomputed under the new weights. | miles/SGLang default; no vLLM P/D user yet | P1, needs invalidate-without-reclaim (#64865 / #64900) |

### Motivation.

Fully-async RL frameworks update the policy while rollouts are still generating. On P/D disaggregation the update looks like this. prime-rl runs it in production on GLM-5.x with NIXL, xPyD and DP/EP.

```
pause(mode="keep", clear_cache=False)   on every P and D engine
broadcast the new weights               to every P and D engine
update_weight_version(step)
resume()
```

In-flight requests keep their KV and continue under the new weights. Tokens are labelled with `weight_versions`, and the trainer masks or corrects stale ones. New rollouts carry a `cache_salt` that includes the policy version, so they never hit KV computed with old weights. The prefix cache is never reset. miles/SGLang uses the same scheme (`in_place` pause plus a namespaced radix cache).

For this to work, a keep pause on P/D has to be safe in any order and short. On main it is neither:

1. **A P pause waits for D.** A keep pause completes only when the engine has no work (`EngineCoreProc._pause_complete` → `not has_work()`). On P, prefill requests whose KV is retained for a remote reader keep `Scheduler.has_finished_requests()` true. So P's pause lasts until D has read every export, or until the lease expires.
2. **A paused D goes dark.** In `PAUSED_ALL`, `get_num_unfinished_requests()` returns 0, so D stops stepping. It stops issuing reads, reporting completions, and renewing leases (NIXL and Mooncake both send their D→P renewals from `build_connector_meta`, which only runs inside a step). P reaps leases by wall clock, so a pause longer than the lease frees blocks D will read after resume.
3. **Aborts during a transfer are fragile.** #46240: a completion for a request the scheduler already freed kills EngineCore. On Mooncake, a request aborted before its KV is exported leaves D's pull unanswered until a timeout (see "Measured" below).

prime-rl works around (1) and (2) by pausing all P engines before any D engine, and around (3) with a monkey-patch. With the ordering, their slowest pause went from 30 s to 14.3 s and "Potentially invalid KV blocks" from 354 to 0 (prime-rl #4059). P's pause still lasts until D has drained P's exports.

### Measured on main, on a glue fix, and on this proposal.

Setup: one H20 node, 1P1D (one GPU each), Qwen3-8B, RoCE, D capped at `--max-num-seqs 32` so that P holds exports D has not read yet (the prime-rl situation), lease 30 s on both connectors (`kv_lease_duration=30` for Mooncake). 600-request load at concurrency 96. A case passes if every control call returns 200, the load finishes, both engines go idle and healthy, and greedy probes with a fresh `cache_salt` match a pre-load reference. S1 cases also require every pause to finish in < 3 s and zero lease expiries.

We built two variants from the same base (main 5cdeea9b1):

- **A, structure (this proposal):** the three scheduler-side structures in "Proposed Change". +416/-48 excluding tests on the branch, of which +15/-4 is the Mooncake fix (step M).
- **B, glue:** no change under `vllm/v1/core/`; a worker-side lease-renewal thread plus a relaxed pause predicate. +275/-9. Details and why it is not proposed are in the collapsed section below.

**S1 matrix** (keep pause, no clear; pause order {concurrent, P→D, D→P} × length {2 s, 45 s} under load, plus two idle cases):

| | main | B (glue) | A (structure) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mooncake | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |
| NIXL | 4/8 | 5/8; 8/8 only with `kv_unclaimed_grace=300` | **8/8** |

- On main with NIXL, every case where D pauses before or with P fails the same way: P's pause takes 31 s (the lease) and 19 leases expire.
- A passes all 8 with no knob: P pause 0.9–1.7 s, D pause 0.03 s, 0 expiries, including the 45 s pauses.
- On Mooncake, where lease expiry is enforced, a D paused longer than the lease fails all 12 requests it holds on main; A serves all 12 (stale-read probes below).
- No cost without a pause: the no-pause load takes 56.5–57.1 s on main, B and A, on both connectors.

<details><summary>S2/S3 probes (regression check only; out of scope for this RFC)</summary>

Run to check that the S1 structures do not regress these scenarios and that they extend to them. S2: `abort_P_midxfer`, `pause_wait_clear_P`, `pause_abort_PD`, `sleep1_abort_PD`, `resume_during_wait_D`. S3: `pause_keep_clear_D`.

| | main | B (glue) | A before Mooncake fix | A |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mooncake | 1/6 | 5/6 | 1/6 | **4/6** + 1 intended 500 |
| NIXL | 6/6 | 5/6 | 5/6 + 1 intended 500 | 5/6 + 1 intended 500 (NIXL code untouched) |

- **Mooncake D gets stuck on main** under abort mid-transfer, wait+clear on P, pause(abort) and sleep(abort). D waits on a pull that P never answers: `record_send_reqs` drops the aborted transfer without waking the waiter (or raises `KeyError` if the worker never saw it; #65672 fixes that), and a later pull recreates a placeholder. D then waits out `VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (480 s by default). Our probes give up after 120 s and count that as a failure; with the timeout lowered to 60 s, D drains. This is a connector bug independent of the pause design. With the Mooncake fix (step M), all four cases pass on A: pause(abort) of P and D takes 1.7 s / 0.9 s, where main's D pause had not finished within the probe's 120 s.
- **NIXL sleep(abort) on P and D:** P's sleep takes 33 s on main (until D's leases lapse), >120 s on B (D's worker keeps renewing for requests D abandoned), and 3.8 s on A.
- **`resume` during a pending pause** now fails that pause with 500 "Resumed before the pause completed" instead of a late 200 for a pause that never held (decision 3). This is intended and counted as a failure in the table. On Mooncake, one run in three also left one request waiting on D forever (544 ok, 55 client disconnects, 1 stuck); two reruns finished cleanly. Not yet root-caused; tracked as a step-2 review item.
- **`keep` + `clear_cache=True` on D** returns 500 on Mooncake everywhere. That is S3, out of scope here.

</details>

<details><summary>Stale-read probes (checking "no request reads invalid KV")</summary>

Twelve copy-task requests ("repeat these 24 random 5-digit numbers") are sent while D is paused, so P exports their KV and D holds them. Then the control sequence runs and D resumes. Each request either errors (an honest failure) or must copy its list exactly. A copy task is used because free-form greedy text is not batch-invariant: in a first version of the probe, 4–8 of 12 free-form outputs differed from the no-load reference by a word or two, also in runs with no abort and no lease expiry. The copy task is 12/12 in a no-pause control on every variant. Sequences:
- `abort`: P pause(abort) and resume while D is paused. Run with and without `clear_cache`.
- `dpause`: D alone stays paused 40–45 s, longer than the lease.
- Each sequence runs once at full KV size and once with P's pool cut to 4096 blocks (65k tokens), with a flood of local requests to P of 1× and 4× its pool before D resumes, so that freed blocks get reused before D reads.

| | main | B (glue) | A |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mooncake, `abort` | 12 errors (P pause 25 s, leases lapse) | 12 errors | 12 errors (P pause 1.4 s) |
| Mooncake, `dpause` | **12 errors** (leases lapse while D is paused) | — | **12/12 correct** (paused D keeps renewing, P3) |
| NIXL, `abort` | 12/12 correct (P pause 31 s) | 12/12 correct (P pause 30 s) | 12/12 correct (P pause 1.4 s) |
| NIXL, `dpause` | 12/12 correct, 95–119 leases expired | 12/12 correct, 92–118 expired | 12/12 correct |
| silently wrong output | 0 in all runs | 0 | 0 |

- No variant returned a wrong copy in any of these runs, including runs where P had freed and reused the blocks of an export D read later. On NIXL that is not explained yet: on main, P reaps 67–95 leases while D is paused (which should include the probes'), seconds before D reads them, P then serves 4× its pool of other requests, and D's reads still return the right KV. We do not want to rely on this and will instrument D (checksum of the received blocks against P's at export) before calling it safe.
- The other side of P3: on A, P's blocks stay reserved for a paused D's backlog for as long as D is paused.
