title: [RFC]: Packed-weight INT4 GEMM (W4A16 / W4A8) for RDNA4 (gfx1200/gfx1201)
author: jeffreylowzg
body:
### Motivation.


On RDNA4 (Radeon AI PRO R9700, gfx1201), W4A16 decode runs on `RDNAHybridW4A16LinearKernel` (#40977): `wvSplitK_int4_g` for up to 5 rows, Triton above. #62708 extends it to an INT4 `lm_head`, and #63562 retunes the gfx12 Triton tiles for small M. I have a set of RDNA4 kernels (HIP, opt-in, gfx1200/gfx1201 only). Against current main + #63562, with the model's numerics unchanged (W4A16), my branch decodes RedHatAI's Qwen3.8-27B-INT4 1.12× faster at batch 1, 1.65× at batch 16 and 1.51× at batch 64. It decodes Muse-Glimmer-30B-INT4 at the same speed at batch 1 and 1.71× faster at batch 16 and 64. An opt-in W4A8 mode raises batch 64 to 1.84× (Qwen) and 2.30× (Muse). The branch sits on an Oct 16 base, so these are not yet like-for-like; numbers on main will come with PR 1. I'd like to agree on how to upstream them without duplicating or conflicting with the PRs above.

The core idea differs from the existing path. Weights are repacked once at load time into WMMA fragment order, with each group's scales and zero points interleaved in the same stream. One HIP decode kernel family then covers 1–448 tokens, with variants chosen by M. Above 448 tokens the weights are dequantized into a packed BF16 prefill GEMM. The existing path reads the GPTQ/AWQ layout directly instead, using `wvSplitK` for M ≤ 5 and Triton for everything else.

**Setup:** 1× R9700 (32 GB) capped at 250 W to reduce run-to-run variance, ROCm 7.2.1. Models: `RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-INT4` and `RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-INT4` (compressed-tensors, symmetric INT4, group 128). FP8 KV cache, 1024-token prompts, `max_num_seqs` 64; BF16 SSM state for Qwen. Decode tok/s = batch / per-step decode time. No row below preempted or ran in waves. Main is 7871c62b61; #63562 (c066a2949a) is applied on top of it. Repeats of the same cells were within 0.2 % (0.5 % for one b1 cell). "All on" rows include the opt-in W4A8 mode, which quantizes activations to INT8 for 33–448 tokens; the "without W4A8" rows leave it off, so their numerics match W4A16.

**Qwen3.8-27B-INT4** (hybrid Gated DeltaNet + attention):

| setup | b1 ms (tok/s) | b16 ms (tok/s) | b64 ms (tok/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 28.53 (35.1) | 75.65 (211.5) | 96.30 (664.6) |
| main + #63562 | 28.53 (35.1) | 51.99 (307.7) | 94.91 (674.3) |
| **this work, without W4A8** | **25.38 (39.4)** | **31.49 (508.1)** | **63.03 (1015.4)** |
| this work, all on | 25.47 (39.3) | 31.36 (510.2) | 51.50 (1242.7) |

**Muse-Glimmer-30B-INT4** (52 attention layers, 39 of them with a 2048-token sliding window):

| setup | b1 ms (tok/s) | b16 ms (tok/s) | b64 ms (tok/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | 29.21 (34.2) | 75.35 (212.3) | 89.94 (711.6) |
| main + #63562 | 29.19 (34.3) | 51.91 (308.2) | 88.58 (722.5) |
| this work, all on, sliding-window layers on Triton | 33.00 (30.3) | 34.42 (464.8) | 45.38 (1410.3) |
| **this work, without W4A8** | **29.08 (34.4)** | **30.32 (527.7)** | **51.58 (1240.8)** |
| this work, all on | 29.09 (34.4) | 30.28 (528.4) | 38.50 (1662.3) |

With 4096-token prompts, longer than the window, Muse decodes at 29.57 ms (33.8 tok/s) at b1 and 31.79 ms (503.3 tok/s) at b16 with this work, against 29.51 ms (33.9) and 76.81 ms (208.3) on main.

This work is on an older base (1a5b187066, Oct 16), so here is its ablation from that base on Qwen. Each row adds one piece to the row above:

| this work, cumulative (Qwen) | b1 ms (tok/s) | b16 ms (tok/s) | b64 ms (tok/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| base 1a5b187066, all flags off | 40.55 (24.7) | 93.79 (170.6) | 144.64 (442.5) |
| + packed W4A16 GEMM | 40.72 (24.6) | 53.40 (299.6) | 112.91 (566.8) |
| + W4A16 epilogue fusion (add+RMSNorm, SiluAndMul) | 40.74 (24.5) | 54.40 (294.1) | 113.03 (566.2) |
| + W4A8 for 33–448 tokens (opt-in, changes numerics) | 40.37 (24.8) | 54.62 (292.9) | 104.04 (615.1) |
| + RDNA4 paged decode + prefill attention | 28.40 (35.2) | 34.29 (466.6) | 54.00 (1185.2) |
| + INT4 `lm_head` | 25.47 (39.3) | 31.36 (510.2) | 51.50 (1242.7) |

What the ablation shows:

- **W4A16 GEMM** is the main piece for batches: −43 % step time at b16 and −22 % at b64 on the old base. On the old base it reaches 53.4 ms at b16, close to main + #63562 (52.0 ms), even though the old base's attention is much slower than main's. A like-for-like number against #63562 will come from PR 1 rebased on main.
- **Epilogue fusion** shows no gain here (+0.0 to +1.9 %). I propose leaving it out.
- **W4A8** only pays off at b64, because it only applies from 33 tokens: −8 % on the old base, and −18 % on Qwen (63.03 → 51.50 ms) and −25 % on Muse (51.58 → 38.50 ms) once attention is fast. It is off by default because it quantizes activations to INT8.
- **Attention** drives b1. Main already closed most of that gap (#63735 et al.: 28.5 ms vs the old base's 40.6 ms), so against main the gains are mostly at batch. On Muse, the attention kernels need sliding-window support: without it, the 39 windowed layers fall back to Triton, which costs 3.9 ms per step at b1 and 6.9 ms at b64.

**Accuracy** (GSM8K, 1319 questions, chat template):

| model | main | this work, all on |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B-INT4 (thinking off) | 0.953 | 0.952 |
| Muse-Glimmer-30B-INT4 (`--reasoning-parser muse_glimmer`, reasoning strength low, 4096 max tokens) | 0.870 | 0.890 |

### Proposed Change.

A series of small, opt-in PRs, each gated to gfx1200/gfx1201, with kernel tests and `benchmarks/kernels/` scripts:

1. **Packed W4A16 GEMM** as an `MPLinearKernel` (group 64/128, with or without zero points, BF16/FP16 activations). It covers decode for 1–448 tokens, plus the packed BF16 prefill GEMM it dequantizes into above 448. Off by default via an env flag at first. The open question is whether it should later outrank `RDNAHybridW4A16LinearKernel` on gfx12 when it is built.
2. **INT4 `lm_head`**: reuse #62708's `lm_head` quantization config rather than adding a second flag, with the packed kernel as the gfx12 backend. This would build on #62708 once it lands. It must find the head on models whose language model is the bare decoder: on Muse-Glimmer, `get_language_model()` has no `lm_head`.
3. **RDNA4 paged decode attention** (BF16/FP8 KV, sliding windows, speculative verification), then **prefill attention**. This overlaps in goal with #58156 and #34741, so I'll compare against them before opening anything.
4. **W4A8 (INT8 activations) for 33–448 tokens**, opt-in only.

Not proposed: the epilogue fusion, which shows no measurable gain on one GPU.

One finding about hardware queues needs a decision. HIP maps streams onto `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES` hardware queues, 4 by default. On RDNA4 some processes then fall into a slow mode that lasts for the whole process. On Muse with the packed GEMM alone at b1, 6 of 9 launches in one session ran at about 47 ms per step instead of 37 ms. The kernel times are identical in both modes; the host waits about 10 ms longer for each step's sampled tokens. With 1 or 2 queues, every launch was fast. My branch therefore defaults RDNA4 to 1 queue, and the Muse "this work" rows use it. The Qwen "without W4A8" row also uses 1 queue. The other Qwen rows and every main row use the default 4. With our attention, Qwen measures the same at 1 and 4 queues in the fast mode (all on at 1 queue: 25.37 / 31.45 / 51.67 ms), but in a later session it fell into the slow mode at 4 queues too. Main stays at 4 because 1 queue slows upstream's Triton paged attention by 28 % at b1 (40.2 → 51.5 ms per step). I'd propose the queue default as a separate change once it is clear which attention path it applies to.

Questions for reviewers:

- Is a separate packed-weight kernel acceptable next to the hybrid kernel, or should it plug in as a backend of `RDNAHybridW4A16LinearKernel`?
- Opt-in env flag or automatic selection on gfx12? What CI coverage for gfx12 kernels is expected?
- Should W4A8 be a quant-config option instead of an env flag?
- Has anyone else seen the 4-queue slow mode on gfx12, and is a `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES` default in `platforms/rocm.py` acceptable?

### Feedback Period.

One week

### CC List.

@mgehre-amd (#40977) @daibenzhe #63562

### Any Other Things.

- All runs used a single GPU at a 250 W cap (stock is 300 W) to reduce variance; every row was measured under the same cap. I haven't measured at 300 W.
- The main and #63562 rows ran from a separate worktree with its own venv.
- Size: the kernels live in one new HIP file. On my branch it covers BF16, FP8 and INT4 (~2,600 lines); PR 1 needs only the INT4 and BF16 prefill parts. Tests are in `tests/model_executor/layers/test_rocm_unquantized_gemm.py` and, for attention, `tests/kernels/attention/test_attention.py`. vLLM's AMD CI doesn't cover gfx12, so I'd run the tests and benchmarks on an R9700 for each PR.
- AI assistance was used for the kernels, the benchmarks and this write-up. I reviewed the results and am responsible for them.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Define an Optional In-Tree Integration Path for Hardware Backends
author: a120092009
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM's hardware plugin system enables independent backend development. However, an optional in-tree path could improve coordination during upstream refactors for vendors willing to provide sustained maintenance and hardware CI.

Two examples illustrate the adaptation work involved:

1. KV cache spec refactoring ([#51704](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51704)): Introduced backend-published packing through customize_spec() and fields such as state_content_bytes, moving format-specific sizing out of spec subclasses. Downstream backends need to align their custom cache specifications and packing logic with this contract.

2. Memory profiling changes ([#49208](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49208)): Added torch_allocated, total_consumed, and transient_peak_headroom, and changed how non-KV memory is calculated and consumed by the worker. Backends maintaining their own profiling utilities need to update both data structures and accounting semantics.

These changes improve vLLM, but adapting out-of-tree implementations can require a separate cross-repository update and validation cycle.

In-tree implementations are more readily included in repository-wide impact analysis, maintainer review, and coordinated updates within the same PR. With vendor-provided CI, affected backends could be validated before merging. Out-of-tree plugins can also participate in upstream PR testing, but coordinated fixes still span repositories.

The hardware-specific model separation discussed in #42770 provides an additional reason to revisit integration boundaries, while recognizing that model separation alone does not isolate every runtime dependency.

### Proposed Change.

Define an optional, case-by-case in-tree integration path alongside plugins. Vendors could build hardware-specific adaptations using the current flat model structure, while keeping shared runtime changes aligned with upstream architecture. Optimizations that require incompatible architectural changes could remain in out-of-tree plugins.

Requirements for in-tree backends would include, but are not limited to:

1. Dedicated backend maintainers responsible for reviews and compatibility fixes.

2. Vendor-provided hardware CI with an agreed test scope.

3. Hardware-specific code and dependencies isolated from unrelated platforms.

### Feedback Period.

One week

### CC List.

@youkaichao @simon-mo @WoosukKwon @kzawora-intel @wangxiyuan @zou3519

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Async CPU tier setup for OffloadingConnector
author: Etelis
body:
## Motivation.

With a large CPU tier, startup waits for every worker to pre-fault and pin its share of `/dev/shm` before the engine can serve. Two examples from our experiments:

- GLM-5.3 with 16 H100s (DP16/EP, 4 pods), a 280 GiB tier per rank. Pre-fault takes 117 s and pinning 12 s, all of it on the startup critical path.
- Qwen3-8B (dummy weights) with TP=4 and a 1,250 GiB tier on one H100 node. Startup is 241.5 s, and most of that is the CPU tier.

#62337 adds a core ready state for connectors. #54578 adds async init to OffloadingConnector with the same `async_init` option, and #42632 and #54792 cover SimpleCPUOffloadConnector. This RFC covers what OffloadingConnector needed on top at these sizes: a graph-capture guard, paced pinning, and Tiering support, which #54578 rejects. Problems came up in four parts of the connector.

### CPU tier setup (worker)

1. **CUDA graph capture.** A `cudaHostRegister` on another thread during a global-mode capture invalidates the capture. That race is what reverted #45850 (#46933, #46958). 

2. **Serving stalls.** Back-to-back `cudaHostRegister` calls hold a CUDA driver lock and starve the serving thread's CUDA calls.

   | Background thread (microbenchmark) | Median step time vs. no thread (3.7 ms) |
   |---|---|
   | Pins 9 MiB slots back to back | 303x |
   | Pins 1 GiB chunks | ~5,800x |
   | Pins 9 MiB slots, then sleeps 1x the call time | 1.8x |
   | Pins 9 MiB slots, then sleeps 4x the call time | 1.2x |

### Readiness (scheduler)

3. **Readiness from many workers.** The tier is usable only when every worker (TP x PP) has finished. Fault-tolerance recovery can replay a worker's output, so the scheduler should count ranks, not reports.

4. **Idle engines.** Readiness travels with engine steps. An idle engine therefore turns offloading on, and attaches secondary tiers, only with its first request. That is harmless for a cache. For the P2P tier's P/D mode it means the first requests to an idle engine always arrive before its tier is attached (problem 8).

### Tiering secondary tiers

Tiering (`TieringOffloadingSpec`) uses the CPU tier as its primary tier and adds secondary tiers, such as the P2P tier.

5. **Registering an empty region.** The P2P tier registers the whole CPU region when the scheduler starts. If the workers have not faulted the region in yet, that registration faults every page on one thread. That is the cost #66391 removes from the synchronous path, and it comes back here. Secondary tiers have to be attached after the workers are ready. #54578 rejects `async_init` with Tiering, which is the configuration we run.

6. **Requests that predate a tier.** A tier attached later never saw `on_new_request` for requests already running, so it must not get lookups, stores or finish calls for them.

### P2P tier

The P2P tier moves KV from one instance's CPU tier to another's over NIXL. Which of its two modes a request uses depends on its `kv_transfer_params`.

7. **Prefix sharing (`remote_kv_source`).** An instance asks a peer which blocks it holds, and fetches only the ones the peer confirms. It needs no change:
   - Lookups miss until the tier is attached and the peer handshake is done.
   - If a peer's tier is not up yet, the handshake cannot finish until it attaches, so its prefixes are recomputed until then.

   A late tier costs recomputed prefixes, not errors or stalls.

8. **P/D mode (`remote_decoder` / `remote_prefiller`).** This is an alternative to NixlConnector for the handoff. The proxy marks the prefill instance's request (P) with `remote_decoder` and the decode instance's request (D) with `remote_prefiller`. D's lookup reports a hit for every block right away, without asking P. Two things can go wrong at startup:
   - **P's tier is not attached yet, or the request reached P before the attach.** P never holds the blocks for D. D waits up to 30 s for them, then prefills the whole prompt itself.
   - **D's tier is not attached yet.** D prefills locally, while P keeps the blocks it held for D pinned in its CPU tier for 60 s.

9. **No readiness signal.** `/health` is OK before the secondary tiers are attached, so a router cannot tell when the P/D mode is safe to use.

## Proposed Change.

### Milestone 1: background CPU tier setup

**Worker side** (`CPUOffloadingWorker`):
- With `async_init`, the region is mapped without pre-faulting or pinning. A background thread then does the following:
  - sets the device and switches itself to relaxed capture mode (problem 1);
  - pre-faults the region in 1 GiB steps with `madvise` through ctypes, which releases the GIL;
  - pins it one small call at a time, sleeping `async_init_pin_pace` times each call's duration after it (default 2.0; problem 2). A call is this worker's slot in one row, or whole rows up to 8 MiB when the region is pinned as a whole;
  - marks the worker ready.
- Shutdown stops the thread between steps and unregisters whatever it already pinned.
- If setup fails, it logs an error and offloading stays off; the engine keeps serving.
- Memory is committed after the engine is healthy, so an undersized pod limit shows up as an OOM kill while serving, not at startup.
- CUDA only. Other platforms log a warning and set up synchronously.
- This covers `CPUOffloadingSpec`. Tiering moves its CPU tier to the background in milestone 2, together with its secondary tiers, since deferring one without the other brings back problem 5.

**Gate.** Until every worker is ready, lookups return no hits and no store jobs are built. For requests still running when the tier turns on, skipped chunks are offered again, because stored-chunk indices don't move.
- Each worker reports its rank in `OffloadingWorkerMetadata`, and ranks are merged as a set (problem 3).
- The scheduler turns offloading on once it has seen every rank, and tells the workers through `OffloadingConnectorMetadata`.

The gate lives in the connector so this can land before #62337, and it goes away once #62337 merges (see below). Until then it needs no changes to the connector base API, the core scheduler or the model runner. The offloading API gets `OffloadingWorker.start_background_setup()` and `is_ready()`, plus `OffloadingManager.on_workers_ready()` in milestone 2, all no-ops by default.

Pinning gradually and letting transfers wait on the blocks they touch, as suggested in #46933, would bring the tier up sooner, but every transfer would need a readiness check. Turning the whole tier on at once keeps the change inside the gate.

### Milestone 2: Tiering secondary tiers

- With `async_init`, Tiering sets its CPU tier up in the background as in milestone 1.
- Secondary tiers are not built at scheduler start. Once every worker is ready, a background thread builds them and attaches them under the manager lock (problem 5). If building fails, the engine keeps running on the CPU tier alone.
- Each request remembers how many tiers existed when it arrived, so a tier attached later never sees a request that `on_new_request` did not announce to it (problem 6).
- Shutdown waits up to 120 s for an attach that is still registering the region before it unmaps the region.

**Results** (milestones 1 and 2; Sync and async_init are time to `/health` OK):

| Setup | Sync | async_init | Tier ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.3, 16 H100 (4 pods), 280 GiB/rank, Tiering + P2P | 439 s | 334 s | ~104 s after healthy (P2P ~138 s) |
| Qwen3-8B (dummy weights), TP=4, 1,250 GiB, Tiering + P2P | 241.5 s | 57-61 s (3 runs) | ~160 s after healthy (P2P ~197 s) |

```mermaid
gantt
    title GLM-5.3 startup, seconds from container start
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %s
    section Sync
    Start to KV cache init                 :s1, 0, 205s
    Pre-fault                              :crit, s2, after s1, 117s
    Pin                                    :crit, s3, after s2, 12s
    Warmup                                 :s4, after s3, 86s
    Ready to healthy, P2P registration     :crit, s5, after s4, 19s
    Healthy at 439 s                       :milestone, after s5, 0s
    section async_init
    Start to KV cache init                 :a1, 0, 230s
    Warmup                                 :a2, after a1, 100s
    Ready to healthy                       :a3, after a2, 4s
    Healthy at 334 s                       :milestone, after a3, 0s
    Pre-fault and pin, background          :active, a4, after a1, 208s
```

Pre-fault, pinning and P2P registration leave the critical path. Two things went the other way in the async run: its slowest pod took 101 s to load weights against 66 s in sync, and warmup took 14 s longer. This run also used an earlier build that pinned without pacing. Pinning started after healthy on every rank, so healthy times are unaffected, but with the default pacing the tier comes up later.

### Milestone 3: P2P tier P/D mode

This milestone matters only for deployments that hand off through the P2P tier instead of NixlConnector. It is not implemented yet. We run prefix sharing with NixlConnector for the handoff, so we have not tested the P/D mode with `async_init`.

- **Readiness gauge.** Each engine exports a gauge, such as `vllm:kv_offload_tier_ready`. It turns 1 once the CPU tier is ready and the secondary tiers are attached, and within a process it only goes from 0 to 1. Without `async_init` it reads 1 from the start (problem 9).
- **Router gating.** The router uses the P/D mode only when both P and D report 1. Before that it hands off through NixlConnector if the deployment runs it. Otherwise D prefills alone, and P needs problem 4 solved to come up without traffic (question 1). Prefix sharing is no fallback here, since it also needs both P2P tiers attached.

Together these cover problem 8:
- A request sent in the P/D mode reaches P after P's tier is attached, so P holds its blocks for D.
- D's tier is attached too, so P's held blocks are fetched instead of pinned for 60 s.
- A stale scrape only delays the switch, as long as the router resets an instance's value when it restarts.

### Open questions

1. **Idle engines.** Should an idle engine keep stepping until the tier is ready, so offloading turns on without traffic? Returning True from `has_pending_push_work()` until then would do it with no core change, at the cost of empty engine steps for the minutes setup takes. #62337 has the same limitation.
2. **Readiness signal.** We plan a gauge, not a new probe:
   - `/health` has to stay OK during setup, or `async_init` gains nothing.
   - KV-cache-aware routers, such as llm-d's and Dynamo's, learn about CPU tier blocks from KV events. There are none before the tier is on, so they already route correctly.
   - The P2P tier's P/D mode is the only case that needs an explicit signal.

   Is a gauge enough there, or would routers rather poll an endpoint?
3. **Fail fast for the P/D mode.** Should D's P/D lookup miss until its session to P has finished the handshake, as prefix sharing does since #64501? A 30 s wait on an unattached or restarted P would become an immediate local prefill. But sessions open on the first request, so the first requests on every new session would prefill on D and pin P's blocks for 60 s. That is why #64501 kept the eager hit.

## CC List.

@orozery @NickLucche @YannikHinteregger @ivanium @liranschour @nilig @ronensc

title: [RFC]: Classify GPU faults in fault-tolerance status and mark sticky CUDA errors dead
author: harche
body:
### Motivation. I work on GPU device health in Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA): resource health status in kubelet ([KEP-4680](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4680)) and the device health monitor for the NVIDIA DRA driver ([kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu#1525](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/pull/1525)). That monitor decides whether a GPU is healthy from the [NVML recovery action](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvml-api/latest/api/group__nvmlFieldValueEnums.html#c.NVML_FI_DEV_GET_GPU_RECOVERY_ACTION). One class of faults is invisible there, and only the inference engine can report it. The fault-tolerance framework from [#44428](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44428) and [#46370](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46370) is the natural place to do so. **Faults caused by the application leave the GPU healthy but the process unusable.** - **CUDA:** for `cudaErrorIllegalAddress` (700), the [CUDA runtime documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#_CPPv4N9cudaError23cudaErrorIllegalAddressE) says it "leaves the process in an inconsistent state and any further CUDA work will return the same error. To continue using CUDA, the process must be terminated and relaunched." [`cudaErrorAssert`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#_CPPv4N9cudaError15cudaErrorAssertE) (710) says "The device cannot be used again" and requires the same relaunch. - **Device:** NVIDIA's [Xid catalog](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/xid-errors/analyzing-xid-catalog.html) lists `RESTART_APP` as the immediate action for Xid 31. For Xid 43 it says the application "must terminate. The GPU remains in a healthy state." - **Node:** NVML reports the recovery action as `NONE`, so the DRA health monitor treats the event as non-fatal and keeps the device schedulable ([device_health.go#L548-L550](https://github.com/harche/k8s-dra-driver-gpu/blob/256a484c073bb2421338ff2a32ed48747dc73a34/cmd/gpu-kubelet-plugin/device_health.go#L548-L550)). Measured on an A10G (driver 595.112.07, torch 2.14, CUDA 13). The node view column follows from the recovery action; I did not run the DRA driver in this test. | Fault | Exception in the worker | Xid | NVML recovery action | Node view | CUDA context | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Illegal address | `torch.AcceleratorError`, `error_code=700` | 31 | `NONE` | Healthy | Unusable | | Device-side assert | `torch.AcceleratorError`, `error_code=710` | 43 | `NONE` | Healthy | Unusable | | Out of memory | `torch.OutOfMemoryError` | None | `NONE` | Healthy | Usable | **The fault-tolerance status cannot tell these apart today.** PyTorch puts the CUDA error code on the exception ([Exceptions.cpp#L294-L303](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/0eeca006d930450cf7b950a3532228b84026d9f1/torch/csrc/Exceptions.cpp#L294-L303)), but vLLM drops it on the way to the sentinel: 1. The worker converts the exception to a string ([multiproc_executor.py#L1154-L1156](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py#L1154-L1156)). 2. The executor raises `RuntimeError("One or more workers failed")` ([multiproc_executor.py#L572](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py#L572)). 3. The sentinel sets `unhealthy` and stores only the class name in `fault_info` ([engine_core_sentinel.py#L152-L170](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py#L152-L170)). Fault-tolerance deployments use the multiprocess executor by default, because external-LB mode requires more than one DP rank ([parallel.py#L589-L592](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/config/parallel.py#L589-L592), [parallel.py#L1147](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/config/parallel.py#L1147)). So every worker fault reaches the orchestrator as `RuntimeError`. An orchestrator that follows the contract from [#46370](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46370) sees all ranks `unhealthy`, the only status that accepts commands ([engine_core_sentinel.py#L115-L118](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py#L115-L118)), and with no dead rank to remove it sends `retry`. After a sticky error `retry` cannot succeed, and the orchestrator then resets the whole group. [#27866](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/27866) defines `retry` for "transient and recoverable faults". A sticky CUDA error is neither, but the status gives the orchestrator no way to know that. ```mermaid flowchart LR W["Worker
AcceleratorError
error_code=700"] -->|"str(exc)"| E["Executor
RuntimeError
'One or more workers failed'"] E --> S["Sentinel
status: unhealthy
fault_info: 'RuntimeError'"] S --> O["Orchestrator
retry, then group reset"] ``` Outside fault-tolerance mode the result is similar: a GPU fault and an ordinary Python exception look the same from outside the process. Both return HTTP 500 and raise `EngineDeadError`, the server exits with status 0 ([#48966](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48966)), and nothing is written to the container's [termination message](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/determine-reason-pod-failure/) ([core.py#L1726-L1732](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/engine/core.py#L1726-L1732)). ### Proposed Change. Carry the classification that the worker can make at the point of failure up to the status API, and report a fault that requires a restart as `dead`. The engine reports what happened. The orchestrator still owns the decision. ```mermaid flowchart LR W["Worker
classifies the exception
at the point of failure"] -->|"classification"| E["Executor
failure carries
the classification"] E --> S["Sentinel
status: dead
gpu_fault: {...}"] S --> O["Orchestrator
scale_down the rank"] E -.->|"fatal error"| T["Termination message"] ``` **What the worker records.** At the point of failure the worker holds both the exception and the device. It records: - the CUDA error code, from `error_code` on `torch.AcceleratorError`, with no message parsing; - whether the code is sticky. The set is 700, 702, 710 and 714 to 719, the kernel-execution errors for which the [CUDA runtime documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/group__CUDART__TYPES.html#_CPPv4N9cudaError22cudaErrorLaunchFailureE) says the process must be "terminated and relaunched"; - the GPU UUID, so the fault can be matched with node-side health for the same device; - the NVML recovery action, read once after the fault with the same query the DRA driver uses ([device_health.go#L472-L493](https://github.com/harche/k8s-dra-driver-gpu/blob/256a484c073bb2421338ff2a32ed48747dc73a34/cmd/gpu-kubelet-plugin/device_health.go#L472-L493)). NVML stays usable after the CUDA context has faulted. **The decision rule.** A fault requires a restart when the error is sticky or the recovery action is anything other than `NONE`. Every worker failure path must carry the classification. That includes the KV connector path, which today also reduces the exception to a string ([multiproc_executor.py#L1138-L1147](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py#L1138-L1147)). **The status contract.** A restart-required fault reports `dead`. Both `unhealthy` and `dead` carry a structured `gpu_fault` object. `fault_info` stays a string, because existing consumers decode it as one ([llm-d resiliency operator, driver.go#L62](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator/blob/02fc86cf9c213002a519bca20d8a6309bddd2ee4/internal/engine/vllm/driver.go#L62)), and gains a readable summary: ```json { "status": "dead", "fault_info": "AcceleratorError: GPU fault: cuda_error=700 sticky=True gpu=GPU-5f1c... recovery_action=NONE; restart required", "gpu_fault": { "cuda_error": 700, "sticky": true, "gpu_uuid": "GPU-5f1c...", "recovery_action": "NONE", "restart_required": true } } ``` **The termination message.** On a fatal engine error, the engine writes the same classification to `/dev/termination-log` as `{"gpu_faults": [...]}`. Kubernetes then shows it in the container's last state. This applies to plain `vllm serve` as well, independent of fault-tolerance mode. #### Goals and non-goals Goals: - An orchestrator, such as the [llm-d resiliency operator](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator), can distinguish a sticky GPU fault from a transient one using the status API alone. - A rank whose CUDA context is unusable is never offered `retry`. - The fault class is visible after the process exits. Non-goals: - Hardware monitoring in the engine. Xid events and ECC counters belong to the node layer, which already watches them. - Recovery policy in the engine. vLLM does not cordon, restart or exclude devices. - New FT commands. #### Design decisions - **`dead` rather than a new status.** In [#46370](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46370), `dead` accepts no commands and covers two cases: - the engine process is gone; - a `scale_down` failed, after which, in the words of that PR, "the instance has to be restarted" ([engine_core_sentinel.py#L455-L458](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py#L455-L458)). A rank with a sticky CUDA error is in the second situation even though its process is still running. Orchestrators already exclude `dead` ranks. The llm-d resiliency operator treats a `dead` rank as terminal ([vllm.go#L110-L112](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator/blob/02fc86cf9c213002a519bca20d8a6309bddd2ee4/internal/engine/vllm/vllm.go#L110-L112)) and removes terminal ranks with `scale_down` ([policy.go#L49-L52](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator/blob/02fc86cf9c213002a519bca20d8a6309bddd2ee4/internal/engine/vllm/policy.go#L49-L52)) instead of retrying ([policy.go#L54](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator/blob/02fc86cf9c213002a519bca20d8a6309bddd2ee4/internal/engine/vllm/policy.go#L54)). A new status would make every orchestrator change its policy for the same outcome. - **Recovery action alongside stickiness.** A non-sticky error on a GPU that NVML says needs a reset (for example Xid 79, whose catalog action is `RESTART_BM`) must not be retried either. The engine uses the same signal as the DRA driver, which treats `GPU_RESET`, `NODE_REBOOT`, `DRAIN_P2P` and `DRAIN_AND_RESET` as fatal ([device_health.go#L521-L563](https://github.com/harche/k8s-dra-driver-gpu/blob/256a484c073bb2421338ff2a32ed48747dc73a34/cmd/gpu-kubelet-plugin/device_health.go#L521-L563)), so the node and the engine agree on the class. - **A structured field next to `fault_info`.** Changing `fault_info` to an object would break existing clients. Today `fault_info` is sent only with `unhealthy` ([engine_core_sentinel.py#L235-L241](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py#L235-L241)). With this change it is sent with `dead` as well, together with `gpu_fault`. - **No Xid in the engine.** Reading Xids needs an always-on NVML event subscription ([device_health.go#L195-L196](https://github.com/harche/k8s-dra-driver-gpu/blob/256a484c073bb2421338ff2a32ed48747dc73a34/cmd/gpu-kubelet-plugin/device_health.go#L195-L196) shows the node-side one), and an Xid does not identify the process that caused it. - **The process lifecycle is unchanged.** After `on_fault`, the busy-loop wrapper waits `engine_recovery_timeout_sec` for a command and then exits ([engine_core_sentinel.py#L524-L534](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py#L524-L534)). An executor-failed `dead` rank already behaves this way. During that window the orchestrator can read `dead` and the classification while it removes the rank from the survivors. Exiting immediately would replace a precise status with a connection error. - **Platform scope.** Classification is a per-platform hook that reports nothing by default. CUDA is the first implementation. ROCm and NPU workers can add their own, and the field can take a device-neutral name at that point. - **The termination message is written only if `/dev/termination-log` exists.** Kubernetes creates that file in every container by default (`terminationMessagePath`). Outside Kubernetes the file is normally absent, so nothing is written. #### Validation I validated the design with a proof of concept on vLLM [ff74259](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/ff74259da320420d481d0d59970d6ec0c8fad242), AWS g5.xlarge (A10G). Faults were injected inside `Worker.execute_model`: an out-of-bounds Triton store for an illegal address, and an out-of-range index for a device-side assert. **Termination message.** Default `vllm serve`, with both the single-process and the multiprocess executor. The server exit status stays 0 in every case ([#48966](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48966)). | Injected fault | Stock vLLM | With this change | |---|---|---| | Illegal address | no message | `{"gpu_faults": [{"cuda_error": 700, "sticky": true, ..., "restart_required": true}]}` | | Device-side assert | no message | same, with `cuda_error: 710` | | Python `RuntimeError` | no message | no GPU fault recorded | **Fault-tolerance decision with an external orchestrator.** I ran the [llm-d resiliency operator](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator)'s controller and vLLM driver at [02fc86c](https://github.com/llm-d-incubation/llm-d-resiliency-operator/commit/02fc86cf9c213002a519bca20d8a6309bddd2ee4), unmodified, against two ranks: - one real fault-tolerance engine taking a real sticky fault; - one emulated surviving rank. The real engine ran with DP=1, which needed a local relaxation of the check that fault tolerance requires external-LB mode ([arg_utils.py#L2484-L2488](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/vllm/engine/arg_utils.py#L2484-L2488)), because the hardware available could not run a DP=2 pair (see Limits). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant R0 as Rank 0 (CUDA 700) participant O as Orchestrator participant R1 as Rank 1 (emulated survivor) alt Stock vLLM R0->>O: unhealthy, fault_info "AcceleratorError" O->>R0: retry O->>R1: retry R0-->>O: retry failed, illegal memory access O->>O: reset the whole group else With this change R0->>O: dead, gpu_fault cuda_error=700 sticky O->>R1: scale_down, removed_dp_ranks [0] R1-->>O: serving end ``` The `retry` on the faulted rank failed with "CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered", which confirms on hardware that in-place recovery cannot work after a sticky error. With the change, the faulted rank was excluded and the group was never reset. In this single-worker setup `fault_info` starts with `AcceleratorError`. With two or more DP ranks it starts with the executor's error class: `RuntimeError` in stock vLLM, and its subclass `WorkerFailedError` in the proof of concept. #### Limits I have not run a real surviving rank executing `scale_down` after a peer's GPU fault. That needs two or more H100-class GPUs on one host: - the `nixl_ep` wheel ships kernels for sm_90, sm_100, sm_103 and sm_120 only; - on sm_120 the low-latency combine kernel needs about 196 KB of shared memory against a 99 KB limit; - two DP ranks cannot share one GPU. The fault-tolerance e2e step is currently disabled ([fault_tolerance.yaml#L5-L6](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/b2094acc88a7f76b49332ebc91a34887272e36c8/.buildkite/test_areas/fault_tolerance.yaml#L5-L6)). If anyone with such a host can run the proof of concept there, I would be grateful. #### Follow-ups - A Prometheus counter for faults and recoveries, labeled by `cuda_error` and `restart_required`, as requested in the [#44428 review](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44428#pullrequestreview-4738185221). #### Related work - [#64249](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64249) and [#64254](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64254) cover the opposite direction: an external signal, such as DRA device health, tells healthy survivors to pause. Together with this RFC, health information flows both ways between the node and the engine. - [#50265](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50265) (`on_fault`), [#60940](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60940) (executor failure path) and [#62235](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62235) (status cache) touch the same code. The design needs to be coordinated with them. cc @fangyuchu @tlrmchlsmth @njhill @tzulingk @Etelis @ruisearch42 @Jeffwan ### Any Other Things. - Proof of concept: [harche/vllm@gpu-fault-classification](https://github.com/harche/vllm/tree/gpu-fault-classification) ([diff against main](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...harche:vllm:gpu-fault-classification)). It does not yet cover the KV connector path. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Draft Window KV: Dual-Boundary Recovery and Sparse P/D Page Fill
author: SSSunzt
body:
### Motivation.

Main attention requires the full reusable history, while a sliding-window Draft model reads only the most recent `W` tokens. In the original shared-pool design, Main KV and Draft KV share the same physical block pool, cache-hit boundary, and lifetime. This forces Draft to retain history outside its window. When Draft cache state diverges from Main, it can also trigger unnecessary target-forward replay, block allocation, and Main KV writes.

The shared cache-hit boundary also couples Main reuse to Draft availability. A missing Draft page may move the combined hit boundary backward, preventing the system from reusing otherwise valid Main KV and causing unnecessary replay, block allocation, and Main KV writes.

In a prefill/decode-disaggregated deployment, P and D may hold different Draft pages for the same request. Transferring the full Draft history or a coarse-grained contiguous range wastes bandwidth when D needs only a small set of logical pages.

An internal production implementation validates the feasibility and potential benefits of this design. For the recovery requests that entered window replay, the actual replay range was reduced from 75.00M to 3.94M tokens, a 94.75% reduction. Under equivalent throughput, TTFT P50/P95 improved by 31.7%/47.9%, while the observed TTFT capacity knee moved outward by at least 7.7% in offered load.

### Proposed Change.

This RFC proposes a Draft Window KV protocol that separates Main and Draft cache lifetimes and defines recovery when their cache states diverge.

The proposed changes are:

1. **Independent Main and Draft cache pools.** Main retains the full reusable history, while Draft retains only the most recent sliding window. Draft blocks outside the window can be reclaimed without affecting Main KV.
2. **Separate recovery boundaries.** The scheduler tracks the combined cache hit `J`, the Main hit endpoint `M`, and the Draft recovery start `D` independently. A missing Draft page does not force an otherwise valid Main block table to roll back to `J`.
3. **Main KV write protection during Draft recovery.** When recovery replays `D → M` to regenerate the hidden states required by Draft, Main KV slots that already hit are set to `PAD_SLOT_ID`. They are neither allocated nor written again.
4. **Logical and non-contiguous Draft gaps.** The required Draft window is represented as complete logical pages and exact missing ranges rather than as one contiguous cache-hit length.
5. **Consumer-driven sparse page fill for P/D disaggregation.** D generates a missing-page plan from its own cache state. P sends the Main suffix and only the Draft logical pages missing on D. The metadata describes logical page indexes, valid token ranges, layer ranges, dtype, tensor-parallel layout, version, and completion state without exposing allocator-local physical block IDs.
6. **Completion-gated publication.** A Draft page becomes eligible for cache hits only after its local computation or remote transfer has completed.

This RFC overlaps with #64109 and #64611 on windowed Draft storage and independent Draft cache lifetimes. #60320 reduces Draft context-projection and KV computation and is complementary. The additional scope of this RFC is the end-to-end recovery protocol for divergent Main/Draft cache states: the `J/M/D` recovery model, non-contiguous Draft gaps, Main KV write protection, consumer-driven sparse P/D page fill, and support for different parallel layouts such as P/TP4 to D/TP1.

---

**Full RFC**

# Draft Window KV: Dual-Boundary Recovery and Sparse P/D Page Fill

- Author: @SSSunzt
- Co-authors: @maplestarplayl @haoxli0412-spec
## Abstract

Main attention requires the full history, whereas a sliding-window Draft model reads only the most recent `W` tokens. Placing these two semantics in the same pool creates two forms of waste:

1. **Excess storage and recovery work:** Draft retains history outside the window, while divergent Main/Draft hits can trigger unnecessary replay, allocation, and Main KV writes.
2. **Excess transfer:** In a prefill/decode-disaggregated (P/D) deployment, the system may transfer the full Draft history or a coarse-grained contiguous range instead of only the pages actually missing on D.

This RFC proposes a complete Draft Window KV protocol:

- Main and Draft use independent cache pools.
- Main retains the full reusable history, while Draft retains only the most recent sliding window.
- During recovery, the system tracks the combined cache hit `J`, the Main hit endpoint `M`, and the Draft recovery start `D` separately.
- When Draft KV is missing, the system replays the required range and continues to execute the target forward pass needed by Draft, while using a slot mask to prevent duplicate allocation and writes to Main KV entries that already hit.
- D reports gaps in terms of logical pages, and P sends only the Main suffix and the missing Draft pages.
- A Draft page becomes eligible for cache hits only after its computation or transfer has completed.

This is not merely an optimization that makes Draft store only a window. It is an end-to-end protocol covering cache-pool separation and recovery when Main and Draft cache hits diverge.

## 1. Original Shared-Pool Baseline and Core Problem

### 1.1 Original Implementation

The original implementation places Main KV and Draft KV in the same physical block pool. For a given request, both allocate, hit, and reclaim blocks over the same token range:

```text
One shared pool
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ request block 0 ... N                                       │
│ Each block stores KV for both Main and Draft layers         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Shared hit boundary J: both Main and Draft are considered hits only up to J
Shared lifetime: while either side still needs the history, the block cannot
                 be reclaimed independently
```

This design is valid when both Main and Draft require the full history. A sliding-window Draft model, however, reads only the tail window. A shared pool therefore forces it to retain history it does not need. Conversely, a missing Draft page within the window shortens the shared hit boundary, preventing the system from reusing otherwise valid Main KV.

This RFC directly replaces four behaviors in the original implementation:

| Original shared-pool behavior | This RFC |
|---|---|
| Main and Draft share one physical pool | Main pool and Draft window pool are independent |
| Only a shared hit boundary `J` is tracked | Track `J`, the Main endpoint `M`, and the Draft recovery start `D` |
| A Draft miss causes Main to be replayed, allocated, and written again | Repair only Draft; use write protection for Main slots that already hit |
| Transfer the full history or a contiguous suffix | D requests the exact gaps in the current window by logical page |

### 1.2 Two Attention Semantics Should Not Share One Cache Lifetime

```text
Request tokens: [----------------------------------------------------------]

Main KV:        [==========================================================]
                 Retains the full reusable history

Draft KV:                                                  [================]
                                                            Retains only the
                                                            most recent W tokens
```

For example, consider a request with 1M tokens of history and a Draft window of 4,096 tokens. Draft reads only the final 4,096 tokens. Retaining the rest of the history has no semantic value, but consumes GPU memory over the long term and displaces the Main Prefix Cache.

### 1.3 Main Hits and Draft Recovery Do Not Share the Same Boundary

For a request being restored, define three boundaries:

- `J`: the current combined cache hit;
- `M`: the endpoint of valid Main KV hits;
- `D`: the first position still missing within the Draft window currently required.

If `J < D < M`:

```text
Combined path: J ----------------------------------------> M
Window recovery path:                 D -----------------> M
```

The system should preserve the Main block table at `M` and replay only from `D` to `M`. This replay still requires target forward passes to generate the hidden states needed by Draft. However, the Main KV slots that already hit within `D → M` must be masked: they must not be allocated or written again.

This path therefore reduces all of the following:

- target-forward replay over `J → D`;
- Main block allocation over `D → M`;
- Main KV writes over `D → M`;
- storage and transfer outside the Draft window.

## 2. Design

### 2.1 Independent Main and Draft Cache Pools

- The Main pool follows full-history and Prefix Cache semantics for allocation, hits, and eviction.
- The Draft pool covers only the most recent sliding window of active requests.
- As the window advances, old Draft blocks can be reclaimed independently without affecting Main blocks.
- The budget previously used for long-lived Draft history can be reassigned to the Main pool.

The purpose of independent pools is to give the two caches genuinely different lifetimes.

### 2.2 Dual-Boundary Recovery

Recovery proceeds as follows:

1. Query the combined hit `J` and Main hit `M`.
2. Compute the Draft window currently required: `[max(0, M - W), M)`.
3. Scan the completed Draft logical pages in the window and produce an exact missing-page plan.
4. Apply any available remote page fills first.
5. Recompute `D`, the first page that remains missing.
6. If `D → M` is shorter than `J → M`, replay the contiguous range from `D` to `M`.
7. During replay, preserve the Main block table and set the Main KV slots that already hit to `PAD_SLOT_ID`.
8. If the dual-boundary path offers no benefit, fall back to the existing combined-hit path.

This preserves two independent facts: how far Main has already hit, and what the current Draft window still lacks. A shorter combined hit must not overwrite either fact.

### 2.3 Sparse Page Fill in P/D Disaggregation

P and D may hold different Draft pages for the same request. D must produce a missing-page plan based on its own state:

```text
D: compute the required window and report missing logical pages
                         │
                         ▼
P: send the Main suffix and the Draft pages missing on D
                         │
                         ▼
D: write the destination pages, wait for completion, then publish
   them as eligible for cache hits
```

Missing-page metadata describes logical meaning rather than exposing allocator physical addresses. At a minimum, it includes:

- request/sequence identity;
- window start/end;
- logical block index;
- valid token range within the page;
- KV type, dtype, layer range, and tensor-parallel layout;
- version and completion state.

This protocol allows Mooncake, NIXL, shared memory, or other connectors to use different transfer implementations while presenting the scheduler with consistent semantics for which Draft pages are complete and usable.

## 3. GPU Memory Savings

The MiniMax M3.1 production configuration uses the TS Draft backend with FP8 Draft KV:

| KV type | Logical size per token |
|---|---:|
| Main KV, NVFP4 | 33.75 KiB |
| Draft KV, FP8 | 5 KiB |
| Main + Draft | 38.75 KiB |

When a system that retains Main + Draft for the full long-term history switches to retaining only Main for that history, the theoretical capacity increase is:

```text
38.75 / 33.75 - 1 ≈ 14.81%
```

After accounting for the fixed Draft window, block alignment, and scheduling headroom, the effective Main-history capacity in the production configuration is expected to increase by approximately **13%–14%**.

| Context | Full Draft history | 4,096-token Draft window | Ideal savings |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 32K | 160 MiB | 20 MiB | 140 MiB |
| 1M | 5 GiB | 20 MiB | approximately 4.98 GiB |

These figures apply only to the TS + FP8 geometry described above. They must be recalculated if the backend, dtype, layer count, number of KV heads, or head dimension changes.

## 4. Relationship to Existing Proposals

This RFC shares the same high-level goal as existing proposals: align Draft KV storage and computation with the sliding window actually used by the Draft model. Existing work covers individual parts of this problem:

- [#64109](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64109) retains only the tail window for DFlash/DSpark Draft KV and adds window-aware allocation, eviction, and prefix-hit queries.
- [#60320](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60320) restricts Draft context projection and KV computation to the tail window, reducing computation that Draft attention will never read.
- [#64611](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64611) by @Dao007forever builds on #64109 by adding an independent Draft block pool, allowing Main and Draft to use different physical cache capacities and eviction policies.

These PRs are not three components of a single complete end-to-end protocol. #60320 is an independent model-execution optimization, while #64109 and #64611 form a stacked storage and cache-management proposal. They primarily answer how Draft KV can store and compute less. They do not fully define the recovery protocol for divergent Main/Draft hits, non-contiguous gaps within the Draft window, or mismatched cache state between P and D.

### 4.1 Overlapping Scope

This RFC overlaps with #64109/#64611 in the following goals:

1. Draft KV retains only the tail window that can actually be read.
2. Main and Draft use different physical cache lifetimes.
3. Blocks outside the Draft window can be reclaimed independently.
4. Prefix Cache queries understand Draft window semantics.

### 4.2 Material Differences

This RFC is an independent implementation. It does not depend on the PRs above landing first, nor does it require their allocator, window manager, or prefix-hit implementation. Its principal differences are as follows.

1. **Unified dual-boundary model for Main and Draft**

   The scheduler tracks all of the following simultaneously:

   - combined cache hit `J`;
   - Main hit endpoint `M`;
   - Draft recovery start `D`.

   A missing Draft page does not force the scheduler to roll an otherwise valid Main block table back to `J`. This is not a local adjustment to window-aware prefix hits. It is a recovery contract jointly honored by the scheduler, cache manager, and model executor.

2. **Draft gaps represented as logical pages**

   This RFC does not model the Draft window as a single contiguous hit length. Instead, it records the complete logical pages and non-contiguous gaps within the required window for each Draft group.

   Local replay uses a contiguous safe range beginning at the first missing page. P/D transfer preserves the exact set of non-contiguous gaps. Both use the same recovery plan but execute at different granularities.

3. **Main KV write protection**

   Draft recovery may still require target forward passes to regenerate the hidden states needed by Draft. For Main tokens in `[D, M)` that already hit, this RFC uses a slot mask to prevent duplicate allocation and Main KV writes.

   Recovery computation, Main KV ownership, and Draft KV writes can therefore be planned independently instead of being determined implicitly by a single shared cache-hit length.

4. **Consumer-driven sparse page fill in P/D disaggregation**

   D generates the missing-page plan from its own Draft cache state. P sends the Main suffix and the Draft logical pages that D actually lacks, rather than assuming identical windows on P and D or sending a coarse-grained contiguous Draft range.

   Transfer metadata uses logical page indexes, valid token ranges, layer ranges, dtype, version, and completion state. It does not expose allocator-local physical block IDs. The protocol supports differing parallel layouts, such as P/TP4 to D/TP1.

## 5. Test Plan

| Scenario | Setup | Required assertions |
|---|---|---|
| Full Draft-window hit | All pages in `[start, M)` are `COMPLETE` | No replay; preserve `M`; allocate no Draft repair blocks |
| Single missing page | Remove one page from the middle of the window | `D` points to that page; replay only `D → M`; Main block table remains unchanged |
| Non-contiguous gaps | Remove two non-adjacent logical pages | The missing-page plan preserves two ranges rather than merging them into one contiguous hit |
| Main write protection | `D < M` and Main has already hit | Replay slots for Main entries that already hit use `PAD_SLOT_ID`; no duplicate Main KV writes |
| Remote page-fill completion | A page first enters `WRITING` | The page is ineligible for hits before its completion event and is atomically published as `COMPLETE` afterward |
| Remote page-fill failure | The connector fails or times out | Remove incomplete visibility, replan local replay, and produce output identical to full prefill |
| CoW/shared prefix | Multiple requests reference a Draft page | Do not switch the block table or release the old block before CoW completes |
| Preemption and cancellation | Preempt or cancel during a write | Remove the page from the visible set first; reclaim it only after asynchronous references have ended |
| TP1/TP4 | Run the local-completion and collective paths separately | Both paths wait for local completion events; TP1 does not issue meaningless collectives |
| TP4 → TP1 | Map four producer ranks to one consumer | Reassemble K/V, layer ranges, and token ranges correctly; reject incompatible metadata |
| Capacity planning | Fixed GPU memory budget and Draft window | Main/Draft block counts match the formula; arbitrary pool-splitting ratios are not allowed |
| Metric semantics | Direct hit, replay, remote fill, and failure | Counters increase only on the corresponding state transition; candidate and admitted populations are not mixed |

Recommended direct test commands:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/core/test_draft_window_recovery.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_block_table.py \
  tests/v1/metrics/test_stats.py -v

.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_connector.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_connector_hma.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_stats.py -v
```

Real GPU completion, Main slot masking, and TP mapping cannot be validated solely with mocks. The corresponding tests must run on CUDA GPUs and synchronize the relevant streams/events before the tests finish.

## 6. Production Validation and Evaluation Plan

### 6.1 Internal Mechanics: Fixed Production Window

The following data comes from a production traffic window selected in advance, rather than from a best-performing interval chosen after the fact:

- Time: 2026-11-05 19:46–20:46 CST;
- Topology: 24× B300, 2P1D; 4 Prefill Engines and 8 Decode Engines;
- Draft: MiniMax M3.1 TS backend with FP8 Draft KV;
- Sample: 83,476 requests; this window is used only for aggregate mechanism counters, not for comparing mean end-to-end latency;
- Input: 10.07B tokens/h; output: 72.05M tokens/h; input/output ratio approximately 139.8×.

Prometheus `increase()` extrapolates at scrape boundaries, so aggregate counts may contain fractional values. Request, page, and token counts in this document are rounded as appropriate.

#### Less Computation and Fewer Writes: Shrinking `J → M` to `D → M`

On the Prefill side, 81,974 requests directly hit the Draft Cache, for a direct-hit ratio of **98.75%**. Only 1,036 requests entered window replay. For this subset of recovery requests that were actually admitted:

| Metric | Shared-endpoint path | Window-recovery path | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Replay tokens | 75.00M | 3.94M | 71.06M fewer, **94.75%** reduction |
| Mean per replayed request | approximately 72.37K | approximately 3.80K | approximately **19×** reduction |

These counters measure token positions processed during target-forward replay: the candidate combined-hit path would process `J → M`, whereas actual window recovery processes only `D → M`. The 71.06M tokens represent target-forward replay avoided under real production traffic. For the remaining 3.94M replay tokens, target forward is used to generate Draft hidden states, while Main KV entries that already hit are neither reallocated nor rewritten. This path therefore reduces computation, block-management overhead, and KV write bandwidth at the same time.

### 6.2 Serving Performance: Steady-State Gains and the Capacity Knee

End-to-end serving performance is not evaluated using the average over the entire load-test period. The full period mixes cache warm-up, load ramp-up, and the saturated phase after queuing begins. Averaging across these phases would obscure the actual difference under equal load. We therefore select the steady state after A/B cache warm-up and compare two configurations under the same production-shaped traffic:

| Metric | Sliding window disabled | Sliding window enabled | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| RPS | 22.39 | 22.38 | Essentially unchanged |
| Total TPM | 143.32M | 143.47M | Essentially unchanged |
| TTFT P50 | 1.26 s | 0.86 s | **-31.7%** |
| TTFT P95 | 4.77 s | 2.49 s | **-47.9%** |
| TPOT P50 | 5.21 ms | 4.92 ms | **-5.7%** |
| TPOT P95 | 9.74 ms | 8.76 ms | **-10.1%** |
| Cached/input tokens | 90.75% | 93.62% | **+2.87 percentage points** |

Both traffic groups sustain the same 22.4 RPS and approximately 143.4M Total TPM, so the latency improvement is not obtained by sacrificing throughput. Within the equal-load steady-state interval, windowed Draft KV reduces TTFT P50/P95 by **31.7%/47.9%**, respectively, and TPOT P50/P95 by **5.7%/10.1%**.

The cached/input token ratio rises from 90.75% to 93.62%. This indicates that end-to-end Prefix Cache performance does not regress after windowing Draft KV, and is consistent with the expected increase in Main-history capacity.

#### TTFT Capacity Knee

As production-shaped load continues to increase, the two configurations exhibit different TTFT knee points:

- With the sliding window disabled, TTFT P50 begins a sustained rise at approximately **23.3 RPS**.
- With the sliding window enabled, TTFT P50 still does not enter a sustained rise at the test peak of **25.1 RPS**.
- This observation therefore demonstrates that the TTFT knee moves outward by at least **7.7%** in offered load.

Based on the KV accounting for the TS + FP8 configuration, releasing Draft KV outside the window is expected to increase effective Main-history capacity by approximately **13%–14%**. When KV pressure is the system's primary bottleneck, the TTFT knee may theoretically move by a similar amount. The realized improvement will still depend on prefill compute, scheduling, networking, and the request-length distribution. The current data directly supports at least **7.7%** additional load headroom; **13%–14%** remains a testable expectation derived from the KV capacity model.

The production data above comes from an internal company implementation and is included to validate the design's feasibility and benefits.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks, until November 24, 2026.

@maplestarplayl @haoxli0412-spec @Dao007forever

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Tree speculative decoding in vLLM
author: chenaoxuan
body:
### Motivation.

Recent work has made tree-based drafting a major direction in speculative decoding. By proposing multiple continuations per step, a draft tree can increase the number of tokens accepted in one target verification pass. [PCTree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02123), [DARTree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13524), [PRESTO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22634)

This RFC builds on [vLLM RFC #65813](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/65813) and details how vLLM schedules, verifies, and commits draft trees, drawing on the Ascend prototype. [vLLM-Ascend RFC #18797](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/issues/18797)

### Proposed Change.

### Execution flow

| Stage | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Propose | Produce a bounded tree of candidate continuations. Publish flattened candidate token IDs and retain their topology with the matching worker request state. |
| Schedule and prepare inputs | Account for the candidate rows and their KV slots. When trimming a tree to fit, retain an ancestor-closed subset. Keep the flat candidates and topology associated with the same request and draft step. |
| Verify | Assign position IDs by depth and distinct temporary KV slots by node. Each query can attend to the committed prefix and its own path through the tree, including itself. |
| Select a path | Starting from the root, match each token selected by the target to a child. Stop at a missing match or a leaf and emit the target token, subject to normal stop and length handling. |
| Commit | Keep the root and commit the accepted nodes in path order. Update request state and gather any target hidden states needed for the next draft in that same order. |
