title: [RFC]: KV Trace monitoring
author: Tjh-UKN
body:
## Summary

**KV Trace monitoring** connects request scheduling, KV-block lifetimes, and model-runner address plans. A developer should be able to start with a request or block and inspect its history across these boundaries.

> **Status:** Seeking agreement on the problem and first implementation scope. No upstream acceptance is recorded yet.  
> **Reference implementation:** My [vllm-ascend PR #17833](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/17833), head `a0d8bef0b2ef`. Evidence and CI status below were checked on **2026-11-11**.

## 1. Problem and evidence

### The missing debugging view

An allocated block can still be the wrong token destination. For example, A and B own blocks 1 and 2, but their write slots are swapped. Allocation logs alone cannot identify the mismatch. This is an illustrative failure, not measured production incidence.

Diagnosing such behavior requires connecting three views:

- **Request history:** scheduled ranges, block bindings, preemption/resume, and completion.
- **Block history:** allocation, reference changes, sharing, and reuse across allocation generations.
- **Execution plan:** request/row order, block tables, slot mappings, and read lengths.

Repeated text alone does not prove a KV fault; conclusions need trace evidence, with missing observations identified.

### Evidence available today

The linked PR's [guide at the referenced commit](https://github.com/Tjh-UKN/vllm-ascend/blob/a0d8bef0b2efb7ed9da31ba683671e462e8e3080/docs/source/user_guide/feature_guide/kv_cache_guard.md) documents scheduler-to-metadata checks and their supported paths.

| Evidence | What it establishes | Remaining limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current head: 181 focused tests + 4 Mooncake contracts reported passing | Implemented address/lifecycle checks | Current-head NPU functionality and service overhead remain unverified. |
| Historical head `c95f8b060806`: 36 normal + 4 injected invalid-address requests, V1/V2, eager/FULL | Injected faults detected before output consumption | Not a natural-failure reproduction on current upstream. |
| Historical performance: maximum mean throughput decrease 0.71%; TTFT increase up to 6.70% | Results for that workload and revision | Not current-head or upstream performance evidence. |

**K1 still needs:** a minimized real-failure replay on pinned upstream, its impact, and the diagnostic gap. Problem acceptance remains pending.

## 2. Goals and first scope

| First slice proposed for discussion | Follow-up coverage |
| --- | --- |
| V2, dense paged attention, one device, eager/graph, prefix caching on/off | Other layouts, parallelism, speculation, and connectors through explicit adapters |
| Bindings, allocation/reference/reuse changes, final per-group address plans | Additional execution/transfer evidence at reliable native boundaries |
| Structured records and request/block queries | Further checks supported by those records |

This proposed scope differs from the reference PR. Unobserved paths must be identified without blanket startup rejection of valid inference configurations.

## 3. Proposed design

### 3.1 Observe native boundaries

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Scheduler] -->|native scheduling output| R[Model Runner V2]
    S -->|request bindings| T[KV Trace records]
    P[Block pool] -->|allocation and reference changes| T
    R -->|final address plans| T
    T --> Q[Request and block queries]
```

Reuse existing observation interfaces; propose minimal callbacks for missing boundaries. Observe final runner metadata once per cache group. The first slice requires no per-layer attention instrumentation.

### 3.2 Correlate records without inventing state

Records carry operation, source, sequence, and available request/step, engine/process, rank, pool/group, and block identities. Allocation generation requires observed reassignment. Names and encoding remain open for review.

| Observed operation | Required interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Allocation or reassignment | Identify the new block lifetime. |
| Prefix sharing | Preserve the lifetime and record the added reference. |
| Reference release | Record the reference change; request completion alone does not prove physical release. |
| Reuse | Separate the new lifetime from earlier bindings to the same numeric block ID. |
| Read/write plan | Record supplied addresses; do not label them as completed kernel accesses. |

Snapshots retain their original step across async retrieval and graph replay, preserving native output order. History is bounded; overflow or observation loss produces an explicit gap.

### 3.3 Keep collection and diagnosis distinct

Queries show records and association sources; address checks can annotate expected/observed mismatches. Monitoring is disabled by default, with no KV-content copies or automatic repair in the first slice. Address plans do not prove kernel accesses or KV numerical correctness.

## 4. Alternatives and trade-offs

| Approach | Benefit | Cost or limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Component logs and local assertions | Smallest integration; already available | Cross-component request/block history still has to be reconstructed manually. |
| Full tensor dumps or per-layer instrumentation | More information about contents and individual operations | More data movement, synchronization, storage, and backend-specific maintenance. |
| **Boundary-based KV Trace** | Connects lifecycle and address-plan records with a smaller data footprint | Requires maintained observation points and cannot prove actual kernel memory behavior. |

K2 requires demonstrating the chosen trace's diagnostic value and acceptable cost.

## 5. Validation and operating cost

The PoC should retain its workload, expected records, raw trace, and assertions. Test legal sharing/reuse, request reordering, padding/dummy calls, wrong write destinations, and stale-generation bindings; verify both diagnostics and supporting history, including gaps.

Compare enabled/disabled output behavior, async handling, eager/graph execution, false positives, CPU/memory/synchronization cost, throughput, TTFT, and ITL. Disabled tracing should create no trace buffers or device copies.

**Proposed budget:** at most 2% throughput decrease on an agreed workload. Upstream agreement, including latency and memory limits, is still needed. Publish revisions, hardware, workloads, all valid runs, and variation; report latency separately.

## 6. Delivery plan and acceptance gates

- [ ] **Problem accepted — K1:** explicit maintainer agreement on the problem and relevance.
- [ ] **Design accepted — K2–K3:** agreement on the approach and first scope, with conditions recorded.
- [ ] **Implementation accepted — K4–K6:** useful PoC, controlled risks, agreed budgets, and passing required checks.
- [ ] **Community accepted — K7–K8:** required approvals and merge completed.

Silence, an open PR, and bot reviews do not establish acceptance. Unmet gates require evidence, revision, or a narrower proposal.

<details>
<summary>K1–K8 deliverables and current position</summary>

| Stage | Exit criterion | Current position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **K1 · Problem** | Concrete failure, impact, diagnostic gap; maintainer agreement | Real upstream replay and acceptance pending. |
| **K2 · Alternatives** | Evidence supports the integration/cost trade-off | Comparison above; validation pending. |
| **K3 · Design** | Accept record contract, lifecycle interpretation, architecture impact, and first scope | Proposed; acceptance pending. |
| **K4 · PoC** | Reproducible faults and legal cases validate records/checks | Reference evidence available; upstream PoC pending. |
| **K5 · Risk** | Correctness, compatibility, false-positive, and performance matrix meets budgets | Current reference-head NPU/performance work remains open. |
| **K6 · PR** | Focused code, tests, docs, self-review, and passing required CI | No upstream PR linked. Reference-head `pre-commit` and `ci-gate` fail. |
| **K7 · Review** | Resolve blockers, rerun affected checks, obtain approvals | No upstream approval recorded. |
| **K8 · Merge** | Verify target branch, update RFC, record follow-up ownership | Pending. |

</details>

## 7. Decisions requested

1. Is the diagnostic gap worth addressing upstream, and which real failure should anchor K1?
2. Is the V2-first scope above the right first contribution?
3. Which existing interfaces should supply the observations, and which minimal callbacks would make downstream wrappers removable?
4. What workload and performance budgets should govern acceptance?

Feedback period: two weeks from publication. Record scope decisions and conditions here before splitting implementation into PRs.

<details>
<summary>Submission checks</summary>

- [x] Searched existing issues and reviewed the relevant source and documentation.
- [ ] Consulted the documentation chatbot. No chatbot entry point was available on the documentation pages accessible while preparing this RFC.

</details>

title: [RFC]: DWDP: Distributed Weight Data Parallelism for MoE Prefill
author: qianlihuang
body:
### Motivation.

**Central question: Can Distributed Weight Data Parallelism achieve higher sustainable prefill request throughput under strict TTFT SLAs than the best existing EP-based approaches on high-bandwidth scale-up systems?**

MoE prefill commonly distributes expert weights across GPUs and dispatches token activations to expert owners. Efficient EP backends reduce communication costs, but dispatch/combine and coordination across ranks remain in the execution path. Unequal prompt lengths, prefix-cache hits, and request arrivals can leave ranks with different amounts of work.

DWDP separates expert-weight ownership from request execution: expert weights remain distributed, while each GPU runs its own prefill batch and fetches peer weights for local MoE computation. High-bandwidth scale-up systems make this trade-off worth evaluating.

There is relevant prior work in [TensorRT-LLM's DWDP design and implementation](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/docs/source/blogs/tech_blog/blog19_DWDP_Distributed_Weight_Data_Parallelism_for_High_Performance_LLM_Inference_on_NVL72.md), the [TokenSpeed Kimi K3 AgentX report](https://lightseek.org/blog/tokenspeed-kimi-k3-agentx.html), and [SGLang's DWDP implementation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29778). TokenSpeed's AgentX report evaluates a complete prefill/decode system with shared caching; its output-throughput gains do not establish an isolated prefill improvement at a matched TTFT SLA. The [TokenSpeed implementation PR](https://github.com/lightseekorg/tokenspeed/pull/3086) also reports configurations where weight streaming loses to its EP baseline. These results motivate measuring the crossover in vLLM.

### Proposed Change.

#### Execution strategy and initial scope

Explore an opt-in DWDP execution path for MoE prefill:

- Partition persistent routed-expert weights across a group of peer GPUs.
- Keep each rank's requests and token activations local, and execute attention and MoE locally.
- Prefetch remote expert weights into bounded staging buffers, overlapping transfers with computation where possible.
- Remove per-layer cross-rank activation dispatch/combine and lockstep scheduling within that DWDP group.

A starting point is layer-wise peer-weight prefetch with alternating buffers, as in the reference implementations. Selectively fetching only routed experts needs separate evaluation: a layer's exact routing is known only after its router runs, so selective fetching cannot assume the same lookahead window as whole-layer prefetch.

Independent execution still requires local weight-readiness dependencies and safe buffer lifetimes. Expert owners must keep source weights resident while peers read them, even when the owner's execution is idle. NVLink/HBM contention and exposed copies remain potential costs.

The first scope should be immutable inference weights, one NVLink domain, and prefill workers in a disaggregated deployment. Full rank independence assumes attention/dense execution can run locally; any later TP/PP composition must account for its remaining collectives. Memory accounting must include resident expert shards, replicated non-expert weights, prefetch buffers, KV cache, and workspaces. CUDA graphs, weight updates, and EPLB interactions need explicit compatibility decisions.

Feedback is welcome on how to fit this into vLLM's existing MoE, model-runner, and DP lifecycle abstractions, and whether the independent execution work below can be reused. This RFC proposes an exploration and evaluation, with integration details to follow from the agreed design.

#### Relationship to existing vLLM work and alternatives

A search of public vLLM issues/PRs and the forum did not find a DWDP-specific proposal. Related work includes:

- [MoonEP integration RFC #52095](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52095) and [initial integration #52101](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52101): balanced EP using dynamic redundant experts and weight prefetch, while retaining token dispatch/combine. This is an important baseline and a source of related integration experience.
- [Independent MoE data parallelism #66671](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/66671): independent replicas with complete model weights per replica/TP group. DWDP instead shares distributed expert storage to reduce persistent per-rank weight residency.
- [Expert offloading RFC #38256](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38256): host-backed expert caching and prefetch. DWDP's initial backing store is peer GPU HBM, with a different communication and scheduling trade-off.

Other alternatives include tuned conventional EP with communication/computation overlap, and fully replicated DP when the model fits. DWDP should be compared against the strongest applicable configurations under the same hardware budget. MoonEP should be included where it supports the chosen model/precision; its end-to-end standing on these workloads should be established by measurement.

#### Evaluation

**Primary objective:** maximize sustainable prefill RPS while meeting a defined end-to-end TTFT SLA, including queueing and tail latency.

- Use [InferenceX AgentX](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/agentx) as a representative agentic workload.
- Report client-observed TTFT P50/P95/P99 and maximum sustainable completed RPS/TPS without queue growth.
- Compare against the strongest applicable EP baselines, including MoonEP where supported, under matched GPU budgets, model configurations, precision, and cache settings. Tune each approach independently.
- For disaggregated serving, keep the decode pool and KV-transfer path fixed, and report both end-to-end TTFT and prefill completion latency.
- Use open-loop load sweeps and AgentX replay. Profile weight-transfer overhead, compute overlap, and EP synchronization to identify the performance crossover.

Publish benchmark configurations and reproduction commands.

#### Target models

The approach is not model-specific. Candidate evaluation models are:

- [moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro)
- [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017)
- [zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash)
- Other large MoE models with suitable local execution and weight layouts.

### Any Other Things.

This is a design/evaluation proposal; no vLLM DWDP benchmark results are claimed here. Feedback on existing efforts, suitable baselines, and representative workloads is welcome.

References:

- [TensorRT-LLM DWDP technical introduction](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/docs/source/blogs/tech_blog/blog19_DWDP_Distributed_Weight_Data_Parallelism_for_High_Performance_LLM_Inference_on_NVL72.md)
- [TokenSpeed: Kimi K3 AgentX](https://lightseek.org/blog/tokenspeed-kimi-k3-agentx.html)
- [TokenSpeed DWDP PR #3086](https://github.com/lightseekorg/tokenspeed/pull/3086)
- [SGLang DWDP PR #29778](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29778)
- [MoonEP](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/MoonEP)
- [vLLM MoonEP integration #52101](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52101)

AI assistance was used to organize this author-provided proposal, check public references, and prepare the RFC.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched relevant issues/PRs and the public forum, and asked the [documentation chatbot](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/).

title: [RFC]: Shared stream conformance cases for `vllm bench serve` and `vllm-bench`
author: dilberx
body:
### Motivation.

`vllm bench serve` (Python) and `vllm-bench` (Rust) each parse the same SSE streams and decide the same things: which chunk sets TTFT, which chunks add an ITL sample, and whether the request succeeded. The two parsers are written and tested separately, so each rule gets fixed twice, weeks apart:

| Rule | Python | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| Role-only and empty chunks carry no token | #62341 | #64626 |
| Tool-call deltas count as output (Responses) | #62753 | #64557 |
| `reasoning_content` deltas count as output | #64937 | #64626 |
| A stream with no token fails (chat) | already | #59736 |
| A stream without `[DONE]` or with an error object fails | #64703 (open) | #65301 (open) |
| CRLF and split separators | #61534 (open) | #60177 |

With `VLLM_USE_RUST_BENCH=1`, `vllm bench serve` hands the same command line to the Rust client, so any difference between the two changes reported numbers for the same run.

CLI flags already have a parity check: `rust/src/bench/tests/python_serve_flags.txt` is a snapshot of the Python parser that `cli_parity.rs` and `tests/benchmarks/test_rust_bench_cli_parity.py` both read. Stream handling has nothing like it.

### Proposed Change.

One data file of stream cases that both test suites run.

- `tests/benchmarks/stream_cases.json`, with the Python tests. Each case has a backend (`openai`, `openai-chat`, `openai-responses`), the response as a list of raw chunks, and the expected result: `success`, a substring of `error`, number of ITL samples, `generated_text`, `output_tokens`, `prompt_len`. Because the chunks are raw, a case can cover where a stream is split and which line endings it uses.
- Python: one parametrized test serves each case from a local socket and checks the `RequestFuncOutput`.
- Rust: one test reads the file with `include_str!`, serves each case from a raw socket and checks the same fields.
- Timings aren't compared.
- A case can list a client under `known_gap` with the PR that closes it. When that client starts passing the case, its test fails until the entry is removed.

The implementation is in #67043: 83 cases, six of them streams captured from a real vLLM server. 61 cases pass on both clients and 22 are known gaps. Most of the gaps map to the open PRs in the table, plus #64143 for `event:`/`id:` lines in Python. Three have no PR yet:

- A usage chunk with `prompt_tokens: 0`: Python reports 0 input tokens, Rust keeps the client estimate.
- Usage on the same chunk as a token: Rust reads it, Python ignores it.
- `data:` with no space after the colon: Rust rejects it (Python is covered by #64143).

The six vLLM streams (chat, completions, Responses, with and without usage, `continuous_usage_stats`) pass on both clients, so these three only show up with other servers and proxies.

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@esmeetu @DarkLight1337

### Any Other Things.

- The case file sits in `tests/benchmarks/` and the Rust test reads it from there, as suggested in the first comment. The Rust cargo CI step lists it in `source_file_dependencies`, so a change to it runs both suites.
- Scope is the three streaming backends both clients have. `openai-audio` exists only in Python, and the pooling backends don't stream.
- The existing per-client unit tests stay. New stream fixes add a case to the shared file.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to build the implementation and write this up.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Async EPLB: one owner for all state, worker runs self-contained jobs
author: latioswang
body:
### Motivation.

**One owner for all async EPLB state: the main thread. The worker thread only runs self-contained jobs.**

Today the main thread and the async EPLB worker hand work to each other through seven pieces of shared mutable state. Fault recovery has to patch that state while the worker keeps running.

In this proposal the worker thread runs one job per MoE layer. A job takes all its inputs as arguments and returns a result or raises. The main thread keeps each cycle as a plain list of layers still to do, and takes the next one once every EP rank has finished the same job.

The goal is to simplify the hand-off and change as little observable behaviour as possible. Every chart below compares main with the proposal. "Main" here means main plus the fix for the fault-tolerance silent stall (#66144, PR #66146). The few visible differences are listed in "Visible changes".

- Draft PR: #67020. It is stacked on #66146 and should land after it.
- Not in this proposal: reporting a main-thread failure (while submitting a job or applying a layer) to the other ranks. Main does not do this either.
- AI assistance was used for this proposal and its implementation.

#### Problem

The worker is a `while True` loop on a daemon thread. It shares the following with the main thread:

| state | written by | read by |
|---|---|---|
| `rearrange_event` (CPU + GPU event) | main, `rearrange()` | worker, top of the loop |
| `rebalanced` per model | main and worker | both, plus a per-layer all-reduce in the worker |
| `pending_result` per model (one-slot mailbox) | worker | main, `step()` |
| `consumed_event` per layer | main, at 3 `record()` sites | worker |
| `ft_reset_epoch` | FT reset | worker |
| `async_worker_error` | worker, FT reset | main |
| `async_cycles_pending` and its condition | main, worker | FT reset |

The three `record()` sites are the normal consume in `_move_to_workspace`, `drain_async` for elastic EP, and the FT reset, which wakes the worker with a fake "consumed" signal.

Correctness depends on the exact order of statements on both threads. The code relies on the GIL for that ordering and nothing enforces it.

### Proposed Change.

## Main and the proposal, side by side

### Who touches what

Main: both threads read and write the same fields. Filled boxes are shared mutable state.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph MAIN[main thread]
        R[rearrange]
        S[step]
        F[FT reset]
        D[drain_async]
    end
    subgraph SHARED[shared mutable state]
        E1[rearrange_event]:::shared
        RB[rebalanced per model]:::shared
        PR[pending_result per model]:::shared
        CE[consumed_event per layer]:::shared
        EP[ft_reset_epoch]:::shared
        ER[async_worker_error]:::shared
        CP[async_cycles_pending + condition]:::shared
    end
    subgraph WORKER[worker thread, endless loop]
        W1[wait for rearrange_event]
        W2[plan]
        W3[all-reduce rebalanced, per layer]
        W4[transfer layer]
        W5[wait for consumed_event]
    end
    R -->|record| E1
    R -->|set| RB
    R -->|increment| CP
    F -->|wait for zero| CP
    F -->|clear| ER
    W5 -->|decrement at cycle end| CP
    S -->|read, clear| PR
    S -->|record| CE
    S -->|read| ER
    F -->|bump| EP
    F -->|clear| PR
    F -->|fake record| CE
    D -->|record| CE
    E1 --> W1
    RB --> W3
    W3 -->|clear| RB
    W4 -->|write| PR
    CE --> W5
    EP -->|compare| W4
    W2 -->|write on failure| ER
    classDef shared fill:#D55E00,stroke:#a84a00,color:#ffffff
```

Proposal: the runner on the main thread owns everything. A job going in and a `Future` coming out are the only things that cross the thread boundary.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph MAIN[main thread]
        RE[rearrange]
        S[step]
        F[FT reset]
        D[drain_async]
        subgraph RUNNER[AsyncEplbRunner, private fields]
            L[_layers_left]
            J[_job Future]
            ERR[_error]
        end
    end
    subgraph WORKER[worker thread, one job at a time]
        Q[job queue]
        JOB[job: plan if first layer, barrier, transfer layer]
    end
    RE -->|start| RUNNER
    S -->|poll| RUNNER
    F -->|reset, waits for the job| RUNNER
    D -->|drain| RUNNER
    L -->|submit first layer + event| Q
    Q --> JOB
    JOB -->|result or exception| J
```

### One cycle on a timeline

Two MoE layers, one model, no failure. The two charts have the same rows, in the same order, with the same lengths: nothing on this path changed. Blue is the main thread, green is the worker working, orange is the worker syncing with the other ranks, and red is the worker waiting for the main thread. The sync is drawn far wider than it is: it takes milliseconds, a transfer takes seconds.

Main:

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'taskBkgColor':'#0072B2','taskBorderColor':'#005a8c','activeTaskBkgColor':'#009E73','activeTaskBorderColor':'#007a59','doneTaskBkgColor':'#E69F00','doneTaskBorderColor':'#b87f00','critBkgColor':'#D55E00','critBorderColor':'#a84a00','taskTextColor':'#ffffff','taskTextLightColor':'#ffffff','taskTextDarkColor':'#ffffff','taskTextOutsideColor':'#7a7a7a','taskTextClickableColor':'#ffffff','sectionBkgColor':'#56B4E922','altSectionBkgColor':'#00000000','sectionBkgColor2':'#56B4E922','gridColor':'#9aa0a6','titleColor':'#7a7a7a'}}}%%
gantt
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %s
    section Main thread
    rearrange, signal worker                 :m1, 0, 2s
    steps, all-reduce failed and pending     :m2, after m1, 7s
    step, apply L0, release buffer           :m3, after m2, 2s
    steps, all-reduce failed and pending     :m4, after m3, 5s
    step, apply L1, cycle done               :m5, after m4, 2s
    section Worker thread
    wait for main, start signal              :crit, w1, 0, 2s
    plan                                     :active, w2, after w1, 2s
    sync with other workers                  :done, w3, after w2, 1s
    transfer L0 into buffer, stream sync     :active, w4, after w3, 4s
    wait for main, L0 applied                :crit, w5, after w4, 2s
    sync with other workers                  :done, w6, after w5, 1s
    transfer L1 into buffer, stream sync     :active, w7, after w6, 4s
    wait for main, L1 applied                :crit, w8, after w7, 2s
```

Proposal:

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'taskBkgColor':'#0072B2','taskBorderColor':'#005a8c','activeTaskBkgColor':'#009E73','activeTaskBorderColor':'#007a59','doneTaskBkgColor':'#E69F00','doneTaskBorderColor':'#b87f00','critBkgColor':'#D55E00','critBorderColor':'#a84a00','taskTextColor':'#ffffff','taskTextLightColor':'#ffffff','taskTextDarkColor':'#ffffff','taskTextOutsideColor':'#7a7a7a','taskTextClickableColor':'#ffffff','sectionBkgColor':'#56B4E922','altSectionBkgColor':'#00000000','sectionBkgColor2':'#56B4E922','gridColor':'#9aa0a6','titleColor':'#7a7a7a'}}}%%
gantt
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %s
    section Main thread
    rearrange, signal worker                 :m1, 0, 2s
    steps, all-reduce failed and busy        :m2, after m1, 7s
    step, apply L0, release buffer           :m3, after m2, 2s
    steps, all-reduce failed and busy        :m4, after m3, 5s
    step, apply L1, cycle done               :m5, after m4, 2s
    section Worker thread
    wait for main, start signal              :crit, w1, 0, 2s
    plan                                     :active, w2, after w1, 2s
    sync with other workers                  :done, w3, after w2, 1s
    transfer L0 into buffer, stream sync     :active, w4, after w3, 4s
    wait for main, L0 applied                :crit, w5, after w4, 2s
    sync with other workers                  :done, w6, after w5, 1s
    transfer L1 into buffer, stream sync     :active, w7, after w6, 4s
    wait for main, L1 applied                :crit, w8, after w7, 2s
```

| row | main, in code | proposal, in code |
|---|---|---|
| signal worker | `rearrange_event.record()` | `runner.start()`: record a `torch.Event`, submit the L0 job |
| wait for main, start signal | `rearrange_event.wait(stream)` | `queue.get()`, then `after.synchronize()` |
| sync with other workers | gloo all-reduce of `rebalanced` on the EPLB CPU group | `torch.distributed.barrier` on the EPLB CPU group |
| release buffer | `consumed_event.record()` after `move_from_buffer` | record a `torch.Event` after `move_from_buffer`, submit the next job |
| wait for main, layer applied | `consumed_event.wait(stream)`, `stream.synchronize()` | `queue.get()`, then `after.synchronize()` |

### What the main thread does each step

Main, the async part of `step()`:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[step] --> M{next model with rebalanced set?}
    M -->|none left| RET[continue step]
    M -->|yes| AR["all-reduce (worker error set, pending_result empty)"]
    AR --> F{any rank failed?}
    F -->|yes| RAISE[raise on every rank]
    F -->|no| B{any rank pending?}
    B -->|yes| M
    B -->|no| APPLY[_move_to_workspace: copy out of buffer, commit maps]
    APPLY --> LAST{last layer?}
    LAST -->|yes| CLR[clear rebalanced]
    LAST -->|no| REC
    CLR --> REC[clear pending_result, record consumed_event]
    REC --> M
```

Proposal, all of `poll()`:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[step calls poll] --> E{_error set?}
    E -->|yes| RAISE0[raise _error]
    E -->|no| J{_layers_left empty?}
    J -->|yes| RET[continue step]
    J -->|no| AR["all-reduce (job failed, job not done)"]
    AR --> F{any rank failed?}
    F -->|yes| RAISE[store _error, clear _layers_left, raise on every rank]
    F -->|no| B{any rank busy?}
    B -->|yes| EXTRA
    B -->|no| APPLY[_move_to_workspace: copy out of buffer, commit maps]
    APPLY --> LAST{_layers_left empty?}
    LAST -->|yes| DONE[cycle done]
    LAST -->|no| NEXT[record event, submit next layer job]
    NEXT --> EXTRA[one more all-reduce per model still waiting]
    EXTRA --> RET
```

### FT reset with a job in flight

Rank 0's worker is still inside a transfer of the old cycle. Rank 1 has finished it. Then every rank resets and the next cycle starts.

Main:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M0 as rank 0 main
    participant W0 as rank 0 worker
    participant W1 as rank 1 worker
    participant M1 as rank 1 main
    Note over W0: old transfer still running
    M1->>W1: reset: clear rebalanced, bump epoch, fake consumed record
    W1->>W1: sees new epoch, leaves the cycle
    W1-->>M1: cycles pending is 0, reset returns
    M0->>W0: reset: clear rebalanced, bump epoch
    Note over M0: blocked, waits for cycles pending to reach 0
    W0->>W0: old transfer ends, sees new epoch, leaves the cycle
    W0-->>M0: cycles pending is 0, reset returns
    Note over M0: or RuntimeError after the cpu group timeout
    Note over M0,M1: FT rebuilds the groups, then the next rearrange
    W0->>W1: worker sync, then new L0 transfer on both
```

Proposal:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M0 as rank 0 main
    participant W0 as rank 0 worker
    participant W1 as rank 1 worker
    participant M1 as rank 1 main
    Note over W0: old job still running
    M1->>M1: reset: clear _layers_left
    W1-->>M1: job already done, reset returns
    M0->>M0: reset: clear _layers_left
    Note over M0: blocked, waits for the job's Future
    W0->>W0: old job ends, result never read
    W0-->>M0: Future done, reset returns
    Note over M0: or RuntimeError after the cpu group timeout
    Note over M0,M1: FT rebuilds the groups, then the next rearrange
    W0->>W1: worker sync, then new L0 transfer on both
```

The order of events is the same. Main counts running cycles under a condition variable; the proposal waits on the `Future` it already has. Both use `cpu_distributed_timeout_seconds` and raise `RuntimeError` when it runs out.

### Elastic EP drain

Main, `drain_async()`:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D[drain_async] --> M{model with rebalanced set?}
    M -->|no| END[return]
    M -->|yes| AR[all-reduce: every rank has a result?]
    AR -->|no| SL[sleep 1 ms]
    SL --> AR
    AR -->|yes| DISC[discard the result, record consumed_event]
    DISC --> LAST{last layer of the model?}
    LAST -->|yes| CLR[clear rebalanced]
    LAST -->|no| AR
    CLR --> M
```

Proposal, `drain()`:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D[drain] --> M{_layers_left empty?}
    M -->|yes| END[return]
    M -->|no| AR[all-reduce: every rank's job done?]
    AR -->|no| SL[sleep 1 ms]
    SL --> AR
    AR -->|yes| DISC[discard the result, drop the layer]
    DISC --> LAST{_layers_left empty?}
    LAST -->|no| NEXT[record event, submit next layer job]
    NEXT --> AR
    LAST -->|yes| END
```

Same behaviour: every remaining transfer runs, none is applied, and the weights and maps stay where the last normal step left them.

## The whole state of the runner

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `_layers_left` | layers of the running cycle that are not applied yet; the job of the first one is running or finished |
| `_job` | the last submitted job, kept until its cycle ends; after a reset or a failure its result is never applied |
| `_error` | the failure, raised by every `poll()` and `start()` until `reset()` |

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> IDLE
    IDLE --> RUNNING: start()
    RUNNING --> RUNNING: every rank done, apply first layer, submit next
    RUNNING --> IDLE: last layer applied
    RUNNING --> FAILED: job failed on any rank
    RUNNING --> IDLE: reset(), after the job ends
    FAILED --> IDLE: reset()
```

| state | encoding |
|---|---|
| IDLE | `_layers_left` empty, `_error` not set |
| RUNNING | `_layers_left` not empty |
| FAILED | `_error` set; `poll()` raises on every rank |

| removed | what replaces it |

## Blocking syncs: main thread and worker

| | main | proposal |
|---|---|---|
| Main thread, each step while a cycle runs | one CPU all-reduce per model being rebalanced | the same count: one for the model whose job is running, one for each model still waiting |
| Main thread, FT reset | condition wait until the worker leaves its cycle, up to `cpu_distributed_timeout_seconds` | `Future` wait until the job ends, same timeout |
| Main thread, GPU sync | none | none (`Event.record()` does not block; `Future.result()` is read only when done) |
| Worker, per layer | gloo all-reduce, `stream.synchronize()`, `consumed_event.wait`, `stream.synchronize()` | `after.synchronize()`, barrier, `stream.synchronize()` |

## Design

- **`AsyncEplbExecutor`:** one daemon thread bound to the device, with one side stream, returning `concurrent.futures.Future`s. The stdlib `ThreadPoolExecutor` is not used: its threads are joined at exit, so a job stuck on a dead peer would hang shutdown.
- **`AsyncEplbRunner`:** lives on the main thread and owns all cycle state as private fields. Its API is `start(model_states)`, `poll()` (once per `step()`), `cycle_running`, `reset(timeout)` (FT) and `drain()` (elastic EP).
- **Plan:** there is no separate plan job. The job of a model's first layer gets `plan=None`, computes the plan and returns it; later layer jobs receive it as an argument.
- **GPU ordering:** before every submit, the main thread records an event on its stream, and the worker synchronizes on it before the job. The record happens before the submit on the same thread, so record-before-wait holds by program order. This replaces `CpuGpuEvent`.
- **Lockstep:** a CPU all-reduce of two flags, `(failed, busy)`, on the main thread each step, and one barrier per job on the worker.
- **No interruption:** a job is never told to stop. After a reset or a failure its result is not applied. `reset()` waits for it.
